ingredients.name: Pork shoulder or pork neck (with some fat marbling)
Fermented red bean curd (nan ru), mashed smooth

steps:
Slice the pork shoulder into strips approximately 4 cm wide, 4 cm thick, and 15–20 cm long, following the grain of the meat. Mix all marinade ingredients — honey, hoisin, soy sauce, mashed red bean curd, Shaoxing wine, brown sugar, five spice, and garlic — in a bowl and whisk until smooth. The fermented red bean curd (nan ru) should fully dissolve into the mixture, turning it a distinctive reddish-brown that will deepen to the characteristic char siu red during roasting. Add the pork strips to the marinade and turn to coat every surface thoroughly. Press the marinade into any crevices with your fingers. Transfer to a zip-lock bag or covered container and refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours — overnight is strongly preferred and will produce a markedly more complex result. The longer marinade time allows the salt to penetrate deep into the meat and the sugars to begin their chemical interaction with the proteins, which accelerates Maillard browning during roasting.
Visual cue: Pork strips are evenly coated in a thick, reddish-brown marinade with no dry patches visible. The marinade should look glossy and slightly syrupy on the meat surface.
Underdone: Marinade is sitting in pools at the bottom of the bag without adhering — the pork surface is still pale and under-coated. Massage the bag vigorously for 2 minutes to work the marinade into the surface. Let rest for at least 30 minutes before the next check.
Perfect: Every surface is coated in an even, thick, reddish-brown layer. The marinade has been absorbed at the edges, darkening the outer millimeter of the pork. When you open the bag, the smell is sweet, funky, and faintly spiced. Refrigerate for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.
Overdone: Pork has been marinating longer than 36 hours — the surface looks slightly cured and dry, and the texture may be mushy from extended salt contact. Proceed with cooking

immediately. The flavor will be intense but the texture may be slightly soft.
Feel cue: When you press a marinated strip, it should feel tacky and slightly dense on the outside — the surface sugars and soy are beginning to denature the outermost proteins. The interior should still feel like raw pork — yielding and cold.

Preheat your oven to 220°C (425°F). Place a wire rack over a foil-lined baking tray — the rack elevates the pork so heat circulates underneath, and the foil catches the inevitable sugary drips that would otherwise carbonize directly on your tray. Remove the pork from the marinade, reserving all of the marinade, and lay the strips on the rack with at least 2 cm of space between each. They should not touch. Roast for 15 minutes. Meanwhile, pour the reserved marinade into a small saucepan and bring to a boil for 2 minutes — this makes it safe to use as a glaze on cooked meat. After the first 15 minutes, flip each strip using tongs and brush the top generously with the cooked marinade. Return to the oven for another 10 minutes. The alternation of high heat and glaze application is what builds the layered, crackling lacquer that defines char siu.
Visual cue: Strips are deeply caramelized on all surfaces — the edges closest to the rack edges will be darker, approaching char. The color should range from deep amber at the sides to reddish-mahogany at the center.
Underdone: Surface is still pale reddish-tan without significant caramelization. The glaze is still tacky and wet rather than set and lacquered. Return to the oven for 5 more minutes and apply another coat of glaze.
Perfect: Deeply mahogany-red, almost lacquered, with charred edges where the honey has caught. The surface is set and no longer sticky to a finger lightly touched — it has dried into a glaze. An instant-read thermometer reads 68–72°C internal. Apply the final honey glaze and proceed to the finish glaze step.
Overdone: Black at the edges, acrid smell of burnt sugar. The glaze has carbonized into a hard, bitter crust. Trim the blackest edges. The interior remains excellent — char siu can handle significant edge charring before the flavor crosses into unpleasant bitterness.
Feel cue: After flipping, press

the top surface of a strip with a finger — it should feel set and firm like the surface of a drumhead, not soft and yielding. The surface should be dry and slightly tacky, not wet. You should smell toasted honey and five spice in the kitchen air.

Brush the reserved honey (the second portion set aside for glazing, not the used marinade) generously over every surface of the still-hot pork strips. Return to the oven under the broiler — with the oven rack in the upper third — for 3–4 minutes, watching constantly. The honey will bubble and caramelize at the surface in real time, producing the final high-shine lacquer glaze that char siu is famous for. Pull the strips out when the glaze is bubbling vigorously and the surface looks wet and glossy but the edges nearest the heat are just beginning to turn very dark. The glaze will set and harden slightly as it cools. Do not skip this step — the pre-glaze roasting develops the crust; this final honey application provides the shine and the final layer of sweetness.
Visual cue: Strips are glossy and lacquered, almost reflective, with a visible sheen. The surface is set hard, like varnished wood. Edges are dark with char. Color is deep reddish-mahogany to near-black at the very tips.
Underdone: Honey glaze is still pale and transparent — the broiler has not caramelized it. The surface looks wet rather than lacquered. Return under the broiler for 2 more minutes, watching every 30 seconds.
Perfect: Dark, high-gloss lacquer with a slight shatter quality when tapped with a fingernail. Edges are charred in a controlled way. The pork looks like something hanging in a Cantonese roast window. Remove and rest for 5 minutes before slicing across the grain.
Overdone: Glaze has crossed into carbon — black rather than dark mahogany, with a sharp burning smell. Trim the blackest parts. The char at reasonable levels is desirable; true carbon bitterness is not. Slice immediately.
Feel cue: Tap the glazed surface with a fingernail — it should have a faint resistance and produce a subtle sound, like tapping on hard candy. That is the lacquer set. Let it cool 5 minutes before slicing or the
glaze will smear.

Transfer the rested strips to a cutting board. Slice each strip across the grain into pieces 8–10 mm thick — cutting with the grain produces tough, stringy pieces; cutting across it produces the clean, yielding bite that is the whole point. Each slice should reveal a cross-section of pale-pink, juicy interior ringed by a band of deep mahogany glaze. Fan the slices slightly overlapping on a plate. Drizzle any drippings from the pan over the top. Serve with steamed white rice, or use as a filling for steamed bao buns, over lo mein noodles, or alongside congee.
Visual cue: Slices show a clean cross-section: blush-pink to rose-red interior, ringed by a dark, mahogany glaze layer 2–3 mm thick. Grain is clearly visible running perpendicular to the cut. Each slice glistens from the fat and glaze.
Underdone: Interior is pale and raw-looking, with no blush pink — it looks beige or grey, and the juices run clear but there is a slight resistance when you cut. Return the strips whole to the oven at 200°C for 8–10 more minutes and check internal temperature.
Perfect: Rose-pink interior with juices that are slightly orange-tinted from the marinade. The exterior ring of glaze is distinct and dark. Each slice is moist-looking at the cut surface. Fan onto a plate, drizzle with pan drippings, and serve.
Overdone: Interior is grey-white and dry-looking at the cut surface. No juice visible. The meat feels dense and pulls apart in dry strands. Slice thin and serve with extra sauce or drizzle with a small amount of sesame oil to compensate for lost moisture.
Feel cue: Slice through a strip and listen — a good char siu makes a faint crackling sound as the knife breaks through the lacquered crust before gliding through the tender interior. The resistance changes in two distinct stages: crust, then meat.

name: Chard with Currants and Pine Nuts
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

description: Wilted rainbow chard braised with golden raisins and pine nuts in olive oil — the sweet-and-savory Sicilian agrodolce that turns a humble green into something worth seeking out.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Rainbow chard, stems separated and sliced into 2 cm pieces, leaves roughly torn

steps:
Place the pine nuts in a dry skillet over medium-low heat. Shake or stir constantly for 2–3 minutes until they turn a deep golden color. Watch without distraction — they go from pale to burnt in under 30 seconds. Tip immediately onto a cool plate to stop cooking.
Visual cue: Pine nuts are a warm, even golden-tan throughout — the color of polished wood — with a few darker freckles and a distinctly nutty, rich aroma.
Underdone: Nuts are still pale ivory and taste raw and resinous. Continue over medium-low heat, stirring constantly.
Perfect: Deep tan with a few darker spots. The kitchen smells of warm, roasted nuts. Remove immediately from the pan onto a plate — they will continue cooking in residual heat if left in the pan.
Overdone: Brown to near-black with a bitter, oily smell. Discard and toast a fresh batch — burnt pine nuts will make the dish acrid.
Feel cue: Perfectly toasted pine nuts feel slightly oily when rubbed between fingers and give off warmth — they should smell like a warm bakery, not like paint.

In a large, wide pan over medium heat, warm the olive oil until it shimmers. Add the garlic slices and cook, stirring, until they are pale gold and fragrant — about 1 minute. Do not let them brown. Add the chard stems and cook, stirring, for 3 minutes until beginning to soften. Add the chard leaves in large handfuls, wilting each before adding the next. Once all leaves are wilted, add the golden raisins, white wine vinegar, and red pepper flakes. Stir to combine and cook for 1 more minute. Season with salt.
Visual cue: Chard is fully wilted and deeply colored — the rainbow stems still visible as jeweled streaks of red, yellow, and white through a tangle of glossy dark green leaves. Raisins are plump and golden.
Underdone: Some leaves are still raw and standing upright. Stems are crunchy and taste raw. Continue tossing over medium heat with a splash of water if needed — add more leaves only once the previous batch has wilted.
Perfect: All leaves are collapsed and tender. Stems are soft but still have a slight bite. Raisins are plumped. The dish is glossy with olive oil and fragrant with garlic and vinegar. Scatter pine nuts and serve immediately or at room temperature.
Overdone: Chard is very dark, khaki-green, and has released so much water the pan is soupy. Stems are mushy. Raise the heat and cook off the excess liquid, stirring vigorously, until the pan is just glossy again.
Feel cue: A wilted chard leaf should offer gentle but distinct resistance when you press it between spoon and pan — it yields without dissolving, with just enough structure to feel like food rather than compost.

Taste for seasoning — the agrodolce balance should be present but subtle. If it tastes flat, add a few more drops of vinegar; if too sharp, a small pinch of sugar. Transfer to a serving plate and scatter the toasted pine nuts over the top. Serve warm or at room temperature.
Visual cue: A glossy, dark-green tangle of chard studded with golden raisins and scattered with warm-tan pine nuts. The plate looks rustic and jeweled at once.
Underdone: Dish looks unfinished — pine nuts missing, no contrast in color or texture. Add the pine nuts. Without them the sweet-bitter balance reads only as flat.
Perfect: Deep green, golden raisins, tan pine nuts. The plate smells of garlic, vinegar, and olive oil. A spoonful delivers sweet, savory, and slightly bitter in the same bite. Serve.
Overdone: Pine nuts have been stirred in and are now soft from sitting in the warm moisture. They are less crunchy but still add flavor. Toast a few extra to scatter over at the last moment for texture.
Feel cue: The dish should feel glossy and substantial when you spoon it up — not dripping with oil, not dry, but coated with that particular Sicilian richness where olive oil and vegetable juice have become one.

name: Chawanmushi
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Eggs (large, room temperature): 3 eggs
Ichiban dashi (warm, not hot): 1.5 cups
  Alternatives: kombu dashi (vegan); light chicken stock
Soy sauce (light, usukuchi preferred): 1 tsp
  Alternatives: tamari
Mirin (hon-mirin): 1 tsp
Fine sea salt: 0.25 tsp
Raw shrimp (peeled, deveined, tail on): 6 pieces
  Alternatives: scallop slices; chicken breast, thin strips
Kamaboko (fish cake), sliced: 4 slices
  Alternatives: shiitake mushroom caps
Mitsuba (Japanese parsley) or trefoil, leaves: 6 sprigs
  Alternatives: watercress leaves; flat-leaf parsley; chervil
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Silky Japanese steamed egg custard set with ichiban dashi — so delicate it barely holds its form, trembling when the cup is tilted, filled with shrimp and mitsuba.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Beat the eggs gently with chopsticks or a fork in a cutting, slicing motion — do not whisk vigorously. The goal is to break the yolks and blend the whites and yolks into a uniform mixture without incorporating any air, which would create bubbles in the steamed custard. In a separate bowl or jug, combine the warm dashi, soy sauce, mirin, and salt and stir to blend. Pour the seasoned dashi into the beaten eggs gradually, stirring gently as you pour. The dashi-to-egg ratio of roughly 2.5:1 by volume is what produces the barely-set, trembling consistency — more egg and the custard becomes firm; less and it won't set. Strain the entire mixture through a fine-mesh sieve into a pouring jug, pressing the chalazae through with a spoon, then strain once more through cheesecloth if possible for an impeccably smooth result.
Visual cue: A perfectly smooth, pale golden liquid with no visible bubbles, no white streaks, and no foam — uniform from top to bottom when the jug is gently swirled.
Underdone: Mixture has visible white streaks of unblended albumen, undissolved salt crystals are visible, and the surface is foamy with air bubbles. Strain again through a fine sieve and pop any remaining bubbles with a paper towel pressed gently to the surface. Bubbles in the mixture become holes in the custard.
Perfect: Smooth, shimmering, uniformly pale gold. Flows silently off a spoon in a thin, even sheet. No foam, no streaks, no particles. Pour into the prepared cups immediately and proceed. Do not let the mixture sit long, as the egg proteins will begin to coagulate at the bottom.
Overdone: Egg mixture has been left standing and a thin, slightly coagulated layer has formed at the bottom of the jug. Stir gently to re-incorporate and strain once more before pouring into cups. Pour cups immediately after.
Feel cue: Rub a drop of the strained mixture between your fingers: you should feel
absolute smoothness, like cold cream. Any graininess is undissolved seasoning; any stringiness is unstrained egg cord. Both will mar the finished custard.

Divide the shrimp and kamaboko slices evenly among 4 chawanmushi cups (or any deep, heatproof cups or ramekins with lids). Arrange them with some care — in traditional service, the shrimp curl attractively against the cup wall where they can be seen through the custard once it sets, acting as a visual indicator of quality. If using shiitake, place them cap-side down. Leave space at the top — fill cups only to 80% capacity, as the custard needs room to set without touching the lid. Do not add the mitsuba yet; it will go on just before serving.
Visual cue: Cups with the fillings arranged in an attractive, non-crowded pattern, filling no more than one-third of the cup's height.
Underdone: Fillings are raw and unprepped — shrimp still undeveined, shiitake uncleaned, added in a messy heap rather than arranged. Chawanmushi is an elegant dish — the presentation of the filling matters. Arrange neatly; the custard will set around the filling as a transparent window into the cup's interior.
Perfect: Two to three items per cup, arranged intentionally, with the shrimp curved nicely and the kamaboko placed flat. The cups look like they have been staged before the custard enters. Pour the strained egg mixture over the fillings slowly, ideally through the back of a spoon to minimize disturbance and bubbles.
Overdone: Cups are overfilled with fillings, leaving little room for custard — the set chawanmushi will be mostly filling with thin veins of custard rather than a unified, delicate dish. Remove some filling. The fillings should accent the custard, not crowd it out.
Feel cue: Hold an empty cup in your palm and feel its weight — chawanmushi cups are intentionally light. The filling inside should not make the cup feel front-heavy when tilted. A well-loaded cup feels balanced, not top-heavy.

Pour the strained egg mixture slowly into each cup over the back of a spoon to prevent disturbing the fillings or creating bubbles. Fill to about 1 cm below the rim. Skim any bubbles off the surface with a paper towel or the edge of a spoon — any bubble on the surface will leave a crater when it pops during steaming. Cover each cup with its lid (or foil wrapped tight). Place in a bamboo steamer or a pot with a steaming rack. Steam over medium-low heat — not a rolling boil, just a gentle, steady steam. A violent boil will cause the custard to cook too fast at the edges, creating a pocked, spongy texture called 'su' (holes). Steam for 12–15 minutes. Check at 12 minutes: the custard should tremble as a single unit when gently shaken, with the center just barely set.
Visual cue: A smooth, pale ivory-gold surface on the set custard, with no surface holes or bubbles, and a uniform, barely-set trembling when the cup is gently moved.
Underdone: Custard is still liquid in the center — waves move independently across the surface when shaken, and a skewer inserted in the center comes out coated in liquid egg. Re-cover and steam for 3 more minutes. Check again with the shake test. Over-steaming is a worse outcome than the short additional time.
Perfect: The surface is smooth and ivory, trembling as one single mass when tilted — not waves, but a single unified wobble, like cold firm jelly. A skewer inserted pulls out clean or with just a small amount of clear liquid. Remove immediately from the steamer. Set any longer and the silky texture is gone. The residual heat in the cup will continue to set the center.
Overdone: The surface has visible pitting and holes (su), the custard has pulled away from the sides of the cup, and the texture is grainy and slightly rubbery — it has been overcooked and the proteins have over-tightened. Nothing to restore. Serve topped generously with

garnish to disguise the pitting. Next time: lower the steam temperature and check earlier.
Feel cue: Hold the cup steady in your palm and give it a single firm quarter-turn and stop — you want the custard to tremble and then settle immediately, like a snow globe after one shake. If it sloshes liquidly, it needs more time. If it barely moves, it is overcooked.

Remove the cups from the steamer and let them sit for 2 minutes — the custard will firm the final degree of setting from residual heat. Remove the lids and add 1–2 mitsuba sprigs to each cup, pressing the stems gently into the custard surface so they stand slightly upright. Serve immediately in the cup, with small spoons. Chawanmushi is eaten with a spoon by breaking through the smooth surface and scooping custard and filling together. It is served hot in winter and chilled (cold chawanmushi requires a firmer egg ratio) in summer. The mitsuba will wilt quickly — serve without delay.
Visual cue: A pale ivory custard surface with the green mitsuba leaves pressed in, the cup still steaming gently, the shrimp visible as a warm pink curve through the sides of the custard.
Underdone: Custard is still liquid in the center when the garnish is added and it flows to the edges when tilted — the garnish sinks. Return the cup to the steamer (without the mitsuba) for another 3 minutes and check again.
Perfect: The mitsuba stands gently in the barely-firm surface, the custard is still warm and steaming, and the shrimp is visible as a pink arc through the translucent wall of egg dashi. Perfect. Serve within 5 minutes. Chawanmushi at its peak is served moments out of the steamer.
Overdone: Custard has been left to cool and has set stiff, shrinking from the cup walls, with a watery liquid pooling around the edges. Serve as-is — it is still delicious, just not at its ethereal best. Pour off any weeping liquid before presenting.
Feel cue: Break the surface with a spoon: you should feel only the gentlest resistance, like breaking through the skin of a very ripe peach. The interior should yield without any spring-back — just quietly collapsing into a soft, silky cloud that slides off the spoon rather than holding its shape.

description: North Africa's all-purpose wet rub and marinade — cilantro and parsley pounded with cumin, paprika, and garlic, loosened with preserved lemon and olive oil into a vivid paste that perfumes fish, chicken, and vegetables alike.

ingredients.name: Fresh cilantro, leaves and tender stems
Flat-leaf parsley, leaves and tender stems

steps:
Place the garlic cloves in a mortar with the salt. Pound with a circular and downward motion until the garlic breaks down completely into a sticky, smooth paste — the salt acts as an abrasive, drawing out the garlic's moisture and accelerating the process. This should take about 90 seconds of sustained effort. The paste should show the faint translucency of crushed raw garlic with no visible fibrous strands.
Visual cue: A smooth, pale-cream garlic paste with no visible chunks. The salt has dissolved into the garlic's released moisture, and the paste clings to the pestle.
Underdone: The garlic is finely broken but still in discrete pieces — the mortar shows chunky, wet garlic rubble rather than a smooth paste. Continue pounding, working the pestle in tight circular strokes and pressing down firmly on each rotation.
Perfect: The paste is completely smooth, sticky, and translucent — it clings to the pestle and pulls away in strings. A sharp, clean garlic fragrance fills the kitchen. Add the herbs and spices directly to the mortar.
Overdone: The garlic paste has been worked so long it is beginning to turn from white to a faintly grey tinge and is releasing a slightly bitter, harsh aroma. Proceed immediately. The herbs will temper the harshness. Use the chermoula right away rather than letting it sit.
Feel cue: The paste should feel tacky and grab your fingertip with a slight resistance — like a very firm, smooth glue. Roll a tiny amount between fingers and it should leave a clean, intensely aromatic residue.

Add the cilantro and parsley to the garlic paste in the mortar and pound together — the herbs will release their oils quickly and the mixture will turn bright green almost immediately. Add the ground cumin, paprika, cayenne, and lemon zest. Continue pounding and working the pestle, alternating between crushing and stirring motions. The goal is a coarse, fragrant paste: not a smooth puree, but not a rough chop either — something with visible herb texture and fully integrated spices. If the mortar is too small, transfer to a food processor and pulse briefly, being careful not to over-process.
Visual cue: A coarse, vivid green paste with rust-red flecks of paprika and cumin visible throughout. The color is intensely green — darker than a pesto but brighter than a mole.
Underdone: The herbs are still in large, poorly broken-down pieces. The spices are dry and powdery rather than integrated into the herb paste. The mortar smells of each component separately. Continue pounding. The herbs need sustained pressure to release their oils and merge with the garlic and spice base.
Perfect: A cohesive, coarse-textured green paste where the herbs are well broken down but still identifiable. The paprika and cumin are fully integrated, giving the paste a warm reddish-green undertone. Add the lemon juice and olive oil to loosen the paste to a saucy, spreadable consistency.
Overdone: The paste has been pounded to a completely smooth, wet puree — all texture lost. The herbs may be starting to oxidize from the heat of friction, turning from bright green to olive. Proceed immediately. Add the liquids and use right away. The flavor will be excellent even if the texture is smoother than traditional.
Feel cue: Press a finger into the paste and lift — it should pull up in a single, cohesive mound and release with a faint suction, fragrant with cumin, herbs, and raw garlic simultaneously.

Add the lemon juice and olive oil to the herb and spice paste. Fold and stir together — the acid and fat will loosen the paste into a spreadable, saucy consistency. Add the oil in increments, stirring after each addition, until you reach the texture you need: thicker if using as a marinade or rub, looser if spooning over cooked fish. Taste and adjust: more salt if it tastes flat, more lemon if it needs brightness, more cayenne if it needs heat. Chermoula is immediate — use it within an hour for the brightest color and freshest flavor.
Visual cue: A vivid green sauce with a loose, drizzleable consistency and rust-red spice flecks visible throughout. The lemon juice lightens the paste slightly to a brighter green.
Underdone: The chermoula is too thick and paste-like — more oil or lemon is needed. The spices taste sharp and unintegrated rather than mellowed by the fat and acid. Add olive oil a tablespoon at a time, stirring well, until the sauce flows easily. A rest of 5 minutes also helps the spices settle into the base.
Perfect: The chermoula flows from a spoon in a thick but steady drizzle, vivid green with visible herb texture and a heady aroma of cumin, lemon, and fresh herb. Use immediately as a marinade for fish, chicken, or vegetables, or as a sauce spooned over anything that has come off a grill.
Overdone: The chermoula is thin and oily — too much olive oil has diluted the flavor and made it pool rather than cling. The color may be starting to fade. Pound in a small handful of fresh parsley or cilantro to restore body and color. Taste: the flavor should reassert itself with the fresh herbs.
Feel cue: A finished chermoula drizzled over the back of your hand should cling and coat without running — slightly thick, slightly sticky from the garlic, bright and aromatic from the lemon and cumin.

name: Chicken Bone Broth
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Chicken carcasses and bones (roasted): 1500 g
  Alternatives: raw chicken backs and feet (more gelatin)
Yellow onion (halved, skin on): 200 g
Carrots (roughly chopped): 150 g
Celery stalks (roughly chopped): 100 g
Garlic cloves (halved, unpeeled): 6 cloves
Apple cider vinegar: 30 ml
  Alternatives: white wine vinegar; lemon juice
Bay leaves: 3 leaves
Black peppercorns, whole: 10 whole
Fresh thyme sprigs: 4 sprigs
  Alternatives: 1 tsp dried thyme
Cold filtered water: 3000 ml
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 14 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A deeply nourishing, collagen-rich broth drawn from roasted chicken bones over 12–18 hours — it gels solid when cold, turning a shallow bowl of liquid into something that wobbles like aspic, the gelatin coating your lips with every sip.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Spread chicken bones and carcasses in a single layer on a heavy rimmed baking sheet. Add halved onion (cut-side down) and carrot pieces. Roast at 220 C (425 F) for 35–45 minutes, turning once, until the bones are deep golden-brown with dark edges and the onion is caramelized black on the cut face. Dark coloring means Maillard flavors — these give bone broth its depth. Do not skip this step; unroasted bones yield a pale, thin broth.
Visual cue: Bones are deeply golden-brown with dark edges and blistered joints. Onion cut-face is nearly black and caramelized.
Underdone: Bones still pale or blond. Onion barely caramelized. No visible browning on the bone joints. Return to oven for 10 more minutes. The Maillard reaction needs high heat and time — this determines broth color and depth.
Perfect: Bones are deep golden-amber with almost-black tips and joints. Onion cut-face is charred to black. A rich roasted smell fills the kitchen. Transfer to the stockpot. Deglaze the roasting pan with water and add every bit of fond to the pot.
Overdone: Bones are completely black. Bitter acrid smell from burnt fats. Discard the most charred pieces. Scrub burnt fond from the pan before deglazing — burnt fond makes bitter broth.
Feel cue: The roasted bone joints should feel almost crispy on the outside and still faintly wet at the center — the marrow should have started to melt and run at the cut ends.

Place roasted bones and aromatics in a large stockpot or slow cooker. Add celery, garlic, vinegar, bay leaves, peppercorns, and thyme. Cover completely with cold water. The vinegar is key — even one tablespoon creates an acidic environment that draws minerals and collagen from the bones without affecting the final flavor. Bring slowly to a boil, then immediately reduce to the barest possible simmer — single bubbles breaking the surface every few seconds, no boil. Skim all grey foam that rises in the first 15 minutes. Simmer uncovered (or with lid cracked) for 12–18 hours.
Visual cue: A slow, lazy simmer — single bubbles breaking the surface irregularly, not a rolling boil. Liquid stays clear, not cloudy.
Underdone: Less than 4 hours of simmering. Broth is thin, pale, and watery. Does not gel when chilled. Continue simmering. Collagen extraction requires sustained low heat over many hours — there is no shortcut.
Perfect: After 12–18 hours: golden-amber broth, slightly viscous when hot. A tablespoon on a chilled plate gels completely within 5 minutes. Smells deeply of roasted chicken. Strain through fine-mesh strainer lined with cheesecloth. Chill overnight.
Overdone: Boiled vigorously rather than simmered. Broth is cloudy, milky white, greasy. Though still nutritious, it has lost its clarity. Strain through multiple layers of damp cheesecloth to clarify. The flavor is still there, but transparency is lost.
Feel cue: Run a drop of hot broth between your fingers after 12 hours — it should feel slightly viscous and tacky compared to plain water, a sign that gelatin is dissolving from the collagen in the bones.

Pour the broth through a fine-mesh strainer lined with a double layer of damp cheesecloth. Do not press the bones — gravity is the only force here. Discard the solids. Cool the broth to room temperature, then refrigerate overnight. The next morning, lift off and discard the solidified fat cap from the surface. The broth beneath should be solidly gelled, like brown aspic. Season lightly with salt only when ready to serve — salt concentrates as the broth reduces in subsequent cooking.
Visual cue: After chilling: a solid, amber-brown gel with a clean, removable fat cap on the surface.
Underdone: Still liquid when cold, or barely thickened like chicken stock. The gel is the measure of success. The simmer time was insufficient or heat was too high (boiling destroys some collagen structure). Still usable as stock.
Perfect: Solidly gelled — the pot can be tilted and nothing moves. Amber-brown, glossy, with clean fat on top. Smells intensely of chicken and roasted aromatics. Remove fat cap, portion into containers, and refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze 3 months.
Overdone: Over-reduced to a very dark, intensely strong concentrate. Less than a third of the starting volume remains. Dilute 1:1 with water before using. The flavor is intense but concentrated bone broth still excels as a base.
Feel cue: A correctly made bone broth, set and cold, has the wobble of firm jelly — you can run a spoon across it and it holds a line, snapping back elastically, rather than running like water.

name: Chicken Katsu
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Boneless, skin-on chicken thighs (or skinless): 100 parts
  Alternatives: boneless chicken breast, pounded thin
Plain (all-purpose) flour: 15 parts
  Alternatives: rice flour
Whole eggs, beaten: 10 parts
Panko breadcrumbs (Japanese-style, coarse): 25 parts
Neutral oil for shallow frying (rice bran or canola): 30 parts
Fine salt and white pepper: 1 parts
Worcestershire sauce (for tonkatsu sauce base): 8 parts
Ketchup (for tonkatsu sauce base): 5 parts
Oyster sauce: 3 parts
  Alternatives: hoisin sauce
Shredded green cabbage, to serve: 20 parts
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 40 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Chicken thighs pounded to an even thickness, coated in panko breadcrumbs, and shallow-fried until deep golden — shatteringly crisp exterior, moist interior — served with tonkatsu sauce.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Neutral oil for shallow frying (rice bran or canola)

steps:
If using skin-on thighs, leave the skin on — it fries up into a crackling layer that contrasts beautifully with the panko crust. Open the thigh flat and trim any large pockets of fat from the interior that would not render during shallow frying. Place between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound gently with the flat face of a meat mallet from the center outward until the thigh is an even 1.5 cm thickness throughout — thick patches will not cook through by the time the crust reaches full color. Season both sides with fine salt and white pepper immediately before dredging.
Visual cue: A flat, even chicken thigh of uniform 1.5 cm thickness, with no dramatically thick or thin patches. The skin, if present, is intact and smooth rather than torn.
Underdone: Thick ridge in the center or uneven lumps — the center muscle is still significantly thicker than the edges. Focus mallet blows on the thick areas. Work slowly — chicken tears more easily than pork.
Perfect: Uniform 1.5 cm throughout. Skin intact. Smooth surface that will hold the dredge evenly. Season immediately and begin dredging.
Overdone: Chicken has been pounded to 8–10 mm and is tearing — the muscle fibers are separating and there are visible holes. Proceed — thin katsu fries slightly faster and is still delicious. Adjust fry time down by 1 minute per side.
Feel cue: Press across the surface with two fingers: even pressure should produce even give throughout. A spot that bounces back harder than the surrounding area is still too thick.

Combine the Worcestershire sauce, ketchup, and oyster sauce in a small bowl. Stir well to combine. Taste — the sauce should be sweet, tangy, and deeply savory with a slight fermented undertone. Adjust ratios to personal taste: more Worcestershire for depth and tang, more ketchup for sweetness and body, a touch more oyster sauce for umami. This is a quick approximation of commercial Bull-Dog sauce. Allow to sit for 5 minutes for the flavors to integrate.
Visual cue: A dark brown, glossy sauce about the consistency of thin ketchup — pourable but not watery. The aroma is tangy, sweet, and umami-rich simultaneously.
Underdone: The sauce tastes thin and one-dimensional — predominantly ketchup without depth. Add more Worcestershire sauce and oyster sauce. The Worcestershire is the backbone that gives it complexity.
Perfect: Balanced sweet-sour-savory-umami. It tastes rich and slightly caramelized even at room temperature, with a pleasant tang. Set aside. It is ready immediately and needs no cooking.
Overdone: The sauce is too sharp and vinegary — Worcestershire has dominated. Add more ketchup to balance sweetness and body against the acidity.
Feel cue: Dip a fingertip — it should leave a thin, glossy coat that clings for a moment before dripping off. If it slides off instantly, it needs more body (more ketchup). If it doesn't drip at all, thin with a drop of water.

Set up three shallow dishes: flour, beaten egg, and panko. Dredge each thigh in flour, patting off every trace of excess. Dip into beaten egg, letting the excess drip for 2 seconds. Press firmly into the panko, then flip and press again — unlike schnitzel, katsu benefits from a thick, pressed panko coating that builds a robust, shattering crust rather than a delicate one. The coating should be visibly thick. Heat oil to 170°C / 340°F in a heavy pan — enough oil to come halfway up the thigh. Fry skin-side down (or top-side down) for 4 minutes until deep golden. Flip carefully and fry 3 minutes on the second side until deep golden and the thickest part reads 74°C / 165°F. Drain on a rack.
Visual cue: Deep golden-amber panko crust, uniformly colored across the entire surface. The crust looks thick and robust, with the irregular pointed tips of the panko crumbs clearly visible as individual golden spires.
Underdone: Panko is pale yellow and still looks raw and white in the recesses. The oil sizzle is sluggish. Check oil temperature — it may have dropped below 160°C. Allow to recover and continue frying. The crust will color quickly once temperature returns.
Perfect: Deep, rich golden-amber with the individual panko crumbs forming a spiky, three-dimensional surface. The chicken feels firm and springy through the crust when gently pressed. Interior reads 74°C. Remove and drain upright on a rack for 1 minute before slicing.
Overdone: Panko is uniformly deep brown and the recesses are starting to blacken. The oil may be smoking and the crumbs smell sharp. Remove immediately. Slice quickly to release steam and prevent carryover cooking. The chicken will be dry but safe.
Feel cue: Press the katsu gently through the crust — it should spring back firmly but not feel hard as a rock. A slight give tells you the chicken inside is cooked and juicy, not still raw and yielding.

Rest the fried katsu on the rack for 2 minutes — this allows the crust to set and the interior to equilibrate. Using a sharp, heavy knife with one clean downward press per cut (not a sawing motion, which tears the crust), slice into 2–3 cm strips across the width, keeping the slices in the original shape of the thigh. Reassemble the sliced pieces on the cutting board and slide as a unit onto warmed plates beside a mound of shredded cabbage. Drizzle tonkatsu sauce across the slices or serve alongside for dipping.
Visual cue: Evenly sliced strips showing a white, moist, juicy interior against the thick golden panko crust. The crust has not shattered or separated from the chicken in the slicing.
Underdone: Interior is pink or raw-looking at the center when sliced. The juices run pink. Return the slices skin-down to the hot oil for 2 more minutes. Thin slices will cook through quickly from residual heat.
Perfect: White, juicy interior with slight glistening from fat. Golden crust remains intact on each slice. Tonkatsu sauce drizzled creates an aromatic sweet-savory steam. Serve immediately with rice and miso soup.
Overdone: Interior is dry and white throughout with no visible moisture. Crust may have separated from the meat during slicing. Serve with extra tonkatsu sauce. The thick panko crust traps steam and katsu is rarely as dry as it appears — taste before writing it off.
Feel cue: Pick up a slice by pinching the crust between your thumb and forefinger: a perfect katsu slice holds together — the crust grips the chicken. If the crust slides off, the egg wash was too thin or the dredge was improperly ordered.

name: Chicken Marsala
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: chicken cutlets; veal scallops

  Alternatives: rice flour

Olive oil: 2 tbsp
  Alternatives: neutral oil
Cremini mushrooms, sliced 1/4 inch thick: 8 oz
  Alternatives: shiitake caps; button mushrooms
Shallots, finely minced: 2 medium
  Alternatives: 1 small yellow onion, minced
Garlic cloves, minced: 3 cloves
Dry Marsala wine: 0.75 cup
  Alternatives: medium-dry sherry; Madeira
Chicken stock: 0.25 cup
Fresh thyme leaves: 1 tsp

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Pounded chicken cutlets seared in a ripping hot pan, then swathed in a sauce of Marsala wine and earthy cremini mushrooms that reduces to a deep amber lacquer. The wine's caramel-oxidized sweetness plays against the savory fond in a way that makes a thirty-minute dinner taste like it spent the afternoon on the stove.

ingredients.name: Boneless skinless chicken breasts, pounded to 1/4 inch

steps:
Season pounded cutlets with salt and pepper. Dredge in flour, shaking off all excess. Heat 2 tablespoons butter and all the olive oil in a large, wide skillet over medium-high heat until the butter foam subsides. Sear the cutlets in a single layer, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply golden on both sides. Do not crowd the pan — work in batches. Transfer to a plate and loosely tent with foil.
Visual cue: A rich, amber-gold crust on both sides with a flour-thickened fond building on the pan bottom. The chicken edges are white, indicating the interior is cooked.
Underdone: The cutlets are pale blond with minimal browning. They resisted when you tried to flip them — the crust was not yet set. Return to heat. A properly hot pan with the right fat ratio is essential — reheat if the pan has cooled.
Perfect: Deep, even gold on both sides. Crisp at the edges. The pan bottom shows a rich, flour-and-butter fond that smells nutty and sweet. The chicken is fully cooked through at 1/4-inch thickness. Remove to a plate. Cook mushrooms in the same pan.
Overdone: Dark brown approaching burnt. Flour has scorched and the fond is bitter and black in patches. Remove chicken. If the fond is truly burnt, wipe the pan and start fresh. A slightly dark fond will still yield a good sauce.
Feel cue: The finished cutlet should have a light, papery crust that crackles when you press it — the flour-butter crust is only a few millimeters thick but adds all the textural contrast.

Add remaining butter to the pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer — do not stir for the first 2 minutes, letting them make contact with the hot pan. Once browned on one side, stir and add shallots and garlic. Cook, stirring, until the shallots are soft and the mushrooms are fully golden and have released and reabsorbed their liquid, about 4-5 minutes total. Add thyme.
Visual cue: Deep golden-brown mushrooms that have released and reabsorbed their moisture, now caramelized and reduced in volume by half. Soft, translucent shallots clinging to the mushrooms.
Underdone: Mushrooms are pale and swimming in liquid they have released but not reabsorbed. They are soft but not browned. Increase heat and cook without stirring. Stirring extends the time before browning begins.
Perfect: Mushrooms are deep gold to brown, shrunken, and meaty. The pan is nearly dry. A savory, earthy smell fills the kitchen. Shallots are tender. Deglaze with Marsala immediately.
Overdone: Mushrooms are very dark and slightly dry at the edges. The shallots have begun to burn in places. Deglaze immediately with Marsala to rescue the fond before it crosses into bitter.
Feel cue: Properly browned mushrooms feel solid and meaty when pressed with a spoon — they bounce back rather than collapsing under pressure, signaling that their moisture has cooked off.

Pour the Marsala into the hot pan all at once — it will spatter and steam dramatically. Scrape up all the fond from the pan bottom. Add the chicken stock. Bring to a boil and reduce by half over high heat, about 3-4 minutes. The sauce should thicken enough to coat a spoon and turn a deep amber color as the Marsala's sugars concentrate.
Visual cue: A deep amber sauce, glossy and slightly thickened, with mushrooms distributed throughout. The color is like dark honey — translucent but rich.
Underdone: Sauce is light amber and watery — it runs freely off the back of a spoon. Tastes of raw wine. Continue reducing over high heat, watching the edges of the pan where reduction is most visible.
Perfect: Deep amber, glossy, coating the back of a spoon with a thin, even film. The Marsala flavor is concentrated — sweet, nutty, slightly oxidized. Smells like the inside of a wine barrel. Return chicken to the pan and finish with butter.
Overdone: Sauce is very thick and dark — nearly a glaze. The sweetness has become cloying. Add a splash of chicken stock to loosen and balance.
Feel cue: Dip a finger into the cooled edge of the sauce — it should cling to your fingertip in a thin film and taste intensely of wine, mushroom, and caramelized meat juices all at once.

Nestle the seared chicken cutlets back into the Marsala sauce. Simmer over low heat for 2-3 minutes to rewarm the chicken and meld the flavors. Off heat, swirl in the remaining butter until the sauce becomes glossy and unified. Scatter fresh parsley. Serve immediately over egg noodles, polenta, or mashed potatoes.
Visual cue: Glossy, mahogany-amber sauce clinging to the chicken cutlets. Parsley bright green against the dark sauce. The sauce moves as a unified sheet when the pan is tilted.
Underdone: Sauce is broken or thin — butter has not emulsified. The chicken looks pale sitting in a separated, oily liquid. Remove from heat and swirl the pan vigorously. Add a teaspoon of cold water if needed to help re-emulsify.
Perfect: Glossy, unified sauce that coats the chicken in a thin amber lacquer. The butter has enriched the sauce without making it heavy. Parsley is vibrant. Plate immediately.
Overdone: Sauce has broken from too much heat after adding butter — pools of clear butter float on a dull sauce. Remove from heat. Add 2 tsp cold water and swirl aggressively off heat to bring it back together.
Feel cue: Tilt the pan and watch how the sauce moves — a finished, properly mounted marsala should flow in a single glossy sheet, not in separated pools of fat and liquid.

Complex without being complicated: every step has a purpose.

ingredients.name: Chipotle chiles in adobo (or 2 dried morita chiles)
Dark chocolate (70% cacao minimum), roughly chopped
Stale white bread slice, fried in lard until golden
Ripe roma tomatoes (charred whole under broiler until blackened)
White onion half (charred cut-side down in a dry skillet)
Garlic cloves (charred unpeeled in a dry skillet, then peeled)

steps:
Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium heat until it almost smokes. Working one or two at a time, press each dried chile flat against the hot surface with a spatula for 10–15 seconds per side. They will puff slightly, release an intoxicating roasty-chocolate aroma, and turn a shade darker — not black, not soot, just a shade. Transfer each toasted chile immediately to a large bowl and pour boiling water over them. Weight them down with a small plate and soak for 20 minutes until completely softened and pliable.
Visual cue: Dried chiles that have puffed and blistered slightly, releasing a rich chocolate-roasted aroma, still deep red-brown not black, now soaking until fully supple.
Underdone: Chiles are barely warm, still leathery and stiff, with no fragrance released — the comal is too cool. Increase the heat; you need direct contact with a hot dry surface, not gentle warming.
Perfect: Each chile puffs in 10–15 seconds, smells of chocolate and dried fruit, darkens one shade — then immediately into the water. Move quickly from comal to water; lingering even 5 seconds past perfect causes bitterness.
Overdone: Chiles have turned black and smell acrid — the capsaicin and chlorophyll have burnt to bitter compounds. Discard those pieces; over-toasted chiles cannot be rescued and will ruin the mole's balance.
Feel cue: A properly toasted, soaked chile should be completely pliable — fold it in half and it bends without cracking, feeling like soft wet leather. Any stiffness means more soak time is needed.

Drain the soaked chiles, reserving the soaking liquid. In a blender, combine the chiles, fried bread, toasted pumpkin seeds, sesame seeds, charred tomatoes and onion, peeled charred garlic, cinnamon, cloves, cumin, peppercorns and dark chocolate. Add 200 ml of the warm chicken stock. Blitz at high speed for 3 full minutes, scraping down twice, until completely smooth — the paste should have the consistency of thick hummus. For a silkier mole, pass through a medium sieve.
Visual cue: A thick, dark brown-to-near-black paste that is completely smooth, fragrant with chocolate, dried chile and spice, dense enough to mound on a spoon.
Underdone: Paste is still visibly grainy with whole spice fragments, seeds not fully broken down, and the texture is rough rather than smooth. Blend another 2 minutes; add stock in tablespoon increments to keep the blade moving through thick paste.
Perfect: Completely smooth, deeply dark, an aroma layered with chile, chocolate, spice and the roasted char of the tomatoes. Moves like thick tahini. Fry the paste in hot lard before adding the stock.
Overdone: Over-blending with too much liquid has thinned the paste to a runny sauce before it has been fried. Proceed to the frying step; the water will cook off in the hot fat.
Feel cue: Rub between your fingers — the paste should feel perfectly smooth and slightly oily from the seeds, with a chocolate-chile fragrance that catches in the back of the throat.

Heat the lard in a deep, wide pot over medium-high heat until shimmering. Carefully pour or spoon the mole paste into the hot fat — it will spatter and spit violently as the moisture hits the oil. Fry the paste, stirring and scraping constantly, for 5–8 minutes. This is the most important step: frying drives off water, deepens the colour from brown to nearly black, concentrates the flavour and marries the fat with the solids into a unified paste that will later emulsify with the stock.
Visual cue: A very dark, near-black paste bubbling and frying in its own fat, reduced and thickened from the blended version, with a concentrated, complex aroma.
Underdone: The paste is still sputtering with water and has not changed colour; the aroma is still raw chile rather than toasted and complex. Keep frying; the water has not driven off and the paste has not properly caramelized.
Perfect: The paste has darkened by two shades, the spattering has calmed, and it moves like thick chocolate ganache when stirred. The aroma is deeply roasted, complex and fragrant. Begin adding the warm chicken stock in increments.
Overdone: The paste has scorched on the bottom, turning from chocolate-dark to carbon-bitter, and the kitchen smells of burnt chile. Pull from the heat, add a splash of stock to stop the cooking, and taste — a small amount of burned paste can be masked by the remaining stock and chocolate.
Feel cue: Draw a wooden spoon through the fried paste — it should leave a clean channel that closes slowly, like thick mud. The spoon should meet steady, even resistance, not a thin, liquid swirl.

Add the warm chicken stock to the fried mole paste in three additions, whisking thoroughly after each to fully incorporate before adding the next. Season with salt. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered, stirring frequently, for 30 minutes until the sauce reduces slightly and the individual flavours knit into something unified, complex and rounded. Taste: mole should be bitter (chile), sweet (chocolate and dried fruit), earthy (spices), with heat in the back of the throat — adjust with a pinch more salt or a small square of chocolate.
Visual cue: A smooth, deep mahogany-black sauce of medium body, coating a spoon with a glossy, faintly shimmering surface, the aroma layered and complex.
Underdone: The sauce tastes of separate notes — raw chile, sharp chocolate, raw spice — rather than a unified whole. Simmer another 15 minutes; mole flavours need time to knit and the sharp edges to round.
Perfect: A deeply complex, unified sauce — bitter, sweet, earthy, faintly smoky — that coats the spoon and tastes of something irreducible. Add the chicken to the mole and finish cooking.
Overdone: The sauce has reduced too far, concentrating to a bitter, thick paste that overwhelms the other flavours. Thin with warm stock or water in splashes; taste to re-balance with a pinch of sugar if bitterness dominates.
Feel cue: Taste a spoonful and breathe out through your nose — the aroma released retronasal should be all chocolate and dried fruit, with the heat building slowly in the throat 10 seconds later. That slow build is the correct signature.

Nestle the raw chicken thighs into the mole sauce, skin-side up. The sauce should come about two-thirds of the way up the chicken. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover loosely with a lid slightly ajar, and cook for 35–40 minutes until the chicken is cooked through and beginning to pull from the bone. Remove the lid and simmer 10 more minutes to caramelize the exposed skin. Taste the sauce one final time and adjust salt. Let the pot rest off the heat for 10 minutes before serving.
Visual cue: Chicken thighs partially submerged in glossy near-black mole, the exposed skin caramelized to a deep, crackling finish, the meat visibly pulling from the bone.
Underdone: The chicken still shows a pink interior when pierced at the thigh joint and the juices run pink. Cover and simmer another 10–15 minutes; probe at the deepest point near the bone.
Perfect: Meat pulls cleanly from the bone with gentle fork pressure; juices run clear; skin is caramelized; mole clings to every surface. Rest 10 minutes and serve with white rice, black beans, and warm tortillas.
Overdone: Chicken has lost all its fibrous structure and is shredding into the mole, the bone floating free. Serve as a shredded mole chicken — equally delicious if somewhat less elegant.
Feel cue: Insert a thin skewer near the thigh bone — it should slide in with minimal resistance and the juices should run a clear amber. The mole should cling to the skewer as you withdraw it in a dark, glossy coat.

ingredients.name: Bone-in chicken pieces (legs, thighs, and drumsticks)
Mole negro paste (Oaxacan or commercial, e.g. Doña Maria)

steps:
Pat the chicken pieces completely dry and season all over with salt. Heat the lard or oil in a wide, heavy pot (Dutch oven or cazuela) over medium-high heat until shimmering. Working in batches, sear the chicken skin-side down for 4–5 minutes without moving it until the skin is golden-brown and releases cleanly from the pan. Flip and sear the underside for 2 minutes. Remove and set aside. This browning is not about cooking the chicken through — it is about building Maillard-browned fat and fond in the pot that will marry into the mole.
Visual cue: Chicken skin is golden-brown and glistening, not blond or pale. The pot has a golden fond on the bottom — not burnt, but richly coloured.
Underdone: Skin is pale gold, slightly flabby, and still sticking slightly to the pan. The fond is very thin and blonde. Give each piece 2 more minutes, undisturbed. Pale skin will leach excess moisture into the mole rather than contributing richness.
Perfect: Skin is deep golden-brown, rendered, and releases cleanly. A good layer of dark gold fond coats the bottom of the pot. Remove all chicken pieces, pour off all but a thin film of fat, and move to frying the mole paste.
Overdone: Skin is very dark brown to black in spots. Fond is beginning to scorch and smell bitter. Remove chicken immediately and deglaze the pot with a splash of stock, scraping up the fond. Proceed, but taste the liquid — if bitter, discard and start with a clean pot.
Feel cue: Press the back of a spoon on the browned skin — it should feel dry and papery, not soft or wet. A skin that sounds slightly hollow when tapped has rendered its fat properly.

In the same pot over medium heat, add the mole negro paste directly into the remaining fat. Fry the paste, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, for 3–5 minutes. The paste will sputter and spit at first, then gradually quiet as its moisture evaporates. You are frying out the raw, flat flavour of the paste ingredients and developing a deeper, more complex base. The paste will darken by one shade and smell toasted, smoky, and bittersweet — like dark chocolate and dried chile.
Visual cue: Paste has deepened from its original dark reddish-brown to near-black, smells of toasted chile and cocoa, and has reduced noticeably in volume.
Underdone: Paste is still the original colour and smells raw and slightly muddy. It is still sputtering heavily with moisture. Continue frying, stirring constantly. The paste must be fried until the moisture is gone and the fat begins to glisten on the surface.
Perfect: Paste is near-black, aromatic, and moving as a single mass rather than spattering. A glossy film of separated fat appears around the edges. Begin adding the warm chicken stock gradually, one ladle at a time, whisking each addition fully into the paste before adding the next.
Overdone: Paste is smoking, smells acrid, and has stuck to the bottom of the pot in a carbonised layer. Remove from heat immediately. The bitterness may be unrecoverable in the sauce — taste as you proceed. If very bitter, dissolve a small amount of sugar or use a fresh pot.
Feel cue: Lean over the pot during frying and breathe in — the correct smell is rich, dark, smoky, and slightly sweet, like the interior of a quality chocolate shop. An acrid or burning smell means reduce the heat immediately.

With the fried mole paste over medium heat, add the warm chicken stock one ladle at a time, whisking each addition fully into the paste before adding the next. This gradual incorporation prevents lumping and helps the sauce develop a smooth, velvety body. After all the stock is incorporated, bring the sauce to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered for 15 minutes, stirring frequently to prevent the thick sauce from catching on the bottom. Taste and adjust salt.
Visual cue: Sauce is uniformly dark, glossy, and coats the whisk in a thick, flowing layer. No lumps of paste remain. The surface shows lazy, slow bubbles rather than a rolling boil.
Underdone: Sauce is lumpy with unincorporated paste, or thin and watery from too much stock added too fast. Separating into oily and watery patches. Whisk vigorously off the heat to break up lumps. If too thin, simmer 10 more minutes uncovered to concentrate. If oily, the paste fat has split — add stock and whisk from the center outward.
Perfect: Sauce is the colour of very dark mahogany and has a lacquer-like sheen. It nappés a spoon in a thick, even layer and flows slowly. The taste is complex: bitter, sweet, smoky, and spiced. Return the browned chicken to the sauce, nestling pieces until submerged.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced to a very thick paste and is beginning to stick and scorch on the pot bottom between stirs. Add additional stock 50ml at a time and stir from the bottom to loosen. Keep heat very low going forward.
Feel cue: Drag a spoon across the surface of the sauce — it should fill back slowly over 2–3 seconds, like hot tar, not instantly like water. That viscosity tells you the sauce has body enough to braise in.

Nestle the browned chicken pieces into the mole sauce, turning each piece to coat. The sauce should come three-quarters up the sides of the chicken. Cover with a lid, reduce to the lowest possible simmer, and cook for 1.5 hours, turning the chicken gently every 20 minutes and spooning the sauce over any exposed skin. The low heat is critical — a rolling boil will make the chicken tough and crack the mole sauce. Uncover for the last 15 minutes to thicken the sauce slightly and glaze the chicken.
Visual cue: Chicken skin is deeply stained near-black by the mole, glistening, and starting to pull back from the ends of the drumsticks. The sauce has visibly thickened around the pieces.
Underdone: Chicken skin is still brown and not yet fully stained by the mole. Meat at the drumstick joint still resists twisting when tested. Replace the lid and continue braising. At 1 hour, twist a drumstick — if it offers resistance at the joint, it needs 20 more minutes.
Perfect: Chicken is near-falling-off-the-bone — the drumstick twists easily at the joint with little resistance. Skin is deeply mole-stained and glistening. The sauce is thick and coats every surface. Serve immediately, ladling extra sauce over each piece and scattering sesame seeds on top.
Overdone: Chicken has fully fallen apart — bones are separating from the meat. The sauce may have reduced so much it is sticky. Serve as a rustic pulled chicken with the mole. Add a splash of warm stock to the sauce to restore consistency. The flavour is glorious.
Feel cue: Grip a drumstick and twist the joint near the knuckle — at perfect doneness it rotates about a quarter-turn with moderate pressure before yielding. It should feel like loosening a bottle cap that was sealed but not torqued tight.

Transfer the chicken pieces to warm plates or a warm serving platter. Ladle the mole sauce generously over each piece — the chicken should be nearly submerged in sauce. Scatter toasted sesame seeds over the top. Serve immediately with freshly made white rice (which absorbs the mole beautifully), warm corn tortillas for tearing and scooping, and a garnish of finely chopped white onion. Mole negro is meant to be tasted in quantity — do not be restrained with the sauce.
Visual cue: Each piece of chicken sits in a dark pool of sauce, glistening with the chile oil floating on the surface. White sesame seeds dot the black surface like stars.
Underdone: Too little sauce on the plate — the chicken looks dry and the mole is being rationed. The experience will be dominated by protein rather than the sauce. Ladle more sauce — this dish lives or dies by the mole, not the chicken. There is no such thing as too much.
Perfect: Chicken half-submerged in dark, glistening sauce. Sesame seeds visible. The steam rising from the plate carries chocolate, chile, and smoke. Bring to the table immediately with accompaniments.
Overdone: Sesame seeds added too early and have absorbed moisture and lost their crunch. The surface of the mole has developed a dry skin. Stir a tablespoon of warm stock into the mole on each plate to restore the sheen, and add a fresh pinch of sesame seeds.
Feel cue: Before serving, taste a small spoonful of the mole alone — it should hit your tongue in waves: first smoke and heat, then bitterness like dark chocolate, then sweetness and depth. If any single note dominates completely, adjust with salt, a pinch of sugar, or a drop of lime juice.

ingredients.name: Boneless skinless chicken breasts (pounded to 1/4 inch)

steps:
Butterfly each chicken breast or halve horizontally to create two thin cutlets. Place between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound with a meat mallet or rolling pin to an even 1/4-inch thickness. Season both sides generously with salt and pepper. Dredge in flour, shaking off all excess — a bare, dusty coat is what you want, not a thick crust.
Visual cue: Even, thin cutlets with a ghostly film of flour on each side. No clumps. The chicken shape is visible through the flour.
Underdone: Cutlets are still thick in the center — the breast hump is intact. Flour is patchy. Return to the plastic wrap and pound the thick center more aggressively. Re-dredge after pounding.
Perfect: Uniform 1/4-inch thickness edge to edge. A fine, even flour coat that adheres to the tacky surface. Shaking leaves no puff of loose flour. Sear immediately — do not let the floured cutlets sit or they will steam and turn gluey.
Overdone: Cutlets have torn holes in the center from over-pounding. Thick flour crust from excess dredging. Work with what you have — cook carefully to avoid the torn spots drying out faster.
Feel cue: Pounded correctly, the cutlet feels like a thick piece of chamois cloth — pliable, slightly springy, with no thick center ridge when you run your thumb across it.

Heat 2 tablespoons butter and all the olive oil in a wide, heavy skillet over medium-high heat until the butter foam subsides and the pan shimmers. Lay cutlets away from you in a single layer. Do not crowd — cook in batches if needed. Sear 3-4 minutes without moving until deep golden. Flip and cook 1-2 more minutes. Transfer to a warm plate and tent loosely.
Visual cue: Deep golden-brown crust on the first side with defined edges. The top turns from pink to white as the heat climbs through.
Underdone: The cutlet is still pale blond and releases from the pan with resistance when you try to flip it. Steam is rising. Leave it alone — it is still releasing moisture. The protein will naturally release when the crust is set.
Perfect: Rich amber-gold on the bottom, releasing cleanly. The edges have turned fully white and the center is pale pink. Smells of toasted flour and butter. Flip and cook 1-2 minutes on the second side. Remove to a warm plate.
Overdone: Brown crust turning dark, edges blackening. Smoke rather than steam coming from the pan. Flip immediately and remove from heat 60 seconds later. The fond will still make a good sauce.
Feel cue: Press the thickest part of the seared cutlet — it should give like a firm sponge and spring back. If it feels hard, it is overcooked; if it feels raw and squishy, it needs more time.

Pour off excess fat from the pan, leaving the golden fond. Return the pan to medium-high heat. Add the white wine and stock, scraping all the browned bits from the bottom with a wooden spoon. Reduce by half — about 2 minutes of vigorous boiling. The liquid should concentrate and the alcohol smell should have fully cooked off.
Visual cue: A thin, rapidly bubbling liquid with a golden tinge from the fond. Visible reduction in the pan as it boils down.
Underdone: Liquid is still light colored and smells sharply of raw wine. Pan bottom not fully scraped. Increase heat and scrape more aggressively. Cook another 60-90 seconds.
Perfect: Liquid has reduced by half. Golden, syrupy at the edges of the pan. Smells of concentrated chicken and cooked wine — no raw alcohol sharpness. Add lemon juice and capers.
Overdone: Liquid has reduced to a dark glaze clinging to the pan bottom. Beginning to smoke. Add a splash of stock immediately to loosen. The deep color will still give flavor.
Feel cue: Dip a spoon and let a drop fall back into the pan — reduced correctly, it should pool for a moment before spreading, rather than running immediately like water.

Reduce heat to low. Add lemon juice and capers to the reduced sauce base. Return the chicken cutlets to the pan and simmer 1 minute to rewarm. Remove from heat and add the remaining cold butter in pieces, swirling the pan constantly until each piece melts and incorporates. Add parsley. The sauce should look glossy and slightly thickened — opaque, not transparent. Serve immediately.
Visual cue: A glossy, opaque pale-gold sauce that coats the back of a spoon. The butter has fully emulsified — no visible fat pools or streaks.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and transparent, running off the cutlets like water. Butter has not emulsified — you can see fat droplets. Keep swirling the pan off the heat. If it has broken, add a teaspoon of cold water and swirl vigorously.
Perfect: Sauce is pale gold, glossy, and coats the back of a spoon. It clings to the chicken in a thin, glistening layer. Smells of lemon, butter, and capers. Plate immediately — butter sauces break when they sit.
Overdone: Sauce has broken — you can see a pool of clear butter separated from the white solids. The sauce looks oily and thin. Remove from heat. Whisk in 1-2 tsp cold water or a splash of cold stock and swirl aggressively to re-emulsify.
Feel cue: Tilt the pan — the sauce should move in a single, unified sheet, coating the pan bottom as it slides rather than separating into oily and watery zones.

name: Austrian Chicken Schnitzel
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Boneless, skinless chicken breasts: 600 g
  Alternatives: chicken thighs, butterflied and pounded
Fine dried breadcrumbs (not panko): 100 g
Plain flour (all-purpose): 60 g
Eggs, beaten with a splash of milk: 120 g
Fine sea salt and white pepper: 5 g
Clarified butter (Butterschmalz): 150 g
  Alternatives: neutral oil; lard
Lemon, cut into wedges: 60 g
Flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped: 8 g
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A chicken breast pounded to translucency, dressed in fine breadcrumbs, and shallow-fried in clarified butter until the coating billows away from the meat like a souffleed golden shell — the quintessential Vienna technique applied to poultry.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
