ingredients.name: 五花肉（Pork belly, skin-on, cut into 4cm cubes）

steps:
Place the pork belly cubes in a pot of cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat. Boil for 5 minutes — you will see grey foam rising. This is myoglobin and impurities. Drain, discard the water, and rinse each cube of pork under cold running water. This step is not optional — it ensures a clear, clean-tasting braising liquid rather than a murky, funky one. Pat the pork dry with paper towels.
Visual cue: Grey foam at the surface of the blanching water. Clean, white-and-pink pork cubes after rinsing.
Underdone: Only 2 minutes of blanching — limited foam has appeared. The pork is still raw at the core. Continue boiling until the foam is profuse and the pork surfaces are no longer raw-red.
Perfect: 5 minutes of vigorous boiling has extracted the foam. After rinsing, the pork cubes are clean and odorless. The skin is opaque and slightly tightened. Pat dry and proceed to caramelizing.
Overdone: Pork has blanched more than 10 minutes and the exterior is fully cooked and grey. Proceed — the exterior will be re-flavored during the long braise. It won't affect the final result significantly.
Feel cue: The rinsed pork should feel clean and neutral — no off-odor, no slickness of myoglobin. If it still smells funky, rinse again.

Heat the oil in a wok or heavy pot over medium heat. Add the rock sugar and stir until it melts into a golden caramel — about 3 minutes. The caramel should be amber, not dark. Immediately add the pork belly cubes and turn them to coat in the caramel. The skin side should spend the most time in contact with the pan. Cook for 3–4 minutes, turning, until the pork is lightly caramelized and the skin is turning golden.
Visual cue: Pork cubes with a thin, golden caramel coating. The skin is turning from white to amber.
Underdone: Sugar is still in chunks and not fully melted. Continue stirring over medium heat. Do not rush with high heat or it will burn instantly.
Perfect: A thin, amber caramel coats all surfaces. The skin is beginning to color. The pot smells of burnt sugar and pork fat. Add the Shaoxing wine — it will hiss dramatically. Add the soy sauces and remaining ingredients.
Overdone: Caramel has turned very dark and is smoking. The pork skin has dark burnt spots. Add the Shaoxing wine immediately to stop the cooking. The caramel will still dissolve into the braise.
Feel cue: The pork should feel tacky and glazed as you turn it — the caramel is coating every surface. The sound is a rich, sticky sizzle.

Add the Shaoxing wine to the pot — it will sizzle and steam dramatically. Add the dark soy, light soy, scallion knots, ginger coins, star anise, cinnamon stick, and enough water to just cover the pork. Bring to a boil, then reduce to the lowest possible simmer. Cover and braise for 1.5 hours, turning the pork every 30 minutes. Remove the lid for the final 20–30 minutes and increase heat to medium-low to reduce the sauce to a glossy, lacquer-like consistency that coats each cube heavily. Remove the whole spices and scallions before serving.
Visual cue: After 2 hours of braising and reducing, each cube of pork is coated in a thick, mahogany-red glaze. The skin is deeply colored and translucent.
Underdone: After 1 hour the pork is tender at the surface but the fat layer still feels waxy and the skin is opaque and rubbery. Continue braising. The fat layer needs another 30–45 minutes to fully convert.
Perfect: The fat layer is translucent and trembling. The skin is deeply colored and cuts with a spoon. The sauce has reduced to a glossy glaze that coats the pork thickly. The dish smells of star anise, soy, and sweet pork. Remove the spices and scallions. Serve immediately over white rice.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced completely to a sticky paste. The pork skin has collapsed and the cubes are breaking apart. Add 2–3 tbsp of hot water and stir gently. Serve immediately.
Feel cue: Press a cube with a spoon — the skin and fat should give completely and the lean meat beneath should be just barely yielding. The entire cube should feel like it might dissolve.

name: Chinese Steamed Egg Custard
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Large eggs: 3 whole
Warm water or dashi (around 60°C): 240 ml
  Alternatives: warm chicken stock (unsalted) for extra umami
Light soy sauce (for custard): 8 ml
  Alternatives: salt to taste
Fine salt: 1 pinch
Light soy sauce (finishing drizzle): 5 ml
Toasted sesame oil (finishing drizzle): 3 ml
Spring onion, finely sliced on the bias: 5 g
  Alternatives: fried shallot; thin-sliced chili
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 25 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Zhēng dàn — a savory custard so silky it trembles at the touch of a spoon, its surface smooth as polished jade, topped with a few drops of soy and sesame oil that pool into dark, fragrant islands.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Spring onion, finely sliced on the bias

steps:
Beat the eggs gently with chopsticks using a side-to-side motion — the goal is full integration without incorporating air. Add the warm (not hot) water and soy sauce. The water must be warm, not boiling: hot liquid pre-cooks the proteins and cold water sets them unevenly. Beat gently to combine, then strain through a fine-mesh sieve into the steaming bowl or individual cups. The sieving is non-negotiable — it removes chalazae and bubbles that create pitting and air holes in the finished custard. Skim off any foam from the surface with a spoon and cover tightly with cling film to prevent condensation from dripping onto the surface.
Visual cue: A completely smooth, pale gold liquid with zero bubbles on the surface, fully covered with cling film.
Underdone: Visible white strands from chalazae, or a layer of foam on the surface from over-beating. Strain again through a fine sieve and use a paper towel to dab off any remaining surface bubbles.
Perfect: Crystal-clear, uniform amber-gold with zero foam. Pours like light cream. Surface is mirror-smooth under the cling film. Place into the steamer immediately.
Overdone: The water was too hot when added and the eggs have begun to scramble — visible white lumps in the mixture. Strain very well — small pre-cooked pieces can be removed. The custard will still set, just with a less uniform texture.
Feel cue: The mixture should feel barely thicker than water when poured into the bowl — the egg-to-liquid ratio is deliberately high for maximum silkiness.

Set up your steamer with boiling water but immediately reduce to the lowest possible simmer before adding the custard. The enemy of smooth custard is aggressive steam. Place the covered bowl in the steamer, then turn the heat down so only a whisper of steam circulates. Steam on low for 12–15 minutes. Do not open the lid more than once to check. The custard is done when it no longer sloshes as one liquid but jiggles as a unified, soft gel. If your stove cannot sustain low enough heat, crack the steamer lid open 1–2 cm to let excess steam escape — this keeps the temperature from climbing too high.
Visual cue: A set, slightly domed surface that is completely smooth, pale gold, with no pitting, craters, or bubbles — like a mirror coated in custard.
Underdone: The center is still liquid and sloshy when the bowl is gently moved. The edges may be set but the middle is runny. Re-cover and steam another 3–4 minutes. Test again by gently shaking.
Perfect: The entire surface is set and trembles as one solid jelly when the bowl is moved. Surface is smooth as glass. Pale amber-gold throughout. Remove from steamer immediately and top with finishing sauces and garnish.
Overdone: Surface has honeycombed into a cratered, bubbly landscape — the custard cooked too hot and proteins have contracted and expelled liquid. Still edible — the texture is spongy rather than silky. Add finishing sauces to add moisture. Lower heat next time.
Feel cue: Gently tap the rim of the bowl: the custard should shimmer and tremble as a single mass, like a very soft panna cotta. If ripples cross the surface as separate waves, it is not yet set.

Remove the cling film carefully — the accumulated steam and condensation will roll off. Drizzle the finishing soy sauce and sesame oil across the surface in two or three passes — they will pool into dark, fragrant islands on the pale custard. Scatter the spring onion across the top. Serve immediately in the steaming bowl, scooping portions at the table with a spoon. The custard is best the moment it's made; it begins to weep liquid as it cools.
Visual cue: A pale gold, mirror-smooth surface dotted with dark pools of soy and sesame oil, scattered with bright green spring onion rings.
Underdone: Custard surface has broken or dimpled where the cling film stuck and was pulled off too abruptly. The flavor is unchanged — the visual is the only loss. Next time, spray the cling film lightly with oil before covering.
Perfect: Smooth, glossy surface with the garnishes sitting cleanly on top. The whole bowl trembles gently as you carry it to the table. Serve at once.
Overdone: Custard has begun to weep clear liquid from resting too long. Surface looks slick and wet. Tilt the bowl gently to drain excess liquid, then add garnishes and serve.
Feel cue: A perfectly set custard yields to a spoon with almost no resistance — it parts like very firm silken tofu, quivering at the edges of the cut.

name: Chocolate Fondant (Molten Lava Cake)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing: 100 g
Dark chocolate (70% cocoa solids), chopped: 100 g
  Alternatives: bittersweet chocolate 66-72%
Whole eggs: 2 whole
Egg yolks: 2 whole
Caster sugar: 60 g
Plain flour, plus extra for dusting: 20 g
  Alternatives: rice flour (gluten-free)
Fine sea salt: 1 g
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A deeply dark individual chocolate cake with a barely-set shell that collapses on the plate to release a river of liquid ganache from the centre — the margin between triumph and disaster is exactly two minutes in the oven.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing
Plain flour, plus extra for dusting

steps:
Melt butter and chocolate together in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water (bain-marie). Do not let the bowl touch the water. Stir gently until fully melted and glossy. Remove from heat and set aside to cool slightly — you want it warm, not hot (around 40 C). Meanwhile, butter and flour six individual dariole moulds or ramekins (100 ml), tapping out excess flour.
Visual cue: A uniformly glossy, fluid ganache with no lumps or graininess. The surface shines like lacquered wood and falls in a smooth ribbon from the spoon.
Underdone: Butter is melted but chocolate still has lumps. The mixture looks broken and grainy. Continue stirring over gentle heat — even gentle heat will melt remaining pieces.
Perfect: Smooth, glossy, fluid. Temperature feels warm but not burning when tested on the inner wrist. Remove from heat and cool 5 minutes before adding eggs.
Overdone: The mixture has seized — it is thick, grainy, and dull. Chocolate has burned. A seized ganache cannot be recovered. Start again with fresh chocolate and butter, using lower heat.
Feel cue: The base should flow like thick cream and smell intensely of dark chocolate, with a hint of warm dairy — not smoky, not sharp.

In a large bowl, whisk together the whole eggs, egg yolks, and caster sugar vigorously by hand (or with an electric whisk) for 3–4 minutes until the mixture is pale, thick, and falls from the whisk in a wide ribbon that holds its shape on the surface for 2–3 seconds before dissolving. This aeration is what gives the fondant its thin, souffle-like shell.
Visual cue: A pale, creamy-yellow mixture that falls from the lifted whisk in a thick, slow ribbon, writing on itself for a moment before sinking back in.
Underdone: Still liquid and yellow, no change in volume or colour. Drips off the whisk in thin threads. Keep whisking — the sugar needs to dissolve and the eggs need aeration.
Perfect: Pale and doubled in volume. Ribbon holds for 2-3 seconds. The mixture feels significantly thicker when the whisk lifts. Fold in the chocolate base immediately.
Overdone: Over-whisked by machine: very stiff and mousse-like, leaving stiff peaks. It will be difficult to fold without deflating. Fold very gently — the fondant will still work but may have a drier shell.
Feel cue: When you lift the whisk, the ribbon should fall slowly and with weight, like a wide satin ribbon rather than a thread of water.

Pour the warm chocolate-butter base into the egg-sugar ribbon. Fold with a large spatula using wide, deliberate scooping motions from the bottom of the bowl — do not stir. When almost combined, sift over the flour and salt, then fold until just incorporated with no dry streaks visible. The batter should be glossy, fluid, and airy. Divide evenly between the prepared moulds, filling to 1 cm below the rim. Refrigerate for at least 20 minutes (up to 24 hours).
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy, dark batter with no streaks of flour or egg. It pours cleanly into the moulds and the surface is level and even.
Underdone: Streaks of pale egg mixture and streaks of dark chocolate still visible. Unmixed pockets of flour. Continue folding with 4-5 more strokes — each fold incorporates roughly 10%.
Perfect: Uniformly dark and glossy. Batter holds its level in the mould without doming or sinking. It smells deeply chocolatey. Refrigerate until ready to bake.
Overdone: Batter has deflated — it is dense and liquid, no longer airy. Over-folded. Bake anyway. The shell will be denser and the liquid centre smaller but the fondant will still work.
Feel cue: The batter should pour from the spatula like thick double cream — not as fluid as water, but not stiff enough to hold a shape. You should see small bubbles suspended throughout.

Preheat oven to 200 C (fan 190 C). Place moulds on a baking tray and bake for exactly 10–12 minutes (10 for a very liquid centre, 12 for a fudgey-flowing one). The exterior should be set and pulling away from the mould sides very slightly; the centre should still wobble. Run a knife around the edge, invert onto warmed plates, and wait 5 seconds before lifting the mould. Serve immediately — the centre begins to set within 2 minutes of leaving the oven.
Visual cue: Fully risen with a domed, matte, set surface. The mould lifts cleanly to reveal a glossy dark cake that holds its shape for 3–4 seconds before the centre begins to flow.
Underdone: The top is still shiny and liquid. The cake collapses completely when inverted — more a puddle than a cake. Return the mould to the oven for 2 more minutes. The line between raw and right is narrow.
Perfect: Domed and set on top, matte, pulling from the mould. Inverts cleanly. The centre flows slowly and glossily when cut or pressed. Plate immediately and bring to the table at once.
Overdone: The top is fully set and dry-looking. When cut, the interior is uniformly sponge with no liquid centre — a chocolate cake, not a fondant. Accept the result. Serve with warm caramel sauce to compensate for the lost centre.
Feel cue: Tap the top of the mould gently with a fingertip — the shell should feel set and spring back, but the mass beneath it should shift and ripple slightly, like tapping a water balloon.

name: Dark Chocolate Ganache
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Dark chocolate (70% cacao), finely chopped: 2 parts
  Alternatives: 60% bittersweet chocolate; milk chocolate (reduce cream by 20%)
Heavy cream (36% fat): 1 parts
  Alternatives: full-fat coconut cream for vegan version
Unsalted butter, room temperature, cubed: 0.1 parts
  Alternatives: cold-pressed coconut oil
Light corn syrup (for gloss and shelf life): 0.05 parts
  Alternatives: glucose syrup; honey
Flaky sea salt: 0.005 parts
  Alternatives: smoked salt
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 25 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Cream and chocolate collapse into each other in a glossy, jet-black emulsion that clings to a spoon like liquid velvet. At room temperature it pours like a mirror glaze; chilled, it sets to a truffle-firm fudge you can slice clean.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Light corn syrup (for gloss and shelf life)

steps:
Pour the heavy cream and corn syrup into a small heavy-bottomed saucepan. Set over medium heat and bring to a full simmer — you want small, insistent bubbles breaking across the entire surface, not a rolling boil that would scorch the fat. Watch the edges of the pan: cream scalds quickly once it reaches a gallop. The moment you see a confident simmer with steam rising in a column, remove from heat. The corn syrup dissolves invisibly but is doing important work: it disrupts sugar crystallisation and gives the finished ganache that jewel-like sheen that makes mirror glazes sing. Do not stir once it approaches heat — just watch. Total time on heat: 2–3 minutes.
Visual cue: Small bubbles forming a ring around the edge, breaking toward the center. Surface is shimmering and a thin wisp of steam rises steadily.
Underdone: Cream is warm but flat — no bubbles at the edges, no steam. Chocolate will not melt evenly when poured. Return to heat for another 60 seconds. The cream must be genuinely hot.
Perfect: A confident ring of small bubbles at the edges racing inward. Steam curls up. The cream has just puffed and risen slightly. Remove from heat immediately and pour over the chocolate.
Overdone: A hard rolling boil with large, violent bubbles. The cream is losing water as steam and may scorch. Remove from heat. Let it settle for 30 seconds before pouring — some water loss is acceptable, the ganache will be slightly firmer.
Feel cue: Hold your hand 10 cm above the pot — you should feel firm, dry heat pushing up, not a moist cloud. That dry radiant heat means the cream is hot enough without having boiled off.

Place the finely chopped chocolate in a deep, heatproof bowl — a deep bowl concentrates the heat and prevents splashing. Pour the hot cream over the chocolate in one confident pour, making sure all the chocolate is submerged or in contact with the cream. Do not stir yet. Wait 90 seconds, letting the residual heat of the cream melt the chocolate from the outside in. This patience is the secret: if you stir immediately, you introduce cold air before the chocolate has melted, risking a grainy, broken ganache. After 90 seconds, begin stirring with a silicone spatula from the very center of the bowl, making small, tight concentric circles. You will see a glossy, dark emulsion form in the center — keep working outward until the ganache is completely uniform, glossy, and no streaks of cream remain. This should take about 2 minutes of gentle, deliberate stirring.
Visual cue: A completely uniform, deeply glossy, dark brown emulsion with no white cream streaks and no visible chocolate chips remaining.
Underdone: The mixture is streaky — pale cream and dark chocolate have not fully combined. Some chips still visible. Keep stirring from the center outward. If chips remain after 3 minutes, set the bowl over a pot of barely simmering water for 20 seconds and stir again.
Perfect: The ganache is glossy, uniformly dark, and flows slowly off the spatula in a thick, continuous ribbon. It moves like warm fudge sauce. Add the butter and salt in the next step.
Overdone: The ganache looks greasy or grainy — the emulsion has broken. Fat has separated and pools on the surface. Add a tablespoon of warm cream and whisk vigorously. If still broken, add another tablespoon. The emulsion can almost always be recovered.
Feel cue: Drag the spatula through the center — it should feel like pulling through warm honey, coating the spatula in a smooth layer with no graininess when you rub a small amount
between your fingertips.

While the ganache is still warm (but not burning hot — ideally around 40°C / 104°F), drop in the room-temperature butter cubes one at a time, stirring each in completely before adding the next. Room-temperature butter is critical: cold butter will not emulsify smoothly and can make the ganache seize. Add the pinch of flaky sea salt and stir it through — the salt performs two functions: it amplifies the chocolate's fruitiness and balances the sweetness so the ganache tastes complex rather than simply sweet. The finished ganache should be poured immediately if using as a glaze, or left at room temperature for 2 hours until it firms to a spreadable truffle consistency. For chocolate truffles, cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours until scoopable. The ganache keeps at room temperature for 48 hours or refrigerated for two weeks.
Visual cue: The ganache deepens in gloss after the butter is incorporated — it should look lacquered, almost wet, and flow slowly off the spatula in a wide, glossy curtain.
Underdone: The butter has not fully incorporated — the ganache looks pale or slightly mottled where butter pockets remain. Keep stirring gently. Add butter cubes one at a time, not all at once.
Perfect: Deep, mirror-like gloss. The ganache falls off the spatula in a single, slow, unbroken curtain. When a drop lands, it spreads and smooths itself. Pour immediately as a glaze, or cover and let set for your intended use.
Overdone: The ganache has been stirred too vigorously and has cooled and thickened unevenly. Surface looks dull and the texture is lumpy. Gently reheat over a double boiler, stirring slowly, until fluid and glossy again. Do not overheat.
Feel cue: At the perfect warm temperature, a drop on the inside of your wrist should feel neutral — neither cold nor hot — and it should sit on your skin for 3 seconds before it begins to spread, which tells you the emulsion
is stable and the fat is properly distributed.

name: Chocolate Lava Cake
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Unsalted butter, plus extra for ramekins: 60 parts
Dark chocolate (70% cacao), roughly chopped: 60 parts
  Alternatives: bittersweet chocolate chips
Large eggs (whole): 40 parts
Egg yolks: 20 parts
Powdered (icing) sugar: 30 parts
  Alternatives: caster sugar
All-purpose flour: 12 parts
  Alternatives: cake flour
Fine sea salt: 1 parts
Pure vanilla extract: 2 parts
  Alternatives: vanilla bean paste
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A paradox in a ramekin — a cake with a fully set chocolate shell that conceals a dark, flowing center of pure molten ganache, the interior flowing out in a slow, warm river when the spoon breaks through the thin crust.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, plus extra for ramekins

steps:
Butter four 180ml (6oz) ramekins generously and dust with cocoa powder or flour, tapping out the excess. The butter-cocoa coating must be thorough and even — any bare spot and the cake will stick, ruining the unmolding. Refrigerate the prepared ramekins while you make the batter. Cold ramekins help the outer shell set quickly in the oven, creating the temperature differential that keeps the center liquid.
Visual cue: The interior of each ramekin is uniformly coated in a thin, matte cocoa-brown film. No bare or shiny patches. The coating extends all the way to the rim.
Underdone: Thin coverage with visible bare or shiny patches. Butter looks streaky rather than uniform. Cocoa hasn't adhered in spots. Butter and dust again — this step is the insurance policy for a clean unmold. Never rush ramekin prep.
Perfect: Complete, matte, uniform coverage from base to rim. When you tip the ramekin, no cocoa falls — it has adhered to the butter completely. Refrigerate the ramekins while making the batter.
Overdone: Heavy, thick layer of cocoa with clumps. Will leave a gritty, powdery exterior on the baked cake. Tap firmly to shake out the excess before refrigerating.
Feel cue: Run a finger along the interior wall — it should feel slightly dry and grippy, like fine-grit sandpaper coated in fine cocoa, not slick or bare.

Combine the butter and chopped chocolate in a heatproof bowl over a pot of barely simmering water (bain-marie). The water should not touch the bottom of the bowl. Stir gently and frequently until the mixture is completely melted and smooth — remove from heat the moment the last solid piece has melted, as continuing to heat will make the chocolate grainy. The finished mixture should be glossy, fluid, and smell deeply of dark chocolate.
Visual cue: A glossy, smooth, uniformly dark chocolate mixture with no lumps or graininess. It should flow like a thin, velvety sauce when the bowl is tilted.
Underdone: Lumps of partially melted chocolate still visible. Butter and chocolate have not fully incorporated — they look separated or streaky. Continue stirring over barely simmering water. Move the bowl off the steam occasionally to avoid overheating.
Perfect: Perfectly smooth, glossy, and homogenous. Flows in a continuous ribbon from a spoon. A deep, clean chocolate scent with no bitterness. Remove from heat and cool to room temperature before adding eggs.
Overdone: The chocolate has seized — it looks grainy, dull, and stiff rather than glossy and fluid. It may have a slightly scorched smell. Add a tablespoon of warm cream and stir vigorously — this can sometimes rescue seized chocolate. If it smooths out, proceed.
Feel cue: The melted chocolate should feel warm but not hot on the inside of your wrist — approximately body temperature. Hotter than that and it will cook the eggs when added; cooler and it will be thick and hard to incorporate.

In a large bowl, whisk the whole eggs, yolks, powdered sugar, salt, and vanilla vigorously by hand for 2 full minutes until the mixture is pale, thick, and ribbon-like. This step aerates the batter and gives the outer shell its slightly cakey structure — without this whipping, the cake will be more like set ganache throughout rather than having a defined shell. The mixture should lighten in color noticeably.
Visual cue: The mixture has turned from deep gold to a pale, creamy yellow and has roughly doubled in volume. When the whisk is lifted, it falls back in thick, lazy ribbons that hold briefly before dissolving.
Underdone: Still deeply golden and thin. No ribbon formation. Bubbles are large and unstable rather than fine and persistent. Continue whisking — this needs 2 full minutes of vigorous activity. Use an electric hand mixer if your arm is tiring.
Perfect: Pale, creamy, and aerated. Ribbon test passes — the mixture holds its shape briefly when drizzled from the whisk. Volume has increased visibly. Fold in the cooled chocolate mixture.
Overdone: The mixture has been beaten so long it looks stiff and slightly dry, and is not flowing smoothly. Over-aerated egg foam. Proceed — the excess air will escape during baking and the structural outcome is the same.
Feel cue: When you let the whisk drip over the surface, the ribbon should sit on top for a moment before slowly sinking back in — this is the visual test that the eggs have trapped enough air to build the structure.

Pour the cooled chocolate mixture into the egg mixture and fold gently with a spatula until just combined. Sift the flour over the top and fold again with minimal strokes — 8–10 folds maximum. Overmixing develops gluten and toughens the exterior shell. The batter should be smooth, dark, and just barely homogenous — stop the moment no flour streaks remain.
Visual cue: Smooth, dark, glossy batter with no flour streaks visible. It pours in a slow, thick ribbon. No large bubbles or streaks of unmixed chocolate.
Underdone: Flour streaks still visible as pale ribbons through the dark batter. Chocolate and egg layers still marbled rather than combined. Fold 3–4 more times, turning the bowl as you go. Keep strokes large and deliberate.
Perfect: Uniformly dark and glossy. No flour streaks. No chocolate streaks. Falls in a slow, even ribbon from the spatula. Divide into prepared ramekins and bake or refrigerate.
Overdone: Batter has been over-folded and is smooth to the point of being elastic — you can see the batter pulling slightly when dropped. Gluten has developed. Bake immediately — the exterior will be slightly denser but the molten center will still work.
Feel cue: The batter should feel almost airy when you fold it — the egg foam is still present, and the batter should feel lighter than it looks. A heavy, dense batter means the eggs were cold or under-whisked.

Fill each prepared ramekin three-quarters full. Bake at 220°C (425°F) for exactly 10–12 minutes — the timing is everything. The edges should be set and pulling away from the ramekin walls, but the center should visibly jiggle when the pan is shaken. Run a thin knife around the edge of each cake, place a warm plate on top, and invert in one decisive movement. Wait 10 seconds, then lift the ramekin. Serve immediately — the center will continue to set within 2 minutes.
Visual cue: Set, slightly domed top with matte dry surface. When the pan is shaken gently, the center of each cake wobbles distinctly while the edges remain firm.
Underdone: The entire top surface wobbles when shaken. The edges haven't pulled away from the ramekin walls. The batter may still look wet and shiny in the center. Return for 2 more minutes. The difference between underdone and perfect here is approximately 2 minutes of baking time.
Perfect: Edges set and matte. Center jiggles but doesn't ripple like liquid. Top is domed and dry-looking. The aroma is intense dark chocolate. Remove from oven. Wait 1 minute, then invert onto warm plates.
Overdone: The entire top is firm and no jiggle remains. The edges have pulled fully away and may be slightly cracked. No movement at all. Invert anyway — you have a dense, fully baked chocolate cake. Still delicious, just not lava.
Feel cue: When you invert the ramekin and lift it away, a warm dome of chocolate cake should release cleanly. Within 5 seconds, a crack should appear at the top as the molten center begins to push through — that is the moment to serve.

name: Chocolate Mousse
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Bittersweet chocolate, 64–70% (finely chopped): 200 g
  Alternatives: a blend of 70% and 55% for a rounder finish
Unsalted butter (soft, cubed): 40 g
Egg yolks (room temperature): 80 g
Egg whites (room temperature): 120 g
Caster sugar (for the meringue): 60 g
  Alternatives: superfine sugar
Heavy cream, 35% fat (cold): 120 g
  Alternatives: crème fraîche, softly whipped, for a tangy edge
Fine sea salt: 1 g
  Alternatives: flaky salt, to finish
Pure vanilla extract: 3 g
  Alternatives: a splash of dark rum, Cognac, or strong espresso
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 4 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The classic mousse au chocolat — bittersweet chocolate enriched with egg yolks, then lifted by a glossy meringue and softly whipped cream into a cloud that holds a swooped peak yet dissolves the instant it touches the tongue. Dark, deep, and barely sweet.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Set the chopped chocolate and butter in a bowl over a pan of barely steaming water — the bowl should not touch the water. Stir gently and let them melt together into a single, glossy mass. Pull the bowl off the heat the moment the last shards disappear; chocolate scorches and grain the instant it overheats. Let it cool to just warm to the touch, around 40°C, before anything else goes in.
Visual cue: A smooth, mirror-glossy chocolate that ribbons off the spatula and falls back into itself without a trace of unmelted fleck.
Underdone: Tiny solid bits still cling to the spatula and the surface looks dull and granular. Keep stirring off the heat — residual warmth usually finishes it. Return to the steam only briefly if it stalls.
Perfect: Uniformly fluid, deeply shiny, and warm but not hot to a fingertip. It coats the spatula in a thin, even sheet. Set aside to cool to body temperature before folding in the yolks.
Overdone: The chocolate looks thick, matte, and grainy, or has split into a greasy puddle with dark specks — it overheated and seized. Whisk in a teaspoon of hot water at a time to bring a seized mass back; if scorched and bitter, start over.
Feel cue: Dip a fingertip — it should feel warm, never hot. The kitchen smells of pure cocoa with no acrid, burnt edge.

Whisk the egg yolks, vanilla, and salt together, then whisk them into the warm (not hot) chocolate in one go. The mixture will thicken and pull together into a dense, deeply shiny paste — almost like a soft ganache. Work quickly and confidently; if the chocolate is too hot the yolks will scramble, and if it sits too long it stiffens. You want a base that is supple and pourable, ready to receive air.
Visual cue: A thick, satiny, near-black base that falls in a heavy, glossy ribbon and smells intensely of chocolate.
Underdone: Streaks of loose yolk still marble the chocolate and the mixture looks uneven. Whisk a few seconds more until completely homogeneous, but stop the moment it is uniform.
Perfect: A uniform, glossy, supple paste with the sheen of melted satin. It holds a slow ribbon on the surface before sinking in. Set aside at room temperature while you whip the meringue and cream — do not chill it or it will set too firm to fold.
Overdone: The base has stiffened into a dull, claggy mass, or shows tiny scrambled flecks of cooked yolk. If merely stiff, warm gently over steam to loosen. If the yolks scrambled, strain through a sieve and accept a slightly less rich result.
Feel cue: The whisk meets sudden resistance as the yolks bind the chocolate — that thickening is the sign it has come together. It should taste bittersweet and round, just shy of bitter.

In a spotlessly clean, grease-free bowl, whip the egg whites until frothy, then rain in the caster sugar a spoonful at a time as you beat. Continue to a soft, glossy meringue that holds a peak which curls gently at the tip. Stop short of stiff and dry — an over-beaten meringue turns grainy and refuses to fold in smoothly, leaving white specks through the mousse.
Visual cue: A billowy, glossy meringue that holds a soft peak with a tip that bends over on itself like a wave about to break.
Underdone: The whites are foamy and loose; peaks collapse back into the surface and the sugar feels gritty. Keep whipping to dissolve the sugar and build structure until soft peaks form.
Perfect: Smooth, shiny, and thick, holding a peak that curls gently at the tip. Rubbed between fingers it feels silky, with no sugar grit. Use immediately — meringue weeps and deflates if it sits.
Overdone: The meringue looks dry, cottony, and dull, breaking into clumps rather than a smooth mass. Whisk in an extra spoonful of un-whipped white to bring it back, or re-whip a fresh white and fold a little in.
Feel cue: Rub a dab between two fingers — no sugar grain should remain. Lift the whisk and the peak should nod over softly rather than stand stiff and pointed.

Whip the cold cream to soft, droopy peaks — barely past pourable, what the French call 'à la chantilly molle'. It should mound but still flow when the bowl is tilted. Stop early; cream that is whipped stiff makes a heavy, buttery mousse and risks turning grainy when folded.
Visual cue: Softly thickened cream that leaves a slow-fading trail from the whisk and folds over itself in lazy mounds.
Underdone: The cream is barely thickened and still pours in a stream. Whip a few seconds more, watching closely — it firms up fast at this stage.
Perfect: Soft, billowy mounds that just hold their shape and droop at the peak. The whisk leaves a soft, slowly closing trail. Fold in immediately while it is loose and supple.
Overdone: The cream is stiff, clumpy, and looks slightly grainy or dull — on the edge of butter. Whisk in a splash of fresh cold cream to loosen it back to a smooth, soft texture.
Feel cue: The cream should still wobble and flow when you tilt the bowl. Stop the moment it holds a soft shape; another ten seconds and it stiffens.

First whisk a third of the meringue vigorously into the chocolate base to slacken it — this sacrificial third makes the rest fold in without deflating. Then add the remaining meringue and the whipped cream together and fold with a large spatula, cutting down through the center, sweeping along the bowl, and turning over, rotating the bowl as you go. Stop the instant no streaks remain. Spoon into glasses or a serving bowl and chill at least 3 to 4 hours, or overnight, until set but still pillowy.
Visual cue: A uniform, airy, mocha-dark mousse with no marbling of white, that mounds softly and holds the swoop of a spoon.
Underdone: Pale streaks and ribbons of meringue and cream still run through the dark base. Fold a few more gentle strokes — but chase out the last faint streaks rather than over-working it.
Perfect: Evenly colored, light, and voluminous, dropping from the spatula in a soft, aerated mound that holds its shape. Portion immediately and chill to set — handling it longer knocks the air out.
Overdone: The mousse looks dense, deflated, and slack, with a soupy, liquid edge — it was over-folded and the air collapsed. There is no full recovery, but chilling will still firm it; next time fold less and stop at the first uniform color.
Feel cue: Each fold should feel light, the spatula meeting almost no resistance as the mass stays buoyant. Set, a spoonful should give a faint resistance then collapse instantly into silk on the tongue — bittersweet, cool, and clean-finishing.

name: Choron
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Egg yolks: 3 yolks
Clarified butter (warm): 8 parts
  Alternatives: warm melted ghee
Salt: 0.2 part
  Alternatives: fine sea salt
Cayenne pepper: 0.05 part
  Alternatives: pinch of white pepper
White-wine vinegar: 3 parts
  Alternatives: tarragon vinegar; champagne vinegar
Shallot (minced): 1 part
Tarragon (plus stems for the reduction): 1 part
  Alternatives: chervil (milder)
Cracked black peppercorns: 0.3 part
  Alternatives: white peppercorns
Tomato paste (cooked, concentrated): 1 part
  Alternatives: reduced tomato purée
Active time: 35 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Béarnaise tomatée — the classic béarnaise tinted blush-pink and rounded with a spoonful of concentrated cooked tomato, lending color and a softer, sweeter acidity. The traditional partner to grilled beef.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine the vinegar, minced shallot, tarragon stems (reserve the leaves), and cracked peppercorns in a small saucepan. Simmer gently until the liquid reduces to about two tablespoons of intensely flavored, syrupy essence. Strain out and press the solids, discarding the stems, shallot, and pepper — you want only the perfumed, acidic liquid. Let it cool to warm before it meets the yolks; hot reduction would start to cook them.
Visual cue: About two tablespoons of cloudy, pale-amber liquid that smells sharply of vinegar, anise-sweet tarragon, and pepper. It is reduced but still clearly liquid — not a glaze.
Underdone: Still a thin, watery pool with little aroma — barely reduced from its starting volume. The vinegar smell is raw and harsh. Keep simmering gently. The harsh edge of the vinegar should mellow as it concentrates and the aromatics infuse.
Perfect: Reduced to roughly two tablespoons, syrupy at the edges, deeply fragrant with tarragon and pepper. The vinegar has lost its raw bite. Strain through a fine sieve, pressing the solids. Let the liquid cool to warm, then move to building the sabayon.
Overdone: Reduced past two tablespoons into a sticky, dark, near-dry glaze stuck to the pan — or burnt and acrid. Loosen by whisking in a tablespoon of water or vinegar off the heat. If it has burnt and smells acrid, start the reduction again — scorched aromatics will taint the whole sauce.
Feel cue: The kitchen should fill with the sharp, sweet-herbal smell of tarragon and hot vinegar. The reduction should still slosh in the pan, not cling like syrup.

Set a heatproof bowl over a pan of barely simmering water — the bowl must not touch the water, and the water must steam, not boil. Add the yolks and the cooled tarragon reduction. Whisk constantly and vigorously, lifting the bowl off the heat every few seconds to control the temperature, until the yolks triple in volume and thicken to a pale sabayon that holds a ribbon. Too much heat scrambles the yolks; too little and they never thicken enough to carry the butter.
Visual cue: Pale, glossy, and tripled in volume, faintly flecked with the reduction. When you lift the whisk, the sabayon falls in a thick ribbon that sits on the surface for two or three seconds before melting back in.
Underdone: Still loose, dark-yellow, and watery. The whisk leaves no trail — the mixture runs flat the instant it falls. Keep whisking over the heat. It needs more time and a touch more warmth — but keep lifting off the heat so it thickens gradually rather than cooking.
Perfect: Pale, voluminous, and thick enough to ribbon. You can see the bottom of the bowl for a beat when the whisk passes through. It is warm to the touch but not hot — body temperature, around 65 C / 150 F. Pull the bowl off the heat. Begin streaming in the warm butter immediately, while the sabayon is still warm.
Overdone: Grainy, lumpy, or visibly scrambled — pale curds forming around the edge or on the whisk. It smells of cooked egg. If only just starting to grain at the edges, pull off the heat instantly and whisk in a teaspoon of cold water to drop the temperature. If it has truly scrambled into curds, start over — there is no recovery from cooked yolk.
Feel cue: The whisk should meet steadily growing resistance as the yolks aerate. The bowl should feel warm against your palm but never so hot you must let go — if it stings, you are seconds from scrambling.

Off the heat (or with the bowl resting on a damp towel for stability), begin adding the warm clarified butter in a thin, steady stream while whisking without pause. Start drop by drop until the emulsion takes and visibly thickens, then increase to a slow trickle. Keep the butter warm, not hot — around 40-50 C / 105-120 F — and the sabayon warm too, so droplets disperse evenly. Add butter faster than the yolks can absorb it, or let either component get cold, and the emulsion breaks.
Visual cue: A thick, glossy, opaque pale-gold sauce that coats the whisk and falls in slow, smooth folds. It mounds softly and holds a clean line when you draw the whisk across the surface.
Underdone: Thin and pourable, like loose cream — not all the butter is in yet, or it is going in too slowly to build body. Keep streaming butter steadily while whisking. The sauce thickens as fat accumulates; it will reach nappe consistency as the last of the butter goes in.
Perfect: Lush, thick, and glossy — it clings to the whisk in a smooth sheet and holds soft peaks. Drawn across a spoon, it coats the back and you can draw a clean line through it. Move on to finishing. Whisk in the chopped tarragon, salt, and cayenne, then the tomato paste.
Overdone: Broken: the sauce has gone thin, greasy, and curdled-looking, with butter pooling and separating from the yolk. It looks like oily scrambled egg in liquid fat. Rescue it: in a clean bowl, whisk a fresh egg yolk (or a tablespoon of warm water) and dribble the broken sauce into it drop by drop, re-emulsifying as you go. If the break came from overheating, a splash of cold water whisked in hard can also pull it back together.
Feel cue: The whisk drag grows heavier with every addition — the sound shifts from a thin splash to a thick, slapping fold. If you suddenly feel the resistance drop and hear it go watery, the emulsion is breaking; stop adding butter
and whisk hard to recover before continuing.

Whisk in the reserved fresh tarragon leaves, finely chopped, then season with salt and a small pinch of cayenne. Off the heat, whisk in the cooked, concentrated tomato paste a spoonful at a time until the sauce takes on an even blush-pink color and a rounded, slightly sweet acidity. The tomato must be cooked down and concentrated first — raw paste is watery and sour and can slacken or break the emulsion. Add it warm and gently; just enough to tint and round, not to turn the sauce into tomato sauce.
Visual cue: A thick, satiny sauce of an even, pale salmon-pink, flecked green with tarragon. It naps a spoon in a glossy sheet and smells of butter, anise, and sweet cooked tomato.
Underdone: Streaky and uneven — pale gold marbled with unmixed tomato, or barely tinted with no rounded tomato note on the palate. Whisk in the tomato paste more thoroughly, a little at a time, until the color is uniformly blush-pink and the acidity tastes round and soft rather than sharp.
Perfect: Evenly blush-pink, glossy, and thick enough to nap a spoon yet loose enough to spoon over beef. Rich and tangy with a soft, sweet tomato roundness behind the tarragon. Serve immediately over grilled beef, or hold gently warm until needed.
Overdone: Slackened, thin, or beginning to break from too much tomato or paste added too cold or too raw — the color is deep red-orange and the sauce tastes of tomato rather than béarnaise. Stop adding tomato. If it has loosened, whisk hard to retighten; if it has broken, re-emulsify the sauce drop by drop into a fresh yolk in a clean bowl. The tomato should round the sauce, never dominate it.
Feel cue: The sauce should taste rich first, then tangy, then bloom into a soft sweet-tomato roundness with tarragon behind it. On the spoon it should feel like warm pink velvet, never thin or watery.

name: Choucroute Garnie
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Sauerkraut (fermented cabbage), rinsed and squeezed: 1200 g
Smoked pork knuckle (Eisbein): 1 piece
  Alternatives: smoked pork ribs
Smoked Strasbourg or Frankfurter sausages: 6 sausages
  Alternatives: bratwurst; weisswurst
Smoked lardons: 200 g
  Alternatives: smoked bacon slices
Alsatian Riesling: 300 ml
  Alternatives: dry Pinot Gris; dry white wine
Onions, sliced: 2 large
Juniper berries, lightly crushed: 10 berries
Bay leaves: 3 leaves
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 3 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Alsatian braised sauerkraut — rinsed to tame its sharpness, then slow-cooked in Riesling with juniper and bay until silk-tender, piled high with smoked pork knuckle, sausages, and lardons. A dish that makes winter honorable.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
In a large, deep pot or Dutch oven over medium heat, cook the lardons for 5 minutes until the fat begins to render and they are lightly golden. Add the sliced onions and continue cooking, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the onions are soft and translucent. They should not colour significantly — keep the heat medium at most.
Visual cue: Soft, translucent onions in a pool of rendered smoky fat. Lardons are golden. No browning on the onions.
Underdone: Onions are still firm and opaque. The lardon fat is not yet fully rendered. Continue cooking — raw onion will create a harsh base note that the wine cannot soften.
Perfect: Onions are silky, translucent, and yielding. The lardons are golden and the pan smells of smoke and sweet onion. Add the sauerkraut and aromatics.
Overdone: Onions have browned significantly. The pan smells of caramelization. Proceed — the sweetness from browned onions works well here, but the dish will be slightly richer and sweeter than the traditional version.
Feel cue: Press an onion slice against the side of the pot — it should flatten without resistance and feel completely limp, like cooked pasta.

Add the rinsed and well-squeezed sauerkraut to the pot, nestling the smoked pork knuckle into the center. Scatter the juniper berries and bay leaves over the top. Pour the Riesling over everything — it should come about halfway up the sauerkraut. Bring to a simmer, then cover tightly and cook over very low heat (or in a 150 C / 300 F oven) for 2 hours. The sauerkraut should braise gently, not boil.
Visual cue: After 2 hours: the sauerkraut has gone from pale white to a soft, creamy-ivory colour, lying in a reduced wine broth. The pork knuckle skin is beginning to loosen.
Underdone: Sauerkraut is still bright and firm, retaining most of its acidic sharpness. The pork knuckle skin is tight. Continue braising. The sauerkraut needs time to mellow and absorb the wine and pork fat.
Perfect: Sauerkraut is creamy-ivory, soft, and mellow — still tangy but without the raw harshness of fresh kraut. The wine has reduced to a fragrant broth. The pork knuckle yields when pressed. Nestle the sausages in and continue for the final step.
Overdone: Sauerkraut has completely lost its structure and dissolved into the broth. The liquid has reduced to almost nothing. Add a splash of water or white wine to reconstitute. The kraut may be mushy but the flavour is good.
Feel cue: Taste a strand of sauerkraut — after proper braising it should feel completely tender on the tongue, with only the faintest resistance, like well-cooked pasta. The acidity should be mellow and integrated, not sharp and immediate.

Nestle the smoked sausages into the sauerkraut so they are half-submerged. Cover and cook for a further 20–25 minutes at a gentle simmer until the sausages are heated through and have absorbed some of the kraut perfume. To serve, make a bed of sauerkraut on a large warmed platter, tear the pork knuckle meat from the bone in large pieces, and arrange everything — knuckle, sausages, lardons — over the sauerkraut. Serve with boiled potatoes and Dijon mustard.
Visual cue: Sausages are plump and the skin is tight, pulling slightly at the ends. The sauerkraut beneath them is fragrant with juniper and Riesling.
Underdone: Sausages are barely warm at the center. When squeezed with tongs, the center feels cool and firm. Continue simmering covered. Cold sausage in a hot dish is the only failure here.
Perfect: Sausages are plump and evenly heated. The skin is taut and lightly shiny. Juices run clear when pierced. The sauerkraut has taken on the sausage's smoke. The knuckle meat pulls away from the bone in large silky pieces. Plate immediately on a large warmed platter.
Overdone: Sausage skins have burst and the meat inside is contracting and dry. The fat has rendered out. Serve quickly — burst sausages are not a failure but they look less elegant. The flavour remains good.
Feel cue: Squeeze a sausage gently with tongs — it should feel uniformly yielding from end to end, plump and springy like a taut balloon. Any cold firmness in the center means more time is needed.

name: Churros con Chocolate
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Water: 240 ml
Unsalted butter: 60 g
  Alternatives: lard (traditional); neutral oil
Fine sea salt: 3 g
All-purpose flour: 150 g
Eggs (large): 2 unit
Caster sugar: 50 g
  Alternatives: white sugar
Ground cinnamon: 5 g
Vegetable oil for frying: 1 L
  Alternatives: sunflower oil; light olive oil
Cornstarch: 20 g
  Alternatives: potato starch
Whole milk: 300 ml
  Alternatives: oat milk for dairy-free
Sugar (for chocolate sauce): 30 g
Dark chocolate 70%, finely chopped: 100 g
  Alternatives: bittersweet chocolate chips
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Crisp, ridged ropes of fried choux dough — golden and shattering at the ridges, yielding within — dusted in cinnamon sugar and plunged into a cup of velvet-thick, bittersweet Spanish hot chocolate.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine water, butter, and salt in a medium heavy-bottomed saucepan over high heat. Bring to a full rolling boil, stirring until the butter is completely melted and incorporated. The entire surface should be turbulent — no butter slicks should float on top. Remove from heat the moment it hits a full boil; a moment of over-boiling evaporates too much water and throws off your flour ratio.
Visual cue: A vigorously boiling, uniform liquid with no visible butter separation. Steam billows generously.
Underdone: Butter pools on the surface and the liquid is gently simmering, not boiling. Keep the heat on high and wait for a true rolling boil before adding flour.
Perfect: Full boil across the whole surface, butter completely emulsified into the water, no separation. Remove from heat immediately and add all the flour at once.
Overdone: Liquid has reduced visibly; the saucepan bottom is visible through a thin layer. Steam is excessive. Add a tablespoon of hot water to compensate, return briefly to boil, then proceed.
Feel cue: Hold your hand above the pan — you should feel fierce, steady heat radiating up before the liquid even comes into view.

Tip all the flour into the boiling liquid in one go. Switch immediately to a stiff wooden spoon or silicone spatula and stir vigorously, pressing the dough against the sides of the pan. Within 60–90 seconds the mixture will pull away from the sides and form a single cohesive ball. Continue drying the dough over medium heat for another 2 minutes, stirring constantly. This step drives out excess moisture and cooks the starch so the dough can absorb eggs without becoming soupy.
Visual cue: A smooth, matte ball that pulls cleanly away from the pan walls and gathers around the spoon. A thin, dry film forms on the pan base.
Underdone: Dough is still sticky and clings to the pan in wet streaks. No film on the pan bottom. Continue stirring over medium heat — the dough needs more drying time before eggs can be added.
Perfect: A glossy-then-matte cohesive mass. A thin starchy film (panada) coats the bottom. Dough does not stick to the spoon when it stands upright in the mass. Transfer to a stand mixer bowl or wide bowl and cool 5 minutes before adding eggs.
Overdone: Dough has turned crumbly and gritty; it crumbles rather than holding together. Smells of scorched starch. Discard and start over — over-dried panade will produce grainy churros.
Feel cue: Press your palm lightly on the dough ball — it should feel dry and almost waxy, like firm mashed potato, with no moisture transferring to your hand.

Beat the eggs one at a time into the cooled panade using a hand mixer, stand mixer with a paddle, or strenuous hand-beating with a wooden spoon. After each egg the dough will look broken and slippery — keep beating until it fully absorbs before adding the next. When both eggs are incorporated the dough should be smooth, glossy, and just stiff enough to hold a piped shape. Test by lifting the spoon: the dough should fall in a slow, thick ribbon and hold a V-shape at the tip.
Visual cue: Glossy, smooth dough that falls from the spoon in a slow, heavy V-shaped ribbon without snapping off or pouring freely.
Underdone: Dough is too stiff — it falls in chunky lumps, not a ribbon. Piping will be difficult and churros may crack while frying. Beat in an additional egg yolk or a tablespoon of water to soften the consistency.
Perfect: Pipe-able, smooth, and glossy. The dough holds a star-tip shape when piped and does not slump. Falls as a slow, defined V-ribbon. Fill a piping bag fitted with a large open-star tip (1.5 cm) and heat the oil.
Overdone: Dough is too loose and flows like thick batter; it will not hold the ridged star shape in the oil. The dough cannot be thickened once thinned; the resulting churros will still taste good but be round ropes without defined ridges.
Feel cue: The dough should resist the spoon with each beat and then release with a shiny, satisfying plop — like a very stiff cake batter.

Heat vegetable oil to 175–180°C (350°F) in a deep saucepan or wok — use a thermometer. Pipe 15–20 cm lengths of dough directly into the hot oil using scissors or a knife to snip each rope. Fry in small batches of 3–4 without crowding, turning once with tongs after 2 minutes. Total fry time is 4–5 minutes per batch until deeply golden. The oil temperature will drop when you add dough; adjust heat to maintain 170°C. Drain on a wire rack, not paper — paper traps steam and softens the crust.
Visual cue: Rich amber-gold churros with clearly defined star-tip ridges that are darker at the peaks. The surface should be evenly colored, not blotchy.
Underdone: Pale golden, almost yellow. The ridges are lightly colored but the body is still blond. Interior will be doughy and greasy. Return to the oil for another 60–90 seconds per side; the exterior must be deep gold for the interior to cook through.
Perfect: Deep amber-gold. The ridges are darker — almost mahogany — and the body is evenly golden. They audibly sizzle and feel rigid when tapped with tongs. Drain on a wire rack and immediately roll in cinnamon sugar while piping hot.
Overdone: Dark brown to reddish-brown. Ridges are charring. Smells of burnt dough. Pull immediately; brush off the darkest exterior and taste — if bitter throughout, those pieces are lost, but the interior may be salvageable as churro pieces in ice cream.
Feel cue: A perfect churro rings hollow and feels rigid when tapped with a fingernail — the wall should have set into a crisp shell you can hear.

Mix the caster sugar and ground cinnamon in a wide, shallow bowl — about 10 parts sugar to 1 part cinnamon. Roll each hot churro through the mixture immediately after draining, turning to coat every ridge. The residual oil acts as a binder; if the sugar slips off, the churro has cooled too much. Work quickly. Arrange on a plate without stacking to preserve the crust.
Visual cue: Every ridge and groove is coated in sparkling cinnamon sugar. The churro glints under light.
Underdone: Sugar is only on one side or slides off in places. Bare patches of uncoated dough visible. Re-roll while still warm, pressing gently to help the sugar adhere.
Perfect: Full, even coating of sparkling cinnamon sugar on all surfaces. The crust stays crisp. You can hear a faint crunch when the churro flexes. Serve immediately with the hot chocolate.
Overdone: Sugar has formed a thick, cloying crust that obscures the ridges; bitter burnt-sugar taste if the sugar hit the hot oil. Nothing to do once over-sugared — just note the proportion for next time and serve as-is.
Feel cue: Roll the churro between your fingers in the sugar bowl — the ridges should catch the crystals like a file, giving a gentle gritty rasp.

Whisk the cornstarch into about 50 ml of the cold milk until fully dissolved — no lumps. Pour the remaining milk and sugar into a small saucepan over medium heat and warm until steaming. Add the dissolved cornstarch slurry, whisking constantly. When the mixture begins to steam and thicken, reduce heat to low and add the finely chopped dark chocolate all at once. Stir slowly until the chocolate fully melts and the sauce coats the back of a spoon thickly — this is meant to be far thicker than hot cocoa. It should mound slightly when dropped from a spoon.
Visual cue: A glossy, dark brown sauce that coats the spoon in a thick, opaque layer and falls in slow ribbons. It should be thick enough that a spoon dragged through holds a line for 2 seconds.
Underdone: Thin and runny, like chocolate milk. The spoon leaves no clear coating. Continue cooking over low heat, stirring constantly, until the sauce thickens to the ribbon stage — usually another 3–5 minutes.
Perfect: Thickly coats the spoon. A finger drawn through the back leaves a clean line that holds. Deep brown, not black, with a glossy sheen. Pour into serving cups immediately and keep warm.
Overdone: Sauce has seized into a grainy, stiff paste. Lumps of chocolate have scorched on the bottom. Whisk in a tablespoon of hot milk off the heat to loosen; if grainy, strain through a fine sieve.
Feel cue: Dip a teaspoon and let the chocolate fall back into the pan — it should fall in thick, molten sheets, not drops or streams.

name: Spanish Churros
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
All-purpose flour (plain): 1 parts
Boiling water: 1 parts
Fine salt: 0.01 parts
  Alternatives: fleur de sel
Olive oil (or unsalted butter): 0.05 parts
  Alternatives: neutral vegetable oil; lard for a more traditional flavour
Ground cinnamon: 0.01 parts
  Alternatives: canela (softer Mexican cinnamon)
Granulated sugar (for coating): 0.15 parts
  Alternatives: caster sugar; vanilla sugar
Neutral oil for deep-frying: 2 parts
  Alternatives: sunflower oil; refined olive oil; lard
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Crisp-ridged, grease-free fried dough piped star-shaped and rolled in cinnamon sugar — the breakfast of Madrid, best plunged still hot into a cup of thick, almost-solid hot chocolate, the batter inside still just slightly damp at the centre.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Bring water to a rolling boil in a saucepan. Add the salt and oil and let them dissolve in the water, then pull the pan off the heat and tip in all the flour at once. Stir immediately and vigorously with a wooden spoon — the boiling water cooks the starch in the flour (this is a pâte à choux relative), creating a smooth, stiff dough that pulls away from the sides of the pan cleanly. Continue stirring for 1 to 2 minutes until no raw flour remains and the dough forms a single cohesive mass.
Visual cue: A smooth, stiff, non-sticky dough that holds its shape in the pan and pulls away from the walls cleanly. No dry flour patches, no lumps. Pale ivory.
Underdone: Lumpy and heterogeneous. Dry pockets of uncooked flour visible. The dough doesn't hold together when pressed. Keep stirring over residual heat for another minute. The starch needs to cook fully — underdone dough will burst in the oil.
Perfect: Smooth, homogeneous, and stiff enough that a spoon dragged through it leaves a clean channel that slowly fills back. Smells like cooked dough. Transfer to the piping bag fitted with a large star nozzle (1 cm minimum) and rest for 5 minutes to cool slightly before piping.
Overdone: Dough has dried out on the stovetop, gone crumbly, or stuck and scorched on the pan bottom. Add a tablespoon of hot water and stir to rehydrate. A slightly over-dried dough is still pipeable if rehydrated carefully.
Feel cue: The dough should feel dense and warm when pressed — like stiff mashed potato. It should not be sticky on your fingers, but it should leave no dry flour residue either. Stiff enough to pipe without collapsing, supple enough to extrude through the star tip cleanly.

Transfer the dough to a large piping bag fitted with a large star nozzle — a 6-point or 8-point star with at least a 1.5 cm opening. Twist the top shut and rest for 5 minutes. The brief rest allows the dough to cool just enough that it will not soften the bag, and gives the gluten a moment to relax so the dough extrudes evenly. Meanwhile, mix the cinnamon and sugar in a shallow tray and set it next to the stove. Heat the frying oil in a deep, wide pot to 180°C (356°F).
Visual cue: The piping bag is firm and taut. The oil thermometer reads 180°C and the surface of the oil shimmers but does not smoke.
Underdone: The dough is still too hot — it softens the piping bag and the oil has not reached temperature yet. Wait a few minutes more. Piping into under-temperature oil causes the churros to absorb oil before the crust sets.
Perfect: Dough has cooled to a handleable temperature. Oil is at 180°C — a breadcrumb dropped in sizzles vigorously and rises within 2 seconds. Test-pipe one churro. It should sizzle firmly on contact and hold its star-ridged shape in the oil.
Overdone: The dough has cooled too long and become very stiff and hard to pipe. Oil is smoking and approaching 200°C. Knead the dough briefly to warm it. Drop the oil temperature by removing from heat for 30 seconds before frying.
Feel cue: The piping bag should feel warm but not hot against the palm of your hand — a temperature you could hold comfortably. If the nozzle is too hot to touch, wait another minute.

Holding the piping bag over the hot oil, pipe 10–15 cm lengths directly into the oil, using scissors or a knife to snip the dough cleanly at the nozzle. Fry in small batches — no more than 4 to 5 at a time — for 2 to 3 minutes per side, turning once, until deep golden-brown on all sides. The ridges from the star nozzle are the churro's crust — they crisp before the dough's interior sets. Lift with a spider or tongs and drain on a rack or paper towel for no more than 30 seconds before coating.
Visual cue: Deep, even golden-brown across all ridges and grooves. The star cross-section is pronounced and holds its shape. No pale patches, no dark spots. The inside is still slightly soft.
Underdone: Pale blond and soft on all surfaces. The churros feel light and bouncy but greasy when pressed — the crust has not set and they will become soggy rapidly. Return to the oil. Churros need deep colour — pale churros are almost always also greasy and soft inside.
Perfect: Rich amber-gold with a crisp, audible crust when tapped. The ridges are slightly darker than the grooves. Inside, when torn open, the dough is set and barely moist at the centre. Drain briefly and move immediately to the cinnamon-sugar coating — the sugar adheres best to the hot, oily surface.
Overdone: Dark mahogany-brown, very hard. The ridges are nearly burnt and the sugar you add will melt and burn immediately. Eat them quickly — they have a short window before they harden completely. Next time, reduce oil temperature by 10°C or shorten the fry time.
Feel cue: A perfect churro straight from the oil sounds hollow when tapped — a quiet click rather than a dull thud. It should feel rigid enough to hold its shape when lifted from one end, but the interior should have a faint give when you squeeze it gently between two fingers.

Drop the hot drained churros immediately into the cinnamon-sugar mixture and toss to coat, or roll them quickly in the tray. The residual oil on the surface is the glue — the coating will not adhere well once they cool. Serve within 10 minutes of frying. Churros do not keep well: they begin losing their snap within 20 minutes as steam migrates from the interior to the crust.
Visual cue: A uniform, sparkly coat of cinnamon sugar on every surface, the warm oil acting as adhesive. The sugar glistens slightly from the heat of the churros.
Underdone: The cinnamon sugar is patchy or has mostly fallen off. Bare gold surfaces visible between the ridges where no sugar clung. Roll while the churro is still hot and oily. Press the sugar lightly into the surface with your palm if needed.
Perfect: Every groove and ridge is sugar-dusted. The cinnamon smell rises as the warmth blooms the spice. A pinch of the coating between the fingers feels gritty-sweet. Serve immediately with thick hot chocolate for dipping. Do not pile the churros on top of each other — they steam each other soft.
Overdone: The churros were coated while wet (not well-drained) and the sugar has dissolved into a sticky paste rather than a dry sparkle. Drain more thoroughly next time. The coating is cosmetic — it won't affect flavour much, but the sticky texture is unpleasant.
Feel cue: Pick up a coated churro and tap it on the counter — it should ring lightly with a crisp shell. The cinnamon-sugar should feel dry and sparkling between your fingers, not damp or syrupy.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

description: The slipper loaf — a wet, slack dough fermented with a poolish and folded rather than kneaded, baked into a blistered, flour-dusted crust over a crumb shot through with glassy, irregular holes. Tear it open and it should steam, smell of cream and wheat, and tug back like wet lace.

ingredients.name: Water (cool, for the poolish and dough)

steps:
The night before, build a poolish: whisk together a third of the flour, an equal weight of the water (so roughly 30% flour at 100% hydration), and a pinch of the yeast — about a fifth of the total. It should be a loose, pancake-thick batter. Cover and leave at cool room temperature for 12 to 16 hours. This long, slow pre-ferment is where the bread's flavor and extensibility are built; rushing it gives a bland, tight loaf.
Visual cue: A domed, bubbly batter laced with bubbles across the whole surface, just starting to sink in the center, smelling sweet, yeasty, and faintly of yogurt or beer.
Underdone: The surface is mostly flat with only a few scattered bubbles. It smells of raw flour, not fermentation. Leave it longer in a warmer spot. A cold kitchen can need the full 16 hours or more before the poolish is ready.
Perfect: Risen and domed, the whole top covered in bubbles, with the center just beginning to dimple downward. Aroma is winey and lactic. Use it now — at peak it has maximum strength and the best flavor. Mix the final dough immediately.
Overdone: The poolish has fully collapsed into a flat, deflated, sharply sour and alcoholic batter, sometimes with a grayish skin. Still usable if only just collapsed — proceed but expect a tangier loaf. If it smells like nail polish, it over-fermented; the dough will be slack and weak.
Feel cue: Tap the bowl — a ripe poolish jiggles like a loose, airy mousse and is webbed with bubbles all the way through, not just on top. It smells closer to beer than to dough.

Add the remaining flour, water, yeast, and the olive oil to the poolish and mix to a shaggy, sticky mass — no real kneading, just enough to hydrate every bit of flour. Cover and rest 20 minutes (an autolyse) so the flour fully absorbs water and the gluten begins to organize on its own. Then sprinkle the salt over the top and squeeze it through the dough with wet hands until evenly distributed. The dough will be very wet and slack; that high hydration is what makes ciabatta's open crumb, so resist adding flour.
Visual cue: A wet, sticky, cohesive dough that pulls away from your fingers in long sticky strands but still pools and spreads in the bowl — too slack to hold a ball.
Underdone: Dry flour streaks remain and the dough breaks into lumpy clumps rather than a single sticky mass. Keep gently mixing with wet hands until no dry flour is left, then give it the autolyse rest.
Perfect: A uniform, very wet dough that clings and stretches off the fingers, glossy where the oil and salt have worked in. It spreads to fill the bowl. Cover and move to the bulk fermentation with stretch-and-folds.
Overdone: The dough has gone soupy and batter-like with no stretch, often from over-mixing a wet dough or adding extra water. Build strength back with extra folds in the next step, spaced closer together. Avoid adding flour, which kills the open crumb.
Feel cue: Wet your hands before touching it — the dough should feel like thick, tacky paste that grabs at your fingers. It will seem alarmingly loose; that is correct for ciabatta.

Bulk-ferment in an oiled tub for about 2 to 3 hours at warm room temperature, building strength with stretch-and-folds instead of kneading. With a wet hand, grab one side of the dough, stretch it up, and fold it over the center; rotate the tub and repeat on all four sides. Do a full set of four folds every 30 minutes for the first 90 minutes, then leave the dough to rise undisturbed. Each fold tightens the gluten and traps gas; over the session the slack dough transforms into something jiggly, billowy, and full of air.
Visual cue: A puffy, domed dough roughly doubled, jiggly and alive when the tub is nudged, with large bubbles visible through the sides and surface.
Underdone: The dough is still flat and slack with few bubbles, and tears rather than stretches during a fold. Give it more time and another gentle fold. Warmth speeds it — find a spot around 24-26°C.
Perfect: Roughly doubled, airy and quivering, holding loose folds when handled and domed with big bubbles under the surface. Stop folding and proceed to dividing and proofing. The dough should feel strong but extensible.
Overdone: The dough has risen and then begun to slump and spread flat, smelling sharply sour, with a fragile slack surface that deflates at a touch. Move to shaping immediately and handle gently — over-proofed dough has little oven spring left. Reduce bulk time next batch.
Feel cue: By the last fold the dough should feel supple and balloon-like, stretching thin without tearing and pulling back with a soft elastic tension. It will billow and slowly relax when you let go.

Generously flour your work surface and a couche or floured towel with the semolina or rice flour. Tip the dough out without punching it down — you want to keep the gas. Dust the top, then with a bench knife cut it into two or three rough rectangles, handling as little as possible. Stretch each gently into a slipper shape, transfer (flour-side down, then flipped at baking) onto the floured couche, and pleat the cloth between loaves. Proof 30 to 45 minutes until puffy and pillowy. Meanwhile heat the oven to 245°C (475°F) with a baking stone or steel and a steam pan.
Visual cue: Soft, puffy, dimpled rectangles that have relaxed and spread slightly, wobbling like a water balloon and dotted with bubbles just under the floured surface.
Underdone: The loaves are dense and firm, holding sharp cut edges and feeling solid rather than airy. Give them another 10-20 minutes. They should look noticeably puffed and feel light before baking.
Perfect: Pillowy and jiggly, spread to a relaxed slipper shape with surface bubbles showing. A floured fingertip leaves a dent that springs back slowly. Bake right away on the hot stone with steam. Don't degas — gentle handling keeps the holes.
Overdone: The loaves have spread thin and flat, the surface gone fragile and bubbly, and a poked dent does not spring back at all. Bake immediately and skip moving them around. Expect flatter loaves but still good flavor; shorten the proof next time.
Feel cue: A ready loaf feels like a gas-filled cushion — light, wobbly, and tender. A gentle poke leaves a dent that fills back slowly and only partway; if it springs right back it needs more time, if it stays put it's overproofed.

Flip each loaf flour-side up onto a peel or parchment and slide onto the hot stone, keeping the slipper shape. Pour boiling water into the steam pan (or spritz the oven walls) and shut the door fast. Bake with steam for the first 10 minutes for maximum oven spring and blistering, then vent the steam and bake another 10 to 15 minutes until deeply golden and crackling. The loaves are done at an internal temperature of about 96-99°C (205-210°F). Cool fully on a rack — at least an hour — before tearing; the crumb is still setting inside.
Visual cue: A burnished, blistered, golden-brown crust dusted with flour, crackling audibly as it cools, with an airy crumb full of glossy irregular holes when torn.
Underdone: The crust is pale blond and soft, the loaf light for its size, and the bottom sounds dull when tapped. Bake longer with the oven vented. A proper ciabatta needs deep color and a crisp, resonant crust.
Perfect: Deep golden with darker blisters, a crackly thin crust, and a hollow drum-like thump on the bottom. Torn open, the crumb is open, glossy, and elastic. Cool fully on a rack before slicing so steam escapes and the crumb sets — cutting hot makes it gummy.
Overdone: The crust is very dark to scorched and tastes acrid and bitter, the crumb dry near the edges. Pull it sooner next time and lower the heat slightly after the steam phase. A dark crust is good; a black one is burnt.
Feel cue: Listen for the crust singing — a faint crackle as it cools is the sign of a thin, crisp shell. Squeeze gently; it should give with a slight crunch over a springy, light interior. The bottom should sound hollow when knocked.

name: Cider-Braised Pork Shoulder with Apples
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Pork shoulder (butt), boneless, cut into 4 large pieces: 1800 g
  Alternatives: 2.2 kg bone-in shoulder (add 30 min)
Kosher salt: 20 g
Black pepper, freshly ground: 1 tsp
Neutral oil: 30 ml
