ingredients.name: Jumbo lump blue crab meat (picked for shell)

steps:
In a large bowl, whisk together the beaten egg, mayonnaise, Old Bay, Dijon mustard, and chopped parsley until smooth and uniform. This is the entire binding and seasoning base — taste it on a cracker to calibrate the salt and spice before it touches the crab. The mixture should taste bright, slightly sharp from the mustard, and warmly spiced.
Visual cue: A smooth, pale-yellow emulsion with green flecks of parsley distributed evenly. No lumps of undissolved mustard, no streaks of unmixed egg.
Underdone: Yolk and white still visible as separate streaks; mustard pools in the center. Whisk more vigorously until the mixture is fully homogeneous.
Perfect: Uniform pale gold, fragrant with Old Bay. A line drawn through it with a whisk holds for a second. Fold in the crab and breadcrumbs gently.
Overdone: Over-whisked into stiff foam — air bubbles visible. This is not a concern here; any amount of whisking is fine at this stage. Proceed; over-whisking the binder alone does not damage the final cake.
Feel cue: The binder should feel silky and a little slippery between two fingers — the mayo and egg forming a unified emulsion before the crab is introduced.

Add the crab meat and breadcrumbs to the binder. Using a large spatula or clean hands, fold very gently — five to eight slow, sweeping folds maximum. The goal is to coat the crab in the binder while leaving the lumps as intact as possible. Every time you stir, you break crab. Stop the moment the mixture barely holds together. It should look loose and shaggy, not smooth and paste-like.
Visual cue: Large, intact white and pearlescent crab lumps barely coated in a thin film of binder. The mixture holds a clump when squeezed but falls apart if not compacted. You can see individual lump pieces clearly.
Underdone: Mixture crumbles apart even when squeezed firmly — not enough binder, or the binder is not distributed yet. Fold two or three more times, targeting the dry patches, but stop as soon as it holds.
Perfect: Just barely cohesive — a handful squeezed will hold a patty shape but the surface looks textured and chunky, not smooth. The lumps are still largely intact. Refrigerate the mixture for 30 minutes before shaping to help it firm up.
Overdone: The crab has been broken down into a smooth, paste-like mince with no visible lumps — over-mixed. The cakes will still taste good but lose the textural soul of the dish. Form immediately and cook; further handling makes it worse.
Feel cue: The mixture should feel like loosely packed snow — it holds when you press it but has no spring or stickiness of its own. If it feels like smooth putty, you have folded too many times.

Divide the mixture into six equal portions (roughly 100–120 g each). Gently press each into a thick disc about 4 cm high — do not compress too firmly. Place on a parchment-lined tray and refrigerate uncovered for 30 minutes minimum, up to 4 hours. The cold firms the binder and makes the patties dramatically easier to flip without falling apart in the pan.
Visual cue: Pale, chunky discs with a slightly tacky, matte surface after chilling. They hold their shape when the tray is tilted but still look fragile and textured rather than smooth.
Underdone: Patties still feel soft and squishy; they slump when tilted. Not cold enough. Return to the fridge for another 15–20 minutes. Rushing this step is the most common cause of cakes disintegrating in the pan.
Perfect: Firm enough to pick up cleanly without distorting. Cold to the touch, surface slightly dried from the fridge air. They feel like a just-set custard when pressed. Cook in batches immediately, keeping uncooked patties refrigerated while others cook.
Overdone: Left overnight uncovered: surface has dried to a crust and the interior is rock-cold. Not a failure — they will cook fine, just slightly slower. Cook as normal; the crust that formed will actually help them hold together in the pan.
Feel cue: Pick up a patty: it should sit flat and hold its edge without flowing over your fingers. If your hand's warmth makes it immediately soften and sag, back in the fridge it goes.

Heat a heavy skillet (cast iron or stainless) over medium heat. Add the butter and oil together — the oil raises the smoke point, the butter brings color and flavor. When the butter foam subsides and the fat shimmers, carefully lower the patties in, leaving space between them. Do not move them. Cook 3–4 minutes per side. Resist flipping early — they will release cleanly once a golden crust has formed. Use a thin fish spatula and flip once only.
Visual cue: A deep golden-brown, evenly crusted disc on both sides. The crust is crisp and dry, not wet or greasy. The sides remain slightly underdone-looking — that is correct; the center should be barely set.
Underdone: Surface is pale blonde, the crab still looks raw and wet. The patty sticks to the pan when you try to lift it — the crust has not formed. Leave it alone. The cake will release naturally when the crust sets. Attempting to lift it now will tear it apart.
Perfect: Deep golden-brown, releasing cleanly from the pan. A tap on the surface sounds hollow and crisp. The interior feels yielding but not raw when probed gently. Flip once and cook the second side. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Crust has gone dark brown or black; butter is smoking and smells acrid. The exterior is scorching before the interior can warm through. Lower the heat immediately. The next batch should go into a cooler pan.
Feel cue: Press the center of a cooked patty lightly: it should give a little — yielding like a just-set custard, not springy like rubber or squishing like putty. That gentle, barely-set give is the interior you are aiming for.

Transfer to warm plates immediately — do not rest them on a rack or they will steam and soften the crust. Serve with lemon wedges and a remoulade or simple tartar sauce alongside. The cakes are best eaten within two minutes of leaving the pan, while the contrast between the crisp exterior and the barely-bound interior is at its peak.
Visual cue: Two deep-gold discs per plate, crusts intact and dry, the broken edge revealing large, ivory crab lumps barely held in a thin binder. Steam rising from the cut.
Underdone: Interior is cold and raw-looking, the binder still liquid and the crab pale. Return to the pan or to a 180 C / 350 F oven for 4–5 minutes to finish through.
Perfect: Crust shatters at the fork's edge; inside is warm, moist, crabby, and barely cohesive — the lumps hold their shape but yield at the slightest pressure. Squeeze lemon over the top and eat immediately.
Overdone: The whole cake is dry and crumbly; no moisture remains in the center, the lumps have broken down into a firm, uniform mass. Serve with extra sauce and a piece of lemon squeezed over — nothing will restore the lost texture, but the flavor is still good.
Feel cue: A well-made Maryland crab cake should feel fragile and almost improper — like it might fall apart at any moment. That precariousness is the point. If it feels solid and safe to eat, it has too much filler.

ingredients.name: Short pasta (penne, fusilli or casarecce), dry
Kosher salt, for the pasta water
Boneless skinless chicken breasts, cut into 2.5 cm pieces
Kosher salt, for the chicken and sauce

steps:
Bring about 4 l (4 qt) water to a boil in a large pot and add the salt. Cook the pasta 1 minute less than the package directions, stirring in the first minute. Before draining, scoop out a mug of the starchy cooking water (you need about 180 ml), then drain.
Visual cue: Pasta bent easily but with a thin white core visible when bitten.
Underdone: Pasta stiff with a thick chalky center. Boil another minute and taste again.
Perfect: Tender outside, firm thread of white at the center — it will finish in the sauce. Reserve the water and drain.
Overdone: Soft all the way through, surface swollen and starting to split. Drain immediately and toss into the sauce for as short a time as possible.
Feel cue: The pasta water should taste pleasantly salty, like mild broth.

While the water heats, pat the chicken dry and season with 3/4 tsp kosher salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a 12-inch (30 cm) skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chicken in a single layer and cook without stirring 3 minutes until golden underneath, then turn and cook 2–3 minutes more until cooked through to 165°F (74°C) — check the largest piece. Transfer to a plate.
Visual cue: Golden-brown faces on the chicken pieces, opaque white throughout when cut.
Underdone: Pale surfaces and a glossy pink center; below 165°F (74°C). Cook 1 minute more and recheck the largest piece.
Perfect: Browned on two sides, opaque and juicy inside, 165°F (74°C). Remove to a plate.
Overdone: Shrunken, stringy and dry at the edges. Slice smaller and let the sauce do the work of moistening them.
Feel cue: A cooked piece feels firm with a slight spring when pressed, not soft and wobbly.

Lower the heat to medium, add the butter to the same skillet and, once it foams, add the garlic and pepper flakes; cook 45 seconds until fragrant. Pour in the cream and the lemon zest, scraping up the browned bits, and simmer gently 2–3 minutes until slightly thickened.
Visual cue: A pale ivory sauce, faintly flecked with garlic and zest, bubbling gently around the edges.
Underdone: Cream thin and runny, no body. Simmer another minute.
Perfect: Sauce lightly coats a spoon and small bubbles rise lazily. Add the pasta right away.
Overdone: Thick and pasty, butter fat separating at the edges. Whisk in a few tablespoons of pasta water to bring it back.
Feel cue: Run a finger across the coated back of the spoon: the line should hold for a second before softening.

Add the drained pasta and 120 ml of the pasta water to the skillet and toss over medium-low heat for 1–2 minutes until the pasta is al dente and the sauce clings. Take off the heat, add the Parmesan in handfuls, tossing to melt, then add the spinach and chicken and toss until the spinach just wilts. Stir in 2 tbsp lemon juice, taste, and add more lemon, salt, pepper or a splash of pasta water to loosen. Serve immediately.
Visual cue: Glossy, creamy pasta with bright green spinach wilted through and chicken evenly distributed.
Underdone: Sauce watery and pooling at the bottom of the pan. Toss over low heat another 30–60 seconds; the starch will tighten it.
Perfect: Sauce clings to every piece in a silky coat, no pooling, spinach just collapsed. Serve right away — it thickens as it sits.
Overdone: Sauce gluey and the cheese clumped or stringy. Loosen with warm pasta water, off the heat, tossing vigorously.
Feel cue: The sauce should feel silky rather than heavy on the tongue, with lemon lifting the richness at the end of each bite.

name: Crema Catalana
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Whole milk: 100 %
  Alternatives: half-and-half for a richer result
Egg yolks: 25 %
Caster sugar (plus extra for the crust): 20 %
  Alternatives: superfine sugar
Cornstarch (cornflour): 5 %
  Alternatives: potato starch
Cinnamon stick: 1 %
  Alternatives: ceylon cinnamon; cassia bark
Lemon zest (1 large lemon, no pith): 1 %
  Alternatives: orange zest; Meyer lemon zest
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 4 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Catalonia's ancient answer to crème brûlée — a silky egg-yolk custard perfumed with lemon zest and cinnamon rather than vanilla, set in shallow terracotta dishes and finished with a brittle caramel crust burned with a red-hot iron.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Caster sugar (plus extra for the crust)
Lemon zest (1 large lemon, no pith)

steps:
Combine the whole milk with the cinnamon stick and lemon zest in a heavy-bottomed saucepan. Set over medium heat and bring slowly to a bare simmer — small bubbles forming at the edge, not a rolling boil. Remove from heat the moment it steams and the first bubbles appear. Cover the pot and let it steep for 20 minutes off the heat. The milk will absorb the fragrant oils from the lemon zest and the warm spice of the cinnamon, building the aromatic base that defines crema catalana from crème brûlée. Strain the milk through a fine sieve to remove the zest and cinnamon, pressing lightly to extract the flavored oils. The milk should smell unmistakably of warm citrus and spice.
Visual cue: Pale, faintly ivory milk with a delicate lemony fragrance and a suggestion of cinnamon warmth — the aroma should be more perfume than food at this stage.
Underdone: Milk smells clean and barely different from raw milk — the flavors have not had time to extract. Re-cover and steep another 10 minutes. A 20-minute steep is the minimum; 30 is better.
Perfect: A distinct, citrus-forward fragrance with cinnamon warmth behind it. The milk looks barely changed in color but tastes transformed. Strain and proceed immediately to the custard base.
Overdone: Milk was brought to a full boil — it has taken on a faintly cooked or skin-like quality and the lemon zest has turned bitter from prolonged heat. Strain immediately and use the milk anyway, but note the bitterness. A small extra pinch of sugar in the yolk mixture can help compensate.
Feel cue: Hold your palm over the strained warm milk and breathe in — you should smell lemon first, then cinnamon rising behind it. This layered fragrance is your north star for the finished custard.

In a large bowl, whisk the egg yolks with the caster sugar until the mixture turns pale, thick, and ribbony — lift the whisk and the mixture should fall back in a slow, fat ribbon that holds its shape for 2–3 seconds before dissolving. This takes about 3 minutes of vigorous whisking. Then whisk in the cornstarch until no dry lumps remain. The cornstarch is what differentiates crema catalana from a pure yolk custard — it gives a firmer, slightly starchier set that holds up in the shallow terracotta dishes and allows the crust to be applied without the custard collapsing. Do not skip this step or substitute with flour.
Visual cue: A pale, creamy-yellow, thick mixture that falls from the whisk in a wide, slow ribbon and holds its shape briefly on the surface — no undissolved sugar granules visible, no dry cornstarch streaks.
Underdone: Mixture is still thin and bright yellow — the sugar has not dissolved and no ribbon forms; it falls like liquid. Continue whisking. The pale color and ribbon stage require the sugar to be fully dissolved into the yolks.
Perfect: Pale, thick, and glossy. Ribbon holds its shape for 2–3 seconds. Cornstarch is fully incorporated with no dry lumps. Have the strained warm milk ready and temper immediately.
Overdone: Mixture is foamy and has increased dramatically in volume from over-whisking — this introduces excess air that will create bubbles in the set custard. Let it settle for 5 minutes before proceeding, and tap the finished custard dishes on the counter before chilling to pop surface bubbles.
Feel cue: Rub a small amount between your fingertips — it should feel smooth and slightly slippery, with no graininess from undissolved sugar or dry starch. The warmth of your fingers should not change the texture noticeably.

Reheat the strained infused milk over medium heat until it's steaming and just below a simmer. Slowly pour a small ladle of hot milk into the yolk mixture while whisking constantly — this is the temper, which raises the egg temperature gently without scrambling. Pour in a second ladle, then return the entire mixture to the saucepan. Cook over medium-low heat, whisking constantly and making sure to cover every part of the bottom and corners of the pan. The custard will thicken quickly — within 3–4 minutes it will begin to coat the back of a spoon. As soon as it thickens noticeably and the first large bubble pops at the surface, remove from heat. The cornstarch needs to reach just past gelatinization temperature, which happens around the first boil. Pour immediately into shallow terracotta or ramekin dishes. Chill uncovered for at least 3 hours until completely cold and set.
Visual cue: A smooth, velvety custard that coats a spoon heavily and leaves a clean line when a finger is drawn through it — no lumps, no streaks, no scrambled yolk bits, and an evenly pale golden color.
Underdone: Custard is still thin and liquid — the cornstarch has not reached gelatinization and it flows off a spoon like cream. No coating yet. Return to medium heat and whisk continuously. It will thicken suddenly — keep the heat moderate and do not walk away.
Perfect: Thick, smooth, and glossy — coats a spoon and leaves a clean line when a finger is drawn through. One or two bubbles just breaking the surface. Remove from heat immediately and pour into dishes. Do not delay or the residual heat will continue to cook the eggs.
Overdone: Custard has scrambled into lumpy, curdled fragments — the eggs have cooked too fast or the heat was too high. Immediately pour through a fine-mesh strainer into a cold bowl and press through with a spatula. Small lumps can be smoothed out this way, though large

curds cannot.
Feel cue: Drag a wooden spoon through the custard and hold it up horizontally — a finger drawn through the coating should leave a line that holds cleanly for at least 5 seconds without the sauce closing in. That is nappe — the custard is done.

Remove the chilled custard dishes from the refrigerator. Sprinkle an even, thin layer of caster sugar over each custard — about 1 teaspoon per 10 cm dish — and tilt the dish to spread it uniformly to the edges with no bare patches and no thick mounds. The sugar must be dry and even, like a thin sheet of paper. Traditionally crema catalana is finished with a red-hot iron (ferro), but a kitchen torch works perfectly: hold the flame 2–3 cm from the surface and move in tight circles, watching the sugar melt, bubble, and caramelize from the center outward to the edges. Stop the moment the surface turns amber-brown — it continues to darken for a second after the flame moves away. The crema should be served within 10 minutes of caramelizing, before the sugar absorbs moisture and softens.
Visual cue: A smooth, glassy amber disk of caramel with no white sugar patches, no black spots, and a uniformly thin surface that taps hard and shatters when tapped with a spoon.
Underdone: Sugar has melted but is still pale gold and soft — it will not crack when tapped and still tastes of raw sugar rather than caramel. Continue with the torch, working inward from where it has already caramelized. Aim for a uniform amber, not just melted.
Perfect: Deep amber, glossy, and stone-hard when cool — shatters cleanly with a spoon tap, revealing the cold custard below. A faint bitter caramel fragrance rises. Serve within 10 minutes while the contrast between hot brittle crust and cold creamy custard is at its peak.
Overdone: Surface is dark brown to black in patches and smells acrid — burnt caramel is irreversibly bitter. Scrape off the burnt sugar with a spoon, re-chill the exposed custard for 10 minutes, apply a fresh layer of caster sugar, and caramelize again more gently.
Feel cue: Tap the center of the caramel with the back of a spoon — it should ring like glass and shatter cleanly into
shards. The spoon should meet resistance and then break through in a single crisp crack, revealing the cold, silky custard underneath. That textural contrast is everything.

name: Crème Anglaise
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Whole milk: 1 parts
  Alternatives: oat milk (thinner result)
Heavy cream (36% fat): 1 parts
Large egg yolks: 6 yolks per 500ml liquid
Caster sugar: 0.4 parts
  Alternatives: honey
Vanilla bean, split and scraped (or 2 tsp pure extract): 1 bean per 500ml
  Alternatives: vanilla paste; tonka bean
Fine sea salt, one small pinch: 0.005 parts
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 40 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The mother of all dessert sauces — a slow-cooked ribbon of egg yolks, milk, cream, and vanilla that pours over a warm pudding like liquid cream and coats every surface in a thin, trembling veil. It exists in the narrow corridor between raw custard and scrambled egg, and cooking it well is the mark of a trained hand.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Vanilla bean, split and scraped (or 2 tsp pure extract)
Fine sea salt, one small pinch

steps:
Combine the whole milk and heavy cream in a medium heavy-bottomed saucepan. Split the vanilla bean lengthwise with a sharp paring knife and scrape out the seeds — drag the back of the knife along the cut face to lift the fine black paste. Add both the seeds and the empty pod to the milk. Heat over medium heat until the mixture reaches a full simmer — you will see the vanilla seeds dispersing into tiny black dots throughout the milk. Turn off the heat, cover the pot, and let the vanilla infuse for 15 minutes. This off-heat infusion extracts the full aromatic complexity of the vanilla without cooking out the volatile top notes that make it smell floral rather than simply sweet. If using extract, add it after the anglaise is cooked and cooled to 60°C — heat destroys the delicate top notes of good extract.
Visual cue: Pale, cream-coloured milk with fine black vanilla seeds distributed throughout. A ring of small bubbles at the edge of the pan indicates it reached the right temperature.
Underdone: Milk is warm but no bubbles appeared. Vanilla aroma is weak. Return to heat briefly until you see bubbles, then cover and infuse.
Perfect: Milk simmered, vanilla seeds are evenly dispersed, and the pot smells powerfully of warm vanilla and fresh cream. Proceed to whisk yolks while the milk infuses.
Overdone: Milk boiled hard and formed a thick skin on the surface. Cream smells slightly cooked. Remove the skin with a spoon. The anglaise will still work; the flavour will be slightly more cooked.
Feel cue: Remove the lid and hold your face over the pot — the steam should be fragrant with vanilla and cream, not eggy or scorched. That aroma check tells you the milk is ready.

While the milk infuses, place the egg yolks, caster sugar, and pinch of salt in a large heatproof bowl. Whisk vigorously for 2–3 minutes until the mixture reaches the ruban (ribbon) stage — a thick, pale, fluffy foam that falls from the whisk in a wide, slow ribbon that sits on top of itself for two seconds before dissolving. This step partially dissolves the sugar and coats the yolk proteins with a sugar barrier that raises their coagulation temperature, giving you a wider window before the anglaise scrambles on the heat. The mixture will go from a deep orange-yellow to a pale, creamy yellow as you incorporate air. Do not skimp on the whisking — under-developed yolks are the primary cause of grainy anglaise.
Visual cue: A pale, thick, foamy mixture that falls from the lifted whisk in a slow, continuous ribbon resting on the surface for 2 seconds before sinking.
Underdone: The mixture is still orange-yellow and thin. It falls off the whisk in thin drops, not a ribbon. Keep whisking. Your arm will tire — this is normal. The transformation is abrupt; push through.
Perfect: Pale lemon-cream coloured foam. When the whisk is lifted, the batter falls in a thick, slow ribbon that sits on the surface briefly. The mixture has tripled in volume. Temper with the hot milk immediately.
Overdone: You have incorporated too much air — the mixture looks stiff and meringue-like. This is not possible by hand but can happen with an electric mixer at high speed. Proceed — a little extra air will cook out on the heat.
Feel cue: Rub a small amount between your thumb and forefinger — you should feel almost no grit from sugar granules. A slight resistance, but smooth. That tells you enough sugar has dissolved into the yolk fat.

This is the critical step that separates successful anglaise from sweet scrambled eggs. Remove the vanilla pod from the milk. With one hand whisking the yolk mixture constantly, use the other to slowly ladle or pour the hot milk into the yolks — start with just a small splash (about 60ml / ¼ cup) and whisk it in completely before adding more. This gradual addition raises the temperature of the yolks slowly, preventing them from cooking on contact with the hot milk. Add the milk in three additions over 30 seconds of whisking. Once you have incorporated about half the milk, you can pour the remaining milk in a thin, steady stream while whisking. Pour everything back into the saucepan. The mixture will be warm, thin, and faintly foamy on top — this foam dissipates as you cook.
Visual cue: A uniform, pale cream-coloured liquid — slightly thicker than the milk alone — with no white streaks of cooked egg and a faint foam on the surface.
Underdone: You added the milk too slowly and the mixture is still cold. Foam sits thick on top. This is fine — you have simply been careful. Proceed to the heat.
Perfect: A smooth, warm, uniform custard base. Pourable consistency, no lumps, mild vanilla aroma. Pour into the saucepan and cook over medium-low heat.
Overdone: White curds floating in the mixture — you added hot milk too fast and cooked the outer layer of the yolks. Strain immediately through a fine sieve. The curd clumps can be removed; the anglaise is usually saveable.
Feel cue: Hold your hand over the saucepan with the combined mixture — it should feel warm, not hot. If the pot is uncomfortable to hold, it was too hot and you needed to add the milk more slowly.

Cook the custard over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon or silicone spatula, reaching every corner and edge of the pan. This is not a step you can walk away from. The anglaise is done when it reaches 77–82°C (170–180°F) and nappe-coats the back of the spoon — a finger drawn through the coating leaves a clean, distinct line that does not run or fill in. At 83°C the egg proteins begin to scramble rapidly. Use a thermometer if you are new to this technique. Once done, immediately strain through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean bowl sitting over an ice bath. Stir to cool rapidly — the anglaise must drop below 60°C within 10 minutes. Serve warm alongside warm puddings or cakes, or chill completely to pour cold over ice cream as a pouring custard.
Visual cue: The spoon comes out coated in a thick, even, creamy layer of anglaise. A finger drawn through the coating on the spoon leaves a sharp line with clean edges.
Underdone: The spoon comes out with a thin, uneven coating. The drawn line fills in immediately. The surface is still quite foamy. Keep cooking and stirring. The thickening happens gradually and then suddenly. Increase heat slightly if it is taking more than 10 minutes.
Perfect: A thick, even coating on the spoon. Clean line. The surface foam has mostly subsided. A faint ribbon of steam rises but no bubbles break the surface. Strain immediately into the ice bath. Speed matters here.
Overdone: Tiny lumps appear in the mixture. The anglaise smells eggy. Temperature exceeded 83°C. Strain through a fine sieve immediately — the sieve catches the cooked protein clumps. Blend briefly with an immersion blender if needed. It will still be usable.
Feel cue: Dip a clean finger into the strained anglaise — it should feel like warm silk, coating your finger in a thin, trembling veil that clings without dripping. That coating weight is the texture you serve.

name: 法式焦糖布丁 · Crème Brûlée
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。

  Alternatives: half cream, half whole milk for a lighter set
Vanilla bean (split, seeds scraped): 1 pod
  Alternatives: 2 tsp vanilla bean paste; 1 tbsp pure vanilla extract (add off heat)
Egg yolks (large): 100 g
Granulated sugar (for custard): 80 g
  Alternatives: caster sugar
Fine sea salt: 1 g
Granulated sugar (for the brûlée top): 40 g
  Alternatives: turbinado/demerara for a thicker, coarser crack
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 5 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The bistro classic in two textures — a pale, trembling vanilla custard baked just to a quiver in its own water bath, then sealed under a thin lacquer of caramelized sugar that shatters under the spoon like a sheet of glass into the cool cream beneath.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

steps:
Split the vanilla bean lengthwise and scrape the sticky seeds into the cream, then drop in the spent pod too. Warm the cream gently over medium-low heat just until wisps of steam rise and bubbles fringe the edge of the pan — do not let it boil. Pull it off the heat, cover, and let it steep 15 to 30 minutes. This draws the vanilla's perfume and tiny seeds throughout the cream and gives you a warm (not hot) base that won't scramble the yolks.
Visual cue: Cream is steaming with a quivering rim of small bubbles, flecked evenly with thousands of dark vanilla seeds, smelling sweetly floral.
Underdone: Cream is cool to lukewarm, no steam, and the vanilla seeds clump together rather than dispersing. Keep warming gently and stir to break up the seed clumps. You want heat to release the aroma — but stay below a simmer.
Perfect: Steam rises and a ring of fine bubbles laces the edge. The kitchen smells strongly of vanilla and the cream is hot but not boiling. Cover and steep 15–30 minutes, then fish out the pod (scrape any clinging seeds back in) before tempering.
Overdone: The cream has reached a rolling boil and may have foamed up or scorched on the bottom, smelling faintly cooked. If only just boiled, cool it for a few minutes and proceed. If scorched, strain and start over — a burnt-milk note ruins the custard.
Feel cue: Dip a finger (carefully) — the cream should feel hot, around body-warm-plus, not painfully scalding. A long steep is the difference between background sweetness and unmistakable vanilla.

Whisk the yolks with the sugar and salt just until smooth and pale — don't whip in air, you want a flat custard, not a foam. Now temper: pour the warm vanilla cream into the yolks in a thin stream, whisking constantly, so the eggs warm gradually instead of seizing into scrambled curds. Stir, don't froth. Strain the mixture through a fine sieve into a pouring jug to catch the chalaza and any stray cooked bits, then skim off surface foam so the baked tops stay glassy-smooth.
Visual cue: A smooth, pourable, pale-yellow custard with no lumps and only a thin film of foam, lightly speckled with vanilla seeds.
Underdone: Yolks and sugar are still grainy and streaky, or the cold yolks were dumped in all at once and you can see flecks of set egg. Whisk the yolk-sugar smooth before adding cream, and add the cream more slowly. Strain firmly to remove any curdled specks.
Perfect: A uniform, satiny liquid custard that coats the whisk and pours in a smooth ribbon. No visible egg threads after straining. Skim the foam and let any remaining bubbles settle while you prep the water bath.
Overdone: The mixture has visibly scrambled — yellow curds suspended in thin liquid — because the cream was too hot or added too fast. Strain hard to remove the curds; if it's badly cooked through, the custard won't set silky and is best remade.
Feel cue: Add the cream in a thread you can see, whisking the whole time — the bowl should feel only warm, never hot, after tempering. Frothing now means a bubbly, pocked surface later, so stir low and slow.

Set shallow ramekins in a deep roasting pan and divide the custard among them. Slide the pan into a 150°C (300°F) oven, then pour hot water into the pan until it reaches halfway up the ramekins — this bain-marie buffers the eggs from direct heat so they set into satin instead of curdling. Bake 30 to 45 minutes, until the edges are set but the centers still wobble. Lift the ramekins from the water, cool to room temperature, then chill at least 4 hours or overnight so the custard firms and goes cold.
Visual cue: Custards are set at the edges with a center that jiggles like loose jelly — a uniform pale gold, surface matte and unbroken, no cracks or browning.
Underdone: A nudge of the pan sends a liquid ripple across the whole surface and the center looks soupy. Bake another 5–10 minutes and re-check. Residual heat keeps cooking after they leave the oven, so err toward slightly loose.
Perfect: The outer inch is firm and the center wobbles as one soft mass, like the surface of a water balloon — set but trembling. Remove from the water bath immediately so they stop cooking, cool, then chill at least 4 hours until cold and sliceable.
Overdone: The surface has puffed, cracked, or browned, and the whole custard moves stiffly with no wobble — a sign of over-baking or too-high heat. Lower the oven or check earlier next time. They'll taste eggy and the texture turns grainy; still edible, but the silk is lost.
Feel cue: Tap the side of a ramekin — the perfect custard quivers at the center like set jelly while the rim holds firm. The water bath should never simmer; if you see it bubbling, slip an ice cube into the pan to drop the temperature.

Just before serving, blot any condensation from the cold custard tops with a paper towel so the sugar adheres. Sprinkle an even, thin layer of granulated sugar over each — tilt and tap off the excess so no bare or thick patches remain. Sweep a kitchen torch in slow circles a few inches above the surface, melting the sugar until it bubbles, liquefies, and turns deep amber. Let the caramel set for a minute or two until it hardens to a brittle pane, then serve at once while the custard is cold and the crust is crisp.
Visual cue: A continuous, glossy, deep-amber crust — glass-thin and hard — sealing the pale cold custard beneath, with a faint bittersweet smell of toasted caramel.
Underdone: The sugar has only partly melted, leaving pale, grainy, white patches that crunch like raw sugar rather than crack like glass. Keep torching the dull spots until every grain liquefies and colors. Bare sugar tastes gritty and won't form the signature shatter.
Perfect: An even sheet of caramel the color of dark honey, glassy and smooth, that taps hard and cracks cleanly under a spoon to reveal cold custard underneath. Rest 1–2 minutes for the crust to harden fully, then serve immediately before it absorbs moisture and softens.
Overdone: The caramel has gone dark mahogany to black, smoking and smelling acrid — it will taste harshly bitter and burnt. Torch more gently and from farther away. If badly scorched, let it set, lift off the burnt shard, and re-sugar and re-torch the top.
Feel cue: The reward is the sound: tap the cooled crust with the back of a spoon and it should ring slightly, then give way with a sharp crack into the cold cream. Caramelize only at the last minute — a brûlée top weeps and softens within an hour of standing.

name: Creme Caramel
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Whole milk: 100 parts
Whole eggs: 25 parts
Granulated sugar (custard): 18 parts
Granulated sugar (caramel): 15 parts
Vanilla bean (split and scraped): 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: vanilla extract
Water (for caramel): 5 parts
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 5 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A trembling dome of vanilla custard floating on a mirror of bitter caramel — the most elegant dessert that asks nothing of the cook but patience and a gentle hand.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine the caramel sugar and water in a small, light-colored saucepan. Stir once to dissolve, then stop stirring entirely. Place over medium-high heat. The sugar will bubble, then color. Swirl the pan gently — never stir — to ensure even browning. Remove from heat when it reaches a deep amber. Immediately pour into ramekins and swirl to coat the bottoms.
Visual cue: A deep amber caramel the color of dark honey or aged whisky — transparent, with thin, fast-moving bubbles and a faint wisp of smoke.
Underdone: Pale gold, like apple juice. Bubbles are large and slow. Tastes simply sweet, not complex. Continue cooking — the bitter complexity only develops at deeper amber. This is the stage most people stop too early.
Perfect: Deep amber with reddish undertones. Smells like toffee with a slight bitter edge. Bubbles are fine and fast. Thin and liquid, coating the pan glass-smooth. Pour into ramekins immediately — it hardens in seconds.
Overdone: Dark brown to black. Acrid, burnt-sugar smoke. Tastes purely bitter. Discard and start over. Burnt caramel cannot be rescued and will ruin the custard.
Feel cue: The smell is the most reliable guide — it progresses from nothing, to butterscotch, to toffee, to a faint burnt-edge bitterness. Pull it at toffee. The transition from perfect to burnt takes only 10-15 seconds.

Combine milk with the split vanilla bean and its scraped seeds in a saucepan. Heat over medium until steam rises and small bubbles form at the edge — do not boil. Remove from heat, cover, and let the vanilla steep for 15 minutes. Remove the vanilla pod.
Visual cue: Steaming milk speckled with thousands of tiny black vanilla seeds. Surface has a skin just beginning to form at the edges.
Underdone: Milk is lukewarm. No steam, no bubbles. Vanilla seeds are clustered together, not dispersed. Continue heating. The milk needs to be hot enough to extract the vanilla oils.
Perfect: Fine bubbles ring the edge. Steam rises steadily. Vanilla seeds are dispersed throughout. The kitchen smells of warm custard and vanilla. Remove from heat and steep.
Overdone: Milk has come to a full boil. Surface is frothing. A thick skin has formed. Remove from heat immediately. Skim the skin. Boiled milk has a slightly cooked flavor but the custard will still work.
Feel cue: The vanilla-infused milk should smell like ice cream base — warm, round, and floral. If it smells flat, the vanilla was stale. A drop on your wrist should feel comfortably hot, not scalding.

Whisk eggs and custard sugar together gently — combine them without creating foam. Slowly pour the warm milk into the egg mixture in a thin stream, whisking constantly. This tempers the eggs so they do not scramble. Strain the custard through a fine-mesh sieve into a pouring vessel. Let any bubbles settle for 5 minutes.
Visual cue: A smooth, pourable liquid the color of pale cream — no bubbles on the surface, no visible egg strands, no foam.
Underdone: Streaks of unmixed egg visible. Lumps when stirred. Strands of cooked egg white in the mixture. Strain through a fine sieve — this will catch any cooked bits. Whisk the strained liquid smooth.
Perfect: Perfectly smooth, uniform color. Coats the back of a spoon evenly. No foam, no bubbles. Pours like heavy cream. Pour gently into the caramel-lined ramekins.
Overdone: Surface covered in fine bubbles from over-whisking. The custard looks frothy. Let it rest for 10 minutes. Pop surface bubbles with a torch or by passing a flame quickly over the surface. Bubbles bake into pockmarks.
Feel cue: Drag your finger across the back of the coated spoon — it should leave a clean, sharp line that does not bleed back together. If it runs, the mixture is too thin (likely too much milk). If it is thick and sluggish, an egg may have scrambled — strain again.

Pour custard into caramel-lined ramekins, filling to 5mm below the rim. Place ramekins in a deep baking dish and pour hot water into the dish until it reaches halfway up the sides of the ramekins. Bake at 150 C (300 F) for 50-60 minutes. The water bath insulates the custard from direct heat, preventing curdling.
Visual cue: The custard surface is set and matte — it no longer ripples when the pan is gently jostled. The very center may have the faintest jiggle, like set gelatin.
Underdone: The surface ripples in a wave from edge to center when jostled. Liquid visible beneath. More than a 3cm circle of jiggle at the center. Continue baking in 5-minute increments. Underbaked custard will not unmold — it collapses.
Perfect: Edges are firmly set. The center jiggles like jello when tapped — a gentle wobble, not a liquid wave. Surface is smooth, flat, and pale yellow with no browning. Remove from the water bath immediately.
Overdone: Surface has browned or puffed up like a souffle. Tiny bubbles or pockmarks visible. No jiggle at all — completely rigid. The custard has curdled. It will have a grainy, cottage-cheese texture. Lower the oven temperature next time.
Feel cue: Gently tap the side of a ramekin with a spoon — the sound should be a soft, dull thud, not a liquid slosh. The water bath should still be hot but never boiling; if it bubbles, the oven is too hot.

Cool ramekins to room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight. To unmold: run a thin knife around the edge, place a plate on top, and invert confidently in one motion. The caramel will have liquefied in the fridge and will pour down the sides as a sauce.
Visual cue: A smooth, trembling dome of pale custard sitting in a pool of liquid amber caramel. The surface is flawless — no cracks, no bubbles, no marks from the knife.
Underdone: The custard collapses or breaks when unmolded. Caramel is still solid and stuck to the ramekin. It needed more chilling time or was underbaked. Scoop what you can and serve as a broken custard — the flavor is still lovely.
Perfect: A perfect dome that holds its shape but trembles when the plate is nudged. Caramel flows down the sides in a thin, glossy stream. The surface catches light. Serve immediately. One spoon, one plate, no garnish needed.
Overdone: The custard unmolds as a solid, rigid cylinder. When cut, the interior is dense and grainy. Caramel is dark and overly bitter. Serve with whipped cream to soften the texture. The flavor may still be pleasant if the caramel was not burnt.
Feel cue: The first spoonful should feel like silk against the tongue — if it is grainy or rough, the custard was overbaked. The caramel should taste bittersweet, a counterpoint to the vanilla cream — if it tastes only sweet, it was undercooked.

name: Crème Fraîche
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Heavy cream (at least 35% fat, not ultra-pasteurised): 100 parts
  Alternatives: double cream (UK); whipping cream (lower fat, thinner result)
Cultured buttermilk (live cultures): 10 parts
  Alternatives: plain live-culture yogurt; sour cream; existing crème fraîche as a starter
Active time: 5 min
Total time: 16 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Heavy cream inoculated with buttermilk or a spoonful of live culture, left at room temperature for 12–24 hours until it thickens to a tangy, silky, spoonable cream that holds without breaking when heated.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: 淡奶油（Heavy cream (at least 35% fat, not ultra-pasteurised)）

steps:
Pour the heavy cream into a clean glass jar or bowl. Add the buttermilk and stir gently with a clean spoon for 20 seconds — just enough to distribute the cultures evenly throughout the cream. Do not whip or aerate; you are introducing live bacteria, not incorporating air. Ultra-pasteurised cream has been heated to a point that destroys the lipids needed for the cultures to grip, which is why it must be avoided.
Visual cue: A smooth, ivory-white cream with no visible separation between the buttermilk and cream. It pours like a thick liquid, showing no signs of thickening yet.
Underdone: Buttermilk is sitting as a white, watery layer on top rather than integrating — you can see the two liquids clearly separated. Stir more thoroughly for another 30 seconds with a clean spoon to distribute the cultures.
Perfect: A uniform, slightly thickened cream with a clean, fresh dairy smell. No visible separation. The cultures are now distributed and the fermentation can begin. Cover loosely with a clean cloth or plastic wrap (not airtight) and leave at room temperature.
Overdone: Not applicable at the mix stage — there is no way to over-mix at this point beyond introducing too much air. Proceed to fermentation; any bubbles from over-stirring will dissipate as the cream thickens.
Feel cue: The mixture should feel smooth and even on the spoon with no grainy patches or visible curdling — the buttermilk is fully incorporated when the consistency is completely uniform.

Cover the jar loosely — not airtight, as the cultures need to breathe — and leave it in a warm spot at room temperature, ideally 20 to 24 C / 68 to 75 F. Check it after 12 hours. In warm kitchens it may be done in 12 hours; in cooler kitchens it can take up to 24. You are waiting for the cream to thicken to a spoonable, semi-solid consistency and develop a mild, pleasant tang. Do not stir during fermentation.
Visual cue: The cream has set to a thick, spoonable consistency — when you tilt the jar it moves as a single mass rather than sloshing. The surface is smooth and white, possibly with a very slight ivory tint.
Underdone: Still liquid and pourable — the jar sloshes freely when tilted. Tastes like fresh cream with only a faint hint of tang. Replace the cover and leave for another 4 to 8 hours. If your kitchen is very cool, place the jar near a warm spot — on top of the fridge, near a pilot light, or in an oven with only the light on.
Perfect: Thick, spoonable, and gently tangy — it moves as a mass when you tilt the jar and holds a shape briefly when spooned. The flavour is creamy, rich, and pleasantly sour without being acidic. Refrigerate immediately to halt the fermentation. It will thicken a little further as it chills.
Overdone: Very thick, almost curd-like with visible liquid whey separating around the edges. Tastes sharply sour, almost like sour cream or yogurt rather than crème fraîche. Still usable — drain the whey and whisk the curd smooth. It is richer and more sour than ideal, but excellent stirred into soups or baked goods.
Feel cue: After 12 hours, tilt the jar slowly. If the cream barely moves and the surface has a gentle wobble rather than a slosh, the cultures have done their work. If your spoon meets the clean resistance of set cream rather than running clean through liquid, you are there.

Transfer the crème fraîche to the refrigerator, loosely covered. It will firm further over the next 2 to 4 hours as the cold halts the bacterial activity and the fat crystallises slightly. The finished product keeps for 1 to 2 weeks in the refrigerator. To make the next batch, reserve a tablespoon as your starter in place of the buttermilk — the cultures regenerate indefinitely with each batch.
Visual cue: A thick, smooth, ivory-white cream that holds its shape on a spoon and falls in slow, soft folds. It has the consistency of a soft, rich Greek yogurt but with a finer, silkier texture.
Underdone: Still loose and pourable from the refrigerator. The cultures did not have enough time or warmth to set the cream. Return to room temperature for another 4 to 6 hours, then refrigerate again.
Perfect: Thick, spoonable, silky, and tangy. It falls from the spoon in a slow, even sheet. Taste is rich, clean, and gently sour — like cream that has grown up. It will not split or curdle when stirred into a hot sauce. Use as is, or season with salt for a savoury application. Stir into soups, pasta, or spoon over tarts and berries.
Overdone: Grainy or separated with visible whey pooling — over-fermented and close to becoming sour cream or a soft cheese. Whisk smooth and drain any excess whey. Use immediately rather than storing, or use in baking where texture is less critical.
Feel cue: A spoonful of perfect crème fraîche should feel silky and slightly resistant as you scoop — not fluffy or airy, not dense and rubber-like. It should coat the back of the spoon in an even, creamy layer that does not break or weep.

name: Crème Pâtissière (Pastry Cream)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Whole milk: 500 ml
  Alternatives: oat milk (less rich)
Vanilla bean, split and scraped (or 2 tsp extract): 1 whole
  Alternatives: vanilla bean paste (1 tsp)
Egg yolks: 6 whole
Caster sugar: 120 g
Cornflour (cornstarch): 40 g
  Alternatives: plain flour (45 g, less glossy result)
Cold unsalted butter, cubed: 30 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 2 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The workhorse of the French pastry kitchen — a thick, deeply vanilla-scented cream that sets firm enough to pipe into éclairs or crown a tart, yet dissolves on the tongue into pure silk and warmth.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Vanilla bean, split and scraped (or 2 tsp extract)

steps:
Split the vanilla bean lengthwise, scrape out the seeds, and add both pod and seeds to the milk in a medium saucepan. Heat over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the milk just reaches a simmer — small bubbles at the edges, steam rising. Remove from heat, cover, and steep for 10 minutes to deepen the vanilla infusion. Remove the pod (rinse and dry it for vanilla sugar).
Visual cue: Milk with a golden tinge from the vanilla seeds, steaming gently. Vanilla seeds are evenly distributed — visible as tiny black specks throughout.
Underdone: Milk is still cold and the vanilla colour has not developed. Seeds are clumped around the pod. Heat to a proper simmer and steep the full 10 minutes.
Perfect: Creamy, warm milk with a golden cast and fragrant vanilla steam. Vanilla specks evenly distributed. Whisk together the egg yolks, sugar, and cornflour while the milk steeps.
Overdone: Milk has boiled aggressively and reduced slightly. Surface may have a skin. Skim any skin, top up to 500 ml with cold milk, and proceed.
Feel cue: The kitchen should be filled with the warm, almost floral scent of vanilla in warm dairy — not a sharp synthetic note, but a deep, rounded sweetness.

In a large bowl, whisk the egg yolks and sugar together vigorously for 1–2 minutes until the mixture is pale, thick, and forms a ribbon. Sift in the cornflour and whisk again until completely smooth with no lumps. This paste must be completely lump-free or the finished cream will have starchy pockets.
Visual cue: A thick, pale-yellow paste that falls from the whisk in a wide, slow ribbon. Smooth with no cornflour lumps.
Underdone: Still a thin, grainy yellow mixture. Cornflour lumps visible. Whisk more vigorously. All cornflour must be fully incorporated before tempering.
Perfect: Pale, thick, smooth. Falls in a wide ribbon. No lumps when held up to the light. Temper with the hot infused milk.
Overdone: Cannot over-whisk at this stage. Proceed to tempering.
Feel cue: The paste should feel smooth and slightly starchy between the fingers — no grittiness, no powdery pockets. It should be thick enough to hold a soft mound when dropped from a spoon.

Pour a ladleful of the hot infused milk into the egg yolk paste, whisking constantly and vigorously to raise the temperature of the yolks gently without scrambling them. Once combined, pour in the remaining hot milk in a slow, steady stream while whisking. Return the entire mixture to the saucepan.
Visual cue: A smooth, uniform, pale-yellow liquid with vanilla seeds throughout. No scrambled egg bits, no lumps.
Underdone: Only a small amount of milk added and mixture is still cold and thick. Add more hot milk gradually, whisking continuously.
Perfect: Smooth, fluid, warm. All components combined. Vanilla seeds visible throughout. No egg lumps. Pour back into the saucepan and cook to set.
Overdone: Added milk too quickly without whisking — small flecks of cooked egg visible. Strain through a fine sieve before returning to the pan.
Feel cue: The mixture should warm smoothly in the bowl as you whisk in the hot milk — you should feel it thin and loosen as each addition incorporates, with no sudden lumping or resistance.

Return the custard to the saucepan and cook over medium heat, whisking constantly and reaching into every corner of the pan. The mixture will first appear to thicken slightly, then will suddenly seize up and become very thick — keep whisking as it crosses from liquid to thick paste. This is the starch gelatinising. Crucially, once the cream has thickened, continue cooking at a full boil for 1–2 minutes, whisking hard, to cook out the raw starch flavour. Remove from heat, beat in the cold butter, and press cling film directly onto the surface. Refrigerate until cold and firm (at least 1.5 hours).
Visual cue: A thick, glossy, vanilla-specked cream that falls from the whisk in heavy, slow mounds. When a line is drawn through the surface with a finger, it holds cleanly.
Underdone: The mixture is still runny or only loosely thickened. It will not set firm in the fridge. Starchy, raw flavour lingers. Continue cooking and whisking over medium heat — cook for the full 2 minutes at a boil after it thickens.
Perfect: Thick, glossy, and deeply fragrant. Holds its shape on the whisk. A finger drawn across the surface leaves a clean channel. Clean taste — no starchiness. Add cold butter, mix, cover surface with cling film, refrigerate.
Overdone: Cream has begun to stick to the pan and smells slightly of scorched starch. Surface is lumpy. Strain through a fine sieve immediately. Discard any scorched residue.
Feel cue: At the moment the cream fully sets in the pan, the whisk will drag with sudden, dramatic resistance — this is the starch gelatinising all at once. Push through it and keep whisking for the full 2 minutes to cook out the floury taste.

name: Crêpes Suzette
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Plain flour (sifted): 100 parts
  Alternatives: type 45 pastry flour
Eggs (whole, room temperature): 100 parts
Whole milk: 250 parts
  Alternatives: half milk, half water for lighter crêpes
Browned butter (for the batter, cooled): 30 parts
  Alternatives: melted butter
Caster sugar (for the batter): 15 parts
Fine sea salt: 2 parts
Caster sugar (for the caramel sauce): 80 parts
Unsalted butter (for the sauce, cold, cubed): 70 parts
Oranges (zest + freshly squeezed juice): 200 parts
  Alternatives: blood orange
Grand Marnier (orange liqueur): 40 parts
  Alternatives: Cointreau; Curaçao
Active time: 40 min
Total time: 1 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The grand finale of the old French dining room — gossamer-thin crêpes folded into quarters and bathed in a glossy beurre Suzette of caramelized sugar, fresh orange juice and butter, then set alight tableside with a hiss of Grand Marnier until the flames die to a lacquer of warm citrus and toffee.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter (for the sauce, cold, cubed)

steps:
Whisk the flour, sugar and salt in a bowl, make a well, and crack in the eggs. Whisk from the centre outward, drawing in the flour, then pour in the milk in a slow stream to keep the batter lump-free. Whisk in the cooled browned butter. The batter should be thin — the consistency of single cream. Strain it through a sieve and rest, covered, in the fridge for at least 30 minutes to let the gluten relax and the bubbles settle.
Visual cue: A smooth, pourable batter the colour of pale custard that coats the back of a spoon in a thin, even film and runs off in an unbroken ribbon.
Underdone: Batter is lumpy or pasty and thick, clinging to the whisk in clumps; flour streaks remain. Whisk harder or blitz briefly with a stick blender, then thin with a splash more milk and pass through the sieve again.
Perfect: Silky, lump-free and just thin enough to drop off the spoon in a smooth ribbon; bubbles rising slowly to the surface. Cover and rest in the fridge so the crêpes cook tender, not rubbery.
Overdone: Batter is watery and translucent and will not coat the spoon at all. Whisk in a spoonful more sifted flour, rest again, and test-cook one crêpe before committing.
Feel cue: The whisk should move through the batter with almost no drag — it should feel like thin cream, never like a thick pancake mix. Resist the urge to overwork it once smooth; too much beating builds gluten and toughens the crêpes.

Heat a 22 cm crêpe or non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a film of butter. Lift the pan, ladle in just enough batter to coat the base, and immediately swirl it into a thin, even round, pouring any excess back. Cook 45-60 seconds until the edges lift and the underside is lacy and golden, then flip and cook 20-30 seconds more. Stack the finished crêpes on a plate as you go; the first one is always the test.
Visual cue: Paper-thin crêpes, lace-edged and freckled golden-brown on the first side, supple and foldable with no raw, gummy patches.
Underdone: The crêpe is pale, damp and floppy, sticking to the pan, with no colour and a doughy smell. Raise the heat a touch and give it longer — wait until the edges visibly lift and dry before flipping.
Perfect: Thin and even with golden freckles and lacy edges; it releases cleanly and folds without cracking. Flip, cook the second side briefly, then slide onto the stack and continue.
Overdone: The crêpe is dark brown, brittle and crisp at the edges, cracking when folded. Lower the heat and pour the next round more quickly; brittle crêpes can still be used but fold them gently.
Feel cue: Listen for a soft sizzle the instant the batter hits the pan — that tells you it is hot enough to set immediately and stay thin. The crêpe is ready to flip when it shimmies loose as you shake the pan.

Zest the oranges and squeeze the juice. In a wide skillet, melt the sauce sugar over medium heat without stirring, swirling the pan as it liquefies, until it turns a clear amber caramel. Stand back and carefully pour in the orange juice — it will sputter and seize — then add the zest and simmer, stirring, until the hardened caramel dissolves back into a smooth, syrupy sauce.
Visual cue: A glossy, fluid amber syrup, fragrant with orange, that coats a spoon and smells of toffee and citrus with no acrid edge.
Underdone: Sugar is pale straw or still grainy, the sauce thin and one-dimensionally sweet with no toasted depth. Keep cooking the sugar a little longer before adding the juice — the colour is the flavour.
Perfect: Clear amber caramel dissolved into a smooth, glossy orange syrup that lightly naps the spoon. Lower the heat and mount in the butter to build the beurre Suzette.
Overdone: Caramel is dark mahogany and smells sharp and burnt; the sauce tastes bitter. Discard and start the sugar again — burnt caramel cannot be rescued, and bitterness will carry through the whole dish.
Feel cue: Watch the sugar by colour and smell, not the clock — it goes from amber to burnt in seconds. The moment it smells warmly of toffee, the juice goes in; brace for the violent hiss and keep your hand clear of the steam.

Drop the heat to low. Whisk the cold cubed butter into the warm orange caramel a few pieces at a time, letting each addition melt and emulsify before adding more. The sauce should turn satiny, opaque and slightly thickened — a true beurre Suzette. Keep it just warm; do not let it boil hard or the butter will split and the sauce will turn greasy.
Visual cue: A glossy, opaque amber-gold sauce, thickened and satiny, that clings to the spoon and shows no separated pools of oil.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and watery; the butter is melting but not emulsifying into the syrup. Add the butter more slowly off direct heat and whisk constantly to coax the emulsion together.
Perfect: Silky, opaque and lightly thickened, evenly glossy, coating the spoon in a smooth amber sheet. Keep warm and fold the crêpes into the sauce.
Overdone: The sauce has broken — clear melted butter sits on top in greasy pools and the syrup has thinned beneath. Pull off the heat, whisk in a teaspoon of cold water or a fresh cold butter cube to re-emulsify.
Feel cue: Whisk steadily and feel the sauce gain body as each cube melts in — it should thicken under the whisk like a warm emulsion, never feel oily or look broken. Keep the heat gentle; mounted butter splits the instant it boils.

One at a time, lay each crêpe in the warm sauce, turn to coat both sides, then fold in half and in half again into a neat triangle, nudging it to the side of the pan. Repeat until all the crêpes are folded and overlapping in the sauce, basting them with a spoon so each absorbs the orange-butter and glistens.
Visual cue: Glistening folded triangles overlapping in the pan like fallen petals, each one soaked through and lacquered with the amber sauce.
Underdone: Crêpes look dry and pale, sitting on top of the sauce rather than soaked through, with bald patches. Spoon more sauce over each fold and let them sit a minute in the warmth to drink it in.
Perfect: Each triangle is supple, evenly coated and shining, saturated with sauce but still holding its neat folded shape. Bring the pan to the table for the flambé, or finish at the stove.
Overdone: Crêpes have simmered too long and gone soft and torn, breaking apart as you turn them. Stop basting and turning; serve them gently with a spatula even if the folds are a little ragged.
Feel cue: Turn the crêpes with a fork and spoon as if folding linen — they are delicate when soaked. The pan should smell intensely of warm orange and butter, and the sauce should bubble lazily, never boil.

Off the heat, pour the Grand Marnier over the crêpes. Return the pan to the flame and tilt it slightly toward the burner (or touch a long match to the edge) so the warmed alcohol vapour catches and bursts into blue flame. Let it burn down on its own, swirling the pan, until the flames die and the sauce reduces to a final glossy lacquer. Plate the folded crêpes at once and spoon the remaining sauce over the top.
Visual cue: Dancing blue flames that flare and then subside to nothing, leaving the crêpes glazed in a thick, glossy orange-toffee sauce with no raw alcohol bite.
Underdone: The liqueur will not ignite and the sauce tastes sharp with raw alcohol. Warm the pan more before lighting — cold alcohol gives off too little vapour to catch; or simmer briefly to cook off the spirit instead.
Perfect: A brief, theatrical sheet of blue flame that burns itself out in 20-30 seconds, leaving a deep, mellow orange flavour and a glossy reduced sauce. Plate immediately while everything is hot and serve.
Overdone: Flames burn long and the sauce reduces to a sticky, over-caramelized, slightly bitter glaze. Smother the flames with a lid, loosen the sauce with a splash of orange juice, and serve before it tightens further.
Feel cue: Keep your face and hair well back as you tilt the pan — the flames leap higher than you expect, then vanish. When the fire is out, the kitchen smells of caramelized orange and toasted butter, with the sharp edge of the spirit gone soft and round.

name: Slow-Rendered Crispy Duck Legs
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Duck legs, whole (leg and thigh): 1200 g
Flaky sea salt: 20 g
  Alternatives: kosher salt
Fresh thyme sprigs: 15 g
  Alternatives: rosemary; savory
Garlic cloves, halved: 20 g
Black pepper, coarsely cracked: 4 g
Bay leaves: 3 whole
Fleur de sel: 5 g
  Alternatives: Maldon salt
Fresh thyme leaves, stripped: 5 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 10 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Duck legs cured overnight with thyme and salt, then rendered low and slow until the fat is completely liquid beneath a skin that shatters on first bite — the Gascon tradition of patience turning one of the richest cuts in the kitchen into something impossibly light and crisp.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Score the duck skin in a diagonal crosshatch with a sharp knife, cutting through the skin and fat but not the meat beneath. Rub the legs all over with flaky salt, cracked pepper, and thyme, pressing the herbs into the score marks. Tuck garlic halves and bay leaves under and around the legs in a dish. Refrigerate uncovered overnight (8–12 hours). The salt draws moisture from the skin and seasons the meat throughout.
Visual cue: After overnight curing, the skin is completely dry and slightly shrunken over the fat layer. The crosshatch pattern is clearly visible and defined. Moisture has beaded and been reabsorbed.
Underdone: Only 1–2 hours of cure. Skin still feels moist and limp. Extend the cure. The overnight rest is what makes the skin crackle.
Perfect: Skin feels almost papery — dry, slightly stiff, completely matte. Crosshatch cuts are clean and open. The surface looks like it's already been lightly treated. Allow to come to room temperature 30 minutes before roasting.
Overdone: Cured beyond 24 hours — surface has become quite hard and salt-concentrated. Pat off excess salt with a dry cloth and proceed.
Feel cue: Run your fingertip across the cured skin — it should feel like dry parchment paper. Any tackiness or moisture means the skin needs more uncovered refrigeration time to dry.

Place duck legs skin-side down in a cold, dry, oven-proof skillet or roasting pan. Do not preheat — starting cold prevents the skin from buckling. Place in a cold oven and turn to 130 C (260 F). Cook for 3–4 hours, skin-side down the entire time. The duck fat will render out gradually; the legs will sit in an increasing pool of their own golden fat. Occasionally tilt the pan and spoon off excess fat.
Visual cue: After 3 hours, a generous pool of clear golden duck fat has accumulated in the pan. The skin, visible at the edges of each leg, is amber but not yet golden. The meat has begun to pull slightly from the drumstick bone.
Underdone: Very little rendered fat in the pan. Skin still looks white and fatty rather than transparent and rendered. Continue at 130 C. The low-and-slow approach cannot be rushed — the fat needs time to liquefy through the entire layer.
Perfect: Large pool of golden fat. Skin at the edges is amber and beginning to feel firm rather than soft. Meat pulls freely from the drumstick tip. The leg has lost perhaps 20% of its original volume. Increase heat to crisp the skin.
Overdone: Fat has completely rendered and the duck leg is now beginning to fry in its own fat rather than render. Skin is browning unevenly. Move immediately to the high-heat crisping stage.
Feel cue: After 3 hours of low rendering, press the leg firmly — it should feel yielding and jiggly under the skin, with no firm pockets of solid fat remaining. The fat is now all liquid.

Pour off most of the rendered fat into a jar to save. Increase oven to 220 C (425 F) or, for maximum control, transfer legs to a fresh skillet and crisp skin-side down on the stovetop over medium-high heat for 5–8 minutes. Watch attentively — the goal is a shattering, golden-mahogany skin, not burnt. Flip for a final 2 minutes on the meat side.
Visual cue: The skin is a deep, uniform golden-mahogany — not pale gold, not dark brown, but the particular rich amber of perfectly rendered duck skin. It looks visibly dry and crackling.
Underdone: Skin is light gold and slightly soft. Pressing it yields a little rather than shattering. Continue crisping — the skin must lose all its moisture before it will shatter.
Perfect: Skin is deep amber-mahogany and completely rigid when pressed with a spoon. Tapping it makes a hollow sound. The crosshatch pattern is still visible but gilded. Rest 3 minutes then season with fleur de sel.
Overdone: Skin has gone very dark and is beginning to char. The fat beneath may have burnt. Remove immediately from heat. Trim the darkest patches with scissors. The meat inside is still beautiful.
Feel cue: Press the skin with the back of a spoon — a perfectly rendered and crisped duck leg skin does not flex or give. It shatters slightly under pressure, like thin glass.

Rest the duck legs for 3 minutes — just enough for carryover cooking to complete, not long enough for the skin to steam and soften. Sprinkle with fleur de sel and fresh thyme leaves. Serve skin-side up, immediately, with lentils du Puy, sautéed wild mushrooms, or a bitter green salad dressed with the rendered duck fat.
Visual cue: A deep amber leg, skin taut and crackling, with the white crystals of fleur de sel catching the light. A few thyme leaves scattered across the surface.
Underdone: Plated too quickly after the oven. Skin appears moist from steam. Allow the 3-minute rest on a rack, not a plate, so air circulates under the skin.
Perfect: Skin is still crackling and dry, the fleur de sel has not dissolved into moisture. Thyme is fragrant from the residual heat. The meat beneath pulls easily from the bone. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Rested too long or covered. Skin has gone soft. Return to a very hot pan for 90 seconds to restore the crackle.
Feel cue: Cut through the skin with a knife — it should make a clearly audible crack, and the pieces should shatter rather than fold. The meat below should offer mild, yielding resistance.

name: Crispy Pork Belly
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Pork belly (skin-on, bone-out): 100 parts
Fine sea salt: 3 parts
  Alternatives: kosher salt
Five-spice powder: 1 parts
  Alternatives: Chinese five-spice blend
White pepper (ground): 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: black pepper
Rice vinegar: 2 parts
  Alternatives: white vinegar; malt vinegar
Garlic (minced): 2 parts
Baking soda (for skin pricking): 0.5 parts
Active time: 40 min
Total time: 8 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Cantonese siu yuk at its finest — the skin shatters into a thousand lacquered shards, the fat beneath has rendered to a translucent, yielding layer, and the meat below is seasoned deep into the grain.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Using a metal skewer or a fork, prick the skin of the pork belly hundreds of times over its entire surface, going about 5mm deep but not piercing through to the fat layer. Flip the belly and score the meat side in a crosshatch pattern, 2cm deep. This mechanical disruption of the skin creates channels for rendered fat to escape during roasting, which is what causes the skin to blister and shatter.
Visual cue: The skin surface is covered uniformly with tiny puncture holes, showing no large unpierced patches. The meat side has a neat diamond pattern of cuts.
Underdone: Skin has sparse punctures; large areas remain smooth and intact. Continue pricking — even coverage is essential. Unpierced areas will stay tough and chewy.
Perfect: Skin looks like fine-grained sandpaper, evenly pocked. The meat side shows uniform diamond cuts without tearing. Proceed to seasoning.
Overdone: Skin has been pierced so deeply that the fat layer beneath is exposed and beginning to separate. Proceed carefully — the skin may shrink more aggressively; watch closely during roasting.
Feel cue: Run a finger over the pricked skin — it should feel rough and bristly like coarse sandpaper, with no smooth patches. The skin should not flex when you try to bend it.

Flip the belly meat-side up. Rub the five-spice powder, minced garlic, white pepper, and half the salt thoroughly into the meat and into all the score cuts — get the seasoning as deep into the cuts as possible. Flip skin-side up and rub the remaining salt onto the skin evenly. Place skin-side up, uncovered, in the refrigerator for a minimum of 6 hours or overnight. The desiccating air of the refrigerator is what drives the final moisture out of the skin.
Visual cue: After refrigerating, the skin is visibly dry — almost papery — and has tightened. The surface looks translucent and leathery, not moist.
Underdone: The skin still looks moist and plump after refrigeration, with a sheen of moisture. Return uncovered to the refrigerator for several more hours. Do not skip this step.
Perfect: Skin is bone-dry, slightly translucent, and taut. It makes a faint sound when tapped with a fingernail. Proceed with the acid treatment and roasting.
Overdone: Skin is very dark and contracted; it has been in the refrigerator for more than 24 hours. Still fine to proceed — a longer dry will generally yield crispier results.
Feel cue: After overnight drying, the skin should feel like dry parchment — stiff, cool, and almost translucent when held to the light. It should make a soft crinkle sound when flexed.

Dissolve the baking soda in rice vinegar and brush onto the skin generously; the alkalinity raises the pH of the skin, accelerating the Maillard reaction and driving crisping. Place skin-side up on a wire rack over a foil-lined tray. Roast at 180°C (360°F) for 50 minutes to render the fat, then blast at 230°C (450°F) for 20–25 minutes for the crackling. Watch closely in the final stage — the transformation from rendered to blistered is fast.
Visual cue: In the high-heat phase, the skin is actively blistering — small golden-brown bubbles are forming, rising, and turning deep amber across the entire surface.
Underdone: The skin is golden but flat and glassy, with no blistering or bubbling visible. Increase oven temperature to 240°C and continue watching every 5 minutes.
Perfect: The entire surface is covered in golden-amber blisters of varying sizes, like a topographic map. Deep mahogany where blisters have peaked. Remove immediately and rest 10 minutes before slicing.
Overdone: Blisters have blackened; acrid smoke coming from the oven. The skin surface is charred. Remove immediately. Scrape any fully charred areas with a knife before serving.
Feel cue: When you press gently on the skin with a spoon handle, it should sound hollow and crackle audibly — like tapping a glass Christmas ornament. The blisters should feel rigid, not soft.

Remove from the oven and rest on the wire rack — never on a flat surface which would trap steam and soften the crackling. Rest for 10 minutes before slicing. Slice using a sharp cleaver or heavy chef's knife with downward pressure rather than sawing; sawing shatters the crackling unevenly.
Visual cue: The crackling remains rigid and evenly blistered as it rests. No steam escapes from the skin surface. The fat layer beneath the skin is visible as a sheen through the translucent skin.
Underdone: Steam is rising from the skin surface during rest; the crackling feels slightly soft when pressed. Rest longer on the rack — the surface moisture needs to fully evaporate.
Perfect: Crackling is rigid, shatteringly crisp, and completely dry. The fat layer is set and white, not liquid. Slice with confidence and serve immediately.
Overdone: Crackling has sat too long and has begun to absorb ambient humidity, turning slightly leathery. Return to a 230°C oven for 5 minutes to re-crisp.
Feel cue: Press a finger against the crackling — it should shatter inward immediately with a sharp snap. Lift a piece and it should feel weightless and rigid; any flexibility means moisture is still present.

name: Crispy Fried Shallots
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Shallots (small, thin-skinned Asian shallots preferred): 300 g
  Alternatives: European banana shallots; red onion, sliced very thin
Neutral oil (vegetable, rice bran, or peanut): 300 g
Rice flour or plain flour (optional, for extra crunch): 15 g
Fine salt: 3 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 25 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The essential Southeast Asian topping — translucent shallot rings slowly fried in oil from cold until they transform into paper-thin, amber-gold, impossibly crunchy curls that smell like caramelized onion and taste of sweet, savory depth. The finishing touch on nasi goreng, pho, gado-gado, and a hundred other dishes.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
