ingredients.name: 食用油（Neutral oil (vegetable, rice bran, or peanut)）
Rice flour or plain flour (optional, for extra crunch)

steps:
Peel the shallots and slice them into rings approximately 2 mm thick — thin and consistent. A mandoline slicer is ideal for uniformity, which is critical: uneven slices mean some rings burn before others are golden. Separate the rings as you slice. If using the flour method, toss the rings lightly in rice flour, shaking off excess — just a thin coating. Pat the rings dry with a cloth before adding flour, as surface moisture causes violent oil splatter.
Visual cue: Thin, even rings of pale purple-white shallot, separated, dry, possibly dusted lightly with flour.
Underdone: Slices are thick and uneven — some 5 mm, some 1 mm. The thick slices will be undercooked while the thin ones burn. Re-slice the thick pieces, or sort by thickness and fry in separate batches.
Perfect: Consistent 2 mm rings, separated, pale and dry. A thin flour dust clings evenly if using. Proceed to cold-start frying immediately.
Overdone: Shallots have been left out and are weeping moisture from cut surfaces. The rings are soft and damp. Pat very dry with paper towels and proceed. Extra moisture causes the oil to foam aggressively at first.
Feel cue: Thin shallot rings should feel light and papery between your fingers, almost translucent when held to light. If a ring tears the moment you pick it up, the shallot was too moist or sliced too thin — still usable, but handle gently.

Place the shallots in a cold pan and pour the oil over them to submerge them completely. Place over medium heat and begin frying from cold — this is the critical technique of Indonesian bawang goreng. The cold start gently dehydrates the shallots before the oil reaches frying temperature, ensuring they crisp gradually rather than burning outside while remaining soft inside. Stir occasionally. The oil will bubble gently as moisture releases. Gradually increase to medium-high as the bubbling slows. The entire process takes 15 to 20 minutes. Watch intently during the final 3 to 4 minutes — the transition from pale gold to perfect amber to burnt happens within 90 seconds.
Visual cue: Shallots are deep amber-gold, curled and translucent, floating in actively bubbling oil. The bubbling has slowed significantly from its earlier vigorous pace.
Underdone: Shallots are pale gold and still somewhat soft, bending rather than crisping when lifted. The oil is still bubbling vigorously from moisture release. Continue frying. The vigorous bubbling will slow markedly when the shallots are near done. Stay at the pan.
Perfect: Deep amber-gold, curled into tight crisp rings, minimal oil bubbling. If you lift one out it immediately stiffens and crunches — not bends. Remove immediately with a spider strainer to a paper-towel-lined tray. Season with salt while hot. They will crisp further as they cool.
Overdone: Dark brown, smell of burnt onion, rings are beginning to shrink and collapse. The oil smells acrid. Remove immediately. Spread on fresh paper towels. Taste — lightly dark shallots have a pleasant bitter edge; heavily burnt ones should be discarded.
Feel cue: Reach in with a spider or slotted spoon and lift one ring from the oil — it should feel immediately rigid and dry the moment air touches it, crisping up as you watch. If it stays floppy and bends, it needs more time. The oil
color should have deepened and sweetened in smell, infused with shallot.

Transfer the fried shallots immediately to a paper-towel-lined tray in a single layer. Season with a pinch of fine salt while they are still hot. Do not pile them up — they need to stay in a single layer while they cool, or the steam from the inner layers will make the outer ones soggy. Cool completely at room temperature. They will crisp dramatically as they cool from very hot to ambient. Store in an airtight jar at room temperature for up to 1 week. Refrigeration makes them lose their crunch.
Visual cue: Cooled, deep amber-gold rings arranged in a single airy layer. When the jar is tilted, they rattle and crinkle — completely dry and rigid.
Underdone: Shallots are still warm and feel soft and a little oily. They haven't crisped yet. Leave in a single layer and wait — do not touch them for at least 5 minutes while they cool. The crispness arrives with the temperature drop.
Perfect: Completely cool, deeply golden, shatteringly crispy. A pinch produces a satisfying crunch. Smell of sweet, caramelized onion. Store airtight at room temperature. Use as a garnish on soups, noodles, rice, salads, or eat straight from the jar.
Overdone: Stored airtight in the refrigerator or in a damp jar, the shallots have gone limp and chewy. Spread on a tray and re-crisp in a 150°C oven for 5 minutes. Cool on the tray before jarring again.
Feel cue: A properly cooled crispy shallot should shatter when you bite it — not crunch softly, but genuinely shatter into fine amber splinters. They should feel almost weightless in your hand, as if all the moisture has been replaced by crispness. The smell opening a fresh jar is one of the finest in the kitchen.

Butter lettuce, leaves separated and chilled

steps:
Pat the pressed tofu dry and crumble it with your fingers into pea- to chickpea-sized pieces. Heat 30 ml of the oil in a large nonstick skillet or wok over medium-high heat until shimmering (about 350°F / 175°C). Add the tofu in an even layer and cook 10–12 minutes, stirring only every 2 minutes, until the water has cooked off and the crumbles are golden and crisp. Drizzle in 1 tablespoon of the soy sauce for the final minute and toss until absorbed. Transfer to a plate.
Visual cue: Dry, separate, golden-brown crumbles with crisp, craggy edges.
Underdone: Crumbles are pale, steaming, and soft; liquid in the pan. Keep cooking over medium-high and resist stirring too often.
Perfect: Evenly bronzed, rattling in the pan, soy absorbed with no puddle. Remove to a plate.
Overdone: Small bits are dark brown and hard like gravel. Pull off the heat; fine bits can be sifted out.
Feel cue: Stir the pan — the crumbles should skitter and rattle against the metal, not slump.

Add the remaining 15 ml oil to the same pan over high heat. Add the shiitake and cook 3–4 minutes until they release their moisture and brown. Add the garlic, ginger, and scallion whites and stir-fry 45 seconds until fragrant, then add the water chestnuts and toss 1 minute to heat through.
Visual cue: Browned, shrunken minced mushrooms with glistening aromatics and pale water chestnut cubes.
Underdone: Mushrooms are gray and wet. Cook another minute or two over high heat.
Perfect: Mushrooms are brown and glossy; garlic and ginger smell sweet, not raw. Return the tofu and add the sauce.
Overdone: Garlic is brown and bitter-smelling. Add the sauce immediately to stop the browning.
Feel cue: The pan should hiss loudly and smell intensely of ginger within seconds of adding the aromatics.

Stir together the remaining soy sauce, hoisin, rice vinegar, sriracha, and sesame oil. Return the tofu to the pan, pour in the sauce, and toss over high heat for 1–2 minutes until the sauce reduces and clings to every crumble. Take off the heat.
Visual cue: Mahogany, glossy crumbles with no loose sauce left in the pan.
Underdone: Thin sauce pools in the pan; crumbles look wet. Toss 30 seconds more over high heat.
Perfect: Everything is lacquered and sticky; the pan is almost dry. Fill the lettuce cups right away.
Overdone: Hoisin is catching and scorching on the pan base. Pull off the heat and add a splash of water to loosen.
Feel cue: A spoonful should hold together in a loose, sticky pile without dripping.

Arrange the chilled lettuce leaves cup-side up on a platter. Spoon in the hot filling, then top with carrot matchsticks, scallion greens, and cashews. Serve with lime wedges to squeeze over.
Visual cue: Pale green cups holding dark glazed filling, topped with bright orange carrot and green scallion.
Underdone: Lettuce is warm and floppy, tearing when filled. Chill leaves in ice water 5 minutes, then spin dry.
Perfect: Crisp, cold cups hold the filling without tearing. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Cups filled too early have wilted under the heat. Serve filling and leaves separately and build at the table.
Feel cue: The lettuce should snap as you fold it, with the hot, crunchy filling contrasting the cold leaf.

ingredients.name: Extra-firm tofu, pressed and cut into 2 cm cubes
花生酱（Peanut butter, smooth and unsweetened）
黄瓜（Cucumber, cut into thin matchsticks）
香菜（Cilantro, leaves and tender stems）

steps:
Wrap the tofu block in a clean towel and press under a heavy pan for 15 minutes. Cut into 2 cm cubes, sprinkle with a pinch of salt, then toss in a bowl with the cornstarch until every face is dusted. Shake off any clumps.
Visual cue: Dry-looking cubes with a thin, even, matte-white dusting of starch on all sides.
Underdone: Starch is going translucent and pasty on the cubes; water is still weeping out of the tofu. Blot the cubes on a towel and dust again with a teaspoon more starch.
Perfect: Every cube is uniformly frosted, powdery rather than gummy, with no bare wet patches. Fry straight away before the starch absorbs moisture.
Overdone: Thick drifts of loose starch are caked in the corners and falling off in clumps. Tap each cube against the bowl rim to knock off excess — thick starch fries into a gummy shell.
Feel cue: A pressed cube should feel springy and dense, like a firm eraser, and leave your fingers dusty rather than wet.

Heat the oil in a 30 cm nonstick or well-seasoned skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers (about 350°F / 175°C). Add the tofu in a single layer with space between cubes. Fry 3–4 minutes per side, turning with tongs, for 10–12 minutes total, until golden and crisp on at least four faces. Drain on a paper-towel-lined plate.
Visual cue: Deep golden, blistered crust on the cubes with crisp, slightly lacy edges.
Underdone: Faces are pale cream and soft; the starch still looks chalky. Leave the cubes undisturbed another 1–2 minutes per side — moving them early tears the crust.
Perfect: Even amber-gold on most sides, crust visibly blistered, cubes slide freely in the pan. Lift onto paper towels; they crisp further as they cool slightly.
Overdone: Dark brown patches and a bitter, scorched starch smell; oil is smoking. Pull the pan off the heat, remove the tofu, and wipe out burnt starch before any second batch.
Feel cue: Tap a cube with tongs — it should click like a crouton and feel hollow-crisp, not squish.

In a large bowl that will hold the noodles, whisk the peanut butter, soy sauce, rice vinegar, lime juice, maple syrup, garlic, ginger, chili crisp, and sesame oil into a thick paste. It will seize and look stiff at first — that's normal; it loosens with hot water in the next step.
Visual cue: A smooth, thick, caramel-colored paste with flecks of ginger and chili.
Underdone: Streaks of unmixed peanut butter and pools of soy sit separately. Keep whisking firmly; press the peanut butter against the bowl side.
Perfect: Uniform, glossy, spoonable-but-stiff paste; tastes salty, tart, and sweet in balance. Taste — add lime for brightness or maple if it reads harsh.
Overdone: Paste has broken into an oily, grainy slick (usually from too-hot additions). Whisk in a tablespoon of warm water to re-emulsify.
Feel cue: The whisk should drag through with real resistance, like stirring thick hummus.

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil (212°F / 100°C). Cook the noodles according to the package, usually 4–6 minutes, until just tender with a little chew. Scoop out 120 ml of the cooking water before draining. Rinse briefly under warm water to remove surface starch, then drain well.
Visual cue: Noodles evenly opaque throughout, supple, with no chalky white core.
Underdone: Bitten noodle shows a white, dry center line. Boil 30–60 seconds more and test again.
Perfect: Uniformly cooked, springy, bends without snapping. Reserve the water, drain, and move on while hot.
Overdone: Noodles are swollen, slack, and tear when lifted. Rinse in cool water to stop cooking; toss gently so they don't break further.
Feel cue: Pinch a strand between thumb and finger — it should compress and bounce back rather than mush.

Whisk the hot noodle water into the sauce a splash at a time until it pours like heavy cream. Add the noodles and toss with tongs for about 1 minute until every strand is coated. Divide into bowls and top with crispy tofu, cucumber, scallions, peanuts, and cilantro. Add the tofu last so it stays crisp.
Visual cue: Noodles evenly glazed in a light-tan, glossy sauce with no dry spots or pooling.
Underdone: Sauce clumps on some strands and leaves others bare; it looks pasty. Add another tablespoon of hot water and keep tossing.
Perfect: Each noodle is thinly, glossily coated; sauce clings rather than collecting at the bottom. Plate and garnish immediately.
Overdone: A thin, watery pool sits at the bottom of the bowl. Let it stand 2 minutes — the noodles will drink some up — or stir in another spoon of peanut butter.
Feel cue: Lifted with tongs, the noodles should slide as a silky, cohesive mass, not stick together in a brick.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: T55 French flour
Cold whole milk: 55 %
  Alternatives: water (less rich)
Sugar: 10 %
Fine salt: 2 %
Instant yeast: 1.5 %
Unsalted butter (détrempe — dough butter): 8 %
Unsalted European-style butter 84%+ fat (beurrage — lamination butter): 50 %
Egg yolk + whole egg for egg wash: None wash

Total time: 20 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Three days of chilling and folding trap cold butter between hundreds of dough layers — when baked, the butter steams the layers apart into a shattering, honeycomb crumb with a caramel-lacquered crust that perfumes the kitchen for an hour.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Unsalted European-style butter 84%+ fat (beurrage — lamination butter)
Egg yolk + whole egg for egg wash

steps:
Combine flour, sugar, salt, and yeast (keep salt and yeast on opposite sides of the bowl before mixing). Add cold milk and softened dough butter. Mix with a dough hook on low for 3 minutes, then medium for 4–5 minutes — develop the dough only to moderate gluten strength. Unlike bread dough, you do NOT want fully developed gluten here: a tight, over-kneaded dough will tear during lamination. The détrempe should be smooth, cohesive, and only barely tacky. Shape into a flat rectangle, wrap in plastic, and refrigerate for a minimum of 1 hour (overnight preferred).
Visual cue: A smooth, barely tacky rectangle with a matte surface. Does not spring back aggressively when pressed. Has some elasticity but yields.
Underdone: Shaggy and rough. Tears when you stretch it. Dough has not come together. Mix for 2 more minutes. The dough must be cohesive before chilling.
Perfect: Smooth, uniform, slightly elastic but pliable. Springs back slowly — not snapping. Barely tacky. Flatten to a 2 cm rectangle, wrap tightly, and refrigerate at least 1 hour.
Overdone: Very elastic, snaps back immediately, surface is very smooth and tight. The gluten is too developed. Rest in the fridge for 2 hours minimum before laminating — a cold rest relaxes it.
Feel cue: The détrempe should feel like soft, cold leather — pliable and smooth, with just enough resistance that you know gluten is present. Not rubbery, not floppy.

Place the cold lamination butter between two sheets of parchment. Using a rolling pin, beat and roll it into a flat square approximately 18 x 18 cm and exactly 1 cm thick. The butter must be cold but pliable — it should flex without cracking or crumbling. This is the most critical preparation step. Ideal butter temperature is 15–17 C. If the butter is too warm it will smear into the dough; too cold and it will shatter and create holes during lamination, ruining the layers.
Visual cue: A flat, even, 18 x 18 cm square of butter that bends slightly without cracking. Edges are clean and the block holds its shape at room temperature for at least 60 seconds.
Underdone: Butter is very cold and snaps or crumbles when you flex the parchment. Leave at room temperature 5–10 minutes. Lightly tap with the rolling pin to make it pliable without warming it.
Perfect: Butter flexes like cold clay — bends 45 degrees without cracking. Cool to the touch but not hard. Work quickly. Begin laminating with the détrempe immediately.
Overdone: Butter has softened and is greasy, spreading beyond the parchment edges. Return to the fridge for 10 minutes. Never laminate with warm butter.
Feel cue: Press your fingertip against the butter block — it should leave a clean indent without the butter smearing or sticking. Like pressing into cold wax.

Roll the chilled détrempe on a lightly floured surface into a rectangle that is exactly twice the width of the butter block and the same height. Place the butter block on one half of the dough. Fold the other half over to encase the butter completely. Press the edges to seal. You have now created the initial butter package. Roll the package carefully, always away from you, into a long rectangle 8–10 mm thick. Work fast and confidently — hesitant rolling causes tearing. Complete 3 book folds (double folds) with 30–60 minutes refrigeration between each fold: after the first fold, wrap and chill for 45 minutes; after the second, chill 30 minutes; after the third, chill for 30 minutes before cutting.
Visual cue: After rolling and folding, the dough shows a clean marble-pattern of butter layers when viewed from the cut edge. No butter smearing or bleed-through. Edges stay clean and squared.
Underdone: Butter has fractured into chunks. You can see large solid butter pieces rather than even layers when you peek at the edge. The butter was too cold. Chill the dough and let it rest 30 minutes. On the next fold, roll more gently to break up chunks gradually.
Perfect: Fine, even layering visible at the cut edge. Dough is cold, firm, rolls smoothly. No butter breaking through the surface. Chill for the required resting period before the next fold.
Overdone: Butter has melted and smeared into the dough — no visible layers, greasy surface, dough looks wet. The dough is too warm. Chill immediately for 1 hour. If the butter is fully absorbed, the lamination is lost — the croissants will bake without layers.
Feel cue: After each fold, the dough should feel cold, firm, and slightly resistant under the rolling pin — never warm, never soft. If your hand warms the dough through the parchment in less than 30 seconds, it is too warm to work with.

Roll the fully laminated dough to 4–5 mm thickness in a long rectangle. Cut triangles with a base of 10 cm and sides of 20 cm. Stretch each triangle gently to 25 cm. Starting from the wide base, roll forward firmly without squeezing — the pressure should be confident but never crushing. 7–8 rolls should bring you to the tip. Curve the two ends toward you to create the classic crescent. Place on a parchment-lined pan with the tip tucked underneath (tip touching the pan prevents unrolling during proofing). Space 6 cm apart.
Visual cue: A tightly wound crescent with the tip secured underneath. The dough strands wrap visibly around the body, even in thickness from end to end.
Underdone: Croissant is loosely wound — strands are uneven and the body is thick in the center but thin at the ends. Unroll and start again. Press from the base and roll with consistent, even pressure.
Perfect: Compact, even crescent. Tip is tucked. The multiple dough layers are just barely visible at the cut ends as fine rings. Egg wash once lightly and let proof at 25–27 C.
Overdone: Rolled so tightly the croissant is dense and sausage-like. Layering compressed. Allow to proof longer — extra proofing time may open the layers back up. They may not shatter as dramatically.
Feel cue: A correctly shaped croissant feels lighter than it should for its size — the laminated layers have air between them. When you lift it, there is almost a papery quality to the outside while the body feels substantial.

Proof shaped croissants at 25–27 C (no warmer — above 29 C the butter melts and the layers collapse) for 2–3 hours until visibly puffed and jiggling when the pan is shaken. They will not double in height — they expand outward and the layering relaxes. Apply egg wash (1 yolk + 1 whole egg, strained) very gently with a brush, avoiding the cut edges (sealing the layers prevents rise). Let rest 10 minutes, apply a second wash. Bake at 190 C (375 F) for 18–22 minutes, rotating once at 10 minutes. The butter must steam the layers apart — this happens in the first 5 minutes.
Visual cue: Deep amber-brown with a lacquered gloss. Individual layers are visibly separated and standing at the cut ends. The crescent has expanded and the tail points stick out from a puffy, layered body.
Underdone: Pale gold, no layer separation visible at the ends. Feels soft and yielding — butter has not steamed the layers open. Bake another 3–5 minutes. Pale croissants are undercooked; their interior will be raw and doughy.
Perfect: Rich amber-brown, gloss, clear layer separation at the cut ends showing a honeycomb crumb pattern. The croissant rattles slightly when shaken — hollow sound inside. Shatters when you break it. Cool 10 minutes on the rack. Eat within 2 hours for maximum shatter.
Overdone: Very dark brown, almost burnt on the crescent tips. Bitter caramel smell. Layer ends are crisp-hard. The interior may still be excellent. Trim the darkest tips. The shatter is now maximum — enjoy immediately.
Feel cue: A perfect croissant breaks with a shattering crunch that sends flakes of laminated crust flying. The interior is a honeycomb of fine, buttery layers — pull one apart and count 27 or more. The smell should be sweet butter, caramel, and bread all at once.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: T55 French flour

  Alternatives: water

Fine salt: 2 parts
Instant dry yeast: 1.5 parts
Unsalted butter (détrempe, soft): 5 parts
European unsalted butter (beurrage, 84% fat, cold): 50 parts
Active time: 3 hr
Total time: 18 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Laminated dough layered with European-style butter through dozens of turns — the result is a crescent of shattering honeycomb layers that hisses when you bite, fragrant with browned butter and lactic acid.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine flour, sugar, salt, yeast, cold milk, and soft butter in a stand mixer. Mix on low 3 minutes until combined, then on medium for 4–5 minutes only — stop while the dough is still slightly under-developed (rough surface, barely passing windowpane). Over-kneading the détrempe makes it too elastic to roll easily later. Shape into a rectangle, wrap tightly, and refrigerate overnight or at least 6 hours. Cold détrempe is easier to laminate and helps maintain the butter layers.
Visual cue: A smooth but slightly under-developed dough. Surface should look mostly smooth with very faint roughness. Not fully elastic.
Underdone: Rough, shaggy surface. Tears on short stretches. Does not hold together well. Mix 1–2 more minutes on low.
Perfect: Mostly smooth surface with a few rough patches. Only slightly elastic — when you pull a piece it stretches a bit then tears. This is intentional. Shape into a flat rectangle, wrap, and refrigerate minimum 6 hours.
Overdone: Very smooth, elastic dough that springs back aggressively. Will resist rolling later. Refrigerate immediately. The cold will slow gluten activity.
Feel cue: The détrempe should feel cool, slightly stiff, and only minimally elastic — it should not fight back like a mature kneaded dough. When cold, it should feel like firm clay that holds an impression.

Remove the butter from the refrigerator 15 minutes before lamination. Beat it between two sheets of parchment with a rolling pin until it forms a 20×20cm square, 5–6mm thick. The butter must be pliable but cold — 16°C (60°F) is ideal. It should bend without cracking and should not be greasy. If it cracks when bent, it is too cold. If it smears and softens immediately when handled, it is too warm. Proper butter plasticity is the most critical variable in lamination.
Visual cue: A neat 20×20cm square of uniform thickness, 5–6mm throughout. No cracks visible. Opaque, matte, and firm.
Underdone: Butter is cracking and crumbling when beaten. White flakes visible. Rest at room temperature 5 more minutes. The butter is too cold.
Perfect: Pliable, smooth 20×20cm square. When a corner is bent 90°, it bends without cracking or breaking. Cool to the touch. Proceed to envelope the butter in the dough immediately.
Overdone: Butter is greasy and smearing. Your hands are warming it. Butter temperature above 20°C. Refrigerate the butter block for 10 minutes before proceeding.
Feel cue: The butter block should feel like cold wax or thick cold clay — firm but plastic, not brittle. When you press a finger into it it should leave a clean impression without the butter cracking around the edges.

Roll the cold détrempe into a 40×20cm rectangle. Place the butter block in the center, fold the dough ends over to completely encase the butter, and pinch the seams closed. Roll out to 60×20cm and perform a letter fold (three-fold). Return to refrigerator for 30 minutes. Repeat this roll-and-fold cycle three more times (4 total), chilling 30 minutes between each turn. After 4 turns of a letter fold you have 3×3×3×3 = 81 layers. Work quickly — if the butter breaks through the dough or you see it smearing, chill immediately.
Visual cue: After the final fold, the edges of the dough should show distinct layer lines when viewed from the cut edge — like looking at laminated plywood.
Underdone: Layers not yet distinct. Butter and dough seem merged. Not enough folds completed. Complete remaining fold cycles with adequate chilling between each.
Perfect: Distinct layer lines at the cut edge — multiple visible strata of butter and dough. No butter breaks visible on the surface. Dough cold and firm. Final chill 30 minutes, then cut and shape.
Overdone: Butter has broken through the dough surface, or layers have merged from warmth. Greasy, smearing surface. Refrigerate immediately for 1 hour. Some layer integrity may be lost but croissants will still be good.
Feel cue: After lamination, the dough feels distinctly stiffer and more stacked — you can feel the resistance of the layers when you press into it. The surface should be cold, dry, and smooth, with no butter visible through the dough skin.

Roll the laminated dough into a 60×25cm rectangle, 4mm thick. Use a ruler and sharp knife to cut long triangles with a 12cm base. Stretch each triangle gently to 25cm long. Starting at the base, roll firmly toward the point without compressing too hard. The roll should be tight but not squeezing the layers flat. Curl the ends slightly toward you to form the crescent. Place on parchment-lined trays, with the point tucked under. Proof at 75°F (24°C) for 2–3 hours until nearly doubled and visibly layered.
Visual cue: Proofed croissants look jiggly, airy, and full. When the tray is shaken gently, they wobble noticeably. Visible layer definition at the cut ends.
Underdone: Croissants are dense and don't jiggle. Feel heavy and compact when lifted. Continue proofing. Croissants need a full 2–3 hours at 24°C. Do not rush with heat.
Perfect: Full, airy, jiggling croissants with visible layers at the open ends. The crescent shape is maintained. When poked, springs back slowly. Egg wash gently and bake.
Overdone: Croissants are very puffy and the layers are beginning to separate or meld. Butter visible pooling on the parchment. Bake immediately. Reduce oven temperature by 10°C to account for excess butter.
Feel cue: Fully proofed croissants feel impossibly light and tremble when you shake the tray — they should feel like they are barely there, full of air trapped between the layers. Press one very gently: it should yield like a foam pillow.

Apply a thin, careful egg wash (egg + milk, well-beaten), brushing with the layers not against them to avoid deflating. Bake at 400°F (200°C) for 18–22 minutes until deep amber-brown. Croissants should puff dramatically in the oven — the butter creates steam that forces the layers apart. If they look pale at 18 minutes, increase to 410°F for a final 3 minutes. A properly baked croissant will leave a visible ring of clarified butter on the parchment.
Visual cue: Deep amber honeycomb exterior. Layers visibly separated and distinct. A pool of clarified butter on the parchment beneath each croissant. The smell of browned butter is unmistakable.
Underdone: Pale golden. Layers barely separated. No butter pool. Interior may be wet and doughy between layers. Continue baking 4–5 more minutes. The interior must dry out.
Perfect: Deep amber. Distinct, shattered layers like a honeycomb visible at the cut ends. Butter pool on parchment. Sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom. Cool on a rack for 15 minutes before eating.
Overdone: Dark brown with some burnt edges. Excessive butter on parchment. Layers are very dark. Still delicious — the burnt layers add a pleasant bitterness. Just avoid the darkest bits.
Feel cue: Lift a finished croissant and it should feel shockingly light — dramatically lighter than its size suggests. Tap the bottom and it rings hollow. Squeeze it gently: you should feel the resistance of dozens of distinct layers, and then hear a faint, satisfying crackle.

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The Parisian café sandwich elevated by proper béchamel — buttery bread, good ham, nutmeg-scented white sauce, and Gruyère that bubbles and blisters under the broiler into a savoury, slightly charred crust that crackles when you press down on it.

ingredients.name: Thick-cut white bread (pain de mie preferred)
Gruyère, coarsely grated (Comté or Emmental work too)
盐（Salt, white pepper, and freshly grated nutmeg）

steps:
Melt butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add flour all at once and stir vigorously with a wooden spoon or whisk for 90 seconds — the roux should turn pale blonde and smell faintly nutty, not raw. Gradually pour in warm milk, whisking constantly to prevent lumps. Stir over medium heat until the sauce thickens to a consistency that coats the back of a spoon heavily. Season with salt, white pepper, and a generous grating of nutmeg.
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy white sauce that coats the back of a spoon in a thick, even layer and holds a line when you draw your finger through it.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and milky. No coating on the spoon — it runs off immediately. Floury taste when sampled. Continue stirring over medium heat. Béchamel needs to reach near-boiling to fully cook the starch and thicken properly.
Perfect: Thick, glossy, smooth. A finger drawn through the coat on a spoon leaves a clean line that holds for 5+ seconds. Tastes rich with a warm nutmeg note, no floury raw edge. Remove from heat. Stir in a handful of the Gruyère if a cheesier sauce (Mornay) is desired.
Overdone: Sauce is very stiff and gluey — it mounds on the spoon rather than flowing. Lumps may appear from sticking to the pan bottom. Whisk in warm milk a tablespoon at a time to loosen. Pass through a sieve if lumps remain.
Feel cue: Rub a small amount of béchamel between your fingers — the properly cooked sauce should feel silky-smooth with no gritty floury granules, and it should cling to your skin in a thin, even film.

Spread butter on one side of each bread slice. Toast buttered-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat for 2–3 minutes until golden and fragrant. This step is often skipped in shortcuts, but pre-toasting prevents the bottom bread from going soggy under the wet béchamel. Remove from heat.
Visual cue: The buttered side is an even, pale golden brown — not dark brown. The bread smells toasted and nutty. The unbuttered side remains soft and white.
Underdone: The buttered side is still white or very pale yellow. Bread is soft throughout with no crust formed. Return to heat. Untoasted bread will become soggy and collapse under the béchamel.
Perfect: Even, golden-blonde color on the buttered surface. The bread is rigid and slightly crisp to the touch. Smells of brown butter. Remove from pan and assemble.
Overdone: Buttered side is dark brown, bordering on burnt. Bitter smell. Bread is very hard. Proceed — the béchamel and broiler will mask some bitterness, but be gentle with heat during the broil step.
Feel cue: Tap the toasted surface with a fingernail — it should give a light, dry click, like tapping a wooden cutting board, not the soft thud of untoasted bread.

Spread a generous layer of béchamel on the untoasted side of the bottom bread slice. Lay ham slices to cover completely. Add a layer of grated Gruyère. Place the second slice on top, toasted side up. Spread more béchamel over the top of the sandwich — this is the defining move of the croque-monsieur — and pile the remaining Gruyère on top.
Visual cue: A well-built sandwich with béchamel extending to the edges of the top surface and an even mound of Gruyère covering the top entirely. No bare bread visible through the cheese.
Underdone: Too little béchamel on top — bread still visible. Not enough cheese. The top will dry out under the broiler rather than forming a crust. Add more béchamel and cheese. There should be no skimping — the excess is what creates the golden crust.
Perfect: Béchamel reaches the edges and cheese fully covers the top in an even mound. The sandwich looks slightly over-built — this is correct. Transfer to a baking sheet and broil.
Overdone: So much béchamel that it's sliding off the sides before even reaching the oven. Extremely difficult to handle. Refrigerate 5 minutes to firm up the béchamel before broiling.
Feel cue: Pick up the assembled croque — it should feel satisfyingly heavy for its size, the cheese and sauce creating real substance, not a lightweight dry sandwich.

Place the assembled croque on a baking sheet under a hot broiler set to high, positioned 15 cm from the element. Broil for 3–5 minutes, watching constantly, until the Gruyère on top is bubbling, golden-brown, and developing dark spots. The edges of the béchamel should be caramelizing. Serve immediately — the crust is best in the first 90 seconds.
Visual cue: Gruyère is bubbling vigorously across the entire surface, with golden-brown patches and a few charred dark spots scattered throughout. The béchamel edges are caramelized and slightly darker.
Underdone: Cheese has melted but is pale and barely golden. No bubbling spots. The surface looks damp and glistening but not browned. Continue broiling. The flavour transformation happens in the last 90 seconds when the cheese begins to colour.
Perfect: Deep golden bubbling across the surface. Dark spots visible — these are the best bites. Edges of the sauce are amber and slightly caramelized. An overwhelming smell of browned cheese fills the kitchen. Remove immediately. Transfer to a plate and serve within 90 seconds.
Overdone: Cheese is uniformly dark brown or black. Smoke is rising from the baking sheet. The acrid smell of burnt dairy fills the kitchen. Remove immediately. Scrape off the topmost blackened layer — the middle is likely still fine and melted underneath.
Feel cue: Press the top of the finished croque lightly with a fingertip — the cheese crust should crack and give a slight crunch before yielding to the molten layer beneath, like pressing the surface of a freshly baked gratin.

name: Crumpets
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=bakers_percentage）；不是经核对的人均用量。
All-purpose flour: 100 %
Warm water (105°F / 41°C): 80 %
Warm whole milk (105°F / 41°C): 30 %
  Alternatives: all water for dairy-free
Instant dry yeast: 1.5 %
Baking soda: 0.5 %
Fine salt: 1.5 %
Sugar: 1 %
Butter (for greasing rings and griddle): 3 %
  Alternatives: neutral oil
Warm water (2 tbsp, for baking soda slurry): 5 %
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 2 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Batter-poured rounds cooked in rings on a griddle until a lacework of holes forms on top, leaving a moist, spongy interior and a crisply-toasted base perfect for soaking butter.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: 黄油（Butter (for greasing rings and griddle)）
Warm water (2 tbsp, for baking soda slurry)

steps:
Whisk together the flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a large bowl. Add the warm water and warm milk and whisk vigorously until you have a very smooth, thick batter with no lumps. The batter at this stage should be notably thicker than pancake batter — more like a thick milkshake. Cover with plastic wrap or a damp cloth and leave to ferment at room temperature for 1–1.5 hours. The batter will rise, become very bubbly and frothy, and the volume will roughly double. The yeast activity is what creates the hole structure: when the batter hits the hot griddle, the CO2 dissolved in it rises and punches through the surface, forming the characteristic crumpet holes.
Visual cue: A frothy, actively bubbling batter that has visibly risen in the bowl. Lifting the whisk, the batter falls in thick, bubbly ribbons. The surface should look like a foam of tiny bubbles — a sign of active yeast and sufficient fermentation.
Underdone: Batter looks flat and dense with no surface bubbles. It has barely risen. The yeast is under-active — either the water was too hot (killed the yeast) or too cold (yeast not activated). Move to a warmer spot (75–80°F / 24–27°C) and wait another 30–45 minutes. If still flat, the yeast may be dead — start again with fresh yeast.
Perfect: Batter has doubled or nearly so, surface is a foam of small bubbles. When stirred, the batter falls from the whisk in bubbly ribbons with visible trapped air. Smells of fresh yeast and faintly tangy. Dissolve the baking soda in 2 tablespoons of warm water and stir into the batter. Immediately proceed to cooking.
Overdone: Batter has over-fermented — it smells aggressively sour or alcoholic, has begun to deflate, and the bubbles have coalesced into large irregular pockets. Proceed immediately. The crumpets will have an aggressively tangy flavor (not necessarily unpleasant) but the hole structure may be irregular. Reduce

fermentation time next batch.
Feel cue: Stir the fermented batter slowly and feel the air trapped in it — the whisk should pull through with the soft resistance of something full of bubbles, like stirring a slightly thick foam. Taste a small amount: it should be yeasty, faintly sour, and alive. Not sour like vinegar but bright and tangy like a young sourdough, with a wheaty backbone.

Dissolve the baking soda completely in 2 tablespoons of warm water, then stir it into the fermented batter quickly and thoroughly. The baking soda creates an immediate reaction with the acids from the yeast fermentation, producing extra CO2 bubbles — you will see the batter immediately become even frothier. This dual leavening (yeast + baking soda) is what gives crumpets their characteristic deep, open hole structure. Cook within 5–10 minutes of adding the baking soda, while the reaction is still active. The batter at this stage should be thick enough to hold its shape in the ring mold without flowing under the ring, but pourable — about the consistency of slightly-thinned yogurt.
Visual cue: A noticeably frothier, more aerated batter after the baking soda addition. Small bubbles cover the entire surface. When you pour a ladleful, it should fall in a thick, bubbly sheet, not a thin stream.
Underdone: Batter looks unchanged after adding the baking soda — no increase in froth or aeration. The reaction did not occur because the baking soda was not fully dissolved, or there was insufficient acid from fermentation. Stir more vigorously for 30 seconds. If still flat, proceed anyway — the yeast bubbles alone may produce adequate holes, though they will be smaller.
Perfect: Noticeably frothier after the soda addition. Surface covered in small bubbles. Batter pours in a thick, aerated sheet and holds a slight mound in the ladle. Cook immediately on a preheated, buttered griddle with greased crumpet rings.
Overdone: Batter poured too long after adding baking soda — 20+ minutes — and the reaction has dissipated. The batter looks flat again and the soda flavor may be detectable as a slightly metallic taste. Proceed regardless. The yeast activity will still produce some holes. If the metallic flavor is present, add a few drops of lemon juice to balance the residual

alkalinity.
Feel cue: Immediately after stirring in the baking soda, the batter should feel lighter under the ladle — the increased gas makes it almost feathery. Pour a small amount on the back of your hand: it should feel cool and smooth, and the air bubbles should be visible as tiny, tight specks throughout the coating. This aeration is what makes the hole structure possible.

Heat a flat griddle or heavy skillet over low-medium heat (325°F / 163°C). Butter the inside of 3.5-inch / 9 cm crumpet rings (or egg rings) generously. Place the rings on the griddle and butter the griddle surface lightly inside each ring. Fill each ring to about two-thirds full with batter — roughly 3–4 tablespoons. The batter should not overflow but should have room to rise. Cook uncovered for 8–12 minutes without disturbing. Within 2–3 minutes the surface will begin to set at the edges while the center remains liquid; over the next several minutes, bubbles will rise through the batter and burst on the surface, forming the characteristic holes. When the entire surface looks set and matte with a defined lacework of holes, and the top looks nearly dry (not shiny), remove the rings with tongs and flip the crumpets. Cook the second side for 1–2 minutes until the base is golden-crisp. Cool on a rack and toast before serving.
Visual cue: A fully formed crumpet with a dense lacework of small, distinct holes covering the entire top surface, a matte, set appearance, and a crisply golden bottom. The holes should be clean and open, not collapsed or wet-rimmed.
Underdone: The top surface still looks shiny and wet in the center. Holes have started to form but many are still open bubbles, not dry holes. The crumpet feels squishy and floppy when you try to remove the ring. Continue cooking uncovered. Do not rush by raising the heat — higher heat burns the base before the top sets. Patience is the crumpet's requirement. Cook 2–3 more minutes and check again.
Perfect: Entire top surface is matte and set, covered in open, clean holes of varying sizes. The ring releases easily and the crumpet holds its shape. Bottom is golden brown when flipped — a firm, toasted base that contrasts with the soft, holey interior. Flip, cook 1–2 minutes on the top side for a light color, then cool on

a rack. Toast before serving.
Overdone: Bottom is dark brown or burnt. The crumpet smells of scorched butter. Top surface may be over-set and look almost like a fried egg in texture — solid rather than spongy. Reduce griddle heat significantly for the next batch. English crumpets need very gentle, sustained heat — not the medium-high heat used for pancakes. If the bottom is merely dark (not burnt), the interior is likely fine; the char can be scraped away.
Feel cue: A properly finished crumpet should feel substantial but yielding when you press the top — like pressing a firm sponge. The base should feel crisp and rigid, with a dry crackle when you press it. When you split or bite into a toasted crumpet, the interior should give with the soft, tender squish of bread soaked in butter — the holes drawing the butter deep inside. That butter absorption is the soul of a good crumpet: without open holes, there is nowhere for the butter to go.

ingredients.name: Dried black beans (soaked overnight, or canned)
Apple cider vinegar or dry white wine

steps:
If using dried beans (soaked overnight), drain and rinse. Place in a large pot and cover with 8cm of cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook for 60-90 minutes until beans are completely tender throughout — they should crush easily between two fingers. Season with salt only when completely soft; salt added before tenderness toughens the skin and extends cooking time significantly. Reserve 2 cups of the bean cooking liquid before draining.
Visual cue: Beans are uniformly tender and have swollen to approximately twice their dry size. The cooking liquid has turned deep purple-black and is slightly thick.
Underdone: Beans are still chalky and firm at the center when bitten. The skin is intact but the interior is not soft. Continue simmering and test every 15 minutes. Do not salt yet.
Perfect: Beans crush completely between two fingers without resistance. Cooking liquid is deep, inky black. Season with salt now. Reserve 2 cups of cooking liquid and drain.
Overdone: Beans have split and are beginning to dissolve into the cooking liquid. Liquid is very thick. Proceed — partly dissolved beans will make the final dish creamier. Use all the liquid and reduce less at the end.
Feel cue: Take a bean between your thumbnail and forefinger and apply gentle pressure — a perfectly cooked bean should collapse completely with minimal force, leaving no chalky center.

Heat olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add diced onion and green pepper. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 8-10 minutes until completely soft and beginning to turn golden — the onion should be translucent throughout, not just at the edges. Add garlic and cumin. Cook for another 90 seconds, stirring constantly, until the garlic is fragrant and the cumin blooms in the fat, smelling toasty and warm. The sofrito should look like a thick, golden-green jam.
Visual cue: A soft, jammy paste of onion and pepper — translucent, golden, and significantly reduced in volume from the raw state. No white or crunchy pieces remain.
Underdone: Onion and pepper are still crunchy and opaque white. The mixture looks watery, not jammy. Continue cooking over medium heat. Undercooked sofrito gives the finished dish a raw, harsh flavor.
Perfect: Completely translucent, golden onion and pepper that have melted into a cohesive, fragrant base. The fat has separated slightly around the edges. Add garlic and cumin, then immediately add the beans.
Overdone: Sofrito is darkening at the edges and beginning to stick to the pot. Garlic may be browning. Reduce heat and add a splash of water to deglaze. Brown sofrito will make the beans taste slightly bitter.
Feel cue: A properly cooked sofrito should smell sweet and savory simultaneously — caramelized onion sweetness, the slight bitterness of cooked pepper, and a warm cumin bloom that rises in a single aromatic wave.

Add the cooked beans to the sofrito pot along with the reserved cooking liquid. Stir to combine and bring to a simmer. Cook uncovered for 20-30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the liquid has reduced and thickened considerably — it should coat the back of a spoon and look glossy. In the final 2 minutes of cooking, add the vinegar or white wine. Do not cook after adding the vinegar; you want the brightness to be present in the finished dish, not cooked away. Taste and adjust salt.
Visual cue: An intensely dark, glossy, thick sauce enveloping plump beans. The surface of the liquid barely moves when the pot is nudged. A spoon dragged through it leaves a trail that fills slowly.
Underdone: The liquid is watery and dark but not thick. It runs quickly off the spoon. The beans taste separate from the sauce. Continue reducing over medium heat, uncovered. Stir more frequently as it thickens to prevent sticking.
Perfect: Thick, glossy, deeply flavored broth that clings to each bean. The surface is slightly viscous. The taste is complex: earthy, savory, with a clean acidic lift. Remove from heat. Add vinegar if not already done, stir, and serve.
Overdone: Beans are sitting in a thick paste. The bottom is beginning to stick and scorch. Add water or stock to loosen, stir from the bottom to incorporate any stuck bits, and remove from heat.
Feel cue: Stir the pot and listen — properly thickened frijoles negros make a heavy, slow gurgling sound as bubbles push through the viscous liquid, not a thin, rapid boiling.

name: Cucumber Raita
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: regular whole-milk yogurt, strained 30 min

  Alternatives: Persian cucumber; seeded regular cucumber

  Alternatives: 1/2 tsp ground cumin

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: India's great cooling counterpoint — cold thick yogurt folded with grated cucumber, bloomed cumin, fresh mint, and coriander into a condiment that brings peace to any fiery curry or biryani it accompanies.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Full-fat plain yogurt (strained or Greek style)
English cucumber, grated on large holes

steps:
Grate cucumber on the large holes of a box grater. Sprinkle with half the salt and toss. Place in a colander or wrap in a clean kitchen towel and squeeze out as much liquid as possible — really compress it. Let drain for 10 minutes, then squeeze again. A single cucumber holds a surprising amount of water; releasing it prevents a watery raita.
Visual cue: Cucumber reduced to roughly half its original volume, pale green, compacted — still identifiable as cucumber but much drier.
Underdone: Cucumber still wet and dripping. You can wring more water out. Continue squeezing. Press between two plates with a weight on top for 10 minutes.
Perfect: Cucumber barely drips when squeezed in the fist. Still green and fresh-smelling. Feels like a compressed sponge. Fold into yogurt.
Overdone: You cannot over-drain cucumber — but if it's been sitting in salt more than 30 minutes, it tastes excessively salty. Rinse quickly under cold water and squeeze again before adding to yogurt.
Feel cue: Squeeze the grated cucumber in your fist — it should feel like wet sand compressing, and a stream of pale green water should run out.

Toast cumin seeds in a small dry skillet over medium heat for 60-90 seconds, shaking constantly, until they darken and begin to pop. Immediately grind coarsely in a mortar or between two spoons. The heat transforms the raw, slightly harsh flavor of cumin into a warm, nutty, aromatic note.
Visual cue: Seeds darkened to a warm brown, no black, releasing a warm spice aroma.
Underdone: Seeds still pale and grassy-smelling. No visible darkening. Continue over medium heat.
Perfect: Dark brown, fragrant, one or two have popped. Kitchen smells of warm spice. Grind immediately and add to yogurt.
Overdone: Black and smoking. Acrid, bitter smell. Discard and start again.
Feel cue: The smell of toasted cumin is unmistakable — earthy, warm, faintly smoky. If you can't smell it strongly from arm's length, it needs more heat.

In a bowl, combine yogurt, drained cucumber, bloomed cumin, mint, coriander, ground coriander, and remaining salt. Fold gently — don't overstir into a smooth paste. The texture should be spoonable with visible herb flecks and cucumber strands. Taste and adjust salt. Refrigerate for 15 minutes before serving — the rest allows the flavors to meld.
Visual cue: A thick, white-green speckled condiment — clearly yogurt-based with visible mint, coriander, cucumber, and cumin throughout.
Underdone: Cucumber still too wet — raita pools liquid after 2 minutes in the bowl. Drain the raita by pressing through a strainer, or add more yogurt to absorb the liquid.
Perfect: Thick, cool, aromatic. Holds its shape on a spoon. Visible flecks of green herb throughout. Tastes simultaneously cooling and flavored. Serve cold alongside biryani, curry, or grilled meats.
Overdone: Over-stirred into a smooth puree. Texture uniform and herb flecks unrecognizable. Still delicious. Add a last-minute fold of fresh mint for texture.
Feel cue: A spoonful should feel cool and thick, with a slight resistance — yogurt-thick, not pourable. If it runs off the spoon, the cucumber wasn't drained enough.

ingredients.name: 胡萝卜（Carrots, peeled and sliced into coins）
Red lentils, rinsed until the water runs clear

steps:
Heat oil in a 5–6 litre pot over medium heat. Add cumin seeds and let them sizzle 20–30 seconds until they darken a shade. Add onion with a pinch of salt and cook 7–8 minutes until soft and golden at the edges. Stir in garlic, ginger, and curry powder and cook 60 seconds, stirring constantly.
Visual cue: Golden onion coated in a turmeric-yellow paste that smells toasty and sweet.
Underdone: Curry powder still looks dusty and dry; raw, chalky spice smell. Add a spoonful of oil and stir 20–30 seconds more.
Perfect: Spices have turned to a glossy paste clinging to the onion; aroma is warm and rounded. Add carrots, lentils, and liquid immediately.
Overdone: Paste is dark brown and sticking, with a bitter, scorched smell. Deglaze at once with a ladle of stock. If it tastes acrid, start the base over.
Feel cue: Listen: cumin seeds should crackle like light rain; if they go silent and smoke, the oil was too hot.

Add carrots, lentils, and stock. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then simmer partially covered 25–30 minutes, stirring the bottom every so often (red lentils sink and catch), until carrots are completely tender and the lentils have dissolved.
Visual cue: Lentils vanished into a thick golden broth; carrots soft enough to crush against the pot wall.
Underdone: Lentils still hold their lens shape; carrot coins have a firm core. Simmer 5–10 minutes more, adding water if the pot gets thick.
Perfect: Lentils have melted to mush; a carrot coin crushes under the spoon with no resistance. Blend.
Overdone: Lentils have caught and browned on the bottom; faint scorched smell. Don't scrape. Pour the soup into a clean pot, leaving the stuck layer behind.
Feel cue: Drag the spoon across the pot bottom — it should glide, not grab on a sticky layer.

Purée with an immersion blender until completely smooth (or blend in batches, filling the jar no more than half full and venting the lid). Stir in coconut milk and warm through without boiling. Add lime juice and salt to taste — usually 1.5–2 tsp. Thin with water to a pourable consistency. Garnish with cilantro and chili flakes. To freeze: cool in shallow containers, refrigerate within 2 hours, and freeze up to 3 months. It sets up thick when cold; loosen with water as it reheats and add fresh lime.
Visual cue: Glossy, sunset-orange soup that pours in a thick ribbon.
Underdone: Flecks of carrot and a grainy texture remain; coconut milk streaks. Blend another minute and stir thoroughly.
Perfect: Silky and uniform, coating the back of a spoon; bright from lime, gently sweet from carrot. Serve.
Overdone: Stiff enough to hold a spoon upright after standing. Whisk in hot water 100 ml at a time and re-season with salt.
Feel cue: On the tongue it should feel like velvet with no grit; the ginger should warm the throat after you swallow.

ingredients.name: Green cabbage, cored and finely shredded
胡萝卜（Carrot, peeled and julienned or grated）
White onion, thinly sliced into half-moons
Red pepper flakes or dried chile de árbol, crumbled

steps:
Place shredded cabbage in a large bowl. Pour the boiling water over the cabbage, toss to coat, and let it sit for 3 minutes. Drain immediately and rinse under cold water to stop any cooking. The goal is just-wilted cabbage — still crunchy but pliable, with the raw-vegetal harshness softened.
Visual cue: Cabbage has lost its stiff rigidity and gone slightly translucent at the cut edges while remaining pale green. It piles loosely rather than standing up in stiff shreds.
Underdone: Cabbage is still raw and very stiff. The boiling water didn't penetrate. It will be too crunchy and slow to absorb the brine. Pour more boiling water over and let sit 2 more minutes before draining.
Perfect: Slightly softened but still holding a definite crunch. The translucent green of wilted cabbage. Pliable but not limp. Rinse with cold water to stop the wilting and drain well before combining.
Overdone: Cabbage has gone limp, olive-drab, and wet — it was left too long in hot water or the water was too voluminous. Drain very well, squeeze out excess water with your hands, and proceed. The texture will be softer than ideal, but the curtido will still be good.
Feel cue: Grab a small handful of the drained cabbage and squeeze — it should give freely without crunch but then spring back partially, like squeezing a slightly damp sponge. No water should drip out without squeezing.

In a large bowl, combine the wilted cabbage, julienned carrot, and sliced onion. Pour over the vinegar and sprinkle on the salt, dried oregano, and pepper flakes. Toss thoroughly with clean hands or tongs until everything is evenly combined and the vegetables are coated. Taste and adjust: it should be clearly tart, lightly salty, and have a herbal oregano warmth.
Visual cue: A colorful, evenly combined slaw — pale green cabbage threaded with bright orange carrot and white onion rings, glistening with a light vinegar coat. The oregano flecks are evenly distributed.
Underdone: The carrot and onion are pooled at the bottom, the vinegar has not coated the cabbage. The mixture looks dry on top. Toss more thoroughly, lifting from the bottom and turning over the top. Use your hands for the most thorough mixing.
Perfect: Every shred of cabbage and every carrot stick is glistening. The vegetables are evenly distributed throughout. It smells of vinegar, oregano, and fresh vegetables. Pack into a jar or container and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, ideally overnight.
Overdone: The salt has drawn so much water from the vegetables that the mixture is swimming in liquid and the cabbage looks very limp and pale. Drain the excess liquid, add a tablespoon of fresh vinegar, and refrigerate. The curtido will be softer but still good.
Feel cue: Toss the curtido and then smell your hands — you should catch a bright hit of oregano and vinegar together, a combination that smells clean and sharp, like the counter of a very good pupusería.

Pack the curtido tightly into a clean jar, pressing down so the vegetables are submerged in their own released liquid (or under the vinegar brine). Cover loosely — not airtight — and leave at room temperature for 12-24 hours. This brief room-temperature rest jumpstarts a very light lacto-fermentation that adds just a touch of natural tang beyond the vinegar. Then refrigerate. It is ready to eat right away but improves dramatically overnight. Keeps for 2 weeks refrigerated.
Visual cue: After 24 hours total (room temp + fridge): the cabbage is pale, slightly translucent, and well-compressed. The liquid in the jar has gone from clear to a slightly cloudy, pale amber. The smell is sharply vinegary with a warm oregano note.
Underdone: Still bright white with raw cabbage crunch and no tanginess beyond the added vinegar. The flavors haven't melded. Leave at room temperature for the full 24 hours, then refrigerate. The transformation is in time, not technique.
Perfect: Pale, translucent, well-compressed cabbage. Tangy, bright, herbal, with a clean crunch that gives almost no resistance. The liquid is slightly cloudy and deeply flavored. Tastes essential alongside a pupusa. Refrigerate and use within 2 weeks.
Overdone: Left at room temperature for 3+ days: very sour and funky, onions have softened to mush, vinegar has been overwhelmed by lactic acid tang. The smell is powerful. Still edible — curtido can ferment all the way to a sauerkraut-style preserve. Drain and serve as a more aggressively fermented condiment, or use in cooked dishes.
Feel cue: Pinch a strand of curtido from the jar after a day — it should snap cleanly with a small crunch, not squish between your fingers. Hold it to the light: the translucency of just-fermented cabbage is distinctly different from raw, with a watercolor quality at the edges.

name: Hazelnut Dacquoise
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Egg whites (large, room temperature, no trace of yolk): 6 whites
Caster sugar: 150 g
Hazelnut flour (toasted, skins-on ground hazelnut): 150 g
  Alternatives: almond flour
Icing (powdered) sugar: 100 g
Fine sea salt: 1 g
Unsalted butter (softened, for praline buttercream): 250 g
Praline paste (hazelnut, store-bought or home-made): 120 g

Egg yolks (for pâte à bombe base): 3 yolks
Active time: 60 min

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Crisp, cloud-light meringue discs bolstered by toasted hazelnut flour, layered with praline buttercream — crunchy at the edges, chewy at the center, and with a richness that slowly gives way to the clean lift of whipped sugar.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: 蛋清（Egg whites (large, room temperature, no trace of yolk)）
蛋黄（Egg yolks (for pâte à bombe base)）

steps:
If starting from whole hazelnuts: roast at 175 C (350 F) for 12-15 minutes, rub in a kitchen towel to remove skins, then pulse in a food processor with the icing sugar until fine but not paste. If using pre-ground hazelnut flour: spread on a tray and toast at 160 C for 8-10 minutes, stirring once, until fragrant and lightly golden. Cool completely before using.
Visual cue: Fine, dry hazelnut flour with a warm tan color — visibly darker than raw, with small golden-brown flecks. The smell is rich, nutty, and warm.
Underdone: Flour is still pale ivory. The raw, slightly bitter smell of untoasted nuts remains. Return to the oven for 3-5 more minutes, watching closely.
Perfect: Golden-tan color with dark flecks from toasted skins. Fills the kitchen with a warm, roasty hazelnut aroma. Dry to the touch. Cool to room temperature before folding into meringue — hot flour will deflate the whites instantly.
Overdone: Dark brown, approaching burnt. Bitter rather than nutty smell. Discard and re-toast with a new batch — burnt hazelnut flour ruins the dacquoise with bitterness.
Feel cue: Properly toasted hazelnut flour pinched between two fingers feels dry and light, releasing an immediate wave of roasted nut smell — like freshly ground espresso, but warmer.

In a scrupulously clean, dry bowl, whip egg whites with salt on medium speed until frothy and opaque. Increase to medium-high and add caster sugar one tablespoon at a time over 3-4 minutes. Continue whipping until the meringue is stiff, very glossy, and the sugar is completely dissolved (rub between fingertips — no grittiness). The meringue should stand in firm peaks that do not droop at all.
Visual cue: Bright white, glossy meringue that stands in firm, upright peaks — the peak curls back slightly but the body holds completely rigid. Looks like polished white satin.
Underdone: Peaks fold over softly and the meringue feels gritty when rubbed — undissolved sugar. The meringue looks dull and slightly wet. Continue whipping on medium-high for 2-3 more minutes. Test for dissolved sugar by rubbing between finger and thumb.
Perfect: Firm, glossy, and completely smooth. Stiff peaks stand upright without drooping. No grittiness. When the bowl is tipped, the meringue does not slide. Fold in the hazelnut mixture immediately.
Overdone: Meringue is dry, lumpy, and no longer glossy. It looks like fluffy cotton wool and tears when lifted. Unfortunately cannot be recovered — over-whipped whites produce a dacquoise that crumbles rather than having the characteristic chewy-crisp bite.
Feel cue: Rub a small amount of meringue between your index finger and thumb — it should feel silky-smooth and cool, with zero graininess. Any trace of sugar crystals means another two minutes of whipping.

Sift icing sugar over the toasted hazelnut flour and stir to combine. Working quickly, fold the hazelnut mixture into the meringue in three additions using a large metal spoon or flat spatula. Cut through the center, sweep under, and flip — do not stir in circles. The mixture will deflate somewhat; this is expected. Stop when no streaks of white meringue are visible.
Visual cue: A thick, spoonable batter of pale beige color — darker than pure meringue, lighter than the hazelnut flour alone. Holds a shape when dolloped but is not stiff.
Underdone: White meringue streaks still visible throughout. The batter is still two-toned when scooped. Three more deliberate cuts-and-folds. Work decisively but not hastily.
Perfect: Uniform pale-beige color. The batter holds a soft mound when spooned but slowly levels out over 10 seconds. Pipe or spread into circles immediately — the batter deflates if left waiting.
Overdone: Batter has become runny and spreads immediately flat on the spoon. The meringue structure has been destroyed. Spread immediately in thin layers and bake as-is — the dacquoise will be denser but still edible.
Feel cue: Each fold should meet light resistance and then yield softly — the rhythm is slow and deliberate, like turning over a large dune of snow without collapsing it.

Preheat oven to 150 C (300 F) fan. Draw three 20cm circles on baking paper, flip the paper over. Pipe or spread the batter evenly within the circles to about 1.5cm thick. Bake 30-35 minutes until lightly golden on the surface and firm to the touch. Turn off the oven and prop the door open 2cm; leave the dacquoise inside for 30 minutes to dry out slowly. This gives the characteristic dry crust with chewy interior.
Visual cue: Pale ivory-beige discs with a dry, lightly golden surface. The edges are slightly darker. The surface should feel firm and papery when tapped — not sticky.
Underdone: Surface is still tacky and yields to light finger pressure like a marshmallow. The dacquoise will stick to the paper when peeled. Return to the oven for 5-8 more minutes and then rest in the open oven again.
Perfect: Light golden surface, paper-dry to the touch. Lifts cleanly from baking paper. The underside has a thin caramel-brown crust. Smells of toasted hazelnut and sugar. Cool completely on a rack before layering — warm dacquoise absorbs moisture from the cream and softens.
Overdone: Surface is deeply golden-brown and the edges are dark. The disc has flattened and is fully dry and brittle throughout with no chew. Use immediately — over-baked dacquoise becomes very brittle and the layers will shatter when cut.
Feel cue: A properly dried dacquoise sounds hollow when tapped — a light, dry click rather than a dull thud. The underside should peel away from the paper with a satisfying snap at the edges.

Beat softened butter until very pale and fluffy, about 5 minutes. In a separate bowl, whisk egg yolks until pale. Make a pâte à bombe: boil caster sugar with a little water to 121 C (250 F) soft-ball stage, then pour slowly onto whisking yolks. Whip until cool. Beat the pâte à bombe into the butter gradually, then beat in the praline paste. The buttercream should be smooth, pipeable, and hold a firm peak. Assemble the dacquoise: dacquoise disc, buttercream, dacquoise, buttercream, dacquoise. Chill 1 hour before cutting.
Visual cue: Pale caramel-golden buttercream that holds clean, defined peaks when the paddle is lifted. Smooth and silky with no visible butter lumps or air pockets.
Underdone: Buttercream looks broken and curdled — yellow butter chunks floating in liquid. The butter was too cold when added to the warm pâte à bombe. Continue beating on medium speed. It will emulsify as the temperature equilibrates. If still broken after 5 minutes, gently warm the bowl with a hair dryer while beating.
Perfect: Creamy, smooth, holds a firm ribbon. Golden from the praline paste. Tastes of hazelnut caramel and butter. Use immediately or refrigerate, beating briefly again before use.
Overdone: Greasy, grainy texture. The buttercream has been beaten too long and the butter has separated to the edges. Refrigerate 20 minutes and beat again on medium speed to re-emulsify.
Feel cue: Properly made praline buttercream should feel like cool, thick velvet on the spatula — it holds a clean groove when dragged, and the praline gives a faint grittiness that melts instantly on the tongue.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

Katakuriko or cornstarch (dusting): 0.5 cup
  Alternatives: rice flour

  Alternatives: food-grade sakura powder; black sesame paste

Total time: 1 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Pillowy rounds of sweet glutinous rice dough — chewy and yielding like nothing else on earth — stretched thin around a generous ball of sweet red bean paste until the filling is completely enveloped and the seam is sealed tight. Dusted in rice flour so the skin stays soft and dry to the touch, each piece is a quiet study in contrasting textures.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Tsubuan or koshian (sweet red bean paste)

steps:
In a microwave-safe bowl, combine mochiko, sugar, and water (add matcha now if using). Whisk until completely smooth and no dry powder remains. The batter will be thin and milky-white.
Visual cue: A smooth, slightly viscous, pure white (or pale green if matcha is used) liquid batter with no lumps.
Underdone: Dry flour pockets at the bottom or edges, batter not fully homogeneous. Whisk more thoroughly; scrape the bottom of the bowl to catch any unmixed flour.
Perfect: Completely uniform, flows smoothly off the whisk in a thin ribbon with no breaks. Matcha (if used) fully dissolved without green flecks. Cover loosely and microwave in stages.
Overdone: N/A — there is no way to over-mix a thin batter at this stage. Proceed.
Feel cue: Tilt the bowl and listen — smooth batter pours silently. Lumpy batter makes a slight gritty scraping sound.

Loosely cover the bowl with plastic wrap. Microwave on high for 1 minute. Remove, stir vigorously with a wet silicone spatula. Microwave again for 1 minute. Stir again. Microwave for a final 30–60 seconds until the dough is fully translucent and sticky throughout, with no white, raw-looking patches. Alternatively, steam over boiling water for 20 minutes, stirring halfway through.
Visual cue: Fully translucent, shiny, pale grey-white (or vibrant green) dough that stretches without tearing when pulled. Extremely sticky.
Underdone: Parts of the dough are still white and opaque — uncooked starch. The texture is wet and loose rather than stretchy. Microwave in 30-second bursts, stirring between each, until fully translucent throughout.
Perfect: Completely translucent. Pulls away from the bowl in long elastic strings when stirred. The spatula lifted slowly draws a continuous ribbon. Soft sheen, slightly glossy. Transfer immediately to a surface generously dusted with katakuriko to cool and divide.
Overdone: Dough is very stiff, rubbery, and has begun drying at the edges. Loses its stretch. Wet your hands and knead in a teaspoon of warm water while the dough is still hot to restore elasticity.
Feel cue: When you stir a fully cooked mochi with a wet spatula, it should pull at you — thick, slow, enormously resistant. Like stirring chewing gum.

While the mochi is still warm (it becomes stiffer as it cools — work quickly), portion the bean paste into balls of about 25 g each (roughly 1 tbsp). Set aside. Dust your work surface and hands generously with katakuriko. Divide the mochi into 8–10 equal portions with a bench scraper or oiled scissors. Flatten each piece into a disc 7–8 cm across using floured fingertips or a rolling pin. Place a bean paste ball in the centre, gather the edges of the mochi disc up around it, and pinch firmly to seal the seam.
Visual cue: Smooth, plump mochi balls with no visible seam. The skin is thin but unbroken, the filling completely enclosed.
Underdone: Mochi skin is too thick or uneven, or seam has opened leaving the filling exposed. Re-seal the seam by pinching firmly; roll gently between cupped palms to redistribute the skin.
Perfect: The skin is uniformly thin (about 3 mm), the ball feels firm and springy, the seam is tight and invisible. The bean paste can just be felt as a gentle resistance when pressed. Place seam-down on dusted parchment. Dust the tops lightly with additional katakuriko.
Overdone: Mochi has been overworked, is sticky despite the flour, and the skin is tearing or the filling is visible. Chill hands briefly, re-dust with starch, and work more quickly on the remaining pieces.
Feel cue: A properly wrapped daifuku feels like pressing a firm stress ball — the mochi skin taut, the filling giving just slightly at the centre.

Rest the completed daifuku at room temperature for 20–30 minutes to allow the surface to dry slightly and the filling to settle. Do not refrigerate — cold hardens mochi to an unpleasant rubbery stiffness. Serve within 8 hours of making; mochi stales quickly at room temperature.
Visual cue: Soft, rounded spheres with a dry, matte surface free of cracks. A slight translucency at the thinnest points of the skin.
Underdone: Surface is still wet and sticky to touch, transferring starch to everything it contacts. Dust more liberally with katakuriko and rest for another 10 minutes.
Perfect: Dry to the touch, soft when pressed, springs back slowly. The dusting starch gives a clean, professional-looking white bloom. Serve immediately or within 8 hours.
Overdone: Left too long at room temperature — surface has developed fine cracks and the skin feels tough. Consume immediately; even slightly stale mochi can be toasted briefly over a gas flame to restore chewiness.
Feel cue: The finished daifuku should bounce back when pressed — a soft, decisive rebound. If it stays dented, the filling has shifted or the mochi is too cold.
