ingredients.name: Floury potatoes (Russet or Maris Piper, peeled)
Garlic cloves (1 halved for rubbing, 2 minced)
Unsalted butter (for the dish and dotting)

steps:
Peel the potatoes. Using a mandoline set to 2–3mm, slice each potato into uniform thin rounds. Do not rinse the sliced potato — the surface starch is what causes the cream to thicken and bind the gratin as it bakes. Place slices in a bowl as you work. The mandoline setting is not a suggestion: 4mm slices will still be firm in the center when the top is golden; 1mm slices will dissolve entirely.
Visual cue: A pile of translucent, paper-thin rounds, uniform in thickness, slightly gummy to the touch from surface starch.
Underdone: Slices are thick and uneven — some 4–5mm, some thinner. Will not cook evenly. Use a mandoline consistently set at 2–3mm. Inconsistent slices create a gratin with crunchy pockets inside a soft matrix.
Perfect: Uniformly thin, semi-translucent. When held to the light you can nearly see through them. Slightly sticky on the surface. Season the slices and build the gratin immediately.
Overdone: Sliced so thin the rounds are tearing and fragmenting. Adjust mandoline slightly thicker. Fragmented potato is harder to layer cleanly but still perfectly edible.
Feel cue: The sliced potatoes should feel like pages of a heavy book between your fingers — thin but not fragile, with a slight tackiness from the starch that makes them cling together slightly when stacked.

In a wide saucepan, combine the cream, milk, minced garlic, salt, pepper, and a generous grating of nutmeg. Bring to a bare simmer over medium-low heat, stirring to dissolve the salt. Taste the cream — it should taste slightly overseasoned because the potato will absorb salt significantly. Do not boil. Remove from heat and set aside.
Visual cue: Cream is steaming and at a bare simmer — small bubbles appearing at the edges, not a rolling boil. The garlic is fragrant.
Underdone: Cream is barely warmed. Salt has not fully dissolved. Garlic aroma is raw. Continue warming gently. The cream must be hot when it goes into the dish to ensure even cooking.
Perfect: Steaming, at a bare simmer, garlic fragrant and beginning to turn translucent. Cream is well-seasoned throughout. Use immediately or hold at a low simmer.
Overdone: Cream has come to a full boil and is beginning to reduce. The fat is starting to separate. Remove from heat immediately. Stir well to re-emulsify and add a splash of cold milk to bring the temperature down.
Feel cue: Dip a clean finger into the cream — it should feel distinctly hot, thin but coating, and intensely flavored. The seasoning should make your eyes slightly widen — it needs to be boldly seasoned to season the potato.

Preheat oven to 160°C (320°F). Rub a baking dish generously with the halved garlic clove, then butter it liberally. Layer potato slices evenly across the bottom, overlapping like scales. Season the layer lightly. Continue layering and seasoning until all the potato is used. Pour the hot cream mixture over the top — it should come about two-thirds up the depth of the potato. Dot with butter.
Visual cue: Neat, overlapping rows of potato, uniformly cream-submerged to two-thirds depth, with butter dots glistening on the surface.
Underdone: Potatoes are haphazardly piled rather than layered. Cream is well below or well above the two-thirds mark. Even layers ensure uniform cooking. Press down gently to flatten the top and distribute cream if needed.
Perfect: Clean overlapping layers, cream visible at the sides, butter evenly distributed. The dish looks promising. Place in the oven immediately.
Overdone: Cream fills to the very top — will overflow in the oven. Remove some cream with a ladle. The baking dish needs headspace for the bubbling expansion.
Feel cue: Press down on the assembled gratin with the flat of your hand — the potato layers should compact slightly and cream should well up around your hand. The dish should feel substantial and dense.

Bake at 160°C (320°F) for 60–75 minutes. For the first 45 minutes, do not open the oven — the potato is slowly absorbing the cream and the starch is thickening the matrix. At 45 minutes, increase heat to 190°C (375°F) and bake another 15–20 minutes until the top is deeply golden-brown and bubbling at the edges. Test doneness by inserting a thin knife into the center — it should slide through with zero resistance.
Visual cue: Top is deeply golden-brown, almost caramelized in patches. The cream is visibly bubbling and thickened at the edges. The surface has a slight skin with dark gold patches.
Underdone: Top is pale gold, cream is still liquid and thin at the edges. Knife meets resistance at the center. Continue baking. Cover loosely with foil if the top is coloring too fast while the interior finishes.
Perfect: Deep golden-brown, bubbling, knife slides in like butter. The whole dish trembles slightly when the rack is nudged — the cream has set to a silky, stable gel. Remove from oven. Rest 15 minutes before serving.
Overdone: Top is very dark brown to black in patches. Edges have dried and shrunk from the dish sides. Smell of scorched cream. Cover with foil immediately and remove from oven. The interior is likely fine — remove the darkest top layer before serving.
Feel cue: After baking, nudge the dish gently — the gratin should tremble like set gelatin, not slosh like liquid. That tremor means the cream has fully absorbed into the potato starch and set into the classic silky texture.

Allow the gratin to rest at room temperature for 15–20 minutes before serving. This rest period allows the cream matrix to firm up enough to slice cleanly. Serve in portions using a wide spatula, lifting from the bottom. The gratin reheats beautifully the next day — covered with foil at 160°C for 20 minutes.
Visual cue: When cut, the gratin holds its shape as a clean slice with visible layers. The cream matrix is set — no liquid pooling on the plate.
Underdone: Cut immediately from the oven, the gratin slumps and cream floods the plate. Structure has not set. Rest longer. 20 minutes minimum — the cream matrix needs time to firm after the heat is removed.
Perfect: Clean slice with distinct layers visible. Cream is set to a silky, not runny, consistency. Top crust is intact and golden. Serve alongside roast meat, or simply with a green salad.
Overdone: Rested too long and cooled completely. Cream has set very firm and the gratin has dried out at the edges. Reheat covered at 160°C for 15 minutes with a splash of cream added around the edges.
Feel cue: The serving spatula should slide cleanly beneath a slice and the slice should hold together without crumbling — a test of whether the cream has properly thickened and set. The interior should feel soft and yielding when pressed, like a firm custard.

name: Scandinavian Gravlax
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。

  Alternatives: sea trout fillet; Arctic char

  Alternatives: kosher salt

  Alternatives: light brown sugar (adds depth)

  Alternatives: black pepper

  Alternatives: gin (adds botanical note)
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 48 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Salmon cured raw in equal parts salt and sugar with masses of fresh dill — no heat, no smoke, just chemistry and time turning the flesh translucent and silken over two days.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Coarse sea salt (not table salt, not iodised)
Fresh dill, large bunch, roughly torn

steps:
Combine the coarse salt, sugar, and cracked white pepper in a small bowl. Stir together until evenly mixed. The ratio of salt to sugar should be 1:1 by weight — this is not negotiable. More salt produces a firmer, saltier cure; more sugar keeps the flesh softer but can make it cloying. Taste a pinch: it should be distinctly salty with a backing sweetness.
Visual cue: A uniform sandy mixture of equal white crystals — no visible separation of salt and sugar layers.
Underdone: Salt and sugar are still in visible separate piles or layers in the bowl. Mix more thoroughly. An uneven cure will create saltier patches and under-cured patches across the fish.
Perfect: Uniformly blended pale mixture — the two are indistinguishable by eye. Smells clean with a faint peppered sharpness. Proceed to curing immediately.
Overdone: You have added too much pepper and the ratio is visibly off — the mixture looks grey rather than white. Add more salt and sugar in equal measure to bring the pepper ratio back in balance.
Feel cue: Pinch the cure — it should feel like coarse sea sand between your fingers, the two crystals distinguishable only by feel, not by sight.

Lay a double sheet of cling film on a large tray. Scatter half the curing mixture in the centre in the shape of the fillet. Lay the salmon skin-side down on the cure. Drizzle the aquavit or vodka over the flesh if using. Press the remaining cure firmly onto every centimetre of the flesh side — the belly flaps and the thin tail end will cure faster than the thick centre, so use less cure there. Pile the dill in a thick, fragrant mass covering the entire flesh surface. Wrap the whole package tightly in the cling film, then again in a second layer.
Visual cue: A firmly wrapped parcel with the fish completely enclosed, green dill visible through the cling film, cure visible against the skin beneath.
Underdone: Cure is only on one side of the fish. Dill is sparse and covers less than half the flesh. Package is loosely wrapped with air pockets. Unwrap and redistribute the cure to coat all flesh surfaces. Pack the dill more generously and wrap tightly — air in the package allows uneven curing.
Perfect: Salmon completely sealed in two tight layers of cling film. Cure visible coating both the skin and the flesh (through the bottom layer). Dill densely packed against the flesh, bright green. Transfer to a rimmed tray, place a heavy pan or books on top, and refrigerate.
Overdone: Cure has been applied so thickly (more than 5 mm deep all over) that the surface will over-cure and turn unpleasantly hard and salty. Scrape off the excess, leaving a thin, even coating no thicker than a knuckle.
Feel cue: The wrapped parcel should feel firm and cold — as dense and compact as a wrapped cheese. No sloshing or air movement inside.

Place the wrapped salmon on a rimmed tray in the refrigerator. Set a heavy weight directly on top — a cast iron pan, heavy books, or a brick. The weight presses the curing liquid back into the flesh rather than letting it pool below. After 24 hours, flip the entire package over. After 48 hours total, the gravlax is ready. The cure can safely stretch to 60 hours for a firmer, saltier result, or be stopped at 36 hours for a more delicate texture.
Visual cue: At 48 hours: the flesh has changed from translucent deep-pink to a darker, slightly waxy, opaque-at-the-surface salmon-coral. The skin is rigid and shrunken.
Underdone: At 24 hours: flesh is still bright pink and raw-looking when unwrapped. The surface feels yielding and almost raw. Cure liquid is pooling but hasn't been re-absorbed. Re-wrap, flip, re-weight, and return for another 24 hours. Under-cured gravlax is raw salmon with salt on it — not the same thing.
Perfect: At 48 hours: flesh surface looks slightly glossy and darker, as if lacquered. The texture when pressed with a finger is firmer than raw — it resists the finger before springing back slowly. Smells intensely of dill and sweet brine. Unwrap, scrape off the cure and dill, pat dry, and slice immediately or refrigerate uncovered for 30 minutes to dry the surface further before slicing.
Overdone: At 72+ hours: flesh surface is quite firm, almost hard. The cure has drawn out a great deal of moisture. Colour is quite dark and the smell is intensely salty. The gravlax is still edible but will slice very thin and taste quite salt-forward. Serve with generous blini, crème fraîche, and something acidic to balance.
Feel cue: Press the flesh at the thickest point with one finger — at 24 hours it still feels almost raw; at 48 hours it should feel like firm, cold rubber, springing back slowly.

Scrape off all the dill and cure with the back of a knife and discard. Pat the flesh completely dry with paper towels. Place skin-side down. Using a long, thin, sharp knife (a carving knife or salmon slicer), angle the blade at 45 degrees and slice as thinly as possible — 2–3 mm at most — in long strokes, separating each slice from the skin. Work from the tail to the head. The slices should be almost translucent. Arrange overlapping on a cold plate and serve within 30 minutes of slicing.
Visual cue: Near-translucent paper-thin slices of deep coral-pink salmon, draped slightly to show their length and silken texture.
Underdone: Slices are too thick (5 mm or more) and look like raw salmon chunks rather than translucent sheets. The cure has not penetrated these thick slices evenly. Angle the knife lower to the fish (more horizontal) and use long, smooth strokes rather than short chopping ones.
Perfect: Slices are 2–3 mm thick, visibly translucent at the edges, holding together without tearing. Deep coral with darker edges where the cure concentrated. Surface is silken and glistening. Arrange immediately — slices begin to dry out within 20 minutes at room temperature.
Overdone: Slices are so thin they tear apart on the knife or fall to pieces. Alternatively, the knife is dragging rather than slicing cleanly and the slices are ragged. Ensure your knife is very sharp and make long, confident strokes without sawing. A sharp knife cuts; a dull one tears.
Feel cue: Lift a slice with a palette knife and it should drape over the blade like a sheet of fine silk — holding together yet clearly delicate enough to melt on the tongue.

ingredients.name: Fine sea salt and freshly ground black pepper

steps:
Preheat the oven to 180°C (350°F). In a large roasting dish or oven-safe skillet, layer the potato slices across the bottom. Add the onion rings, tomato slices, and garlic over the top. Season generously with salt and pepper. Pour 60ml of olive oil and the white wine over the vegetables. Add the thyme sprigs. Bake for 25 minutes until the potatoes have begun to soften and the tomatoes are beginning to collapse. The preliminary bake ensures the potatoes are cooked through — they need more time than the fish.
Visual cue: Potatoes are semi-tender and the tomatoes have collapsed, releasing their juices into a fragrant, wine-scented base.
Underdone: Potatoes are still firm and raw at the center; tomatoes barely softened. Continue baking for 10 more minutes before adding the fish.
Perfect: Potatoes yield to a knife tip but hold their shape. Tomatoes are collapsing and juicy. Onions are translucent and soft. Lay the scored fish on top of the vegetable bed.
Overdone: Potatoes are very soft and the tomato juices have reduced to a dry, concentrated layer. Add 100ml of hot water before placing the fish to restore moisture.
Feel cue: The vegetable bed should smell of baking wine and tomato — sweet, acidic, and warm — filling the kitchen before the fish even arrives.

Score the fish 3 times on each side. Season inside and out with salt and pepper. Stuff the cavity with parsley, lemon rounds, and a drizzle of olive oil. Lay the fish on top of the partially cooked vegetable bed. Drizzle the remaining olive oil over the fish. Arrange the remaining lemon rounds on top. Return to the oven for 30–35 minutes until the fish is cooked through. Spoon the pan juices over the fish twice during cooking.
Visual cue: Fish skin is golden and slightly blistered; score cuts have opened and reveal opaque, white flesh. Pan juices are bubbling around the fish.
Underdone: Score cuts are still closed; flesh inside the body cavity looks translucent pink. Return for 10 more minutes. Test with a skewer at the thickest point — it should pass through without resistance.
Perfect: Skin is golden with lightly blistered patches. Score cuts gape open with white, opaque flesh. The fish lifts cleanly from the backbone when tested with a spoon. Rest 5 minutes and serve directly from the roasting dish.
Overdone: Fish is pulling away from the bones spontaneously; flesh looks dry at the surface. Serve immediately with extra pan juices ladled over to restore moisture.
Feel cue: The fish is done when you can slide a fork into the thickest score cut and feel it yield completely with no resistance — like pushing through warm butter.

Bring the entire roasting dish to the table — this is the way plaki is served. Scatter fresh parsley over the top. Each person takes a portion of fish and a spoonful of the vegetables and fragrant pan juices beneath. Serve with crusty bread to mop up the juices.
Visual cue: Golden fish resting on a bed of collapsed tomatoes and tender potatoes, with a pool of olive oil and tomato juices surrounding it all.
Underdone: Juices are thin and watery; the dish looks unfinished and underdressed. Return to a 200°C oven for 5 minutes uncovered to concentrate the pan juices.
Perfect: Pan juices are a deep, brick-orange color and slightly thick — a natural sauce. Fish is golden, vegetables are tender and glossy. Serve directly at the table.
Overdone: Pan juices have dried completely; the vegetables are sticking to the pan. Add a splash of warm water, scrape up the fond, and pour over the fish as a sauce.
Feel cue: The pan juices should taste simultaneously of olive oil, tomato sweetness, white wine acidity, and the clean mineral note of the sea bass — a simple but complete sauce that needs nothing added.

name: Galaktoboureko
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Whole milk: 1000 ml
Fine semolina: 120 g
Caster sugar (for custard): 180 g
Eggs: 4 pieces
Unsalted butter (for custard): 30 g
Pure vanilla extract: 8 ml
  Alternatives: vanilla bean seeds from 1 pod
Filo pastry sheets: 400 g
Unsalted butter, melted (for filo): 150 g
  Alternatives: clarified butter
Sugar (for syrup): 300 g
Water (for syrup): 200 ml
Lemon peel strip: 1 piece
Fresh lemon juice: 15 ml
Active time: 1 hour
Total time: 2 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Shatteringly crisp filo leaves encasing a thick, trembling vanilla semolina custard, drenched at the moment of emergence from the oven with cold lemon-scented syrup so it hisses and absorbs.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine the sugar, water, and lemon peel strip in a saucepan. Heat over medium, stirring only to dissolve the sugar. Once boiling, stop stirring and cook for 8-10 minutes until slightly syrupy. Remove the lemon peel, add the lemon juice, cook 1 minute more. Remove from heat and cool to room temperature. This syrup must be cold when it meets the hot pastry — make it first or at least 1 hour ahead.
Visual cue: A clear, pale-golden syrup that coats the back of a spoon. Has a lemon aroma.
Underdone: Watery and thin. No viscosity at all. Runs off a spoon immediately. Cook for 3-5 more minutes. Syrup should be slightly thicker than water.
Perfect: Pale gold and lightly viscous — coats the back of a spoon. Single-thread stage. Smells of lemon and plain sugar. Must be completely cold when used. Remove from heat, cool to room temperature. Refrigerate if needed.
Overdone: Thick, multi-thread stage or beginning to caramelize. Too concentrated. Add 50ml of warm water and stir to thin.
Feel cue: A cooled drop between moistened fingertips should feel barely tacky — slicker than water, less sticky than honey.

Heat the milk in a large, heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium heat until just simmering. Whisk the semolina, sugar, and eggs together thoroughly in a bowl. Slowly pour a ladleful of the hot milk into the egg mixture while whisking constantly (tempering). Pour the tempered egg mixture back into the hot milk, whisking constantly. Cook over medium heat, whisking without stopping, until the mixture thickens dramatically — it should pull away from the sides of the pan and hold a shape when a spoon is drawn through it, about 8-10 minutes. Remove from heat, stir in butter and vanilla. Immediately cover the surface with plastic wrap touching the custard to prevent a skin.
Visual cue: A thick, smooth, glossy custard that holds a clear trail when a spoon is drawn through and falls from the spoon in heavy, slow dollops.
Underdone: Thin and pourable like béchamel. Flows freely and runs off a spoon. Will make the filo soggy rather than setting inside. Return to medium heat and whisk constantly until the mixture visibly thickens and begins to pull from the pan sides.
Perfect: Very thick, glossy custard. A spoon dragged through leaves a clear trail that holds. Falls in heavy dollops. Surface steams and bubbles have disappeared. Smells of vanilla and warm milk. Cover immediately with plastic wrap touching the surface. Allow to cool for 10 minutes before using.
Overdone: Custard is seizing and beginning to dry out, pulling from the pan in solid sheets. Egg scrambling smell. Remove from heat immediately and whisk vigorously with 2 tbsp of warm milk to smooth out. If lumpy, strain through a sieve.
Feel cue: The finished custard should feel heavy in the pan — when you lift it with a spoon and let it fall back, it should take a full 2 seconds to slide off.

Preheat oven to 180°C (350°F). Butter a 30x20cm baking pan generously. Layer 8-10 sheets of filo in the base, brushing each sheet generously with melted butter before adding the next — including the very first sheet on the pan bottom. Let the edges hang over the sides. Pour the warm custard over the filo base and spread evenly. Fold the overhanging filo edges over the custard. Layer the remaining 8-10 filo sheets on top, again brushing each layer generously with butter. Tuck the edges down into the sides of the pan. Brush the top layer very generously with remaining butter. Score the top layers (not all the way through to the custard) in diamond or square shapes with a sharp knife.
Visual cue: A well-buttered, multi-layered pastry case with an even layer of thick custard visible at the cut sides. Top layer is smooth and thoroughly buttered.
Underdone: Filo sheets are dry in places — white, unbuttered patches visible on several sheets. Custard is very hot and has melted several layers. Butter all uncoated areas now, before baking. Let the custard cool more before assembly next time.
Perfect: Every filo layer glistens with butter. No dry white patches. Custard is evenly distributed. Top is uniformly coated and the score marks are clean. The whole thing smells of warm butter. Bake immediately.
Overdone: Filo has been over-handled, tearing and bunching. Layers are wrinkled and inconsistent. Proceed to bake — torn filo will still crisp. The result may not look perfect but will taste correct.
Feel cue: Each filo layer should feel slippery and well-coated when you place the next sheet — if any sheet feels dry or rough under your fingertips, add more butter.

Bake at 180°C for 45-55 minutes until the top is deeply golden and the filo is crisp all over. The custard filling will have puffed slightly and the pastry will be blistered and golden at the scored edges.
Visual cue: An evenly deep-golden, blistered filo top with visible score marks and lightly darker edges.
Underdone: Pale golden, soft filo that gives when pressed. Custard still visibly jiggly inside. Baking not complete. Bake for another 10 minutes. The top must be genuinely crisp and golden to handle the syrup.
Perfect: Deep golden-brown filo with flaky, blistered layers. Score marks are clearly visible. Edges are slightly darker. The custard below has set — the pan does not wobble liquid. Remove from oven. Immediately pour the cold syrup over the hot pastry.
Overdone: Very dark edges approaching burnt. Top filo is very rigid and crumbly. Remove at once and pour syrup to prevent further drying. Trim the darkest edges before serving.
Feel cue: The filo top should sound hollow when tapped with a knuckle — a dry, crackling sound that signals all moisture has been expelled from the pastry.

This is the defining moment. The pastry must be smoking hot and the syrup must be completely cold. Pour the cold syrup evenly and slowly over the entire surface of the just-from-the-oven galaktoboureko. The pastry will hiss, steam, and splutter — this is correct. Pour along the score marks first, then over the entire surface. Use all the syrup. Allow to rest for at least 45 minutes before cutting — the syrup needs time to penetrate the layers and the custard needs time to set firmly enough to slice.
Visual cue: A glistening, syrup-drenched pastry that has absorbed the liquid without becoming soggy. Score lines are defined. Surface is glossy.
Underdone: Syrup is pooling on the surface and running down the sides without absorbing. Too much syrup applied too fast. Slow the pour. Allow each ladleful to absorb before adding the next.
Perfect: Surface is uniformly glossy and glistening. No pools of syrup. The score lines have absorbed the syrup deeply and look darker. The aroma is of lemon, butter, and warm vanilla custard. Rest for at least 45 minutes. Slice along score marks with a sharp knife.
Overdone: Syrup was applied when the pastry was already cold — it sits on the surface refusing to absorb. The filo has softened unevenly. Warm the galaktoboureko briefly at 160°C for 10 minutes to help absorption.
Feel cue: After resting, the cut edge should reveal distinct filo layers above a clean-edged custard slab — the syrup has penetrated but not dissolved the pastry.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

ingredients.name: Dried gigantes beans (giant white beans), soaked overnight

steps:
Drain the soaked beans and rinse well. Cover with fresh cold water in a large pot by at least 5 cm. Bring to a boil, skim off any white foam that rises in the first 5 minutes. Reduce to a vigorous simmer and cook for 45 to 60 minutes until the beans are tender but still slightly firm at the center — they will finish in the oven. Drain and reserve.
Visual cue: The beans are plump and creamy white, expanded to roughly double their dry size. They hold their shape but squash easily between two fingers.
Underdone: The beans are still dense and chalky at the center. They resist firm pressure between fingers. Continue boiling — partially cooked beans will never soften fully in the acidic tomato sauce in the oven.
Perfect: Squash completely between two fingers with light pressure. No chalkiness. The skin is intact but relaxed. Drain immediately and proceed to the sauce.
Overdone: The beans are very soft and some skins have split. They are beginning to fall apart. Drain immediately and handle very gently. They will break down more in the oven — the result will be creamier rather than distinct beans.
Feel cue: Press a bean between thumb and index finger — it should yield completely with moderate pressure, leaving a smooth, dense smear. No grit or chalkiness.

Preheat oven to 180 C (350 F). In a large, wide oven-safe pan or skillet, heat half the olive oil over medium heat. Add onion, garlic, and celery. Cook, stirring, for 12 to 15 minutes until everything is very soft, sweet-smelling, and just beginning to turn golden at the edges. Do not rush this step.
Visual cue: Translucent, jammy onion and celery with a hint of gold at the edges. The mixture has shrunk by half and looks glossy.
Underdone: The onion is still opaque and the celery is bright green and crunchy. Raw, pungent smell. More time over medium heat — raw alliums will make the sauce taste harsh and sharp, not sweet and mellow.
Perfect: All three vegetables are completely limp, sweet-smelling, and slightly golden. The mixture looks like a soft, fragrant pile. Celery has lost its bright green, turning a muted jade. Add tomato paste to pinch.
Overdone: The onion is deeply caramelized and brown. The garlic has begun to crisp. Proceed — the extra caramelization will make the sauce sweeter and richer. Just watch the garlic.
Feel cue: Drag a wooden spoon through the soffritto — it should move easily like a soft paste, leaving a trail that slowly closes. If it resists, cook longer.

Add the tomato paste to the soffritto and stir for 2 minutes until it darkens from bright red to rust-brown (this is pinçage — it mellows the acidity). Add the crushed tomatoes, sugar, salt, pepper, and water or stock. Stir to combine. Simmer for 10 minutes until slightly thickened.
Visual cue: A thick, burgundy-red sauce with visible vegetable pieces. The surface is gently bubbling. The color is darker than raw canned tomatoes.
Underdone: The sauce is bright, thin, and watery. It smells raw and acidic. Simmer more — the sauce needs to concentrate slightly before the beans go in or it will be too liquid in the oven.
Perfect: Deep burgundy, gently thickened, smelling of sweet cooked tomato and celery. Tastes pleasantly sweet-sour, well-seasoned. Add the beans and transfer to the oven.
Overdone: The sauce is very thick and dark, sticking to the pan. Slightly bitter. Add another 100 ml of water, stir, and proceed.
Feel cue: The sauce should coat the back of a spoon in a thin, even layer — not transparent and watery, not so thick it clumps.

Gently fold the parboiled beans into the tomato sauce in the pan. Drizzle the remaining olive oil over the top. Transfer to the preheated oven uncovered. Bake for 50 to 60 minutes, turning the beans once at the halfway point, until the sauce is thick and jammy and the top layer of beans has formed a slightly caramelized, darkened crust. Scatter fresh parsley over the top just before serving.
Visual cue: A pan of glossy, sauce-lacquered beans with some split skins and caramelized tops. The sauce is visibly thick and barely pourable — it clings to each bean. Bright green parsley punctuates the surface.
Underdone: The sauce is still loose and watery. The beans look pale and are not absorbing the sauce. The top layer has not caramelized. Return to the oven for another 15 minutes uncovered. The beans need to drink in the sauce.
Perfect: The sauce is thick and jammy, nearly absorbed by the beans. The top layer has a slightly darkened, caramelized crust. The kitchen smells of sweet tomato and olive oil. Each bean is tender throughout, its interior creamy. Scatter parsley and serve warm or at room temperature.
Overdone: The sauce has completely reduced and the beans at the top are dry and crispy. The edges of the pan are dark. Add 100 ml of hot water, stir gently, and return to the oven for 5 minutes with foil over the top.
Feel cue: Pick up a bean and bite it in half — the interior should be creamy and yielding, almost like a dense, savory custard, with no firm or chalky center.

name: Greek Souvlaki
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Pork shoulder, cut into 3cm cubes: 700 g
  Alternatives: pork loin; chicken thigh
Extra-virgin olive oil: 60 ml
Fresh lemon juice: 40 ml
  Alternatives: white wine vinegar
Dried Greek oregano (rigani): 6 g
  Alternatives: Italian oregano (use more)
Garlic cloves, minced: 10 g
Salt and black pepper: 8 g
Fresh thyme sprigs: 4 g
Lemon wedges, for serving: 50 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 8 hours 20 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Pork shoulder cubes soaked overnight in olive oil, lemon, and oregano, then threaded onto skewers and grilled over high heat until the exterior chars and the interior remains tender and juicy — Athenian street food at its most elemental.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Whisk together the olive oil, lemon juice, oregano, minced garlic, thyme, salt, and pepper in a bowl. The emulsion won't hold long but that's fine — it just needs to coat. Add the pork cubes and toss thoroughly. Transfer to a zip-lock bag or sealed container. Marinate in the refrigerator for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight (8–12 hours). The lemon juice will begin to denature the surface protein, which creates a better texture for charring. Beyond 24 hours the acid becomes aggressive and the texture suffers.
Visual cue: Pork cubes coated in a fragrant, golden-green marinade with visible herbs and garlic.
Underdone: After only 1–2 hours the marinade hasn't penetrated. The pork looks pale and the coating is thin. Continue marinating. The minimum for meaningful flavor penetration is 4 hours.
Perfect: After 8–12 hours the pork has taken on a slightly tightened texture and the olive oil has soaked in. The cubes smell strongly of oregano and lemon. Remove from the refrigerator 30 minutes before grilling to take the chill off.
Overdone: After 24+ hours the surface of the pork looks grey and slightly cooked from the acid. Cook immediately and expect the texture to be slightly softer than ideal.
Feel cue: The marinated pork should feel firm but slightly slick with olive oil. If it feels soft and mushy, the acid has gone too far and broken down the protein.

Thread the pork cubes onto metal skewers (or soaked wooden ones), 5–6 pieces per skewer, leaving a small gap between each cube. Heat the grill or grill pan to its highest setting — you want immediate searing, not slow cooking. Grill for 3–4 minutes per side (12–15 minutes total, turning every 3 minutes through all four faces). The goal is char on the exterior while the interior remains just cooked through and moist. Do not cover the grill — you want direct radiant heat, not the steaming effect of a closed lid.
Visual cue: Deep char marks on each face. The exterior edges are darkened and fragrant with scorched oregano.
Underdone: Pale, grey, steamed-looking surface. No char marks. The pork is releasing water rather than caramelizing. Increase heat dramatically. Souvlaki needs violence — not gentle cooking.
Perfect: Bold char marks on each face. Edges are dark and fragrant. When cut, the interior is off-white and juicy, not pink. The oregano and lemon smell is toasted and heady. Remove from grill and rest 2 minutes before serving.
Overdone: Cubes are very dark all over, shrunken significantly. They feel hard when pressed with tongs. Serve immediately with plenty of lemon juice to reintroduce acid and moisture.
Feel cue: Press a cube with your tongs — it should give with moderate resistance, like a firm pillow, not a rock or a sponge. Feel the heat radiating off the char when your hand passes 5cm above the skewer.

Serve the skewers immediately with lemon wedges, warmed pita bread, tzatziki, sliced tomato, and red onion. In the Greek street food tradition, the pork can be slid off the skewer directly into the pita. Squeeze lemon generously at the table — the fresh acid is essential to balance the char.
Visual cue: Deep-charred pork cubes glistening with their own juices, scattered with dried oregano.
Underdone: Pork has sat and is cooling on the skewer. Steam is no longer rising. Return to the grill for 60 seconds per face to reheat.
Perfect: Pork is hot, steaming, fragrant. Char is crisp and audible when bitten. Interior is moist and just cooked through. Serve immediately with lemon.
Overdone: Pork has continued cooking off-heat or sat too long and is now dry. Drizzle with olive oil and lemon to reintroduce moisture before serving.
Feel cue: The souvlaki should smell like a Greek summer: charred meat, scorched oregano, and the bright sting of fresh lemon — all at once.

name: Green Goddess Dressing
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Mayonnaise (good quality, egg-yolk based): 100 parts
  Alternatives: vegan mayo
Sour cream: 60 parts
  Alternatives: full-fat Greek yogurt; crème fraîche
Fresh tarragon leaves: 15 parts
  Alternatives: dried tarragon (use 1 tsp, not a full substitution)
Flat-leaf parsley, leaves and stems: 20 parts
Fresh chives, roughly chopped: 15 parts
  Alternatives: green onion tops
Anchovy fillets in oil, drained: 20 parts
  Alternatives: 1 tsp Worcestershire sauce for a milder umami
Garlic clove: 5 parts
  Alternatives: roasted garlic for a sweeter result
White wine vinegar: 15 parts
  Alternatives: Champagne vinegar
Fresh lemon juice: 15 parts
Fine sea salt: 2 parts
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A 1920s San Francisco blender sauce of mayonnaise, sour cream, anchovy, and a generous fistful of tarragon, chives, and parsley — blended smooth to a vivid, herb-electric green.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Add the tarragon, parsley, chives, anchovy fillets, garlic, white wine vinegar, and lemon juice to a blender. Blend on high for 30–45 seconds until the herbs are completely pulverized and the mixture is smooth. The blend will be intensely green at this point — almost luminous — and the raw garlic and anchovies will have dissolved completely into the herb puree. Scrape down the sides once if needed.
Visual cue: A vivid, electric-green smooth liquid with no visible herb chunks or anchovy pieces — the color of a high-summer garden in blended form.
Underdone: Visible herb pieces still identifiable. The liquid is green but speckled rather than uniformly colored. Anchovy may still be in chunks. Blend for another 20–30 seconds at full speed, stopping to scrape down the jar walls if herbs are clinging.
Perfect: Completely smooth, uniform, vivid green. The color is deep and saturated — brighter than a pesto, more transparent than a puree. The kitchen smells intensely of fresh tarragon and parsley. Add the mayonnaise, sour cream, and salt and blend again briefly.
Overdone: The herb mixture has been blended so long that the friction is heating it slightly, causing the fresh herbs to oxidize and the green to dull slightly toward olive. Proceed immediately. The dairy components added in the next step will cool and stabilize the mixture.
Feel cue: Rub a drop of the herb blend between your fingers — it should feel slightly oily from the herb oils, completely smooth, and leave a vivid green stain on your fingertip.

Add the mayonnaise, sour cream, and salt to the blender with the herb mixture. Blend on high for 20–30 seconds until completely smooth and uniformly colored. The dairy will turn the intense herb green into a lighter, slightly more pastel sage-green. Taste immediately and adjust: more vinegar or lemon juice if it needs brightness, more salt if it tastes flat, more anchovy if the umami backbone is missing. The dressing should be pourable but thick — similar in consistency to a light ranch dressing.
Visual cue: A smooth, uniformly sage-green dressing — lighter and slightly creamier-looking than the pure herb blend, opaque from the mayo and sour cream.
Underdone: The dressing shows swirls of white mayo and cream against the green herb puree — the two have not fully incorporated. The texture is uneven. Blend for another 15 seconds. The mayonnaise emulsion needs a moment to break down and re-emulsify with the herb liquid.
Perfect: Completely smooth, uniform sage-green dressing that flows from the blender jar in a slow, steady pour. The flavor hits with bright herb and acid, followed by creamy richness, followed by a faint umami echo from the anchovy. Refrigerate for at least 15 minutes before serving to let the herb flavors meld and the dressing thicken slightly.
Overdone: The dressing is too thin — the blender has whipped in air and thinned the dairy components. It runs like water rather than pouring like cream. This is hard to fix without adding more mayo. Stir in an additional tablespoon of mayonnaise and whisk by hand to restore body without further thinning.
Feel cue: Dip a finger and coat it lightly — the dressing should cling in a thin, uniform layer that doesn't immediately run. The tarragon should be the most prominent herb flavor on the palate.

Transfer the dressing to a sealed container and refrigerate for a minimum of 15 minutes before serving — ideally 30 minutes. The cold thickens the mayo-sour cream base slightly and allows the raw garlic to mellow and the fresh herbs to release more of their aromatic oils into the surrounding fat. The color will deepen slightly as it rests. Green Goddess can be refrigerated for up to 3 days; the herb flavors actually develop and intensify on day two.
Visual cue: A cold, thickened sage-green dressing that pours in a viscous, unbroken stream and clings generously to greens, vegetables, or a dipped crudité.
Underdone: The dressing is still at room temperature — it pours too thinly, the garlic tastes raw and sharp, and the herbs have not yet fully integrated with the creamy base. Refrigerate for at least 15 minutes. The cold both thickens and harmonizes this dressing in ways that room-temperature resting cannot.
Perfect: Cold, slightly thickened, vivid sage-green. The flavors are harmonious — the tarragon is prominent but balanced by parsley freshness, the anchovy is present as a background depth rather than a fishiness, and the acid is bright and clean. Serve over butter lettuce, romaine, cucumber, or asparagus. It is also excellent as a dip for crudités or a spread for cold chicken sandwiches.
Overdone: The dressing has been refrigerated for more than 24 hours and the fresh herb color has faded from sage-green to olive-grey. The garlic flavor has become dominant. The flavor remains good for up to 3 days, though the color will not recover. Stir in a tablespoon of freshly chopped parsley before serving to restore some brightness.
Feel cue: The chilled dressing should feel cold, thick, and slightly resistant — dragging a spoon through it should require a gentle push, unlike a vinaigrette which flows immediately.

ingredients.name: Green (unripe) papaya, peeled and shredded into matchsticks
Thai bird's eye chilies (2-5, adjust to tolerance)
鱼露（Fish sauce (or soy sauce for vegan)）
Dried shrimp (kung haeng) — optional for Isan style
Long beans or green beans, cut into 3cm pieces

steps:
In a large clay or stone mortar, add chilies and garlic. Pound with the pestle until broken down into a coarse paste — not smooth, but no large chunks. The breaking of the cells releases volatile compounds that make the salad fragrant and permeating. A wooden salad bowl and spoon cannot replicate this; the mortar is not optional.
Visual cue: Garlic and chilies are bruised and broken, releasing oils — you should see a slightly moist, fragrant paste with visible texture.
Underdone: Garlic is still in whole pieces; chilies are cracked but not broken open. Continue pounding — 15-20 firm strikes with the pestle.
Perfect: Coarse paste — garlic mashed to a pulp with some fibrous bits, chilies split and releasing orange-red oil. Smells sharply of raw garlic and chili. Add long beans and tomatoes.
Overdone: Smooth, wet paste with no texture — the garlic bitterness is overextracted. This is fine; the flavors will balance once the dressing is added.
Feel cue: Your eyes should be watering slightly from the volatile chili compounds released into the air — that's the mortar working correctly.

Add long beans and cherry tomatoes to the mortar. Use the pestle to bruise them — press and lightly pound the tomatoes until they release juice, and crack the beans open slightly. Then use a large spoon to toss everything together. The mortar technique simultaneously bruises and dresses — the vegetables should crack open, not disintegrate.
Visual cue: Tomatoes are lightly crushed and releasing red juice; long beans are cracked at intervals but still hold their shape.
Underdone: Tomatoes are intact with no juice released; beans are whole and impermeable — they won't absorb the dressing. Bruise more firmly with the pestle, pressing down rather than striking.
Perfect: Tomatoes are split and juicy, long beans cracked in several places. The bottom of the mortar has a puddle of mixed tomato juice and chili-garlic paste. Add papaya and dressing.
Overdone: Tomatoes are completely mashed into pulp; beans are mushy — texture is lost. Continue with the recipe. The sauce will be thicker and more tomato-forward.
Feel cue: Press a bruised bean between your fingers — it should flex and bend without snapping, meaning it's cracked open but still has structural integrity.

In a small bowl, combine lime juice, fish sauce, and palm sugar. Stir until sugar dissolves. Taste — it should be aggressively sour with a savory backbone and a subtle sweetness. This dressing ratio is a starting point; adjust to your preference before adding to the salad. In Thailand, som tam is adjusted to order at the mortar.
Visual cue: Clear golden dressing with dissolved sugar — no crystals visible.
Underdone: Sugar granules still visible at the bottom of the bowl. Stir more vigorously or warm briefly in the microwave for 5 seconds.
Perfect: Fully dissolved, smooth, bright yellow-gold. Tastes sour-first, savory-second, barely sweet. The lime aroma is vivid. Pour over the papaya.
Overdone: Not applicable for a cold dressing, but if the ratio is wrong — too sweet or too salty — adjust now before adding to the papaya, which is hard to fix once combined. Adjust with more lime juice or fish sauce as needed.
Feel cue: Taste the dressing alone — it should be too much of everything, which is correct, because the green papaya is very neutral and will absorb and temper all the flavors.

Add shredded papaya and dried shrimp to the mortar. Pour dressing over the top. Using both the pestle (lightly) and a large spoon, toss and bruise everything together for 1-2 minutes — simultaneously mixing and pressing to help the papaya absorb the dressing. Taste, adjust, and serve immediately alongside sticky rice.
Visual cue: Papaya strands are glistening with dressing, slightly wilted but still with crunch — vivid white-green against red tomato and orange dried shrimp.
Underdone: Papaya strands are still dry and pale; dressing pools at the bottom of the mortar rather than clinging to the papaya. Continue tossing and lightly pounding for another minute; the papaya needs to be slightly bruised to absorb.
Perfect: Every papaya strand glistens with dressing and has absorbed the lime-sour flavor. Crunch is present but slightly yielded. Colors are vivid. The smell is lime, fish sauce, and chili. Plate and serve immediately.
Overdone: Papaya has wilted to limpness; texture is lost and the salad looks waterlogged. Serve immediately regardless — wilted som tam is still delicious, just softer. Next time, serve faster after mixing.
Feel cue: Grab a pinch of dressed papaya — it should feel cool and crisp with a slight moisture, the papaya releasing a small amount of juice when squeezed but not turning to mush.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

  Alternatives: orange zest (milder); grapefruit zest (bitter)

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Three ingredients, one minute, and the entire register of a braise shifts — Milanese lemon zest, raw garlic and flat-leaf parsley crushed together into a condiment of extraordinary aromatic brightness.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

steps:
Zest the lemon directly onto the chopping board using a Microplane or fine grater — use only the yellow outer layer, never the white pith. Peel and finely mince the garlic to a near-paste. Pick the parsley leaves and chop finely until almost a powder. Combine all three on the board and chop together briefly to marry the elements. The finished gremolata should be finely textured but not a wet paste — individual flecks should be distinct. Use immediately, or refrigerate for up to 1 hour; longer and the garlic becomes acrid and the lemon oils dissipate.
Visual cue: A bright green-flecked mixture with yellow zest threads visible throughout. Finely textured but not homogeneous — each element still identifiable at close inspection.
Underdone: Ingredients chopped too coarsely — large leaf chunks, whole zest strips, visible garlic pieces. Will be unbalanced on the palate. Continue chopping until all three elements are the same fine, even texture.
Perfect: Fine, even, bright green with yellow and white flecks. Smells sharp, citrusy and intensely herbal when a pinch is rubbed between the fingers. Dry enough to scatter, not wet. Scatter directly onto braises, risotto or soup just before serving.
Overdone: Chopped to a wet paste — juices have released and the mixture is weeping green liquid. Use immediately. Over-chopped gremolata oxidises quickly and loses its aromatic brightness.
Feel cue: Rub a small pinch between your fingers and smell — the oils should release in a sharp, multi-layered burst: citrus first, then green herb, then a warm garlic note that follows after a beat.

name: Sauce Gribiche
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Hard-boiled eggs (large): 100 parts
Dijon mustard: 8 parts
  Alternatives: whole-grain mustard
White wine vinegar: 15 parts
  Alternatives: Champagne vinegar
Neutral oil (sunflower or grapeseed): 75 parts
  Alternatives: light olive oil
Capers, rinsed and roughly chopped: 15 parts
  Alternatives: caper berries, sliced thin
Cornichons, finely sliced into rounds: 20 parts
  Alternatives: small dill pickles
Flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped: 10 parts
Fresh tarragon, finely chopped: 5 parts
  Alternatives: dried tarragon (use half)
Fresh chervil, finely chopped: 5 parts
  Alternatives: extra flat-leaf parsley
Fine sea salt: 1 parts
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A cold French sauce built on hard-boiled egg yolks emulsified like a mayonnaise, then tumbled with capers, cornichons, and a tangle of fine herbs — briny, bright, and satisfyingly textured.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Lower eggs gently into boiling water and cook for exactly 11 minutes. Transfer immediately to an ice bath for 5 minutes — this stops carryover cooking and makes peeling easier. Peel under cold running water. Halve each egg and carefully lift the yolks out whole. Set the whites aside on a cutting board. The yolks should be fully set but still waxy in the center, not chalky or crumbly.
Visual cue: Yolk is a uniform pale gold throughout, with no grey-green ring at the edge and no translucent wet center.
Underdone: The yolk has a translucent, jammy orange core that hasn't fully set. The white may still be slightly soft near the yolk. Return eggs to simmering water for 2 more minutes, then plunge back into the ice bath.
Perfect: Yolk is fully set and waxy, pale yellow-gold throughout, with a slightly powdery, almost crumbly exterior when pressed lightly. Proceed to separate and sieve the yolks; chop the whites into rough 5 mm pieces and reserve.
Overdone: Yolk is completely dry and mealy with a telltale grey-green sulfurous ring at the edge. Smells faintly of hard-boiled excess. The sauce will still work, but the emulsion will be slightly grainier. Proceed and whisk vigorously to smooth it out.
Feel cue: Press a peeled egg firmly between thumb and index finger — it should yield without shattering, dense and slightly springy, not spongy or wet-soft inside.

Press the egg yolks through a fine-mesh sieve into a bowl, or mash them very thoroughly with a fork until absolutely no lumps remain — any lump will create a grainy break-point in the emulsion. Add the Dijon mustard and white wine vinegar. Season with salt. Whisk vigorously until the mixture is smooth, thick, and completely homogeneous — it will look like a very stiff, pale-yellow paste.
Visual cue: A smooth, cohesive pale-yellow paste with no visible yolk lumps, thick enough to mound on a spoon without sagging.
Underdone: Lumps of yolk are still visible throughout the paste. The mixture is uneven in color and texture. Pass through the sieve again, or continue mashing and whisking. Lumps will create broken spots in the finished emulsion.
Perfect: Completely smooth, uniform pale-gold paste. It holds its shape on a whisk but drops slowly when the whisk is inverted. No graininess whatsoever. Begin adding oil drop by drop while whisking constantly.
Overdone: Over-whisked before any oil was added — the paste looks thin and wet, as though it has already started to separate. Add a pinch more mustard and a few more drops of vinegar and continue whisking to re-tighten before adding oil.
Feel cue: Run a finger through the paste — it should drag cleanly like thick hummus, leaving a distinct trail with defined edges that hold their shape for several seconds.

Working exactly as for a mayonnaise: begin adding the neutral oil in a thin, steady trickle while whisking constantly. The first 30 ml is critical — add it drop by drop to establish the emulsion. Once the mixture turns thick and opaque and the whisk leaves furrow-marks, you can add the remaining oil in a thin, steady stream. Total whisking time is 3–4 minutes. Do not rush the oil addition.
Visual cue: A thick, creamy, ivory-yellow emulsion that holds stiff peaks on the whisk and doesn't flow when the bowl is tilted — identical in body to a firm mayonnaise.
Underdone: Oil is pooling on the surface or the sauce looks broken — a slick, greasy yellow puddle with white curds. Stop adding oil immediately. Whisk a fresh egg yolk with a pinch of mustard in a clean bowl, then slowly whisk the broken sauce back into it to rescue the emulsion.
Perfect: The emulsion is opaque, creamy, and stiff. When a spoon is drawn through it, the furrow holds clean, sharp edges for several seconds. The base is ready. Fold in the garnishes in the next step.
Overdone: Too much oil added too quickly — the emulsion has become waxy and solid, or it has broken under the weight of excess fat. Whisk in a teaspoon of cold water or vinegar to loosen. If broken, restart with a fresh egg yolk as above.
Feel cue: The resistance on the whisk should build noticeably as the emulsion tightens — by the end it takes real physical effort to drag the whisk through the sauce.

Finely chop the reserved egg whites to a rough 5 mm dice — not a fine mince, you want texture. Using a rubber spatula, fold the chopped egg whites, capers, cornichon rounds, parsley, tarragon, and chervil into the emulsion base. Fold gently with a scooping motion from the bottom of the bowl — you want even distribution without deflating the sauce. Taste and correct: more vinegar if it needs lift, more salt if it tastes flat. Serve at room temperature within an hour of making.
Visual cue: An ivory-cream sauce visibly studded with green herb flecks, white egg pieces, dark caper rounds, and pale cornichon discs — distinctly textured, not smooth.
Underdone: The sauce is uniform and creamy with garnishes barely visible, clumped at the surface rather than distributed throughout the base. Continue folding — make sure the spatula reaches the bottom of the bowl on each stroke. Rotate the bowl as you fold.
Perfect: Every spoonful shows a mosaic of herbs, capers, cornichons, and egg white pieces distributed evenly through the creamy, mustard-scented base. Rest at room temperature for 10 minutes to let the flavors meld before serving alongside poached fish, cold meats, or asparagus.
Overdone: The sauce has been stirred rather than folded — the texture has become homogeneous and paste-like, the egg whites disintegrated into the base. The flavor will be excellent. Serve as-is, or fold in a few extra chopped egg whites to restore textural contrast.
Feel cue: The finished sauce should coat the back of a spoon heavily and hold the herb pieces in suspension — not watery, not stiff, somewhere between a loose mayonnaise and a thick ravigote.

name: Grilled Asparagus with Lemon and Parmesan
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

  Alternatives: thin asparagus (halve the grill time)

Parmesan, shaved: 30 g
  Alternatives: Pecorino Romano; nutritional yeast (vegan)

description: Thick asparagus spears rolled in olive oil and grilled at high heat until the tips blister to a charred, crispy fringe and the stalks take on sweet, smoky char while remaining tender enough to snap cleanly — finished with bright lemon and nutty shaved parmesan.

ingredients.name: Thick asparagus spears, woody ends snapped off

steps:
Bend each asparagus spear gently near the base — it will snap naturally at the point where woody fibre gives way to tender stalk. Discard the woody ends (or use for stock). Toss the spears in olive oil until each one glistens. Season with salt. The asparagus must be dry before you add oil — any water will steam the grill grate and the spears will steam rather than char.
Visual cue: Glistening, evenly-coated asparagus spears with no dry patches. All the same length, arranged neatly.
Underdone: Spears are wet with condensation or unevenly coated — some have oil pooled, others look dry. Pat dry thoroughly and re-toss with oil. Uneven oil means uneven charring.
Perfect: Each spear has a thin, even coat of oil — shiny all over without dripping. Looks like it has been polished. Place immediately onto a very hot grill.
Overdone: Too much oil — the spears are dripping. This will cause flare-ups on the grill. Hold each spear over the bowl and let excess drip back. A thin coat, not a drench.
Feel cue: Rolled in oil, a properly dressed asparagus spear should feel slippery and smooth in your fingers, but not dripping — the oil should form a continuous, barely visible film.

Place spears perpendicular to the grill grates on a very hot grill or ridged cast-iron grill pan (preheated to screaming hot). Grill without moving for 2–3 minutes until char marks develop, then roll 90 degrees and grill a further 2 minutes. The asparagus should show distinct char at the grill marks and the tips should be frizzled and blistered. Total cook time: 4–6 minutes for thick spears.
Visual cue: Distinct dark grill marks perpendicular to the stalk's length. Tips frizzled and charred. Stalk still vivid green between the char marks.
Underdone: Only light yellow grill marks with no char. Asparagus still completely rigid and raw-tasting. Increase heat. The grill must be very hot for asparagus — it cooks quickly and chars even faster.
Perfect: Bold, dark char marks. Tips are frizzled to a near-crisp. The stalk between marks is bright green and yields to gentle pressure with a slight snap. Smells of sweet char. Transfer immediately to a plate and dress.
Overdone: Asparagus is limp and collapse when lifted. The entire surface is charred, not just the grill-mark lines. Smells acrid. Dress quickly with lemon and serve — the flavor underneath the char is still good, and the lemon will brighten it.
Feel cue: Roll an asparagus spear between your thumb and finger at the center of the stalk — a perfect grilled spear will feel firm but bend slightly without snapping, with a slight give that raw asparagus does not have.

Arrange the hot spears on a serving plate. Squeeze lemon juice generously over all of them and zest the lemon directly over the top. Drape shaved parmesan ribbons over the spears while still hot so they soften slightly. Crack fresh black pepper over the top. The acid and salt of the lemon must be applied while the asparagus is still hot enough to absorb it.
Visual cue: Char-marked green asparagus spears topped with translucent parmesan ribbons, glistening with lemon juice, and dusted with black pepper.
Underdone: Underdressed — looks dry and the parmesan hasn't softened at all on the asparagus. Add more lemon juice and let the parmesan sit another minute to soften with the residual heat.
Perfect: Bright, vivid presentation. Parmesan ribbons softened and slightly translucent. Glistening with lemon juice and oil. Char marks visible. Smells bright and nutty. Serve immediately — asparagus cools quickly and loses its vitality.
Overdone: Asparagus has sat too long — it has gone cold and limp, the parmesan hard and unmelted. Re-warm briefly under a hot grill for 1 minute, then redress with fresh lemon and parmesan.
Feel cue: Eat a spear immediately — the contrast between the slight char bitterness of the tip and the bright acid of lemon and the salty, nutty parmesan is the entire point. It should hit in waves: char, lemon, umami.

ingredients.name: Lamb loin chops (2–3 cm thick, frenched)

steps:
Combine the olive oil, smashed garlic, rosemary, thyme, lemon zest, and lemon juice in a shallow dish or zip-lock bag. Add the lamb chops and turn to coat every surface. The olive oil carries the aromatic compounds of the rosemary and garlic into the meat; the lemon juice tenderizes the surface proteins and brightens the finished flavor. Marinate at room temperature for 1–2 hours or refrigerated for up to 8 hours. If refrigerated, bring to room temperature for 30 minutes before grilling — cold meat seizes on contact with heat and cooks unevenly.
Visual cue: Each chop is well-coated in olive oil and scattered with herb flecks and lemon zest. The oil has taken on a faint green tint from the rosemary. The meat looks glossy, not pooled in marinade.
Underdone: Chops are barely coated — oil slides off, herbs have not adhered, and the meat looks dry in patches. Toss more thoroughly and press the herbs against the surface. A zip-lock bag ensures full contact with minimal marinade.
Perfect: Every surface glistens with herbed oil; garlic and rosemary are visibly embedded. The oil smells fragrant from the aromatics releasing their oils. Leave to marinate the full time and remove from marinade before grilling, wiping off excess herbs to prevent burning.
Overdone: Chops have marinated over 12 hours; surfaces look pale and slightly mushy where lemon acid has begun to denature the proteins. Cook them as-is — the flavor is still good but they may not develop as strong a crust. Pat dry aggressively before grilling.
Feel cue: Press the raw chop through the bag: the meat should feel dense and spring back firmly. After marinating, it will feel slightly softer at the very surface — a sign the marinade has penetrated.

Prepare a very hot charcoal or gas grill — you want direct high heat that chars immediately on contact, not medium heat that dries. Wipe the excess marinade and herbs from the chops with paper towels (wet herbs and oil cause flare-ups and bitter char). Season generously with kosher salt on both sides immediately before grilling. Grill the chops 2–3 minutes per side for medium-rare — do not move them during each side. Use tongs to sear the fat cap along the edge for 1 minute. For 2 cm chops, total grill time is 5–7 minutes; for 3 cm, 7–9 minutes. Internal temperature should read 57–60°C / 135–140°F for medium-rare.
Visual cue: Bold crosshatch char marks on both faces, fat cap crisped and amber. The sides show a cooked band 60–70% through the thickness. Internal color is a vivid rose-pink throughout when cut.
Underdone: Grill marks are pale, the exterior feels soft and tacky. The cut interior is red and cool at the center. Return to the grill for another 60–90 seconds per side. Lamb is safe to eat at rare but the texture improves at medium-rare.
Perfect: Bold char marks with a faint orange glow between them. The interior reads 57–60°C. The fat cap is amber and partially rendered. The meat springs back firmly when pressed. Remove to a rack over a plate and tent loosely with foil. Rest for 5 minutes minimum.
Overdone: Interior is uniformly grey-brown when cut, reads above 68°C. The meat has tightened and exuded juices visibly during grilling. Fat cap may be scorched. Slice immediately and serve with extra sauce — dry lamb benefits from a good deal of acid and fat alongside it.
Feel cue: Press the center of a chop with your fingertip: medium-rare lamb should push back with moderate resistance, like pressing the base of your thumb when your hand is relaxed. The surface should sizzle, not steam.

Transfer the chops to a rack set over a plate and tent loosely with foil — not sealed tight, which traps steam and softens the crust. Rest for 5 minutes per 2 cm of thickness. During resting, the muscle fibers relax and the juices redistribute from the center outward; cutting too early sends them flooding onto the board. The internal temperature will rise 2–3°C during rest from carryover cooking.
Visual cue: The foil tent looks damp on the inside from escaping steam. The plate beneath collects 1–2 tablespoons of amber-pink resting juices. The meat looks slightly more uniform in color when cut after resting versus immediately after grilling.
Underdone: Rest time under 3 minutes — the meat releases a rush of red juices when cut and the interior is still very hot at the center. Allow the full rest. Patience here is the difference between good lamb and great lamb.
Perfect: Resting juices collected on the plate are clear amber-pink, not bloody red. Cutting now reveals a uniform rose-pink interior with no hot spot at the center. Collect the resting juices to spoon over the plated chops.
Overdone: Rested too long — more than 15 minutes — and the chops have cooled significantly. The crust has softened. Flash the chops on the grill for 30 seconds per side to reheat the crust. Serve immediately.
Feel cue: Pick up a chop after resting: it should feel heavy and dense, not tight. Press it — it yields more than on the grill and the juices do not spring to the surface.

Arrange the chops on warmed plates, leaning against each other or upright so the charred faces and interior color are visible. Spoon the collected resting juices over them — do not waste a drop. Scatter torn fresh mint leaves over. Serve with grilled flatbread, tzatziki, or a simple salad of tomato and herbs.
Visual cue: Bold char marks, glistening resting juices, vivid rose interior visible at the bone. Mint leaves bright green and fresh against the brown crust.
Underdone: The plate is cold and the resting juices have congealed. Warm the plates in an oven at 80°C / 175°F for 5 minutes before plating. Always plate on warm surfaces.
Perfect: Warm plate, glistening chops, bright garnish. The aroma of char, rosemary, and lamb fat fills the immediate vicinity. Serve at once.
Overdone: Chops have been left plated too long — juices have run off and the crust is soft. Accept the loss and serve anyway. Next time: plate and serve within 2 minutes of resting.
Feel cue: The bone should feel warm in your fingers but not burn them. Lift a chop by the bone — it should feel substantial and weighty, not light and hollow.

ingredients.name: Whole octopus, cleaned (mantle and beak removed)

steps:
Place the cleaned octopus in a pot large enough to hold it comfortably. Add the white wine, bay leaves, celery, garlic, and peppercorns. Cover with cold water — start from cold; this allows the proteins to relax gradually rather than seizing in boiling water. Bring slowly to a simmer over medium heat, then reduce to the lowest possible setting: a barely trembling surface, not a boil. Cover with a tight lid. Cook for 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours depending on size. The collagen in the mantle needs a long, gentle poach to convert to gelatin; a boil will tighten and toughen the flesh irreversibly. Begin checking at 1 hour 30 minutes by piercing the thickest part of a tentacle with a thin knife.
Visual cue: The tentacles have curled and the skin is uniform deep purple; a thin knife slides into the thickest tentacle with no resistance, like warm butter.
Underdone: The knife meets a rubbery resistance at the center of the tentacle. Skin may be patchy between purple and translucent-white. Replace lid and continue poaching, checking every 15 minutes.
Perfect: Knife enters with zero resistance. Tentacle yields when gently tugged from the body. Flesh is evenly purple-mauve with no raw white center. Remove from heat and allow the octopus to cool in its poaching liquid to room temperature — this keeps it moist.
Overdone: Tentacle flesh has pulled away from the sucker rings, which are falling off, and the flesh is mushy or shredding. Remove immediately. Cool and grill quickly — the texture will be soft but flavor excellent. Serve with more lemon to brighten.
Feel cue: Press a tentacle gently between thumb and forefinger — a perfectly poached octopus yields like set panna cotta: slight resistance at the surface, soft and giving inside, never rubbery or springy.

Allow the octopus to cool completely in its poaching liquid. This resting period is not optional — the octopus reabsorbs moisture and the proteins fully relax as the temperature falls. Once at room temperature (about 45 minutes), transfer to a tray and pat the tentacles dry with paper towels. You can refrigerate at this point for up to 24 hours; resting overnight actually improves the texture for grilling, as the surface dries slightly and forms a better crust. If you wish, cut the head from the tentacles and split the tentacle cluster into individual pieces or pairs for easier grilling.
Visual cue: Surface of the octopus is matte-dry, not wet, and the tentacles hold their curled shape without flopping.
Underdone: Octopus is still warm and wet — surface steaming, skin slick with liquid. Allow more cooling time on the tray. Pat dry again just before grilling.
Perfect: Room temperature, dry to the touch, tentacles firm and holding their curl. Skin is intact, uniform deep purple. Brush with olive oil and grill immediately or refrigerate overnight.
Overdone: Over-rested and dried in the open fridge more than 24 hours — skin has begun to tighten and crack, surface chalky. Rehydrate very briefly by dipping in warm poaching liquid for 30 seconds, then pat dry and grill immediately.
Feel cue: The cooled tentacles should feel firm and slightly tacky under your fingers — not wet and slippery, not papery-dry. Like cool, lightly oiled leather.

Heat a charcoal grill or gas grill to its absolute maximum, ideally 270 C (520 F) and above — cast-iron grill grates are preferred for maximum heat retention. Brush the octopus pieces generously with olive oil and season with flaky salt. Place on the hottest part of the grill. Do not move them for the first 2 minutes. You will hear aggressive sizzling and some flaring from the fat — this is correct. After 2 minutes, the tentacles in contact with the grill should be charred with defined grill marks; flip and repeat on the second side. Add the lemon halves to the grill cut-side down alongside. Total grill time: 4–6 minutes. You are not cooking the octopus — it is already cooked. You are creating char, crust, and smoke flavor.
Visual cue: Deep char marks on two sides, sucker rings slightly blackened, a curl of light smoke, and the lemon halves are caramelized and golden on the cut face.
Underdone: Tentacles are still pale purple with no char, grill marks faint or absent. Smells steamed, not grilled. Leave them alone and increase heat. Do not move the pieces — contact time creates crust.
Perfect: Dramatic crosshatch char on two sides, sucker tips blackened, skin blistered and pulling in places. Caramel smoke aroma. Remove from grill and rest 1 minute before dressing.
Overdone: More than half the tentacle surface is blackened, flesh underneath beginning to dry out and shrink. Remove immediately. Trim the most charred tips with scissors — the flavor underneath is still excellent.
Feel cue: When you pick up a grilled tentacle, it should feel firm and slightly resistant at the charred crust but warm and yielding when you squeeze the thicker body — like biting through a well-seared steak.

Transfer the grilled octopus to a warm platter. Immediately dress while still sizzling-hot: drizzle generously with extra-virgin olive oil, squeeze the grilled lemon halves over everything (grilling concentrates and sweetens the juice), scatter the rinsed capers, and tear or roughly chop the flat-leaf parsley leaves over the top. Give the whole thing a final pinch of flaky salt. Eat at once — the contrast of smoky-charred crust against the tender, briny interior exists only for about 5 minutes before the crust softens.
Visual cue: Glistening, oil-sheened tentacles with visible char, bright green parsley, and capers scattered across a pool of olive oil and lemon.
Underdone: Octopus is dressed but cold — the oil is not being absorbed and the lemon is not integrating. Return to the grill for 1 minute each side to reheat before re-dressing.
Perfect: The olive oil is sizzling slightly against the hot flesh, lemon juice hissing, capers and parsley bright and vivid. Aroma is smoky, briny, grassy. Serve immediately on warm plates.
Overdone: Octopus has sat dressed for more than 5 minutes — the crust has softened, caper brine has diluted the lemon, and everything looks steamed. Serve regardless — return to the grill next time and dress at the absolute last moment.
Feel cue: Bite through a tentacle: the very outside should snap and char against your teeth, then give way to tender, yielding flesh that tastes of the sea, smoke, and bright lemon all at once.
