ingredients.name: Whole wheat flour (or half white, half wholemeal)
Cold unsalted butter, cubed (optional, for richness)

steps:
Preheat the oven to 220°C (425°F). In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, baking soda, and salt until evenly combined. If using butter, rub it into the flour using your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs. Work quickly — you do not want the butter to melt from the heat of your hands. The dry mix should be aerated and loose.
Visual cue: A pale, aerated mixture with no clumps of flour or butter visible. If using butter, no pieces larger than a pea remain.
Underdone: Large chunks of butter are still visible. Baking soda is not fully distributed — visible white streaks. Continue rubbing the butter in and whisk the dry ingredients more thoroughly. Undistributed baking soda creates bitter, alkaline pockets in the baked loaf.
Perfect: Flour looks sandy and aerated. Butter (if used) is rubbed in to fine crumbs with no visible chunks. The mixture feels light and flows freely through your fingers. Add the buttermilk immediately — speed matters now. Baking soda activates the moment it contacts acid.
Overdone: The mixture has been worked so long that the butter has melted into the flour from your hand's warmth, forming a paste. Chill the bowl for 5 minutes. The fat in the crumb will not create the same flaky structure but the bread will still rise.
Feel cue: Plunge your fingers into the dry mix — it should feel cool, light, and slightly gritty from the flour particles, like beach sand. If it feels dense and heavy, it needs more aerating.

Make a well in the center of the dry mix. Pour in all the cold buttermilk at once. Using a large fork or your hand held flat like a paddle, stir in large circular motions from the inside out — 15 to 20 strokes maximum. Stop as soon as the dough just comes together. It will be shaggy, rough, and slightly sticky — this is correct. Over-mixing develops gluten and toughens the crumb fatally. The reaction between the soda and buttermilk has already begun.
Visual cue: A rough, shaggy dough that holds together in one mass but looks ragged at the edges. Dry flour streaks may still be visible on the edges — this is acceptable.
Underdone: Dough is still crumbly and will not hold together when picked up. Dry flour pockets remain throughout. Fold 3–4 more times until it just coheres. A splash more buttermilk may be needed if the flour is particularly absorbent.
Perfect: Dough holds together as one rough, lumpy mass. It looks messy but can be lifted from the bowl without falling apart. Bubbles may already be visible from the baking soda reaction. The surface is slightly tacky. Turn onto a floured surface and shape immediately — the leavening is already working.
Overdone: Dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls cleanly away from the bowl. It has been over-mixed and developed gluten. The baking soda has had time to activate and may partially exhaust before baking. Shape and bake immediately. The bread will be chewier and denser than ideal but will still rise.
Feel cue: The dough should feel slightly tacky when you press it with a floured finger — it clings very gently but releases without tearing. If it pulls like elastic, gluten has developed too much. If it crumbles, it needs a little more liquid.

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and shape quickly and gently into a round about 20cm in diameter and 5cm thick — use the minimum number of touches needed. Place on a parchment-lined baking tray. Using a sharp knife or blade, cut a deep cross into the top, nearly all the way through — this allows heat to penetrate the dense interior and is said traditionally to let the fairies out. Dust lightly with flour.
Visual cue: A rough, dome-shaped round with a deep, clean cross cut across the top. The surface is dusted with flour and slightly cracked from the cross.
Underdone: The cross is too shallow — less than 1cm deep. Heat cannot penetrate the center and the interior will remain underbaked. Re-cut the cross more deeply. The knife should go through about 80% of the loaf depth.
Perfect: Cross is cut nearly to the base of the loaf. The four quadrants open slightly from the cut, like a flower about to bloom. The loaf is approximately round and evenly domed. Bake immediately on the center shelf.
Overdone: The loaf has been handled too much during shaping and is now smooth and flat — the dough has over-developed and spread. The baking soda has exhausted further. Bake immediately. Prioritize oven time — speed matters more than perfect shape at this stage.
Feel cue: Pick up the shaped loaf gently — it should feel airy and springy, not dense or heavy. Press the center lightly with a floured finger; it should indent and spring back slowly, a sign the leavening is actively working.

Bake at 220°C (425°F) for 20 minutes. Without opening the oven, reduce the temperature to 200°C (390°F) and bake for a further 20–25 minutes. To test doneness, lift the loaf and tap the base firmly with your knuckle — a fully baked soda bread sounds hollow, like an empty wooden box. If it sounds dense and dull, return to the oven for 5 more minutes base-side up. Cool on a wire rack for at least 20 minutes before cutting.
Visual cue: Deep golden-brown crust all over with the cross spread open. The four quadrants have bloomed out and risen separately. No pale patches remain.
Underdone: Crust is pale gold and the cross has not fully opened. A tap on the base sounds dull and dense, not hollow. Return to the oven at 200°C for 10 more minutes, placing the loaf directly on the oven rack for a crisper base.
Perfect: Even dark golden-brown crust, open cross with each quarter slightly curled outward. The base tap produces a clear, hollow sound — like tapping an overturned ceramic bowl. The aroma is toasted grain and buttermilk tang. Cool on a wire rack. Cutting too early creates a gummy interior — the steam is still finishing the crumb.
Overdone: Crust is very dark brown or cracking. The cross quarters have split all the way and the bread has an almost hard exterior. The base smells slightly of char. The interior is likely still good. Slice off the very darkest crust to reveal the tender crumb beneath. Serve with plenty of butter to compensate.
Feel cue: The tap test is the most reliable: hold the loaf on your palm and knock the center of the base firmly with your knuckle — a baked-through soda bread resonates with a clear, ringing hollow knock. An underbaked loaf thuds flatly like tapping a block of wood.

name: Isicia Omentata
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Beef mince (chuck, 20% fat, coarse-ground): 100 parts
  Alternatives: minced lamb; minced pork
Garum / liquamen (fermented fish sauce): 8 parts
  Alternatives: colatura di alici; Thai nam pla

  Alternatives: sweet white wine; dry vermouth

  Alternatives: long pepper

  Alternatives: pistachios; chopped almonds
Cumin & lovage seed (ground): 1 parts
  Alternatives: celery seed for lovage; caraway
Stale bread soaked in wine (squeezed dry): 10 parts
  Alternatives: fresh breadcrumbs
Caul fat (omentum, rinsed): 15 parts
  Alternatives: thin streaky bacon; extra olive oil
Olive oil (for the pan): 4 parts
  Alternatives: lard
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Rome's answer to the burger, lifted straight from Apicius: minced beef pounded with pepper and pine nuts, soused with salty garum and a splash of wine, then wrapped in lacy caul fat that bastes the patty as it sears into a crisp, savoury shell. Smoky, funky, and unmistakably ancient.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Dry white wine (Roman passum if you have it)
Stale bread soaked in wine (squeezed dry)

steps:
In a dry pan over medium heat, toast the pine nuts until they turn pale gold and smell nutty, 2-3 minutes, shaking constantly. Tip them out, then briefly warm the cracked pepper, cumin and lovage seed in the residual heat just until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Crush the cooled pine nuts coarsely so they keep some bite.
Visual cue: Pine nuts are evenly straw-gold with a few amber edges; the spices smell sharp and warm, with no smoke rising from the pan.
Underdone: Pine nuts are still chalky white and the spices smell flat and raw. Keep toasting and shaking — the nuttiness only blooms once they take on colour.
Perfect: Even gold colour on the nuts, a toasty aroma, spices fragrant and bloomed. Cool slightly, then crush the nuts and move on to the mix.
Overdone: Nuts are dark brown and bitter, spices acrid and starting to smoke. Discard scorched nuts and re-toast a fresh batch; burnt pine nuts will sour the whole patty.
Feel cue: Listen for a faint crackle as the pine nuts heat and breathe in for that buttery, resinous smell — the moment it turns sharp or smoky, they have gone too far.

In a wide bowl, combine the beef mince with the toasted pine nuts and spices, the wine-soaked bread, garum and wine. Work the mixture with your hands for about a minute until the garum is evenly distributed and the meat just begins to feel tacky and cohesive. Do not overwork it into a paste — you want a tender, open crumb, not a dense sausage.
Visual cue: A glossy, evenly flecked forcemeat that holds together when pressed but still shows the texture of the mince and flecks of pine nut.
Underdone: The mix is loose and crumbly, garum pooling at the bottom, and a pinch falls apart instantly. Keep working gently and add a touch more soaked bread until a pinch holds its shape.
Perfect: Cohesive and slightly tacky, seasoning evenly dispersed, the mince still visible and the smell deeply savoury. Divide and shape the patties.
Overdone: The meat has turned smooth and pasty, dense and rubbery, like an over-kneaded sausage. Stop mixing at once; fold in a little more coarse mince to reopen the texture before shaping.
Feel cue: The forcemeat should feel cool, springy and just sticky enough to cling to your fingers — when it starts to smear instead of clump, stop working it.

Divide the forcemeat into 4-6 portions and shape each into a plump patty about 2 cm thick. Lay a piece of caul fat flat, set a patty in the centre, and fold the lacy membrane snugly around it, trimming any excess so it overlaps once on the underside. The caul will melt as it cooks, basting and crisping the surface.
Visual cue: Each patty is sealed in a single translucent layer of caul, the lacy veins of fat visible across a smooth, taut surface with the seam tucked underneath.
Underdone: Caul is bunched in thick folds or gaping open, leaving bare meat exposed. Unwrap and re-lay the caul flat so a single thin layer hugs the whole patty with the seam underneath.
Perfect: A snug, single-layer veil of caul over the entire patty, seam-side down, surface smooth and taut. Rest the wrapped patties seam-side down while the pan heats.
Overdone: Caul wound on in many heavy layers; it will turn gummy and refuse to render. Peel back the excess to a single layer — thick wads of caul stay rubbery and greasy.
Feel cue: Stretch the caul gently between your fingers; it should feel cobwebby and slightly sticky, clinging to itself so the patty stays sealed without any string.

Heat the olive oil in a heavy pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Lay the patties seam-side down and sear undisturbed for 3-4 minutes until a deep crust forms, then flip and cook the second side 3-4 minutes more, until the caul has rendered and crisped and the centre reaches a juicy 60-63°C / 140-145°F. Rest 5 minutes before serving with extra garum on the side.
Visual cue: A glossy mahogany crust where the rendered caul has crisped, juices running clear-amber, and the patty springing back firmly when pressed.
Underdone: Surface is pale and flabby, the caul still white and slippery, and the patty feels soft and squishy. Keep searing without moving it — the caul must fully render and brown before you flip.
Perfect: Deep brown crisp crust, caul melted into a lacquered skin, centre juicy and just firm to the touch. Rest the patties 5 minutes so the juices settle, then serve.
Overdone: Crust is blackening and the patty feels hard and dry, juices gone and the smell scorched. Pull off the heat immediately; serve with a generous spoon of garum and a little wine to bring back moisture.
Feel cue: Press the centre with a fingertip — at the right point it springs back with a gentle resistance, like the pad of your palm below the thumb, and smells of toasted fat and fermented depth.

name: Italian Acqua Pazza
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: fish fillets (reduce time by 5 min)
Extra-virgin olive oil: 80 ml
Cherry tomatoes, halved: 250 g
  Alternatives: datterini tomatoes

Dried peperoncino (red chili flakes): 2 g
  Alternatives: fresh red chili

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Fish poached in 'crazy water' — a bubbling broth of cherry tomatoes, white wine, and olive oil that drives itself to a boil in the pan, perfuming the fish with the sea breeze of the southern Italian coast.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Whole fish (sea bream, snapper, or sea bass), cleaned

steps:
In a wide, lidded skillet or shallow casserole, warm the olive oil over medium heat. Add the bruised garlic and peperoncino and cook gently for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the cherry tomatoes cut-side down and cook for 3 minutes until they begin to blister and collapse. Add the white wine and let it bubble for 1 minute. Add the water or fish stock and the capers. Season with salt. Bring to a vigorous simmer.
Visual cue: A lively, bubbling broth with cherry tomatoes beginning to collapse and release their juice into the wine-oil liquid.
Underdone: Tomatoes are still whole and firm; broth is thin and pale. Insufficient flavor development. Cook 2 more minutes over medium-high heat, pressing the tomatoes gently with a spoon to encourage them to burst.
Perfect: At least half the tomatoes have burst, releasing their juice into the broth. Broth is a light pink-orange color and smells of white wine, tomato, and garlic. Add the fish immediately.
Overdone: All tomatoes have completely dissolved into the broth; it has become too thick and reduced. Add 100ml of water to restore volume before adding the fish.
Feel cue: The broth should bubble vigorously and smell simultaneously of sea, wine, and tomato — a pure distillation of the southern Italian coast.

Score the fish 3 times on each side. Season inside and out. Lower the fish into the simmering broth. Cover the pan and cook over medium heat for 8–10 minutes per 500g of fish. Spoon the broth over the fish every 3 minutes. The fish is cooked when the score cuts have opened and the eye of the fish has turned white and opaque — this is the Neapolitan fisherman's traditional indicator of doneness.
Visual cue: The fish eye is opaque white; score cuts gape open revealing white, cooked flesh; skin has taken on color from the tomato broth.
Underdone: Eye of the fish is still dark and translucent. Score cuts are closed. Flesh inside the body cavity is pink. Cover and continue poaching for 4–5 more minutes.
Perfect: Eye is cloudy-white. Score cuts open fully with opaque white flesh. Skin has absorbed the pink-orange tomato color. Fish lifts easily from the bone. Serve immediately directly from the pan.
Overdone: Fish is pulling away from the bones spontaneously; the flesh looks dry at the tail end. Serve immediately — lift the fish out gently to avoid further toughening in the residual heat.
Feel cue: Press the thick dorsal area of the fish — it should yield completely without any springback, like pressing into room-temperature butter, a sign that the flesh has fully relaxed and cooked through.

Scatter torn fresh parsley leaves over the fish and drizzle a final thread of raw olive oil over the broth. Serve directly from the pan at the table. Provide good crusty bread for the broth — the acqua pazza (crazy water) is the real treasure: a light, herb-bright, tomato-scented essence that should be drunk from the bowl at the end.
Visual cue: Fish in a gleaming pink-orange broth with green parsley, collapsed tomatoes, and the glistening thread of raw olive oil across the surface.
Underdone: Broth is pale and barely flavored; dish looks washed-out and wan. Increase the tomato component or simmer the broth 5 minutes longer before adding fish next time.
Perfect: Vivid pink-orange broth with distinct pools of olive oil, fragrant parsley, and a fish that holds its shape while looking completely yielding. Smells of the sea and summer. Bring to the table immediately.
Overdone: Broth has reduced to a thick sauce rather than a light poaching liquid. Add a splash of hot water and stir; serve without further cooking.
Feel cue: The acqua pazza broth should feel weightless on the spoon — light as water but with a round, saline sweetness from the fish and a clean wine acidity. Nothing heavy, nothing thick.

name: Japanese Cotton Cheesecake
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Full-fat cream cheese (room temp): 250 g
Unsalted butter: 50 g
Whole milk: 100 g
Egg yolks (large): 6 unit
Plain flour (cake flour preferred): 60 g
  Alternatives: plain flour sifted 3 times
Cornflour (cornstarch): 20 g
Egg whites (large, cold): 6 unit
Caster sugar: 130 g
Cream of tartar: 1 g
  Alternatives: 1 tsp lemon juice
Vanilla extract: 5 g
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 3 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A cake that trembles like set custard, its surface burnished to deep amber, its crumb so aerated it yields to a spoon like foam — a soufflé's lightness married to cream cheese's gentle tang, impossibly sustained.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Place cream cheese, butter, and milk in a large heatproof bowl set over a saucepan of barely simmering water (bain-marie). Whisk gently until the cream cheese has melted completely and the mixture is smooth, silky, and uniform — no lumps, no streaks. Remove from heat and cool to 40-45 C before adding yolks. If the mixture is too hot it will scramble the yolks.
Visual cue: A smooth, homogeneous, pale cream-coloured mixture with no lumps, streaks of cream cheese, or separated fat. Silky and uniform in texture.
Underdone: Lumps of un-melted cream cheese remain. Mixture looks curdled or uneven. Continue whisking over the bain-marie. Cold cream cheese takes 5-7 minutes to fully dissolve — patience is required.
Perfect: Perfectly smooth, silky, pale-cream mixture. Flows off the whisk in a smooth, uniform stream with no lumps visible. Cool to 40-45 C by placing the bowl in a bowl of cool water, then add yolks.
Overdone: Mixture is beginning to simmer or shows signs of scorching. It smells of overheated dairy. Remove from heat immediately. The fat in cream cheese can separate if overheated — whisk vigorously and cool fast.
Feel cue: Dip a fingertip into the cooled base — it should feel warm but not hot, around body temperature or slightly above. Smooth as warmed lotion, with no graininess.

Whisk the egg yolks into the cooled cream cheese base one at a time. Sift together the flour and cornflour and fold into the mixture in two additions until completely smooth with no lumps. Add vanilla. The batter should be thick but pourable — like thick pancake batter. Any lumps of flour will show as dense spots in the finished cake.
Visual cue: A pale, smooth, lemon-cream batter with a thick, flowing consistency. When the whisk is lifted, it falls in a thick ribbon that holds on the surface for 2 seconds.
Underdone: Lumps of flour visible in the batter. Mixture looks rough and uneven. Whisk more vigorously and strain through a sieve if lumps persist.
Perfect: Perfectly smooth, thick, pale batter with a glossy sheen from the egg yolks. Ribbons slowly off the whisk. Set aside while you whip the egg whites.
Overdone: Batter has been over-mixed and looks very tight. Or it was mixed while too hot and shows signs of the eggs beginning to cook. Pass through a sieve to smooth and cool in an ice bath if needed.
Feel cue: The yolk batter should feel like thick, cold cream when you run a finger through it — smooth, slightly resistant, and leaving a clean channel that slowly fills back in over 3 seconds.

In a scrupulously clean bowl, whip cold egg whites with cream of tartar at medium speed until foamy. Add the caster sugar gradually while continuing to whip. Increase to medium-high and whip to firm peaks — the meringue should be stiff enough to hold a peak but still smooth and glossy, not dry or grainy. The critical point: do not over-whip. The meringue should be just firm, with a slight curl at the peak tip, not completely rigid.
Visual cue: A glossy, bright-white meringue with firm peaks that hold their shape but have a gentle curl at the very tip — not stiff and straight, not soft and drooping.
Underdone: Peaks are soft and droop over. Meringue has a watery quality and runs off the whisk. Continue whipping. The meringue is not yet stiff enough — fold in too early and the soufflé effect will not develop.
Perfect: Stiff, glossy peaks with a very slight curl at the tip. When you lift the whisk, the peak stands and then the very tip gently curves over. Brilliant white. Fold into the yolk batter immediately in three additions.
Overdone: Meringue looks dry, grainy, and cottage-cheese-like. Peaks are stiff and straight with no gloss. Dry meringue cannot be saved — it will fold in as lumps, ruining the texture. Start again.
Feel cue: Dip a clean finger into the meringue and pull away — the peak left on your finger should hold upright for 2 seconds and then the very tip should droop over gently. It should feel like incredibly smooth, cold, stiff foam.

Add the meringue to the yolk batter in three additions. The first addition: stir in roughly to lighten the batter without concern for preserving air. The second and third additions: fold with a wide rubber spatula, scooping from the base and folding over, rotating the bowl. Stop as soon as no white streaks remain. Pour into a parchment-lined 20 cm round tin. Tap the tin once on the counter to release large bubbles.
Visual cue: A light, airy, pale-cream batter with no white meringue streaks. Noticeably more voluminous and airy than the yolk batter alone — holds a gentle mound in the tin.
Underdone: White meringue streaks are still visible in the batter. One or two more deliberate fold strokes — scoop from the base and fold over.
Perfect: Uniform, airy, light batter. No streaks. The batter has a buoyant, cloud-like quality as it falls from the spatula. Fills the tin with a gentle mound. Place in water bath and bake immediately.
Overdone: Batter is flat and liquid — over-folding has deflated the meringue. The cake will not soufflé. Bake anyway. It will be denser than ideal but still delicious.
Feel cue: When you scoop a spatula of batter and let it fall, it should land with a soft, cushioned sound and barely spread — like spooning a thick, airy cloud.

Wrap the base and sides of the tin tightly in two layers of foil. Place in a deep roasting tray and fill with boiling water to reach halfway up the tin sides (water bath / bain-marie baking). Bake at 160 C (320 F) for 55-65 minutes. The surface should be a deep amber-brown and the cake should tremble as a whole when the tin is gently shaken — not sloshing liquid, but a unified jiggle. Turn the oven off and leave the cake inside with the door ajar for 30 minutes before removing. Cool completely at room temperature before refrigerating overnight.
Visual cue: Deep, even amber-brown dome. When the tin is shaken, the entire cake trembles as a cohesive unit — like watching a very firm jelly. No liquid sloshing at the centre.
Underdone: Centre sloshing as liquid when shaken. Surface is still pale. The batter has not set. Continue baking. Do not open the oven — sudden temperature changes cause cracking and collapse.
Perfect: Deep amber dome, trembles as a cohesive unit, does not slosh. A skewer at the edge comes out clean; a skewer in the centre comes out with a few moist crumbs. Turn off oven, leave the door ajar, and cool gradually inside for 30 minutes.
Overdone: A large crack has appeared across the top and the dome has started to pull away from the sides. Remove from the oven. A crack is cosmetic and does not affect flavour. Dust with icing sugar to disguise it.
Feel cue: After overnight refrigeration, the surface should feel smooth, cool, and lightly springy when pressed very gently — it yields 2 mm under a fingertip and springs back completely. Cutting into it with a clean, hot knife reveals a crumb so fine it looks like compacted cotton.

name: Japanese Curry
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: beef chuck; pork shoulder; firm tofu (vegan)

  Alternatives: shallots

  Alternatives: kabocha squash; carrot + potato

  Alternatives: parsnip
Japanese curry roux blocks (S&B Golden Curry or similar): 12 parts
  Alternatives: homemade roux: 2 tbsp butter + 2 tbsp flour + 2 tsp curry powder
Water or chicken stock: 120 parts
  Alternatives: dashi
Neutral oil: 5 parts
  Alternatives: butter (richer)
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 1 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The most comforting dish in the Japanese home kitchen: golden-brown chicken and sweet potato disappearing into a glossy, deeply spiced sauce that straddles the line between curry and gravy — warming, mildly sweet, and built for bowls of short-grain rice on cold evenings.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: 鸡腿（Chicken thigh, bone-in or boneless (cut into large chunks)）
Japanese curry roux blocks (S&B Golden Curry or similar)

steps:
Heat oil in a large heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Pat chicken dry with paper towels and season generously with salt and pepper. Sear in a single layer, skin-side down if bone-in, for 3-4 minutes without moving until golden-brown. Flip and sear the other side for 2 minutes. Remove and set aside — chicken will not be cooked through at this point. The fond left in the pot is flavor gold.
Visual cue: Chicken pieces are golden-brown on both seared sides with some charred edges. The pot bottom has a layer of brown fond.
Underdone: Chicken is pale yellow-white. No browning has occurred. Fond is minimal or absent. Increase heat and wait. The sear is contributing depth of flavor to the entire curry, not just the chicken.
Perfect: Deep golden-brown on the seared faces, with aromatic fond coating the pot bottom. Smells like roasted chicken. Remove chicken and proceed to the onions immediately before the fond burns.
Overdone: Chicken skin is very dark and the fond has turned black and smells bitter. Deglaze immediately with a splash of water, scraping up what you can. Discard any fully burnt black pieces of fond.
Feel cue: The chicken should release cleanly from the pan when it is ready to flip — if it resists and tears, the sear is not complete and will leave the crust behind.

Reduce heat to medium. Add onions to the same pot with the chicken fond. Cook, stirring regularly, for 12-15 minutes until the onions are deeply golden-brown and have reduced dramatically in volume. This extended caramelization of the onion is the secret to a rich, sweet Japanese curry base. Do not rush this step — pale, underdone onions produce a sharp, raw flavor that does not mellow in the sauce.
Visual cue: Onions have reduced to about one-third their original volume. Color is deep golden-brown, almost amber. No white or pale pieces remaining.
Underdone: Onions are still pale and have only softened slightly. Volume is almost unchanged from raw. Flavor is sharp and raw. Continue cooking. Turn down heat to prevent burning and stir more frequently. Patience here is repaid in the final dish.
Perfect: Deeply amber, jammy, sweet-smelling. Onions stick slightly to the pot. When you drag a spoon through them, they flow back slowly. Add potato and carrot, stir to coat in the onion, and proceed.
Overdone: Onions are dark brown to black and smell bitter. They have stuck firmly to the pot. Deglaze with a small splash of water, scraping up the fond. The slightly bitter notes may add complexity or may be too much depending on how dark.
Feel cue: The kitchen should smell of sweet, toasted onion — that caramel-savory aroma signals the Maillard reaction has run its course and the sugars are fully developed.

Add potato/sweet potato and carrot to the pot. Stir to coat in the caramelized onion. Return the seared chicken. Pour in water or stock, enough to just cover. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Skim any foam that rises. Simmer uncovered for 20-25 minutes until potatoes and carrots are completely tender when pierced with a skewer, and the chicken is cooked through. If using bone-in chicken, the meat should begin to pull away from the bone.
Visual cue: Vegetables are completely tender. Skewer inserts without resistance. Broth is lightly golden and has reduced by about a quarter from the boiling level.
Underdone: Skewer meets resistance in the center of the potato. Broth is still very thin and pale. Chicken may still be pink inside. Continue simmering for 5-10 more minutes and re-test. Potato starch needs full gelatinization before adding roux.
Perfect: Everything is tender. Broth has a slight body from the potato starch leaching into it. Chicken is cooked through. Remove from heat before adding curry roux.
Overdone: Potatoes are beginning to fall apart and dissolve into the broth. Chicken is drying out. Add roux immediately. The dissolved potato will actually thicken the sauce more, which you need to account for.
Feel cue: Dip a spoon into the broth and feel it between your fingers when cool — it should feel slightly slippery from the dissolved starch, not watery like plain water.

Break the curry roux blocks into the pot, distributing them evenly. Stir gently over low heat until the blocks have completely dissolved — about 3-5 minutes. Return to a very gentle simmer, stirring frequently, for 5 more minutes as the starch in the roux thickens the sauce. The curry should be glossy and coat a spoon thickly. Taste and adjust with a little extra soy sauce for saltiness, or grated apple for sweetness. Serve over short-grain white rice with fukujinzuke pickles and tonkatsu sauce on the side.
Visual cue: Curry is thick, glossy, and uniform in color — a deep amber-brown with no visible lumps of roux remaining. It falls from a ladle in a thick, slow stream.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and watery. Pieces of undissolved roux are still visible. Curry smells raw and spicy rather than cooked and rounded. Keep stirring over low heat. Roux lumps need full heat and stirring to dissolve completely.
Perfect: Thick, glossy, uniformly amber-brown. Sauce coats the back of a spoon and the line you draw with your finger through it stays clean. Smells of spice, sweetness, and meat. Serve immediately over rice, or rest for 5 minutes — the flavor improves as it sits.
Overdone: Curry is very thick and begins to stick to the pot bottom. When stirred, it moves as a single mass rather than a flowing sauce. Add hot water or stock, 2 tablespoons at a time, and stir to loosen to the correct consistency.
Feel cue: Japanese curry should have a faintly tacky, almost velvety texture on your tongue — thicker than a broth, thinner than a gravy, with a lingering warmth that builds slowly rather than hitting immediately.

name: Kinpira Gobo (Braised Burdock and Carrot)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Burdock root (gobo), scrubbed, julienned: 200 g
  Alternatives: celery root (celeriac); parsnip
Carrot, peeled, julienned: 100 g
Soy sauce (tamari for gluten-free): 25 ml
Mirin: 25 ml
  Alternatives: 1 tbsp sugar + 1 tbsp water
Sake (or dry sherry): 20 ml
  Alternatives: dry white wine
Toasted sesame oil: 15 ml
Dried red chili flakes (togarashi, optional): 1 g
Toasted sesame seeds: 5 g
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 35 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Julienned burdock root and carrot sautéed in sesame oil and simmered in a sweet soy glaze until each strand is tender but still has the faintest, satisfying resistance — a Japanese comfort side that rewards patience with the knife.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Scrub the burdock root with a stiff brush under cold water — do not peel, the skin carries earthiness and nutrition. Cut into 5cm matchsticks (julienne), approximately 3–4mm square. As you cut, immediately transfer to a bowl of cold water with a splash of rice vinegar or lemon juice to prevent oxidation. Burdock discolors dramatically and quickly when exposed to air — within minutes it will turn from cream to dark brown. Drain and pat dry just before cooking.
Visual cue: Cream-colored, uniform matchsticks submerged in acidulated water. When drained, the color should be pale cream, not grey or brown.
Underdone: Gobo has not been soaked and is already turning brown on the cut surfaces. Soak in acidulated water for 5–10 minutes. Some browning is cosmetic only — the flavor is unaffected.
Perfect: Uniform, pale cream matchsticks of consistent size. After draining, they hold their color. When bent, they have a woody, firm flexibility. Pat dry and proceed to cooking.
Overdone: Gobo has soaked so long that it has become water-logged and soft. Drain and pat very dry. The cooking time will be slightly shorter.
Feel cue: Hold a matchstick of gobo and try to bend it — it should flex significantly before breaking, like a fresh twig. This fibrous resilience is what gives kinpira its characteristic slight resistance even when cooked.

Heat the sesame oil in a wok or medium skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chili flakes and stir for 10 seconds until fragrant. Add the drained, dried burdock matchsticks and the julienned carrot. Stir-fry over high heat for 3–4 minutes, tossing regularly, until the vegetables are beginning to pick up color and the burdock has softened slightly at the surface but is still firm at the center. The sesame oil should smell nutty and toasty.
Visual cue: Burdock strands beginning to turn slightly golden at the edges. Carrot is vivid orange and slightly softened. Both are beginning to glisten from the sesame oil.
Underdone: Vegetables are pale and still very raw. No color from the sesame oil. Increase heat and continue tossing. The sesame oil should be smoking lightly.
Perfect: Burdock has the faintest gold tinge at the edges. Carrot is bright orange. Both are coated in sesame oil and smell nutty and slightly earthy. Add the sake, mirin, and soy sauce.
Overdone: Vegetables are deeply browned and beginning to stick. The sesame oil has burnt. Add the liquids immediately. The browning will add depth to the finished dish.
Feel cue: Listen for a sustained high-pitched sizzle when the vegetables are in the hot sesame oil — if the sound is muted, the pan isn't hot enough.

Add the sake first — it will sizzle and reduce in 30 seconds. Add the mirin and soy sauce. Reduce heat to medium. Toss the vegetables in the glaze, then cook, stirring regularly, for 4–5 minutes until the liquid has reduced to a thin, glossy glaze that coats every strand. The burdock should be tender but with a slight, distinctive resistance at the core — kinpira is never soft. Taste for seasoning — it should be sweet, salty, and faintly earthy.
Visual cue: Each strand of burdock and carrot coated in a thin, mahogany-colored glaze. No pooling liquid — it has all reduced and adhered to the vegetables.
Underdone: Liquid has not yet reduced — the vegetables are swimming in thin soy-mirin. The burdock is still very firm throughout. Continue cooking, tossing regularly. Increase heat slightly to speed the reduction.
Perfect: A glossy, thin glaze coats every strand. The burdock is tender with just a slight bite. The carrot is yielding but still holds its shape. The dish smells of caramelized soy and sesame. Remove from heat. Scatter sesame seeds and serve.
Overdone: The glaze has reduced to a sticky, salty paste. The vegetables are very soft. Add a teaspoon of water and stir to loosen. Remove from heat immediately.
Feel cue: Bite a strand of cooked burdock — it should have a slight resistance, like biting through a firm noodle. If it's completely soft with no push-back, it's overcooked.

Transfer to a small serving dish or bowls. Scatter toasted sesame seeds generously over the top. Serve at room temperature as a banchan alongside rice. Kinpira gobo keeps refrigerated for 3–4 days and actually improves overnight as the glaze penetrates deeper into the burdock.
Visual cue: Mahogany-glazed strands of burdock and orange carrot in a small dish, crowned with white sesame seeds.
Underdone: Dish looks wet and unglazed. Sesame seeds missing. Return to heat for 2 more minutes to reduce. Then garnish.
Perfect: Every strand glossy and well-glazed. The contrast of mahogany burdock and orange carrot is visually striking. Sesame seeds add texture and aroma. Serve.
Overdone: The glaze has thickened and clumped the strands together. Gently separate with chopsticks. A few drops of water stirred through will loosen it.
Feel cue: Lift a serving of kinpira with chopsticks — the strands should separate and fall cleanly, not clump or stick together. Each piece should glisten independently.

name: Japanese Matcha Latte
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Ceremonial-grade matcha powder: 4 g
  Alternatives: culinary-grade matcha (more bitter, brighter green)
Hot water, 70–75°C (NOT boiling): 30 ml
Oat milk, barista-style: 200 ml
  Alternatives: whole dairy milk; almond milk (less foam)
Maple syrup or simple syrup: 8 ml
  Alternatives: honey; agave for vegan
Active time: 8 min
Total time: 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Ceremonial-grade matcha whisked to a frothy jade paste with a few drops of water, then drowned in gently steamed oat milk — grassy, slightly bitter, and warming, with a foam cap that holds the ghost of a chasen whisk pattern.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Sift the matcha powder through a fine strainer directly into a warmed ceramic bowl (chawan) or wide mug — sifting breaks up clumps that will never dissolve once milk is added. Add a splash of the 70–75°C water (about 10 ml) and use a bamboo chasen (matcha whisk) to work the powder into a smooth paste, pressing and working the bristles against the clumps. Once a uniform dark-green paste forms, pour in the rest of the water and whisk in a rapid W or M motion — not circular — for 20–30 seconds until a dense, uniform foam covers the surface and the matcha turns from dark forest green to a bright, cloudy jade.
Visual cue: A vivid jade-green foam covering the entire surface of the bowl, with no dark-green clumps visible and no dry powder at the edges.
Underdone: Dark green clumps float or sit at the bottom. Powder has not fully hydrated. The surface looks matte and streaky. Keep whisking with the W-motion for another 20 seconds, focusing the chasen on any visible clumps.
Perfect: A bright, uniform jade foam covers the entire surface. The matcha below is fully dissolved and deeply colored. Smells grassy and fresh. Pour in the hot oat milk immediately.
Overdone: The foam has collapsed from over-whisking in a circular motion. The matcha looks dark and flat. It is fine to drink — just less visually appealing. Next time use the W-motion and stop when foam forms.
Feel cue: The water temperature matters enormously — above 80°C, the catechins in matcha turn bitter and harsh. At 70–75°C, the whisk releases only sweetness and umami.

Heat the oat milk in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring constantly, until it reaches 60–65°C — steaming, with tiny bubbles appearing around the edges but not boiling. If you have a steam wand, steam to the same temperature. Remove from heat and froth vigorously with a handheld milk frother for 20–30 seconds until the volume increases by one-third and a dense microfoam forms on top. Barista-style oat milk contains extra fats that help it foam — regular oat milk will foam less but still works.
Visual cue: A pale, creamy-white milk with a layer of dense, velvety microfoam on top — fine bubbles, no large gaps, the surface moving slowly when tilted.
Underdone: The milk is warm but unfoamed — it looks like plain warm milk with no texture. Froth with the handheld frother for 20 more seconds.
Perfect: A glossy, thick foam cap that clings to the jug walls. The milk below is steamy and uniform. The foam pours slowly. Pour over the whisked matcha immediately.
Overdone: The milk has boiled — large bubbles and a scorched-milk smell. The foam is thin and watery. Allow to cool slightly and re-froth. Boiled oat milk loses its sweetness and foaming ability.
Feel cue: Well-frothed barista oat milk should feel almost velvet-thick when swirled in the pitcher — heavy and slow-moving, not thin and sloshy.

Add the sweetener to the whisked matcha in the bowl and stir briefly to combine. Hold the matcha bowl or pour it into a warmed mug. Pour the steamed oat milk in a slow, steady stream from a height of about 10 cm, holding back the foam with a spoon until the last moment, then allow the foam to flow over the top. The matcha and milk will swirl together into an ombré of jade and cream. For a layered presentation, pour the milk slowly over the back of a spoon held at the surface to keep them distinct. Serve immediately.
Visual cue: A deep jade-green drink with a cream-white foam cap — ombré where milk and matcha meet, the surface slightly mounded with foam.
Underdone: The matcha and milk haven't integrated — dark green sinks, white foam floats separately with a harsh separation line. Stir gently with a spoon once before drinking. The layers are pretty but meant to be blended.
Perfect: A seamless jade-to-cream gradient with a velvety foam dome. The aroma is grassy and milky. The jade color is vivid and saturated. Serve immediately — matcha oxidizes and dulls quickly.
Overdone: The matcha has sat too long. The surface is dull olive-brown rather than bright jade and the foam has deflated. Stir and add a fresh pinch of sifted matcha on the foam for color, then serve.
Feel cue: The first sip should deliver the vegetal sweetness of matcha and the creamy round body of oat milk simultaneously — not bitter-then-sweet, but unified and smooth from the first taste.

description: A silkier, richer, more intensely umami mayonnaise than its Western cousin — made with egg yolks only, rice vinegar instead of white, a whisper of MSG, and a touch of dashi — pale ivory, voluptuous, and deeply savory.

ingredients.name: 蛋黄（Egg yolks, large (at room temperature)）
食用油（Neutral oil (rice bran or light grapeseed)）

steps:
Ensure your egg yolks are at room temperature — cold yolks resist emulsification and will break more easily when the oil is added. Place the yolks in a medium bowl set on a damp cloth to prevent it sliding. Add the rice vinegar, Dijon mustard, MSG, and salt. Whisk vigorously for 60 seconds until the mixture is pale, slightly thickened, and completely homogenous. The mustard is not just for flavor — it contains lecithin, a natural emulsifier that reinforces the lecithin already in the yolks and gives you more leeway when adding the oil. The preliminary whisking begins to form the emulsion matrix before any oil is added.
Visual cue: A pale yellow, slightly foamy mixture that falls off the whisk in a thick, slow ribbon rather than running off like liquid.
Underdone: Mixture is thin, watery, and still separates when the whisk is lifted — yolks not yet properly beaten. Whisk more vigorously for another 30–45 seconds until the mixture thickens and turns paler.
Perfect: Pale yellow, slightly thickened. Falls from the whisk in a slow, thick ribbon that holds its shape on the surface for a moment before folding back in. Begin adding oil in a very thin, slow stream.
Overdone: Very thick and very foamy — excessively beaten. The emulsion matrix will still work but the mayo will be less smooth. Proceed — the foam will integrate during the oil addition.
Feel cue: Rub a drop of the yolk base between your fingers — it should feel slightly slick and coat your skin in a thin, persistent film, unlike the liquid feel of an unbeaten yolk.

The oil addition is the critical step: the first 25% of the oil must go in extremely slowly or the emulsion will break. Begin by adding the oil drop by drop — literally one drop at a time — while whisking constantly. Continue drop by drop for the first 50–75 ml of oil. As the emulsion establishes and the mixture visibly thickens and turns paler, you can increase to a very thin, steady stream. Once you have added half the oil and the mayonnaise looks thick and stable, you can add the remaining oil in a thin but steady stream, whisking continuously. If at any point the mixture looks glossy, greasy, or starts to pool with oil rather than incorporating, stop adding oil and whisk vigorously for 30 seconds before continuing. If you have a stand mixer or immersion blender, you can add the oil in a thin stream while the machine runs — the constant agitation is equivalent to whisking.
Visual cue: A thick, pale ivory, glossy mayo that clings to the bowl walls and pulls away cleanly from the whisk in thick ribbons.
Underdone: Mayo is still thin and slightly transparent — not enough oil incorporated yet, or it's too cold. Continue adding oil very slowly. The emulsion will thicken as more oil is incorporated.
Perfect: Thick, pale ivory, voluptuous. Clings to the bowl sides. Falls from the whisk in thick, glossy dollops. Holds its shape when a spoon is dragged through it. Add the optional dashi, taste, and adjust seasoning.
Overdone: The emulsion has broken — the mixture looks greasy, curdled, or the oil is pooling on the surface and separating. In a clean bowl, whisk a fresh yolk with a teaspoon of mustard. Then very slowly whisk the broken mixture into the fresh yolk, drop by drop, to re-emulsify.
Feel cue: Drag a spoon through the finished mayo — it should move through with gentle resistance, like a firm cream, and the channel left behind should hold its shape rather than
collapsing immediately back.

Stir in the dashi (if using) — add it a teaspoon at a time, tasting after each addition. The dashi adds a subtle background umami that rounds and deepens the flavor, characteristic of the complexity that makes Kewpie-style mayo so compelling. Taste the finished mayo carefully: it should be rich and deeply savory, with a bright, mild acidity from the rice vinegar (noticeably gentler than Western mayonnaise), and a longer umami finish from the MSG. Adjust with more salt, rice vinegar, or MSG as needed. Transfer to a clean, airtight jar. Japanese-style mayo keeps refrigerated for up to 2 weeks. It can also be transferred to a squeeze bottle for the distinctive Kewpie serving style.
Visual cue: Pale ivory to soft yellow, very thick and glossy, with a slight sheen. Falls from a spoon in a slow, unbroken dollop.
Underdone: Mayo tastes flat, only of oil — not enough acid, salt, or MSG to bring up the flavor. Add rice vinegar a few drops at a time, tasting until the flavor brightens. Add more MSG for umami depth.
Perfect: Rich, voluptuous, mildly tart, deeply savory, with a clean, lingering umami finish. Pale ivory, glossy, and very thick. Transfer to an airtight jar and refrigerate.
Overdone: Too sour or too salty from over-seasoning. Whisk in a small amount of fresh neutral oil to dilute the excess seasoning. Adjust balance accordingly.
Feel cue: Take a small taste on the tip of your finger — the mayo should coat your tongue in a rich film that melts away slowly, leaving a long savory finish rather than immediately disappearing like a thin sauce.

description: Hokkaido shokupan — a pillowy, impossibly soft Japanese white bread built on the tangzhong technique, where a small portion of flour is cooked into a gel that locks moisture into the crumb, resulting in a loaf that tears into cloud-white, gossamer sheets and stays fresh for days.

ingredients.name: Warm whole milk (38 C) for main dough

steps:
Whisk the tangzhong flour with the cold milk in a small saucepan until completely smooth and lump-free. Place over medium-low heat and cook, stirring constantly with a silicone spatula, for 3–5 minutes until the mixture thickens into a thick, glossy, pudding-like paste and a thermometer reads 65 C (150 F). At this temperature the starch granules fully gelatinize, and in this gelatinized state they can absorb and lock in far more water than raw starch — this is the scientific reason shokupan stays softer longer than any other bread. Remove from the heat, press a sheet of plastic wrap directly onto the surface to prevent a skin forming, and cool to room temperature.
Visual cue: A thick, smooth, ivory-white paste that holds a clear trail when the spatula is drawn across the pan bottom and temperature reads 65 C.
Underdone: Still thin and milk-like. No trails form when stirred. Below 60 C. Continue cooking and stirring — the transformation from liquid to gel happens over a narrow temperature window near 65 C, so be patient.
Perfect: Thick and glossy, like a pastry cream without eggs. Holds its shape briefly, then settles slowly. Trail left by spatula closes in 2–3 seconds. 65 C. Press plastic wrap to the surface and cool completely before adding to the dough.
Overdone: Very stiff, gummy, and pulling away from the pan sides in a rubbery lump. Whisk in a teaspoon of milk to loosen, then proceed. The paste is still functional.
Feel cue: Cool tangzhong pressed between two fingers feels smooth, thick, and slightly elastic — not gummy like over-cooked pudding, and not liquid. It should hold a fingerprint briefly before slowly filling back in.

In a stand mixer bowl, combine the bread flour, sugar, salt, and instant yeast (keep salt and yeast on opposite sides of the bowl before mixing). Add the warm milk, egg, and cooled tangzhong. Using the dough hook, mix on low speed for 2 minutes until combined, then increase to medium for 5 minutes. The dough will be shaggy and sticky at first — resist adding extra flour. It will come together as the gluten develops and the tangzhong integrates. After 5 minutes it should begin to pull away from the bowl sides.
Visual cue: Dough that is clinging to the hook and pulling away from the bowl sides, not yet smooth, still somewhat sticky.
Underdone: Dough is splashing around the bowl and not cohering. Flour is not fully incorporated. Let it mix on low speed for 1–2 more minutes before increasing speed.
Perfect: Dough clings to the hook and clears the bowl sides (mostly — some sticking at the bottom is fine). Looks rough and slightly shiny. Begin adding butter in the next step.
Overdone: Already smooth and pulling fully clean before butter is added. Proceed to butter addition — no harm done.
Feel cue: At this stage the dough should feel quite sticky to a finger pressed into it — this is correct and expected. Shokupan is a high-hydration enriched dough and the stickiness will resolve completely once the butter is fully incorporated.

With the mixer running on medium, add the softened butter in small pieces, about 1 tablespoon at a time, waiting for each addition to be fully absorbed before adding the next. This will take 8–10 minutes of mixing in total after the butter is all in. The dough will go through an ugly phase — looking greasy and broken — before it comes back together into a silky, elastic ball that pulls completely clean from the bowl. Increase to medium-high for the final 2 minutes. The windowpane test should be very easy to pass: a small piece stretches to nearly translucent without tearing.
Visual cue: A silky, smooth, ivory-white ball of dough that pulls completely clean from the bowl and the hook. Surface looks almost shiny.
Underdone: Still slightly greasy or breaking apart. Windowpane tears immediately. Continue kneading — the gluten network is not yet strong enough to hold the fat in suspension. Give it 3 more minutes.
Perfect: Silky smooth, springs back quickly, clears the bowl completely, and passes the windowpane test easily. Surface almost looks like skin. Shape into a ball and bulk-ferment.
Overdone: Extremely tight and stiff, no longer tacky at all. Has a slightly rubbery quality. Rest 15 minutes covered and proceed. Over-worked enriched dough still bakes beautifully.
Feel cue: Fully developed milk bread dough is the softest bread dough you will ever handle — it should feel like warm, silky putty, smooth and non-sticky, yielding to pressure like a firm marshmallow.

Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let it rise at room temperature (24–26 C) for 1 to 1.5 hours, until doubled in size. Because of the tangzhong and high butter content this dough rises more slowly than a lean dough. Punching it down once at the halfway point (45 minutes) helps develop a more even, fine crumb by redistributing the yeast and redistributing gas. After the full rise, chill the dough in the refrigerator for 20 minutes to firm it up, which makes the sticky dough much easier to divide and shape cleanly.
Visual cue: Dough has clearly doubled — dome above the bowl rim. Surface is smooth and pillowy. The bowl shakes with a soft jiggle.
Underdone: Less than 50% growth. Dense and firm. Poke fills back immediately. Return to a warmer spot — enriched doughs need warmth and time to overcome the fat's effect on the yeast.
Perfect: Doubled. A two-finger poke fills slowly, halfway. Dough is light and airy. Smells of warm milk and bread. Chill briefly, then divide and shape.
Overdone: More than doubled, surface showing large bubbles. Smells somewhat alcoholic. Punch down, shape, and proceed. Over-fermented milk bread is still very good.
Feel cue: Stick your fist gently into the doubled dough — it should deflate slowly like a punctured tire, giving a soft sigh of gas. Over-fermented dough collapses instantly and flatly; under-fermented dough barely dents.

Divide the chilled dough into 4 equal pieces. Flatten each piece into a rectangle, fold the long sides in toward the center, and roll it into a tight cylinder. Place all 4 cylinders side by side in a greased 9x5 Pullman loaf pan (or a standard loaf pan), seam-side down. For a classic shokupan dome, leave the pan uncovered. For a flat-topped Pullman loaf, slide the lid on. Cover and proof at room temperature for 1 to 1.5 hours, until the dough crests 2 cm above the rim (dome) or fills the Pullman pan 90%.
Visual cue: Four evenly sized rolls filling the pan side by side, domed above the rim after proofing. Surface is smooth and slightly shiny from the egg/cream wash.
Underdone: Rolls haven't crested the rim yet. Dense and tight. Wait another 20–30 minutes. Enriched doughs are slow at the final proof stage.
Perfect: Cresting 2 cm above the rim (or 90% filling the Pullman). Jiggle-jiggly. A poke springs back halfway. Brush with cream and bake.
Overdone: Jelly-like, almost trembling, and extremely soft. Poke doesn't spring back. Bake immediately — wait any longer and the dough will collapse.
Feel cue: Brush the cream or milk onto the proofed surface: it should glide on easily without tearing the delicate skin. The surface should feel almost impossibly soft and light — like touching a baby's cheek.

Brush the proofed loaf with cream or milk for a shiny, deep golden crust. Bake at 180 C (355 F) for 30–35 minutes for a dome loaf, or 35–40 minutes with the Pullman lid on. The loaf is done when the top is a rich, even golden-brown (no pale doughy patches), the internal temperature reads 93–96 C (200–205 F), and the sides pull away from the pan. Remove from the pan immediately and cool completely on a wire rack for at least 1 hour before slicing. The crumb will be dense and gummy if cut hot — it continues to set as it cools.
Visual cue: Even, glossy golden-brown dome. No pale patches. Internal temperature 94 C. When lifted from the pan, sides are golden and the bottom sounds hollow.
Underdone: Pale gold with white patches on the dome or sides. Internal temperature below 90 C. The loaf feels soft and heavy when thumped. Return for 5 more minutes. Tent with foil if top is already dark to finish cooking the interior.
Perfect: Rich, even, deep-golden dome. 94 C internal. Hollow bottom tap. The kitchen smells of warm milk, butter, and caramelized sugar. Cool 1 hour before slicing. Patience here is not optional.
Overdone: Dark brown or cracked dome. Stiff, hard crust. The interior may still be perfect — shokupan's enriched crust toughens quickly when over-baked, but the crumb usually survives.
Feel cue: A cooled shokupan compressed between two palms should spring back completely and almost silently — the tangzhong crumb is so elastic it absorbs the pressure and releases it. Tear off a slice: the crumb should pull apart in long, silky, cotton-candy-like threads, not crumble.

name: Japanese Miso-Glazed Black Cod
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Black cod (sablefish) fillets, skin-on: 600 g
  Alternatives: Chilean sea bass; salmon
White miso paste (shiro miso): 120 g
  Alternatives: yellow miso (slightly less sweet)
Mirin: 60 ml
Sake: 60 ml
  Alternatives: dry sherry
Sugar: 30 g
Pickled ginger (gari): 20 g
Thinly sliced green onion: 10 g
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 72 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Black cod marinated for three days in a sweet white miso paste until the flesh is perfumed to the bone, then broiled until the glaze caramelizes to a shatteringly lacquered surface over butter-soft fish.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

steps:
In a small saucepan, combine the mirin and sake. Bring to a boil over medium heat for 1 minute to cook off the alcohol. Reduce heat to low and whisk in the white miso and sugar until completely smooth. Cook, stirring, for 2–3 minutes until the mixture is glossy and thick. Remove from heat and cool completely to room temperature before using — adding hot marinade to the fish will begin cooking the exterior prematurely.
Visual cue: Smooth, glossy, caramel-tan paste that runs slowly off a spoon in a thick ribbon.
Underdone: Marinade is thin and watery; sugar has not fully dissolved. Continue cooking over low heat for 2 more minutes, whisking constantly.
Perfect: Thick, smooth, glossy paste — the consistency of a thick peanut butter. Deep golden-tan color. Tastes sweet-salty-umami in equal measure. Cool completely before applying to fish.
Overdone: Marinade has scorched on the bottom and smells faintly burnt; miso has caramelized past its ideal. Strain through a fine mesh; the top portion is likely salvageable. Reduce cooking time next batch.
Feel cue: The marinade should feel thick and clingy when rubbed between your fingers — more like a paste than a liquid, with a sweet miso fragrance that is unmistakably Japanese.

Coat each cod fillet generously on all sides with the cooled miso marinade. Place in a container, seal tightly, and refrigerate for 2–3 days (48–72 hours). The long marination is the signature of this preparation — the salt in the miso gently draws moisture from the fish while the sugars and umami compounds diffuse deep into the flesh. After marination, the fish will be notably firmer and more deeply flavored throughout.
Visual cue: After 72 hours: fillet is firmly coated in a thick, darkened miso crust. The marinade has visibly thickened on the surface.
Underdone: After only 24 hours: marinade is still thin and the fish interior has not been affected. The glaze will not behave correctly. Marinate for at least 48 hours; 72 is the target.
Perfect: At 72 hours: marinade is thick and set on the fish's surface. The fish feels firmer and denser than fresh. The color has deepened to a caramel-tan. Scrape off excess marinade before broiling — the residue will burn, not caramelize.
Overdone: Beyond 4 days: the salt has over-firmed the flesh, which feels compressed and dense rather than supple. Cook immediately; the texture will be denser but the flavor will be exceptional.
Feel cue: A properly marinated black cod fillet should feel like a firm gel when you press it — the miso salt cure has tightened the proteins just enough to hold their shape when touched.

Remove the cod fillets from the marinade and wipe off most (not all) of the miso with your fingers or a spatula. A thin layer should remain. Place skin-side down on a foil-lined, lightly oiled baking sheet. Broil at the oven's highest setting (230–260°C) for 8–10 minutes, watching constantly. The miso glaze will darken dramatically and some sections will look nearly burnt — this is the Maillard reaction and caramelization of the sugars, and it is the correct result. The fish is done when the glaze is deeply caramelized and the flesh flakes when a fork is pressed at the thickest point. Serve with pickled ginger and green onion.
Visual cue: Deep mahogany glaze with caramelized brown and black highlights — dramatic, almost alarming color on the surface, with ivory-white flesh just visible beneath the crust.
Underdone: Glaze is still pale golden-yellow and has not caramelized. Fish interior is underdone. Return to the broiler for 2–3 more minutes — the transition from underdone to perfect is fast.
Perfect: Glaze is a dramatic dark caramel-brown to near-black with burnished highlights. Fish flakes into large, buttery sections at the fork. The skin is crisp. The flesh is impossibly rich and sweet. Serve immediately with pickled ginger and green onion.
Overdone: Glaze has blackened entirely and smells of pure carbon rather than sweet caramel; the skin has dried to a hard shell. Remove, let rest 1 minute, and gently scrape off the top layer of char — the flesh beneath is likely still excellent.
Feel cue: The finished fillet should collapse under the gentlest fork pressure, breaking into large, glossy white flakes that look almost translucent in the center — the ultimate expression of fat-rich sablefish at its peak.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

description: Vegetables buried in a seasoned rice bran bed and left to ferment overnight — emerging the next morning transformed, with compressed texture, a faint funkiness, and the earthy depth of the nuka itself.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Vegetables for pickling: cucumber, carrot, daikon, eggplant
Extra salt (for vegetable salting before burial)

steps:
Toast the rice bran in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring constantly, for 5-8 minutes until golden and fragrant (nutty, not burnt). Cool completely. Dissolve the salt in warm water. In a large, deep, non-reactive container (ceramic crock, enamel pot, or food-grade plastic tub), combine the cooled toasted bran with the salted water. Mix thoroughly with clean hands until it resembles damp sand that holds together when pressed. Bury the kombu, dried chilis, and dried shiitake in the bed. The nukadoko (bran bed) should be moist throughout but not wet or sloshy.
Visual cue: A damp, golden-brown bran bed that holds together when pressed but is not wet or sticky.
Underdone: Dry, powdery bran that doesn't hold its shape when pressed. The water has not been fully absorbed. Add water tablespoon by tablespoon and continue mixing until the bed clumps when squeezed.
Perfect: Moist, brown bed that holds its shape when a handful is squeezed but doesn't leave water on your palm. Texture like barely damp beach sand. Smells of toasted grain and salt. Begin the conditioning phase: bury scrap vegetables for the first 7 days.
Overdone: The bed is wet and sloshy — excess water added. Leaves a muddy residue on your palm when squeezed. Add more dry toasted bran a handful at a time and mix until the correct consistency is achieved.
Feel cue: Squeeze a handful — it should hold together in a clump and feel moist but release no water when squeezed firmly. Like moist potting soil.

For the first 7 days, the nukadoko must be conditioned to establish a healthy microbial culture. Twice daily (morning and evening), mix the entire bed with clean hands from the bottom up, burying the surface into the center and turning the bed completely. This aerates the bed, prevents harmful anaerobic bacteria, and distributes the cultures evenly. Bury kitchen vegetable scraps (carrot tops, cabbage leaves, cucumber peels — whatever you have) each day to feed the developing cultures. After each mixing, press the bed smooth. Keep the container at 18-25°C. The bed is ready to use when it smells pleasantly funky and slightly sour — not off-putting, but alive.
Visual cue: A bed that has darkened slightly, developed a more complex aroma, and has a slightly tacky, unified texture.
Underdone: After 2-3 days, no aroma change. Still smells of raw toasted bran and salt only. No visual change. Continue the twice-daily mixing. The culture is developing slowly — be patient. Warmth accelerates it.
Perfect: After 5-7 days, the bed smells pleasantly complex — earthy, slightly sour, faintly funky, never unpleasant. The color has darkened slightly. It feels sticky and unified when mixed rather than sandy. Discard the conditioning vegetables and begin pickling real vegetables.
Overdone: Strong ammonia smell or putrid odor. Black or pink surface mold visible. A surface ammonia smell can be addressed by stirring in more salt (20g) and leaving uncovered in a cool spot for a day. Black or pink mold means discard and start over.
Feel cue: Properly conditioned nukadoko feels unified and cohesive when turned — not sandy or crumbly. It has a distinctive living aroma: pleasant, complex, earthy, not unpleasant.

Rub the vegetables lightly with the extra salt before burying — this removes surface moisture and helps them absorb the nuka flavors faster. For cucumbers: leave whole or halve. For carrots and daikon: cut into sticks. For eggplant: halve, cut slashes across the flesh. Bury the vegetables completely in the nukadoko, pressing the bed back smooth over them. Mark the position of buried vegetables. Store at 18-22°C or refrigerate (pickling will be slower but more controlled in the refrigerator). Mix the bed twice daily even when vegetables are buried.
Visual cue: Vegetables fully buried with a smooth bed surface and no visible items above the bran.
Underdone: Vegetables partially buried with some surface exposed to air. Press the bran firmly over the vegetables and add more bed material if needed to cover completely.
Perfect: Vegetables fully buried, bed surface smooth. The salt-rubbed vegetables begin to visibly weep moisture into the bed as you press them in. Mark the location and leave until the following day.
Overdone: Too many vegetables buried at once — bed is overcrowded and the salt balance will be disrupted. Remove some vegetables and pickle them separately in plain brine. Bury fewer items at once.
Feel cue: Press the bed over a buried vegetable — you should feel the firm resistance of the vegetable below the surface of the yielding bran bed.

Pickling times vary by vegetable and temperature: cucumbers at room temperature, 12-24 hours; carrots and daikon, 24-48 hours; eggplant, 12-18 hours. At refrigerator temperature, multiply times by 2-3. Remove the vegetables, scrape off the nuka bed (return it to the container), rinse or wipe the vegetables gently with a damp cloth, and slice to serve. The bed should be mixed thoroughly after each use. Continue the twice-daily mixing of the nukadoko indefinitely — a maintained bed improves over months and years.
Visual cue: Vegetables have changed color — cucumber has yellowed slightly, daikon has become translucent, eggplant has darkened and softened.
Underdone: Vegetables taste mostly of salt only — no nuka flavor has penetrated. Texture is unchanged. Return to the bed for another 12-24 hours. The bed temperature and culture strength affect how fast flavor develops.
Perfect: Vegetables have taken on a complex, earthy, mildly sour nuka flavor beneath the salt. Cucumber is yellow-tinged. Texture is firmer and more compressed than raw. Flavor is savory, funky in the best way, and refreshing. Rinse, slice, and serve immediately as a side dish or with rice.
Overdone: Vegetables are very soft and have an aggressive, overpowering fermented flavor. Sour enough to be unpleasant. Left too long in the bed. Use very sparingly as a condiment. Shorten pickling time next time.
Feel cue: A properly nukazuke vegetable feels firmer and more dense than raw — moisture has been drawn out and replaced with brine. It should snap cleanly when broken, not bend.

name: Japanese Onigiri
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。

  Alternatives: Calrose rice
Water: 360 ml
Fine sea salt (for hands and rice): 8 g
Nori sheets, cut into strips: 2 sheets
Umeboshi (pickled plum) or tuna mayo: 40 g
  Alternatives: salted salmon flakes; seasoned cod roe
Soy sauce (for wet hands, optional): 5 ml
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 50 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Warm seasoned rice compressed into a firm triangle, its salty nori exterior crackling at the first bite to reveal a savory filling hidden at the center — Japan's perfect portable meal.

ingredients.name: Fine sea salt (for hands and rice)
酱油（Soy sauce (for wet hands, optional)）

steps:
Rinse the rice until the water runs nearly clear (5–6 rinses). Drain and let the rice sit dry in the pot for 10 minutes — this pre-resting firms the exterior. Add the measured water, cover tightly, and bring to a boil over high heat. As soon as you hear the boiling, reduce to the absolute lowest simmer and cook for 12 minutes. Remove from heat without lifting the lid and steam for 10 minutes. The rice is ready when you open the lid to a puff of steam with no visible water at the surface.
Visual cue: Grains are glossy, fully cooked, and slightly sticky, with a clean, sweet fragrance.
Underdone: Grains still have a chalky, hard center. Surface looks dull. Re-cover and steam off-heat for another 5 minutes.
Perfect: Grains are plump, glossy, and cling together when pressed but individual grains are still distinct. Smells clean and sweet. Allow to cool slightly until just warm enough to handle (not hot) before shaping.
Overdone: Grains have burst and the rice has become very soft and gluey. Bottom layer smells slightly scorched. Use for onigiri anyway — overcooked rice forms very well, it will just be denser.
Feel cue: Run a rice paddle through the cooked rice from the bottom up — it should fold in clean ribbons that glisten with steam and cling gently without being gummy.

While the rice is still warm, turn it into a large flat bowl using a rice paddle. Sprinkle the salt evenly over the surface. Fold the rice using a cutting-and-folding motion (not stirring) to distribute the salt without crushing the grains. Fan or let cool to a temperature where you can comfortably handle it — just above body temperature, around 40°C.
Visual cue: Rice grains are evenly distributed, glossy, and slightly separated — no clumps, no dry spots.
Underdone: Salt is unevenly distributed; some bites will be bland, others too salty. Fold more times using the cutting motion.
Perfect: Every grain glistens slightly and the rice tastes evenly seasoned — mildly salty and sweet at once. Shape immediately while still warm.
Overdone: Rice has been stirred too aggressively and grains have broken and become pasty. Proceed — the texture is slightly compromised but onigiri will still hold shape.
Feel cue: Warm, properly seasoned rice should feel like a gently damp clay between your palms — yielding but with spring, not wet or gluey.

Wet both palms with cold water and rub with a generous pinch of salt — this prevents sticking and adds flavor to the exterior. Take about 120g of warm rice and form a loose ball in one palm. Press a shallow indentation in the center and place your filling (umeboshi, tuna mayo, or salmon flakes) inside. Close the rice around the filling. Cup both hands into a V-shape and press firmly from the sides while rotating, forming a compact triangle with three flat faces and three ridges. Wrap the base with a strip of nori. Repeat for remaining rice and fillings.
Visual cue: A firm, compact triangle with flat faces, three defined ridges, and a strip of nori at the base.
Underdone: Triangle is loose and crumbling; filling falls out when picked up. Rice hasn't compressed enough. Re-compress with firmer palm pressure — 6–8 decisive squeezes, rotating 120 degrees between each.
Perfect: Onigiri holds its triangle shape firmly when picked up, with a slight give when squeezed. Nori adheres cleanly. Filling is centered and invisible. Serve immediately or wrap tightly in plastic for later.
Overdone: Rice has been compressed into a hard, dense block with no lightness. The triangle is too rigid and the rice texture is dense. Serve immediately — dense onigiri is still delicious, just less elegant.
Feel cue: A well-made onigiri should feel like a firm handshake — solid and confident, but not painfully hard. It should yield slightly when you squeeze without crumbling.

description: Thick salmon fillets lacquered in a four-ingredient teriyaki glaze until the skin crackles and the glaze turns to a mahogany, bittersweet varnish that shatters at the fork.

ingredients.name: 食用油（Neutral oil (sunflower or rice bran)）

steps:
Combine the soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small saucepan. Bring to a boil over medium heat and stir to dissolve the sugar. Simmer for 3–4 minutes until reduced by one-third and the glaze coats the back of a spoon with a thin sheen. Remove from heat. The glaze thickens further as it cools.
Visual cue: Glaze is dark amber and coats the spoon in a thin, even film that runs slowly off the edge.
Underdone: Glaze is thin and watery; runs off the spoon immediately without coating. Continue simmering for 2 more minutes.
Perfect: Leaves a clean, slow-dripping coat on the spoon. Deep amber-brown. Smells of caramelized soy and sweet rice wine. Remove from heat. It will thicken further as it cools.
Overdone: Glaze has become very thick and sticky while hot — it will set rock-hard as it cools. Add 1 tbsp of water and stir over low heat to loosen.
Feel cue: Dip a spoon and drag your finger through the coating — a properly reduced teriyaki should hold a clean line for 3–4 seconds before it flows back together.

Pat the salmon fillets completely dry with kitchen paper — any moisture creates steam and prevents a crust. Score the skin 3 times diagonally to prevent curling. Heat the oil in a non-stick or cast-iron pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Place the salmon skin-side down and press firmly with a spatula for 10 seconds to prevent curling. Cook skin-side down for 4 minutes until the skin is deeply golden and crisp and the flesh has turned opaque 2/3 of the way up the sides. Flip once.
Visual cue: Skin is a deep, golden-brown with crisp, rendered edges; the flesh has turned opaque from the bottom up, leaving a translucent orange band at the top.
Underdone: Skin is pale and sticking to the pan; flesh is still fully translucent. Salmon will tear if you try to flip it. Wait — salmon releases naturally when the skin is properly seared. Do not force it.
Perfect: Skin is deep golden-brown and releases cleanly. Flesh is opaque 60–70% of the way through. Edges are just beginning to turn white. Flip and reduce heat to medium.
Overdone: Flesh has gone fully opaque and white all the way to the top before flipping. Skin may be too dark. Flip immediately and apply glaze. The center will be cooked through but not dry yet.
Feel cue: Press the thickest part of the salmon with your fingertip — skin-down, it should feel firm at the base but spring back like a muscle at rest in the upper half.

After flipping, cook the flesh side for 1 minute. Reduce heat to low. Pour the teriyaki glaze over and around the salmon. As it bubbles, spoon it over the top of the fillets repeatedly for 1–2 minutes. The glaze will reduce and lacquer the salmon in a shiny, mahogany coating. Remove from heat and spoon any remaining glaze over the top. Scatter green onion and sesame seeds. Rest 1 minute before serving.
Visual cue: Salmon is coated in a deeply shiny mahogany glaze with caramelized edges and the skin is visibly crisp beneath.
Underdone: Glaze is still thin and running off; the salmon looks pale and under-lacquered. Baste more aggressively over low heat for 1–2 more minutes.
Perfect: Salmon glistens with a thick, dark glaze that barely moves when the pan tilts. Smells of caramelized soy and sake. Flesh is just set and yields to gentle pressure. Rest 1 minute and serve immediately.
Overdone: Glaze has blackened and turned bitter-sharp; salmon interior is chalky and dry. Remove from heat immediately. Serve with extra plain rice to balance the intense, slightly bitter exterior.
Feel cue: The finished fillet should offer a distinct two-texture experience — a barely yielding press on the surface followed by a clean, buttery give as the fork enters the flesh.

name: Japanese Teriyaki Sauce
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

description: A four-ingredient glaze reduced to a mahogany lacquer — soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar cooked together until they thicken into a glossy, clingy sauce that chars to a sweet-salty shellac on grilled fish or chicken.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
