steps:
Pulse almond flour and icing sugar together in a food processor for 30 seconds to eliminate any lumps and evenly combine. Sift through a fine-mesh sieve. Discard any large almond pieces that won't pass. The mixture should feel like talc — if it clumps, your almond flour is too moist; spread it on a sheet tray and dry in a 100 C oven for 10 minutes.
Visual cue: A perfectly uniform, fluffy, off-white powder with no lumps, no coarse almond slivers, no icing-sugar clumps.
Underdone: Coarse almond pieces or visible sugar lumps remain after sifting. Re-process and re-sift. Lumps prevent a smooth shell surface.
Perfect: Silky, dusty powder that cascades through the sieve without effort. Consistent pale cream colour. Set aside and prepare the Italian meringue.
Overdone: Mixture looks oily and clumped — almond fat has been released by over-processing. Discard and start with fresh almond flour. Once oily, it cannot be corrected.
Feel cue: Rub a pinch between your fingers — it should feel like smooth face powder, with no graininess and no oily residue.

Cook caster sugar and water in a small saucepan to 118 C (soft-ball stage), without stirring. Meanwhile, whip the aged egg whites with salt to soft peaks on medium speed. When the syrup hits 118 C, increase mixer to high and pour the syrup in a thin, steady stream down the bowl wall (not onto the whisk). Whip on high for 8-10 minutes until the bowl is no longer hot to the touch and the meringue is stiff and glossy.
Visual cue: A stiff, brilliant white meringue that forms sharp, upright peaks. The bowl should feel no warmer than body temperature.
Underdone: Peaks flop over softly. Meringue feels warm. Surface is still slightly grainy from undissolved sugar. Continue whipping on high — the meringue must cool and reach full stiffness before macaronage.
Perfect: Peaks are stiff and slightly curled at the very tip. Meringue is silky-smooth and brilliant. When you lift the whisk, a beak forms and holds. Begin macaronage immediately while meringue is still at its peak.
Overdone: Meringue looks curdled, watery, or separating at the bowl edges. Peaks are crumbly, not silky. Overwhipped meringue cannot be fixed — start again. The macarons will spread and crack.
Feel cue: Press the meringue between your thumb and forefinger — it should feel like satin, completely smooth, with zero graininess. If you feel sugar crystals, whip longer.

Add the tant-pour-tant to the Italian meringue in two additions. Macaronage: using a wide rubber spatula, fold by pressing the batter flat against the side of the bowl, then scooping from the bottom and folding over. Work decisively — this is not a gentle fold. You are deliberately deflating the meringue to achieve the correct flow. Perform roughly 40-50 strokes. Stop when the batter flows from the spatula in a thick, continuous ribbon that disappears back into the bowl within 10 seconds.
Visual cue: A flowing, lava-like batter. When the spatula is lifted and batter falls, it forms a thick continuous ribbon that ribbon folds back and becomes smooth within 10 seconds.
Underdone: Batter is stiff and lumpy. When spatula is lifted it breaks off in clumps rather than ribboning. Continue folding — under-macaronaged batter makes lumpy, peaked shells.
Perfect: Thick flowing lava. Ribbon disappears back to a smooth surface in 8-10 seconds. Batter is shiny and flows uniformly. Transfer to a piping bag and pipe immediately.
Overdone: Batter is runny, spreads immediately when the spatula is lifted. No ribbon forms — it just pours. Over-macaronaged batter cannot be saved. The shells will spread flat. Start again.
Feel cue: When you scoop a spatula-full and let it fall back into the bowl, it should flow off the spatula in a wide, glossy cascade, not drip in individual drops.

Pipe 3.5 cm rounds onto silicone-mat-lined baking sheets, spacing 3 cm apart. Tap the sheet firmly on the counter 3-4 times to release large air bubbles. Let rest at room temperature for 30-45 minutes until the surface forms a dry skin — it should not stick to your fingertip. Bake one sheet at a time at 150 C (fan-forced) for 14-16 minutes. Shells are done when they slide cleanly off the mat with no resistance at the base.
Visual cue: Smooth, matte-surfaced domes with a ruffled 'foot' (pied) around the base and no cracks on the crown.
Underdone: Shells stick to the mat. The foot is there but the base is still soft and comes away in pieces. Return to the oven for 2 more minutes. A proper shell releases cleanly when the mat is peeled back.
Perfect: Smooth, uncracked dome. A proud, even foot. The shell slides off the mat cleanly when cool. Hollow sound when tapped. Cool fully on the mat before filling — minimum 30 minutes.
Overdone: Shells are ivory or tan on top, not pale — the almond is browning. Texture will be dry and crumbly. Reduce oven temperature by 5 C next batch. Overly browned shells lose their chew.
Feel cue: Tap a cooled shell on its back — it should sound faintly hollow like a tiny ceramic bead, not dull and dense. Press the side gently: it should give slightly, like pressing a firm grape.

Beat the softened butter alone for 3 minutes until very pale and fluffy. Add icing sugar in three additions, beating for 1 minute between each. The finished buttercream should be smooth, ivory, and stiff enough to hold a peak but soft enough to pipe easily. Add 1 tsp of vanilla or other flavouring, and a pinch of salt to balance.
Visual cue: Very pale, almost white buttercream that holds a stiff, smooth peak. No graininess visible.
Underdone: Buttercream looks yellow and grainy — butter not yet fully aerated, sugar not fully incorporated. Beat for 2 more minutes. Properly creamed butter is nearly white, not yellow.
Perfect: Pale ivory, silky-smooth, holds shape when piped. Springs back when pressed with a fingertip. Transfer to a piping bag and fill the macaron shells.
Overdone: Buttercream looks curdled or soupy — either over-beaten or butter was too warm. Chill the bowl in the fridge for 10 minutes, then re-beat. If soupy, the butter was too hot — chill until firm and retry.
Feel cue: Taste a small amount — it should dissolve smoothly on the tongue with no graininess. If you can feel sugar crystals, beat longer.

Match shells by size into pairs. Pipe a generous, even disc of buttercream onto the flat side of one shell, leaving a 2 mm border. Sandwich with its pair and press gently until the filling reaches the edge. Refrigerate, uncovered, for 24 hours — this is the 'maturation' step. The moisture from the filling softens the shell interior to its characteristic chewy texture. Bring to room temperature for 20 minutes before serving.
Visual cue: Uniform, neat sandwiches with filling visible in an even ring at the edge. Shells are smooth and uncracked.
Underdone: Filling is squeezed to one side, sandwich is lopsided. Filling visible unevenly at edges. Apply filling more centrally next time. Gently press again to even out.
Perfect: Filling forms a neat, even halo at the equator. Top and bottom shells aligned. Sandwich feels substantial but not heavy. Refrigerate for 24 hours to mature before serving.
Overdone: Too much filling applied — it bulges beyond the shell edges and the sandwich feels cumbersome. Scrape back some filling and re-press. Ratio should be roughly 1:1 shell:filling by volume.
Feel cue: After 24 hours in the refrigerator, the macaron should yield to gentle pressure with a slight resistance — the shell exterior is still faintly crisp but the interior has softened to a chew that gives like a ripe fig.

name: Classic Madeleines
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
All-purpose flour: 120 g
  Alternatives: cake flour for a more tender crumb
Unsalted butter: 115 g
  Alternatives: European-style butter for richer noisette

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Shell-shaped, honey-golden sponge cakes with a distinctive hump — a fleeting warmth of browned butter and lemon zest that perfumes the kitchen for only a few minutes after leaving the pan, best eaten while still crackling at the edges.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Place the butter in a light-coloured saucepan over medium heat. It will melt, foam, subside, then foam a second time. At the second foam, swirl constantly and watch the milk solids on the bottom: they will turn from blonde to golden to hazelnut-brown (noisette). At the first scent of toasty hazelnuts, immediately pour the butter into a cold bowl to stop cooking. Cool to room temperature — it should be liquid but not warm.
Visual cue: Golden-amber liquid with a scattering of dark-brown milk solids on the bottom of the receiving bowl. The kitchen smells of toasted hazelnuts and caramel.
Underdone: Butter is fully melted and clear yellow but the milk solids are still pale and blonde. Little aroma beyond fresh butter. Return to heat and continue swirling. The noisette colour happens quickly — watch closely and don't walk away.
Perfect: A clear amber-gold liquid with dark-brown flecks settled at the bottom. Smell is unmistakably nutty and caramel-sweet. Pour immediately into a cold bowl. Don't leave it in the hot pan — it will continue to darken from residual heat.
Overdone: Butter has gone past amber to dark brown and smells acrid or burnt. The milk solids are nearly black. Discard and start again — burnt beurre noisette will make every madeleine bitter. The window between perfect and overdone is about 15 seconds.
Feel cue: The second foam is quieter and more golden than the first — when the sizzling softens and you smell something like roasted nuts, you have five seconds to act.

In a large bowl, whisk together the eggs, caster sugar, and honey. Whisk vigorously — by hand for 3 to 4 minutes, or with an electric whisk on high for 2 minutes — until the mixture has roughly doubled in volume, turned pale ivory, and falls from the whisk in a thick ribbon that holds its shape on the surface for a few seconds before dissolving.
Visual cue: A pale, creamy-ivory, billowing mixture that falls from the whisk in a slow, thick ribbon and sits on the surface for 3–4 seconds before sinking.
Underdone: Still golden-yellow and liquid. The whisk leaves no trail. Mixture is thin and homogeneous. Keep whisking — you need to dissolve the sugar fully and incorporate enough air to give the madeleines their lift. Under-aerated batter bakes flat.
Perfect: Pale, thick, almost mousse-like. Holds a clear ribbon. The volume is about double what you started with. Stop whisking. Now add the dry ingredients and aromatics — over-whisking from this point collapses the air you just built.
Overdone: Mixture has become stiff, meringue-like, and the whisk leaves rigid peaks. Bright white and grainy. You've over-aerated. Fold in the dry ingredients gently to deflate to a reasonable consistency — the madeleines may still be fine, but slightly drier.
Feel cue: Lift the whisk and draw a figure-eight in the batter with the falling ribbon. If the line holds for a moment before melting back in, you're there.

Sift the flour, baking powder, and salt directly over the ribbon mixture. Add the lemon zest and vanilla extract. Using a large spatula, fold gently with wide, sweeping, under-over strokes until just combined — no dry streaks, but don't over-mix. Finally, pour the cooled browned butter around the edge of the batter and fold it in the same way until fully incorporated. The batter will be smooth, glossy, and noticeably heavier.
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy, pale batter — slightly heavier than the ribbon stage, with a subtle shimmer from the butter. Smells of lemon and hazelnuts.
Underdone: Streaks of flour still visible, or the butter is pooled at the base rather than incorporated. Looks streaky and uneven. Fold a few more strokes, focusing on the bottom of the bowl where flour hides. Be deliberate but not vigorous.
Perfect: Uniform, smooth, and glossy. Falls off the spatula in a slow ribbon. No flour streaks, no butter pools. Cover the bowl tightly with cling film and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or up to 24 hours. The cold rest is essential for the signature hump.
Overdone: Batter looks deflated, flat, and dense. Vigorous stirring has popped all the air bubbles and developed the gluten. Proceed — the rest in the fridge may help recover some structure, but the hump will be smaller and the crumb tighter.
Feel cue: The batter should pour slowly off a spoon in a single, unbroken ribbon — not drip, not flow. If it runs like water, the butter was too warm; if it sits in stiff mounds, it was over-worked.

Press cling film directly onto the surface of the batter and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or up to 24 hours. Meanwhile, butter the madeleine molds generously and dust with flour, tapping out the excess; refrigerate the prepared pan too. The cold shock when cold batter meets a hot oven creates the distinctive hump — do not skip this step.
Visual cue: The batter has firmed slightly and is noticeably cold. It holds its shape when piped or spooned into the mold without spreading immediately.
Underdone: Batter is still warm or room temperature. It flows too easily into the molds and spreads thin before the oven can set it. Return to the fridge. An hour is the minimum — overnight rested batters often produce a more defined hump than a 1-hour rest.
Perfect: Cold, firm, thick. Holds its shape in the mold for a few seconds before settling. The butter in the molds has set solid. Fill the molds to three-quarters full and bake immediately from cold. Have the oven pre-heated to 200°C for at least 20 minutes.
Overdone: You rested the batter for several days — it may have absorbed too much liquid or begun to smell sour from the eggs. The batter is best used within 24 hours. Beyond that, it still bakes but the lift is diminished.
Feel cue: Scoop the batter cold and it should hold a small dome in the mold for 2–3 seconds before slowly relaxing — a sign the fat has solidified enough to create a temperature shock in the oven.

Preheat the oven to 200°C (390°F) for at least 20 minutes. Fill the chilled, floured molds to three-quarters full. Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until the edges are deep golden and pulling away from the shell, the hump has risen fully and the peak is just set. Remove immediately and turn out onto a rack. Eat within 30 minutes — they are a different food after an hour.
Visual cue: The classic hump has risen clearly above the rim. Edges are deep golden-brown; the hump peak is pale gold and just dry. The shell-side is richly caramelised and patterned.
Underdone: The hump looks raw and damp at the peak. Shell-side is pale blond. The madeleine springs back loosely when pressed. Add 1–2 more minutes. The hump should be dry to the touch at its highest point and the edges visibly darker than the centre.
Perfect: Hump stands high and firm, dry at the top. Edges and shell underside are deep golden. The kitchen smells of warm butter, honey, and lemon. They release from the mold cleanly. Turn out shell-side up immediately onto a rack. They are at their peak for the next 20 minutes.
Overdone: Edges are dark brown approaching burnt, the hump is cracked, and the aroma tips from caramel toward bitter biscuit. They are still edible — trim the darkest edges and dip in chocolate to rescue. Lower oven or reduce time by 2 minutes next time.
Feel cue: Freshly unmolded, the shell underside should feel warm and slightly tacky with caramelised butter. The hump should be springy, not soft. Press it gently: it should push back immediately like a sponge, not collapse.

name: Mafé (West African Groundnut Stew)

quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: lamb shoulder; chicken thighs

Garlic cloves, minced: 3 parts
Fresh ginger, grated: 2 parts
Sweet potato, cubed 3cm: 20 parts
  Alternatives: white potato; cassava
Fine sea salt: 2 parts
Dried chile flakes or scotch bonnet: 1 parts
Beef or vegetable stock: 40 parts
  Alternatives: water
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 2 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A stew built on a foundation of natural peanut butter — not the sweetened, industrial kind, but the raw, oily, slightly bitter groundnut paste that bubbles into something nutty and profound when it meets beef, tomato, and the slow heat of a heavy pot. It is the kind of stew that improves every hour it sits, and the kitchen smells like it has been cooking since morning, even if you started at noon.

ingredients.name: Canned whole tomatoes, crushed by hand
Dried chile flakes or scotch bonnet

steps:
Pat the beef cubes completely dry with paper towels — moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Season aggressively with salt. Heat a heavy pot or Dutch oven over high heat until a drop of water evaporates on contact. Add oil and sear the beef in a single layer, without crowding, for 3–4 minutes per side until deeply browned on all surfaces. Work in batches. The goal is a dark mahogany crust on every face, not grey steaming.
Visual cue: Deep mahogany-brown crust on all sides of the beef. No steaming, only sizzling.
Underdone: Beef is releasing moisture and steaming. Pan is full of water. Meat is grey. Remove half the meat. Overcrowding is causing steaming. Increase heat.
Perfect: Aggressive sizzle. Each face of the beef is a deep mahogany with a caramelized crust. The pan has developed a dark fond. Remove beef and deglaze pan with a splash of stock.
Overdone: Beef is black and the fond is verging on burnt. Deglaze immediately with water, scraping. Add less oil and lower heat for the next batch.
Feel cue: When a cube of beef releases naturally from the pan without sticking, the Maillard crust has fully formed — forced release before that point tears the crust and wastes the flavor.

In the same pot with the beef fond, add the diced onion and cook over medium heat, scraping up the fond constantly, for 8–10 minutes until deeply golden and translucent. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for another 2 minutes, stirring, until fragrant. The onion should be well beyond translucent — approaching golden-amber — before the liquids are added. This caramelization provides the sweet, savory undertone that balances the peanut butter.
Visual cue: Onion is golden-amber and translucent, soft throughout. Garlic is fragrant but not browned.
Underdone: Onion is still white and crunchy. Fond has not been fully incorporated. Continue cooking with a tablespoon of water to help lift the fond. Do not rush this step.
Perfect: Onion is soft, amber, and jammy. The fond from the beef is fully incorporated into the onion. The pot smells of sweet caramelized allium and spice. Add tomatoes and peanut butter.
Overdone: Garlic has browned and smells bitter. Add the tomatoes immediately to stop the cooking. The slight bitterness will be absorbed into the stew.
Feel cue: When the onion is ready, it should feel completely soft when pressed against the side of the pot with a spoon — no crunch, no resistance, just yielding, sweet softness.

Add the crushed tomatoes to the aromatics and cook 5 minutes, stirring, until the tomatoes darken and the oil separates at the edges — this is pinçage, even if the French don't claim this stew. Add the peanut butter and stir until fully dissolved into the tomato base. The paste will initially resist blending — press it against the hot pot wall and stir until smooth. Return the seared beef, add the stock and chile, bring to a boil, then reduce to the lowest simmer. Cook partially covered for 60 minutes.
Visual cue: A thick, orange-brown stew that flows slowly. The peanut butter has fully homogenized — no oily slicks or white chunks.
Underdone: Peanut butter is still visible in white lumps. Stock is thin and watery. Beef is still firm. Continue simmering. Stir frequently to break down the peanut butter.
Perfect: Stew is thick, glossy, and deep orange-brown. Beef yields when pressed with a spoon. Oil from the peanuts has risen and can be skimmed if desired. Add sweet potato and continue.
Overdone: Stew has reduced to a very thick paste and is beginning to scorch at the bottom. Add hot stock or water and stir from the bottom. Reduce heat significantly.
Feel cue: When the peanut butter has fully dissolved into the stew, the sauce should feel uniformly silky on the tongue — that smoothness tells you the emulsion has held and the groundnut oils are fully incorporated.

Add the cubed sweet potato to the stew. Stir to submerge and coat in the peanut sauce. Continue simmering uncovered for 25–30 more minutes, until the sweet potato is fully tender and beginning to break down at the edges — those broken edges will thicken the stew further. Taste aggressively: mafé needs significant salt. Adjust with salt and chile. Serve over white rice or with thiéboudienne bread for soaking.
Visual cue: Sweet potato is tender and breaking at the edges. Stew is thick and glossy. A spoon dragged through leaves a clear channel for 2 seconds before closing.
Underdone: Sweet potato resists a knife. Centers are still hard. Stew is thinner than desired. Continue simmering uncovered for 10 more minutes.
Perfect: Sweet potato is fully yielding and the edges have dissolved slightly into the stew, thickening it further. The sauce is deep orange-brown and glossy. Serve immediately over rice.
Overdone: Sweet potato has entirely dissolved. Stew is very thick and paste-like. Add hot stock or water to loosen to a pourable consistency.
Feel cue: The finished mafé should be heavy on the ladle — that weight from the peanut proteins and dissolved sweet potato starch is what distinguishes a proper groundnut stew from a thin soup.

name: Maître d'Hôtel Butter
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Unsalted butter, at room temperature (very soft but not melted): 100 parts
Flat-leaf parsley, very finely chopped: 10 parts
  Alternatives: chives (alone or combined); tarragon (smaller amount)
Fresh lemon zest, finely grated: 3 parts
Fresh lemon juice: 4 parts
Shallot, very finely minced (almost to a paste): 5 parts
  Alternatives: chives, finely snipped
Fine sea salt: 2 parts
  Alternatives: flaky sea salt, folded in gently
White pepper, freshly ground: 0.3 parts
  Alternatives: black pepper
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 1 hour 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The simplest and most elegant of compound butters — soft unsalted butter beaten with flat-leaf parsley, lemon zest and juice, and shallot, rolled into a cylinder and chilled until firm — a medallion of this melted over a hot steak or grilled fish becomes its own instant sauce.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, at room temperature (very soft but not melted)
Shallot, very finely minced (almost to a paste)

steps:
The quality of the finished butter depends entirely on the fineness of the chopping. For the parsley: strip the leaves from the stems and gather into a tight pile. Chop repeatedly with a sharp chef's knife, rocking the blade, until the parsley is almost a green powder — at the finest level of chopping, the parsley releases a small amount of green juice and the individual pieces are nearly indistinguishable. Coarsely chopped parsley gives the butter an uneven, ragged appearance and releases a harsh grassy bitterness. For the shallot: halve, peel, and mince as finely as possible until it is nearly a paste. If the minced shallot still has a sharp, raw burn when tasted, rinse briefly under cold water and squeeze dry in a cloth — this removes some of the harsh sulfur compounds without losing flavor.
Visual cue: Parsley reduced to an almost-paste consistency, vivid green, intensely fragrant; shallot invisible as individual pieces, almost a fine paste.
Underdone: Parsley still in recognizable leaf pieces. Shallot in chunky dice. Both will produce an uneven, bitter butter. Continue chopping until both are almost unrecognizable as pieces. This takes patience and a truly sharp knife.
Perfect: Parsley is a vivid green powder, slightly damp from its own juice. Shallot is a fine paste, barely visible. Both smell intensely fresh. Combine with the butter immediately — the parsley will begin to oxidize and darken if left too long.
Overdone: Parsley has been worked so long it has turned dark, oxidized olive-green and lost its fresh fragrance. Proceed. The flavor is slightly less bright but still excellent. For next time, chop just before combining with butter.
Feel cue: Run the flat of the blade through the chopped parsley — at the right fineness it will smear slightly on the board, leaving a green film. That release of juice is the signal it is fine enough.

Place the soft butter in a medium bowl. Beat it briefly with a wooden spoon or silicone spatula until smooth and slightly fluffy — do not use a mixer, which incorporates too much air. Add the minced parsley and shallot, lemon zest, lemon juice, salt, and white pepper all at once. Beat together until completely and evenly combined — the butter should be uniformly green from the parsley, with no white streaks of plain butter remaining, and should smell intensely of parsley and lemon. Add the lemon juice slowly if the butter starts to look slightly wet or broken — citric acid at high quantities can cause butter to break. Taste for seasoning: the raw butter should taste aggressively seasoned — generously salty and lemon-forward — because when a cold slice melts over hot food, the dilution effect from the heat will soften those flavors considerably.
Visual cue: Uniformly green, slightly fluffy, intensely fragrant butter — no white streaks, no visible shallot pieces, parsley distributed evenly throughout.
Underdone: White streaks of plain butter still visible — aromatics not evenly distributed. Continue beating until every streak of white is incorporated and the color is uniform green.
Perfect: Uniform vivid green, light and slightly fluffy, smells intensely of fresh parsley and lemon. Tastes bright, savory, and lemon-forward. Transfer to cling film and roll into a cylinder.
Overdone: Butter has been beaten too long and looks separated or greasy — butter fat beginning to break from over-agitation. Refrigerate for 10 minutes until it firms slightly, then fold gently. The cylinder form and chilling will recover the texture.
Feel cue: Taste a small amount of the compound butter on your fingertip — it should melt quickly from body heat and leave a full, complex coating: creamy richness, bright lemon, herbal parsley, and a clean salt finish all present at once.

Lay a piece of cling film (plastic wrap) about 30 cm long on the work surface. Spoon the compound butter in a rough cylinder along the center of the wrap, approximately 4–5 cm in diameter. Fold the wrap over the butter, then roll it away from you while simultaneously pressing gently on the roll through the wrap to compact it into a tight, even cylinder — the same technique used for a sausage. Twist the ends like a cracker wrapper and tie or tuck them. Refrigerate for at least 1 hour until completely firm. The butter keeps refrigerated for up to 1 week, or frozen for 2 months. To serve: unwrap and slice into rounds 5–8 mm thick with a sharp knife. Place a cold disc directly on a just-rested steak, piece of grilled fish, or steamed vegetables — it will melt into a pool of aromatic, lemony butter within 30 seconds.
Visual cue: A firm, tight, uniform green cylinder that slices cleanly into perfect rounds with no crumbling or tearing.
Underdone: Butter is still soft and the cylinder sags or squashes rather than holding its shape when sliced. Refrigerate for another 30 minutes until firm enough to slice cleanly.
Perfect: Firm and cold, slices cleanly into rounds that hold their circular shape. Vivid green throughout with no white patches. Smells of parsley and lemon even when cold. Store refrigerated. Slice to order and place on hot food to serve.
Overdone: Over-chilled and very hard — shatters rather than slicing cleanly, and pieces scatter. Allow the cylinder to sit at room temperature for 3–4 minutes to soften slightly, then slice.
Feel cue: A properly chilled maître d'hôtel butter should feel like cold modeling clay — firm and yielding a little under firm pressure, slicing with a clean sound through a sharp blade rather than crumbling or smearing.

name: Malabi
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Whole milk: 500 ml
  Alternatives: oat milk (slightly less rich set)
Heavy cream: 100 ml
  Alternatives: coconut cream for dairy-free
White sugar: 60 g
Cornstarch: 45 g
  Alternatives: potato starch (use 40 g)
Rose water: 20 ml
  Alternatives: orange blossom water (use half quantity)
Orange blossom water: 10 ml
Sugar (for rose syrup): 80 g
Water (for rose syrup): 80 ml
Rose water (for syrup): 15 ml
Pomegranate molasses or grenadine: 15 ml
  Alternatives: a few drops of natural red food coloring
Shelled pistachios, roughly chopped: 40 g
  Alternatives: crushed walnuts
Dried rose petals: 5 g
Desiccated coconut: 20 g
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 2 hr 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A milk-white pudding that trembles like moonlight — set with cornstarch to a delicate, custard-soft consistency, perfumed with rose water and orange blossom, and served cold under a river of pink rose syrup and crushed pistachios.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Measure out 100 ml of the cold milk into a small bowl. Add all the cornstarch and whisk vigorously until not a single lump remains — the mixture should look like thin white paint with no dry powder specks floating at the surface or clinging to the bowl. This slurry technique prevents the starch from seizing into lumps when it hits the hot liquid. The remaining 400 ml of milk goes into the saucepan.
Visual cue: A smooth, completely lump-free white liquid the consistency of thin cream. Poured over a dark counter it should leave no lumps behind.
Underdone: White lumps of undissolved cornstarch are visible at the bottom of the bowl or floating in the milk. Whisk more vigorously for another 60 seconds; press any visible lumps against the bowl wall with the whisk.
Perfect: Perfectly smooth, uniform milky-white liquid. No texture, no lumps, no dry powder specks. Set aside and prepare the saucepan with remaining milk and cream.
Overdone: Not possible to over-dissolve a cold slurry — this step cannot be overdone. Proceed.
Feel cue: Rub a drop of the slurry between your fingertips — it should feel as smooth as lotion, not at all gritty.

Pour the remaining 400 ml of milk into a medium saucepan along with the cream and sugar. Warm over medium heat, stirring gently until the sugar dissolves. When the mixture is steaming and just below simmering, pour in the cornstarch slurry in a thin, steady stream while whisking continuously and vigorously. Do not stop whisking. The mixture will begin to thicken within 2–3 minutes. Continue whisking over medium-low heat until the first large, lazy bubbles break the surface — this activates the starch fully. Remove from heat immediately and whisk in rose water and orange blossom water. The residual fragrance is delicate; heat destroys it quickly, so add off the flame.
Visual cue: A thick, smooth, opaque white pudding that falls from the whisk in slow, heavy ribbons and holds a faint surface pattern for 2–3 seconds before settling.
Underdone: Mixture is still thin and runny — it coats the whisk in a thin, watery layer that drips off quickly. Has not yet thickened to a pudding consistency. Keep whisking over medium heat — the starch needs to reach full gelatinization temperature (~95°C). A few more minutes will bring it together.
Perfect: Thick enough to fall in slow, heavy sheets off the whisk. Opaque and silky white. The first lazy bubbles have broken the surface. The kitchen smells sweetly of milk. Remove from heat immediately and whisk in rose water and orange blossom water. Pour into cups.
Overdone: Mixture is a very thick, nearly solid mass — it clumps rather than pours. Starch has fully over-gelatinized. Thin with a tablespoon of cold milk and whisk vigorously, then pour immediately — the set texture will still be acceptable.
Feel cue: Dip a clean spoon in and run your finger across the back — the line should hold clean and firm without the pudding flowing back across it.

Pour the hot pudding into individual serving cups or glasses — about 120–150 ml per cup. If the surface has a skin forming, pass it through a fine sieve as you pour for a perfectly smooth top. Tap each cup gently on the counter to settle. Leave uncovered at room temperature for 15 minutes until the surface is no longer steaming, then cover with plastic wrap pressed directly onto the surface (to prevent a skin) and refrigerate for at least 2 hours. The pudding is best served cold — the rose water and orange blossom flavors bloom more clearly when chilled.
Visual cue: Perfectly smooth, white, firm-set puddings with no surface skin or cracks. They should tremble like panna cotta when the cup is gently shaken.
Underdone: Pudding still moves loosely like a thick liquid when shaken after 2 hours of chilling. Has not fully set. Refrigerate another hour; the starch needs more time to fully gel at refrigerator temperature.
Perfect: Firm with a delicate, gentle jiggle. Surface is matte-smooth and snow-white. Holds a slight indent when pressed with a fingertip before springing back. Top with rose syrup and garnishes just before serving.
Overdone: Pudding is very hard and stiff, like a rubber ball. Does not jiggle at all. Over-starched or too much cooling time. Serve anyway — the flavor is unaffected. Increase ratio of cream to milk next time for a more delicate set.
Feel cue: Tilt the cup gently — the pudding should slide fractionally and then catch itself, like a very firm blancmange, not like gelatin.

Combine sugar and water in a small saucepan over medium heat. Stir until the sugar dissolves then bring to a simmer for 3 minutes without stirring. Remove from heat and stir in rose water and pomegranate molasses or grenadine. The syrup should be a soft blush-pink or dusty rose color. Cool to room temperature — do not pour hot syrup over the cold pudding or it will melt the surface and create a watery pool. The contrast between the cold white pudding and the fragrant rose syrup is the entire point.
Visual cue: A clear, pale rose-pink syrup that runs freely off a spoon in a thin thread. Fragrant with roses and just faintly tart from the pomegranate.
Underdone: Syrup is thin and watery; it runs instantly off the spoon with no body. Return to heat and simmer 2 more minutes to concentrate slightly.
Perfect: Lightly viscous, blush-pink, and beautifully fragrant. Coats the back of a spoon faintly. Tastes floral-sweet with a whisper of tartness. Cool to room temperature before pouring over the chilled malabi.
Overdone: Syrup is thick and candy-like — when cooled it will harden on the pudding surface rather than pool gracefully. Thin with a tablespoon of water, stir, and cool.
Feel cue: A drop of cooled syrup on your wrist should feel like rose-scented water — light and clear, not at all sticky.

Just before serving, spoon 2–3 tablespoons of the room-temperature rose syrup over each chilled malabi cup, letting it pool at the surface edges and seep slightly down the sides. Scatter roughly chopped pistachios over the center — they provide the textural contrast that makes the dessert. Add a few dried rose petals and a pinch of desiccated coconut. Serve immediately while the pudding is still cold and the garnishes are fresh and crisp. Malabi does not wait well once garnished — the nuts soften in the syrup.
Visual cue: A snow-white pudding cup wearing a crown of pink syrup with bright green pistachios, deep-red rose petals, and white coconut snow on top.
Underdone: Not enough syrup — the pudding surface looks dry and plain. Garnishes look sparse. Add more syrup; the pudding can take more than you expect without becoming overly sweet.
Perfect: The syrup pools beautifully at the top and drips attractively down the inside edge of the cup. Pistachios are vivid green, rose petals dramatic red-pink, coconut white. Visually striking. Serve immediately.
Overdone: So much syrup the pudding is drowning and the garnishes have sunk and softened. Nothing to do post-plating — serve immediately and note to use less syrup next time.
Feel cue: Tap the pudding with a spoon — it should give a faint, satisfying resistance before the spoon breaks through to the cool, silky interior.

name: Manakeesh
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=bakers_percentage）；不是经核对的人均用量。
All-purpose flour: 100 %
  Alternatives: bread flour; tipo 00
Warm water (38-40 C): 60 %
Extra-virgin olive oil: 8 %
  Alternatives: neutral oil
Instant yeast: 1.5 %
  Alternatives: active dry yeast (proof first)
Fine sea salt: 2 %
Sugar: 1 %
  Alternatives: honey (same weight)
Za'atar spice blend: 30 %
Extra-virgin olive oil (for the topping): 20 %
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 1 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Lebanon's beloved morning flatbread — pillowy yeasted dough flattened into rounds and painted with a paste of za'atar and olive oil, then baked until the edges crisp and the herb-oil bubbles into a fragrant, dark-green crust.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
In a large bowl, combine warm water, sugar, and yeast. Stir and let sit for 5 minutes if using active dry yeast (instant can go straight in with the flour). Add flour, salt, and olive oil. Mix with your hand or a wooden spoon until no dry flour remains and a shaggy, cohesive dough forms. The dough should be soft, slightly tacky, and pull together into one mass. Turn out onto an unfloured surface and knead for 6–8 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should not stick aggressively to the surface — a light tack is correct.
Visual cue: A smooth, slightly tacky ball of dough that springs back when poked. The surface is soft and slightly shiny from the olive oil. No dry patches, no tears.
Underdone: Rough, shaggy, and pulling apart when stretched. Dry flour still visible. Tears rather than stretches. Knead for 3 more minutes. The gluten network is not yet developed — the dough needs more working to become extensible and smooth.
Perfect: Smooth, supple, slightly tacky surface. Pulls away cleanly from the work surface with each push. Springs back when poked. Form into a ball, oil the bowl lightly, cover, and let rise in a warm spot.
Overdone: Dough is tight, rubbery, and resists every stretch. Bounces back aggressively when poked — over-kneaded gluten. Let it rest uncovered on the bench for 15 minutes to relax before rounding and proofing. Over-kneaded dough bakes fine, just needs rest.
Feel cue: Take a small piece of dough and stretch it gently between two hands — after proper kneading it should stretch into a thin, semi-transparent membrane without tearing. This windowpane test confirms gluten development.

Form the dough into a smooth ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, and cover with a damp cloth or plastic wrap. Proof in a warm spot (28–32 C) for 45–60 minutes, until doubled in size. Street bakers in Beirut do a single warm rise at 40 C for 30 minutes; home bakers can also proof in a cold fridge overnight for a better flavour and a slower rise. The dough is ready when it looks puffy and jiggly and a finger poke leaves a slow-filling indent.
Visual cue: A rounded, dome-shaped mass that has clearly doubled in volume — the dough fills the bowl where before it sat in the bottom third. The surface is smooth and slightly translucent where large bubbles push outward.
Underdone: Dough is barely 25% larger. Dense, heavy, resistant when poked — the finger indent fills back immediately. Smells only of flour and yeast, not yet fermented. Cover and wait. A cold room stalls yeast dramatically. Move the bowl to a warmer location: on top of the oven, in a turned-off oven with just the light on, or in a bowl of warm water.
Perfect: Doubled, jiggly, dome-topped, and smelling lightly of beer and fresh bread. A poke leaves a slow-filling dimple that returns about halfway in 5 seconds. Divide and shape immediately — the dough is at peak gas retention and will spread beautifully.
Overdone: The dome has collapsed back into a flat, spreading mass. The dough smells sharply alcoholic. The surface may be slightly sticky and clings to the bowl. Deflate, reshape, and bake as soon as possible. Overproofed manakeesh will still taste good — sour and complex — but will be harder to shape thinly without tearing.
Feel cue: Press a floured fingertip 1 cm into the proofed dough and watch the indent. It should fill back slowly, about halfway in 5 seconds, then stop. This is the perfect gas-retention moment — the gluten is relaxed but the yeast hasn't exhausted the sugar.

Combine za'atar spice blend and olive oil in a small bowl and stir into a thick, spreadable paste. The ratio should be roughly 3 parts za'atar to 2 parts oil — thick enough to coat a spoon and not run freely, but fluid enough to spread easily without tearing the dough. Taste the paste: it should be assertively herby, sour, and savory. Add more za'atar if it tastes only of oil; add more oil if it clumps dryly. Let the paste rest for 2 minutes for the herbs to hydrate slightly.
Visual cue: A thick, dark olive-green paste that falls from a spoon in a slow, lumpy drizzle rather than flowing like a liquid. The sesame seeds are visible throughout, suspended in the herb-oil.
Underdone: Too much oil — the paste runs freely and pools on the surface. It will slide off the dough and puddle at the edges rather than coating the bread. Add more za'atar a teaspoon at a time until the paste thickens to the right consistency. You need it to hold its position on the dough.
Perfect: Spreadable but not runny — applies like a thick jam. Clings to the back of a spoon. The oil coats the herbs without drowning them. Use immediately. The paste settles if left too long — stir before spreading on each round.
Overdone: Too much za'atar — the paste is dry and crumbly, stiff on the spoon, and will tear the dough surface when spread. Stir in more olive oil a teaspoon at a time until spreadable. The za'atar should be well-wetted with oil for even cooking.
Feel cue: Spread a small amount on the back of your hand with a butter knife — it should glide smoothly and leave a uniform, fragrant green-red coating, not drag and clump. The hand should smell like an herb garden after rain.

Preheat your oven to its maximum temperature — 250–270 C — with a baking stone or heavy baking sheet on the center rack for at least 30 minutes. Divide the proofed dough into equal balls (about 150 g each for individual portions). On a lightly floured surface, press and stretch each ball into a round disc 5–6 mm thick and roughly 20 cm in diameter. The edge should be slightly thicker than the center. Spoon 2–3 tablespoons of za'atar paste onto the center of each round and use the back of the spoon to spread it to within 1 cm of the edge in an even layer.
Visual cue: A thin, round disc of dough with a generous, even layer of dark green za'atar paste covering the surface to within 1 cm of the edge. The dough edge is a bare, pale rim that will puff and brown as it bakes.
Underdone: Dough is only 1 cm thick and hasn't been spread thin. The za'atar paste is in a blob in the center rather than spread evenly. The round is misshapen and thick. Press and stretch more aggressively — use the knuckles of both hands to stretch from the center outward. Spread the topping to the edge before baking.
Perfect: 5–6 mm thin round, even za'atar coverage right to the edge, a bare rim. The whole piece is about the size of a salad plate. Transfer to a hot baking stone or sheet immediately — the dough will begin to relax and puff slightly on the bench.
Overdone: Dough has been stretched paper-thin and tears through in the center. Za'atar paste applied so thick it's mounded at the center. Gently press the tear together and use less topping. A mound of za'atar paste will be raw and oily in the center while the edges burn.
Feel cue: Lift the topped manakeesh by the edge — it should flex but not droop completely through; a little sag is fine, but if it stretches and tears under its own weight, the dough is too thin. The za'atar layer should feel slightly tacky to a fingertip pressed on it, not
wet.

Slide the topped manakeesh onto the screaming-hot baking stone or preheated sheet. Bake at maximum oven heat for 6–8 minutes, until the edges are golden-brown and crisped, the za'atar paste is bubbling and fragrant, and the underside is golden-brown and pulls away from the surface with a crunch. The za'atar topping will darken noticeably — this is expected and correct. Serve immediately: manakeesh is a bread that must be eaten hot, folded in half like a soft taco, and consumed within minutes of baking.
Visual cue: Golden-brown, slightly charred edges. The za'atar topping is a deep, glistening dark green — bubbly at the edges where the oil has toasted into the bread. The underside is firm and crisp, not pale or soft.
Underdone: Edges are pale blond, the za'atar topping looks wet and raw, and the underside is soft and white. The bread bends without resistance. Return to the oven for 2–3 more minutes. Manakeesh needs high heat quickly — a hot oven is non-negotiable for a crunchy edge and properly cooked topping.
Perfect: Golden-brown rim, fragrant dark green topping with bubbled oil at the edges, crisp underside that lifts cleanly from the stone. The kitchen smells of toasted thyme and olive oil. Remove and serve immediately, folded in half or flat with fresh tomatoes and white cheese tucked inside.
Overdone: The edges are dark brown to black, the za'atar topping has gone from green to near-black with a sharp, burnt herb smell rather than a toasty one. Trim the burnt edge with a knife or scissors. The center is likely fine. A splash of fresh lemon juice on the too-dark topping helps cut the bitterness.
Feel cue: Pick up the baked manakeesh by its edge — it should be crisp enough to hold its shape horizontally for a few seconds before bending. Fold it in half to eat: the inside should steam gently against your hand, the za'atar paste fragrant and warm, the edge crackling
satisfyingly between your teeth.

name: Mango Chutney
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

  Alternatives: cane sugar; jaggery
White wine vinegar: 25 parts
  Alternatives: cider vinegar; malt vinegar

Garlic (finely minced): 3 parts
Dried red chili flakes: 1 parts
  Alternatives: fresh red chili, minced; cayenne
Ground cumin: 1 parts
Ground coriander: 1 parts
Fine salt: 1.5 parts

Active time: 20 min
Total time: 1 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Diced mango cooked down with vinegar, sugar, ginger, and chili into a thick, jammy preserve — sweet-sharp-spiced and golden, equally at home with cheese, cold meats, or alongside curry.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Firm ripe mango (peeled, diced into 1 cm cubes)

steps:
Combine the diced mango, sugar, vinegar, ginger, garlic, chili flakes, cumin, coriander, salt, and water in a wide, heavy-based saucepan. Stir together over medium heat until the sugar dissolves — 2 to 3 minutes. The mango will begin to release its own juice into the syrup.
Visual cue: A slick, golden-syrup pool surrounding the mango cubes, bubbling gently at the edges. The sugar has dissolved and you see no granules.
Underdone: Sugar granules still visible, mixture looks cloudy and stiff. Keep stirring over medium heat until the sugar is fully dissolved before raising the temperature.
Perfect: Clear, pale amber liquid surrounding the mango pieces; first gentle bubbles forming at the edge of the pan. Raise heat to a steady simmer and proceed to the cook-down step.
Overdone: Heat was too high before dissolving — syrup is already reducing unevenly around raw-tasting mango. Lower the heat and add a splash of water to slow the reduction while the mango catches up.
Feel cue: The spoon should move easily through the mixture. No gritty resistance from undissolved sugar.

Raise the heat until the chutney reaches a rolling simmer, then reduce to medium-low. Cook uncovered, stirring every 5 minutes, for 30 to 40 minutes. The mango will gradually break down: the outer flesh collapses into the syrup while some cubes hold their shape. You are driving off water and concentrating the sugars into a jammy preserve.
Visual cue: A deeply golden, jammy mass — some mango cubes intact, others dissolved into a glossy, thick sauce. The surface sputters with slow, heavy bubbles rather than a vigorous rolling boil.
Underdone: Still watery and pourable; the mango looks parboiled and pale, not jammy. The spoon leaves a trail that instantly fills back in. Continue simmering uncovered; it needs more time to reduce. Stir more frequently to prevent sticking at the base.
Perfect: Thick and slow-moving, a deep amber gold. A spoon dragged across the base leaves a clean trail that holds for 3 to 4 seconds. Mango is translucent and deeply flavoured. Remove from heat. The chutney thickens further as it cools — do not over-reduce.
Overdone: Dark brown, sticky, and very stiff. The chutney is catching on the base and smells of burnt sugar. The mango has completely disintegrated. Pull off the heat immediately and add a splash of vinegar or water to loosen, stirring vigorously to rescue the texture.
Feel cue: Tilt the pan — the chutney should flow slowly like warm honey, not slosh like water. When it barely moves under its own weight, it is done.

Taste the chutney while still warm. The balance you are looking for is sweet first, then a clean sharp note of vinegar, and a background warmth from the chili and ginger. Adjust with a pinch more salt to sharpen the other flavours, a splash of vinegar if it tastes flat or cloying, or a pinch of chili if you want more heat. The flavours will meld and deepen over 24 hours.
Visual cue: A glossy, translucent amber-gold chutney with a rich, jammy sheen. The surface holds its shape when you press the back of the spoon gently against it.
Underdone: Tastes sharp and one-dimensional — too much raw vinegar edge, insufficient depth from the sugar caramelizing. Return to a gentle simmer for 5 more minutes to mellow the acid and integrate the sweetness.
Perfect: Sweet, sharp, warmly spiced, and complex. No single note dominates. A hint of lingering chili warmth in the throat. Pour into sterilised jars while still hot, or allow to cool before refrigerating.
Overdone: Tastes flat, cloying, and one-dimensional — the acidity has been cooked off and the sugar dominates. Stir in a measured tablespoon of vinegar and a pinch of salt off the heat to restore the brightness.
Feel cue: Touch a small spoonful to the back of your wrist — it should feel thick and warm, cooling quickly to a sticky-jammy texture rather than running off like a sauce.

Ladle the hot chutney into sterilised glass jars, filling to within 1 cm of the rim. Seal immediately with sterilised lids. As the chutney cools the lid will dimple inward, creating a vacuum seal. Unopened, the chutney keeps for up to a year in a cool, dark place. Once opened, refrigerate and use within 8 weeks. The flavour improves significantly after resting for 48 hours as the spices fully integrate.
Visual cue: Jars filled with a jewel-gold, thick, jammy chutney with visible mango pieces and no air pockets. Lids sealed with a soft dimple inward after cooling.
Underdone: Chutney is too liquid — it will pool in the jar with the solids floating and a watery syrup layer forming below. Return to the pan and simmer a further 10 minutes before re-potting.
Perfect: Thick enough to hold its shape in the jar but with an even distribution of mango throughout. Lid seals cleanly on cooling. Label with the date and rest for at least 48 hours before opening.
Overdone: Chutney is so thick it is hard to ladle — it has set near-solid in the pan. Warm gently with a splash of vinegar to loosen before potting, or serve as a thick spread rather than a pourable condiment.
Feel cue: Press the sealed lid once cool — it should not flex. A drum-tight, concave lid means a good seal. If it still flexes after 30 minutes, the jar has not sealed; refrigerate and use first.

name: Mango Lassi
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Ripe Alphonso mango pulp (fresh or canned Kesar): 2 parts
  Alternatives: ripe Ataulfo mango; frozen mango chunks, thawed
Full-fat plain yogurt, cold: 2 parts
  Alternatives: whole-milk kefir; coconut yogurt
Whole milk, cold: 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: cold water for lighter body
Sugar or honey: 0.1 parts
  Alternatives: agave nectar
Ground cardamom (freshly ground from green pods): 0.01 parts
  Alternatives: a strip of cardamom steeped and removed

Active time: 5 min
Total time: 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The chilled Punjabi yogurt drink made with ripe Alphonso mango — thick, sweet, and faintly tart, with the dairy's richness cooling the palate like nothing else on a hot day.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Ripe Alphonso mango pulp (fresh or canned Kesar)
Ground cardamom (freshly ground from green pods)
Pinch of saffron threads, bloomed in 1 tsp warm milk

steps:
Crumble a small pinch of saffron threads into one teaspoon of warm (not boiling) milk or water. Stir and leave to steep for 5 minutes. The liquid will turn golden-orange and the room will fill with a faintly floral, honeyed scent. This brief blooming extracts both the color and the aroma compounds that a blender alone cannot release. If using canned mango pulp (which is already deep golden), you can skip this step — the saffron is primarily a luxury flourish.
Visual cue: The small amount of milk has turned a vivid golden-orange from the saffron; the threads themselves have softened and release color evenly when stirred.
Underdone: Liquid is still pale; saffron threads look dry and have not fully released color. Wait another 2–3 minutes; the blooming is passive — do not rush it with boiling liquid.
Perfect: Vivid golden-orange liquid; threads are plump and stained pale orange; aroma is distinctly floral and saffron-sweet. Set aside until blending.
Overdone: Liquid has cooled; no harm done — saffron does not burn in liquid. Oversteeping in warm liquid only deepens the color slightly. Use as-is.
Feel cue: A properly bloomed saffron suspension smells like warm honey meeting a wildflower meadow — a scent that feels expensive and sunny. If you smell nothing, the saffron may be old or adulterated.

Combine the mango pulp, cold yogurt, cold milk, sugar, cardamom, and rose water in a blender. Add the bloomed saffron and all its liquid. Blend on high for 60–90 seconds until completely smooth, frothy, and homogeneous. Taste and adjust: add more sugar if the mango is tart, more yogurt if you want a thicker, more tangy result, or a splash more milk if you prefer it to pour like a drink rather than be eaten with a spoon. Serve immediately or refrigerate for up to an hour — longer and the foam collapses and the mango can separate.
Visual cue: A thick, frothy, vivid golden-orange drink with a rich foam cap; no visible lumps of mango or streaks of white yogurt; color is uniform mango-gold.
Underdone: Mixture is lumpy; white yogurt streaks visible; blender ran for too short a time. Blend for another 30–60 seconds on high until perfectly smooth.
Perfect: Thick, homogeneous, golden, and foamy; pours slowly; tastes balanced between sweet mango and tangy yogurt with a floral cardamom lift. Pour into tall glasses over ice or serve chilled as-is.
Overdone: Blended so long the foam has already started to deflate; temperature has risen and the lassi tastes warm and flat. Add a small handful of ice, blend for 10 seconds to re-chill and re-froth.
Feel cue: The lassi should pour like a thick milkshake — not as watery as juice, not as solid as smoothie. It should coat the inside of the glass slightly before sliding down. A good lassi sits on your palate for a moment before cooling the throat.

If serving immediately, pour into chilled glasses over a few cubes of ice. If making ahead, transfer to a pitcher, cover, and refrigerate for up to 1 hour. Give the pitcher a vigorous shake or a 10-second re-blend before pouring, as the mango pulp and yogurt can settle in layers. The lassi should arrive at the table cold enough to fog the glass — its entire purpose is thermal relief.
Visual cue: A tall, fogged glass of dense golden drink; condensation forming on the outside; a faint froth cap of pale foam; color a rich saffron-mango gold.
Underdone: Lassi is room temperature or only slightly cool; foam has collapsed; glass is not cold. Add ice and refrigerate the glasses for 5 minutes before serving.
Perfect: Deeply cold, condensation on the glass, still frothy at the top, vivid golden color. Serve at once and drink slowly.
Overdone: Separated after more than 2 hours in the fridge; top layer is thin and watery, mango solids sunken. Re-blend for 20 seconds to recombine before serving.
Feel cue: Hold the glass for a moment — you should feel the chill immediately through the glass. On the first sip, the cold hits first, then sweetness blooms, then the yogurt tang arrives at the back of the throat. That sequence is the whole point.

name: Thai Mango Sticky Rice
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Glutinous (sweet) rice, soaked 2+ hours and drained: 100 parts
Full-fat coconut milk: 80 parts
  Alternatives: coconut cream (dilute slightly)
Palm sugar or light brown sugar: 25 parts
  Alternatives: white sugar; coconut sugar
Fine sea salt: 2 parts
  Alternatives: kosher salt
Ripe Ataulfo (honey) mangoes, peeled and sliced: 80 parts
  Alternatives: Nam Dok Mai mango; ripe Alphonso mango
Toasted sesame seeds: 3 parts
  Alternatives: toasted mung beans
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 1 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Glossy, coconut-drenched sticky rice crowned with sweet ripe mango and a trickle of salted coconut cream — the summer dessert that tastes of Bangkok's night markets at their best.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Glutinous (sweet) rice, soaked 2+ hours and drained
Palm sugar or light brown sugar
Ripe Ataulfo (honey) mangoes, peeled and sliced

steps:
Cover the raw glutinous rice with cold water by at least 5 cm and soak for a minimum of 2 hours, ideally overnight. Drain completely through a fine-mesh sieve before steaming. Do not skip this step — soaking allows the rice to steam evenly all the way through without drying out.
Visual cue: Rice grains are swollen and opaque white throughout, with no visible dry cores. They feel soft when pressed between your fingers but still hold their shape.
Underdone: Grains still translucent or chalky at the center when held to the light. Snap when pressed. Soak longer. Inadequately soaked grains steam unevenly, giving a gummy exterior with a hard, chewy core.
Perfect: Uniformly opaque white grains that yield softly under finger pressure without crumbling. Drain through a fine sieve and proceed to steaming.
Overdone: Grains have begun to break down, releasing starch into the soaking water which is now milky and thick. Drain immediately. Over-soaked rice will steam to mush, but proceed — the flavor will be fine.
Feel cue: A fully soaked grain pressed between the thumb and finger should give with barely any resistance — soft, but still whole.

Line a bamboo or metal steamer basket with damp cheesecloth or a banana leaf. Spread the drained rice in an even layer no more than 4 cm deep. Steam over briskly boiling water for 20–25 minutes, flipping the rice mass halfway through. The rice is done when the grains are translucent, sticky, and tender all the way through.
Visual cue: Grains are fully translucent — no white, chalky centers visible. The mass is cohesive and glossy, clinging together in a soft, sticky slab.
Underdone: Centers still white and opaque. Grains feel firm and separate when tossed. Continue steaming 5 more minutes. Uncooked glutinous rice has an unpleasant raw starch texture.
Perfect: Fully translucent, evenly sticky, the grains hold together but can be separated cleanly with a spoon. Steam rising freely from the mass. Transfer immediately to a bowl and fold in the hot coconut cream.
Overdone: Rice has collapsed into a gluey, formless mass. Sticking heavily to the cloth. Proceed — overcooked sticky rice is still delicious, just denser. Use a wet spatula to fold in the coconut cream.
Feel cue: A pinch of steamed sticky rice should cling to itself and to your fingers with a satisfying, elastic pull — not wet and slick, not dry and falling apart.

Combine the coconut milk, sugar, and salt in a small saucepan. Warm over medium-low heat, stirring, until the sugar and salt are fully dissolved. Do not boil — you want a warm, fluid cream, not a reduced sauce. Reserve 4 tablespoons of this liquid in a small bowl to use as the thin drizzle sauce for plating; keep the rest warm.
Visual cue: A smooth, lightly steaming liquid with no visible sugar grains. The cream should be fluid and just beginning to release steam — not simmering.
Underdone: Sugar grains still visible catching the light. Liquid is cold or room temperature. Stir and warm further over low heat until you can no longer feel graininess when rubbing the spoon on the pan.
Perfect: Smooth, silky, faintly sweet and salty cream that coats the spoon lightly. Just warm to the touch — not scalding. Fold immediately into the hot steamed rice. The heat of the rice and the warm cream work together.
Overdone: Coconut milk has boiled and separated — visible pale watery liquid with a yellowish fat layer on top. Whisk vigorously to re-emulsify, then cool slightly before using. The flavor is unaffected but the texture will be slightly oilier.
Feel cue: Dip a fingertip — the cream should feel warm and silky, coating the skin lightly. It should taste distinctly salty-sweet in balance, not purely sweet.

Transfer the hot steamed rice to a wide bowl. Pour the warm seasoned coconut cream (reserving the 4 tbsp set aside earlier) over the rice all at once. Fold gently with a wooden spoon or rice paddle — cut through the center and fold the sides over, rotating. Don't stir vigorously or the rice will turn gluey.
Visual cue: Rice grains are evenly coated and glistening, the mass is cohesive and glossy. No pools of unabsorbed cream sitting at the bottom of the bowl.
Underdone: Coconut cream still pools at the bottom. Some grains dry and uncoated. Continue folding gently. The hot rice needs more turning to absorb the liquid evenly.
Perfect: Uniformly glossy rice that holds together in a soft mound. All cream absorbed. The mass is fragrant with coconut. Cover tightly with a lid or plastic wrap and rest 15 minutes.
Overdone: Over-folded — rice has become a gluey, uniform paste. Lost individual grain definition. Proceed. Over-worked sticky rice is less elegant but the flavor is the same. Don't fold further.
Feel cue: The dressed rice should feel heavy and yielding in the spoon — rich with absorbed coconut cream, not liquidy, not dry.

Cover the bowl tightly and rest for 15 minutes at room temperature. This allows the rice to fully absorb the coconut cream and the texture to stabilize — freshly dressed rice is too soft and wet to plate neatly.
Visual cue: Rice has firmed slightly into a cohesive, moldable mass. The surface is glossy and the cream is no longer visibly liquid.
Underdone: Rice is still very wet, cream runs when the bowl is tilted. Cover and rest longer. 15 minutes is the minimum — 20 is fine.
Perfect: Rice holds its shape when scooped with a spoon, with a gently yielding, almost set texture. Fragrant, glossy, and cohesive. Plate immediately or hold warm for up to 30 minutes.
Overdone: Rice has cooled fully and stiffened into a dense block, losing its yielding, molten quality. Warm briefly over the steamer basket for 2–3 minutes to restore texture.
Feel cue: The rested rice should give slightly when pressed with a spoon — yielding, not stiff, with a gentle spring-back. It holds a mold but isn't rubbery.

Mound a generous portion of warm sticky rice onto a shallow plate or bowl. Arrange sliced mango alongside or fanning over the rice. Drizzle the reserved thin coconut sauce (the 4 tbsp set aside in step 3) over the rice and mango. Scatter sesame seeds over the top. Serve immediately.
Visual cue: A glistening mound of ivory coconut rice beside vivid golden-yellow mango slices, threaded with a thin coconut drizzle and flecked with toasted sesame.
Underdone: Mango is unripe — pale yellow or green, firm, sour, lacking fragrance. Use a riper mango. Ataulfo mangoes are ready when the skin is slightly wrinkled at the shoulders and the fruit yields under gentle thumb pressure.
Perfect: Deep golden mango, fragrant and juicy, in contrast to the glistening ivory rice. A thin, fluid coconut drizzle pools around the rice. Serve at once — the warm rice and cold mango contrast is the point of the dish.
Overdone: Rice has cooled and stiffened, mango has oxidized and browned, coconut drizzle has congealed. This dish does not hold well. Prep just before serving; do not assemble ahead.
Feel cue: The mango should yield under a fork like very ripe butter — silky, not fibrous. The warm rice against cool mango creates the essential temperature contrast that makes this dessert.
