ingredients.name: All-purpose flour or low-protein Chinese white flour (medium gluten)

steps:
Dissolve the sugar in the warm milk, then add the yeast and let it bloom for 5 minutes until foamy. Combine with the flour and salt in a bowl. Bring together into a rough dough, then turn out and knead for 10-12 minutes by hand, or 6-8 minutes in a stand mixer with a dough hook, until perfectly smooth and elastic. Add the oil in the last 2 minutes of kneading. Unlike bread dough, mantou dough should be dry enough to handle without sticking — if it sticks, dust with flour, not water.
Visual cue: A smooth, slightly tacky dough with a matte surface — no rough patches, no tears, and no stickiness. When pulled, it stretches without tearing.
Underdone: Dough surface is rough, tears easily, and feels dense and inelastic. Windowpane test fails. Continue kneading for 3-5 more minutes; the gluten needs more development.
Perfect: Dough is smooth as a baby's cheek, springs back when poked, and passes the windowpane test — stretched thin, a translucent membrane holds without tearing. Form into a ball, cover, and proof.
Overdone: Dough is very tight, springs back aggressively, and is warm to the touch from overworking. Cover and rest for 15 minutes to allow the gluten to relax before shaping.
Feel cue: Well-kneaded mantou dough feels alive in your hands — smooth, resilient, and slightly warm from the friction of kneading, with a faint, clean yeast fragrance.

Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a damp cloth, and proof in a warm place (28-30 C) for 60 minutes, or until doubled in size. Do not rush this proof — a slow, even rise develops a more uniform, finely bubbled crumb than a fast one.
Visual cue: Dough has visibly doubled in size; pressing a floured finger into the center leaves an indent that slowly (not immediately) fills back about halfway.
Underdone: Dough has barely grown; poke test indent fills back immediately and springily. Return to a warmer spot and wait; yeast needs consistent warmth above 25 C.
Perfect: Clearly doubled, dough is pillowy and light, the poke leaves a gentle indent that slowly recovers; the interior when torn shows a fine web of small bubbles. Punch down gently and shape.
Overdone: Dough has more than doubled and smells strongly of yeast alcohol; poke indent does not recover at all. Punch down and shape immediately; buns may be slightly denser but are still good.
Feel cue: A properly proofed mantou dough feels like a cloud — feather-light and airy under gentle pressure, with a faint yeasty-sweet fragrance.

Turn the dough out onto a clean surface. Roll it into a flat rectangle about 1 cm thick. Roll it up tightly from one short end into a log — this lamination creates the layered internal structure. Cut the log into 6-8 equal oval portions. Place each bun cut-side up on a small square of parchment paper. Cover with a damp cloth and let rest for 25-30 minutes for the second proof.
Visual cue: Shaped buns that are smooth on top, slightly domed, and visibly puffier than when first cut; the spiral pattern of the lamination is visible on the cut ends.
Underdone: Buns look dense and flat; they have not relaxed and risen after shaping. Give them more time — 10-15 more minutes of resting; cold kitchen slows this proof.
Perfect: Buns are plump and lightly domed; they jiggle gently when the tray is moved; the surface is smooth and slightly taut. Steam immediately over already-boiling water.
Overdone: Buns are over-proofed and very puffy with a wrinkled, loose surface skin. Steam immediately; do not wait any longer or they may collapse during steaming.
Feel cue: A correctly proofed mantou bun feels like a soft balloon — gentle pressure compresses it and it springs back slowly, full of the gas that will give it its signature pillow-soft texture.

Bring the steamer water to a rolling boil before placing the buns inside. Leave 3-4 cm space between each bun as they expand. Cover with a tight lid and steam over high heat for 12-15 minutes depending on size. Critical: do not lift the lid during steaming. When the time is up, turn off the heat and leave the lid on for 5 full minutes before opening — the rest prevents the sudden temperature drop that causes the surface to shrink and wrinkle.
Visual cue: Perfectly white, smooth-surfaced buns that have expanded by about 30% and look uniformly plump with no wrinkling, pitting, or yellowing.
Underdone: Buns are slightly dense and the dough feels gummy at the center when prodded; surface may have small damp patches. Re-cover and steam for 2-3 more minutes.
Perfect: Buns are pure white, shiny, and perfectly smooth; they spring back immediately when pressed with a finger; the interior is fine-crumbed, soft, and slightly sweet. Serve immediately or allow to cool and reheat by steaming 3-5 minutes.
Overdone: Surface is wrinkled and pitted; buns have shrunk slightly — the lid was lifted too soon and cold air hit the hot surface. They taste fine; the wrinkling is only cosmetic — re-steam for 2 minutes to partially smooth the surface.
Feel cue: A properly steamed mantou feels impossibly light for its size — like holding a warm cloud — and pressing it gently leaves a fingertip impression that almost instantly bounces back to a perfect dome.

name: Mantu
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
All-purpose flour: 6 parts
Warm water: 2.5 parts
Fine sea salt (for dough): 0.15 parts
Ground beef (20% fat): 5 parts
  Alternatives: ground lamb
Yellow onion, finely diced: 4 parts
Ground coriander: 0.3 parts
Ground cumin: 0.3 parts
Cayenne pepper: 0.2 parts
Fine sea salt (for filling): 0.3 parts
Full-fat plain yogurt: 4 parts
Garlic, minced: 0.5 parts
Dried mint: 0.2 parts
Active time: 90 min
Total time: 3 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Afghan steamed dumplings filled with spiced ground beef and caramelized onion, served over a pool of split-pea sauce and tangy yogurt, then crowned with dried mint and a blushing thread of tomato.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine flour and salt, make a well, and pour in the warm water gradually, mixing with a fork until a shaggy dough forms. Turn onto a work surface and knead for 8-10 minutes until smooth, elastic, and not sticky. Mantu dough should be slightly stiffer than pasta dough — it needs to hold its pleats under the pressure of steaming. Form into a ball, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and rest for at least 45 minutes.
Visual cue: A smooth, taut dough ball that springs back slowly when indented — slightly stiffer than an earlobe.
Underdone: Dough is shaggy, tears when pulled, and sticks to hands. Knead for another 3-5 minutes, adding flour by the teaspoon only if essential.
Perfect: Smooth, slightly tacky but not sticky. When you pull a piece, it stretches without immediately tearing. Springs back halfway when poked. Cover and rest 45 minutes minimum.
Overdone: Dough is very firm and has become elastic and resistant — snaps back instantly. Rest covered for 30 minutes. Over-kneaded gluten needs time to relax before rolling.
Feel cue: After kneading, press your thumb into the center — it should leave a clean indent that slowly fills back halfway over about 10 seconds. That slow recovery is the gluten working.

In a wide skillet, cook the diced onion in a small amount of oil over medium heat, stirring frequently, for 15-20 minutes until deeply caramelized and sweet — golden-brown, not pale. Add the ground beef, breaking it into fine crumbles, and cook until no pink remains. Add the spices and salt, stir for 2 minutes, then taste. The filling should be highly seasoned, as the dumpling dough dilutes the flavor. Spread on a plate to cool completely before filling.
Visual cue: A dark, fragrant filling of fine-crumbled beef and deep golden onion — no pink meat, no pooled oil.
Underdone: Onions are pale and translucent; beef is just-cooked without any browning. The filling will taste bland inside the wrapper. Cook longer over medium heat. The caramelization of the onion is essential to the sweetness of mantu.
Perfect: Onions are deeply golden-brown. Beef is fully cooked with some slightly crisp edges. Spices smell toasted and warm. Spread to cool. Do not fill dumplings with warm filling — it steams the dough from inside.
Overdone: Onions are starting to char and the beef is dry. Add a tablespoon of water to the pan, stir, and remove from heat.
Feel cue: Press the filling between your fingers — it should hold together slightly when pressed (from the fat) but crumble apart freely. No pink, no raw smell.

Divide the rested dough into manageable portions. On a lightly floured surface, roll each portion as thin as possible — aim for 2mm, almost translucent. Cut into squares of 8-10cm. Mantu wrappers are slightly thicker than Chinese dumpling wrappers to withstand steaming, but thin enough to be delicate. Keep cut wrappers under a damp cloth.
Visual cue: Thin, even squares of dough that flex and drape when lifted, with slight translucency.
Underdone: Dough is thick and opaque — more than 3mm. Cooked mantu will have a doughy, bread-like wrapper. Roll thinner. Use a long pasta-style rolling pin and roll from the center outward.
Perfect: Thin and slightly translucent when held to the light, but not paper-thin — it should not tear when folded. Even thickness across the square. Keep under damp cloth and fill promptly.
Overdone: Dough rolled too thin — tearing when handled. Set these aside for irregular dumplings. Re-roll the scraps slightly thicker.
Feel cue: Lift a wrapper and drape it over your hand — it should fall with its own weight and cling softly to your palm, like a silk handkerchief.

Place a generous teaspoon of cooled filling in the center of each square — do not overfill or the pleats will split. The traditional mantu fold: bring all four corners up to meet at the top, then pinch the four seams shut, creating a 'four-petal' shape with a gathered top. Press the seams firmly so no steam can escape during cooking. Place formed mantu on a lightly oiled surface.
Visual cue: Compact, well-sealed square parcels with four pleated seams meeting at a gathered top — like a small wrapped gift.
Underdone: Seams are not firmly sealed — gaps visible when the dumpling is gently squeezed. Wet your fingertip with water and re-press the seam firmly. Unsealed mantu burst open in the steamer.
Perfect: Firm, compact parcels with all seams tightly pinched. They hold their shape when placed on the tray. A slight dome from the filling. Place on oiled steamer basket immediately.
Overdone: Wrappers have dried out from sitting too long — they are cracking at the pleats. Brush with water to rehydrate the dough, then re-seal the cracked areas.
Feel cue: Squeeze a formed mantu very gently — if it feels firm and yields only slightly, the filling is correct. If it feels flabby or the seams gap, there is too much air inside.

Stir together the yogurt, minced garlic, and a pinch of salt in a small saucepan. Warm very gently over the lowest possible heat, stirring constantly — yogurt must never boil or it will curdle. The goal is warmed through, not hot: 40-45 C (104-113 F). Taste and adjust salt. The sauce should be pourable and smooth.
Visual cue: A warm, smooth, ivory-white sauce that pours in a thin, even stream.
Underdone: Yogurt is still cold and thick — it will chill the mantu immediately. Warm further over the lowest heat, stirring constantly.
Perfect: Warm to the touch, fluid, no graininess. Smells gently of garlic and clean dairy. Keep warm off the heat until the mantu are steamed.
Overdone: Yogurt has curdled — grainy, separated, with whey pooling. There is no recovery for curdled yogurt sauce. Start fresh, keeping temperature below a simmer.
Feel cue: Dip a finger — the yogurt sauce should feel warm but not hot, the way you would test baby formula temperature on your wrist.

Oil the steamer basket generously to prevent sticking. Place mantu with space between each — they expand as they steam. Steam over vigorously boiling water for 20-22 minutes until the wrappers are translucent and cooked through, not gummy. To serve: spread warmed garlic yogurt on the plate, arrange the steamed mantu on top, and finish with a drizzle of olive oil, a shower of dried mint, and optionally a spoonful of tomato-based chili oil. The mantu arrive at the table glistening.
Visual cue: Translucent, glistening dumplings with no white floury spots — fully cooked wrapper that clings to the filling.
Underdone: Wrapper is still white and slightly opaque, with a raw-flour taste when bitten. Steam for 3-5 more minutes. Check the water level — it may have run low.
Perfect: Wrappers are fully translucent and glossy with steam. The filling inside has set and holds the shape. A bite reveals juicy, fragrant beef within. Serve immediately over yogurt sauce with mint and olive oil.
Overdone: Wrappers have become very soft and are beginning to split — over-steamed. Serve immediately and handle gently. The flavor is still excellent.
Feel cue: A properly steamed mantu pressed gently between finger and thumb should give with slight resistance then feel soft — the wrapper should cling to your finger for a moment.

name: Maple Bourbon Glaze
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Pure maple syrup (Grade A dark, robust taste): 4 parts
  Alternatives: Grade A amber (lighter flavor); honey (floral but works)
Straight bourbon (100-proof preferred for flavor retention after cooking): 2 parts
  Alternatives: rye whiskey (spicier); apple cider (non-alcoholic, add 1 tsp lemon juice)
Soy sauce: 1 parts
  Alternatives: fish sauce (more umami, less clean); Worcestershire sauce
Whole-grain or Dijon mustard: 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: smooth Dijon (finer texture); English mustard (sharper)
Garlic (minced fine): 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: garlic powder (large pinch)
Fine sea salt and cracked black pepper: 0.25 parts
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Dark amber maple syrup and straight bourbon reduce together into a lacquer of extraordinary depth — the alcohol strips the raw sweetness and leaves behind toffee, vanilla, and oak that clings to pork ribs, caramelizes on Brussels sprouts, and gives roasted salmon a glassy, sweet-bitter finish. A spoon of Dijon and a pinch of salt tie it together.

ingredients.name: Pure maple syrup (Grade A dark, robust taste)
Straight bourbon (100-proof preferred for flavor retention after cooking)
Fine sea salt and cracked black pepper

steps:
Whisk together the maple syrup, bourbon, soy sauce, mustard, garlic, salt, and pepper in a small saucepan until fully combined and smooth. The mustard will need a few extra seconds of whisking to fully integrate. Taste the raw mixture — it will be intensely sweet with raw alcohol and sharp mustard. These edges will round significantly during cooking.
Visual cue: A smooth, dark amber liquid with no visible separation or mustard clumps. The bourbon will lighten the color of the maple slightly.
Underdone: Mustard clumps are still visible and the mixture is separated — oil from the mustard floating on top. Whisk more vigorously until fully emulsified and smooth.
Perfect: Uniform deep amber, smooth and flowing. Smells of raw bourbon and sweet maple with a sharp mustard note. Place over medium heat.
Overdone: Nothing can be overdone in mixing — proceed to heat. Proceed.
Feel cue: The raw mixture should feel watery and thin between your fingers — much thinner than the finished glaze will be. The alcohol makes it flow freely before the heat concentrates it.

Bring the mixture to a boil over medium heat, stirring frequently. Once boiling, reduce to a steady simmer and cook for 8–12 minutes, stirring every 30 seconds, until the glaze has reduced by approximately half and coats the back of a spoon heavily. Watch carefully in the last 2 minutes — maple syrup glazes go from perfect to scorched very quickly. The alcohol will burn off in the first 2–3 minutes of simmering. Remove from heat when a finger drawn through the spoon coating holds a clean line for 5 seconds.
Visual cue: Deep, burnished amber-brown glaze, significantly darker and more opaque than the raw mixture. It flows slowly off a spoon in a single thick sheet.
Underdone: Still thin and watery, runs off the spoon quickly. Raw bourbon smell still dominant. Continue reducing. The glaze needs more time — the color should deepen noticeably as the sugar concentrates.
Perfect: Deep burnished amber, glossy, and flowing like warm caramel. A finger line through the spoon coating holds cleanly. Smells of caramelized maple, oak, and sweet soy. The bourbon is present as warmth and complexity, not raw alcohol. Remove from heat and use immediately or cool to room temperature.
Overdone: Glaze has seized and formed a stiff candy in the pan. Very dark, bitter caramel smell. Add 2 tablespoons of warm water and stir gently over low heat to dissolve. Next time remove from heat earlier.
Feel cue: At the moment of perfect reduction, the glaze will stretch between two fingers in a thin, sticky thread before breaking cleanly. The kitchen fills with the smell of warm vanilla, caramel, and woodsmoke from the evaporating bourbon — a smell that should make anyone in the room stop what they are doing.

name: Mapo Tofu Sauce
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Doubanjiang (Pixian chili bean paste): 3 parts
  Alternatives: gochujang + miso (approx substitute)
Ground pork (or beef): 4 parts
  Alternatives: ground chicken; crumbled firm tofu (vegan)
Fermented black beans (douchi), minced: 1 parts
  Alternatives: 1 tsp soy sauce as substitute
Garlic cloves, minced: 1 parts
Fresh ginger, minced: 0.5 parts
Sichuan peppercorns, toasted and ground: 0.3 parts
Chicken or pork stock: 8 parts
  Alternatives: water
Cornstarch slurry (2:1 water to starch): 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: potato starch slurry
Chili oil or neutral oil: 1 parts
Light soy sauce: 0.5 parts
Scallions, white and green parts separated: 1 parts
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 35 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A deep-red Sichuan sauce built from doubanjiang, fermented black beans, and ground pork — the finished bowl delivers a simultaneous assault of chili heat and Sichuan peppercorn numbness that the Chinese call ma la, leaving lips tingling long after the last bite.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: 花椒（Sichuan peppercorns, toasted and ground）
葱（Scallions, white and green parts separated）

steps:
Place Sichuan peppercorns in a cold, dry wok or skillet. Heat over medium-low, shaking and stirring constantly. Toast until the peppercorns are fragrant — about 2–3 minutes. They should smell citrusy, floral, and slightly camphoraceous. Be careful: over-toasted Sichuan pepper turns bitter and loses the numbing hydroxy-alpha-sanshool compound that defines ma la. Immediately remove from the heat and grind coarsely in a mortar. The ground pepper should look like coarse black pepper.
Visual cue: Peppercorns have darkened from brick-red to deep mahogany, and the kitchen smells intensely floral and citrusy.
Underdone: Peppercorns still smell raw and piney, little floral aroma. Exterior still dull brick-red. Continue toasting over low heat. Under-toasted pepper lacks the numbing quality.
Perfect: Deep mahogany, intensely aromatic — floral, lemony, slightly resinous. First wisps of fragrant smoke. Remove immediately and grind while hot.
Overdone: Dark brown, smells acrid and bitter rather than floral. Discard — burnt Sichuan pepper is unpleasantly astringent. Start with fresh.
Feel cue: Crush one toasted peppercorn on your tongue — within 10 seconds you should feel a distinct tingling-numbing sensation on the tip of your tongue. If there is no numbing, the peppercorns are old and need replacing.

Heat oil in a wok over medium heat. Add doubanjiang and stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until the oil turns deep red and the paste separates slightly. This step — frying the bean paste in oil — is called chao hong you ('frying red oil') and it is the flavor foundation of mapo tofu. Add minced garlic, ginger, and fermented black beans. Stir-fry for another 90 seconds until everything is aromatic and the raw garlic smell has mellowed. The paste will smell deeply savory, fermented, and slightly sharp.
Visual cue: The oil in the wok has turned a brilliant, translucent crimson-red. The paste is fragrant and sizzling, oil visibly separated and pooling at the edges.
Underdone: Oil is still pale and the bean paste smells raw and sharp. Garlic is still pungent and biting. Continue frying — the color change in the oil is the reliable indicator. Underdone doubanjiang tastes harsh.
Perfect: Oil has bloomed to a deep, transparent red. Garlic is golden and fragrant. Kitchen smells of fermented chili, garlic, and ginger. Add the pork and stir-fry.
Overdone: Paste is darkening and beginning to stick. Oil is turning dark red-brown. Add the pork immediately and deglaze with stock — this will stop the burning.
Feel cue: Lean over the wok and take a careful breath — the steam should be powerfully savory and spicy, almost eye-watering from the fermented chili paste. If it smells flat, the heat is too low.

Increase heat to high and add ground pork. Stir-fry briskly, breaking up any clumps, until the pork is fully cooked through and no pink remains — about 3 minutes. The pork should be in small, separate granules coated in the red chili paste, not large clumps. Each grain of pork should be individually seasoned by the doubanjiang. Once cooked, add the white parts of the scallions and stir for 30 seconds.
Visual cue: Fine, separate granules of cooked pork, each coated in deep red paste, sizzling and aromatic. No pink remaining, no large meat clumps.
Underdone: Pink pork visible in clumps. Meat has steamed rather than seared. Increase heat and break up clumps. Do not cover — steam prevents browning.
Perfect: Fully cooked, granular pork coated in red paste. Hissing and slightly caramelized at the wok edges. Add stock and simmer.
Overdone: Pork is beginning to dry out and stick to the wok. Add stock immediately.
Feel cue: The wok should be extremely hot and smoking slightly — you want the aggressive heat of a restaurant wok station. The hissing should be loud and constant, not occasional.

Add stock and soy sauce. Bring to a boil, stirring to incorporate all the stuck-on paste from the wok bottom. Reduce heat to a steady simmer and cook for 5 minutes to allow the flavors to meld. The sauce will be a rich, deep red. Taste and adjust salt with soy sauce. This is the moment to add silken tofu if serving as mapo tofu: add 400g silken tofu cut into 2.5 cm cubes, pushing them gently into the sauce with a spoon (never stirring or they will break). Simmer 3–4 minutes to heat the tofu through.
Visual cue: A deep, glossy, red-orange sauce simmering gently. If tofu is added, white cubes float just below the surface, the sauce stained slightly around their edges.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and the flavors taste separate — chili paste sharp, soy sauce dominant, stock flat. Simmer another 3–5 minutes. The meld requires time on heat.
Perfect: Unified, complex sauce: spicy, salty, deeply savory, with a full-body depth. All elements integrated. Add cornstarch slurry to thicken.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced to a thick paste — overly concentrated, too salty. Add 4 tbsp fresh stock and stir to thin.
Feel cue: Dip a spoon and taste — the sauce should hit with immediate chili heat, then a wave of fermented umami, then the back of the palate with a building heat. If any single flavor dominates too much, balance is off.

Give the cornstarch slurry a final stir (starch settles quickly). Pour in a slow, steady stream around the edges of the sauce, stirring gently. The sauce will thicken almost immediately. For tofu: use the back of a spoon to gently push the tofu, never stir. The sauce should be thick enough to coat tofu cubes and not pool excessively on the plate. Ladle into bowls. Finish with a generous shower of ground Sichuan peppercorns and the sliced green scallion tops. The pepper should be added last — heat destroys its numbing compounds.
Visual cue: The finished sauce is glossy, thick enough to coat a spoon, and deep crimson-red with visible dark specks of Sichuan pepper and bright green scallion.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and runs immediately off the back of a spoon. Add another small slurry addition. Stir gently and test again.
Perfect: Sauce coats tofu cubes with a thick, glossy layer. A spoon drawn through the sauce leaves a trail that closes slowly. Deep, complex red with visible aromatics. Serve immediately — mapo tofu does not hold.
Overdone: Sauce has become a thick, gloopy paste that mounds on the tofu. Add 2 tbsp stock and stir gently. The texture should flow, not sit solid.
Feel cue: The finished dish should feel warm and slightly oily on the lips, with the Sichuan peppercorn tingling beginning on the front of the tongue within 15–20 seconds of eating. The numbing sensation builds over the first three or four bites.

description: Silken tofu bobbing in a rust-red sea of doubanjiang, fermented black beans, and ground pork — fiery, tingling, deeply savoury, and almost dangerously moreish. The Sichuan peppercorn delivers its signature ma (numbing) alongside the la (heat) of the chilies.

ingredients.name: 豆瓣酱（Doubanjiang (Pixian broad bean chili paste)）
花椒（Sichuan peppercorns, toasted and ground）
鸡高汤（Chicken stock (or unsalted vegetable stock)）
玉米淀粉（Cornstarch, mixed with equal water (slurry)）
Scallion, green parts only, thinly sliced

steps:
Cut the tofu into 2cm cubes and place carefully in a bowl. Bring a pot of lightly salted water to a gentle boil. Slide the tofu cubes in and blanch for 2 minutes — do not stir aggressively, as silken tofu shatters easily. Drain with a spider or slotted spoon onto a plate lined with kitchen paper. This step firms the tofu surface slightly, seasons it from within, and removes any beany off-flavours — it is the difference between mapo tofu with clean, distinct cubes and a broken, murky mess.
Visual cue: Tofu cubes that hold their shape, look slightly firmer on the outside surface, and have a faint creamy sheen from the light salting.
Underdone: Tofu went straight from the packet into the wok — cool, slightly sour, very fragile. Breaks at a breath. Always blanch. Even 1 minute in hot salted water transforms the texture and eliminates off-flavours from the packaging brine.
Perfect: Cubes hold their shape cleanly. The outer surface is very slightly set — still yielding inside but no longer raw-fragile. Smell is neutral and clean. Set aside on paper and keep at room temperature. Do not refrigerate or the tofu will weep water into the sauce.
Overdone: Tofu has been boiled hard and the surface has puffed and toughened. Cubes look pockmarked. Proceed, but lower the wok heat when adding the tofu — it will not absorb sauce as beautifully.
Feel cue: Lift a cube gently with a spoon and press lightly with a fingertip — it should compress about 30% before you feel resistance, then spring back partially. Completely firm cubes were over-blanched; cubes that collapse to the touch were never blanched at all.

Heat the oil in a wok or wide heavy pan over high heat until wisps of smoke appear. Add the ground pork and spread it into a thin layer. Let it sear undisturbed for 90 seconds until the bottom is golden and fat has rendered. Break it up and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3–4 more minutes until all pink is gone and the pork has rendered its fat and some pieces are golden and slightly crisp. Do not drain the fat — it carries the chili and fermented flavour into the sauce.
Visual cue: Golden-brown ground pork with some crisped, caramelised edges. Significant fat in the wok. No pink remaining.
Underdone: Pork is grey and steamed. Still some pink. Fat hasn't fully rendered — the meat looks wet. Increase heat. Cook until the pan is sizzling and the pork begins to show some golden-brown colour.
Perfect: Golden in places, no pink visible. Pork fat is pooled in the wok, shimmering and golden. Smells of caramelised meat. Add the doubanjiang and fermented black beans without draining.
Overdone: Pork is very dark brown and the small pieces have dried out and turned hard. Add the stock (ing_09) 2 tablespoons early to re-moisten before continuing.
Feel cue: Listen to the wok: the crackling pop of fat rendering is distinctly higher-pitched than the wet steam hiss of grey, underdone pork. Chase the crackle, not the hiss.

Add the doubanjiang to the wok and stir-fry with the pork for 2 minutes over high heat until the paste darkens from red to a deep rust-brown and the oil in the wok turns a vivid crimson — this is the hallmark of properly fried doubanjiang. Add the fermented black beans, garlic, and ginger; stir-fry for 1 more minute. Add the dried chili flakes. The wok should smell intensely of fermented chili, garlic, and caramelised pork — deeply savoury and slightly harsh in the raw stage, which will mellow once the stock goes in.
Visual cue: The oil in the wok has turned a vivid brick-red to crimson. The doubanjiang has darkened and fried, no longer a raw red paste. The pork and paste are inseparable.
Underdone: Doubanjiang is still bright red and the oil is barely tinted. The paste has not fried — it has only warmed. The raw fermented smell is harsh. Fry for another 2 minutes over high heat, stirring constantly. The oil must turn red — this signals that the chili oils and fermented compounds have dissolved.
Perfect: Deep rust-red oil. Doubanjiang has darkened and caramelised. The wok smells of umami, chili, and caramelised fermented complexity — harsh edge is gone. Add stock immediately and scrape up any fond from the wok bottom.
Overdone: Doubanjiang has burned — dark brown to black at the edges, bitter smoke rising. Lower heat immediately and add stock. If very bitter, start again — burnt doubanjiang cannot be salvaged.
Feel cue: The wok should feel actively hot and the handle almost too warm to hold comfortably without a cloth. The sizzling when you add the garlic should be immediate and violent — a loud, fragrant explosion of steam.

Pour the stock into the wok and scrape up any stuck bits from the bottom. Bring to a simmer, then gently slide in the blanched tofu cubes using a spatula. Add the soy sauce. Stir by gently rocking the wok and using a spatula to move the sauce — never stir through the tofu with a spoon or it will shatter. Simmer gently for 4–5 minutes so the tofu absorbs the sauce from the outside inward. The sauce will thin from the tofu's water — the cornstarch slurry in the next step will bring it back.
Visual cue: Vivid crimson broth at a lazy simmer with tofu cubes just visible beneath the surface, intact and uniformly stained a faint red at the edges.
Underdone: Tofu cubes are white and have not absorbed any colour. The sauce looks pale and watery. Only 2 minutes in. Simmer for the full 4–5 minutes, rocking the wok gently — the crimson colour migrating into the tofu surface is the sign of proper absorption.
Perfect: Tofu cubes have reddened at the edges and hold their shape. Sauce is a vivid, bubbling crimson. The broth smells of all the aromatics working together. Proceed to thickening with the cornstarch slurry.
Overdone: Hard boiling has broken the tofu apart into ragged fragments. The sauce is milky from dissolved tofu protein. Keep heat very low for the remaining steps. The flavour is fine — just the texture has suffered.
Feel cue: Tilt the wok to check the sauce level — it should pool in a crimson lake beneath the tofu, neither dry nor watery. The tofu should be bobbing gently with the simmer, each cube still distinct.

Give the cornstarch slurry a quick stir (it settles fast) and pour it around the edge of the wok in a slow, thin stream, gently rocking the wok as you add it. Cook for 30–60 seconds until the sauce thickens to a glossy, coating consistency that clings to the tofu. Remove from heat. Sprinkle the toasted, ground Sichuan peppercorn over the top — do not add it during cooking, or the numbing compounds will dissipate. Scatter the sliced scallion. Serve immediately over steamed rice. The ma (numbing) sensation builds over 30–60 seconds after eating.
Visual cue: A glossy, lacquer-red sauce that coats the tofu cubes completely. Visible flecks of green scallion and pale Sichuan peppercorn powder. The sauce should not run freely from a tilted spoon — it should drip slowly.
Underdone: Sauce is still thin and watery — cornstarch slurry was not enough or was added too slowly. The tofu swims loosely. Mix another teaspoon of cornstarch with cold water and stir in. Do not boil hard — thicken gently.
Perfect: Glossy, coating, deeply red sauce. It falls from a spoon in slow, thick drops. Every tofu cube is lacquered. Sichuan peppercorn visible as grey-green powder. Scallion is bright green. Serve immediately in a warmed bowl over rice.
Overdone: Too much cornstarch added — the sauce has set into a thick, gluey paste. The wok may show sauce pulling from the edges. Add hot stock or water a spoonful at a time and stir gently until the sauce loosens to a coating consistency.
Feel cue: Take a bite: the tofu should be cool and silky at its core and warm at the edges. The sauce coats the mouth for a moment, then the Sichuan peppercorn hits — a buzzing, electric tingle along the sides of the tongue and lips that starts subtle and builds for 30 seconds. If you feel nothing, the peppercorn was stale.

name: Masala Chai
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Water: 100 parts
Whole milk: 100 parts
  Alternatives: full-fat oat milk; buffalo milk for a richer pot
Strong black tea (Assam CTC): 8 parts
  Alternatives: any robust loose-leaf black tea; two strong tea bags
Green cardamom pods: 2 parts
  Alternatives: a pinch of ground cardamom added late
Fresh ginger (peeled): 6 parts
  Alternatives: 1/4 tsp dried ginger powder
Black peppercorns: 1 parts
  Alternatives: a small pinch of long pepper
Whole cloves: 0.5 parts
Cinnamon bark (cassia): 1 parts
  Alternatives: true Ceylon cinnamon for a lighter note
Sugar: 12 parts
  Alternatives: jaggery; honey stirred in off the heat
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The roadside kettle distilled to its essentials — black tea and milk simmered hard with hand-crushed cardamom, ginger, and cracked peppercorns until the whole pot turns the deep tan of caramel and throws a fragrant, peppery steam. Sweet, spiced, and strong enough to stand a spoon.

steps:
Crack the cardamom pods open and tip in their black seeds along with the husks. Add the peppercorns, cloves, and a snapped piece of cinnamon bark, and pound everything coarsely in a mortar — you want the spices bruised and broken open, not powdered. Smash the peeled ginger separately to a fibrous pulp. Crushing fresh releases volatile oils that a pre-ground masala has long since lost, and the coarse texture steeps cleanly without clouding the chai.
Visual cue: A rough, fragrant rubble of split cardamom, cracked peppercorns, and broken cinnamon, with the ginger reduced to a wet, stringy pulp that smells sharp and bright.
Underdone: Pods are still whole and peppercorns intact, rolling around the mortar unbroken. Keep pounding. The pods must split and the peppercorns crack — sealed spices barely flavor the pot.
Perfect: Every cardamom pod is open, peppercorns are cracked into halves and quarters, cinnamon is in splinters, and the kitchen smells of warm spice and ginger. Scrape it all — husks, seeds, ginger pulp, and any juices — straight into the water.
Overdone: The masala is a fine, dusty powder and the ginger is liquefied. Usable, but it will cloud and slightly muddy the brew. Strain extra carefully at the end.
Feel cue: The pestle should meet a satisfying crunch as the pods and peppercorns give way. A whiff at this stage should make your nose tingle — that pepper-and-cardamom hit is the soul of masala chai.

Tip the crushed masala into the water in a small saucepan and bring it to a rolling boil. Let it bubble hard for 2 to 3 minutes — this is a true decoction, drawing the heat and aroma out of the spices into the water before any milk goes in. The water will tint pale gold and the steam will turn unmistakably peppery and gingery.
Visual cue: A vigorously bubbling, faintly golden water carrying flecks of spice, throwing a sharp, warm-scented steam.
Underdone: The water is still clear and the steam smells of little more than hot water. Keep boiling. The spices need a hard, open boil to surrender their oils — a gentle simmer is not enough.
Perfect: The water has turned pale straw-gold, the spices are dancing in a rolling boil, and the aroma is pungent and spiced. Add the tea leaves and let it boil on.
Overdone: The pan has nearly boiled dry and the spices smell scorched. Top up with a splash of water and lower the heat before adding tea — burnt masala turns the chai bitter.
Feel cue: Lean over the pan: the steam should sting faintly with ginger and pepper. The sound is a busy, full-throated boil, not a lazy simmer.

Stir the tea leaves into the boiling spice water and keep it at a brisk boil for 1 to 2 minutes. CTC leaf brews fast and dark; you want a strong, almost inky liquor because the milk to come will dilute and pale it considerably. The colour should deepen to a rich mahogany.
Visual cue: A dark, reddish-brown brew at a steady boil, the leaves swollen and tumbling, the surface carrying a thin tannic foam.
Underdone: The liquid is a weak amber and you can still see clearly to the bottom of the pan. Boil another half minute. Under-brewed tea makes a thin, milky chai with no backbone.
Perfect: A deep mahogany, nearly opaque brew with a tight foam — it looks too strong on its own, which is exactly right. Pour in the milk and sugar.
Overdone: The brew has boiled long and hard and smells harshly astringent and bitter. Move straight to the milk — dairy and sugar will mask some bitterness, but next time shorten the tea boil.
Feel cue: It should look almost aggressively dark and tannic. Trust it — the moment milk hits, that intensity becomes the perfect strength.

Pour in the milk and add the sugar, then bring the whole pot back to a boil. Watch it closely — as it climbs the pan and threatens to foam over, pull it briefly off the heat to settle it, then return it. Repeat this rise-and-settle two or three times over 2 to 3 minutes; each boil-up thickens the chai and melds the tea, spice, and milk into one. Pour from a height through a fine strainer into cups to leave the leaves and spices behind and build a little froth on top.
Visual cue: A uniform warm-tan chai, the colour of milky caramel, frothing up the sides of the pan and giving off a sweet, spiced, milky steam.
Underdone: The chai is pale and looks thin and watery, with the milk not yet fully boiled into the tea. Let it rise to a full boil at least once more. The boil-ups are what give chai its body and round, cooked-milk flavour.
Perfect: A rich, even tan with a frothy collar, having boiled up and settled a few times. It smells sweet, gingery, and fully integrated. Strain and pour at once, from a height, into warmed cups.
Overdone: The chai has boiled over or reduced too far, tasting cooked, overly sweet, and faintly scalded. Cut it with a splash of hot milk or water and re-balance the sweetness before serving.
Feel cue: The classic moment is the foam racing up the pan — pull it off just before it spills. Finished chai should coat the cup with a faint clinging film and taste sweet, strong, and warming, with the pepper landing as a gentle afterglow in the throat.

description: Split red lentils that melt into golden silk in under thirty minutes, then meet a tarka of mustard seeds, cumin, and dried chili that hits the surface with a hiss and an aroma that fills the kitchen before the spoon reaches the bowl.

ingredients.name: Tarka spices (mustard seeds, cumin seeds, dried red chili, turmeric)

steps:
Combine rinsed lentils, tomatoes, ginger-garlic paste, and 2.5 parts water in a medium saucepan. Add a pinch of turmeric. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat, then reduce to a brisk simmer. Cook uncovered for 15–20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until lentils have completely dissolved into the tomatoes and the mixture is thick and smooth. The lentils will turn from orange-red to golden yellow as they cook.
Visual cue: The dal is uniformly smooth and golden-yellow with no visible distinct lentils. The consistency is between a thick soup and a porridge — it flows slowly from a stirred spoon.
Underdone: Individual lentils are still visible and hold their shape. The liquid is thin and orange-red, with a grainy rather than smooth texture. Continue simmering uncovered for 5–8 more minutes. Stir to prevent sticking. The lentils dissolve quickly once they reach temperature.
Perfect: Completely smooth and golden — no visible lentil shapes. Thick enough to mound slightly when a spoon is dragged across the surface. Smells lightly of cooked tomato and earth. Season with salt. The tarka will go on top — have the oil and spices ready before the next step.
Overdone: Dal is very thick and sticking to the bottom of the pan, producing a burnt smell. It has the consistency of mashed potatoes. Add 60ml water and stir vigorously, scraping the bottom. Thin to desired consistency and reduce heat immediately.
Feel cue: Drag a spoon across the surface of the cooked dal — the trail should slowly fill back in over 3–4 seconds. Too fast and it is too thin; if it holds rigid, it is too thick.

In a small pan or ladle, heat mustard oil over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly (smoking point neutralizes mustard oil's harsh raw flavour). Add mustard seeds and wait for them to pop and splutter. Add cumin seeds — they will darken within 10 seconds. Add dried red chili and fry for 5 seconds. The entire tarka happens in under 30 seconds — have all spices measured and ready before heating the oil.
Visual cue: The oil is shimmering, mustard seeds are popping audibly, cumin seeds are dark brown and fragrant, and the chili has puffed and darkened slightly.
Underdone: Oil is not hot enough — seeds sink and sit quietly in the oil rather than popping. The tarka will smell raw and oily rather than toasted. Wait for the oil to reach smoking point. High heat is mandatory for proper tarka — tempering at low heat produces flat, greasy flavour.
Perfect: Mustard seeds are popping vigorously like tiny firecrackers. Cumin seeds are dark golden-brown and filling the kitchen with a toasted, nutty aroma. Chili has expanded and darkened. Pour immediately over the dal — do not delay. The spices continue cooking in the residual oil heat.
Overdone: Mustard seeds have stopped popping and are charred. Cumin is black. Chili is blackened and smoking. The tarka smells bitter and acrid. Discard and start again. Burnt tarka will ruin the dal — the acrid bitterness cannot be masked.
Feel cue: You should hear the tarka before you see it — the aggressive pop and crackle of mustard seeds in very hot oil is unmistakable and should start within 3–5 seconds of the seeds hitting the oil.

In the same dal pot, if including raw onion sauté it until golden in 1 tbsp oil, then combine with the dal. Pour the sizzling tarka directly over the surface of the dal in one decisive move. The oil will hit the dal with a dramatic hiss. Stir to incorporate. Add lemon juice, taste and adjust salt. The acidity brightens and lifts the entire dish — add it at the end, never during cooking.
Visual cue: The golden dal now has swirls of dark aromatic oil on the surface, dotted with visible cumin seeds, chili pieces, and popped mustard seeds.
Underdone: The dal looks unchanged — tarka was not hot enough when poured and has sunk in without a visible reaction. The dal smells like plain cooked lentils. If the tarka cooled before pouring, reheat the dal and make a fresh tarka. Cold oil and spices won't bloom properly in the dal.
Perfect: The surface shows a vivid aromatic sheen with a complex landscape of spices. One stir releases a bloom of warm, toasted, smoky fragrance. The flavour is deep, balanced, and bright with lemon. Serve immediately in bowls with steamed rice. The tarka fragrance dissipates within minutes.
Overdone: Too much lemon juice added — the dal tastes aggressively sour and the spice balance is drowned. The colour has shifted towards tan from the acid. Add a small pinch of sugar and extra salt to rebalance. A tiny knob of butter will also smooth the sharpness.
Feel cue: The moment the tarka hits the dal, the kitchen should flood with a wave of fragrance — toasted cumin, smoky chili, and the grassy punch of mustard. If the aroma is flat, the tarka was not hot enough.
