ingredients.name: Dried guajillo or dried red Thai chilies, seeded and soaked 20 min
Lemongrass stalks, white part only, thin-sliced
Galangal, fresh or frozen, peeled and rough-chopped
Shallots, halved and dry-roasted in a pan until charred outside
Garlic cloves, dry-roasted in shell until soft
Warm spice blend: cardamom pods (seeds only), cinnamon, cloves

steps:
Place a dry skillet over medium heat. Add coriander seeds and toast, shaking frequently, for 2–3 minutes until they begin to pop and smell of warm citrus and earth. Add cumin seeds for the last 60 seconds — they toast faster and burn easily. In the final 30 seconds, add the cardamom seeds, a piece of cinnamon, and 2 cloves. Tip everything onto a cold plate immediately and let cool completely before grinding. A mortar and pestle or spice grinder will work; grind to a fine powder.
Visual cue: Coriander seeds are pale golden-brown, cracked at the seams, with a visible deepening of color. The kitchen smells unmistakably of warm curry.
Underdone: Seeds are still pale, smell raw and starchy with no warmth. Coriander tastes faintly soapy. Return to the pan on medium heat, watching constantly — another 60 seconds.
Perfect: Seeds are amber at their equators, dark at the tips. They smell like warm orange peel and dried flowers. A cracked seed reveals a golden interior. Tip onto a cold plate immediately to stop cooking.
Overdone: Seeds are dark brown or black. Smoke rising. Bitter, acrid smell. Discard and start again — burnt spices will make the whole paste bitter beyond rescue.
Feel cue: A toasted coriander seed should crumble between your thumbnail and forefinger, not bounce. If it bounces, it needs more heat.

Place shallots (halved, skin on) and whole unpeeled garlic cloves in a dry skillet or directly over a gas flame. Cook over medium-high heat, turning occasionally, until the outsides are blackened in patches and the flesh inside is soft and caramelized — 8–12 minutes. Peel and discard the charred skins; the flesh underneath should be jammy and sweet with bitter edges. This char is essential: it builds the smoky depth characteristic of Thai curry pastes made by street vendors who hold aromatics over an open flame.
Visual cue: Shallots are black and blistered on the cut face, soft when squeezed. Garlic cloves give when pressed and the skin peels away to reveal ivory-golden flesh.
Underdone: Shallots are barely colored, flesh still firm and sharp. Garlic skin hasn't softened. Continue dry-roasting, pressing down with a spatula to increase contact with the heat.
Perfect: Exterior black and papery, interior soft, sweet, and jammy with a caramel aroma. Peel slips off easily. Cool slightly, peel, and set aside for pounding.
Overdone: Interior flesh is also darkened and tastes purely bitter, not sweet. You can salvage mildly burnt alliums by soaking briefly in cool water — it won't fix badly burnt ones, so use judgment.
Feel cue: Squeeze a roasted shallot half — it should give completely, like a ripe grape, with jammy flesh yielding under your fingers.

Drain the soaked chilies and squeeze out excess water. Tear into pieces and place in the mortar with the sliced lemongrass, galangal, and salt. Begin pounding with a rhythmic downward motion — not stirring, pounding. Rotate the pestle to ensure even pulverization. This will take 10–15 minutes of committed work. Add the fibrous materials first: the salt acts as an abrasive, the lemongrass and galangal must be completely broken down to fiber-free smoothness before anything else goes in. If using a food processor, pulse in bursts, scraping down frequently.
Visual cue: A deep brick-red paste with no visible chili skin shreds or lemongrass strings. The paste holds together in a cohesive mass when pressed.
Underdone: Visible threads of lemongrass fiber, chili skin pieces, and chunky galangal. Paste looks stringy and uneven. Keep pounding — the fibrous aromatics need full mechanical breakdown to release their oils.
Perfect: Smooth and cohesive, deep brick-red with a matte surface. When smeared on the back of a spoon, no strings remain. Intensely fragrant. Begin adding the roasted alliums.
Overdone: Paste is watery and over-worked, sticking to the mortar walls rather than clumping. Add a pinch more salt to help it cohere, and continue briefly.
Feel cue: The mortar should ring with a thud, not a click — you want the pestle to strike paste, not stone. When the fibrous resistance disappears and each blow lands soft, the paste is ready.

Add the peeled roasted shallots and garlic to the mortar and pound them into the paste until fully incorporated. Add the toasted shrimp paste and ground warm spices. Continue pounding until everything is unified — the paste will deepen from brick-red to a dark reddish-brown, almost mahogany, as the shrimp paste and spices integrate. Taste and adjust: it should be complex, fragrant, slightly sweet, earthy, with gentle heat that builds slowly. Store in a jar under a thin layer of oil in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks, or freeze in tablespoon portions.
Visual cue: A unified dark mahogany paste, dense and aromatic, with no visible lumps of allium or spice specks. It holds its shape when scooped.
Underdone: Lumps of shallot still visible, spices not integrated, color is uneven — brick-red in patches, dark in others. Pound methodically, rotating the pestle in wide arcs to drag all components together.
Perfect: Smooth, dark mahogany, and intensely aromatic. A complex bloom of cardamom, galangal, chili heat, and roasted garlic. Dense enough to hold a groove from the pestle. The paste is finished. Use immediately or store.
Overdone: Paste has become oily and separated, releasing aromatic oils in a puddle around the mass. This is actually acceptable — the released oil is pure flavor. Mix back in before using.
Feel cue: Rub a little paste between your fingers — it should feel dense and slightly oily, not gritty or wet. The heat hits your fingertips a few seconds after contact.

name: Matcha Castella
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Bread flour (strong, 12-13% protein): 100 parts
  Alternatives: all-purpose flour (less bouncy result)
Large eggs (whole, room temperature): 200 parts
Caster sugar: 130 parts
Honey: 30 parts
  Alternatives: mild-flavored honey
Ceremonial-grade matcha powder: 12 parts
  Alternatives: culinary matcha (greener color, slightly more bitter)
Whole milk (warm, 40 C): 20 parts
Fine salt: 1 parts
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 2 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A fine-textured, honey-sweetened sponge cake with the grassy bitterness of ceremonial matcha — moist and springy, with a characteristic dark crust.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Warm the whole eggs (in their shells) in hot tap water for 5 minutes. Combine the warmed eggs, sugar, and honey in the bowl of a stand mixer (or use a hand mixer). Beat at high speed for 8-10 minutes until the mixture is very pale, tripled in volume, and holds a thick ribbon that dissolves back in about 10 seconds when the whisk is lifted. The warm eggs help dissolve the sugar and retain air. Do not rush this stage — the aerated egg foam is the only leavener in castella.
Visual cue: A very pale, almost white foam that falls from the lifted whisk in a thick, slow ribbon, writing a visible trail on the surface for 8-10 seconds.
Underdone: Mixture is still yellow and pours off the whisk in a thin stream — not enough air incorporated. Continue beating for 2-3 more minutes at high speed.
Perfect: Pale ivory, very thick foam. Ribbon holds its shape on the surface for 8-10 seconds before dissolving. Volume has tripled. Sift the matcha-flour mixture in and fold immediately.
Overdone: Over-beaten — foam is dry and appears to break into large curds at the edges. Fold in the dry ingredients immediately and gently; deflating some foam is better than a grainy batter.
Feel cue: A properly beaten castella base feels like warm, dense shaving foam — it holds the impression of the whisk and trembles slightly when the bowl is moved.

Sift the bread flour and matcha powder together twice to ensure even distribution. Sift one-third of the matcha-flour over the egg foam and fold with a large spatula in slow, sweeping movements from the bottom of the bowl — cut down the center, sweep along the bottom, fold up over the top. Rotate the bowl and repeat. Add the remaining flour in two more additions. Fold in the warm milk with the last addition. Stop as soon as no dry streaks remain — every additional fold deflates the foam.
Visual cue: A uniformly deep jade-green batter with no streaks of white flour or paler yellow — smooth, thick, and still airy with visible large bubbles.
Underdone: Pale yellow streaks or white flour pockets still visible in the batter. Fold 3-4 more times, targeting the unincorporated areas.
Perfect: Even jade green throughout. Batter falls off the spatula in a thick ribbon. Still holds volume — not deflated. Pour into the prepared pan immediately.
Overdone: Batter has become thin and pourable, having lost its foam; color may be very dark green. Bake anyway — the castella will be denser but still good; matcha flavor will be excellent.
Feel cue: The folded batter should feel substantial and mousse-like — it resists the spatula gently, a sign the foam is still intact, and drops off in heavy waves rather than pouring.

Line a 21 x 10 cm loaf tin with baking paper (parchment), leaving overhang on all sides. Pour in the batter and gently tap the tin on the counter twice to release large air bubbles. Run a skewer through the batter in a figure-eight motion to break any visible bubble clusters. Bake at 160 C (320 F) for 50-60 minutes, rotating once at 30 minutes. The top should be a deep, dark brown — this is correct for castella, not a sign of overcooking. A skewer inserted in the center should come out clean.
Visual cue: A dark mahogany-brown domed top that has settled back level (not cracked), with lightly browned sides visible through the paper.
Underdone: Top is pale brown; skewer comes out wet; center jiggles when the tin is moved. Return to oven for 10 more minutes; cover with foil if the top is already dark.
Perfect: Dark, mahogany-brown top that springs back when pressed gently. Skewer emerges clean. Sides are pulling slightly away from the paper. The cake smells of honey and green tea. Remove from oven and immediately wrap tightly in cling film while hot.
Overdone: Top has cracked and is very dark with a slight burnt smell. Trim the top crust away with a bread knife; the interior will be excellent.
Feel cue: Pressing the top of a perfect castella feels like pressing a firm, deep sofa cushion — it compresses under your finger and springs back with gentle elasticity, the honey-scented steam rising through the paper.

Immediately upon removing from the oven, lift the castella out by the paper overhang and wrap the entire loaf tightly in plastic wrap while still hot. The steam trapped inside creates the characteristic moist, tight crumb of authentic castella. Place wrapped in the refrigerator for at least 1 hour (overnight is better). Slice into 2 cm rectangles with a wet knife, wiping the blade between cuts for clean edges.
Visual cue: After chilling, the castella cross-section reveals a deep jade-green interior with an even, fine crumb and a distinct darker crust line at the top and base.
Underdone: Crumb is open and uneven with large holes; exterior crust has not set. Slices crumble. Return to the fridge wrapped for another hour.
Perfect: Dense, even, fine-grained green crumb. Cuts cleanly with a wet knife. Moist to the touch, slightly springy. Dark crust is thin and distinct. Serve at room temperature or slightly chilled. Keeps 3 days wrapped at room temperature.
Overdone: Over-rested and dried — crumb is compact and dry, crust is hard. Brush slices with a light syrup (1:1 honey and warm water) and rest 30 minutes before serving.
Feel cue: A slice of rested castella has a faint tackiness from the honey — it slightly resists being pulled apart before giving cleanly, with a springy, fine-grained resistance unlike any Western sponge cake.

name: Ceremonial Matcha
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Ceremonial-grade matcha (sifted): 2 g
  Alternatives: high-quality culinary matcha for a more robust, slightly more bitter result
Water at 75–80°C (just off the boil): 70 ml
  Alternatives: spring water is ideal — highly chlorinated tap water dulls the flavour
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The heart of the Japanese tea ceremony — ceremonial-grade matcha sifted fine, whisked with a bamboo chasen in just-below-boiling water into a bowl of vibrant, vegetal green with a cap of fine, persistent foam. Sweet and savoury at once, it tastes of the shaded tea field in early spring.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Pour a small amount of the 80°C water into the chawan (tea bowl) and swirl it around to preheat the vessel. Tip the water out and dry the bowl thoroughly with a clean cloth. A cold bowl will instantly drop the water temperature and prevent the foam from forming properly. While you work, let the just-boiled water rest uncovered in the kettle or a jug for 2 to 3 minutes to reach the target temperature of 75–80°C — an instant-read thermometer is helpful, but the moment active boiling stops and the first wisps of rising steam soften, you are close.
Visual cue: A dry, warm ceramic bowl — touch the outside and it should feel pleasantly warm, not neutral or cold.
Underdone: The bowl is still cool to the touch and the warm water has been tipped out too quickly. Add the hot water again and hold it in the bowl for 20 seconds before drying — it needs to absorb the heat.
Perfect: The outside of the bowl feels consistently warm when you cup it in both hands, and the interior is completely dry with no condensation. Proceed to sifting immediately — the bowl is ready for the matcha.
Overdone: Water too hot (still boiling) was used; the bowl is uncomfortably hot to hold. Let the bowl cool to warm-to-comfortable and let your water cool another minute before proceeding — above 85°C turns matcha bitter.
Feel cue: Cup the bowl in both hands the way you would receive it at a tea ceremony. The ceramic should feel like a warm stone — present but gentle.

Measure 2 g of matcha (about one heaped chashaku scoop, or one level teaspoon) and pass it through a very fine sieve directly into the warmed, dry chawan. Matcha clumps on contact with humidity, and unsifted matcha whisked into water produces lumps that float stubbornly on the surface rather than dispersing into foam. Use the back of a small spoon to press the powder through if it resists. The sifted matcha should settle in the bowl as a thin, even, vivid green layer with no visible clumps.
Visual cue: A thin, even dusting of vivid emerald-green powder on the floor of the bowl — fine as eyeshadow, with no white or yellow-tinged clumps.
Underdone: Large clumps have passed through the sieve unbroken and sit in the bowl like small green pebbles. Press them firmly through the sieve with a spoon or use a finer mesh. Clumps will not dissolve in the whisk step.
Perfect: An even, perfectly smooth layer of fine green powder, the colour a clear, saturated jade-green — no yellow or brown tinge. Add the water in a thin, careful stream immediately.
Overdone: The powder has been exposed to heat or humidity and has taken on a dull, slightly brownish tinge. The matcha is past its peak but still drinkable. Store all remaining matcha sealed and refrigerated to slow further oxidation.
Feel cue: Tap the sieve gently — the powder should fall through freely, as fine and weightless as talc. Resistance means the mesh is blocked or the matcha is clumping from moisture.

Pour the 80°C water in a thin, slow stream over the matcha, aiming for the side of the bowl rather than directly onto the powder to avoid splashing. Take the chasen (bamboo whisk) and, holding the bowl steady with one hand, whisk in a rapid W or M motion across the surface — not circular, which creates large bubbles — moving the wrist quickly from side to side. Whisk for 20 to 30 seconds until a layer of fine, tight, uniform foam covers the entire surface. The bowl should stay still; only the wrist moves. Lift the chasen gently at the end to avoid leaving a hole in the foam.
Visual cue: A rich, opaque jade-green liquid with an even cap of fine, tight, light-coloured foam that completely covers the surface and holds without immediately collapsing.
Underdone: The surface shows large, uneven bubbles with patches of dark, un-foamed liquid visible beneath. The matcha is not yet fully dissolved. Whisk faster and more vigorously in the W motion for another 15 seconds, focusing on the patches without foam.
Perfect: A complete, uniform cap of small, uniform, cream-coloured bubbles sits over the vivid green liquid below. Lifting the chasen draws a thin foam thread that holds briefly before breaking. The colour is a clear, saturated green. Set the chasen aside gently and drink at once — foam is at its best in the first 90 seconds.
Overdone: The foam has collapsed into large, flat bubbles and the surface looks greenish-brown and oily from over-whisking with water that was too hot. Drink immediately regardless — the taste is largely unaffected even if the aesthetics are not ideal. Use cooler water next time.
Feel cue: The chasen should move fast enough to feel slight resistance from the liquid — a soft, swishing drag, never a heavy stir. When you lift it, the tines should come away clean, not trailing thick green threads.

name: No-Bake Matcha Cheesecake
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Digestive biscuits (crushed fine): 100 parts
  Alternatives: graham crackers; Hobnobs; sable shortbread
Unsalted butter (melted): 40 parts
Full-fat cream cheese (room temperature): 200 parts
  Alternatives: mascarpone for a richer, less tangy version
Heavy cream (cold): 100 parts
Icing sugar (sifted): 40 parts
  Alternatives: caster sugar
Ceremonial-grade matcha powder: 8 parts
  Alternatives: culinary-grade matcha (increase to 10 parts)
Hot water (just off the boil, for matcha paste): 12 parts
Lemon juice (freshly squeezed): 5 parts
Sheet gelatin (gold, 200 bloom): 4 parts
  Alternatives: 1.5 tsp powdered gelatin bloomed in 2 tbsp cold water
Matcha powder (for dusting): 2 parts
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 5 hr 25 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A cool, dense Japanese-style cheesecake with the quiet bitterness of ceremonial-grade matcha cutting through rich cream cheese, set just enough to slice clean on a crumbled digestive biscuit base — vivid green, barely sweet, deeply fragrant.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Hot water (just off the boil, for matcha paste)

steps:
Crush the digestive biscuits in a food processor to a fine, even sand — no large chunks or sandy dust, a uniform medium crumb. Alternatively, seal them in a zip-lock bag and roll with a rolling pin. Stir in the melted butter until every crumb is evenly coated — the mixture should look like damp sand that just clumps when pressed. Tip into the base of a 20 cm (8 inch) springform tin lined with baking parchment. Use the flat base of a glass to press the crumbs into a compact, even, level layer. Refrigerate for 15 minutes to set the butter.
Visual cue: An even, compact, flat biscuit layer that holds its shape when the tin is tilted and doesn't crumble when the edge is pressed with a fingernail.
Underdone: Crumbs are too coarse or the layer is uneven, with visible mounds and valleys. Press more firmly and evenly with the glass base. A loose base crumbles when sliced.
Perfect: Compact, flat, even, and slightly dark from the butter. Firm to the touch and holds a clean edge when pressed. Refrigerate while making the filling.
Overdone: Too much butter has made the base greasy — it pools at the edges and the surface looks shiny and wet. Blot gently with paper towel and refrigerate — the excess butter will firm up when chilled.
Feel cue: Press your palm flat on the chilled base — it should feel cold, firm, and faintly gritty, like cool, compacted sand. If it yields or feels soft, refrigerate longer before adding the filling.

Submerge the gelatin sheets in cold water for 5–8 minutes until completely floppy and translucent. Lift them out and squeeze out the excess water — the gelatin should weigh almost nothing in your palm. Set aside. For powdered gelatin, sprinkle it over 2 tablespoons of cold water and leave it to absorb into a firm sponge before heating. Gelatin enables the no-bake filling to hold its shape while maintaining a creamy, barely-set texture rather than a rubbery one.
Visual cue: Fully floppy, translucent gelatin sheets that drape over the fingers — no stiff or opaque spots remaining.
Underdone: Sheets are still stiff and opaque at the edges, not fully hydrated. Return to the cold water for another 2 minutes.
Perfect: Fully limp, clear, and cool. Drapes without resistance. Easy to squeeze dry. Squeeze gently and melt into warm cream in step 3.
Overdone: Sheets have begun dissolving into the water, leaving a cloudy bloom. If mostly intact, proceed. If dissolved significantly, start with fresh sheets — you've lost gelatin strength.
Feel cue: A bloomed gelatin sheet feels like a cool, wet piece of plastic film — completely pliable, weightless, and slightly slippery between the fingers.

Sift the matcha powder into a small bowl — sifting is non-negotiable, as matcha clumps badly and will leave green specks in the filling if not dispersed. Add the hot water (about 70–80°C, just off the boil — not boiling, which degrades the vivid green and the delicate flavor). Using a small whisk or matcha chasen, whisk in tight 'M' or 'W' motions until the powder is fully dissolved into a smooth, vivid green paste with no lumps. Melt the squeezed gelatin in 2 tablespoons of warm cream in a small saucepan over very low heat, swirling until dissolved. Stir the gelatin into the matcha paste.
Visual cue: A smooth, intensely vivid jade-green paste with no lumps, clumps, or floating powder — uniform and glossy.
Underdone: Green specks and lumps of powder are still visible — it looks mottled, not smooth. Sift the matcha first and whisk more vigorously. Lumps in the paste will show as dark spots in the finished cheesecake.
Perfect: Bright, even jade-green, smooth and lump-free. The aroma is grassy, vegetal, and intensely fragrant. Cool the paste slightly before folding into the cream cheese mixture.
Overdone: Matcha was mixed with boiling water and has gone an olive-drab, dull green. Still usable but the color and delicate flavor are compromised. Keep the water temperature at 70–80°C.
Feel cue: Taste a tiny amount of the paste on a fingertip — the bitterness should be immediate and intense, then give way to the grassy, umami sweetness. This concentrated paste is what gives the cheesecake its assertive matcha character.

Beat the room-temperature cream cheese with the icing sugar and lemon juice until completely smooth and lump-free — 2 minutes with a hand mixer. Fold in the matcha-gelatin paste until evenly colored. In a cold bowl, whip the cold heavy cream to firm peaks. Fold the whipped cream into the matcha cream cheese mixture in three additions, from the bottom up, cutting and folding gently to retain the volume. The final filling should be airy, vivid green, and hold a soft peak.
Visual cue: A smooth, vivid jade-green mousse-like filling — uniformly colored, airy, and holding a soft peak — with no white streaks of cream cheese or whipped cream.
Underdone: White streaks of unmixed cream cheese or whipped cream are visible through the green. The texture is uneven. Fold 2–3 more times, scraping the bottom of the bowl to catch unmixed white patches.
Perfect: Uniformly jade-green, smooth, billowy, holds a soft peak. Smells strongly of matcha. Falls off the spatula in slow, airy folds. Pour onto the chilled base and smooth the surface.
Overdone: The cream has been over-folded and deflated — the filling looks dense and heavy, barely holding its structure. Still functional; the cheesecake will be denser and creamier rather than airy. Pour immediately.
Feel cue: Lift a spatula full: the filling should hold a soft, lazy mound for a moment before slowly settling — airy and cool, like mousse. If it runs off the spatula, it has been over-folded or the cream wasn't whipped enough.

Pour the filling over the chilled biscuit base and smooth the top with an offset spatula, spreading to the edges. Tap the tin gently on the counter twice to settle any air bubbles. Cover with cling film and refrigerate for a minimum of 4 hours, or overnight — the gelatin needs time to set fully and the flavors to develop. Before serving, dust the surface lightly with sifted matcha powder through a fine-mesh sieve. Release the springform and cut with a hot, wiped knife for clean slices.
Visual cue: A smooth, vivid green cheesecake with a flat, even surface and a clean green matcha dusting — set firmly enough to hold clean edges when sliced.
Underdone: The filling trembles too much when the tin is nudged — center is still very soft and would slump when unclipped. Refrigerate longer — at least another 2 hours. Rushing a gelatin set results in a cake that flows rather than holds.
Perfect: Holds its dome cleanly, just trembles at the center when tapped, slices with a clean, smooth face. The green is vivid, the dusting matte and even. Serve cold. Keeps refrigerated for up to 2 days.
Overdone: Set for too long or too much gelatin — rubbery, bouncy, and holds a sharp shape with no trembling. Still tastes correct; texture is less refined. Use slightly less gelatin next time.
Feel cue: Press the surface gently with a fingertip: it should give just slightly and spring back — not hard like rubber, not liquid soft. Cold, creamy, and faintly yielding, like the best cheesecake always is.

name: Matcha Ice Cream
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Whole milk: 240 g
  Alternatives: oat milk (texture will be slightly icier)
Heavy cream (35%+ fat): 360 g
  Alternatives: coconut cream for dairy-free (distinct flavour)
Egg yolks (5 large): 90 g
Caster sugar: 150 g
  Alternatives: light muscovado (adds a molasses note that competes with matcha)
Ceremonial-grade matcha powder (Uji preferred): 20 g
  Alternatives: culinary grade matcha (use 25g; flavour is coarser and more bitter); premium culinary grade (25g)
Flaky sea salt (a small pinch): 1 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 5 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Ceremonial-grade Uji matcha — astringent, vegetal, the colour of moss after rain — churned into a rich custard base until it freezes into a bittersweet cream that coats the tongue in green tea tannins before the dairy sweetness follows. The tension between bitter and sweet is what makes this ice cream feel like it belongs in a tea ceremony, not just a dessert bowl.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Sift the matcha powder into a wide, shallow bowl to break up any clumps — matcha is finely milled and prone to lumping. Add 3 tablespoons (about 45g) of the measured whole milk, warm but not hot (around 60 C). Using a bamboo chasen (matcha whisk) or a small balloon whisk, whisk the matcha and milk in rapid 'M'-and 'W'-shaped strokes until a smooth, lump-free paste forms. Add the remaining milk gradually, whisking to maintain smoothness. Matcha paste must be completely homogeneous before being added to the custard — a single undissolved lump will leave a bitter green streak in the finished ice cream.
Visual cue: A vivid, uniformly green liquid with no lighter or darker patches, no floating clumps, and a thin layer of fine foam from the whisking.
Underdone: Small dark green lumps visible floating in the milk. Streaks of unmixed powder on the bowl sides. Continue whisking in the 'W' pattern — undissolved matcha will not dissolve once added to the custard and will create bitter flecks.
Perfect: Uniformly vivid green throughout, thin foam on top, no lumps. Smells of fresh-cut grass, seaweed, and milk. Add to the remaining cream and heat for the custard base.
Overdone: You over-whisked and the milk is now very foamy — difficult to weigh and will add air to the custard. Let stand 2 minutes for foam to subside before proceeding.
Feel cue: Run the back of a spoon through the matcha milk — it should leave a clean, vivid jade-green channel that holds its edges for 2 seconds before the milk flows back. No streaks, no islands of darker powder.

In a medium heatproof bowl, whisk the egg yolks and caster sugar together vigorously for about 2 minutes until the mixture has turned pale, noticeably thickened, and falls from the whisk in a slow, wide ribbon. This is the ribbon stage — it indicates that enough air and emulsification have occurred to give the custard body. The yolks will be ready when they have doubled in volume, turned from deep orange to pale cream-yellow, and the ribbon holds on the surface for 3 seconds before sinking. This step also helps buffer the yolks against scrambling when the hot matcha milk is added.
Visual cue: A pale, airy, cream-coloured foam that falls from the whisk in a thick, slow ribbon and holds a trail on the surface of the bowl for 2 to 3 seconds.
Underdone: Mixture is still yellow and liquid — has not changed in colour or volume. Falls from the whisk in an immediate drip. Continue whisking — the sugar has not yet fully dissolved into the yolks and the mixture will be thin if used now.
Perfect: Pale cream-yellow, doubled in volume, ribbon holds 3 seconds. A lifted spoonful falls back in a folded pattern rather than dissolving immediately. Have the matcha milk heating and tempering tools ready — this should be used quickly while airy.
Overdone: Mixture is white, very stiff, and has begun to grain or separate. Warm the bowl briefly over a pan of hot water and whisk again to re-combine. The slight over-beating is inconsequential for the final custard.
Feel cue: Dip your finger in — it should taste intensely sweet and eggy, coating your fingertip in a thin film. The texture under your finger should feel like very loose, aerated condensed milk.

Combine the matcha milk and remaining heavy cream in a medium saucepan. Heat over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the mixture just begins to steam and small bubbles appear at the edge — about 75 C. Do not boil. Slowly pour about one-third of the hot matcha cream into the yolk mixture while whisking constantly — this is tempering: gradually raising the egg temperature to prevent scrambling. Pour the tempered yolk mixture back into the saucepan with the remaining hot cream. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a silicone spatula in figure-eight patterns and scraping the bottom and corners, until the custard reaches 82 C and coats the back of a spoon cleanly. Add the pinch of salt. Immediately strain through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean bowl set over an ice bath.
Visual cue: A thick, vivid green custard that coats the spatula in a distinct, opaque film — running a finger across the back leaves a clean line that holds without dripping.
Underdone: Custard is thin and drips freely off the spatula. Line drawn on the back disappears in less than 1 second. Temperature is below 79 C. Continue cooking, stirring constantly. Custard thickens suddenly in the 80-82 C range — be ready.
Perfect: Nappe consistency — spatula coating holds a clean line for 5+ seconds. Temperature 82 C. Deep jade green throughout. Smells of grassy matcha and cream. Strain immediately through a fine sieve into a bowl over an ice bath. Stir to cool, then refrigerate until completely cold before churning.
Overdone: Scrambled green egg visible — small curds forming. Grainy texture. Temperature above 85 C. Strain through a very fine sieve immediately — the curdled proteins will be caught. Blend the strained custard with a hand blender to restore smoothness. Slightly less rich than ideal but usable.
Feel cue: Run your finger across the back of the custard-coated spoon — if the line
stays crisp and doesn't fill in when you tip the spoon, the custard is ready. If it floods back across your finger, keep cooking.

Cool the custard base completely over the ice bath, stirring occasionally, then refrigerate for at least 2 hours or overnight until it is thoroughly chilled — around 4 C. Churn in an ice cream machine according to the manufacturer's instructions until the ice cream is the consistency of thick, scoopable soft-serve (about 20 to 25 minutes). Transfer to a chilled container, press parchment paper directly onto the surface to prevent ice crystal formation, and freeze for at least 3 hours before scooping. For a no-churn version: whip 200g of the heavy cream to medium peaks separately, fold into the chilled custard, and freeze in a loaf pan for 5 hours.
Visual cue: A deep, matte jade-green ice cream with a dense, smooth texture that holds a scoop shape cleanly — not icy or crystalline, but velvety and opaque.
Underdone: Ice cream is still soft and pale — melts immediately when scooped, has a liquid core. Not enough freezing time. Return to the freezer for another hour. The custard ratio is high and needs full freezing time to set.
Perfect: Scoops cleanly with a warm scoop, holds its round shape for 60+ seconds at room temperature before softening, and the interior is uniformly dense with no icy cores or white frost patches. Serve immediately in chilled bowls. Pairs with sesame brittle, sweet red bean (anko), or mochi.
Overdone: Ice cream is rock-hard — a warm scoop drags rather than curls. Icy, crystalline shards visible on the cut face. Transfer to the refrigerator for 15 minutes to temper. Icy texture can indicate the base was too diluted or the cream fat percentage was too low.
Feel cue: Take a tiny taste straight from the churning bowl before the final freeze — it should taste exactly like how a Japanese teahouse smells: intensely vegetal green tea, slightly bitter, with the cream coming in as a soft landing on the finish.

name: Matcha Latte
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Ceremonial-grade matcha powder (sifted): 1 part
  Alternatives: culinary-grade matcha (stronger, more bitter)
Hot water (70–80°C / 158–175°F, not boiling): 2 parts
Whole milk (steamed or frothed): 8 parts
  Alternatives: oat milk (froths well); almond milk; coconut milk
Simple syrup or honey (optional): 0.5 part
  Alternatives: maple syrup; agave
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Ceremonial-grade matcha whisked with a small measure of hot (not boiling) water into a smooth, foam-flecked concentrate, then poured over steamed milk — bitter, grassy, and creamy.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Sift the matcha powder through a fine-mesh sieve into a small ceramic bowl (chawan) or a regular bowl. This single step is more important than most cooks expect: matcha clumps aggressively due to its ultra-fine particle size and the natural static electricity of the dry powder. Unsifted matcha forms stubborn lumps that no amount of whisking will fully dissolve, producing a visibly grainy drink with an uneven bitter hit. Even freshly opened tins should be sifted. Use 1–2 grams (about 1 teaspoon) per serving — this quantity is critical, as ceremonial matcha is potent and expensive.
Visual cue: A fine, even, dry layer of vivid jade-to-forest-green powder in the bowl, with no visible clumps. The color should be intensely, evenly green — bright and slightly luminous, not dull or yellowish.
Underdone: Visible clumps remain after sifting — they look like tiny dark-green pebbles or irregular specks in the fine powder. They will not dissolve cleanly in the next step. Press them through the sieve with the back of a spoon. Every clump must be broken down before adding water.
Perfect: A perfectly even, silky-fine green powder with no clumps whatsoever. Runs through your fingers like the finest flour. Color is uniformly bright, vivid green. Proceed to mixing with hot water immediately. Sifted matcha is ready to hydrate.
Overdone: Sifted into a warm or moist environment — the matcha has begun to absorb ambient moisture and will be slightly harder to fully dissolve. Not a failure, but ideal conditions are dry and cool. Proceed quickly. Do not let sifted matcha sit in a humid kitchen for more than a few minutes.
Feel cue: Touch the sifted matcha with a dry fingertip: it should feel impossibly soft and fine — lighter than cornstarch, leaving an intense green stain on the skin that washes off with water but not with a quick wipe. No lumps, no grit.

Pour the hot water (70–80°C / 158–175°F) over the sifted matcha. The temperature is non-negotiable: boiling water denatures the amino acids (especially L-theanine and the chlorophyll) that give ceremonial matcha its sweet, umami edge, producing an acrid, vegetal drink that tastes like hot lawn clippings. Using a bamboo chasen (matcha whisk), whisk briskly in a W or M motion — not a circular stirring — for 20–30 seconds until a fine, stable foam forms on the surface with no visible powder clumps. The W-pattern breaks the surface tension and aerates; circular stirring only moves liquid without creating the micro-foam that defines a proper bowl of matcha.
Visual cue: A smooth, vivid jade-green liquid covered with a fine, uniform layer of small, stable bubbles — the foam should look like a soft green carpet across the whole surface, not large bubbles at the edges.
Underdone: Large bubbles at the rim, dry powder visible at the bottom, foam thin and immediately collapsing. The liquid below the surface looks streaky rather than uniformly green. Continue whisking in the W-pattern, faster and with more wrist action. The chasen should feel like it is barely touching the bottom — you are frothing the surface, not scraping the bowl.
Perfect: Dense, fine-bubbled jade foam covering the entire surface. The liquid below is uniformly green with no powder spots. The aroma is grassy, sweet, and slightly marine — umami-green, not vegetal or bitter. Pour over steamed milk immediately. Matcha foam begins to settle within 30–60 seconds — move quickly.
Overdone: Whisked so long and hard that the foam has collapsed back to liquid and re-formed as larger, coarse bubbles. The matcha may also have been whisked with too-hot water, giving the surface a darker, slightly dull green. Give one final burst of W-whisking and pour immediately. The quality of the foam affects aesthetics more than flavor

— proceed.
Feel cue: A properly made matcha concentrate smells of fresh green leaves, the sea (from L-theanine and umami compounds), and a faint sweetness — it should smell enticing, not sharp or grassy-acrid. If it smells acrid, the water was too hot.

Steam or heat the milk to 60–65°C / 140–150°F. If using an espresso machine steamer, introduce the steam wand just below the surface and incorporate air in the first few seconds before submerging to create a microfoam with fine, even bubbles. If no steamer: heat in a small saucepan over medium heat until steaming (do not simmer), then transfer to a jar and shake vigorously for 30–45 seconds to create a coarse foam, or use a handheld frother for 20 seconds. Oat milk and whole milk produce the best foam; skim milk foams but yields watery texture; plant milks vary — oat milk is remarkably close to whole milk.
Visual cue: Steamed milk with a glossy, thick microfoam — the surface should look like wet paint: smooth, shiny, and slightly viscous. The foam should pour as part of the milk, not float separately like shaving cream.
Underdone: Milk is warm but not steamed — it has no foam, just warm liquid. The latte will be flat and the matcha will not blend attractively without the foam layer. Steam or froth until you achieve visible foam. Even a small amount of foam transforms the texture of the final drink.
Perfect: Glossy, fine-bubbled microfoam with a silky, almost pourable texture. Tipped, the pitcher should show the foam moving slowly as a unified mass, not sloshing like water. Pour over the matcha concentrate immediately before the foam settles.
Overdone: Scalded milk — milk boiled past 70°C / 160°F loses sweetness and develops a cooked, slightly sulfurous taste. The foam is large-bubbled and rapidly collapsing. Discard scalded milk and steam a fresh portion. Scalded milk cannot be fixed and will make the latte taste flat and slightly stale.
Feel cue: Test the steaming pitcher against your palm: it should be almost too warm to hold comfortably but not burn. That warmth — sustained for 3 seconds of contact — is 60–65°C. Any hotter and the milk is scalded.

Add simple syrup or honey to a pre-warmed cup or glass if using, then pour the matcha concentrate over it and stir briefly. Pour the steamed milk from a low height at first to combine, then raise the pitcher to layer the foam on top. For an iced matcha latte: fill a tall glass with ice, pour the matcha concentrate over, then pour cold milk (no steaming needed) from a height. Stir before drinking — iced matcha separates as it sits. The contrast of bitter-umami matcha against sweet, creamy milk is the whole point; resist the urge to fully homogenize them into a uniform green drink.
Visual cue: A two-tone drink: a deep jade-green matcha layer beneath a creamy, golden-white milk and foam layer, with a gradient halo where they meet. The foam cap should hold a faint green tinge from the matcha below.
Underdone: Milk poured too quickly and stirred too aggressively — the drink is now a uniform, pale sage-green without the striking contrast layers. Still tastes correct but loses the visual appeal. No fix needed — drink as-is. Next time, pour the milk from a low height and angle to achieve layering.
Perfect: Visible gradient from deep green at the base to creamy white at the top, with the foam cap dusted with a faint green trace from the matcha below. It looks like a Japanese aesthetic composition. The first sip is pure milk foam; the second is the bittersweet green layer beneath. Stir once lightly before the second sip to blend, or drink layered for the full experience.
Overdone: Too much matcha or too little milk — the drink tastes aggressively bitter and the matcha flavor overwhelms the milk entirely. Ceremonial matcha should balance, not dominate. Add more steamed milk or a touch more sweetener to tame the bitterness. Culinary-grade matcha particularly benefits from a higher milk ratio.
Feel cue: The finished latte should feel silky and slightly coating in the mouth — the

fat of the milk blending with the fine particle suspension of the matcha creates a texture that is fuller than either alone. The warmth should linger after swallowing, with a sweet-grassy aftertaste that fades slowly.

name: Mayonnaise
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Egg yolk (large, room temperature): 18 parts
  Alternatives: 1 whole egg for a lighter, more pourable sauce
Dijon mustard: 5 parts
  Alternatives: English mustard powder bloomed in a little water
White wine vinegar: 5 parts
  Alternatives: fresh lemon juice
Neutral oil (grapeseed or canola): 200 parts
  Alternatives: part olive oil for a more assertive sauce
Fine sea salt: 2 parts
Fresh lemon juice (to finish): 4 parts
Cold water (as needed to loosen): 6 parts
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The mother of cold sauces — a single egg yolk coaxed into accepting its own weight many times over in oil, beaten drop by drop into a thick, glossy emulsion that stands in soft peaks, sharpened with mustard, lemon, and just enough salt to make it taste of nothing but itself.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Set a medium bowl on a damp folded towel so it cannot spin while you whisk one-handed. Add the egg yolk, mustard, vinegar, and salt and whisk for a full 30 seconds until the mixture is smooth, slightly paler, and slightly thickened. Everything must be at room temperature — a cold yolk emulsifies sluggishly and is far quicker to break. The mustard is not just flavor here: it is a second emulsifier that makes the sauce far more forgiving.
Visual cue: A smooth, homogeneous, pale-yellow base with the gloss of the mustard worked fully in and no streaks of separated vinegar pooling at the edges.
Underdone: The yolk, mustard, and vinegar sit in distinct streaks and the surface looks broken and watery. Keep whisking another 15 to 20 seconds until it pulls together into one uniform color.
Perfect: A single glossy, pale-yellow liquid that coats the whisk in a thin even film and smells sharply of mustard and vinegar. Begin adding oil — start at a literal drop at a time.
Overdone: You cannot really over-mix this step; at most the bowl warms slightly from effort. Proceed. If the kitchen is hot, the base is fine as-is.
Feel cue: The whisk should move freely with almost no resistance — this is a thin, loose base, not yet a sauce. It will smell bracingly of raw mustard and vinegar.

This is the whole game. Whisking constantly and hard, add the oil drop by drop for the first quarter of it — wait until each addition has fully disappeared before adding more. As the mixture thickens and lightens, you can relax to a thin, steady thread of oil, still whisking without pause. The base is grabbing oil droplets and locking them apart in a network; rush it and the network never forms. By the time the oil is in, you will have a thick, pale, jiggling mound.
Visual cue: A thick, opaque, ivory emulsion that mounds on the whisk, holds the marks of the wires, and slowly falls back on itself rather than running.
Underdone: The sauce is still thin, sloshy, and translucent-yellow — the emulsion has not taken hold yet. Stop adding oil. Whisk hard until what you have visibly thickens, then resume adding oil even more slowly, drop by drop.
Perfect: A glossy, billowing, pale ivory mass that holds soft peaks and clings thickly to the whisk. The oil thread vanishes on contact. Stop adding oil once it is as thick as you want, then move to finishing and seasoning.
Overdone: The sauce suddenly turns greasy, curdled, and slick, with free oil weeping out and the structure collapsing — it has broken. Put a fresh egg yolk (or a teaspoon of mustard and a splash of water) in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it drop by drop to re-emulsify it.
Feel cue: You will feel the exact moment it 'takes' — the loose slosh under the whisk firms into a heavy, dragging resistance within the first tablespoon or two of oil. From there it only gets thicker and harder to whisk.

Taste the emulsion — it will be flat and oily-rich and need brightening. Whisk in the lemon juice for acidity and lift, then adjust salt. If the mayonnaise is stiffer than you want, or looks dull and greasy, whisk in cold water a few drops at a time: it both loosens the sauce and re-tightens a slightly oily-looking emulsion, restoring the satin sheen. Chill at least an hour before serving; the flavors round out and it firms slightly.
Visual cue: A satiny, spoonable, off-white mayonnaise that holds a soft peak, tastes clean and balanced — rich but bright — and shows no beads of free oil on the surface.
Underdone: It tastes flat, heavy, and one-note, or sits too stiff and claggy on the spoon. Add lemon juice and salt to taste, then a few drops of cold water to loosen and lighten until it tastes alive and spreads easily.
Perfect: Glossy and just firm enough to hold its shape, with a clean balance of richness, acidity, and salt and a faint mustard warmth on the finish. Cover tightly and refrigerate. Use within three to four days.
Overdone: It has gone slack and runny from too much water or lemon, or tastes sharp and sour. Whisk in a little fresh oil drop by drop to rebuild body, or balance excess acid with a pinch more salt.
Feel cue: A finished spoonful should fall in a soft, glossy dollop and hold a gentle peak. On the tongue it is rich but never greasy, with the acid hitting first and the egg-and-mustard depth lingering behind it.

name: Maza
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: stone-ground barley flour (skip the roast-and-grind, toast the flour dry instead)
Warm water: 70 %
  Alternatives: watered-down wine for an ancient touch

Extra-virgin olive oil: 8 %

  Alternatives: omit for the plain soldier's loaf
Toasted sesame seeds: 6 %
  Alternatives: ground coriander seed; omit

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The unleavened backbone of the ancient Greek table — coarse-roasted barley meal kneaded with little more than water, oil, and salt, then baked on a stone into a dense, nutty griddle-cake. Plain, portable, and faintly sweet from the toasted grain, it was the everyday bread of farmers, soldiers, and philosophers alike.

ingredients.name: Barley grains (hulled, for roasting and grinding)
蜂蜜（Honey (optional, for a richer cake)）

steps:
Spread the hulled barley grains in a dry, heavy pan over medium heat and toast, shaking and stirring constantly, for 8 to 12 minutes. The grains darken from pale straw to a warm tan and throw off a popcorn-like, nutty aroma — this roasting (the ancient ?lphita process) is what gives maza its signature toasted flavor and was traditionally how the grain was prepared before milling. Let cool completely before grinding.
Visual cue: Grains are an even golden-tan throughout, glossy and dry, smelling strongly of toasted nuts and fresh bread crust.
Underdone: Grains are still pale and the pan smells only faintly grainy, like raw cereal. Keep toasting and stirring. The color and aroma develop suddenly near the end — don't walk away.
Perfect: A uniform warm tan, with a few grains just beginning to show darker freckles and a rich, nutty perfume filling the kitchen. Tip immediately onto a cold plate to stop the carryover heat, and cool fully before grinding.
Overdone: Grains are dark brown to scorched, the aroma sharp and acrid, and bitterness has set in. Discard any black grains and reduce the heat for the next batch — burnt barley will make the whole maza taste harsh.
Feel cue: A finished grain crunches crisply and snaps between the teeth rather than chewing soft. The pan sounds active with a steady gentle ticking as the grains heat.

Grind the cooled roasted barley to a coarse meal in a mortar, hand mill, or pulse-grinder — aim for a texture between fine flour and cornmeal, with some grit left in. Ancient maza was deliberately coarse, not silky; that rustic body is part of its character. Sift out only the largest unbroken hulls.
Visual cue: A pale brown meal with a sandy, slightly uneven texture — flour-fine in part but flecked throughout with small cracked grains.
Underdone: The meal is full of whole and barely-cracked grains and will not hold together when wetted. Keep grinding in batches. You need enough fine flour to bind the coarser bits.
Perfect: Mostly fine meal carrying a generous scatter of fine grit, like damp sand — coarse enough to feel, fine enough to clump when pressed. Move on to mixing the dough.
Overdone: The meal is a uniform fine powder with no grit at all. Still usable — the cake will just be denser and smoother. Mix in a spoon of cracked barley if you want the traditional texture back.
Feel cue: Rubbed between the fingers the meal feels sandy and dry, never powdery-soft like wheat flour, and smells like toasted bread.

Dissolve the salt (and honey, if using) in the warm water. Tip the barley meal into a bowl, add the olive oil and sesame, then pour in the liquid and work it together with your hands. Barley has almost no gluten, so this will never become a smooth elastic dough — instead knead just until it forms a cohesive, dense, slightly tacky mass that holds a shape. Press it together for a minute or two; over-working only dries it out. Let it rest 10 minutes so the meal fully hydrates.
Visual cue: A stiff, claylike dough that just holds together in a single mass, matte and tan, with flecks of sesame and grain visible throughout.
Underdone: The mixture is crumbly and dry, breaking apart and refusing to come together into one mass. Add warm water a teaspoon at a time and keep pressing — barley drinks slowly, so give it a moment between additions.
Perfect: A dense, pliable dough that holds a fingerprint, feels barely tacky, and forms a smooth ball without cracking at the edges. Rest it briefly, then shape into a flat round or small cakes.
Overdone: The dough is wet, slack, and sticks to everything, slumping rather than holding its shape. Work in a little more barley meal until it firms up to a moldable consistency.
Feel cue: It should feel like soft modeling clay — heavy and dense, holding whatever shape you press it into, with none of the springy pull-back of a wheat dough.

Pat the dough into a flat round about 1.5 cm thick (or several small cakes) and bake on a hot stone or in a dry heavy skillet over medium heat, 6 to 9 minutes per side, until the surface is firm and freckled with golden-brown spots. Without leavening it stays dense and flat — a hearty griddle-cake rather than a fluffy loaf. Eat warm with olive oil and honey, or let it cool and pack it for the road as the ancients did.
Visual cue: A firm, flat cake with a dry, lightly crisp crust mottled deep golden-brown, the interior set and tender but dense throughout.
Underdone: The surface is pale and soft and the center is still damp and pasty when pressed or split. Lower the heat slightly and keep cooking — a too-hot pan browns the outside before the dense middle sets.
Perfect: Golden-freckled and firm to the tap, with a center that is cooked through, tender, and steamy but no longer wet. Pull it off and let it cool a few minutes before tearing — it firms as it rests.
Overdone: The crust is dark and hard, the edges crumbling to dry crumbs, and the whole cake feels like a brick. Wrap it briefly in a damp cloth to soften, or break it up and steep in broth or watered wine as a porridge — exactly how leftovers were used.
Feel cue: Tapped on the bottom it sounds firm and a little hollow; torn open it should be dense and slightly moist, never gummy. The crust carries a nutty, faintly sweet toasted-barley smell.

name: Menemen
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

Breakfast, lunch, or late night — eaten from the pan with white bread.

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes, cored and roughly chopped
Green sivri peppers or Italian frying peppers, sliced
Aleppo pepper (pul biber), or mild red pepper flakes

steps:
Heat the butter and olive oil together in a wide, shallow pan — ideally a sahan (copper pan) or small cast-iron skillet, 22–24cm — over medium heat. If using onion, add it first and cook for 3–4 minutes until translucent. Add the sliced sivri peppers and cook, stirring occasionally, for 5–7 minutes until the peppers are completely soft, limp, and faintly blistered at the edges. The peppers should be almost sweet by this point — green pepper's bitterness cooks away with time. Season with a pinch of salt.
Visual cue: Peppers are fully limp and dark green, with faint brown blistering at the tips. The butter has taken on a faint green tint from the pepper juices. Onion (if used) is fully translucent.
Underdone: Peppers are still bright green and firm, resisting a wooden spoon. They smell raw and slightly grassy. Lower the heat and cook another 3 minutes. Raw-pepper menemen is the most common mistake — the peppers must be fully cooked before the tomatoes are added or they stay raw in the final dish.
Perfect: Peppers are dark olive-green, completely limp, and smell sweet and slightly caramelised. They collapse under a spoon with no resistance. Add the chopped tomatoes and seasoning immediately.
Overdone: Peppers have begun to brown and stick to the pan. Some are very dark at the edges and beginning to taste bitter. Proceed — the tomatoes will deglaze the pan and the deeper flavour actually adds complexity. Just ensure no parts are truly burned.
Feel cue: Press a pepper slice against the pan wall with a spoon — at the right stage it should collapse completely with no resistance, leaving a glossy smear. Any springiness or crunch means more time.

Add the roughly chopped tomatoes to the peppers, along with half the Aleppo pepper, the salt, and the black pepper. Stir to combine. Increase the heat to medium-high and cook, stirring occasionally and breaking up the tomato pieces with a wooden spoon, for 8–12 minutes until the tomatoes have completely collapsed and the mixture is thick, jammy, and reduced — the water has evaporated and the mixture is clinging to the pan rather than flowing freely. The sauce should be deeply coloured and fragrant.
Visual cue: Tomato and pepper mixture is thick, glossy, and dark red-orange. It sits in the pan without flowing when the pan is tilted. A wooden spoon dragged through it leaves a clean line that fills back slowly.
Underdone: Mixture is still very liquid and pale — the tomato water has not evaporated. It pours easily when the pan is tilted. Adding eggs now will make watery, scrambled-in-soup menemen. Continue cooking on medium-high, uncovered. Stir more frequently as it reduces. The water must leave before the eggs go in.
Perfect: Thick, reduced, nearly jam-like. Deep orange-red. Trails of sauce left by the spoon fill back in over 3–4 seconds. The smell is intense: sweet tomato, Aleppo pepper, and butter. Reduce heat to medium-low and add the eggs.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced to a very thick paste that is beginning to stick and scorch on the pan bottom. Smells slightly caramelised. Add a tablespoon of water, stir to loosen, and proceed to the eggs. The caramelisation is actually flavour.
Feel cue: Drag a wooden spoon across the bottom of the pan and lift it — the sauce should coat the back of the spoon in a thick, glossy layer and drip off slowly, not run off like water. That's the sign to add the eggs.

Beat the eggs lightly in a bowl — just enough to break the yolks and roughly combine, leaving streaks of white visible (these streaks create a marbled effect in the finished dish). Pour the eggs directly over the tomato and pepper base. Using a silicone spatula, fold the eggs gently through the tomato base in slow, wide strokes — pull from the edges inward, letting the tomato base streak through the eggs. Alternatively, leave the eggs mostly whole for a different style: nest the eggs whole on top and cover with a lid for 3 minutes until the whites set but the yolks remain runny.
Visual cue: Eggs have just set into soft, glossy, custardy folds that are streaked with red-orange tomato. The yolk is still visibly yellow in places. No liquid egg remains pooled.
Underdone: Liquid egg is still pooling at the base of the pan and raw egg white is clearly visible running freely. Continue folding over medium-low heat for 30 more seconds. Do not rush with higher heat — the eggs will curdle and seize.
Perfect: Eggs are just barely set — glossy, soft, and creamy with no liquid pooling but still moist and slightly trembling when the pan is nudged. The tomato-streaked scramble holds its shape on a spoon. Remove from heat immediately. Residual heat will carry-cook the eggs another 10–15 seconds.
Overdone: Eggs are fully set, dry, and separating from the tomato. The mixture looks crumbly and the egg has seized into tight, dry curds. Serve immediately with a drizzle of good olive oil over the top to restore some richness. Next time, remove from the heat 15 seconds earlier.
Feel cue: Tilt the pan gently when the eggs are folding — the mixture should move as a single, barely-set mass, not slosh like raw egg and not hold completely rigid. It should feel like a very soft, heavy custard.

Remove the pan from the heat. Scatter the remaining Aleppo pepper generously over the top — it should look like a dusting of dark rust-red across the yellow-orange surface. Scatter the chopped parsley. Serve immediately in the pan — menemen is traditionally brought to the table in its cooking vessel with a stack of white bread alongside for tearing and scooping. Do not let it sit: the carry-over heat from the pan will continue cooking the eggs, and the difference between perfect and overcooked is measured in minutes.
Visual cue: Vivid red-orange egg scramble blanketed in rust-red Aleppo pepper and bright green parsley. Still gently steaming. The butter and olive oil glisten slightly at the edges of the pan.
Underdone: Garnish not yet added. The dish looks monochrome and flat without the Aleppo pepper — and more critically, the heat of the pepper is missing from the flavour profile. Add the Aleppo pepper and parsley now. They are not optional decoration.
Perfect: Glossy, custardy eggs streaked with tomato, generously dusted with Aleppo pepper, and flecked with parsley. Steam rising. The butter is still foaming faintly at the edges. Serve immediately with white bread, sliced tomatoes, and white cheese alongside.
Overdone: The eggs have continued cooking from pan heat and are now dry and fully set. Parsley has wilted. The Aleppo pepper has absorbed the surface moisture. Add a small knob of fresh butter to the pan's edge and let it melt over the surface — it will restore some gloss and richness. Serve immediately.
Feel cue: Scoop a spoonful of menemen from the centre of the pan and hold it over the vessel — the eggs should fall back off the spoon slowly, in a creamy, cohesive ribbon, not drip off like liquid or hold stiffly like a solid. That slow ribbon is perfect menemen.

name: Mexican Carnitas
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: 2 tsp sugar + 2 tsp milk

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Pork shoulder braised low and slow in lard with orange and bay until it surrenders completely, then crisped under the broiler into shatteringly caramelized shards — the essential Michoacán street taco filling.

ingredients.name: Pork shoulder (bone-in preferred), cut into 8cm chunks

steps:
Place the pork chunks in a wide, heavy Dutch oven or deep skillet. Add the lard, orange juice, orange peel halves (squeezed side down), smashed garlic, bay leaves, oregano, cumin, and salt. Add just enough cold water to barely cover the pork — about 500ml. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook uncovered, maintaining a moderate simmer throughout. Do not cover — you want the liquid to evaporate. After 1 hour, add the condensed milk. Continue cooking for another 1.5–2 hours. As the water evaporates, the pork will transition from braising to frying in the rendered lard.
Visual cue: After 2.5 hours, the liquid has fully evaporated and the pork is frying in its own lard. The pieces are golden and beginning to caramelize.
Underdone: After 1.5 hours there is still significant liquid. Pork resists a fork — collagen hasn't converted. Continue simmering. Do not increase heat — the gradual transition from braising to frying is the method.
Perfect: Liquid has evaporated. Pork is golden and beginning to develop caramelized spots in the lard. It shreds easily when pressed with a spatula. Begin stirring every few minutes to caramelize evenly. Proceed to crisping.
Overdone: All liquid evaporated too early — pork is still tough and now frying hard in the lard. Add a splash of orange juice or water and continue cooking, covered, for 30 minutes.
Feel cue: At the end of the braise, press a chunk of pork with a wooden spoon — it should split apart with no resistance, falling into natural, striated shards.

Once the liquid has evaporated and the pork is frying, begin turning the pieces every 2–3 minutes. The condensed milk will caramelize with the orange sugars, creating dark, lacquered spots. Break larger pieces apart with a spatula as you go. When the pork is a patchwork of deep golden and dark caramelized spots — or transfer to a foil-lined baking sheet and finish under the highest broiler for 5–7 minutes for extra shattering crispiness.
Visual cue: Shredded pork in irregular shards — some pieces pale gold, some mahogany, some with crisp dark edges. A variety of textures from tender interior to crackled exterior.
Underdone: All pieces are uniformly blond. No caramelization. The flavor is still mild and steamed. Increase heat slightly and stir less — let the pork make contact with the hot pan for longer between turns.
Perfect: A textural mosaic: crisp caramelized edges, dark mahogany spots, pale tender interior. The kitchen smells of orange caramel and roasted pork. Each piece is self-basting in the lard. Remove from heat. Squeeze remaining orange juice over the top. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Pieces are uniformly very dark and dry. Caramel has burned bitter. Lard may be smoking. Remove from heat. Add a squeeze of fresh lime juice to introduce fresh acid and cut bitterness.
Feel cue: Pick up a piece of carnitas — the exterior should feel rigid and papery, while the interior gives immediately under pressure. If it's all crisp and no yield, it's overdone.

Taste the carnitas and adjust salt. Squeeze the remaining fresh orange juice over the hot meat — the acid will sizzle against the hot lard and brighten the flavor dramatically. Serve immediately on warm corn tortillas with diced white onion, fresh cilantro, salsa verde, and lime wedges. Carnitas are best within 30 minutes of cooking — the texture changes as they cool.
Visual cue: Glistening shards of pork with visible golden, mahogany, and dark crisp patches. Steam rising when the orange juice hits.
Underdone: Carnitas appear pale and moist. The flavor is mild and porky without caramelized depth. Return to high heat for 5 more minutes, or finish under the broiler.
Perfect: A mosaic of textures and colors — crisp edges, tender core. The bright acid of the orange juice cuts through the rich lard. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Carnitas are dry throughout, no textural contrast. Add a very small drizzle of fresh lard or oil before serving to restore some richness.
Feel cue: The smell at this moment should be extraordinary — roasted pork, caramelized citrus, and toasted lard. If it doesn't make you want to eat immediately, it needs more color.

description: Charred corn kernels tossed warm with crema, lime, cotija, and chile powder — all the drama of elote in a cup, the kernels popping with sweetness against the salty, creamy, spicy dressing.

ingredients.name: Fresh corn kernels (from 4 ears) or frozen

steps:
Heat a wide, dry cast-iron skillet or heavy pan over the highest possible heat until you can hold your palm 5cm above the surface for only 1–2 seconds. Add the butter, let it foam and begin to brown, then add the corn kernels in a single, uncrowded layer — you may need to do this in two batches. Do not stir for 2 full minutes. Let the bottom layer of corn make hard contact with the hot pan and char. Then toss once and let it sit for another 90 seconds. The goal is visible black charring on some kernels with others remaining golden — a variety of char is more interesting than uniform browning.
Visual cue: A mosaic of golden-yellow, deep amber, and char-black corn kernels. The pan should have a dark, fragrant fond.
Underdone: All kernels are pale yellow and steaming. No char anywhere. The pan is too cold or the corn is too wet. Remove half the corn if overcrowded. Increase heat. Wait until the pan is screaming hot before adding corn.
Perfect: A spectrum of char — some kernels black, some amber-gold, some pale. The kitchen smells of popcorn and butter char. The corn has dried slightly and concentrated in sweetness. Transfer to a bowl and proceed while still hot.
Overdone: Most kernels are uniformly black. The pan has burnt fond. The corn is fine — very charred corn is intentional in Mexican street food. Proceed with the recipe.
Feel cue: Listen for a constant, aggressive pop and hiss when the corn is in the hot pan — it should sound like popcorn about to pop. Silence means the pan isn't hot enough.

While the corn is still hot, transfer to a bowl. Add the crema, mayonnaise, lime juice, chile powder, and sliced scallions. Toss immediately — the heat from the corn will warm the dressing and help it coat every kernel. Taste and adjust: more lime for brightness, more chile for heat, a pinch of salt if needed. The dressing should be creamy, tangy, and spicy — each bite should have all four elements simultaneously.
Visual cue: Charred corn kernels fully coated in a creamy, pale-yellow dressing with visible chile-red specks and green scallion.
Underdone: Dressing is not fully coating the corn — some kernels are dry and uncoated. Toss more vigorously. If the dressing is too thick, a few drops more lime juice will loosen it.
Perfect: Every kernel is coated. The mixture is warm, steaming, and the char smell mingles with lime and cream. The scallion is distributed throughout. Plate and finish with cotija and herbs.
Overdone: The dressing has gone from creamy to thin from too much lime juice. Add an extra tablespoon of crema to restore body.
Feel cue: Taste a spoonful — the first flavor should be sweet corn, then cream, then the brightness of lime cutting through, then a heat build from the chile. If one element dominates, adjust.

Transfer to cups or a serving bowl. Scatter the crumbled cotija generously over the top — it should look like a snow of salty cheese. Add the chopped cilantro. Finish with an extra dusting of chile powder on top for visual contrast and an additional hit of heat. Serve immediately — this is a hot dish and the textural contrast of the charred kernels diminishes as they cool.
Visual cue: Creamy, charred corn in a cup or bowl with a generous cap of white cotija, vivid green cilantro, and a rust-red dusting of chile.
Underdone: Little garnish — the dish looks monochromatic and flat. Be generous with the cotija. It is not merely garnish — it is a main flavor component.
Perfect: Abundant cotija, bright cilantro, and visible chile red. The colors are vivid and appetizing. Steam still rising from the corn. Serve within 5 minutes of dressing.
Overdone: Corn has cooled and is no longer steaming. The dressing has absorbed and the kernels look dry. A 30-second blast in a hot pan with a drop of butter revives it. Add fresh cotija and herbs after reheating.
Feel cue: Scoop a spoonful and let it fall — the corn should fall in a creamy cascade, not a dry clatter. Each kernel should glisten with dressing.

name: Basbousa
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Fine semolina: 250 g
  Alternatives: coarse semolina (texture will be grainier)
Caster sugar: 100 g
  Alternatives: granulated sugar
Plain yoghurt: 200 g
  Alternatives: sour cream
Unsalted butter, melted: 80 g
  Alternatives: neutral oil; coconut oil
Baking powder: 5 g
Rose water: 10 ml
Blanched almonds, whole: 30 pieces
  Alternatives: pine nuts; pistachios
Sugar (for syrup): 200 g
Water (for syrup): 150 ml
Orange blossom water: 15 ml
  Alternatives: rose water
Fresh lemon juice: 10 ml
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 1 hour
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A golden, grainy semolina cake soaked with orange blossom syrup — dense yet tender, with a faint crunch at the surface and the heady perfume of rose water in every bite.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine the semolina, sugar, and baking powder in a large bowl. Add the yoghurt, melted butter, and rose water. Mix well with a spatula until fully combined — the batter will be thick and grainy, not smooth. Unlike a standard cake batter, it should hold its shape when mounded. Grease a 23x23cm baking pan. Spread the batter evenly with a wet spatula, pressing it into an even layer about 2cm thick. Let rest 15 minutes to allow the semolina to hydrate.
Visual cue: A thick, uniform, grainy batter spread evenly in the pan — matte surface, no liquid pooling.
Underdone: Batter is lumpy and uneven. Dry semolina still visible as separate grains at the surface. Mixture has not fully come together. Mix more thoroughly until all dry spots are incorporated. The butter and yoghurt need to coat every grain.
Perfect: Thick, uniform batter that holds its shape in the pan. Surface is matte and even. Smells of rose and butter. Place an almond on each pre-scored square and bake.
Overdone: Batter is very thin and runny — too much yoghurt was added, or the yoghurt was very liquid. Add 2-3 tbsp more semolina and stir in. Batter should be thick enough to hold a spoon upright briefly.
Feel cue: The batter should feel grainy and thick when stirred — like wet sand mixed with fat, not a smooth cake batter.

Preheat oven to 180°C (350°F). Score the rested batter into diamond or square shapes with a wet knife, cutting almost all the way through. Press a whole blanched almond into the center of each piece. Bake for 25-30 minutes until the top is golden and the edges are beginning to pull away from the pan. The surface should look slightly firm and dry.
Visual cue: An even golden top with slightly darker edges. Surface is firm and dry to the touch. Almonds are lightly toasted.
Underdone: Pale, soft top that gives when pressed. Interior still wet and custard-like. Edges not pulling from the pan. Bake for another 5-8 minutes. The cake must be fully set before the syrup is added.
Perfect: Golden top with the slightest resistance to a gentle press. Edges have pulled cleanly from the pan. A toothpick comes out mostly clean with a few moist crumbs. Almonds are light caramel in color. Remove from oven and immediately pour the hot syrup over the hot cake.
Overdone: Very dark golden edges approaching brown. Very firm, dry surface. Almonds are dark brown. Pour syrup immediately and generously — a dry basbousa needs more syrup to compensate.
Feel cue: Tap the center — it should sound slightly hollow and feel set, not wet. The aroma should be warm semolina and toasted almond, not raw flour.

Combine sugar and water in a small saucepan. Bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring only until the sugar dissolves. Once boiling, stop stirring and cook for 5-7 minutes until slightly thickened. Add the lemon juice and cook for 1 more minute (the acid prevents crystallization). Remove from heat and stir in the orange blossom water. The syrup should be ready just before the cake comes out of the oven — it must go hot onto hot.
Visual cue: A clear, slightly viscous syrup with light orange-blossom fragrance — not colored, not thick enough to thread.
Underdone: Thin, watery syrup that runs immediately off a spoon. Has not concentrated. Simmer for another 2-3 minutes. Test: a drop on a cold plate should hold its shape slightly.
Perfect: Lightly viscous, clear syrup that coats the back of a spoon thinly. Fragrant with orange blossom. Still hot and fluid. Add orange blossom water and pour immediately over the hot baked cake.
Overdone: Thick, golden syrup beginning to caramelize. Threads form between finger and thumb. Add 50ml hot water and stir to thin. The syrup must be fluid enough to soak in, not sit on top.
Feel cue: The syrup should feel barely slick between moistened fingertips — slightly thicker than water, but nowhere near honey.

Pour the hot syrup slowly and evenly over the hot basbousa in a thin, steady stream. Pour in the scored lines first, then over the whole surface. The cake will sizzle and absorb the syrup immediately. You should use all the syrup. Allow to rest at room temperature for at least 30 minutes until fully absorbed and the cake has cooled slightly. Cut along the score lines to serve. Basbousa improves after several hours as the flavors meld.
Visual cue: A glistening, lightly sticky surface with no pooling liquid — the syrup has fully absorbed into the semolina.
Underdone: Syrup is still pooled in the score lines and on the surface. The cake looks wet and waterlogged. Wait 20-30 more minutes for absorption. The semolina will continue to drink in the liquid.
Perfect: Surface is uniformly glistening but not wet. No puddles. Each piece has an even sheen. The bottom of the pan shows just a thin residue of syrup. Serve at room temperature. Each piece should feel moist but intact when lifted.
Overdone: Syrup was added cold to a cold cake and sits on the surface refusing to absorb, making the top soggy while the interior remains dry. Warm the pan briefly in a 160°C oven for 5 minutes to re-melt and drive the syrup in.
Feel cue: A perfect piece of basbousa should feel slightly dense and moist in the hand — not heavy with syrup, not dry, but with that characteristic yielding semolina texture.

name: Mujaddara (Lentils and Rice with Crispy Onion)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Brown or green lentils, rinsed: 200 g
  Alternatives: French Puy lentils (hold shape better)
Long-grain white rice (basmati), rinsed: 150 g
  Alternatives: short-grain rice (use less water)
Large yellow onions, halved and thinly sliced: 500 g
Olive oil: 80 ml
Ground cumin: 5 g
Ground coriander: 3 g
Ground allspice: 2 g
Water: 700 ml
Salt: 8 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 1 hour
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Earthen brown lentils and rice cooked together until they absorb and then share everything — finished with a crown of deeply caramelized onions so crisp they shatter and so sweet they taste of burnt sugar.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
