ingredients.name: Large yellow onions, halved and thinly sliced

steps:
Heat the olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat. Add all the sliced onions — the pan will be very full. Cook, stirring every 3–4 minutes, for 35–45 minutes. The onions will shrink dramatically, releasing water first, then slowly browning as the water evaporates. In the last 10 minutes, increase heat to high and stir more frequently as the onions caramelize. The goal is deeply browned, almost crispy onions that are sweet and complex. Remove two-thirds of the onions and set aside as the topping. Leave one-third in the pan.
Visual cue: Deep mahogany-brown onions that have shrunk to about 20% of their original volume. Some are crispy at the edges.
Underdone: After 20 minutes the onions are golden and sweet but not yet deeply colored or crispy. Continue cooking. Increase heat in the final 10 minutes. The crispy edges are the signature of mujaddara.
Perfect: Deep mahogany throughout. Some pieces are genuinely crispy. They smell of caramelized onion with a hint of pleasant bitterness. Remove two-thirds to a plate. Proceed with the remaining third.
Overdone: Onions have gone past caramel to burnt-black. Bitter and acrid smell. Discard the very darkest pieces. The slightly over-caramelized onions are still good — start a new batch for the topping if needed.
Feel cue: The fully caramelized onions should crunch slightly when you press one between your fingers — like a very thin, slightly soggy potato chip. The thinnest edges should be genuinely brittle.

In the same pan with the remaining one-third of the caramelized onions, add the ground cumin, coriander, and allspice. Stir for 30 seconds. Add the rinsed lentils and the water. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook for 15 minutes until the lentils are partially tender but still have a slight bite — they are not done yet. Season generously with salt.
Visual cue: Lentils that have swollen and turned from their raw color to a slightly muted brown-green, still holding their shape.
Underdone: After 10 minutes the lentils are still chalky at the center when bitten. Continue simmering. They will finish with the rice.
Perfect: Lentils have a slight resistance when bitten — tender at the outside, just barely cooked at the center. They need 10–12 more minutes with the rice. Add the rinsed rice and proceed.
Overdone: Lentils are fully soft and some are beginning to break apart. Add the rice and water immediately. The lentils will mash into the rice during the final cooking — still delicious, more of a porridge consistency.
Feel cue: Bite a lentil — it should offer real resistance at the center, like biting a firm chickpea. This is the target before the rice goes in.

Add the rinsed basmati rice to the partially cooked lentils and stir to combine. Check the water level — there should be enough to just cover the mixture by 1cm. Add a splash more if needed. Bring to a boil, then cover tightly and reduce heat to the lowest setting. Cook for 15 minutes. Do not lift the lid. Remove from heat and let steam, covered, for 10 more minutes. Fluff with a fork. The lentils and rice should be cooked through and have absorbed all the liquid.
Visual cue: Fluffy, separate grains of rice interspersed with intact, soft lentils. All liquid absorbed. No mushy spots.
Underdone: Rice is still chalky at the center. Some liquid remains at the bottom. Cover and cook for 5 more minutes on very low heat, then steam for 10 minutes off heat.
Perfect: Rice grains are fluffy and separate. Lentils are soft throughout. The mixture smells of cumin and caramelized onion. All water has been absorbed. Fluff with a fork and plate. Top with reserved caramelized onions.
Overdone: The bottom has scorched slightly. Rice is mushy. Remove from heat immediately. Place a clean kitchen towel under the lid to absorb steam for 5 minutes. The scorched bottom layer is a bonus — in the Middle East it is called qalaya and is prized.
Feel cue: Drag a fork through the finished mujaddara — the rice should separate cleanly and not clump. The texture should be fluffy and distinct, each grain and lentil independent.

Plate the mujaddara in a wide, shallow bowl or deep plate. Pile the reserved caramelized onions on top — do not stir them in; the contrast of the soft, spiced rice-and-lentil base with the crispy, sweet onion crown is the dish. Serve with plain yogurt, a salad of chopped tomato and cucumber, and warm flatbread.
Visual cue: A mound of earthy-brown rice and lentils crowned with dark, almost-crispy caramelized onions.
Underdone: The onion topping is still pale or the mujaddara base looks wet. Reheat the base if needed. The onions can be crisped in a dry pan for 2 minutes.
Perfect: The crown of dark, sweet onions contrasts visually and texturally with the soft, spiced base. The aroma is of warm cumin and caramelized onion. Serve immediately.
Overdone: The onion topping has softened from the steam of the mujaddara and is no longer crispy. Spread the onions on a baking sheet and toast at 200°C for 5 minutes to re-crisp, then plate.
Feel cue: Scoop through both layers with a serving spoon — you should feel the resistance of the crispy onions, then the yielding softness of the lentil-rice base. The contrast is the entire point of the dish.

name: Pocket Pita Bread
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=bakers_percentage）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Bread flour: 100 %
  Alternatives: all-purpose flour (less puff)
Warm water (38 C): 63 %
Fine sea salt: 1.8 %
Instant yeast: 1 %
Sugar: 0.5 %
Olive oil: 3 %
  Alternatives: neutral oil
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 1 hour 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A pillowy, steaming pita with a perfectly formed pocket — the result of a thin disc hitting a blazing stone or pan, where the surface sets before the interior can, trapping steam that inflates the bread into a hollow sphere.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine flour, salt, yeast, and sugar. Add warm water and olive oil. Mix until a rough dough forms, then knead by hand for 8 minutes (or 6 minutes in a stand mixer on medium) until smooth and elastic. The dough should be soft but not sticky — it should clear the bowl sides cleanly. Divide into 8 balls (about 90 g each). Cover with a damp towel and rest 10 minutes, then place on a lightly oiled tray, cover, and proof for 1 hour at room temperature until puffy.
Visual cue: A smooth, supple dough ball that holds its round shape and springs back slowly when poked.
Underdone: Still rough, slightly tacky surface. Tears when stretched. Knead 3 more minutes. The gluten network needs to develop fully for the pocket to form in baking.
Perfect: Smooth, slightly tacky but not sticky. Passes the stretch test — a small piece stretches thin without tearing. Springs back within 3 seconds when poked. Divide, ball, rest, and proof as directed.
Overdone: Tight, dry, springs back immediately when poked. Rest covered 15 minutes and proceed. Over-kneaded dough will relax during the proof.
Feel cue: The dough should feel like soft clay — smooth, cool, and responsive, yielding gently under the palm without sticking.

Place a baking stone or heavy inverted baking sheet in the oven and preheat to the maximum temperature (250–260 C / 480–500 F) for at least 45 minutes. On a lightly floured surface, roll each dough ball into a thin round 20–22 cm in diameter and about 3–4 mm thick. Even thickness is critical — thick spots won't puff. Transfer to a peel dusted with semolina or cornmeal, or a piece of parchment. Let the rolled pitas rest 5 minutes before baking.
Visual cue: Thin, even rounds with no thick spots or tears. Surface is lightly dusted and holds its round shape without springing back.
Underdone: Thick disc (6+ mm) that springs back to the center after rolling. Uneven thickness. Let it rest 5 more minutes and roll again. Gluten tension needs to relax.
Perfect: 4 mm even disc that holds its shape when lifted. No tears, no thick patches. Faintly translucent in the thinnest spots. Rest 5 minutes and slide onto the screaming-hot stone.
Overdone: Torn holes or paper-thin patches under 2 mm. Steam will escape through tears and the pocket won't form. Fold and re-ball the torn pita. Rest 10 minutes and re-roll.
Feel cue: The rolled pita should feel like a soft chamois cloth — flexible, barely stiff, draping easily over your palm without springing back.

Slide pitas directly onto the preheated stone or sheet pan. Bake for 3–4 minutes — do not open the oven. Watch through the oven glass: within 60–90 seconds the pita should begin to puff up into a balloon. Once fully inflated and lightly spotted with golden-brown, remove with tongs. Stack the hot pitas under a clean towel immediately — the steam inside softens the crust as they cool, creating the signature soft, pliable texture.
Visual cue: Each pita inflates into a taut, golden-spotted sphere within 90 seconds of hitting the stone.
Underdone: Pita has barely puffed. Looks like an irregular flatbread with some bubbles but no full pocket. The stone wasn't hot enough or the dough was too thick. Bake 1–2 more minutes. Fully puffed pitas have the cleanest pockets.
Perfect: Pita inflates fully into a balloon shape, golden-tan with scattered brown spots. After 3 minutes, the puff begins to subside slightly. Remove immediately with tongs. Stack under a towel — pockets remain as the pita deflates and cools.
Overdone: Pita has browned too darkly. The crust is rigid and crackly rather than soft and pliable. Reduce baking time to 2.5 minutes next time. Wrap overbaked pitas in a damp towel for 5 minutes to soften.
Feel cue: A properly baked pita is warm and pillow-soft after resting under the towel — gently squeezing it between two fingers reveals the hollow interior, a paper-thin wall flexing under the pressure.

name: Middle Eastern Rice Pilaf with Vermicelli
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Long-grain white rice (basmati): 300 g
  Alternatives: Egyptian short-grain rice
Fine vermicelli noodles, broken: 60 g
  Alternatives: angel hair pasta broken into 2cm pieces
Unsalted butter: 40 g
  Alternatives: olive oil for vegan version
Chicken or vegetable broth: 550 ml
  Alternatives: water with a pinch of turmeric
Fine sea salt: 8 g
Pine nuts: 40 g
  Alternatives: slivered almonds; toasted pumpkin seeds
Ground allspice (bahar): 2 g
  Alternatives: mixed spice
Fresh flat-leaf parsley, chopped: 10 g
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 35 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Thin vermicelli threads toasted in butter until amber, then cooked with long-grain rice into a fragrant pilaf scattered with golden pine nuts — the backbone of the Levantine table.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Rinse the rice in several changes of cold water until the water runs clear, releasing excess surface starch that would make the pilaf gluey. Cover with cold water and soak for 20 minutes. Drain thoroughly in a fine-mesh strainer and pat lightly dry — residual moisture will cause the butter to spatter.
Visual cue: Water runs clear when poured over rice; grains look white and slightly swollen.
Underdone: Water still runs milky-white, loaded with surface starch. Rinse 2–3 more times with cold water, agitating the grains each time.
Perfect: Water is nearly clear, grains are slightly translucent at the edges from soaking. Drains freely. Drain well and proceed to toast the vermicelli.
Overdone: Rice has been soaking too long (over 2 hours) and has begun to soften and break. Drain and reduce cooking time by 2 minutes.
Feel cue: Rinsed, soaked rice should flow through your fingers like fine sand with no stickiness — any tackiness means more rinsing is needed.

Melt the butter in a heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium heat. Add the pine nuts and toss for 1–2 minutes until golden. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside — they burn quickly. Add the broken vermicelli to the remaining butter and toss constantly for 3–4 minutes until the noodles turn a deep amber-brown and smell of toasted hazelnuts. This is the defining character of the dish.
Visual cue: Vermicelli is a deep, uniform amber-brown — darker than you'd think safe, almost russet.
Underdone: Vermicelli is still pale or only faintly yellow — it will be flavorless and contribute no nuttiness. Continue toasting over medium heat, stirring constantly.
Perfect: Deep amber to chestnut brown, smells intensely of toasted nuts and butter. Crackles faintly when stirred. Add the drained rice immediately.
Overdone: Vermicelli has gone past brown to black and smells burnt and bitter. Remove the burnt threads, wipe out the pan, and start again with fresh vermicelli in fresh butter.
Feel cue: The butter in the pan should smell of hazelnut browned butter — nutty and rich, not sharp or acrid — that is the moment to stop and add the rice.

Add the drained rice to the toasted vermicelli and stir to coat in the butter for 1 minute. Pour in the hot broth, add salt and allspice. Stir once. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to the lowest simmer, cover tightly, and cook for 15 minutes. Remove from heat and steam, covered, for 10 minutes. Do not lift the lid during cooking or steaming.
Visual cue: Each rice grain is separate and fluffy; amber vermicelli threads are woven throughout without becoming mushy.
Underdone: Rice still has a chalky bite; wet patches visible on the surface of the pot. Re-cover and steam off-heat for 5 more minutes — the residual heat will finish the rice.
Perfect: Grains are separate, fluffy, and fragrant with allspice. Vermicelli threads are tender but distinct. No liquid at the bottom. Fluff with a fork and plate.
Overdone: Rice grains have blown out and clumped; vermicelli has dissolved into the mass. Spread on a baking sheet to dry slightly; the flavors are intact even if the texture is softer.
Feel cue: Lift the lid after steaming and take a deep breath — the pilaf should exhale a warm cloud of allspice and toasted butter, the hallmark of a properly rested rice.

Fluff the pilaf with a fork, turning gently from the bottom up. Mound onto a warmed serving platter. Scatter the reserved golden pine nuts over the top and finish with the chopped parsley. Serve immediately.
Visual cue: A mound of amber-flecked white rice crowned with golden pine nuts and bright green parsley.
Underdone: Pine nuts are pale and mealy rather than golden; they add no flavor. Toast separately in a dry pan for 1 minute before scattering.
Perfect: Golden pine nuts glow against the rice; parsley is vivid green and fresh-smelling. The mound holds its shape but is not compressed. Serve within 10 minutes for best texture.
Overdone: Pilaf has been plated too long; the vermicelli has continued to absorb moisture and the dish looks heavy. Serve immediately — pilaf is a dish of immediacy.
Feel cue: The finished pilaf should feel light and airy on the serving spoon, each forkful revealing threads of toasted noodle and the occasional crunch of pine nut.

name: Misir Wot (Red Lentil Stew)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Red lentils (masoor dal), rinsed: 300 g
  Alternatives: split yellow lentils (longer cook time)
Yellow onions, finely minced: 400 g
  Alternatives: red onion
Niter kibbeh or clarified spiced butter: 60 g
  Alternatives: coconut oil + pinch turmeric + pinch cardamom (for vegan)
Berbere spice blend: 40 g
Garlic cloves, minced: 15 g
Fresh ginger, grated: 10 g
  Alternatives: ground ginger (3 g)
Water or light vegetable stock: 700 g
Fine sea salt: 8 g
Fresh lemon juice: 15 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 50 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Ethiopia's everyday vegan red lentil stew — red lentils cooked down in a base of caramelized onion and niter-kibbeh, spiced with berbere until the lentils dissolve into a thick, earthy, brick-red mass full of aromatic depth.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Niter kibbeh or clarified spiced butter

steps:
Place the finely minced onions in a heavy-bottomed pot with no oil over medium heat. Stir every 2–3 minutes for 20–25 minutes — the onions will first release water and steam in it, then dry out and begin to colour. The goal is a reduced, dark-tan, sweet-smelling onion base. This dry caramelization without fat is the traditional Ethiopian method (called 'dry frying' the onions) that gives misir wot its characteristic depth. The onions should shrink to about one-third of their starting volume and turn a warm golden-brown before any fat is added.
Visual cue: A reduced, golden-tan jammy mass of onion, roughly one-third of the original volume, clinging together in a soft pile. The pot bottom has light brown fond. The smell is sweet and savory — nothing sharp.
Underdone: Onions are still white to light tan, wet and soft, steaming actively. The volume has barely reduced. The flavor is sweet but flat and one-dimensional. Continue cooking. The caramelization only begins after all the water has evaporated — which takes at least 15 minutes. Be patient and keep stirring.
Perfect: Golden-tan, reduced by two-thirds, slightly sticky to the spoon, and smelling intensely of caramelized sweetness with a savory undertone. Fond forming on the pot bottom. Add niter kibbeh, berbere, garlic, and ginger immediately — the hot, dry pan will bloom the spices perfectly.
Overdone: Onion mass has gone dark brown to black at the edges, and the pot bottom has dark, bitter-smelling burnt fond rather than sweet caramel fond. Add 2 tablespoons of water and scrape the bottom immediately. Taste the onion: if it's mostly sweet with only slight bitterness, proceed. If it tastes bitter throughout, start the onion step again.
Feel cue: Stir the onions and listen — during the first 10 minutes they sound like steaming vegetables. During the last 5 minutes before adding fat, they should sound like gentle
frying, soft and slightly crackly. That transition in sound is your signal.

Add the niter kibbeh to the caramelized onions and stir until melted. Add the berbere, garlic, and ginger. Stir vigorously and cook over medium heat for 4–6 minutes, stirring constantly — the berbere will foam slightly as it hits the hot fat, then the fat will begin to separate at the edges as the spices cook. The mixture will become a very thick, dark, fragrant paste. The cooking of berbere in fat is non-negotiable: raw berbere tastes sharp and acrid; bloomed berbere tastes rounded, deep, and complex.
Visual cue: A thick, very dark brick-red paste with orange-red niter kibbeh fat beginning to pool at the edges. The smell is deep and complex — not the raw sharpness of berbere from a jar, but something richer and rounded.
Underdone: Berbere added just 1–2 minutes ago and still smells raw — sharp, acidic, and acrid. The fat hasn't separated and the paste looks grainy rather than glossy. Keep cooking. The raw sharpness of berbere takes 4–5 full minutes of heat in fat to mellow. Do not rush this step — it defines the flavor of the finished dish.
Perfect: Glossy, dark paste with fat separation visible at the edges. Smell is deeply savory, warm, and complex — heat without sharpness, spice without rawness. Add the rinsed lentils and stir to coat them in the spice base before adding water.
Overdone: The paste is burning — sticking aggressively, smoking, and smelling acrid. The berbere has carbonized. Add water immediately and reduce heat. Scrape the bottom. Taste: burnt berbere in small amounts is survivable in a stew; large amounts of carbonized spice will make the whole dish bitter.
Feel cue: Press a small amount of the bloomed paste onto your fingertip and smell it — if the berbere is properly bloomed, the warmth and fragrance should bloom immediately into the air around your hand. If it smells sharp and catches in your throat, give it 2 more minutes.

Add the rinsed red lentils to the spiced base and stir to coat them in the dark paste — they should turn a dark brick-red immediately. Add the water or stock and the salt. Stir to combine, scraping any stuck paste from the bottom. Bring to a boil over high heat, stirring occasionally. Reduce to a medium simmer, cover partially, and cook for 20–25 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes to prevent sticking. Red lentils cook quickly and dissolve completely — misir wot is not chunky; the lentils should entirely melt into the sauce to form a thick, uniform, porridge-like texture.
Visual cue: A thick, uniform, dark brick-red stew with no visible intact lentils. The texture resembles a very thick, smooth soup — it holds a spoon groove for 3–4 seconds before settling. The oil is visible as a sheen at the surface.
Underdone: After 15 minutes: lentils are still visible as individual shapes, the sauce is thin, and the lentils are only half-dissolved. Tasting a lentil reveals a still-chalky, undercooked center. Continue cooking, stirring more frequently to encourage dissolution. Red lentils fully dissolve at 20–25 minutes; if they're not dissolving, the heat may be too low.
Perfect: No intact lentils visible, thick and uniform texture, rich red-brown color that coats a spoon in a heavy layer. Tastes earthy, spicy, deeply savory, and slightly smoky from the berbere. Add the lemon juice, taste for salt and berbere, and adjust before serving. The lemon brightens the finished stew significantly.
Overdone: Lentils have stuck and burnt at the bottom — the stew smells slightly scorched, and lifting the spatula from the bottom shows dark, gluey stuck residue. Do not scrape the bottom — transfer the unstuck portion to a fresh pot. The scorched layer contaminates everything if stirred in.
Feel cue: Drag a spoon through the center of the simmering stew and watch the groove — it should fill back
in within 3–4 seconds. If it fills immediately, reduce without the lid to thicken. If it never fills (the stew is stiff), add 50 ml of water and stir.

Add the lemon juice and stir through. Taste and adjust: more berbere for heat and depth, more salt for savory presence, more lemon for brightness. Let the stew rest for 5 minutes off the heat — it will thicken slightly as it sits. Serve on injera: spoon the misir wot in a mound on top of a large round of injera and allow it to spread and be absorbed. The injera tears into pieces that scoop the stew. Traditionally served alongside other wots on a single large shared plate.
Visual cue: A mound of thick, dark brick-red stew sitting on the spongy surface of injera, the edges spreading slowly into the bread. The surface glistens with a thin sheen of niter kibbeh oil.
Underdone: Stew poured while still very hot and watery — it spreads too thin across the injera and soaks through rather than sitting in a mound. The injera becomes soggy rather than pleasantly saturated. Remove from heat and rest the stew for 5 minutes to thicken slightly before serving. A thick misir wot should hold its shape on the injera initially.
Perfect: A thick, glistening mound of dark red stew on injera. The earthy, spicy, complex smell of berbere and niter kibbeh is forward. The injera slowly absorbs the stew from the bottom, turning dark red at the contact point. Serve immediately with other Ethiopian side dishes. The stew is eaten by tearing pieces of injera and using them to scoop the wot — no utensils.
Overdone: Stew has been left to sit and has thickened to an unworkable, stiff paste that mounds but doesn't spread and is difficult to eat with injera. Stir in 2–3 tablespoons of warm water over low heat until loosened to the correct consistency. The stew should be thick but not gluey.
Feel cue: Tear a piece of injera and use it to scoop a spoonful of misir wot — the stew should cling to the injera piece completely, not drip off. The first bite delivers the spongy sourness of the teff bread
against the earthy, spiced warmth of the lentils, then the heat of the berbere builds slowly over 20–30 seconds.

name: Miso-Marinated Black Cod (Gindara Saikyo Yaki)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Black cod (sablefish) fillets, skin-on, pin-bones removed: 600 g
  Alternatives: salmon fillets (reduce marination to 1 day); Chilean sea bass
Saikyo (Kyoto white) miso: 200 g
  Alternatives: any white shiro miso
Mirin (hon mirin preferred): 60 g
Sake: 45 g
  Alternatives: dry sherry
Granulated sugar: 15 g
Pickled ginger (gari), finely sliced: 20 g
  Alternatives: fresh ginger, very thinly sliced
Yuzu zest or lemon zest: 3 g
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 3 days 20 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Black cod fillets buried in white miso and mirin for three days, then broiled until the miso caramelizes into a lacquer of bittersweet umami and the fish beneath is silky, rich, and nearly dissolves on contact with the tongue.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Black cod (sablefish) fillets, skin-on, pin-bones removed

steps:
Combine white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small saucepan over medium-low heat. Stir until the sugar dissolves and the mixture is smooth and slightly warmed (do not boil). Remove from heat and cool completely to room temperature. The marinade should be thick and spreadable, slightly thicker than heavy cream.
Visual cue: A pale, creamy beige marinade that flows slowly off a spoon in thick sheets. Smells of sweet rice wine, fermented soybean, and alcohol.
Underdone: Sugar not fully dissolved — granules visible at the bottom. Stir over gentle heat until fully smooth.
Perfect: Uniform, smooth, glossy marinade. No graininess. Sweet-savory smell with a clean miso base. Cool to the touch. Coat fish and marinate.
Overdone: Marinade has been cooked too hot and reduced significantly — thicker and darker than intended. Add a splash of sake or mirin to thin back to the right consistency.
Feel cue: The marinade should feel like smooth yogurt on your fingers — thick, uniform, and slightly sticky from the miso and mirin. If it feels watery, reduce slightly.

Pat the cod fillets completely dry with paper towels. Coat the flesh side generously with marinade, pressing it into the fish surface. A thin layer on the skin side is fine. Place in a zip-lock bag or container, making sure each piece is well-coated. Refrigerate for 2–3 days (72 hours for the full effect). The longer the marination, the deeper the flavor penetration and the more dramatic the miso lacquer during cooking.
Visual cue: After 3 days, the fish is deeply stained — the flesh under the miso looks slightly translucent and pale beige where the marinade has penetrated. The miso coating has adhered firmly and looks darker than when applied.
Underdone: Marinated less than 24 hours. Flavor is surface-only. Fish interior will taste of plain cod rather than miso. The dish works at 24 hours but is transformative at 72. The extra days are worth it.
Perfect: After 72 hours, the miso has slightly 'cured' the fish surface — it looks translucent where it meets the flesh. The coating has darkened and adhered firmly. Fish feels slightly firmer than raw. Scrape off excess marinade before broiling.
Overdone: Marinated beyond 5 days. The fish has become over-cured and the texture may be mealy. Cook regardless — it will still be exceptional. Reduce future marination time.
Feel cue: After 72 hours, the fish feels slightly firmer and denser than when you started — the miso enzymes have gently restructured the surface proteins, pre-seasoning the flesh all the way through.

Remove fillets from the marinade and gently scrape off the excess with a spoon or your fingers — do not rinse. Excess miso will burn, not caramelize. Place skin-side down on a foil-lined baking sheet lightly oiled. Broil 15–18 cm from the element for 8–12 minutes, watching constantly. The miso should caramelize to a deep golden-mahogany — not burnt, not pale.
Visual cue: The miso glaze has caramelized to a deep, blistered, uneven mahogany — darker at the thin edges of the fillet, lighter at the thickest part. The fish beneath is opaque and firm but still glistening.
Underdone: Miso glaze is still pale and wet-looking. Has not caramelized. Fish may still be raw at the center. Continue broiling. Watch every 30 seconds — the transition from perfect to overdone is rapid.
Perfect: Deep mahogany caramelization, slightly blistered and darker at the edges. The glaze looks dry and slightly charred at the very thin points. Fish flakes easily and the flesh is opaque throughout. Remove immediately and serve.
Overdone: Miso is black and burned. Bitter, acrid smell. A very dark char has appeared across the whole fillet. Scrape the most burnt bits with a spoon and serve the flesh beneath — black cod is so rich the underlying fish is likely still excellent.
Feel cue: Press the thickest part of the fillet with a finger — it should yield with almost no resistance, like pressing ripe avocado. If it springs back firmly, it needs another 2 minutes.

Transfer each fillet carefully — they are extremely delicate — to a warm plate using a wide spatula. Add a small pile of sliced pickled ginger beside the fish. Grate a tiny amount of yuzu or lemon zest over the top. Serve immediately with steamed rice and a simple cucumber vinegar salad to cut the richness.
Visual cue: A glistening dark-caramelized fillet, skin crisped, with the blushing pink of pickled ginger and a faint yellow confetti of yuzu zest against the mahogany.
Underdone: Fillet fell apart during transfer — the flesh is very flaky and delicate. Use the widest spatula you own and support the full fillet. Serve on the foil and slide onto the plate.
Perfect: Fillet transferred intact, mahogany glaze shining, garnishes vivid. The fish glistens with its own rich fat. Eat immediately — black cod at its peak is extraordinary.
Overdone: Fish has been sitting and begun to dry out. This is best served the moment it leaves the broiler. No resting needed.
Feel cue: A perfect bite of miso black cod should offer almost no resistance — the fork should glide through the flesh and it should dissolve on the palate like warm butter, leaving behind the lingering umami of the miso and the sweetness of the mirin.

ingredients.name: Salmon fillets, skin-on, about 150 g each

steps:
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the upper-middle position. In a small bowl, mash the miso, softened butter, honey and grated garlic with a fork until completely smooth and uniform.
Visual cue: A smooth, pale-caramel paste with no streaks of plain butter or lumps of miso.
Underdone: White butter streaks and beige miso lumps visible. Keep mashing; if the butter is too cold, set the bowl near the warm oven for 1 minute.
Perfect: Uniform, spreadable paste the color of peanut butter. Set aside while the beans start roasting.
Overdone: Butter has fully melted and the miso has separated into a grainy layer. Chill 5 minutes and stir again; or just brush it on as a thinner glaze.
Feel cue: It should spread like soft frosting on the back of a spoon and smell sweet, salty and faintly funky.

On a rimmed sheet pan, toss the green beans with the oil and 1/2 tsp kosher salt and spread them out. Roast for 8 minutes to give them a head start.
Visual cue: Beans turning a brighter, glossier green with the first small blisters appearing.
Underdone: Beans unchanged, dull green, no sizzle. Give them 2 more minutes before adding the fish.
Perfect: Vivid green with a few browned freckles; still firm. Push to the edges and add the salmon.
Overdone: Beans already shriveled and brown throughout. Move them to a plate and return them to the pan for only the last 3 minutes of the salmon's roast.
Feel cue: The pan should be sizzling faintly when you open the oven, and a bean should bend slightly but still snap.

Pat the salmon dry. Push the beans to the edges of the pan and lay the fillets skin-side down in the center. Spread the miso butter thickly over the tops and sides of the fillets. Roast 9–12 minutes, depending on thickness, until the salmon flakes easily and is opaque at the center or reads 145°F (63°C) in the thickest part. If the tops are pale, switch to the broiler for the final 1–2 minutes, watching constantly — miso burns quickly.
Visual cue: Salmon with a bronzed, bubbling miso crust, flesh opaque and just separating into flakes, butter pooling around the beans.
Underdone: Center still deep translucent orange and the flesh resists a fork. Return to the oven for 2 minutes and check again.
Perfect: Opaque pale-coral flesh that separates into large moist flakes under gentle fork pressure, 145°F (63°C) at the thickest point; glaze caramelized at the edges. Remove immediately.
Overdone: White albumin beading heavily on the sides, flakes dry and chalky, glaze blackened. Spoon extra pan butter over the fish and scrape off any burnt glaze.
Feel cue: Press the top of a fillet with a fingertip: it should give and begin to separate into layers, like pressing a stack of cards, not spring back firmly.

Drizzle the rice vinegar over the green beans and toss them in the melted miso butter on the pan. Plate the salmon with the beans, spoon over any remaining pan juices, and scatter with scallions and sesame seeds. Serve with steamed rice if you like.
Visual cue: Beans glistening with miso butter, salmon glazed and topped with fresh green scallion rings.
Underdone: Beans dry and plain while the butter sits pooled under the fish. Tilt the pan and roll the beans through the juices.
Perfect: Everything coated in a thin, savory gloss with a bright hit of vinegar. Serve hot.
Overdone: Too much vinegar pooling and making the beans sour. Add a small pat of butter and a pinch of salt to rebalance.
Feel cue: A bite of bean should taste deeply savory first and then clean and bright from the vinegar.

name: Homemade Miso
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Dried soybeans: 10 parts
  Alternatives: chickpeas (shiro-miso style); black soybeans
Dry rice koji (Aspergillus oryzae): 10 parts
  Alternatives: barley koji for mugi miso
Non-iodized sea salt: 4.5 parts
Reserved soybean cooking liquid: 2 parts
Soybean cooking liquid (tamari): 0.1 parts
Active time: 3 hours
Total time: 90 days
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Cooked soybeans inoculated with koji and packed under salt ferment over months into a dense, amber paste — concentrated umami, roasted earthiness, and a complexity that only time can build.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Rinse soybeans under cold water, sorting out any shriveled or discolored beans. Cover with at least three times their volume in cold water and soak for 18–24 hours at room temperature. The beans will roughly double in size and the skins will become taut. Drain and discard the soaking water — it contains flatulence-causing oligosaccharides. The beans are ready when a fingernail presses through one easily with minimal resistance.
Visual cue: Plump, pale-golden beans, fully round and smooth, with taut skins. The soaking water has turned slightly tan.
Underdone: Beans are still wrinkled, feel hard when squeezed, and the soaking water is still nearly clear. Soak 4–6 more hours. Cooler water slows absorption significantly.
Perfect: Beans have doubled in size, feel firm but yield gently under thumbnail pressure. Drain and cook.
Overdone: Skins are splitting open, beans feel very soft and waterlogged. Cook immediately — they are just over-soaked, not ruined. Reduce cooking time slightly.
Feel cue: A soaked bean pressed between thumb and forefinger should flatten with moderate resistance — like pressing a soft rubber eraser. A hard bean will crack; a perfect bean will yield smoothly.

Cover soaked soybeans with fresh cold water by 3 inches and bring to a boil over high heat. Skim and discard the grey foam that rises in the first 10 minutes — this is bitterness. Reduce to a vigorous simmer and cook for 3–5 hours until the beans are very soft: they should crush completely between two fingers with no resistance. Reserve 2 cups of the cooking liquid (tamari-like, deep amber, savory). The beans must be soft enough to mash — under-cooked beans create a lumpy, gritty miso that ferments poorly.
Visual cue: Beans are pale gold, completely tender, and crush between two fingers into a smooth paste with no graininess.
Underdone: Center of the bean is still slightly firm or chalky when bitten. Bean holds its shape under pressure. Continue cooking. Check every 30 minutes. Hard beans produce gritty miso.
Perfect: Bean crushes to a smooth paste between fingers. Entire bean is the same pale golden color throughout. Drain, reserve cooking liquid, and allow to cool to 40°C (104°F) before adding koji.
Overdone: Beans are falling apart, skins all burst, cooking water is very thick. Proceed — this is actually fine for miso. More surface area for koji to work.
Feel cue: Pick up a single cooked bean and press it between your thumb and forefinger until it collapses — the paste should feel like smooth hummus with no grit. The reserved cooking water will be dark amber and taste deeply savory.

Drain the cooked soybeans (reserving cooking liquid) and spread on a sheet pan to cool to below 40°C (104°F) — hot beans will kill the koji mold spores. Once cool enough to hold comfortably, mash using a potato masher, food mill, or by pressing in a zip-lock bag. The goal is a smooth, uniform paste with minimal bean chunks. Some texture is acceptable in country-style miso; total smoothness is the goal for refined miso.
Visual cue: A pale, smooth golden paste — slightly sticky, uniform in color, no visible whole beans. Texture resembles thick peanut butter.
Underdone: Half the beans are still whole or chunky. Paste is lumpy and uneven. Continue mashing — lumpy miso ferments unevenly and can harbor dry pockets.
Perfect: Smooth, sticky, uniformly golden paste. A handful pressed between palms holds its shape. Cool to 40°C or below before proceeding.
Overdone: Paste is so thoroughly worked it has become warm from friction. Spread thin and allow to cool below 40°C before adding koji — heat kills Aspergillus.
Feel cue: The mashed paste should feel warm but not hot against the inside of your wrist — like a comfortable bath, not a shower. If it burns, wait longer. The paste will be sticky and cling to your palms.

In a large bowl, combine rice koji and salt. Toss with your hands until fully mixed — the salt coats each grain of koji. Add this koji-salt mixture to the cooled bean paste. Mix thoroughly with your hands, kneading and squeezing until the koji is fully incorporated and no white koji clumps remain. If the mixture feels too stiff and crumbly, add reserved cooking liquid tablespoon by tablespoon until the paste holds together when squeezed into a ball. The mixture should hold its shape like wet clay.
Visual cue: A uniform, earthy-tan paste with occasional visible rice grains from the koji. Neither too wet (slumps immediately) nor too dry (cracks when squeezed).
Underdone: White koji grains still visible as distinct lumps. Salt streaks visible in the paste. Continue kneading for 5 more minutes — even distribution is critical for uniform fermentation.
Perfect: Consistent pale amber color throughout. Holds a firm ball when squeezed. Koji grains are evenly distributed. Form into dense balls and pack into fermentation vessel.
Overdone: Mixture is very wet and loose from too much added liquid. Spread thin, allow to firm up slightly, then proceed — excess moisture slows fermentation.
Feel cue: The miso mixture should feel like firm, slightly sticky modeling clay — cohesive, not crumbly, with the koji grains giving it a slightly granular texture against your palms. It should smell faintly sweet from the koji, earthy from the beans, and sharply salty.

Sterilize your fermentation crock or container with a clean cloth dampened with shochu or vodka. Form the miso mixture into baseball-sized balls and throw them firmly into the vessel — this packing motion eliminates air pockets, which cause mold growth. Press each layer firmly flat with a flat spatula or your fist. When all the miso is packed, smooth the surface completely flat. Sprinkle a thin layer of salt (about 2 tbsp) over the entire top surface as a protective barrier. Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface, then add a weight (a sealed bag of salt works well).
Visual cue: A smooth, flat surface of miso in the vessel with no cracks or depressions. Salt barrier visible as a thin white crust on top. Plastic wrap pressed directly to the surface with no air gaps.
Underdone: Visible air pockets, surface is uneven and pitted. Re-pack firmly. Every air pocket is a mold colony waiting to form.
Perfect: Dense, smooth, uniform surface. Container sealed with a direct-contact cover and a weight. No visible cracks. Label with the date and store in a cool, dark place.
Overdone: Miso has been packed so firmly the container is dangerously full. Remove some to a second container — miso expands slightly as it ferments.
Feel cue: Press your palm flat onto the packed miso — it should feel dense and unyielding, like firm clay. Any give or sponginess suggests air pockets that need to be pressed out.

Store at cool room temperature (60–75°F / 15–24°C), away from direct light. White or tan surface mold (tamari) is normal and expected — scrape and discard at the 30-day mark when you inspect. Shoyu-like liquid that pools on the surface is tamari: stir it back in. Check monthly: at 45 days the miso is a young shinshu style — golden, mildly sweet, and light-bodied. At 90 days it becomes a rounded, complex pale yellow miso. At 6 months: full-bodied aka miso. At 1 year: robust, dark, concentrated hatcho-style depth.
Visual cue: At 90 days: the miso has darkened from pale gold to a deep amber-tan. Scraping the surface reveals a paste that smells powerfully of soy sauce and roasted grain.
Underdone: At 30 days: still pale and smells of salty soy paste with little complexity. Tastes raw and harsh. Reseal and continue fermenting. Miso cannot be rushed.
Perfect: At 90 days: deep golden-amber, smells intensely savory with sweetness. Tastes rounded, salty, and complex on the tongue. Taste weekly from this point and harvest when you reach your desired depth.
Overdone: After 12+ months: very dark, almost black. Overpoweringly salty and concentrated. This is intentional for hatcho miso style — use in small quantities as a seasoning paste, diluted.
Feel cue: Ready miso yields slowly to a spoon pressed into the surface, leaving a glossy impression that holds its shape. It should smell like a sophisticated, savory version of soy sauce — never rancid, never putrid, always somehow edible and inviting.

name: Miso-Glazed Black Cod
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Black cod fillets (sablefish), skin-on, pinbones removed: 600 g
  Alternatives: sea bass; salmon
White miso (shiro miso): 120 g
  Alternatives: sweet yellow miso
Sake: 60 ml
  Alternatives: dry sherry
Mirin (hon-mirin): 60 ml
  Alternatives: 2 tsp sugar dissolved in 60 ml sake
Caster sugar: 20 g
  Alternatives: honey
Fine sea salt (for patting fish dry): 3 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 3 days (marinade)
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Nobu's iconic preparation — sablefish fillets submerged in sweet white miso, sake, and mirin for two to three days until the glaze becomes part of the fish, then broiled to a caramelized, lacquer-like sheen that shatters gently at the touch of a fork.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Black cod fillets (sablefish), skin-on, pinbones removed
Fine sea salt (for patting fish dry)

steps:
Combine sake, mirin, and sugar in a small saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 2-3 minutes, stirring, until the sugar dissolves and the alcohol cooks off — the raw boozy smell will mellow to a soft, sweet aroma. Do not boil vigorously. Remove from heat and allow to cool to room temperature completely before adding the miso.
Visual cue: A thin, pale amber liquid that coats a spoon faintly. Sugar is fully dissolved — no visible granules when tilted in the light.
Underdone: Raw alcohol smell still sharp and biting. Sugar granules visible when you tilt the pan. Continue simmering and stirring for another minute. Reduce heat if it threatens to boil hard.
Perfect: Liquid smells sweet and faintly vinous — like warm dessert wine. Fully clear. Cool enough to touch. Whisk in the miso off the heat.
Overdone: Liquid has reduced by more than a third and begun to caramelize — darkening to amber. Add a splash of sake or water to loosen, stir well, and remove from heat. The flavor is more concentrated but still good.
Feel cue: The liquid should feel slightly more viscous than water against your fingertip — warm honey-thin, not syrupy.

Add the white miso to the cooled sake-mirin base and whisk vigorously until the paste is completely dissolved and the mixture is uniformly smooth and creamy. There should be no lumps of miso visible. The finished marinade is sweet-salty, intensely savory, and pale ivory in color. Cool completely before use.
Visual cue: A smooth, creamy, pale ivory paste with no darker miso lumps. Runs off a whisk in a slow, steady ribbon.
Underdone: Streaks of undissolved miso visible. Mixture is lumpy or uneven in color. Keep whisking. If paste is very cold and stiff, set the bowl over warm water briefly while stirring.
Perfect: Uniformly pale ivory, silky, and slightly glossy. Smells deeply of fermented rice and sweet mirin. Use immediately to coat the fish, or refrigerate up to one week.
Overdone: Over-whisked — air has been incorporated and the marinade is foamy. Set aside for 5 minutes for the foam to subside before coating the fish.
Feel cue: The marinade should glide between your fingertips like thin hummus — creamy with faint resistance, not gritty.

Pat the cod fillets completely dry with paper towels, then lightly salt both sides and let them sit 10 minutes. The salt draws out surface moisture that would dilute the marinade. Wipe the salt and any exuded moisture away. Spread the miso marinade generously over all surfaces of each fillet, working it gently into the flesh. Place in a sealed container or zip-lock bag, pressing out air, and refrigerate for a minimum of 24 hours — 48-72 hours is ideal and transforms the fish.
Visual cue: Every surface evenly coated with a thick ivory-cream layer of miso. No bare patches. Fish is barely visible beneath the coating.
Underdone: Less than 24 hours — glaze sits on the surface without having penetrated. Flavor will be surface-level only. Extend the marinating time. This dish rewards patience — 2-3 days is the sweet spot.
Perfect: After 48-72 hours, the miso has stained the fish golden-ivory and the flesh feels slightly firmer. The fillet smells deeply of fermented sweetness. Wipe off excess marinade and proceed to broiling.
Overdone: More than 4 days — the miso's salt has begun to cure the fish excessively. The flesh feels dense and slightly rubbery. The flavor is intensely savory and the texture will be firmer than ideal, but still delicious. Wipe clean and broil as normal.
Feel cue: After 2-3 days, the fillets feel subtly firmer under the coating — the miso's salt has gently cured the outermost layer, giving it a silky, set quality.

Preheat the broiler to maximum heat with the rack 10-12 cm (4-5 inches) from the element. Wipe away excess marinade from each fillet with your fingers — too thick a layer burns before the fish cooks through. Place fillets skin-side down on a foil-lined tray. Broil for 8-12 minutes, watching constantly. The glaze will bubble, caramelize, and turn a deep amber-to-mahogany in patches. The fish is done when it is opaque throughout and flakes easily with a fork at the thickest point.
Visual cue: The glaze is caramelized to a deep amber, nearly mahogany at the edges, with a glossy sheen that catches the light like lacquer. The flesh beneath is opaque ivory and separates into large, glistening flakes.
Underdone: Glaze is still pale and matte — the Maillard reaction has barely begun. The center of the fillet resists the fork. Broil for another 2-3 minutes. If the glaze is coloring faster than the fish is cooking, lower the rack one position.
Perfect: Glaze is dark amber with charred spots at the highest points. Flesh flakes into large moist, glistening pieces with the faintest translucency at the very center. Remove immediately and serve without delay.
Overdone: Glaze has blackened and smells acrid. Flesh is dry and separating into small, tight flakes rather than large pillowy ones. Scrape the darkest crust gently. The fish oil-rich nature of sablefish means the interior is more forgiving than leaner fish.
Feel cue: Press the thickest part of the fillet gently with a fingertip — it should give way like soft butter, yielding in distinct planes of flesh rather than pressing to a uniform mass.

Serve immediately on warmed plates. The fish needs nothing beyond itself, though a small mound of pickled ginger and a few stems of blanched broccolini complete the plate. If the fillet sticks to the foil, slide a thin spatula between skin and foil — the skin sometimes adheres. Serve skin-side down and eat the caramelized glaze first — it is the crown of the dish.
Visual cue: A fillet of deep amber lacquer over ivory flesh, with the distinct planes of sablefish flake visible at the edge where it has been gently parted. Steam rising softly.
Underdone: Fish has cooled on the tray and the glaze has stiffened to a matte film. Flash under the broiler for 60 seconds to rewarm and revive the gloss.
Perfect: Glaze is glossy and molten-looking at the edges. Fish releases steam when the fork parts it. Plate is warm. Serve at once.
Overdone: Fish sat too long and has dried out. The glaze has fully set and lost its gloss. A brush of mirin warmed with a drop of soy, painted on before serving, restores some gloss.
Feel cue: When the fork slides into the fillet it should meet almost no resistance — the oil-rich sablefish flesh yields like cold butter, parting into translucent, yielding layers.

ingredients.name: Black cod (sablefish) fillets, skin-on, 150–180 g each

steps:
Combine mirin and sake in a small saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 2 minutes to burn off the alcohol — this prevents the marinade from tasting raw and sharp on the finished fish. Remove from heat. Whisk in the white miso paste until completely smooth with no lumps. Whisk in the sugar until dissolved. The marinade should be thick, silky, and uniformly tan-gold. Cool to room temperature before using.
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy, uniformly tan-gold paste — thick enough to coat a spoon heavily and fall in a slow, unbroken ribbon.
Underdone: Alcohol still sharp and raw in the aroma. Miso lumps visible. Sugar granules settled at the bottom. Continue heating and whisking. The alcohol needs at least 2 minutes at a simmer to volatilize.
Perfect: Deeply fragrant with a rounded, sweet-salty-fermented aroma — no raw alcohol sharpness. Perfectly smooth, glossy, honey-like consistency. Cool completely to room temperature before coating the fish. Hot marinade will begin cooking the proteins.
Overdone: Marinade has reduced too far — very thick and already beginning to caramelize at the pan edges. Dark patches in the paste. Add 1 tablespoon of water and whisk off the heat to restore consistency.
Feel cue: Rub a small amount between your fingers — it should feel silky, dense, and slightly sticky. When you release your fingers, it should pull in slow strings rather than dripping. Taste: assertively sweet, salty, and complex.

Pat the cod fillets completely dry — any surface moisture will dilute the marinade and prevent even coating. Coat each fillet generously on all sides with the cooled miso marinade. The coating should be visible and substantial, about 3–4 mm thick. Place in a non-reactive container (not aluminum — the miso acid will react), cover, and refrigerate. Marinate for a minimum of 2 days; 3 days is the traditional preparation. The miso enzymes will deeply penetrate the fish, converting some proteins and creating the characteristic silky texture.
Visual cue: Fillets completely encased in a thick tan-gold miso coating. After 2+ days: the coating has partially absorbed into the fish surface, which has taken on a deeper golden color.
Underdone: Thin, patchy coating. Pink fish flesh visible through the miso in several spots. Under 24 hours of marinating. Apply a second coat of marinade where gaps exist. Marinate at least another 24 hours.
Perfect: After 2–3 days: thick coating has partially absorbed. The fish beneath the coating has firmed slightly and taken on a golden stain. Aroma is intensely fermented and sweet. Remove from fridge 30 minutes before broiling. Wipe off excess marinade carefully before cooking.
Overdone: Marinated more than 5 days — the miso enzymes have broken down the surface proteins too far. Fish feels mushy and slides away in sheets. Cook immediately. The texture will be very delicate — handle with a fish spatula and serve directly from the pan.
Feel cue: After 3 days, press a fillet through the container — it should feel denser and firmer than fresh fish, like the coating has bound to the surface. The miso should have changed color from tan to a slightly darker gold where it contacts the fish.

Preheat the broiler to maximum heat. Very gently wipe each fillet with your fingers or a dry paper towel to remove the bulk of the miso marinade — leave a thin, even coating behind. Excess marinade will burn black under the broiler before the fish cooks through. Brush a broiler-safe pan with a thin film of neutral oil. Place fillets skin-side down. Broil 10–15 cm from the heat element for 5–7 minutes, watching constantly. The miso sugar will caramelize rapidly. You are looking for a lacquered, deep amber glaze with some dark caramelized spots — not charred black.
Visual cue: A deep amber-to-caramel lacquered surface with concentrated dark spots where the sugar has caramelized furthest. The flesh beneath should be barely opaque throughout — black cod is done at the first sign of flaking.
Underdone: Surface is pale gold, not lacquered. No deep caramelization. Fish is translucent and raw in the center. Continue broiling. The caramelization happens in a rush at the end — watch every 30 seconds.
Perfect: Deep amber glaze with dark spots. Fish lifts from the pan at the edges and the center is just barely opaque. A chopstick inserted in the center meets no resistance. The kitchen smells of caramelized miso. Remove immediately. Black cod overcooks in under 30 seconds.
Overdone: Surface has gone black and bitter. Fish has contracted and is pulling away from the skin. Scrape off the most bitter surface with a palette knife. The flesh beneath will be fine.
Feel cue: Press the thickest part of a fillet with a fingertip — it should give with the lightest pressure and the flesh should separate into its natural flakes without effort. Black cod at perfect doneness feels like pressing into firm, cool butter: yielding, smooth, almost no resistance.

Transfer the fillets immediately from the pan to warmed serving plates using a thin fish spatula — black cod is fragile at this point and will break apart if manhandled. The skin, having rendered its fat, should release easily from the pan. Serve immediately with steamed Japanese rice, pickled ginger, and a simple dashi broth alongside. No garnish is needed — the lacquered surface is the presentation.
Visual cue: A glossy, deeply caramelized amber fillet on a white plate, skin side down. The surface has a lacquered sheen, not a matte finish. Pale ivory flesh visible at the edges where it has just barely flaked.
Underdone: Fish transferred while the glaze is still sticky and tearing. Surface looks dull and wet. The fish should rest in the pan 30 seconds after removing from the broiler before sliding the spatula underneath.
Perfect: Glaze is set and lacquered. Fillet holds its shape on the plate. The first flake at the edge is visible and pearlescent-white. Serve within 90 seconds — the texture changes rapidly as it cools.
Overdone: Fish has cooled too long and the fat has set in white globules on the surface. Return to the broiler for 60 seconds to re-melt the fat and revive the glaze.
Feel cue: Slide a chopstick between the flakes — they should separate in thick, pearl-white sheets with no resistance. Each flake should feel moist and gelatinous, coated in its own rendered fat. The skin should peel away in a single piece, crackly-dry on the outside, silky on the underside.

name: Nasu Dengaku
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: Chinese eggplant; Italian eggplant (halved lengthwise, scored deeper)

  Alternatives: honey; light brown sugar
Sesame oil: 15 ml

  Alternatives: shiso chiffonade; micro shiso

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Halved Japanese eggplant lacquered in a sweet-savory white miso glaze, broiled until the surface caramelizes to deep amber and the flesh beneath collapses to yielding silk. A dish of opposites — bitter char over honeyed umami, firm skin over trembling interior.

steps:
Halve the eggplants lengthwise. Using a sharp paring knife, score the cut face in a deep crosshatch pattern — cut about two-thirds into the flesh at 1 cm intervals in both directions without piercing the skin. This scoring is critical: it allows heat to penetrate and sesame oil to seep into the flesh, preventing steam from splitting the skin and dramatically shortening the roasting time. Press the cut face lightly to open the grid slightly.
Visual cue: A diamond grid of cuts visible across the pale ivory flesh, roughly 1 cm apart, deep enough to see the depth of the cut but not breaking the purple skin.
Underdone: Cuts are shallow, only scratching the surface. The grid is barely visible and the flesh is still tightly closed. Re-score more deeply — the knife should enter at least half the thickness of the eggplant.
Perfect: Clear, confident diamond grid, cuts deep but skin intact. The flesh opens slightly like a waffle pattern when the halves are pressed. Brush with sesame oil and proceed to roasting.
Overdone: Cuts have pierced the skin in places, creating holes in the purple exterior. Proceed — the eggplant will still taste excellent, the skin will just be less intact when served.
Feel cue: The blade should glide through the spongy, seed-flecked flesh with almost no resistance, like cutting through dense foam.

Brush the scored cut face generously with sesame oil, working the oil into the crosshatch cuts with the brush. Flip and brush a thin layer over the skin side as well. The sesame oil serves double duty: it prevents sticking and imparts a deep, nutty fragrance that suffuses the flesh during roasting. Line a baking tray with foil and place eggplant halves cut-side down.
Visual cue: The cut faces glisten with a thin even coat of oil, the diamond cuts slightly pooled with oil. The flesh shows no dry white patches.
Underdone: Pale, dry-looking flesh with the oil only on the surface. The cuts look dry and tight. Apply another pass of oil, pressing the brush into the scored cuts.
Perfect: Every cut holds a tiny pool of oil. The surface shines evenly without dripping excess onto the tray. Place cut-side down on the foil-lined tray.
Overdone: Oil is pooling heavily on the tray beneath the eggplant, not staying in the flesh. Tip slightly to let excess oil drain — proceed, the eggplant will not suffer.
Feel cue: The brush should glide across a lightly resistant, spongy surface. The scored flesh drinks in the oil — if it pools and runs off immediately, the cuts are too shallow.

Roast cut-side down in a 220°C (425°F) oven for 12–15 minutes, until the flesh is completely tender when pierced with a chopstick or skewer and the cut faces have taken on a light gold color from contact with the tray. This initial roasting collapses the air pockets in the spongy eggplant flesh and drives out moisture, which concentrates the flavor and creates the right base for the glaze to adhere to. Do not rush this step — underdone eggplant will have a bitter, spongy bite.
Visual cue: The eggplant has shrunk noticeably and the cut faces show light golden-brown color where they contacted the tray. A chopstick meets no resistance when pushed through.
Underdone: Eggplant still holds its original shape, feels firm when pressed. Cut faces are pale and steamed-looking rather than colored. Return to the oven for 3–4 more minutes. The eggplant must be fully yielding before glazing.
Perfect: Eggplant has collapsed and softened, the skins are slightly wrinkled, the cut faces show a light gold fond. A skewer passes through with zero resistance. Flip, apply the dengaku glaze, and move to the broiler.
Overdone: Eggplant is very dark underneath, skins are breaking down and starting to shrivel aggressively. Flesh is mushy. Pull immediately and glaze — the broiler step will be short. The extra softness is forgiving in the final dish.
Feel cue: Press the skin side with a finger — the eggplant should give completely, collapsing like a soft pillow with no firm resistance at the core.

While the eggplant roasts, combine white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small saucepan over very low heat. Whisk constantly as the mixture warms — the goal is just to dissolve the sugar and bring everything into a smooth, homogeneous paste, not to cook it. The glaze should be warm, fluid, and spreadable, the consistency of thick yogurt. Remove from heat as soon as it is smooth. Taste: it should be deeply savory, sweetly balanced, and intensely fragrant.
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy amber paste that falls from the whisk in a thick, slow ribbon. No lumps of miso visible.
Underdone: The glaze is lumpy and the sugar hasn't dissolved. The miso is not fully incorporated. Continue whisking over low heat until fully smooth.
Perfect: Glossy, fluid, uniform amber paste. Drops from the whisk in a slow, thick ribbon that dissolves back into itself. Remove from heat and set aside for glazing.
Overdone: The glaze has begun to bubble, darken at the edges, and thicken too much. It smells toasty rather than just fragrant. Remove from heat immediately. It will relax as it cools — thin with a splash of sake if too stiff.
Feel cue: The whisk should meet gentle resistance that disappears — you are looking for the moment the paste becomes uniformly smooth and fluid rather than grainy or separated.

Flip the roasted eggplant halves so the cut face is now up. Spoon the dengaku glaze generously over each half, spreading it to the edges with the back of the spoon. The layer should be thick enough to be opaque — roughly 3–4mm — so it caramelizes and chars slightly rather than burning off thin. Do not be timid: a thick, generous glaze is what makes this dish.
Visual cue: Each eggplant half is blanketed in a thick, even amber glaze that reaches the edges of the flesh. No bare patches visible.
Underdone: Thin, uneven smear of glaze, flesh visible through it in patches. Spoon more glaze on and spread again. Err on the side of generosity.
Perfect: Opaque, even amber blanket. The glaze sits thick and slightly domed at the center, thinning toward the edges. Place under the broiler immediately.
Overdone: So much glaze it is pooling on the tray and sliding off. The eggplant is drowning in the paste. Use a spoon to remove a little from the tray — but honestly, a little extra caramelized glaze on the tray is delicious scraped back.
Feel cue: The spoon should glide smoothly over the soft eggplant surface, the glaze spreading like cool honey — thick and yielding, not watery.

Broil the glazed eggplant halves under a hot broiler (or salamander) for 3–5 minutes, watching constantly. The glaze should bubble, then caramelize to deep amber-brown with slightly charred edges and spots — this Maillard browning and mild caramelization is the defining character of dengaku. Remove from the broiler and let rest for 1 minute on the tray. Transfer to serving plates, scatter toasted sesame seeds generously, and finish with sliced scallion. Serve immediately while the eggplant is still trembling-soft and the glaze is warm.
Visual cue: Deep amber to dark brown glaze with charred edges and dark spots. The surface should be matte and caramelized, not glossy and wet.
Underdone: Glaze is warm but still pale and glossy, no browning or charring. Looks identical to before broiling. Return under the broiler for 1–2 more minutes. Watch closely — the line between perfect and burnt is narrow.
Perfect: Deep amber-brown, blistered in spots, matte and slightly tacky. Edges show darker char. The kitchen smells intensely of caramelized miso. Remove immediately. Rest 1 minute, then garnish and serve.
Overdone: Black patches across most of the surface. Acrid, burnt-miso smell rather than toasty. Scrape the most burnt areas off carefully with a spoon. The flesh beneath is excellent and the slightly bitter char may even be welcome in small amounts.
Feel cue: The broiler will make the glaze hiss and bubble — the sound of active caramelization. The moment the bubbling subsides and the surface goes quiet and matte, it is ready.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

  Alternatives: black cod (sablefish); mahi-mahi
White shiro miso: 20 parts
  Alternatives: awase miso
Mirin: 10 parts
  Alternatives: sake + 1 tsp sugar
Sake: 8 parts
  Alternatives: dry sherry; dry vermouth
White sugar: 4 parts
  Alternatives: brown sugar
Fine salt: 1 parts
Thinly sliced scallion greens: 3 parts
  Alternatives: toasted sesame seeds
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 1 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Salmon fillets marinated in white miso, mirin, and sake, then broiled until the glaze caramelizes to a burnished lacquer and the interior flakes into rich, lustrous layers.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Whisk together the white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar until fully smooth and the sugar has dissolved. The marinade should be a pale caramel paste that flows like thick honey. Taste it: it should be intensely savory and sweet, with the faint sting of alcohol — the sake and mirin will carry the volatile top notes away as the fish broils, leaving the miso caramelized and fragrant.
Visual cue: A uniform, glossy, pale-amber paste with no lumps of undissolved miso. It pours in a slow, thick ribbon from the whisk.
Underdone: Lumpy with flecks of unmixed miso; the sugar is gritty at the bottom. Keep whisking and add a few drops more sake to help the paste loosen and the sugar dissolve.
Perfect: Silky, glossy, uniformly amber — the whisk leaves a brief trail. The smell is sweet, yeasty, and umami-rich. Pour over the salmon fillets and proceed to marinate.
Overdone: Thinned to a watery liquid — too much sake added. The marinade will run off the fish without adhering. Whisk in a little more miso to thicken it back to a coating consistency.
Feel cue: The marinade should cling to the whisk rather than drip freely — somewhere between heavy cream and smooth peanut butter in body.

Season the salmon lightly with salt, then coat each fillet on all sides with the miso marinade. Place in a shallow dish or zip-lock bag, making sure the marinade contacts every surface. Refrigerate for at least 1 hour and up to 24 hours — the longer the rest, the deeper the savory penetration and the more intense the caramelized crust. Wipe off the excess marinade before broiling; any thick layer will burn before the fish cooks.
Visual cue: Fillets evenly coated in a pale amber veil — no bare patches, no thick pooled clumps. After resting, the surface looks slightly tacky and the marinade has tightened where it touches the flesh.
Underdone: Marinade is thin and mostly dripped off; fish looks pale and barely colored. Spoon the pooled marinade back over the fish and return to the fridge for a longer rest.
Perfect: An even, amber-tinted coat that clings firmly. The flesh has taken on a slightly firmer texture at the edges from the salt and enzymes. Wipe away the excess with a finger or paper towel, then broil immediately.
Overdone: Marinated beyond 36 hours: the flesh looks grey and mushy at the surface, texture broken down by the salt and miso enzymes. Wipe the surface clean, cook promptly, and keep a closer eye on texture during cooking. The flavor will still be good.
Feel cue: The coated fillets should feel slightly sticky to the touch, the marinade gripping your fingertip before releasing — that tack is what will bond the glaze to the fish under the broiler's heat.

Position an oven rack about 15 cm from the broiler element and preheat the broiler to maximum. Line a baking sheet with foil and lightly oil it. Wipe the excess marinade from the salmon, place skin-side down, and broil 8–12 minutes depending on thickness — no flipping needed. Watch continuously: the miso sugars move from golden to burnt in under a minute at this heat. The skin should crisp and the glaze should bubble, bronze, and develop dark caramelized spots at the edges.
Visual cue: A deep mahogany-lacquered surface with dark caramelized flecks at the edges, the center a burnished amber-gold. The skin is crisp and slightly charred. The flesh beneath has gone from translucent to barely opaque at the very center.
Underdone: Surface is pale yellow, no caramelization, the glaze looks wet and steamed rather than bronzed. The flesh is soft and translucent at the center. Continue broiling, watching every 30 seconds — the browning accelerates quickly once the surface dries.
Perfect: Deep, burnished mahogany crust with concentrated dark edges, the interior just turning opaque and flaking under gentle pressure of a fork. The skin crisps and pulls slightly from the flesh. Transfer immediately to plates; the fish continues cooking briefly off the heat.
Overdone: Black and acrid-smelling surface; the miso sugars have burnt past caramelization to carbon. Flesh is chalky and dry underneath. Scrape away any fully carbonized bits; the fish beneath may still be salvageable but will be dry. Next time, wipe off excess marinade more thoroughly and watch the broiler constantly.
Feel cue: Prod the thickest part with the tip of your finger: perfectly cooked salmon yields and just begins to separate into flakes, with the faintest resistance at the very center — not rock-solid (overcooked) and not a slippery give (raw).

Slide the fillets onto warm plates using a thin spatula. The skin may stick to the foil — use the spatula to separate it cleanly. Scatter thinly sliced scallion greens over the top. Serve immediately with steamed short-grain rice and a small mound of pickled ginger or a wedge of sudachi if available.
Visual cue: A lacquered, deep amber fillet contrasted with bright green scallion ribbons. The glaze shimmers under the light. Pressed with a fork, the flesh separates into rich, lustrous flakes.
Underdone: Flesh parts reveal large, glassy, translucent sections — the interior is raw. Return to the oven (not the broiler) at 180 C / 350 F for 2–3 minutes to finish gently without burning the glaze further.
Perfect: Flakes separate cleanly into large, moist, ivory-pink layers. The glaze is glossy, tacky, and fragrant — sweet, savory, and smoky from caramelization. Serve at once — the glaze sets and loses its sheen as it cools.
Overdone: Flesh crumbles into dry, fine-grained pieces with white albumin pressed out; the color has gone pale and chalky. Flake the fish and serve over rice with extra warm miso broth to compensate for the lost moisture.
Feel cue: The finished fillet should offer almost no resistance to a fork — the flakes should release with a gentle nudge, each one glistening with its own fat. If you have to push, it has gone too far.

name: Homemade Shiro Miso
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Dried soybeans: 10 parts
  Alternatives: chickpeas (for shiro-style chickpea miso)
Rice koji (steamed rice inoculated with Aspergillus oryzae, fresh or dried): 10 parts
  Alternatives: barley koji (mugi koji, for a deeper, more robust miso)
Non-iodized sea salt or kosher salt: 3.5 parts
Soybean cooking water (reserved from boiling): 2 parts
  Alternatives: filtered water if soybean water unavailable
Additional salt (for the crock surface crust): 0.5 part
Active time: 2 hr
Total time: 90 days
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Cooked soybeans blended with koji rice and salt, then packed into a crock and weighted for 3–6 months — slowly transforming into a sweet, pale miso with a mellow, savory depth that no commercial paste can match.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
