ingredients.name: Rice koji (steamed rice inoculated with Aspergillus oryzae, fresh or dried)
Non-iodized sea salt or kosher salt
Additional salt (for the crock surface crust)

steps:
Rinse the dried soybeans thoroughly and soak in three times their volume of cold water for 16–24 hours. The soybeans will absorb water and more than double in size — use a sufficiently large container, as they expand dramatically and can overflow an undersized bowl. The soaking water will turn pale beige to yellow from the surface proteins and phytates leaching out; this is normal. Drain and discard the soaking water. Well-soaked soybeans are essential: insufficiently soaked beans will not cook evenly and will produce a rough, gritty miso base with a raw-soybean edge that no amount of fermentation will fully smooth out.
Visual cue: After 18–24 hours, soybeans have swelled to nearly double their dried size, turning from wrinkled and dense to plump and smooth-skinned. When you cut one in half, the cross-section should be uniformly pale yellow with no visible dry center.
Underdone: After only 8–10 hours, soybeans are still visibly wrinkled and smaller than fully soaked beans. When cut, the center shows a dry, starchy white dot. They will not cook evenly. Continue soaking for at least 6–8 more hours. Undersoaked soybeans will remain hard in the center even after prolonged cooking and produce a rough miso.
Perfect: Plump, smooth, uniformly swollen soybeans that nearly fill the soaking vessel. Cut in half: uniformly pale yellow throughout, no white dry center. The soaking water is yellow-beige. Drain, discard the soaking water, and proceed to cooking immediately.
Overdone: Soaked more than 36 hours at room temperature in warm weather — some beans may have split or even begun to ferment (faint sour smell). Not a catastrophe, but cook immediately. Drain and proceed to cooking. Slightly over-soaked beans cook very quickly — check for doneness earlier than usual.
Feel cue: Squeeze a fully soaked soybean between your thumb and index finger — it should yield and split cleanly
with moderate pressure. If it resists and feels hard inside, it needs more soaking time.

Cover the drained soybeans with fresh cold water (three to four times their volume) in a large pot and bring to a boil. Skim the foam that rises aggressively in the first 10–15 minutes — this foam is saponins and surface proteins that would make the miso bitter and the broth murky. Reduce to a gentle simmer and cook for 2–4 hours until the soybeans are completely tender all the way through. Test by mashing a single bean between two fingers: it should collapse into a smooth paste with zero resistance. Reserve about 2 cups of the cooking liquid — it is rich in amino acids and dissolved soybean proteins and will be used to adjust the texture of the miso base. Drain the rest.
Visual cue: Fully cooked soybeans are uniformly soft, pale yellow-to-golden, and yield instantly to slight pressure — no hard center whatsoever. The cooking water is a warm amber-golden color, slightly thick from dissolved soybean proteins.
Underdone: After 2 hours, the beans still have a slight bite — not hard, but not fully yielding. There is resistance when you press one between your fingers. The miso will have a slightly grainy texture. Continue simmering. Soybeans can take up to 4 hours depending on their age (older beans take longer). Don't rush — they must be completely, effortlessly soft.
Perfect: Beans collapse with the lightest pressure into a smooth, even paste. No grit, no resistance. The cooked aroma is of warm, slightly nutty soybeans — mild and pleasant. Reserve the cooking liquid before draining. Reserve cooking liquid, drain the beans, and let them cool to around 40°C / 104°F (warm to the touch) before mixing with koji — too hot will damage the koji enzymes.
Overdone: Beans have cooked to the point of disintegrating — the pot is a porridge of collapsed soybean pulp rather than identifiable beans. This is actually fine and even slightly beneficial for miso, as the paste will be

smoother. Proceed as normal — drain the cooking liquid and use the bean mush directly. The miso base will be smoother than average, which is not a problem.
Feel cue: Press a cooked soybean between your molars — it should dissolve into an even, smooth paste with no hard or chalky bits. The cooking water should feel slightly slick between your fingers from dissolved soybean proteins, like a very thin, gelatinous stock.

While the cooked soybeans are still warm (not hot — around 40°C / 104°F; if too hot the heat will damage the koji enzymes), mash them thoroughly by hand with a potato masher, a food mill, or a food processor until they form a smooth, fairly uniform paste. A few larger pieces are acceptable, but the goal is a relatively smooth, consistent texture. In a large bowl, combine the mashed soybeans with the rice koji and all but a pinch of the salt. Mix thoroughly by hand — the traditional Japanese method of miso-making, called tameshitate, involves vigorous kneading and squeezing the mixture between your hands to fully integrate the koji with the soybean paste. Add cooking liquid as needed to reach a consistency like a stiff, moldable dough — firm enough to hold a ball shape, not sticky or loose. The koji provides the enzymes (amylases and proteases) that will gradually break down proteins and starches into the glutamates and sugars that define miso's deep flavor.
Visual cue: A dense, pale yellow paste with a slightly rough, grainy texture from the koji rice still visible as distinct cooked grains throughout the soybean mass. It looks like a very dense, savory almond paste.
Underdone: Soybeans not fully mashed — large chunks of intact bean are visible and the paste is uneven, with distinct lumps rather than a relatively uniform texture. Mash more thoroughly. For a completely smooth miso (the style of most commercial shiro miso), pass the mashed beans through a food mill or process in a food processor before mixing with koji.
Perfect: A stiff, dense paste that holds a molded ball shape without slumping or sticking to your hands. Pale yellow-to-cream in color, with tiny white rice koji grains visible throughout. Tastes assertively salty and mildly soybean-ish — nothing like finished miso yet. Roll into balls and proceed to crock packing. The ball-rolling helps reveal any

remaining air pockets before packing.
Overdone: Added too much cooking liquid — the paste is now too wet and soft, slumping from a ball shape. It will ferment fine but the texture will be looser than ideal. Incorporate more koji or let the paste rest uncovered for 15 minutes to firm slightly. Do not add more salt to compensate — the salt ratio is precisely calibrated.
Feel cue: The miso base should feel like stiff raw cookie dough when you roll it — firm enough to hold its shape when pressed into a ball, slightly yielding when squeezed, and leaving a clean impression of your fingerprints without sticking to your palms.

Sterilize a ceramic crock, glass jar, or food-grade container by rinsing with boiling water or a dilute alcohol solution (sake works perfectly). Roll the miso base into balls roughly the size of a tennis ball — rolling expels air pockets. Slam each ball into the crock firmly (the Japanese call this action 'tama-nage', or 'ball throwing') — the impact packs the miso tightly and expels trapped air that would create anaerobic pockets where unwanted mold can form. Pack layer by layer, pressing each layer flat and firm before adding the next. Once all the miso is packed, press the surface completely flat and smooth. Sprinkle the remaining salt over the surface to form a protective crust. Press a layer of plastic wrap directly onto the surface, then place a heavy weight on top (a plate and full bottles of water work well). Cover the crock with a cloth and secure it.
Visual cue: A tightly packed crock with a flat, smooth miso surface dusted with a thin salt crust, a layer of plastic wrap pressed directly on the surface, and a visible weight on top pressing the miso down. No gaps, no air pockets visible at the edges.
Underdone: Loosely packed miso with visible air gaps between layers — the balls were placed rather than slammed, and the layers were not thoroughly pressed flat. Re-pack by pressing the miso down firmly with a dampened fist. Any visible gaps at the crock walls should be pressed closed. Air is the enemy.
Perfect: Dense, flat-packed miso with no visible gaps. When you press on the plastic wrap layer, you feel solid, consistent resistance — no spongy air pockets. The weight is stable and level. Mark the crock with the date. Store in a cool, stable-temperature location (ideally 15–20°C / 59–68°F) for the duration of fermentation.
Overdone: Packed so forcefully that the miso has smeared up the crock walls past the salt-crust line, creating unprotected exposed

surfaces above the brine level. Wipe the inner crock walls above the miso surface clean, re-apply a dusting of salt at the surface level, and re-lay the plastic wrap.
Feel cue: Press your palm firmly on the weight atop the crock — it should feel completely immovable and solid. Any give or wobble means the miso beneath is not uniformly packed. A properly packed miso crock feels like pressing on packed earth.

Ferment in a cool, stable location at 15–20°C / 59–68°F. Shiro miso (white miso) is a short-ferment style: 3–6 months is typical, with the lower end of the temperature range extending the timeline and producing more complex flavor. Darker, longer-fermented aka miso requires 12–24+ months. Check the crock every 2–4 weeks: if any mold (white, green, or black fuzzy growth) appears on the surface, scrape it off cleanly, re-smooth the surface, re-apply the salt crust, and re-weight. A thin flat white kahm yeast is common and harmless. The miso will slowly darken from cream to pale gold and the aroma will shift from raw-soybean and salty to deeply savory, sweet, and fermented. At 3 months, taste a small portion: shiro miso is ready when it tastes rounded, sweet-savory, and deeply umami — with none of the raw-soybean sharpness present at packing.
Visual cue: At 3 months: the miso has darkened from pale cream to a golden tan-to-light-amber color, and the surface may show a faint tamari liquid (dark, intensely savory liquid) pooling at the edges. The aroma is deeply savory, mildly sweet, and complex — recognizably miso.
Underdone: At 6 weeks, tasting reveals a still-sharp, one-dimensionally salty paste with the raw-soybean edge clearly present. The color is still cream-white. The koji has not yet produced sufficient glutamates. Re-seal and continue fermenting. The most dramatic transformation in shiro miso happens between months 2 and 4. Resist early tasting and be patient.
Perfect: At 3–6 months: a pale golden-amber paste with a smooth, spreadable texture and a complex aroma — sweet from enzymatic starch breakdown, deeply savory from glutamate production, and faintly fruity from ester fermentation. Tastes mellow, rounded, and unmistakably miso. Transfer to smaller jars, seal, and refrigerate. The miso is fully ready and will keep refrigerated for 12+ months.
Overdone: Left

fermenting past 8 months at room temperature — the miso has darkened significantly toward a reddish-brown and the flavor has become more intense, more sour, and more complex than classic shiro miso. Not wrong — it has become a medium miso. Transfer to refrigerator to halt fermentation at its current point. The deeper, darker miso is equally delicious — use in heartier applications like braises, ramen tare, and marinades.
Feel cue: Finished shiro miso should feel like thick, smooth, slightly grainy cream cheese — yielding but dense, spreading with a small amount of pressure but holding its shape when scooped. When you taste it cold, it should dissolve on the tongue into a wave of savory sweetness with a lingering, complex umami echo.

name: White Shiro Miso
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Dried soybeans: 500 g
  Alternatives: yellow soybeans; chickpeas (for a lighter flavored miso)
Rice koji (fresh or dried): 500 g
  Alternatives: barley koji (gives slightly earthier miso)
Fine non-iodized sea salt: 150 g
  Alternatives: non-iodized kosher salt — never iodized salt, which inhibits fermentation
Reserved soybean cooking water, cooled: 100 g
  Alternatives: filtered water
Active time: 1 hr
Total time: 4 weeks
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Short-fermented, mild, and sweetly umami — white miso made from steamed soybeans, rice koji, and salt aged weeks rather than years for a pale, paste-smooth result.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

steps:
Rinse the dried soybeans thoroughly. Place in a large bowl and cover with cold water by at least 10 cm — the beans will roughly double in size overnight. Soak for a minimum of 12 hours, ideally 18. Drain and discard the soaking water.
Visual cue: Fully hydrated soybeans that have plumped to roughly twice their original size. Skins are smooth and taut, no wrinkling. Opaque pale yellow throughout.
Underdone: Beans still show wrinkling or are noticeably smaller than twice their dry size. Hard at the center when bitten. Soak longer — ideally overnight (12–18 hours). Under-soaked beans cook unevenly and produce a gritty miso paste.
Perfect: Plump, smooth-skinned, and uniformly pale. Yield cleanly when split — no hard center, no wrinkled skin. Drain and proceed to cooking.
Overdone: Beans have begun to ferment in the soaking water — skins have split, liquid is slightly bubbly or sour-smelling. Drain and cook immediately. The fermentation is harmless but indicates the beans have soaked too long in warm conditions.
Feel cue: A fully soaked soybean pressed between the thumb and forefinger should yield readily and split cleanly, feeling much like a firm cooked bean — soft, not starchy or powdery.

Transfer soaked beans to a large pot and cover with fresh water by 5 cm. Bring to a boil, skim the foam, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook for 3–4 hours until the soybeans are completely soft — they should crush between thumb and ring finger with almost no effort. Taste one: it should be creamy, not starchy. Reserve 100 g of the cooking water before draining.
Visual cue: Soybeans that have swelled further and turned a deeper, creamy yellow. The cooking water is lightly cloudy and golden-tinted.
Underdone: Beans are still firm at the center when crushed. Starchy, chalky taste. Continue simmering — under-cooked soybeans produce a grainy, poorly textured miso and ferment unevenly.
Perfect: The bean crushes completely under gentle thumb-ring-finger pressure, feeling like soft butter. Taste is nutty and creamy. Reserve cooking water, drain, and cool to room temperature before blending.
Overdone: Beans have broken apart in the water and partially disintegrated. Proceed — the miso paste will be slightly more liquid but will still ferment and taste correct. Use less cooking water to compensate.
Feel cue: The thumb-ring-finger test is definitive: if the bean disappears into a smooth paste between those two fingers with no resistance, it is ready.

While still warm, blend or pound the cooked soybeans to a smooth paste using a food processor, blender, or traditional suribachi (grinding bowl). Add the reserved cooking water a little at a time to achieve a smooth, thick consistency — similar to very stiff hummus. No visible bean pieces should remain.
Visual cue: A thick, completely smooth, pale amber paste that mounds on a spatula and drops slowly. No visible skins or bean pieces.
Underdone: Paste is grainy or lumpy — bean pieces still visible. Skin fragments in the mixture. Continue blending. Pass through a coarse sieve if needed to remove any skins that resist blending.
Perfect: Completely smooth, thick, and glossy. When you run a spatula through it, the trail holds cleanly. Drops from a spoon in slow, heavy blobs. Cool fully to room temperature before combining with the koji-salt mixture.
Overdone: Paste is thin and soupy — too much cooking water added. Spread on a flat tray and let cool — the starch will thicken it slightly. Proceed with less cooking water compensation.
Feel cue: Rub a little soybean paste between your fingertips — it should feel completely smooth, with no granular texture whatsoever, like very thick pudding.

Combine the rice koji and the fine salt in a large bowl. Rub the salt into the koji with both hands for 2–3 minutes, squeezing and pressing to ensure every grain of koji is coated in salt. The salt both seasons the miso and protects against harmful bacteria during fermentation.
Visual cue: A slightly damp, uniformly salted koji mixture. Every grain coated in white salt. The koji should be fragrant — faintly sweet, mushroom-like, and slightly floral.
Underdone: Salt and koji appear separate — pockets of white salt visible sitting on top of the koji grains. Rub and squeeze with both hands until the salt is fully and evenly distributed through the koji.
Perfect: Uniform, slightly damp mixture with every grain of koji coated. The mass is cohesive and smells of sweet rice and salt. Combine immediately with the cooled soybean paste.
Overdone: Koji has been crushed to a powder from over-vigorous rubbing. Proceed — powdered koji still ferments correctly, though the final texture may be slightly denser.
Feel cue: Grab a handful of the koji-salt mix and squeeze — it should clump together momentarily, then crumble apart, each grain distinct but salt-coated.

Combine the cooled soybean paste and the koji-salt mixture in a large bowl. Mix thoroughly with your hands, squeezing and pressing until completely uniform — no streaks of pale soybean paste visible, no unmixed pockets of koji. Form the mixture into balls roughly the size of a tennis ball by pressing firmly.
Visual cue: A uniform, pale, slightly grainy-textured paste with no streaks or unmixed pockets. Can be formed into cohesive balls without crumbling.
Underdone: Streaks of pale soybean paste and darker koji-salt visible. Mixture crumbles when formed into a ball. Continue mixing with both hands. Every gram of koji must have direct contact with the soybean paste to ferment evenly.
Perfect: Uniform color and texture throughout. The mixture holds a ball shape under light pressure without cracking. Begin packing firmly into the sterilized fermentation crock.
Overdone: Mixture has been warmed from too much hand contact, becoming slightly greasy or sticky. Cool the mixture for 10 minutes in the refrigerator, then continue. Warm miso mixture packs poorly.
Feel cue: The miso mixture should feel like dense, slightly wet clay — malleable, cohesive, and willing to be formed without sticking aggressively to your hands.

Sterilize a crock or large jar with boiling water. Throw each ball of miso mixture into the crock with force, pressing firmly to eliminate all air pockets. Smooth the surface flat. Sprinkle a thin layer of salt over the entire surface to protect it. Press plastic wrap directly against the surface, then place a weight on top. Cover the crock with a cloth and store at room temperature (18–22°C) for 3–4 weeks, tasting weekly. Refrigerate once the flavor is mild, sweet, and satisfyingly salty-umami.
Visual cue: After 3–4 weeks: a darker, deeper amber surface with a clean, miso-like aroma. The paste has contracted slightly from the crock walls. No mold beneath the protective salt layer.
Underdone: After 3 weeks: paste still tastes raw and salty with no sweet umami development. Pale, almost identical to when packed. Leave for another 1–2 weeks. Temperature below 18°C slows fermentation significantly.
Perfect: Pale golden-brown with a sweet, mild, savory depth. Umami is present but not aggressive. Salt rounds into the background. Texture is smooth and spreadable. Refrigerate immediately to arrest fermentation. White miso will keep refrigerated for 3 months.
Overdone: Very dark surface, intensely salty, sour or alcoholic smell. Possible dark mold growth at the edges (scrape away before tasting). Taste below the surface — if still pleasant, refrigerate now. Salty miso can be used as a seasoning paste rather than a soup base.
Feel cue: Properly fermented shiro miso should feel smooth and cohesive when smeared across a fingertip — silky, not grainy — and the aroma should make your mouth water before you even taste it.

ingredients.name: Japanese sweet potatoes (Satsumaimo) or orange-flesh sweet potatoes
Thinly sliced spring onion (green part only)

steps:
Preheat the oven to 180 C (355 F). Place the whole, unpeeled sweet potatoes directly on the oven rack with a foil-lined tray below to catch drips. Roast for 55–75 minutes depending on size (a chopstick pressed into the thickest part should meet no resistance). The skin will blister and deflate; a dark, caramelised syrup will drip from the ends.
Visual cue: Whole sweet potato in the oven
Underdone: Skin is still taut and bright. No syrup has dripped. Centre still firm when pressed. Continue roasting. Sweet potatoes need time — the sugars must migrate and concentrate slowly. A 200 g potato typically takes 60–65 minutes.
Perfect: Skin is wrinkled, slightly deflated, and very dark in places. A caramelised amber syrup has crystallised around the ends and dripped onto the tray. A chopstick glides in with zero resistance anywhere, including the centre. The potato feels very soft when squeezed gently. Remove from the oven and let rest 5 minutes before splitting.
Overdone: Skin is blackened and dry. Syrup has burnt on the tray. Interior may have dried out near the skin. The interior is likely still excellent. Discard the outermost 3–4 mm if it tastes bitter, then proceed.
Feel cue: Squeeze the hot potato gently through a folded kitchen towel — it should feel like a soft beanbag with no firm spots anywhere. Any hardness is undercooked flesh that needs more time.

While the potatoes roast, combine the softened butter, white miso, and mirin in a small bowl. Stir vigorously until completely smooth and homogenous. The mixture will be a pale amber paste. Set aside at room temperature.
Visual cue: Miso butter paste
Underdone: Butter and miso are still separate — streaks of white butter visible in the brown miso. Stir more vigorously until completely unified. Cold butter will not blend easily — let it soften fully first.
Perfect: A smooth, pale amber paste that holds its shape on a spoon. Smells of fermented soy, dairy, and faint sweetness from the mirin. Set aside. It will melt on contact with the hot potato.
Overdone: N/A — this step cannot be overdone. Proceed.
Feel cue: The finished paste should feel silky and cohesive when rubbed between your fingers — no graininess from undissolved miso, no separation from the butter.

Split each sweet potato lengthwise with a sharp knife — but not quite all the way through. Press the two ends toward each other to open up the split and create a cavity. Spoon or pipe a generous amount of the miso butter into the cavity. Finish under the grill (broiler) at high heat for 3–4 minutes until the glaze is bubbling and caramelised. Scatter flaky salt, sesame seeds, and spring onion.
Visual cue: Glazed sweet potato under the grill
Underdone: Miso butter has not yet caramelised — it is still pale and melted but not bronzed. Return under the grill for 2 more minutes. The sugars in both the miso and mirin need direct radiant heat to caramelise.
Perfect: The miso butter has bubbled and set into a deep, glossy amber-brown glaze with darker caramelised patches. The edges of the split potato are golden and slightly crisped. The kitchen smells of toasted soy and sweet caramel. Plate immediately and garnish. Eat while hot — the contrast between the caramelised exterior and the creamy interior is at its best right now.
Overdone: Glaze is dark brown and beginning to smell burnt. The miso's sugars have crossed from caramel to bitter. Remove immediately. Scrape off the darkest parts of the glaze and add a small knob of fresh plain butter to soften the bitterness.
Feel cue: Scoop into the split with a spoon — the interior should part like warm silk, yielding to the lightest pressure, with the glossy glaze pooling into the hollow and the whole thing collapsing gently into itself.

name: 味噌汤 · Classic Miso Soup

Dashi stock: 100 parts
  Alternatives: kombu-shiitake dashi
Awase miso (blended): 8 parts
  Alternatives: shiro miso; aka miso
Silken tofu: 12 parts
  Alternatives: firm tofu
Wakame (dried seaweed): 1 parts
  Alternatives: fresh wakame
Scallion (green part): 2 parts
  Alternatives: mitsuba
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 20 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The quiet heartbeat of a Japanese breakfast — dashi softened with fermented soybean paste, served the moment it is ready, never a minute later.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

steps:
Place dried wakame in a small bowl of cold water. Let it soak until it has fully expanded and turned silky — about five minutes. Drain and gently squeeze out excess water.
Visual cue: Wakame has tripled in volume and turned a deep, translucent green — each frond is pliable and slightly slippery.
Underdone: Pieces are still dark, shriveled, and leathery at the center. Continue soaking. Dried wakame reconstitutes unevenly, so give it another minute or two.
Perfect: Uniformly green, soft, with a slight sheen. Tears easily between fingers. Drain and set aside.
Overdone: Slimy, mushy, with a dull olive color. Falls apart when lifted. Use it — the flavor is intact, but cut back the amount slightly as it will dissolve into the broth.
Feel cue: Properly rehydrated wakame feels like wet silk between your fingers — if it feels gritty or stiff, it needs more time.

Bring dashi to a gentle simmer over medium heat. You want steam and faint movement at the surface — never a rolling boil, which destroys the delicate aromatics.
Visual cue: Wisps of steam rising from the surface. Tiny bubbles forming around the edges of the pot but not breaking at the center.
Underdone: No steam, no bubbles. Surface is still. Increase heat slightly and wait.
Perfect: Gentle steam, occasional small bubbles at the perimeter. Surface shimmers but does not churn. Reduce heat to low and add tofu.
Overdone: Full rolling boil with aggressive bubbling. Remove from heat immediately and let it settle — boiling muddies the clarity.
Feel cue: Hold your hand six inches above the pot — you should feel steady warmth, not blasting heat. The dashi should smell oceanic and clean.

Cut tofu into 1.5cm cubes and lower them gently into the dashi with a spoon. Let them warm through for two minutes on the lowest heat. Never stir — push gently if needed.
Visual cue: Tofu cubes are floating just below the surface, warmed through, with clean white edges intact.
Underdone: Tofu cubes have sunk to the bottom and feel cold when one is fished out. Give them another minute. They are dense when cold and will rise slightly as they warm.
Perfect: Cubes are suspended in the broth, edges sharp, surface smooth. A test cube is warm all the way through. Proceed to dissolve miso.
Overdone: Cubes have developed a pockmarked, cratered surface. Broth around them is cloudy. The tofu boiled — it will be spongy. Lower heat and proceed. Flavor is still fine.
Feel cue: Lift a cube with a spoon and touch it — it should be bath-temperature warm, with a custard-like give, not rubbery resistance.

Place miso in a ladle or small strainer. Submerge it halfway into the broth and stir with chopsticks until the paste has fully dissolved. This prevents lumps and keeps the broth from boiling. Never boil miso — it kills the living cultures and turns the flavor flat.
Visual cue: Broth has turned an opaque tawny-amber. No miso lumps visible. A gentle haze hangs evenly throughout — not settling to the bottom.
Underdone: Streaks of undissolved miso swirling in the broth. Gritty patches near the bottom. Return the ladle and continue stirring through it. Some misos are stubborn — pressing against the mesh helps.
Perfect: Uniformly cloudy, warm amber throughout. Tastes balanced — salty, round, and deep. Remove from heat immediately.
Overdone: Broth has boiled after miso was added — surface roiling. Flavor tastes flat and one-dimensional. Cannot undo, but a tiny splash of fresh miso stirred in off-heat can partially restore depth.
Feel cue: The aroma should bloom the moment the miso dissolves — earthy, warm, and slightly sweet, like a barn in autumn. If it smells sharp or acrid, the broth was too hot.

Add the drained wakame to the pot. Ladle the soup into warm bowls. Float thinly sliced scallion greens on the surface. Serve immediately — miso soup is a dish that cannot wait.
Visual cue: A warm bowl of amber broth with white tofu cubes, dark-green wakame fronds, and bright scallion rings floating on the surface.
Underdone: Broth looks thin and watery. Garnishes have sunk. Check the miso ratio — you may need more. Scallions should be added last so they stay afloat.
Perfect: Broth has body and opacity. Each ingredient is distinct and visible. The surface has a gentle sheen. Bring to the table. This is ready.
Overdone: Wakame has broken down into the broth. Scallions are wilted and dull. Garnish with fresh scallion on top. The soup itself is still perfectly fine to eat.
Feel cue: The first sip should feel like a warm blanket — gentle heat, soft salinity, and a lingering sweetness at the back of the throat. If the salt hits first, the miso ratio was too high.

description: A concentrated seasoning paste of white and red miso, mirin, and sake simmered together and enriched with sesame — used to season ramen broth, marinate proteins, or finish vegetable dishes.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Shiro miso (white miso, mild and sweet)
Aka miso (red miso, robust and salty)

steps:
Combine the mirin and sake in a small saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat and simmer for 3-4 minutes to cook off the raw alcohol. You can carefully tip the pan to ignite the vapor if cooking over gas — the flame will be brief and blue. If flambéing makes you nervous, simply simmer until the alcohol sharpness disappears from the steam. The liquid will reduce slightly and the aroma should smell sweet and gently caramelized, not boozy and raw. This step is non-negotiable — raw alcohol gives the tare a harsh edge that doesn't belong.
Visual cue: The simmering liquid has reduced by about 20%, looks glossy and amber-gold, and no longer releases sharp alcohol fumes when you wave your hand over it — only a gentle, sweet-savory steam.
Underdone: Still smells sharply of raw sake — hold your hand above the pan and the fumes will sting the eyes slightly. The alcohol hasn't cooked off yet. Continue simmering for another 1-2 minutes. The transition from raw to cooked is unmistakable in the aroma.
Perfect: Sweet-smelling, slightly reduced, clear gold. No sharp alcohol fumes. Tastes sweet with a clean, gentle warmth — not boozy. Remove from heat and allow to cool for 2 minutes before whisking in the miso.
Overdone: Reduced too far — the sugars are beginning to caramelize into a thick syrup with a darker color and slightly bitter edge. Add a small splash of water to bring the volume back up and proceed.
Feel cue: Test a drop on the inside of your wrist — it should feel warm and sweet, and the alcohol tingle that raw sake leaves should be completely absent. If it stings slightly, it needs more time on the heat.

Add the white miso and red miso to the slightly cooled sake-mirin mixture. Whisk vigorously until completely smooth with no lumps — miso can be stubborn and hide clumps if you rush this step. Add the garlic and ginger if using and whisk through. Return to the lowest possible heat and stir continuously for 5-6 minutes — do not let the mixture boil. The goal is a gentle, brief cooking that marries the miso with the mirin and sake, mellows the raw miso edge, and creates a unified paste. Watch carefully: miso scorches at very low temperatures and should never bubble.
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy, dark amber-tan paste — the white and red miso merged into a single color between honey and caramel. No lumps, no beige streaks of unincorporated miso.
Underdone: Paste is streaky — visible pale and dark zones where the white and red miso haven't fully combined. Tastes slightly discordant, with the red miso arriving as a separate bitter note. Whisk more vigorously, or press any lumps through a fine sieve. The blending must be thorough.
Perfect: Uniform, glossy, smooth. The aroma is sweet, deeply savory, and fermented in the best sense — like a very refined, concentrated miso soup base. The color is even amber-tan throughout. Remove from heat and stir in the sesame oil and sesame seeds.
Overdone: The mixture has boiled — there are bubbles on the surface and the edges are beginning to stick. Overheated miso loses its beneficial enzymes and develops a harsh, metallic edge. Remove from heat immediately, cool for 2 minutes, and proceed. Don't discard it — the flavor impact of a brief boil is minor.
Feel cue: The whisked miso paste should feel dense and smooth coating the whisk — if you can feel graininess when you press the whisk against the bowl, there are still undissolved lumps and more whisking is needed.

Remove from the heat and stir in the toasted sesame oil and sesame seeds. The sesame oil must go in off the heat — it is intensely aromatic and its fragrance dissipates rapidly when cooked. Stir to incorporate fully. Allow to cool completely before transferring to a sealed jar. The tare will keep refrigerated for up to a month. To use: stir a heaped tablespoon into a bowl of hot ramen broth, whisk into a marinade with soy sauce and oil, or use as a glaze for roasting root vegetables and tofu.
Visual cue: A rich, dark, glossy paste with visible sesame seeds throughout. The sesame oil gives the surface a subtle sheen. Spooned into a jar, it holds its shape but is soft enough to scoop easily with a spoon.
Underdone: Sesame oil not yet stirred in — the paste lacks the final aromatic lift and the nutty, roasted sesame richness that defines miso tare. Stir in the sesame oil and seeds thoroughly off the heat.
Perfect: Dense, fragrant, glossy. The sesame aroma is immediately present — toasted and rich. On a spoon it holds a slow, heavy mound. One tablespoon stirred into hot dashi broth transforms it completely. Cool and transfer to a sealed jar. Refrigerate for up to 1 month.
Overdone: Tare has been stored too long or improperly sealed — surface has oxidized darker and the flavor is sharp and astringent rather than mellow and sweet. Discard and make a fresh batch — miso tare past its prime will make any dish it touches taste harsh.
Feel cue: A teaspoon of finished tare pressed to the roof of the mouth should be intensely savory — almost overwhelming as a pure paste — with the sesame oil providing a round, softening warmth. This concentration is the point: you'll use just a small amount to season an entire bowl of broth.

name: Strawberry Daifuku Mochi
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

ingredients.name: Tsubuan or koshian (sweet red bean paste)

steps:
Divide the anko (bean paste) into portions — approximately 25g per daifuku. Flatten each portion into a disc in your palm. Place a hulled strawberry point-down in the center and wrap the anko up around it, pinching to seal at the base of the strawberry. The strawberry tip should just be visible or barely covered. Refrigerate wrapped strawberries for 15 minutes to firm.
Visual cue: A smooth, compact ball of bean paste fully encasing the strawberry, with a slight point at the top where the hull was — no tears, no gaps.
Underdone: Anko disc is too thick and the strawberry pokes through one side; coverage is uneven. Re-wrap with a thinner, wider disc of anko and press more carefully.
Perfect: Smooth, seamless anko exterior. The ball sits flat on the base. When pressed very gently, you can feel the strawberry inside. Refrigerate for 15 minutes; cold anko is firmer and easier to handle when wrapping mochi.
Overdone: Anko applied in too thick a layer; the ratio of paste to strawberry is out of balance. Trim excess anko from the seam side before wrapping in mochi.
Feel cue: The chilled anko-wrapped strawberry should feel solid and slightly cool in the hand — a quiet, dense weight, smooth without tackiness.

Whisk shiratamako, sugar, and water together in a microwave-safe bowl until smooth with no lumps. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and microwave on high for 2 minutes. Remove, stir thoroughly with a wet spatula, then microwave for a further 1 minute. Stir again — the mochi should be fully translucent with no white, opaque patches. If white patches remain, microwave in 30-second bursts, stirring each time. Alternatively, steam in a covered steamer for 20 minutes, stirring halfway through.
Visual cue: A fully translucent, uniformly glossy mass with no white or opaque spots — stretchy and pulling away from the bowl cleanly.
Underdone: White, chalky opaque patches throughout; mochi tears easily and feels grainy. Continue microwaving in 30-second increments, stirring vigorously between each, until fully translucent.
Perfect: Shiny, fully translucent, elastic mass. Stretches smoothly without tearing. Smells faintly of warm cooked rice. Very hot. Work quickly while hot — mochi stiffens rapidly as it cools.
Overdone: Mochi has dried and begun to skin over; surface is tacky but the interior is stiff. Dip hands in water and knead briefly; add 1 tsp water and microwave 20 seconds to soften.
Feel cue: Properly cooked mochi is intensely hot and stretches like warm bubble gum — it resists pulling, then yields smoothly, with a satisfying elastic tension.

Dust a work surface generously with katakuriko. Turn the hot mochi out onto the dusted surface — it will be extremely sticky and very hot, so work quickly. Dust the top and your hands. Divide into equal portions (approximately 40g each) using a dusted dough cutter or scissors. Stretch each portion into a disc about 10 cm wide. Place an anko-wrapped strawberry in the center, point-down. Gather the mochi edges up and over, pinching firmly to seal at the base. Pinch point downward. Dust the finished daifuku with more katakuriko to prevent sticking.
Visual cue: A smooth, round pillow of white mochi with a clean sealed base, coated in a fine dusting of potato starch — barely tacky to the touch.
Underdone: Mochi tore during shaping and the anko is visible; seal is broken. Press the torn edges together and pinch firmly; a small patch of double-layered mochi at the seal is normal.
Perfect: Smooth, domed top. Sealed base is tidy. Mochi is yielding when pressed and springs back. Dusting of starch is even, not clumped. Allow to rest 5 minutes at room temperature before serving. Best eaten within 4 hours.
Overdone: Mochi cooled too much before shaping — it tore or cracked at the edges and is stiff. Microwave the remaining mochi for 15 seconds to restore pliability.
Feel cue: A finished daifuku should give under a gentle squeeze and push back slowly — a soft, yielding resistance, like pressing a firm marshmallow, with the subtle firmness of the strawberry inside.

ingredients.name: 玉米淀粉（Cornstarch (katakuriko) for dusting work surface）

steps:
Combine the glutinous rice flour and sugar in a microwave-safe bowl. Add the water gradually while stirring with a spatula until completely smooth and lump-free. The batter will be thin — like very thick cream — and should pour off the spatula in a slow, even sheet. Pass it through a fine strainer if any lumps remain. Cover loosely with microwave-safe plastic wrap or a damp paper towel.
Visual cue: A uniformly smooth, thin, milk-white batter with no lumps or undissolved sugar grains. Falls in a slow, even sheet from the spatula.
Underdone: Lumpy and heterogeneous. Sugar has not fully dissolved. Dry flour clumps float on the surface. Stir more vigorously and ensure the sugar has fully dissolved before microwaving. Lumps that remain will become chewy, rubbery patches in the finished mochi.
Perfect: Pourable, silky-smooth, uniformly white. Leaves the spoon cleanly. Tastes faintly sweet and floury. Cover and microwave on high for 2 minutes for the first burst.
Overdone: You've added too little water and the mixture is thick and dough-like before cooking — not a pourable batter. Add water a tablespoon at a time, stirring between additions, until the batter pours freely.
Feel cue: The batter should flow off the spatula in a smooth, even curtain — not drip in separate drops, but not pour like water. Between milk and condensed milk in viscosity.

Microwave the covered batter on HIGH for 2 minutes. Remove, uncover, and stir vigorously — the outer edge will have cooked to a translucent, rubbery mass while the centre remains white and liquid. Stir to combine them, re-cover, and microwave again for 1 to 2 minutes until the entire mass is translucent, pulling away from the bowl sides, and glistening. Stir well between each burst. The dough should look uniformly glossy and slightly translucent, not chalky or opaque. Total microwave time: 4 to 6 minutes in 1-2 minute bursts.
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy, fully translucent (not chalky) mass that is uniformly cooked and pulls away from the bowl walls cleanly. Glistens in the light.
Underdone: Opaque white patches remain, especially at the centre. The dough is two-toned and the uncooked parts look chalky and feel cold relative to the outer edges. Re-cover and microwave in further 1-minute bursts, stirring between, until the entire mass is uniformly translucent. Raw mochi starch is unpleasant and will be hard to work with.
Perfect: Fully translucent, glossy, and smooth. The mass pulls away from the bowl as a single elastic unit. Very sticky and hot. Smells faintly like cooked rice. Let it cool in the bowl for 5 minutes, then transfer to a cornstarch-dusted surface to work while still pliable but cool enough to handle.
Overdone: The mochi has gone rubbery, dense, and extremely tough. It resists stretching and has dried patches from repeated microwaving. A slightly over-cooked mochi can sometimes be rescued by kneading in a few drops of water on a wet surface. But severe over-cooking makes it unworkably stiff.
Feel cue: Poke the cooked mochi with a wet fingertip — it should feel uniformly elastic throughout, like a firm gummy bear, not firm on the outside and squishy in the middle. No cold or chalky spots.

Dust a clean work surface generously with cornstarch. Turn the hot mochi out onto the surface and dust the top as well. Let it cool for 5 to 10 minutes — it should be warm but comfortable to handle. Do not let it cool completely: cold mochi becomes stiff and tears when portioned. Divide into 8 equal pieces using a bench scraper or a knife dusted with cornstarch. Flatten each piece into a round disc about 8 cm in diameter, working quickly.
Visual cue: A warm, pliable, ivory-white mass that stretches smoothly without tearing. The cornstarch forms a dry, non-sticky coating on the surface. Pieces pull apart cleanly.
Underdone: The mochi is still too hot to handle — steam rises and it sticks aggressively to hands and bench even with dusting. Wait 2 to 3 more minutes. Working too-hot mochi causes it to tear and the steam can burn. It also won't hold the filling shape.
Perfect: Warm, smooth, and elastic. Pulls without tearing. Cornstarch dusting keeps it completely non-sticky. Feels like smooth, warm playdough. Portion and flatten the discs now — fill within the next 5 to 8 minutes before the mochi stiffens from cooling.
Overdone: The mochi has cooled to room temperature and is now stiff, reluctant to stretch, and tears at the edges when flattened. Microwave for 15 to 20 seconds to rewarm and restore pliability. Re-dust with cornstarch before proceeding.
Feel cue: Press the mochi disc with three fingers — it should stretch evenly in all directions with gentle resistance, like stretching warm gum, without snapping back or tearing at the edges.

Roll a tablespoon-sized ball of anko between your palms to a smooth sphere and place it at the centre of each mochi disc. Gather the edges of the mochi up around the filling and pinch firmly together at the top, rotating and pleating as you go, until the seam is completely sealed with no filling visible. Pinch the seam tightly — a loose seam opens during handling. Turn seam-side down and roll gently between cupped palms to smooth the surface. Roll in kinako to coat. Arrange seam-side down on a tray. Eat at room temperature on the day they are made.
Visual cue: Smooth, slightly oval spheres with no visible seam. A uniform, matte, pale-tan kinako coat on every surface. No cracks or thin spots where the filling might be seen.
Underdone: The seam is open or only loosely pinched. The mochi disc was not stretched thinly enough over the filling and the anko is pushing through a weak spot. Pinch the seam closed firmly and roll between cupped palms to seal. If the mochi has torn, press it gently together — it will re-fuse if still warm.
Perfect: A smooth, unblemished exterior with the filling fully concealed. Even kinako coating. When held up to a light, you can faintly see the darker anko through the translucent mochi skin. Serve within 4 hours at room temperature. Do not refrigerate — cold stiffens the mochi and makes it unpleasantly tough.
Overdone: The mochi skin was stretched so thin you can see the anko clearly through it, or it has split. Alternatively, the filling overpowers the delicate mochi texture. Use slightly less filling next time. A 1:1 ratio by weight of mochi to anko is the maximum — many prefer more mochi than filling.
Feel cue: A well-made mochi should feel cool and slightly yielding when pressed — not hard, not soft. The kinako coat should feel dry and powdery, like a gentle dusting of flour, not greasy or damp.

ingredients.name: Dried mulato chilies, stems and most seeds removed
Dried pasilla negro chilies, stems and most seeds removed
Dried ancho chilies, stems and most seeds removed
Dried chihuacle negro chilies, stems removed
Ripe plantain, peeled and sliced thick
Dark chocolate (70% cacao minimum), roughly chopped
Day-old corn tortilla, torn into pieces

steps:
Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium-high. Working in batches, toast each chili variety: press them flat against the hot surface for 15–20 seconds per side until they blister, puff, and release a deep, smoky fragrance — not the acrid scent of burning. Immediately submerge toasted chilies in a bowl of very hot water and weigh them down with a plate; soak 25–30 minutes until fully soft. In the same dry pan, toast cumin seeds until fragrant (30 seconds), then cinnamon, peppercorns, sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds, and torn tortilla pieces separately, each until golden and aromatic. Toast the reserved chili seeds if you want more heat (optional). Keep all toasted dry components together.
Visual cue: Each chili should show blistered, puffed skin with small dark spots — deeply fragrant, not black or ashy. Soaked chilies are fully pliable, dark, and almost silky.
Underdone: Chilies are flat and matte with no blistering. The pan smells of dried pepper but not of smoke or depth. Seeds and sesame are still pale and raw-tasting. Increase the heat and continue pressing — the comal must be hot enough to generate immediate contact with the chili skin. Listen for a faint sizzle when they touch the surface.
Perfect: Chilies have puffed, showing small blistered dark patches on the skin and a mahogany-brown interior when torn open. The kitchen smells of smoky dried fruit and spice. Sesame and pumpkin seeds are golden and smell nutty. Soak the toasted chilies immediately while they are still hot; this is when they rehydrate most efficiently.
Overdone: Chilies are black in patches, brittle, and smell acrid. The scorched flavor will make the entire mole bitter in a way that can't be corrected. Discard the burnt chilies — bitterness from char cannot be masked even by chocolate. Start with fresh dried chilies and reduce the heat before proceeding.
Feel cue: A fully soaked chili should
feel completely pliable, almost silky between the fingers — no stiff or papery patches anywhere along the skin. Tear one open; the flesh inside should be dark, moist, and intensely fragrant.

Place tomato halves, quartered onion, and unpeeled garlic directly on the same dry comal over high heat. Char them without moving: you want dramatic blackening on at least one side — this char is structural flavor, not a mistake. Turn once and char the other side. Garlic is done when its papery skin is blackened and the cloves feel soft inside when pressed. In a small pan with a splash of lard or oil, fry plantain slices over medium heat until deeply caramelized and bronze on both sides (3–4 min per side). Add raisins to the pan in the last minute and fry until they puff. Peel the garlic; do not peel the onion char.
Visual cue: Tomatoes have blackened, collapsed skins with juices bubbling out. Onion quarters are charred black on the cut faces with softened interiors. Garlic papery skins are fully black. Plantain slices are a deep amber-brown.
Underdone: Tomatoes are merely softened with pale, unchanged skin. Onion and garlic show light browning rather than char. Plantain is golden but not caramelized. Return to high heat without moving — the char must be genuine. A properly hot pan with no oil is required.
Perfect: Tomatoes are collapsed and black-skinned with juices caramelized at the edges. Onion faces are mahogany-black. Garlic skins are fully charred, cloves tender inside. Plantain is deep caramel. Leave all components with their charred skins for the blending stage — the char contributes the mole's characteristic dark color and bitter base note.
Overdone: Components have crossed from char into ash — tomatoes are dry and shrunken, onions carbonized to a powder. Plantain is burnt-sweet and acrid. Discard and start the wet components again. Some char is essential; complete carbonization is not recoverable.
Feel cue: Press a charred garlic clove through its blackened skin — it should yield completely, squeezing out like soft butter. If there is any resistance,
return it to the heat.

Drain the soaked chilies, reserving the soaking liquid (but use sparingly — it can be very bitter). Working in batches in a blender: combine soaked chilies, charred tomatoes and onion, peeled charred garlic, toasted spices, sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds, tortilla pieces, fried plantain, and raisins. Add warm broth as needed (not chili soaking liquid) to get the blades moving — typically 3–4 ladles per batch. Blend each batch for at least 2 full minutes until completely smooth. Pass through a medium sieve if you want a very refined texture; leave it as-is for a more rustic, textured mole.
Visual cue: A thick, jet-black to very dark brown paste that moves like molasses when the blender is stopped — viscous, completely smooth, and so dark it is nearly opaque.
Underdone: The paste is grainy and speckled with visible chili skin pieces, seed fragments, or green patches of unblended herbs. The color is reddish-brown rather than true black. Blend longer — 2 full minutes at high speed per batch is the minimum. Add more broth to free the blades if needed.
Perfect: The paste is completely smooth, deeply dark (black-brown), and flows off a spatula in a slow, thick ribbon. The smell is extraordinary — chocolate, smoke, dried fruit, and spice simultaneously. Proceed immediately to frying — the paste must be cooked in hot fat to develop its final flavor.
Overdone: The paste has been blended so long and with so much broth that it is thin and watery rather than thick. Reduce the paste in a saucepan over medium heat, stirring constantly, until it thickens back to a mole-paste consistency before frying.
Feel cue: Rub a little paste between your fingers — it should feel velvet-smooth with absolutely no graininess. If you feel any roughness, it needs more blending.

Heat the lard in a large, heavy-bottomed pot (preferably clay or enameled cast iron) over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly. Pour the mole paste in all at once — it will spit violently, so stand back and have a lid ready. Fry the paste, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, for 10–15 minutes until it darkens another shade, thickens, and the fat separates visibly at the edges. This frying step is what transforms a blended mixture into a true mole. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add warm broth one ladle at a time, stirring well after each addition. Add dried thyme, oregano, and salt. Simmer gently for at least 1 hour, skimming any fat that rises. Add the chopped chocolate in the final 5 minutes, stirring until fully melted. Taste and adjust salt.
Visual cue: A sauce the color of polished obsidian — almost black — that coats the back of a spoon completely and falls in a single unbroken, heavy curtain when the spoon is lifted.
Underdone: The mole is reddish-brown rather than black and tastes raw and harsh — the paste hasn't been fried long enough, and the flavors haven't unified. The consistency is too thin. Fry the paste for another 5–10 minutes on higher heat, and continue simmering to reduce and concentrate.
Perfect: Deep, near-black color. The mole coats a spoon thickly and falls off in an unbroken curtain. The flavor is extraordinarily complex — you taste layers: first heat, then chocolate bitterness, then dried fruit sweetness, then smoke, then umami depth. The mole is done. It will hold refrigerated for 5 days and improve. Thin as needed with warm broth when reheating.
Overdone: The mole has reduced too far — it is stiff, clinging, and salty, with the chocolate dominating and the broth flavor gone. Whisk in warm broth, a ladle at a time, until the consistency returns to coating-spoon weight. Taste for salt after each addition.
Feel cue: The properly
finished mole clings to every surface it touches — spoon, pot, tongue — with a weight that feels almost substantial, like a liquid you can lean against.

ingredients.name: Firm white fish fillets (e.g. sea bass or cod), 4 cm chunks
Red and green bell peppers, thinly sliced
Fresh cilantro, stems and leaves separated

steps:
Toss fish chunks with lime juice, a pinch of salt, and minced garlic (half the garlic). Cover and refrigerate for 20-30 minutes. The acid will begin to set the exterior proteins, helping the fish hold together in the stew without falling apart.
Visual cue: Fish slightly opaque and white at the edges where the lime juice has contacted — otherwise still translucent and raw in the center.
Underdone: Fish still fully raw-looking and glossy — acid hasn't had time to act. Wait the full 20 minutes.
Perfect: Edges turned opaque white, interior still raw. Fish holds its shape when lifted. Proceed to build the base.
Overdone: Fish has been in the acid too long and is white and firm throughout — essentially ceviche. Cook quickly to warm through only — it will toughen further with heat.
Feel cue: The fish should feel slightly firmer at the edges than at its core — there's a tension to the outer layer that wasn't there before.

Heat dendê oil in a heavy clay pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add onion and cook 5 minutes until soft and turning golden. Add remaining garlic and bell peppers and cook 3 more minutes. The dendê oil will turn the whole base a vivid orange — this is correct and beautiful.
Visual cue: Onions and peppers soft and glistening, the whole base turned a rich saffron-orange from the dendê oil.
Underdone: Onions still translucent and crunchy, no color developed. Cook longer — don't rush the softening.
Perfect: Onions translucent-to-golden, peppers soft, everything stained a deep orange. Kitchen smells earthy and fruity. Add tomatoes.
Overdone: Onions browning and beginning to stick; dendê oil smoking. Deglaze with a splash of water and reduce heat.
Feel cue: The dendê oil has a distinctive smell — earthy, faintly fruity, reminiscent of carrots and forest floor. If you've never smelled it before, it's assertive. Trust it.

Add tomatoes and cilantro stems to the sofrito. Cook 5 minutes until tomatoes begin to dissolve. Pour in coconut milk and stir. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. Season well with salt and taste — the broth should be rich, sweet from coconut, and slightly acidic from the tomato.
Visual cue: A deeply orange-red broth with visible tomato pieces, steaming gently, coconut milk swirled into the dendê into a sunset gradient.
Underdone: Coconut milk and oil not fully combined — visible white streaks. Stir and give it 2 more minutes of gentle heat.
Perfect: Uniform golden-orange, gently simmering at the edges. Smells of coconut, tomato, and the sea. Taste for salt and add the fish.
Overdone: Broth boiling hard — coconut milk has broken and looks grainy. Reduce heat immediately. Boiling splits coconut milk. It will re-integrate with gentle heat.
Feel cue: The broth should coat a spoon in a thin, silky layer — richer than water but lighter than cream. Tasting it raw tells you everything about where the finished stew is going.

Nestle the marinated fish gently into the simmering broth in a single layer. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 8-12 minutes, depending on thickness. Do not stir — use the lid to baste. The fish is done when it flakes easily at the thickest point and is opaque throughout. Scatter cilantro leaves over the top and serve straight from the clay pot.
Visual cue: Fish opaque and beginning to flake at the edges, broth still vivid orange and gently bubbling, cilantro green against the golden surface.
Underdone: Fish still translucent in the center when a fork is pressed into the thickest point. Cover and cook 2 more minutes. Check again.
Perfect: Opaque throughout, flaking into large, moist, clean plates when probed. Broth simmering gently. Cilantro fragrant. Serve immediately over white rice.
Overdone: Fish has broken apart and turned dry and stringy, sinking into the broth. Serve anyway — it becomes a thick, rich stew rather than intact pieces.
Feel cue: A fish chunk pulled from the broth should offer gentle resistance and then give way in large, moist flakes — never cottony, never wet and raw.

name: Moqueca de Peixe

ingredients.name: Thick white fish fillets (cod, sea bass, or grouper)
White onion, sliced into thin rounds
Red and green bell peppers, sliced into thin strips
Malagueta chillies or scotch bonnet, finely sliced

steps:
Cut the fish fillets into large portions (approximately 150 g each). In a bowl, combine with the lime juice, half the garlic, and salt. Toss gently to coat. Marinate for 20–30 minutes in the refrigerator. The lime juice will begin to denature the surface proteins, giving the fish a slightly opaque look and a more flavourful surface.
Visual cue: Fish in the lime marinade
Underdone: Fish is still completely translucent and raw-looking after only 5 minutes. Not enough time for the marinade to penetrate. Marinate for the full 20 minutes minimum.
Perfect: Fish surface is slightly opaque — lightly 'cooked' by the acid. Flesh is firm and fragrant with lime and garlic. No browning or graying. Proceed to building the stew.
Overdone: Fish has been marinating for over 2 hours in the lime juice. Surface is white and 'cooked' throughout, crumbling when touched. Reduce the simmering time significantly — the fish will need very little heat to cook through.
Feel cue: Press a piece of marinated fish gently — it should feel slightly firmer than raw fish but still fully yielding, like firm tofu rather than meat.

In a heavy clay pot (ideal) or wide, heavy-bottomed pan, pour the dendê oil. Layer the onion rounds across the base, then the tomato rounds, then the pepper strips, then the chilli. This layered approach is traditional — the vegetables cook in sequence from the heat of the oil below.
Visual cue: Layered vegetables in the pan
Underdone: N/A — this is a cold-assembly step. Ensure the layers are even and cover the entire base of the pan so the fish cooks surrounded by vegetables on all sides.
Perfect: Distinct, even layers of red-orange onion, red tomato rounds, and multicoloured pepper strips. The dendê oil at the base is a vivid orange-red. Scatter the remaining garlic over the top and lay the fish pieces on top of the vegetable layers.
Overdone: N/A at assembly stage. Proceed.
Feel cue: The layered pan should feel cold and wet when you place the fish on top — the moisture from the vegetables and the raw fish will create the steam that begins the cooking process.

Lay the marinated fish pieces on top of the layered vegetables. Pour the coconut milk over everything — it should nearly submerge the fish. Cover tightly and cook over medium heat for 15–20 minutes, without stirring, until the fish is just cooked through and the coconut milk has combined with the vegetable juices and palm oil to create a brilliant orange-red broth. Add most of the coriander in the final 2 minutes. Taste and adjust salt.
Visual cue: Moqueca broth and fish during cooking
Underdone: Fish is still translucent at the centre. Broth is pale and has not yet emulsified the palm oil and coconut milk. Cover and continue simmering — the broth will turn orange as the dendê emulsifies into the coconut milk.
Perfect: Fish is opaque all the way through but still holds its shape in large, moist flakes. Broth is a vivid, cloudy orange-red — the dendê and coconut have emulsified into a rich, aromatic sauce. Coriander floats on top. The pot smells of tropical richness. Serve directly from the pan at the table. Scatter remaining coriander over the top.
Overdone: Fish has broken apart into flakes and disintegrated into the broth. Broth has separated — the oil floating on the surface of the coconut milk. Serve immediately and very gently. Do not stir. The flavour is intact but the fish texture is gone.
Feel cue: Use a large spoon to pull a piece of fish from the broth — it should break into large, moist, separate flakes rather than one cohesive piece. If it resists and feels rubbery, it needs more time; if it dissolves in the spoon, it is overcooked.

ingredients.name: Garlic cloves (the poem's four heads — fresh, pungent)

steps:
Peel the garlic and drop it into a heavy mortar with the coarse salt. The salt is both seasoning and abrasive: its crystals tear the garlic cells open and stop the cloves from skidding under the pestle. Pound with a firm circular grind — not a stamp — until the garlic breaks down to a wet, smooth, ivory paste with no visible chunks. The poem's Simylus weeps at the fumes; expect a sharp sting in the nose.
Visual cue: A smooth, glistening, pale paste pooling at the bottom of the mortar, with the salt fully dissolved into it and no recognizable pieces of clove.
Underdone: Garlic is mashed but still lumpy, with pale chunks rolling away from the pestle and skidding on the stone. Keep grinding in slow circles and press the pestle's weight down. If it keeps sliding, add a few more grains of salt for grip.
Perfect: A uniform, slick paste that coats the mortar walls and smells aggressively of raw garlic. It smears flat with no resistance. Stop here and add the herbs — overworking now only sharpens the burn.
Overdone: The paste has gone thin, almost watery, and smells acrid and hot rather than pungent. Move straight on; the cheese and herbs will absorb the excess moisture and tame the harshness.
Feel cue: The pestle should glide once the cloves give way, the paste tacky and cool against the stone. Your eyes will water — that is the sign the garlic's oils have been fully released.

Add the celery leaf and coriander, then just a few leaves of rue — it is intensely bitter and the poem warns to hold back its 'biting power.' Pound them into the garlic, grinding the leaves against the grit until they bruise, darken, and release their oils, streaking the paste a deep mottled green. Work them in fully so no whole leaf survives. A safety note: rue is potent — use only a few leaves, and avoid it entirely if pregnant or trying to conceive, as it can act as a uterine stimulant; skin contact with the fresh plant in sunlight can also cause photosensitivity.
Visual cue: A dense, dark-green herb paste flecked with paler garlic, fragrant and faintly bitter, with the leaves entirely crushed into the mass.
Underdone: Whole and half leaves are still visible, sitting on top of the garlic rather than blended in, and the green is patchy and bright. Keep pounding and scrape down the sides. The leaves must be bruised, not merely chopped, to give up their aroma.
Perfect: A cohesive deep-green paste with a savory, herbal, slightly bitter scent and no intact leaves. Proceed to fold in the cheese.
Overdone: The paste smells harshly bitter and tastes medicinal — too much rue has been worked in. Add an extra spoonful of grated cheese in the next step to mute the bitterness; in future use even less rue.
Feel cue: The aroma shifts from pure garlic to a green, grassy bitterness as the leaves break. The paste should feel slightly looser and wetter from the herbs' juices.

Add the grated aged cheese a large handful at a time, pounding and folding it into the green paste. As Virgil's poem describes, the mass will resist and crumble at first, then suddenly catch and pull together — the cheese's fat and protein binding the herbs and garlic into one body. Keep working until it forms a single rough ball that lifts cleanly from the mortar in one piece.
Visual cue: A single cohesive, marbled green-and-cream ball clinging together in the mortar, no longer loose or crumbly, holding its shape when nudged.
Underdone: The mixture is dry and crumbly, breaking into clumps that won't gather, with dry pockets of unmoistened cheese. Keep pounding and pressing; the friction warms the cheese's fat and helps it bind. A few drops of oil now will help it come together.
Perfect: One smooth, marbled ball that holds together and pulls cleanly off the pestle, smelling of sharp cheese, garlic, and herbs at once. Slacken it with vinegar and oil to the spreading consistency you want.
Overdone: The ball has gone greasy and slick, weeping oil from the cheese where it was overworked and warmed too much. Stop pounding immediately and add the vinegar to tighten and brighten it; serve at cool room temperature.
Feel cue: Watch for the moment of binding — the loose rubble suddenly grabs and rolls into a ball under the pestle. It should feel firm, tacky, and unified, like a stiff dough.

Sprinkle in the wine vinegar and pour in the olive oil, then grind and stir them through until the stiff ball loosens into a thick, spreadable paste. Taste and balance: it should be loud and assertive — sharply garlicky, salty from the cheese, sour from the vinegar, with a bitter green undertone. Scrape it out and roll into a rough mound. Serve at room temperature smeared thickly on coarse, warm country bread.
Visual cue: A thick, glossy, mottled-green spread that holds soft peaks and ribbons slowly off a spoon, with oil just visible at the edges.
Underdone: Still stiff and ball-like, too dense to spread and tasting flat without the brightening acid. Add a little more vinegar and oil and work it in until it spreads easily and the flavor sharpens.
Perfect: A cohesive, spreadable paste with a satiny sheen that catches the bread without tearing it, tasting balanced — pungent, salty, sour, and green. Mound it up and serve at once with warm bread; it is best fresh, while the garlic is at its brightest.
Overdone: The spread has gone slack and oily, with free oil pooling and a flat, greasy mouthfeel. Pound in a little more grated cheese to reabsorb the oil and rebuild body, then re-balance with a touch of salt.
Feel cue: The spread should pull at a knife with a slight tack, then release smoothly onto the bread. On the tongue it hits hot and sharp from the garlic first, then settles into salty cheese and a clean vinegar tang.

description: Béchamel's richest child: the velvet base melted through with Gruyère and Parmigiano and bound glossy with an egg yolk. This is the sauce under a croque-monsieur's bronzed lid and inside every great gratin.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

steps:
Melt the butter over medium-low heat until it foams but does not brown. Whisk in the flour all at once and cook, stirring constantly, for 2-3 minutes to cook out the raw-flour taste while keeping the roux pale. Keep it white — a Mornay should taste of cheese, not toasted flour.
Visual cue: A smooth, pale paste the color of wet sand, loosening as it cooks and smelling faintly of pie crust.
Underdone: The paste still smells raw and floury, with no aroma rising from the pan. Keep stirring over the heat another minute to cook off the raw smell.
Perfect: Loose and gently bubbling, the color of bone, smelling of warm shortcrust. It moves like lava under the whisk. It is ready for the milk.
Overdone: Tanned to blond and smelling nutty. Start over for a clean cheese flavor — a toasted roux muddies the Gruyère.
Feel cue: The roux drags against the whisk like thick batter, then relaxes. It hisses softly and should never crackle.

Stream in the warm milk, whisking hard and constantly — the first third slowly to build a smooth paste, then the rest in a steady pour. Constant whisking is what keeps it lump-free.
Visual cue: A thin, uniform, lump-free liquid the color of cream, just beginning to steam, with the whisk leaving fading trails.
Underdone: Lumps of roux bob in thin milk; the sauce looks grainy and broken. Whisk hard to break them up or pass through a fine sieve before continuing.
Perfect: Completely smooth and pourable like heavy cream, with a faint sheen. Whisk trails close slowly. Bring to a gentle simmer to thicken.
Overdone: Milk added too fast and hot has scorched the bottom, flecking the sauce brown. Pour into a clean pan, leaving the scorched layer behind.
Feel cue: Each splash of milk loosens the resistance under the whisk until the thick squelch of paste becomes a soft slosh.

Simmer gently 8-10 minutes, whisking often, until the sauce thickens to nappe consistency — thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Build it slightly thicker than a plain béchamel; the cheese will loosen it later. Season lightly with salt, nutmeg, and white pepper, remembering the cheeses bring their own salt.
Visual cue: A glossy, thick sauce that coats the spoon; a finger drawn through leaves a clean channel that holds and does not flood back.
Underdone: Thin and watery, running off the spoon as the channel closes instantly. Simmer longer to evaporate water and gelatinize the starch — it must be thick before cheese goes in.
Perfect: Velvety and thick enough to nappe, falling from the whisk in a smooth ribbon, the salt restrained. Pull from the heat and let the bubbling stop before adding cheese.
Overdone: Gluey and stiff, mounding like paste, the surface dull. Whisk in a splash of warm milk to bring back a pourable ribbon.
Feel cue: The whisk meets steady, even resistance; the sauce blurps lazily with slow, heavy bubbles and smells of sweet cooked milk.

Off the heat — and this matters, because boiling cheese turns greasy and stringy — whisk in the Gruyère and Parmigiano a handful at a time until each melts. Temper the yolk: whisk a ladle of the warm sauce into the yolk, then whisk that back into the pot. The residual heat cooks and thickens the yolk without scrambling it. Adjust salt last.
Visual cue: A deeply glossy, lacquered sauce the color of pale straw that falls in a thick, satiny sheet — no oil slick on the surface, no strings trailing the whisk.
Underdone: Grainy with undissolved cheese, or thin and pale because the yolk hasn't set; cheese clumps cling to the whisk. Whisk patiently off the heat; if it has cooled too much, return to the gentlest heat for seconds at a time until smooth.
Perfect: Uniformly smooth, glossy, and thickened by the yolk — it sheets off the spoon and tastes of nutty Gruyère and savory Parmesan over the cream. Use immediately over gratins or croques, or hold warm with plastic pressed to the surface.
Overdone: Broken and oily, with cheese fat pooling on top and stringy curds — the sauce was too hot, or it boiled. Pull off heat and whisk in a splash of cold milk to re-emulsify; whisk hard to pull it back together.
Feel cue: As the cheese melts the sauce turns heavier and silkier under the whisk and the aroma blooms — sweet, nutty, savory. It should pour like warm satin, never rubbery or weeping fat.

ingredients.name: Whole sea bream or sea bass (1–1.2kg), cleaned and scored

steps:
Combine all chermoula ingredients in a food processor or pound in a large mortar. Process until a thick, bright-green paste forms — it should have body and cling to a spoon, not be a smooth liquid. Taste: it should be intensely herby, sour from the preserved lemon, and earthy-warm from the cumin. A traditional chermoula made in a mortar will have more texture; a processor gives a smoother result. Both are correct.
Visual cue: A thick, vivid green paste speckled with darker herb flecks and pale preserved lemon.
Underdone: Paste is still chunky with visible large herb pieces and unbroken garlic. Continue blending or pounding until cohesive and spreadable.
Perfect: Thick, bright-green paste that holds its shape on a spoon. Smells powerfully of cumin, cilantro, and lemon. Divide: two-thirds for marinating the fish, one-third reserved for basting.
Overdone: Paste is watery and thin from over-processing; the herbs have released too much moisture. Squeeze through a cloth to remove excess liquid; the paste will be denser and more concentrated.
Feel cue: The chermoula should feel slightly gritty from the herb stems and spices — a living, aromatic paste rather than a smooth sauce. Rub a small amount between your fingers; you should be able to smell it across the room.

Score the fish deeply on both sides — 4–5 diagonal cuts per side, down to the bone. This is essential for two reasons: it allows the chermoula to penetrate deep into the flesh, and it prevents the skin from buckling in the oven. Rub two-thirds of the chermoula aggressively into every surface of the fish: inside the body cavity, into every score cut, and over the skin. Marinate for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 4 hours in the refrigerator.
Visual cue: Fish is entirely coated in green paste, with chermoula visible deep in every score cut and throughout the body cavity.
Underdone: Chermoula is only on the surface; score cuts are not filled. Use your fingers to press and force the paste into every cut and crevice.
Perfect: Fish is completely green. Score cuts are packed with paste. Cavity is generously coated. The fish smells intensely herby. Allow to marinate. Preheat oven to 200°C.
Overdone: Fish has marinated more than 6 hours in lemon-heavy chermoula; the acid has begun to 'cook' the surface flesh. Rinse off the marinade, pat dry, apply fresh chermoula, and bake immediately.
Feel cue: Work the chermoula into the score cuts firmly with your thumb — you should feel each cut open and accept the paste rather than sealing over it.

Place the fish on a lightly oiled baking sheet or in a tagine. Spoon the reserved chermoula over the top. Bake at 200°C (400°F) for 20–25 minutes depending on thickness (10 minutes per 2.5cm of thickness at the widest point). The fish is done when the score cuts have opened and the flesh inside is white and opaque, and the skin is lightly blistered. Rest 5 minutes before serving. Garnish with lemon wedges and fresh cilantro.
Visual cue: Skin is blistered and slightly charred at the score cut edges; chermoula has darkened to a deep green-brown. Score cuts gape open revealing white, opaque flesh.
Underdone: Score cuts are still closed; flesh inside shows translucent pink sections. Skin has not blistered. Return to the oven for 5 more minutes. Test with a skewer at the thickest point — it should pass through without resistance.
Perfect: Score cuts have opened fully; every cut reveals bright white, fully opaque fish. Chermoula is dark and fragrant. The fish peels away from the bone cleanly. Rest 5 minutes before bringing to the table.
Overdone: Flesh is beginning to pull away from the bone spontaneously; the outside looks very dry. Serve immediately with a drizzle of raw olive oil and extra lemon to restore moisture.
Feel cue: Slide a spoon or knife into the thickest score cut — perfectly baked fish should part cleanly in large, glistening flakes, each one still moist and tender rather than dry and stringy.
