steps:
Combine warm milk, sugar, and yeast in a large bowl and let stand 5 minutes until foamy (if using instant yeast, add directly to the flour). Add eggs, softened butter, flour, and salt. Mix until a rough dough forms, then knead by hand for 8–10 minutes or with a dough hook for 6–8 minutes. The dough should be soft, smooth, and slightly tacky — enriched with butter and egg but not wet.
Visual cue: A smooth, supple, slightly tacky dough that is softer than bread dough but holds a ball shape. Faintly golden from the egg yolks.
Underdone: Rough, uneven surface. Dough tears when stretched. Butter may be visible in smeared streaks. Knead longer. The butter needs to be fully worked into the flour matrix.
Perfect: Smooth, golden-tinged, slightly tacky but not sticky. Windowpane: stretches thin without tearing. Springs back slowly. Smells of butter and fresh dough. Proof in a covered bowl until doubled, about 1–1.5 hours.
Overdone: Dough is warm, somewhat wet-looking, and the butter has separated, leaving oily patches. Chill the dough for 20 minutes. Cold will re-solidify the butter and allow you to continue kneading.
Feel cue: The finished dough should feel like the softest, most supple bread dough you have ever touched — almost silky, giving way under gentle pressure like a soft pillow. It should barely cling to your hand and pull away cleanly when you lift your palm.

Cover the dough tightly and let it rise at room temperature until doubled, about 1–1.5 hours. Gently turn the risen dough out onto a lightly floured surface. Roll out to about 1 cm thickness. Using a round cutter (6–7 cm), cut out rounds. Brush each round with melted butter, then fold it in half so the butter is on the inside and the top edge slightly overhangs the bottom by about 5 mm.
Visual cue: Folded half-moon shapes with a clean fold at the top and the top half slightly overhanging the bottom, each one glistening with butter on the inner fold.
Underdone: Dough is stiff and has not doubled. Rounds spring back when rolled. Let the dough continue rising. Enriched doughs rise more slowly than lean doughs.
Perfect: Dough is doubled and pillowy. Rounds roll out easily and the fold holds its shape. Butter visible at the seam. Arrange closely together in the baking dish and let proof for 45–60 minutes.
Overdone: Dough over-proofed and is very slack and sticky. Falls apart when folded. Chill the dough for 15 minutes to firm it slightly before rolling and cutting.
Feel cue: When you fold the butter-brushed round, press the top half down gently — the butter should be contained inside, creating a slick interior layer that will become the feathery separation between the two halves after baking.

Arrange the folded rolls tightly in a buttered baking dish or on a baking sheet, with the fold facing the same direction and the rolls just touching each other. Cover loosely and let proof until noticeably puffed and beginning to press against their neighbors, about 45–60 minutes. They should look full and pillow-like before going into the oven.
Visual cue: A pan of closely packed, puffy, folded rolls that have risen into each other, each one clearly domed and soft-looking.
Underdone: Rolls have gaps between them and look flat. Have not filled the pan. Rest longer. The rolls need to press against each other — that contact is what creates the characteristic pull-apart texture.
Perfect: Rolls are touching and pressing gently against neighbors. Each one is domed and visibly puffy. A poke springs back about halfway over 2 seconds. Brush gently with melted butter and bake immediately.
Overdone: Rolls are very puffy and have begun to overflow the pan. Surface looks fragile. Bake immediately, very gently. The over-proofed rolls will still be delicious but will be less defined.
Feel cue: Gently press the top of a proofed roll with one fingertip — it should give way with barely any resistance, like pressing a marshmallow, and spring back with a slow, airy rebound. That almost-nothing resistance tells you the gas structure is fully formed and ready for the oven.

Gently brush the proofed rolls with melted butter. Bake at 190 C (375 F) for 18–22 minutes until deeply golden-brown on top and the rolls sound hollow when tapped. Immediately brush again with melted butter the moment they come out of the oven. Scatter flaky salt on top. Serve warm.
Visual cue: Deeply golden-brown, glossy, pull-apart rolls with defined folds visible at the seam and an even color across the top.
Underdone: Pale gold tops. The interior is soft and may be slightly doughy at the fold. Bake 3–5 more minutes. Enrich the color — the egg and sugar in the dough need heat to fully caramelize.
Perfect: Deep amber-gold. The fold line is visible. Each roll has a defined domed top and is pressed against its neighbors. Interior is soft and feathery when pulled apart. Smells intensely buttery. Brush immediately with more butter while hot. The hot surface will absorb it completely.
Overdone: Very dark brown, edges slightly burnt. Interior may be drying out. Tent with foil for the last 5 minutes of baking. Brush with extra butter when done to re-add moisture.
Feel cue: Pull a roll from the pan and separate it at the fold — the interior should spring apart in soft, feathery layers with the buttered layer separating cleanly. The crumb inside is cottony-white, fine-grained, and springs back immediately when gently compressed. Hold it up: it should feel almost weightless for its size.

description: Rome's most demanding pasta — spaghetti cloaked in a trembling, egg-yolk-rich sauce that exists in the razor-thin margin between silky cream and scrambled catastrophe, punctuated by shards of crisped guanciale and a snowfall of aged Pecorino.

ingredients.name: Guanciale (cured pork cheek), cut into lardons
黑胡椒（Black pepper, coarsely ground and toasted）
Pasta cooking water, starchy and salted

steps:
Place the guanciale lardons in a cold, dry skillet — no oil. Start over medium-low heat and cook slowly for 8-12 minutes, turning occasionally. The fat must render gently; high heat will make the exterior tough before the interior fat has melted. Cook until the fat is fully translucent and the meat portions are crisp and golden at the edges. Remove the pan from the heat and use a slotted spoon to transfer the guanciale to a paper towel briefly, then return to the pan with all the rendered fat. The pan and fat must be warm but not hot when the sauce is made.
Visual cue: Lardons that are golden-amber and crisp at the edges, with translucent rendered fat pooling in the pan. The fat is clear and shimmering, not dark or smoking.
Underdone: Fat is still white and opaque. Meat is soft and chewy throughout with no crisp edge. Continue on medium-low heat. The fat must be fully rendered before the meat crisps.
Perfect: Edges are deep golden and crisp; the interior portions are still slightly tender. Fat in the pan is clear, golden, and fragrant with pork sweetness. Remove from heat. Keep the pan warm — it will be needed for the sauce.
Overdone: Guanciale is uniformly dark brown and hard throughout. Fat has begun to smoke and smells burnt. Remove immediately. If the fat is not burnt, it can still be used. Let the pan cool more before adding the egg mixture.
Feel cue: The rendered fat should smell sweet and clean — like warm pork candy, not acrid. The guanciale pieces should click lightly against the pan, not squish.

While the guanciale renders, combine the egg yolks and whole egg in a bowl large enough to eventually hold all the pasta. Add half the finely grated Pecorino and a generous amount of freshly coarsely ground black pepper. Whisk vigorously until the mixture is smooth, thick, and pale yellow — the consistency of heavy cream. It should fall from the whisk in a thick, continuous ribbon. Do not add salt — the guanciale fat and Pecorino provide all the salt this dish needs.
Visual cue: A thick, smooth, pale yellow cream with the consistency of heavy cream or loose custard. Falls from the whisk in a thick ribbon.
Underdone: Egg yolks and cheese are not fully incorporated — white streaks of cheese are still visible in the yellow base. Whisk more vigorously. The friction of whisking begins to emulsify the mixture.
Perfect: Uniform pale yellow, thick, creamy consistency. Cheese is fully incorporated. Falls from the whisk in a slow, heavy ribbon. Set aside near the stove. It needs to be room temperature when it meets the pasta.
Overdone: Over-whisked; mixture is frothy with large air bubbles. Let it rest and the foam will settle. This is not a problem.
Feel cue: The sauce base should feel almost like thick yogurt when stirred with a spoon — there should be resistance when you drag it across the bowl.

Cook the pasta in a large pot of well-salted water (the water should taste pleasantly salty, like a mild sea). Cook to 1 full minute less than the package's al dente time — it will finish cooking in the sauce off-heat. Before draining, scoop out at least 1 cup (240ml) of pasta cooking water — this cloudy, starchy water is the linchpin of the sauce. Drain the pasta but do not rinse.
Visual cue: Pasta that is just barely underdone — firm with a very faint white line when bitten through. It will finish in the sauce.
Underdone: Significant white core when bitten. Still chalky and floury tasting. Cook for another 30 seconds and check again. The pasta needs to be almost done before it leaves the water.
Perfect: Barely underdone — tender exterior, slight firmness throughout, tiny white thread at the center. The pasta has absorbed flavor from the salty water. Reserve the pasta water immediately, then drain and transfer to the pan.
Overdone: Fully soft with no resistance. Will turn completely soft in the final sauce step. Move quickly through the remaining steps — do not let this pasta cool.
Feel cue: Bite a strand against your front tooth — you should feel a firm 'snap' through about 80% of the thickness, then a last thin thread of resistance. That thread is the margin between al dente and overcooked.

Transfer the drained pasta directly to the pan with the guanciale and its rendered fat over medium heat. Toss vigorously for 30 seconds, making sure every strand is coated in pork fat and has had contact with the hot pan. This step flavors the pasta before the egg sauce arrives. Add 2-3 tablespoons of the reserved pasta water to the pan and toss again — the starch in the water begins building the emulsion.
Visual cue: Pasta shiny and evenly coated in rendered guanciale fat. Each strand glistens. Guanciale pieces are distributed throughout.
Underdone: Pasta looks dry and mat. Fat has not coated the strands. Guanciale all sitting at the bottom. Toss more actively — lift and toss rather than just stirring. Add a splash more pasta water.
Perfect: Every strand coated and glistening. Steam rising. Guanciale evenly distributed. Pan is hot but not screaming. Remove the pan from the heat before adding the egg sauce.
Overdone: Pan is too hot and the pasta is beginning to dry out and stick. Add pasta water and immediately remove from heat. The pan must cool before the egg sauce goes in.
Feel cue: The pasta should sound like a quiet, moist sizzle as it tosses in the fat — not a hard sear. If you hear crackle or see smoke, the pan is too hot for the egg sauce.

This is the critical step. Remove the pan from the heat entirely and let it rest 30 seconds off the burner. Pour the egg-cheese mixture over the pasta, and immediately begin tossing vigorously with tongs while simultaneously adding pasta water a tablespoon at a time. The residual heat from the pasta and pan will gently set the eggs into a sauce — but only if you keep moving. The pasta water both lubricates the sauce and prevents the eggs from scrambling by distributing heat. Aim for a consistency between thick cream and loose custard — it should flow when the pan is tilted but cling to every strand. Add the remaining Pecorino in two additions, tossing between each. Taste and adjust pepper.
Visual cue: A glossy, creamy, pale-yellow sauce that clings to every strand of pasta and flows slowly when the pan is tilted. No visible curds. No pooling liquid.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and watery. Egg has not emulsified — it runs freely to the bottom of the pan. The pasta looks undressed. Toss more vigorously and move the pan back over a very low flame for 10 seconds, tossing constantly. The starchy pasta water will help bind.
Perfect: Thick, glossy, uniform pale-yellow cream coating every strand. Flows like heavy cream when tilted. No liquid pooling at the base of the pan. Plate immediately in warm bowls and serve.
Overdone: Visible yellow curds. Sauce has scrambled and separated. Liquid has pooled at the base. You cannot unscramble eggs, but the flavor is intact. Toss in a generous splash of hot pasta water off-heat and keep moving — the starch can partially re-emulsify mild scrambling.
Feel cue: Tilt the pan — the dressed pasta should slowly slide as one cohesive mass, not separate into pasta strands swimming in liquid. It should feel and look like a single, glossy entity.

ingredients.name: Dried borlotti or cannellini beans, soaked overnight
Short pasta: ditalini, tubettini, or broken spaghetti
芹菜（Celery, finely diced (including the pale inner leaves)）
Extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish

steps:
Drain and rinse the soaked beans. Place them in a large pot and cover with fresh cold water by 6 cm. Add the rosemary sprig and a generous pinch of salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, skim any grey foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered for 60-90 minutes until the beans are completely tender — no chalkiness at the center when bitten. Do not rush this step with a hard boil, which can split the bean skins and make the broth cloudy. Reserve all the cooking liquid. Remove the rosemary. Using a potato masher or the back of a spoon, roughly mash about one-third of the beans directly in the pot to create a naturally thick, creamy broth.
Visual cue: Tender beans with no chalky center in a cloudy, starchy broth. One-third of the beans partially mashed to create thickness.
Underdone: Beans have a firm, chalky center when bitten. Broth is thin and clear. Continue simmering and test every 10 minutes. Old beans can take up to 2 hours.
Perfect: Beans crush completely between fingers with no resistance. Broth is cloudy and slightly thick from dissolved starch. One-third mashed into the broth. Set aside and begin the soffritto.
Overdone: Most beans have burst and dissolved into the broth. Liquid is very thick. This is fine — the dissolved beans enrich the broth. Proceed.
Feel cue: Pinch a bean — it should collapse instantly to a smooth paste without any grit or resistance, like pressing a ripe grape.

Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy pot over medium-low heat. Add the diced onion, celery, carrot, garlic, and red pepper flakes. Season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 10-12 minutes until the vegetables are completely soft and the onion is translucent and just beginning to turn gold. Add the tomato paste and stir to coat all the vegetables. Cook for 3-4 minutes, stirring constantly, pressing the paste against the hot pot until it darkens slightly from bright red to brick-red and smells sweet and caramelized.
Visual cue: Completely softened, glossy vegetables in a fragrant base, with a brick-red tomato paste coating fully incorporated.
Underdone: Onion still has a raw bite. Tomato paste still bright red and smells raw. Continue cooking. The tomato paste especially needs time on the heat to develop sweetness.
Perfect: Vegetables completely tender and glossy. Tomato paste darkened to brick red. Smells sweet, savory, and complex. Add the beans and their cooking liquid.
Overdone: Tomato paste has scorched to black spots. Bitter smell. Add a small splash of water to deglaze any scorched spots before adding the beans.
Feel cue: Press a piece of onion against the side of the pot — it should smear entirely without resistance. The soffritto should smell like the beginning of every good Sunday sauce.

Add the cooked beans and all their reserved cooking liquid to the soffritto. Stir together and bring to a gentle simmer. If the broth is too thick, add water until you reach a consistency slightly thinner than your target finished soup — the pasta will thicken it further. Simmer for 15 minutes to allow the flavors to meld. Taste and adjust salt. The broth should now taste deeply savory with a faint sweetness from the soffritto and a lingering heat from the peperoncino.
Visual cue: A creamy, rose-tinted broth — somewhere between a cream soup and a thin broth — with whole and mashed beans visible throughout.
Underdone: Broth still tastes separately of beans and tomato. The flavors haven't melded. Simmer for 10 more minutes and taste again.
Perfect: Unified, deeply savory broth with a slight sweetness and heat. The bean starchiness and soffritto are fully integrated. Add the pasta directly to the pot.
Overdone: Broth has reduced too far and is very thick and starchy. Add water to loosen before adding the pasta — the pasta will thicken it further.
Feel cue: Taste a spoonful of broth — it should coat the back of the spoon slightly, with a warm, savory, slightly sweet weight that feels substantial even without the pasta.

Add the dry pasta directly to the simmering bean broth. Stir immediately and frequently — the pasta will absorb the broth aggressively, so check consistency every 2 minutes and add water as needed to keep it soupy throughout cooking. Cook until the pasta is al dente — it will continue softening in the residual heat. The final dish should be thick enough that a spoon dragged through it leaves a clear channel that fills back slowly. Remove from heat. Taste and adjust salt generously. Drizzle a generous amount of olive oil over the surface and stir it in. Let the soup rest for 2-3 minutes before serving.
Visual cue: A thick, creamy rose-pink soup with pasta and beans evenly distributed. The surface shimmers with olive oil. A spoon-trail closes slowly.
Underdone: Pasta is still very firm or chalky at the center. Broth is thin. Continue cooking, adding a splash of water if the broth has absorbed too quickly.
Perfect: Pasta is just al dente. The soup is thick enough to hold a spoon-trail but loose enough to pour into a bowl. Rich, creamy, shimmering with olive oil. Let rest 3 minutes off-heat, then serve in warm bowls.
Overdone: Pasta has absorbed all the broth. The dish has become a thick, starchy paste. Pasta overcooked. Add warm water and stir vigorously — pasta e fagioli is very forgiving. A wetter version is still delicious.
Feel cue: Ladle into a bowl and tilt — the soup should flow slowly as a single, unified mass, neither running freely like water nor sitting immovably like polenta. This is the perfect 'lagane' consistency Neapolitans call 'né troppo asciutta, né troppo brodosa.'

name: Fresh Egg Pasta
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: all-purpose flour; half 00 / half semola
Whole eggs (large, room temperature): 55 g
  Alternatives: 1 whole egg per 100 g flour
Egg yolk (for richer, more golden dough): 9 g
Extra-virgin olive oil: 3 g
Fine sea salt: 1 g
Semola rimacinata (for dusting & dredging): 8 g
  Alternatives: fine semolina

Total time: 1 hr 30 min

description: The golden foundation of every Italian table — soft tipo 00 flour and whole eggs worked by hand into a single supple dough, rested until it relaxes, then rolled into sheets thin enough to read a newspaper through. The base for tagliatelle, pappardelle, and tender ravioli alike.

ingredients.name: Egg yolk (for richer, more golden dough)

steps:
Mound the flour on a clean work surface and whisk the salt through it, then sweep out a wide well in the centre. Crack the whole eggs and the extra yolk into the well, add the olive oil, and beat them with a fork. Working the fork in slow circles, draw flour from the inner wall of the well into the eggs a little at a time. When the centre is too thick to stir, switch to a bench scraper and chop the wet, ragged mass together with the remaining flour until it forms a rough, shaggy dough with no loose dry pools.
Visual cue: A craggy, cohesive ball of dough — moist but not wet, holding together when pressed, with the surrounding flour mostly absorbed.
Underdone: The mixture is wet and sticky, smearing on your fingers, with the well's walls collapsed into a soup before the flour was worked in. Scatter in flour a tablespoon at a time, chopping with the scraper, until the mass firms into a workable shaggy ball.
Perfect: A rough, slightly tacky dough that clumps into one mass and pulls cleanly from the board, with only a light dusting of flour left behind. Begin kneading to develop the gluten.
Overdone: The dough is dry and crumbly, cracking apart and refusing to gather, with loose flour that won't absorb. Wet your hands and work the dampness in, or add a few drops of water, until the crumbs come together.
Feel cue: The fork should meet rising resistance as more flour is pulled in. The finished shaggy mass feels cool, slightly tacky, and clings to itself more than to your hands.

Knead the dough on a lightly floured surface with the heel of your hand: push the dough away from you, fold it back over itself, give it a quarter turn, and repeat. Keep a steady rhythm for 8-10 minutes. At first it will tear and feel stiff; as the gluten develops it tightens, smooths, and springs back. Add flour only a pinch at a time if it stays stubbornly sticky.
Visual cue: A smooth, satiny ball with a faint sheen — uniform in colour, no dry seams, springing back slowly when pressed with a finger.
Underdone: The surface is still lumpy and torn, the dough feels slack, and a finger-poke leaves a dent that does not recover. Keep kneading — the gluten needs more time. The transformation to smoothness happens suddenly near the end.
Perfect: Silky and elastic, the surface taut and smooth like an earlobe, springing back slowly and evenly when pressed. Wrap and rest the dough to relax the gluten.
Overdone: The dough fights back hard, the surface beginning to dry and resist any reshaping; it has been worked too long and too dry. Stop kneading, wrap tightly, and rest longer than usual so the tight gluten can relax.
Feel cue: The dough shifts from rough and sticky to firm and bouncy under your palm. When it pushes back gently and the surface feels like the lobe of your ear, the kneading is done.

Wrap the dough tightly in cling film or seal it under an inverted bowl so it cannot dry out. Let it rest at room temperature for at least 30 minutes, up to an hour. This hydrates the flour evenly and relaxes the gluten so the dough will roll thin without snapping back. Do not skip this — a rested dough rolls effortlessly where a fresh one fights you.
Visual cue: A relaxed, supple dough that yields easily and stretches without immediately recoiling when you press a corner.
Underdone: Pressed dough snaps back instantly and feels tight and springy; it has not rested long enough to relax. Re-wrap and give it another 15-20 minutes — the gluten is still too tense to roll thin.
Perfect: The dough is soft and pliable, holding a gentle dent and stretching smoothly without tearing or pulling back. Roll the dough out into sheets.
Overdone: The surface has dried and crusted because it was left exposed, with a leathery skin that will crack when rolled. Trim or knead away any dry skin, then wrap properly and rest a few minutes more to even out the moisture.
Feel cue: After resting, the dough should feel softer and looser than when you wrapped it — a gentle press leaves a slowly filling dimple, a sign the gluten has surrendered.

Cut the dough into quarters, keeping the unused pieces wrapped. Flatten one piece into a disc and pass it through the widest setting of a pasta machine (or roll by hand with a long pin). Fold it in thirds like a letter, give it a quarter turn, and pass it through the widest setting two or three more times to laminate and square it. Then roll it through progressively narrower settings, dusting lightly with flour to prevent sticking, until the sheet is thin enough to see your hand through.
Visual cue: A long, even, satiny sheet of pasta — thin enough that you can see the shadow of your fingers through it, smooth and unbroken at the edges.
Underdone: The sheet is thick and opaque, with ragged or cracked edges, and feels heavy and stiff to lift. Continue rolling down through the settings; if the edges crack, fold and laminate once more before going thinner.
Perfect: A smooth, translucent ribbon of even thickness, supple and silky, holding together as you lift it. Cut, fill, or shape the pasta as desired.
Overdone: The sheet has gone so thin it tears under its own weight or sticks and wrinkles, becoming impossible to handle. Stop at the previous setting next time; patch tears by pressing the dough together and re-rolling, or dust more flour to stop sticking.
Feel cue: Each pass should glide more easily as the dough relaxes and lengthens. The finished sheet feels cool, smooth, and faintly elastic, draping over your hand like fine fabric.

Let the sheets dry on a floured cloth for 5-10 minutes until the surface is tacky-dry but still flexible — this keeps the cut ribbons from gluing together. Pass the sheets through the cutter or roll them loosely and slice by hand into tagliatelle or pappardelle. Toss the ribbons generously with semola rimacinata, lift and fluff them into loose nests, and either cook within the hour in heavily salted boiling water (2-3 minutes) or let dry for later.
Visual cue: Loose, separate nests of golden ribbons dusted with semola, each strand distinct and not clumping to its neighbours.
Underdone: The cut strands stick together in a damp, fused mass because the sheet was too wet when cut. Toss more aggressively with semola and gently tease the strands apart; let future sheets surface-dry a little longer before cutting.
Perfect: Silky, even ribbons that fall apart into loose nests with a light coat of semola, flexible but not tacky. Cook in well-salted boiling water for 2-3 minutes, or dry for storage.
Overdone: The strands have over-dried and turned brittle, snapping into short pieces when handled. Handle gently and accept some breakage; if cooking soon, the brief boil will soften them again.
Feel cue: The ribbons should feel cool, smooth, and just dry enough not to cling. A handful lifted and dropped should cascade into airy nests, dusted strands whispering against each other.

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, softened to room temperature
Plain flour (for custard thickening, small amount)
Lemon zest strip and cinnamon stick

steps:
Mix the flour with a pinch of salt and enough cold water (roughly 50 parts) to form a shaggy dough. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth. Rest 10 minutes, then roll into a large rectangle on a floured surface. Spread two-thirds of the softened butter in an even, thin layer across the surface. Fold into thirds (letter fold), rotate 90 degrees, roll out again, and repeat with remaining butter. Fold into thirds one final time. Chill for 20 minutes before shaping.
Visual cue: A layered dough package that, when cut at the edge, reveals distinct strata of pale dough and white butter with clean, separate lines.
Underdone: Butter has smeared into the dough rather than layering — the cut edge shows a uniform pale yellow, not distinct stripes. The dough feels greasy. Chill for 15 minutes and try rolling more gently. Warm butter breaks down layers; cold butter maintains them.
Perfect: Clean, distinct layers visible when the folded block is cut at the edge. The dough is smooth on the outside, cool, and pliable but not sticky. The butter is in thin, flat sheets between the dough layers. Chill 20 minutes, then roll into a log and cut into rounds for the tart tins.
Overdone: Dough has been over-worked and is becoming elastic, springing back when rolled. Butter layers are beginning to merge. Gluten is developing excessively. Rest the dough in the fridge for 30 minutes. Over-kneaded laminated dough will never be as flaky but will still produce an acceptable pastry.
Feel cue: The laminated dough, when pressed with a fingertip, should feel cool and firm at the surface with a slightly yielding interior — like pressing on a closed paperback book. It should not leave a grease mark on your fingers when you pick it up.

Roll the chilled dough into a tight cylinder about 4cm in diameter. Slice the cylinder into rounds 2cm thick. Press each round into a lightly greased tart tin, working from the center outward with your thumbs to line the sides, creating a thin, even shell that extends just above the tin rim. The walls should be thinner than you think — the butter layers will puff in the oven. Refrigerate the lined tins for 15 minutes before filling.
Visual cue: Evenly lined tins with thin walls (about 3mm) that come up just above the rim. The cut layers of dough are visible at the top edge.
Underdone: Pastry shell walls are too thick (6mm+) and uneven. The bottom is thick and the sides are thin. Thick pastry will not cook through before the custard sets. Work the dough thinner by pressing more firmly from the center. Aim for translucence — you should almost see your fingers through the dough at the sides.
Perfect: Walls are a uniform 3mm with clean visible lamination layers. The top edge is slightly uneven and textured from the cut cylinder — this is correct and will form the most flaky edge. Chill 15 minutes before filling.
Overdone: Pastry has been handled so much it is very soft and greasy from warm hands melting the butter. The layers have begun to merge. Return to the freezer for 10 minutes. The butter must re-solidify before baking or the pastry will not puff.
Feel cue: Run your thumb around the inside of the tin after lining — you should feel a uniform resistance and the layered dough should feel cool and slightly papery, not warm and greasy. Any thick spots will bake dense and raw.

Warm the milk in a saucepan with the lemon zest and cinnamon stick until steaming but not boiling. In a separate bowl, whisk together the sugar, flour, and egg yolks until pale and smooth. Remove aromatics from the milk. Stream the hot milk gradually into the egg mixture, whisking constantly — never add hot milk to cold eggs all at once. Return the mixture to the saucepan and cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, until it just begins to thicken and the first bubbles appear. Remove from heat immediately. The custard will look too loose — this is correct; it will set in the oven.
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy, pale-yellow custard that coats a spoon but flows freely. When you draw a finger across the back of the spoon, the line holds for 3–4 seconds before the custard creeps back.
Underdone: Custard is thin and watery. No coating on the spoon. Line drawn in it disappears instantly. Flour has not cooked and will leave a raw starchy taste. Return to medium heat and stir until the coating consistency is reached. Do not stop stirring or the bottom will curdle.
Perfect: Custard coats the spoon in a thin, even layer. When poured, it falls in a steady ribbon, not a stream. It smells of warm milk, egg, and cinnamon. Color is deep golden-yellow from the yolks. Pass through a fine sieve into a jug for easy pouring. Use while warm.
Overdone: Custard has scrambled — yellow eggy lumps are visible. The mixture smells of cooked egg rather than custard. It is grainy when stirred. Pass urgently through a fine sieve, pressing hard. Some custard can be rescued this way if the lumps are not too large. Reduce oven temperature by 20°C when baking to prevent the pre-scrambled custard from completely setting hard.
Feel cue: Dip a clean finger into the warm custard — it should feel silky and coating, like heavy cream, with no graininess on your fingertip. The warmth should be pleasantly
hot but not scalding, around 60–65°C.

Preheat your oven to its maximum temperature — at minimum 240°C (465°F), ideally 260°C or higher. The high heat is non-negotiable: it is what creates the characteristic leopard-spot caramelization on the custard surface. Fill the chilled pastry shells three-quarters full with warm custard. Bake on the top shelf for 12–15 minutes until the pastry is golden-brown and the custard surface is blistered with dark caramelized spots. Allow to cool for 5 minutes before eating.
Visual cue: Pastry shells are deep golden-brown with visible flaky layers. The custard surface has irregular dark brown to black caramelized spots, like a leopard's skin. The custard should still wobble slightly in the center when the tin is shaken.
Underdone: Custard surface is pale yellow with no caramelized spots. The pastry is blond but not golden. The custard center feels completely liquid when the tin is gently shaken. Return to the oven for 3–5 more minutes. The caramelized spots are not optional — they are the defining character of the pastel de nata.
Perfect: Pastry is deep amber-gold and flaky at the visible edges. The custard has a dramatic pattern of dark spots from intense caramelization. When the tin is shaken, the center wobbles slightly like barely set gelatin — not liquid, not rigid. Cool for at least 5 minutes before eating — the custard is liquid-hot and will burn. They are best warm, eaten within 30 minutes of the oven.
Overdone: Custard has puffed dramatically and then collapsed, leaving a sunken center. The spots have merged into an entirely black, burnt surface. The custard edges have gone rubbery. The caramelized center may be salvageable if you peel away the worst of the surface. Reduce oven time by 3 minutes next batch.
Feel cue: Lift a cooled tart from its tin — the bottom of the pastry should feel rigid and dry, not soggy. Tap the base with a fingernail and it should sound
hollow, like a good cracker. The top custard, when touched with a fingertip, should resist gently and then slowly spring back.

name: Pastel de Nata
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Plain flour (all-purpose): 250 g
Cold water: 125 g
Fine sea salt: 3 g
Lard (or unsalted butter, softened): 150 g
  Alternatives: vegetable shortening
Whole milk: 250 g
Caster sugar (for custard): 200 g
Water (for sugar syrup): 60 g
Plain flour (for custard thickening): 15 g
Egg yolks (large): 6 unit
Cinnamon stick: 1 unit
Lemon peel strip (no pith): 1 unit
Active time: 60 min
Total time: 4 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A cupped shell of shatteringly crisp laminated pastry cradling a custard so silky and trembling it barely holds its shape — caramelised black on top where the fierce heat of the oven turned sugar to lacquer.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine flour, water, and salt to form a smooth, supple dough. Knead for 5-6 minutes until it is soft, non-sticky, and has some elasticity. It should feel like very soft plasticine. Do not over-knead. Wrap in cling film and rest in the refrigerator for 30 minutes. This gluten rest is essential — it allows the dough to roll out without springing back when laminated.
Visual cue: A very smooth, soft dough ball with a slightly silky surface. When pressed, it holds the indent of a thumbprint cleanly.
Underdone: Dough is rough, uneven in texture, and tears when stretched. Gluten is underdeveloped. Knead for 2-3 more minutes. The surface should be smooth and the dough should stretch without tearing.
Perfect: Smooth, uniform, very soft and pliable. Almost silky. Holds a fingerprint indent cleanly. Not sticky. Wrap and refrigerate for 30 minutes before laminating.
Overdone: Dough has become tough and elastic — it springs back aggressively when pressed. Refrigerate for 1 hour. Over-kneaded dough needs a longer rest to relax the gluten.
Feel cue: The dough should feel like a warm earlobe — incredibly soft and yielding with a smooth, slightly tacky surface that doesn't cling to your palms.

On a lightly floured surface, roll the rested dough into a large rectangle, about 40 x 30 cm. Spread the softened lard or butter evenly across the surface, leaving a 1 cm border. Roll up the dough tightly into a log from the short end. Slice the log into 12 equal rounds. Press each round flat between your fingers, then press it into a muffin tin to line the base and sides, pressing the pastry up above the rim. Refrigerate the lined tins for 20 minutes.
Visual cue: Muffin tin cups lined with a thin pastry shell that shows the swirled cross-section of the roll. The pastry layers are visible as concentric rings when looked at from above.
Underdone: Pastry is too thick in places, especially the base. The layers are bunched rather than evenly spread. Use your thumb to thin the base further, pressing from the centre outward and working the pastry up the sides evenly.
Perfect: Thin, even shells with visible laminated layers from the swirl cut. The pastry extends just above the rim of each cup. Refrigerate and prepare the custard while chilling.
Overdone: Pastry has been worked too warm and the fat has melted in, losing the distinct layers. Refrigerate for 20 minutes before any further shaping — fat must be cold to create distinct layers.
Feel cue: Properly chilled pastry shells should feel cool and very firm when you press the side — almost rigid. Any warmth or softness means the fat has softened and the layers will merge in the oven.

Heat milk with the cinnamon stick and lemon peel strip over medium heat until steaming and just below a simmer. Remove from heat and steep for 15 minutes. Remove the cinnamon stick and lemon peel. Meanwhile, cook the sugar and water in a separate small saucepan to 104 C (the soft thread stage), without stirring. This is the sugar syrup that will sweeten and enrich the custard with a faintly caramelised note.
Visual cue: Milk that smells of warm cinnamon and citrus. The syrup at 104 C will form thin threads when a small amount is dropped into cold water.
Underdone: Milk has not fully infused — faint cinnamon scent only. Syrup below 100 C is still watery. Steep the milk longer with the spices and ensure the syrup reaches temperature.
Perfect: Milk smells strongly of cinnamon with a background of lemon. Syrup is clear and lightly viscous at 104 C. Combine with the flour and yolks to form the custard base.
Overdone: Syrup above 110 C will begin caramelising — the custard will taste of caramel rather than being subtly sweet. Add a tablespoon of cold water immediately to stop the cooking and lower the temperature.
Feel cue: The steeped milk should smell like a Portuguese pastelaria — warm cinnamon-spice with a citrus whisper. Taste a small spoonful — it should be subtly flavoured, not aggressively perfumed.

Whisk the flour into the infused milk until completely smooth. Pour in the hot sugar syrup, whisking constantly. Place over medium heat and stir constantly until the custard just begins to thicken — remove from heat the moment it thickens, while it is still pourable (do not let it set fully on the stove). Whisk in the egg yolks off the heat. Pass through a fine sieve into a jug. The custard should be thin enough to pour, not thick like a set pudding — it sets in the oven.
Visual cue: A thin, pourable custard that coats the back of a spoon with a thin, translucent layer. Still more liquid than a thick cream.
Underdone: Custard is water-thin with no body — the flour has not begun to thicken it. Return to heat briefly, stirring. The starch needs to reach around 80 C to begin gelling.
Perfect: Lightly thickened, pourable, coats a spoon in a thin, translucent layer. Colour is pale yellow from the yolks. Pass through a sieve and pour into lined pastry shells.
Overdone: Custard has set into a thick, pudding-like mass. Cannot be poured into the shells. Whisk vigorously off heat and thin with a little warm milk. Strain again. This custard will set very stiff in the oven.
Feel cue: Pour a thin stream of the custard from the sieve back into the jug — it should fall in a wide, smooth, barely viscous stream, like very thin cream. Thicker than water, thinner than cream of soup.

Pour the custard into the chilled pastry shells, filling to within 3 mm of the rim. Bake in the highest position of a very hot oven — 240-260 C (460-500 F) — for 12-15 minutes. The pastry should be golden-brown and deeply blistered. The custard surface should have dramatic black blisters and patches of deep amber caramelisation over a set, trembling custard below. Serve warm, dusted with ground cinnamon.
Visual cue: Black blistered patches across the custard surface — not uniform brown, but dramatic charred spots over an amber base, with the custard set but trembling. The pastry is golden, blistered, and crisp.
Underdone: Custard surface is pale yellow and has not caramelised. Pastry is blond. Custard may still be liquid in the centre. Return to oven. The defining feature of a pastel de nata is the black caramelisation — do not remove too early.
Perfect: Dramatic black blisters and deep amber caramelisation across the custard. Pastry is deeply golden and blistered. The custard jiggles softly when the tray is moved. Cool for 5 minutes in the tin, then remove. Serve warm with cinnamon.
Overdone: Entire custard surface is uniformly black and smells acrid rather than caramel-sweet. Pastry is very dark at the edges. Reduce the oven temperature by 10 C and shorten by 2 minutes next time. The line between perfect and burnt is narrow at this temperature.
Feel cue: Hold a finished tart at its rim and tip it gently — the custard centre should tremble and wobble visibly, like a barely-set flan. A custard that doesn't move at all has been overbaked and will be rubbery.

name: Patatas Bravas Sauce
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Extra-virgin olive oil: 3 parts
Garlic cloves, finely minced: 0.5 parts
Sweet smoked paprika (pimentón dulce): 1 parts
Hot smoked paprika (pimentón picante): 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: cayenne, use half the quantity
Crushed canned tomatoes: 8 parts
  Alternatives: fresh tomatoes, grated on a box grater
Sherry vinegar: 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: red wine vinegar
Fine sea salt: 0.1 parts
Granulated sugar: 0.1 parts
Full-fat mayonnaise (for aioli layer): 4 parts
Fresh lemon juice: 0.25 parts
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 35 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A bold, paprika-red sauce with the smoky ferocity of dried chilis and the cool, garlic-sharp counterpoint of aioli — each bite of potato arrives in two temperatures, two textures, two temperaments.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Warm the olive oil in a small saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the minced garlic and cook for 60-90 seconds, stirring constantly, until it is fragrant and just starting to turn golden at the edges — not browned. Remove from heat and immediately add both paprikas. Stir vigorously for 30 seconds; the residual heat will bloom the spices without burning them. Burning paprika is irreversible and produces a sharp, acrid bitterness.
Visual cue: The oil is stained a deep brick-red, the paprika fully wetted and fragrant. Garlic is gold at the edges but not brown.
Underdone: Garlic is translucent and raw-smelling. Paprika sits in clumps, not fully dispersed in the oil. Return to low heat for 30 more seconds, stirring constantly.
Perfect: Oil is vivid orange-red, uniformly tinted. Smells of sweet smoke, toasted spice, and gentle garlic. Add the tomatoes immediately to halt cooking.
Overdone: Garlic is brown or the paprika smells sharp and acrid. Dark flecks in the oil. Discard and start over — burnt paprika ruins the entire sauce and cannot be fixed.
Feel cue: Hold your palm over the pan — you should feel warmth but not scorching heat. The spices should hiss gently when they hit the oil, not snap and spit.

Add the crushed tomatoes, sherry vinegar, salt, and sugar to the saucepan. Stir to combine with the bloomed paprika base. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, then reduce to low. Cook uncovered for 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has thickened to a loose paste that mounds slightly on a spoon and no longer tastes raw.
Visual cue: A thick, glossy, deep-red sauce that coats the back of a spoon and leaves a clean line when you draw a finger across it.
Underdone: Sauce is still thin and watery. Tomatoes taste bright and raw. Surface bubbles actively. Continue simmering. Stir more frequently to prevent sticking on the bottom.
Perfect: Sauce pulls away from the sides of the pan when stirred. Spoon-dragged line holds clean for 3 seconds. Flavor is deep, smoky, and balanced. Taste and adjust — more vinegar for brightness, sugar to tame acidity. Cool slightly before serving.
Overdone: Sauce is very thick and dark, sticking aggressively to the pan. May have a slightly caramelized or bitter edge. Thin with a splash of water and stir vigorously over low heat to reincorporate.
Feel cue: Drag a wooden spoon across the bottom of the pan — if the sauce closes back slowly over 2-3 seconds, it is ready. A rapid flood means it needs more time.

For a restaurant-smooth sauce, carefully transfer the warm sauce to a blender and blend on high for 60 seconds until completely smooth. Alternatively, use an immersion blender directly in the pan. This is optional — the sauce is excellent either chunky or smooth — but the smooth version clings better to fried potatoes.
Visual cue: A uniformly glossy, deeply coloured sauce with no visible tomato seeds or skin fragments.
Underdone: Sauce has a rough, granular texture. Tomato skin pieces visible. Blend longer. If using an immersion blender, move it through the whole volume of sauce.
Perfect: Sauce runs off the blender in a smooth, shining sheet. Rich, even color throughout. Return to the pan to reheat gently before serving, or cool and refrigerate.
Overdone: Sauce has been over-blended and is now frothy and pale from aeration. Let it rest for 5 minutes. The foam will settle and the color will deepen again.
Feel cue: Run a finger across the back of a spoon — it should feel completely smooth, like painted lacquer, with no grit or texture.

For the aioli layer: stir the mayonnaise with a small additional minced garlic clove and the fresh lemon juice until smooth. Taste — it should be sharp with garlic, bright with lemon, and creamy. This is a shortcut aioli; for the full version, emulsify from egg yolk. Refrigerate until service.
Visual cue: A thick, pale cream with tiny garlic flecks, glossy and smooth throughout.
Underdone: Garlic and lemon are not fully incorporated. Streaks of plain mayo visible. Stir more vigorously for another 30 seconds.
Perfect: Uniform, ivory-white, sharply garlicky with a bright lemon lift. Holds a soft peak when dragged. Cover and refrigerate until needed.
Overdone: Too much lemon has thinned the mayo to a runny consistency. Stir in a spoonful of fresh mayo to rebalance the texture.
Feel cue: The aioli should fall from a spoon in a thick, slow ribbon — substantial enough to pool on the sauce without immediately sinking.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

description: Madrid's beloved bar tapa — thick-cut potatoes twice-fried to a craggy, crisp exterior and a fluffy center, served doused in a spicy tomato-paprika brava sauce and a drizzle of aioli.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Floury potatoes (Maris Piper or Russet), peeled and cut into 3 cm chunks
Olive oil or sunflower oil for frying
Ripe tomatoes, roughly chopped (or canned whole plum tomatoes)
Olive oil for the brava sauce

steps:
Place the potato chunks in a large pot and cover generously with cold salted water. Bring to a boil over high heat and cook for 12–15 minutes until the potatoes are just cooked through but not falling apart — a skewer should slide in with slight resistance at the center. Drain in a colander and shake the colander vigorously 5–6 times to rough up the edges. This roughing-up shatters the exterior starch into jagged, uneven points that will turn into the craggy, shattery crust that defines great bravas. Spread the roughed-up potatoes in a single layer on a rack and let them steam-dry for at least 10 minutes. The drier the surface, the more ferocious the crust in the fry.
Visual cue: Potato chunks with shaggy, roughed-up edges and a dry, matte, chalky exterior from the steam-drying — they should look almost frosted with surface starch.
Underdone: Potato chunks are still hard at the center — a skewer meets significant resistance. The exterior will not fluff during frying. Return to boiling water for another 3–4 minutes. The parboil must go far enough for the center to be fully tender.
Perfect: Just yielding at the center with a chalky, roughed exterior. They hold their shape but the edges are visibly shaggy from shaking. Steam-dry on a rack for 10 minutes minimum before the first fry.
Overdone: Potatoes have boiled too long and are crumbling apart — the chunks cannot hold together for frying. Handle very gently during frying. A crumbled bravo is less tragic than it sounds — the rough pieces still fry well and the irregular shapes can be charming.
Feel cue: Pick up a potato chunk and shake it — it should feel light for its size, like the moisture is already leaving the surface. The exterior should feel dry and slightly powdery under your fingers, not damp or slick.

Heat the olive oil for the sauce in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook for 1–2 minutes until pale gold. Add both paprikas and stir for 30 seconds — the paprika blooms almost immediately, turning the oil a vivid red-orange. Add the chopped tomatoes and a pinch of salt and cook, stirring occasionally, for 15–20 minutes until the tomatoes have broken down completely and the sauce has thickened and darkened. Add the sherry vinegar, stir to combine, and taste. The sauce should be bold, smoky, and hot — not just mildly spiced but genuinely brava (brave, ferocious). Blend until smooth with a stick blender or pass through a sieve. Keep warm.
Visual cue: A deep, mahogany-orange sauce with a glossy, slightly oily surface, thick enough to coat the back of a spoon heavily without running. The aroma should be intensely smoky-sweet with a background heat.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and still tastes of raw tomato — the moisture hasn't cooked off and the paprika hasn't integrated with the tomato. Continue cooking over medium heat, stirring occasionally. It needs to reduce by roughly half from where it started.
Perfect: Thick, glossy, deeply colored, and intensely flavored — smoky paprika dominant, with sweet tomato body and a vinegar brightness at the end. Remove from heat, blend smooth, and keep warm until the potatoes are fried.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced too far and is sticking to the pan, becoming grainy and bitter-smelling from scorched paprika. Add a splash of water or tomato juice to loosen and remove from heat. The burnt flavor is difficult to mask — better to strain and accept a thin sauce than to serve a scorched one.
Feel cue: Dip a finger and rub the sauce — it should feel silky and coat the skin evenly, not greasy or watery. The heat should arrive a second after the sweet smoke — first the paprika, then the burn climbing.

Heat the frying oil in a wide, heavy pan to 150C / 300F. Add the potato chunks in batches and fry for 4–5 minutes until they have a pale, set exterior but no color — this is the first fry, which drives out any remaining surface moisture and begins to build the interior structure. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel. Raise the oil temperature to 190C / 375F. Return the potatoes in smaller batches and fry for 3–4 minutes until they turn deep gold, with a craggy, puffed, irregular crust. Remove and drain immediately. Season with flakes of sea salt the moment they leave the oil while the surface is still wet with fat — the salt will stick. Do not pile the finished potatoes — they lose their crust in seconds against each other's steam.
Visual cue: Potatoes with a deeply golden, craggily irregular exterior — the surface should look almost blistered in places, with shaggy ridges from the roughing-up catching and crisping in the hot oil.
Underdone: Pale gold and soft — the exterior has not formed a proper crust and the potatoes feel hollow when pressed. They will go soggy quickly. Return to the hot oil for another 2 minutes. The oil must be genuinely hot (190C) for the crust to form.
Perfect: Deep gold with an irregular, craggy crust that sounds hollow when tapped and shatters under slight pressure. Interior is fluffy and steaming. Season immediately with salt and serve within minutes, sauced at the table.
Overdone: Dark brown or beginning to look oily, with a hard, thick crust that tastes bitter rather than toasty. The interior has dried out. Drain and season; cut one open to assess — if the interior is still fluffy and pale, only the exterior is overdone. The sauce will help.
Feel cue: Tap a finished potato with your fingernail — it should ring slightly hollow, like tapping a thin ceramic tile. That hollow ring is the sound of the crisp exterior and the
gap of steam it has made between crust and fluffy interior.

Arrange the fried potatoes in a shallow dish or cazuela in a single loose layer. Spoon the warm brava sauce generously over the top — not a thin drizzle but a proper coating, enough that every potato gets touched. The sauce should puddle slightly in the gaps between the potatoes. Serve immediately. Bravas should always arrive at the table hot — the window between perfect and soggy is narrow. If serving with aioli (traditional in some regions), drizzle it over the sauce in thin lines or zigzags. The dual-sauce version (bravas with both brava and aioli) is called bravas 'ali-oli' and is a common Madrid tapas bar offering.
Visual cue: Craggy golden potatoes half-submerged in deep red brava sauce, the sauce still glistening and pooling, steam rising from the potatoes underneath.
Underdone: Sauce applied too sparingly — potatoes are mostly bare and the brava impact is lost. The dish looks and tastes dry. Add more sauce. Bravas should be sauced generously enough that you scoop sauce with every potato piece.
Perfect: Every potato is coated in bold, spicy sauce; the crust is still audible when a potato is picked up; the heat of the sauce and the crunch arrive simultaneously. Eat immediately — this dish waits for no one.
Overdone: Potatoes sauced and left to sit for 10+ minutes — the crust has absorbed the sauce's moisture and gone soft and heavy. Nothing to recover here. For next service, keep potatoes and sauce separate and combine at the last moment.
Feel cue: Bite through a sauced potato — you should hear the crack of the crust a fraction of a second before the interior gives way and the heat of the sauce lands on your tongue. The crunch should survive the sauce. That's the whole point.

name: Pâte à Choux
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Whole eggs, lightly beaten, room temperature: 1 parts by weight of egg to flour
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 1 hr 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A paradox of a dough — cooked twice, enriched with eggs added one at a time, it bakes into hollow golden shells that are simultaneously crisp as a cracker on the outside and utterly empty within, waiting to be filled with crème pâtissière, ganache, or whipped cream. The oven transforms a gluey paste into architecture.

ingredients.name: Whole eggs, lightly beaten, room temperature

steps:
Combine the water, cubed butter, salt, and sugar in a medium heavy-bottomed saucepan. Place over medium heat and bring to a full, rolling boil. The objective here is to melt the butter completely before the water boils — if the water boils first and begins to evaporate before the butter is melted, the fat-to-water ratio of the dough is compromised and the choux will be unpredictable. Watch carefully: as the butter melts you will see the water turn from clear to a slightly milky white emulsion. As it approaches the boil, the emulsion will foam up. The moment it reaches a full boil, proceed immediately to the next step — every extra second of boiling evaporates water and changes the dough's consistency.
Visual cue: A vigorous, rolling boil with milky-white butter-water emulsion foaming up in the pan. All butter is melted and fully emulsified.
Underdone: Butter is not fully melted — you can see butter chunks still floating. The water has not yet boiled. Wait. Do not add flour until both boiling and full butter melt are achieved simultaneously.
Perfect: A full rolling boil — not a gentle simmer, but a vigorous, aggressive bubble across the entire surface. All butter is dissolved into the water. Add all the flour at once and stir immediately.
Overdone: The mixture has been boiling for more than 30 seconds. Steam and bubbling have reduced the water significantly. The liquid level is visibly lower. Proceed, but add 2 tablespoons of additional water to the panade during the drying step to compensate.
Feel cue: The pan should feel uncomfortably hot to hold bare-handed. The vigorous boil sounds like a rapid, insistent rattling — not a gentle murmur but a full, churning roar.

Remove the pan from the heat and add all the sifted flour in one go. Beat immediately and vigorously with a wooden spoon — this is urgent. The hot butter-water must hydrate every flour particle in the first few seconds, and the starch must gelatinise instantly in the residual heat. Beat until no dry flour remains, then return the pan to medium heat. Cook the panade (the dough ball), stirring and pressing constantly, for 2–3 minutes. You are driving off moisture — the panade is ready when it pulls away completely from the sides of the pan, forms a cohesive ball in the center, and leaves a thin, dry film on the bottom of the pan. This film is the sign that enough water has evaporated. The dough will be very stiff and non-sticky at this point.
Visual cue: A single, smooth, stiff dough ball sitting in the center of the pan, completely pulled away from the sides, with a dry white film on the pan bottom.
Underdone: The dough is still sticky and clinging to the sides of the pan. The bottom shows no dry film. The dough looks wet and shiny. Keep cooking and stirring over heat. The drying takes 2–3 minutes of active cooking — do not rush it.
Perfect: A stiff, smooth, unified ball. Completely releases from the sides. Clear dry film on the pan bottom. The dough feels like thick, stiff mashed potato. Transfer to the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment (or a large bowl for hand mixing) and cool for 5 minutes before adding eggs.
Overdone: The film on the bottom is getting dark or the dough is cracking on the surface. Overcooked. Remove from heat immediately. The choux may still work but will be drier — add eggs carefully to adjust consistency.
Feel cue: Press the back of the spoon into the dough — it should resist firmly and spring back very slightly. If it sticks to the spoon and strings away, it needs more drying. The dough should smell of warm, slightly nutty
cooked flour.

This is the most nuanced step in choux. Allow the panade to cool for 5 minutes (so it does not cook the eggs on contact), then begin adding the beaten eggs gradually — a tablespoon at a time for the first few additions, beating vigorously between each addition. The dough will at first look broken and curdled as the egg tries to separate from the fat in the panade. Keep beating — it will come back together. Do not add all the egg at once. The total egg needed varies with the exact water content of your panade, the protein content of your flour, and the ambient humidity. Stop adding egg when the dough reaches the correct consistency: when you lift the spatula and allow the dough to fall, it should drop in a slow, heavy 'V' shape that bends but does not break — the beak should be 2–3 cm long before it drops. Test by pulling the spatula through the dough: it should form a smooth channel that slowly closes.
Visual cue: Smooth, glossy, pipeable dough that hangs from the spatula in a slow V-shaped drip (2–3 cm beak) without snapping off. Glossy surface, not dull or matte.
Underdone: The dough is stiff and breaks off cleanly when lifted on the spatula. It does not flow. Too little egg added. Add more beaten egg, a tablespoon at a time, and beat well between additions.
Perfect: The dough is glossy and smooth. When a spatula is lifted slowly, it forms a long inverted V-shape (the 'beak') that holds for 2–3 seconds before dropping. The channel test shows slow closing. Transfer to a piping bag fitted with a 1.5 cm round or star tip and pipe immediately.
Overdone: The dough is runny and flows off the spatula in a liquid stream. It spreads flat when piped. Too much egg. Unfortunately this cannot be recovered by adding more panade — make a second small batch of panade and fold the runny dough into it to re-stiff it.
Feel cue: The dough should feel like a firm, heavy, warm batter
when you press it between your fingers — smooth and glossy, never gritty or grainy. It should peel cleanly off a spatula with a satisfying, slow resistance.

Pipe the choux onto parchment-lined baking sheets: for profiteroles, make 3 cm rounds spaced 4 cm apart; for éclairs, pipe 10 cm lines. Dampen your fingertip and smooth any peaks. Bake at 200°C (390°F) for 10 minutes without opening the oven — the initial blast of heat causes rapid steam expansion that puffs the shells. Then reduce to 180°C (356°F) and bake for a further 15–20 minutes until the shells are deep golden-brown all over, not just on top. The shells must be fully coloured before you open the oven: a pale shell will collapse when it meets the cool air. In the final 5 minutes, crack the oven door open 5 cm to allow steam to escape and the shells to dry completely inside. Transfer to a wire rack and pierce each shell with a skewer at the base to vent remaining steam.
Visual cue: Deep, even golden-brown shells that have puffed to 2–3 times their piped size, with no pale patches. They look like hollow domes or pillows.
Underdone: Pale golden shells with a matte, damp-looking surface. They feel soft when pressed and will deflate if removed from the oven now. Return to the oven for 5 more minutes. Do not open the oven early — the collapse from cool air is irreversible.
Perfect: Deep, even golden-brown all over, including on the sides. Shells feel hollow and light when picked up. Tapping the base produces a dry, hollow sound. Pierce with a skewer to vent steam and cool on a wire rack. Fill within 4 hours for maximum crispness.
Overdone: Very dark brown, almost mahogany. Shells may be cracked on the sides. Smell of toasted egg. They are still usable — trim any very dark spots. The flavour will be more nutty and caramelised, which many people prefer.
Feel cue: A perfectly baked choux shell weighs almost nothing — it should feel startlingly light for its size, as though the oven ate the inside and left only the crust. Squeeze gently: it should feel rigid, not
yielding.

name: Pâte Brisée (Shortcrust Tart Pastry)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=bakers_percentage）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Plain flour (all-purpose): 100 %
  Alternatives: half plain, half almond flour (for richer shell)
Cold unsalted butter, small cubes: 50 %
  Alternatives: cold lard (flakier, less buttery)
Fine salt: 0.5 %
Ice-cold water: 15 %
Egg yolk: 5 %
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 1 hour 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A tender, crumbly French shortcrust — barely any water, cold butter rubbed to sand — that bakes to a pale, biscuity shell with enough structure to hold the wettest custard without turning to paste.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Place the flour and salt in a large bowl (or food processor). Add the cold butter cubes. Rub the butter into the flour with your fingertips, lifting and dropping the mixture from a height to aerate it, until the mixture resembles coarse, damp sand with no individual butter pieces larger than a pea. Work quickly — if your hands are warm, press the bowl against a cold surface. Alternatively, pulse in a food processor 8–10 times.
Visual cue: A pale, dry, coarse-sand texture with no visible butter lumps — but not yet a fine powder. Some larger pea-sized clumps are acceptable.
Underdone: Large, identifiable butter pieces still visible among the flour. The mixture looks floury with butter lumps. Continue rubbing, focusing on breaking down each butter cube individually.
Perfect: The mixture resembles damp breadcrumbs or coarse sand. Butter is distributed but not invisible. Lifts and falls freely. Make a well in the centre and add the egg yolk and water.
Overdone: The mixture looks uniform and pale — butter has melted into the flour. Feels greasy and warm. Refrigerate the entire mixture for 15 minutes before adding water. The pastry will be less crumbly but can still be used.
Feel cue: Work with cold hands and a light touch — the mixture should feel cool and dry, flowing between your fingers like wet sand, with very faint oiliness from the butter coating the flour particles.

Beat together the egg yolk and ice-cold water in a small bowl. Make a well in the flour-butter mixture and pour in the egg-water. Using a fork or a pastry cutter, bring the dough together with minimal mixing — use a chopping and stirring motion, not kneading. The dough will look shaggy and barely coherent. As soon as it comes together when you squeeze a handful in your fist, stop. Turn out onto a lightly floured surface and press together into a flat disc. Do not knead.
Visual cue: A rough, shaggy disc that barely holds together when pressed — not a smooth ball. There should still be visible texture on the surface.
Underdone: Mixture is still very crumbly and will not hold together even when squeezed. Dry and powdery. Add ice-cold water, one teaspoon at a time, mixing with the fork.
Perfect: Shaggy and rough-surfaced but cohesive when pressed firmly. No wet, sticky patches. Holds its shape as a disc. Wrap and refrigerate for at least 45 minutes.
Overdone: Dough has been over-worked and is smooth like bread dough. It may look elastic. Refrigerate for 1 hour. The gluten needs to relax or the pastry will shrink dramatically in the tin.
Feel cue: The dough should feel almost crumbly in your hands — press a piece firmly and it holds, but it has no give or elasticity. It is cool, slightly rough-textured, and holds its shape without sticking to your palms.

Wrap the disc tightly in cling film and refrigerate for at least 45 minutes, or up to 3 days. This rest allows the gluten to relax (so it does not shrink when baked) and the butter to firm up again (so it stays in distinct layers). Remove from the fridge 5–10 minutes before rolling if very hard.
Visual cue: A firm, cold disc of dough that holds its shape when pressed and shows no sign of the butter melting or the dough warming.
Underdone: Dough is still pliable and slightly warm from handling. Rolling now will cause shrinkage. Refrigerate for the full 45 minutes minimum.
Perfect: Firm, cold, and slightly resistant to pressing. The butter is re-solidified throughout. Roll out on a lightly floured surface to 3–4 mm thickness.
Overdone: The dough is very hard and cracks at the edges when pressed — it has been refrigerated too long or is too cold. Allow to soften at room temperature for 5-10 minutes before rolling.
Feel cue: A properly rested pâte brisée feels like cold plasticine — firm but manageable, with no stickiness and no elasticity fighting back when you press it.

Roll the rested dough on a lightly floured surface to 3–4 mm thickness. Line a 23 cm tart tin, pressing gently into the corners. Trim the edge and prick the base lightly with a fork. Freeze for 15 minutes. Line with parchment and fill with baking beans or rice. Blind bake at 180 C for 15–18 minutes, remove beans, brush the base with a little beaten egg, and return for 5–8 minutes until the base is dry and golden. The egg wash seals the pastry against wet fillings.
Visual cue: A dry, evenly pale-gold shell that releases cleanly from the tin and shows no grey wet patches. The base is firm and sounds hollow when tapped.
Underdone: The base remains pale and soft — grey or translucent in colour. Flexes when pressed. Return to the oven without the beans until fully dried. A wet base ruins the tart.
Perfect: Pale gold, dry, firm. The sides are lightly coloured. A hollow tap on the base. Egg-washed base has a faint sheen. Fill with desired filling and finish baking, or allow to cool and fill with a no-bake filling.
Overdone: Edges and base are deeply golden, approaching biscuit-brown. The pastry smells nutty. Still excellent. A slightly darker shell adds flavour that complements most fillings.
Feel cue: Lift the shell — it should feel crisp and rigid, with no soft flex at the base. The sides and base should be uniform in colour and temperature, not pale and cold in the centre.

name: Patina de Piris
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Ripe pears (peeled, cored, soft-fleshed): 100 parts
  Alternatives: quince (longer cook); apples
Honey (Roman would use defrutum-sweetened): 18 parts
  Alternatives: passum (raisin wine); grape must syrup
Eggs (lightly beaten): 35 parts
  Alternatives: extra yolks for a richer set
Black pepper (freshly cracked): 1 parts
  Alternatives: long pepper (more authentic)
Garum / liquamen (fish sauce, a few drops): 1 parts
  Alternatives: colatura di alici; a pinch of salt
Ground cumin (a small pinch): 1 parts
  Alternatives: caraway
Olive oil (to oil the dish): 3 parts
  Alternatives: butter (anachronistic but works)
Black pepper (to finish, optional): 1 parts
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 1 hr 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A pear custard from the kitchens of imperial Rome, transcribed in Apicius — orchard pears pounded smooth with honey and a startling lick of black pepper, bound with eggs and a splash of fish sauce, then baked into a trembling, savoury-sweet flan that sets like a soufflé and slumps softly under the spoon.

ingredients.name: Garum / liquamen (fish sauce, a few drops)
橄榄油（Olive oil (to oil the dish)）

steps:
Peel and core the pears and cut them into rough chunks. Simmer them gently with the honey and a splash of water in a covered pan until completely tender and translucent, 12-15 minutes. The honey draws out their juice and seasons the flesh from within. Drain off most of the loose liquid so the finished custard will set.
Visual cue: Pear chunks are glassy and yielding, slumping when nudged, swimming in a thin amber syrup smelling of warm honey and orchard fruit.
Underdone: Pears are still firm and opaque white at the centre, the syrup thin and watery. Cover and keep simmering — hard fruit will leave fibrous threads in the custard.
Perfect: Flesh is translucent and soft enough to crush against the pan with a spoon; syrup is fragrant and lightly thickened. Drain off excess liquid and pound the fruit smooth.
Overdone: Pears are collapsing into mush and the syrup is darkening and caramelising at the edges. Pull off the heat at once and proceed; a little caramelisation is fine, scorching is not.
Feel cue: A spoon should sink through the fruit with almost no resistance, and the kitchen smells of honey and ripe pear with no green, raw edge.

Tip the drained pears into a mortar (or food processor) and pound to a smooth purée. Crack the pepper and grind the cumin fresh, then work them through the warm fruit. Apicius is emphatic about pepper here — it should be present, a gentle prickle that lifts the sweetness rather than a sting. Let the purée cool to just warm before adding the eggs.
Visual cue: A smooth, pale-gold purée flecked with black pepper, loose enough to fall from the spoon in a ribbon, warm but no longer hot.
Underdone: Purée is lumpy with stringy pieces of fruit, and the pepper sits in one corner unmixed. Keep pounding and stirring until uniform — lumps will scramble or weep in the bake.
Perfect: Silky, evenly speckled purée that ribbons off the spoon; pepper aroma rises warmly from the bowl. Cool slightly, then beat in the eggs and garum.
Overdone: Purée has been pounded so long it has gone gluey, or is still hot enough to cook the eggs on contact. Stop working it and let it cool; whisk in a spoon of the reserved syrup to loosen if needed.
Feel cue: Rub a little between your fingers — it should feel smooth and creamy, not grainy, and feel warm rather than hot so the eggs will not seize.

Beat the eggs until smooth and stir them steadily into the warm pear purée so they thicken it without scrambling. Add just a few drops of garum — enough to deepen and round the flavour, not to taste of fish. Taste: it should read sweet first, then savoury, with a peppery warmth underneath. Whisk to a loose, pourable batter.
Visual cue: A glossy, homogeneous custard base the colour of pale caramel, pourable and faintly foamy on top, smelling sweet with a savoury undertone.
Underdone: Egg streaks of clear and yellow remain visible; the batter looks separated rather than unified. Keep whisking until no streaks remain — uneven egg sets unevenly in the oven.
Perfect: Fully emulsified, smooth and pourable, balanced on the tongue between honeyed pear and savoury depth. Pour into the oiled dish and bake.
Overdone: Tiny cooked-egg flecks have formed because the purée was too hot, giving a curdled texture. Pass the batter through a sieve to catch the flecks before baking.
Feel cue: Drag a spoon through it — it should flow back together smoothly with no graininess, and the smell of fish from the garum should be undetectable, present only as savoury roundness.

Brush a shallow baking dish with olive oil and pour in the batter. Bake at 170°C / 340°F until the patina is just set with the faintest wobble at the centre, 30-35 minutes (a water bath gives the silkiest set). Crack a little more pepper over the top. Cool until barely warm — it firms as it rests — and serve in soft spoonfuls.
Visual cue: The surface is set and lightly puffed with a pale-gold skin; a gentle shake sends a soft wobble through the centre, and a knife slid into the edge comes out clean.
Underdone: The whole custard sloshes loosely when shaken and a tester comes out wet and milky. Return to the oven in 5-minute checks until only the very centre trembles.
Perfect: Edges are set and just blushing gold, the centre quivers softly like a panna cotta, the smell is sweet and peppery. Remove, finish with pepper, and let it cool until barely warm before serving.
Overdone: The custard has puffed high, cracked across the top and is weeping liquid — the eggs have overcooked and curdled. Take it out immediately; it will be firmer and slightly grainy but still good served cool with extra honey.
Feel cue: Nudge the dish — the right patina answers with a single soft jiggle at its heart while the rim stays still. It should smell of warm honey and pepper, never of sulphur or overcooked egg.

name: Pavlova
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Egg whites (room temperature, no trace of yolk): 6 large
Caster sugar (superfine): 300 g
Cornstarch: 2 tsp
  Alternatives: arrowroot
White wine vinegar or lemon juice: 1 tsp
  Alternatives: cream of tartar (1/4 tsp)

Heavy whipping cream (cold): 400 ml
Vanilla extract (for cream): 0.5 tsp

Active time: 25 min
Total time: 4 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A crisp, snowy meringue shell giving way to a marshmallow-soft interior, topped with billowing cream and vivid fresh fruit — the balance of crunch, yielding sweetness, and tart fruit is the whole art of this continent-defining dessert.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
