ingredients.name: 蛋清（Egg whites (room temperature, no trace of yolk)）
White wine vinegar or lemon juice

steps:
Ensure the mixing bowl, whisk, and all utensils are completely clean, dry, and free of any trace of fat — even a drop of egg yolk or a smear of butter will prevent the whites from whipping. Wipe everything with a cut lemon half and dry thoroughly. Beat the room-temperature egg whites on medium speed until they form soft peaks that droop at the tip when the whisk is lifted. Begin adding the caster sugar one tablespoon at a time — this slow addition is non-negotiable. After each addition, beat for 30 seconds before adding more. The process takes 10–12 minutes total, and the patience is what creates a stable, dense meringue rather than a brittle shell.
Visual cue: A stiff, brilliantly white, glossy meringue that holds sharp, upright peaks with no droop whatsoever. When the bowl is inverted, the meringue does not move. The surface looks like shaving cream — satiny, not dull.
Underdone: Soft, glossy peaks that curve over at the tip. The meringue slides when the bowl is tilted. Sugar is still partially undissolved — the meringue feels grainy when rubbed between fingers. Continue beating, adding no more sugar. Test by rubbing a small amount between index finger and thumb — beat until no grittiness remains.
Perfect: Stiff peaks stand bolt upright. When rubbed between fingers: silky-smooth, no grit. When the bowl is inverted: the meringue sits still. Brilliant white and satiny. It takes some force to pull the whisk free. Fold in the cornstarch, vinegar, and vanilla, then shape.
Overdone: The meringue looks dry, lumpy, and curdled — like cottage cheese. It does not flow when the bowl is tilted but breaks apart in chunks. The proteins have been over-beaten and the foam has collapsed. This cannot be recovered. Start again with clean equipment and fresh egg whites.
Feel cue: Pinch the meringue between thumb and forefinger and pull away slowly — it should form a firm, clean peak
that stands on its own without slumping, like stiff whipped butter.

Sprinkle the cornstarch and vanilla extract over the meringue and pour in the vinegar. Fold with a large metal spoon or rubber spatula using exactly three or four large, sweeping motions from the bottom of the bowl up and over the top. Do not stir or beat. This technique is intentionally under-mixed — a few unincorporated streaks are perfectly fine. The cornstarch and vinegar work together with the egg proteins to create the marshmallow interior: the starch gelatinizes and the acid keeps the proteins tender, preventing the meringue from setting entirely solid.
Visual cue: The meringue with a few faint streaks of cornstarch visible but mostly incorporated. The texture is unchanged from before folding — still stiff and glossy, not deflated.
Underdone: Large white clumps of dry cornstarch still visible and vinegar visibly pooled in the bowl. The meringue looks marbled. One or two more gentle folds — just enough to incorporate the dry spots and pooled vinegar.
Perfect: Meringue is still stiff and glossy. The cornstarch and vinegar are mostly incorporated with perhaps a faint streak or two remaining. The meringue holds its shape when a spoon is dragged through it. Spoon immediately onto the prepared baking sheet.
Overdone: The meringue has deflated from over-folding. It looks softer and less voluminous. Peaks no longer hold shape. Shape and bake quickly — deflated meringue will spread more and may crack, but will still taste good.
Feel cue: Lift a large spoonful — the meringue should hold its shape on the spoon for several seconds before slowly sinking, dense and pillowy like a cloud made solid.

Draw a 22cm circle on a sheet of parchment paper (trace a dinner plate), flip the parchment so the pencil is face-down, and place on a baking sheet. Spoon the meringue onto the circle in a mounded pile. Using the back of a spoon, shape it into a disc with slightly raised sides and a shallow indent in the center — the well is where the cream and fruit will pool. Bake at 140°C (285°F) for 1 hour and 15 minutes. Turn the oven off completely and leave the pavlova inside with the door closed for at least 2 hours — overnight is ideal. Do not open the oven during this time.
Visual cue: After the oven rest: an ivory-white meringue shell that has dried to a crisp, slightly chalky exterior. The surface may have fine cracks — this is traditional and beautiful. The base is dry and sounds hollow when tapped.
Underdone: The meringue is still soft and sticky to the touch. The exterior has not set to a crisp shell. It will stick to the parchment and collapse when moved. Close the oven and leave for another hour. The resting time is as important as the baking time — never rush this stage.
Perfect: The exterior is bone-dry, crisp, and ivory-white. Fine cracks may appear on the surface — this is characteristic, not a failure. The pavlova lifts cleanly from the parchment. The interior, when the well is probed with a spoon, is soft and marshmallow-like. Leave at room temperature until ready to top. Do not refrigerate.
Overdone: The pavlova has taken on a yellow or brown tinge and the exterior is very hard throughout with no marshmallow interior remaining. The oven was too hot or the bake too long. Top and serve anyway — the flavor is still meringue, just without the yielding interior contrast.
Feel cue: Tap the surface with a fingernail — you should hear a crisp, dry click, and the exterior should yield slightly under pressure but not sink in, like tapping on a hollow eggshell.

Just before serving — not hours ahead — beat the cold heavy whipping cream and vanilla extract in a chilled bowl until the cream reaches medium-firm peaks. The cream should hold its shape when the bowl is tilted but still have a slight jiggle at the top of the peaks. Stop before the cream becomes stiff or grainy. The target is a cream that billows generously rather than standing in rigid blocks — it will settle slightly on the meringue, which is the correct look.
Visual cue: Soft, billowing, ivory-white cream with peaks that curl gently at the tip. When spooned onto the pavlova it settles into gentle mounds rather than rigid peaks.
Underdone: Cream still pourable and does not hold peaks. It will slide off the meringue and pool around the base. Continue beating for 30-second intervals until medium peaks form — peaks that hold when the whisk is held upright but curl at the tip.
Perfect: Cream holds a soft, curved peak that just droops slightly at the tip. Billowy and voluminous. Pure white with a satiny sheen. Spoon immediately onto the pavlova and top with fruit.
Overdone: Cream is stiff, grainy, and beginning to look yellow. It has started to turn into butter. Fold in 2 tablespoons of fresh cold cream to soften. Use quickly.
Feel cue: Run a spoon through the cream — it should leave a clean, smooth track that gradually softens at the edges, like drawing through very cold clotted cream.

Transfer the cooled pavlova shell to a serving plate. Pile the whipped cream into the center well in generous, billowing mounds, allowing it to spread naturally toward the raised edges without spilling over. Arrange the strawberry halves and kiwi slices first, then scatter the blueberries and finally spoon the passionfruit pulp over everything — the golden, seedy pulp running down over the cream and fruit is the signature finish. Serve immediately or within 30 minutes — the pavlova softens quickly once topped.
Visual cue: A stunning arrangement: snow-white meringue shell, cloud of cream, and a cascade of bright fruit — red, green, blue, and gold passionfruit — creating a vivid contrast of textures and colors.
Underdone: Cream has been applied too sparingly and the fruit sits directly on the meringue. The visual layers of cream between shell and fruit are lost. Add more cream generously — pavlova should be abundant, not restrained.
Perfect: The meringue shell is visible around the edge, the cream billows generously in the center, and the fruit is piled with abandon on top. The passionfruit pulp runs in golden rivulets over everything. Serve within 30 minutes. Bring to the table immediately.
Overdone: The pavlova was topped hours ahead and has sat in the refrigerator. The meringue has absorbed moisture from the cream and fruit and the crisp shell has become soft and chewy throughout. It still tastes good but loses the textural contrast. Serve remaining portions immediately and do not refrigerate once topped.
Feel cue: The first spoon through a perfect pavlova gives you three resistances in sequence: the light crunch of the shell, the yielding softness of the marshmallow interior, and the cool slip of cream.

  Alternatives: nectarines; yellow peaches

Vanilla bean (split & scraped): 1 parts
  Alternatives: 1 tsp vanilla paste
Lemon (juice & a peel strip): 4 parts
Fresh raspberries (for the melba sauce): 50 parts
  Alternatives: frozen raspberries, thawed
Icing sugar (for the sauce, to taste): 12 parts
  Alternatives: caster sugar
Best vanilla ice cream: 80 parts
  Alternatives: vanilla gelato
Toasted flaked almonds: 6 parts
  Alternatives: slivered almonds
Active time: 40 min
Total time: 2 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Escoffier's tribute to a soprano — ripe peaches poached whole in vanilla syrup until they slip from their skins, set over a quenelle of cold vanilla ice cream, and veiled in a raw raspberry melba sauce that bleeds crimson down the sides of the coupe.

ingredients.name: Icing sugar (for the sauce, to taste)

steps:
Combine the water and caster sugar in a saucepan just wide enough to hold the peaches snugly. Scrape in the vanilla seeds and drop in the pod, add the strip of lemon peel and a squeeze of the juice, and warm over medium heat, stirring, until the sugar fully dissolves. Bring to a gentle simmer so the syrup is clear and fragrant before the fruit goes in.
Visual cue: A clear, pale syrup flecked with vanilla seeds, steaming gently with tiny bubbles rising at the edge — no undissolved grains on the spoon.
Underdone: Syrup is cloudy and you can feel sugar crystals grinding when you stir; it has not yet steamed. Keep stirring over the heat until every grain dissolves and the liquid turns glassy and clear.
Perfect: Crystal-clear syrup, faint vanilla perfume rising with the steam, a lazy simmer breaking at the surface. Lower the heat and slide in the peaches to poach.
Overdone: Syrup is reducing hard and starting to thicken or colour at the edges before any fruit is added. Add a splash of water to bring it back to a thin poaching consistency and turn the heat down.
Feel cue: Dip the spoon and feel for grit — when it drags smoothly with no sandy resistance, the sugar is gone and the syrup is ready.

Lower the whole peaches into the barely-simmering syrup, cover with a round of parchment to keep them submerged, and poach gently for 12-18 minutes depending on ripeness, turning once. They are done when a paring knife slides into the flesh with no resistance. Lift them out, and once cool enough to handle, slip off the skins — they should peel away in sheets. Halve and stone them, then chill the peaches in their syrup.
Visual cue: Tender peaches whose skins pucker and split, with a knife tip sinking to the stone like into soft butter and no firm core remaining.
Underdone: Skins still cling tightly and a knife meets a crunchy, resistant core near the centre. Return them to the syrup and poach a few minutes more, testing again at the thickest point.
Perfect: Skins loosen and slip off cleanly, flesh is silky and translucent at the edge, a knife glides to the stone unobstructed. Lift out, peel, halve and stone, then chill the peaches submerged in their syrup.
Overdone: Peaches are collapsing, mushy and breaking apart as you lift them, the flesh waterlogged and shapeless. Remove at once and handle gently; serve the softest ones broken into the coupe rather than as neat halves.
Feel cue: Keep the syrup at a whisper of a simmer, never a boil — a hard boil bruises the fruit. The peach should feel like it surrenders to the knife rather than fighting it.

Blitz the raspberries with the icing sugar and a few drops of lemon juice to a smooth purée — no cooking, to keep the colour vivid and the flavour fresh. Pass it through a fine sieve, pressing hard to extract every drop and leaving the seeds behind. Taste and adjust the sugar so the sauce is sweet but still bright with acidity. Chill until cold.
Visual cue: A glossy, intensely crimson sauce, smooth and seedless, thick enough to coat a spoon yet still pourable in a ribbon.
Underdone: Sauce tastes sharp and thin, or is still flecked with seeds and pale pulp that wasn't pressed through. Sieve again more firmly and whisk in a little more icing sugar until it rounds out without losing its tang.
Perfect: Deep ruby, silky and seedless, balanced between sweet and tart, falling from the spoon in a glossy ribbon. Chill the sauce until you are ready to plate.
Overdone: Sauce is cloyingly sweet and dull, the fresh raspberry brightness flattened by too much sugar. Sharpen it with a few more drops of lemon juice or a handful of crushed fresh berries to revive the acidity.
Feel cue: Press the purée through the sieve until only dry seeds remain — the back of the spoon should come away clean. The finished sauce smells purely of fresh raspberry, never cooked or jammy.

Chill your coupes or shallow glasses. Set a generous scoop of cold vanilla ice cream in the base of each, arrange two peach halves cut-side down over the top, then spoon the cold melba sauce over the fruit so it bleeds down over the ice cream. Scatter with toasted flaked almonds and serve at once, before the ice cream begins to soften.
Visual cue: A glossy crimson sauce streaming down rounded golden peach halves onto a firm white quenelle of ice cream, finished with a crackle of toasted almonds.
Underdone: Ice cream is rock-hard and frosted, the peaches still warm from the syrup melting it into a puddle, sauce sliding off too thin. Let the ice cream temper a minute for a clean scoop and make sure the peaches are fully chilled before plating.
Perfect: Cold, scoopable ice cream holding its shape, cool glossy peaches, ribbons of ruby sauce pooling at the base, almonds crisp on top. Serve immediately while everything is cold and the contrast is sharpest.
Overdone: Ice cream has melted into soup and the whole coupe is a slumped pink pool with the peaches sinking in. Plate over a fresh scoop and work quickly; keep assembled coupes in the freezer for only a moment before serving.
Feel cue: Everything should meet cold — the spoon hits firm ice cream, yielding peach, and cool sauce in one stroke. Serve the instant it's built, while the sauce still streams and the almonds still crunch.

name: Peanut Sauce
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Raw skinless peanuts: 100 parts
  Alternatives: unsalted dry-roasted peanuts (skip the roasting step)
Thai red curry paste (krueng gaeng phed): 35 parts
  Alternatives: Massaman curry paste for a milder, warmer note; homemade pounded paste
Coconut cream (thick, top of the can): 120 parts
  Alternatives: full-fat coconut milk reduced harder to split
Coconut milk (or water): 80 parts
  Alternatives: unsalted chicken or vegetable stock; plain water
Tamarind paste (seedless, sour): 25 parts
  Alternatives: fresh lime juice added off the heat
Palm sugar (shaved): 30 parts
  Alternatives: light brown sugar

Toasted peanuts, roughly chopped: 12 parts

Active time: 30 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Nam jim satay, the way it should be — dry-roasted peanuts pounded coarse, simmered with cracked red curry paste in split coconut cream until the oil rises red and slick, then balanced sharp-sweet-salty with tamarind, palm sugar, and fish sauce into a glossy, nutty dip that clings to charred skewers.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Thai red curry paste (krueng gaeng phed)
椰浆（Coconut cream (thick, top of the can)）

steps:
Dry-roast the raw peanuts in a heavy pan over medium-low heat, shaking constantly, 8 to 12 minutes, until golden and fragrant with dark freckling. Let them cool completely — they crisp as they cool. Pound in a granite mortar (or pulse in a processor) to a coarse rubble: about two-thirds gritty meal and one-third pea-sized pieces. You want texture, not peanut butter; over-grinding releases oil and turns the sauce pasty and flat.
Visual cue: Peanuts are evenly honey-gold with scattered toasty-brown spots, smelling deeply nutty and almost popcorn-sweet, and the pounded result is a coarse two-tone rubble of meal and crunchy bits.
Underdone: Peanuts are still pale and taste raw and beany, with no roasted aroma. Pounded, they smell green. Keep roasting and stirring over low heat — color and aroma develop slowly. Raw peanut flavor will dull the whole sauce.
Perfect: Golden with brown freckles, snapping crisp when bitten, smelling like roasted nuts. The pound yields gritty meal studded with crunchy fragments. Set aside. Reserve a small handful coarsely chopped for the final garnish.
Overdone: Peanuts are scorched dark brown to black and smell acrid and bitter; pounded, they weep oil into a sludge. Discard burnt nuts — bitterness carries straight through the sauce. If only the pound went oily, stir in a spoon of the dry meal to bring back texture.
Feel cue: A properly roasted peanut snaps cleanly between the teeth, never bends. Under the pestle it should crack and crumble dry, not smear; the moment it starts to slick the mortar with oil, stop.

Put the thick coconut cream alone in a wide pan over medium heat and let it bubble and reduce, stirring, 4 to 6 minutes, until it 'cracks' — the cream splits and a slick of clear oil pools at the edges. Stir in the red curry paste and fry it in that coconut oil, pressing and turning, 3 to 5 minutes, until the raw garlic-and-galangal smell cooks off and the oil glows red and aromatic. This frying of the paste (pad prik gaeng) is what builds depth; skip it and the sauce tastes flat and dusty.
Visual cue: A thick, brick-red paste sizzling in a visible pool of glossy orange-red oil that has separated from the solids, smelling fragrant and toasty with no harsh raw-spice edge.
Underdone: The coconut is still soupy and white and hasn't split; the paste sits in liquid and smells sharply raw. Keep cooking over medium heat and be patient — the cream must reduce and crack before the paste can fry. Lower the heat if it threatens to scorch.
Perfect: Glossy red oil has separated and the paste is thick, darkened, and intensely aromatic, sizzling rather than boiling. Proceed immediately to add the peanuts and liquid before the paste catches.
Overdone: The paste is dry, dark, and sticking, with a burnt, bitter smell starting to rise from the pan. Pull off the heat at once and add the coconut milk to stop the cooking. If it tastes scorched, start the paste again — burn doesn't wash out.
Feel cue: Listen for the change from a wet rolling boil to a sharp, oily sizzle — that crackle is the cream splitting. The paste should leave a clean trail when you drag the spoon, and the kitchen should smell of toasted chili and galangal, not acrid smoke.

Stir the pounded peanuts into the fried paste so every grain is coated in the red oil, then pour in the coconut milk (or water). Bring to a gentle simmer and cook 8 to 12 minutes, stirring often as the peanuts drink the liquid and thicken the sauce. It will go from loose to luxuriously thick; thin with a splash more coconut milk or water whenever it gets too tight to fall off the spoon. The peanut starch and oil now carry the chili heat and give the sauce its body.
Visual cue: A thick, terracotta-colored sauce, slightly grainy from the peanuts, with beads of red oil glistening on the surface and a slow, lava-like blup as it simmers.
Underdone: The sauce is thin and watery, the peanuts loose and the flavors not yet melded; it tastes of separate parts. Keep simmering to let the peanuts swell and thicken and the flavors marry. Resist over-thinning early.
Perfect: Thick enough to coat the spoon and mound softly, glossy with surfaced oil, the peanut and chili flavors now reading as one. Move to the final seasoning — tamarind, palm sugar, and fish sauce.
Overdone: The sauce is stiff and claggy, almost a paste, threatening to catch on the pan bottom. Loosen with coconut milk or warm water a splash at a time, stirring, until it flows again. Lower the heat to stop it sticking.
Feel cue: Drag the spoon across the pan — when it leaves a slow-closing channel that shows the base for a beat, the body is right. It should feel velvety with a pleasant peanut grit, never gluey.

Off a vigorous simmer, stir in the tamarind, palm sugar, and fish sauce. Let it melt together for a minute, then taste and tune: it should hit sweet first, then salty and sour close behind, with the chili heat blooming at the back. Adjust in small amounts — palm sugar to round, tamarind to brighten, fish sauce to deepen — until no single note dominates. Loosen to a thick-but-pourable dipping consistency. Spoon into a bowl, scatter the reserved chopped peanuts over the top, and serve warm with grilled satay.
Visual cue: A glossy, deep russet-brown sauce that ribbons thickly off the spoon and slowly settles flat, an oil sheen on top and a crown of chopped peanuts catching the light.
Underdone: The sauce tastes flat or one-dimensional — overly nutty, or sharp from raw fish sauce, with the sweet-sour balance not yet locked in. Add palm sugar and tamarind in small increments, tasting between each. Sweet and sour together are what make it sing; under-seasoned satay sauce tastes muddy.
Perfect: Balanced and rounded — sweet, salty, and sour layered over deep roasted peanut and chili, thick enough to cling to a skewer without sliding off. Garnish with chopped peanuts and serve warm. It thickens as it cools, so leave it a touch loose.
Overdone: The sauce is cloyingly sweet or aggressively salty, or so thick it sits in a stiff clump. Pull it back with a squeeze of lime or a little tamarind for sweetness, water for salt, and loosen with coconut milk. Re-taste until balanced.
Feel cue: A correct satay sauce coats the back of a spoon and drips slowly, with that characteristic grainy-silky peanut texture. On the tongue the sweetness should arrive first and the heat last; if it tastes flat, it usually wants tamarind and salt, not more sugar.

name: Pear Ginger Crisp

description: Juicy pears baked down into a honeyed, gently spiced filling with a double hit of ginger — warm fresh root and chewy candied bits — under a buttery, crunchy oat topping.

ingredients.name: Pears, ripe but firm, peeled, cored, cut into 2 cm chunks
Fresh ginger, peeled and finely grated
Unsalted butter, cold, cut into 1 cm cubes

steps:
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) with a rack in the middle. In a large bowl, toss the pears with the lemon juice, 50 g brown sugar, cornstarch, fresh ginger, and crystallized ginger until the cornstarch disappears. Spread evenly in a 9 × 9 in (23 × 23 cm) or 2 qt (2 l) baking dish.
Visual cue: Pear chunks evenly glossed with no white patches of cornstarch.
Underdone: Dry white streaks of cornstarch cling to the fruit. Toss again; the pear juice will dissolve it within a minute or two.
Perfect: Glossy, lightly syrupy fruit with specks of ginger throughout, spread in an even layer. Make the topping.
Overdone: Sat for over an hour — a pool of thin juice has collected at the bottom. Pour off half the juice; the filling will still set.
Feel cue: A pear chunk should resist a knife slightly — ripe enough to smell sweet but firm enough to hold its shape.

Stir the flour, oats, 100 g brown sugar, cinnamon, and salt together in a bowl. Add the cold butter cubes and rub them in with your fingertips (or a pastry cutter) until the butter is in pea-sized pieces and the mixture holds together in clumps when squeezed, 3–4 minutes. Chill 10 minutes if the butter feels soft.
Visual cue: Moist, irregular clumps from pea- to hazelnut-sized, with little loose flour left.
Underdone: Mostly loose, dry flour and oats with large butter chunks. Keep rubbing in the butter.
Perfect: Clumpy and sandy, holds together when pinched, with small visible bits of butter. Scatter over the fruit.
Overdone: Butter has warmed and the topping has become one greasy mass. Chill 15 minutes, then break it into clumps by hand.
Feel cue: A pinch squeezed in your fist should hold together like damp sand and crumble when you poke it.

Scatter the topping evenly over the pears, leaving it in clumps rather than pressing it down. Set the dish on a foil-lined sheet pan to catch drips. Bake 45–55 minutes, until the topping is deep golden brown and the filling is bubbling thickly at the edges — a knife should slide into the pears with no resistance. Tent with foil if the topping browns before the filling bubbles.
Visual cue: Golden-brown crunchy topping with thick, glossy juice bubbling up around the edges.
Underdone: Topping is pale and the juices are thin and cloudy, or not bubbling. Keep baking 10 minutes and check again — the cornstarch only thickens once it boils.
Perfect: Deep golden topping; juices bubble slowly and look glossy and syrupy at the edges; pears are tender. Remove and rest.
Overdone: Topping edges are dark brown to black, and juices have caramelized hard on the rim. Scrape off any scorched bits; the filling will still be good.
Feel cue: The bubbles at the edge should be slow and thick, popping lazily like simmering jam.

Cool on a rack for at least 20 minutes so the juices thicken as they cool. Serve warm with vanilla ice cream or lightly sweetened whipped cream.
Visual cue: A spoonful that holds together, with thick juices, not a watery pool.
Underdone: Served straight from the oven, and the juices run thin across the plate. Let the rest of the dish sit a little longer.
Perfect: Warm, with juices that are thick and glossy and a topping that stays crisp. Serve.
Overdone: Covered in the fridge overnight, and the topping has softened. Reheat uncovered at 350°F (175°C) for 15 minutes to re-crisp.
Feel cue: The dish should feel warm but comfortable to hold with bare hands at the edges.

name: Pecan Pie Filling
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Dark corn syrup: 4 parts
  Alternatives: golden syrup (less sweet, more complex)
Dark brown sugar, packed: 2 parts
  Alternatives: light brown sugar (less molasses depth)
Large eggs, room temperature: 3 parts
Unsalted butter, melted and cooled: 1 parts
  Alternatives: browned butter for nuttier depth
Pecan halves: 5 parts
  Alternatives: walnuts (more bitter, less rich)
Fine kosher salt: 0.1 parts
Pure vanilla extract: 0.2 parts
  Alternatives: bourbon (same quantity, more adult flavor)
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 75 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A deep amber, caramel-scented custard bound with corn syrup and whole eggs, poured over toasted pecans that rise to the surface and lacquer to a glossy, crackle-topped crown.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Spread the pecan halves on a dry sheet pan in a single layer. Roast at 175 C (350 F) for 8–10 minutes, stirring once halfway through. You are not just toasting for color — you are driving off moisture so the nuts stay crisp through a long bake inside a wet custard.
Visual cue: Pecans are uniformly one shade deeper — a warm, reddish-brown rather than the pale tan they started as. The kitchen smells of warm butter and caramel.
Underdone: Nuts are still pale and smell raw and green. No color change on the flat faces. Return to the oven for 3 more minutes. Watch closely — they go from underdone to overdone quickly.
Perfect: Deeply fragrant, mahogany-tinged, and oily on the surface. A broken half reveals a consistently toasted interior, not just a toasted skin. Remove and cool completely on the pan before using.
Overdone: Nuts are dark brown to black at the edges. The smell is bitter and acrid rather than caramel-sweet. Discard and start again — burnt pecans will ruin the finished pie with persistent bitterness.
Feel cue: A perfectly toasted pecan snaps cleanly when broken and feels dry between the fingers — no waxy raw fat. Rub one between your palms; the released oil should smell immediately of caramel, not raw nut.

In a large bowl, whisk together the dark corn syrup, brown sugar, melted (not hot) butter, salt, and vanilla until the sugar has partially dissolved and the mixture is uniform in color. The butter must be cooled to below 50 C or it will begin to cook the eggs when they are added. Rub a drop between your fingers — you should not feel undissolved sugar crystals, though some is acceptable at this stage.
Visual cue: A deep amber, glossy liquid with no visible butter separation. The brown sugar streaks have been whisked into a uniform dark caramel color.
Underdone: Brown sugar is still in visible lumps or unmixed streaks. Butter is floating on the surface. Whisk vigorously for another 30 seconds. Slightly warm the bowl from underneath if the sugar is very cold and crystalline.
Perfect: Glossy, uniformly dark amber with no visible streaks. Falls off the whisk in a smooth, unbroken ribbon. Add eggs one at a time and continue.
Overdone: N/A — you cannot over-mix this stage. However, if the bowl still feels very hot from the butter, wait for it to cool further before adding eggs. Set the bowl in a cold-water bath for 3–4 minutes to cool before adding eggs.
Feel cue: The mixture should feel like liquid caramel — slightly tacky on the fingertips, with the dense, viscous drag of a syrup rather than the thin slip of water.

Add the eggs one at a time, whisking each in fully before adding the next. Do not beat aggressively — you are incorporating eggs, not building foam. Excess air creates a soufflé-like filling that puffs and cracks dramatically in the oven. Whisk gently, just until each egg is fully absorbed and the mixture is homogeneous.
Visual cue: A smooth, homogeneous, pourable batter that is a uniform deep amber-brown with no egg streaks. No foam or bubbles on the surface.
Underdone: Visible yellow streaks of egg yolk running through the dark syrup. The mixture looks marbled. Continue whisking gently until fully uniform — marbling means uneven custard set.
Perfect: Smooth, deep amber, with a satiny surface and very few bubbles. Pours evenly off a spoon in a steady stream. Pour over the toasted pecans in the unbaked pie shell.
Overdone: The batter is frothy and full of fine bubbles from over-whisking. The surface looks like beaten egg white foam. Let sit 10 minutes for the foam to settle before baking — bubbles baked in will create a spongy, airy texture instead of dense custard.
Feel cue: Dip a fingertip in — the batter coats your finger like warm honey, neither too thin (watery) nor too thick (caramel-stiff). It should drip off your raised finger in a slow, unbroken thread.

Arrange the toasted pecan halves in concentric circles in an unbaked 9-inch pie shell, flat side down, covering the entire bottom. Pour the filling batter gently over them — the pecans will float up and redistribute. Do not try to hold them in place; they will self-arrange as they bake. Fill to within 1 cm of the crust rim.
Visual cue: Pecans are floating near the surface in an even layer, partly submerged in the amber filling. The shell is filled to just below the rim with no gaps.
Underdone: Shell is less than 75% full. Too few pecans — the nut-to-custard ratio will be wrong. Add more filling or more pecans. Do not exceed the rim.
Perfect: Pecans form a nearly continuous, overlapping layer just below the surface of the filling. Filling reaches within 5–8 mm of the crust edge. Bake immediately at 175 C (350 F).
Overdone: Filling is at or over the rim of the shell. Risk of overflow in the oven. Carefully remove a small amount of filling with a spoon. Place a sheet pan on the rack below as a catch.
Feel cue: Tilt the dish gently — the filling should move slowly and settle with a slight tremor, like panna cotta before it is set. If it sloshes freely, it has not been mixed thickly enough.

Bake at 175 C (350 F) on the lower-middle rack for 50–60 minutes. Shield the crust edge with foil or a pie shield after the first 20 minutes. The custard sets from the outside inward — the edges will firm up while the center still appears liquid. Do not overbake waiting for the center to set firm in the oven; it will finish cooking off-heat.
Visual cue: The pecan top is a deep, lacquered mahogany. The edges of the filling are fully set. The center wobbles like gelatin — a slow, unified wobble across the whole pie, not a liquid splash.
Underdone: The center wobbles loosely and independently like a raw egg, and the filling looks opaque and bubbling. Bake 5 more minutes and re-check. Use a thermometer — the center should reach 85 C (185 F).
Perfect: Edges are firm and matte. Center has a slow, jiggly wobble that moves the whole pie as one mass. Pecans are deeply lacquered and fragrant. Cool completely on a wire rack — minimum 2 hours — before slicing.
Overdone: Filling has puffed up beyond the crust edge and cracked across the surface. The custard has scrambled rather than set smoothly. Allow to cool — the filling will deflate and the cracks may close slightly. The texture will be grainy, but the flavor is usually still good.
Feel cue: Place your palm 5 cm above the center of the pie — you should feel strong residual heat radiating upward. The smell should be intensely caramel-sweet with toasted nut, not eggy or sulfurous.

name: Peking Duck
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Whole Pekin duck (2.2–2.5 kg), cleaned: 2300 g
Maltose syrup: 60 g
  Alternatives: honey (less viscous)
Shaoxing rice wine: 30 ml
  Alternatives: dry sherry
Light soy sauce: 30 ml
  Alternatives: tamari (gluten-free)
Boiling water (for blanching): 2000 ml
Five-spice powder: 5 g
Fine salt: 10 g
Fresh ginger, sliced: 20 g
Spring onion, cut into lengths: 30 g
Active time: 1 hour
Total time: 30 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The pinnacle of Chinese roast cookery — a whole duck air-dried over 24 hours, lacquered with maltose and soy until the skin shatters at a touch, the fat rendered completely away beneath a burnished mahogany shell.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

steps:
Mix five-spice and salt. Remove the neck and giblets. Dry the duck cavity thoroughly with paper towels. Rub the five-spice-salt mixture inside the cavity. Stuff the cavity with ginger and spring onion. Truss the opening with a skewer. Using a bicycle pump or air compressor nozzle inserted under the skin at the neck opening, inflate the skin away from the breast — this separates subcutaneous fat from flesh, the key to shatteringly crisp skin.
Visual cue: The duck's breast skin should look visibly puffed and separated from the meat beneath, like a small pillow.
Underdone: Skin still lies flat against the flesh — the air didn't penetrate far enough. Re-insert the nozzle at the neck and pump slowly while pressing the neck skin closed around it. Work air toward the legs too.
Perfect: The breast skin has separated visibly, the thigh skin looks taut. The duck looks inflated and round, not flat. Move immediately to blanching.
Overdone: Skin has torn in a spot where too much pressure built up. Patch with a toothpick to hold the skin. The tear will seal during drying and roasting.
Feel cue: When you press the inflated breast skin, it should feel like a ripe grape — taut and springy, with a distinct air pocket between your finger and the meat beneath.

Hold the duck over a large pot or wok by its trussed neck. Ladle boiling water slowly and evenly over the entire skin surface for 2–3 minutes — the skin will tighten and turn opaque white. This opens the pores and tightens the protein matrix, allowing better lacquer adhesion and a crisper final skin.
Visual cue: The skin transforms from pale ivory to tight, opaque white all over, pulling slightly away from the legs.
Underdone: Patches of skin still look loose, yellowish, and slightly translucent. Continue ladling boiling water, focusing on the pale patches.
Perfect: Uniformly tightened, white, and visibly contracting. The duck now looks leaner. Allow to drain well before lacquering.
Overdone: Skin is starting to cook through and blister from too much boiling water. Move quickly to lacquering. The skin will still crisp in the oven.
Feel cue: After blanching, the skin should feel like taut parchment when you run a finger along the breast — stiff and papery, not soft.

Warm the maltose in a small pan over very low heat until it just flows. Stir in the Shaoxing wine and soy sauce to make a lacquer. Brush a thin, even coat over the entire duck skin. Hang the duck in a cool, airy spot (or in front of a fan) and repeat the lacquering every 4 hours for a total of 3–4 coats over 24 hours. The skin must be fully dry between coats. This is non-negotiable — moisture trapped under the lacquer steams the skin during roasting instead of crisping it.
Visual cue: After 24 hours, the duck skin should look dark amber-mahogany, dry as drum skin, and slightly tacky to the touch.
Underdone: The skin is pale golden and still feels soft or leathery. Only one or two coats applied. Continue drying and apply more lacquer coats. Do not roast until the skin is tight and dark amber.
Perfect: Deep mahogany-brown, uniformly dry, and tight. Tapping the breast makes a faintly hollow sound. No sticky patches. Proceed to roasting at high heat.
Overdone: Lacquer has built up unevenly — thick, almost black patches alternating with lighter areas. Use a clean brush to lightly redistribute before the final drying hour. Uneven color is cosmetic but uneven crisping is not.
Feel cue: The dried lacquered skin should feel like stiff vinyl — smooth, cool, and completely inelastic. If it bends slightly under your fingers, it needs another hour of drying.

Preheat oven to 220 C (430 F). Place the duck breast-side down on a wire rack set over a deep tray with 2 cm of water beneath (to catch dripping fat and prevent smoking). Roast 25 minutes. Flip to breast-side up, increase to 240 C (465 F), and roast a further 20–25 minutes until the skin is shatteringly crisp and deeply lacquered.
Visual cue: Glistening mahogany skin with a lacquer-mirror sheen, bubbled and blistered at the high points of the breast. The drip tray below should hold a pool of clear rendered fat.
Underdone: Skin looks matte and dark but has not bubbled or blistered. It flexes when pressed. Increase oven to 250 C and roast a further 10 minutes, watching closely.
Perfect: Bubbled, blistered, shatteringly brittle skin. Tapping with a spoon produces a sharp 'click'. Deep mahogany with golden-amber highlights where the fat pooled. Rest for 5 minutes, then carve skin and meat separately.
Overdone: Skin has blackened and the lacquer has burned to a bitter char. Use a sharp knife to scrape the blackened top layer away — the layer beneath is often still good. Serve immediately.
Feel cue: Tap the finished duck skin with a fingernail — it should produce a sharp, resonant click, like tapping the back of a phone. If it sounds dull, it needs more time at high heat.

ingredients.name: Mixed sweet bell peppers (red, yellow, orange — halved, seeded, cut into 1cm strips)

steps:
Heat olive oil in a wide, heavy pot or deep skillet over medium-low heat. Add sliced onion and garlic. Season with a pinch of salt. Cook very gently, stirring occasionally, for 15 minutes until the onion is completely soft, sweet, and golden — not browned, just deeply cooked. Peperonata is a slow recipe; do not rush this step.
Visual cue: Onion strands are completely limp, translucent, and golden-yellow. Garlic is soft and fragrant. The oil in the pan is perfumed and slightly golden.
Underdone: Onion is still partly crisp and white. The raw allium sharpness is present in the smell. Lower the heat and continue cooking. The onion's sweetness must fully develop before the peppers go in.
Perfect: Completely soft, golden, and sweet-smelling. Garlic has turned pale gold and fragrant. No sharpness remains. Add peppers.
Overdone: Onion has browned significantly and smells caramelized. Garlic is darkening. Add the peppers immediately and a splash of water — the browned onion will contribute a slightly more robust, sweet flavor which is acceptable.
Feel cue: Taste a strand of onion at this stage — it should taste sweet, almost jammy, with none of the sharp eye-watering pungency of a raw onion. That transformation is the green light.

Add all the pepper strips to the pot. Season with salt. Stir to coat in the oil and onion. Cover with a lid and cook over medium-low heat for 20 minutes, lifting the lid and stirring every 5 minutes. The peppers will release a great deal of liquid — this is correct. The steam and pepper juice create the braising liquid.
Visual cue: Peppers have dramatically wilted and reduced in volume by about half. A generous pool of bright-colored, sweet-smelling liquid has accumulated in the pot.
Underdone: Peppers are still firm, holding their strip shape, and the pot is relatively dry. Continue braising covered. The peppers are releasing their liquid slowly — give them time.
Perfect: Peppers are noticeably limp, colors are still vivid (red, orange, yellow), and a substantial pool of sweet pepper liquid fills the pot. They are tender but still have some structure. Add tomatoes and braise uncovered.
Overdone: Peppers are completely collapsed and the liquid has begun to reduce away. Some peppers are sticking. Add a splash of water and reduce heat before adding tomatoes.
Feel cue: Lift the lid and inhale — the concentrated steam should smell powerfully of sweet pepper, almost like a fresh-squeezed juice. This is the natural sugar of the peppers concentrating as they cook down.

Add the chopped tomatoes. Stir to combine. Remove the lid and cook over medium-low heat for 20–25 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes, until the tomatoes have completely collapsed, the liquid has reduced to a thick, jammy, glossy sauce that just coats the peppers, and the whole pot is a unified, glistening compote. The peppers should be completely tender and silky.
Visual cue: The pot holds a glistening mass of collapsed pepper strips and tomato, barely distinguishable from each other, in a thick amber-red sauce. The olive oil shimmers at the surface.
Underdone: Tomatoes are still in distinct pieces. The liquid is watery and has not reduced. Peppers still have some bite. Continue simmering uncovered. Stir more frequently to prevent sticking as it reduces.
Perfect: The compote is thick and glossy, with the consistency of soft jam. When you draw a spoon through it, the path closes slowly. The peppers are completely silky. The color is a beautiful deep amber-red-orange. Finish with vinegar and basil.
Overdone: Peperonata has reduced too far and is sticking to the pot. The sweetness has turned to a concentrated, slightly burnt caramel. Add a tablespoon of water and stir well. The flavor may have some bitterness from caramelization — a touch of vinegar will balance it.
Feel cue: Spoon some peperonata onto the back of your hand — it should flow slowly and coat the skin in a shining, thick film. If it runs off like water, keep reducing. If it holds stiffly in a mound, add a splash of water.

Off the heat, add a small splash of red wine vinegar if using — it lifts and brightens the sweetness. Taste and adjust salt. Tear fresh basil and stir through. Serve warm, at room temperature, or cold. Peperonata is extraordinarily versatile: use it as a side dish, bruschetta topping, pasta sauce, pizza base, or accompaniment to grilled meats and fish.
Visual cue: A beautiful, glossy, ruby-amber compote flecked with fresh basil. The surface shimmers with olive oil. The whole pot smells sweet, herbaceous, and deeply of summer.
Underdone: Tastes flat and one-dimensionally sweet, lacking brightness. The vinegar is the bridge — add it in drops, tasting after each, until the sweetness has a counterpoint lift.
Perfect: The sweetness of the peppers is the primary note, lifted by the acid, deepened by tomato, rounded by olive oil. Each spoonful is a concentrated hit of summer. Serve at room temperature — peperonata is always best this way.
Overdone: Too tart from vinegar or too sweet from excessive reduction. Balance with a pinch of sugar if too tart, or a splash of water and a squeeze of lemon if too sweet and concentrated.
Feel cue: A spoonful of finished peperonata should feel velvety and dense on the tongue — not watery, not dry, but that perfect middle register where concentrated vegetable sweetness coats every taste receptor all at once.

name: Peri-Peri Chicken
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Whole chicken, spatchcocked (backbone removed, flattened): 10 parts
  Alternatives: bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks
African bird's eye chilies (piri-piri), stemmed: 2 parts
  Alternatives: red Thai chilies; fresh cayenne (milder)
Garlic cloves: 1 parts
Lemon juice and zest: 2 parts
  Alternatives: lime juice
Smoked paprika and dried oregano: 0.5 parts
Olive oil: 2 parts
Salt: 0.5 parts
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 2 hrs 20 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A whole spatchcocked chicken marinated in a ferocious sauce of African bird's eye chilies, garlic, lemon, and smoked paprika — then grilled low and slow until the skin is lacquered and blistered and every bite delivers heat that builds from the back of the throat forward.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Blend the chilies, garlic, lemon juice and zest, smoked paprika, oregano, olive oil, and salt in a blender or food processor until smooth. The sauce should be a vivid red-orange. Taste carefully — it should be very hot, punchy with acid, and deeply savory. Adjust salt and lemon to balance. For a milder result, remove seeds before blending. For maximum heat, use the whole chili including seeds.
Visual cue: A smooth, vivid orange-red emulsion with no visible chunks of chili skin or garlic. Slightly thicker than a vinaigrette.
Underdone: Sauce is chunky with visible pieces of chili and garlic. It won't penetrate the chicken evenly and will burn in patches during grilling. Blend for another 30–60 seconds. Scrape down the sides and blend again. The sauce needs to be smooth to form a proper lacquering marinade.
Perfect: Smooth, uniformly emulsified sauce that pours in a steady stream. Deep orange-red color. Smells intensely of chili, garlic, and citrus all at once. Proceed to coat and marinate the chicken.
Overdone: Blended too long — the sauce has aerated and lightened to a foam, losing density. It will coat less effectively. Let it sit in the blender for 2 minutes without running to allow the foam to subside. The sauce is still usable.
Feel cue: Dip a fingertip — you should feel immediate, building heat within 10 seconds. If the heat doesn't arrive, the sauce needs more chili. If your eyes are watering immediately, you are on track.

Score the chicken skin in a crosshatch pattern with a sharp knife — 4–5 cuts per side, slicing through the skin to the flesh. This allows the marinade to penetrate deeply. Rub the peri-peri sauce all over the chicken: under the skin where possible, into all scoring lines, into the cavity. Reserve about 3 tablespoons of the marinade for basting during grilling. Place the chicken in a container, cover, and refrigerate for a minimum of 2 hours or overnight.
Visual cue: Chicken is uniformly coated in vivid orange-red marinade. The scoring marks are filled with sauce. No pale spots of unmarinated skin.
Underdone: Marinade is dripping off the surface rather than clinging. Pale, unmarinated patches of skin visible. Score marks are empty. Ensure the chicken skin is dry before applying marinade — moisture prevents it from adhering. Pat dry and re-apply.
Perfect: Even, vibrant coating on all surfaces. The marinade has begun to stain the flesh visible through the score marks. Chicken looks deeply colored and glossy. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours before grilling.
Overdone: Marinated more than 12 hours — the acid in the lemon has begun to denature the chicken surface proteins, making the outer flesh pale and slightly mushy. Proceed to grilling immediately. The flavor will be excellent but the texture of the surface may be softer than ideal.
Feel cue: Press the marinade-coated skin with your finger — the sauce should cling to your fingertip and leave a clean, uniform orange-red stain on your skin, indicating even, thorough penetration.

Prepare a two-zone grill: direct high heat on one side, indirect medium heat on the other. Start the chicken skin-side up on the indirect side and cook with the lid closed for 35–40 minutes, basting every 10 minutes with the reserved marinade. The lower, slower indirect heat allows the interior to cook through before the exterior burns. When the internal temperature reaches 68 °C in the thickest part of the thigh, move the chicken to direct heat skin-side down for 5–8 minutes to lacquer and char the skin.
Visual cue: Skin is deeply burnished, moving from orange-red to a charred, lacquered mahogany. Irregular black char spots across the raised skin areas. Leg joints move freely.
Underdone: Skin is still pale and pink-orange, soft, and not yet lacquered. Leg joint is stiff and the thigh flesh is pink when pierced near the bone. Continue on indirect heat, basting every 10 minutes. The chicken needs both internal temperature (74 °C) and external color.
Perfect: Mahogany, lacquered skin with charred high spots. Leg joint moves freely and the thigh runs clear juices when pierced. Internal temp 74–76 °C at the thickest point. Remove from heat, rest 10 minutes before carving.
Overdone: Skin is uniformly black and the chicken smells of bitter char. Leg meat may be beginning to shred involuntarily. Remove from grill immediately. Trim the worst char with a knife. The interior meat is likely still excellent — the skin is the sacrifice.
Feel cue: Wiggle the drumstick — if the leg joint moves with minimal resistance, like a door hinge that needs oil, the chicken is cooked. If the leg pulls straight and stiff, it needs more time.

Rest the chicken breast-side down on a cutting board for 10 minutes — resting breast-side down keeps the breast meat basted in its own juices. Carve and serve with Portuguese rolls, chips, and a simple salad. Drizzle any resting juices over the carved meat. The heat from peri-peri builds slowly — warn guests that the full effect arrives 30 seconds after the first bite.
Visual cue: Carved chicken shows a deeply charred, lacquered skin and juicy, pale flesh beneath that runs clear at the thigh joint. The skin holds its rigid, charred character even after resting.
Underdone: Juices at the thigh joint run pink or red-tinged when the chicken is carved. Flesh is still distinctly pink near the bone. Return to the grill on indirect heat, or cover loosely with foil and rest in a warm oven at 160 °C for 10 minutes.
Perfect: Clear juices at every cut. Flesh is opaque throughout, white at the breast and pale rose at the thigh (safe at 74 °C). Skin is rigid and crackling. The resting liquid on the board smells of chili, char, and citrus. Serve immediately — this is best within 5 minutes of carving.
Overdone: Breast meat is dry and stringy when carved. No pooling juices on the board. Skin may have partially fallen off during carving. Serve with extra peri-peri sauce on the side for moisture. Thigh meat will still be juicy even when breast is overdone — route the white meat portions to those who want it.
Feel cue: Press the center of the breast immediately before carving — it should feel firm but yield with a definite spring, not spongy (undercooked) and not board-hard (overcooked). The char on the skin should crackle audibly when pressed.

name: Pernil (Puerto Rican Slow-Roasted Pork Shoulder)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

description: A bone-in pork shoulder buried in garlic-sazón adobo and marinated for 24 hours, then roasted low and slow until the meat is fall-apart tender — then blasted high to transform the thick skin into the crunchy, shattering cuerito that is the most coveted part of the entire dish.

ingredients.name: Bone-in pork shoulder (picnic or Boston butt), skin-on
Fresh cilantro with stems, roughly chopped

steps:
Using a pilón (mortar and pestle) or food processor, pound the garlic, oregano, salt, pepper, and cumin to a rough paste. Add vinegar and olive oil and mix to a thick, pungent adobo. Stir in the sazón and cilantro. The paste should be thick enough to press into incisions without falling out.
Visual cue: A thick, rough orange-yellow paste flecked with oregano and cilantro. Strong garlic and herb aroma. Thick enough to hold its shape on a spoon.
Underdone: Garlic is still chunky and not fully incorporated into a paste. Pound or process more. Garlic lumps burn in the oven and taste acrid.
Perfect: Smooth-ish paste with some texture. Vivid orange from sazón. Pungently garlicky and herbal. Apply immediately to the pork.
Overdone: N/A — raw paste. Proceed.
Feel cue: The adobo should feel thick enough to mound on a spoon — if it slides off immediately, it's too thin and will run out of the incisions rather than staying in place.

Score the skin in a crosshatch pattern, cutting through skin and fat but not meat. Using a thin, sharp knife, make 20–30 deep incisions all over the meat (under and around the skin flap) and push a generous amount of adobo into each with your finger. Rub remaining adobo all over the meat. Rub coarse salt all over the skin only. Place in a roasting pan, skin-side up, uncovered, in the refrigerator for 24–36 hours.
Visual cue: After marination, the skin is dry and pale, the crosshatch cuts clearly visible. The meat visible around the skin edges has darkened from the adobo.
Underdone: Marinated less than 8 hours. Adobo flavor will be surface-only, not deep. The 24-hour minimum is essential for a shoulder this large. Plan ahead.
Perfect: Skin is dry and matte after 24 hours. Crosshatch cuts are dry at the edges. The exposed meat is deeply stained with the adobo paste. Remove from fridge 1 hour before roasting.
Overdone: Marinated beyond 48 hours. Still excellent — pernil is very forgiving on marination time.
Feel cue: After 24 hours, drag a finger across the skin — it should feel completely dry, like thick paper. Any moisture means the skin won't crackle properly.

Place pork skin-side up on a rack in a deep roasting pan. Add 2 cups of water to the pan bottom. Cover tightly with foil. Roast at 160 C (325 F) for 5–6 hours (approximately 1.5 hours per kilogram). The pork is done when an instant-read thermometer reads 90 C (195 F) at the thickest part — this temperature ensures all collagen has converted to gelatin.
Visual cue: After 5 hours, lifting the foil reveals a shoulder that has visibly contracted and slumped. The skin looks pale and steamed. Juices in the pan are rich and fragrant.
Underdone: Internal temperature below 85 C. Meat still holds its shape firmly and doesn't shred easily. Continue roasting. Do not rush — the collagen conversion is temperature-dependent, not time-dependent.
Perfect: Meat falls in large shreds when probed with a fork. The bone can be wiggled freely. Juices run clear. Internal temp 90–95 C. Remove foil and blast the skin at high heat.
Overdone: Meat has dried at the edges from oven heat despite the foil. Has lost some juiciness. Baste with the pan drippings and proceed to high-heat crisping immediately.
Feel cue: After 5 hours, press the shoulder through the foil with your hand — it should feel like a pillow of rendered fat and tender meat, completely yielding. No resistance means the collagen has done its work.

Remove the foil and increase oven to 230 C (450 F). Roast uncovered for 30–45 minutes, watching constantly, until the skin bubbles and shatters into golden cuerito (crackling). Rotate the pan every 10 minutes. The skin should go from pale and steamed to blistered and golden — listen for the crackling, popping sound.
Visual cue: The skin is a uniform golden-mahogany, completely blistered and puffed into individual crackling bubbles. It looks like a vast, crispy expanse of golden domes across the shoulder.
Underdone: Skin is still pale and chewy. Bubbles haven't formed in sections. Continue at high heat. If uneven, rotate the pan more frequently.
Perfect: The entire skin surface is golden and blistered. Tapping with a knuckle makes a hollow crackle. The most coveted part of the dish — distribute fairly. Rest 15 minutes before carving.
Overdone: Skin is very dark brown and edges are burning. Bitter smell. Tent loosely with foil and remove from oven immediately. Trim the darkest edges.
Feel cue: Tap the cuerito — it should sound like knocking on a hard-boiled egg shell, dry and resonant. Any soft, dull tapping sound means there are pockets that haven't crisped.

Rest uncovered for 15 minutes. Carve by pulling the meat in large chunks with two forks — pernil should not be sliced, it should be pulled. Keep the cuerito intact and break it into pieces separately, distributing equitably. Serve with arroz con gandules and tostones.
Visual cue: Pulled pork in large, juicy shreds, dark with adobo. Broken cuerito pieces are golden-mahogany, shattering when pressed. Pan drippings are rich and orange-tinted.
Underdone: Meat is sliced rather than pulled — holds together in firm chunks rather than yielding to forks. If meat needs slicing, return to the oven at 160 C for 30 more minutes.
Perfect: Meat pulls in long, moist, fragrant shreds. Cuerito is golden and shatters. The pan drippings, drizzled over the meat, are the best sauce possible. Serve.
Overdone: Cuerito has gone soft from the resting steam. Blast under the broiler for 2 minutes to re-crisp before serving.
Feel cue: The rested meat should pull apart in long shreds with essentially no resistance from two forks — if you have to tug hard, the shoulder needed another 30 minutes in the oven.

ingredients.name: Neutral oil or clarified butter (for pot)

steps:
Rinse the basmati in cold water, changing the water 4-5 times until it runs clear. Cover the rinsed rice with cold water, add 1 tsp of salt per cup of rice, and soak for at least 30 minutes — ideally 1-2 hours. The soaking whitens the grains, separates them during cooking, and cuts the final steam time.
Visual cue: Grains are visibly swollen and have turned from translucent-ivory to a more opaque, bright white after soaking.
Underdone: Grains are still translucent and have not visibly swollen — under 15 minutes of soaking. Continue soaking; 30 minutes minimum is required for proper texture.
Perfect: Grains are white and slightly plump — each one distinct, not clumping. When you break one between your fingers, the center is still firm. Drain and proceed to parboiling.
Overdone: Soaked more than 4 hours: grains are beginning to break and feel mushy when pressed. Drain immediately and parboil briefly — reduce parboil time to avoid over-cooking.
Feel cue: A soaked grain should bend slightly before snapping — no longer bone-hard, but with a distinct bite remaining at the center.

Bring a large pot of generously salted water (as salty as pasta water) to a rolling boil. Drain the soaked rice and add to the boiling water. Parboil for exactly 5-7 minutes, stirring once. Test frequently from minute 5: the rice should be cooked on the outside but still have a distinct chalky white line at the very center when bitten. Drain immediately through a fine colander and rinse with cold water to stop cooking.
Visual cue: Grains are elongated, almost doubled in length, with a tiny opaque chalk-white core visible when bitten — the outer third is cooked, the core is raw.
Underdone: Grain is still crunchy through — more than half the cross-section is chalky and hard. Return to the boil for 1-2 more minutes; the parboil stage has a tight window.
Perfect: Cooked on the exterior, firm and chalky at the very core. The grain bends and is stretching to its full length. Drains and separates easily. Drain through colander, rinse cold, and proceed immediately.
Overdone: Grains are fully cooked through — no chalkiness remaining. They may be slightly sticky. Drain and proceed, but handle gently — the final steam will make them very soft, possibly mushy.
Feel cue: The drained rice should feel like loose dry gravel in the colander — individual grains that bounce off each other, not a sticky mass.

Heat the oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot (nonstick or well-seasoned) over medium-high heat until shimmering. Whisk the yogurt with a ladleful (about 15 parts) of the drained parboiled rice and the bloomed saffron water. Spread this yogurt-rice mixture across the bottom of the hot pot in an even layer — this forms the tahdig. Mound the remaining parboiled rice over the top in a pyramid, keeping it away from the pot sides. Drizzle the remaining saffron water over the top. Wrap the lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel (to absorb steam) and place on the pot. Cook over medium-high heat for 10 minutes to set the crust, then reduce to the lowest possible heat.
Visual cue: Steam is escaping around the towel-wrapped lid; the sides of the pot show a faintly golden line near the base where the crust is forming.
Underdone: No steam, no golden edge visible — heat is too low or the pot hasn't come up to temperature. Increase heat to medium-high for 3-5 minutes to establish the crust before reducing.
Perfect: Steady, gentle steam around the lid; the side of the pot shows a golden color at the base; the pyramid of rice is fluffy and dry at the top. Reduce to minimum heat and steam 35-45 more minutes undisturbed.
Overdone: Acrid scorching smell and dark smoke from the lid cracks — the tahdig has gone past golden to burnt. Remove from heat immediately and place pot in a sink of cold water to arrest the burn.
Feel cue: The kitchen should fill with a warm, nutty, almost caramel scent — not smoke, but the smell of golden starch forming. If it smells sharp or acrid, reduce the heat.

After 45-55 total minutes of steaming, remove the lid. Scoop out the fluffy upper rice onto a serving platter and scatter the saffron-stained grains and barberries over the top for color. Now the moment of truth: place a large flat platter over the mouth of the pot and invert in one decisive motion. The tahdig should release as a single, golden disc — crackling and glossy. If it sticks, return to low heat for 2 more minutes.
Visual cue: A burnished, golden-amber disc of crust — uniformly colored, intact, crackling as it cools, the underside a continuous golden-brown sheet.
Underdone: Tahdig is pale blonde or white, soft and sticking to the pot — not crisped. Return to medium heat for 5 more minutes, checking every 2 minutes.
Perfect: Deep golden, crackling crust — releases cleanly from the pot in a single piece or large sections. The crust makes an audible cracking sound as you break it. Place on the serving platter beside the fluffy rice. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Tahdig is dark brown with black patches and smells acrid — over-crisped beyond the golden stage. Trim off any fully black sections; the golden portions are still excellent.
Feel cue: A perfect tahdig makes a sound like breaking a cracker when you snap off a piece — dry, crisp, hollow. If it feels soft and bendy, it needed more time.

ingredients.name: Fine sea salt (for soaking and parboiling)

steps:
Rinse the basmati in cold water until the water runs clear — at least 5-6 rinses. Soak in cold water with 1 tablespoon of salt for 30 minutes minimum (up to 4 hours). The soaking hydrates the grain, which allows it to elongate dramatically during steaming. Drain and rinse once more.
Visual cue: Rice grains that have visibly swollen and appear slightly translucent, with the water from the final rinse running clear with no starch cloudiness.
Underdone: Grains are still opaque white, hard when bitten. Water is still milky with starch. Soak for another 30 minutes. Unsoaked basmati will not elongate and the tahdig method will produce uneven results.
Perfect: Grains have lengthened slightly, feel firmer but slightly springy, and the rinse water is clear. A bitten grain is almost tender at the outside but still firm at the core. Parboil immediately.
Overdone: Grains have soaked for 6+ hours and are very soft, easily crushed. The outside is waterlogged. Proceed but reduce the parboiling time significantly — these grains will cook faster.
Feel cue: Squeeze a soaked grain between your fingernails — it should offer distinct resistance at the core but yield at the outer edge. Still firm, but no longer hard.

Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to a rolling boil (should taste like seawater). Add the drained rice. Parboil uncovered for exactly 5-7 minutes, stirring gently once. A grain is ready when it has elongated and is tender at the outside but still has a firm, white core when bitten — like pasta 2 minutes before al dente. Drain immediately into a sieve and rinse with cold water to stop cooking. The rice is only half done at this point.
Visual cue: Long, elegant grains that have elongated and whitened throughout, still holding their shape cleanly but bending slightly rather than snapping when curved between finger and thumb.
Underdone: Grains are very firm throughout. Snaps rather than bends. Still opaque and starchy-tasting. Return to the boiling water for another 2 minutes. The grain must be half-cooked before steaming.
Perfect: Grains are elongated, bright white, and bend without snapping. The outside is tender but the centre has a visible white opaque core when bitten. Drain immediately in a sieve and rinse with cold water.
Overdone: Grains are fully cooked and soft all the way through. They will become mushy during steaming. Proceed very quickly to the steaming step — reduce steam time to 20-25 minutes.
Feel cue: Pinch a grain between two fingers after parboiling — the outside should feel smooth and tender, but applying pressure from both sides should reveal a firm, chalky resistance at the centre.

Melt the butter in a heavy-bottomed non-stick pot over medium-high. Layer sliced potato in a single even layer on the bottom. Mound the parboiled rice on top in a gentle pyramid — do not press it. Drizzle the bloomed saffron over the top third. Wrap the pot lid in a clean cloth to absorb condensation, place on tight. Cook on medium-high for 3 minutes, then reduce to the lowest possible heat. Steam for 35-45 minutes. To serve: invert the entire pot onto a serving platter so the golden tahdig comes out on top.
Visual cue: When inverted: a dome of elongated, separate, steamed rice grains with a vivid saffron-gold crown, surrounded at the base by a perfectly golden, intact potato tahdig.
Underdone: Potato tahdig is pale and has not crisped. When inverted, it sticks to the pan and tears. Grains are still slightly firm. Return to medium heat, covered, for 10 more minutes. The tahdig needs colour and the grains need more steam time.
Perfect: Golden-amber potato tahdig that releases in a single intact layer when the pot is inverted. Grains are separate, elongated (up to 3x their dry length), and fluffy — each grain distinct and not sticky. Serve the tahdig as the centrepiece and the rice mounded alongside.
Overdone: Tahdig is dark brown to black. Burnt potato smell. Some grains may be slightly dry. Serve the rice, discard the burned tahdig layer. Salvage by adding a drizzle of melted saffron butter over the plated rice.
Feel cue: After inverting, press one corner of the tahdig — it should crackle and sound hollow, like pressing through a thin layer of fried food. If it feels soft and flexible, it is not done.

name: Persian Saffron Rice (Chelow)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Extra-long basmati rice (aged preferred): 100 parts
Sea salt: 3 parts
Unsalted butter: 10 parts
  Alternatives: ghee (more traditional)
Neutral oil (for tahdig): 8 parts
Saffron threads, bloomed in 3 tbsp hot water: 0.5 parts
Hot water (for blooming saffron): 5 parts
Lavash bread or thin flatbread (optional tahdig base): 15 parts
  Alternatives: potato slices; thick yogurt layer
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 2 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The crown jewel of Iranian cooking — long-grain basmati that has been soaked, parboiled, and then steamed over a low flame wrapped in a cloth to create a golden, shatteringly crisp crust called tahdig at the bottom of the pot while the rice above remains separate, elongated, and perfumed with saffron.
