ingredients.name: Desalted salt cod (bacalao), skin-on fillets, soaked 48 hr in cold water
Dried guindilla chili peppers (or dried cayenne)
Fine sea salt (taste before adding — the cod carries salt)

steps:
If not already desalted, submerge the salt cod in a large bowl of cold water in the refrigerator. Change the water every 8–12 hours for 48 hours. The fish is ready when a small piece tastes pleasantly salty rather than overwhelming. After desalting, remove the fillets from the water and pat them completely dry on multiple layers of paper towel, then leave them uncovered on a rack at room temperature for 20 minutes. This drying step is critical: surface moisture is the enemy of the emulsion — it will cause the gelatin to dilute into water rather than binding with the oil. Run your fingers over the skin; the fillets should feel dry and faintly tacky, not wet.
Visual cue: Fillets are pale ivory-white, uniformly moist but not glistening wet. The surface texture is slightly fibrous and the fish holds its shape firmly without being stiff.
Underdone: Fillets still taste aggressively salty — the water hasn't penetrated to the core. The flesh is dense, almost hard. Continue soaking with more frequent water changes. A still-salty fillet will make an inedibly salty sauce.
Perfect: Pleasantly salty, like well-seasoned fish. Flesh is supple and peels in long, meaty flakes. Surface is dry and faintly tacky. Pat dry thoroughly and rest on a rack before confiting.
Overdone: Fillet tastes bland and waterlogged after too long a soak, and the flesh is soft and starting to fall apart. Proceed but handle gently. The sauce may need salt added at the finish to compensate.
Feel cue: Run a fingernail lightly along the grain of the flesh — it should separate into clean, long filaments without crumbling. The skin side should feel slightly rubbery and dry, ready to release gelatin without steaming.

In a wide, shallow clay cazuela or heavy skillet, combine the olive oil, sliced garlic, and dried chilis over the lowest possible heat. When the garlic begins to sizzle gently (about 2 minutes), nestle the cod fillets in skin-side up. The oil should never bubble aggressively — it should hover around 60–70C / 140–160F, which is well below a fry. Cook for 12–15 minutes, periodically tilting the pan to baste the fish with the warm oil. You will begin to see small white droplets forming at the edges of the fillets — this is the gelatin leaching from the fish into the oil. This is the raw material for the emulsion. When the fish is just cooked through and beginning to flake, gently remove the fillets with a slotted spatula onto a warm plate. Reserve every drop of the oil with its garlic and gelatin droplets.
Visual cue: Small, milky-white droplets of gelatin are visible at the edges of each fillet and scattered through the oil; the garlic has turned pale gold but not brown; fish flesh lifts at the edge in loose, moist flakes.
Underdone: No white droplets visible yet in the oil; fish is still translucent at the center and the flesh is firm and unyielding. Continue at the lowest heat. The gelatin needs time and gentle warmth to migrate out of the collagen — do not rush with higher heat.
Perfect: White gelatin droplets visible throughout the oil, garlic pale gold, fish just opaque through to the center but still very moist. Remove fish carefully and begin the emulsification swirl immediately while the oil is still hot.
Overdone: Fish has broken into dry flakes, the gelatin has cooked out completely and the oil looks slightly cloudy from over-extraction. Garlic is brown. The sauce will still emulsify but the fish will have a drier texture. Remove garlic if brown to avoid bitterness.
Feel cue: Nudge the fish gently with a spatula — it should yield and begin to separate at the
natural flake lines, but still hold together as one piece. The oil in the pan should feel slightly thicker than when you started, almost silky on a spoon.

This is the defining technique of the dish. With the reserved warm oil still in the pan over the lowest heat, begin moving the pan in slow, continuous circles — tilting it forward, sideways, backward, in a hypnotic, patient swirl. Do not stir, do not whisk. Just swing the pan. As you do this, the gelatin droplets begin to bind with the olive oil, and after 5–10 minutes a pale, creamy emulsion starts forming at the edges of the pan and slowly spreading to the center. The sauce goes from oily to ivory-white and slightly thickened, like a very loose aioli. If at any point it looks like it's about to split — the oil separates from the white mass — add a teaspoon of cold water and slow down the swirl. Taste and adjust salt very carefully. A pil-pil sauce that holds is one of the great quiet miracles of the kitchen.
Visual cue: A pale ivory emulsion with a glossy, creamy sheen that coats the bottom of the pan evenly and holds its shape for a second when the pan is still — not a greasy oil with white flecks, but a unified, creamy sauce.
Underdone: The pan still shows a clear separation between the oily liquid and the white gelatin droplets — no creaminess has formed yet. Continue swirling patiently. The emulsification typically begins at the 5-minute mark. Make sure the pan is warm but not hot.
Perfect: Smooth, pale ivory sauce that trails and drapes when the pan is tilted — looks like a loose cream sauce but contains no cream. Tastes savory, garlicky, faintly oceanic. Return the cod fillets gently to the sauce skin-side up and serve immediately from the cazuela.
Overdone: The emulsion has broken: oil has separated to the top and a dense, rubbery gelatin mass has sunk to the bottom. Remove from heat. Add 1 tablespoon of cold water and restart the gentle circular swirl away from heat. Most broken pil-pils can be rescued this way — patience is the cure.
Feel cue: Dip a spoon

and hold it horizontally — the sauce should coat the back in a layer thick enough to leave an opaque trail when you drag a finger through it. If the oil beads and runs off the spoon, it hasn't emulsified yet. If it coats like cream, you are there.

Gently lower the reserved cod fillets back into the emulsified sauce, skin-side up, and tilt the pan to baste them with the sauce. The residual heat of the sauce will warm the fish through without further cooking. Taste the sauce carefully and add a pinch of salt only if needed — the fish and oil will have already contributed significant salt. To serve, bring the cazuela directly to the table. Tear crusty bread and drag it through the ivory sauce. The dish should be served warm, not hot — pil-pil breaks at temperatures above 80C, so never return it to a burner at this stage.
Visual cue: Cod fillets resting in a pool of ivory-cream sauce, skin gleaming on top, the sauce quivering slightly when the dish is moved — a dish that looks both rustic and almost impossibly elegant.
Underdone: Sauce is warm but the fish is cold at the center — the heat exchange wasn't long enough. Let the fillets rest in the warm sauce (off heat) for another 3–4 minutes, tilting the pan to baste continuously.
Perfect: Fish is warm throughout, flaking in large, moist chunks at the touch of a fork; sauce is glossy and ivory, pooling around the fish. Serve immediately in the cazuela with bread.
Overdone: Sauce has been returned to active heat and broken — oil pooling, sauce grainy and separated. Off the heat: add a splash of cold water and swirl patiently to re-emulsify. The broken state is rarely permanent.
Feel cue: Drag a crust of bread through the finished sauce — it should coat the bread in a thick, shiny layer that clings rather than soaks. The flavor on your lips should be oceanic, garlicky, and richly olivey, with a low tingle from the guindilla warming the back of the throat.

name: Butter Pilaf

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The pillar of Central Asian and Turkish cooking — long-grain rice toasted in butter until translucent and nutty, then steamed in stock with onion and carrot until each grain is firm, separate, and fragrantly golden.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Rinse the rice under cold running water, swirling with your hand, until the water runs nearly clear — this removes excess surface starch that would cause the grains to clump. Transfer to a bowl and cover with cold water. Soak for 30 minutes. This hydrates the outer layers of the grain so they can expand uniformly under steam without the center remaining chalky. Drain thoroughly before cooking.
Visual cue: Rinse water has gone from cloudy white to nearly translucent. Soaked grains are slightly swollen and uniformly opaque white.
Underdone: Rinse water is still milky white and the grains remain glassy and translucent at the center. Continue rinsing. The milky water is surface starch — it must go or the pilaf will be gluey.
Perfect: Water runs almost clear after 4-5 rinses. Grains are uniformly chalk-white and slightly swollen from soaking. Drain completely in a fine-mesh sieve and allow to sit 2 minutes so excess water drips off.
Overdone: Rice has soaked more than 1 hour and grains are beginning to break when pinched. Drain and proceed — cook slightly more gently and reduce the stock by 30 ml.
Feel cue: After soaking, a grain pinched between fingertips should feel slightly springy and moist, bending rather than snapping — it has absorbed enough water to cook evenly.

Melt the butter in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot with a tight-fitting lid over medium heat until it foams and then settles — this is clarified butter temperature, ideal for frying. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring often, for 5-6 minutes until completely soft and just beginning to turn golden at the edges. Add the carrot julienne and cumin seeds and cook for 3 more minutes until the carrot softens slightly. The pot should smell of warm butter, sweet onion, and earthy cumin.
Visual cue: Onion is completely translucent and soft, tinged gold at the edges. Carrot has softened and the cumin seeds have darkened and become fragrant.
Underdone: Onion is still white and firm in the center, with no golden color. Carrot is raw and hard. Continue cooking — undercooked alliums will leave a sharp, harsh note in the finished pilaf.
Perfect: Onion is soft, translucent, with gold fringing. Carrot is flexible and slightly shrunken. Cumin seeds are fragrant and a shade darker. Add the drained rice immediately and begin toasting.
Overdone: Onion edges are dark brown and beginning to crisp. Cumin seeds are very dark and smell sharp. Reduce heat immediately and add the rice to stop the cooking — the slight bitterness will be absorbed by the grain.
Feel cue: The butter should still smell clean and nutty — if it smells sharp or burnt, the heat is too high; lower it before adding the rice.

Add the drained rice to the pot with the aromatics and stir to coat every grain in the butter. Spread the rice in an even layer and cook over medium heat, stirring frequently, for 2-3 minutes. The grains will turn from opaque white to a slightly translucent, glassy appearance, and the pot will smell of warm, toasted grain — like popcorn but delicate. This toasting step coats each grain in fat, which keeps them separate during steaming.
Visual cue: Rice grains appear glassy and slightly translucent, glistening with butter. The mass looks like polished glass beads mixed through the aromatics.
Underdone: Grains are still chalky white with no translucency. No toasted aroma. Continue stirring over medium heat — the translucency is the visual cue that the starch has been coated with fat.
Perfect: Grains are uniformly translucent with a butter sheen. The pot smells of warm, popcorn-like grain. Nothing has browned. Add the hot stock and proceed immediately.
Overdone: Some grains are beginning to turn golden-brown and the pot smells of toasted grain verging on nutty. Add the stock at once — a little extra toasting is fine and adds nuttiness, but stop before anything browns further.
Feel cue: Stir the translucent rice with a spoon and listen — it makes a dry, glassy, whisper-like sound as the fat-coated grains slide against each other rather than clumping wetly.

Pour the hot stock over the toasted rice — it will hiss and steam immediately. Add salt and black pepper. If using, nestle the whole unpeeled head of garlic into the center of the rice, cut side down (it perfumes the steam without making the pilaf garlicky). Stir once to distribute everything. Bring to a full boil over high heat, then immediately reduce to the absolute lowest setting. Cover tightly with the lid and cook for 15 minutes without lifting the lid once.
Visual cue: Boiling starts within 2-3 minutes, then subsides to a quiet simmer hidden under the lid. No steam should escape — a tight lid is essential.
Underdone: After 15 minutes the lid lifts to reveal standing liquid still pooled across the surface. Replace the lid and continue on the lowest heat for 3-5 more minutes, then check again.
Perfect: After 15 minutes, all liquid has been absorbed. The rice surface is dimpled with small steam-hole craters. Grains at the edges are fluffy and separate. Remove from heat without lifting the lid and allow to rest for 10 minutes.
Overdone: A burning smell rises from the pot before the 15 minutes are up. Remove from heat immediately. The bottom may have formed a slight crust — leave the lid on and rest off heat, which will allow steam to loosen it.
Feel cue: After 10 minutes of cooking, press your palm flat against the lid — you should feel the rhythmic warmth of rising steam but no liquid condensation dripping back; that means the rice is properly steam-cooking rather than boiling.

Remove the pot from heat and let it rest, completely undisturbed with the lid on, for 10 minutes. This is not optional — it is the moment the steam redistributes through the grains, equalizing moisture and ensuring even texture. After 10 minutes, remove the lid and the garlic head (if used). Using a fork or the handle of a wooden spoon, gently fluff the rice from the bottom up with light, lifting motions — never press down or stir aggressively, which would crush the grains.
Visual cue: Each grain is distinct, elongated, fluffy, and completely separate. The rice pours off the fork in a gentle cascade of individual grains, not clumps.
Underdone: Some grains in the center are still slightly firm and not quite fluffy. The rice seems a little dense. Re-cover and rest another 5 minutes — the residual heat will finish the center grains gently.
Perfect: Every grain is tender, fluffy, and completely separate. Carrot and onion are distributed throughout. The bottom has a very thin, lightly golden crust that releases cleanly. Serve immediately or keep covered with a clean cloth under the lid to hold heat for up to 20 minutes.
Overdone: Grains are soft and beginning to clump. The bottom crust is dark brown. Fluff immediately and serve at once — the texture will not worsen but it will not improve with more time.
Feel cue: A perfectly rested pilaf grain, pressed between thumb and forefinger, should give with a gentle sigh of yielding starch — fully cooked, never mushy, like pressing a tiny pillow.

name: Pineapple Upside-Down Cake
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Canned or fresh pineapple rings: 60 parts
  Alternatives: mango slices; peach halves
Dark brown sugar (for caramel base): 40 parts
  Alternatives: light brown sugar
Unsalted butter (for the caramel base): 30 parts
Plain (all-purpose) flour: 100 parts
Caster or granulated sugar: 80 parts
Eggs, at room temperature: 50 parts
Baking powder: 5 parts
Unsalted butter, softened (for the sponge batter): 80 parts
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 55 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A golden sponge baked over a glossy layer of caramelised pineapple rings and brown sugar, then inverted to reveal a lacquered, jewel-bright topping that smells of caramel and tropical fruit.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Unsalted butter, softened (for the sponge batter)

steps:
Preheat oven to 175°C (350°F). Place a 24cm oven-safe skillet or round cake tin directly on the stovetop over medium heat. Add the butter and let it melt. Add the dark brown sugar and stir briefly to combine, then leave undisturbed for 2 minutes until it bubbles and darkens slightly. The caramel does not need to be fully made at this point — it will finish in the oven — but the butter and sugar should be melted and fragrant. Remove from heat.
Visual cue: A dark, glossy, bubbling mixture of butter and brown sugar covering the base of the pan. It smells of deep toffee with a hint of bitterness.
Underdone: Butter and sugar have barely combined — still looks sandy and pale. Stir briefly and continue heating for 1 more minute. The mixture needs to be fully melted and beginning to bubble before adding the pineapple.
Perfect: Dark, glossy, and bubbling. Toffee aroma fills the kitchen. The mixture is uniform with no visible sugar crystals. Remove from heat and arrange pineapple rings immediately.
Overdone: Caramel is very dark and smells slightly burnt. It is beginning to separate and look oily. Remove from heat immediately. If it smells acrid, discard and start again — bitter burnt caramel will dominate the entire cake.
Feel cue: The caramel at this stage should smell like warm toffee sauce — deeply sweet with a faint edge of bitterness. If it smells predominantly sweet and buttery, give it another 30 seconds of heat.

Lay the pineapple rings over the hot caramel in the pan, fitting them snugly — one in the centre and as many as will fit around the edge without overlapping. Press them gently into the caramel. If using canned pineapple, pat the rings thoroughly dry first — excess juice will water down the caramel and prevent the fruit from browning properly. Place a maraschino cherry or dried cherry in the centre of each ring if desired.
Visual cue: Pineapple rings are flat against the caramel base with no gaps between them. The caramel is visible at the edges and between the rings. The rings look slightly golden from the caramel heat.
Underdone: Rings are sitting loosely on top and the caramel around them is still very fluid and separating. Press the rings down more firmly. Wet rings are also floating — pat them drier and replace.
Perfect: Rings are flush with the pan, caramel has crept up slightly around their edges. The arrangement looks neat and the rings have a slight gloss from the caramel. Pour the sponge batter immediately and evenly over the top.
Overdone: The caramel has hardened while arranging the fruit and the rings are sitting on a solid toffee disc. Very gently warm the pan base for 30 seconds to soften. Proceed — the fruit will still caramelise beautifully in the oven.
Feel cue: When pressed gently, the pineapple rings should have a slight resistance — not the springiness of cold tinned fruit, but a settled, flush contact with the caramel beneath them.

In a bowl, beat the softened butter and caster sugar together with an electric mixer for 3 minutes until pale and fluffy. Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each addition. Sift in the flour and baking powder and fold until just combined — a few turns with a spatula rather than vigorous beating. The batter should be smooth, thick, and fall from the spatula in slow ribbons. A small splash of milk or pineapple juice from the tin can loosen it to the right consistency.
Visual cue: Pale, creamy batter that falls from a spoon or spatula in thick, slow ribbons. No flour streaks visible. Batter is smooth and glossy.
Underdone: Butter and sugar are not fully creamed — the mixture is dense and yellowish rather than pale and fluffy. Flour streaks visible. Beat butter and sugar longer before adding eggs. Fold the flour more completely.
Perfect: Pale, very smooth batter that falls in thick ribbons. Slightly thicker than double cream — it holds a figure-eight pattern briefly when dropped. Pour evenly over the arranged pineapple and caramel.
Overdone: Batter has been over-mixed and looks slightly dense and gluey. It does not fall smoothly. Proceed. The texture may be slightly less tender but the caramelised topping is the star of this cake.
Feel cue: A ribbon of batter dropped from a spoon should hold its shape on the surface for 2–3 seconds before slowly dissolving back — this viscosity ensures the sponge will bake with an even, fine crumb.

Pour the batter carefully over the pineapple arrangement, spreading gently to the edges to cover everything evenly without disturbing the fruit arrangement. Bake at 175°C for 30–35 minutes until the sponge is deep golden and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean. Remove from the oven and rest for 5 minutes — not longer. Run a knife around the edge, place a large serving plate on top, and invert decisively in one motion. Lift the pan straight up. Any caramel clinging to the pan can be scraped off and poured over the top.
Visual cue: After inversion: a glossy lacquer of amber caramel and golden pineapple rings facing upward on a dark, beautifully coloured sponge base.
Underdone: After inversion, the centre of the sponge is sunken and raw-looking. The batter may have partially adhered to the pan. Re-cover with the pan and return to the oven for 10 minutes. The caramel can be re-warmed if needed.
Perfect: A perfect circle of glossy amber caramel and fruit rings resting on a golden sponge. The caramel has set to a glaze. No raw spots visible. Serve warm with cream or ice cream.
Overdone: The caramel has hardened to a dark, almost brittle toffee. Sponge edges are very brown and dry. The flavour is still good. Warm slices briefly in the microwave before serving, or serve with extra cream to moisten.
Feel cue: The five-minute resting period before inversion is critical — the caramel needs to set slightly from its boiling state. If you invert immediately, it will pour off the cake; wait too long and it bonds to the pan.

description: A vivid, oil-bright red sauce from the African bird's eye chili — simultaneously fiery and fruity, with a lemon-garlic sharpness that makes grilled chicken sing and your lips tingle long after the last bite.

ingredients.name: Bird's eye chilies (fresh or dried and rehydrated), stems removed
Red bell pepper, roughly chopped and roasted
食用油（Neutral oil (sunflower or light olive)）

steps:
Place the red bell pepper pieces and whole garlic cloves on a baking tray under a very hot broiler (240C/460F) or directly over a gas flame using tongs. Roast until the pepper skin is blackened and blistered in patches and the garlic is golden-brown and soft inside. The pepper takes 10-15 minutes, the garlic 8-10 minutes. Transfer to a bowl, cover with cling film, and steam for 5 minutes. Peel the pepper skin off — the char and steam loosens it.
Visual cue: Pepper skin is 50-60% blackened with blistered, collapsed flesh beneath. Garlic is golden-brown and yielding.
Underdone: Pepper skin has only softened but not blistered. Garlic is still firm and pungent-raw. Return to the broiler for 3-5 more minutes. A fully hot broiler is essential.
Perfect: Pepper is dramatically blistered with char in patches. Flesh is soft and collapsing. Garlic is fragrant and yielding when pressed. Steam in the covered bowl then peel the pepper before blending.
Overdone: Pepper is entirely black throughout. Garlic is deeply browned with bitter notes. Use anyway but reduce the quantity slightly. The bitterness will be offset by lemon and vinegar.
Feel cue: Press the pepper through the film — it should collapse immediately, completely soft with no resistance. The garlic clove should yield like a cooked potato.

Combine the chilies, peeled roasted pepper, roasted garlic, lemon juice, vinegar, oil, salt, oregano, and paprika in a blender or food processor. Blend on high for 2 minutes until completely smooth and emulsified. If the sauce is too thick, add a tablespoon of water and blend again. Taste carefully — the heat will be significant. Adjust with more lemon for brightness or more salt for depth.
Visual cue: A vivid brick-red, glossy, smooth sauce that pours in a fluid stream with a slight emulsified opacity from the oil.
Underdone: Sauce has visible chili skin pieces and a chunky texture. Oil not emulsified — floating in pools. Blend for another 60 seconds on the highest setting. A tamper helps with thick sauces.
Perfect: Silky, bright red, uniformly colored with a slight sheen from emulsified oil. Flows off a spoon in a smooth sheet. Complex on the tongue — heat, acid, smoke. Taste and adjust seasoning, then use or jar up.
Overdone: Sauce is pale orange-pink from over-blending with air, or the oil has broken and separated on the surface. Let it rest 2 minutes. If broken, add a splash of lemon juice and briefly re-blend.
Feel cue: Place a drop on your wrist — within 5 seconds you should feel a spreading heat that intensifies to a clean burn, not a dull ache. Sharp, not heavy.

For a cooked piri piri (preferred for marinating and shelf stability): pour the blended sauce into a small saucepan and simmer over low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Cooking mellows the raw chili edge, deepens the roasted pepper flavor, and extends refrigerator life to 2 weeks. For a fresh, vibrant table sauce, skip this step and use raw. Cool completely before jarring.
Visual cue: The sauce darkens very slightly and the surface becomes more glossy as it cooks. Aroma shifts from raw to deeply roasted and complex.
Underdone: Sauce is still bubbling vigorously and smells very raw and sharp. Oil starting to separate at the edges. Reduce heat to the lowest setting and stir. A gentle simmer, not a boil.
Perfect: Surface is barely moving — a gentle shimmer rather than a boil. Color has deepened. Aroma is rounded, smoky, fruity. No raw chili sharpness. Cool and jar. Keeps refrigerated for up to 2 weeks.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced too much and is thick, sticky, and very dark. Has a slight caramelized note. Thin with a tablespoon of water and stir in a squeeze of fresh lemon to brighten.
Feel cue: After cooling, rub a drop between your fingers — it should feel silky and oily with a faint lingering heat spreading across the fingertips.

name: Pisco Sour
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Peruvian pisco (quebranta or acholado): 60 ml
  Alternatives: Chilean pisco (fruitier); unaged brandy as a last resort
Fresh lime juice (key lime preferred): 30 ml
  Alternatives: fresh lemon juice
Simple syrup (1:1 sugar:water): 22 ml
  Alternatives: gomme syrup for extra body
Egg white, fresh (one egg): 30 ml
  Alternatives: aquafaba (chickpea water) for vegan
Angostura bitters: 3 drops
  Alternatives: Amargo Chuncho bitters (more authentic)
Ice cubes (for shaking): 1 handful
Active time: 8 min
Total time: 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Peru's national cocktail — a dry, citrus-bright pisco shaken hard with fresh lime juice, simple syrup, and raw egg white until it froths into a cloud, served in a chilled coupe with three drops of Angostura bitters bleeding into the foam.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine the pisco, lime juice, simple syrup, and egg white in a cocktail shaker with no ice. This is the 'dry shake' — shaking without ice to build a preliminary foam from the egg white protein before dilution with ice. Shake as hard and as long as you can for 30–45 seconds. The shaker will feel almost impossible to open from the vacuum. The egg white requires the heat and full force of this dry shake to denature and foam — a half-hearted shake produces a thin, watery foam cap that collapses in seconds.
Visual cue: When the shaker is briefly opened, the contents appear thick and foamy — visibly increased in volume and a paler color than when it went in.
Underdone: The liquid is still thin and unfrothy, smelling strongly of raw egg. The dry shake was too short or too gentle. Close and shake harder for another 20 seconds. The foam needs sustained force to form.
Perfect: The mix has thickened noticeably and a persistent foam is visible when the lid is briefly loosened. Volume has increased. Smells citrusy and slightly eggy. Add ice and shake again.
Overdone: Not possible to over-dry-shake. Continue with confidence. Proceed to the ice shake.
Feel cue: The shaker should rattle very little compared to a normal wet shake — the foam-thickened liquid doesn't slosh; it churns. Your arms should feel the effort.

Add a generous scoop of ice cubes to the shaker containing the dry-shaken base. Shake vigorously again for 15–20 seconds. This second shake chills, dilutes, and further aerates the cocktail. The colder temperature helps set the foam into a more stable structure. The shaker will frost over on the outside — this is your cue that the drink is cold enough.
Visual cue: The outside of the shaker is frosted white with condensation and feels very cold — near-frozen to the touch.
Underdone: The shaker is cold but not frosted. The drink inside is not cold enough and will melt the ice too fast in the glass. Shake for another 10 seconds.
Perfect: The shaker is frosted and feels near-frozen. When you shake near your ear, the ice sounds dense and compact — little slosh. Strain immediately into the chilled coupe.
Overdone: Over-dilution from shaking too long with ice — the drink tastes watery and pale. Use more ice next time and shorter second shake. The dry shake does the heavy lifting.
Feel cue: The shaker should feel uncomfortably cold to hold with bare hands — the metal contracts in your grip. That is the right temperature.

Double-strain the cocktail through a Hawthorne strainer and a fine-mesh sieve into a chilled coupe glass — the fine strainer catches ice shards that would crater the foam. Pour from a low height so the foam lands cleanly on top rather than splashing against the sides. The foam should dome slightly above the rim of the glass. Immediately add three drops of Angostura bitters to the center of the foam. Use a cocktail pick or toothpick to drag the drops through the foam in a spiral or line — the bitters bloom in the white foam like ink in water, creating the classic pisco sour pattern.
Visual cue: A pale gold cocktail visible through the glass, topped by a thick, slightly domed white foam with three dark amber bitters drops arranged on the surface.
Underdone: The foam is thin, barely 3 mm, and already dissolving. Bitters drops are sinking through it. The dry shake was insufficient. Serve as is — the flavor is correct, just the texture is compromised.
Perfect: A firm, dense white foam dome at least 1 cm thick, holding the bitters drops on its surface like ink on velvet. The foam does not dissolve for 3–4 minutes. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Too much foam has formed, overflowing the glass. The cocktail to foam ratio is off. Gently lift the foam layer with a spoon if needed, or serve in a larger glass.
Feel cue: The foam should feel like stiff whipped cream on the tongue — airy and immediate — followed by the sharp hit of lime, the dry warmth of pisco, and a whisper of bitters on the finish.

name: Pistou
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Fresh basil leaves (packed, no stems): 60 g
Garlic cloves: 3 cloves
Extra-virgin olive oil (best quality): 100 ml
Coarse sea salt: 5 g
Squeeze of lemon juice (optional): 5 ml
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Provence's uncooked basil paste — raw garlic pounded with fresh basil and olive oil into a vivid green sauce that smells like a garden in August. Unlike its Ligurian cousin pesto, pistou contains no nuts and no cheese, meaning all the flavors are immediate and transparent, with nowhere for the basil to hide.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
In a mortar, pound the garlic cloves with the coarse salt until a completely smooth, white paste forms. The salt crystals act as an abrasive and draw out the moisture from the garlic. This step is crucial — any remaining garlic chunks will make the sauce harsh and unpleasant. If using a food processor instead, mince the garlic as fine as possible before proceeding.
Visual cue: A smooth, translucent white-cream paste. No visible garlic chunks. Intense, clean garlic aroma without any acrid bitterness.
Underdone: Chunks of garlic still visible. Texture is rough. Continue pounding — the garlic must be fully reduced to a paste to distribute evenly.
Perfect: Completely smooth, almost sticky paste. Salt crystals fully dissolved. Smells of pure, clean garlic. Add basil and begin incorporating.
Overdone: Garlic has oxidized and turned slightly gray. Very pungent. Acrid notes. Proceed — the basil will temper the harshness. Add a drop of lemon juice to stabilize.
Feel cue: Drag your finger across the mortar — the paste should feel like cool butter: smooth, cohesive, with no grit from the salt or garlic fibers.

Add basil leaves to the mortar in two or three batches. Pound and grind with a circular pressing motion — not sharp strikes — until each batch is completely incorporated before adding the next. The goal is to bruise and crush the cells to release the oils, not to create friction heat. If using a food processor, pulse briefly in short bursts — blending too long heats the basil and turns it black.
Visual cue: A dense, brilliantly green paste. No whole leaves remaining. A pool of dark green oil begins to separate around the edges of the mortar.
Underdone: Leaves still partially whole or very chunky. Paste is rough and poorly integrated. Continue pounding — the sauce needs fully macerated basil.
Perfect: Vivid green paste, dense and smooth. Green oil weeping at the edges. Fragrance is intensely floral and herbal — summer in a bowl. Stream in the olive oil immediately.
Overdone: Basil is turning from bright green to dark olive and black. Cell walls fully oxidized. Work faster — add oil immediately to slow oxidation. A squeeze of lemon juice will also help preserve the green.
Feel cue: The paste should smell like a crushed basil plant — intensely herbal and floral, with a slight anise sweetness that fills the whole room.

Stream in olive oil a little at a time, stirring and pressing the paste against the sides of the mortar to incorporate. The sauce will loosen and become glossy as the oil emulsifies with the water content of the basil. Add a small squeeze of lemon juice if using. The consistency should be thick enough to coat a spoon but fluid enough to pour. Use immediately — pistou begins to oxidize and lose its vivid color within 30 minutes.
Visual cue: Vivid, brilliant emerald-green sauce. Pours from a spoon in a slow, oil-thick ribbon. No separation.
Underdone: Oil pooling separately rather than integrating. Sauce looks broken. Stir more vigorously, pressing paste against the sides. Add a drop of water to help emulsify.
Perfect: Uniform, flowing emerald-green sauce. Completely emulsified. An explosion of basil-garlic-oil fragrance. Coats a spoon and slides off slowly. Use within 20 minutes for best color and flavor.
Overdone: Sauce is very dark olive green and oxidizing. Flavor turning slightly bitter. Use immediately. Add a touch more fresh basil if available to revive the color.
Feel cue: Taste a small spoonful straight — it should feel coating and rich from the oil, with an immediate bright basil hit followed by the slow, clean warmth of raw garlic.

name: Greek Pita Bread

Total time: 2 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Soft, pillowy rounds that inflate into perfect steam-pockets in a furiously hot oven — they emerge with a pale gold crust, a tender crumb, and a hollow belly just waiting to be torn open and filled.

steps:
Combine flour, instant yeast, and salt in a large bowl. Add warm water and olive oil. Mix with a wooden spoon until no dry flour remains, then use your hand to bring it into a rough ball. The dough should be moderately soft and slightly sticky — noticeably softer than pizza dough but not as wet as focaccia. Turn out onto a lightly floured surface.
Visual cue: A slightly sticky, shaggy ball that holds together and pulls cleanly away from the bowl sides.
Underdone: Dry pockets of flour at the bowl bottom; dough is crumbly and doesn't hold together. Add warm water 1 teaspoon at a time and fold until cohesive.
Perfect: Soft, slightly sticky ball. Pulls away from the bowl but sticks a little to your hand. No dry patches. Turn out and begin kneading.
Overdone: Soupy and wet — pours rather than holds a shape. Add flour a tablespoon at a time. Pita dough should be soft but shapeable.
Feel cue: Pita dough should feel like a soft earlobe — yielding, slightly warm, just barely tacky. A little stickier than commercial bread dough is correct and desirable.

Knead for 8 minutes on a lightly floured surface using a push-fold-rotate motion. The dough will transform: from sticky and rough to smooth, elastic, and barely tacky. After 8 minutes it should pass the basic stretch test — pull a small piece and stretch it a few inches without it tearing immediately. Shape into a ball, lightly oil the surface, and place in a clean bowl.
Visual cue: A smooth, satiny ball with a slightly shiny surface. Springs back halfway when poked. No tears or rough patches.
Underdone: Surface still rough and bumpy; tears when stretched 3 cm. Dough sticks to the bench continuously. Continue kneading — check again every 2 minutes.
Perfect: Smooth and elastic, barely tacky. Stretches to 5–7 cm without tearing. Feels alive and slightly warm from the friction. Place in an oiled bowl and cover for the first rise.
Overdone: Dough is very tight and snaps back immediately — difficult to stretch at all. Cover and rest 20 minutes. Gluten will relax on its own.
Feel cue: Properly kneaded pita dough should feel like a smooth, flexible rubber band — it resists and then gives, stretching without snapping, springing back slowly rather than instantly.

Cover the bowl with a damp towel or plastic wrap. Let rise at room temperature (22–25 C) for 60–75 minutes until doubled. While the dough rises, place a heavy baking stone or inverted cast-iron pan on the top rack of the oven. Preheat the oven to its maximum temperature — 260 C (500 F) or higher — at least 30 minutes before baking. A screaming-hot surface is essential for pita to puff.
Visual cue: Dough has doubled in volume. The bowl shows clear expansion marks, the dough domes above the rim, and jiggling the bowl makes the mass quiver.
Underdone: Dough has barely grown — less than 30% larger. Dense and tight. Poke returns immediately. Give it more time in a warmer spot. Cold rooms slow yeast dramatically.
Perfect: Doubled, jiggly, and domed. Poke leaves a slow-fading dimple that returns about halfway after a few seconds. Punch down gently, divide, and roll out pita rounds.
Overdone: Dough has collapsed, smells strongly of alcohol, surface is wet and sticky. Divide and shape immediately. Pitas may be slightly denser but will still puff.
Feel cue: Properly proofed pita dough feels airy and fragile — handle it gently when dividing or it deflates. It should feel almost weightless for its size.

Punch down the dough and divide into 8 equal portions (about 70 g each). On a lightly floured surface, roll each portion into a smooth ball. Cover and rest 10 minutes so the gluten relaxes. Then roll each ball with a rolling pin into a round 18–20 cm across and about 4–5 mm thick. Do not roll too thin — a pita that is too thin won't form a proper pocket. Place on a sheet of parchment and rest 15 minutes before baking.
Visual cue: Even round discs, 18–20 cm across and uniform in thickness — no thick center and thin edges. Surface is smooth with no tears.
Underdone: Rounds are thick and oval rather than circular. Center is much thicker than edges. Continue rolling with even pressure. Rotate the disc a quarter-turn after every few passes.
Perfect: Even circles of uniform 4–5 mm thickness. Surface smooth. Hold up to the light — thickness is consistent across the disc. Rest on parchment 15 minutes before baking.
Overdone: Rounds are paper-thin (less than 3 mm) and have developed tears. Use carefully — thin pitas may not form a pocket. They will still taste good as flatbreads.
Feel cue: A well-rolled pita round feels substantial but pliant — it flops gently rather than holding stiffly. If you press it, it springs back slowly, a sign the gluten is relaxed enough to puff.

Working in batches of 2–3 (however many fit on your baking stone), use a peel or the back of a flat baking sheet to slide pita rounds directly onto the screaming-hot stone. Bake for 3–4 minutes — no more. You will see the pita begin to puff dramatically about 60–90 seconds in, inflating into a dome. Once fully puffed and barely pale gold on top, remove. Do not over-bake — the goal is a soft, pliable pita, not a crisp one. Wrap immediately in a clean towel to keep soft.
Visual cue: A fully inflated dome — the pita has puffed into a complete balloon shape, pale gold with no dark spots. When removed from the oven it deflates into a soft round with a hollow interior pocket.
Underdone: Pita has barely puffed — maybe a small bubble in the center but not a full dome. Doughy and pale. Bake 60–90 seconds more. Check that the stone is hot enough — surface temp should be 260 C+.
Perfect: Full inflation into a round dome, pale gold. Deflates into a flat round when removed; interior is hollow and steam-soft. Tears open easily into two layers. Wrap in a cloth immediately to keep pliable. Best eaten within 30 minutes.
Overdone: Golden-brown to dark, crust has crisped. Will not be soft and pliable. The pocket may have sealed shut. Serve as flatbread — split manually if needed. Lower baking time for the next batch.
Feel cue: A just-baked pita should feel like a warm, inflated pillow — light and hollow when you tap it, soft as a cloth when you press it. The steam inside is what forms the pocket.

name: Polenta
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Water (or half water, half milk): 500 parts
  Alternatives: light chicken stock; whole milk
Stone-ground coarse cornmeal (polenta): 100 parts
  Alternatives: polenta taragna (corn + buckwheat); medium-grind cornmeal
Fine sea salt: 2 parts
Unsalted butter: 12 parts
  Alternatives: extra-virgin olive oil
Parmigiano-Reggiano (finely grated): 15 parts
  Alternatives: Grana Padano; aged Montasio
Whole milk (to finish, optional): 30 parts
  Alternatives: heavy cream
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 50 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Coarse cornmeal stirred into a slow whirlpool until the grains burst, swell, and pull away from the pot in a single glossy mass — patient, golden, and finished with a knot of butter and a storm of cheese.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Pour the water into a heavy-bottomed pot — copper or thick-clad steel holds heat best and resists scorching. Add the salt and bring to a bare simmer over medium heat. The water should be hot and lazily steaming, with small bubbles trembling at the edges, NOT at a rolling boil. A violent boil flings cornmeal everywhere and seizes it into lumps.
Visual cue: Wisps of steam rise steadily and a few small bubbles break the surface near the rim. The salt has fully dissolved and the water moves with a slow, glassy convection.
Underdone: Water is warm but still, no steam, salt grains visible on the bottom. Keep heating and stir once to dissolve the salt before adding cornmeal.
Perfect: Hot, gently steaming, a quiet shimmer of small bubbles around the edge — a 'smiling' simmer, not a boil. Begin streaming in the cornmeal.
Overdone: Rolling, splashing boil with large bubbles bursting across the whole surface. Lower the heat and let it settle for 30 seconds before adding the cornmeal, or it will spit and clump.
Feel cue: Hold your hand over the pot — you should feel soft, even warmth and hear a faint hiss, not the loud rumble of a hard boil.

Stir the simmering water into a slow whirlpool with a whisk. While it spins, add the cornmeal in a thin, steady rain from your fist — never dump it. Whisk constantly as you pour so each grain disperses before the next lands. Once all the cornmeal is in, switch to a sturdy wooden spoon. The mixture will look loose and milky, like thin cream.
Visual cue: A smooth, lump-free, pourable slurry the color of pale custard. The whisk leaves momentary trails that fill back in instantly.
Underdone: Visible lumps or a dry skin of cornmeal floating on top; the meal was added too fast or the whisk stopped moving. Whisk hard to break up clumps now, while it is still thin — lumps set permanently once it thickens.
Perfect: Uniform, silky, and just-pourable. No dry pockets, no lumps, a faint sweet corn aroma rising. Reduce heat to low and settle in for the slow cook.
Overdone: Already stiff and gluey before any real cooking, because too much meal went in too soon. Whisk in a splash of hot water to loosen it back to a pourable slurry.
Feel cue: The whisk should move freely with almost no resistance — like stirring loose batter. If it drags this early, you've added the cornmeal too quickly.

Drop the heat to its lowest setting so the polenta blips rather than boils — a thick bubble should heave up and burst every few seconds, like a slow mud pot. Cook 35-45 minutes, stirring every few minutes with the wooden spoon, scraping the bottom and corners to prevent scorching. The polenta is done when the grains have lost all grittiness and the mass pulls cleanly away from the sides of the pot as you stir.
Visual cue: Thick, glossy, deep-gold polenta that mounds on the spoon and pulls away from the pot wall in a single sheet, briefly exposing the bottom before flowing back.
Underdone: Still soupy and pale; a spoonful rubbed on the lip of the pot feels sandy and gritty between the teeth. Keep cooking — the grains need more time and water to fully gelatinize. Add a splash of hot water if it thickens before the grit is gone.
Perfect: Spoon stands a moment before slowly falling. The polenta tastes sweet and smooth with no graininess, and the surface glistens. It sheets off the pot wall. Mantecatura — stir in the butter and cheese.
Overdone: Stiff, dry, and pasty, cracking at the edges of the pot, possibly with a scorched smell from the bottom. Stir in hot water or milk a little at a time to bring back a soft, flowing texture; do not scrape up any burnt layer.
Feel cue: The stir gets heavier minute by minute — at the start the spoon glides, near the end it leaves a clean valley that holds for a second before closing. That fading trail is your timer.

Off the heat, beat in the cold butter and grated Parmigiano, stirring vigorously until both melt into a glossy, unified cream. For a soft, spoonable polenta, loosen with the warm milk until it slumps slowly off the spoon. Taste and adjust salt. Serve at once in warm, shallow bowls — polenta stiffens fast as it cools.
Visual cue: Lustrous, smooth, pale-gold polenta that flows in a slow ribbon and settles into a flat pool, with a rich, buttery sheen on the surface.
Underdone: Butter and cheese sit in visible streaks; the polenta looks dull and matte rather than glossy. Keep beating — the fat needs to emulsify into the starch. A splash of hot milk helps it come together.
Perfect: Glossy and flowing, holding a soft mound that slowly relaxes flat. Buttery and savory, with the Parmigiano humming in the background. Plate immediately in warmed bowls.
Overdone: Thick, stiff, and pasty, holding a hard shape and turning gummy as it sits. Beat in more hot milk or water to restore the flow — soft polenta should pour, not stand.
Feel cue: On the tongue it should be velvety and clean, never grainy or chalky. If it coats your palate like paste, loosen it with hot liquid; if it pools like soup, give it a minute to set.

name: Pollo a la Brasa (Peruvian Rotisserie Chicken)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Whole chicken (1.6–2 kg): 1800 g
Soy sauce: 80 g
  Alternatives: tamari
Garlic cloves, minced to a paste: 30 g
Ground cumin: 10 g
Aji panca paste (or dried aji panca, rehydrated): 40 g
  Alternatives: ancho chili paste + 1 tsp paprika
Smoked paprika: 8 g
Fresh lime juice: 30 g
  Alternatives: lemon juice
Fine sea salt: 15 g
Black pepper, ground: 5 g
Dried oregano: 5 g
Neutral oil: 30 g
Fresh mint leaves (for aji verde): 20 g
Fresh cilantro (for aji verde): 30 g
Fresh jalapeño or aji amarillo (for aji verde): 20 g
Mayonnaise (for aji verde): 80 g
Lime juice (for aji verde): 15 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 26 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A whole chicken brined in soy sauce, cumin, aji panca, and garlic for 24 hours, then roasted on a rotisserie or in the oven until the skin is burnished and crackled and the meat inside is so juicy and aromatic it needs nothing beyond the bright green aji verde served alongside.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Garlic cloves, minced to a paste
Aji panca paste (or dried aji panca, rehydrated)
Fresh jalapeño or aji amarillo (for aji verde)

steps:
Whisk together soy sauce, garlic paste, cumin, aji panca paste, smoked paprika, lime juice, salt, pepper, oregano, and oil until uniform. The mixture should be thick, dark, and deeply aromatic — the soy and aji panca together create the characteristic mahogany color of pollo a la brasa.
Visual cue: A dark mahogany marinade, slightly thicker than water, with a reddish undertone from the aji panca and paprika. Smells of earthy cumin, soy, and chili.
Underdone: Marinade looks thin and pale. Not fully combined. Whisk more vigorously. The aji panca should be fully incorporated, not floating in patches.
Perfect: Dark, unified marinade. Tastes assertively of soy, cumin, and chili. It will be diluted somewhat by the large chicken — it should taste strong. Apply to chicken.
Overdone: N/A — raw marinade. Proceed.
Feel cue: The marinade should taste dramatically seasoned on its own — salty, aromatic, and complex. If it tastes balanced at this stage, it won't be flavorful enough once distributed across 1.8 kg of chicken.

Dry the chicken thoroughly inside and out. Using your fingers, carefully separate the skin from the breast and thigh meat and push half the marinade directly under the skin, massaging it over the meat. Rub remaining marinade all over the exterior and inside the cavity. Place in a large zip-lock bag or covered dish. Refrigerate 12–24 hours, turning once.
Visual cue: The chicken is deeply stained mahogany-red everywhere, including under the skin where the marinade bulges slightly against the breast. After 24 hours, the skin looks dark and matte.
Underdone: Marinade only on the surface. Skin hasn't been separated to allow under-skin seasoning. Lift the skin gently with fingers, being careful not to tear. The under-skin application is what makes the breast moist and flavored.
Perfect: Even dark staining inside and out. Under-skin marinade has seeped into the flesh. Skin is dark and slightly tacky. Remove from fridge 1 hour before roasting.
Overdone: Over-24 hours. High soy content may start to darken the flesh. Still excellent. Proceed.
Feel cue: After 24 hours, the breast meat under the skin should feel slightly firmer and denser — the soy and salt have done a light cure, improving the texture and ability to retain moisture during roasting.

Place chicken breast-side up on a rack in a roasting pan (or on a rotisserie spit). Roast at 200 C (400 F) for 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes. Every 20 minutes, baste with pan drippings. Rotate the pan if using a regular oven. The chicken is done when the thigh joint reads 82 C (180 F) and the skin is deeply burnished. Rest 10 minutes before carving.
Visual cue: A deeply mahogany-brown chicken with crackled, burnished skin. The wings and drumstick tips are very dark — nearly black — while the breast skin is deep amber. The thigh joint shows no pink juice when pierced.
Underdone: Skin is a pale copper-red and soft. Juices at the thigh joint run pink. Internal temp below 74 C at breast. Continue roasting and basting. The skin needs more time to set and crackle.
Perfect: Deeply burnished, mahogany-to-dark-brown skin. Skin crackles when pressed with a spoon. Clear juices at the thigh joint. Internal breast temp 74 C, thigh 82 C. Rest 10 minutes tented loosely with foil.
Overdone: Skin is very dark, crackling, and dry. Breast meat beginning to dry at the edges. Rest immediately under foil. The breast may be marginally dry but the thigh will be excellent.
Feel cue: After resting, press the skin — it should feel taut and papery, not soft or oily. A perfectly roasted pollo a la brasa skin should rustle faintly when pressed.

Blend mint, cilantro, jalapeño, mayonnaise, and lime juice in a blender until completely smooth and vivid green. Season with salt. The sauce should be bright, herby, creamy, and slightly spicy — the essential accompaniment to cut the richness of the chicken.
Visual cue: A vivid green, completely smooth sauce with no visible herb chunks. The color should be a bright, clean green, not grey-green.
Underdone: Sauce is still chunky with visible herb pieces and jalapeño skin. Blend longer. The sauce must be silky and uniform.
Perfect: Vivid, smooth green. Tastes bright, herby, slightly spicy, with a creamy richness from the mayonnaise. Balances the richness of the chicken. Refrigerate until ready to serve.
Overdone: Sauce is grey-green — over-blended and oxidized, or left too long before serving. Add a squeeze of fresh lime to brighten the color and serve immediately.
Feel cue: The aji verde should feel creamy but not heavy on the tongue — the herb freshness should dominate, with the mayonnaise as a background emulsifier, not a dominant element.

Carve the rested chicken: separate the legs, split the breast, cut the wings. Arrange on a warm platter skin-side up so the burnished skin remains visible. Serve the aji verde in a bowl alongside, with fried yuca or papas fritas and a simple salad.
Visual cue: Carved chicken pieces arranged skin-side up, deeply mahogany, alongside a bowl of vivid green aji verde. The contrast between the dark chicken and bright green sauce is striking.
Underdone: Skin is facing down or not prominent. The visual appeal of pollo a la brasa is the burnished skin. Always present skin-side up.
Perfect: Mahogany chicken carved and arranged, vivid green sauce, warm sides. The kitchen smells of cumin, roasted garlic, and caramelized soy. Serve.
Overdone: Chicken was carved before resting. Juices ran out of the carving board rather than into the meat. Always rest 10 minutes before carving.
Feel cue: A piece of perfectly rested pollo a la brasa should feel moist and juicy to the touch — pressing the breast gently shouldn't cause juice to stream out, because the rest has retained it within the muscle fibers.

name: Pollo en Adobo
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Bone-in chicken pieces (thighs and legs): 1000 g
  Alternatives: pork shoulder cut into chunks
Dried ancho chiles (stems and seeds removed): 4 whole
  Alternatives: mulato chiles
Dried guajillo chiles (stems and seeds removed): 4 whole
  Alternatives: New Mexico chiles
White onion, quartered: 150 g
Garlic cloves: 5 cloves
Apple cider vinegar: 45 ml
  Alternatives: white wine vinegar
Cumin seeds, toasted: 1 tsp
  Alternatives: ground cumin (½ tsp)
Dried Mexican oregano: 1 tsp
  Alternatives: dried marjoram
Cinnamon stick: 1 small
  Alternatives: ¼ tsp ground cinnamon
Whole cloves: 3 whole
  Alternatives: pinch ground cloves
Chicken stock: 300 ml
  Alternatives: water
Lard or neutral oil: 30 ml
  Alternatives: vegetable shortening
Fine sea salt: 10 g
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 3 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Bone-in chicken braised in a deep brick-red Mexican adobo — ancho and guajillo chiles toasted, rehydrated, and blended with vinegar, garlic, cumin, and oregano into a glossy, chile-thick sauce that clings to the meat like varnish.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Dried ancho chiles (stems and seeds removed)
Dried guajillo chiles (stems and seeds removed)

steps:
Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium heat until very hot. Toast the stemmed, seeded ancho and guajillo chile pieces in batches by pressing them flat against the hot surface for 10-15 seconds per side — you will see them puff slightly, change color, and release an intoxicating smoky-sweet fragrance. Do not scorch them black: a toasted chile smells of raisin, chocolate, and dried fruit; a burnt chile smells of acrid carbon and will make your sauce bitter. Once toasted, transfer immediately to a bowl and cover with boiling water. Soak for 20-30 minutes until completely soft and pliable.
Visual cue: Chiles are deeply fragrant, slightly blistered, and have changed to a brighter, more vivid brick-red or dark red-brown. They should feel pliable, not papery.
Underdone: Chiles are still papery and dull in color. No aroma released. The interior moisture hasn't activated. Return to the hot surface for a few more seconds per side. The pan must be properly preheated.
Perfect: Blistered slightly, vivid red-brown, fragrant with dried fruit and mild smoke. Pliable when bent but not black anywhere. Transfer immediately to a bowl and cover with boiling water to rehydrate.
Overdone: Black patches on the surface. Sharp, acrid, burnt-coffee smell. Surface is stiff and carbonized. Discard these pieces and start fresh. One burnt chile can make the entire adobo bitter.
Feel cue: A properly toasted chile presses flat under your finger with a leathery, warm flexibility — like warm dried leather, not papery stiffness.

Drain the rehydrated chiles, reserving 120 ml of the soaking liquid (it has flavor but can be bitter — taste before using). Place the chiles in a blender with the quartered onion, garlic, apple cider vinegar, toasted cumin, oregano, cinnamon, and cloves. Add 60 ml of the soaking water and 60 ml fresh water. Blitz to a completely smooth, thick paste, 2-3 minutes on high. The finished adobo should be the color of dark brick, intensely aromatic, slightly sour from the vinegar, and thick enough to coat a spoon. Pass through a fine-mesh strainer if desired for a smoother texture.
Visual cue: A deep brick-red paste with a velvety surface. No visible chile skin or seed fragments. Thick enough that it does not pour freely from the blender.
Underdone: Still chunky with visible chile pieces. Pale and uneven in color. The spices have not fully integrated. Blitz longer, scraping down the sides every 30 seconds. Add soaking liquid a tablespoon at a time if the blender struggles.
Perfect: Completely smooth, deep brick-red paste. Falls from the blender in slow, heavy waves. Taste is complex: smoky, vinegary, earthy, slightly sweet. Fry the paste immediately for the best flavor development.
Overdone: Over-thinned with too much liquid — paste is watery and pale. Fry the paste as normal; the extra moisture will evaporate quickly in the hot fat.
Feel cue: The finished adobo paste should feel thick and slightly gritty between your fingertips from the dried chile solids — more like thick hummus than a liquid sauce.

Heat the lard in a large, heavy pot (Dutch oven) over high heat until smoking. Working in batches, sear the salted chicken pieces skin-side down for 4-5 minutes without moving until deeply browned. Turn and sear the other side for 2 minutes. Remove and set aside. Reduce heat to medium. Add the adobo paste to the hot fat — it will splatter furiously. Stand back, then stir constantly for 3-4 minutes, frying the paste in the fat. This step, called freír el adobo, transforms the raw chile paste into a deep, complex sauce: the color darkens, the sharp raw smell mellow to something round and toasted, and the fat begins to bleed out visibly — the Mexican equivalent of bhunao.
Visual cue: The paste has darkened to a very deep red-brown and is visibly frying in the fat — you can see small bubbles of fat emerging through the surface of the paste.
Underdone: Paste is still the bright brick-red of the blended chiles. It looks raw and wet. The vinegar is still sharp on the nose. Continue frying for another 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly. The adobo needs to cook down and concentrate.
Perfect: Paste has darkened to a deep mahogany and is visibly frying — small fat beads on the surface. Smells earthy, complex, and round. No raw chile sharpness. Return chicken to the pot, add stock, and braise.
Overdone: Paste is sticking and scorching at the edges. Smells bitter and burnt. Deglaze immediately with a splash of the chicken stock. Reduce heat significantly before returning chicken.
Feel cue: When the adobo is properly fried, a wooden spoon dragged across the pot bottom leaves a clean trail that fills back slowly — the paste has thickened and begun to separate from the fat.

Return all the seared chicken pieces to the pot with the fried adobo paste. Pour in the chicken stock and stir to combine — the liquid should come about halfway up the chicken. Bring to a simmer, cover the pot, and cook over low heat for 45-60 minutes until the chicken is completely tender at the bone. The adobo will penetrate every surface of the chicken. A fork inserted at the thigh joint should meet no resistance and the meat should want to pull from the bone.
Visual cue: Chicken partially submerged in a brick-red adobo that clings to every surface. The liquid is at a gentle trembling simmer — not a boil. The kitchen smells of dried chile and vinegar warmth.
Underdone: Less than 30 minutes. Meat near the bone is still firm and resists a fork. The adobo sauce is still thin. Continue braising covered. Bone-in chicken needs full time for the connective tissue to break down.
Perfect: After 45-60 minutes, the meat pulls away from the bone with light fork pressure. The sauce has reduced and thickened to coat every piece. Uncover and proceed to the final reduction.
Overdone: Chicken has fallen apart completely and the sauce is very thick and beginning to stick. Remove the largest pieces carefully. Thin the sauce with a splash of stock and serve immediately.
Feel cue: After full braising, insert a fork into the thigh joint — it should slide through the meat with the sensation of parting warm, yielding clay rather than cutting muscle fibers.

Remove the lid and increase heat to medium-high. Cook uncovered for 10-15 minutes, turning the chicken pieces frequently and spooning sauce over them. The adobo will reduce and glaze: each piece of chicken becomes lacquered in a thick, glossy, brick-red coating. The sauce should be thick enough that it coats the back of a spoon and holds for a moment. Taste and adjust salt. Serve over rice or with warm tortillas, with pickled jalapeños and sliced white onion alongside.
Visual cue: Each chicken piece lacquered in a thick, glossy brick-red adobo. The sauce barely pours — it glides. The chicken is deeply colored and shiny.
Underdone: Sauce is still thin and watery, running off the chicken. The chile color has not concentrated. Continue reducing, turning pieces every 2-3 minutes to promote even glazing.
Perfect: Each piece is deeply glazed in an almost sticky adobo. The sauce at the base of the pot is thick and barely pourable. Color is a deep, dark brick-red. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced to a near-paste and is beginning to scorch. The vinegar and sugar have concentrated too far — sauce tastes very intense. Add 50-80 ml of warm water or stock, toss to coat, and remove from heat.
Feel cue: Drag a wooden spoon through the sauce at the base of the pot — a perfect adobo parts cleanly and the channel holds for 3-4 seconds before slowly filling back in.

name: Ponzu
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Yuzu juice (freshly squeezed): 50 parts
  Alternatives: sudachi juice; a mix of lemon and lime juice; kabosu juice
Rice vinegar: 20 parts
  Alternatives: sushi vinegar (reduce mirin slightly)
Soy sauce (koikuchi): 50 parts
  Alternatives: usukuchi for a paler, saltier ponzu; tamari for gluten-free
Mirin (hon-mirin): 15 parts
  Alternatives: mirin simmered 1 min to burn off alcohol; a pinch of sugar dissolved in water
Kombu (dried kelp, 5 cm square): 5 parts
  Alternatives: rishiri or ma-kombu
Katsuobushi (dried bonito flakes): 8 parts
  Alternatives: shiitake dashi powder for a vegan ponzu (omit bonito)
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 24 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The bright, savory backbone of the Japanese table — sour citrus juice married to soy and steeped over kombu and katsuobushi until it deepens into a tart, mahogany dressing that wakes up everything from chilled tofu to seared fish and shabu-shabu hot pot.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

steps:
In a clean glass jar or non-reactive bowl, combine the yuzu juice, rice vinegar, soy sauce, and mirin. Do not heat the citrus — raw juice keeps its high, perfumed top note, and cooking would dull the sourness into something flat and stewed. Stir gently to blend. The liquid should be a deep amber that smells equally of sharp citrus and salty soy, neither one drowning the other.
Visual cue: A clear, dark-amber liquid with no oil sheen or cloudiness, smelling brightly of citrus over a savory soy base.
Underdone: The mix smells overwhelmingly of raw soy with little citrus lift, or tastes harshly alcoholic from the mirin. Add yuzu juice a teaspoon at a time until the citrus reads clearly on the nose. If sharply boozy, use mirin that has been simmered one minute to cook off the alcohol.
Perfect: Balanced on the nose — citrus and soy in equal measure — tasting bracingly sour and salty with a faint sweet edge from the mirin. Add the kombu and katsuobushi and move it to steep.
Overdone: The base tastes cloying and flat, the sweetness or vinegar dominating and the citrus lost. Pull it back with more fresh yuzu juice and a splash of soy to restore the sour-salty backbone.
Feel cue: It should taste aggressively tart and salty at this raw stage — almost too sharp to sip neat. The umami steeping to come will round and deepen it, so resist the urge to soften it now.

Wipe the kombu lightly with a damp cloth (never rinse off the white powdery mannitol — that is pure umami) and submerge it in the base along with the katsuobushi. Cover and refrigerate for at least 24 hours, ideally 2 to 3 days. This cold infusion draws glutamate from the kelp and inosinate from the bonito into the acidic liquid, building the deep savory undertone that defines true ponzu. The flakes will swell and slowly sink as they saturate.
Visual cue: The kombu has softened and expanded, the bonito flakes have darkened and mostly sunk, and the liquid has deepened to a richer, rounder mahogany.
Underdone: The flakes still float dry on top and the liquid tastes thin and one-dimensionally sour, with no savory depth. Keep steeping. Cold infusion is slow — give it the full day or more, and gently press the flakes under the surface.
Perfect: A pronounced savory roundness now sits beneath the citrus tang, and the bonito and kelp have given up their flavor. The aroma is layered: tart, salty, and deeply oceanic. Strain immediately to stop the infusion before it turns muddy or fishy.
Overdone: Steeped too long, the ponzu tastes overly fishy, bitter, or musty, with a slick, slightly cloudy look. Strain at once and brighten with a little fresh yuzu and a splash of soy. In future, strain at the 2 to 3 day mark.
Feel cue: Lift the lid each day and smell — you want the marine, savory note to grow steadily without ever crossing into sharp fishiness. The kombu will feel supple and slippery, no longer brittle.

Set a fine-mesh sieve lined with a paper towel or cheesecloth over a clean jar and pour the ponzu through, letting it drip without pressing — squeezing the solids forces through bitter, cloudy fines. Discard the spent kombu and bonito. Bottle the strained ponzu and let it rest in the refrigerator at least a few hours so the flavors settle and marry. It keeps refrigerated for several weeks and only improves over the first week.
Visual cue: A clean, glossy, translucent mahogany liquid with no floating particles, pouring in a clear bright stream.
Underdone: The strained liquid is cloudy and flecked with fine sediment that won't settle. Strain again through a fresh paper-lined sieve without pressing, and let it stand undisturbed so any remaining fines drop to the bottom.
Perfect: Crystal-clear, deep amber-mahogany ponzu that coats a spoon thinly and tastes vividly sour, salty, and savory all at once with a long umami finish. Bottle and refrigerate. Use within a few weeks, shaking gently before each use.
Overdone: Pressed too hard, the ponzu is murky and carries a bitter, dusty edge from the crushed flakes. Let it settle overnight in the fridge and carefully decant the clear liquid off the sediment, leaving the murk behind.
Feel cue: The finished ponzu should feel light and watery on the tongue, never thick or syrupy, then bloom into layered sourness and savory depth. A single drop on the back of the hand should taste complete — bright, salty, and deeply savory, needing nothing more.

ingredients.name: Skin-on pork belly, deboned, butterflied flat
Fresh fennel fronds or wild fennel
Fennel seeds, toasted and coarsely ground

steps:
The night before: lay the pork belly skin-side down. Score the flesh side in a crosshatch pattern about 5 mm deep (this is where the filling will cling). Season the flesh generously with salt — use about half the total salt. Flip the belly and score the skin with a sharp knife in parallel lines about 1 cm apart, cutting only through the skin and just into the fat — do not cut into the flesh. Salt the skin lightly, rub in, and refrigerate uncovered overnight. Dry skin is the key to crackling.
Visual cue: Skin is pale and completely dry after overnight refrigeration. Score lines are visible across both skin and flesh.
Underdone: Skin is still moist or tacky. Scoring cuts are too shallow. Pat with paper towels and return uncovered to the fridge for another hour, or score deeper.
Perfect: Skin feels like dry paper. Score lines are deep, even, and clean. Flesh is firm and cold. Proceed to building the filling.
Overdone: Not possible — the longer the skin dries, the better. 48 hours is fine. Proceed.
Feel cue: Run your finger across the scored skin — it should feel like dry parchment, with no moisture transferring to your finger.

Roughly chop rosemary, fennel fronds, and garlic together on a cutting board until finely minced. Transfer to a bowl. Add ground fennel seeds, black pepper, and olive oil. Stir into a fragrant, moist paste. Taste — it should be aggressively herby and garlicky. This is the soul of the porchetta.
Visual cue: A dense, moist, dark green paste with visible fennel seed specks. Intensely fragrant.
Underdone: Herbs are too coarsely chopped — large pieces will fall out when rolling. Continue chopping until everything is very fine.
Perfect: Fine, cohesive paste. Sticky from the natural oils in the herbs. Deeply fragrant when you stir it. Apply immediately to the pork — the paste must stay moist for rolling.
Overdone: Over-chopped into a near-liquid puree. Add a few whole fennel seeds to restore texture. Proceed.
Feel cue: The paste should feel like cool, gritty butter when you press it between two fingers — moist and cohesive, not dry and crumbly.

Spread the herb paste evenly over the entire scored flesh side, pressing it into the crosshatch cuts. Roll the belly tightly from one short end, keeping the tension even, ensuring the roll is tight with no air pockets. Tie with kitchen twine at 3 cm intervals — tight enough that the roll holds a drum-like firmness. Rub remaining salt all over the skin. Refrigerate uncovered for at least 2 hours, or overnight if possible.
Visual cue: A tight, drum-like cylinder with parallel twine loops. Skin smooth and dry. No gaps visible at the seam.
Underdone: Roll is loose, seam gaping, filling falling out at the ends. Re-tie more firmly, starting at the center and working outward. Tuck filling back in at the ends.
Perfect: Firm cylinder, evenly tied, no sag between loops. Seam tightly closed. Skin dry and pale. Rest uncovered in fridge until ready to roast.
Overdone: Tied so tightly the meat is bulging between loops. Retie with slightly looser tension — uneven pressure creates uneven cooking.
Feel cue: Squeeze the roll — it should feel as firm and solid as a magazine rolled tight, with no give or shift between the skin and filling.

Take porchetta from the fridge 1 hour before roasting. Preheat oven to 230 C (450 F). Place porchetta on a wire rack over a roasting pan, seam-side down. Roast at 230 C for 30 minutes — this blast of heat begins the crackling. Reduce heat to 160 C (325 F) and roast for 2 to 2.5 more hours until internal temperature reaches 70 C (158 F) at the center.
Visual cue: After the blast heat: skin is blistered, bubbled, and starting to turn golden. After slow roast: deeply amber with dramatic bubbled blisters covering the entire surface.
Underdone: Skin is still flat and pale golden after the blast heat period. Internal temp below 65 C. Continue slow-roasting and check temperature every 20 minutes.
Perfect: Skin is covered in dramatic, amber-gold bubbles — each blister a tiny pocket of crackle. Internal temp 70–75 C. Fat rendered clear. Rest for 20 minutes before slicing. The crackling continues to crisp as it rests.
Overdone: Skin is very dark brown, some areas blackened. Possible burnt smell. Tent with foil for the rest of the cook. The interior is likely still moist.
Feel cue: Tap the skin with a knife — fully rendered crackling rings with a hollow, crisp click, not a dull thud. If it thuds, return to high heat for 10 more minutes.

Rest the porchetta on a wire rack (not a cutting board) uncovered for 20–30 minutes. Resting lets the juices redistribute through the fat and flesh. Do not tent with foil — steam will soften the crackling you worked so hard for. Slice with a sharp, serrated bread knife using a sawing motion — a chef's knife will crack and shatter the crackling rather than cut through it cleanly.
Visual cue: Cross-section reveals alternating rings of herb-flecked meat, rendered white fat, and a shattering amber crackling crust.
Underdone: Juices run freely when cut — meat is not rested. Interior is slack. Patience — rest 10 more minutes. Cutting now wastes juice.
Perfect: Juices stay in the meat. Crackling shatters at the first touch of the knife. Layers of fat, herb, and meat visible in the cross-section. Slice immediately and serve.
Overdone: Rested too long, gone cold. Crackling has softened from surface steam. Blast under the broiler for 3–4 minutes to re-crisp the skin before slicing.
Feel cue: The crackling should shatter with a sound like breaking a thin sheet of caramel — if it bends, it needs more heat.

Cassia bark (or cinnamon stick): 1 parts

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Thick-cut pork belly caramelized in rock sugar and braised in soy, Shaoxing wine, and star anise until the fat layers quiver like warm amber silk and the sauce reduces to a dark, lacquered glaze.
