ingredients.name: 五花肉（Pork belly (skin-on), cut in 4 cm cubes）

steps:
Place pork belly cubes in a cold pot, cover with cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat and blanch for 5 minutes, skimming the grey foam vigorously. Drain and rinse each piece under cold running water to remove all grey protein residue. Pat completely dry with paper towels. This step is essential for a clean, clear braising sauce with no off-flavors.
Visual cue: Uniformly pale grey pork cubes, clean and dry, with no blood or foam residue. The skin should be intact.
Underdone: Grey foam still rising in the pot. Pork still partially pink at the interior. Blanch another 2–3 minutes. The grey proteins must fully coagulate before proceeding.
Perfect: Pale, clean, uniformly grey. Water runs completely clear when rinsed. Skin is intact and firm. Pat dry aggressively — any surface water will cause dangerous spatter when the pork hits the caramel.
Overdone: Pork is beginning to tighten and firm from the blanching water. No harm done — the long braise ahead will completely re-tenderize the meat.
Feel cue: The blanched, dried pork cubes should feel dry and almost papery on the outside — like cold deli meat that has been briefly air-dried. Any moisture on the surface will cause the caramel to seize and splatter.

In a wide, heavy pot or wok, heat the neutral oil over medium heat. Add the rock sugar and cook, stirring gently, until it melts and turns a deep amber color — like old whiskey. This takes about 4–6 minutes. Do not walk away. The caramel transitions from clear to pale gold to amber to dark amber very quickly.
Visual cue: A fluid, deep amber caramel with wisps of smoke beginning to rise. Color of strong black tea.
Underdone: Caramel is pale gold, barely amber. Still tastes primarily sweet without bitter complexity. Continue cooking. Pale caramel will make the final dish taste flat and sweet.
Perfect: Deep amber — strong tea color. Faint bitter note on tasting. Thin wisps of smoke just beginning. Smells of butterscotch and toasted sugar. Add pork belly immediately, standing back — it will spit violently.
Overdone: Caramel has gone dark brown with acrid smoke. Tastes burnt and bitter. Discard caramel and wipe the pot. Start again — burnt caramel will make the entire braise bitter.
Feel cue: Hold your hand 30 cm above the pot — you should feel distinct radiant heat without touching the surface. At that heat level, the caramelizing sugar will spit and hiss the moment the pork hits it, which is exactly what you want.

Add the pork belly to the hot caramel and toss to coat (stand back — it will spit). Add Shaoxing wine, dark and light soy sauces, star anise, cassia, ginger, and scallion knot. Pour in enough water to just barely cover. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a very low simmer. Cover and braise for 1.5–2 hours, turning the pork every 30 minutes.
Visual cue: Pork cubes in a deep mahogany braising liquid. The fat layers have softened visibly and the skin has relaxed into a glossy, trembling surface.
Underdone: Pork is firm. Chopstick inserted meets resistance. Fat layers are still solid and white. Cover and continue braising. The fat needs time to fully render and the collagen to dissolve.
Perfect: Pork is very tender. Chopstick slides in with almost no resistance. Fat layers are translucent and quivering. Sauce is deep mahogany. Uncover to begin the final glaze reduction.
Overdone: Pork has begun to fall apart. Cubes are losing their shape. Remove pork carefully to a plate and reduce the sauce separately. Reunite for glazing.
Feel cue: Pierce the skin side with a chopstick — it should slide through the fat layers and skin as if through room-temperature butter, meeting only a slight catch at the lean meat below. Two distinct textures in one probe.

Uncover the pot and increase heat to medium-high. Baste the pork continuously with the braising liquid as it reduces and concentrates. Cook for 10–15 minutes, turning the pork gently, until the sauce is thick, glossy, and sticky — it should coat each pork cube in a shiny, lacquered shell. Remove the whole spices, ginger, and scallion knot.
Visual cue: Each pork cube is entirely coated in a mirror-glossy, deep mahogany lacquer. The fat surface is quivering and translucent. Sauce in the pot is thick enough to coat a spoon heavily.
Underdone: Sauce still thin and runs off the pork. Color is medium brown, not deep mahogany. Continue reducing with heat raised, basting every minute. The sugars must concentrate.
Perfect: Deep mahogany lacquer on every cube. Sauce barely moves in the pot. When you tilt a cube, the glaze moves slowly like warm honey. Sweet-soy perfume. Plate and garnish with scallion greens.
Overdone: Sauce has burned and seized. Pork cubes are sticking to the pot. Remove pork immediately. Add a splash of water to the pot and scrape up what you can. The pork will still have great flavor.
Feel cue: Take a piece of the finished pork belly between two fingers and gently press — you should feel the fat layer give and quiver like warm wax, while the skin offers the faintest bite of resistance before yielding completely. If the fat feels solid, it needs more time.

name: Chashu Pork Belly
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。

  Alternatives: skinless pork belly; pork shoulder for a leaner chashu
Soy sauce (regular / shoyu): 15 parts
  Alternatives: tamari for gluten-free
Mirin (hon-mirin): 15 parts
  Alternatives: dry sherry + 1 tsp sugar
Sake (cooking or drinking grade): 15 parts
  Alternatives: dry sherry; dry white wine
White sugar (or light brown sugar): 5 parts
  Alternatives: honey
Green onion / scallion (whole stalks): 3 parts
Fresh ginger (thick slices, unpeeled): 2 parts
Neutral oil (for searing): 2 parts
Water: 10 parts
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 3 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A rolled pork belly tied tight, seared golden, and braised in soy, mirin, sake, and sugar until the fat is trembling and translucent — the canonical ramen topping.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Lay the pork belly skin-side down on a clean board. Roll it tightly from one short end into a compact cylinder, keeping the roll as even in diameter as possible. Tie at 2 cm intervals with butcher's twine — snug but not so tight that it cuts into the fat. The tight roll ensures even slices for ramen, and the twine holds the shape through the braise. If the belly is very thick or the skin tough, score the skin lightly at 1 cm intervals before rolling to help it render and soften evenly.
Visual cue: A compact, neat cylinder of pork belly, tied at even intervals, with the skin forming the outside of the roll and the meat tightly wound within. In cross-section it should look like a neat spiral of alternating meat and fat.
Underdone: The roll is loose and uneven, with gaps between the layers and twine tied haphazardly — it will unravel and cook unevenly during the braise. Untie and re-roll more tightly. Squeeze the roll between both palms as you tie each piece of twine to compress it.
Perfect: A firm, evenly cylindrical roll that holds its shape when you pick it up. The twine sits snug along its length, and the roll feels dense and compact. Proceed to searing immediately, or refrigerate the tied roll uncovered for up to 24 hours to firm up further.
Overdone: The roll has been tied so aggressively that the twine is cutting into the flesh and distorting the shape into an hourglass. Loosen the offending ties slightly. The roll should be snug, not constricting — it needs to expand slightly as the fat renders during cooking.
Feel cue: The rolled belly should feel dense and heavy for its size, with the skin springy and taut under your fingers. When you squeeze it gently, it should not give much — there should be real resistance from the tightly wound layers.

Heat the oil in a heavy pan or Dutch oven over high heat until shimmering. Place the rolled belly in the pan and sear, turning every 2 to 3 minutes with tongs, until every surface including the two flat ends is golden-brown. This takes about 10 to 12 minutes total. The skin side will sputter and contract energetically — use a splatter screen if needed. The Maillard crust built here contributes the roasted, caramelized notes that distinguish chashu from a simple braised pork roll.
Visual cue: The entire outside of the roll — skin, fat, and ends — is evenly golden to deep amber, with a crisp, lightly textured crust. The pan has a coating of golden-brown fond and the kitchen smells of caramelized pork fat.
Underdone: The roll has only been seared on one or two sides and the rest is still raw-white or pale. It went into the braise too quickly. Continue turning and searing until every surface has good color. Do not rush: pale chashu lacks the caramelized depth that makes it distinctive.
Perfect: Deep, even golden-amber all around — no pale patches, no raw-looking fat. The skin has tightened and browned slightly and is starting to blister in places. The fond in the pan is brown, not black. Remove the roll and deglaze the pan with the sake before building the braise liquid.
Overdone: Some sections are dark brown to black and the fond is burning. Acrid smoke rises from the pan. Pull the roll out and immediately deglaze with the sake, scraping up the fond. Trim any truly carbonized patches from the roll before braising.
Feel cue: Listen for the sound of the sear: loud, aggressive spitting from the skin as the fat and moisture volatilize. As the surfaces dry and brown, the sound shifts from a wet hiss to a drier, hollow sizzle. When you hear that shift on each side, it is ready to turn.

Remove the seared roll to a plate. Deglaze the hot pan with the sake, scraping all the fond from the bottom. Add the soy sauce, mirin, sugar, water, scallion stalks, and ginger slices. Stir to dissolve the sugar. Return the roll to the pan — the braising liquid should come about halfway up the roll. Bring to a bare simmer, then cover with a tight-fitting lid or a cartouche of parchment paper. Cook over the lowest heat that maintains a gentle simmer, turning the roll every 30 minutes so all sides have equal time submerged, for 2 to 2.5 hours total.
Visual cue: The braising liquid is a dark, glossy soy-mirin sauce, steadily bubbling at the lowest possible simmer. The roll is basting in the liquid, turning progressively darker as the sugar and soy lacquer onto the surface.
Underdone: After 1 hour, the fat inside the roll is still firm and white when probed with a skewer. The roll has not yet reached the fully yielding stage. Continue braising. The transformation of the fat from opaque and solid to translucent and trembling happens between 1.5 and 2.5 hours depending on the thickness of the belly.
Perfect: After 2 to 2.5 hours, a skewer slides into the center of the roll with no resistance. The fat layers are translucent and jiggly, not opaque. The outside of the roll is dark mahogany and glossy from the braising liquid. The braising liquid has reduced slightly and is thick enough to coat a spoon. Remove the roll and let it cool to room temperature in the braising liquid, then refrigerate overnight.
Overdone: The braising liquid has reduced to a very thick, almost jammy glaze that is beginning to stick and scorch. The roll is falling apart or the twine has loosened from the fat having completely dissolved. Add water to the pan to rescue the sauce, and remove the roll from the heat. The meat is likely very tender — handle with care and proceed directly to chilling.
Feel

cue: After 2 hours, probe the center of the roll with a thin metal skewer. It should slide in and out with no resistance whatsoever — like pushing through cold butter. Hold the skewer against your wrist: it should feel quite warm at the center (indicating the core has reached temperature). If there is any springiness or resistance, give it another 20 minutes.

Allow the chashu to cool in the braising liquid to room temperature, then transfer the roll (still in its braising liquid) to the refrigerator and chill overnight, or at minimum 4 hours. Chilling accomplishes two things: the fat solidifies, making clean slicing possible (warm chashu is too soft to slice neatly), and the roll continues to absorb the braising liquid as it cools, deepening the flavor penetration. The chilled braising liquid will set to a dark, jiggly gel — reserve it as a tare or glaze for other applications.
Visual cue: The chilled chashu roll is a deep mahogany, the surface lacquered and glossy. When sliced cold, each round shows a perfect spiral of dark, caramelized exterior meat and pale-to-translucent fat layers. The braising liquid has gelled around it.
Underdone: The roll is still warm and the fat is too soft to slice cleanly — it smears and squashes rather than cutting in a clean round. Return to the refrigerator for at least 3 more hours. Patience here directly determines the quality of the final slices.
Perfect: Cold, firm, sliceable. Each 1 cm slice cuts cleanly and holds its spiral shape. The fat is set but still trembles slightly when handled — translucent and almost gelatinous rather than white and solid. Slice to desired thickness and reheat in the braising liquid or sear briefly in a hot pan before serving.
Overdone: The roll has chilled so long (more than 3 days) that the fat has begun to dry out and the exterior has lost its gloss and become slightly grey. Remove the twine, re-submerge in the braising liquid, and gently warm to refresh the surface before slicing and serving.
Feel cue: A properly chilled chashu roll feels dense and heavy, with the fat layers set but just barely — press a finger against the surface and it yields slightly before springing back. If it feels completely rigid like refrigerator-cold butter, let it temper at
room temperature for 10 minutes before slicing for cleaner, more even cuts.

To serve, cut the twine with scissors and slice the chilled roll into rounds of 8 to 12 mm thickness. For ramen service, heat a small non-stick or cast-iron pan over medium-high heat until it just begins to smoke. Lay the chashu slices in without oil — they carry enough rendered fat from the braise. Sear for 45 to 60 seconds per side until the edges caramelize and char at the points and the surface takes on a glorious, lacquered char. Alternatively, brush the slices with a little of the gelled braising liquid and briefly torch them or place under a very hot broiler for 60 seconds to lacquer and caramelize the surface.
Visual cue: Each finished chashu slice is a dark, glossy, caramelized round with a char at the edges. The fat is translucent and trembling, the meat dark mahogany. In the bowl it glistens like lacquered wood.
Underdone: The slices are merely warmed through — pale, without any caramelized color on the surface. They look grey rather than lacquered. Return to a hotter pan or give them 30 more seconds under the broiler. Chashu needs surface heat to caramelize and lacquer, not just warmth.
Perfect: Deep mahogany edges with points of char, a glossy, lacquered surface, and a fat layer that is translucent and quivering. The aroma is of soy-caramel and roasted pork. Placed in a ramen bowl, it causes the broth to bloom with a trail of golden pork fat. Place immediately in the ramen bowl, or serve as a donburi topping with steamed rice and a drizzle of braising liquid tare.
Overdone: The slices are uniformly black, the fat has rendered out completely, and the meat is dry and chalky. The sugar in the braising liquid has burned to bitterness. Trim the carbonized surfaces. The interior may still be edible — serve with extra braising liquid on the side to add moisture.
Feel cue: A perfect chashu slice, held between chopsticks, should feel heavy with its own fat,

barely holding together. The fat layer should look almost translucent when held against the light — like amber. When you eat it, the fat should dissolve instantly on the tongue, rich but not heavy, followed by the deep, sweet soy-mirin char of the meat.

name: Pork Belly Confit
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: duck legs for classic confit

  Alternatives: kosher salt

  Alternatives: brown sugar

Fresh thyme sprigs: 5 sprigs
  Alternatives: dried thyme (1 tsp)
Bay leaves: 3 whole
Black peppercorns, lightly crushed: 1 tsp
Juniper berries, lightly crushed: 0.5 tsp
Rendered pork fat or duck fat: 1000 g
  Alternatives: a mix of lard and vegetable oil
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 18 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Skin-on pork belly cured overnight in salt and aromatics, then slow-cooked submerged in its own rendered fat until the collagen surrenders completely — pressed flat overnight and finished with a skin so crisp it shatters like a pane of amber glass.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Rendered pork fat or duck fat

steps:
Mix together the salt, sugar, lightly crushed garlic, thyme, bay leaves, cracked peppercorns, and juniper berries in a small bowl. Score the skin of the pork belly in a crosshatch pattern with a sharp knife or Stanley blade — cuts 1 cm apart, through the skin and just into the fat layer but not reaching the meat. This scoring promotes even crackling later. Rub the cure mixture thoroughly over every surface of the belly, working it into the score cuts and pressing the aromatics firmly into the flesh. Place skin-side up on a wire rack set over a tray, cover loosely with cling wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8-12 hours).
Visual cue: Belly coated in an even white-grey cure crust. Score lines visible through the cure. Tray beneath shows a small amount of drawn-out pink brine by morning.
Underdone: Less than 4 hours of curing. Little or no brine at the base of the tray. The salt has not drawn moisture and begun to cycle back in as a concentrated brine. Return to the fridge. Overnight is necessary for the cure to penetrate through the fat to the meat layers.
Perfect: After 8-12 hours. The tray has a visible pool of pink brine. The cure has partially dissolved. The skin feels slightly tacky and firm. Rinse the belly under cold water, pat bone-dry with paper towels, and proceed.
Overdone: More than 24 hours. Belly is overly salty and the texture of the meat at the edges is dense and slightly translucent — beginning to cure rather than just season. Soak in cold water for 30 minutes to draw out some excess salt before continuing.
Feel cue: After curing, the belly feels noticeably firmer to the touch than raw — the salt has tightened the protein structure slightly and the skin has taken on a dry, papery texture.

Preheat the oven to 90°C (195°F). Melt the pork fat in a deep roasting dish or Dutch oven large enough to hold the belly. Place the belly skin-side down, pour in enough warm fat to completely submerge it — the fat should cover the belly by at least 1 cm. Place a piece of parchment over the surface and then the lid or tight foil. Transfer to the oven and cook for 6-8 hours. Do not rush this with higher heat. At 90°C, the collagen in the connective tissue and skin gradually converts to gelatin without ever forcing the fat to fry — the distinction between confit and poaching in fat.
Visual cue: The belly has turned from pale pink to an opaque, ivory-cream color throughout. Surrounded by gently trembling, clear fat — not bubbling or frying. A thin probe inserted into the meat meets almost no resistance.
Underdone: Interior temperature below 70°C. Meat is still slightly pink at center. A skewer meets firm resistance. The connective tissue between fat layers has not softened. Continue confiting. At 90°C you cannot overcook the exterior while the center slowly comes up. Check at 7 hours, then again at 8.
Perfect: After 6-8 hours, the belly is completely ivory and tender. A thin wooden skewer slides through every layer — meat, fat, and between — with no resistance. The skin is translucent and gelatinous. Lift carefully from the fat and proceed to pressing.
Overdone: Fat was too hot (above 110°C). The belly has fried slightly — exterior is yellowed and the fat layers have begun to render out excessively. Press and chill as normal. The crackling step will still work — in fact a slightly drier belly crisps more readily.
Feel cue: After 7 hours, press the back of a spoon against the meat side — it should yield with almost no pressure, sinking gently like pressing into cold butter, each layer distinct but utterly tender.

Line a small baking dish or loaf tin with cling wrap, leaving an overhang on all sides. Lift the belly from the fat and place it skin-side down in the lined tin. Fold the cling wrap over the top. Place another baking sheet directly on the cling wrap and weigh it down with heavy cans — at least 2 kg of weight. Refrigerate for a minimum of 6 hours, ideally overnight. The pressing compacts the belly into a uniform slab for clean portioning and forces the fat and gelatin to redistribute evenly throughout.
Visual cue: After pressing, the belly has become a compact, even-thickness slab. The skin is smooth and flat on the bottom. Cross-section shows defined, even layers of skin, fat, and meat.
Underdone: Less than 4 hours of pressing. The belly is still rounded and uneven. The layers have not set firmly. Return to the fridge with the weight. The setting happens as the gelatin firms in the cold.
Perfect: A clean, rectangular slab that holds its shape when unmoulded. Layers are clearly defined. The skin is tight and smooth on the underside. Unmould, peel off cling wrap, and portion into squares or rectangles with a sharp knife.
Overdone: Not possible to over-press. More pressing time only improves the result. Proceed at your convenience — the pressed belly keeps refrigerated for up to 3 days before the final sear.
Feel cue: The pressed slab should feel cold, dense, and uniform under your palm — like a block of cold butter rather than yielding meat, the gelatin and fat having fully set.

Portion the pressed belly into individual serving pieces (typically 5-6 cm squares). Place a heavy oven-safe skillet — cast iron ideal — over medium-low heat. Do not add fat; the belly itself will render immediately. Place the portions skin-side down, pressing firmly with a spatula. Cook over medium-low heat for 12-18 minutes without moving — patience here is essential. The fat will slowly render and the skin will progressively crisp and turn translucent amber. It should crackle like glass underfoot when tapped with a spoon. Flip for the final 2 minutes to lightly colour the meat side.
Visual cue: The skin has transformed from gelatinous and pale to a deep amber, blistered, and puffed surface. When tapped with a spoon it rings and resists — it should shatter when bitten.
Underdone: Skin is still pale and slightly tacky. Makes a soft, yielding sound when pressed. Has not reached the shattering stage. Continue on medium-low heat. Do not increase heat — rushing the render causes the fat to fry before the water escapes the skin, making rubbery crackling instead of glass.
Perfect: Deep amber-gold, dramatically blistered skin that makes an audible tap-tap when pressed with a spoon. The pan is full of rendered lard. Meat side is warm and glistening. Remove and blot the skin surface with a paper towel. Serve immediately — crackling degrades within minutes in humid air.
Overdone: Skin has crossed from amber to dark brown. Smaller pieces may be beginning to char. Smells of burnt fat. Remove immediately. The skin is likely still delicious — the Maillard reaction on pig skin is forgiving — but do not let it go further.
Feel cue: Press the skin with the flat of a spoon during searing — the resistance increases minute by minute from soft and giving, to springy, to the final glass-hard tap that tells you it is done.

name: Chashu Pork Belly
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Pork belly slab, skin-on, 600–800 g: 700 g
  Alternatives: skinless pork belly; pork shoulder (less fat layers but works)
Soy sauce: 80 ml
  Alternatives: tamari; dark soy sauce (use 50 ml — much more intense)
Mirin (hon-mirin preferred): 60 ml
  Alternatives: sweet rice wine; dry sherry + 1 tsp sugar
Sake: 60 ml
  Alternatives: dry sherry; Chinese Shaoxing rice wine
White sugar: 20 g
  Alternatives: brown sugar; honey
Water: 200 ml
  Alternatives: chicken stock (richer)
Scallions, roughly cut in 5 cm sections: 3 pcs
  Alternatives: leek, white part
Fresh ginger slices, unpeeled, 5 mm: 30 g
  Alternatives: ground ginger (5 g, less fresh)
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 4 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Rolled and tied pork belly braised in soy, mirin, sake, and sugar until lacquered, sliceable, and deeply caramel-sweet — the ramen topper that makes the bowl.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: 葱（Scallions, roughly cut in 5 cm sections）

steps:
Lay the pork belly flat, skin-side down. Starting from the shorter end, roll the belly tightly into a compact cylinder, trapping as many fat-to-meat layers as possible within the roll. Tie at 2–3 cm intervals with butcher's twine, pulling each loop firmly so the roll holds its circular cross-section during cooking. A loose roll will unravel and produce uneven slices. The goal is a tight, even cylinder that will hold its shape through 3 hours of braising.
Visual cue: A tight, even cylinder of pork belly, skin wrapped to the outside, held by evenly spaced loops of twine. No fat or skin visible at the ends.
Underdone: Roll is loose and oval in cross-section. Skin gap visible at one end. Twine loops spaced too far apart. Untie and re-roll more tightly. Add twine loops every 2 cm. Start the roll from the opposite end for a tighter core.
Perfect: A firm, even cylinder with the skin forming a smooth exterior. Each twine loop slightly compressed. Cross-section shows concentric layers of fat and meat. Sear immediately while the roll is cold and firm.
Overdone: Tied so tightly the skin is splitting and the fat layers are squeezing out the ends. Loosen 2–3 loops at the tightest points — a little give is fine. The roll will firm up during braising.
Feel cue: Grip the roll and squeeze gently — it should feel dense and unyielding, like a cold cylinder of butter. If it flattens under your grip or the layers separate, it is not tight enough.

Heat a Dutch oven or heavy pot over medium-high heat with no oil — the belly's own exterior fat will render immediately. Place the roll in and sear, turning with tongs every 90 seconds, until all sides are evenly golden-brown, including the flat cut ends. This sear builds the Maillard flavor base that enriches the braising liquid and creates the lacquered exterior. Total searing time: 8–10 minutes.
Visual cue: Even golden-brown on all surfaces, including both flat ends. The skin side should be the deepest color — near caramel.
Underdone: Pale gold on only one or two sides. The skin is still white and flabby in places. Rendered fat in the pan but no Maillard browning. Continue rotating — every side needs direct contact with the hot pan base for at least 90 seconds.
Perfect: Uniform deep gold-to-caramel across all sides. The skin has tightened and is just beginning to crisp. Pan base has a layer of golden-brown fond. Remove the roll to a plate while you build the braising liquid in the same pot.
Overdone: Skin has browned to very dark brown on one side; fat pooling and smoking. Reduce heat and continue rotating more frequently. Dark skin color will still produce good results — the exterior flavors the braise.
Feel cue: The outside of the seared roll should feel firm, slightly tacky from the rendered fat, and warm throughout. The skin side should feel tight and papery-dry under your fingertip.

Pour the sake into the hot pot and bring to a boil, scraping up the fond from the bottom. Add soy sauce, mirin, sugar, water, scallion, and ginger. Return the pork roll to the pot — the liquid should come about two-thirds of the way up the roll. Bring to a very gentle simmer (90°C, barely bubbling — large bubbles will cause the roll to turn tough and the skin to contract unevenly). Cover and braise for 2.5–3 hours, turning the roll every 45 minutes so all sides spend time submerged. The liquid will reduce and deepen.
Visual cue: After 3 hours: the roll is dark mahogany-brown all over, sitting in a glossy, reduced, syrup-like braising liquid. The twine is cutting slightly into the swollen, tender flesh.
Underdone: Roll still has some spring when pressed. Braising liquid still thin and light amber. Internal temperature below 85°C. Continue braising. Check that the liquid is at a bare simmer, not a boil — boiling toughens the collagen.
Perfect: Roll yields completely with gentle pressure — feels like braised collagen all the way through. Braising liquid has reduced to a dark, glossy, almost syrupy consistency. Mahogany-brown exterior. Remove from heat. Cool the roll in the braising liquid to room temperature, then refrigerate.
Overdone: Roll has partially unrolled in the pot. Exterior is very dark and the liquid has reduced to a sticky paste on the pan bottom. Remove the roll carefully, add 50 ml water to deglaze the remaining glaze. Cool and refrigerate both.
Feel cue: Press the center of the roll through the pot lid gap — it should feel like pressing into firm gelatin: yielding, gelatinous, giving without bouncing back. The collagen has fully converted.

The key: refrigerate the chashu roll in its braising liquid overnight before slicing. Cold fat and gelatin give the roll structural integrity — room-temperature chashu collapses under the knife. Remove from the liquid (reserve the liquid: it becomes your tare for ramen). Remove all twine. Using a very sharp, thin-bladed knife, slice rounds 1.5–2 cm thick in a single confident stroke — no sawing. For ramen, sear each cold slice in a screaming-hot dry pan for 30 seconds per side to reheat and caramelize the glaze before placing in the bowl.
Visual cue: Perfect rounds of alternating fat-and-meat layers, each slice a mahogany exterior transitioning to ivory-pink center. The gelatin layer is visible as a translucent ring just inside the skin.
Underdone: Sliced while warm — roll has compressed and deformed under the knife. Fat layers are smearing rather than cutting cleanly. Chill the remaining roll at least 2 hours before continuing to slice.
Perfect: Clean, even rounds. Fat layers bright white against pink-mahogany meat. Each slice holds its circular shape without falling apart. Reheat slices in a hot pan for 30 seconds per side immediately before serving in ramen.
Overdone: Sliced too thin — rounds are falling apart and the gelatin layer is crumbling. For ramen, crumbled chashu is still delicious; just arrange the pieces rather than placing whole rounds.
Feel cue: A properly chilled slice should feel like firm, cold butter — it should hold its shape when picked up with chopsticks but yield immediately on the tongue. The fat should feel smooth and waxy-cold, not greasy or liquid.

name: Pork Bone Broth
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Pork neck bones or knuckles (split): 50 parts
  Alternatives: pork spare ribs; pork trotters
Pork back ribs (for gelatin): 20 parts
Cold water: 100 parts
Fresh ginger (thick slices, unpeeled): 5 parts
Spring onion / scallion (whole): 3 parts
Shaoxing rice wine: 4 parts
  Alternatives: dry sherry
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 5 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A Cantonese broth of crystalline clarity and extraordinary depth, achieved by blancing bones meticulously and simmering at the precise point where convection lifts collagen but never clouds the liquid — the restraint is the technique.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Place all bones in a large pot and cover with cold water. Bring to a full boil over high heat and boil vigorously for 5 minutes. You will see large quantities of grey scum (blood proteins and impurities) accumulate on the surface. Drain the bones and rinse each one individually under cold running water, removing all grey deposits. Also scrub the pot clean. This blanching step is the single most important technique for achieving clear, clean-tasting Cantonese broth — skipping it results in murky, gamy-smelling stock.
Visual cue: After blanching and rinsing, bones should be visibly clean and slightly pink with no grey-brown deposits clinging to them.
Underdone: Bones still have grey-brown scum attached. The boil did not last long enough to fully purge the blood proteins. Boil another 3–5 minutes and rinse thoroughly again.
Perfect: Clean, pinkish-white bones. No visible scum. Boiling water was grey and murky — that murk is now discarded. Bones smell clean and faintly porky. Transfer to a clean pot and begin the long, slow simmer.
Overdone: Bones boiled too long in the blanch (15+ minutes) — some collagen has already released into the murky water. Rinse well and proceed. The broth will still be excellent.
Feel cue: Run your fingers along a blanched, rinsed bone — it should feel smooth and clean, with no sticky or slippery deposits. The bone surface should feel almost chalky in spots where the marrow has started to melt out.

Return the rinsed bones to the clean pot. Cover with fresh cold water and bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. As it approaches simmer, skim any remaining foam from the surface. Add ginger slices, whole scallions, and Shaoxing wine. Reduce to the lowest possible simmer — the surface should show lazy ripples and occasional bubbles at the edges, but never a rolling boil. A boiling stock becomes cloudy; a simmering stock stays clear. Maintain this temperature for 3.5–4 hours.
Visual cue: A golden-amber broth with lazy surface ripples and edge-only bubble activity. The liquid should be increasingly golden and translucent, never grey or murky.
Underdone: Broth is still very pale and thin at 2 hours. Flavor is light and watery. Gelatin not yet extracted. Continue simmering. Pork collagen needs minimum 3 hours at a gentle simmer.
Perfect: Golden amber, clear or near-clear. Lazy surface movement only. Tastes deeply porky and round. When a small amount is cooled on a spoon and refrigerated, it sets to a light jelly. Strain and season.
Overdone: Broth has been boiling rather than simmering — it is grey and murky. Or simmered so long it has reduced by more than half. Strain immediately. The flavor will be good even if the clarity is gone. Use for braising rather than clear soups.
Feel cue: After 3 hours of proper simmering, the broth should smell like concentrated, sweet pork — a clean, almost caramel-like umami aroma with the ginger providing a warm green note. No gaminess, no liver-like odors. If it smells gamy, the blanching was insufficient.

Remove the bones with tongs and discard. Line a fine-mesh strainer with a single layer of cheesecloth. Strain the broth slowly, without pressing. Allow to cool slightly, then refrigerate uncovered for 1–2 hours until the fat solidifies on the surface as a cream-colored cap. Remove the solidified fat layer. The broth beneath should be clear, golden, and slightly gelatinous when cold. Season with salt only at the point of use, never in the base stock.
Visual cue: After defatting, the chilled broth should be clear and golden, with a slight wobble when the container is shaken — indicating adequate gelatin content.
Underdone: Broth is thin and watery when cold — does not gel. Color is pale. Flavor is light. Insufficient collagen was extracted. Return to the pot and simmer an additional hour. Add a split pig's foot if available for gelatin boost.
Perfect: Clear, golden broth. Gels to a soft jello when cold — holds its shape when spooned but melts immediately when warmed. Tastes clean, deep, and savory. Store up to 5 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen.
Overdone: Broth gels into a very firm, dense block when cold. Very concentrated. This is a bonus — dilute 1:1 with water when using. It is essentially a demi-glace.
Feel cue: Spoon a small amount of the chilled, set broth — it should tremble like firm gelatin when the spoon is shaken and melt immediately on contact with your warm tongue. A broth with good gelatin feels silky and rich rather than watery, coating the inside of your mouth with a pleasant, lingering savory weight.

name: 墨西哥慢炖猪肉 · Pork Carnitas
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: pork leg; pork picnic shoulder

  Alternatives: 1/2 orange + 1 lime

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Michoacán's definitive taco filling — pork shoulder braised slowly in its own rendered lard with orange, cinnamon, bay, and garlic until meltingly tender, then fried in that same fat until the edges shatter into mahogany-brown crackle while the center stays irresistibly juicy.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Pork shoulder (boston butt, cut into large 6cm chunks)
橙子（Orange (1 large — halved, juice squeezed, shells reserved)）
Mexican cinnamon stick (canela, one small piece)

steps:
Pat the pork chunks thoroughly dry with paper towels — surface moisture is the enemy of both rendering and browning. Toss generously with the salt until every surface carries a visible, even coating. Leave at room temperature for 20 minutes while you gather the aromatics. The salt draws the barest trace of moisture to the surface, then the surface dries: this tack helps the lard cling and the seasonings penetrate.
Visual cue: Pork pieces look matte and dry, salt evenly distributed, each piece roughly the same size to ensure even cooking.
Underdone: Pieces are visibly wet and the salt is sliding off rather than dissolving into the surface. Pat more thoroughly and wait — surface moisture must be removed before proceeding.
Perfect: Tacky and dry, with fine salt crystals just beginning to dissolve into a slight sheen. All pieces uniform in size. Transfer to the wide heavy pot with the lard.
Overdone: Sat too long, surface looks grayish and dehydrated with a small puddle of liquid in the bowl. Drain off any liquid, pat dry, and proceed — the result will still be fine.
Feel cue: The meat should feel sticky and slightly grippy, not slippery. A faint, clean pork smell — nothing sour, nothing sharp.

Nestle the pork chunks in a single layer in a heavy wide pot or Dutch oven. Add the lard, then squeeze the orange juice over the top and drop in the spent orange shell halves. Tuck in the onion, garlic, bay leaves, and cinnamon stick. Add just enough cold water to come level with the top of the meat — the water will cook off first, and when it does, the lard takes over. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered on the lowest heat, never letting it boil, for 1.5 to 2 hours. The water gradually evaporates over the first hour; the pork then quietly poaches in clear lard for the second hour until fork-tender.
Visual cue: After the water has cooked away, the liquid in the pot has turned from milky and cloudy to crystal-clear golden fat, with lazy oily bubbles drifting up around tender, pale pork.
Underdone: Liquid is still cloudy and watery, bubbling actively; a fork meets firm resistance in the meat. Keep the heat low and patient — the water must fully evaporate before the pork is done. Hard boiling toughens the meat.
Perfect: Clear, golden lard, slow oily bubbles, orange and bay perfuming the kitchen. A fork sinks into a chunk with no resistance and the piece holds together but yields completely. Raise the heat to fry — the critical final stage.
Overdone: The water cooked off before the pork was tender; pieces are browning in dry lard before the connective tissue fully broke down. Add a splash of water to reset, lower heat, and continue braising covered.
Feel cue: Early on the pot sounds like a steady watery simmer; as the water leaves, that sound gradually shifts to the quieter, deeper crackle of fat frying. That audible transition is your signal to watch closely.

Once the water is fully gone and the pork sits in clear lard, raise the heat to medium-high. If using condensed milk, drizzle it in now and stir — the trace of dairy sugar accelerates browning in the authentic Michoacán way. Cook, turning the pieces only every 3 to 4 minutes, until deeply browned and crisp at all the exposed edges and high points. The fat will bubble vigorously around the pieces. Resist the urge to stir constantly — extended contact between meat and hot metal is what builds the crust. Total frying time 8 to 15 minutes.
Visual cue: Edges and angular surfaces of each chunk are deep mahogany-brown and visibly crisp, crackling when tapped with a spoon; the interior stays glistening and juicy.
Underdone: Meat looks pale and soft, boiled-looking, with no browning; it releases little aroma. Raise the heat and stop stirring — the pieces need sustained contact with the hot surface.
Perfect: Burnished, crackling edges; a piece pressed with the back of a spoon yields softly in the center. The kitchen smells of caramelized pork fat and orange. Lift with a slotted spoon, draining fat back into the pot, and transfer to a board.
Overdone: Uniformly dark-brown and hard throughout; the fat smells scorched; pieces crumble rather than shred. Remove immediately; chop fine and mix with any still-juicy pieces. Even overcooked carnitas fold into good tacos.
Feel cue: Tap a piece with the back of a spoon — a perfect piece of carnitas sounds crisp but gives: like tapping a well-done crouton that still has a soft interior. The lard should smell nutty and sweet, never acrid.

Transfer the carnitas to a large cutting board and let them rest 5 minutes. The resting is important — the residual heat finishes any remaining pink interior, and the crust sets rather than steaming back soft. Using two forks or your fingers, roughly pull and chop each piece into a mix of large crispy shards and tender shreds. Spoon a tablespoon of the warm reserved lard back over the top to gloss them. Taste and season with a pinch of flaky salt and a squeeze of fresh lime. Serve immediately on warm corn tortillas with white onion, cilantro, lime, and your salsa of choice.
Visual cue: A craggy, textured tangle of golden-mahogany shards and juicy shreds, slicked with rendered fat, looking like the best thing on any taco menu.
Underdone: Mostly soft shreds, few crisp edges, pale and a little greasy-looking rather than caramelized. Return to the hot fat for 2 to 3 more minutes before shredding.
Perfect: Mixed textures throughout: crisp, mahogany edges contrasted with juicy, tender shreds; savory-sweet with a citrus backnote. Pile into warm tortillas and serve at once — carnitas are best in the first 15 minutes.
Overdone: Dry and crumbly with no juicy interior; falls to dust rather than tearing into fibers. Toss with a splash of orange juice and a spoonful of warm lard to revive some moisture and gloss.
Feel cue: The finished carnitas should feel rich but clean — the fat coating your fingers but not leaving a heavy grease. Each bite should give both the snap of a crust and the yielding comfort of braised meat: that duality is the whole point.

ingredients.name: Bone-in pork rib chops, about 2.5 cm (1 inch) thick
Firm, tart-sweet apples (such as Honeycrisp or Pink Lady), cored and cut into 1 cm wedges
Green cabbage, cored and thinly sliced

steps:
Pat the chops dry. If there is a thick fat cap, slash it every 2–3 cm to keep the chops from curling. Season generously on all sides with about 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt total and pepper. Let stand at room temperature 10–15 minutes while you slice the apples, cabbage and shallot.
Visual cue: Chops evenly coated in salt, surfaces starting to look slightly damp as the salt draws moisture then begins to dissolve.
Underdone: Salt sitting in dry, visible crystals, surface bone-dry, straight from the fridge. Let them stand the full 10–15 minutes.
Perfect: Salt mostly dissolved into a faint sheen on the surface. Blot away any beads of moisture right before searing.
Overdone: Puddles of liquid under the chops. Pat thoroughly dry — wet surfaces will not brown.
Feel cue: The surface should feel slightly tacky under a fingertip, not wet.

Heat the oil in a 12-inch (30 cm) heavy skillet (cast iron or stainless) over medium-high heat until it just smokes. Lay the chops in, pressing lightly so they make full contact, and sear without moving 4–5 minutes until deeply browned. Flip, reduce the heat to medium, and cook 3–5 minutes more, turning once more if needed, until an instant-read thermometer inserted near (not touching) the bone reads 140°F (60°C). Stand the chops on their fat edges for the last minute to render it. Transfer to a plate and rest 5 minutes; carryover heat brings them to the USDA-safe 145°F (63°C).
Visual cue: A deep golden-brown crust on both faces, fat edge rendered and crisp; juices pooling lightly on the resting plate.
Underdone: Crust only lightly tan; thermometer below 135°F (57°C) near the bone. Keep cooking over medium, flipping every minute, and recheck.
Perfect: Burnished crust, 140°F (60°C) at the pull rising to 145°F (63°C) after resting; center pale pink and juicy when cut. Rest while you cook the apples and cabbage in the same pan.
Overdone: Chops read above 155°F (68°C), feel stiff, and the pan fond is blackening. Slice thinly and serve with extra sauce; wipe out any black fond before continuing.
Feel cue: Press the thickest part: a properly cooked chop feels like the fleshy base of your thumb when you touch thumb to middle finger — resilient, not squishy or rock-hard.

Pour off all but about 1 tbsp fat from the skillet. Over medium-high heat, add the apple wedges in a single layer and cook 2 minutes per side until caramelized at the edges. Add the shallot, cabbage and a pinch of salt and cook, tossing, 4–5 minutes until the cabbage is wilted and browned in spots but still has some bite.
Visual cue: Apple wedges golden on their cut faces and holding their shape; cabbage slumped and flecked with brown.
Underdone: Apples pale and crisp, cabbage stiff and squeaky. Give it 1–2 more minutes, tossing occasionally.
Perfect: Apples tender at the edges but intact, cabbage soft with a gentle crunch and caramelized patches. Deglaze for the sauce.
Overdone: Apples collapsing into sauce, cabbage limp and scorched. Proceed — it becomes more of a compote, which still pairs well.
Feel cue: A wedge of apple should yield to a fork at the edge but resist at the center, like a just-baked tart filling.

Pour in the cider and stock, add the thyme sprigs, and scrape up the browned bits. Boil 4–5 minutes until reduced by about half. Reduce the heat to low, stir in the mustard and the resting juices from the chops, then swirl in the cold butter a piece at a time until glossy. Stir in the cider vinegar, discard the thyme stems, and season. Return the chops to the pan for 30 seconds to warm, spooning sauce over them, and serve over the apples and cabbage.
Visual cue: A glossy, amber sauce with visible mustard seeds, coating the apples and clinging to the chops.
Underdone: Sauce thin and watery, running straight off the spoon; taste is sweet and flat. Keep boiling another 1–2 minutes before adding the butter.
Perfect: Sauce coats a spoon lightly and looks satiny; sweet-tart and sharp from the mustard. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Sauce reduced to a sticky syrup or the butter has broken into greasy beads. Whisk in 2–3 tbsp water off the heat to bring it back together.
Feel cue: Taste the sauce on a spoon: sweet from the cider first, then a nose-tingling mustard sharpness and a clean vinegar finish.

name: Wiener Schnitzel
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Pork loin cutlets (180–200g each): 4 cutlets
  Alternatives: veal leg cutlets (the original); chicken breast, butterflied
All-purpose flour: 100 g
Eggs, lightly beaten with a fork (not whisked): 3 large
Fine, dry white breadcrumbs (not panko): 150 g
  Alternatives: fine panko (produces a coarser crust)
Clarified butter or lard: 300 ml
  Alternatives: a mix of clarified butter and neutral oil
Fine sea salt: 6 g
White pepper, freshly ground: 2 g
  Alternatives: black pepper
Lemon wedges, for serving: 2 wedges
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 40 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Pork loin pounded thin as a page, encased in three precise coats of flour, egg, and breadcrumb, then fried in a deep wave of clarified butter until the crust billows away from the meat in a golden, gossamer shell that crackles on the first cut.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: 鸡蛋（Eggs, lightly beaten with a fork (not whisked)）

steps:
Place a cutlet between two sheets of plastic wrap or inside a zip-lock bag. Using a meat mallet or the bottom of a heavy pan, pound the meat to an even 3mm thickness with firm, outward strokes — starting from the center and sweeping toward the edges to stretch rather than tear the meat. A properly pounded schnitzel should be uniformly thin across its entire surface, with no thick center or torn holes. Season both sides with salt and white pepper, then let rest for 5 minutes at room temperature so the salt begins to draw moisture to the surface.
Visual cue: A very thin, near-transparent veil of pork — the same thickness as a pound coin across its entire width. The grain of the meat should have visibly elongated from the pounding.
Underdone: Cutlet still has a thick center and thinner edges. The pork springs back noticeably when pressed. Pound the thick areas with direct, firm blows. Work the mallet outward from the center. A 3mm cutlet should not spring back at all.
Perfect: Uniform thickness across the entire surface. Semi-translucent at the thinnest points. Lies completely flat with no curl or spring. Season both sides and let rest 5 minutes before breading.
Overdone: Cutlet has holes or tears from over-pounding. The edges have separated from the meat. Patch tears by pressing the edges back together. The breading will hold small tears together during frying.
Feel cue: The pounded cutlet should feel like a damp chamois cloth when held — supple and yielding, with almost no spring or thickness. Fold a corner over itself: it should drape, not fold with resistance.

Set up three separate wide dishes: flour in the first, beaten eggs in the second, breadcrumbs in the third. Working one cutlet at a time: first dredge in flour, pressing to adhere and shaking off every grain of excess — you want a ghostly, light dusting, not a thick coat. Dip immediately into the egg, allowing the excess to drip off for 3 seconds. Lay in the breadcrumbs and, critically, do NOT press the crumbs into the meat — scatter them over the top, and shake the tray to set them. This loose, unpressed crumb is what allows the crust to soufflé away from the meat in the fat, creating the billowing effect.
Visual cue: A lightly, evenly coated cutlet with crumbs adhering loosely all over. The surface looks matte and irregular — not smooth or tightly pressed. Crumbs should not clump.
Underdone: Bare patches of egg showing through where crumbs didn't adhere. Parts of the meat are visible through the coating. Sprinkle crumbs over the bare spots and shake the tray gently. Do not press — that undoes the loose coating.
Perfect: Uniform loose crumb coat. Slightly irregular surface. No bare patches and no areas where the crumb has been pressed into a dense layer. Fry within 5 minutes. Do not refrigerate — a cold, compressed crust will not soufflé.
Overdone: Crumbs have been pressed firmly into the egg — the surface looks smooth, dense, and compact. The schnitzel will still fry fine but the crust will be stuck tightly to the meat rather than billowing. Taste is unaffected.
Feel cue: Pick up a breaded cutlet and hold it horizontal — the crumbs should stay in place but feel loosely attached, not anchored. A gentle shake should make a few crumbs drift off. That fragility is what produces the famous crust.

Pour clarified butter into a wide pan to a depth of 8–10mm. Heat to 160–170°C — test with a breadcrumb: it should sizzle immediately and turn golden in 30 seconds. Slide in the breaded cutlet. Immediately begin spooning hot butter over the top of the cutlet in a continuous stream while gently moving the pan to keep the fat agitated. This constant basting and movement is how the crust inflates. Fry 2–3 minutes per side until deep golden-amber. Never crowd the pan — fry one cutlet at a time if necessary. Remove to a wire rack (never paper) to drain.
Visual cue: A golden-amber schnitzel with a visibly inflated, rippled crust that has detached from the meat surface in places — it looks like a crinkled golden map rather than a flat slab of breading.
Underdone: Pale gold, flat crust still touching the meat uniformly. Fat may not have been hot enough. The crust is soft rather than set. Increase heat and continue frying with constant basting. The temperature was too low — 160°C minimum is essential.
Perfect: Deep golden-amber, rippled, billowing crust with visible air pockets between the crumb and the meat. The schnitzel has inflated noticeably. Sounds hollow when tapped. Drain on a wire rack and season immediately with a pinch of salt. Serve within 2 minutes.
Overdone: Dark brown crust with some charred spots. Crust has contracted back against the meat from over-frying. The cutlet inside is still good — the outside will taste somewhat bitter. Avoid this by using a thermometer.
Feel cue: Gently press the crust with the back of a spatula — it should resist and spring back, like pressing a crisp autumn leaf. Any softness means more time in the fat. Listen: the sizzle should be a steady, vigorous hiss throughout — anything weaker means the fat has cooled.

Transfer immediately to warmed plates — schnitzel waits for no one and softens within minutes. Place one lemon wedge alongside, not squeezed over. Serve with potato salad, parsley potatoes, or lingonberry jam. The lemon is squeezed at the table by the diner, and only directly over their portion. Schnitzel eaten 10 minutes after frying is a different, lesser dish — time it to the moment the plates hit the table.
Visual cue: A golden-amber, crackling schnitzel on a warm plate with a bright yellow lemon wedge. The crust should be dry and rippled — not glistening with fat.
Underdone: Schnitzel is sitting in a pool of fat on the plate, and the crust is already softening from steam. Drain on a wire rack, not paper, for 30 seconds before plating. Paper traps steam and destroys the crust.
Perfect: Dry, crackly crust. The plate shows no pool of fat. A squeeze of lemon causes an immediate sizzle as the acid hits the hot crust. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Schnitzel has been held too long — the crust has gone soft and the meat inside has dried out. The breading looks pale and steamy. Serve immediately regardless — there is no recovery from a held schnitzel, only speed going forward.
Feel cue: Cut the schnitzel with a knife: the crust should shatter with a clean crack before the knife reaches the meat beneath. If it compresses and squashes rather than cracks, the crust was never crisp to begin with.

name: Pan-Seared Roasted Pork Tenderloin
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Pork tenderloin (silver skin removed): 600 g
Kosher salt: 8 g
  Alternatives: fine sea salt (use half the weight)
Black pepper, coarsely ground: 4 g
Smoked paprika: 4 g
  Alternatives: regular paprika
Garlic powder: 3 g
Neutral high-smoke-point oil (avocado or grapeseed): 20 g
  Alternatives: clarified butter
Unsalted butter: 30 g
Fresh thyme sprigs and rosemary: 10 g
  Alternatives: fresh sage
Garlic cloves, crushed: 15 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The most forgiving of the lean cuts — seared in a searing hot pan until mahogany on all sides, finished in a hot oven, then rested until the juices redistribute into a blush-pink, impossibly tender centre.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Remove the silver skin: slide the tip of a thin knife under the silver membrane and angle the blade slightly upward, sawing forward while pulling the skin taut with your other hand. It should come off in one or two strips. Pat the tenderloin completely dry. Combine salt, pepper, smoked paprika, and garlic powder and rub evenly over every surface. Rest uncovered at room temperature for 20 minutes.
Visual cue: The tenderloin is a uniform rose-red, evenly dusted in a rust-coloured spice rub with no silver membrane remaining and no bare patches of seasoning.
Underdone: Silver skin still present — visible as a shiny, whitish, translucent strip along the top. Patchy seasoning. Remove the silver skin first — it will tighten during cooking and cause the tenderloin to curl and cook unevenly.
Perfect: Completely trimmed, uniformly seasoned in a rust-red crust, surface dry to the touch. The spice fragrance is immediate. Rest 20 minutes at room temperature while you preheat the oven and pan.
Overdone: Salted too far in advance (over 2 hours at room temperature). Surface looks damp and discoloured. Pat dry once more before searing. The surface moisture will cause the crust to steam rather than sear.
Feel cue: Run your finger along the top of the tenderloin — no ridges, no slick spots. The surface should feel dry and slightly gritty from the spice rub.

Preheat the oven to 220 C (425 F). Heat an oven-safe skillet (cast iron preferred) over high heat for 3 minutes until screaming hot. Add the oil — it should shimmer immediately. Sear the tenderloin for 90 seconds per face, rotating through all four broad faces until every surface is mahogany brown. Use tongs and apply firm downward pressure to maximise contact.
Visual cue: A uniform mahogany-brown crust covering every face of the tenderloin, with no grey or pale patches remaining. The spice crust is caramelised and fragrant.
Underdone: Colour is pale tan or grey rather than mahogany. Meat is still releasing moisture and steaming. Increase heat and wait. The spice rub needs high, dry heat to caramelise. Do not flip until the meat releases cleanly.
Perfect: A deep, even mahogany crust on all four sides. Drippings in the pan are dark bronze, not black. The tenderloin has contracted slightly and holds its shape firmly. Add butter, thyme, rosemary, and garlic to the pan. Move immediately to the oven.
Overdone: Crust is black and drippings are burning. Bitter, acrid smell. Remove tenderloin, wipe pan, and add fresh fat. The exterior char will be partially masked by the butter basting in the oven. Shorten oven time by 2 minutes.
Feel cue: Hold the tenderloin against the pan with tongs — you should hear a continuous assertive sizzle, not sputtering. Lift after 90 seconds: if the crust releases cleanly and is mahogany, it is ready to rotate.

Add the butter, thyme, rosemary, and crushed garlic to the pan. Transfer the skillet to the preheated oven. Roast for 10–12 minutes, basting once halfway through by tipping the pan and spooning the melted herb butter over the tenderloin. Remove when an instant-read thermometer reads 60 C (140 F) at the thickest point — carry-over cooking will bring it to 63 C (145 F).
Visual cue: The tenderloin has firmed and tightened in the oven. The herb butter is bubbling in the pan. When probed, the centre of the thickest point registers 60 C.
Underdone: Internal temperature below 55 C. The thickest section still feels very soft when pressed with a fingertip through an oven mitt. Return to the oven for 3–4 more minutes. Check temperature again at the thickest point, not the centre of the log.
Perfect: 60 C internal. The tenderloin feels firm but with a slight give when pressed. The flesh has set but not tightened. Herb butter is golden and fragrant. Remove from oven and transfer tenderloin to a cutting board to rest. Pour the pan butter over it.
Overdone: Internal temperature above 70 C. Tenderloin feels rigid and hard when pressed. Juices on the pan floor are beginning to brown and scorch. Remove immediately. Let the residual heat finish — don't return it to the oven. The rest period will help retain any remaining juices.
Feel cue: Press the centre of the tenderloin firmly with your thumb through a cloth — at 60 C it should feel like pressing on the fleshy base of your thumb with your hand relaxed open. Spring and resistance, not rigidity.

Transfer the tenderloin to a warm cutting board and tent loosely with foil. Rest for exactly 8 minutes. Do not cut earlier — the temperature will rise 3 degrees and the juices need time to redistribute from the contracted muscle fibres back into the interior.
Visual cue: The tenderloin appears to deflate very slightly as the fibres relax, and a small pool of pink-gold juice forms on the cutting board beneath it.
Underdone: Cutting too soon (under 5 minutes). Juices pour out immediately when cut — the fibres are still contracted. You cannot undo this, but next time, rest longer. Slice quickly and serve immediately to minimise further juice loss.
Perfect: After 8 minutes, the tenderloin has relaxed visibly. A small puddle of rosy juice has collected on the board. The crust is still warm and fragrant. Interior registers 63 C. Slice and serve.
Overdone: Rested beyond 20 minutes with no foil — the exterior has cooled and the crust softened. Slice and flash briefly under a grill for 60 seconds to re-warm the surface and re-crisp the crust.
Feel cue: Gently press the rested tenderloin — it should feel noticeably softer and more yielding than it did straight from the oven, a sign that the muscle fibres have released their grip on the juices.

Using a sharp slicing knife, cut the tenderloin into medallions 1.5–2 cm thick, slicing on a slight diagonal for a broader face. Each slice should reveal a uniform pale-rose interior surrounded by the dark seared crust. Spoon the resting juices and any remaining herb butter over the slices. Serve immediately.
Visual cue: Medallions showing a blush-pink interior (the exact shade of a pale pink rose) from edge to edge, surrounded by a thin ring of mahogany-brown crust.
Underdone: Interior is deep red-pink and shiny at the centre, resembling raw meat. Temperature below 58 C. Fan the slices on an oven-proof plate and return to a 180 C oven for 5 minutes. The pink will even out without further drying.
Perfect: A uniform pale rose-pink throughout, like pale salmon. Moist but not weeping. The crust ring is intact on every slice and the slices hold their shape. Spoon resting juices over and serve immediately.
Overdone: Interior is white-grey throughout. Slices feel dry and tight under the knife. No juice on the board. Serve with a pan sauce made from the deglazed drippings or with a generous drizzle of olive oil. The flavour of the crust is still excellent.
Feel cue: The knife should glide through each medallion with minimal resistance — a gentle forward press, not a sawing motion. If you feel the meat pushing back against the blade, the fibres are overcooked and tight.

ingredients.name: Ground cinnamon and icing sugar, to finish

steps:
Combine sugar, water, cinnamon stick, lemon peel, and vanilla bean in a small saucepan. Bring to a boil without stirring and simmer for 3 minutes at 107 C (a light syrup). Remove from heat and steep for 10 minutes to allow the aromatics to infuse deeply. Discard the cinnamon, lemon peel, and vanilla pod — reserve the vanilla seeds if you scraped them in. Cool to room temperature.
Visual cue: A clear, lightly golden syrup with a thin viscosity — just thicker than water. The kitchen smells of vanilla, cinnamon, and lemon peel.
Underdone: Syrup is still thin and watery. Sugar barely dissolved. Simmer for 2 more minutes. The syrup needs to reach 107 C to have the right sugar concentration for the custard.
Perfect: Glossy, thin but not watery. A drop on a cold plate sets to a soft, slightly sticky film within 30 seconds. Fragrant with lemon and vanilla. Cool completely before adding to the egg yolk mixture.
Overdone: Syrup is thick and pulling in strings — it has concentrated too much. Add 30ml hot water and stir to thin before using.
Feel cue: The cooled syrup should feel like very thin honey between the fingers — slippery and slightly tacky, but not thick enough to leave a visible thread when you pull your fingers apart.

Whisk together egg yolks and cornflour in a bowl until smooth. In a saucepan, combine milk, cream, and the cooled syrup. Bring to just below a simmer (small bubbles at the edge). Slowly pour the hot milk over the yolk mixture, whisking constantly. Return the whole mixture to the saucepan and cook over medium heat, whisking constantly, until it just begins to thicken to a pourable custard — remove immediately. Strain through a fine sieve.
Visual cue: A smooth, pale gold custard that coats the back of a spoon lightly — thinner than double cream but thicker than milk. Silky and completely lump-free.
Underdone: Custard is still thin as milk. No coating on the back of a spoon. Cornflour hasn't reached gelatinisation temperature. Return to gentle heat and whisk continuously — it will thicken quickly once it reaches 82 C.
Perfect: Thin nappe consistency — coats the back of a spoon, and a line drawn through it holds cleanly. Pours easily. Smells of vanilla and cream. Strain immediately and pour into prepared pastry shells.
Overdone: Custard has scrambled — visible yellow flecks and grainy texture. Smells eggy. Discard and start again — scrambled custard will bake unevenly and with an unpleasant grainy texture.
Feel cue: Draw a finger across a spoon dipped in the custard — the line should hold clean and sharp for 5 seconds. The custard should feel silky, with absolutely no graininess on the fingertip — not even a hint.

Roll puff pastry into a tight log, then slice into 12 equal discs about 1.5 cm thick. Press each disc into the base of a greased standard muffin tin, using your thumbs to work the pastry up the sides evenly — it should be thicker at the base than the sides, and the sides should come right to the top of the tin. The pastry will be thin and slightly translucent at the sides. Refrigerate for 20 minutes.
Visual cue: Thin, even pastry shells that reach the top of each muffin cup with no gaps, tears, or visible thick patches. The layered cross-section of the puff pastry is visible at the cut edge.
Underdone: Pastry is too thick at the base and too thin at the sides, or doesn't reach the top of the tin. Work the pastry more with your thumbs — think of throwing a pot, working from the centre outward and upward.
Perfect: Uniform shells with an even wall of approximately 3mm. Layered pastry visible at the rim. No holes. Slightly translucent at the sides when held to the light. Refrigerate for 20 minutes to relax the gluten before baking.
Overdone: Pastry has been handled so much it has torn or the butter has melted — pastry feels greasy and is beginning to lose its layered structure. Refrigerate immediately for 30 minutes before proceeding. Cold butter is the foundation of puff pastry.
Feel cue: Press your thumbnail gently into the side of a chilled shell — the pastry should feel firm and cold, not soft or greasy. The layered structure should be perceptible as a slight springiness.

Preheat oven to its maximum temperature — ideally 250 C (480 F) or higher. Fill each chilled shell three-quarters full with custard. Bake on the highest rack for 13–17 minutes, watching carefully. You are chasing the classic dark amber leopard-spots across the surface — the tops will blister and char in places and the custard will wobble alarmingly. Pull when the tops are darkly blistered but the custard is still trembling. Cool for 10 minutes and dust with ground cinnamon.
Visual cue: Custard surface is a constellation of dark amber to near-black caramelised spots across a pale cream background. The pastry is deeply golden and blistered. The custard still trembles at the centre when tapped.
Underdone: Custard surface is uniformly pale — no blistering or browning. Custard jiggles as one liquid mass. Pastry is pale and soft. Return to the highest rack for 3–5 more minutes. A lower oven temperature is your enemy here — these tarts need ferocious heat.
Perfect: Dark, dramatic caramelised spots across the custard. Pastry is crispily golden and separating into flaky layers. The custard centre trembles independently when the tin is tapped. Smells of caramelised sugar and vanilla. Cool in the tin for 5 minutes then transfer to a rack. Serve warm, dusted with cinnamon.
Overdone: Custard is completely set — no tremor. Surface is uniformly dark. Pastry is very dark at the edges. The tarts will still be delicious, just fully set rather than creamy. Serve immediately and adjust time next batch.
Feel cue: Tap the side of the tin gently — the custard in the centre should shimmer and wobble with a loose, liquid movement separate from the set edges. This wobble is the soul of a pastel de nata.

ingredients.name: Marrow bones (5–6 cm sections, tied in muslin)
Large yellow onion (halved, cut-side charred dry in a pan)
Bouquet garni (thyme, bay leaf, parsley stalks, black peppercorns)
韭葱（Leeks (white and pale green, tied)）
Dijon mustard, cornichons, fleur de sel, and toasted baguette (to serve)

steps:
Place the beef shin and marrow bones in a large pot, cover with cold water, and bring to a full boil over high heat. Boil for 5 minutes — a grey scum will rise aggressively. Drain, rinse the meat and bones under cold running water to remove all impurities, and scrub the pot clean. This blanching step is not optional — it is what allows the final broth to be clear rather than grey.
Visual cue: Meat and bones rinsed clean, with no traces of grey scum, and the cooking pot scrubbed of all residue.
Underdone: Only a light scum has risen and the water is still fairly clear — not all impurities have been purged. Continue boiling for another 2–3 minutes until the scum has stopped rising aggressively.
Perfect: The water is thick with dark grey foam. When drained and rinsed, the meat looks grey-brown but clean. The pot is clear of residue. Return the cleaned meat to the clean pot and cover with fresh cold water.
Overdone: Meat has been boiled far too long in the blanching stage and is beginning to look dull and fibrous. Proceed quickly to the simmer stage — do not repeat the blanch.
Feel cue: The meat after blanching and rinsing should feel cold and slightly sticky from the collagen beginning to release — run your fingers along the shin and feel the slight tackiness.

Return the blanched meat and bones to the clean pot. Add the charred onion halves (hold them cut-side down in a dry pan over high heat for 3–4 minutes until blackened — this gives the broth its golden color). Add the bouquet garni and enough cold water to cover everything by 5 cm. Bring slowly to a simmer over medium heat — this should take 20 minutes. Skim any remaining scum carefully as it rises. Reduce to the lowest possible simmer — the surface should barely tremble, just an occasional lazy bubble breaking through. Cook for 2 hours before adding any vegetables.
Visual cue: A gently trembling, golden-amber broth with no visible roiling boil, and a clean surface with only an occasional slow bubble.
Underdone: Water is barely warm and scum is still rising heavily. The broth has no color or body yet. Continue over medium heat, skimming steadily. The broth needs patience — a full slow warm-up is essential for clarity.
Perfect: A quiet, trembling simmer. The surface is nearly still. Broth is already deepening to amber from the charred onion. Smells deeply of beef and herbs. Maintain this simmer for 2 hours before adding vegetables.
Overdone: Broth is at a rolling boil — it will become cloudy and greasy as fat is emulsified into the liquid. Reduce heat immediately. Add a splash of cold water to shock the temperature down. Skim the surface thoroughly.
Feel cue: Dip a clean spoon into the broth at the 2-hour mark and taste — it should already have a clear, golden beef flavor that coats the back of the spoon with barely perceptible viscosity.

Add the vegetables to the simmering broth in stages by their cooking time: add turnips first (30 minutes to cook), then carrots and celery root (20 minutes), and finally leeks (15 minutes). The goal is for all vegetables to be perfectly tender at the same time. Do not add them all at once. The broth should remain at a gentle simmer throughout — never a boil.
Visual cue: Vegetables that are completely tender but still holding their shape — a knife passes through a carrot without resistance, the cut surface is clean, not fibrous.
Underdone: Carrots or turnips resist a thin skewer. The centers feel cool to the touch when pressed. Continue simmering. Test each vegetable individually with a thin skewer or knife — they will not all be done at the same time.
Perfect: All vegetables yield to a knife with no resistance. Leeks are completely limp but not disintegrating. Carrots have a slight golden gleam from the broth. Lift everything from the broth. Serve the strained broth first, then the meat and vegetables.
Overdone: Leeks have collapsed into strands, turnips are falling apart, and the broth has absorbed their flavor to the point of muddiness. Serve immediately. Drain the vegetables quickly and present them on a platter; they are not irreparably lost.
Feel cue: Press a carrot with your thumb against the side of the pot — it should yield completely with barely any pressure, like pressing into soft butter.

Lift the meat and vegetables carefully from the broth with a slotted spoon onto a warmed platter. Untie and remove the muslin from the marrow bones. Strain the broth through a fine sieve lined with dampened muslin or a clean cloth. Taste and correct the salt. Serve the clear broth first in warmed soup bowls with a few small pasta or toasted bread. Follow with the meat, sliced thick, and the vegetables, accompanied by Dijon mustard, cornichons, coarse salt, and horseradish if desired.
Visual cue: A clear, jewel-like amber broth with no visible fat globules or cloudiness, and a platter of deeply colored, tender meat and vibrant vegetables.
Underdone: Broth is grey and cloudy with floating fat and particles. It was boiled too hard at some stage. Strain through muslin a second time. The taste may still be excellent even if the appearance is compromised.
Perfect: The broth is a clear amber, almost like dark tea, with no cloudiness. Light shimmers through it. It has a gentle, rich, clean depth. Serve at once in the traditional two-service format.
Overdone: Broth has reduced too much from prolonged cooking and tastes salty and intensely concentrated. Add a small amount of hot water to balance. Taste again before serving.
Feel cue: Ladle the strained broth slowly — it should have the faintest resistance as it flows off the ladle, the earliest hint of gelatin, proof that the collagen has given itself to the pot.
