ingredients.name: Coarse non-iodized sea salt or kosher salt
Fresh lemon juice (from additional lemons for brine)

steps:
Scrub the lemons thoroughly under warm water to remove any surface wax or pesticide residue — unwaxed lemons are strongly preferred, as the rind is the prize and you want nothing between the salt and the natural lemon oils. Cut each lemon nearly into quarters from the top, stopping 1–2 cm before the base so the lemon holds together in a fan shape. This quartered-but-hinged cut maximizes the surface area exposed to the salt while keeping the lemon whole for an attractive presentation. Pack 1–2 tablespoons of coarse salt generously into the opening of each quartered lemon, pressing the salt into the flesh. The quantity of salt is not negotiable — undersalting will allow harmful bacterial growth rather than the desired fermentation.
Visual cue: Each lemon splayed open like a four-petaled flower, densely packed with white coarse salt that is pressed into every crevice of the cut surfaces. The lemon should look almost crystallized at the cut faces.
Underdone: Too little salt in the cuts — the lemon surfaces are only lightly dusted and the salt has not been pressed into the flesh. Insufficient salt creates conditions for harmful mold rather than safe fermentation. Open the cuts wider and pack in additional salt. You cannot over-salt at this stage — the lemons will ultimately be rinsed before use, and the salt is the preservation mechanism.
Perfect: Every cut surface is thickly coated in salt, pressed into the flesh, with visible salt crystals packed into the opening. When you squeeze the lemon gently, a tiny amount of juice beads at the cut — the salt is already beginning to draw moisture. Proceed to packing the jar.
Overdone: Lemon cut all the way through into four separate quarters — they are no longer held together. Not a catastrophe, but whole-hinged lemons pack more tightly and look more traditional. Pack the separated quarters into the jar anyway — they will still

work perfectly, just with a less traditional appearance.
Feel cue: When you squeeze a salt-packed lemon, it should feel already yielding — more pliable than a fresh lemon, because the salt has begun drawing juice from the flesh. That softening is the start of the preservation process.

Sterilize a wide-mouth glass jar (large enough to hold all the lemons tightly) by boiling or running through a dishwasher's hot cycle. Place a bay leaf, a small piece of cinnamon, a pinch of peppercorns, and the cloves in the base of the jar. Pack the salt-stuffed lemons into the jar as tightly as possible, squeezing them in and pressing down so the lemons compress and release their juice. Tuck additional spices between the lemons as you layer. Once all lemons are packed, press down firmly with your fist — you want the jar to be so tight the lemons cannot rattle or move. Pour fresh lemon juice over the top until the lemons are fully submerged. If needed, add a small amount of additional salt dissolved in lemon juice. Seal tightly.
Visual cue: A tightly packed jar of lemons compressed to the point of releasing visible juice into the jar. The lemon juice rises around and over the packed lemons. The jar looks dense and full, with no air gaps between the lemons.
Underdone: Lemons packed loosely with empty gaps between them and the jar — they will float above the juice level as it rises, exposing the top lemons to air and potential mold. Add more lemons (even thin slices can fill gaps), press more firmly, or add a fermentation weight on top before sealing.
Perfect: Lemons packed so tightly they can't move. The jar juice level reaches or covers the top lemon. Bay leaves and spices visible between the lemons. The jar lid closes with resistance from the compressed contents. Seal and store at room temperature or in a cool pantry.
Overdone: Jar over-packed and the lid cannot close without crushing the lemons to a broken pulp. While not harmful, a crushed lemon jam rather than whole preserved lemons is the result. Remove one lemon to allow the lid to close properly. The slightly crushed lemons will still preserve well.
Feel cue: Press the sealed jar down on a countertop and
shake gently — you should not hear or feel the lemons shifting. A jar that rattles has loose lemons that will bob above the brine. Re-open and pack more tightly.

Store the sealed jar at room temperature (18–24°C / 65–75°F) for 30 days minimum, turning the jar upside down once daily for the first week to redistribute the salt and juices, ensuring all lemon surfaces are bathed in the brine. The lemons will gradually sink as they soften and the juice level will look different from day to day — this is normal. After a week, the turning is less critical, but occasional rotation helps. At 30 days, taste: the rind should be tender, translucent, and mellow — not sharply bitter but savory-salty-fragrant. The flesh is typically discarded when using preserved lemons in cooking; only the rind is used.
Visual cue: After 30 days: the lemons have softened and sunk, their rinds translucent and slightly golden-amber from the salt and their own juices. The brine in the jar is now a cloudy, golden syrup — thicker than plain lemon juice.
Underdone: At 2 weeks, the lemon rinds are still firm and opaque when cut open — they taste sharply bitter and salty rather than mellow and silky. The pith still has its aggressive white bitterness. Seal and continue curing. Two weeks is the halfway point — the real transformation happens in weeks 3–4. Patience is the only ingredient you need here.
Perfect: At 30+ days: the rind is translucent, tender to a clean cut with a knife, and tastes intensely savory-salty-fragrant with only a hint of pleasantly mellow bitterness. The pith has softened from stark white to a gelatinous, mellow texture. Refrigerate. The preserved lemons are ready to use and will keep refrigerated for 6–12 months.
Overdone: Left at room temperature past 60 days — the lemons may develop a very strong, almost fermented-alcoholic brine and the rinds can become mushy rather than silky-firm. The flavor becomes more intensely funky than fragrant. Transfer to refrigerator immediately. Very over-cured preserved lemons are still useful — particularly

in slow braises and stews where the extra fermented depth integrates well.
Feel cue: At 30 days, slice open a preserved lemon: the rind should give to a sharp knife with no resistance and the pith should look translucent-gelatinous rather than chalky-white. Press a small piece between your fingers — it should squish easily, like cooked vegetable, not resist like raw peel.

Once cured, refrigerate the jar. To use: remove a lemon quarter, rinse the salt from the rind under cold water, then scrape away and discard the flesh and pith — only the silky, translucent rind is used. Slice or mince the rind and use in tagines, grain salads, pasta, compound butters, or dressings. The brine in the jar is also excellent: use it as a seasoning salt substitute in sauces and braises. Preserved lemons can transform a dish from good to memorable with just a small amount — their flavor is concentrated, so use with restraint until you understand their potency.
Visual cue: A jar of ready-to-use preserved lemons shows translucent, amber-tinted rinds submerged in a thick, golden, cloudy brine. When you remove a quarter and rinse it, the rind should look almost lacquered — sleek and slightly glossy.
Underdone: The rind, after rinsing, still looks opaque and white in patches — the pith has not fully transformed. The taste is sharp and bitter rather than silky and savory. Return the lemon to the jar and cure for another 1–2 weeks. Not all lemons soften at the same rate — thin-skinned Meyers preserve faster than thick-skinned Eurekas.
Perfect: The rinsed rind is translucent, soft, and fragrant — intensely lemon-forward but with no harsh bite. It smells of concentrated lemon zest and salt. Sliced thin, it dissolves almost on the tongue, releasing a burst of savory lemon flavor. Use immediately or keep refrigerated. Add to any dish that needs a deep, savory-citrus accent.
Overdone: Rind has broken down to a mushy, almost paste-like texture — difficult to slice cleanly. Still flavorful but not the silky strips that make preserved lemons so elegant. Use as a paste stirred into vinaigrettes, hummus, or compound butter where the texture is irrelevant.
Feel cue: A perfectly preserved lemon rind, pinched: it should feel like a thin piece of silicone — flexible, smooth,
slightly waxy, with no grit or roughness from unbroken cell walls. It should slide between your fingers rather than drag.

name: Pretzel Rolls
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=bakers_percentage）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Bread flour (12–13% protein): 100 %
  Alternatives: all-purpose flour (slightly less chew)
Warm whole milk (38 C): 55 %
  Alternatives: water (less tender crumb)
Instant yeast: 1.5 %
  Alternatives: active dry yeast (proof first)
Fine sea salt: 2 %
Unsalted butter, softened: 5 %
  Alternatives: lard (more traditional)
Baking soda (for the lye bath): 12 %
  Alternatives: food-grade lye 3% solution (true Laugengebäck, use with extreme caution)
Water (for baked-soda bath): 500 %
Coarse pretzel salt (or flaky sea salt): 1 %
  Alternatives: Maldon salt; coarse kosher salt
Active time: 1 hour
Total time: 3 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: German Laugenbrötchen — dense, mahogany-dark rolls submerged in a baked-soda lye bath that turns the outer starch into a crackle-crisp, bitterly savory shell over a chewy, pillowy interior, finished with coarse pretzel salt that glints under kitchen light.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Coarse pretzel salt (or flaky sea salt)

steps:
Combine the flour, yeast, and salt in a large bowl, then add the warm milk. Mix until a rough dough forms, then add the softened butter in pieces. Knead by hand for 10 minutes or in a stand mixer with the dough hook at medium speed for 7 minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and only faintly tacky. Pretzel dough is intentionally stiffer than a typical bread dough — the lower hydration is what allows the rolls to hold their shape during the lye bath and develop that distinctive dense, chewy crumb. The dough should pass the windowpane test: stretch a small piece thin and it should be nearly translucent without tearing.
Visual cue: A smooth, elastic ball of dough that holds its shape on the counter. Slightly stiffer than sandwich bread dough. Surface is glossy and taut.
Underdone: Still rough and slightly ragged. Tears when pulled. Doesn't hold a round shape. Knead for 2–3 more minutes — the gluten needs more development for the rolls to hold their shape in the bath.
Perfect: Windowpane test passes. Smooth, elastic, only slightly tacky. Springs back within 2 seconds when poked. Surface looks almost glossy. Round into a ball and place in an oiled bowl to bulk ferment.
Overdone: Very stiff and tight, fighting back when kneaded. Snaps back immediately. Cover and rest 15 minutes. Over-developed gluten needs time to relax.
Feel cue: Pretzel dough should feel like a firm handshake — not as soft as brioche, not as stiff as pizza dough, but somewhere confidently in between. Pull a piece: it should stretch without effort into a long ribbon before tearing.

Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let it rise at room temperature for 1 to 1.5 hours until 50% larger (not doubled — pretzel dough is kept relatively under-fermented by design). This controlled fermentation keeps the crumb dense and chewy rather than airy. Meanwhile, prepare the baked-soda bath: spread the baking soda on a foil-lined sheet pan and bake at 250 C (480 F) for 1 hour until it turns from white powder to a yellowish crust. Baked soda is significantly more alkaline than regular baking soda and gives a much closer result to a real lye bath.
Visual cue: Dough has grown about 50% and feels lighter. Surface is domed and smooth. Not doubled — deliberately under-proofed.
Underdone: Dough looks and feels identical to when it went in. No growth visible. Firm and dense. Move to a warmer place and wait. Under-fermented dough produces rolls too dense to enjoy.
Perfect: 50% larger, feels slightly lighter and airier. A poke leaves a lazy-filling indent. Divide and shape into rolls while the oven heats and the lye bath is prepared.
Overdone: Doubled or more. Smells strongly of yeast. Very soft and gas-filled. Proceed quickly. Over-fermented pretzel rolls will be softer and more bready — still delicious, but less chewy.
Feel cue: Properly fermented pretzel dough still feels relatively dense and firm compared to a sandwich loaf at the same stage — this is correct. It should feel like a soft stress ball, not a pillow.

Divide the dough into 8 equal pieces (about 80–100 g each for a typical batch from 500 g flour). To shape a round roll: flatten each piece into a disc, fold the edges toward the center all around, then flip it over and roll it under your cupped palm on the counter with firm downward pressure, moving in tight circles. The goal is a taut, smooth ball with a sealed seam on the bottom. Alternatively, score a deep cross on top with a sharp knife or lame after shaping — this gives the classic Laugenbrötchen look. Place shaped rolls seam-side down on a parchment-lined sheet and refrigerate uncovered for 30 minutes — cold rolls hold their shape better during the lye bath.
Visual cue: Tight, smooth spheres with a sealed seam on the bottom. No tears or loose dough. Refrigerated rolls are firm and hold their shape when picked up.
Underdone: Loose, floppy balls with visible seams and tears on the surface. They sag and flatten on the sheet. Reshape each one — flatten, fold, and re-roll with more downward pressure to build tension.
Perfect: Firm, taut balls that hold their round shape when set on the tray. Seam is invisible or sealed tightly. Refrigerate 30 minutes before the lye bath.
Overdone: Shaped rolls are warm and already proofing fast — surface looks puffy and soft. Get them into the refrigerator immediately to firm up before the lye bath.
Feel cue: A well-shaped pretzel roll should feel solid and taut when squeezed lightly — not springy and puffy, not hard, but like a firmly packed snowball that holds its form.

Dissolve the baked baking soda in 1 liter of water in a wide, non-reactive pot (stainless steel or enameled — no bare aluminum). Bring to a gentle simmer. Wearing rubber gloves (baked soda solution is still caustic to skin), lower the cold rolls into the simmering bath one or two at a time. Simmer 20–30 seconds per side, turning once. The surface will turn a slightly tan, rubbery, tight skin. Lift out with a slotted spoon or spider and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Scatter coarse salt over the tops immediately while the surface is tacky.
Visual cue: Each roll emerges from the bath with a tight, slightly tanned, rubbery-looking skin that catches coarse salt immediately and holds it.
Underdone: Still looks pale and doughy after 15 seconds in the bath. Surface has not tightened. Leave in the bath a full 30 seconds per side — the alkaline reaction takes time to gelatinize the exterior starch.
Perfect: Slightly tan, taut, rubbery surface — looks like a damp chamois skin. Salt sticks immediately. Will turn deep mahogany brown in the oven. Salt immediately and load into a 220 C (425 F) oven.
Overdone: More than 60 seconds in the bath — surface starts to dissolve and becomes slimy or cracked. Bake it anyway and score deeply before baking to let steam escape. The flavor will be fine; the crust may be irregular.
Feel cue: Fresh from the lye bath, the surface of each roll feels rubbery and slightly slimy under a gloved finger — that gelatinized outer starch is the direct precursor to the crackle-crisp mahogany pretzel shell in the oven.

Bake on the upper-middle rack at 220 C (425 F) with no steam for 18–22 minutes until deeply, uniformly dark mahogany-brown — much darker than you would ever take a regular roll. The lye reaction produces the characteristic dark color and bitter-savory flavor as the gelatinized exterior caramelizes aggressively. The coarse salt should be lightly toasted but intact. Let the rolls cool on a rack for at least 15 minutes before eating — the interior crumb needs time to firm up and the crust to crackle fully as it cools.
Visual cue: Deep mahogany-brown all over — not golden, not tan, but genuinely dark. Coarse salt glints. The surface is hard and crackle-crisp. The natural splits or scores show an inner pale crumb.
Underdone: Golden-tan color. The crust is soft and the distinctive pretzel bitterness is missing. Doesn't look like a pretzel. Return to the oven for 3–5 minutes. Pretzel rolls must be baked much darker than normal bread — you're looking for mahogany, not gold.
Perfect: Uniformly dark mahogany with a crackle-hard crust that gives a sharp click when tapped. The kitchen smells of toasted malt and caramelized starch. Coarse salt toasted golden. Cool on a rack 15 minutes. The crumb will be dense and chewy under the brittle shell.
Overdone: Black or very dark brown with a burnt, harsh smell. Salt may be charred. The outer layer may be discardable; check the interior. If the crumb is good, remove the darkest bits of crust.
Feel cue: Tap the bottom of a pretzel roll: it should sound like tapping a hard stone, not a hollow drum. The crust is its own layer — dense and rigid — and when you tear the roll open, it should resist and then snap apart rather than pull apart.

name: Bavarian Soft Pretzel
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=bakers_percentage）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Bread flour (12–13% protein): 100 %
  Alternatives: all-purpose flour
Warm water (32 C): 58 %
Instant yeast: 1.5 %
  Alternatives: active dry yeast (proof first)
Fine salt: 2 %
  Alternatives: kosher salt
Unsalted butter, softened: 3 %
  Alternatives: neutral oil
Baking soda (for alkaline dipping bath): 10 %
  Alternatives: food-grade lye 1% solution
Coarse pretzel salt: 1 %
  Alternatives: flaky sea salt
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 2 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A Bavarian soft pretzel — arm-thick arms of bread, deeply mahogany from its alkaline dip, with a dense satisfying chew that yields to a cloud-soft interior dusted with coarse salt crystals that crunch under the tooth.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine warm water, instant yeast, and softened butter in a large bowl; stir briefly. Add flour and salt. Mix until a rough, stiff dough forms — this dough is noticeably firmer than a typical bread dough. It should clean the sides of the bowl. If still sticky, add flour one tablespoon at a time.
Visual cue: A cohesive, smooth-ish ball that barely sticks to the bowl sides. Stiffer and drier than a focaccia or sourdough dough.
Underdone: Wet and sticky, clings to the bowl in sheets, won't hold a shape. Add flour 1 tablespoon at a time and continue mixing until it clears the bowl.
Perfect: Firm, slightly tacky ball. Holds its shape when dropped. Not as smooth as kneaded dough yet. Transfer to a work surface and begin kneading.
Overdone: Crumbly and stiff, difficult to bring together, cracking at the edges. Add warm water 1 teaspoon at a time and knead to bring it together.
Feel cue: Pretzel dough should feel like firm modeling clay — noticeably stiffer than pizza dough. It should hold a fingerprint without collapsing.

Knead on an unfloured surface for 8–10 minutes by hand, or 5 minutes in a stand mixer with a dough hook on medium speed. The dough is stiff — use the heel of your hand to push-fold-turn. It will become smooth and elastic as the gluten develops. The dough should pass the windowpane test: stretch a small piece thin enough to see light through without tearing.
Visual cue: A smooth, satiny ball with no visible lumps or tears. Surface is taut and slightly shiny. The dough stretches without immediately snapping back.
Underdone: Surface still rough and bumpy; dough tears when stretched; windowpane test fails — it rips immediately. Continue kneading — gluten needs more work. Check after every 2 minutes.
Perfect: Satiny smooth surface, passes the windowpane test: stretches into a thin, translucent membrane without tearing. Round into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover and proof.
Overdone: Dough has become tough and rubbery, very resistant, tears when pulled. Cover and rest 20 minutes — overworked gluten needs to relax.
Feel cue: Well-kneaded pretzel dough has the firmness of a tennis ball and the smoothness of warm leather. It bounces back slowly when pressed.

Cover the dough and let it proof at room temperature (22–24 C) for 45–60 minutes until noticeably puffed. It will not double like a lean bread dough — the fat and stiff hydration slow fermentation. While the dough proofs, bring 1 liter of water to a boil in a wide saucepan and dissolve the baking soda — it will bubble furiously. Reduce to a steady simmer.
Visual cue: Dough has increased roughly 50% in volume. Surface is smooth, slightly pillowy, and springs back when poked.
Underdone: Barely grown; dense and stiff; poke leaves a permanent dent rather than springing back. Move to a warmer spot and give it another 20 minutes — yeast needs warmth to activate.
Perfect: Noticeably puffed, poke springs back slowly but completely. Smells lightly yeasty. Divide, roll into ropes, and shape into pretzels.
Overdone: Dough is very puffy, deflates when touched, smells strongly of alcohol. Shape immediately. Reduce the second rest after shaping to 10 minutes.
Feel cue: Proofed pretzel dough should feel pillowy but with backbone — press it and it slowly returns, unlike an overproofed dough that collapses and stays flat.

Divide dough into 8 equal pieces. Roll each into a 60 cm rope, thicker in the center and tapered at the ends. Form a U shape, twist the ends twice around each other, fold down and press to the bottom arch. Place on parchment-lined baking sheets and chill uncovered in the freezer 15 minutes — cold pretzels hold their shape during dipping. Working one at a time, submerge each pretzel in the simmering baking soda bath for 30 seconds per side, turning once. The alkaline solution is what creates the mahogany crust and distinctive chew. Place on the baking sheet, cut 3 shallow slashes across the thick belly, and scatter coarse pretzel salt generously.
Visual cue: Each pretzel holds its classic shape after dipping — the dough has a matte, slightly tacky surface from the alkaline bath, the color shifted from ivory to a pale tan.
Underdone: Pretzels skipped the dip or were submerged too briefly — surface looks pale and unchanged, glossy. Submerge again for a full 30 seconds per side in a simmering (not boiling) baking soda bath.
Perfect: Matte tan surface, slightly tacky, holds its pretzel shape. Arms and belly clearly defined. Salt crystals adhering to the surface. Bake immediately at 220 C (425 F).
Overdone: Pretzels were dipped in boiling (not simmering) solution and began falling apart, or dipped too long and are disintegrating. Salvage by placing on the pan and baking — they may look irregular but will still taste correct.
Feel cue: After the baking soda dip the dough surface feels slightly slippery and almost soapy — that's the alkalinity doing its work. Handle with care and work quickly.

Bake at 220 C (425 F) for 14–18 minutes until deeply mahogany — darker than you think is right. Pretzel crust should be nearly the color of dark chocolate at its best. The alkaline coating Maillard-browns at a lower temperature than regular bread, so the color comes fast. Rotate the pan halfway through. Cool on a wire rack for 5 minutes before serving warm.
Visual cue: Deep mahogany-brown crust — the color of dark chocolate or dark molasses, not caramel. The slashes on the belly have opened and the interior shows pale, steaming bread beneath.
Underdone: Pale amber or golden crust. The pretzel will be soft and bland — it hasn't developed the bitter-edged Maillard crust that defines a Bavarian pretzel. Return to the oven for 3–5 minutes. Pretzel crust should be fearlessly dark.
Perfect: Dark mahogany-brown, belly slashes open and pale. Inside is fluffy, steam rises when broken. Salt crystals still whole and crunchy. Rest 5 minutes and serve warm. Eat within 2 hours for the best crust texture.
Overdone: Black, bitter-smelling crust, salt has dissolved and burned into the surface. Trim the darkest exterior with a knife. Interior is likely still good.
Feel cue: A finished pretzel feels heavy for its size and firm all over — no soft, squishy spots. The crust should resist the fingernail rather than yield. Break one open to a cloud of steam and pull-apart softness.

name: Profiteroles with Chocolate Sauce
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
All-purpose flour (sifted): 125 g
Unsalted butter (diced): 80 g
  Alternatives: European-style butter for richer flavour
Water: 200 g
  Alternatives: half water, half whole milk for a more tender shell
Eggs (large, lightly beaten): 160 g
Fine salt: 3 g
Granulated sugar: 10 g
Heavy cream (35%+ fat): 300 g
Dark chocolate 70% finely chopped: 150 g
  Alternatives: bittersweet 60% for a sweeter sauce
Vanilla extract: 5 g
  Alternatives: vanilla bean paste
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 2 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Airy choux puffs, hollow at the centre, filled with billowing vanilla chantilly and drowned under a silky warm chocolate sauce — the unreasonably perfect Parisian bistro dessert, made from nothing more than flour, butter, eggs, and chocolate.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine the water, diced butter, salt, and sugar in a heavy saucepan. Set over medium heat and stir occasionally until the butter melts completely. Increase the heat and bring to a full, rolling boil — every bubble breaking the surface. Do not let it reduce; have the flour ready and act immediately when it boils. A partial boil is not sufficient — the entire liquid must be at a true boil when the flour goes in, or the starch will not cook properly.
Visual cue: A vigorous, churning, white-foam boil across the entire surface of the pan. The butter is fully emulsified into the water — no clear fat layer.
Underdone: Butter has melted but the liquid is only simmering, not boiling. Small bubbles fringe the edge. Steam rises but no vigorous activity at the centre. Increase heat and wait for a full rolling boil. Adding flour to simmering liquid does not cook the starch properly and the choux will not set.
Perfect: The liquid is boiling vigorously across its entire surface, not just at the edges. Steam and foam rising. The butter and water are fully blended. Remove from heat and add all the flour at once in a single motion.
Overdone: The liquid has been boiling too long and has reduced noticeably — the pan looks half-empty compared to when you started. The ratio of liquid to flour has changed. Add 20-30ml of water and bring back to a boil before adding the flour.
Feel cue: You should feel the heat radiating from the pan before you get close — a vigorous, aggressive boil, not a gentle simmer. The moment it boils, act without hesitation.

Tip all the flour into the boiling liquid at once. Stir immediately and vigorously with a wooden spoon — the mixture will seize into a rough, shaggy mass, then smooth out within 30 seconds into a ball. Return to medium heat and continue stirring, pressing the paste against the bottom of the pan, for 1 to 2 minutes to dry it out — a thin skin should form on the pan base. Transfer to a stand mixer bowl or large bowl and beat briefly to cool, then add the beaten eggs in 6 to 8 additions, beating well after each. Stop when the paste falls from the beater in a slow V and holds its shape when piped.
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy, cohesive paste that falls from the beater in a slow, heavy, inverted V-shape and holds piped ridges without spreading.
Underdone: The paste is too stiff — it breaks away from the beater in chunks rather than flowing in a V. Piped shapes would crack rather than puff. Not all the egg has been added. Add another 20g of egg and beat thoroughly. Test again — the V-drop test is the only reliable indicator. Each addition of egg loosens and glosses the paste.
Perfect: A smooth, glossy paste the colour of pale gold. Falls from the beater in a slow, unbroken V. When piped onto a baking sheet, it holds ridges and doesn't slump. Transfer immediately to a piping bag with a plain 1 cm nozzle and pipe at once. Choux paste dries quickly and should not rest.
Overdone: The paste is too slack — liquid, shiny, and flowing. It cannot hold a piped shape and spreads flat on the baking sheet immediately. You added too much egg. There is no remedy for over-thinned choux paste — the puffs will be flat and dense. Next time, add the egg more slowly and stop the V-test at the right moment.
Feel cue: Scoop up a dollop of choux paste on a wooden spoon and tilt it — it should slide off slowly as a clean, unbroken ribbon ending in a point. If it drops immediately or doesn't move,
it's wrong.

Preheat the oven to 200°C (390°F). Pipe the choux paste onto lined baking sheets in rounds of about 3 cm diameter, spaced 5 cm apart. Wet a finger and smooth any peaks. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until puffed, deeply golden brown, and rigid. Do not open the oven in the first 15 minutes. After the puffs are golden and holding their shape, reduce the heat to 170°C and bake for a further 5 minutes to dry the interior. Transfer to a rack and pierce the base of each puff with a skewer to release steam. Cool completely before filling.
Visual cue: Deeply golden, well-rounded puffs with a rigid shell and a hollow interior audible when tapped. The shells hold their shape without any softening or collapsing when removed from the oven.
Underdone: The puffs look puffy and golden but collapse within 5 minutes of leaving the oven, falling flat and soft. The interior is still wet and unset. Return to the oven immediately — collapsed puffs can sometimes be rescued if caught early. They need more time at the lower temperature to dry the interior fully.
Perfect: Firm, deep amber-gold, hollow-sounding when tapped. Hold their shape after 15 minutes at room temperature. The base is dark brown and dry. Pierce the base with a skewer, cool completely, and fill within 30 minutes of filling. Filled puffs soften after 1 hour.
Overdone: Very dark brown approaching burnt, very rigid and hard. The interior may be over-dried and fragile. They are still usable — the chocolate sauce will mask a slightly bitter shell. Trim the very darkest bases if needed. Reduce oven temperature by 10°C next time.
Feel cue: Pick up a cooled puff and shake it gently — you should hear and feel the hollow space inside, like rattling an empty box. If it feels solid or dense, it has not dried out sufficiently. A firm, dry, airy shell is the goal.

Heat half the heavy cream in a small saucepan to just below a boil — wisps of steam and a quiver of surface movement, no rolling bubbles. Pour the hot cream over the finely chopped dark chocolate in a heatproof bowl and leave undisturbed for 90 seconds. Stir from the centre outward in slow circles until the ganache is completely smooth and glossy. The sauce should be pourable and warm but not runny — if too thick, add a splash of cream. Keep warm over a pot of hot water.
Visual cue: A deep, glossy, flowing chocolate sauce — the colour of a dark mirror, smooth with no lumps or streaks of unmelted chocolate. Falls off a spoon in a thick, even ribbon.
Underdone: Lumps of unmelted chocolate remain visible. The sauce looks broken, oily, or grainy. This means the cream was not hot enough or the chocolate was not fine enough. Stir gently over very low heat or warm gently in the microwave in 10-second bursts until the lumps dissolve. If broken (oil separated), add a teaspoon of warm cream and stir in circles.
Perfect: Glossy, dark, and smooth. Flows off a spoon in a slow, unbroken ribbon with a wet shine. Smells intensely of dark chocolate. Keep warm. Pour over the filled profiteroles at the last possible moment — the sauce firms as it cools.
Overdone: The cream was too hot and scorched, giving a slight bitter, burnt-milk undertone. Or the sauce has sat too long and set to a thick, fudgy glaze. If fudgy, reheat gently with a splash of cream. A scorched cream cannot be fixed — remake if the burnt note is strong.
Feel cue: The finished ganache sauce should feel warm (not hot) and coat the back of a spoon in a layer you can draw a clean line through with a finger. If you can see your fingertip through the sauce on the spoon, it is too thin.

Using cold cream, cold bowl, and cold beaters, whip the remaining heavy cream with the vanilla extract to firm but not stiff peaks — it should hold its shape when piped but feel airy, not grainy. Transfer to a piping bag. Make a small incision in the base of each puff with a serrated knife and pipe in the cream until the puff feels noticeably heavier. Arrange in a bowl or on a plate, pile generously, and pour the warm chocolate sauce over at the table so guests hear the sauce hitting the cream. Serve immediately.
Visual cue: Filled puffs sitting on a cloud of extra cream, the warm chocolate sauce glossing over the tops and pooling around the bases, still flowing when served.
Underdone: The cream inside the puffs is still liquid — it was under-whipped and runs out of the incision when the puff is tilted. The sauce is cold and set, not flowing. Whip the cream further before filling. Reheat the sauce. Profiteroles are at their best served immediately while the sauce is liquid and the puffs are fresh.
Perfect: Each puff is noticeably heavy with cream and holds it when tilted. The warm sauce flows smoothly and glossily over the tower. The temperature contrast between cold cream and warm chocolate is immediate. Eat within 10 minutes — the cream begins softening the puff shells after that.
Overdone: The puffs were filled more than an hour ago and the shells have gone soft and soggy from the cream's moisture. The sauce has firmed to a cold glaze. Fill and sauce profiteroles only at the moment of serving. Assemble puffs, sauce, and cream can all be prepared up to 4 hours ahead and assembled to order.
Feel cue: A freshly filled profiterole should feel weightier than you expect — light shell, heavy with cream inside. Bite into it and the shell should give a brief crunch before yielding to the cold cream. The hot sauce hitting the cold cream is the point of the whole dish.

name: Provençal Tian
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Zucchini, sliced 5 mm rounds: 35 parts
  Alternatives: yellow squash; aubergine
Ripe plum tomatoes, sliced 5 mm rounds: 35 parts
  Alternatives: heirloom tomato
Waxy potato, peeled, sliced 5 mm rounds: 30 parts
  Alternatives: sweet potato
Extra-virgin olive oil: 15 parts
Garlic cloves, thinly sliced: 4 parts
Fresh thyme and rosemary, stripped from stems: 2 parts
  Alternatives: herbes de Provence
Flaky sea salt and black pepper: 2 parts
Extra olive oil for finishing: 5 parts
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 1 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Rounds of zucchini, ripe tomato, and waxy potato arranged in overlapping spirals in an olive-oil-slicked earthenware dish, then baked until every edge catches colour and the vegetables melt into each other at their touching faces.

ingredients.name: Ripe plum tomatoes, sliced 5 mm rounds
Waxy potato, peeled, sliced 5 mm rounds
Fresh thyme and rosemary, stripped from stems
Flaky sea salt and black pepper

steps:
Use a mandoline or very sharp knife to slice all vegetables to a uniform 5 mm thickness. Consistency is what makes the tian visually cohesive — irregular slices bake unevenly, leaving raw patches beside overdone edges. Lay slices on a clean surface and assess for uniformity.
Visual cue: The vegetable slices laid flat
Underdone: Slices vary in thickness from 3 mm to 10 mm — the thinner ones will char while thick ones are raw. Re-slice the thicker pieces. The mandoline is your friend here.
Perfect: Each round is translucent at its thin edges, consistent in thickness, and holds its circular shape without cracking or bending. The potato rounds are opaque; tomato rounds show their seed chambers. Proceed to the oil-and-herb bed.
Overdone: Slices are wafer-thin (under 3 mm) and already beginning to weep moisture, especially the tomato. Proceed carefully; thin tomatoes will melt faster than potato — layer in two separate rows in the dish rather than alternating.
Feel cue: A well-sliced tomato round should hold its shape when lifted from one edge — if it flops and tears, it was sliced too thin.

Coat the bottom of a wide earthenware gratin dish with a third of the olive oil. Scatter garlic slices across the oil. Arrange the vegetable rounds standing upright in overlapping rows — potato, zucchini, tomato, repeating — tilting each round slightly so it leans on the one behind it. Drizzle the remaining olive oil over the top, scatter herbs throughout the slices, and season generously with flaky salt and pepper.
Visual cue: The arranged tian before baking
Underdone: Vegetables are laid flat in a single layer rather than upright — they will steam instead of roast. Re-stand the slices on their edges in the dish, overlapping like scales.
Perfect: Concentric rows of alternating colours — deep green zucchini, bright red tomato, pale potato — standing upright and overlapping by half. Oil glistens in the crevices. Herb sprigs peak between slices like small green flags. Cover with foil and bake at 180 C (350 F) for 40 minutes.
Overdone: The rounds are packed so tightly they are not overlapping but compressed, walls parallel — the steam cannot escape. Use the handle of a spoon to gently create small gaps between rows.
Feel cue: Run a finger along the top of the arranged slices — there should be resistance, like a row of standing books. No slices should fall flat without prompting.

Cover the dish with foil and bake at 180 C (350 F) for 40 minutes to steam the vegetables through. Remove the foil and raise the oven to 220 C (425 F). Bake a further 25–35 minutes until the tops are deeply golden and the tomato has caramelised at its edges. The dish should be bubbling gently at the perimeter. Rest 10 minutes before serving.
Visual cue: The top edges of the vegetable rounds
Underdone: The exposed tops are still the raw colours of the raw vegetables — no browning, no caramelisation. A pool of unabsorbed olive oil sits undisturbed in the dish. Return uncovered for another 15 minutes at 220 C.
Perfect: The top 5 mm of each round has caramelised to amber and gold, with the tomatoes showing dark, jammy edges and the zucchini and potato lightly crisped. The dish smells of toasted olive oil, Provençal herbs, and concentrated tomato. The base of the dish shows a thickened, golden-brown vegetable liquid. Remove from oven and rest 10 minutes; the tian sets as it cools.
Overdone: The top rounds are uniformly dark — charred rather than caramelised — and the tomato has dried to a papery disc. Cover loosely with foil for the last few minutes of any remaining cook time to protect the tops.
Feel cue: Press the centre of the tian with a finger through a cloth — it should give with no resistance from the potato, the most stubborn vegetable in the dish. If the potato still pushes back, more time under foil is needed.

name: Pulled Pork Shoulder
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Bone-in pork shoulder (Boston butt, 2–2.5 kg): 100 parts
  Alternatives: boneless pork shoulder, netting removed
Smoked paprika: 4 parts
  Alternatives: sweet paprika + a drop of liquid smoke
Ground cumin: 2 parts
Freshly ground black pepper (coarse): 2 parts
Garlic powder: 2 parts
Onion powder: 1 parts
Cayenne pepper: 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: chipotle powder for more smoke
Dark brown sugar: 3 parts
  Alternatives: light brown sugar; muscovado
Fine salt (kosher or sea salt): 3 parts
Apple cider vinegar (for spritzing): 5 parts
  Alternatives: apple juice; water
Hardwood chunks (oak, hickory, or apple wood): 6 parts
  Alternatives: wood chips, soaked 30 min for gas grills
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 14 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A pork shoulder rubbed with spices, smoked low and slow for hours until the bark is mahogany and the interior pulls apart in long, silky, juicy threads with zero effort.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Hardwood chunks (oak, hickory, or apple wood)

steps:
Mix all the spices, sugar, and salt together into a uniform rub. Pat the pork shoulder completely dry with paper towels — surface moisture prevents the rub from adhering and forms steam instead of bark during cooking. Apply the rub in a thick, generous, even layer across every surface of the shoulder, pressing and patting it in firmly. Do not neglect any surface, including the fat cap and under any folds. Wrap the rubbed shoulder in plastic wrap or place in a large zipper bag and refrigerate for at least 8 hours, ideally overnight (12 hours). The salt in the rub draws out moisture, dissolves into a brine, and is reabsorbed — seasoning the meat deeply rather than just the surface.
Visual cue: The rubbed shoulder is completely coated in a dark, rust-red rub — no bare patches, no pooled rub at the bottom. After resting, the surface looks slightly damp as the salt has drawn moisture to the surface and the rub has begun to adhere.
Underdone: The rub is thin, applied in a light dusting that barely covers the surface. The pork fat is still clearly visible through the coating and the rub will not form a proper bark during cooking. Apply more rub generously. You want a thick, encrusting layer that makes the shoulder look like it has been dredged in spiced earth.
Perfect: A thick, even, dark rust-red coat across every surface. The shoulder looks almost black from the combination of paprika and dark brown sugar. The rub sticks without clumping or sliding off. Wrap and refrigerate for at least 8 hours before smoking.
Overdone: The rub has been applied in such a thick, crusty layer that it is beginning to fall off in clumps and the underlying fat is not visible. The salt ratio may overwhelm the meat. Brush off the most excessive accumulations and proceed. A slightly heavy rub is far better than a light one.
Feel cue: Press your palm flat against the rubbed surface — the rub

should feel gritty and slightly moist from the sugars, and it should cling to your skin when you lift your hand. If it feels powdery and dry and does not adhere, add a very thin brushing of neutral oil to the surface before applying the rub.

Set up the smoker or grill for indirect heat at a stable temperature of 107 to 120 C / 225 to 250 F. This is the low-and-slow window — above 135 C / 275 F the exterior dries before the interior collagen has had time to dissolve. Add hardwood chunks to the fire: oak and hickory are traditional for a bold, Southern BBQ character; apple and cherry are milder and pair beautifully with pork's sweetness. Place the shoulder fat-cap side up on the grate over the indirect zone. Smoke for 6 to 8 hours, maintaining the temperature window and adding wood as needed. Spritz with apple cider vinegar every 90 minutes after the first 3 hours to keep the surface moist and promote bark formation without washing the rub away.
Visual cue: After 6 to 7 hours, the bark is a deep, cracked mahogany — nearly black in the thicker areas, caramelized and lacquered-looking. The fat cap is translucent and rendered. White smoke drifts from the vents rather than thick billowing blue-grey smoke.
Underdone: The surface is still mostly red-orange from the paprika, with no crust and no significant darkening. Less than 4 hours have passed and the bark has not formed yet. Maintain the temperature and continue smoking. Bark typically begins forming after 4 to 5 hours. Do not raise the temperature to speed things up.
Perfect: A hard, crackling, mahogany bark that does not give when pressed. The shoulder has stalled (the temperature plateau, typically at 68 to 74 C / 155 to 165 F) and then powered through. The internal temperature should be approaching 88 C / 190 F. Check the internal temperature and begin the wrap phase if the bark is fully formed and the internal temperature is between 74 and 82 C / 165 to 180 F.
Overdone: Thick, black, and acrid-smelling smoke has been present throughout — a sign of incomplete combustion. The bark has become bitter rather than savory from the creosote in the smoke. Open

the vents to improve combustion and reduce fuel, aiming for thin, blue-white smoke. The bark may carry some bitterness — rest and pulling will distribute it and moderate its impact.
Feel cue: After 6 hours, knock on the bark with your knuckle — it should make a hollow, hard sound, like knocking on wood, not a wet, dull thud. The bark should feel completely dry and hard, like a crust. If it flexes or dents under your finger, it is not yet fully formed.

Once the bark is fully formed and the internal temperature is between 74 and 82 C / 165 and 180 F, wrap the shoulder tightly in two layers of heavy-duty foil (the Texas Crutch). Add a small splash of apple cider vinegar into the foil before sealing. Return to the smoker at the same temperature. The foil traps moisture and steam, rapidly converting remaining collagen to gelatin and driving the internal temperature through the stall. Cook until the internal temperature reaches 95 to 97 C / 203 to 207 F — the bone-probe temperature. At this temperature, the probe or a skewer should slide into the meat with the resistance of soft butter.
Visual cue: The foil package is tightly sealed. On unwrapping, the shoulder has softened visibly — the bark has relaxed slightly from the steam, the fat is completely rendered and trembling, and liquid has collected in the bottom of the foil package.
Underdone: The internal temperature is still below 90 C / 195 F and a probe or skewer meets distinct resistance in the thickest part. The shoulder does not wobble when you shake the rack. Return to the heat. The collagen has not yet fully converted. The shoulder may sit in the stall for another 1 to 2 hours before the temperature rises again — this is normal, do not raise the heat.
Perfect: Internal temperature at 95 to 97 C / 203 to 207 F and a probe slides in and out with no resistance — like pushing through soft peanut butter. The shoulder wobbles visibly when you shake the rack. The bone will feel loose in the meat. Remove from heat and move to the rest phase immediately.
Overdone: The internal temperature has exceeded 100 C / 212 F and the meat is beginning to dry out — the muscle fibers have contracted and squeezed out the moisture beyond recovery. Pull immediately and serve quickly; the meat may still be acceptable but will lack the full succulence of a properly cooked shoulder.
Feel

cue: Shake the foil package gently while it is on the grate — a perfectly cooked shoulder wobbles and jiggles with an almost liquid quality, the internal structure having fully given way. If it feels solid and unmoving, it needs more time. When you unwrap it, liquid should pool in the foil — that is the rendered collagen, and you should pour it back over the meat.

Transfer the wrapped shoulder (still in its foil) to a clean, empty cooler. Close the cooler and rest for a minimum of 1 hour, ideally 2 hours. This rest is not optional — it is what transforms the shoulder from simply cooked to superlative. During the rest, the internal temperature equalizes, the muscle fibers relax and reabsorb their juices, and the collagen that converted to gelatin coats every fiber, making the final pull glossy and self-saucing. A properly rested shoulder held in a cooler maintains temperature for up to 4 hours, so you can rest it comfortably while preparing everything else.
Visual cue: On unwrapping after the rest, the shoulder looks deflated and soft, the bark slightly steamed from the foil. The bone can be pulled free with two fingers and almost no effort — it slides out cleanly.
Underdone: The shoulder was rested for less than 30 minutes and is still steaming when unwrapped. The juices run clear and watery when cut — they have not had time to reabsorb. Re-wrap and continue resting. The difference in juiciness between a 30-minute and a 2-hour rest is dramatic.
Perfect: The bark has tightened back slightly after resting and the shoulder holds its shape when unwrapped. The bone pulls free cleanly. The juices released during the rest have pooled in the foil as a thick, gelatinous, mahogany liquid. Unwrap over a tray to catch the juices and begin pulling immediately.
Overdone: Rested too long (more than 4 hours in the cooler) and the shoulder has dropped below safe serving temperature and is cold to the touch. Return to the oven or smoker at 120 C / 250 F for 30 minutes to bring it back to serving temperature before pulling.
Feel cue: Touch the bark after the rest — it should have firmed back from the steamed texture it had immediately after unwrapping from foil. It should feel slightly crisp at the surface but give way immediately underneath.
The meat below the bark should feel soft and yielding, like clay.

Pull the pork using two forks or your hands (with clean heat-resistant gloves). Start from the bone and work outward, pulling the meat apart into long, natural strands — follow the grain of the muscle. Avoid chopping or shredding too finely; long, silky strands are the ideal. Pour the collected resting juices over the pulled meat and toss to coat. Chop the darkest pieces of bark into small bits and fold them through the pulled meat — these dark, intensely flavored bits are called 'burnt ends adjacent' and are prized for the concentrated spice-smoke flavor they add to the final mix. Taste and add salt or a splash of apple cider vinegar if needed.
Visual cue: A pile of long, glistening, mahogany-to-bronze threads of pulled pork, with darker bits of bark distributed throughout. The meat looks moist and self-saucing from the rendered fat and gelatin coating every fiber.
Underdone: The meat is still in chunks rather than pulling into strands — it is resistant to pulling and requires significant force. It is not done. Do not pull yet. Return any uncooperative sections to the oven at 120 C / 250 F for 30 to 45 minutes, wrapped, and try again.
Perfect: The meat pulls apart effortlessly into long, natural strands with the lightest touch, each strand glistening with rendered fat. Bark bits mixed through add dark, caramelized intensity. The pile holds moisture and does not look dry. Serve in sandwiches, bowls, or tacos. The fat and gelatin will keep the pulled pork moist for hours at room temperature on a tray.
Overdone: The meat has shredded to a mushy, paste-like consistency — the fibers have broken down entirely and the texture is more akin to tinned meat than pulled pork. Serve it as-is but sauce generously to compensate for the lost texture. Avoid this by pulling promptly and not overcooking past 97 C / 207 F.
Feel cue: Take a strand of pulled pork and stretch it gently

between your fingers — a perfect piece should elongate a little before tearing cleanly, like pulling apart a piece of cooked fish. It should feel slick and slightly tacky from the dissolved collagen, not dry or stringy.

name: Low-and-Slow Smoked Pulled Pork
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Bone-in pork shoulder (Boston butt), 4–5 kg: 1 whole
  Alternatives: boneless pork shoulder (reduce cook time by ~1 hr)
BBQ dry rub (see bbq-dry-rub recipe): 6 tbsp
  Alternatives: store-bought competition rub
Yellow mustard (binder): 2 tbsp
  Alternatives: hot sauce as binder
Apple cider (for spritzing): 120 ml
  Alternatives: apple juice; diluted ACV
Hickory or oak wood chunks: 4 chunks
  Alternatives: pecan wood; apple wood (milder, sweeter)
Apple cider vinegar (for finishing): 2 tbsp
  Alternatives: white wine vinegar
Flaky salt (for finishing pull): 1 tsp
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 14 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A bone-in pork shoulder wrestled down to collapse over ten to fourteen hours of hardwood smoke — the kind of cook where patience is the only active ingredient. Bark dark as mahogany, interior that pulls apart in long, silk-threaded ropes with nothing more than two forks and a light touch.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Pat the pork shoulder completely dry with paper towels. Using your hands, coat every surface — sides, fat cap, bone — with a thin, even layer of yellow mustard (this acts purely as a binder and disappears during cooking; you will not taste it). Immediately apply the dry rub generously over all surfaces, pressing it firmly into the flesh. Wrap tightly in plastic and refrigerate overnight, or at minimum 4 hours. Remove from the fridge 1 hour before cooking to temper slightly.
Visual cue: A uniformly coated shoulder with no bare skin. The rub should look opaque and tacky after refrigerating, not dry and powdery.
Underdone: Visible bare patches of meat or thin, dusty rub layer. Apply more rub and press firmly. The mustard helps it stick — add more if needed.
Perfect: Thick, even mahogany crust clinging to the meat surface. Slightly tacky to the touch after resting. Proceed to the smoker.
Overdone: Rub so thick it is sliding off in sheets. Surface is wet with drawn-out moisture. Pat excess rub back on gently. Some falling-off is normal on wet cuts.
Feel cue: After overnight resting, the rub should feel almost paste-like — the salt has drawn moisture out and the surface is damp and clingy rather than dry and granular.

Preheat your smoker to 107–121 C (225–250 F). Place the shoulder fat-cap up directly on the grate. Add wood chunks for steady thin blue smoke — not white billowing smoke, which turns bark bitter. Maintain temperature and smoke for 6–8 hours. Every 90 minutes after the first 3 hours, spritz all surfaces with apple cider to keep the bark moist and encourage smoke absorption. The internal temperature will stall around 68–74 C (155–165 F) and plateau for 2–3 hours — this is the collagen rendering. Do not raise the heat.
Visual cue: Bark has turned a deep mahogany-to-black on the exterior. Fat cap has partially rendered down. The meat probe slides in with minimal resistance at the stall.
Underdone: Bark is still reddish and soft. Meat is pulling back from the bone only slightly. Continue smoking. You have not yet reached the stall — do not rush with higher heat.
Perfect: Dark mahogany-black bark, firm and slightly crisp. Meat has shrunk visibly from the bone end. Internal temp hovering 68–74 C. Wrap in butcher paper to push through the stall (the Texas crutch).
Overdone: Bark is black and ashy with a harsh, acrid smell. Bark is flaking off in dry chunks. Wrap immediately and do not add more wood. The interior will still be good.
Feel cue: Grip the bone end with a towel — by the time you hit the stall, it should have just the faintest wobble, like a loose tooth, but not yet pulling free.

Wrap the shoulder tightly in two sheets of uncoated butcher paper (or foil as a fallback). Return to the smoker at the same temperature. Continue cooking until a probe thermometer slides into the thickest part of the shoulder with zero resistance — like pushing into soft butter — at approximately 93–96 C (200–205 F) internal temperature. This typically takes another 3–5 hours after wrapping. The bone should be completely loose.
Visual cue: Probe thermometer registers 93–96 C and slides into the meat with no push-back at all.
Underdone: Probe meets firm resistance or reads below 90 C. Bone still feels anchored. Rewrap and return to the smoker for another 30–60 minutes. Check again.
Perfect: The probe slides in like warm custard — no resistance. Bone can be twisted and pulled free with a gentle tug. Internal temp 93–96 C. Transfer (still wrapped) to a cooler with towels to rest for at least 1 hour.
Overdone: Meat feels mushy and liquid is pouring out of the paper wrap. Internal temp above 99 C. Pull immediately and rest in a cooler. It will still pull well — the texture is just slightly softer.
Feel cue: Lift the wrapped shoulder — it should feel dramatically heavier and more liquid-filled than when it went in, shifting and sloshing slightly inside the paper.

Transfer the wrapped shoulder, still sealed, into a clean cooler lined with folded towels. Close the cooler. Rest for a minimum of 1 hour, up to 4 hours. This rest is not optional — it allows the internal juices to be reabsorbed into the muscle fibers. Cutting too early results in juice running out onto the board, not staying in the meat.
Visual cue: The wrapped package holds its shape but feels somewhat yielding when gently pressed — the meat is relaxing.
Underdone: Only 15–20 minutes of rest. The package is still very hot and rigid. Continue resting. The cooler will hold temperature easily for 3–4 hours.
Perfect: After 1–2 hours, the package has stopped steaming when opened. Meat holds its shape when the paper is peeled back but separates easily when pulled. Unwrap and pull the meat.
Overdone: Rested more than 4–5 hours in the cooler. Internal temp may have dropped below 60 C (140 F) food-safety threshold. Check temperature before serving. Reheat in a covered pan with a splash of apple juice if needed.
Feel cue: After a proper rest, the meat surface will feel warm but not hot to the back of the hand — like a thick-quilted comforter, not a hot pan.

Unwrap the shoulder over a large cutting board to capture the juices. Remove and discard the bone — it should slide free with zero effort. Using two forks or heat-proof gloves, pull the meat apart in long strands, working with the grain of the muscle. Roughly chop any large bark pieces and fold them back through the pulled meat for texture contrast. Drizzle the collected board juices back over the meat. Finish with a light splash of apple cider vinegar and a pinch of flaky salt. Taste and adjust.
Visual cue: Long, silk-like strands of pork with dark bark pieces folded throughout, glistening with the collected cooking juices.
Underdone: Meat requires significant effort to pull — it tears in chunks rather than long strands. The shoulder likely needed another 30–60 minutes of cooking. Chop rather than pull for serving.
Perfect: Meat falls into long, moist strands with gentle fork pressure. Dark bark flecks distributed throughout. Glistening with juice. Serve immediately on buns, or hold in a covered pan.
Overdone: Meat crumbles to mush with no strand structure — almost paste-like. Still delicious. Serve it chunky-chopped style, Carolina-hash style, or pile it on nachos.
Feel cue: Properly pulled pork should feel silky and slightly sticky between the fingers — each strand separating cleanly without shredding to fluff. Squeeze a small handful: it should hold together briefly then fall apart.

This is the legionary's bowl, older than bread in the Roman kitchen and the bedrock of the Mediterranean table.

ingredients.name: Emmer wheat / farro (whole or coarsely cracked)
Fresh lovage or celery leaf, chopped

steps:
Rinse the emmer in cold water until it runs clear, then cover it generously with part of the water and leave it overnight, 8 hours or more. Whole emmer is a tough, hulled grain; the long soak rehydrates the bran and lets the kernels swell so they will cook down sweet and tender rather than staying chalky at the core. Reserve the rest of the water for the cook.
Visual cue: Plumped, glossy kernels that have visibly swollen and softened at the edges, sitting in faintly cloudy, starch-tinged water.
Underdone: Grains are still small, hard, and dry-looking, and the soak water is nearly clear. Keep soaking. Old or very whole emmer can need a full 12 hours — give it more time in a cool spot.
Perfect: Kernels are noticeably swollen and bend slightly under a fingernail without splitting. The water has gone cloudy with released starch. Drain off the soak water (or keep it for extra body) and move to the simmer.
Overdone: Water smells sour or yeasty and bubbles cling to the surface — the grain fermented in a warm room. If only faintly sour, rinse very well and proceed. If clearly fermented, discard and start again with a cooler soak.
Feel cue: A soaked kernel should feel leathery and yielding, not glassy-hard. Bitten, it gives a chewy resistance with no dry, powdery center.

Put the drained emmer in a heavy pot with the reserved water and the salt. Bring to a boil, then drop to the barest simmer and cook uncovered, stirring often as it thickens, 45 minutes to over an hour depending on the grain. As the kernels burst they release starch and the pot turns from soupy to a thick, spoon-coating pottage. Add hot water as needed; you want the grains broken and creamy, not dry. Salting now seasons from within as the starch absorbs the liquid.
Visual cue: A thick, oatmeal-like porridge where many kernels have split open into a creamy starch matrix, and a dragged spoon leaves a slowly closing trail across the bottom.
Underdone: Grains are still distinct and firm with a chalky center, swimming in thin, watery liquid. Keep simmering low and stir more often. The porridge thickens only once the kernels burst — be patient and top up with hot water if it tightens too soon.
Perfect: A cohesive, creamy pottage that mounds softly on the spoon; the grains are tender with a pleasant chew and the liquid has all but vanished into a glossy body. Pull from the heat and move to finishing while it is still loose and hot — it firms quickly as it cools.
Overdone: The puls is stiff and gluey, sticking to the pot bottom and threatening to scorch. Stir in a splash of hot water to loosen and scrape the pot off the heat before it catches and turns bitter.
Feel cue: The pot should burble lazily, not boil, and the porridge will pull heavier on the spoon as it goes. Crush a kernel against the side — it should smear to a soft, sweet-smelling paste with only a gentle chew left.

Off the heat, beat in the olive oil and most of the grated cheese until the puls turns glossy and rich; the residual heat melts the cheese into the starch for savory depth. Stir through the chopped lovage and a heavy grind of pepper. Taste and correct the salt. Spoon into bowls, scatter the remaining cheese over the top, and finish with a thread of olive oil — or, for the full Roman effect, a few drops of garum.
Visual cue: A glossy, cohesive porridge flecked green with herb, its surface sheened with oil and dotted with half-melted cheese, mounding softly without weeping liquid.
Underdone: The puls tastes flat and starchy, the oil and cheese sitting on top rather than blended in. Stir more vigorously to emulsify the oil into the hot starch and add salt or a little more cheese until it tastes savory and rounded.
Perfect: Rich, glossy, and well seasoned — nutty grain, salty-sharp cheese, green herb, and warm pepper in balance, loose enough to fall softly from the spoon. Serve at once while hot and yielding, with the final drizzle of oil or garum.
Overdone: Stirred too long off the heat, the puls has cooled and stiffened into a dense, claggy mass. Loosen with a splash of hot water or broth and warm gently, stirring, to bring back its soft, spoonable texture.
Feel cue: It should slump, not pour — thick enough to hold a shape on the spoon yet soft enough to spread. The first taste is nutty and warm, then the cheese hits salty and sharp, with the lovage lifting it like wild celery.

name: German Pumpernickel
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=bakers_percentage）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Coarse rye meal (pumpernickel grind): 100 %
  Alternatives: whole rye flour (denser result)
Whole rye berries (soaked overnight): 30 %
  Alternatives: cracked rye
Boiling water: 90 %

Fine salt: 2 %
Caraway seeds: 1 %
  Alternatives: fennel seeds; anise seeds
Dark malt extract or blackstrap molasses: 5 %
  Alternatives: treacle; dark barley malt syrup
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 24 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Dense, midnight-dark, and profoundly complex — this Westphalian rye brick steams for sixteen hours until every grain is saturated with malt depth, subtle sourdough tang, and an undercurrent of dark chocolate and coffee that has no parallel in other breads.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Dark malt extract or blackstrap molasses

steps:
In a large heatproof bowl, combine the coarse rye meal and the pre-soaked whole rye berries. Pour the boiling water over both and stir vigorously until the rye meal has absorbed all the water. The mixture will look like a very thick, sticky porridge — almost like wet concrete. Cover tightly and let stand at room temperature for 1 hour. This scalding step gelatinizes the rye starches, kickstarts enzymatic breakdown of the complex rye sugars that become the bread's distinctive malt-dark sweetness, and softens the whole berries.
Visual cue: After 1 hour: a thick, dark, uniform mass that has absorbed all the water. No pools of standing liquid. Rye berries visible throughout like small dark pearls.
Underdone: Still watery — standing liquid on the surface, rye meal not fully hydrated, coarse granules still gritty. Stir vigorously and wait another 30 minutes — the rye meal needs time to absorb fully.
Perfect: Dark, thick, uniform porridge. No standing water. Whole rye berries distributed evenly throughout. Has a faint, toasted-rye smell. Cool to below 35 C before adding the sourdough starter.
Overdone: Mass is very dense and has stiffened into a paste that barely stirs. Almost cold. Proceed — this is normal. Add a small amount of water (5%) if the starter won't incorporate.
Feel cue: The soaked grain mass should feel like cold, dense porridge — thick enough to mound on a spoon without running, with the faint rough texture of the rye berries throughout.

Once the soaked grain has cooled to below 35 C (check with your wrist), add the rye sourdough starter, salt, caraway seeds, and dark malt extract or molasses. Stir everything together vigorously with a heavy wooden spoon or stiff spatula until completely uniform. This is not a dough in the conventional sense — there is no gluten network to develop. It is a thick, dense batter that barely holds a shape. The color will be very dark brown. Taste: it should be savory, subtly sweet, malty, and smell complex.
Visual cue: A uniform dark-brown mass — every dark ingredient blended in without visible streaks of lighter rye meal or lighter starter. Dense enough to hold a mound when dropped from a spoon.
Underdone: Paler streaks of starter or unmixed rye meal visible; malt extract has not fully incorporated; dough looks marbled. Continue mixing vigorously until completely uniform in color.
Perfect: Uniformly very dark brown, almost black-brown. Dense but stirrable. Smells of rye, caraway, and dark malt. Tastes deeply savory with a background sweetness. Transfer immediately to a loaf tin and proceed to baking.
Overdone: You have overmixed with a machine and the mass has become slightly aerated or stringy. Unlikely by hand. Proceed — minor overmixing doesn't harm pumpernickel, which has no gluten structure to damage.
Feel cue: Pumpernickel dough feels impossibly dense and sticky — it clings to your spoon in long, reluctant threads and takes real effort to stir. If your arm is tired, you're doing it right.

Line a small loaf tin (approximately 20 x 10 cm) with parchment on all sides. Grease the parchment lightly. Spoon the pumpernickel dough into the tin, pressing firmly into the corners with a wet spatula or wet hands to eliminate air pockets. Smooth the top flat. Tap the tin firmly on the counter several times to release trapped bubbles. The tin should be filled to within 1 cm of the top. Cover tightly with an oiled piece of foil, crimped tightly around the rim to trap steam during baking.
Visual cue: A smooth, flat-topped dark mass filling the tin to within 1 cm of the rim. No visible air holes or craters in the surface. Foil seal is tight.
Underdone: Air pockets visible on the surface; corners are not fully filled; the top surface is uneven with craters. Press the surface smooth with a wet spatula and tap the tin again to settle the dough.
Perfect: Smooth, flat, matte-black surface filling the tin evenly. Foil crimped tight. The tin feels heavy for its size. Place in a water bath or steam oven and bake at 120 C (250 F) for 16 hours.
Overdone: You've overfilled the tin — dough is level with or above the rim and will overflow during baking. Remove a spoonful or two, then seal with foil and proceed.
Feel cue: When you press the pumpernickel dough into the tin, it feels like pressing very dense, cold clay — it holds the indentation of your fingers and does not spring back at all.

Preheat the oven to 120 C (250 F). Place the covered loaf tin inside a deep roasting pan. Pour boiling water into the roasting pan to reach halfway up the sides of the loaf tin — this creates the steam environment essential for pumpernickel. Bake covered with foil for 16 hours. Yes, sixteen hours. The low heat and steam slowly caramelize the rye sugars through the Maillard reaction and enzymatic browning — this is what creates the characteristic near-black color and complex, malt-chocolate flavor without any added colorants. After 16 hours, remove the foil, raise oven to 180 C (350 F), and bake uncovered for 30 minutes to set the crust. Cool completely in the tin before unmolding. Slice paper-thin — pumpernickel is best the day after baking.
Visual cue: After 16 hours under foil: the loaf has shrunk slightly from the tin walls and the surface is very dark brown, almost black. After the uncovered 30-minute finish: a firm, very dark crust with a matte surface.
Underdone: After 16 hours the loaf center still feels soft and wet when pressed; internal temp below 95 C; the color is more dark-brown than near-black. Return covered at 120 C for another 2–4 hours. Pumpernickel cannot be rushed.
Perfect: Near-black exterior, firm throughout when pressed. Internal temp 96–98 C. When unmolded and sliced, the crumb is dense, moist, and very dark — the color of dark chocolate. Rye berries visible as slightly paler dots. Cool completely — ideally overnight — before slicing. Wrap in paper and serve in thin slices.
Overdone: Crust is charred or cracked; edges have dried to a hard, brittle shell. Trim the dried edges. The interior is almost certainly perfect — pumpernickel's dense structure protects it from overbaking.
Feel cue: A finished pumpernickel loaf feels like a dense, moist brick — far heavier than a wheat bread of the same size. Slice it paper-thin with a sharp serrated
knife: each slice should flex slightly rather than crumble.

name: Pumpkin Pie
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: graham cracker crust; gingersnap crust

  Alternatives: roasted butternut squash puree; kabocha squash puree

  Alternatives: evaporated milk (more traditional); coconut cream

  Alternatives: 3 whole eggs (less rich)

  Alternatives: granulated sugar; maple syrup (reduce cream slightly)

Active time: 25 min
Total time: 1 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A silky, trembling custard of pumpkin and warm spice set in a buttery, shatteringly crisp crust — the pie that makes an entire holiday smell like cinnamon and brown sugar from the moment it goes into the oven.

ingredients.name: Pumpkin pie spice (cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, clove, allspice)

steps:
If using a raw pie shell, line it with parchment and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake at 190°C for 15 minutes. Remove weights and parchment and bake a further 5 minutes until the base is just set and dry, but not browned. This par-baking prevents the classic soggy bottom. Cool slightly before filling.
Visual cue: The crust bottom looks dry and matte — no raw, doughy sheen. The edges are barely starting to turn a light golden color.
Underdone: Crust bottom still looks wet and shiny. Raw dough visible. It will turn soggy under the wet pumpkin filling. Return to oven for 3–5 more minutes. The base must look dry and slightly set before you pour in the custard.
Perfect: Base is dry and matte-looking with very light color at the edges. The dough no longer looks raw. Cool to the touch. Reduce oven to 165°C and fill with custard.
Overdone: Crust is already golden-brown and baked through before the custard has even been added. It will over-brown significantly during the filled bake. Tent the edges with foil strips during the custard bake to prevent burning.
Feel cue: Press the base of the par-baked crust gently with a finger — it should feel firm and dry, not soft or give way. The edges should feel set but pale, not crumbly or crisp.

In a large bowl, whisk together the pumpkin puree and brown sugar until no lumps remain. Add the spice blend, salt, and vanilla and whisk to combine. In a separate bowl, whisk the eggs and extra yolk until smooth, then add the heavy cream and whisk to combine. Pour the egg-cream mixture into the pumpkin mixture and whisk until completely smooth. Do not over-whisk or you will incorporate air that causes cracking during baking.
Visual cue: A smooth, uniform, deep orange custard that flows like thick cream. No lumps, no bubbles on the surface, uniform in color throughout.
Underdone: Lumps of unmixed pumpkin or undissolved brown sugar visible. The mixture looks streaky — orange swirls in a lighter background. Whisk more gently until uniform. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve if lumps persist — pumpkin custard should be silky-smooth.
Perfect: Smooth, deep orange, flowing custard. No lumps. When you hold a whisk above it, the custard falls in a smooth ribbon, not in drops. Strain through a sieve for extra smoothness, then pour into the par-baked crust.
Overdone: The custard has lots of bubbles on the surface from vigorous whisking. These bubbles will set into the pie and create an uneven, pockmarked surface. Let the custard stand for 5 minutes to allow most bubbles to dissipate before pouring. Or torch the surface briefly after pouring into the shell.
Feel cue: Run a clean finger through the custard and taste — you should taste earthy pumpkin, warm spice in this order: cinnamon, then ginger warmth, then a distant heat from clove. If one spice dominates, the blend is off.

Pour the custard into the par-baked shell, filling to within 5mm of the top edge. Tent the crust edges with foil or a pie shield. Bake at 165°C for 50–60 minutes until the edges of the custard are set but the center 5cm still jiggles when the pie is gently shaken. Remove and cool completely at room temperature for 2 hours, then refrigerate.
Visual cue: The custard surface is set and matte with a slight dome. The edges are completely firm. The center 5cm jiggles as a single mass — like jello — when the pan is gently shaken.
Underdone: The center half of the pie is still liquid and moves like water when shaken, not as a single jiggly mass. The surface looks wet and shiny throughout. Return to oven for 5–10 minute intervals. Check often — the window between underdone and overdone is narrow.
Perfect: Edges are completely set and matte. The center 5cm jiggles as one unified mass. A paring knife inserted 2cm from the edge comes out clean, but the very center still looks underdone. Trust the jiggle. Remove immediately. The center will finish cooking from carryover heat.
Overdone: The entire pie is firm, even the center. The surface has cracked across the middle. The edges may be puffed and separating from the crust. Cool and refrigerate — cracked pies still taste good. Cover cracks with whipped cream. Next time, pull 10 minutes earlier and trust carryover heat.
Feel cue: Gently shake the pie pan while it's still in the oven — rest your fingertips on the rack and tilt slightly. The center should move as a single disc, not as a liquid wave. The moment you feel one unified jiggle rather than a liquid slosh, pull it.

Cool the pie on a wire rack at room temperature for 2 full hours. Do not refrigerate immediately — rapid temperature change causes cracking. After 2 hours, refrigerate uncovered for at least 2 hours before slicing. The filling must be completely cold before cutting — warm pumpkin pie filling is still technically liquid and will collapse when cut.
Visual cue: After cooling, the custard surface is completely matte, slightly shrunk from the edges, and firm with a very slight bounce when tapped. The pie holds its shape when sliced.
Underdone: Pie was cut while still warm — the custard collapses out from the slice, pooling on the plate. Surface looks wet in the cut. Refrigerate the remaining pie and serve the collapsed slice as a 'deconstructed' portion. Slice cold next time.
Perfect: Cold pie slices cleanly, holding its triangular shape. Cut edge is smooth and firm, showing the deep orange custard and flaky crust at the base. Serve with whipped cream.
Overdone: Pie has been refrigerated for more than 2 days. The crust is slightly soft from moisture migration. The custard surface may have a slight sheen. Serve anyway — flavor is unaffected. Next time, store covered loosely with plastic wrap, not sealed, to reduce moisture condensation.
Feel cue: Press the center of the cooled pie gently with one finger — it should spring back immediately with a faint bounce, like pressing a firm cheek. If it holds a dent, it needs more time in the refrigerator.
