ingredients.name: Whole cauliflower head (leaves trimmed, stem cut flat)
柠檬（Lemon (half juiced, half for serving)）
Flaky sea salt and black pepper (to finish)
Chopped parsley and toasted pine nuts

steps:
Bring a large, deep pot of water to a rolling boil and season it aggressively with the kosher salt and the juice of half the lemon — it should taste like seawater. Lower the trimmed whole head in stem-side down, cover, and simmer 8 to 12 minutes. This seasons the cauliflower to its core and softens the dense stem so it cooks through before the surface scorches in the oven. Lift it out carefully with two slotted spoons or a spider and set it stem-down on a rack to drain and steam-dry completely.
Visual cue: The head has dulled from chalk-white to a faint ivory and a paring knife slides into the core stem with light resistance, like a barely-done potato.
Underdone: A knife meets a hard, crunchy core at the stem and the florets still feel rigid and squeaky. Simmer another few minutes. The stem must yield or the center will be raw when the outside is browned.
Perfect: A blade meets gentle, even resistance at the core and the florets feel tender but still fully intact and holding their shape. Drain stem-down on a rack and let it steam-dry for several minutes — surface moisture is the enemy of browning.
Overdone: Florets are slumping, the head feels loose and waterlogged, and pieces break away when lifted. Handle very gently and drain longer. It will still roast beautifully — just expect a softer, more spoonable result than a carvable one.
Feel cue: Lifted from the water the head should feel heavy and supple, not stiff. Let it sit until it stops steaming and the surface looks matte and dry to the touch — wet curds will steam instead of brown.

Whisk the olive oil with the garlic paste, cumin, and smoked paprika into a loose, rust-colored slurry. Set the drained head in an oven-proof skillet or on a lined sheet and massage the spiced oil over every surface, working it down into the crevices between florets and over the cut stem. Be generous — the oil is both the seasoning and the frying medium that crisps the crown.
Visual cue: The whole head glistens an even terracotta-red, with oil pooled slightly in the folds and no dry, pale patches showing through.
Underdone: Chalky white gaps show between florets and the spice rub sits only on the domed top. Tilt the head and brush oil into the seams and underside. Uncoated spots stay pale and bland in the oven.
Perfect: A uniform glossy, spice-stained coat clings to the entire surface, from crown to stem, and the kitchen smells of toasted cumin. Set it crown-up in the pan and move straight to the oven.
Overdone: Oil runs off in a puddle around the base and the rub looks washed-out and pale. Pour off excess oil and add another light dusting of paprika and cumin directly onto the wet surface.
Feel cue: The surface should feel slick and fully saturated under your fingers, the rub gripping rather than sliding off. The raw garlic and smoked paprika should smell vivid and sharp — they mellow and sweeten in the heat.

Roast in a hot oven at 220C / 425F for 30 to 40 minutes, basting once or twice with the oil that collects in the pan. The Maillard browning turns the surface curds deeply golden and concentrates the sugars into a nutty, almost popcorn sweetness. The head is done when the crown is bronzed and crackly and a skewer slides through the center without resistance.
Visual cue: A burnished mahogany-gold dome with crisp, lacquered floret tips and a few dark, blistered edges, while the interior is meltingly soft.
Underdone: The surface is pale gold and still soft, with no crisp edges or browning on the floret tips. Return to the oven and raise the heat if needed. Color is flavor here — push it well past blond.
Perfect: Deep golden-brown all over with shatter-crisp tips, the odd charred edge, and a skewer gliding through the center with no resistance. Pull it now, squeeze over the remaining lemon, and rest five minutes before carving.
Overdone: Large patches have gone past brown to bitter black and acrid smoke is rising from the pan. Remove immediately and trim the scorched tips. A cooler oven and a tent of foil will save the next one.
Feel cue: Tap the crown — it should sound and feel crisp, the tips snapping slightly, while a skewer through the heart meets the soft give of butter. The aroma turns sweet and toasty, the raw-garlic edge long gone.

Transfer the rested head to a warm platter. Squeeze over the juice of the remaining lemon half, scatter with flaky salt and a few grinds of black pepper, then shower with chopped parsley and toasted pine nuts. Bring it whole to the table and carve into thick wedges from the crown down through the tender stem, spooning the spiced pan oil over each portion.
Visual cue: A glistening bronze head bright with green herbs and golden pine nuts, cutting into wedges that hold together from crisp crown to soft, seasoned core.
Underdone: The cauliflower tastes flat and one-note, with no brightness cutting the richness of the oil. Add more lemon and flaky salt right at the table — the acid and crunch wake the whole dish up.
Perfect: Each wedge is crisp-edged and creamy-centered, savory and lightly smoky, lifted by lemon and salt and finished with fresh herbs and crunch. Serve at once while the crown is still crackling, with the pan oil spooned over.
Overdone: The head has cooled and gone soft and oily, the crisp crown turned chewy. Flash it back into a hot oven for a few minutes to re-crisp, then re-dress with fresh lemon and herbs.
Feel cue: The first cut should give a faint crackle at the crown then yield to a soft, steamy interior. On the palate it runs nutty and savory, brightened by lemon, with the pine nuts adding a buttery crunch against the tender curds.

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Parsnips, carrots, and beetroot — peeled and cut to size, tossed in a generous coat of oil, and roasted at high heat until their sugars have caramelized to a deep, bittersweet char — the most honest and satisfying way to eat the vegetables of an English autumn.

ingredients.name: 胡萝卜（Carrots (peeled, halved or quartered lengthwise)）
Fresh thyme sprigs and bay leaves
Flaky sea salt and black pepper

steps:
Peel all vegetables. Cut into pieces of approximately equal size and similar surface area so they roast at the same rate — this is the single most important prep step. Parsnips halved lengthwise; carrots halved or quartered depending on size; beetroot into 6–8 wedges. Toss in a large bowl with the oil, coating every surface — do not season with salt yet, as salt draws moisture and creates steam in the early roasting stage.
Visual cue: Uniformly sized pieces across all three vegetable types, each surface glistening with an even coat of oil. The pieces should look roughly the same size when mounded together.
Underdone: Pieces are of vastly different sizes — some large beetroot wedges alongside thin carrot strips. Re-cut the oversized pieces to match the smaller ones. Uneven sizes guarantee some pieces will burn while others undercook.
Perfect: Consistent size throughout. Even oil coat on every face. The vegetables look plump and glistening. Spread onto the roasting tray immediately.
Overdone: Vegetables have been sitting in oil for too long and some pieces appear waterlogged. Proceed — the oil absorption won't significantly affect the result.
Feel cue: Pick up a piece of oiled parsnip — it should feel slick and the oil should not drip off when held for 5 seconds. The cut surfaces should feel smooth and slightly tacky from the oil.

Preheat the oven to 220°C (430°F) with a large, heavy roasting tray inside. The preheated tray is essential — vegetables placed in a cold tray steam rather than roast. Spread the vegetables in a single layer with the cut sides down, with space between each piece — touching vegetables steam each other. Scatter thyme and bay leaves throughout. Roast for 25 minutes without opening the oven.
Visual cue: After 25 minutes, the cut sides in contact with the tray should show deep caramelization — golden to dark-brown. The vegetables are beginning to shrink and the edges have started to color.
Underdone: After 25 minutes, the cut sides are pale and the vegetables look steamed — no caramelization visible. The tray was likely not hot enough or the oven temperature was too low. Turn up to 230°C and return to oven.
Perfect: Cut sides are deeply golden to brown with distinct caramelization. The kitchen smells of caramelized carrot and earthy beetroot. Parsnips at the tips are beginning to char. Turn pieces over, season with salt, and return to oven.
Overdone: The cut surfaces have blackened and the vegetables are beginning to shrink dramatically. Remove immediately and serve. Deeply caramelized root vegetables are still delicious even at the border of charred.
Feel cue: Open the oven after 25 minutes and you should hear a steady, moderate sizzle from every piece. The released steam should carry the sweet smell of caramelizing parsnip and carrot sugars.

Turn each piece over to expose an unbrowned side. Season now with flaky sea salt and black pepper. Drizzle honey or maple syrup over the pieces in the tray. Return to the oven for 15–20 more minutes until everything is tender, deeply caramelized, and the honey has darkened and concentrated. The sugar in the glaze accelerates the Maillard reaction on the freshly exposed surfaces.
Visual cue: Deep amber-brown caramelization on multiple sides, with the honey glaze forming a shiny, dark, concentrated coat on the exposed surfaces. Parsnip tips may be very dark — this is desirable.
Underdone: Pale second side with honey not yet caramelized — it looks pale and liquid on the surface. Return to the oven. The honey needs heat to concentrate and caramelize.
Perfect: Multiple deep-caramelized sides. Honey has darkened and adhered to the vegetables, forming a sticky, shiny coat. Parsnip tips are dark, almost charred. A fork passes through all pieces with almost no resistance. Serve immediately from the tray.
Overdone: Honey has burnt to a black, bitter film and the vegetables are very dark and dry. Remove immediately. Scrape off the worst of the burnt honey. The underlying vegetable may still be excellent.
Feel cue: Press a parsnip with the back of a fork — it should yield completely with a slight give, like pressing into firm butter. The honey glaze on the surface should feel tacky and slightly sticky, not wet.

name: Roasted Tomato & Garlic Soup
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Plum (Roma) tomatoes, halved lengthwise: 1800 g
  Alternatives: 2 x 800 g cans whole peeled tomatoes, drained (juice reserved for the liquid)
Yellow onions, cut into thick wedges: 300 g
Red bell pepper, seeded and quartered: 1 whole
  Alternatives: 1 large carrot, sliced thin
Garlic, unpeeled: 10 cloves
Extra-virgin olive oil: 60 ml
Kosher salt: 10 g
Fresh thyme: 4 sprigs
  Alternatives: 1/2 tsp dried thyme
Vegetable stock: 750 ml
  Alternatives: chicken stock; water
Fresh basil: 12 leaves
Red wine vinegar: 10 ml
  Alternatives: balsamic vinegar
Sugar (only if the tomatoes are sharp): 0 to taste
Heavy cream: 120 ml
  Alternatives: coconut milk; omit for a lighter soup
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 1 hr 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Tomatoes, onion, and a whole head of garlic roasted until blistered and caramel-edged, then blended into a thick, brick-red soup that tastes of late summer, with basil and a swirl of cream.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Yellow onions, cut into thick wedges
Red bell pepper, seeded and quartered
糖（Sugar (only if the tomatoes are sharp)）

steps:
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Divide tomatoes (cut-side up), onion, pepper, and garlic between two rimmed sheet pans, drizzle with oil, sprinkle with the salt, and tuck in thyme sprigs. Roast 45–55 minutes, rotating the pans halfway, until the tomatoes are slumped and blackened in spots and the garlic is soft.
Visual cue: Collapsed, wrinkled tomatoes with dark caramelised edges and jammy juices; onion charred at the tips.
Underdone: Tomatoes still plump and wet, no browning; pans full of watery juice. Roast 10–15 minutes more; the juice needs to reduce before it caramelises.
Perfect: Tomatoes deflated with charred freckles; juices thick and sticky at the pan edges; garlic squeezes out like paste. Scrape everything, juices included, into a pot.
Overdone: Pan juices burnt black; tomatoes leathery. Leave the burnt pan residue behind and add a splash more stock for body.
Feel cue: Press a roasted garlic clove — the soft centre should slip out of the skin with a gentle squeeze.

Squeeze the garlic from its skins and discard the skins and thyme stems. Scrape everything into a 5 litre pot, pour a little of the stock onto the hot pans to loosen the stuck juices, and add it all with the remaining stock and the basil. Simmer 10 minutes to marry the flavors.
Visual cue: A chunky, deep-red mixture barely bubbling, basil wilted through.
Underdone: Roasted flavor sits on top; liquid tastes thin. Simmer 5 minutes more.
Perfect: Liquid tinted brick-red and smelling sweet and smoky. Blend.
Overdone: Reduced to a sticky sauce. Add stock or water to loosen.
Feel cue: The kitchen should smell like concentrated tomato paste and roasted garlic rather than fresh tomato.

Blend until smooth with an immersion blender (or in batches in a vented blender). For a silkier soup, press through a sieve to remove skins. Stir in vinegar, then taste: add a pinch of sugar only if it's sharp, and adjust salt. Stir in cream and warm gently without boiling. To freeze: freeze before adding cream (dairy can separate) — cool quickly, refrigerate within 2 hours, freeze up to 4 months, then add cream after reheating.
Visual cue: Thick, velvety orange-red soup with a satin sheen from the oil and cream.
Underdone: Flecks of skin and chunks of pepper remain; texture grainy. Blend longer, or pass through a sieve.
Perfect: Smooth and pourable, coating a spoon; sweet, tangy, and deeply savoury. Serve with a torn basil leaf and grilled cheese.
Overdone: Cream curdled from boiling after the vinegar went in. Blend again briefly — it usually smooths back. Warm gently from here on.
Feel cue: Drag a finger across the back of a coated spoon — the line should hold clean for a second before closing.

name: Roasted Vegetable Stock
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Leek (halved lengthwise, washed): 15 parts
Fennel bulb and fronds (roughly chopped): 10 parts
Dried mushroom skins or shiitake stems (or 30g dried porcini): 8 parts
Garlic head (halved horizontally, unpeeled): 5 parts
Olive oil or neutral oil: 5 parts
Bay leaves, flat-leaf parsley stems, fresh thyme: 5 parts
Black peppercorns (whole): 1 parts

Active time: 20 min
Total time: 2 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Onion, carrot, celery, leek, fennel, and mushroom skins roasted to deep golden-brown and then simmered with herbs and black peppercorns — the roasting gives this vegan stock a depth and body that makes it genuinely useful in place of light meat stocks.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Dried mushroom skins or shiitake stems (or 30g dried porcini)
Bay leaves, flat-leaf parsley stems, fresh thyme
番茄膏（Tomato paste (for colour and depth)）

steps:
Preheat oven to 220°C (425°F). Spread all vegetables on two large sheet pans — do not crowd them. Drizzle with oil and toss to coat. Dot the tomato paste in spoonfuls across the vegetables. Roast for 35–40 minutes, tossing once at the 20-minute mark, until the vegetables are deeply caramelized and dark at the edges — golden-brown onions, nearly blackened carrot edges, dark-spotted leeks. The deeper the color here, the richer and more complex the stock.
Visual cue: Vegetables are deeply caramelized and dark — golden-brown to mahogany edges on the onion and carrot, with some char on the leek and fennel edges. The tomato paste has turned brick-red and concentrated.
Underdone: Vegetables are golden but not caramelized. Onion is still white inside. No charred edges. Return to the oven for 10–15 more minutes. Pale-roasted vegetables produce pale, thin stock. Commit to the color.
Perfect: Deep mahogany color on the cut faces, black char at the exposed edges of leek and fennel. Tomato paste has darkened to a brick-brown. The tray smells intensely caramelized and savory. Deglaze the pan and transfer to the stockpot.
Overdone: Vegetables are uniformly black and smell acrid and bitter rather than caramelized and sweet. Discard the most heavily burned pieces. The slightly-too-dark ones are fine — a small amount of bitterness is okay. Start again with better oven management if all is burned.
Feel cue: The roasted vegetables should release from the pan easily — if they stick and tear, they need more time in the oven. The pan surface will have dark, caramelized fond stuck to it — this is liquid gold for the stock.

Remove the pans from the oven. Add a small amount of cold water (about 2 tablespoons per pan) to each hot pan and scrape vigorously with a wooden spoon or spatula to dissolve all the dark caramelized fond from the pan surface. This concentrated caramelized material is extremely rich in Maillard reaction products and is a primary driver of stock depth.
Visual cue: The dark caramelized crust lifts from the pan in the liquid, turning the small amount of water into a deep brown, intensely fragrant glaze.
Underdone: The fond is not dissolving — water is not hot enough or you are not scraping vigorously enough. Use a metal spatula and more physical pressure. The fond is bonded to the pan and must be mechanically lifted and dissolved.
Perfect: All dark bits are dissolved and the water has turned into a rich, dark brown liquid with an intensely savory caramel aroma. Transfer everything to the stockpot.
Overdone: The fond was burnt, not caramelized, and the deglaze tastes bitter and acrid. Discard the deglaze liquid from this pan. The bitter compounds from burnt fond will ruin the stock.
Feel cue: The deglaze liquid should feel slightly thick and sticky on your fingers — the dissolved Maillard compounds give it a body and richness. Smell it: if it smells sweet and caramelized, use it. If it smells acrid and burnt, discard.

Transfer all roasted vegetables and deglaze liquid to a large stockpot. Add dried mushrooms, herb bundle, peppercorns, and cold water. Bring to a boil, then immediately reduce to a bare simmer — just occasional bubbles breaking the surface. Simmer for 1 hour 30 minutes. Skim any foam that forms in the first 15 minutes. Do not stir — stirring makes the stock cloudy. Do not let it boil hard at any point after the initial come-up.
Visual cue: A steady, calm simmer — a bubble every 2–3 seconds at the surface. The liquid is deep golden-amber and clear, not cloudy. Vegetables are slowly giving up their color and flavor to the broth.
Underdone: After 1 hour, the stock is still pale golden and thin-tasting. Little depth or body. Continue simmering. Vegetable stock develops flavor quickly in the first hour but needs the full 90 minutes for depth.
Perfect: Deep golden-amber, clear, with a complex savory aroma and good body. Tasted, it should coat the tongue lightly. Strain and cool.
Overdone: Stock has reduced significantly and become very dark and bitter from over-extraction of the vegetables. Dilute with water until the flavor balances. Strain and cool. For future batches, maintain a bare simmer and limit to 90 minutes.
Feel cue: At the 1-hour mark, taste the stock and notice if it has transitioned from thin to something with actual depth — a coat on the tongue, a savory resonance that lingers. That transition is your landmark.

Set a fine-mesh sieve over a large bowl or pot. Ladle the stock through the sieve — do not pour directly from the pot, which would force cloudy liquid through. Do not press the vegetables. Let gravity drain the stock for 5 minutes. Discard the exhausted vegetables. Allow stock to cool at room temperature for 1 hour, then refrigerate. Skim any oil from the surface when cold. Use within 5 days or freeze in 500ml portions for up to 6 months.
Visual cue: The finished stock is a clear, deep amber-gold, shimmering when the bowl is tilted. No cloudiness, no floating debris.
Underdone: Stock is pale and thin, lacking body. When tasted, it has little depth beyond watery vegetable flavor. Return to the pot and reduce by one-third over medium-high heat to concentrate.
Perfect: Deep, clear amber-gold, with a full, rounded savory flavor that coats the tongue. When reduced by half it becomes a vegetable demi-glace of remarkable intensity. Cool and refrigerate or freeze.
Overdone: Stock is very dark and slightly bitter from extended roasting and simmering. Dilute by 25–30% with additional cold water and taste. The balance should restore. Very bitter stock may need a small amount of cream or butter when used in sauces to mellow it.
Feel cue: Dip a clean finger into the cooled, finished stock — at room temperature, good stock should feel slightly more substantial than water, with the faintest suggestion of body. Run your finger across your palm: it should leave a very light coating, not nothing, not a film.

name: 瑞士土豆饼 · Rösti
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Waxy potatoes (Yukon Gold or Charlotte): 100 parts
  Alternatives: boiled-and-chilled floury potatoes (Bernese method)
Clarified butter (or ghee): 8 parts
  Alternatives: duck fat; lard
Fine sea salt: 1.5 parts
Freshly ground black pepper: 0.5 parts
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 50 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A Swiss potato cake of elemental satisfaction — waxy potatoes grated raw, pressed into a cast-iron pan with clarified butter until the bottom crust is a shattering, tawny-gold disc and the interior remains steaming, creamy, and fragrant.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Peel the potatoes. Grate them on the coarse side of a box grater into a large bowl. Working quickly (grated potato oxidizes and discolors), gather handfuls of the grated potato and squeeze them as hard as you can over the sink. Remove as much starch-water as possible — this is critical for crispness. If the potato releases a bluish-purple liquid, it contains excess starch: squeeze more. Season the dry-ish grated potato with salt and pepper and toss to distribute evenly.
Visual cue: Long, uniform white shreds of potato piled loosely in a bowl. The shreds are slightly damp but not dripping. No pooling liquid at the bottom of the bowl.
Underdone: Grated potato is very wet. A squeeze produces streams of starchy liquid. The bottom of the bowl has puddles. Continue squeezing in handfuls — inadequately dried potato will steam rather than fry and never develop a crust.
Perfect: Shreds are dry to the touch but pliable. A hard squeeze yields only a few drops. The potato surface looks slightly chalky, not wet. Season and press into the pan immediately before oxidation occurs.
Overdone: Potato has been squeezed so much the shreds are compacted into dense, waterlogged-looking mats. Loosen with your fingers before pressing into the pan — good rösti needs air between the shreds.
Feel cue: A handful of properly prepared grated potato should feel like damp straw — not wet fabric, not dry paper. When you open your fist, the shreds fall apart rather than holding together in a matted ball.

Heat a 24–26cm cast-iron or heavy non-stick pan over medium heat. Add the clarified butter and swirl to coat. When the butter is hot and shimmering but not smoking, add all the grated potato at once. Immediately use a wide spatula to press the potato into a firm, even disc, extending it to the pan edges. Do not touch it again. Cook on medium-low heat for 10–12 minutes. The goal is a deep golden-brown crust built slowly from even, patient heat.
Visual cue: The edges of the rösti disc have turned golden-brown and are visibly crisping. The top surface, though still raw-looking, shows steam escaping, indicating the interior is cooking through.
Underdone: After 10 minutes, the bottom is still pale and the rösti slides freely in the pan with no color. Increase heat very slightly. The butter may have been insufficient or the heat too low. Wait longer — do not flip yet.
Perfect: A gentle shake of the pan reveals that the rösti slides as a single unit. The visible edges are deep amber-gold. A peek with a spatula confirms a mahogany crust. Flip onto a plate, slide back butter-side down, and cook the second side.
Overdone: The edges are very dark brown, edges smell of burnt butter, and the crust is dark brown-black. Flip immediately onto a plate. The bottom may be saved; the edges can be trimmed after. Reduce heat significantly for the second side.
Feel cue: Shake the pan gently — a properly formed rösti moves as one solid disc, like a pancake, with no loose potato shifting underneath. If any part drags or tears, it is not yet set. Wait and trust.

To flip: invert a large plate over the pan and, in one confident motion, flip both together so the rösti drops onto the plate crust-side up. Add the remaining clarified butter to the pan. Slide the rösti back in, uncooked side down. Increase heat to medium. Cook 8–10 minutes until the second side is equally golden and crisp.
Visual cue: The second side builds the same deep, even amber-gold crust as the first. Both sides should look equally browned when done.
Underdone: Second side is still pale and steamy-soft when pressed. The potato interior feels dense and slightly raw. Continue cooking. Check every 2 minutes by lifting an edge with a spatula.
Perfect: Both sides are a matching deep amber gold. The rösti is firm to the touch, holding its disc shape. Tap the crust with a knuckle — it sounds hollow. Slide onto a board and rest 2 minutes before cutting.
Overdone: Second crust is browning too quickly from the higher heat. Dark patches forming. Reduce heat to low and cover for the last 3 minutes to finish the center gently.
Feel cue: After the flip, press the center of the rösti with your palm — there should be firm resistance, not a soft give. As the second crust sets, you'll hear the sizzling change from a wet, steamy sound to a dry, crackly crispness.

Slide the finished rösti onto a wooden board. Season lightly with additional flaky salt. Rest for 2 minutes before cutting into wedges — this allows the interior steam to redistribute and the crust to firm completely. Serve immediately. Classic accompaniments are fried eggs, smoked salmon, applesauce, or alpine cheese.
Visual cue: A golden-amber disc with a uniformly crisped top and bottom. Cut cross-section reveals steaming, creamy potato interior against the dark-gold crust.
Underdone: Interior is gluey and dense when cut. The potato shreds are fused into a soft, starchy paste rather than tender individual shreds. The center needed more time. Next time, lower heat and extend cooking time. For now, return the cut wedges face-down to a hot buttered pan for 3 minutes.
Perfect: Crust shatters like a biscuit when tapped. Interior is creamy and yielding, with individual potato shreds still visible. Steam escapes from the cut face. Eat immediately — rösti waits for no one.
Overdone: Both crusts are very dark and taste of over-browned butter. The interior is dry. Trim the darkest exterior edges. The interior is likely fine and the flavor salvageable.
Feel cue: The perfect rösti offers two textures in one bite — the brittle shattering of the exterior crust giving way immediately to the soft, steamy, creamy interior. Your knife should pass through it with an audible snap at the crust.

name: Romesco Sauce
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Red bell peppers (large): 300 g
  Alternatives: jarred roasted peppers (drained)
Sun-dried tomatoes (oil-packed): 60 g
  Alternatives: ripe Roma tomatoes, halved and roasted
Blanched almonds (or marcona): 80 g
  Alternatives: hazelnuts; a mix of both
Garlic cloves: 4 cloves
Smoked paprika (pimentón de la Vera): 8 g
  Alternatives: sweet paprika + pinch of cayenne
Cayenne pepper: 1 g
  Alternatives: dried chili flakes
Sherry vinegar: 25 ml
  Alternatives: red wine vinegar; lemon juice
Extra-virgin olive oil: 80 ml
Fine sea salt: 6 g
Day-old sourdough bread, crusts removed (use GF bread to keep GF): 40 g
  Alternatives: gluten-free bread (for strict GF)
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The great Catalan sauce — a smoky, brick-red emulsion of charred peppers, toasted almonds, and sun-dried tomato, thickened by pounded bread and brightened by a jolt of sherry vinegar, tasting of fire and earth in equal measure.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Day-old sourdough bread, crusts removed (use GF bread to keep GF)

steps:
Char the bell peppers directly over a gas flame or under a screaming-hot broiler, turning with tongs until completely blackened on all sides — this takes 10–15 minutes. Place in a sealed bag or covered bowl for 15 minutes to steam. Peel off the charred skin (a little residue adds flavor), remove the seeds and core. Wrap the garlic cloves unpeeled in foil with a drizzle of oil and roast at 200 C for 20 minutes until completely soft. Squeeze from skins.
Visual cue: Peppers completely black on the outside, soft enough to collapse when pressed. Garlic caramel-golden and yielding.
Underdone: Patches of red still visible. Skin hasn't blistered fully. The pepper still holds its shape rigidly. Continue charring — you need aggressive heat. Underdone peppers taste raw and lack the caramelized depth that defines romesco.
Perfect: Completely black exterior. Soft, steam-collapsed interior. The steamed skins slip off easily. Garlic is golden-amber and completely tender. Peel, deseed, and reserve. Toast almonds and bread while waiting.
Overdone: Peppers have dried out or the interior has burnt through to the flesh. Salvage any unburnt flesh. Scrape the worst burnt areas. Interior should be soft and sweet.
Feel cue: The steamed peppers slip out of their skins like velvet — the charred exterior releases with almost no resistance, revealing glistening, mahogany-sweet flesh beneath.

In a dry skillet over medium heat, toast the almonds for 4–6 minutes, tossing frequently, until golden-brown and fragrant. Set aside. In the same pan with a splash of oil, fry the torn bread pieces until golden and crisp on all sides, 3–4 minutes. The toasted bread is the thickener — it emulsifies the sauce and gives it body.
Visual cue: Almonds: deep golden-tan all the way through. Bread: golden-brown and completely dry/crisp.
Underdone: Almonds still pale in the center. Bread is soft and white. Continue toasting on medium heat. Remove from heat and they will continue to color from residual heat.
Perfect: Almonds are deep golden, fragrant with a toasty, slightly bitter aroma. Bread is dry and golden, crunching when pressed. Remove from heat immediately — residual heat will continue the browning process.
Overdone: Almonds are dark brown, smelling acrid. Bread is black at the edges. Discard burnt almonds and start over — burnt almonds make the sauce bitter beyond recovery.
Feel cue: The toasted almonds crunch loudly when you press one between two fingers — completely dry all the way through with no give, and the skin flakes off easily.

In a food processor or blender, pulse the almonds and toasted bread first until coarsely ground. Add the roasted peppers, garlic, sun-dried tomatoes, smoked paprika, cayenne, sherry vinegar, and salt. Process until a rough, textured paste forms. With the motor running, drizzle in the olive oil to emulsify. Process to your preferred consistency — classic romesco is chunky, not smooth. Taste and adjust: more vinegar for acidity, more paprika for smoke, more oil for richness. The sauce should taste bold enough to be slightly overwhelming on its own.
Visual cue: A brick-red, rough-textured sauce with visible almond and pepper pieces — not a smooth puree.
Underdone: Still chunky with large visible almond pieces. Sauce separates immediately on the plate. Process another 30 seconds. The bread needs time to fully integrate and emulsify.
Perfect: Brick-red, chunky but cohesive. The sauce holds together on a spoon but has visible texture. Glossy from the olive oil. A spoonful tastes smoky, rich, and sharp simultaneously. Taste and season. Let rest 10 minutes for flavors to meld before serving.
Overdone: Completely smooth, pale orange, sauce-like rather than paste-like. Lost all texture. No recovery — serve as-is. The flavor will be the same; only the textural drama is lost.
Feel cue: A proper romesco coats the back of a spoon thickly without being gluey — it should hold a tongue-smear of vibrant red color on white china, fading at the edges to orange.

name: Romesco
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。

  Alternatives: jarred roasted piquillo peppers

  Alternatives: choricero pepper; 1 tsp sweet smoked paprika

  Alternatives: canned whole tomatoes, drained

  Alternatives: hazelnuts; half almonds half hazelnuts
Day-old country bread (fried in olive oil): 18 parts
  Alternatives: toasted baguette slice

  Alternatives: roasted garlic
Extra-virgin olive oil: 50 parts
Sherry vinegar (Jerez): 8 parts
  Alternatives: red wine vinegar
Flaky sea salt: 2 parts
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 1 hour
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The brick-red sauce of Catalonia — sweet roasted red peppers and rehydrated ñora chiles pounded with charred tomato, toasted almonds, and fried bread, then loosened with fruity olive oil and sharpened with sherry vinegar into a rustic, nutty, smoky paste that clings to grilled calçots, fish, or roasted vegetables.

ingredients.name: Day-old country bread (fried in olive oil)

steps:
Roast the bell peppers over a flame or under a hot broiler until the skins blacken and blister all over, then steam them in a covered bowl for 10 minutes and slip off the skins; discard stems and seeds. Roast the whole tomatoes the same way until collapsed and charred. Meanwhile, stem and seed the ñora chiles, cover with hot water, and soak 20 minutes until soft; scrape the softened flesh from the skins with a spoon and discard the papery skins.
Visual cue: Peppers are slumped and silky with their skins gone, flesh deeply colored and sweet-smelling. Tomatoes are soft and smoky with blistered patches. The ñora flesh is a thick, dark-red scrapeable paste.
Underdone: Pepper skins are merely golden, not blistered, and cling stubbornly. Ñora flesh is leathery and won't scrape free. Return peppers to the flame until the skins blacken; soak the ñoras longer in hotter water until the flesh yields.
Perfect: Skins peel away in sheets leaving glossy, smoky flesh. Tomatoes are jammy and charred. Ñora paste scrapes cleanly off the skins in a deep red smear. Set the cleaned produce aside and toast the almonds and fry the bread.
Overdone: Pepper flesh has gone gray and papery, scorched right through; tomato is bitter and acrid from over-charring. Trim away any ashen, bitter flesh. A little char is flavor; carbonized flesh is not — discard the worst of it.
Feel cue: The peeled pepper should feel slippery and limp like wet silk, and the kitchen should smell of sweet smoke. The ñora paste should be tacky and stain your spoon a deep burgundy.

Toast the blanched almonds in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking constantly, until golden and fragrant, 4–6 minutes; tip out and reserve. In the same pan, warm a third of the olive oil and fry the bread slice and whole garlic cloves until both are deep golden and the garlic is soft, about 3 minutes per side. The bread will thicken the sauce; the fried garlic gives mellow sweetness without raw bite.
Visual cue: Almonds are evenly tan with a toasted-nut aroma. Bread is crisp and golden-brown, saturated with oil. Garlic cloves are soft, golden, and sweet-smelling, with no scorched spots.
Underdone: Almonds are still pale and taste raw and grassy. Bread is soft and oil-logged rather than crisp; garlic is sharp and white inside. Keep toasting the almonds until they color; fry the bread and garlic longer over gentle heat until golden.
Perfect: Almonds snap with a clean toasted flavor. Bread is crisp-edged and richly golden. Garlic is buttery-soft and sweet. Combine everything in the mortar or food processor.
Overdone: Almonds are dark brown and acrid; garlic is browned to the point of bitterness. Discard burnt almonds and garlic and re-toast a fresh batch — bitterness here taints the whole sauce.
Feel cue: Listen for the almonds to start crackling faintly and smell nutty just before they color — pull them then. The garlic should give no resistance when pressed against the pan.

Traditionally done in a large mortar: pound the toasted almonds, fried garlic, and a pinch of salt to a coarse meal, then work in the fried bread, the ñora flesh, the roasted peppers, and the charred tomato, pounding until you have a thick, textured paste. A food processor works too — pulse the nuts and bread first, then add the rest and pulse, keeping some grit. You want texture, not a smooth purée.
Visual cue: A thick brick-red paste, coarse and rustic, with visible flecks of almond. It mounds on a spoon and holds its shape.
Underdone: Large chunks of almond and pepper remain; the mixture is loose and falls off the spoon in pieces rather than holding together. Keep pounding or pulsing until the nuts break down into a meal and the paste coheres.
Perfect: Cohesive, spoonable paste, deep red, with a pleasant grit from the almonds. It holds a soft peak. Begin emulsifying in the olive oil.
Overdone: Smooth, pasty, and pale — pounded into a homogenous purée with no texture, almost gummy from over-worked bread. Accept it as a smoother style, or fold in a few extra hand-crushed toasted almonds to rebuild texture.
Feel cue: The paste should feel grainy and slightly sandy from the almonds when you rub a little between your fingers — that grit is the signature of real romesco.

With the mortar or processor running, drizzle in the remaining olive oil in a slow stream so it emulsifies into the paste, thickening it to a loose, glossy sauce. Sharpen with the sherry vinegar, then taste and adjust salt and vinegar — romesco should taste sweet, nutty, and faintly smoky with a bright acidic lift. Let it rest 30 minutes before serving so the flavors marry.
Visual cue: A glossy, cohesive, brick-orange sauce that coats a spoon and slowly settles back to level. It tastes balanced: sweet pepper up front, nutty middle, a clean vinegar finish.
Underdone: Oil pools separately on the surface and the sauce tastes flat and dull, lacking acidic lift. Keep streaming the oil while the machine runs to emulsify it in, then add vinegar a few drops at a time until the flavor brightens.
Perfect: Thick but pourable, uniformly glossy with no free oil, balanced between sweet, nutty, smoky, and sour. Rest 30 minutes, then serve with grilled calçots, fish, or roasted vegetables.
Overdone: Broken and greasy, with oil weeping out, or so sharp from excess vinegar it makes you wince. Whisk in a spoonful of the reserved paste or a little extra fried bread to re-bind; balance harsh acidity with a pinch of salt and a touch more oil.
Feel cue: Drag a spoon through it — the sauce should close back over the trail slowly and leave a glossy coating on the spoon. On the tongue it should feel rich and faintly granular, finishing clean and bright, never oily.

name: Rose Lassi
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Full-fat plain yogurt (room temperature): 400 g
  Alternatives: Greek yogurt thinned with 100g milk; coconut yogurt (vegan)
Whole milk (cold): 150 g
  Alternatives: water for a lighter lassi
Rose syrup (Rooh Afza or similar): 40 g
  Alternatives: 2 tbsp sugar + 1 tsp rose water
Rose water (pure, food-grade): 10 g
  Alternatives: rose extract, use half the amount
Green cardamom pods, seeds ground: 3 g
  Alternatives: 1/4 tsp pre-ground cardamom
Saffron threads: 0.1 g
  Alternatives: a pinch of turmeric for color only
Warm milk (for blooming saffron): 30 g
  Alternatives: warm water
Dried rose petals and crushed pistachios: 5 g
  Alternatives: a pinch of ground cardamom
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A cooling North Indian yogurt drink perfumed with rose water and green cardamom, tinted a blush pink by a spoonful of rose syrup, and finished with a pinch of saffron bloomed in warm milk — simultaneously cooling and aromatic, its floral complexity deepening with each sip.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Dried rose petals and crushed pistachios

steps:
Crush the saffron threads between your fingers to break them into smaller pieces — this dramatically increases the surface area and the amount of color and flavor extracted. Add to the warm (not boiling) milk and stir. Leave to bloom for 5–10 minutes. The milk will turn a deep golden-orange and the room will fill with the unmistakable honeyed, slightly medicinal fragrance of good saffron. A small pinch of saffron is potent — more than 5–6 threads for this quantity will make the lassi bitter and medicinal rather than fragrant.
Visual cue: The warm milk has turned a deep amber-gold, with visible saffron threads floating. The color is vivid and saturated, not pale yellow.
Underdone: Milk is barely tinted, pale yellow, after less than 2 minutes of blooming. Little aroma released. Wait the full 10 minutes. Saffron needs time and warmth to release its color and volatile aromatic compounds.
Perfect: Deep amber-gold color. Rich, complex floral-honey smell. Threads have given most of their color to the milk. Use immediately or cool and use later.
Overdone: The milk was too hot (boiling) and the saffron's most volatile aromatics have cooked off. Color present but fragrance diminished. The color and a baseline saffron flavor remain — use it. Next time, use warm (65 C) not boiling milk.
Feel cue: Press a saffron thread between your fingers before adding: it should stain your fingertips deep orange immediately — that's the crocin pigment. A thread that barely stains is either old or low quality; genuine saffron (Kashmiri or Spanish) stains vividly.

Combine the yogurt, cold milk, rose syrup, rose water, and ground cardamom in a blender. Add the bloomed saffron milk. Blend on high for 90 seconds until completely smooth, frothy, and well-combined. Taste after blending: the rose should be prominent but not soap-like, the cardamom a warm whisper on the finish, and the saffron should add a golden depth rather than a medicinal note. Adjust sweetness with a touch more rose syrup if needed. The lassi should be pourable but creamy — if too thick, add cold milk a tablespoon at a time.
Visual cue: A frothy, blush-pink to pale orange drink with a thick foam cap, blended so smoothly it shows no yogurt lumps or unmixed streaks.
Underdone: Thick, lumpy, unblended. Visible yogurt curds. Layers of ingredients not fully mixed. Blend another 60 seconds on high speed until completely smooth and frothy.
Perfect: Uniformly pink-orange, frothy, smooth. Tastes floral, sweet, cool, and complex. Pours smoothly without any gluey resistance. Pour over ice and garnish.
Overdone: Over-blended until warm from friction — the ice will melt immediately. Rose flavor muted from heat. Refrigerate for 15 minutes before serving over ice.
Feel cue: Pour a small amount into your palm: it should flow like heavy cream — smooth, slightly thick, with no graininess. The aroma off the foam should be immediately and unmistakably floral: rose dominant, with cardamom rising beneath it.

Fill tall glasses with crushed ice. Pour the blended lassi over the ice. The foam will settle in a thick cap on top. Scatter a few dried rose petals and crushed pistachios across the foam for color and texture contrast. Serve immediately with a long spoon or wide straw. Rose lassi does not hold well — the foam settles and the ice dilutes within 10 minutes, so serve it the moment it is made. In Punjab, it is served in tall clay glasses (kulhads) that add an earthy, mineral note; a chilled glass is a good substitute.
Visual cue: A tall glass layered with crushed ice and blush-pink lassi foam, crowned with vivid dried rose petals and pale green pistachio crumble.
Underdone: Served without enough ice or at room temperature. Flat, warm, and heavy. Add more crushed ice and serve in chilled glasses. The cold is not aesthetic — it changes the texture and the perceived sweetness.
Perfect: Ice-cold, frothy, aromatic, pink, and decorated. The first sip is cold and floral; the finish is warm from cardamom and saffron. Drink within 5–10 minutes.
Overdone: Left standing too long — ice has melted, foam has collapsed, and the drink is now watery and diluted. If this happens, re-blend with fresh ice and serve again.
Feel cue: The first sip should deliver an immediate cold shock followed by a rapid expansion of rose fragrance at the back of the nose — that retronasal rose bloom is what distinguishes a real rose lassi from a sweetened yogurt drink.

name: Malaysian Roti Canai
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
All-purpose flour: 4 parts
  Alternatives: bread flour (slightly chewier)
Warm water (35 C): 1.5 parts
Large egg, beaten: 0.5 parts
Ghee (clarified butter): 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: neutral oil plus a knob of butter
Fine salt: 0.05 parts
Sugar: 0.05 parts
  Alternatives: condensed milk (classic Mamak variation)
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 4 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Flaky, gossamer-thin flatbread slapped and spun on the tawa until translucent as a windowpane, then coiled and smashed flat before frying in ghee to a shatteringly crisp exterior with a honeyed, pull-apart interior of a hundred paper layers.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine flour, salt, and sugar in a large bowl. In a measuring jug, mix warm water, beaten egg, and half the ghee. Pour the wet ingredients into the flour and mix with your hand in circular strokes until a shaggy dough forms. The dough will be soft, slightly sticky, and richer than a standard bread dough thanks to the egg and ghee. Do not add extra flour. Knead briefly in the bowl until it just comes together — about 2 minutes.
Visual cue: A soft, slightly tacky ball that just holds its shape. Lighter and more pliable than bread dough. Slightly golden from the egg.
Underdone: Dough is wet, won't hold shape, streams between fingers like thick batter. Add flour 1 tablespoon at a time and mix until it holds together. Roti dough is soft — do not over-correct.
Perfect: Soft, smooth ball; slightly tacky but doesn't stick to dry hands; a light golden tinge from the egg. Pulls away from the bowl cleanly. Transfer to a lightly oiled surface and knead to develop gluten.
Overdone: Dough is stiff and firm, almost bread-like. Will not stretch thin without tearing. Add warm water 1 teaspoon at a time and knead in until soft and pliable.
Feel cue: Roti canai dough should feel luxuriously soft — like baby's skin or warm plasticine. It should stretch a few inches between your fingers without resistance.

Knead the dough on a lightly oiled surface (not floured — oil keeps it extensible) for 10 minutes by hand. Use a push-pull-fold motion. The goal is to develop just enough gluten for the dough to stretch paper-thin without tearing, while remaining soft and supple — not a tight, elastic bread dough. Toward the end of kneading, the dough will become notably smoother and almost silky.
Visual cue: A smooth, satiny ball with a slight sheen from the ghee. When you stretch a small piece, it thins into a near-translucent membrane before tearing.
Underdone: Dough tears immediately when stretched even slightly. Surface is rough. Windowpane test fails at a very short stretch. Continue kneading for another 3–4 minutes. Gluten extensibility takes time.
Perfect: Silky, smooth, slightly warm. Stretches several centimeters into a thin veil before tearing. The surface is unmarked and almost glossy. Divide into balls, coat in ghee, cover and rest.
Overdone: Dough has become springy and snaps back aggressively when stretched — too much elasticity. Rest covered for 30 minutes uncovered — overdeveloped gluten needs to relax before it will stretch.
Feel cue: Well-kneaded roti dough feels alive in your hands — it gives immediately, stretches without any snapping sensation, and almost seems to want to spread itself.

Divide the dough into 8 equal balls (roughly 80 g each). Coat each ball generously in ghee, turning it until completely slicked. Arrange in a single layer on an oiled tray, ensuring the balls are not touching. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and rest at room temperature for at least 3 hours, or refrigerate overnight. The gluten relaxes completely during this rest, making it possible to stretch each ball to an almost see-through thinness without tearing. Do not skip or shorten this step.
Visual cue: Each ball has relaxed and spread slightly into a thick disc. The surface is slick with ghee and the dough no longer bounces back when poked — it holds the indent.
Underdone: Balls spring back immediately when poked. Dough is still elastic. Attempting to stretch will tear it. Rest longer — roti needs a minimum of 2 hours to become extensible enough. 3 hours is ideal.
Perfect: Balls have relaxed into flatter, wider discs. Poke leaves a permanent dimple. Surface feels silky rather than springy. Begin the stretch-and-layer step.
Overdone: Dough has been sitting so long (12+ hours unrefrigerated) it smells fermented and is very slack. Still usable — just handle very gently. Proceed to shaping quickly.
Feel cue: After the long ghee rest, picking up a dough ball should feel like picking up a water balloon — it wants to spread and sag in your hand, heavy with its own relaxed weight.

Oil your tawa or work surface lightly. Place one ball and begin pressing it out flat with oiled fingers. Then use the back of your hand and a slapping motion to stretch it outward — rotate constantly, slap from underneath, let gravity thin it. Work until the dough is nearly paper-thin and you can see the surface below through it (roughly 45–50 cm diameter). Smear a thin film of ghee across the entire surface. Fold in from two opposite sides like a letter, then fold again to create a square packet. Coil the square into a tight snail. Let all 8 coils rest 5 minutes before flattening. Press each coil down firmly with your palm into a flat round, 15–18 cm diameter.
Visual cue: Each stretched sheet is nearly see-through before folding. After folding and pressing, a round 15 cm disc with visible layering at the edges.
Underdone: Sheet is thick and uneven; you can't see through it; edges are much thicker than the center. Keep slapping and stretching, focusing on the thick spots. Patience — the technique takes a few attempts to learn.
Perfect: Nearly translucent over most of its area; tears only at the very thinning edges. After folding and coiling, the round shows distinct layer lines at the edge when pressed. Cook immediately on a hot tawa for best results, or refrigerate the shaped rounds up to 30 minutes.
Overdone: Sheet has torn in multiple places from over-stretching. Fold the torn sheet as-is — the layers will still be flaky; just the shape will be imperfect.
Feel cue: A stretched roti sheet should feel lighter than air — so thin it moves in the draft from your hands. You should feel the warmth of the work surface through it as you work.

Heat a tawa or flat cast-iron pan over medium-high heat until very hot. Add a generous spoonful of ghee — it should shimmer instantly. Place a shaped roti round on the pan. Cook 1.5–2 minutes until the bottom is golden-brown and the roti has puffed in places. Flip, add another dab of ghee, and cook 1–2 minutes more. Immediately remove from heat and 'scrunch' the roti with both hands (like clapping it accordion-style) to separate the layers and release steam. This is the signature move — it turns a flat disc into a pillowy, flaky cloud.
Visual cue: Golden-brown and crisp on both sides with irregular darker spots. After scrunching, the roti puffs into a layered, crinkled mass with a flaky, shatteringly thin exterior and a soft, honeyed interior.
Underdone: Pale and doughy; the interior is still raw and dense when you tear it open. No flaky layers visible. Return to the pan over medium heat for another minute per side. Ensure the pan is properly preheated.
Perfect: Golden-brown with amber spots; crust shatters when torn; layers pull apart in ribbons; steam rises from the interior. Smells of toasted ghee. Scrunch immediately while hot and serve with dhal or curry.
Overdone: Dark brown or blackened in spots; crisp but not flaky; has a bitter, burnt-ghee smell. Serve anyway — many people prefer darker roti. Lower heat slightly for the next batch.
Feel cue: A perfectly cooked roti canai shatters when you tap it with a finger and then gives way to a soft, pull-apart interior that almost melts. The contrast between the crisp crust and the layered interior is the whole point.

name: Rouille
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Egg yolks: 2 pcs
Extra-virgin olive oil: 150 ml
  Alternatives: 50/50 olive oil and neutral oil for milder flavor
Garlic cloves: 4 pcs
Saffron threads: 0.3 g

Piment d'Espelette or cayenne: 2 g

description: Provence's vivid rust-red saffron-and-garlic aioli — the essential companion to bouillabaisse, smeared thickly on grilled croutons and set afloat in the broth until it melts into the soup in golden ribbons.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Crumble saffron threads between your fingers into the hot water. Steep for 10 minutes until the water turns a vivid burnt-orange and the threads become translucent. This infusion is what colors and perfumes the rouille — do not skip or rush it.
Visual cue: Water turned deep amber-orange, saffron threads now pale and translucent after surrendering their color.
Underdone: Water only faintly yellow, threads still bright red-orange. Not enough steep time. Wait the full 10 minutes.
Perfect: Water deeply golden-orange. Threads translucent and faded. Smells floral, honeyed, and slightly metallic. Proceed to the mortar.
Overdone: Saffron has over-steeped and turned slightly bitter and medicinal. Still usable — dilute the infusion with a teaspoon more water.
Feel cue: Rub a thread between two fingers — when the color transfers strongly to your skin, the threads have given their color to the water.

In a large mortar, pound garlic cloves with a pinch of salt into a completely smooth paste. The salt acts as an abrasive, tearing apart the cells. Grind in a circular motion, pressing and dragging the pestle. The paste should be completely smooth — no chunks — as any unbroken garlic cell will not emulsify properly.
Visual cue: A completely smooth, white garlic paste — almost liquid, sticky, with no chunks.
Underdone: Garlic still in small pieces, not fully broken down. Continue pounding and grinding. Add another pinch of salt as abrasive.
Perfect: Completely smooth, sticky, nearly fluid. Forms a thin film on the mortar walls. Aggressively garlicky aroma. Add roasted pepper and yolks.
Overdone: You cannot over-pound garlic paste — keep going. Proceed.
Feel cue: Press your fingertip into the paste — it should be sticky and creamy, with no graininess. If you feel any fiber or crunch, keep pounding.

Add roasted pepper and Espelette to the garlic paste and pound to a smooth paste. Work in egg yolks and all of the saffron infusion. Begin adding olive oil, drop by drop at first, pounding and stirring constantly. As an emulsion forms and the mixture thickens, you can add oil in a thin stream. Finish with lemon juice. The rouille should be thick enough to hold its shape on a spoon — significantly thicker than mayonnaise.
Visual cue: A vivid rust-red to deep orange mayo — thick, glossy, holding a mound. The saffron and pepper give it an unmistakably dramatic color.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and greasy — emulsion hasn't fully formed yet. Continue adding oil drop by drop while stirring constantly. The emulsion will form.
Perfect: Thick, glossy, rust-red. Holds its shape on a spoon. Smells of garlic, saffron, and pepper simultaneously. Tastes rich, garlicky, with a warm heat finish. Serve alongside bouillabaisse or spread on grilled croutons.
Overdone: Rouille has broken — yellow oil pooling around the sides. Start with a fresh yolk in a clean bowl, then slowly whisk in the broken rouille as you would oil.
Feel cue: Spread a teaspoon on bread — it should sit on the surface without running, thick enough to require spreading with a knife.

quantity_notes:

description: Tiny enriched yeast cakes soaked in warm rum syrup until fully saturated and dripping — Italian in origin, Parisian in execution, best crowned with Chantilly and a cherry.

ingredients.name: 淡奶油（Heavy cream (35%+ fat), very cold）
Vanilla pod or 1 tsp vanilla extract

steps:
In a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine flour, sugar, salt, and instant yeast. Add the warm milk and then the eggs one at a time with the mixer running on medium. Beat for 8–10 minutes until the batter is smooth, shiny, and elastic, pulling cleanly away from the bowl sides. The mixture is wetter than a bread dough — closer to a thick batter.
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy, elastic batter that slaps the sides of the bowl and leaves the bowl walls clean. Stretches into long, shiny ribbons when a spoon is lifted.
Underdone: Rough, lumpy texture. Batter still sticks heavily to the bowl walls. No elasticity when stretched. Continue beating on medium speed. Gluten development is essential — the structure must be built before butter is added.
Perfect: Smooth, shiny, and elastic. When you lift a spoonful and drop it, it falls in a thick, even ribbon. Slight sheen from developed gluten. Begin adding the soft butter a tablespoon at a time.
Overdone: Batter has become very tight and elastic, forming a ball that climbs the hook. Smell of warming dough. Proceed carefully — add butter quickly to loosen the structure before gluten becomes too tight.
Feel cue: A fingerful of batter stretched between two fingers should form a thin, translucent membrane before tearing — the windowpane test in miniature.

With the mixer running on medium-low, add the very soft butter one tablespoon at a time. Wait until each addition is fully incorporated before adding the next — this takes patience, about 15 minutes total. The batter will loosen dramatically at first, then tighten into a smooth, glossy, enriched dough that pulls cleanly from the bowl.
Visual cue: A glossy, smooth, very soft dough with a silky sheen. Pulls away from the bowl in one cohesive, elastic mass when the hook is lifted.
Underdone: Butter visible in streaks or pools. Dough is greasy and broken-looking, not cohesive. Continue beating — the butter will eventually emulsify into the dough. Do not add more flour.
Perfect: Smooth, glossy, elastic. The dough slaps the bowl sides and springs back when poked. Smells richly of butter and yeast. Cover the bowl with cling film and let it proof at room temperature until doubled.
Overdone: The dough has warmed from friction, butter is greasing the bowl. Slightly tacky and slack. Refrigerate the bowl for 15 minutes to firm the butter, then continue.
Feel cue: The finished enriched dough should feel like very soft, warm velvet — yielding and smooth, with just enough body to be scooped with a spoon rather than flowing freely.

Cover the bowl and let the dough proof at room temperature until doubled, 45–60 minutes. Then butter individual baba molds (or a muffin tin) generously. Fill each mold halfway with batter using a piping bag or spoon. Let proof again until the dough crests just above the rim, 20–30 minutes.
Visual cue: Molds filled and domed above the rim like small mushroom caps. Surface is smooth and pillowy, with visible bubbles beneath the skin.
Underdone: Batter barely reaches the mold rim, flat on top, no visible activity. Wait in a warm spot — baba dough is heavily enriched and rises slowly. 20–30 minutes is the minimum second proof.
Perfect: Batter domes 1–2 cm above the mold rim, smooth and pillowy. A gentle poke slowly springs back. Bake immediately in a preheated 190°C (375°F) oven.
Overdone: Domes have collapsed or the batter has begun to run over the mold edges. Smells strongly of alcohol. Bake immediately — overproofed baba will still bake, but the texture will be coarser.
Feel cue: A proofed baba mold should feel light relative to its size — the dough has trapped so much air it almost seems to float when picked up.

Bake at 190°C (375°F) for 18–22 minutes until deeply golden on top and pulling away from the mold sides. A skewer inserted in the center should come out clean. Turn onto a rack immediately and let cool for 15 minutes before soaking — they must be warm but not hot.
Visual cue: Deep golden-brown, domed babas with a small, even crack around the waist where the dough broke from the mold. Firm to the touch, springing back immediately when pressed.
Underdone: Pale gold, giving when pressed, skewer comes out with wet batter. Return to the oven for 3–5 more minutes. Underbaked babas will collapse into wet mush when soaked.
Perfect: Rich golden-brown, fully pulled from the mold sides, firm and springy. A skewer comes out clean. Turn out immediately and cool on a rack 15 minutes before soaking.
Overdone: Dark brown, hard crust that resists the skewer. Smell of burnt sugar. Proceed — a well-baked crust actually soaks more evenly. Trim any very dark bits.
Feel cue: A perfectly baked baba sounds hollow when the bottom is tapped — a light, resonant knock, not dense and thuddy.

Combine water, caster sugar, honey, and the vanilla pod in a wide, shallow saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring until the sugar and honey dissolve completely. Simmer 2 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in the rum. Keep the syrup warm — it must be hot when the babas are soaked.
Visual cue: A clear, barely amber syrup with no visible sugar granules. Smells of warm vanilla and rum. Surface shimmers but does not bubble.
Underdone: Sugar granules still visible, syrup looks cloudy. Rum added while still over heat — alcohol has evaporated. Stir over low heat until sugar dissolves fully, then add rum off-heat.
Perfect: Clear, lightly fragrant syrup that flows easily. A drop on the back of a spoon coats thinly — not viscous, just lightly sweet. Add the rum off-heat and begin soaking the warm babas.
Overdone: Syrup has reduced and thickened, coating the spoon like honey. Smells intensely caramelized. Add 50 ml of hot water and stir to thin back to a light, mobile syrup.
Feel cue: A drop of correct syrup on the wrist should feel warm — comfortably hot, like a bath — never cold or scalding. The rum should be just perceptible as fragrance, not sharp on the nose.

Place the warm babas into the wide pan of warm syrup (having added the rum to the syrup base). Spoon syrup over continuously, turning the babas, for 2–3 minutes until each one has absorbed the maximum syrup it can hold. A fully soaked baba should feel waterlogged and heavy, and syrup should run from it when pressed gently.
Visual cue: Babas are deeply mahogany-golden, visibly swollen from syrup absorption. When pressed lightly, syrup weeps from the surface.
Underdone: Babas feel dry and springy. Center is still pale and dry when probed. Syrup has barely penetrated the crust. Continue spooning syrup and turning for 2 more minutes. Some babas absorb quickly; others need patient, repeated basting.
Perfect: Plump, deeply colored, and heavy. Syrup pools freely around each baba in the pan. The texture is moist all the way through. Transfer to plates and spoon extra syrup over just before serving.
Overdone: Babas are falling apart in the syrup, losing their structure. Pieces floating in the pan. Lift gently with a slotted spoon and plate immediately. Serve with extra syrup on the side.
Feel cue: A properly soaked baba in the palm of your hand feels unexpectedly heavy — dense with absorbed syrup, yielding, like pressing a saturated sponge.

Combine the very cold heavy cream with a small amount of sugar and vanilla extract (if using extract rather than pod) in a chilled bowl. Whip to soft, billowing peaks — Chantilly for baba should be cloud-light, not stiff or butter-like.
Visual cue: Soft, billowing peaks that droop gently when the whisk is lifted. The cream is airy and bright white, with a silky rather than grainy texture.
Underdone: Cream still pours freely, peaks collapse immediately. Liquid pools at the bottom. Continue whipping. Cold cream and a cold bowl are essential — put both back in the fridge for 5 minutes if needed.
Perfect: Soft peaks that fold gently over but hold a shape for several seconds. The cream is voluminous and smooth. Spoon or pipe immediately over the soaked babas.
Overdone: Cream is grainy, yellow-tinged, starting to look curdled and buttery. Fold in 2 tbsp of cold liquid cream to smooth it back. If fully split, it cannot be repaired — start over.
Feel cue: Chantilly at the right stage feels weightless on a spoon — it barely depresses under the lightest touch, like stable foam.

Place each soaked baba on a shallow plate. Spoon or pipe a generous dome of Chantilly cream directly on top. Drizzle any remaining warm rum syrup around the base. Serve immediately while the baba is warm and the cream is cold — the contrast is essential.
Visual cue: A deep mahogany-gold baba glistening with syrup, topped with a white cloud of Chantilly. Syrup pools at the base, catching the light.
Underdone: Baba looks dry and the cream has been assembled too far in advance, causing it to weep. Serve rum babas immediately after soaking and topping with cream.
Perfect: Glistening, plump baba with a snowy cream crown. A puddle of amber syrup at its base. The smell is of warm rum, vanilla, and butter. Serve at once.
Overdone: Baba has been assembled and has sat too long — syrup continues to pool, the cream has melted into the syrup, the baba has gone cold. This dish does not hold. Soak and plate to order.
Feel cue: The finished baba should yield immediately under a spoon, releasing a rush of warm rum syrup — the sensation of saturated, yielding sponge is the entire point of the dish.

name: Scandinavian Rye Bread
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

Sunflower seeds: 10 %
  Alternatives: pumpkin seeds; sesame seeds

description: A dense, dark, tangy loaf of rye flour, whole grains, and seeds, long-fermented with a sourdough rye starter into a moist, sliceable crumb that keeps for weeks.

ingredients.name: Cracked rye or rye berries (soaked 12 hr)

steps:
Cover the cracked rye berries or whole rye berries with cold water and leave to soak for 12 hours or overnight. They will absorb a significant amount of water and soften considerably. Drain before using. This soaker adds texture, moisture, and a nutty chew to the finished loaf — unsoaked grains would be unpleasantly hard and would steal hydration from the dough itself during baking.
Visual cue: Plump, softened rye grains that press flat between two fingers without crunching. They look dull and swollen compared to raw berries and have nearly doubled in size.
Underdone: Grains are still hard at the center — they crunch or resist when bitten. Only the outer shell has softened. Soak for another 4–6 hours. Cold water slows absorption; switch to room-temperature water to speed it up.
Perfect: Grains press flat without resistance but still hold their shape. They have absorbed water throughout. The soak water is starchy and slightly cloudy. Drain and add directly to the dough. The grain moisture is now calculated into the dough hydration.
Overdone: Grains have fermented slightly in the soaking water — it smells sour or alcoholic. The grains are mushy and may fall apart. Drain and rinse. The grain is still usable and may add a pleasant tang, but reduce the overall hydration by 2–3% as they will release more free water into the dough.
Feel cue: Properly soaked rye berries should feel like cooked lentils — soft enough to squish, firm enough to hold their shape. Bite one: no hard crunch at the center, just an even, yielding chew.

Combine all the flours, the rye starter, remaining water (adjust for grain moisture), salt, and molasses in a large bowl. Mix vigorously with a wooden spoon or dough scraper — rye dough contains almost no gluten and behaves more like thick batter than bread dough. No kneading is needed or useful: rye proteins do not form gluten strands. Fold in the drained soaker, sunflower seeds, and caraway seeds until evenly distributed. The dough will be very sticky and stiff-heavy — it should hold its shape when scooped but not stretch. Cover and ferment at room temperature 8–12 hours.
Visual cue: A dense, sticky, very dark dough with visible grain and seed inclusions evenly throughout. It holds a peak when you scoop it with a spoon — it does not flow but it does not stretch either. Surface looks matte and heavily textured.
Underdone: Mixture looks streaky — dark rye flour and pale bread flour have not been fully integrated. Pockets of dry flour are visible. Starter is not distributed. Mix for 3–5 more minutes with the spoon. Rye dough is fully mixed when the color is uniform dark brown with no pale streaks and the seeds are evenly dispersed.
Perfect: Uniform, deeply brown, sticky mass with evenly distributed grains and seeds. It holds its shape when scooped and the spoon pulls cleanly. Smells tangy and malty. Transfer to the loaf tin and smooth the top with wet hands. Mark and ferment.
Overdone: Dough looks thin or pourable — too much water was added or the soaker was not drained. The seeds sink to the bottom rather than staying suspended. Work in a tablespoon more rye flour at a time until the dough holds a peak again. The fermentation will still proceed normally.
Feel cue: Rye dough should cling to the spoon and require a firm pull to release. When you drag the spoon across the surface, it should leave a wake that fills slowly, like stiff hummus. If it snaps back like wheat
dough or runs flat like pancake batter, something is off in the ratio.

Transfer the dough to a well-oiled 9 × 5-inch loaf tin. Dip your hands or a spatula in water and smooth the top into an even dome — rye dough cannot be shaped in the traditional sense; the tin does all the work. Sprinkle a few extra sunflower seeds or caraway on the surface. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and proof at room temperature until the dome crowns about 1 cm above the tin rim and cracks appear in the surface, 2–4 hours. Rye dough will not achieve the dramatic rise of wheat bread — a 20–30% increase is ideal. Preheat the oven to 425°F / 220°C.
Visual cue: The dough crown has risen 1–2 cm above the tin rim and the surface shows small cracks — a natural sign the interior is gassing and the surface skin is drying slightly. The loaf should be domed and matte, not flat.
Underdone: Dough still sits below the tin rim, surface is flat and uniformly damp. No cracks visible. Proof longer. Move to a warmer spot — 75°F / 24°C is ideal. Check again in 1 hour. Under-proofed rye bakes dense with a gummy streak.
Perfect: Crown crests just above the rim; surface cracks are visible but the loaf has not spread over the sides. Interior smells actively tangy. Bake immediately, uncovered, at 425°F / 220°C.
Overdone: Dough has spread over the sides of the tin, surface cracks are large and the dough looks sunken in the center — fermentation has peaked and the structure is collapsing. Bake immediately regardless. The loaf will have a flatter top and more sour flavor. Reduce proof time next time.
Feel cue: Touch the crown gently with a wet fingertip — it should feel slightly firm and springy on the surface but yield softly underneath, like a thick damp sponge. If it feels uniformly dense and resists the touch, it needs more time. If it collapses at the faintest touch, it has over-proofed.

Bake at 425°F / 220°C for 15 minutes, then reduce to 375°F / 190°C and bake a further 45–55 minutes. The internal temperature should reach 205°F / 96°C. The loaf will shrink slightly from the tin sides when done. Turn out and cool completely on a wire rack — at least 8 hours, preferably 24 hours — before slicing. The crumb is gummy and unset when hot; slicing too soon produces a sticky, undercooked interior regardless of the actual bake level. The loaf's interior continues to set as it cools.
Visual cue: A firmly domed, dark chocolate-brown loaf with a dry, slightly cracked crust and a firm, matt finish. Tapped on the bottom it sounds hollow. The sides and bottom should be even and deep brown, not pale.
Underdone: Top is browned but sides are pale and soft. Interior temperature below 200°F / 93°C. When pressed the loaf feels springy and squishy rather than firm. Return to the oven without the tin, directly on the rack, for 10–15 more minutes to develop the side and bottom crust.
Perfect: Uniformly dark brown all over, firm and rigid. Sounds hollow on all sides when tapped. Internal temperature 205–210°F / 96–99°C. The loaf is pulling cleanly away from the tin sides. Cool completely — minimum 8 hours. Wrap in parchment and rest. Rye bread improves dramatically over 24 hours as the crumb firms and flavors meld.
Overdone: Crust is very dark, nearly black in places, with a bitter aroma. The loaf has shrunk noticeably and feels extremely hard and dense. Cool as normal. The interior is likely fine despite the hard crust. A dark rye loaf can absorb significant color before becoming truly burnt. If the crust tastes bitter, slice thinner.
Feel cue: A cooled rye loaf should feel dense and substantial — noticeably heavier than a wheat loaf of similar size. Press the center: it should not give at all. When you finally slice it 24 hours later, the crumb should feel moist and
slightly waxy rather than crumbly or gummy — like pressing a thick, firm gel.

ingredients.name: Waxy potatoes (Desiree or Charlotte), cut into 3 cm cubes

steps:
Place the cubed potatoes in a saucepan of cold salted water. Bring to a boil and cook for 8–10 minutes until just tender — a skewer meets slight resistance at the center. Drain and allow the steam to escape for 2 minutes so the surface dries slightly.
Visual cue: Cubes are pale gold, edges just beginning to look fluffy, and a skewer slides in with the faintest resistance.
Underdone: Centers are dense and starchy; a skewer stops hard at the middle. Return to simmering water for 3 more minutes.
Perfect: Cubes yield to a skewer with gentle pressure but hold their shape. Edges are beginning to look slightly rough. Drain and rest — they will finish in the sauce.
Overdone: Cubes are crumbling and waterlogged. Corners have disappeared. Drain very carefully; handle gently. They will break up in the sauce but the flavor will still be good.
Feel cue: A cube should feel like a firm grape when pressed — yielding on the outside but with a detectable firmness at the core.

Heat the ghee in a wide, heavy pan over high heat until shimmering and a mustard seed dropped in skips and pops. Add the mustard seeds — cover immediately and let them pop for 30 seconds. Reduce heat to medium, add cumin seeds and let sizzle for 15 seconds. Add onion and cook, stirring, until deep golden and beginning to crisp at the edges, 10–12 minutes. Add ginger, garlic, green chili, and turmeric; cook 2 minutes until the raw smell disappears.
Visual cue: Onion is deeply golden with brown edges. The masala paste is fragrant, sticking slightly to the pan, and the oil is beginning to separate at the edges — this is the key moment.
Underdone: Onion is pale and translucent; spices smell raw and sharp. No oil separation. Cook longer on medium heat — rushing this step produces a flat-tasting curry.
Perfect: Onion is jammy and dark gold. Oil glistens in a ring at the pan edge. The kitchen smells of bloomed cumin and sweet, caramelized onion. Add spinach immediately.
Overdone: Onion is very dark brown or black in patches. Spices smell bitter. Add a splash of water and scrape up the dark bits. Proceed — some fond adds depth.
Feel cue: The masala should feel almost sticky when stirred — it clings to the spoon and pulls slightly as you lift it, telling you the water has cooked off and the flavors have concentrated.

Add the spinach in large handfuls to the pan, stirring between each addition until each batch wilts before adding the next. Once all spinach is wilted (about 3 minutes), transfer half of it to a blender or use a hand blender to blitz it to a smooth, vivid-green purée — leave the other half whole for texture. Return the purée to the pan. Add the parboiled potatoes, garam masala, and salt. Stir gently to coat, then simmer on low heat for 5 minutes so the potatoes absorb the sauce. Taste and adjust salt.
Visual cue: A vivid emerald sauce coats each potato cube. The dish is neither watery nor dry — the sauce is thick enough to mound slightly when spooned.
Underdone: Potatoes are still separate from the sauce, which is thin and pale green. Flavors taste raw. Simmer 5 more minutes, stirring gently, to let the potatoes absorb the sauce.
Perfect: Potatoes are glazed with deep green sauce. Whole spinach leaves are visible in a sea of smooth purée. The color is vivid, not khaki. Serve immediately with roti or rice.
Overdone: Sauce has turned from bright green to olive-brown. Potatoes are mushy and indistinct. The flavor is still good. Serve topped with a squeeze of lemon and a drizzle of fresh ghee to brighten it.
Feel cue: The sauce should coat the back of a spoon without dripping immediately — it pauses, then slides. The potatoes should feel firm through the spoon but yield gently when you press.

name: 菠菜奶酪咖喱 · Saag Paneer
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

The finished dish tastes like the forest floor and the hearth at the same time.
