ingredients.name: Fresh spinach (palak), washed, tough stems removed
印度奶酪（Paneer, cut into 2 cm cubes）

steps:
Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a fierce rolling boil. Add all the spinach at once — it will seem like an enormous volume, but it collapses dramatically. Push the spinach below the surface and cook for exactly 2 minutes: no more, or it will lose its vivid green color and turn a muddy army-green. Immediately drain and plunge into a bowl of ice-cold water, holding for 1 full minute to arrest all cooking. Lift the spinach from the cold water and squeeze firmly with both hands to remove as much liquid as possible — excess water will thin the final sauce. Transfer to a blender and blitz until completely smooth, about 2 minutes, adding just 2–3 tablespoons of the blanching water if the blade struggles. The puree should be electric green and pourable.
Visual cue: A brilliantly vivid, almost neon-green spinach puree with no visible fiber. The color should resemble fresh grass rather than dried herbs.
Underdone: The puree is still fibrous and chunky. The blender has left stringy bits. Color is good but texture is coarse. Continue blending on high. Add water one tablespoon at a time to get the blades moving.
Perfect: Silk-smooth, electric green, pours in a steady ribbon. Smells grassy and fresh, almost sweet. Set aside and begin the masala base.
Overdone: The spinach was not immediately shocked in cold water and has turned from bright green to a dull, gray-green. The oxidized color is permanent. Proceed — the flavor is unaffected. A pinch of baking soda in the pot next time will help preserve color.
Feel cue: After squeezing, the spinach ball should feel almost dry between your palms — if water runs freely through your fingers, keep squeezing. The kitchen smells of hot, fresh vegetables, clean and slightly mineral.

Heat the ghee in a wide, heavy pan over medium-high heat. When it shimmers, add the cumin seeds and let them crackle and darken for 20 seconds. Add the onion and cook, stirring frequently, for 10–12 minutes until it is deeply golden and caramelized at the edges — do not rush this step; the sweetness of properly browned onion forms the flavor backbone of the entire dish. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for 2 more minutes until the raw smell vanishes and the mixture turns a pale golden paste. Add the ground coriander, cumin, chili powder, and turmeric; stir constantly for 90 seconds, toasting the ground spices in the fat without letting them scorch. The masala is ready when the fat separates visibly around the edges of the spice mixture — an old cook's signal called 'bhunoing' that the rawness has been driven off.
Visual cue: A deep amber paste of onion, ginger, and garlic with a ring of clear golden ghee separating from the solid spice mass around the pan edges.
Underdone: Onions are translucent and pale, barely softened. No separation of fat yet. The spice smell is sharp and raw, like powdered seasoning rather than cooked depth. Lower the heat and continue cooking. Rushing the onion is the most common mistake in Indian cooking.
Perfect: Onions are a deep tawny gold, almost jammy. Fat pools visibly around the edges. The smell is mellow, toasty, and deeply savory — nothing raw or harsh. Add the spinach puree.
Overdone: Onions are dark brown and bitter. Spices are beginning to smoke and smell acrid. The mass is sticking to the pan. Deglaze with a tablespoon of water to arrest the browning. The bitterness will be partly masked by the spinach, but use a more gentle heat next time.
Feel cue: Press a wooden spoon into the onion mass — it should yield without resistance, like pressing through soft clay. The aroma transitions from sharp and onion-forward to sweet, toasty,
and complex as the caramelization progresses.

Pour the spinach puree into the hot masala base — it will sputter and steam dramatically. Stir to combine thoroughly and reduce the heat to medium-low. Simmer uncovered for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the saag has darkened slightly from its electric green to a richer forest green and has thickened to the consistency of a pourable sauce. Season with salt. Stir in the garam masala and swirl in the cream or yogurt — the dairy tempers the sharpness and adds body. If using yogurt, lower the heat to minimum before adding to prevent curdling. The sauce should now taste fully seasoned, warmly spiced, and rich without heaviness.
Visual cue: A thick, dark forest-green sauce that coats the back of a spoon and holds its shape when you drag a finger through it. Small pools of ghee are visible on the surface.
Underdone: Sauce is still very thin and pale green, with the raw spinach and masala not yet integrated. The flavor is flat and vegetal. Continue simmering — the integration takes time. The color should deepen visibly over 5 minutes of cooking.
Perfect: Thick, glossy, and deeply flavored. Coats the spoon in a velvety layer. The color is a rich, saturated forest green with golden ghee flecks. Add the paneer.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced to a very thick paste and is spitting. The color has gone toward a muddy brown-green. Add hot water 2 tablespoons at a time until the sauce loosens to a pourable consistency. Taste for salt.
Feel cue: The sauce should smell layered and complex — green and grassy from the spinach, toasty from the spices, sweet from the cream. It should cling to a spoon in a sheet, not drip like water.

In a separate small pan, heat 1 tablespoon of ghee over medium-high heat. Add the paneer cubes in a single layer — they should sizzle immediately on contact with the fat. Let them sit undisturbed for 90 seconds until the bottom face is golden, then flip each cube and repeat on the adjacent side. You are only browning the surface — the interior of paneer does not need cooking, only the exterior needs color and a slight crust to help it hold its shape in the sauce. Work in batches if your pan is small. Drain on a paper towel.
Visual cue: Paneer cubes with at least two golden-brown faces. The crust should be visibly set and slightly darker than the white interior.
Underdone: Paneer is still pure white on all faces, soft, and breaking apart when moved. Has not developed any color. Increase heat. Paneer must be dry (pat it with paper towel) for the surface to brown rather than steam.
Perfect: Two or three faces have a golden, slightly crisp crust. The interior is still white and firm. Cubes hold their shape when nudged. Add to the saag sauce immediately — add them off the heat if the sauce is very hot to prevent breaking.
Overdone: Paneer is deeply brown and has become rubbery and tough. The crust is hard. Add the paneer to the sauce now and let it simmer for 5 minutes — the moisture will rehydrate the surface slightly.
Feel cue: A well-seared paneer cube feels firm and springy when pressed, not soft and collapsing. The surface has a faint give, like pressing a firm rubber eraser, and the kitchen smells of browned dairy — warm, slightly sweet, nutty.

Gently fold the golden paneer cubes into the hot saag sauce, being careful not to break the cubes. Turn the heat to low and let the paneer warm through in the sauce for 3–4 minutes — this allows the cheese to absorb the spiced sauce at the surface while remaining firm at the center. Do not boil the sauce after adding paneer, as high heat will make it rubbery. Taste the final dish for salt. Serve with a final swirl of cream or a small knob of butter over the top, accompanied by hot naan, paratha, or steamed basmati.
Visual cue: Ivory-gold paneer cubes cradled in a velvety, dark-green sauce. Each cube retains its shape and has a distinct golden crust visible where it was seared. The sauce coats every cube without drowning them.
Underdone: Paneer cubes are still cold in the center and haven't absorbed any of the sauce's color or flavor. The dish looks assembled rather than cohesive. Continue on low heat for 3–4 more minutes. Cover with a lid to trap steam and gently warm the cheese through.
Perfect: Paneer is heated through, the exterior has taken on a faint green tint where the sauce has been absorbed, and each cube is structurally intact. Sauce and cheese are unified on the spoon. Serve immediately, before the cheese tightens.
Overdone: Paneer has become rubbery from prolonged heat. Cubes are shrinking and weeping liquid into the sauce, thinning it. Remove from heat immediately. The dish is still good — serve promptly before the cheese tightens further.
Feel cue: Stir the finished saag paneer with a spoon — it should move as a unified, glossy, thick sauce, and each paneer cube should remain whole as the spoon passes around it. The smell is deeply savory, green, and warming.

name: Chelow ba Tahdig
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Saffron threads (highest quality, loosely packed): 0.5 g
Boiling water (for blooming saffron): 60 ml
Fine salt (for soaking and parboiling water): 25 g
Neutral oil or unsalted butter: 60 ml
  Alternatives: ghee for a richer tahdig
Plain whole-milk yogurt (for tahdig binder): 60 g
  Alternatives: one egg yolk + 2 tbsp oil for a crispier crust; thin potato slices for potato tahdig
Ground turmeric (optional, for golden color): 1 g

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Persian saffron rice — the parboil-and-steam technique that produces rice of extraordinary refinement, each grain separate and impossibly light, perfumed with bloomed saffron, and crowned with a golden, shattering tahdig crust that the cook claims as their prize.

ingredients.name: Fine salt (for soaking and parboiling water)

steps:
Place the basmati rice in a large bowl. Dissolve 15 g of salt in 1 liter of cold water and pour over the rice — the water should be as salty as the sea; this salting firms the grain structure and prevents the rice from becoming mushy in later steps. Soak for a minimum of 30 minutes and ideally 1 hour. Soaking allows the grain to hydrate slowly and evenly so the parboiling step can cook the outside while the center remains firm. Drain and rinse gently with cold water.
Visual cue: Rice grains are uniformly swollen, chalk-white, and slightly elongated from the soak. The soaking water is cloudy from leached starch.
Underdone: Grains are still glassy and translucent at the center — only the outer layer has hydrated. Soak for at least 30 more minutes. Under-soaked rice will take longer to parboil and may end up unevenly cooked.
Perfect: Grains are uniformly opaque white, slightly elongated, and have swollen noticeably. They are firm but have taken on water throughout. Drain and proceed to parboil within 10 minutes.
Overdone: Grains have soaked 3+ hours and are beginning to break when pinched. Drain immediately and reduce the parboiling time to 3-4 minutes.
Feel cue: A soaked grain snapped between fingernails should break cleanly with a soft snap — not shattering like dry rice, not squashing wetly — confirming even hydration throughout.

Crush the saffron threads between fingertips or in a small mortar to a fine powder — whole threads release color and flavor incompletely. Place the saffron powder in a small glass or cup. Pour 60 ml of water that is just off the boil (not violently boiling — around 90°C) over the saffron. Stir once and cover the cup. Let steep for a minimum of 15 minutes. The water will turn a deep, glowing amber-orange and smell of hay, honey, and something metallic and floral. This bloomed saffron is used in two places: mixed into the tahdig, and drizzled over the finished rice.
Visual cue: A deeply concentrated, glowing amber-orange liquid with a rich, distinct floral-metallic aroma. The exhausted threads at the bottom are nearly colorless.
Underdone: The water is pale yellow and the saffron threads are still bright red — they have not fully released their color or flavor. Wait at least 10 more minutes. Saffron cannot be rushed — the color compounds are slow to dissolve.
Perfect: Deep amber-orange, rich and saturated. Smells of saffron distinctly. Threads are pale gold or nearly white at the bottom. Divide: use half for the tahdig, reserve half for the final drizzle.
Overdone: The saffron water has gone slightly bitter from over-steeping with water that was too hot. Still usable but add less — the bitterness will be apparent at high concentration. Dilute with a tablespoon of water.
Feel cue: Properly bloomed saffron water applied to the back of a hand should stain a vivid amber-orange that takes 30 seconds to even begin to fade — the color and the flavor are one; intense color means intense flavor.

Bring a large pot of water to a vigorous rolling boil — use at least 2 liters of water for 400 g of rice; Persian rice demands space to move freely. Add the remaining salt (10 g). Add the drained rice and stir gently once. Boil uncovered for exactly 5-7 minutes. Test the rice by removing a grain and biting it in half: the outside should be fully cooked and soft, but a small white line should still be visible at the center — the grain is two-thirds cooked. This is the parboil stage. Drain immediately and run cold water over the rice for 15 seconds to stop cooking.
Visual cue: Drained rice grains are elongated, fully white on the outside, with a visible thread of uncooked white starch at the very center when bitten in half.
Underdone: The grain center is large and chalky — more than half the grain is still uncooked. Return to the boiling water for 1-2 more minutes and test again. The outside must be fully cooked.
Perfect: Soft, fully cooked exterior with a thin, white, uncooked line at the center. The grain has lengthened significantly. Drain immediately and rinse with cold water. Do not let it sit in the pot.
Overdone: The grain is fully cooked all the way through — no white center visible. Grains may be starting to stick together. Drain and rinse immediately with cold water. Steam very gently for a shorter time to avoid total mushiness.
Feel cue: Parboiled rice in the colander should feel almost dry and slightly firm when you run a hand through it — slippery from the starch, but each grain distinct and separate, not clumping.

Pour the oil into a wide, heavy-bottomed pot (non-stick or well-seasoned) and heat over medium heat. In a bowl, mix 3 large spoonfuls of parboiled rice with the yogurt, half the saffron water, and turmeric if using — this is the tahdig mixture. Spread it in a thin, even layer across the bottom of the hot oil. Listen: it should sizzle gently. Now pile the remaining rice on top in a pyramid shape — do not press down. Make 5-6 holes through the mound with the handle of a spoon to allow steam to circulate. Drizzle a thin stream of oil or melted butter over the pyramid.
Visual cue: A pyramid of loose rice grains rising above a thin, golden-saffron base layer. The sides of the pyramid look airy and the steam-hole channels are visible.
Underdone: The tahdig mixture was spread in too thick a layer — over 1 cm. The oil was not hot enough when the mixture went in and it didn't sizzle. Proceed but expect a softer, less crispy tahdig. The heat was insufficient for initial crust formation.
Perfect: Thin, even tahdig layer that sizzled when it hit the oil. Rice mound is loose and airy, pyramid shape with clear steam channels. The pot smells of hot oil and saffron. Wrap the lid in a clean kitchen towel and cover the pot tightly.
Overdone: The tahdig is already browning aggressively and the oil is smoking before the lid goes on. Reduce heat immediately. The bottom will cook too fast without the top layers being ready.
Feel cue: The saffron tahdig mixture should feel like a very loose, golden-yellow rice porridge as you spread it — just fluid enough to find its own level but thick enough to hold the grains together.

Wrap the pot lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel — the cloth absorbs condensation and prevents water droplets from falling back onto the rice, which would make it wet rather than fluffy. Place the lid on tightly. Cook over medium heat for 5 minutes (this starts the tahdig crisping), then reduce to the lowest possible heat and cook for 40-45 minutes without lifting the lid. To unmold: place the pot on a cold, damp cloth or a pot holder for 2 minutes — the thermal shock helps release the tahdig. Remove the lid, place a large flat platter firmly over the pot, and flip in one confident movement. The tahdig should slide out golden and intact onto the platter. Drizzle the remaining saffron water over the white rice.
Visual cue: The inverted rice is a white mountain with strands of golden saffron across the top, resting on a golden-brown, intact tahdig crust the color of autumn leaves.
Underdone: The tahdig is pale and soft — it did not crisp, and it clings to the pot rather than releasing cleanly. Next time: ensure the oil was hot enough before the tahdig went in, and use medium heat for the first 8 minutes before reducing.
Perfect: The tahdig releases cleanly in one intact, golden-brown, shattering crust. The rice is white, fluffy, and fragrant with saffron. Individual grains are visible and distinct. Drizzle saffron water over the white rice and serve the tahdig pieces alongside as the prize.
Overdone: The tahdig is very dark brown, almost black, and smells sharp and burnt rather than golden and toasty. Serve the rice without the tahdig, leaving the burnt crust behind in the pot. Still an excellent rice.
Feel cue: When you tap the bottom of an unmolded tahdig with a knuckle, it should ring with a hollow, glassy sound — like knocking on a ceramic tile — confirming the thin, crisp crust that is the hallmark of a perfect chelow.

description: Oaxaca's oil-based chile-nut condiment — dried árbol and mulato chiles bloomed in hot oil with toasted pumpkin seeds, peanuts, and garlic until the oil itself becomes an aromatic, rust-red medium carrying smoky, nutty, slow-building heat. More oil than sauce, more condiment than salsa, entirely irreplaceable.

ingredients.name: Dried chiles de árbol (stemmed, seeded or not)
Dried mulato or ancho chile (stemmed, seeded, torn)
食用油（Neutral oil (vegetable or avocado oil)）

steps:
In a dry skillet over medium heat, toast the pepitas and peanuts separately, each stirring constantly. Pepitas first: 3 to 4 minutes until they inflate, turn golden-green, and begin to pop. Remove. Peanuts: 4 to 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until they smell of roasted peanuts and turn a uniform golden-brown. Remove. Do not mix them during toasting — they finish at different times. Cool both completely. The dry-toasting before the oil fry builds a layer of nutty flavor that the oil alone cannot achieve.
Visual cue: Pepitas are puffed and golden-olive green; peanuts are evenly golden-brown with no pale or dark spots.
Underdone: Pepitas are still flat and green; peanuts are pale and still taste raw. The salsa will lack its characteristic roasted-nut depth. Continue toasting in the dry pan. Both will signal doneness with aroma and color — wait for both.
Perfect: Pepitas are golden and fragrant of toasted squash; peanuts smell of roasted nut butter. Both feel dry and crisp when bitten. Cool completely before adding to the hot oil step — warm nuts will over-cook in the oil.
Overdone: Peanuts have gone dark brown, some are nearly black. Pepitas smell bitter. Discard and start over. Burnt nuts are unrecoverable — the bitterness will be the dominant flavor of the finished salsa.
Feel cue: A properly toasted peanut should crack cleanly in half when bitten, showing a uniformly golden-tan interior with no pale center. A raw peanut shows a white center; an overtoasted one shows brown throughout.

In a small saucepan, heat the oil over medium heat. When a piece of garlic dropped in sizzles immediately, add all the garlic slices and fry 60 to 90 seconds until golden — do not let them darken further. Remove garlic with a slotted spoon to a blender. Reduce the oil to medium-low and add both types of dried chiles. They should sizzle gently, not violently. Stir and press them into the oil for 30 to 60 seconds until they turn a darker shade and the oil takes on a deep red color and smells of bloomed dried chile. Watch carefully — dried chiles burn in seconds. Remove chiles immediately with a spider to the blender with the garlic. Reserve the now red-tinged oil.
Visual cue: The oil is deeply colored red-orange from the chile bloom; the garlic is golden; the chiles are a shade darker and puffed.
Underdone: Oil is still pale gold, chiles barely sizzled. The oil has not picked up the chile's color or flavor. The salsa macha will taste of raw oil. Increase the heat slightly and give the chiles longer contact. The oil should visibly color within 30 seconds of the chiles entering.
Perfect: Oil is a gorgeous terra-cotta red. Chiles are slightly puffed and darker. Garlic is deep golden. The kitchen smells of toasted chile and roasted garlic. Remove the chiles and garlic immediately to the blender. Keep the red oil for the final blend.
Overdone: Chiles have gone dark brown to black, the oil smells acrid and burnt, and the garlic is dark brown. If only slightly overdone, the salsa will have extra bitterness — balance it with sugar and extra vinegar. If severely burnt, discard and start again.
Feel cue: The bloom is complete when the oil itself turns visibly red-orange and the chile aroma in the room shifts from raw dried-chile smell to something warm, toasted, and slightly smoky. This transformation happens fast — the window between perfect and burnt is 20 to 30 seconds.

To the blender with the fried garlic and chiles, add the toasted pepitas and peanuts, vinegar, salt, and sugar (if using). Pour in the reserved red chile oil. Pulse 8 to 12 times — the goal is a very coarse texture, not a smooth puree. Each pulse should break down the nuts and chiles further without turning the whole thing into a paste. The finished salsa macha should have visible nut and chile fragments in a red oil — it is an oil-based condiment, not a thick paste. Taste and adjust salt, vinegar, and sugar. Pour into a jar and seal. The oil and solids will separate on standing — stir or shake before each use.
Visual cue: A rust-red oil studded with nut fragments, chile flakes, and sesame-seed-sized fragments. The oil itself is deeply colored, the solids suspended loosely within it.
Underdone: After only 3 to 4 pulses, nuts are still in large pieces and the components haven't begun to integrate into a cohesive condiment. Pulse 5 more times. Salsa macha should look like a thick, rustic relish in oil — not a pile of ingredients in oil.
Perfect: Red oil with coarsely blended nuts and chile pieces. Pours from a tilted jar in a thick stream with visible texture. Tastes of roasted nut, dried chile heat, and a bright vinegar lift. Jar and refrigerate. Use within 1 month. Drizzle on tacos, eggs, rice, grilled meat, or eat on a tortilla with salt.
Overdone: Blended to a smooth, uniform paste — all texture lost. The salsa macha has become more of a chile nut butter. Still delicious — use as a spread. For next time, stop pulsing earlier. The texture is what makes salsa macha distinctive.
Feel cue: Salsa macha on the spoon should feel heavy and oily, with a satisfying textural crunch from the nut and seed fragments. Taste the oil alone, separately from the solids — it should be deeply flavored and red-tinged, acting as both a cooking medium and a condiment in its own right.

ingredients.name: Serrano chilies (whole, with seeds for heat)

steps:
Heat a dry comal, cast-iron skillet, or griddle over high heat until it is very hot — a drop of water should evaporate instantly. Place the whole tomatoes, serrano chilies, onion wedges, and unpeeled garlic directly on the dry surface. Do not add oil. Leave undisturbed for 3-4 minutes per side until deeply blackened in places. The tomatoes will collapse and weep juice; the onion and garlic skins will char and blacken. Turn each piece once, and char the second side equally. This is not burning — it is tatemado, the technique of charring aromatics to build depth.
Visual cue: Tomatoes are collapsed and blackened on at least two sides, weeping juice into the pan. Onion wedges have char marks and softened interior. Garlic skins are papery black.
Underdone: Tomatoes are soft but uniformly red; no char. Onion is warm but not dark. This salsa will taste like cooked tomato sauce, not tatemada. Increase heat to its maximum. The comal must be very hot before charring begins.
Perfect: All vegetables show dramatic black charred patches alongside collapsed, jammy red-orange flesh. Tomatoes have burst and released juice that has charred on the comal itself. The kitchen smells of smoke, sweet tomato, and roasted garlic. Peel the garlic and transfer all vegetables to a blender or molcajete.
Overdone: Vegetables are uniformly black and completely carbonized — nothing red or orange remains. Smell is purely acrid. Salvage by removing the blackest outer layers; the interior flesh beneath the char is still usable.
Feel cue: A perfectly charred tomato feels completely soft when pressed with a spoon — it collapses immediately like a water balloon, the skin black and paper-thin over jelly-like flesh.

Peel the charred garlic cloves. Transfer all the charred vegetables and any juices on the comal (scrape them in — that char is flavor) to a blender or food processor. Add salt. Pulse in short bursts — do not puree — until you reach a chunky, coarse texture with distinct bits of tomato and chili still visible. Add cilantro and pulse once more. Taste and adjust salt. The salsa should be bold, smoky, and chunky.
Visual cue: A chunky, textured, deep-red salsa with visible black char flecks throughout — not a smooth purée but a rough, country-style sauce.
Underdone: Only one pulse — large pieces still present, onion is in large shards, tomato skin is in distinct strips. Inconsistent texture. Pulse 3-4 more times in short bursts; you want chunky, not whole pieces.
Perfect: Coarse, thick, deeply red-orange salsa with small, distinct vegetable pieces and black char flecks dispersed throughout. Smells of smoke, tomato, and garlic. Heat from the serranos is present but not numbing. Taste and serve immediately at room temperature, or refrigerate up to 3 days.
Overdone: Salsa has been pulsed to a smooth, thin purée — all texture is gone. Looks like ketchup. Stir in a finely diced fresh tomato to restore some texture.
Feel cue: Finished salsa tatemada should feel thick and slightly chunky on a spoon — it drops in a single blob rather than running off, and you can see the char flecks without looking hard.

ingredients.name: Dried guajillo chilies (stems and seeds removed)
White onion, cut into thick wedges

steps:
Heat a dry comal or heavy cast-iron skillet over high heat until it starts to smoke. Place the tomato halves cut-side down, onion wedges, and unpeeled garlic directly on the dry surface. Do not add oil. Char everything: tomatoes should develop patches of true black on the cut face and the skins should blister and split; onion wedges should char at the edges and soften through; garlic should darken in the peel and feel soft when squeezed. Turn everything once or twice and remove as it reaches the right level of char. The garlic will take about 6-8 minutes, the tomatoes 5-7, the onion 8-10.
Visual cue: Tomato cut-faces are a patchwork of charred black, blistered skin, and caramelized red flesh. Onion wedges are softened and blackened at their tips. Garlic peel is dark brown and the cloves inside are golden and soft when squeezed.
Underdone: Vegetables are only lightly colored or steam-soft rather than char-roasted. The salsa will lack its characteristic smoky, bitter-sweet backbone. Return to the comal and press firmly to maximize contact. Resist moving them — the char requires sustained contact with the hot surface.
Perfect: All three components carry visible black char alongside caramelized, softened flesh. The kitchen smells of wood smoke and sweet roasted tomato. Peeled garlic cloves are golden and completely soft. Transfer to a blender or molcajete along with the chili and proceed immediately.
Overdone: Tomatoes have collapsed completely and turned to black mush — too charred to provide any tomato body to the salsa. You can still use them — reduce or omit the salt and add a fresh raw tomato to the blender to restore body and balance the bitterness.
Feel cue: Press a tomato half with a spoon: it should give easily, the flesh soft and steaming beneath a charred exterior. The garlic clove squeezed in its skin should pop out as a golden paste — zero resistance.

On the same hot comal, toast the dried guajillo and árbol chilies. Press each chili flat for 10-15 seconds per side using a spatula — you want them to puff slightly, release a toasted chili fragrance, and develop a few darker spots. Do not char them as heavily as the tomatoes; the goal is to wake up their earthy, fruit-dried flavors and soften them slightly. Once toasted, immediately soak in just-boiled water for 10 minutes to rehydrate before blending. Drain and use as is — no need to strain the soaking liquid away unless it is very bitter.
Visual cue: Chilies have puffed slightly and smell toasted and earthy — fragrant like dried fruit and smoke. Their color has deepened to a glossy, dark mahogany. After soaking, they are supple and tear easily.
Underdone: Chilies are still dusty-smelling and stiff, not puffed or fragrant. They'll taste flat and raw in the finished salsa. Press them more firmly on the hot comal and wait for the unmistakable toasted chili fragrance before removing.
Perfect: Puffed, glossy, fragrant. After soaking, they tear like wet leather — supple with no stiffness. Smell is complex: toasted, smoky, and fruity. Drain and add to the blender with the charred vegetables.
Overdone: Chilies are charred black and smell acrid. The soaking water will be bitterly unpleasant and should be discarded. Discard and start with fresh chilies — scorched guajillo in particular becomes harshly bitter and cannot be rescued.
Feel cue: A perfectly rehydrated chili folds in your fingers without cracking or tearing — it has the suppleness of a damp cloth and smells simultaneously like raisins, leather, and a distant wood fire.

Peel the garlic from its charred skins. Add the charred tomatoes (with their skins and any charred bits), onion, garlic, drained chilies, and dried oregano to a blender. Blend at high speed for 30-60 seconds — not too long. A great salsa roja has texture: visible flecks of chili skin, small tomato seed pockets, a slightly coarse consistency. Season with salt and add lime juice. Taste: it should be smoky, deep, and earthy with a bright acid finish and present but not overwhelming heat.
Visual cue: A deep brick-red to near-black salsa with a slightly coarse texture and visible flecks of chili skin. It pours in a loose, scoopable stream — not a smooth purée, not a watery broth.
Underdone: Too coarse and chunky — pieces of onion and tomato are barely broken down, and the sauce lacks cohesion. Pulse the blender a few more times to break down the larger pieces while maintaining texture.
Perfect: Cohesive, slightly coarse, a deep brick-red. It coats a chip evenly and doesn't run off immediately. The color is complex — red, brown, and dark — not flat red. Proceed to the frying step for the final blooming of flavor.
Overdone: Blended to a completely smooth, aerated purée — more like a soup than a salsa. The texture has been lost. You can still use it as is, but call it salsa taquera rather than salsa roja for honesty.
Feel cue: The blended salsa should feel slightly gritty and substantial when rubbed between fingers — not smooth like a purée, not watery like juice. The heat from the chilies should arrive on the palate 2-3 seconds after tasting, not immediately.

Heat the oil in a saucepan over medium-high until shimmering. Carefully pour in the blended salsa — it will spit and hiss violently. Stir and fry, letting the salsa sizzle in the hot oil for 3-5 minutes, stirring frequently. This brief frying — called 'freír la salsa' — deepens the color, concentrates the flavor, and integrates the raw edges. The salsa will darken slightly, reduce a little, and develop a more unified, round flavor. Taste again for salt and lime.
Visual cue: The salsa has darkened 1-2 shades from blending to a deeper brick-red-brown. It is actively sizzling and sputtering in the oil, and the aroma is roasted and concentrated rather than raw.
Underdone: The salsa still tastes sharp and raw — the chili and tomato haven't integrated. It looks the same as it did when first blended. Continue frying — the transformation takes the full 3-5 minutes of active sizzling in hot oil.
Perfect: Slightly darker, unified, and round — a single cohesive flavor rather than distinct notes of tomato, chili, and char. The smell is deeply savory and roasted. Remove from heat, cool slightly, and serve at room temperature as a table salsa or taco condiment.
Overdone: Salsa has reduced to a thick paste and is beginning to stick and scorch at the bottom of the pan. The water has cooked off too quickly. Add a splash of water, stir to deglaze and loosen, and immediately reduce heat.
Feel cue: The frying salsa should gradually quiet down from a violent spitting sizzle to a gentler, slower bubble. When it stops sounding like a rainstorm and begins sounding like a slow simmer, the freír is done.

name: Salsa Verde Cruda
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Fresh tomatillos (husked and rinsed): 300 g
Jalapeño pepper (stemmed, rough chop): 40 g
  Alternatives: serrano for more heat; poblano for less
White onion, roughly chopped: 60 g
Garlic clove: 5 g
Fresh cilantro (leaves and stems): 25 g
Fresh lime juice: 20 g
Fine salt: 5 g
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The raw Mexican green salsa — tomatillos, jalapeño, onion, and cilantro blended entirely without heat, yielding a grassy, bracingly tart sauce with a crunch of freshness that cooked versions cannot touch. The verde in every taquería worth visiting.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

steps:
Remove the papery husks from the tomatillos and rinse them under cold water, rubbing off the sticky, slightly waxy coating on their skin. This coating is mildly bitter and slightly acidic — removing it ensures the salsa doesn't carry an unwanted soapy note. Quarter them. Taste a small piece raw: the tomatillo should taste bracingly sour with a fruity, apple-like undertone. If they taste flat, they are under-ripe; very ripe tomatillos are better for cooked salsa.
Visual cue: Tomatillos are rinsed and clean with a slight sheen, pale lime-green, quartered and ready.
Underdone: Still a sticky, slightly tacky coating on the skin. The papery remnants of husks still visible on some. Rinse more thoroughly under warm water, rubbing the skin until it feels smooth and not tacky.
Perfect: Smooth, bright green, clean-smelling. The cut surface reveals pale cream flesh with tiny seed chambers. Proceed to blending — no further prep needed.
Overdone: Tomatillos are overripe — yellow, very soft, smell fermented rather than fresh and tart. Use them for a roasted salsa verde instead. Overripe raw tomatillos will make this salsa taste muddy, not bright.
Feel cue: A properly rinsed tomatillo should feel slightly firm and smooth, like a small firm plum. The cut surface is pale and moist. A bite is immediately sour and clean, like unripe apple crossed with green tomato.

Combine the tomatillos, jalapeño, onion, garlic, cilantro, lime juice, and salt in a blender. Pulse 8 to 12 times — do not blend continuously. The texture should remain slightly chunky, not pureed. Cruda means raw and it means textured. Taste after the first few pulses and adjust: more jalapeño for heat, more lime for brightness, more cilantro for green flavor. The salsa will seem thin but will thicken as it rests.
Visual cue: A bright, vivid green salsa with visible herb and vegetable texture — chunky enough that you can see pieces, fluid enough to pour.
Underdone: After only 2 to 3 pulses, still large chunks of tomatillo and rough onion pieces. Not cohesive — the flavors haven't begun to integrate. Pulse 5 more times. The goal is a coarse, slightly broken-down texture, not identifiable large chunks.
Perfect: Uniformly textured, bright green, slightly chunky. Smells overwhelmingly of cilantro, lime, and tomatillo. Pours from the blender in a loose stream. Taste for salt and lime. Rest 5 minutes before serving so the onion's sharpness softens slightly.
Overdone: Blended into a completely smooth, aerated, foamy green puree. Has lost its raw texture and looks more like a green smoothie than a salsa. Still good — stir in a finely diced fresh tomatillo and a spoonful of fresh cilantro to restore texture.
Feel cue: Finished salsa verde cruda on the tongue delivers a sharp, high-pitched tart note first — the tomatillo's malic and citric acid — followed by an herbal green wave of cilantro, then the creeping heat of jalapeño. If the sequence is reversed and the heat arrives first, add more lime.

name: Italian Salsa Verde
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Flat-leaf parsley, leaves only: 100 parts
Anchovy fillets in oil, drained: 40 parts
  Alternatives: anchovy paste (use half the quantity)
Capers, rinsed (salt-packed preferred): 30 parts
  Alternatives: caper berries, roughly halved
Garlic cloves: 15 parts
  Alternatives: roasted garlic for a milder result
Red wine vinegar: 30 parts
  Alternatives: white wine vinegar
Extra-virgin olive oil: 100 parts
Dijon mustard: 10 parts
  Alternatives: whole-grain mustard
Fine sea salt: 2 parts
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A Milanese herb sauce of pounded parsley, anchovy, capers, and garlic loosened with olive oil and red wine vinegar — raw, immediate, and loud enough to cut through the richest braised meats.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

steps:
Place the garlic cloves in a mortar with the salt. Pound in a circular motion, scraping down the walls periodically, until you have a smooth, sticky, slightly translucent paste with no visible garlic chunks remaining. The salt acts as an abrasive — use it generously from the start. This takes about 2 minutes of sustained work. If using a knife instead: mince the garlic fine, then use the flat of the blade to smear it across the board, scraping and repeating until it forms a paste.
Visual cue: A smooth, pale-cream paste with the faint translucency of raw garlic, no fibrous strands, and a piercing raw-garlic scent.
Underdone: Coarse garlic pieces still clearly visible. The paste is chunky and wet, not yet cohesive. Continue pounding. Tilt the mortar to corral the escaping pieces; pound from different angles to break them down evenly.
Perfect: Completely smooth, sticky paste that clings to the pestle in strings when lifted and releases cleanly. No sharp-edged or fibrous pieces remain. Add anchovy fillets, capers, and mustard to the mortar and continue.
Overdone: The garlic has become a watery liquid — all cellular structure obliterated, clear liquid pooling in the bowl of the mortar. This is fine for salsa verde. The garlic flavor will be maximally pungent but slightly less complex. Proceed.
Feel cue: The paste should cling to the pestle like a tacky adhesive — lift the pestle slowly and it comes away trailing strings of garlic before releasing with a small snap.

Add the anchovy fillets to the garlic paste and pound until they completely dissolve into the base — the anchovies should vanish, leaving no visible flesh, only a deeper savory color and scent. Add the capers and pound until they are crushed but retain some rough texture: you want fragments, not obliteration. Add the Dijon mustard and stir it through with the pestle. Taste: it should be intensely savory, salty, and punchy.
Visual cue: A dark, glistening, rough-textured paste with visible caper fragments. No anchovy pieces identifiable — they should have fully dissolved into the garlic base.
Underdone: Anchovy fillets still visible as distinct pink or grey pieces. Capers still whole. The paste lacks cohesion. Continue pounding with patience — anchovies need sustained pressure to break down. Another 60 seconds of consistent work.
Perfect: Anchovies are invisible, fully absorbed. Capers are crushed into rough, dark-green fragments. The paste is cohesive, dark, glossy, and deeply savory. Add the chopped parsley and proceed to assemble the finished sauce.
Overdone: The mixture is completely smooth — all texture lost, capers obliterated into the paste. The flavor will be excellent; the sauce will simply be smoother. Proceed — the parsley will restore some texture.
Feel cue: Taste a small amount on your fingertip — it should hit in distinct waves: first salt and sharp raw garlic, then a round, deep savory cushion from the anchovy, then a brief brine snap from the capers.

Stack the parsley leaves and chop them very finely with a sharp chef's knife — do not use a food processor, which bruises the parsley and turns it grey within minutes. Aim for a near-mince. Add the chopped parsley to the mortar paste and fold together with the pestle. Loosen with red wine vinegar and olive oil, adding each in alternating small additions while tasting after each — the oil brings body and rounds the flavors; the vinegar keeps it alive. The final consistency should be spoonable and flowing, not stiff like a paste and not watery like a dressing.
Visual cue: A vivid, intense green sauce with a clearly visible herb texture, flecks of caper and dark anchovy paste throughout, and a sheen from the olive oil — pourable in a slow, thick ribbon.
Underdone: The sauce is thick and paste-like, clumping on a spoon. The herbs are coarsely chopped and dominate the texture; flavors taste raw and harsh. Chop the parsley more finely, and add olive oil a tablespoon at a time, stirring well after each addition until the sauce loosens to a pouring consistency.
Perfect: The sauce pours slowly from a spoon in an unbroken, heavy ribbon. The color is vivid green, the surface glossy, and texture shows clear parsley specks among the caper fragments. Taste once more for salt — the anchovies and capers carry most of the salt, so add carefully. Serve within the hour to preserve the herb color.
Overdone: The sauce is too thin and oily. The parsley has oxidized from vibrant green to dull army-green. Pound or chop in a fistful of fresh parsley to restore body and color. A small piece of torn day-old bread pounded into the base will also absorb excess oil and add textural body.
Feel cue: The sauce should feel alive on the tongue — raw garlic bites cleanly at the back of the throat, anchovy provides a cushion of umami that lingers, the capers snap with brine, and the parsley fades last
with a vegetal freshness.

ingredients.name: Fresh flat-leaf parsley (leaves and fine stems)

steps:
This sauce must be hand-chopped — not blended, not food-processed. Working on a clean board, roughly chop the parsley leaves and fine stems together until they are finely minced but still have texture, not a wet paste. Chop the capers coarsely; if they are large salt-packed capers, cut them in half or thirds. Lay the anchovy fillets flat and chop them into a rough paste — they will almost dissolve under the knife. Mince the garlic very finely, or press it through a garlic press. Combine everything on the board and run a rocking knife through the combined pile 20-30 times until the mixture is cohesive but visibly rough — every component still identifiable but working as a whole.
Visual cue: A rough, fragrant mound of green-flecked mixture — parsley the dominant presence, with visible pale caper pieces and the anchovy reduced to near-invisible minced shreds throughout. The pile should look textured and rustic, never smooth.
Underdone: The components are barely mixed — large parsley leaves, whole capers, and visible anchovy fillets still separate on the board. Continue chopping in a rocking motion with a large chef's knife, working across the pile repeatedly. The repeated chopping integrates and mingles everything without destroying individual textures.
Perfect: A uniformly minced but still-textured pile — the parsley is fully chopped to a fine mince, the capers are roughly cut into 2-3 pieces each, and the anchovy has essentially dissolved into the parsley. The entire pile smells intensely herbal and savory-salty. Scrape into a bowl. Add the mustard, lemon, and oil. Proceed.
Overdone: The mixture has turned into a green paste from over-chopping — the parsley has released so much liquid it is wet and staining the board, and all textural distinction has been lost. You have made a pesto-adjacent purée. It will taste fine but is no longer salsa verde in texture. Use as is,

or accept the difference.
Feel cue: Run your fingers through the chopped mixture — it should feel like damp, coarsely ground herbs: each piece distinct but the whole cohesive enough to clump lightly when pressed. No large stalks should remain.

Scrape the chopped mixture into a bowl. Add the Dijon mustard and work it into the herbs with a spoon — the mustard acts as a binder, helping the olive oil cling to the parsley rather than pooling at the bottom of the bowl. Stir in the lemon juice and lemon zest. Taste at this stage, before the oil goes in: the mixture should taste intensely salty from the anchovies and capers (this will be attenuated by the oil), aggressively lemon-bright, and herbal-green. If it tastes flat, add more lemon or a tiny pinch of salt.
Visual cue: The chopped herbs and capers glistening lightly with lemon juice, bound by a pale smear of mustard throughout. The mixture is still dry-ish and crumbly, not yet saucy.
Underdone: Mustard is still visible in a single streak rather than integrated throughout. Lemon has not been fully worked in and pools at the bottom of the bowl. Stir more vigorously to fully integrate the mustard and lemon into the herb mixture before adding oil.
Perfect: Everything is evenly distributed — the mustard is no longer visible as a separate element but is coating the herb pieces. The mixture smells of lemon and parsley, sharp and herbal. It tastes aggressively salty-bright. Fold in the olive oil. Proceed.
Overdone: Too much lemon juice has made the mixture watery and the parsley has begun to go dull and slightly gray from the acid. Drain off excess lemon juice and compensate for the brightness loss with a small addition of zest, which carries lemon aroma without additional liquid.
Feel cue: Press a small amount of the herb mixture between your fingers after adding the mustard and lemon — it should clump slightly and feel lightly sticky, like damp coffee grounds, rather than falling apart as dry loose herbs.

Stream the olive oil over the herb mixture in a slow, steady pour while stirring constantly with a fork or spoon. The oil does not need to emulsify here — this is an oil-based suspension, not a creamy emulsion — but it should be evenly distributed so every parsley piece is coated and glistening. Season with a small pinch of salt (the anchovies and capers are already aggressively salty — taste before adding) and black pepper. Stir well and then rest the salsa verde uncovered at room temperature for at least 15 minutes before serving — this rest allows the lemon to mellow, the anchovy to integrate fully, and the oil to absorb some of the parsley's green flavor.
Visual cue: A loose, glistening, bright-green sauce — every herb piece coated in golden oil, the whole looking vivid and alive. It should flow slowly when the bowl is tilted, not pool like water.
Underdone: The oil sits on top of the herbs in a separate layer, or there is too little oil and the mixture is dry and crumbly rather than saucy. Stir more vigorously and add oil gradually until every piece of herb is fully coated and the sauce flows loosely when the bowl is tilted.
Perfect: A bright, glistening, deeply green sauce with a loose, flowing texture — it pours off a spoon in a quick drizzle and leaves a rich green stain on whatever it touches. The flavor is assertively herbal, salty, lemony, and savory. Rest 15 minutes before serving. The sauce is at its peak immediately after this rest; serve the same day.
Overdone: Too much oil has made the sauce thin and oily, with the herbs swimming in a pool of green-tinted olive oil — the herb-to-oil ratio is lost. Add more finely chopped parsley to re-balance the ratio. The sauce can absorb significantly more herb if needed.
Feel cue: Spoon a small amount onto a white plate and tilt the plate — the sauce should flow and spread, leaving vivid green oil trails behind
it. If it sits in a fixed mound, it needs more oil. If it flows like water, it needs more herb.

Allow the sauce to rest at room temperature for 15 minutes minimum — 30 minutes is better. During this time, the acid from the lemon softens the raw edge of the garlic and fully wilts the anchovy into the oil, creating a more cohesive flavor rather than identifiable separate components. Taste once more after resting and adjust: the salsa verde should taste punchy, herbal, savory, and bright — assertive enough to stand alongside a fatty bollito misto or a charred grilled steak. If the flavors have muted during resting, brighten with a final squeeze of lemon.
Visual cue: After resting, the color is slightly deeper and the herbs have absorbed some oil, making the sauce slightly thicker and more cohesive than immediately after mixing. The aroma is more integrated — less sharp garlic-forward, more of a unified herbal-savory impression.
Underdone: Just mixed and served immediately — the garlic is harsh, the anchovy is still a detectable separate note, and the oil and herbs have not fully combined. The sauce is not ruined, but let it rest. Fifteen minutes is a minimum for the salsa verde to become more than the sum of its parts.
Perfect: After resting, the sauce tastes rounded and assertive: herbal, lemony, savory-deep from the anchovy and capers, with the garlic present but not harsh. All components have merged into a cohesive whole. Serve alongside grilled meat, poached fish, bollito misto, or roasted vegetables.
Overdone: Left uncovered for more than 2 hours at room temperature — the parsley is beginning to oxidize to olive-drab, the lemon juice has lost its brightness, and the garlic has mellowed past savory into muted. Add fresh chopped parsley and a squeeze of lemon just before serving to restore vibrancy.
Feel cue: Dip a piece of bread into the rested salsa verde — every bite should deliver an immediate herbal-salty punch followed by the savory depth of the anchovy
and the bright clean lift of lemon. If the bread tastes mostly of oil, the herb-to-oil balance needs adjusting.

name: Salsa Verde (Tomatillo)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

  Alternatives: canned whole tomatillos, drained (char them anyway)

  Alternatives: serrano chiles for more heat, poblano for less

Garlic cloves, unpeeled: 0.2 parts
  Alternatives: roasted garlic for a sweeter note
Fresh cilantro (leaves and stems): 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: flat-leaf parsley for those averse to cilantro

  Alternatives: white wine vinegar in a pinch
Fine sea salt: 0.1 parts
  Alternatives: kosher salt

Total time: 25 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A bright, tangy table sauce from Central Mexico — husked tomatillos and jalapeños blistered under a broiler until their skins blacken and char, then blitzed with raw onion, garlic, and a fistful of cilantro into something vivid and alive. The char is not a mistake; it is the sauce.

steps:
Position an oven rack 4 inches beneath the broiler and set it to high. Arrange the tomatillos, whole jalapeños, onion quarters, and unpeeled garlic cloves on a foil-lined baking sheet in a single layer. Broil for 8-10 minutes, rotating the pan once, until the tomatillos are blackened and blistered in spots, softened and collapsing, and the jalapeño skins are charred. Flip everything once at the halfway mark. The garlic should be soft inside its skin.
Visual cue: Tomatillos with blackened patches on their upper surfaces, soft and weeping juice onto the foil; jalapeños with scorched, blistered skins.
Underdone: The tomatillos are still firm and bright green, the skins unbroken. No blackening. They look raw. Return to the broiler for 3-5 more minutes. Move the pan closer to the element if your broiler runs weak.
Perfect: Tomatillos are softened and slumped, with dark char on their upper faces and a pool of tart green juice on the foil. Jalapeño skins are papery and blackened in places. Let rest 5 minutes, then peel the garlic and pull the stems from the jalapeños — leave the char on everything else.
Overdone: Tomatillos have burst completely and reduced to mush, the juice scorching on the foil. Jalapeños are uniformly blackened. The flavor will be more bitter and smoky than tart. Scrape everything into the blender but add the cilantro and lime juice before tasting — you may need extra to balance.
Feel cue: Press a tomatillo gently with the back of a spoon — it should yield without resistance, like a soft grape, and the skin should slip. If it pushes back, it needs more time under the heat.

Squeeze the roasted garlic from its papery skins directly into a blender. Add the charred tomatillos and their accumulated juices, the jalapeños (seeds and all for full heat, or deseed for milder), and the onion. Pulse 4-5 times to break it down, then add the cilantro, lime juice, and salt. Blend to your preferred texture — a few more pulses for rustic and chunky, a 20-second blitz for a pourable sauce.
Visual cue: A bright olive-green sauce flecked with darker char bits and fresh cilantro, loose enough to pour but not watery.
Underdone: The sauce is still chunky with visible solid pieces of tomatillo; it sits in clumps rather than flowing. Pulse several more times, pressing down large pieces with a spatula between pulses.
Perfect: A slightly rustic, pourable sauce with a few small flecks of char and herb. The color is a vivid, smoky olive-green, neither watery nor thick. Taste for salt and lime. Adjust and let it sit for 10 minutes — the flavor continues to develop.
Overdone: Blended too long into a smooth, uniform purée with incorporated air, turning it a lighter, foam-flecked green. It will still taste correct; the texture is simply restaurant-style rather than molcajete-style. Let it rest to settle.
Feel cue: Run a spoon through the blended salsa — it should flow back into the channel within two seconds. If it stands in a mound, add a tablespoon of water. If it sloshes like water, it over-broiled and lost its body.

Taste the salsa and season in layers: add salt first until the tomatillo flavor snaps into focus, then add lime juice in small increments to amplify the brightness without pushing it into sourness. A good salsa verde should taste bright and tangy, with the heat arriving at the back of the palate. Let it rest at room temperature for 10 minutes before serving — the flavors knit together as it sits.
Visual cue: A vibrant, pooling sauce with an olive-to-jade green color. It smells simultaneously of char, fresh herb, and citrus.
Underdone: Flat and muted; the tomatillo tang is buried and the salsa tastes of nothing in particular. Add salt a pinch at a time, tasting between each addition. The acid will follow once the salt unlocks the flavors.
Perfect: Bright and punchy, the tannin of the tomatillo balanced against the char, the cilantro present but not overwhelming, a clean heat on the finish. Serve immediately or refrigerate. The salsa will keep for 5 days and intensifies overnight.
Overdone: Aggressively sour or salty, the chile heat dominating everything, the tomatillo flavor lost. Add a fresh tomatillo or a small piece of raw onion and re-blend to dilute. A pinch of sugar can tame excess acid.
Feel cue: Dip a clean chip or spoon into the finished salsa. The tomatillo tang should arrive first, the chile heat second, and the herbal lift of cilantro should linger on the exhale. If any single note overwhelms, the sauce needs rebalancing.

name: 墨西哥绿莎莎酱 · Salsa Verde
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: canned tomatillos, drained
Serrano chiles, stems removed: 2 parts

  Alternatives: yellow onion
Garlic cloves, unpeeled: 1 parts
Fresh cilantro, stems and leaves: 1 parts
Fine salt: 0.3 parts
Fresh lime juice: 0.5 parts
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 20 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Bright, tangy tomatillos charred under the broiler with serrano chiles and white onion, then blended raw into a salsa that tastes like green fire — acidic, herbaceous, and dangerously drinkable.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

steps:
Set the oven to broil on high and position a rack 6 inches from the element. Spread the tomatillos (halved if very large), serrano chiles, onion quarters, and unpeeled garlic on a foil-lined baking sheet in a single layer. Broil for 5–6 minutes until the tops are spotted black and blistered. Flip everything with tongs and broil for another 3–4 minutes. The tomatillos should be collapsing and oozing their sticky green juice.
Visual cue: Tomatillos have collapsed, turned dull olive-green, and are pooling their own sticky juice. Serrano skins are blistered and charred. Onion edges are blackened. Garlic skin is papery and golden.
Underdone: Tomatillos are still bright green and firm. No char visible. Skin is intact and shiny. Return to broiler for 2 more minutes. The collapse of the tomatillo is the key indicator — wait for it.
Perfect: Tomatillos are soft and olive-drab, blackened in spots. Juices are running and slightly sticky on the foil. Everything smells sharp and roasted. Let cool 5 minutes, peel the garlic, then blend everything including all the pan juices.
Overdone: Tomatillos have dried out and shrunk. Juices are scorched black on the foil. Serrano is uniformly black and bitter-smelling. Peel the serrano if the skin is fully carbonized. Use the remaining tomatillos — they will taste intense but usable. Add a splash of water when blending.
Feel cue: Press a tomatillo with a spoon — it should offer almost no resistance and leave a trail of sticky greenish juice. A charred exterior with a still-firm interior means more time under the broiler.

Peel the roasted garlic and transfer all roasted vegetables and their accumulated juices into a blender. Add the cilantro, salt, and lime juice. Pulse 4–5 times for a rough texture, or blend for 30–45 seconds for a smoother sauce. Do not over-blend — some texture is traditional and desirable. Taste immediately and adjust salt and lime.
Visual cue: A bright to medium olive-green sauce with visible flecks of dark char and cilantro. Not completely smooth — you can see small pieces throughout. Color is vivid and appetizing.
Underdone: Large chunks of onion and tomatillo are still whole. Texture is more like a rough chop than a sauce. Blend in 5-second pulses until the texture is cohesive but still has some body.
Perfect: Pourable but textured, vivid green-brown with dark flecks. Tastes of bright acid, smoke, heat, and fresh herb all at once. Transfer to a serving bowl. Taste once more and adjust salt. Rest 5 minutes before serving for flavors to meld.
Overdone: Pale, frothy, completely smooth. The color has turned grey-green from over-oxidation. Char flavor has disappeared. The flavor is still good — serve as a smoother style salsa. Add a squeeze of lime to revive the brightness.
Feel cue: A spoonful should taste immediate and bright — the acid should hit first, then the heat builds slowly. If the heat comes first, add more lime. If it tastes flat, add salt in tiny pinches until the brightness snaps back.

Taste the salsa critically. Add salt in small increments (a pinch at a time), stirring and tasting between each addition, until the tomatillo flavor pops and the salsa tastes bright rather than dull. A properly salted salsa verde should make you immediately want another taste. Add more lime juice if the acidity has faded. Let rest at room temperature for 10 minutes before serving to allow the flavors to settle.
Visual cue: Salsa holds its vivid green-brown color. The surface has a very light sheen from the tomatillo pectin. No separation visible — the sauce looks cohesive.
Underdone: Flat, muted taste. Color is bright but the flavor doesn't pop. Feels like something is missing. This is almost always a salt deficiency. Add a pinch, stir, wait 30 seconds, and taste again.
Perfect: Every spoonful is bright, tangy, smoky, herbaceous, and appropriately spicy. You want to eat it with a spoon. Serve immediately or refrigerate. Flavor continues to develop for up to 2 hours.
Overdone: Salty or so spicy it is difficult to eat by the spoonful. Lips tingle immediately on contact. For over-salting: blend in one more roasted tomatillo or a small amount of avocado. For over-spice: the same remedy, or serve with crema.
Feel cue: The finished salsa should have a slight viscous pull when you tilt the bowl — the pectin in tomatillos gives it a natural body. If it runs like water, the tomatillos were underripe or insufficiently roasted.

name: Salt and Pepper Shrimp
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Large shell-on, head-on shrimp (prawns), deveined: 600 g
  Alternatives: large tiger prawns
Cornstarch (cornflour): 40 g
  Alternatives: potato starch
Neutral oil, for wok-frying: 500 ml
  Alternatives: sunflower oil
Garlic cloves, finely minced: 20 g
Spring onions (scallions), thinly sliced: 40 g
Fresh red chillies, thinly sliced (optional but traditional): 15 g
  Alternatives: dried chilli flakes
Fine sea salt: 6 g
Ground white pepper: 5 g
Five-spice powder: 2 g
Sesame oil, to finish: 5 ml
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Cantonese wok-fried whole shell-on shrimp that arrive at the table crackling and fragrant — the shells fried to a shattering crunch you eat whole, the flesh beneath barely cooked and sweet, buried under a confetti of garlic, scallion, and white pepper.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Fresh red chillies, thinly sliced (optional but traditional)

steps:
Pat the shrimp completely dry with kitchen paper — any surface moisture will cause the oil to spit violently and prevent the shell from crisping. Toss in the cornstarch to coat very lightly — just enough for a barely-there dusting, not a thick batter. Mix in half the salt, white pepper, and the five-spice.
Visual cue: Shrimp coated in seasoned cornstarch
Underdone: Shrimp are still visibly wet. Cornstarch is clumping in wet patches. Pat drier and toss again. Wet shrimp will steam instead of fry.
Perfect: Each shrimp has a very faint, even white dusting — barely visible but present. The shells feel slightly tacky to the touch. No clumping. Fry immediately — the cornstarch will absorb moisture quickly and become gluey if left.
Overdone: Shrimp are heavily coated in thick cornstarch — more like a battered prawn. Shake off excess vigorously. A thin coating is the goal, not a coating.
Feel cue: A coated shrimp should feel dry and very slightly powdery on the outside — not slippery or wet. The shell should already feel slightly rigid from the starch.

Heat the oil in a wok over the highest possible heat to 190 C (375 F). Fry the shrimp in batches — 8–10 at a time — for exactly 60–75 seconds. The shells will sizzle aggressively and turn bright orange-red. Remove with a spider and drain on a rack. Do not over-fry — the shrimp continue cooking from residual heat.
Visual cue: Shrimp in the hot oil
Underdone: Shells are pink but still translucent in places. The shrimp float limply in the oil. 60 seconds have not elapsed. Hold longer — but watch carefully. The window between raw and overcooked shrimp is only 30 seconds.
Perfect: Shells are a vivid, even orange-red and have crisped visibly — you can hear them crackle faintly when lifted from the oil. The shrimp have curled into a tight C shape. Heads (if on) are golden and fragrant. Remove immediately and drain. Proceed to the wok-toss step while oil is still hot.
Overdone: Shells are beginning to darken toward red-brown. The shrimp have tightened into a very tight curl and feel firm. Remove immediately. The flesh inside may be slightly overcooked but the shell will still crisp.
Feel cue: Pick up a fried shrimp by the tail — it should feel surprisingly light and rigid, the shell almost papery-crisp. When you bite the shell, it should shatter with a very audible crunch.

Pour off most of the frying oil, leaving about 1 tablespoon in the wok. Return to high heat. Add the garlic, most of the spring onion, and sliced chilli. Stir-fry for 30 seconds until the garlic is golden and fragrant. Add the fried shrimp back to the wok and toss furiously for 30 seconds to coat with the aromatic mixture. Season with remaining salt and white pepper. Drizzle with sesame oil and toss once more. Serve immediately, garnished with remaining spring onion.
Visual cue: Shrimp with aromatics in the wok
Underdone: Garlic is still pale and raw-smelling. The aromatics have not had time to bloom. Toss over high heat for another 30 seconds — the garlic needs to turn golden to lose its rawness.
Perfect: Garlic is golden and fragrant. Each shrimp is glossy with sesame oil and flecked with crisped garlic, green scallion, and chilli. The shells remain audibly crisp. The wok smells of toasted garlic, sesame, and white pepper. Plate immediately and serve at the table without delay.
Overdone: Garlic has darkened to very dark brown or black. Bitter, acrid smell in the wok. Remove the dark garlic pieces if possible. The bitterness will dominate the dish if left.
Feel cue: Eat one shrimp immediately from the wok — the shell should shatter between your teeth with a distinct crack, revealing sweet, barely-cooked flesh beneath. If the shell is soft and leathery, the oil was not hot enough.

description: Rings and tentacles tossed in spiced potato starch and flash-fried until the coating shatters at first bite — finished in the wok with garlic, chili, and spring onion that perfume the crust without softening it.

ingredients.name: Fresh squid tubes and tentacles, cleaned
花椒（Sichuan peppercorns, toasted and ground）
Neutral oil for deep-frying (peanut or sunflower)
Long red chili and green chili, thinly sliced

steps:
Open the squid tubes and score the inside surface in a crosshatch pattern at 5mm intervals — this gives the starch something to grip and helps the squid curl dramatically in the oil. Cut into 4cm pieces. Keep tentacles whole. Dry everything very thoroughly with paper towels.
Visual cue: Diamond-grid score marks covering the entire inner surface. Pieces look dry and slightly tacky.
Underdone: No score marks, surface is still smooth — the coating will slip off. Score deeper, going about halfway through the thickness.
Perfect: Crosshatch grid visible, pieces cut to similar size for even frying. Surfaces matte and dry. Toss in the seasoned starch immediately.
Overdone: Scored too deeply — pieces have been cut through in places. Use as-is; smaller pieces fry faster, so watch the oil more carefully.
Feel cue: The squid should feel cool and slightly sticky from the residual moisture — any visible wetness needs to be dried off before coating.

Combine potato starch, salt, white pepper, and Sichuan pepper in a bowl. Add the dried squid and toss to coat completely. Shake off excess in a sieve — you want a thin, even coating that barely obscures the squid, not a heavy cloak.
Visual cue: Each piece is dusted in a thin, even, opaque white coating. No clumps, no bare patches.
Underdone: Translucent patches where the squid shows through — uneven coating. Toss again and press the starch lightly to adhere, then shake off the excess.
Perfect: A fine, even, matte-white coating on every surface. When you shake the sieve, only loose starch falls away. Fry within 60 seconds of coating — starch absorbs moisture and clumps if it sits.
Overdone: Thick, doughy coating that clumps in places. Looks like battered fish, not salt-and-pepper. Shake vigorously in the sieve to remove the excess. Thin coatings fry crisper.
Feel cue: Run a finger over a coated piece — it should feel chalky and dry, like dusting icing sugar on a pastry.

Heat oil to 200 C (390 F) in a wok or deep pan — higher than most frying, because squid is wet. Fry in small batches for exactly 90 seconds. The squid will curl and the coating will set. Do not stir for the first 30 seconds so the crust can form. Remove to a rack — immediately.
Visual cue: Ivory-white to pale gold coating, tightly curled scored pieces, suckers on the tentacles puffed and crisp.
Underdone: Coating is still pale and soft. Squid has not yet curled. The starch looks wet. Continue 30 more seconds. Ensure oil temp has not dropped below 185 C.
Perfect: Pale gold, shatteringly crisp coating. Scored pieces have curled into tight cylinders. Tentacles are frilly and crunchy. Remove to rack immediately and do not stack — steam will soften the crust.
Overdone: Coating has gone deep gold to brown, squid smells of burnt starch. Remove immediately. The coating will taste slightly bitter but the interior is likely still tender.
Feel cue: Lift a piece of squid on a spider and let it drain — you should hear a hiss and then a dry crackling as the water evaporates from the crust.

Pour off most of the frying oil, leaving a thin slick. Over high flame, add garlic, chili, and spring onion. Stir-fry for 20–30 seconds until fragrant and the garlic is barely golden. Add the fried squid back and toss furiously for 15 seconds — just enough to perfume the crust without steaming it soft.
Visual cue: Garlic is pale gold and fragrant, chili and spring onion are bright and wilted at the edges. Squid crust still looks dry and intact.
Underdone: Garlic is still raw and white, aromatics have barely wilted. Another 10–15 seconds on maximum heat.
Perfect: Garlic pale gold, chili and onion glistening and fragrant. Squid still crisp — toss completed in under 20 seconds. Serve immediately on a hot plate.
Overdone: Garlic is brown and bitter. Squid has steamed in the wok and the crust has gone soft. Serve anyway — the flavor is there even if the texture has suffered. Next time, work faster and hotter.
Feel cue: The final toss should sound like gravel in a pan — that dry rattle is the crust staying crisp.

ingredients.name: Whole branzino (European sea bass), gutted and scaled
柠檬（Lemon, thinly sliced into rounds）

steps:
Preheat the oven to 190°C (375°F). In a large bowl, combine the coarse sea salt with the egg whites. Mix firmly with your hands until every grain of salt is coated and the mixture resembles wet sand — it should clump when squeezed and hold an impression of your fist. This is the mortar that will seal the fish. If it crumbles and won't hold a shape, add a fourth egg white.
Visual cue: A dense, heavy mixture the colour and texture of damp beach sand — clumping easily when squeezed, holding its shape without collapsing.
Underdone: Salt is still dry and granular. Egg whites sit in wet patches rather than coating all the grains. Mixture falls apart when squeezed. Mix more vigorously until all the egg white is evenly distributed. The mixture must hold a squeezed shape or the crust will crack open during baking.
Perfect: Heavy, cohesive, damp throughout. Squeezes into a firm lump that holds its shape when released, like well-packed wet sand for a sandcastle. Work quickly — the egg whites begin to set as they warm up.
Overdone: Mixture has been over-worked and is beginning to feel sticky rather than sandy. Egg whites are slightly frothy. It is still usable — press on. The crust may be slightly less rigid but will still seal adequately.
Feel cue: Squeeze a fistful — it should pack like wet sand, holding the impression of your knuckles without weeping liquid.

Check the fish cavity is clean and dry. Season the interior lightly with a pinch of salt. Lay the lemon rounds in a shingle pattern along the cavity floor. Pack the fennel fronds, thyme, and parsley in on top of the lemon — the cavity should be visibly full. The herbs will steam inside the crust and perfume the flesh from the inside out without penetrating it externally at all.
Visual cue: The fish cavity visibly bulging with green herbs and overlapping lemon rounds. The fish exterior is dry and unadorned.
Underdone: Cavity is only half filled. A few sparse herb sprigs rattle around. Add more herbs — the stuffing expands with heat and releases its aromatics as steam. A sparse stuffing leaves the flesh flavourless.
Perfect: Cavity packed firmly with herbs and lemon, with a faint bulge visible along the belly. The fish holds together when lifted. Transfer to the baking tray over the salt bed immediately.
Overdone: So much stuffing crammed in that the belly has been torn or the fish has been forced open. Herbs are spilling from the cavity. Reduce the quantity slightly and close the belly with a skewer if needed to hold everything in place.
Feel cue: The stuffed fish should feel heavy and dense when you lift it. You can feel the herbs filling out the belly — a reassuring, solid resistance.

Spread a third of the salt mixture onto a rimmed baking sheet in the exact shape and size of the fish, about 1.5 cm thick. Lay the stuffed branzino on top. Pack the remaining salt mixture firmly over the top and sides of the fish, pressing and smoothing it into a solid, even casing at least 1.5 cm thick at every point. Pay special attention to the head and tail — cracks there will let steam escape and dry the flesh. The fish should be completely invisible under the crust. Smooth the surface with wet palms.
Visual cue: A smooth, solid mound of white salt on the baking sheet, clearly fish-shaped, with no cracks, gaps, or exposed fish visible.
Underdone: Salt crust is thin in places, cracking at the edges or tail. Patches of fish skin are still visible through the crust. Press additional salt mixture over any exposed areas and smooth firmly with wet hands. Thin spots will crack open in the oven and dry those sections of fish.
Perfect: A seamless, solid white dome 1.5–2 cm thick all over. No cracks. No visible fish. Surface has been smoothed to a uniform finish. Into the oven — cook immediately before the salt draws moisture out of the fish.
Overdone: Salt crust is excessively thick (over 3 cm) in places, making it very heavy. The fish shape is completely lost and the crust looks like a formless white loaf. It will still work, but take longer to bake and be more difficult to crack. Aim for consistency in thickness next time.
Feel cue: Pat the crust firmly — it should feel as solid and rigid as packed clay, with no soft spots that give when pressed.

Bake at 190°C (375°F) for 25–30 minutes for a 600g fish. The timing scales with fish weight: add 5 minutes per additional 200g. The crust will harden to a rigid, chalky shell and may develop faint ivory-to-beige colouring on top. It will not brown dramatically — the visual cues here are all about the crust hardening. A probe thermometer inserted through the crust should read 58–60°C at the thickest part of the fish. If you do not have a probe, use the timing as your guide.
Visual cue: A chalky-white, hard, rigid shell on the baking tray that resists when tapped with a wooden spoon.
Underdone: Crust is still slightly soft and gives when pressed. Feels like dense, not-yet-set clay. Probe reads below 55°C. Return for 5 more minutes. The crust must be completely rigid before cracking — a soft crust means undercooked fish inside.
Perfect: Crust is hard, chalky, and sounds hollow when tapped with a spoon. Probe at the thickest part reads 58–60°C. A faint smell of herbs escaping around the edges. Bring to the table immediately for the dramatic tableside cracking.
Overdone: Crust has turned a deep beige or pale brown in spots. Probe reads above 65°C. Strong smell of baked salt. The fish may be drier than ideal inside. The crust method protects against extreme overcooking — crack it immediately and assess the flesh.
Feel cue: Knock the crust firmly with a wooden spoon handle — you should hear a solid, resonant 'thunk', like knocking on a thick ceramic pot.

Bring the baking sheet to the table. Using the back of a heavy spoon or a small mallet, crack the crust firmly along the spine of the fish. It will fracture in large shards — peel these away and discard. Carefully lift the top fillet free, then remove the spine in one piece. The bottom fillet sits on the lower salt bed — slide a spatula underneath to lift it clean. Serve the fillets on warmed plates with a generous pour of extra-virgin olive oil and the lemon slices from inside the cavity.
Visual cue: Pearlescent, perfectly cooked fish fillets with a glistening surface and no grey, dry patches. The flesh should pull apart in large, moist, glass-clear flakes.
Underdone: Flesh at the thickest point near the head is still translucent and cool to the touch. Flakes resist separating cleanly. Return the fish in the broken crust to the oven for another 5 minutes — the shell still traps some heat.
Perfect: Flesh is fully opaque, white-to-ivory, and separates in generous, glistening flakes with no dryness at all. Smells intensely of herbs and sea. A slow, clear drop of natural jus beads on the plate. Plate immediately and pour olive oil over the exposed flesh while it is still steaming.
Overdone: Flesh looks dry, chalky, or grainy. Flakes are small and tight rather than large and yielding. Any moisture has been baked away. A generous pour of excellent olive oil at the table can revive the flavour if not the texture. Serve with plenty of lemon.
Feel cue: Press a fillet gently with a fork — it should yield immediately and fall into thick, glossy flakes without any resistance. Resistance means dryness.
