ingredients.name: Whole sea bass, cleaned and scaled (about 700g)
Coarse sea salt (not fine — it must be granular)
Fresh ginger, peeled, sliced into coins
葱（Scallions (spring onions), tied in a loose knot）

steps:
Preheat the oven to 200°C (390°F) with a rack in the centre position. Pat the sea bass completely dry — inside the cavity and all over the outside — with multiple changes of paper towels. Dryness is critical: any moisture on the fish surface will steam inside the salt crust rather than allowing the fish to cook in the dry residual heat of the crust. Inspect the fish for any remaining scales by running a finger from tail to head — any that remain will prevent the crust from sealing properly and can embed in the fish.
Visual cue: Fish skin is completely matte and dry with no glistening or wet patches. The cavity interior is also dry when inspected.
Underdone: Skin still glistens with moisture from the fish monger's ice. Dark wet patches on the skin and wet spots inside the cavity. Pat again with fresh dry paper towels and leave uncovered at room temperature for 5 minutes before encasing. Even a thin film of moisture affects the crust.
Perfect: Skin is completely matte. Running a dry paper towel over it produces no moisture. Inside the cavity is dry to the touch. Stuff immediately and proceed to building the salt crust.
Overdone: Fish has been left uncovered so long the surface has begun to dry and firm slightly at the thinnest points, like the tail. Proceed immediately — superficial drying does not affect the eating. The salt crust will protect it.
Feel cue: Run a dry finger from tail to head across the fish skin — it should catch slightly on the scales and feel completely dry, like touching dry parchment paper, not the slippery wet surface of a fresh-washed fish.

Lay the ginger slices in an overlapping layer along the length of the cavity floor. Place the knotted scallions on top of the ginger, and tuck the cilantro sprigs around them. Drizzle the Shaoxing wine into the cavity — it will perfume the fish as it steams. Close the cavity by pressing the sides of the fish together gently. The aromatics inside do not season the flesh directly; they create a fragrant steam environment that perfumes the fish from within.
Visual cue: Cavity is neatly filled with ginger, scallions, and herbs. Sides of the fish are pressed together. The stuffing is visible if the belly is opened but not spilling out.
Underdone: Too few aromatics — cavity looks sparse and the ginger and scallions cover less than half the interior length. Add more ginger and scallions. The cavity should be generously packed but not so full it cannot close.
Perfect: Cavity neatly and fully packed. Fish sides close together with a gentle press. Faint perfume of ginger and Shaoxing wine already present. Proceed to building the salt crust.
Overdone: Stuffing so abundant that the fish cannot close. Aromatics are bulging out of the cavity opening. Remove a few pieces. An overstuffed fish will not seal in the salt crust properly.
Feel cue: Press the belly of the stuffed fish closed with your palm — it should stay shut with gentle pressure, not spring open. If it springs open, reduce the stuffing slightly.

Mix the coarse sea salt and lightly beaten egg whites together with your hands until the mixture resembles wet sand that holds its shape when squeezed — it should clump, not crumble. Spread a 1.5cm bed of the salt mixture on a baking tray or oven-proof dish. Lay the stuffed fish on the bed. Pack the remaining salt mixture over and around the entire fish, pressing firmly to build a uniform crust 2cm thick on all sides. Seal any gaps, especially around the tail and head. Bake at 200°C for 25–30 minutes (about 20 minutes per 500g of fish weight, plus 5 minutes for the crust).
Visual cue: After baking, the salt crust has hardened to a uniformly pale ivory or lightly golden shell that sounds hollow when tapped. There are no cracks or soft spots.
Underdone: Crust is still somewhat soft and yielding in places — the egg whites have not fully set. Soft spots likely over the thickest part of the fish. Return to the oven for 5 more minutes. A soft crust means the interior is also likely undercooked.
Perfect: Crust sounds hollow and hard when knocked with a knuckle, like tapping a terracotta pot. The surface is bone-dry, off-white, and lightly coloured. A thin crack may appear along the back. Bring the dish to the table immediately and crack the crust theatrically with the back of a large serving spoon.
Overdone: Crust has developed very deep golden to brown colour. The fish inside has likely cooked further than intended. Crack immediately upon removing from the oven. The thick crust insulates the fish and it will continue cooking if left sealed. Serve at once.
Feel cue: Knock the crust sharply with a knuckle after baking — it should ring hollow and hard, like a clay flowerpot, not give under your knuckle. Any softness means it needs more time.

At the table, present the salt-crusted dish. Using the back of a heavy spoon or small hammer, crack the crust along the spine with a few firm blows. Lift off the large pieces of crust — the fish skin will often come away with the top crust, revealing bright, pearlescent white flesh beneath. Brush away any salt granules clinging to the flesh with a pastry brush. The fish will not taste salty — the salt crust seasons it only from the outside through the skin, not into the flesh.
Visual cue: After cracking and removing the crust, the fish flesh is bright white, fully opaque, and moist-looking. It separates cleanly into large, glossy segments when touched with a fork.
Underdone: Flesh at the backbone is still translucent or faintly pink-grey. The segments resist separation when a fork is pressed in at the spine. Replace the crust pieces and return to the oven for 8 minutes. The crust, even cracked, will still conduct heat.
Perfect: Flesh is uniformly bright white throughout, pearlescent and glistening. Segments separate effortlessly. Steam rises gently from the open fish. The ginger and scallion perfume is immediate and beautiful. Drizzle with soy sauce and sesame oil and serve directly from the dish.
Overdone: Flesh looks dry and compact at the thinner areas near the tail. Segments are slightly rubbery rather than glossy. Serve immediately with extra sesame oil drizzled generously. Avoid the driest tail sections.
Feel cue: Touch the exposed flesh lightly with the back of a fork — perfect salt-baked fish should feel warm and yielding with the faintest resistance, like pressing a very soft, ripe mango. Cool or hard flesh means more time was needed.

Working quickly so the fish does not cool, drizzle the soy sauce evenly over the exposed flesh, followed by the toasted sesame oil — the sesame oil should sizzle faintly as it hits the hot fish. Serve directly from the dish with steamed white jasmine rice and a simple stir-fried green vegetable. Use a tablespoon to scoop portions of the flesh off the spine, keeping the segments as large and intact as possible — this fish deserves to be eaten in generous, moist chunks, not shredded.
Visual cue: Flesh is coated in a thin, glistening film of soy and sesame. The dark soy creates a beautiful contrast against the bright white flesh. The kitchen smells of toasted sesame, soy, and ginger.
Underdone: Soy has not been added yet — the flesh looks pale and unseasoned. Without the soy, the dish lacks the savoury depth that ties the sweet fish to the aromatic filling. Add the soy sauce and sesame oil immediately. The fish is cooling fast.
Perfect: Thin even glaze of soy, just enough to season without puddling at the base of the dish. Sesame oil fragrance mingles with the ginger and scallion rising from the opened cavity. Bring to the table and serve immediately.
Overdone: Too much soy sauce — the flesh is swimming in liquid and tastes aggressively salty, overwhelming the subtle sweetness of the bass. Tilt the dish and pour off excess soy. Add a splash of hot water and a few drops of sesame oil to restore balance.
Feel cue: The first bite should taste clean, sweet, and of the sea — with the ginger and sesame oil arriving as a warm, aromatic whisper rather than a shout. If the salt dominates, the crust was too thin or the fish was undersized for the salt ratio.

Fresh lemon juice: 10 ml

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Provençal salt cod pounded or blended with olive oil and warm milk until it becomes a smooth, ivory emulsion — dense, luxurious, faintly fishy in the best possible way. Spread on crostini or gratinéed in a baking dish, it is the taste of the Languedoc coast in winter.

ingredients.name: Whole milk, warmed to hand temperature

steps:
Place the salt cod skin-side up in a large bowl or deep baking dish and cover with cold water. Refrigerate for 24 hours, changing the water at least 3 times — every 6–8 hours is ideal. The water will turn white and cloudy each time, carrying away the curing salt. After the final soak, taste a thin flake from the thickest part: it should taste pleasantly salty, like a well-seasoned fish, not briny or harsh. If it is still harsh, soak 2 more hours.
Visual cue: After the final water change, the flesh has visibly plumped and lightened from its stiff, amber-salted state to a softer, pale ivory fillet.
Underdone: The cod still tastes aggressively salty — almost inedible raw. The flesh is still stiff and slightly translucent. Change the water and soak another 4–6 hours. Under-desalted cod cannot be corrected once cooked.
Perfect: A thin flake tastes like assertively seasoned fish — salty enough to know it is salt cod, but not harsh or mouth-puckering. The flesh is plump and slightly soft. Proceed to poaching.
Overdone: The cod has soaked too long — it tastes flat and fishy with almost no salt character. The flesh is very soft and starting to fall apart. Proceed immediately. Season the final brandade generously with salt to compensate.
Feel cue: After 24 hours the cod should flex when you bend it, no longer rigid as a plank — the texture goes from dry-stiff to supple and slightly yielding, like raw salmon.

Place the desalted cod in a wide pan and cover with fresh cold water. Add the thyme. Bring slowly to a bare simmer — tiny bubbles rising at the edges, the water trembling but not boiling. Poach for 10–12 minutes. Do not boil: boiling at this stage firms the protein into a tough, rubbery slab and breaks the fine flakes. The cod is done when it flakes easily along its natural seams when prodded with a fork. Lift out, discard the poaching water, and let it cool enough to handle.
Visual cue: The cod is uniformly ivory-white and opaque, the flakes opening visibly at the seams when pressed. The skin and bones are easily identifiable for removal.
Underdone: The thickest part of the cod is still translucent in the center and the flakes resist separating. The flesh is springy and not yet tender. Return to the poaching water (off the boil) and let it sit 3 more minutes in the residual heat.
Perfect: Completely opaque and ivory, the flakes separating naturally along their seams. The skin peels off cleanly and the bones lift out without tearing the flesh. Remove the skin and bones, then proceed to the emulsion.
Overdone: The flesh is firm and dry, the flakes very small and tightly compressed. The fish smells strongly — sulfurous notes emerging. Proceed, but add extra warm milk to compensate for the lost moisture. The emulsion will be denser and may need more oil.
Feel cue: Lift a flake of poached cod — it should feel like cooked chicken breast: tender and yielding but still holding form, separating cleanly rather than shredding into mush.

Remove all skin and bones from the cod — run your fingers carefully through the flakes to find every pin bone. Place the cod and raw garlic in a mortar and pound to a paste, or pulse in a food processor. The goal is to break the fish down into a fine, cohesive mass that will absorb the oil and milk. Do not process to a completely smooth paste yet — a slightly grainy, textured base is correct at this stage. The garlic should be fully incorporated and invisible.
Visual cue: A pale, slightly fibrous paste of broken fish, the individual flakes no longer distinct but not yet a smooth cream. Tiny white specks of garlic are invisible in the fish.
Underdone: The cod is still in distinct chunks — large flakes that haven't broken down. The garlic is a separate visible pile. Pound or pulse more aggressively. The cod must be a cohesive paste to emulsify with the oil.
Perfect: A dense, slightly grainy paste — almost like a stiff mashed potato. The garlic is fully incorporated. The color is pale ivory. Begin adding the oil and milk alternately.
Overdone: Over-processing in a food processor has made the cod gluey and slightly gummy, losing all texture. Proceed — the emulsification step with oil and milk will loosen the paste. Reduce the amount of milk slightly.
Feel cue: Press a pinch of the paste between your thumb and forefinger — it should feel like damp sand that holds its shape briefly when squeezed, neither sticky nor crumbling.

With the cod paste in the mortar or a bowl set over gentle heat (or in a stand mixer with paddle), begin adding the warm olive oil in a thin, slow stream, working it in constantly — exactly like making a mayonnaise. When half the oil is incorporated, add a tablespoon of warm milk. Alternate oil and milk until both are fully incorporated. The brandade will transform from a dense paste to a smooth, fluffy, ivory-white emulsion that is light enough to scoop but rich enough to mound. Season with white pepper and lemon juice. Taste: it should be salty, rich, faintly fishy, and deeply satisfying.
Visual cue: A smooth, pale ivory emulsion — lighter and more voluminous than the starting paste, opaque white, glossy, and thick enough to hold a peak when scooped with a spoon.
Underdone: The oil is pooling and the mixture looks broken — greasy pools floating on the cod paste. Not emulsified. Slow down the oil addition and work more vigorously. Add a tablespoon of warm milk to help bind the emulsion.
Perfect: The brandade is white, smooth, light, and fluffy — it ribbons off the spoon in a slow, creamy flow. Tastes balanced between salt and richness, with a clean cod flavor. Transfer to a serving dish and serve warm with crostini, or spread in a gratin dish and brown under a hot broiler.
Overdone: Too much oil or milk has been added — the brandade is very loose and pours rather than mounds. The flavor is diluted. Fold in a little more poached cod (finely broken) to tighten it. Or serve as a sauce rather than a spread.
Feel cue: Scoop a spoonful and watch it fall — it should drop in a slow, heavy ribbon that mounds on itself, not splash like soup. The warmth of the mixture should be pleasantly hand-hot, never too cool to emulsify.

quantity_notes:

Whole sea bass or sea bream (600-800 g), gutted and scaled: 700 g
  Alternatives: snapper; porgy; branzino

  Alternatives: coarse sea salt
Egg whites: 3 pcs
Fresh thyme sprigs: 6 pcs
  Alternatives: rosemary; fennel fronds
Lemon, sliced into rounds: 1 pcs
  Alternatives: orange
Garlic cloves, lightly crushed: 4 pcs
Extra-virgin olive oil, for serving: 30 ml
Lemon wedges, for serving: 2 pcs

Total time: 50 min

description: A whole fish sealed inside two kilos of egg-white-bound salt and baked until the crust rings like plaster — cracked at the table with a mallet, releasing a cloud of herbed steam and the most perfectly seasoned, juicy fish imaginable.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Whole sea bass or sea bream (600-800 g), gutted and scaled

steps:
Whisk egg whites to a light foam — no stiff peaks, just broken and fluid. Pour over coarse salt and work with your hands until the mixture resembles wet sand. It should clump when squeezed and hold the shape of your fist. If it won't clump, add water a tablespoon at a time.
Visual cue: Salt looks like firmly packed damp beach sand — pale, slightly grey from the egg whites, holds its form when squeezed.
Underdone: Salt falls apart when squeezed, too dry to form a crust. Add egg white or water by the tablespoon until it clumps firmly.
Perfect: Holds a firm ball when squeezed in the palm. Slightly grey, no loose crystals escaping the edges. Build the base layer on the baking sheet.
Overdone: Salt paste is too wet and muddy — will crack and run during baking. Add a handful more dry salt and work in.
Feel cue: It should feel like wet sand — gritty, cool, packed with enough density to hold a firm impression of your fingerprints.

Preheat oven to 220 C (425 F). Spread a 1.5 cm layer of salt paste on a baking sheet to form the bed. Stuff the fish cavity with thyme, lemon rounds, and garlic. Lay the fish on the salt bed. Pack remaining salt paste firmly over the entire fish, including head and tail, sealing all seams. Press to compact.
Visual cue: A white mound on the baking sheet — the fish entirely invisible under a smooth, pressed salt shell, at least 2 cm thick everywhere.
Underdone: Thin areas visible where salt paste is sparse — fish skeleton visible through the crust. Patch with more paste and press firmly.
Perfect: A uniform white dome, sealed on all sides, no gaps. The fish is completely entombed. Into the oven immediately.
Overdone: Crust too thick (over 4 cm) — fish may not cook through. It will take longer but still work. Add 10 minutes to cooking time.
Feel cue: Run your palm over the crust — it should feel dense, compact, and cold. Any soft or loose spots need more paste pressed in.

Roast for 25-30 minutes for a 700 g fish. The crust will set and begin to show faint golden spots on its highest points. An instant-read thermometer inserted through the crust into the thickest part of the fish should read 55-60 C (130-140 F). The fish steams inside its own armor.
Visual cue: The salt dome is firm and dry to the touch, showing golden tinges at its crown. No steam escaping from the edges — the seal has held.
Underdone: Crust still feels slightly soft when tapped. Thermometer reads below 50 C. Return to oven for 5 more minutes.
Perfect: Crust rings hard when knocked with a knuckle — like plaster. Thermometer reads 57 C. Kitchen smells of herbs and sea salt. Bring to the table for dramatic cracking.
Overdone: Crust has cracked on its own and steam has escaped; fish smells very strong. Still salvageable — crack and serve immediately.
Feel cue: Knock the crust with your knuckle — when done, it sounds like rapping on a clay pot, dense and resonant, not hollow.

At the table, crack the crust with the back of a heavy spoon or a small mallet, following the line of the fish's spine. Lift away the top half of the crust in large pieces — it comes off in satisfying slabs. Brush away any salt crystals with a pastry brush. Peel back the skin and serve the fillets with olive oil and lemon wedges. The flesh will be luminous, juicy, and perfectly seasoned.
Visual cue: Pearl-white fish beneath the broken crust — skin peels cleanly away, flesh glistens with its own juices, no dried edges.
Underdone: Flesh still translucent and slightly gel-like near the backbone. Reassemble the crust and return to a 180 C oven for 5 more minutes.
Perfect: Opaque, glistening flesh that separates from the bone in clean, moist plates. Herbs and lemon fragrant from the cavity. Fish smells of the sea, not of fishiness. Serve immediately with olive oil and lemon.
Overdone: Flesh dry and separating from the skin with a chalky texture. Compensate with generous olive oil and a squeeze of lemon.
Feel cue: The fillet should yield under a fish knife like ripe fruit — no tearing, just a gentle give as the flesh parts from the bone.

ingredients.name: Veal escalopes (noce or fesa), 150 g each
Dry white wine (Frascati or Pinot Grigio)
中筋面粉（All-purpose flour, for dusting）

steps:
Place each veal escalope between two sheets of plastic wrap. Using the flat face of a meat mallet or the bottom of a heavy pan, pound with firm, even strokes from the center outward — not vertical blows that tear the meat, but angled slides that stretch the fibers. Target 5–6 mm thickness, roughly even across the whole escalope. Season lightly with white pepper only — the prosciutto will provide all the salt needed.
Visual cue: Translucent pale pink escalopes of even thickness. The surface has a slightly rough, matte texture from the pounding. No holes or tears.
Underdone: Uneven surface with thick ridges. Center still 1 cm+, edges thin and ragged. Will cook unevenly. Continue pounding from the thick center outward, working with the grain of the meat.
Perfect: Even 5–6 mm throughout. Pale pink, slightly translucent at the thinnest point. Surface has a pleasingly roughened texture that will grip the flour. Lay flat and prepare the prosciutto-sage topping.
Overdone: Holes torn through the escalope. Meat has shredded at the edges. Overlap torn sections and press together — the prosciutto will hold them. Very thin sections may cook too fast; watch carefully.
Feel cue: The pounded escalope should feel almost like a piece of chamois leather — supple, thin, and slightly resistant to tearing. No part should feel thick and stiff when you fold it.

Lay 2–3 sage leaves flat on the top (smooth) side of each escalope. Drape one or two slices of prosciutto over to cover the sage and the entire escalope surface — the ham must extend slightly beyond the meat edges. Secure with one or two wooden toothpicks pierced at an angle through ham, sage, and meat. Season the underside (veal side) very lightly with salt only. Dust the veal side in flour and pat off all excess — you want a gossamer coating, not a thick crust.
Visual cue: A neat parcel: prosciutto smooth on top, sage sandwiched between, toothpicks horizontal and flush. The floured veal underside looks matte and dry with no wet patches.
Underdone: Prosciutto bunching up and pulling away from the edges. Sage not secured. Excess flour coating that looks thick and doughy. Re-drape the prosciutto and add a toothpick at each edge. Pat the flour firmly to knock off any excess.
Perfect: Prosciutto flat and taut against the veal. Sage visible as a green shadow through the translucent ham. Flour coating is so thin it barely shows. Refrigerate for 10 minutes to firm up before searing — cold prosciutto holds better in the pan.
Overdone: Over-floured — thick white coating visible, wet in patches where it has absorbed moisture from the meat. Pat vigorously to remove excess. Thick flour coats cook to a gummy paste, not a crisp crust.
Feel cue: Lift an assembled escalope — it should feel light and flat with the prosciutto fitting like a second skin. Press the ham edge: it should adhere rather than slide.

Heat a large stainless or carbon steel pan over medium-high heat. Add butter and let it foam and subside — when the first wisps of color appear in the butter, it is ready. Place escalopes prosciutto-side down. Press them flat with a spatula for the first 10 seconds to ensure full contact. Cook prosciutto-side for 2–3 minutes until the ham crackles and has rendered its fat into the butter. Flip and cook the veal side for just 60–90 seconds — veal is lean and overcooks in moments.
Visual cue: Prosciutto side: golden-copper and slightly crinkled at the edges, having rendered its fat. Veal side: barely golden, still showing pale color in the center.
Underdone: Prosciutto is still floppy and pale pink. No crisping, no fat rendering. Sage not yet fragrant. Continue — you need 1–2 more minutes of contact heat. Ensure pan is truly hot before adding the next batch.
Perfect: Prosciutto edges are deeply golden and crinkled-crisp, releasing a nutty-salty aroma. The sage leaves beneath have turned translucent jade. The veal side is just barely seared. Transfer to a warm plate. Remove toothpicks.
Overdone: Prosciutto is dark brown and chewy-hard. Veal has become dry and fibrous. Pan butter has burnt. Salvage with extra sauce. Wipe the pan, add fresh butter, and deglaze more gently.
Feel cue: Press the center of a cooking escalope — it should feel like a firm but yielding pillow, not rigid. The prosciutto side should crackle slightly when you press it, like stiff paper.

Remove the escalopes to a warm plate. Over high heat, pour the wine into the still-hot pan and immediately scrape up the browned bits from the base — these are the flavor. Let the wine reduce by half, about 90 seconds of vigorous bubbling. Remove from heat, add a cold knob of butter, and swirl constantly until the sauce becomes glossy and emulsified. Pour over the escalopes immediately. The dish is best eaten within 3 minutes of plating.
Visual cue: A thin, glossy amber pan sauce with no separation. It coats the back of a spoon and falls in a slow ribbon, not a splash.
Underdone: Sauce is watery and thin, wine flavor raw and sharp. Not yet reduced. Pooling on the plate rather than coating. Return to high heat for another 30–45 seconds. Do not add butter until the wine has concentrated.
Perfect: Reduced to a light syrup, deeply golden with a rounded wine aroma. Butter has emulsified into a glossy, just-cohesive sauce. Pour immediately over the escalopes — the sauce breaks and loses its emulsion as it cools.
Overdone: Sauce reduced too far and is sticky, bordering on caramel. Flavor is sharp and one-dimensional. Add a tablespoon of cold water and swirl — this will thin it back toward a sauce consistency.
Feel cue: Dip a spoon into the finished sauce and turn it over — it should coat the metal in a thin, even film that holds for 2–3 seconds before starting to run. If it sheets off instantly, it needs more reduction.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

ingredients.name: Fresh red Fresno or Holland chilies (medium heat), stems removed
Fresh red bird's-eye chilies (cabe rawit), for heat boost (optional)
White vinegar or distilled cane vinegar

steps:
Roughly chop the Fresno chilies into large pieces — halve them lengthwise and cut into thirds. If you prefer a milder sambal, scrape out the seeds and white ribs with a spoon; for full heat, leave them in. If using bird's-eye chilies, leave them whole or halve them. Peel the garlic cloves. This rough prep is all that is needed before the mortar does its work — do not fine-mince. Keep seeds and juice from the cutting board; they are flavour.
Visual cue: Rough, large chunks of red chili and whole garlic cloves on the board — vibrantly red, glistening with juice and seeds.
Underdone: Chilies are uncut and whole — they will not fit in the mortar easily and will take forever to pound. Roughly chop into thirds at minimum. The mortar needs surface area to grab.
Perfect: Chunky, irregular pieces about 2–3 cm. Juices are running freely on the board. Seeds scattered throughout. Transfer to the mortar immediately — the juice is volatile and fresh-smelling.
Overdone: Chilies are fine-minced and seeds are already crushed on the board. Proceed directly to seasoning — skip the pounding stage or it will become a liquid purée rather than a coarse paste.
Feel cue: The moment you cut the chilies, the capsaicin oils begin to volatilize — your eyes will know when the chilies are fresh and potent. Wear gloves if your skin is sensitive, and resist touching your face.

Transfer the chopped chilies and garlic to a large granite or stone mortar. Add the salt — salt acts as an abrasive grit that helps break down the fibers faster. Pound with firm, deliberate downward strokes: the pestle should thud, not grind. Begin with harder downward blows to break down the larger pieces, then shift to a rotating, pressing grind for the final paste. The goal is a coarse, rustic paste with visible flecks of chili skin and seeds — not a smooth purée. Sambal oelek's character is its roughness; a blender makes it too uniform and drives off the fresh aroma. Pound for 3–4 minutes total.
Visual cue: A rough, vivid red paste with visible chunks of chili skin, scattered seeds, and a glistening, wet surface — chunky like a fresh salsa, not smooth like ketchup.
Underdone: Large pieces of chili still intact, garlic not yet broken down. The mixture looks more like a rough chop than a paste. Continue pounding with more force. The garlic especially needs to be fully smashed to release its flavour.
Perfect: Coarse, rustic paste — red, glistening, fragrant with chili heat. Seeds and skin flecks visible throughout. Garlic dissolved into the paste. Add the vinegar, stir, and taste for salt before jarring.
Overdone: Paste has become a very smooth, uniform liquid — all texture lost, skin fragments gone. Stir in a few coarsely chopped fresh chili pieces to restore some texture. The flavour is still good, but authenticity is in the chunkiness.
Feel cue: After pounding, drag the pestle through the paste: it should feel like dragging through thick, gritty jam — resistance from chili skin and seeds, with the paste clinging to the stone.

Pour the vinegar over the pounded paste and stir to combine. Taste carefully — it should be fiercely hot, brightly acidic, and cleanly salty, with the fresh, fruity aroma of raw chili dominant. Adjust: more salt for presence, more vinegar for brightness and preservation, more garlic pounded in for depth. Transfer to a clean glass jar and press the surface down to eliminate air pockets. Refrigerate. The sambal keeps for up to 2 weeks refrigerated — the vinegar and salt are natural preservatives. The colour will darken slightly from bright scarlet to a deeper red over the first 24 hours as it rests.
Visual cue: Vivid, scarlet-red, coarse paste glistening under a thin sheen of vinegar. Smells bright, sharp, fruity, and powerfully hot.
Underdone: Paste tastes flat and only hot — no brightness, no salt presence, no acid lift. Add more salt in small pinches and stir, then add more vinegar drop by drop. The acid lifts all the other flavours; without it, sambal tastes one-dimensional.
Perfect: A perfect triangle of heat, salt, and acid, with the raw fruity fragrance of the fresh chili coming through clearly. Burns pleasantly and builds. Jar it and refrigerate. Use immediately as a condiment or as a building block in cooked dishes.
Overdone: Over-salted or the vinegar is so prominent it smells pickled rather than fresh. Add a small amount of freshly pounded chili to dilute and freshen. Once jarred, over-salted sambal cannot be easily fixed — use it sparingly as a seasoning paste rather than a condiment.
Feel cue: Touch a tiny amount to your lower lip with a clean finger — you should feel an immediate, bright sting that spreads rapidly across the lips, followed by a fruity heat that builds for 30 seconds. The vinegar should balance the burn with a clean, sharp brightness rather than muting it.

name: Sambar
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

description: A sour, spiced toor dal broth studded with vegetables and built on a tamarind base — simultaneously soup, sauce, and condiment, poured over rice or alongside idli and dosa. The sambar powder is the soul: make your own if you can.

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables (drumstick, eggplant, pearl onions, tomato)

steps:
Rinse toor dal until water runs clear. Cook in a pressure cooker with water for 3 whistles, or simmer in a covered pot for 30–35 minutes until completely soft. Whisk or mash the cooked dal into a smooth, creamy paste — this will be the body of the sambar.
Visual cue: The cooked toor dal — its texture when mashed.
Underdone: Dal still has a chalky, gritty center when pressed. The water is still mostly clear. Cook for 10 more minutes and test again.
Perfect: Each grain collapses to smooth cream under a spoon. The cooking liquid is thick and golden. Mash or whisk smooth, then add water to desired consistency.
Overdone: Dal has fully dissolved into the water forming a very thick paste — no whole grains at all. Add more water to thin; the sambar base will be richer than usual but still excellent.
Feel cue: Press cooked toor dal between fingertips — it should dissolve completely without any gritty resistance, like smoothing warm clay.

Combine the mashed dal with tamarind paste, sambar powder, salt, and vegetables in a wide pot. Add enough water to make a thin broth. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 15–20 minutes until vegetables are completely tender and the broth has unified into a cohesive, sour-spiced gravy.
Visual cue: The color and body of the broth — it deepens as the tamarind and sambar powder integrate.
Underdone: Broth tastes raw and sour with a flat, gritty spice note — the sambar powder hasn't cooked in. Simmer for 10 more minutes and taste again.
Perfect: Russet-brown broth, slightly thick from the dal, with a rounded sour-spicy-umami profile. Vegetables are completely tender but not falling apart. Proceed to the tadka.
Overdone: Broth has reduced too much and is thickening into a stew; vegetables are mushy. Add water 50ml at a time, stir, and bring back to a simmer briefly.
Feel cue: Taste a spoonful of the sambar base before the tadka — it should hit sour first, then spice, then a warm umami finish from the dal. If one note drowns the others, balance now.

In a small pan, heat oil over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly. Add mustard seeds and cover with a lid — they will pop violently within 10 seconds. Uncover, add curry leaves (stand back — they will splatter) and dried red chilies. Stir for 15 seconds, then pour the entire tadka into the sambar.
Visual cue: The mustard seeds in the hot oil — their color and sound.
Underdone: Seeds have not yet popped — the oil is not hot enough. Cover and raise heat; wait for the first audible pop before adding other aromatics.
Perfect: Seeds are popping rapidly and have turned a shade lighter (from dark to grayish). Curry leaves are translucent and crisp. Red chilies are darker. Pour immediately into the sambar.
Overdone: Seeds are over-popped and beginning to burn; the oil smells bitter. Discard this tadka and repeat in fresh oil — a burnt tadka will ruin the sambar.
Feel cue: When the tadka hits the sambar, step back — it erupts in a fierce sizzle. Stir it in immediately while the aromatic steam is still rising.

ingredients.name: Waxy potatoes (Yukon Gold or similar), boiled whole and peeled
Green peas (fresh shelled or frozen, thawed)
Coriander seeds, lightly crushed in a mortar
Green chilies (serrano or Thai), finely minced
Fresh cilantro leaves and tender stems, finely chopped

steps:
Cover the whole, unpeeled potatoes with cold water in a pot. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer and cook until a thin knife slides through the center with zero resistance — about 20–25 minutes depending on size. Do not rush with high heat or the skins will split and the potatoes will absorb too much water. Drain and immediately peel while hot — the skins slip off easily and the potato flesh sheds moisture better when peeled warm. Spread the peeled potatoes on a tray and leave them uncovered for 5 minutes to steam-dry. Then roughly crush them with a fork or your hands into a mix of small chunks and larger broken pieces. Do not mash smooth — the filling needs texture. Some pieces of potato 1–2 cm across are desirable.
Visual cue: Roughly broken, dry-looking potato pieces of varying sizes, mostly 0.5–2 cm. No smooth mashed sections. The surface looks fluffy and slightly chalky, not wet or glossy.
Underdone: Potato centers are still firm and resist the fork. The flesh looks waxy and translucent rather than fluffy and opaque. Return to simmering water for another 5 minutes. Test again from the center.
Perfect: Fluffy, dry, breaks easily in the hand into irregular chunks. The color is pale yellow-white and opaque. No waxy look. Steam-dry on a tray and begin the spice temper immediately.
Overdone: Potato has become waterlogged and falls apart completely when crushed. Sticks to itself in a sticky mass. Spread on a wide tray and dry in a 150 C (300 F) oven for 10 minutes to drive off excess moisture before adding to the filling.
Feel cue: A perfectly cooked potato should crumble and fall apart at a light press, with a dry, powdery break. If it squashes into a sticky paste, it needs to dry out further. If it bounces back, it needs more cooking.

Heat the oil or ghee in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the cumin seeds and crushed coriander seeds together — they should sizzle immediately and begin crackling. Let them bloom for about 30–40 seconds until the cumin turns a deep chestnut brown. Do not stop here — add the minced ginger and green chili and stir for 1 minute until the raw ginger smell softens to a sweet, fragrant note. Add the ground coriander, amchur, garam masala, and turmeric. Stir constantly for 60 seconds, scraping the bottom — the ground spices will form a thick, fragrant paste in the fat. This step, called the tadka or bhuna, is critical: the oil carries fat-soluble spice compounds directly into the potato and peas at the moment of contact. If your spice paste smells warm and rounded, with no raw edge, it is ready.
Visual cue: A dark, golden-red spice paste in the pan with visible whole cumin and coriander seeds, slightly darkened ginger threads, and a ring of clear oil around the edges.
Underdone: Ground spices are still dry-looking and separate from the oil, sitting on top rather than blooming into a paste. The smell is powdery and raw. Add a teaspoon of water and stir vigorously — the steam will help the spices absorb and cook. Continue for another minute.
Perfect: A unified, glossy, dark paste that moves as a single mass. Smells of toasted cumin and warm, bright coriander. The fat glistens around the edges. Add the peas and potatoes immediately.
Overdone: Spices are dark brown or black, the pan is smoking, and the smell is bitter and acrid. The ground spice paste has scorched. Discard and start fresh. Burnt spices will make the entire filling bitter — there is no recovery.
Feel cue: The kitchen should smell like a spice market at this point — toasty, warm, and complex, with the sharp green note of the chili cutting through. The pan hisses when you drag a spoon across the bottom.

Add the frozen or fresh peas directly to the spiced fat in the pan. Stir and cook for 2 minutes — the peas will warm through and absorb the spiced oil. Add the crushed potatoes all at once and fold everything together using a wide spatula or wooden spoon, working from the bottom of the pan and turning the mixture over itself. You want to evenly coat every piece of potato and pea in the spice blend without turning the mixture into a smooth mash — the filling should retain texture, with visible pieces of potato and peas throughout. Season with salt and stir. Off the heat, fold in the fresh cilantro. Taste: the filling should be intensely flavored — boldly salty, bright with amchur's sour note, and warmly spiced throughout. It needs to be seasoned aggressively because the pastry shell will dilute the intensity. Allow the filling to cool completely before enclosing in pastry — warm filling will steam the pastry and make it soggy.
Visual cue: A fragrant, textured mixture of golden-spiced potato chunks and vivid green peas, uniformly coated in a rust-orange spice blend. Cilantro flecks visible throughout. No smooth, paste-like mashed sections.
Underdone: Spice coating is not uniform — pale potato pieces are visible next to very dark ones. The peas are still separate and pale. The filling tastes bland in spots. Fold more thoroughly, making sure each piece contacts the spiced fat. Cook for 2 more minutes on medium heat.
Perfect: Every piece is uniformly spiced and tinted orange-gold. Texture is varied and interesting. The smell is bright, complex, and deeply appetizing. Fills the mouth with warmth. Spread on a tray and cool completely before using as samosa filling.
Overdone: The mixture has been stirred too aggressively and is now a smooth, pasty mash. Texture is uniform and the peas are broken. The flavor is identical — proceed. The mashed consistency will still work as a

filling, though the eating experience is less varied.
Feel cue: A finished spoonful of samosa filling should feel slightly dry and crumbly in the hand — not wet, not sticky. It should hold a shape when pressed but crumble at a firm push. That dry texture is what prevents the samosa pastry from becoming soggy during frying.

A cup of chai and a plate of these is the perfect North Indian tea-time.

ingredients.name: Waxy potatoes (boiled, cooled, and roughly mashed)
Fine sea salt (for both pastry and filling)
Neutral oil for deep frying (sunflower or vegetable)

steps:
Combine flour and half the salt in a bowl. Rub the ghee or shortening into the flour with your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs and no large fat lumps remain — this is the critical step for a flaky, layered crust. Drizzle in ice-cold water a tablespoon at a time, mixing with a fork after each addition, until the dough just comes together without being sticky. It should feel firmer than a bread dough — this tight, stiff dough is what gives samosas their snap. Knead very briefly — 1 minute only — then wrap tightly and rest for 30 minutes at room temperature.
Visual cue: A pale, firm dough ball that holds its shape and does not crack when pressed but also does not spring back. Smooth surface with no crumbles.
Underdone: Dough is crumbly and falls apart when pressed. Dry flecks around the edges. Add water one teaspoon at a time, kneading briefly after each addition until it coheres.
Perfect: Firm, smooth, and pliable. Presses flat without cracking. Feels like modelling clay — dense and cooperative. Wrap and rest 30 minutes.
Overdone: Dough is soft, sticky, and elastic. Springs back when rolled. Dust with a small amount of flour and rest 30 minutes chilled — gluten needs to relax.
Feel cue: Press a thumb into the dough — it should leave a clean crater without the dough cracking at the edges. Firm, not stiff; dense, not sticky.

Heat 2 tablespoons of the frying oil in a skillet over medium heat. Bloom the cumin seeds for 30 seconds until they crackle and darken. Add the green chili and ginger, fry for 1 minute. Add the mashed potatoes and peas and fold gently to combine, trying to keep some potato texture — do not turn it into baby food. Add amchur, garam masala, and the remaining salt. Mix and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the filling is fragrant and slightly dry. Taste: it should be assertively seasoned, sour from the amchur, and warming with spice. The filling must be fully cool before wrapping — warm filling creates steam inside the samosa and makes the pastry soggy.
Visual cue: A golden-yellow, well-spiced filling with visible pea jewels and potato chunks. Not wet or glossy — dry enough to hold its shape when scooped.
Underdone: Filling is wet and sticky. Raw cumin and ginger smell dominates. Tastes flat. Cook longer over medium heat to drive off moisture. The filling must be quite dry.
Perfect: Dry, well-seasoned, holds its shape when scooped. Each bite has a distinct sour-spice character. Cumin seeds visible throughout. Spread on a plate to cool completely before wrapping.
Overdone: Filling is very dry and sticking in clumps. Beginning to brown. Add a tablespoon of water, stir, and remove from heat. Still fine for wrapping.
Feel cue: Taste a pinch of the filling — the amchur should deliver a bright, citrus-like sourness that catches at the back of your jaw, balanced against earthy cumin and the heat of the chili.

Divide the rested dough into 10 to 12 equal balls. Roll each ball on a lightly floured surface into an oval roughly 15 cm × 8 cm, 2–3 mm thick — thinner than you think you need. Cut each oval in half across the long axis, giving two D-shaped pieces. Fold each D into a cone: moisten one straight edge with water, overlap the two straight edges by 5 mm, and press firmly to seal. Fill the cone two-thirds full with cooled filling — do not overfill. Moisten the open top edge with water and press firmly to seal into a triangle. Press each seam between your fingers and then press lightly against the work surface to create the flat, pyramid shape. Set on a lightly oiled tray. The sealed edges must be completely watertight — test by gently squeezing each samosa over the sink.
Visual cue: Neat, triangular parcels with flat faces, tight sealed seams, and no visible filling gaps. Each one holds its shape when gently squeezed.
Underdone: Seams are pinched but not sealed — you can see gaps at the edges. Filling has overfilled and is pushing through. Re-moisten the seam edges and press more firmly. Remove some filling if needed.
Perfect: Firm triangular parcels with no visible seams. When gently squeezed they hold their shape. Pastry surface is smooth with a slight sheen from the seal water. Rest uncovered 5 minutes before frying.
Overdone: You have handled the dough too much and it has become warm, greasy, and very elastic. Chill the shaped samosas for 20 minutes before frying — the fat needs to firm up.
Feel cue: Hold each sealed samosa in your palm and gently press all three faces — they should feel evenly firm with the filling distributed throughout, not lopsided or hollow in one corner.

Heat the frying oil in a deep, heavy pot to 160°C (325°F) — lower than you expect. Samosas must fry slowly to develop the characteristic blistered crust: high heat seals the outside before the inside cooks through and the pastry has no time to develop its flaky layers. Lower 3 to 4 samosas at a time into the oil and fry, turning every 2 minutes, for 10 to 12 minutes total until they are an even deep amber-gold on all faces. Raise the temperature to 175°C (350°F) for the final 2 minutes to crisp the exterior. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain upright in a rack or colander, not lying flat — this preserves the crust on all sides.
Visual cue: Deep amber-gold on all faces with a crazed, blistered, matte exterior. No wet, pale patches. The pastry surface has the texture of fine cracked earth.
Underdone: Samosas are blond with a smooth, shiny pastry surface. Still floppy when you pick them up. Continue frying at 160°C — they need more time. Check oil temperature with a thermometer.
Perfect: Deep, even amber with a crazed blistered surface that sounds crisp when tapped with a fingernail. Holds its rigid shape when lifted. Drain and serve immediately with mint chutney and tamarind sauce.
Overdone: Dark brown bordering on red-brown, with darker patches at the corners. Still edible but slightly bitter at the tips. Drain immediately on paper towels and serve quickly.
Feel cue: Tap the side of a fried samosa with your fingernail — it should ring with a hollow, papery crack, not a dull thud. The pastry layers have separated in the heat and the samosa is holding itself up with its own rigid crust.

name: 印度咖喱角 · Potato & Pea Samosas
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

description: A shattering pastry shell that gives way to a warmly spiced interior of cumin-fragrant potato and bright peas — the hallmark is the dough made with minimal water for maximum flakiness, and the filling cooled completely so the shell never steams from within.

ingredients.name: Vegetable shortening or ghee (for rubbing into flour)
Russet potatoes, boiled and roughly mashed
Filling spice blend (cumin seeds, coriander, amchur, garam masala, green chili, ginger)

steps:
Combine flour, fat, salt, and 1 tsp ajwain (carom seeds) if available. Rub the fat into the flour with your fingertips for 3–4 minutes until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs with no loose flour remaining — this is the critical step for flakiness. Add ice-cold water 1 tbsp at a time (about 6–8 tbsp total) until the dough just comes together. It should be firm, stiff, and not sticky. Knead for 2 minutes, then rest covered for 20 minutes.
Visual cue: A firm, stiff, smooth dough that holds an impression when pressed but does not stick to hands or surface. Significantly stiffer than bread dough.
Underdone: Dough is crumbly and falls apart when squeezed — the fat and flour have not cohered. Too little water. Add water 1 tsp at a time, kneading after each addition until the dough holds together without crumbling.
Perfect: Smooth, firm, non-sticky dough that holds its shape cleanly when rolled into a ball. When pressed with a finger, it slowly springs back halfway. No stickiness on hands. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 20 minutes. Resting relaxes the gluten and makes it easier to roll thin without shrinking back.
Overdone: Dough is soft and slightly sticky from too much water. It stretches easily rather than feeling firm and stiff. Dust with flour and knead briefly to incorporate. Samosa dough must be stiff — soft dough produces a soft, oily, non-flaky crust.
Feel cue: The properly mixed samosa dough should feel like stiff putty — firm resistance when you press it, but it yields without cracking. It should be notably stiffer than any bread dough you have made.

Heat 1 tbsp oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Add cumin seeds and let them splutter 10 seconds. Add green chili and fresh ginger, cook 30 seconds. Add roughly mashed potato and peas, then all remaining ground spices. Cook for 3–4 minutes, folding rather than stirring to keep some potato texture. Add amchur (dried mango powder) or lemon juice for tartness and salt to taste. Spread on a plate and cool completely before using.
Visual cue: Filling is a golden-yellow with green peas visible throughout. The mixture has some texture — not completely smooth. Peas are intact. The aroma is warm, spiced, and slightly tangy.
Underdone: Spices smell raw and the filling tastes flat. Peas are still frozen-cold and have not absorbed any flavour. Cook for 2 more minutes over medium heat, folding continuously. The spices need to toast briefly in the oil to develop.
Perfect: Vivid golden filling with whole peas visible. The aroma is complex — toasted cumin, warm coriander, sharp amchur tartness. The mash is mostly smooth with deliberate chunky bits. Spread on a tray and cool completely before filling. Hot filling creates steam that softens and splits the dough.
Overdone: Filling is completely smooth and paste-like from over-mashing. Peas have been crushed. The mixture is starting to dry out and stick to the pan. Proceed — the filling will still taste good. The texture will be smoother than ideal but the samosas will be fine.
Feel cue: The cooled filling should hold its shape when pressed into a ball — if it spreads or feels wet, it is too moist and will soften the dough from the inside during frying.

Divide the rested dough into equal portions and roll each into a thin oval about 18–20cm long and 10cm wide. Cut in half to make two semicircles. Form a cone by folding the straight edge over and sealing with a little water. Fill the cone with 2 tbsp of filling — do not overfill. Pinch the open edge closed firmly, pressing the seam flat. The sealed edge must be completely airtight or the samosa will burst during frying.
Visual cue: Samosas are neat, tightly sealed triangular cones with flat pleated seams. The dough is thin and almost translucent at the widest points. No air pockets visible inside when held to light.
Underdone: Seams are poorly sealed with visible gaps or thin spots. The cone walls are thick and uneven. Overfilled samosas bulge at the seams. Press and re-seal any open seams with water and firm pressure. Excess filling makes sealing impossible — remove some if needed.
Perfect: Even, thin walls with a tightly sealed pleated seam. The samosa feels firm and compact when squeezed gently. The weight feels right — not too heavy (overfilled) or light (underfilled). Place on a floured surface, sealed-side down. Fry within 30 minutes or refrigerate up to 4 hours.
Overdone: Dough has been rolled too thin — it tears when filling is added and the seams cannot hold. The cone walls are nearly paper-thin in spots. Patch thin spots with small pieces of dough moistened with water. Re-roll with more flour if the dough continues to tear.
Feel cue: Run your finger along the sealed seam — you should feel a continuous ridge of firmly pinched dough with no gaps or soft spots. Press the samosa gently — it should feel like a tightly packed ball, with no movement of the filling inside.

Heat oil to 160–170°C (325°F) — lower than standard frying temperature. Slide samosas in gently, 3–4 at a time. Fry slowly for 12–15 minutes, turning occasionally, until deep golden. The low temperature slowly renders and crisps the pastry all the way through without burning the exterior before the interior heats. Drain on a wire rack, not paper towels — steam must escape from all sides to keep the crust crisp.
Visual cue: Uniformly deep golden-brown across all surfaces, with a slightly blistered texture on the walls. Colour is the deep gold of good toast, not the pale gold of underfried dough.
Underdone: Pale yellow-gold exterior that looks dry rather than golden. The pastry feels soft rather than firm when tapped. The interior is not yet hot enough. Continue frying at the same temperature. Do not increase heat — this will brown the outside while leaving the inside raw.
Perfect: Deep, even golden-brown with a slightly pebbly, blistered surface. Tapping the samosa produces a hollow sound like tapping a wooden block. The pastry is visibly rigid and shatter-ready. Remove to a wire rack. Taste one immediately — the seam should crack cleanly and the inside should be steaming hot.
Overdone: Dark amber-brown verging on red-brown. Some dark spots forming. The oil smells acrid. The pastry is very rigid and has thickened slightly from overcooking. Remove immediately and drain. The exterior is deeply caramelized but the inside is likely fine. Let cool 2 minutes before eating.
Feel cue: A perfectly fried samosa will produce a shattering crack when you bite through the shell — like breaking a cracker — and release a puff of spiced steam. If it gives silently without cracking, it was fried at too high a temperature and the pastry is dense rather than flaky.

ingredients.name: Lemongrass stalk, white part, finely grated or minced
Palm sugar or light brown sugar
Roasted peanuts, skins removed, finely ground or crushed
椰奶（Coconut milk, additional (for peanut sauce)）
Tamarind water (1 tbsp tamarind paste dissolved in 3 tbsp water)
Dried chili flakes or sambal oelek

steps:
Combine the turmeric, coriander, cumin, grated lemongrass, and palm sugar in a bowl. Pour in the coconut milk and whisk until the spices are evenly dispersed and the sugar is dissolved. The marinade should be a warm golden-yellow — the turmeric stains everything it touches, so use a non-reactive bowl and be careful of clothing. Taste: it should be fragrant with warm spice, mildly sweet, and richly coconutty. This is used to marinate 500 g of thinly sliced chicken, beef, or tofu for at least 1 hour (overnight in the refrigerator is ideal). Thread onto pre-soaked bamboo skewers before grilling.
Visual cue: A smooth, warm golden-yellow marinade with visible specks of lemongrass and spice, uniformly colored with no dry spice clumps floating on the surface.
Underdone: Dry spice clumps are floating on the surface and not integrated, palm sugar is not dissolved. Whisk more vigorously. Warm the mixture gently to 40 C to help the palm sugar dissolve.
Perfect: Uniformly golden, aromatic, smooth. The lemongrass is finely enough minced that it doesn't feel stringy when rubbed between fingers. Smells of turmeric and coconut. Add protein to the marinade, cover, and refrigerate for at least 1 hour.
Overdone: Marinade smells overly pungent from too much raw turmeric or has been over-mixed until frothy. Proceed — frothiness will settle and the raw turmeric will mellow during marinating.
Feel cue: The marinade should feel silky and slightly viscous on your fingers — almost like a light body lotion — from the coconut milk fat. The turmeric will stain your skin yellow within seconds.

Combine the ground peanuts, coconut milk, tamarind water, fish sauce, and chili flakes in a small saucepan. Stir to combine before placing over medium-low heat. Cook, stirring frequently, for 8–10 minutes until the sauce thickens noticeably and the fat begins to separate slightly at the edges of the pan — a ring of golden coconut oil appearing around the peanut sauce is a good sign. The sauce should be thick enough to coat a spoon but still pourable. If it seizes up too thick, add a splash of water. Taste: sweet-salty-sour-spicy in balance, with a deep, toasty peanut character. The sauce should be served warm.
Visual cue: A thick, golden-brown peanut sauce with a faint sheen of coconut oil at the surface, coating a spoon in a heavy, textured layer.
Underdone: Sauce is thin, pale, and raw-smelling. Peanut flavor is not yet developed. Continue cooking over medium-low heat, stirring constantly to prevent scorching on the bottom.
Perfect: Sauce is thick, golden-brown, and aromatic. A ring of coconut oil appears at the edge. Falls from a spoon in slow ribbons. Tastes rich, nutty, slightly sweet and sour with background heat. Remove from heat. Serve warm alongside the grilled skewers.
Overdone: Sauce has thickened to a paste, scorched at the bottom, or smells of burnt peanuts. Deglaze with 2–3 tablespoons of warm water and stir vigorously to loosen. Strain if needed.
Feel cue: The right peanut sauce drips off a spoon in a thick, reluctant thread and holds its shape briefly in the bowl before slowly spreading — heavier than cream, lighter than nut butter.

Thread the marinated meat onto soaked bamboo skewers, 3–4 thin slices per skewer, keeping the meat flat so it makes good contact with the grill. Grill over high heat (charcoal is traditional and dramatically superior) for 2–3 minutes per side. The exterior should char at the tips and edges — caramel-dark, slightly blackened — while the interior remains just cooked through. Baste with remaining marinade during the first turn. The turmeric in the marinade will darken quickly and smell of toasted spice. Watch carefully: thin satay slices overcook in seconds.
Visual cue: Skewers with golden-charred edges, deep mahogany caramelization on the sear face, and tips that are darker still — the color gradient from tip to center tells you they were cooked over serious heat.
Underdone: Pale golden exterior, no char marks, interior still raw. Coconut milk marinade hasn't caramelized. Increase heat dramatically. The grill or pan was not hot enough. Let the marinade caramelize before turning.
Perfect: Visible char marks, caramelized golden-brown on the grill face, tips slightly dark. Meat is just cooked through — internal texture is firm but still juicy. The turmeric has toasted to a deep gold. Serve immediately with warm peanut sauce.
Overdone: Meat is dry and pulling away from the skewer. Exterior is uniformly black. Serve with extra peanut sauce to compensate for dryness. The sauce is forgiving.
Feel cue: A perfectly grilled satay skewer should give the slightest resistance when pressed with a finger, then bounce back firmly — if it doesn't spring back at all, it is overcooked and dry.

name: Satay Peanut Sauce
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Coconut milk, full-fat: 250 ml
  Alternatives: coconut cream (richer, thicker sauce)
Roasted peanut butter, natural (no added sugar): 120 g
  Alternatives: finely ground roasted peanuts

  Alternatives: massaman curry paste (sweeter, deeper)

Tamarind paste, concentrated: 20 ml

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A sauce of roasted peanuts dissolved into coconut milk with red curry paste and palm sugar — thick enough to coat a skewer and leave a trembling drop at the tip, with a warmth that builds slowly from the red curry's dried chilies rather than hitting all at once. This is the sauce that makes satay worth the wait.

ingredients.name: Roasted peanut butter, natural (no added sugar)
Thai red curry paste (store-bought or homemade)
Roasted peanuts, roughly crushed, for topping

steps:
Pour the coconut milk into a small saucepan over medium heat. When it begins to steam and show the first signs of simmering at the edges, add the red curry paste. Whisk constantly to break up the paste and disperse it evenly through the coconut milk. Continue to cook over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring regularly. You are not just dissolving the paste — you are cooking out the raw edge of its dried chilies and spices, blooming them in the coconut fat the way you would bloom spices in oil. The mixture will shift from bright orange-red (raw paste) to a deeper, richer terracotta-orange as the paste cooks. The aroma will change from sharp and raw to roasted and complex. This bloom step is what separates a cooked satay sauce from a merely mixed one.
Visual cue: A deep terracotta-orange liquid that is beginning to separate slightly at the surface — dots of red chili oil appearing in the coconut fat.
Underdone: The paste has dissolved but the mixture is still bright, almost fluorescent orange and smells raw and sharp — like uncooked curry paste. Continue cooking and stirring over medium heat for another 2 minutes. The color deepening is the indicator.
Perfect: The mixture is a deep, slightly smoky terracotta-orange. The surface shows small dots of red chili oil floating in the coconut fat — the paste has released its oils. The aroma is rounded and aromatic, not sharp. Add the peanut butter, palm sugar, tamarind, and fish sauce.
Overdone: The mixture is dark brown and the chili oil is separating heavily. The coconut milk has reduced significantly and the bottom of the pan shows dark paste residue. Add 50ml of water and stir vigorously to re-emulsify. Continue with the recipe.
Feel cue: When you stir the bloomed curry coconut and lift the spoon, it should pull away in a thin, even orange film — more viscous than plain coconut milk, with a glossy surface. The steam
should smell of cooked chili and lemongrass, not raw paste.

Add the peanut butter to the simmering curry coconut mixture. Whisk vigorously to incorporate — the peanut butter will resist at first, then suddenly combine into a thick, uniform sauce. Add the palm sugar, tamarind paste, fish sauce, and salt. Stir constantly over medium-low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until the sugar dissolves and all elements are fully integrated. The sauce will thicken as it heats — adjust consistency with small additions of warm water if it becomes too thick to pour easily. The finished sauce should flow off a spoon in a heavy, slow ribbon. Taste and balance: if too thick and sweet, add a teaspoon more tamarind; if too sharp, add a pinch more palm sugar; if flat, a few more drops of fish sauce. The balance to aim for is rich-sweet-slightly-sour-deeply-savory.
Visual cue: A thick, smooth, warm terracotta-orange sauce that falls from a spoon in a slow, heavy ribbon without breaking.
Underdone: Peanut butter has not fully incorporated — visible pale peanut butter streaks remain in the orange base and the sauce is lumpy. Continue whisking over gentle heat. The peanut butter needs warmth to loosen and incorporate fully.
Perfect: A completely smooth, opaque, terracotta-orange sauce of uniform consistency. It coats the back of a spoon heavily and falls in a slow, unbroken ribbon. The aroma is simultaneously of peanut, coconut, and warm curry spice. Remove from heat, scatter crushed peanuts and chili flakes on top, and serve warm.
Overdone: The sauce has become very thick and stiff — it no longer pours easily and is beginning to resemble peanut paste rather than a sauce. The peanut oil may be separating at the surface. Thin with warm water, adding a tablespoon at a time and whisking until the desired consistency returns.
Feel cue: Dip a satay skewer or the back of a spoon into the finished sauce and lift it straight up — the sauce should cling to the wood
or metal and form a single, slow drop at the tip that holds for 3 to 4 seconds before falling. That drop timing is the consistency test.

Transfer the warm peanut sauce to a serving bowl or pour it into a small clay pot for table presentation. Scatter the roughly crushed roasted peanuts over the surface — they should be chunky enough to provide texture but not so large they fall off a dipped item. Add a small pinch of dried chili flakes for color and a visual hint of heat. Serve warm alongside grilled chicken or pork satay skewers, fresh cucumber rounds, and the traditional Thai ajad (pickled cucumber relish). The sauce can be made up to 3 days ahead and refrigerated — it will thicken on cooling but returns to the correct consistency when gently reheated with a splash of water or coconut milk.
Visual cue: A deep terracotta bowl of glossy orange-brown sauce with visible peanut rubble and flecks of chili on the surface.
Underdone: Sauce is too thin and the garnishes sink immediately rather than sitting on the surface. If serving, the flavor is still correct. Alternatively, return to heat and simmer 2 more minutes to thicken.
Perfect: Sauce has body and holds the peanut garnish at the surface for at least 30 seconds before they slowly sink. The surface is glossy and slightly oily from the peanut and coconut fats. Serve within 30 minutes of making for best texture and temperature.
Overdone: Sauce has been left too long and a skin has formed on the surface. The top layer is dry and matte. Stir the skin back in, add a tablespoon of warm water, and stir to restore the glossy surface.
Feel cue: When you dip a satay skewer into the sauce and pull it through your lips, the sauce should feel thick and slightly oily — coating the inside of your mouth with a warm, peanut-coconut richness that is followed a second later by the slow heat of the red curry.
