ingredients.name: Lemongrass stalks (white and pale-green part only), sliced
Galangal (fresh or frozen), peeled and roughly chopped
Dried red chiles (stemmed and seeded), or 1 tsp sambal oelek
Palm sugar or packed brown sugar
Tamarind paste (from a block, dissolved in warm water)

steps:
Combine the shallots, garlic, lemongrass, galangal, and dried chiles in a blender or food processor. Add a tablespoon of water and blend until you have a rough paste, scraping down the sides as needed. The lemongrass is fibrous and the galangal is woody — blend for at least 2 minutes at high speed, pausing to scrape the sides, until the paste is as smooth as the blender will allow. Some texture is acceptable and even desirable, but the lemongrass in particular must be finely broken down or it will remain fibrous and unpleasant in the finished sauce. A high-powered blender will give a smoother result; a food processor gives a rougher but excellent paste.
Visual cue: A pale golden-brown, rough paste with the consistency of coarse hummus — fragrant with lemongrass, ginger-like galangal, and mild chile. No visible large chunks of lemongrass.
Underdone: Visible chunks of lemongrass — 5mm or larger pieces of fibrous stalk. The galangal is still in identifiable pieces. The paste is rough and chunky. Continue blending. Fibrous lemongrass must be broken down or it will create an unpleasant texture in the finished sauce — no amount of simmering will soften it further.
Perfect: A rough but cohesive paste with no identifiable chunks of lemongrass. The color is pale golden-tan and the smell is intensely aromatic: bright, citrusy lemongrass over warm galangal and mild chile. Proceed to frying the paste.
Overdone: The blender has created a completely smooth, liquid purée rather than a paste, from too much added water. This is fine — the paste will still fry correctly. The extra water will evaporate during cooking.
Feel cue: Rub a small amount of paste between your fingers and press — it should feel slightly gritty from the lemongrass fibers, not completely smooth. Smell your fingers: lemongrass should be the dominant note, not just garlic.

Heat 2 tablespoons of neutral oil or coconut oil in a wok or wide saucepan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the blended aromatics paste and the torn kaffir lime leaves and fry, stirring constantly, until the raw smell of garlic and shallot has cooked out and the paste is fragrant, drier, and deeper in color — 5-8 minutes. Crucially, cook until you can see the oil beginning to separate and collect at the edges of the paste — this is called pecah minyak (oil breaking) in Indonesian and Malay cooking, and it signals that the water in the aromatics has fully evaporated and the paste is truly fried, not merely stewed. This step transforms the raw sharp aromatics into a mellow, complex base.
Visual cue: A drier, deeper golden-brown paste that has visibly shrunk and from which a thin ring of pale oil has separated at the edges of the pan. The raw vegetable smell is gone — replaced by a toasted, sweet, complex aroma.
Underdone: The paste is still light-colored and wet, steaming heavily with no caramelization. The garlic-shallot smell is still raw and pungent. No oil separation visible. Continue frying. Lower the heat slightly if it is spitting aggressively, but keep it moving. The oil separation is the non-negotiable doneness signal for this paste.
Perfect: The paste is golden-brown and significantly drier than when you started. A ring of pale yellow oil has appeared at the edges of the pan. The smell is sweet, toasty, and aromatic — lemongrass forward with a warm underlying garlic depth. Add the ground peanuts and coconut milk immediately. Proceed.
Overdone: The paste has caught on the bottom and is burning — dark brown or black spots and a bitter, acrid smell. Deglaze immediately with a splash of coconut milk and stir vigorously. Lower the heat significantly. If the paste smells genuinely burnt (not just toasted), scrape into a clean pan and proceed — the bottom

layer is sacrificed.
Feel cue: The paste in the pan should make a steady, dry sizzle — not a wet, spitting hiss. When you press it with a spatula, it should spring back slightly rather than collapsing into a wet pool. That spring means the water is gone.

If using whole roasted peanuts, pulse them in a food processor to a rough, crumbly texture — about the size of coarse breadcrumbs, not a paste. Add the ground peanuts to the fried aromatics paste and stir to coat them in the fragrant oil. Pour in the coconut milk and water, stirring to combine everything into a thick, rough soup. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring frequently, and cook for 10-12 minutes until the sauce is thick, glossy, and the peanuts have absorbed the coconut milk and swelled slightly. The sauce should coat a spoon in a heavy, flowing layer — much thicker than pourable cream.
Visual cue: A thick, creamy, pale brown sauce — the peanuts visible throughout as a rough texture, the coconut milk fully integrated rather than separate. The surface should have a faint glossy sheen from the coconut fat.
Underdone: The sauce is thin and watery, with the coconut milk not yet reduced and the peanuts still raw-tasting and floating separately. The flavors have not yet merged. Continue simmering and stirring. The peanuts need sustained heat and moisture to swell and become creamy — at least 10 minutes at a active simmer.
Perfect: A thick, creamy, cohesive sauce — the peanuts swollen and creamy, the coconut milk absorbed into a glossy, rich base. It coats a spoon heavily and flows in a slow, heavy ribbon. Add the seasonings. Proceed.
Overdone: The sauce has reduced too far and is thick and gluey, beginning to stick and scorch at the bottom despite stirring. Add more coconut milk or water, whisking to loosen. The sauce will thicken further as it cools — allow for that when adjusting consistency.
Feel cue: Dip a spoon and lift it above the sauce — the sauce should flow off in a heavy, slow, continuous ribbon rather than dripping in drops. The peanuts throughout should feel softened and creamy rather than crunchy.

Add the palm sugar, fish sauce, tamarind paste, and lime juice to the simmering sauce. Stir to dissolve the palm sugar completely and simmer 2-3 minutes more to integrate everything. Now taste carefully and balance the sauce along four axes: savory-salty (fish sauce), sweet (palm sugar), sour-tamarind (tamarind and lime), and heat (chile). The sauce should be rich and deeply savory first, with the sweetness present but not candy-like, the sourness brightening rather than dominating, and the chile an undercurrent of warmth. Adjust each element incrementally — a satay sauce that tastes sweet and peanut-buttery without complexity is incomplete; one that tastes only fishy has the fish sauce ratio wrong.
Visual cue: After seasoning and final simmering, the sauce takes on a deeper amber color from the palm sugar caramelizing slightly into the coconut base. The surface is glossy and the sauce flows in a rich, heavy pour.
Underdone: The sauce still tastes flat and peanut-buttery without complexity — the fish sauce, tamarind, and palm sugar have not yet been added, or are in insufficient quantity to create the characteristic layered depth. Add each seasoning component in sequence, tasting between each addition. The complex, savory-sweet-sour-spicy balance is what separates a real satay sauce from peanut butter thinned with coconut milk.
Perfect: Rich, glossy, and deeply complex. The taste moves from initial peanut-coconut richness through a savory-sweet middle (fish sauce and palm sugar) to a bright tamarind-lime finish, with chile warmth throughout. It clings to a spoon in a heavy, uniform coat. Thin with warm water if needed for a pourable dipping consistency. Serve warm alongside satay skewers.
Overdone: One element dominates destructively — the sauce tastes only sweet from too much palm sugar, or fishy from excess fish sauce, or mouth-puckeringly sour from too much

tamarind. Counter the dominant note: excess sweetness needs more tamarind and fish sauce; excess fishiness needs more palm sugar and tamarind; excess sourness needs more palm sugar and coconut milk to dilute and round.
Feel cue: Finished satay sauce served over a skewer of grilled chicken should cling to every surface of the meat in a thick, glossy coat without running off. If it pools at the base of the skewer and runs away, the sauce needs further reduction. If it sets like paste on the hot meat, thin with a splash of warm water.

name: Sauce Robert
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Brown stock (veal): 12 parts
  Alternatives: brown beef stock; rich chicken stock
Clarified butter: 1 parts
  Alternatives: rendered beef fat; neutral oil
All-purpose flour: 1 parts
Mirepoix (onion, carrot, celery): 2 parts
Tomato paste: 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: crushed tomato (reduced)
Fine sea salt: 0.1 parts
  Alternatives: kosher salt
Bouquet garni: 0.1 parts
  Alternatives: thyme, bay, parsley stems tied in cheesecloth
Onion (finely diced): 2 parts
  Alternatives: shallot (finely diced)
Dry white wine: 3 parts
  Alternatives: dry vermouth; white wine vinegar (reduced, smaller amount)
Dijon mustard: 0.5 parts
  Alternatives: whole-grain mustard
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 1 hour
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: One of espagnole's oldest children — a brown sauce built on slowly sweated onions, sharpened with reduced white wine, and finished off the heat with a swirl of Dijon. Tangy, mustard-bright, and savory all at once, it is the classic companion to roast pork and grilled meats.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Melt about a third of the clarified butter in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the mirepoix and cook, stirring occasionally, until deeply browned and sweet-smelling — 12 to 18 minutes. Build a rust-colored fond on the bottom of the pot; that caramelization is the backbone of the espagnole base.
Visual cue: Mirepoix softened and collapsed, edges of onion turned golden-amber, with a rust-colored fond forming on the pan bottom. The kitchen smells sweet and savory.
Underdone: Vegetables are translucent and limp but still pale — no color, no fond, and the smell is raw and grassy. Raise the heat slightly and keep cooking. Browning is where the depth comes from.
Perfect: Onions are amber at the edges, carrots glisten and have softened, and a brown fond clings to the bottom of the pot. Push the mirepoix aside and add the remaining butter to begin the roux.
Overdone: Vegetables are blackening, the fond has gone from brown to black, and there is an acrid, scorched smell. Lower the heat at once. If the fond is truly burnt, deglaze with a splash of stock, wipe the pot, and restart the mirepoix.
Feel cue: The vegetables should sizzle steadily, not violently. Dragging a spoon across the bottom should meet the sticky drag of fond, not a smooth slick of fat.

Melt the remaining butter into the cleared part of the pot, sprinkle in the flour, and cook the roux to a deep chestnut brown, stirring almost constantly — 10 to 20 minutes, until it smells nutty and toasty. Stir in the tomato paste and cook it out for 3 to 5 minutes until it darkens to brick-rust and smells sweet rather than sharp. Go low and patient; brown roux scorches in a heartbeat.
Visual cue: A deep chestnut-brown roux smelling of toasted nuts, with the tomato paste cooked into it to a brick-rust color and a sweet, roasted aroma.
Underdone: Roux is pale or blond and smells of raw flour; the tomato paste is still bright orange-red and smells tinny. Keep cooking and stirring over low-medium heat until the roux browns and the tomato turns brick-red and sweet.
Perfect: Chestnut-brown roux carrying a cooked-out, brick-rust tomato paste, smelling toasty and sweet, with a deep fond on the pan. Whisk in the brown stock to build the loose espagnole.
Overdone: Roux or tomato has darkened to black, with an acrid burnt smell and scorched specks throughout. Discard and start the roux over. Burnt roux is bitter and loses its thickening power — it cannot be saved.
Feel cue: The roux moves from gritty sand to silky mud as it cooks, then the tomato paste stiffens and pulls together before it darkens. A soft, steady sizzle is right; a sharp crackle means too much heat.

Pour in the brown stock a few ladles at a time, whisking out lumps before adding more. Add the bouquet garni, bring to the barest simmer, and hold 2 to 3 hours, skimming the fat and froth from the surface and seasoning lightly with salt near the end. When reduced by about a third and coating a spoon, strain through a fine sieve. This is your base espagnole.
Visual cue: A clear, glossy, deep-mahogany sauce that lightly coats the back of a spoon, reduced by about a third, surface clean of fat and scum.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and watery, pale brown, runs off a spoon, and the surface is greasy and cloudy. Keep simmering and skimming. The espagnole needs time to build body and shed impurities before it becomes the base for Sauce Robert.
Perfect: Deep mahogany, glossy and clean, coating the back of a spoon so a finger-line holds. No raw flour or harsh tomato in the taste. Strain through a fine sieve and hold warm while you build the onion and wine reduction.
Overdone: Reduced too far — thick, sludgy, and over-salted. Whisk in a little warm stock to bring it back to a proper nappe and rebalance the seasoning.
Feel cue: A finished espagnole drawn across a spoon leaves a clean, lasting trail. The surface should look polished rather than slick with fat, with a deep roasted aroma.

In a separate clean saucepan, melt a little clarified butter over low-medium heat and add the finely diced onion. Sweat it gently, stirring often, until soft, translucent, and just beginning to turn golden at the edges — 8 to 12 minutes. The goal is sweetness and tenderness without hard browning; keep the heat low so the onion melts rather than crisps.
Visual cue: Onion fully softened, glassy and translucent, with only the faintest golden tinge at the edges and a sweet, mellow aroma — no dark color.
Underdone: Onion is still firm, sharp, and white, with a raw, pungent bite to the smell. Keep sweating gently over low heat. Sauce Robert depends on a soft, sweet onion base — raw onion will taste harsh in the finished sauce.
Perfect: Soft, translucent, glassy onion, just barely golden at the edges, smelling sweet and mellow. Pour in the white wine to deglaze and reduce.
Overdone: Onion has browned hard or scorched, turning bitter and dark. Lower the heat and add the wine immediately to stop the cooking; if badly burnt, start the onions again to keep the sauce clean and sweet.
Feel cue: The onion should hiss softly and turn limp and slippery, almost dissolving when pressed with the spoon. There should be no crackle of browning — only a gentle, sweet sizzle.

Pour the dry white wine over the sweated onions and raise the heat to bring it to a brisk simmer. Reduce, scraping up any fond, until the wine has cooked down to a syrupy glaze barely covering the onions and the sharp alcohol smell has cooked off — 5 to 8 minutes. This reduction concentrates the wine's acidity into a bright backbone for the sauce.
Visual cue: The wine reduced to a scant, syrupy glaze coating the onions, with the raw alcohol smell gone and a bright, mellow, wine-sweet aroma in its place.
Underdone: Still a pool of thin, watery wine around the onions, smelling sharply of raw alcohol. Keep simmering to drive off the alcohol and concentrate the wine; under-reduced wine leaves a thin, boozy harshness.
Perfect: Wine cooked down to a glossy, syrupy glaze just coating the onions, smelling bright and mellow with no alcohol burn. Add the strained espagnole and simmer the two together.
Overdone: The pan has gone dry and the glaze is starting to scorch and turn bitter. Pull off the heat and add the espagnole at once to deglaze and stop the cooking before the bitterness sets in.
Feel cue: As the wine reduces, the brisk simmer slows and the bubbles thicken into a glossy syrup that drags behind the spoon. The sharp vapor of alcohol should give way to a soft, sweet wine aroma.

Pour the strained espagnole into the onion and wine reduction and simmer gently together for 8 to 10 minutes, skimming, until married and smooth. Then pull the pan completely off the heat and let it stop bubbling before whisking in the Dijon mustard. Never let the sauce boil after the mustard goes in — boiling mustard turns harsh and bitter. Taste, adjust the salt, and serve warm.
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy brown sauce flecked with soft onion, with the mustard whisked in off the heat to a bright, tangy, mellow finish — no bitterness, no broken or grainy look.
Underdone: Mustard stirred in but the espagnole and onion reduction have not yet married — flavors taste disjointed and the mustard sits sharp on top. Let the espagnole simmer with the reduction a few minutes longer BEFORE the mustard goes in, so the flavors meld; add the mustard only at the very end, off heat.
Perfect: Glossy, cohesive, mahogany sauce with tender onion throughout and a balanced tang — savory base lifted by bright, mellow mustard. Smooth and warm, not boiling. Taste, correct the salt, and serve immediately over roast pork or grilled meats.
Overdone: The sauce was boiled after the mustard went in — it tastes sharp and bitter, and the mustard has lost its rounded warmth. There is no fully undoing boiled mustard; whisk in a little fresh Dijon off the heat and a pinch of sugar to soften the bitterness, and never let it boil again.
Feel cue: The mustard should disappear into the sauce with a few turns of the whisk, leaving it glossy and smooth. The pan should be hot but still — no bubbles breaking the surface when the Dijon goes in.

name: Sauce Suprême
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
White chicken stock: 12 parts
  Alternatives: white veal stock
Unsalted butter: 1 parts
  Alternatives: clarified butter
All-purpose flour: 1 parts
Fine sea salt: 0.1 parts
  Alternatives: kosher salt
White pepper: 0.02 parts
Heavy cream: 4 parts
  Alternatives: crème fraîche
Butter (cold, to mount/finish): 1 parts
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 50 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A chicken velouté reduced with cream until it turns lush, ivory, and glossy, then mounted with cold butter for a mirror shine. The supreme of the white sauces — built for poached chicken, supreme of fowl, and anything that wants to taste of pure, silken poultry.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Melt the butter over medium-low heat until it foams without browning, then whisk in the flour. Cook, stirring, 4 to 6 minutes until the raw-flour smell turns to toasted hazelnut and the paste is pale straw — a blond roux.
Visual cue: A loose, glossy, pale-straw paste that moves like wet sand and smells of warm toasted nuts.
Underdone: Bright white and pasty, still smelling of raw flour. Stir over the heat another minute until the color shifts to faint straw and the smell turns nutty.
Perfect: Even pale straw, smooth and fluid, faintly nutty. Bubbles lazily at the edges. Pull from the heat and ready the warm chicken stock.
Overdone: Gone golden-brown and strongly toasted. Start over for a true blond — a browned roux would muddy the clean ivory this sauce wants.
Feel cue: The whisk drags through a soft, fluid paste with almost no resistance — if it balls up dry, there is too much flour.

Off the heat, whisk the warm white chicken stock into the roux in three or four additions, letting each disappear before the next. Return to medium heat, bring to a gentle boil whisking, then drop to a bare simmer and skim until the surface runs clean.
Visual cue: A smooth, lump-free, pale ivory chicken velouté, glossy, with a bright clean surface after skimming.
Underdone: Thin and watery, surface still throwing gray foam. Simmer and skim a few minutes longer — the body builds and the foam stops surfacing with time.
Perfect: Smooth, glossy, pale ivory; lightly coats the whisk; surface clear between skims. Pour in the cream and begin reducing.
Overdone: Gluey and paste-thick before the cream is even in. Whisk in a little warm stock to loosen it before adding the cream.
Feel cue: Feel the gentle thickening grab the whisk as it boils — that grab is the starch setting. The simmer should be a lazy blip, never a rolling boil.

Pour the heavy cream into the simmering velouté. Reduce gently over medium-low heat, stirring often and scraping the bottom, until the sauce is enriched, ivory, and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. This cream reduction is what turns a plain velouté into a suprême — expect to lose roughly a third of the volume.
Visual cue: A glossy, ivory sauce reduced until it nappes a spoon — draw a finger across the coated spoon and the line holds clean without flooding back. It falls from the spoon in slow, heavy ribbons.
Underdone: Sauce is pale and loose, runs off the spoon in a thin sheet, tastes more of cream than concentrated chicken. Keep reducing at a gentle simmer, stirring, until the volume drops and the flavor concentrates.
Perfect: Rich ivory, glossy, coats a spoon in a clean nappe. Tastes deeply of chicken rounded by cream. Pull off the heat to mount with cold butter.
Overdone: Reduced too far — heavy, sticky, beginning to catch and brown on the pan bottom, edges turning tan. Whisk in a splash of warm stock or cream at once to loosen, and lower the heat before it scorches.
Feel cue: Stir and you feel the sauce thicken under the spoon and start to whisper against the pan bottom — that drag tells you it is nearly reduced. It smells of concentrated roast-chicken richness.

Off the heat, whisk in the cold butter a cube at a time, swirling the pan, letting each piece melt into the sauce before adding the next (monter au beurre). This gives the suprême its mirror gloss and a final velvet richness. Season with salt and a touch of white pepper. Keep it warm but never let it boil after mounting, or the butter will split.
Visual cue: A flawless, mirror-glossy ivory sauce, thick and lush, that coats poached chicken in a clinging, satiny sheet. The surface shines; it falls from the spoon in heavy, glossy ribbons.
Underdone: Sauce looks matte and flat — the butter has not yet been worked in, or only partly. Keep whisking in cold butter off the heat, cube by cube, until the surface turns glossy and the sauce thickens slightly.
Perfect: High-shine, ivory, velvety; clings to a spoon and to chicken alike; tastes round, rich, and clean. Serve immediately over poultry — it is at its best the moment it is finished.
Overdone: Sauce has been boiled or overheated after mounting — it looks oily and broken, with a slick of fat separating out. Pull off the heat and whisk in a splash of cold cream or a few drops of cold water to bring the emulsion back together.
Feel cue: As the cold butter melts in, the sauce visibly tightens and gleams under the whisk and feels heavier and silkier on the spoon. It should pour like warm satin, never greasy.

name: Sauce Tomate (Classical French)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Ripe tomatoes (or canned San Marzano): 8 parts
  Alternatives: good quality whole peeled plum tomatoes
Salt pork or butter: 1 part
  Alternatives: unsalted butter; pancetta; rendered bacon
Mirepoix (onion, carrot, celery): 2 parts
Garlic: 0.2 part
White stock: 4 parts
  Alternatives: light chicken stock; veal stock
Pinch of sugar: 0.1 part
Salt: 0.2 part
Bouquet garni: 1 bundle
  Alternatives: thyme, bay, parsley stems tied in leek green
Active time: 40 min
Total time: 2 hours 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The Escoffier mother sauce — not a quick marinara. Tomatoes melted into rendered pork fat and mirepoix, moistened with white stock, scented with a bouquet garni, simmered slow until jammy, then passed to a smooth, velvety, deeply rounded red sauce.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Dice the salt pork small and set it in a heavy-bottomed pot over low-medium heat (or simply melt the butter). Let it render slowly without browning, drawing the fat out clear and the scraps to a pale gold. You want a film of clean fat coating the pot, not a fry.
Visual cue: A shallow pool of clear, golden fat across the pot bottom. Pork scraps have shrunk and turned the palest gold; the fat shimmers but does not smoke.
Underdone: Pork is still pink and rubbery, little fat in the pot, surface looks dry. Lower the heat and keep going — rendering is patient work. Stir so nothing sticks.
Perfect: Fat runs clear and golden, scraps are pale and crisp at the edges, the pot smells gently of pork, not of frying. Proceed to sweat the mirepoix in this fat.
Overdone: Scraps are dark brown, fat is browning, an acrid frying smell rises. Pull from the heat at once and lift out the darkest scraps. Browned fat will dull the sauce — proceed gently from here.
Feel cue: The fat should move like thin oil when you tip the pot, and the smell is warm and porky — never sharp or toasted. If using butter, listen for a quiet, even sizzle, not a furious one.

Add the finely cut mirepoix and the garlic to the fat. Sweat over low-medium heat, stirring often, until the onion turns translucent and the whole pot softens and goes silent of its raw bite. Do not let it color — this is a foundation, not a fond.
Visual cue: Mirepoix gone soft and glassy, onions translucent, carrots brightened and yielding, everything slick with fat. No browning anywhere.
Underdone: Onion still white and opaque, vegetables stiff and crunchy, the pot smells raw and oniony. Keep sweating with a lid ajar to trap gentle steam. Stir so the bottom layer does not catch.
Perfect: Onions are translucent and limp, garlic is fragrant and sweet, the mirepoix glistens and the raw smell has given way to a soft, sweet aroma. Add the tomatoes and the pinch of sugar.
Overdone: Edges of onion and garlic have browned and the garlic smells sharp and toasted. Lower the heat immediately and add the tomatoes now — their liquid will arrest the browning. Browned garlic turns bitter, so move quickly.
Feel cue: Drag the spoon across the bottom — the vegetables should part softly with no resistance and no crackle. The kitchen should smell sweet and round, not pungent.

Add the chopped tomatoes (crush canned ones by hand) and the pinch of sugar to correct their acidity. Raise the heat to a lively simmer and cook down, stirring as it thickens, until the watery tomato has collapsed into a thick, jammy base and the bright raw smell turns deep and sweet.
Visual cue: A thick, brick-red mass that mounds on the spoon and pulls away from the sides of the pot. The thin tomato water has cooked off; oil begins to bead at the edges.
Underdone: Tomatoes are loose and soupy, pale orange-red, still smelling green and sharply acidic. A spoon dragged through fills back instantly. Keep reducing over a steady simmer. The flavor cannot round out until the excess water is gone.
Perfect: Deep brick-red and jammy, mounding on the spoon, leaving a clean trail when scraped across the pot. The smell has turned sweet, concentrated, and savory. Moisten with the white stock and add the bouquet garni.
Overdone: The base is darkening, sticking and scorching on the bottom, with a caught, toasted edge to the smell. Stop stirring up the scorched layer — do not scrape it in. Pour the stock in now and transfer to a clean pot if the bottom has truly caught.
Feel cue: The base resists the spoon and clings to it in a glossy clump. When you smell over the pot the sharp raw-tomato note is gone, replaced by something sweet, deep, and almost jam-like.

Pour in the white stock, tuck in the bouquet garni, and season lightly with salt (go easy if you used salt pork). Bring to the barest simmer and hold it there, partially covered, for an hour and a half or more, skimming the fat and scum that gather at the surface. The sauce should ripple, never boil.
Visual cue: A gently rippling, deepening red sauce, clear of foam and surface fat from regular skimming, thickened enough to lightly coat a spoon. The bouquet garni has steeped its perfume through.
Underdone: Thin and watery, tasting of separate parts — stock here, tomato there — with a greasy film and grey scum riding the top. Keep it at a slow simmer and skim patiently. Time married with skimming is what fuses and clarifies the sauce.
Perfect: Glossy, unified deep red, lightly napping the back of a spoon. The surface is clean and the flavor tastes whole — rounded, savory, gently sweet, with the herb perfume woven through. Remove the bouquet garni and pass the sauce.
Overdone: Reduced too far and heavy, edges of the pot crusting dark, the sauce tasting concentrated and dull with a flat over-cooked note. Loosen with a splash more warm stock and pull it off the heat. Pass it promptly before it tightens further.
Feel cue: Only the occasional slow bubble should break the surface — a true simmer, never a boil. Each pass of the skimming ladle should come up with less fat and foam than the last, the surface growing cleaner and glossier.

Discard the bouquet garni and the pork scraps. Pass the sauce through a food mill or push it through a fine sieve with a ladle, working the solids until only dry skins and fibre remain behind. Return it to the heat, taste, and adjust salt and the pinch of sugar to balance the acidity into a smooth, velvety sauce.
Visual cue: A uniformly smooth, glossy, lacquer-red sauce with no visible fibre, skin, or pulp — velvety enough to coat the back of a spoon and hold a clean line drawn through it with a finger.
Underdone: The passed sauce is still flecked with skin and stringy fibre, or it runs thin and watery through the mill. Pass it again through a finer screen, or reduce briefly to bring it back to a napping body. Press the solids harder to claim the pulp still clinging to the skins.
Perfect: Flawlessly smooth and velvety, deep glossy red, coating the spoon and holding a drawn line. Balanced — sweet, savory, and gently acidic all at once. Hold warm over a water bath, or cool and store. It is finished.
Overdone: Over-worked through the mill it has gone pasty and dull, or over-reduced after passing it has turned thick and gluey. Whisk in a little warm stock to bring back a pourable, glossy body, then re-check the seasoning.
Feel cue: Drawn across a plate the sauce should leave a clean, glossy ribbon that holds its shape. On the tongue it is silken and round, with no graininess — the acidity present but tamed, the whole thing rich and complete.

name: 德式酸炖牛肉 · Rhineland Sauerbraten
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Beef bottom round or top round (about 1.5 kg, tied): 1500 g
  Alternatives: beef chuck roast (more marbling, richer result)
Red wine vinegar: 250 ml
  Alternatives: cider vinegar (milder)
Dry red wine: 250 ml
  Alternatives: additional red wine vinegar + 100ml water
Water: 250 ml
White onion, roughly sliced: 200 g
  Alternatives: yellow onion
Celery stalks, roughly chopped: 100 g
Carrot, roughly chopped: 100 g
Bay leaves: 3 ea
Juniper berries, lightly crushed: 8 ea
Whole cloves: 4 ea
Black peppercorns: 10 ea
Sugar: 15 g
  Alternatives: brown sugar
Fine sea salt: 12 g
Lard or neutral oil: 30 ml
  Alternatives: beef tallow; vegetable oil
Gingersnap cookies (Lebkuchen or ginger snaps), crumbled: 80 g
  Alternatives: 2 tbsp dark rye bread crumbs + 1 tsp honey + 0.5 tsp ground ginger
Sour cream (optional, for finishing): 80 g
  Alternatives: crème fraîche
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 4 days (marinade)
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Germany's pot roast nobility — beef marinated for three to four days in red wine vinegar, wine, and a raft of aromatics until the tough outside round transforms into something silken, then braised low and slow with crumbled gingersnaps stirred into the sauce for a haunting, sweet-sour richness unique to the Rhineland.

ingredients.name: Beef bottom round or top round (about 1.5 kg, tied)
Gingersnap cookies (Lebkuchen or ginger snaps), crumbled

steps:
Do not heat the marinade — a cold marinade is traditional for sauerbraten. Combine the red wine vinegar, red wine, water, onion, celery, carrot, bay leaves, juniper berries, cloves, peppercorns, sugar, and salt in a large non-reactive bowl or pot (glass, ceramic, or stainless steel — never aluminium or cast iron at this stage). Stir until the salt and sugar dissolve. Submerge the beef completely, pressing it down. Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate for 3–4 days, turning the meat once per day so all sides marinate evenly.
Visual cue: After 3 days, the surface of the beef has turned from bright red to a dull grayish-brown on all sides — the acid has penetrated the outer 1–2 cm of meat.
Underdone: After only 1 day: beef is still bright red throughout. Only the surface is slightly discoloured. The flavour will be mild and the texture not yet transformed. Return to the refrigerator. Sauerbraten's magic requires time. A minimum of 3 days is non-negotiable for authentic Rhineland flavour.
Perfect: After 3–4 days: outer 2 cm of the beef is uniformly grey-brown from acid. The marinade smells complex — sour, spiced, and wine-dark. The meat feels noticeably firmer and denser than raw beef. Remove from the marinade, pat very dry, and strain the marinade through a sieve, reserving all the liquid.
Overdone: After 5+ days: the acid has penetrated further and the surface meat is beginning to turn mealy and very soft. The marinade smells strongly sour. Proceed — the braising will rescue the texture. The flavour will be very tart; the gingersnaps become even more critical to balance.
Feel cue: On day three, press the surface of the beef with a finger — it feels denser and slightly tighter than fresh beef, almost like cured meat. That resistance tells you the acid has done its work.

Remove the beef from the marinade and pat it completely dry with paper towels — moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Strain and reserve all the marinade liquid. Heat the lard or oil in a heavy Dutch oven or braising pot over high heat until just beginning to smoke. Sear the beef on all sides, including the ends, for 3–4 minutes per side without moving it. You are building deep brown crust for colour and flavour — the Maillard crust will dissolve into the braising liquid and become the backbone of the sauce.
Visual cue: All surfaces of the beef are uniformly deep mahogany-brown with no grey or blond patches. The pot bottom has a dark brown fond stuck to it.
Underdone: Meat is blond or pale grey on some sides — still wet-looking in patches. The fond on the pot bottom is thin and pale. Continue searing, ensuring the heat is high and the surface is bone-dry. Do not rush — a pale sear produces a pale, flat-tasting sauce.
Perfect: Deep mahogany crust on all sides. The pot has a rich dark fond. The kitchen smells of caramelised beef and spice. The meat sizzles loudly when each side first contacts the pan. Remove the beef and set aside. Discard the burned fat if dark; leave if golden.
Overdone: Parts of the crust are black. A scorched, acrid smell in the kitchen. Fond on the pot is black. Wipe the burnt fond from the pot before adding the marinade, or it will turn the sauce bitter.
Feel cue: A properly seared side releases from the pot with zero sticking when you try to lift it — the crust has formed a dry seal. If it sticks and tears, it needs 60 more seconds.

Return the seared beef to the pot. Pour the strained marinade over it — the liquid should come at least halfway up the sides of the meat. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, then cover with a tight lid and reduce to the lowest possible heat (or transfer to a 160°C oven). Braise for 2.5–3 hours, turning the beef every 45 minutes. The meat is done when a carving fork slides in and out without resistance, and the fibres are beginning to separate when pressed.
Visual cue: Beef is deep brown throughout, visibly shrunken from its raw size. A carving fork slides in and out of the thickest point with no resistance — like hot butter.
Underdone: Fork meets significant resistance in the centre. Internal temperature is below 90°C. The fibres are still knitted tightly together. Replace the lid and continue braising. At this low-and-slow temperature, 30 more minutes can transform the texture entirely.
Perfect: Fork slides in effortlessly. Meat shreds at the edges with a gentle nudge. The braising liquid is dark and fragrant. Internal temperature is 93–97°C. Remove the beef and set aside, covered with foil, while you make the sauce.
Overdone: Meat has collapsed and is falling apart. Fibres are completely loose and the roast cannot hold its shape for slicing. Serve it pulled or shredded rather than sliced. The flavour is unaffected — it is arguably even better.
Feel cue: Lift the lid after 2 hours and press the beef with your finger through a folded kitchen towel — perfect sauerbraten yields like memory foam, springing back very slowly. If it springs back fast, it needs more time.

Remove the beef and keep warm under foil. Pour all the braising liquid through a fine strainer into a wide saucepan — discard the spent aromatics. Bring the liquid to a vigorous boil and reduce by one-third, about 10 minutes. Crumble in the gingersnaps and whisk over medium heat until they dissolve completely and the sauce thickens noticeably to a coating consistency. Taste for balance — it should be sweet, sour, warm with spice, and deeply savoury. If it is too tart, add another crumbled gingersnap. Off the heat, stir in the sour cream if using, and reheat gently without boiling.
Visual cue: Sauce coats the back of a spoon in a glossy, brown-mahogany layer that does not run off immediately when the spoon is held upright. The gingersnaps have vanished entirely into the sauce.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and watery, running off the spoon like coloured water. Gingersnaps still visible as lumps or pale patches. Whisk vigorously over medium heat for another 3–4 minutes. Add another crumbled gingersnap if thickness is lacking.
Perfect: Nappe consistency — coats a spoon cleanly. Deep mahogany in colour, glossy, and complex: sour, sweet, spiced, and meaty all at once. Slice the rested beef against the grain and serve napped with the sauce, alongside potato dumplings (Knödel) or braised red cabbage.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced too far — it is thick, sticky, and very sweet from the concentrated gingersnap sugars. Slightly gluey on the spoon. Add a splash of the cooking liquid or hot water and whisk to loosen to the desired consistency.
Feel cue: Dip a clean finger into the sauce — it should leave a visible, glossy coat on your fingertip that clings for a few seconds rather than beading off. That film is the emulsified gelatin, fat, and gingersnap starch binding the Rhineland sweet-sour into one thing.

name: Traditional Sauerkraut
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Green cabbage: 100 parts
  Alternatives: red cabbage; savoy cabbage
Non-iodized sea salt: 2 parts
  Alternatives: kosher salt; pickling salt
Caraway seeds: 0.3 parts
  Alternatives: juniper berries
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 14 days
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Cabbage, salt, time, and trust — a Bavarian fermentation that transforms a humble head into something tangy, probiotic, and profoundly alive.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Quarter the cabbage and remove the core. Slice each quarter into thin ribbons, about 3mm wide. Uniformity matters — uneven shreds ferment at different rates, creating pockets of crunch alongside pockets of mush.
Visual cue: A mound of uniformly thin, pale-green ribbons with no thick chunks or attached core pieces.
Underdone: Thick wedges and irregular chunks. Some pieces are 1cm or wider. Take the time to re-cut. Thick pieces will remain tough while thin ones over-ferment.
Perfect: Consistent thin ribbons, 2-4mm wide. A handful feels light and springy. Weigh the cabbage and calculate salt.
Overdone: Shredded to a fine, almost grated consistency — nearly pulp. Proceed, but expect a softer, mushier kraut with less crunch.
Feel cue: A good shred springs back when you squeeze a handful. If it collapses into a wet clump, the pieces are too fine.

Place shredded cabbage in a large bowl. Sprinkle salt and caraway seeds evenly over the top. Massage with both hands, squeezing and kneading the cabbage firmly. The salt will draw water from the cells. Continue for 8-10 minutes until the cabbage has wilted significantly and sits in its own brine.
Visual cue: Cabbage has reduced to half its volume. A pool of cloudy brine has collected at the bottom of the bowl — enough to submerge the cabbage when packed.
Underdone: Cabbage is still stiff and springy. Only a thin film of moisture on the leaves. Keep massaging. Walk away for 10 minutes and return — salt needs time to osmose. Then knead again.
Perfect: Cabbage is limp and translucent. A generous pool of brine at the bottom. When you squeeze a fistful, liquid streams out. Pack into your fermentation vessel.
Overdone: Cabbage has turned to near-mush. Extremely wet. This is rare with just salt — proceed. The texture will be softer but the flavor fine.
Feel cue: The cabbage transforms under your hands from crisp and squeaky to silky and limp. Your hands will be pruny from the brine — that means there is enough salt and enough liquid.

Transfer the cabbage and all its brine into a clean glass jar or ceramic crock. Push it down in handfuls with your fist, packing as tightly as possible. The brine must rise above the cabbage surface. Place a weight on top — a zip-lock bag filled with brine works well. Cover with a cloth to keep out dust but allow gas to escape.
Visual cue: Cabbage is submerged beneath a layer of brine at least 2cm deep. No leaves are exposed to air. Weight is firmly in place.
Underdone: Cabbage is poking above the brine surface. Air pockets visible between layers. Press down harder. If there truly is not enough brine, dissolve 1 tsp salt in 1 cup water and add it.
Perfect: All cabbage is submerged. Brine is 2-3cm above the surface. Weight sits level. Cover and place in a cool spot (18-22 C) away from direct sunlight.
Overdone: Vessel is filled to the brim with brine overflowing. Remove some brine — you need headspace for the CO2 that fermentation will produce.
Feel cue: When you press the weight down and release, brine should surge up around the edges. If you hear a squelch, the pack is tight enough.

Leave at room temperature (18-22 C) for 3-14 days, tasting every two days after day three. Press the weight down daily and skim any scum from the surface. Bubbling is a sign of active, healthy fermentation.
Visual cue: Fine bubbles rising through the brine when the jar is tapped. Brine has turned cloudy and slightly effervescent. The cabbage has changed from green to a muted golden-straw color.
Underdone: Day 3: No bubbles, brine is still clear, cabbage still green and crunchy. The environment may be too cold. Move to a warmer spot (20-22 C). If no activity by day 5, check that the salt was not iodized.
Perfect: Steady bubbling when agitated. Brine is cloudy. Tasting reveals a clean, tangy sourness with residual crunch in the cabbage. When the flavor pleases you, transfer to the refrigerator to halt fermentation.
Overdone: Extremely sour, almost vinegary. Cabbage is very soft and olive-drab in color. Possibly a pink or fuzzy film on the surface. Skim any mold (surface kahm yeast is harmless). If it tastes good to you, it is done. If too sour, use it in cooked dishes where other flavors will balance it.
Feel cue: Lean close and sniff — early fermentation smells like fresh-cut grass, then shifts to a pleasant pickled tang. If it smells putrid or like rotten eggs, something went wrong. A slight fizz on the tongue when you taste the brine is the sign of healthy lacto-fermentation.

name: 葱油拌面 · Shanghai Scallion Oil Noodles (Cong You Ban Mian)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Fresh thin Shanghai noodles (or dried lo mein): 200 g
  Alternatives: thin spaghetti; ramen noodles
Scallions, cut into 5 cm pieces: 150 g
  Alternatives: Chinese chives (jiu cai); shallots
Neutral oil (vegetable or sunflower): 120 ml
  Alternatives: light peanut oil
Light soy sauce: 20 ml
Dark soy sauce (lao chou): 10 ml
White sugar: 8 g
  Alternatives: rock sugar syrup
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 55 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Plain wheat noodles tossed in a dark, slow-rendered scallion oil that takes forty minutes to build from a bundle of green onions and a cup of oil — the scallions caramelize to a dark, sweet, crispy confetti while the oil absorbs their entire life force, becoming something wholly different from any oil you have ever tasted. A dish of four ingredients that insists on quality in each one.

ingredients.name: Fresh thin Shanghai noodles (or dried lo mein)

steps:
Combine the scallion pieces and neutral oil in a cold small saucepan or wok — starting in cold oil is critical. If you add scallions to already-hot oil they will fry hard and fast, browning too quickly before they have time to release their aromatics into the oil. Place over the lowest heat you can manage and cook for 30–40 minutes. The first 15 minutes will see very little activity — the oil will warm slowly and the scallions will begin to soften and wilt. From 15–25 minutes, the scallions will begin to shrink dramatically and you will see the first signs of browning at the green tips. From 25–40 minutes, the scallions will caramelize progressively from the tips down toward the white roots, going from golden to amber to a deep reddish-brown. The goal is that the scallions go almost fully dark — sweet-bitter, crispy shards — while the oil turns a deep golden-amber and smells like nothing else: sweet, savory, deeply caramelized allium. Stir every 5 minutes, more frequently in the last 10. When the scallion pieces are uniformly dark golden-brown and crispy, remove from heat.
Visual cue: Dark golden-brown scallion pieces that have shrunk to roughly one-quarter of their original size, with crispy, curled edges. The surrounding oil is a deep amber-gold and slightly hazy from the extracted sugars.
Underdone: Scallions are still green and wilted, not yet browned. The oil is still pale and smells raw rather than sweet. Continue cooking on low heat. The color change happens in the last 10–15 minutes — be patient. Do not increase heat to rush it.
Perfect: Scallions are a deep reddish-brown — almost the color of fried shallots — and have become crispy and curled. The oil is deep amber-gold and smells intensely of sweet, caramelized green onion. One piece should shatter between your fingers when cool. Remove from heat and let cool for 5 minutes. Strain into a jar or bowl,

reserving the crispy scallion pieces separately as a garnish.
Overdone: Scallions have gone black and acrid-smelling, and the oil has taken on a burnt note. Any bitterness at this stage will transfer to the noodles. If only a few pieces are black, strain immediately and discard just those pieces. If the oil itself smells burnt, discard everything and start again.
Feel cue: At the 30-minute mark, carefully pluck out one scallion piece with chopsticks and let it cool on the counter for 30 seconds. It should feel rigid and crisp when you pinch it — like a thin chip — not soft and pliable. That crispness tells you the water has been fully cooked out and the sugars have caramelized.

In a large mixing bowl that will also serve as your tossing bowl for the noodles, combine the warm scallion oil (about 3 tablespoons per serving), light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, and sugar. Stir together with a spoon or chopsticks until the sugar is fully dissolved. The sauce will be a dark, glossy, highly aromatic liquid — the dark soy provides color and depth, the light soy provides salinity and brightness. Taste it: it should be very salty and intensely sweet-savory, because it will dilute dramatically when tossed with the starchy noodles. The ratio of scallion oil to soy sauce is important: too much oil and the noodles are greasy; too much soy and they are one-dimensionally salty. Adjust to your preference — more dark soy for a deeper color and molasses-sweet flavor, more light soy for a brighter, saltier result.
Visual cue: A dark mahogany, glossy sauce that swirls together into a uniform deep brown with no visible sugar granules. The oil and soy should be emulsified enough to move together.
Underdone: Sugar is still visibly granular at the bottom of the bowl and the soy and oil are separating — the oil floats on top. Stir vigorously for another 30 seconds until the sugar dissolves. The residual heat from the warm oil helps.
Perfect: Uniform dark mahogany, fragrant with caramelized scallion and soy. The sauce moves as a single, slightly viscous liquid. When you dip a chopstick in and hold it up, the sauce drips in a slow, continuous stream. Add the hot cooked noodles immediately.
Overdone: Not applicable at this mixing stage — but if the scallion oil has cooled completely before mixing, the oil and soy will not emulsify. Warm the oil gently before mixing if this occurs. Warm the scallion oil for 30 seconds over low heat before combining.
Feel cue: Dip a finger into the sauce and rub it between your fingertips — it should feel slick and coating, like a thin
varnish, not watery. That viscosity comes from the caramelized scallion sugars that have dissolved into the oil during slow cooking.

Cook the noodles in a large pot of vigorously boiling, lightly salted water until just done — fresh Shanghai noodles take 2–3 minutes, dried lo mein 4–5 minutes, thin spaghetti 7–8 minutes. Drain well, shaking the colander hard. Transfer immediately to the bowl of scallion sauce while the noodles are still very hot — the heat helps the sauce coat every strand. Toss vigorously and quickly with chopsticks or tongs, lifting and folding the noodles continuously for 60–90 seconds until every strand is evenly coated in the dark, glossy sauce. The hot noodles will absorb the soy quickly, so work fast. Taste and adjust: more soy for salt, more oil for richness, a few drops of scallion oil for aroma. Transfer to a serving plate or bowl and scatter a generous amount of the reserved crispy scallion pieces over the top. Serve immediately — scallion oil noodles are a dish of the moment, and the texture deteriorates rapidly.
Visual cue: Dark mahogany-colored noodles that are glossy and evenly coated, with bright, crispy brown scallion shards scattered over the surface. No pale, undressed noodles visible. The bowl smells intensely of caramelized allium.
Underdone: Noodles are unevenly coated — some dark brown, some still pale and soy-free. The sauce is pooling at the bottom of the bowl. Continue tossing for another 30 seconds, lifting the bottom noodles to the top repeatedly until uniform.
Perfect: Every strand is a deep, uniform mahogany. The noodles are glossy and separate, not clumped. The scallion topping is crispy, dark, and aromatic. When you lift a portion with chopsticks, it comes up in loose strands coated in sauce. Eat immediately, gathering noodles and scallion in each bite.
Overdone: Noodles have been sitting too long after tossing and have absorbed all the sauce — they look dry and the scallion topping has gone limp from the steam. Drizzle a little extra scallion oil

over the top and toss again briefly to re-coat.
Feel cue: When you pick up a tangle of noodles with chopsticks, they should slip and slide against each other slightly — the oil coating each strand keeps them from clumping. If they stick together like pasta left out too long, there is not enough oil in the sauce.

name: Scallion Oil
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Neutral oil (peanut, canola, or grapeseed): 250 g
  Alternatives: rice bran oil; sunflower oil
Scallions (green onions), whole: 150 g
  Alternatives: spring onions; Chinese chives (more assertive)
Fresh ginger, peeled and sliced 5 mm thick: 30 g
Fine sea salt: 4 g
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 25 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Shanghai's most versatile condiment — neutral oil slowly infused with ginger and a mountain of scallions until they turn golden and fragrant, leaving behind an oil that elevates everything it touches.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: 食用油（Neutral oil (peanut, canola, or grapeseed)）
Fresh ginger, peeled and sliced 5 mm thick

steps:
Trim and wash the scallions thoroughly — any trapped moisture will cause the oil to splatter aggressively when they hit the pan. Pat completely dry with paper towels, or better, lay them out for 30 minutes to air-dry. Combine the oil, whole scallions, and ginger slices in a cold wok or medium saucepan. Place over medium-low heat. Starting cold is essential — it gives the scallion and ginger time to slowly release their volatile aromatic compounds into the oil before any browning occurs. As the oil heats, the scallions will begin to wilt, then soften, then bubble. The bubbling is the water content of the scallion cooking off — as long as it is bubbling vigorously, the temperature will stay below browning. Let the oil slowly infuse for 10–12 minutes, turning the scallions occasionally with tongs.
Visual cue: Scallions lying in the oil, fully submerged, actively bubbling (from their own moisture) but not yet browning — they should be limp and jade-green, the oil around them beginning to turn faintly golden and smell distinctly of toasted scallion.
Underdone: Scallions are still stiff and raw-green, the oil is barely warm, and there is no bubbling or aroma. The oil looks and smells completely neutral. Increase heat slightly to medium-low. The infusion requires sustained heat to extract the scallion's aromatic compounds — cold oil cannot do this.
Perfect: Scallions are limp and translucent, submerged in gently bubbling oil. The oil has taken on a faint golden tint and the kitchen smells sweetly of gently cooked scallion and ginger. Continue monitoring closely — once the bubbling slows, browning will begin quickly.
Overdone: Oil has come to a vigorous boil with the scallions and is spattering — the heat is too high and the aromatic extraction is going too fast, risking scorching. Reduce heat immediately to the lowest setting and stir to cool the scallions slightly. Allow

to continue infusing gently.
Feel cue: The oil should feel just barely hot when you hold your hand 15 cm above the surface — not hot enough to flinch from, but warm enough to feel on your palm clearly. This gentle, patient heat is what separates a scallion oil with delicate sweetness from one with a raw or bitter edge.

After the initial infusion, increase the heat to medium and allow the oil to continue cooking the scallions until they transition from jade-green to a pale golden-yellow, with the edges beginning to show the first signs of browning. This stage takes 5–8 minutes after the heat is raised. Watch for the moment the vigorous bubbling slows — this means the scallions have lost most of their moisture and are now beginning to actually fry in the oil rather than steam. This is when browning accelerates rapidly. As soon as the scallions are golden-yellow with pale amber tips, remove from heat — they will continue to cook in the residual heat of the oil.
Visual cue: Scallions that have collapsed from their bright-green stiff state to soft, golden-yellow, slightly translucent ribbons with pale amber at the thinnest ends and tips. The oil surrounding them is a clear, light-amber color.
Underdone: Scallions are still green and limp but not yet golden — the color has not transitioned from jade to yellow-gold, and the bubbling is still vigorous, meaning moisture is still evaporating. Continue frying with patience. The color transition from green to gold is the key signal, not a timer.
Perfect: A uniform pale golden-yellow throughout, amber at the very tips, the oil clearly tinted and smelling of sweet, toasted allium — honeyed and round rather than sharp. The scallions are fully tender and slightly crispy at the thinnest parts. Remove from heat immediately and add salt.
Overdone: Scallions have turned medium to dark brown and smell acrid or bitter. The oil is a deep amber color with a sharp, slightly burnt edge to its scent. Strain the scallions out immediately. The oil may still be usable if the browning was caught early — taste it; if bitter, discard. If merely deeper and more toasted, use it in dishes that can absorb stronger flavors.
Feel cue: Listen carefully as the infusion

progresses: the vigorous crackle of moisture escaping will slow to a quieter, gentler sizzle as the scallions dry out and begin to fry. This quieting of the sound is your cue that browning is imminent — do not leave the pan at this point.

Remove the pan from the heat and immediately stir in the salt — it will dissolve into the hot oil and season it throughout. Let the oil cool slightly for 2–3 minutes (the scallions will continue to cook in the residual heat, deepening slightly from golden to pale amber). Then strain the oil through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean heat-proof jar or container, pressing gently on the solids to extract every drop of flavored oil. Discard the spent scallion and ginger solids — they have given everything to the oil and have nothing left to offer. Let the oil cool to room temperature before sealing. It keeps refrigerated for up to 3 weeks and solidifies slightly when cold; bring to room temperature before using. Drizzle over cold noodles, steamed fish, congee, or use anywhere the gentle, sweet fragrance of scallion should be present without the texture of raw scallion.
Visual cue: A clear, light-amber oil with a warm, golden tint — noticeably deeper than neutral oil but not opaque or dark. The surface is perfectly smooth and clean, with no floating solids. Held to the light, it glows gold.
Underdone: Oil is still pale and nearly clear, barely tinted. The scallions were removed before they transferred sufficient color and aroma. The oil is still useful but mild. To intensify it, heat it again with fresh scallion and re-infuse.
Perfect: A beautiful, clear, warm-amber oil that smells of sweet, caramelized scallion and gentle ginger when held near the nose. A drizzle on a white plate shows its color instantly. Store in a sealed jar. Always use a clean, dry spoon to prevent contamination.
Overdone: Oil is a deep, dark amber approaching brown and has a bitter edge when tasted. The scallions were over-browned before straining. Taste carefully. If merely more intense and toasty without bitterness, use it in marinades or stir-fries where it will be cooked further. If bitter, discard

and start again.
Feel cue: A drizzle of finished scallion oil on the back of your hand should feel silky and clean, not greasy or heavy. It should smell unmistakably of sweet, toasted scallion — if you close your eyes, it should transport you directly to the counter of a Shanghai noodle shop.

name: 葱油饼 · Scallion Pancake (Cong You Bing)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
All-purpose flour: 2 cups
Boiling water (just off the boil): 0.5 cups
Cold water: 0.25 cups
Toasted sesame oil: 2 tbsp
  Alternatives: sesame paste thinned with neutral oil
Neutral oil (for frying): 4 tbsp
  Alternatives: lard for traditional richness
Scallions, thinly sliced: 1 cup
  Alternatives: Chinese chives
Fine sea salt: 1 tsp
Five-spice powder (optional): 0.25 tsp
  Alternatives: white pepper alone
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 1 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Shanghai's beloved street flatbread — a spiral of hot-water dough laminated with sesame oil and a blizzard of dark-green scallion, pan-fried until the exterior shatters into a thousand golden layers while the interior stays yielding and fragrant.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Place flour in a large bowl and make a well in the center. Pour the boiling water directly into the well and immediately stir with chopsticks or a fork in a circular motion from the center outward — the boiling water partially cooks (gelatinizes) the starch, producing a tender, slightly translucent dough. After stirring for 1 minute, add the cold water and continue mixing until a rough ball forms. The combination of hot and cold water produces a dough that is simultaneously soft (from the hot water gelatinization) and elastic (from the cold water activating remaining gluten). The dough will look shaggy at first — this is correct.
Visual cue: A rough dough ball that holds together. No dry flour patches. Steam rising from the mixture.
Underdone: Dry pockets of flour at the base of the bowl. The dough is crumbly and won't hold together. Add cold water one tablespoon at a time, mixing after each addition.
Perfect: A rough but cohesive ball. Slightly sticky but holds its shape. Steam rising — the hot water is still working. Turn out and knead until smooth.
Overdone: Wet and sticky. The dough flows rather than holds. Added too much water. Knead in flour one tablespoon at a time — hot-water doughs absorb flour quickly.
Feel cue: The hot-water dough feels warmer and softer than regular dough immediately after mixing — almost silky from the gelatinized starch. It is not tacky despite the softness.

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 5-7 minutes until the surface becomes very smooth. Hot-water doughs knead faster than cold-water doughs because the heat has already done structural work — do not over-knead or the dough becomes tough. The finished dough should be smooth as a pearl, non-sticky, and extremely pliable — more so than bread dough, closer to fresh pasta. Divide into 4 equal portions, cover with a damp cloth, and rest for 20-30 minutes.
Visual cue: A very smooth, slightly translucent-looking dough that can be stretched thin without tearing. More pliable than bread dough.
Underdone: Small rough spots still visible. Tears within 5 cm when stretched. Knead 2-3 more minutes. The dough is more forgiving than yeast bread — it will smooth quickly.
Perfect: Perfectly smooth, non-sticky. When a piece is pulled, it stretches without tearing to a thin, slightly translucent sheet. Cover and rest before rolling.
Overdone: The dough is warm and slightly tough — has been kneaded too long and the gluten has tightened. Rest 20 minutes before proceeding — the heat will help relax the gluten.
Feel cue: Hot-water dough is remarkably soft — it should yield under the lightest hand pressure, feeling almost like kneading a warm, dense pillow.

Working one portion at a time on a lightly floured surface, roll each piece into a thin rectangle approximately 30 x 20 cm (12 x 8 inches). Brush generously with sesame oil, leaving a 1 cm border. Scatter a quarter of the scallions evenly across the surface and season with salt and five-spice if using. Starting from the long edge closest to you, roll the rectangle tightly into a log — exactly as you'd roll a jelly roll. Then coil the log on itself into a tight spiral, tucking the tail end underneath, and press down gently to seal the coil. Let the coiled discs rest 10 minutes before flattening. Use a rolling pin to flatten each coil to about 6 mm thickness — the layered spiral compresses without losing its laminated structure.
Visual cue: A flat, circular disc showing a spiral pattern of layers when viewed from above or in cross-section. Green flecks of scallion visible throughout.
Underdone: The coil was rolled too loosely — gaps between layers, and the scallion fell out during rolling. Sesame oil pooled at the edges. Re-roll the log more tightly. Seal the edges before coiling — the oil should stay inside the layers, not escape.
Perfect: Tight, even spiral visible from above. Scallion evenly distributed throughout. Disc is uniform in thickness with no thick center mass. Fry immediately or refrigerate up to 30 minutes.
Overdone: The rolling pin has torn through the outer layer, exposing scallion and sesame oil on the surface. Patch exposed spots with a pinch of plain dough. The layers will still form during frying.
Feel cue: When pressing the coil flat with a rolling pin, you feel distinct layers resisting and compressing under the pin — a slight springiness as the spiral absorbs the pressure.

Heat a wide, heavy skillet (cast iron or carbon steel preferred) over medium-high heat until smoking. Add 1 tablespoon of neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place a pancake in the pan and cook for 2-3 minutes until the bottom is deeply golden brown with some darker spots. Flip, add another small splash of oil to the pan, and press the pancake gently but firmly with a wide spatula for 5 seconds to ensure even contact. Cook another 2-3 minutes. Flip again, pressing once more, and cook a final minute if needed. The total cooking time is 5-7 minutes — enough to cook the interior layers through while building a shattering crust. Drain briefly on a rack (not paper towels, which steam and soften the crust).
Visual cue: Deep golden-brown with darker crisped patches. Layers visible at the cut edge. The surface has an uneven, crinkled texture rather than a flat, smooth one.
Underdone: Pale golden, still soft to the touch. The interior may feel doughy when pressed. Scallion has not caramelized. Continue frying on medium heat — do not increase heat, which will burn the outside before the inside cooks.
Perfect: Dark golden to amber. Pressing the surface produces an audible crunch. Layers are visible at the edge. Fragrant with sesame and scallion. Cut reveals flaky, tender interior. Rest on a wire rack 1 minute, then cut into wedges.
Overdone: Dark brown to black in spots. The scallion has burnt rather than caramelized and smells bitter. Cut away the darkest portions. Lower the heat for future pancakes and press less firmly during cooking.
Feel cue: Press the surface of a finished pancake with a knuckle — it should give a satisfying, crisp crackle and spring back slightly, like pressing through a thin shell into a softer core beneath.

name: 葱油饼 · Scallion Pancakes (Cong You Bing)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

  Alternatives: bread flour (chewier result)
Boiling water (100 C): 130 g
Toasted sesame oil: 30 g
  Alternatives: lard for richer flavour
Fine sea salt: 5 g
Scallions (spring onions), thinly sliced: 80 g
  Alternatives: chives
Neutral oil for frying (vegetable or rapeseed): 40 g
Flaky sea salt for layering: 3 g
  Alternatives: Maldon salt
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 1 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A hot water dough is rolled flat, painted with sesame oil and salt, blanketed in scallion, then coiled and re-rolled — the same lamination trick as a croissant, but humble enough to eat on the street. The result is a flaky, chewy, pan-fried flatbread that shatters at the first bite into dozens of separated, fragrant layers.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
