ingredients.name: Neutral oil for frying (vegetable or rapeseed)

steps:
Place the flour in a bowl and pour in the boiling water all at once. Immediately stir with a chopstick or wooden spoon in circular motions until the water is absorbed and the mixture looks like a shaggy, steaming mass. The boiling water partially cooks the starch — this gelatinisation is what makes the dough pliable and the pancake chewy rather than biscuity. Once cool enough to handle (about 2 minutes), knead briefly in the bowl until a smooth dough forms — about 3 minutes. It should feel soft and slightly tacky.
Visual cue: A smooth, elastic dough ball that is noticeably softer and more supple than a standard bread dough — almost silk-like.
Underdone: Dough is still rough, shaggy, and tears when stretched. Knead for 2 more minutes — the gelatinised starch needs more working to become cohesive.
Perfect: Smooth, uniform dough that stretches without tearing, soft to the touch and slightly warm. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 30 minutes.
Overdone: Dough has been over-kneaded and is slightly rubbery, springing back aggressively. Cover and rest for 20 minutes — the gluten will relax before rolling.
Feel cue: The dough should feel distinctly softer and more yielding than pasta dough — almost ear-lobe soft — with a slight warmth still emanating from the hydrated starch.

Divide the rested dough into 4 equal pieces. On a lightly oiled surface (not floured), roll each piece into a thin rectangle about 3 mm thick. Brush generously with sesame oil to within 5 mm of the edges. Scatter salt and sliced scallion evenly across the surface, pressing lightly so they adhere. Now roll the rectangle into a tight log from the long edge, like a Swiss roll. Then coil the log into a tight snail shape and press it flat with your palm. Re-roll the coiled disc to about 5 mm thick. This double-rolling is the technique that creates the layered structure.
Visual cue: A flat disc about 18 cm diameter with visible spiral lines on the surface and faint green flecks of scallion peeking through.
Underdone: Disc is too thick (more than 8 mm) and the layers are too compressed — it will be doughy rather than flaky. Roll more firmly and evenly, working from the centre outward.
Perfect: Roughly 5 mm thick with a clear spiral pattern on the surface, pliable and cooperative under the rolling pin. Fry immediately for maximum layer definition.
Overdone: Dough has been rolled so thin that scallions are bursting through the surface. Proceed carefully — the layers are still there, just very fine. Handle gently when transferring to the pan.
Feel cue: The coiled disc should feel laminated under your palm — press it and you can sense the layered structure resist slightly differently than a single-sheet dough.

Heat a heavy skillet or cast iron pan over medium heat. Add enough neutral oil to coat the bottom with a 2 mm layer. When the oil shimmers, add one pancake. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes on the first side without moving it — the underside should be golden and crisping. Flip and press lightly with a spatula to encourage even contact with the pan. Cook the second side for 2 minutes. The pancake is done when both sides are deep golden-brown with dark, crispy edges and you can hear it crackling and hissing in the oil.
Visual cue: Both sides deep golden-brown with darker, lacey-crisp edges. The surface bubbles and blisters slightly. Scallion appears bright green through the crust.
Underdone: Pale golden, soft when pressed, doughy in the centre — the inside is not cooked. Reduce heat to medium-low, cover the pan, and cook for 2 more minutes to cook the interior without burning the outside.
Perfect: Deep golden-brown exterior, audibly crisp when tapped with a spatula, with visible layers separating at the edges. Inside is chewy and cooked through. Transfer to a cutting board. Cut into wedges and eat immediately.
Overdone: Dark brown verging on burnt, smells of scorched sesame oil, very rigid. Still edible — the char adds a smoky note. Do not cover or steam or you will lose the crispness.
Feel cue: A well-made scallion pancake crackles audibly when bent — the layers shatter like the pages of a book. If it bends silently and pliant, it needs another minute in the pan.

name: Seared Scallops with Pea Purée and Pancetta
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
King scallops, dry-packed, roe removed: 12 whole
  Alternatives: large sea scallops (U10)
Frozen garden peas: 300 g
  Alternatives: fresh peas, shelled; petit pois
Pancetta, finely diced (or lardons): 100 g
  Alternatives: guanciale; smoked bacon lardons
Shallot, finely diced: 1 large
  Alternatives: small onion
Garlic, minced: 1 clove
Unsalted butter: 60 g
Double cream (heavy cream): 60 ml
  Alternatives: crème fraîche
Fresh mint leaves: 10 g
  Alternatives: basil leaves
Fresh lemon juice: 10 ml
Neutral oil (sunflower or grapeseed): 15 ml
  Alternatives: clarified butter
Fine sea salt: 5 g
White pepper: 1 g
  Alternatives: black pepper
Pea shoots or watercress: 20 g
  Alternatives: micro herbs; baby cress
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Pan-seared king scallops with a velvety, sweet pea purée and crispy pancetta — a three-part restaurant classic with a brutally simple margin for error on the sear: golden on one side, translucent at the centre.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Melt 20 g of the butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the diced shallot and garlic with a pinch of salt and sweat gently for 3–4 minutes until completely soft and translucent — no color at all. Add the frozen peas and double cream, bring to a simmer, and cook for 3 minutes until the peas are just tender and brilliant green. Transfer everything to a blender, add the mint leaves, and blend on high until completely smooth. Pass through a fine sieve if you want restaurant-level silkiness. Season with salt, white pepper, and a small squeeze of lemon. Keep warm.
Visual cue: A smooth, vivid green purée with the sheen of a fine vegetable cream. It falls off a spoon in a slow, controlled ribbon.
Underdone: Purée is lumpy and pale — peas were not cooked long enough before blending, and the shallot is still gritty. Return to the blender and process for longer. If still lumpy, push through a fine sieve.
Perfect: The purée is a vivid, uniform spring green with a velvet surface. It falls in a slow ribbon from the spoon and holds its shape on the plate. The mint is present but not dominant. Keep covered in a warm bain-marie or low oven.
Overdone: Purée has turned a dull, grey-green — the peas were overcooked and the chlorophyll has broken down. Proceed. The flavor is still good but the color is lost. Next time, cook peas for only 3 minutes and blend immediately.
Feel cue: The purée should flow off a warm spoon like thick paint — neither so stiff it sits rigid nor so thin it runs into a puddle on the plate.

Place the diced pancetta in a cold dry frying pan and set over medium heat. As the fat renders slowly, the pancetta will crisp evenly without burning. Cook for 5–7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the dice are deeply golden and crispy and the surrounding fat has fully rendered out. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel. Reserve the rendered fat in the pan — this will be used to sear the scallops.
Visual cue: Dice are a deep, even mahogany. Crispy throughout with no soft or chewy centres. Fat has fully rendered clear.
Underdone: Pancetta is golden but still soft and yielding. Fat is not fully rendered — dice will be chewy rather than crispy. Continue cooking over medium heat for 2–3 more minutes.
Perfect: Dice are uniformly dark gold to light mahogany, crispy all the way through, and shatter slightly when pressed. The rendered fat is clear gold. Remove and drain immediately — they will continue to color from residual heat.
Overdone: Dice are very dark brown, beginning to smell acrid. The rendered fat is browning. Remove and drain. Trim any blackened pieces. The flavor will be intensely smoky rather than balanced — use a smaller amount.
Feel cue: Crispy pancetta should shatter with a clean snap between your fingers, not bend or feel leathery. If it bends, it needs more time.

Pat the scallops completely dry with paper towel — this is the single most important step. Any surface moisture will steam rather than sear. Season both flat faces with salt and white pepper. Add the neutral oil to the pancetta-fat pan and heat over the highest possible heat until the oil just begins to smoke. Place scallops flat-side down in the pan, one by one, and do not touch them for exactly 90 seconds to 2 minutes. The sear must be uninterrupted. They are ready to flip when they release easily from the pan — not when the timer says so.
Visual cue: A deep mahogany-gold crust on the bottom face. The sides of the scallop are opaque white and cooked approximately two-thirds of the way up. The very top remains translucent and glossy.
Underdone: The sear is pale gold, patchy, or non-existent. The scallop stuck to the pan when you tried to flip it. Leave it. A scallop releases itself from a hot pan when the crust has formed — it will not release until then.
Perfect: A defined, dark gold caramelized crust on the seared face. Sides are white to two-thirds up. The top center is still translucent and lightly glossy — the scallop is essentially raw at its very heart, which is correct. Flip, cook 30–45 seconds, add cold butter, and baste.
Overdone: Scallop is fully opaque white all the way through. The sear is very dark. The scallop feels firm when pressed. Remove immediately and plate. An overcooked scallop is rubbery — serve it as quickly as possible, the sauce and purée will help.
Feel cue: Press a scallop gently with your fingertip after flipping — it should feel like a soft, resilient pillow with a slight give. Rubbery firmness means it is overcooked.

The moment the scallops are flipped, add the remaining cold butter to the pan in two pieces. It will melt and foam immediately in the residual heat. Tilt the pan and use a spoon to continuously baste the scallops with the foaming butter for 30–45 seconds. Add a tiny squeeze of lemon. Remove scallops the moment the second side shows a pale gold — the center should still feel yielding. Rest on a warm plate for 30 seconds while you arrange the components.
Visual cue: Scallops are golden on both flat faces with white sides. Brown butter foam clings to the surface. The plate beneath them glistens with butter.
Underdone: Second face is still pale and uncrusted. Butter is not foaming — pan has lost too much heat from adding cold butter. Increase heat briefly to restore the foam and continue basting.
Perfect: Both faces are golden. The butter has foamed and turned a pale nut-brown, imparting a hazelnut note. Scallops feel soft and yielding. The center is translucent when sliced. Plate immediately — scallops wait for no one.
Overdone: Butter has burned beyond brown to black. Acrid smell. Scallops feel firm throughout. Plate immediately. Wipe excess dark butter from the scallops with a clean spoon before serving.
Feel cue: The basting butter should foam and hiss constantly — the moment it goes quiet, either the heat is too low or the scallops need to come out.

Working quickly, spoon a swoosh of warm pea purée across each plate using the back of a warm spoon. Arrange three scallops per plate on and around the purée, seared-side facing up to display the crust. Scatter the crispy pancetta dice over and around the scallops. Finish with a small cluster of pea shoots or watercress placed in the center, dressed with a tiny drizzle of olive oil. The three elements must arrive together: any one of them cold ruins the dish.
Visual cue: Vivid green purée, three golden-crusted scallops, mahogany pancetta crumble, and bright green shoots — four distinct colors and textures on the plate.
Underdone: Purée is cold and has formed a skin. Pancetta has softened from humidity. Components feel assembled in stages rather than simultaneously. This dish waits for nothing. Everything must be warm and assembled in under 90 seconds.
Perfect: Purée is warm and vivid green. Scallops are hot with a crackling crust. Pancetta is crispy. Pea shoots are fresh and upright. All three temperatures and textures are present simultaneously. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Pea shoots have wilted over the hot scallops. Purée has spread flat across the plate. Components have merged into each other. Plate more quickly next time. A warm, pre-heated plate helps keep components in place.
Feel cue: When you cut through a perfect scallop it should yield with almost no resistance at the edges, then offer a slight, creamy resistance at the translucent center — like cutting through cold butter that has been left out for ten minutes.

name: Schiacciata
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Type 0 or bread flour: 100 parts
  Alternatives: all-purpose flour
Warm water (32-35 C): 70 parts
Extra-virgin olive oil, plus generous amount for pan and top: 8 parts
Fine sea salt: 2 parts
Instant yeast: 0.8 parts
  Alternatives: active dry yeast, proofed first
Flaky sea salt (Maldon or Fiore di Sale): 0.3 parts
Fresh rosemary leaves (optional): 0.1 parts
  Alternatives: sage leaves; thyme
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 2 hours 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Tuscany's answer to focaccia — thinner, crispier at the edges, and so saturated with good olive oil that the first bite releases a warm, grassy flood — the word 'schiacciata' means crushed, and the flat, dimpled dough delivers exactly that: deliberately pressed-down, maximally crisp.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Extra-virgin olive oil, plus generous amount for pan and top
Flaky sea salt (Maldon or Fiore di Sale)

steps:
Combine the flour, instant yeast, and fine salt in a large bowl, keeping the salt and yeast on opposite sides of the bowl initially. Pour in the warm water and olive oil. Mix with a dough scraper or your hand until no dry flour remains — the dough will be moderately sticky, softer than a bread dough but not as wet as focaccia. It should pull away from the sides of the bowl. Do not add more flour. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.
Visual cue: A rough, cohesive dough with no dry flour pockets. Sticks to the bowl slightly but holds together as a mass.
Underdone: Dry pockets of flour remaining at the base of the bowl. Dough won't come together. Add water a teaspoon at a time and continue mixing until no dry flour remains.
Perfect: Rough, slightly sticky dough that holds together. No dry spots. Pulls away from the sides when pressed. Cover and rest 15 minutes for autolyse.
Overdone: Dough has been over-worked and is already becoming smooth and elastic. This is not a problem at this stage. Proceed to folding.
Feel cue: The dough should feel like a soft, slightly tacky earlobe — pliable and alive, sticking lightly to your fingers but releasing without tearing.

Perform three sets of stretch-and-fold over 60 minutes, one set every 20 minutes. For each set: wet your hand, grab the dough at one side of the bowl, stretch it firmly upward as far as it will reach without tearing, then fold it over the center. Rotate the bowl 90 degrees and repeat until you have completed four folds. After three sets, the dough should be noticeably smoother, more cohesive, and beginning to show bubbles beneath the surface. Cover and let bulk ferment at room temperature for another 30 minutes until puffy.
Visual cue: After the third fold set, a smooth, billowing dough with visible bubbles beneath the surface. When the bowl is tapped, the dough jiggles.
Underdone: Dough still tears easily during folding. No visible bubbles. Flat and dense in the bowl. Continue fold sets. Let the dough rest longer between folds if tearing persists.
Perfect: Smooth, slightly domed, noticeably lighter than when mixing began. Bubbles visible. Stretches extensibly without tearing. Oil the pan and transfer.
Overdone: Over-fermented — very gassy, smells strongly acidic, and deflates when touched. Work quickly — move to the pan immediately and bake as soon as it spreads.
Feel cue: By the third set, folding the dough should feel like working with silk — it stretches generously and resists elastically, and the bowl gives a gentle thud when set down on the counter, heavier than before.

Pour a very generous amount of olive oil onto a half-sheet pan or rimmed baking tray — at least 4-5 tablespoons. Schiacciata is an olive oil bread and should practically float in it. Transfer the dough to the pan and use your fingertips to begin pressing and stretching it toward the edges. If the dough springs back firmly, cover and wait 10-15 minutes, then try again. The dough should eventually be pressed quite flat — roughly 1.5 cm thick throughout. Cover with plastic wrap and proof at room temperature for 30-45 minutes until noticeably puffy and slightly domed.
Visual cue: Dough stretched to fill the pan in a thin, even layer, visibly risen and puffy, pooled in olive oil.
Underdone: Dough has barely spread, still a thick mound in the center. Not yet puffy. Cover and rest 15 more minutes. Proofing at 75 F / 24 C speeds things up.
Perfect: Thin, even layer filling most of the pan. Visibly puffy and alive. Oil has pooled around and under the dough. Press with fingertips to flatten and dimple, then bake immediately.
Overdone: Over-proofed — dough has spread very thin and the surface looks bubbly and collapsed. Bake immediately. Over-proofed schiacciata is still delicious — just slightly denser crumb.
Feel cue: Gently press the surface with one finger — it should indent slowly and spring back about halfway over 3-4 seconds. Instant spring-back means underproofed; no spring-back means overproofed.

Using all ten fingers held flat, press the dough firmly and repeatedly across its entire surface, pushing all the way through to the pan. The dough should be pressed quite flat — flatter than focaccia. This is the 'schiacciata' — the crushing. Drizzle another generous pour of olive oil across the entire surface, letting it pool in the dimples. Scatter the flaky salt and rosemary leaves if using. The salt goes on now, not after baking.
Visual cue: A flat, dimpled landscape of dough with olive oil pooling in every finger-crater. Flaky salt and rosemary evenly distributed.
Underdone: Dough is still too thick and rounded. Dimples are shallow and fill back in immediately. Press more firmly and repeatedly. Schiacciata should be distinctly flatter than focaccia.
Perfect: Flat, deeply dimpled across the whole surface. Oil pooled in every depression. Salt glints on top. 1-1.5 cm thick at the thickest point. Into a 230 C (450 F) oven immediately.
Overdone: Pressed so flat it has torn in places. Very thin, translucent spots. Press the torn spots back together gently. They will heal in the oven.
Feel cue: Your fingers should feel the resistance of the puffy dough and then break through to meet the slick pan — press with the confidence of someone who knows the dough can take it.

Bake at 230 C (450 F) on the lowest rack for 15-20 minutes. Schiacciata bakes hotter and faster than focaccia because it is thinner. Watch carefully after 12 minutes. The edges should be deep brown and very crisp; the center should be golden. Remove from the pan immediately to a wire rack — do not let it cool in the pan or the bottom will steam and soften. Cool for 5 minutes before cutting. Schiacciata is best eaten within 1 hour of baking, while the contrast between the crisp exterior and the moist, oily crumb is still at its peak.
Visual cue: Very deep, almost charred edges, a golden center, and a bottom that is uniformly dark amber and releases from the pan with a crackle.
Underdone: Pale gold, soft crust that bends rather than snaps. Bottom is blond. Return to oven and increase to top rack if the center is pale. Check every 2 minutes.
Perfect: Dark, crisp edges almost verging on charred. Golden center. Bottom is deep amber-brown, crisp, and audibly crackles when lifted. Remove from the pan immediately and cool on a rack.
Overdone: Truly burnt edges — acrid, bitter smell. Edges are black rather than dark brown. Cut off the burnt edges with kitchen shears. The center is likely still perfect.
Feel cue: Pick up a finished piece and squeeze it gently between two fingers — you should hear and feel a crisp crackle followed by a yielding, oily interior. The olive oil should glisten on your fingertips.

ingredients.name: 鸡蛋（Eggs (large, for boiling, very fresh)）
黑胡椒（Black pepper, white pepper, mace blend）

steps:
Lower eggs gently into a pot of vigorously boiling water. Cook exactly 6 minutes 30 seconds for a jammy, coral yolk. Transfer immediately to an ice bath and chill for 10 minutes — this stops the carry-over cook that turns yolks grey. Peel carefully under cold running water, keeping the white intact. Pat dry with paper towels.
Visual cue: Peeled eggs with intact, gleaming whites. The egg, when cut, shows a set outer yolk layer and a flowing, deep-orange interior.
Underdone: White still has translucent patches near the yolk. Egg feels soft all the way through and is difficult to peel cleanly. Boil a replacement egg for 7 minutes — you need structural integrity for wrapping. A too-soft white tears when you apply the sausage.
Perfect: White is fully set, firm enough to hold shape during wrapping. Yolk is custardy at the center, a deep orange-gold. Peels in clean sheets. Ice bath and peel promptly — any delay carries over heat to the yolk.
Overdone: Yolk has fully set to a pale yellow, dry and powdery when cut. Grey-green ring possible if left too long. The egg will still work for a Scotch egg — a fully set yolk is a legitimate style choice — but the runny center is lost.
Feel cue: Hold a peeled egg in your palm and close your fingers gently — it should feel firm but yield very slightly under pressure, like a hard grape, not a ping-pong ball.

Mix sausage meat with salt and spice blend until evenly seasoned. Fry a small patty in a dry pan and taste — the sausage should be boldly seasoned, as the egg and breadcrumbs will dilute its flavor. Adjust. Divide the meat into equal portions — one per egg. Flatten each portion into a thin, even disc on a sheet of cling film.
Visual cue: A uniform, pale-pink disc of sausage meat about 12 cm across and 5 mm thick, with visible fat marbling and no dry or uneven patches.
Underdone: Disc too thick or uneven — one end 1 cm, the other 3 mm. Will leave bare patches on the egg when wrapped. Re-press through the film into an even thickness. Use a rolling pin if needed.
Perfect: Even, pliable disc that clings to the film without tearing. Fat visible as lighter streaks. Smells of pork and spice. Proceed to wrapping immediately — cold sausage meat wraps more cleanly.
Overdone: Overworked into a gummy, dense paste that no longer shows fat marbling. Temperature has climbed above 10 C from hand heat. Refrigerate for 15 minutes before wrapping — warm, overworked sausage sticks to hands and tears.
Feel cue: Pressed between two fingers, the sausage meat should feel tacky and plastic — it grips rather than slides, holds its shape without springing back.

Dust each boiled egg lightly with flour — this helps the sausage grip. Lay a flattened sausage disc on cling film and center the egg on top. Use the film to lift and wrap the sausage around the egg, sealing it with wet hands and pinching any seams closed. Roll in flour, dip in beaten egg, then coat thoroughly in panko, pressing to adhere. Rest in the fridge for 20 minutes.
Visual cue: A smooth, even sphere of sausage-wrapped egg completely encased in panko crumbs with no bare meat patches or gaps.
Underdone: Bare patches of sausage visible through thin or missing breadcrumb coating. Seams not sealed. Re-dip in beaten egg wherever the crumb is thin or absent, then re-roll in panko. Seal any seams firmly — gaps burst open in the fryer.
Perfect: Even, ball-shaped sphere, completely white-gold with panko. No visible meat or egg. Feels firm and slightly heavy when lifted. Refrigerate to firm up the coating before frying.
Overdone: Double-coated and overly thick — the breadcrumb layer is 5+ mm, bulky like a croquette. Will burn before the sausage cooks through. This is almost impossible to over-coat with one pass. If you have thick spots, gently press them thinner.
Feel cue: Holding the breaded egg, it should feel like a cricket ball — smooth, firm, and pleasingly heavy, with a faint give from the sausage layer beneath.

Heat oil to 170 C (338 F) in a deep, heavy pot. Lower Scotch eggs in carefully — do not crowd the pot. Fry for 7–8 minutes, turning every 2 minutes for even color, until the crumb is a deep, even mahogany and the sausage reaches 70 C (158 F) internal. Drain on a rack, not paper towels. Rest 5 minutes before cutting.
Visual cue: A deeply golden-brown, crackling sphere with an even, uniformly dark amber crust — no pale patches, no burnt spots.
Underdone: Pale golden crust with white or light patches. Internal temperature below 70 C — sausage undercooked. Reduce oil temperature 10 degrees (it may have been too hot, cooking the outside fast while the inside lagged) and continue frying. Use a probe thermometer.
Perfect: Deep amber-mahogany all over, crackling audibly when tapped with a fingernail. Sausage at 70–72 C. Cut open: clean white breadcrumb interior around a ring of pink sausage around a coral yolk. Drain on a rack and rest 5 minutes. Serve with English mustard and dressed salad.
Overdone: Very dark brown to near-black crust. Bitter smell of scorched breadcrumbs. Oil may be too hot. The interior may still be fine — cut open and check. Slice off the darkest crust with a sharp knife and serve. Lower oil temperature for subsequent batches.
Feel cue: Tap the surface with a metal spoon — a perfect crust rings back with a dry, sharp knock, not a dull thud. The egg should feel noticeably firm under the crust.

ingredients.name: 鸡蛋（Eggs, for the centres (large, very fresh)）
Good-quality pork sausage meat (or sausages, skinned)
Dijon mustard, fine salt, and black pepper
Fresh sage and thyme, finely chopped together
鸡蛋（Eggs, beaten for the coating (2 eggs)）

steps:
Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Gently lower the eggs on a spoon — do not drop them or the shells will crack. Boil for exactly 6 minutes for a runny-firm yolk that will hold together during frying. Transfer immediately to an ice bath — a bowl of water with as much ice as you can spare — and leave for 5 full minutes. The cold stops the carry-over cooking that would ruin the yolk. Peel carefully under cold running water, starting from the wide air-pocket end. The whites will be very delicate.
Visual cue: Peeled eggs with firm, completely set whites and a golden-orange yolk that is set at the edges but trembling and gel-like at the centre.
Underdone: The white is still soft and tears when handling. Yolk is fully liquid and the egg will not survive being wrapped in sausage meat. At 5 minutes you get a nearly liquid white — if this happens, fry immediately or the egg will be impossible to wrap. Adjust timing to 6 min 30 sec for more substantial whites.
Perfect: White is fully set and peels cleanly without tearing. Yolk is deep orange, gel-like, and trembles when the egg is gently shaken — completely set at the surface but flowing inside. Handle gently — these eggs have delicate whites that bruise easily. Proceed to wrapping within 20 minutes while still cool.
Overdone: Yolk is pale yellow, fully set and chalky throughout. A grey-green ring may be forming around the yolk from the sulphur. A fully cooked yolk inside a Scotch egg is edible but misses the entire point. Next time ice-bath immediately and reduce timing to 6 minutes exactly.
Feel cue: Hold a peeled egg in your palm — it should feel cool and very slightly yielding when you close your fingers, like pressing a water balloon. Solid all the way through means overcooked.

Combine the sausage meat, mustard, chopped herbs, nutmeg, and a generous seasoning of salt and pepper in a bowl. Mix with your hands until the seasonings are fully incorporated and the mixture feels slightly tacky and cohesive — no streaks of mustard visible. Fry a small nugget in a hot dry pan and taste it: the sausage should be boldly seasoned, herby, and slightly mustardy. Season more aggressively than seems right — the breaded exterior and the bland egg will absorb a lot of that punch.
Visual cue: A cohesive, evenly mixed pale-pink sausage paste — no visible streaks of mustard or clumps of herbs, no separate white fat pieces.
Underdone: Yellow mustard streaks clearly visible through the pork. Herb pieces not yet distributed. Mixture is not yet cohesive. Continue mixing with your hands. The heat of your hands helps the fat bind the mixture together.
Perfect: Completely homogenous pale-pink mixture that peels cleanly away from the bowl sides. Holds a shape when squeezed. Smells herby and mustardy. Divide into 6 equal portions and flatten each into a thin round before wrapping the eggs.
Overdone: You have overworked warm sausage meat until the fat is beginning to separate — the mixture looks greasy and slightly grey. Chill in the refrigerator for 15 minutes to firm the fat before wrapping the eggs. Cold sausage meat wraps more cleanly and holds its shape.
Feel cue: The sausage mixture should feel like firm playdough — pliable and smooth, holding the impression of your fingers without sticking to them.

Working with one portion of sausage meat at a time, flatten it in your damp palm into a thin, even oval about 3 mm thick. Set a peeled boiled egg in the centre. Bring the edges of the sausage up and around the egg, pressing gently to seal at the top. Work around the egg, ensuring the sausage layer is even all the way around — thin spots will burst open in the fryer. Roll gently between your palms to even out the surface and seal any seams. The finished shape should be a uniform oval with no visible egg beneath.
Visual cue: A smooth, evenly wrapped oval of pale sausage with no cracks, seams, or visible egg showing through. All six eggs uniform in size.
Underdone: Sausage has thin spots where the egg is visible through the meat, or the top seam has not been properly sealed. The sausage layer is uneven — thick on one side and paper-thin on the other. Pinch and press more sausage over thin spots. Wet hands help prevent sticking. Even thickness is essential — thin spots overcook and burst while thicker sections are still raw.
Perfect: A firm, smooth, uniformly thick sausage casing around each egg. No visible cracks. Uniform oval shape across all 6. The seam is fully pressed closed. Refrigerate for 15 minutes before breading — chilling firms the sausage and makes dredging much tidier.
Overdone: Sausage layer is so thick (over 10 mm) that the centre of the meat will not cook through by the time the outside is deep-golden. Re-wrap using less sausage per egg, aiming for a consistent 5–7 mm layer all around.
Feel cue: Hold a wrapped egg in your hand — it should feel dense and cold, with no soft patches where the sausage is thin. Even firmness all around means even frying.

Set up three shallow bowls: one with flour seasoned with salt and pepper, one with the beaten eggs, one with the panko breadcrumbs. Working one at a time, roll a wrapped egg firmly in the flour, patting off any excess (a thick flour coat creates pastiness). Dip in beaten egg, letting any excess drip for 3 seconds. Roll in panko, pressing the crumbs firmly into every surface — no bare patches. For an extra-crunchy crust, repeat the egg-and-panko dip for a second coat. Set on a rack.
Visual cue: A completely, evenly coated oval with no bare spots, the golden panko crumbs visibly clinging in an even, slightly textured layer.
Underdone: Panko has not been pressed firmly and is falling off in patches. Several bare spots of sausage meat visible. The coating will fall off in the hot oil. Press the crumbs more firmly all over with cupped palms. Re-dip in egg and re-coat in panko any bare areas before the egg dries.
Perfect: Complete, even panko coat with good coverage and visible texture. No bare patches. The oval feels slightly heavier and firmer from the coating. Chill for 10 minutes before frying — a cold, set coating adheres better in the hot oil than a warm, soft one.
Overdone: An excessively thick, lumpy coating from too many layers of egg and crumbs — 3 or more coats. The exterior looks bumpy and uneven. Two coats maximum. A thick coating absorbs too much oil and becomes soggy before the sausage is cooked through.
Feel cue: Squeeze the breaded egg gently — it should feel rigid and fully coated, with no soft yielding spots where crumbs have fallen away to expose sausage.

Heat at least 8 cm of oil in a heavy, deep pot to 170°C (340°F) — slightly cooler than standard frying temperature to allow the thick sausage layer to cook through before the crumbs burn. Carefully lower 2 or 3 eggs at a time (never crowd). Fry for 7–8 minutes, turning every 90 seconds for even colour, until the crust is a deep mahogany-brown and the eggs float freely. Transfer to a wire rack (not paper towels) for 2–3 minutes to let residual heat finish cooking the centre. Test by pressing: the crust should feel rigid, not soft.
Visual cue: Deep mahogany-brown Scotch eggs floating in the oil, with an evenly coloured, crackling-crisp exterior. No pale patches.
Underdone: Crust is pale golden, not yet deep brown. Oil may have been too cool. The sausage layer will still be raw or pink at the centre. Continue frying. If the oil is cool, the crumbs will absorb fat and become greasy before the sausage is cooked. Verify oil temperature with a probe.
Perfect: Deep mahogany brown, floating, turning freely in the oil. Cut open after resting: sausage is fully cooked through with no pink, and the yolk is golden-orange and gel-like at the centre. Rest on a wire rack for at least 2 minutes before cutting — the yolk continues setting and the crust sets firm off the heat.
Overdone: Crust is very dark brown approaching black. A bitter, burnt-crumb smell. The oil temperature was too high or frying time too long. Remove immediately. The sausage interior and egg are likely still fine — peel off the darkest sections of crust before serving if very burnt.
Feel cue: Tap the Scotch egg with a knuckle immediately out of the fryer — it should sound hollow and sharp, like knocking on pottery. A dull thud means the crust hasn't crisped.

name: Scottish Kedgeree
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。

  Alternatives: smoked cod; hot-smoked salmon (flake in after cooking)

  Alternatives: half milk half water

  Alternatives: long-grain white rice

  Alternatives: ghee for more depth
Yellow onion, finely diced: 150 g
  Alternatives: shallots
Mild curry powder (Madras-style): 10 g
  Alternatives: 1 tsp each: turmeric, cumin, coriander
Fine sea salt: 5 g
Eggs, large: 4 whole
Flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped: 20 g
  Alternatives: cilantro for a more Indian note
Lemon: 1 whole
  Alternatives: lime
Heavy cream (optional, for richness): 60 ml
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A colonial-era dish born from Indian khichdi and Scottish smoked haddock — basmati rice scented with curry and butter, folded with flakes of golden haddock and gently hard-boiled eggs, scattered with crisp parsley and a squeeze of lemon.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Place the haddock skin-side down in a wide pan. Pour over the milk — it should just cover the fish. Bring to the barest simmer over medium-low heat. As soon as the milk begins to shiver and small bubbles appear around the edges (not a full boil), turn off the heat, cover the pan, and let the fish poach in the residual heat for 8–10 minutes. Lift the fish out and reserve the poaching milk. When cool enough to handle, peel off and discard the skin, then flake the flesh into large chunks, checking for pin bones.
Visual cue: Large, moist, opaque white-to-pale-gold flakes with no translucency remaining, skin removed cleanly.
Underdone: The flesh is still translucent in the thicker parts and resists flaking — it pulls in strings rather than separating into clean pieces. Return to the covered pan for another 3 minutes. The residual milk heat will be sufficient.
Perfect: The fish flakes into large, moist, golden pieces at the touch of a fork. No raw translucency. The milk beneath is opaque and white with rendered fish oils. Remove fish and reserve the poaching milk for the rice.
Overdone: The fish has broken into tiny shreds and the flesh is dry and stringy. The milk is boiling and curdling. The flavor is intact — proceed with smaller flakes. The dish will be more homogeneous but still delicious.
Feel cue: The thickest part of the haddock should offer no resistance when pressed with a finger — yielding completely, like firmly set tofu.

Bring a pot of water to a full boil. Lower the eggs in gently and cook for exactly 8 minutes for yolks that are set but still have a faintly creamy center — a true soft-set rather than chalky hard-boiled. Transfer immediately to a bowl of ice water for 2 minutes to stop the cooking and make them easier to peel. Peel and cut into quarters lengthwise.
Visual cue: Peeled eggs with fully opaque, set whites and yolks that are pale yellow and fully set but not yet chalky-grey at the edges.
Underdone: Yolk is runny and liquid in the center, making quartering messy — the yolk runs out. Add 1–2 more minutes. A fully soft-set yolk is the target for kedgeree.
Perfect: Yolk is set and yellow throughout with a hint of a slightly creamier center. White is firm and peels cleanly. Quarter and set aside until assembly.
Overdone: A grey-green ring forms around the yolk — the sulfur reaction from overcooking. Yolk is chalky and dry. Still usable. Next time reduce time by 1 minute and use ice bath immediately.
Feel cue: A perfectly cooked egg at 8 minutes feels completely firm when squeezed gently in the shell — no soft spot at the yolk end — yet yields a just-set, slightly yielding yolk when cut.

In a large, wide saucepan, melt the butter over medium heat. Add the diced onion with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring, for 8–10 minutes until soft, translucent, and beginning to turn pale gold at the edges. Add the curry powder and stir for 60–90 seconds until the spices bloom and turn fragrant and dark. Add the rinsed rice and stir to coat every grain in the spiced butter — about 1 minute. Measure 450 ml of the reserved haddock poaching milk (top up with water if needed) and pour it over the rice. Season lightly with salt, remembering the fish and milk are already salty. Bring to a boil, reduce to the lowest simmer, cover tightly, and cook 12 minutes. Remove from heat and steam, lid on, for 5 more minutes.
Visual cue: Rice grains are separate, golden-yellow from the turmeric in the curry powder, with no pooling water or sticky clumping.
Underdone: Rice has a hard, chalky center when bitten. The grains are slightly opaque and pool a little liquid at the bottom of the pan. Add 30 ml more liquid, re-cover, and cook another 5 minutes on the lowest possible heat.
Perfect: Each grain is separate and fully cooked with a slight al dente give. The rice smells of butter, curry, and smoked fish milk. No liquid remains. Fold in the fish, eggs, cream, and parsley.
Overdone: Rice is clumped, mushy, and the grains have broken down. The pan smells of scorched starch on the bottom. Fold in the other ingredients gently to minimize further breakdown. Scorched bottom: spoon from the top only.
Feel cue: Correctly cooked basmati should have the faintest spring when pressed between thumb and forefinger — soft throughout but not squashing to paste.

If using cream, pour it over the rice and fold gently with a wide spatula. Add the flaked haddock in large pieces and fold just twice or three times — you want chunks, not paste. Add half the parsley. Fold once more. Taste and adjust salt and lemon juice — the dish wants brightness. Arrange the egg quarters across the top, scatter the remaining parsley, and bring the pan to the table with lemon halves alongside. Kedgeree is traditionally served at breakfast or brunch, warm but not screaming hot.
Visual cue: Golden rice flecked with large white-and-amber haddock pieces, bright green parsley scattered throughout, and pale egg quarters arranged across the top.
Underdone: The rice looks pale and the fish has disappeared into fine shreds from over-folding. The dish looks grey and homogeneous. Stop folding immediately. Add more parsley for color and arrange egg quarters prominently for visual contrast.
Perfect: Distinct textures visible: separate rice grains, recognizable fish flakes, green herb, golden yolk quarters. The color is warm amber-gold. Smell is rich, smoky, and spiced. Serve immediately or hold covered on very low heat for up to 10 minutes.
Overdone: The rice is clumping from over-stirring. The fish has shredded to paste and the eggs have broken. Press into a serving dish and garnish generously to restore visual appeal.
Feel cue: Each serving should have contrasting textures in a single spoonful — the slight resistance of rice grains, the tender yield of haddock flakes, and the soft give of egg yolk.

ingredients.name: Dry-packed sea scallops (U10, adductor muscle removed)
Neutral oil with high smoke point (grapeseed, avocado)

steps:
This step is the non-negotiable foundation of a well-seared scallop. Lay the scallops on a wire rack set over a baking tray. Season each one lightly on both flat faces with fine sea salt. Refrigerate uncovered for at least 20 minutes, up to 1 hour. The salt draws moisture to the surface through osmosis, which then evaporates in the cold, circulating air of the refrigerator, leaving the scallop surface perfectly dry. A wet scallop surface will steam in the pan rather than sear — the water must flash to steam before any browning can begin, effectively lowering the effective surface temperature below the Maillard threshold. 'Dry-packed' scallops (never treated with sodium tripolyphosphate) are essential — wet-packed scallops have already been soaked in a phosphate solution that prevents browning entirely.
Visual cue: The surface of each scallop looks matte and slightly tacky — not glistening or wet, not powdery-dry.
Underdone: Scallops are still visibly wet and shiny after salting — not enough time or not cold enough. Pat dry with paper towels and return uncovered to the refrigerator for 15 more minutes.
Perfect: Surface looks lightly frosted, matte, and tacky when touched — moisture has been drawn out and evaporated. Remove from the refrigerator 5 minutes before searing to take the chill off the very surface.
Overdone: Over an hour in the refrigerator — scallops have slightly stiffened and lost some of their delicate, translucent quality. Proceed immediately. They will still sear beautifully; the cure is very forgiving up to 1.5 hours.
Feel cue: A properly dry-brined scallop feels tacky when pressed lightly — like the surface of a Post-it note — not slick, not powdery. That stickiness is the protein matrix that will bond to the pan and release cleanly once the crust forms.

Heat a heavy cast-iron or stainless steel skillet over the highest heat for at least 3 minutes — the pan must be thoroughly preheated, not just warm. Add the neutral oil; it should immediately begin to shimmer and whisper. Place the scallops flat-face down, spacing them at least 3 cm apart. You must hear a loud, aggressive sizzle the moment they contact the pan — if you don't, the pan is not hot enough. Do not touch, shake, or move the scallops for a full 90 seconds. Resist every urge to peek underneath. After 90 seconds, gently try to slide a thin spatula under one scallop: if it releases cleanly, the crust has formed. If it resists, wait another 15 seconds. Flip each scallop. The sear should reveal a uniform, mahogany-brown crust across the entire flat face — not patchy, not pale in the center.
Visual cue: A deep, uniform mahogany-brown crust across the entire flat seared face. The sides of the scallop should have changed from translucent to opaque white halfway up.
Underdone: The flat face is pale gold or blond, with patches of pink-translucent where the scallop was curved. The Maillard crust is incomplete. Do not flip. Give it 30 more seconds of undisturbed contact with the hot pan.
Perfect: Uniform deep mahogany on the full flat face, crisp to the touch. Sides show white opaque band reaching halfway up. Caramel-sweet aroma. Flip and proceed to beurre noisette immediately — the second side needs only 30–45 seconds.
Overdone: Dark brown verging on black. Scallop has shrunk significantly and feels firm even at the top. Remove from the pan immediately. The crust will be bitter; the interior may still be correctly cooked. Trim and serve.
Feel cue: Press the top (unseared side) of a scallop lightly with your finger while it cooks on the first side — it should feel completely soft and raw, like pressing a raw prawn. That softness is your control: once the top firms
slightly, the interior is nearly at temperature.

After flipping the scallops, immediately add the cold cubed butter to the pan in one addition. The cold butter hitting the hot pan will erupt with sizzling foam. As soon as the foam subsides and the butter begins to turn golden (this takes about 45–60 seconds), you will see it shift to an amber color and smell a distinctly hazelnut aroma — this is beurre noisette (brown butter): the milk proteins in the butter are caramelizing. Add the rinsed capers. Using a large spoon, immediately begin basting the scallops by tilting the pan slightly toward you and spooning the hot, hazelnut-scented brown butter over each scallop continuously. Baste for 30–45 seconds. Total second-side contact time (including basting): 60–75 seconds. The scallops are done when they still feel slightly soft and yielding at the very center when pressed.
Visual cue: Amber-golden, foamy butter with small brown milk-solid flecks, capers sizzling and jumping in the fat, scallops glistening from basting.
Underdone: Butter is still pale and foamy, not yet noisette — adding capers now will slow browning. Scallops are not yet basted. Wait for the butter to shift to amber before beginning to baste.
Perfect: Butter is a clear amber with dark flecks of toasted milk protein, smelling intensely of hazelnuts. Capers are golden and beginning to open. Scallops shimmer. Remove pan from heat and squeeze lemon immediately to arrest further browning of the butter.
Overdone: Butter has gone from hazelnut to dark brown and smells of popcorn or slightly burnt — beurre noir. Bitter. Pour out the butter immediately and add fresh butter to the pan. The pan's residual heat will brown it in seconds.
Feel cue: Press the very center of the top of a scallop during basting — it should feel like pressing a firm marshmallow: giving but with light resistance. Once it feels like pressing a firm eraser, it is overcooked.

Remove the scallops from the pan and arrange on warm plates, seared-crust side up. Squeeze lemon juice into the remaining brown butter in the pan, swirling to combine — the acid will stop the butter from browning further and lift the pan into a quick pan sauce. Spoon this brown butter-lemon-caper sauce generously over each scallop. Scatter the finely chopped flat-leaf parsley and finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt on each scallop's seared face. Serve within 60 seconds — scallops cool rapidly and the window of perfectly cooked, translucent-centered texture is brief.
Visual cue: Mahogany-topped scallops on a pool of amber butter, golden capers, and bright green parsley. The seared face should be visible and unobscured.
Underdone: Center of the scallop is still cold and raw when bitten — the pale interior is glassy and stiff, not just lightly translucent. Return to the hot pan for 15 seconds each side. This is rare — a well-executed sear is almost always enough.
Perfect: Seared faces mahogany-brown, interior when cut reveals a center that is just barely translucent and pearl-white, yielding and luscious. Brown butter sauce is amber, nutty, and bright with lemon. Serve at once.
Overdone: Interior is fully white and opaque all the way through. Texture is firm, slightly rubbery. The scallop has lost its inherent sweetness. Serve immediately — the brown butter and capers will compensate with richness and acidity. Cut timing on the next round.
Feel cue: The ideal seared scallop resists like a firm grape at the mahogany crust, then transitions in one slow millimeter to the luscious, barely-set interior — you feel both textures in a single bite.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

Eggs, separated: 4 ea
Caster sugar: 150 g

Unwaxed lemons, zest and juice: 2 ea

  Alternatives: toasted pistachios; dark chocolate shavings
Active time: 35 min
Total time: 5 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Italy's answer to frozen mousse — a pillow of whipped cream and meringue suspended in gentle cold, sliced to reveal a cross-section of pale gold lemon cream that yields instantly on the tongue and vanishes without a trace of ice.

ingredients.name: Candied lemon peel or fresh berries

steps:
Place the egg yolks, caster sugar, lemon zest and lemon juice in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of gently simmering water. Whisk vigorously and continuously for 8–10 minutes until the mixture is very thick, pale and has tripled in volume — it should hold a thick ribbon for several seconds when the whisk is lifted. This is the zabaglione base. Remove from the heat and continue whisking until the bowl feels cool to the touch. The cooking stabilises the yolks so the semifreddo stays aerated when frozen.
Visual cue: Pale yellow, thick and voluminous — the whisk leaves a distinct trail that holds for 3–4 seconds before dissolving. The bowl feels no more than body-warm.
Underdone: Mixture is still thin and liquid. Pale yellow but no increase in volume. Ribbon dissolves instantly. Continue whisking over the heat — the yolks need sustained gentle heat to cook and aerate simultaneously.
Perfect: Thick, pale, voluminous. The ribbon test holds clearly. Smells of cooked lemon and egg. Bowl is warm but not hot. Remove from heat and whisk until cool before folding.
Overdone: Small curds of cooked egg are visible. Mixture is grainy or lumpy. Strain through a fine sieve immediately — small curds can be rescued if caught early. Larger curds mean starting again.
Feel cue: Dip a finger into the zabaglione — it should coat your finger in a thick, velvety layer that holds its shape without dripping, like a warm custard.

In two separate bowls: whip the cold double cream to soft peaks — it should hold a shape but still be silky and flowing, not stiff. In a separate grease-free bowl, whisk the egg whites with a pinch of salt until they hold firm, glossy peaks. Do not overwhip either — both should be airy and light, not stiff and dry. Keep both chilled until needed.
Visual cue: Cream holds a soft peak that bends gracefully at the tip. Whites hold a firm peak with a slight bend — glossy and smooth, not dry.
Underdone: Cream barely thickened — pours rather than mounds. Whites are frothy and liquid. Continue whipping both — a few more minutes with a cold bowl will bring cream to the right stage.
Perfect: Cream: soft, billowy, holds a peak that curves gently. Whites: glossy, firm, peaks stand with a slight hook at the tip. Fold immediately into the zabaglione before either loses structure.
Overdone: Cream has become grainy and stiff — beginning to separate toward butter. Whites are dry and clumping. Over-whipped cream cannot be corrected. Whites: add one un-beaten white and fold gently to loosen.
Feel cue: Run a spatula through the cream — it should leave a clean, defined furrow that holds its edges but the cream on either side is clearly light and airy, not dense.

First fold the whipped whites into the cooled zabaglione in two additions, using a large spatula with a cut-and-lift motion. Then fold in the whipped cream in two additions. Be gentle and decisive — the goal is to retain as much air as possible while achieving a fully uniform, streak-free mixture. The finished base should be light, mousse-like and pale yellow. Pour into a loaf tin lined with two layers of clingfilm, with plenty of overhang on all sides.
Visual cue: Pale yellow, mousse-like and airy. No white streaks from the cream or whites. The surface holds its mounded shape when the spatula is lifted.
Underdone: White streaks of cream or whites still visible in the yellow base. Mixture is marbled and uneven. One or two more careful folds — stop immediately when streaks disappear.
Perfect: Uniform pale yellow throughout, airy and voluminous. Slightly thicker than double cream but clearly not dense. Smells of fresh lemon cream. Pour into prepared tin, fold clingfilm over the top and freeze.
Overdone: Mixture has deflated back to a dense, heavy consistency. Volume has reduced noticeably. Proceed — the semifreddo will freeze dense rather than light and mousse-like. Still pleasant but less ethereal.
Feel cue: Scoop a spoonful of the base and let it fall — it should flow in one slow, thick pour and settle with a slight dome, like soft-set custard, not like liquid cream.

Fold the clingfilm over the surface to seal completely. Freeze for a minimum of 4 hours, preferably overnight. To serve: unwrap, invert onto a chilled serving plate and peel off the clingfilm. The semifreddo should hold its shape cleanly and be easy to slice with a warm knife. Decorate the top with candied lemon peel or fresh berries. Slice into 2–3 cm portions and serve immediately — it softens quickly at room temperature.
Visual cue: A firm, pale yellow loaf that holds its shape perfectly when inverted and sliced. Cut surface is smooth and even, not icy or coarse.
Underdone: Interior is still soft and mousse-like when sliced — has not frozen fully. Collapses on the plate. Return to the freezer for at least 2 more hours. A fully frozen semifreddo is firm but not rock-hard.
Perfect: Slices cleanly with a warm knife, holding its shape on the plate. Cut surface is smooth, pale and matte — no ice crystals visible. Melts on the tongue immediately without any cold shock. Decorate and serve immediately. Semifreddo is best consumed within 30 seconds of slicing.
Overdone: Rock-hard — knife struggles to cut and surface shows large ice crystal formation. Gritty on the tongue. Allow to temper at room temperature for 8–10 minutes before slicing. The ideal serving temperature is -8 C, not -18 C.
Feel cue: Press the back of a spoon against a freshly cut surface — it should yield smoothly and leave a shallow impression, then hold that shape without the surface cracking or crumbling.

name: Sfogliatelle Ricce
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Semolina flour (fine): 500 g
Warm water: 180 ml
Fine sea salt: 5 g
Lard (or cold unsalted butter), for laminating: 150 g
  Alternatives: cold unsalted butter (less crisp but more accessible)
Whole milk ricotta, well-drained: 400 g
Fine semolina (for filling cream): 80 g
Whole milk (for filling cream): 250 ml
Caster sugar: 120 g
Candied orange peel, finely diced: 60 g
  Alternatives: candied citron; dried apricot
Pure vanilla extract or vanilla paste: 5 ml
  Alternatives: 1 scraped vanilla pod
Egg (large) for dough binding: 1 whole

Active time: 3 hr
Total time: 6 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Naples' supreme pastry achievement: a layered shell of paper-thin laminated dough, each leaf barely thicker than a page, cradling a filling of ricotta, semolina cream, and candied citrus — the shell shatters into a thousand crisp fragments at the first bite while the interior yields into a dense, fragrant, barely-sweet cream. Every sfogliatella is a feat of patience made edible.

ingredients.name: Lard (or cold unsalted butter), for laminating
Pure vanilla extract or vanilla paste

steps:
Combine semolina flour and salt in a large bowl. Make a well. Add the beaten egg and warm water to the well. Mix by hand until a stiff, cohesive dough forms — this dough should be very firm and smooth, like pasta dough. Knead on the bench for 10–12 minutes until very smooth. The dough will be stiff and fight you — this is correct. A stiff dough extends into very thin sheets without tearing. Wrap tightly in plastic and rest for 30 minutes.
Visual cue: Very smooth, firm dough — stiffer than pasta dough, almost like modeling clay. Completely uniform surface, no stickiness.
Underdone: Dough is still rough and shaggy. Tears when stretched. Continue kneading — this dough needs full development to laminate without tearing.
Perfect: Completely smooth surface, very firm. Does not stick to hands or bench. Can be stretched without tearing. Like thick pastry clay. Wrap and rest 30 minutes.
Overdone: Not really possible to over-knead this stiff dough by hand. Rest the dough — it will relax.
Feel cue: Press a thumb into the rested dough — it should leave a slow-filling indent, like pressing into cool, stiff playdough.

Bring milk to a simmer in a saucepan. Rain in semolina in a thin stream while whisking constantly. Cook over medium-low heat, whisking, for 5–7 minutes until the mixture becomes very thick and pulls away from the sides of the pan. Remove from heat. Beat in sugar, vanilla, and candied orange peel. Spread on a tray, cover with plastic touching the surface, and cool completely in the refrigerator — at least 2 hours.
Visual cue: A very thick, smooth cream that holds a furrow when a spoon is dragged through it. Pulls from the sides of the pan when stirred.
Underdone: Cream is still pourable and thin. Semolina has not fully absorbed the milk. Continue cooking and whisking — the cream must be very thick to pipe cleanly.
Perfect: Very thick, almost solid. Semolina fully hydrated. Smooth, shiny surface. Holds its shape when scooped. Fragrant with orange and vanilla. Cool completely before combining with ricotta.
Overdone: Cream is seizing and sticking hard to the pan. Burnt smell. Remove from heat immediately. Add a splash of milk and stir vigorously to loosen. Strain if necessary.
Feel cue: Press the cooled cream between your fingers — it should feel like firm, cool polenta: dense and yielding but holding a shape completely.

Beat the cold semolina cream to break it up slightly. Add well-drained ricotta (excess liquid will make the filling too wet to hold its shape in the pastry shell) and mix together until smooth and uniform. Fold in candied orange peel and vanilla. Taste — the filling should be sweet, mildly lemony from the orange, and have the grainy-smooth texture of semolina. Refrigerate until needed.
Visual cue: Thick, uniform, creamy filling with visible pieces of candied peel. Holds its shape when spooned — not runny.
Underdone: Filling is too soft and loose from excess moisture in the ricotta. Drain the ricotta in a cheesecloth-lined strainer for 1 hour before mixing.
Perfect: Dense, scoopable, sweet-smelling filling. Holds a spoon standing upright briefly. Flecks of orange peel visible. Refrigerate covered. Use cold.
Overdone: Filling is too stiff and dry. Difficult to spread. Add a tablespoon of milk and mix until smooth.
Feel cue: The filling should feel like thick, cool frosting when pressed between two spoons — dense enough to hold a shape but not crumbly.

Divide the rested dough in half. Using a pasta machine, roll the first piece from the widest setting to the thinnest (setting 7–9 on most machines), stretching into a long, thin sheet. Brush the entire surface generously with very soft (not melted) lard or butter. Fold the sheet like a letter — thirds — and roll again to the thinnest setting. Brush again. Roll the sheet into a tight log from one short end. Refrigerate the log for 30 minutes. Repeat with the second piece.
Visual cue: A tight log of dough with visible spiral layers when viewed from the end. Surface smooth and slightly greasy from the fat.
Underdone: Dough sheet has torn during rolling. Layers are uneven or the log is loosely rolled. Press torn areas together. The lamination is less perfect but the pastry will still be layered.
Perfect: Very thin sheet, almost translucent. Tight, evenly-wound log with many visible spiral layers. Firm after refrigerating. Proceed to slicing and shaping.
Overdone: Sheet is too thin and breaking. Tears as you work. Reset the pasta machine to a slightly thicker setting. The layers will be fewer but the shell will hold.
Feel cue: The rolled sheet should feel like a very stiff, cool piece of waxed paper — firm and barely pliable, with the fat giving it a slight waxy resistance.

Cut the chilled log into 1.5 cm rounds. Using your thumbs, press and stretch each round into a cone shape — the spiral layers will fan out like the pages of a book. Work gently from the center outward, keeping the point of the cone closed while the opening widens into an oval shell. Fill each shell with a heaping tablespoon of the ricotta filling and press the edges firmly shut. Place seam-side down on a parchment-lined baking sheet.
Visual cue: Shell-shaped pastry with visible, fanned layers. Closed seam at the base. Plump with filling.
Underdone: Layers have not fanned out — shell is still a flat disc. Cone not formed. Press more firmly from the center with both thumbs, working outward in a rotating motion.
Perfect: Dramatic shell shape with multiple fanned layers clearly visible. Seam closed and sitting flat. Plump without bursting. Bake immediately or refrigerate up to 2 hours.
Overdone: Dough torn at the edges from pressing too hard. Filling escaping. Pinch the torn edges shut with a little water as glue. Proceed.
Feel cue: When shaped, the sfogliatella should feel like a compact, plump shell with a firm base and a fanned, layered opening — the layers should fan like pages when you peek inside.

Preheat oven to 200 C (400 F). Bake sfogliatelle for 20–25 minutes until deeply golden and the layers have fanned open dramatically and crisped. The pastry will open and separate into distinct shell layers as the fat melts and the steam puffs them apart. Cool for 5 minutes, dust generously with icing sugar, and eat warm — sfogliatelle should be eaten within 30 minutes of baking while the layers are at maximum crispness.
Visual cue: Dramatically fanned layers of golden, crisp pastry. Shell clearly opened. Snow of icing sugar on top.
Underdone: Layers are still pale and not fully separated. Pastry feels soft when tapped. Return to oven for 5 more minutes. The layers need full heat to separate and crisp.
Perfect: Deep golden, dramatically fanned layers — each leaf of dough crisped and separate. The shell shatters when pressed. Filling visible through the opening. Heavy with icing sugar. Eat within 30 minutes.
Overdone: Very dark brown, almost caramelized. Some layers charred. Trim charred tips. The interior and filling are likely fine.
Feel cue: Bite into the end — it should shatter loudly into a cascade of flaky, crisp shards, and then immediately yield to the dense, cool, sweet ricotta cream within.

name: Green Shakshuka
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: canned green chili (2 tbsp)
Ground cumin: 1 tsp
Ground coriander: 0.5 tsp
Extra-virgin olive oil: 3 tbsp
Large eggs: 6 whole

  Alternatives: goat cheese; labneh (dollops)
Fresh cilantro, roughly chopped: 0.25 cup
  Alternatives: flat-leaf parsley
Fine sea salt: 1 tsp
Water or light vegetable stock: 60 ml

Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A tangle of wilted spinach, chard, and charred tomatillo collapses into a bright, acidic, deeply savory green sauce — then eggs are nestled into pockets and covered to set, their whites just barely opaque while the yolks remain trembling and liquid, waiting to break into the green.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Halve the tomatillos and place them cut-side down in a dry, ungreased heavy skillet (cast iron is ideal) over high heat. Do not stir. Let them char for 4-5 minutes until the cut surfaces are deeply blistered and black in spots, and the skins have softened and wrinkled. The sugars at the cut surface caramelize and char, converting tomatillo's raw, astringent sourness into something deeper, slightly sweet, and smoky. When a tomatillo releases from the pan easily when nudged with a spatula, it has charred correctly. Transfer them to a bowl — they will continue to soften from residual heat. The juices that leak into the bowl are precious: add them to the sauce.
Visual cue: The cut faces are mottled black and deep caramel-brown. The skins are wrinkled and slightly translucent. The tomatillos have collapsed by about 30%.
Underdone: The cut faces are barely colored — still pale green-white. The tomatillos are still firm and smell raw and grassy. Return to the hot pan and continue dry-charring. The pan must be genuinely hot — no sizzle means not hot enough.
Perfect: Deep caramel-black char marks cover at least 60% of each cut face. The tomatillos are soft and slumping. The smell is sweet, smoky, and slightly acidic. Transfer to a bowl and proceed immediately to building the sauce base.
Overdone: The tomatillos are black all over and some have begun to dry out. The flesh inside may be stringy and dry rather than juicy. Use them — the char flavor will still be valuable in the sauce. Add an extra tablespoon of water to compensate for the lost juice.
Feel cue: Properly charred tomatillos feel like very soft, warm gel through the tongs — the interior has fully cooked and the membrane is all that holds them together. The pan should smell of scorched sugar and something faintly tropical.

In the same pan (leave any tomatillo char — it adds flavor), heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the diced onion and the chard stems (chopped into 1 cm pieces) and cook, stirring occasionally, for 6-8 minutes until the onion is soft, translucent, and starting to turn golden at the edges. Add the sliced garlic and jalapeño and cook for 2 more minutes until fragrant. The garlic should turn golden at the edges but not brown — once it smells like roasted garlic rather than raw, you're there. Add the cumin and coriander and stir them directly into the oil for 30 seconds — this dry-blooms the spices in the fat and intensifies their fragrance by an order of magnitude. The pan should smell like a Moroccan kitchen.
Visual cue: Soft, translucent-gold onion with slightly caramelized edges. The garlic is golden but not browned. The spices have darkened from their raw color and smell warm and toasty.
Underdone: The onion is still white and firm. The garlic is raw-smelling. The spices haven't toasted — they look dry and raw in the oil. Continue cooking over medium heat. Rushing this step means the onion's sweetness never develops, giving you a raw, sharp-tasting base.
Perfect: The onion is fully tender and beginning to turn amber at the edges. The garlic is golden. The cumin and coriander smell warm, toasted, and slightly sweet — a rich, complex base. Add the greens immediately to prevent the garlic from burning.
Overdone: The garlic has browned and the spices are dark and acrid. The base smells bitter. Lower the heat immediately and add the greens — they will cool the pan and halt the burning. The bitterness will mostly be masked by the greens' volume.
Feel cue: At the correct moment, the onion-garlic-spice base makes a sustained gentle sizzle — not the aggressive crackling of high heat, not the silence of too-low heat, but a steady, soft frying sound that smells deeply
fragrant and sweet.

Add the charred tomatillos (and all their juice) to the pan, pressing them with the back of a spoon to break them into rough pieces. Add the chard leaves (torn large) and the baby spinach — the pan will look impossibly full. Add the water and a generous pinch of salt. Cover and cook over medium heat for 4-5 minutes until the greens have completely wilted and collapsed. Remove the lid and stir everything together, breaking the tomatillos further into the sauce. Cook uncovered for 3-4 more minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has thickened slightly and the greens have fully integrated. Taste and season generously — greens can absorb a surprising amount of salt. The sauce should be vivid green, slightly chunky, pleasantly sour from the tomatillo, and deeply savory.
Visual cue: A vibrant, textured green sauce — not a smooth puree, but also not separate piles of vegetable. The tomatillo chunks are visible but soft. The chard and spinach are fully collapsed and integrated.
Underdone: The greens are still bright green and holding their shape. The tomatillos are still in large pieces. The sauce is very liquid — it hasn't reduced or unified. Continue cooking uncovered for another 3-4 minutes, stirring frequently to help the greens break down.
Perfect: The greens are fully wilted and olive-green in color. The sauce is thick enough that a spoon dragged through the bottom leaves a trail that closes slowly. The tomatillo pieces are soft and have mostly melted into the sauce. Make wells in the sauce for the eggs.
Overdone: The sauce has dried out — it's sticking to the pan and the greens have gone from vibrant to khaki-drab. The tomatillo liquid has evaporated. Add 3-4 tablespoons of water or stock and scrape the pan to re-moisten. The color will have dulled but the flavor intensifies when concentrated.
Feel cue: The green sauce at the right stage makes a slow, lazy
bubble in the center of the pan — not rapid boiling, but a gentle heaving that smells simultaneously of charred tomatillo, wilted spinach, and toasted cumin.

Using the back of a large spoon, make six shallow wells in the green sauce, pressing down to the bottom of the pan. Crack an egg into a small cup first — this gives you control and prevents shell fragments. Slide each egg from the cup into its well. Scatter the crumbled feta around the eggs and into the sauce. Reduce heat to low, cover the pan with a lid or foil, and cook for 5-8 minutes, checking frequently. The whites should be just set — opaque and firm when you press the edge with a spoon — while the yolks remain visibly liquid and trembling. Remove from heat while the yolks still look underdone: residual heat continues cooking them for 1-2 minutes after the pan comes off the stove. Scatter the fresh cilantro over the top and serve directly from the pan with bread.
Visual cue: Six eggs nested in the green sauce, whites fully opaque and set at the edges, yolks still visibly domed and liquid under a thin white film. The feta has softened and some of it has melted into the sauce.
Underdone: The whites are still translucent and jiggle when the pan is gently moved. The yolk is completely bare and fully liquid under no film at all. Cover and cook 2-3 more minutes on the lowest possible heat. Check every 60 seconds.
Perfect: Whites are fully set and opaque — no translucency anywhere. The yolk is still visibly domed and liquid inside but has a thin opaque film across its surface. When pressed very gently with a fingertip, it gives and wobbles. Remove from heat immediately. Garnish and serve within 3 minutes.
Overdone: The yolks are flat and matte — they've set completely. The whites may have developed a rubbery texture from too much heat. Serve immediately — you cannot un-cook an egg. Next time: watch the pan constantly and pull it 30 seconds before you think it's ready.
Feel cue: A perfectly set shakshuka egg pressed lightly with the back of a cold spoon should give a
subtle, liquid wobble at the yolk — like pressing a firm water balloon — while the white resists firmly with no give at all.

Scatter the fresh cilantro generously over the finished pan — the heat of the shakshuka will wilt it slightly on contact, releasing its fragrance. Serve the shakshuka directly from the pan at the table, with warm pita or crusty bread for tearing and dragging through the sauce. The protocol for eating: tear bread, drag through sauce capturing both green and white egg, ensure the final bite has yolk. The shakshuka is at peak quality for approximately 5 minutes after coming off the heat — the egg continues to cook from residual heat and firm progressively. Serve without ceremony.
Visual cue: The pan is a vivid landscape: deep olive-green sauce, six bright white islands of egg white, six golden yolk suns, white crumbles of feta, and a fresh green confetti of cilantro.
Underdone: The garnish is absent or sparingly applied. The visual presentation is monochromatic — just green sauce and egg. Add more cilantro. Add more feta. This dish is meant to be generous with garnish — it contributes flavor and visual contrast equally.
Perfect: Vibrant contrast between the deep green, the white, the gold, and the fresh herb green. The feta sparkles. It smells of cumin and char and fresh cilantro all at once. You want to eat it before you've gotten a plate. Bring the pan to the table immediately.
Overdone: The cilantro was added too early and has wilted brown. The eggs have set to firm yolks while you were plating. Add a fresh scatter of cilantro and serve immediately regardless. The flavor is intact.
Feel cue: The final bite of green shakshuka — sauce, egg white, broken yolk, and bread — should feel simultaneously warm and liquid at the center (yolk), tender but resistant (egg white), silky and acidic (sauce), and crunchy at the rim (bread crust). The cilantro is the last thing your nose registers as you eat.

description: Green shakshuka: tomatillos and charred jalapeños form a bright, tangy, mildly spicy sauce in which eggs are poached just until the whites are set and the yolks still run gold — a pan of morning fire that wakes up slowly, then all at once.
