steps:
Combine the bread flour and whole wheat flour in a large bowl. Pour in the water (holding back about 30 g for the salt later) and mix with your hand until no dry flour remains — squeeze and fold until the mass is shaggy and fully hydrated. Cover and rest 30–60 minutes at room temperature. The autolyse lets enzymes begin degrading the starches and the gluten proteins hydrate and loosely align without mechanical work, making subsequent mixing far more efficient and giving the crumb a silkier extensibility.
Visual cue: A rough, shaggy mass with no dry streaks and no pools of free water. The surface looks matte and somewhat hairy — not smooth. After the rest, the dough will have relaxed and become slightly sticky, with a pliable, cohesive feel.
Underdone: Still has dry flour pockets or clumps that did not absorb water. Surface looks crumbly and patchy. Squeeze and fold more aggressively, pressing the dry pockets into the wet dough until full absorption is achieved. Add a few drops of water if genuinely dry.
Perfect: Fully hydrated, no dry flour, rough and matte. After the rest it should peel cleanly from the sides of the bowl with mild resistance. Gluten strands are already beginning to align. Proceed to add starter and salt when the dough rests cleanly and stretches a couple of centimeters before tearing.
Overdone: Dough has fermented and puffed noticeably during autolyse — means your starter was in the flour or the room is very warm. Gluten may feel slack or tacky-wet. Proceed immediately to avoid over-fermentation. Monitor bulk fermentation time carefully and shorten it.
Feel cue: Press the dough after the rest: it should yield willingly under your palm and bounce back halfway — not spring back hard (under-hydrated) or collapse flat (over-hydrated). It should peel off your hand cleanly rather than stringing.

Dissolve the salt in the reserved water, then pour starter and salt water over the autolysed dough. Use the pinch-and-fold method: pinch the starter through the dough in 10–15 passes until integrated. Then begin the series of stretch-and-folds: every 30 minutes for the first 2 hours, grab one edge of the dough, stretch it up until you feel resistance, and fold it to the opposite side. Rotate the bowl 90° and repeat four times per set. After four sets, leave the dough covered to finish bulk fermentation — roughly 10–14 hours at 68°F / 20°C, or 4–5 hours at 76°F / 24°C. The dough is ready when it has grown by 50–75%, feels airy and domed, and a flap peeled back shows a network of bubbles just below the surface.
Visual cue: Dough has risen 50–75% above its starting volume, is domed and slightly jiggly when the bowl is nudged, and shows a bubbly, webbed structure when you stretch a flap in the light. The surface should be smooth and slightly domed, not flat and dense.
Underdone: Little rise, dough is still dense and compact. No visible bubbles when stretched. Pulls stiffly rather than extending loosely. Give it more time. Move to a warmer spot (oven with light on, ~75°F / 24°C). Check again in 1–2 hours.
Perfect: 50–75% rise, open bubble network visible through a stretched flap, dough domes and wobbles gently. Jiggles like set gelatin when you shake the bowl. A wet finger poked in leaves a hole that fills very slowly. Proceed to pre-shape immediately — do not wait; over-ferment is difficult to recover.
Overdone: Dough has more than doubled, looks flat or collapsed at the top, smells aggressively sour or alcoholic, and has a wet, sloppy structure that breaks apart rather than stretching. Shape immediately and cold-retard for less time (6 hours instead of overnight). The loaf will be very sour and may not hold its shape well but is still edible.
Feel cue: During the

stretch-and-fold sets the dough will transform: early sets feel slack and tear-prone; by the third set it should stretch in a long, translucent windowpane before snapping back. At the end of bulk the dough should feel alive — slightly tacky, gassy, and smooth, leaving a faint residue on your palm that lets go cleanly.

Turn the dough gently onto an unfloured surface. Using a bench scraper and one cupped hand, do a pre-shape: drag the dough toward you while the scraper pushes from behind, rotating to build surface tension into a loose round. Rest uncovered 20–30 minutes (bench rest). Then flour the top of the round generously, flip it, and do the final shape: for a boule, grab the far edge, fold it to the center, then fold left, right, and roll the whole package toward you, using your palms to drag and seal the bottom seam tight against the bench. The surface should be taut like a drum. Drop seam-side-up into a well-floured (rice flour is ideal) banneton or a bowl lined with a floured towel. Pinch the seam closed. Cover and refrigerate 12–16 hours.
Visual cue: A taut, dome-shaped round with a smooth, unbroken surface showing visible surface tension. The seam underneath is sealed tight. No tears or saggy patches on the surface.
Underdone: Surface is loose and saggy, the dough spread sideways on the bench rather than building height. No tension; it looks like a pancake. Use the bench scraper to gather it tighter in the pre-shape stage and rest longer (30 min) before attempting the final shape. Work more decisively — quick, confident moves build more tension than slow cautious ones.
Perfect: Tight, smooth dome that holds its height. The surface skin is taut and springs back to the touch. Drop it in the banneton and it will hold a dome shape rather than slumping. Refrigerate immediately for the cold retard — 12 to 16 hours.
Overdone: Surface has torn — you can see rough rips in the skin, or the dough has de-gassed and feels dense from over-handling. Place as-is into the banneton. A torn surface will give a more rustic crust score but the crumb will be less open. Do not try to re-shape — you will only degas it further.
Feel cue: A correctly shaped boule should resist when you try to

flatten it with your palm — push down and it should push back. The surface skin should feel like stretched cling wrap: smooth, taut, and slightly resistant. If it gives without resistance, the tension is insufficient.

Preheat the oven with a Dutch oven (lid on) inside to 500°F / 260°C for at least 45 minutes. Turn the cold loaf out of the banneton onto a piece of parchment. Working fast, score with a lame or sharp razor blade held at a 30–45° angle: a single ear cut down one side of the dome, or a bold cross-hatch. The cut should be decisive and swift — 5–7 cm deep — not a timid scratch. The cold dough (straight from the fridge) is easiest to score cleanly.
Visual cue: Clean, defined incisions with slightly spread lips. The cut edges should gape open slightly from the surface tension of the dough, revealing the pale interior. Cold dough from the fridge holds its shape and shows cuts clearly.
Underdone: The blade dragged and tore rather than cut — ragged, uneven lips, dough may have deflated slightly where it was dragged. Use a sharper blade (single-edge razor, not a serrated knife). A few drops of water on the blade help. Work faster — hesitation causes dragging.
Perfect: Clean, decisive incisions with visibly open lips. The surface tension causes the cut to gape. Cold dough sits still on the parchment and does not deflate. Lower the loaf immediately into the preheated Dutch oven. Every second counts — oven spring is best when the dough hits maximum heat fast.
Overdone: Scores are too deep, reaching near the bottom crust, or there are too many cuts — the surface tension is compromised and the loaf may spread rather than spring upward. Still bake it — the result will be flatter with less ear, but the flavor will be unaffected.
Feel cue: Cold dough from a 12-hour retard should feel firm and almost stiff under your hand — like cold butter, not like room-temperature dough. That firmness is what allows a clean score. If the dough feels slack and warm, the score will drag.

Using the parchment as a sling, lower the loaf into the screaming-hot Dutch oven and put the lid on. Bake covered at 500°F / 260°C for 20 minutes — steam from the dough trapped inside the pot creates the glossy, extensible crust needed for maximum oven spring. Remove the lid, drop the temperature to 460°F / 238°C, and bake a further 20–25 minutes until the crust is deep mahogany and an instant-read thermometer at the center reads 205–210°F / 96–99°C. Transfer to a wire rack and resist cutting for at least 1 hour — the interior crumb is still setting via residual heat.
Visual cue: A domed loaf with a shattering, deep mahogany crust, a well-sprung ear, and a hollow thunk when tapped on the bottom. The score has bloomed open into a bold ear, caramelized to a deep amber at its lip.
Underdone: Crust is pale gold or tan, sounds dull when tapped. Interior temperature below 200°F / 93°C. The crust yields when squeezed rather than crackling. Continue baking with the lid off, checking every 5 minutes, until deep mahogany is achieved and the bottom sounds hollow. A pale crust means steam never dried the surface properly.
Perfect: Deep mahogany — almost brown-black on the ear and high points, reddish brown on the sides and bottom. Sounds hollow, like a drum. Crust is rigid and crackles audibly as it cools on the rack. Cool on a wire rack 1 hour minimum before cutting. The crackle of the crust as it cools is the sound of success.
Overdone: Crust is uniformly dark brown-black with a bitter, almost charred smell. Bottom may be truly burnt. Trim off any carbonized bottom crust. Reduce oven temperature by 25°F / 15°C next time, or shorten the uncovered bake. The interior is likely fine.
Feel cue: When you tap the bottom of a properly baked loaf it should ring hollow and high-pitched — like knocking on a thin wooden door. A dense, dull thud means the interior is still doughy and needs
more time. The crust should feel rigid and glassy, not soft or pliable, and will audibly crackle and pop as it cools.

name: Sourdough Discard Pancakes
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
All-purpose flour: 1 cup
  Alternatives: whole-wheat flour (denser, nuttier); oat flour
Active sourdough discard (100% hydration): 1 cup
  Alternatives: any hydration starter — adjust liquid accordingly
Whole milk: 0.5 cup
  Alternatives: buttermilk (more tang); oat milk
Large eggs: 2 each
  Alternatives: flax egg (1 tbsp ground flax + 3 tbsp water, 5 min)
Unsalted butter, melted: 3 tbsp
  Alternatives: neutral oil; browned butter (more flavor)
Maple syrup or sugar: 1 tbsp
  Alternatives: honey
Baking soda: 0.5 tsp
Fine salt: 0.5 tsp
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A zero-waste weekend pancake that transforms unfed sourdough discard into tall, fluffy rounds with a subtle tang and a crumb shot through with tiny tunnels from baking soda reacting with the starter's acid.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
In a large bowl, combine the sourdough discard, milk, eggs, melted butter, and maple syrup. Whisk until the discard is fully broken up and the mixture is uniform. The discard should dissolve smoothly into the milk and eggs — if your discard is particularly stiff, whisk it with the milk first until smooth before adding the eggs. The wet mix will smell pleasantly tangy from the discard.
Visual cue: A smooth, pale yellow liquid with a slightly frothy surface from the whisking. No white streaks of unincorporated egg white. Uniformly combined.
Underdone: Lumps of sourdough discard visible. White streaks of egg. Surface not frothy. Whisk more vigorously, breaking up the discard against the bowl sides. A slightly stiff discard can be stubborn — persist.
Perfect: Smooth, uniform pale yellow liquid. Slightly frothy. Smells sour and eggy. Discard fully incorporated. Add the dry ingredients.
Overdone: Over-whisking eggs is not possible here — the fat in the butter prevents over-beating. Proceed.
Feel cue: Dip your finger in the wet mix — it should taste of egg, butter, and a distinct background tang from the sourdough starter. That tang is the acid that will react with the baking soda to lift the pancakes.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the flour, baking soda, and salt. Pour the dry ingredients into the wet all at once. Fold with a rubber spatula using large, sweeping strokes — just 10–15 folds until the dry ingredients are barely incorporated. The batter will be lumpy. This is correct. Over-mixing activates the gluten and produces tough, chewy pancakes instead of tender, fluffy ones. Stop mixing when you still see a few streaks of flour — they will hydrate during the rest.
Visual cue: A lumpy, pourable batter with visible flour streaks and no large pockets of dry flour. A few small lumps are expected and desirable.
Underdone: Large dry pockets of flour at the bottom of the bowl. Dry flour on the surface. A few more gentle folds targeting the dry pockets only. Do not mix globally.
Perfect: Batter is lumpy but no large dry pockets. A poured ladle flows slowly and evenly. A few flour streaks are fine. Rest 5 minutes while the griddle heats.
Overdone: Smooth, thin, lump-free batter. The gluten is developed. Pancakes will be tough. The pancakes are still edible. Next time: 10 folds maximum. Consider this a lesson.
Feel cue: The batter should feel airy and slightly resistant under the spatula — the sourdough discard and baking soda are already beginning to react, producing small bubbles. If you hold the bowl up to your ear and listen carefully, you can sometimes hear the batter quietly fizzing.

Heat a cast-iron or non-stick skillet over medium heat for 3 minutes. Lightly grease with butter or neutral oil, wiping away excess with a paper towel — too much fat causes uneven browning and no crust. Pour a ladleful (about 80 ml) of batter per pancake. Do not spread it — let it pool naturally. Watch the surface: bubbles will appear at the edges first, then march toward the center. Flip when bubbles cover most of the surface AND the edges look set and matte (not shiny). Cook 90 seconds on the second side. Serve immediately — pancakes lose their steam-puffed height within minutes.
Visual cue: A golden-brown bottom and a surface covered in broken and unbroken bubbles with a matte edge ring. After flipping, both sides should be an even medium golden-brown with no raw patches.
Underdone: Flipped too early: the underside is set but pale, the top is still fully wet and shiny with no bubbles. Pancake deflates when flipped. Flip back if possible. Next pancake: wait until bubbles reach the center and edges are matte.
Perfect: Golden-brown bottom, fully bubbled top with matte edges before the flip. After flipping: even golden-brown on both sides. Pancake is thick and springy. Serve immediately. Hold in a 90 C oven if making a large batch.
Overdone: Dark brown bottom before the surface shows bubbles — heat too high. Edges may be dry and overly browned. Lower the heat between batches. Let the pan cool for 60 seconds. Wipe and re-grease.
Feel cue: A perfect sourdough discard pancake should bounce back when you press it gently with a spatula — tall, springy, and slightly resistant. Press your thumb into the top: it should compress and rebound like a very soft sponge. The underside should feel crisp and almost papery, contrasting with the moist, tender interior.

servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

ingredients.name: Active sourdough starter (100% hydration, fed 8–12 hrs ago)
Extra-virgin olive oil (for pan and dimpling)

steps:
Verify the starter is active: it should float in water and smell pleasantly sour and yeasty. Combine warm water, starter, and olive oil in a large bowl. Add flour and salt. Mix with a wet hand or a spatula until no dry flour remains — about 3 minutes. Unlike commercial-yeast focaccia, this dough moves more slowly and benefits from patience. Cover and let rest 30 minutes for autolyse.
Visual cue: A rough, cohesive, very wet dough with a slightly shaggy surface and no dry patches. A starter float in the mixing water confirms readiness.
Underdone: Dry flour pockets remain. Dough is not fully combined. Fold the dry flour into the center with a wet hand. Add a teaspoon of water if genuinely dry.
Perfect: Uniformly combined, shaggy, wet. Smells of the starter's culture — sour and yeasty. No dry patches. Cover and rest 30 minutes, then begin folds.
Overdone: Over-mixed — dough is smooth already and gluten seems very developed. Proceed. The sourdough focaccia will accommodate: it needs strong gluten for the open crumb.
Feel cue: This dough should feel wetter and more fluid than the commercial-yeast version — it clings to the bowl and stretches in long, silky sheets rather than pulling away cleanly. The starter makes it more elastic, almost alive.

Perform four sets of coil folds over 2 hours: wet your hand, slide it under the dough, lift the whole mass, and let it fold under itself. Rotate the bowl 90 degrees and repeat. Perform one set every 30 minutes for the first two hours. After the fourth set, cover and let bulk ferment at room temperature until the dough is 50–75% larger, visibly bubbly, and airy — typically another 3–5 hours depending on room temperature and starter strength.
Visual cue: After bulk ferment: dough has grown 50–75%, is visibly bubbly throughout, domed on top, and jiggles in a wave when the bowl is shaken.
Underdone: Dough barely grown. Less than 30% increase. Few bubbles. Starter may have been weak or room too cold. Continue fermenting. Move to a warmer spot. Sourdough is not on a rigid schedule — it is done when it is done.
Perfect: 50–75% larger, clearly bubbly and airy, dome is formed. Jiggles when nudged. Smells pleasantly tangy. Large bubbles visible along the bowl walls. Transfer to the olive-oil-flooded pan for the final rise.
Overdone: More than doubled, beginning to look flat or collapsed. Very sour smell. Dough is slack and doesn't hold its shape. Transfer to the pan immediately and bake without further delay. Do not dimple until immediately before baking.
Feel cue: By the last fold, the sourdough dough should feel lighter in your hands with each set — as if air is being woven into the fabric of the dough. It stretches farther without tearing and holds its shape briefly before slowly relaxing back.

Pour a generous pool of olive oil (at least 3 tablespoons) into a half-sheet pan. Tip the dough in and gently stretch it toward the edges. Cover loosely with plastic and refrigerate overnight (8–12 hours) for a slow, cold final proof. The next day, remove from the refrigerator 2 hours before baking. The dough should have spread to fill most of the pan and look puffy and airy.
Visual cue: Dough fills the pan, slightly domed and clearly puffy, with visible bubbles under the oiled surface after coming to room temperature.
Underdone: Dough fills less than 70% of the pan and looks dense, not airy, after coming to temperature. Leave it at room temperature for another 1–2 hours. The cold retard slows the yeast significantly.
Perfect: Dough covers 90–100% of the pan, is visibly puffy and bubbly, and jiggles when the pan is nudged. Large bubbles are visible through the oil. Dimple and bake immediately.
Overdone: Dough is very puffy and beginning to look deflated or flat. Bubbles are large and the surface looks fragile. Dimple and bake immediately without delay.
Feel cue: Press the cold focaccia dough with an oily fingertip — after 2 hours at room temperature it should press in slowly and spring back about halfway over 3–4 seconds. If it springs back instantly, give it more time. If it collapses and does not spring back, bake immediately.

Drizzle additional olive oil generously over the surface of the dough. Spread your fingers wide and press them firmly through the dough to the pan bottom, creating deep dimples across the entire surface. Don't be timid — press firmly. Scatter fresh rosemary sprigs and flaky sea salt. The oil will pool in the dimples. Bake immediately at 230 C (450 F).
Visual cue: A landscape of dramatic, deep dimples with olive oil pooling in each crater. Rosemary sprigs scattered throughout. Flaky salt glinting on the surface.
Underdone: Shallow dimples that have mostly sprung back. Oil slides off to the sides. Press harder and deeper — all the way to the pan. The dough can take this force.
Perfect: Deep craters with oil pooling in each one. The dough between dimples has risen into small hills. Rosemary and salt are evenly placed. Into the oven immediately. Every second delays the oven spring.
Overdone: Dimpled too vigorously and torn through the dough in places. Oil leaking under. Gently press torn areas back together. The oven will heal minor tears.
Feel cue: Your fingertips should encounter soft, yielding dough and then suddenly feel the slick resistance of the oil-coated pan bottom. That two-stage feeling — soft dough, then hard pan — is confirmation you have pressed all the way through to create true dimples.

Bake at 230 C (450 F) on the lower-middle rack for 20–25 minutes until the top is deeply golden with darker blistered spots at the dimple peaks and the bottom is crispy and caramelized. Lift a corner with a spatula to check the bottom. Remove from the pan immediately to a wire rack to preserve the crisp bottom.
Visual cue: A deeply golden top with darker blistered peaks and caramelized dimple edges. The bottom is a rich caramel-brown that audibly crackles when the pan is tapped.
Underdone: Pale gold top, soft and blond bottom. No crackle sound. Return to the oven. Drop to the lowest rack for bottom heat. 3–5 more minutes.
Perfect: Rich golden top with charred blisters at the dimple peaks. Bottom is deep caramel-brown and crackles when the corner is lifted. The focaccia sounds hollow when tapped. Transfer immediately to a wire rack. The caramelized bottom will become the pride of this loaf.
Overdone: Dark brown top with very dark edges. Bitter smell from the rosemary. Trim the darkest edges. The interior is likely still excellent.
Feel cue: Tap the bottom of the focaccia — it should ring with a clean, hollow sound, like knocking on wood, rather than a dull thud. The bottom crust should feel rigid and dry under your knuckle: that crispness from the olive-oil caramelization is the crown jewel of sourdough focaccia.

steps:
Combine flour and water. Mix until no dry flour remains. Do not add starter yet — let the flour hydrate alone.
Visual cue: A rough, shaggy mass with no dry patches. Wetter than the yeasted version.
Underdone: Dry pockets visible at the bottom. Add a tablespoon of water and mix again.
Perfect: Shaggy, sticky, no dry flour. Wetter than you'd expect. Cover and autolyse.
Overdone: Soupy — too much water. Add flour a tablespoon at a time.

Cover and let the dough rest for 45-60 minutes. The flour absorbs water and gluten organizes without work.

Underdone: Still rough and shaggy. Wait another 20 minutes.
Perfect: Smooth, extensible, tears less when pulled. Add starter and salt.
Overdone: Starting to ferment on its own (bubbles). Add starter and salt immediately.
Feel cue: Silky compared to the shaggy start. Stretches without snapping.

Add the starter and salt. Squeeze through the dough to distribute, then perform 4 sets of stretch-and-folds at 30-minute intervals.
Visual cue: After 4 fold sets: dough holds shape, surface is smooth, you can see air bubbles through the side of the bowl.
Underdone: Tears when stretched, flattens immediately. Add another fold set and wait 30 minutes.
Perfect: Jiggles when you shake the bowl. Stretches into a thin window. Begin bulk ferment.
Overdone: Tight and springy, won't stretch. Skip the next fold set. Let it relax.
Feel cue: Each fold set should feel easier than the last. By the fourth, the dough feels like stretching warm mozzarella.

Cover. Bulk ferment at room temperature for 6-10 hours (or overnight in the fridge). The dough should grow 50-75%, not double.
Visual cue: Grown 50-75%, domed surface with visible bubbles, slightly sour aroma.
Underdone: Barely risen, dense, no bubbles. Move to a warmer spot and wait.
Perfect: Puffy, domed, jiggly, smells like yogurt and flour. Shape into balls.
Overdone: Collapsed, very sour, sticky and slack. Shape gently. The pizza will be tangier but still good.
Feel cue: Smells like yogurt and fresh bread. A poke returns very slowly — much slower than yeasted dough.

Divide into portions. Pre-shape into rounds, rest 15 minutes, then shape into tight balls. Refrigerate for 12-24 hours before using.
Visual cue: Smooth, taut balls with slight wobble. Surface may show tiny fermentation blisters.
Underdone: Seams visible, not holding shape. Rest 10 minutes, reshape.
Perfect: Taut, smooth, slight jiggle. Blisters forming on the surface. Refrigerate and use within 48 hours.
Overdone: Surface tearing, exposing sticky interior. Rest and reshape gently with wet hands.
Feel cue: Lighter and more airy than yeasted dough. The surface feels like a water balloon — taut but delicate.

description: A soft, Pullman-style American sandwich loaf leavened entirely by an active sourdough starter — tender enough to slice thin for toast yet tangy enough that you taste the ferment on the back of every bite. The crumb is pillowy and close-knit, the crust thin and golden, and the whole kitchen smells like a proper bakery for hours.

ingredients.name: Active sourdough starter (100% hydration, fed 8h ago)

steps:
Combine the flour, water, active starter, and honey in a large bowl. Stir with a wooden spoon or dough whisk until no dry flour remains. The dough will be rough and sticky — resist the urge to add more flour. Cover with a damp towel and let it rest (autolyse) for 30 minutes. This rest allows the flour to fully hydrate and gluten to begin forming without any kneading, which reduces mixing time significantly and improves the crumb structure. Check that your starter is truly active: it should have doubled since feeding and smell yeasty and pleasantly sour.
Visual cue: A rough, shaggy mass that holds together but looks uneven. No dry streaks, some stickiness. Surface is matte and slightly lumpy.
Underdone: Dry flour pockets remain at the bottom or edges. The dough crumbles when pressed. Mix more thoroughly by hand, pressing and folding until completely incorporated. A splash more water (5g) can help if the flour is very thirsty.
Perfect: Uniformly rough and wet with no dry flour. Clings to the bowl sides. Smells of wheat and a hint of ferment from the starter. Cover and rest 30 minutes before adding salt and butter.
Overdone: Dough is already silky smooth from over-mixing — gluten is developed before salt and fat are incorporated. Proceed anyway; add salt and butter in the next step and continue. The loaf will be fine.
Feel cue: The dough should stick aggressively to your hands and pull away in thick, gluey strings — that tackiness is hydration doing its job. If it peels off your palm cleanly, it is too dry.

Sprinkle the salt over the rested dough and squeeze it through the dough with your fingers until evenly distributed — about 2 minutes of aggressive squeezing. Add the softened butter in small pieces and continue squeezing and folding until fully absorbed. Perform stretch-and-folds: wet your hand, grab the far edge of the dough, stretch it up overhead without tearing, and fold it over the center. Rotate 90 degrees and repeat — 4 folds equals one round. Do 4 rounds total, spaced 30 minutes apart, over 2 hours. By the final round the dough should be smooth, strong, and clearly elastic.
Visual cue: A smooth, supple, slightly tacky dough that holds a round shape in the bowl. Surface is nearly silk-smooth. Large bubbles are just beginning to appear underneath.
Underdone: Still ragged, tears easily when stretched, and breaks rather than stretching into a translucent windowpane. Complete all 4 fold rounds before moving on — gluten development is time-sensitive in sourdough; shortcuts show up in the crumb.
Perfect: Stretches into a thin, translucent sheet (windowpane test passes) without tearing. Bounces back slowly when poked. Smooth on the surface. Proceed to bulk fermentation in a lightly oiled bowl.
Overdone: Tight, snapping back instantly when stretched, resisting folds — over-kneaded gluten. Cover and rest 20 minutes uncovered to relax. Then proceed.
Feel cue: After the final fold the dough should feel alive in your hands — slightly warm from fermentation, taut but yielding, like a firm earlobe rather than a rubber band.

Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled container and bulk-ferment at room temperature (21–24 C) for 8–10 hours, or overnight in the refrigerator (4 C) for 12–14 hours. The cold retard slows fermentation and develops deeper sour flavor — for a tangier loaf, always go cold. The dough is ready when it has grown by 50–75% in volume (not doubled, as sourdough is slower), feels lighter and jiggly, and small bubbles are visible along the sides and bottom of the container. Dimples pressed into the surface spring back slowly and lazily.
Visual cue: Dough is visibly puffed — roughly 60–70% larger than it started. Surface is domed and smooth. Bubbles cling to the sides of the container. A poke leaves a slow-filling indent.
Underdone: Barely grown; dense, cold, and tight. Poke fills back immediately and completely. Give it more time at a warmer spot. Sourdough is not the yeast — it needs patience. Cold kitchens need more hours.
Perfect: Grown 60–70%, jiggly when the container is shaken, bubbles visible on sides. A poke fills back halfway and holds for a beat before completing. Shape it while cold — straight from the fridge is ideal.
Overdone: Ballooned and webby with large holes; smells aggressively acidic. Jiggles like loose jelly. Shape it immediately and proof in the pan without delay. A slightly over-fermented dough will be tangier and have a denser crumb but will still bake.
Feel cue: Tip the container and the dough should slowly peel away from the walls like a relaxed, airy mass — not dump out like a dead weight, and not cling stubbornly like raw paste.

Turn the dough onto an unfloured surface. Gently pat it into a rectangle roughly the length of your loaf pan. Fold the long sides in toward the center like a letter, then roll it tightly from the top, sealing the seam with your thumbs as you go. You want surface tension without degassing the crumb — firm but not aggressive rolling. Lower the log seam-side down into a well-greased 9x5 inch (23x13 cm) loaf pan. The dough should fill the pan about 60–65% and sit slightly below the rim.
Visual cue: A tight, evenly shaped log sitting seam-down in the pan, filling it from end to end. The surface is taut and smooth, with no tears or ragged patches.
Underdone: Loose, floppy log with no surface tension. Dough sags and spreads flat in the pan. Remove from the pan, reshape with more tension — fold the seam tightly and roll again, applying downward pressure on the final roll.
Perfect: Tight cylinder with a smooth, taut skin. Springs back only slightly when poked. Fits the pan end to end and sits about 60% full. Cover with oiled plastic wrap and proof until it crests the rim.
Overdone: Surface has torn during shaping, revealing large interior holes. Dough is tight and resists moving. Place in the pan anyway — surface tears do not ruin the loaf, they just change the scoring. Seal any large rips by pinching the dough shut.
Feel cue: A well-shaped loaf feels taut when tapped, like a drum — not hollow but springy, as though the surface is under gentle tension. Run your palm along the top: it should feel uniformly smooth and firm.

Cover the pan with oiled plastic wrap and proof at room temperature (21–24 C) for 3–5 hours, or until the dome of the dough crests about 2 cm above the rim of the pan. If you retarded the bulk in the fridge, the final proof will take the longer end of this range. You can also do a cold final proof overnight in the fridge for baking the next morning — pull it directly from the fridge into the oven. Thirty minutes before baking, preheat the oven to 200 C (400 F).
Visual cue: The dome rises 2 cm above the pan rim, jiggling softly when the pan is nudged. A finger-poke fills back slowly, about halfway, over 10–15 seconds.
Underdone: Dough barely crowns the rim. Poke springs back instantly and completely. Loaf baked now will be dense with large tunnels. Wait longer — sourdough proofing cannot be rushed safely. Check again in 45 minutes.
Perfect: Dome rises confidently above the pan. Gentle jiggle. Poke springs back halfway and holds. Light and pillowy surface. Score a shallow line down the center with a sharp knife and load it into the hot oven.
Overdone: Dome is flat or beginning to dimple inward. Poke leaves a crater that barely moves. Surface looks slightly wrinkled. Bake immediately without scoring. The loaf will still have good flavor but may have a dense crumb. Next time use a slightly cooler room for final proof.
Feel cue: Press the covered surface with one finger: a properly proofed loaf gives like a soft pillow and springs back lazily, as though the gluten is saying 'I'm ready but not in a rush.'

Score a shallow slash down the center of the loaf (optional but gives the crust a controlled split). Bake at 200 C (400 F) for 35–40 minutes, covering the pan loosely with foil for the first 20 minutes to keep the crust from browning too fast before the crumb sets. Remove the foil and continue baking until the internal temperature reads 93–96 C (200–205 F) and the top is a rich golden brown. Let cool in the pan 10 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack. Do not slice for at least 1 hour — the crumb continues to set as the bread cools.
Visual cue: Deep golden-brown domed top with a natural side-bloom split along the score. The crust sounds hollow when the bottom is tapped. Internal temperature 94 C.
Underdone: Pale blond top. Interior temperature below 90 C. Crumb will be gummy and the loaf will compress when sliced. Return for 5–8 more minutes and re-probe. If the top is already dark, tent with foil while the center finishes.
Perfect: Rich amber-gold, hollow on the bottom, 94 C internal. The loaf pulls cleanly from the pan. Crust is thin and snaps gently. Cool 1 hour minimum before slicing — thermal patience is the final ingredient.
Overdone: Very dark, stiff crust. Bitter smell. Interior may be over-dry. Slice and check — if the crumb is fine, the crust was simply dark. Thick crusts mellow when the bread is wrapped.
Feel cue: A properly baked loaf feels surprisingly light when you lift it — the air cells you built over 18 hours are in there, holding up the structure. The crust should crackle softly as it cools on the rack.

name: Sourdough Starter
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A living culture built from nothing but flour and water — coaxed over a week from a flat, lifeless slurry into a billowing, sweet-sour leaven that doubles on schedule and smells of ripe yogurt and green apple. Feed it, watch it breathe, and it will raise bread for a lifetime.

ingredients.name: Whole rye flour (for the first build — high in wild yeast and enzymes)
Unbleached bread or all-purpose flour (for daily feeds)
Mature starter discard (carried forward at each feed)

steps:
In a clean glass jar, stir the whole rye flour and warm water into a thick, lump-free paste — the consistency of pancake batter. Scrape down the sides, mark the level with a rubber band or tape, and cover loosely so gas can escape but the surface stays protected. Rest at warm room temperature, 24–26°C, for 24 hours. Rye carries a dense population of wild yeast and lactic bacteria plus the enzymes that feed them, so it kick-starts a culture faster than white flour ever could.
Visual cue: A smooth, hydrated paste with no dry flour pockets, sitting flat and even at the marked line, just beginning to show a few pinprick bubbles by the end of day one.
Underdone: The mix is stiff and shaggy with dry streaks, or so loose it pours like soup. No bubbles at all and it smells purely of raw flour. Adjust with a teaspoon of flour or water to reach a thick batter, stir smooth, and simply wait — day one is often silent. Make sure the room is genuinely warm.
Perfect: A uniform paste that has lifted very slightly and is freckled with small bubbles. It smells faintly sweet, grassy, and a touch nutty. Leave it another 12–24 hours if needed, then move to the first feed once any bubbling appears.
Overdone: After a couple of days the surface looks gray, alcoholic, or has a thin liquid (hooch) on top and smells sharply of solvent or vinegar. This is normal early hunger, not failure — pour off any hooch, discard down to a spoonful, and proceed straight to feeding. The microbes are awake and need food.
Feel cue: The slurry should feel cool and tacky, dragging slightly on the spoon like thick cream. By the end of day one it may give the faintest hiss of gas when stirred — your first sign of life.

Begin daily feeds. Discard all but about 50 g of the slurry, then stir in equal weights of fresh flour and warm water — roughly 50 g each. Switch to unbleached bread or all-purpose flour now; it builds the gluten strength you want in a leaven. Re-mark the level, cover loosely, and keep warm. Feed once every 24 hours for days 3 and 4. Discarding keeps the culture young and the acid low enough for the yeast to multiply; without it the mixture turns too sour for the yeast to thrive.
Visual cue: Within a day of feeding, the culture climbs noticeably above the mark, domes slightly, and is shot through with bubbles of varying size — clearly fermenting, even if not yet doubling.
Underdone: Little to no rise and only sparse bubbles 24 hours after a feed. The smell is flat or faintly cabbage-like — the false-start lull common around days 3–4. Stay the course and keep feeding on schedule. If it stalls for several days, move it somewhere warmer or add a spoonful of rye to the feed to re-energize it.
Perfect: A visible rise of 30–80% with an open, bubbly body and a slightly domed top. The aroma has turned pleasantly sour and yeasty, like tangy yogurt or beer. Continue feeding once daily. As activity strengthens toward day 5, step up to feeding twice a day, every 12 hours.
Overdone: The culture rose, peaked, and collapsed back down well before the next feed, with hooch pooling on top and a harsh, nail-polish smell. It is fermenting faster than it is fed — shorten the interval to every 12 hours and keep it slightly cooler. This is a sign of strength, not failure.
Feel cue: Freshly fed, the batter is slack and smooth; as it ferments it grows lighter, springier, and webbed with air. A drop on your fingertip should smell brightly sour and clean, never rotten or cheesy.

From around day 5, feed twice daily, every 12 hours, discarding to ~50 g each time and refreshing with equal flour and water. The culture should now be reliable: rising and falling on a predictable rhythm. Watch one full cycle from feed to peak — when it consistently doubles within 4–8 hours and smells sweet-sour and ripe, it is mature. Confirm readiness with the float test: drop a spoonful of peaked starter into water. If it floats, it is buoyant with gas and ready to leaven bread.
Visual cue: A starter that reliably doubles to its peak, full of a tight, even network of bubbles, with a gently domed top that has not yet begun to recede. A spoonful floats in water.
Underdone: It rises only halfway, takes longer than 8 hours to peak, or a spoonful sinks in the float test. The smell is timid. Give it more days of twice-daily feeds. Young cultures gain power gradually — warmth and consistent feeding are all it needs.
Perfect: Doubled or more within 4–8 hours, light and airy throughout, domed and glossy at the peak, and it floats. The aroma is balanced — tangy, sweet, faintly of ripe fruit and yogurt. It is ready to bake with. Use it at or just before peak, when it is at maximum buoyancy and activity.
Overdone: Past its peak: the dome has fallen into a sunken, wrinkled surface, hooch has formed, and the smell is sharply acidic and boozy. Still usable but at its weakest and most sour — feed it and wait for the next peak before baking, or use immediately if you want a more sour loaf.
Feel cue: At peak the starter is light and pillowy, jiggling like a thick mousse and clinging to the jar in airy ribbons. It smells like tart yogurt with a whisper of green apple — appetizing, never offensive.

To keep the starter alive long-term, settle into a maintenance feed: carry forward 50 g of mature starter, discard the rest, and refresh with 50 g flour and 50 g water (a 1:1:1 ratio). If baking often, hold it at room temperature and feed once or twice daily. If baking occasionally, store it in the fridge and feed weekly — let it warm and rise once at room temperature before each bake. A well-kept starter improves for years, deepening in flavor and reliability.
Visual cue: A stable, resilient culture that springs back to a full peak within hours of every feed, with a clean sweet-sour smell — equally happy chilled and dormant or warm and bubbling.
Underdone: Sluggish after fridge storage or a missed feed — slow to rise, with grayish liquid on top and a flat aroma. Revive it with two or three fresh feeds at room temperature, 12 hours apart, discarding well each time. It will rebound to full strength quickly.
Perfect: Predictable and vigorous: doubles on schedule, smells clean and tangy, and floats when peaked. Maintained with minimal effort. Keep your rhythm — daily on the counter or weekly in the fridge — and bake whenever it is at peak. Pass a jar to a friend.
Overdone: Neglected for weeks: dark hooch, an orange or pink tinge, or fuzzy mold on the surface. Pink, orange, or fuzzy mold means contamination — discard entirely and start over. Harmless dark hooch alone just means it is starving; pour it off and resume feeding.
Feel cue: A healthy maintained starter feels lively and elastic, stretching in gluten-laced strands off the spoon and bouncing back at the peak. The smell stays brightly sour and clean year after year — that constancy is the mark of a mature culture.

ingredients.name: White wine vinegar or lemon juice
White bread slices, soaked in milk and squeezed

steps:
Fry the onion in a splash of oil over medium heat until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the spices and fry for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the mince and cook, breaking it up, for 8–10 minutes until browned and cooked through with no pink remaining. Stir in the apricot jam and vinegar. Taste — the filling should be sweet, savory, and warmly spiced with a background sharpness. Season with salt and pepper. The sweetness and acidity are what make this distinctly Cape Malay rather than a standard curry mince.
Visual cue: Meat is fully browned with no pink patches. The filling looks glossy from the jam and is fragrant with warm spice. The color is a warm golden-brown with orange-yellow from turmeric.
Underdone: Pink mince still visible. Spice smells raw. Onions still translucent rather than golden. Continue cooking, breaking up any clumps. The meat must be fully cooked before baking as the custard top sets quickly and won't penetrate the filling.
Perfect: Uniformly brown, glossy, and fragrant. Sweet-savory-spiced aroma fills the kitchen. No liquid pooling in the pan. Fold in the soaked bread and transfer to a baking dish.
Overdone: Meat is very dry and beginning to stick. Jam has caramelized to sticky dark spots. Onions are turning dark. Add a splash of water to loosen. Remove from heat immediately and fold in the bread — the residual heat will continue cooking.
Feel cue: The filling should move as a cohesive mass when the pan is shaken — moist and glossy, not dry and crumbly. If it sounds like it is frying rather than steaming, it is ready.

Squeeze the milk-soaked bread firmly to remove excess liquid, then crumble it into the meat filling and mix well. The bread acts as a binder and moisture reservoir — it keeps the filling from drying out during baking and gives it a slightly soft, yielding texture beneath the custard. Transfer the filling to a buttered oven dish (about 30 x 20 cm), pressing it down into an even layer. Tuck bay leaves on top. Preheat oven to 180 °C.
Visual cue: Filling is pressed into an even, compact layer about 4–5 cm deep in the dish. Surface is level. Bay leaves visible on top.
Underdone: Filling is mounded unevenly with high spots and low spots. The custard will pool in the valleys and be too thin on the peaks. Use the back of a spoon to press and level the surface before adding the custard.
Perfect: Even, compact layer with smooth, level surface. Filling is slightly compressed but still has some give when pressed. Bay leaves lying flat on top. Pour the custard immediately and place in the preheated oven.
Overdone: Filling has been packed so tightly it has become dense and compressed — more like a meatloaf than a bobotie. Use a fork to loosen the top layer slightly before adding custard, which needs to seep into the surface.
Feel cue: Press the surface of the filling with your palm — it should feel firmly padded, like a mattress, yielding 1–2 cm but springing back rather than compressing permanently.

Whisk the eggs and milk together with a pinch of salt and turmeric until smooth and uniformly yellow. Pour the custard mixture slowly and evenly over the meat layer. The custard should cover the surface completely and be visible around the edges — about 1 cm deep. Bake at 180 °C for 35–40 minutes until the custard is just set throughout and golden on top. The center should barely wobble when the dish is shaken.
Visual cue: The custard top is golden yellow with light brown spots where it has caramelized. The entire surface is set — no liquid movement when the dish is gently shaken.
Underdone: Center of the custard is still liquid, sloshing visibly when shaken. The surface is pale yellow and set only at the edges. Return to the oven for 8–10 more minutes and check again. The oven temperature may be too low.
Perfect: Golden, uniformly set surface with a gentle dome. Center barely trembles with a slow, cohesive movement when the dish is moved — like set panna cotta. No liquid visible. Remove from oven and rest 5 minutes before serving.
Overdone: Custard is fully rigid with no wobble. Surface is dark golden with dry, cracked edges. The custard may be beginning to pull away from the sides. Remove immediately. The custard is overcooked but still edible — serve quickly before it continues to tighten from residual heat.
Feel cue: Shake the dish gently — a perfect bobotie custard moves like a very slow-moving lava lamp: cohesive, not sloshy, with the center lagging a half-second behind the edges. That lag is where the perfect texture lives.

Rest the bobotie for 5 minutes out of the oven — this allows the custard to fully set and the filling to firm up so it cuts cleanly. Serve in squares directly from the dish, accompanied by yellow rice (cooked with turmeric and raisins), chutney, and sliced banana. Remove and discard bay leaves before serving. A proper bobotie plate should have sweetness (banana, chutney), warmth (the spiced filling), and the silky custard acting as a gentle, binding crown.
Visual cue: When cut, the bobotie has two distinct layers: a golden custard top and a moist, spiced filling below. The cut edges are clean, not crumbling.
Underdone: Custard top slides off when cut — it hasn't bonded with the filling. The filling is loose and unset. Return to the oven for 5–8 more minutes. Alternatively, rest longer at room temperature, which will allow carryover heat to finish the custard.
Perfect: Clean-cut squares with a distinct golden layer on top and moist, spiced meat below. The custard is soft enough to quiver slightly when the plate is moved. Sweet, spiced aroma. Serve immediately with yellow rice and chutney.
Overdone: Filling is dry and crumbles when cut. Custard is rubbery and separated from the filling. The dish smells slightly scorched. Serve with extra chutney and a generous spoonful of yogurt or cream to restore moisture.
Feel cue: Cut through the custard with the side of a spoon — it should yield with gentle, even resistance, like cutting through a soft terrine, before giving way cleanly to the moist filling beneath.

name: South Indian Idli Batter
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Idli rice (parboiled short-grain rice): 3 parts
  Alternatives: regular parboiled rice; idli rava (rice semolina)
Urad dal (split black gram, husked): 1 parts
Non-iodized salt: 1.5 tsp per cup of batter
Cold water (for grinding): 0.5 parts
Fenugreek seeds (methi): 0.25 tsp per cup of urad
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 16 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Parboiled rice and split black lentils, soaked separately and ground to a silky batter, then left overnight to ferment until airy and slightly sour — the foundation of idli, dosa, and uttapam across South India.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Rinse the rice 3-4 times until the water runs clear. Rinse the urad dal and fenugreek seeds together 2-3 times. Soak them in separate bowls of cold water for 6-8 hours (or overnight). Keep the bowls in a cool spot — not refrigerated. The soaking water should cover the grains by at least 5cm as they will swell significantly. The fenugreek seeds soak with the urad dal. After soaking, drain each bowl but reserve the urad dal soaking water separately — it contains wild yeasts and bacteria that help fermentation.
Visual cue: Plump, swollen grains — rice has turned from translucent to opaque white; urad dal has almost doubled in size and turned very white.
Underdone: Grains are still firm and have barely swelled. Rice is still glassy. Urad dal is not yet doubled. Soak for at least 2 more hours. The grains must be fully hydrated for smooth grinding.
Perfect: Rice has turned opaque and swollen, each grain feeling soft when pressed. Urad dal is plump, white, doubled in volume, and a grain splits easily between fingernails. Fenugreek seeds have swelled slightly. Drain and grind separately.
Overdone: Soaked for 24+ hours — grains smell slightly sour and fermentation has already begun in the water. Drain immediately and use. Pre-fermented soaking water can be used to aid the main fermentation.
Feel cue: A soaked urad dal grain pressed between fingernails should split cleanly with no resistance — fully soft and yielding throughout.

Grind the urad dal and fenugreek seeds first in a wet grinder or high-powered blender with the reserved soaking water (or cold water), adding water tablespoon by tablespoon. Grind for 20-30 minutes in a wet grinder (or 5-10 minutes in a high-speed blender) until the batter is completely smooth, extremely fine, and very fluffy — it should have a whipped, airy quality from the air incorporation during grinding. The traditional wet grinder stone generates minimal heat and grinds ultra-fine. Transfer to a large bowl. Then grind the soaked rice with cold water until smooth but slightly grainy — just a bit of texture is desirable in idli rice batter. Combine both batters and mix well.
Visual cue: Two combined batters: the urad dal portion is snow-white, fluffy, and airy; the rice portion is cream-colored and slightly grainy. Together they form a smooth, pourable batter.
Underdone: Urad dal batter is not airy or white — it looks grey and dense. Rice batter has very visible coarse grain. Batter feels gritty and heavy. Grind for longer. Urad dal must be ground to a very fine, light foam-like consistency. Add water gradually to facilitate grinding.
Perfect: Urad dal batter is white, airy, almost fluffy — it falls off the spoon in light dollops. Rice batter is smooth with only a faint texture. Combined batter is uniform, creamy-white, and pourable, not too thick and not watery. Add salt, stir well, and ferment.
Overdone: Batter is very thin and watery from too much water being added during grinding. The batter will still ferment and work, but the idli will be very flat and slightly rubbery. Use less water next time.
Feel cue: Rub the urad dal batter between your fingers — it should feel silky smooth, with zero graininess. Like the finest foam.

Stir the salt into the combined batter thoroughly — salt helps control unwanted bacteria during fermentation. The batter should be of a consistency that falls off a spoon in a thick ribbon. Transfer to a large container (the batter will roughly double in volume during fermentation — the container must be large enough). Cover loosely with a lid or cloth. Leave in a warm place — 28-32°C (82-90°F) is ideal. In Indian summer climates this happens overnight (8-12 hours). In cooler climates it may take 16-24 hours. The oven with only the light on (around 27°C) works well in cool kitchens. Fermentation is complete when the batter has risen significantly, looks fluffy and aerated, has a pleasant sour smell, and tiny bubbles are visible throughout.
Visual cue: Risen, aerated batter that has at least doubled in volume with visible bubbles throughout and a slightly domed surface.
Underdone: Batter has barely risen. No visible bubbles. Still smells like raw grain and salt. The surface is flat and dense. Move to a warmer location. Fermentation requires warmth — below 24°C it will be very slow or may not start.
Perfect: Batter has roughly doubled or more. Surface is domed and aerated. Fine bubbles visible throughout. Smells pleasantly sour and slightly yeasty — like a mild sourdough. The batter is noticeably lighter in texture and pours fluffy. Stir gently from the bottom and use immediately, or refrigerate for up to 3-4 days.
Overdone: Batter smells aggressively alcoholic and very sour. Has risen, peaked, and collapsed. Liquidy on top. Stir well. The batter is over-fermented but can still make decent idli. Use for dosa (crepes) which are better with sour batter.
Feel cue: Stir the fermented batter from the bottom — it should feel airy and lighter than before fermentation, almost like stirring foam. It should release a faint fizz and a pleasant clean-sour aroma.

Grease the idli molds lightly with oil. Gently stir the batter from the bottom without deflating it too much. Ladle batter into each mold, filling about three-quarters full — they will expand during steaming. Steam over vigorously boiling water for 10-12 minutes. Do not lift the lid during steaming. The idli are done when a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean and the surface is set and slightly dry. Unmold immediately after 2 minutes of cooling by running a wet spoon around each idli. They should pop out cleanly.
Visual cue: Perfectly round, white, slightly domed idli with a smooth surface. No sticking to the mold.
Underdone: Idli are soft and sticky, collapsing when touched. Toothpick comes out wet. Interior is gummy and raw-smelling. Return to the steamer for 3-5 more minutes with the lid on. Maintain vigorous steam throughout.
Perfect: Idli are soft but set — they hold their shape when unmolded and have a smooth, slightly dry surface. Toothpick is clean. Interior is spongy and white with a pleasant mild sour flavor. They release from the mold cleanly. Serve immediately with sambar and coconut chutney.
Overdone: Idli are dry and slightly hard on the surface. Interior is slightly dense. Cover with a damp cloth immediately. They soften as they rest. Over-steaming typically means over-fermented batter or excessive heat.
Feel cue: A perfect idli should feel soft and yielding but not wet when touched — like a dense cloud. It should spring back very slightly when pressed gently.

name: Spanakopita Filling
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Fresh spinach, stems removed (or baby spinach): 100 %
  Alternatives: silverbeet (Swiss chard); frozen spinach (thawed and squeezed)
Feta cheese, crumbled (not pre-crumbled — buy a block): 50 %
  Alternatives: ricotta salata (less salty); goat cheese
Large eggs: 10 %
Scallions (spring onions), thinly sliced: 15 %
  Alternatives: shallots; chives
Fresh dill, finely chopped: 8 %
  Alternatives: fennel fronds
Extra-virgin olive oil: 8 %
Freshly ground black pepper: 0.5 %
Freshly grated nutmeg: 0.2 %
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 35 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The savory filling at the heart of every great spanakopita — wilted spinach wrung bone-dry, crumbled feta, egg, scallion, and dill stirred together into a rich, briny mixture that stays moist inside phyllo pastry.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Fresh spinach, stems removed (or baby spinach)
Feta cheese, crumbled (not pre-crumbled — buy a block)

steps:
Heat a large, dry skillet over high heat until it is very hot. Add the fresh spinach in large handfuls — it will collapse dramatically, reducing to a fraction of its original volume in about 1–2 minutes per batch. Stir and press the spinach to encourage even wilting. Do not add water or oil at this stage; you want the leaves to steam in their own moisture and give up as much liquid as possible. Once all the spinach has wilted, transfer it to a colander and let it cool enough to handle. Then take handfuls and squeeze them with maximum force over the sink — wring them like a wet cloth. The goal is to extract every possible drop of water. The dry spinach should feel almost gritty in your hand, not damp. Then chop the wrung spinach roughly into 1 cm pieces.
Visual cue: A dark green, rough-textured mass of spinach that barely releases any liquid when pressed — the wringing should have removed so much moisture that the pile looks dark and compact, not shiny or wet.
Underdone: Spinach is wilted but still releasing water when squeezed — the pile feels wet and heavy, and liquid pools under it on the board. Wring again in smaller handfuls with more force. This step cannot be rushed or compromised — excess moisture is the single greatest enemy of crispy spanakopita.
Perfect: Dark, cohesive, and barely moist — the chopped pieces separate from each other without clumping, and pressing the pile firmly yields only a few drops of liquid. Proceed with combining. Dry spinach means crispy phyllo.
Overdone: Spinach has been squeezed so aggressively it has broken down to a paste and most of the fresh vegetable texture is gone. This is acceptable — the texture will be more homogeneous but the flavor is the same. Proceed.
Feel cue: Take a large handful and squeeze with both hands as hard as you can. If more than a tablespoon of green liquid runs out, squeeze again. The finished wad in your
hand should feel like dry clay — dense, compact, barely moist. This is the most important step in the whole recipe.

In a small skillet, warm the olive oil over medium heat. Add the sliced scallions and cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they are wilted and sweet-smelling but not browned. The goal is to take the raw edge off the scallion flavor — raw scallion in a baked filling can be sharp and pungent, whereas briefly cooked scallion becomes sweet and integrated. Remove from heat and allow to cool slightly. The scallions will continue to soften in the residual heat. They should look translucent and smell mild and sweet.
Visual cue: Translucent, glistening scallion rings with no browning, smelling sweet and mild rather than sharp and raw — a complete transformation from their raw state.
Underdone: Scallions still have a sharp, raw bite and are only slightly softened — they will taste pungently of raw onion in the finished filling. Cook for another 2 minutes. The goal is translucency and sweetness, not caramelization.
Perfect: Translucent, soft, and mildly sweet. They collapse easily when pressed against the pan. The oil they cooked in smells of sweet allium. Remove from heat and cool before adding to the filling.
Overdone: Scallions have browned and taken on a caramelized sweetness that may overpower the delicate filling. A little browning is not catastrophic — proceed, knowing the filling will be slightly sweeter than intended.
Feel cue: Press a scallion ring with the tip of a spatula — it should yield instantly and completely without any firm resistance. The oil in the pan should feel slippery from the released sugars — slightly thicker than when you started.

In a large bowl, combine the wrung, chopped spinach, cooled sweated scallions, crumbled feta, beaten eggs, chopped dill, black pepper, and freshly grated nutmeg. Mix thoroughly with your hands or a large spoon, breaking the feta into crumbles no larger than a small pea — some very fine feta dust is fine and helps bind the filling. Do not add salt before tasting: the feta carries significant salt and the filling may need none. Taste critically and add salt only if truly needed. The mixture should smell of fresh dill, creamy feta, and cooked spinach — fresh and grassy with a briny background. The texture should be cohesive enough to hold its shape briefly when scooped but not stiff.
Visual cue: A dark green filling generously studded with white feta crumbles and flecked with dill green — the mixture should look vivid and fresh, not grey or watery, and should hold a loose scoop shape.
Underdone: Filling is not thoroughly combined — there are unmixed pockets of spinach, chunks of feta, and the egg hasn't coated everything evenly. Mix more thoroughly, particularly breaking up any large feta chunks and making sure the egg coats all the spinach.
Perfect: Evenly combined, with feta distributed throughout and every piece of spinach coated in egg. The filling holds a scooped shape and smells fresh and herby. Use immediately as a filling or refrigerate for up to 24 hours.
Overdone: Over-mixed to the point where the spinach has broken down and the feta has dissolved into the spinach — the filling is uniformly grey-green rather than spotted with white. Proceed. The texture has changed but the flavor is intact.
Feel cue: Scoop a spoonful and hold it up — it should mound slightly, then slowly slump, not pour. If it pours, the spinach was too wet. Press the back of the spoon into the mixture in the bowl; it should leave a clean impression that holds for a moment before the filling
slowly returns to level.

Leave the combined filling to rest for 10 minutes at room temperature. During this time, the egg will begin to bind more firmly with the spinach and feta, and the dill and scallion flavors will bloom and integrate. After resting, taste once more — flavors will have mellowed and merged. Make any final adjustments: more dill if the herb flavor is too subtle, a few more grinds of pepper if it tastes flat, a drop of lemon juice if it needs brightness. The filling is now ready to be used with buttered phyllo sheets for triangles, a pan pie, or rolled cigars. It holds refrigerated for 24 hours with minimal quality loss; the flavors actually deepen slightly overnight.
Visual cue: After resting, the filling looks denser and more cohesive, with the egg visibly having knit the components together — it holds the shape of a spoon indentation longer than the freshly mixed version.
Underdone: Still freshly mixed and watery at the bottom of the bowl — the components haven't had time to bind and the filling will make phyllo soggy. Rest for the full 10 minutes. If the bottom of the bowl is pooled with liquid, squeeze the whole filling through a clean towel once more.
Perfect: Cohesive, vivid, and fragrant. A scoopful holds its mound shape. No liquid pooling at the base of the bowl. Tastes bright, briny, herby, and deeply satisfying. Proceed immediately to layering with phyllo, or refrigerate covered for up to 24 hours.
Overdone: The filling has been refrigerated for 2+ days and the feta has made the spinach very wet and the dill has turned drab and pungent. Squeeze the filling again through a clean towel to remove excess moisture before using.
Feel cue: After resting, drag two fingers through the filling and press them together — there should be enough body from the egg that the filling briefly strings between your fingers before breaking. That thin, soft thread is the egg binder at
work, and it tells you the filling will stay put inside phyllo rather than oozing out during baking.

name: 希腊菠菜派 · Spanakopita (Greek Spinach Pie)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Phyllo dough (fresh or fully thawed): 400 g
  Alternatives: homemade hand-stretched phyllo if skilled
Fresh spinach (or frozen 500g, fully thawed and squeezed): 1000 g
  Alternatives: Swiss chard; a mix of spinach and chard
Feta cheese, crumbled: 400 g
  Alternatives: a mix of feta and ricotta for a creamier filling
Eggs, beaten: 3 eggs
Spring onions (scallions), thinly sliced: 4 stalks
  Alternatives: 1 small leek, sliced
Fresh dill, roughly chopped: 30 g
  Alternatives: flat-leaf parsley; a mix of dill and mint
Olive oil or melted unsalted butter (for brushing): 120 ml
  Alternatives: a mix of both for richer flavour
Freshly ground black pepper: 2 g
Freshly grated nutmeg: 1 pinch
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 1 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Crisp, golden phyllo pastry layered with a filling of wilted spinach, crumbled feta, dill and egg — each shattering, paper-thin sheet giving way to the creamy, herby, salty filling within. The kind of pie that disappears the moment it reaches the table.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Fresh spinach (or frozen 500g, fully thawed and squeezed)
Olive oil or melted unsalted butter (for brushing)

steps:
If using fresh spinach, wilt it in a dry pan or with a splash of water over high heat until completely collapsed, then tip into a colander and cool. When cool enough to handle, squeeze the spinach in your fists — hard, relentlessly, handful by handful — until almost no water comes out. This is the most critical step in the recipe: residual spinach water makes the filling wet, turns the phyllo soggy, and ruins the finished pie. A kilogram of raw spinach will reduce to about 200g of dry, dark-green paste. Transfer to a large bowl and coarsely chop. Add the crumbled feta, beaten eggs, spring onions, dill, black pepper and nutmeg. Mix together with a fork until cohesive — the filling should look like a rough, green-flecked, salty mixture, not a smooth paste. Taste (carefully — the feta is already salty) and add more pepper or dill as needed. Set aside.
Visual cue: A rough, cohesive filling — dark green spinach, crumbled white feta and flecks of dill — that holds together when you press it in your palm without weeping any liquid.
Underdone: The mixture is wet and pooling — liquid has gathered at the bottom of the bowl and the filling won't hold together. The eggs have not had time to bind it. Squeeze more spinach and drain off the liquid. Add an extra tablespoon of crumbled feta or a handful of breadcrumbs to absorb excess moisture before proceeding.
Perfect: The filling is dense, moist but not wet, holding its shape when pressed. The feta is distributed in visible chunks and the dill is fragrant. No liquid pools. Proceed directly to assembly — the filling is ready.
Overdone: The filling has been over-worked into a homogeneous paste with no visible texture, the feta fully broken down. The texture is lost but the flavour is fine. Proceed — the pie will taste good even if the cross-section looks more uniform.
Feel cue: A handful of the filling pressed into a ball should
just hold together, with the feta crumbles providing resistance and the spinach threading through it. If your palm is wet after pressing, squeeze more spinach.

Preheat the oven to 190°C / 375°F. Brush a 30×22cm (or equivalent) baking pan generously with oil or melted butter. Work with phyllo quickly — it dries and tears within minutes of exposure to air; keep the stack covered with a damp towel between sheets. Lay the first sheet of phyllo in the pan, letting the excess hang over the edges. Brush the entire surface generously with oil or butter, reaching all the way to the edges and corners. Lay another sheet perpendicular to the first, brush again. Repeat this layering and brushing process until you have used roughly half the phyllo sheets (8–10 sheets depending on thickness). The fat between each layer is what creates the shatter-crisp, separated layers of the finished crust — do not skimp.
Visual cue: A glistening, translucent stack of phyllo in the pan, the sheets barely distinguishable as individual layers, each one evenly sheened with oil — no dry, pale or torn patches.
Underdone: Some sheets are barely brushed and show dry, matte patches, or several sheets are layered together unbrused, sticking as a block. Lift the sheets carefully and brush the areas missed. Ungreased sheets bond together and form a thick, doughy layer rather than a crisp one.
Perfect: Each sheet is evenly glistening, the stack translucent and gossamer-thin, the fat distributed across every centimetre of surface. Spoon in the filling and proceed to the top crust.
Overdone: The sheets are dripping and oil is pooling in the base of the pan — each layer has been heavily over-oiled and the phyllo is saturated. Pour off excess oil from the pan before adding the filling. The crust will be greasy rather than crisp if flooded with fat.
Feel cue: Run your palm lightly over the top sheet — it should feel smooth, cool and uniformly slick, like tissue paper coated in a thin film of oil, with no dry crinkle where a spot has been missed.

Spread the filling evenly across the phyllo base using a spatula, pressing it into an even layer and tucking it into the corners. Fold the overhanging phyllo edges inward over the filling — they will form part of the top crust. Now layer the remaining phyllo sheets over the top in the same oiled fashion, sheet by sheet, each one brushed generously. Fold or tuck the overhanging top sheets under the pie to form a neat border. Brush the entire top surface very generously with oil. Score the top layers only with a sharp knife in the portion sizes you want before baking — the classic diamond or square patterns — cutting through only the top 4–5 sheets, not all the way through to the filling. This prevents the crust from shattering uncontrollably when you cut after baking.
Visual cue: A snugly filled pan with a neatly tucked, glistening phyllo top — the scored diamond pattern visible as hairline incisions across the gleaming surface.
Underdone: The filling bulges in the center with the phyllo pulled tight over it, or the top sheets are uneven and bunched at one end. Press the filling to an even thickness and smooth the top phyllo flat by pressing gently with the palm before scoring.
Perfect: Flat, evenly filled, with glistening top sheets that follow the filling's surface, the scored lines showing cleanly through the top layers. Bake immediately at the preheated oven temperature.
Overdone: The knife has been pressed all the way through to the filling, letting filling seep up through the scored channels and preventing the top from crisping. Score very lightly on the next pie. The cuts only need to penetrate the top 3–4 sheets — the idea is to pre-cut the crust, not the filling.
Feel cue: The assembled pie should feel solid and flat under your palm — the filling dense enough to support the top sheets without them dipping. The top should feel smooth and taut, not rucked or
loose.

Bake at 190°C / 375°F for 45–55 minutes until the top is a deep, even golden-brown across its entire surface. Rotate the pan once at the halfway mark to ensure even browning. The pie is done when the scored lines have opened up and the phyllo between them has puffed and crisped, the edges are a slightly darker amber, and the kitchen smells of buttered pastry and herbs. Rest for at least 10 minutes before cutting along the pre-scored lines — the filling needs a moment to firm from liquid-eggy to sliceable. Serve warm or at room temperature; it is equally magnificent both ways.
Visual cue: A uniformly deep golden-brown top, the scored diamonds clearly delineated and puffed open, with slightly darker amber edges and a shatteringly crisp surface.
Underdone: The top is pale golden or ivory, the phyllo still slightly soft and not shattering when pressed. The filling may still be loose. Return to the oven for another 10 minutes. Pale phyllo is not yet crisp and the filling will not have set fully.
Perfect: Deep, even golden-brown, the diamond sections risen and crisp, the edges crisped to amber. A tap on the surface sounds hollow. The filling is fully set and slices cleanly. Rest 10 minutes then cut along the scored lines. Each portion should lift out cleanly with visible layers.
Overdone: The top is darkening to a burnt brown-black and the phyllo is crumbling and powdery rather than crisp. Tent with foil immediately and reduce heat to 160°C for remaining time. Check for burnt spots that must be trimmed before serving.
Feel cue: Tap the surface of the baked pie — it should sound hollow and crackle faintly under the knuckle, like a drum skin. Cut a corner piece and listen for the shatter of phyllo. Each bite should give first crunch then yield to the creamy, salty, herby filling.

name: Spanish Bacalao al Pil-Pil
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Dried salt cod (bacalao), skin-on, bone-in: 600 g
Extra-virgin olive oil: 350 ml
Garlic cloves, thinly sliced: 6 cloves
Dried guindilla or árbol chili: 2 whole
Fine sea salt (for soaking water only): 0 g
Fresh flat-leaf parsley, chopped: 10 g
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 30 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Basque salt cod confited gently in olive oil at a whisper of heat, then coaxed by swirling the pan into a trembling, ivory emulsion from its own collagen — no cream, no flour, nothing but the fish and oil.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
