ingredients.name: Fine sea salt (for soaking water only)

steps:
Submerge the salt cod in a large bowl of cold water, skin side up. Refrigerate for 24–48 hours, changing the water every 8 hours (at least 3 changes). The fish is ready when a small piece, tasted raw, is pleasantly salty — like a lightly seasoned piece of fish, not aggressively briny. The flesh will have rehydrated and turned from stiff board to supple, with a pearlescent color. Cut into 150g portions. Pat completely dry.
Visual cue: Flesh is pearlescent white, supple and pliable, no longer stiff. Soaking water has turned very salty.
Underdone: Flesh is still partially stiff and tasting sharply, aggressively salty (too much for a sauce). Continue soaking with fresh water changes every 6 hours for 12–24 more hours.
Perfect: Flesh is fully supple and pearlescent, tastes pleasantly salty. Returns to its original cream-white color. Pat dry and bring to room temperature 30 minutes before cooking.
Overdone: Fish has been soaked too long (72+ hours) and is now tasteless, having lost all its characteristic salt-dried flavor. Cook immediately; the texture will be fine, though the flavor will be milder than ideal.
Feel cue: Properly desalted bacalao should feel like a thick, supple piece of fresh fish with a slight resistance when bent — not stiff, not watery, but plump and firm.

In a wide, heavy skillet or earthenware cazuela, pour all the olive oil. Add the garlic slices and dried chilies. Over very low heat, slowly bring the oil to 60–65°C — use a thermometer; it must never boil or even simmer. Gently lay the cod portions skin-side up in the oil. Confit for 12–15 minutes at this gentle temperature, carefully turning once. The oil should show only the faintest, laziest movement around the fish — almost still. Remove the cod and set aside, reserving the oil.
Visual cue: Cod is opaque and just set — white and glistening, not flaking apart. The oil is barely moving, showing only the mildest tremor around the fish.
Underdone: Cod is still partially translucent at the center. Oil is too cold — barely above room temperature. Increase heat very slightly and check the temperature — it must reach 60°C.
Perfect: Cod is fully opaque but still holding together in one piece, glistening and supple. Garlic is golden, not brown. Remove the cod and proceed to the emulsification.
Overdone: Oil has boiled and the cod is falling apart; flesh is dry and stringy rather than silky. Proceed to emulsification anyway — the gelatin is still present, just the texture of the fish is compromised.
Feel cue: At the correct confit temperature, the oil should feel barely warm on the back of your hand — almost like a warm bath, not a cooking medium. The fish should look like it is merely resting in oil, not cooking.

Remove the garlic and chilies from the oil and set aside for garnish. Return the cazuela with the oil to the very lowest heat. Return the cod to the pan, skin-side down. Begin swirling the pan in a continuous circular motion, or use a flat-mesh spider to agitate the oil in circles around the fish. The gelatin released from the cod's skin will slowly emulsify with the oil over 8–15 minutes of continuous swirling. Do not stop or add any other ingredient. The sauce will gradually turn from translucent golden oil to an opaque, ivory-cream sauce — the pil-pil.
Visual cue: Oil has transformed into a thick, creamy ivory emulsion that clings to the fish and the sides of the pan.
Underdone: Oil is still clear and golden; no emulsification has occurred despite swirling. The fish may not be releasing enough gelatin. Continue swirling patiently — it can take 12–15 minutes. Add a tablespoon of cold water to trigger the emulsification.
Perfect: Sauce is opaque, ivory-white, and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. It clings to the fish in a silky, trembling layer. The pan moves in slow, heavy waves. Plate the fish and spoon the pil-pil over. Garnish with garlic and chili.
Overdone: Emulsion has broken — the sauce has separated back into clear oil with white flecks. Remove from heat and let cool slightly. Add 1 tbsp cold water and begin swirling again — broken pil-pil can often be rescued with patience and a temperature reduction.
Feel cue: The pil-pil sauce should feel completely smooth on the tongue — no graininess, no oiliness — just a round, almost neutral creaminess with a lingering salt-cod depth. It should shiver when the plate is tapped.

name: Spanish Clams with Chorizo and White Wine
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Littleneck clams, scrubbed clean: 1000 g
  Alternatives: Manila clams; cockles
Spanish chorizo (cured, sliced into coins): 150 g
  Alternatives: Portuguese chouriço
Garlic cloves, thinly sliced: 20 g
Dry white wine (Albariño or Verdejo): 200 ml
  Alternatives: dry vermouth; fish stock
Extra-virgin olive oil: 30 ml
Flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped: 15 g
Fresh lemon juice: 20 ml
Smoked paprika (pimentón de la Vera): 3 g
Black pepper: 2 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 35 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Littleneck clams steam open in a broth of smoky chorizo fat, white wine, and garlic — the most effortless dish in the Spanish canon, and the one most likely to make you forget everything else you planned to cook.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Soak the clams in cold, lightly salted water (30g salt per liter) for 30 minutes. The clams will expel any sand and grit they are holding. Drain and scrub the shells under cold running water. Discard any clam with a cracked shell or any that does not close when tapped — these are dead and will ruin the dish. Sort through them one by one; a single bad clam can make the entire broth bitter and unpleasant.
Visual cue: Clean, tightly closed clam shells with no sand or mud on the exterior.
Underdone: Clams are still gritty when you rub your fingers over the shells. Some may still have sand in their hinges. Change the water and soak for another 20 minutes.
Perfect: Shells are clean and smooth. When tapped, all living clams close tightly. The soaking water has sand and grit at the bottom. Drain and proceed to cooking.
Overdone: Clams have soaked so long in the same water that they are re-ingesting expelled sand. Change the water and give them 5 more minutes in fresh saltwater, then drain.
Feel cue: Run a clean clam shell between your fingers — it should feel smooth and slightly chalky, not gritty. The hinge should feel tight and spring back when pressed.

Heat the olive oil in a wide, heavy pan with a lid over medium heat. Add the chorizo coins and cook for 2–3 minutes until the fat renders and the oil turns a vivid orange-red from the paprika in the chorizo. Add the sliced garlic and smoked paprika, cooking for 60 seconds until fragrant. Do not let the garlic brown. This rendered chorizo fat is the foundation of the entire dish.
Visual cue: The oil in the pan is vibrantly orange-red from the chorizo fat. Garlic slices are golden and translucent at the edges.
Underdone: Chorizo coins are still pale and the oil is clear. The paprika-colored fat has not yet rendered. Continue cooking over medium heat. The fat needs to fully render from the chorizo for the flavor to transfer to the broth.
Perfect: Oil is vivid orange-red. Chorizo coins are slightly firm, not crispy. Garlic is golden at the edges and fragrant. Add the clams and wine immediately — do not let the garlic go further.
Overdone: Garlic is brown and beginning to smell bitter. Chorizo is crispy and dry. Add the wine immediately to stop the cooking. The burnt garlic will slightly bitter the broth; add an extra squeeze of lemon at the end to counteract.
Feel cue: The kitchen should smell of paprika and rendered pork fat — warm, smoky, and intensely savory. This is the moment the dish announces itself.

Add the scrubbed clams to the pan and immediately pour in the white wine. Cover tightly and raise the heat to high. Cook for 4–5 minutes, shaking the pan once or twice. Begin checking at 4 minutes — the moment all (or nearly all) the clams are open, they are done. Remove the lid and add the parsley and lemon juice. Toss quickly and serve in deep bowls with crusty bread to mop the broth. Discard any clam that has not opened after 6 minutes — it was dead before cooking.
Visual cue: All clam shells are open, curled back to reveal the plump, orange-edged meat inside. The broth is a vivid orange-red from the chorizo fat.
Underdone: After 3 minutes, fewer than half the clams have opened. The broth is still barely simmering. Cover and give 2 more minutes on high heat. Do not uncover too early — the steam is essential.
Perfect: Nearly all clams are open, revealing plump, just-cooked meat. The broth is a vivid orange-red and smells of sea, wine, and smoke. The clam meat is still slightly translucent at the thickest point. Add parsley and lemon. Serve immediately — every minute the clams spend on heat after opening toughens them.
Overdone: Clam meat has contracted to a small, rubbery curl. The shells have been open for too long. Serve immediately. Overcooked clams are still good — the broth is the salvation. Provide extra bread.
Feel cue: Lift a cooked clam out of the shell with your fingers — it should feel plump and silky, yielding with very slight resistance. If it feels like a rubber eraser, it has cooked too long.

name: Churros with Chocolate Dipping Sauce
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Water: 240 ml
Unsalted butter: 60 g
  Alternatives: neutral oil
Fine salt: 3 g
Caster sugar (in dough): 10 g
All-purpose flour: 150 g
Neutral oil for frying: 700 ml
  Alternatives: sunflower oil; vegetable oil
Caster sugar (for coating): 60 g
Ground cinnamon (for coating): 5 g
Dark chocolate (70%), chopped: 100 g
  Alternatives: milk chocolate
Whole milk: 200 ml
  Alternatives: oat milk
Caster sugar (for chocolate sauce): 20 g
Cornstarch: 10 g
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 45 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Crisp ridged batons of hot fried choux dough, deeply golden and shattering at the bite, dunked into a thick, dark Spanish-style drinking chocolate.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine water, butter, salt, and sugar in a medium saucepan. Bring to a rolling boil over medium-high heat, stirring to ensure the butter is fully melted. Every granule of sugar and crystal of salt must be dissolved before the flour goes in — the liquid must be at a full boil, not just simmering.
Visual cue: A rapidly boiling liquid, fully clear with no sugar crystals visible. Fat fully melted and incorporated.
Underdone: Only simmering at the edges. Butter partially melted. Sugar granules still visible. Increase heat and wait for a full, rolling boil before adding flour.
Perfect: Vigorous full boil, clear liquid with no crystals, fully emulsified fat. Violent bubbling across the entire surface. Remove from heat immediately and add all the flour at once.
Overdone: Liquid has reduced significantly — too long at the boil. Volume is noticeably less. Add a tablespoon or two of water to restore original volume, then boil again.
Feel cue: The moment the butter melts fully and you can smell a faint sweetness, the liquid is ready — a rolling boil with uniform bubbles across the surface.

Remove the boiling liquid from heat. Add all the flour at once and stir immediately and vigorously with a wooden spoon. The dough will come together almost instantly into a rough, shaggy ball. Return to low heat and cook, stirring and pressing constantly, for 2-3 minutes until the dough pulls away from the sides cleanly and a dry film forms on the pan bottom. The dough must be dried out slightly — this is what makes churros crisp. Transfer to a piping bag fitted with a large star tip (1.5-2cm).
Visual cue: A smooth, stiff, non-sticky ball of dough that pulls cleanly from the pan and holds its shape.
Underdone: Dough is still shaggy and sticks to the pan and spoon. Wet patches visible. Has not fully come together. Continue cooking and stirring on low heat. The dough needs more moisture driven off.
Perfect: Smooth, stiff ball that pulls cleanly away from the pan walls. A dry, thin film coats the pan bottom. Dough does not stick to the spoon when pressed. Has a faint cooked-flour aroma. Pipe immediately into the hot oil. Dough must go in hot — it relaxes as it cools.
Overdone: Dough is grey-tinged, very stiff, and beginning to smell of overcooked flour. Pipe immediately — it will still work but the churros may be denser.
Feel cue: The finished dough should feel like firm, hot Play-Doh — stiff enough to hold a star shape when piped, smooth enough to flow through the tip without tearing.

Heat the frying oil to 180°C (355°F) in a deep pan. Pipe 15-20cm lengths of dough directly into the hot oil, using scissors to cut each churro free from the piping bag. Fry in batches of 4-5 without crowding for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until deeply golden on all sides. The ridges from the star tip should be the darkest points. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain briefly on paper towels.
Visual cue: Deep, even golden-brown churros with crisply defined ridges. No pale patches or raw-looking sides.
Underdone: Pale gold with soft, yielding exterior. Doughy and pale at the ridge tips. Oil not hot enough — churros will be greasy. Increase oil temperature. Remove and test one: it should be crisp and hollow-sounding when tapped.
Perfect: Deep, even golden-brown all over. Ridges are dark and crisp. The churro feels light and rigid. Makes a faint crackling sound when moved. Inside is soft and airy. Drain and toss immediately in cinnamon sugar while still hot.
Overdone: Dark brown to burnt, especially at the ridges. Bitter aroma. Very hard exterior. Reduce oil temperature by 10°C. The star ridges burn faster than the body — keep a close watch.
Feel cue: A perfect churro should feel rigid and crisp when you press the ridges lightly — not give at all like dough. It rattles slightly when shaken.

Combine the caster sugar and ground cinnamon in a shallow bowl or on a plate. Toss the hot churros in the cinnamon sugar immediately after draining — while still hot, so the sugar adheres to the surface. Roll each churro to coat all sides.
Visual cue: Uniformly cinnamon-sugar coated churros with a speckled russet crust on top of the golden fried exterior.
Underdone: Sugar has not adhered — it falls off in clumps because the churros have cooled too much. Toss again and press the sugar into the surface. For cold churros, lightly brush with melted butter before rolling in sugar.
Perfect: Even, speckled coating of cinnamon sugar across every surface of the warm churro. Sugar has dissolved slightly into the hot surface fat. Serve immediately alongside the warm chocolate sauce.
Overdone: Too much sugar applied, creating a very thick crust that falls off in sheets. Shake off the excess. Only a thin, even coating is needed.
Feel cue: The churro should feel warm and slightly gritty from the sugar coating — the sugar has slightly melted into the surface but not dissolved completely.

Whisk the cornstarch into 3 tablespoons of the cold milk until smooth. Heat the remaining milk with the sugar in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the chopped dark chocolate and whisk constantly until melted and smooth. Add the cornstarch slurry and continue whisking over medium heat until the sauce thickens to the consistency of a pourable custard — about 3-4 minutes. The sauce should be thick enough to coat a spoon heavily and not run off immediately when the spoon is tilted.
Visual cue: A thick, glossy, deeply dark chocolate sauce that coats the back of a spoon and falls in slow, heavy drops.
Underdone: Thin and milky, falls off the spoon immediately in a stream. Not enough cornstarch thickening has occurred. Continue whisking over medium heat. The sauce thickens rapidly near the boiling point.
Perfect: Thick, glossy, dark brown. Falls off a spoon in slow, heavy sheets. Coats the back of the spoon and a finger swiped across leaves a clean line. Steaming and fragrant. Pour into a warm cup for dunking. Keep warm over very low heat.
Overdone: Sauce has become stiff and is pulling from the pan in a solid mass. Too much starch has set. Remove from heat, add 2-3 tbsp of warm milk, and whisk vigorously to thin.
Feel cue: The chocolate sauce should pour like thick cream — not quite flowing freely, but not needing to be spooned. It leaves a visible trail on the surface when drizzled.

name: Spanish Gambas al Ajillo
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Large raw shrimp, shell-on or peeled: 400 g
  Alternatives: tiger prawns; langoustine tails
Extra-virgin olive oil: 120 ml
Garlic cloves, thinly sliced: 8 cloves
Dried guindilla or árbol chili, whole: 2 whole
  Alternatives: dried red chili flakes
Fine sea salt: 5 g
Dry sherry (fino or manzanilla): 30 ml
  Alternatives: dry white wine
Fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped: 15 g
Lemon wedges: 1 lemon
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Plump shrimp sizzling in an earthenware cazuela of olive oil so fragrant with garlic and guindilla that the oil itself becomes the sauce you mop up with crusty bread.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Large raw shrimp, shell-on or peeled
Dried guindilla or árbol chili, whole

steps:
Pour the olive oil into an earthenware cazuela (or heavy skillet) and place over medium-low heat. Add the sliced garlic and whole dried chilies. Allow the garlic to gently sizzle in the cold oil as it heats, infusing the oil over 3–4 minutes. The garlic should turn golden but not brown — you want aromatic infusion, not fried garlic. The oil should bubble lazily around the garlic slices.
Visual cue: Garlic slices are pale golden and translucent in the oil, which is visibly bubbling with fragrant steam.
Underdone: Garlic is still white and raw; oil shows no bubbles. The garlic flavor has not infused. Continue on medium-low heat — patience is essential; garlic infuses best in slowly heating oil.
Perfect: Garlic is pale golden throughout, edges just beginning to color. Oil is fragrant and bubbling gently. Chilies are bright red and puffed. Increase heat to high and add the shrimp immediately.
Overdone: Garlic edges are browning to dark gold or brown. Bitter garlic smell from the pan. Add the shrimp immediately — the higher heat of the shrimp will stop the garlic from progressing further.
Feel cue: Stand over the pan and breathe in — the kitchen should fill with a warm, mellow garlic fragrance with a faint pepper heat from the chili. Any sharpness means the heat is too high.

Increase heat to high. Add the shrimp in a single layer and season with salt. They will sizzle dramatically in the hot oil. Add the sherry in a swirl around the pan — it will spatter and steam. Cook without moving for 1 minute until the underside is pink and opaque, then flip each shrimp once. Cook 30–45 seconds more. Total cook time: 2 minutes maximum. Pull from heat the moment all shrimp are pink and just curled.
Visual cue: Shrimp are uniformly pink-orange with tightly curled tails and a light golden edge from the hot oil.
Underdone: Shrimp still show grey-translucent sections at the thickest part. Too much uncoiled tail. Cook 30 more seconds at high heat — shrimp finish quickly.
Perfect: Fully pink from tail to head with a slight curl (C-shape, not O). The flesh is opaque but glistening with oil, not dried out. Remove from heat instantly and add parsley.
Overdone: Shrimp have curled into tight Os and feel rubbery to the touch. Color is dull pink rather than vivid. Serve immediately without further cooking. A squeeze of lemon will help cut the toughness.
Feel cue: A perfectly cooked gambas should press like a just-set gel — firm enough to hold its shape but yielding with a slight snap when bitten, never chewy.

Off the heat, scatter the roughly torn parsley over the shrimp and oil. The parsley will sizzle in the residual heat and release its chlorophyll fragrance into the oil. Bring the cazuela directly to the table while still sizzling. Serve with lemon wedges and crusty bread to soak up every drop of the fragrant garlic-shrimp oil — the oil is not a by-product, it is the point.
Visual cue: Vivid pink shrimp in golden, garlic-studded oil with patches of bright green parsley, still bubbling at the table.
Underdone: Dish is plated cold and still; shrimp look dull rather than glistening. Re-heat briefly in the pan just until sizzling, then add parsley and serve.
Perfect: Cazuela arrives at the table still sizzling, oil bubbling around the shrimp, parsley vivid green and fragrant. The aroma precedes the dish. Eat immediately with bread.
Overdone: Parsley has darkened and wilted completely into the oil; shrimp have toughened from residual heat. Serve immediately — the flavor is intact even if the visual freshness is gone.
Feel cue: The oil in a great gambas al ajillo should feel silky on the lips and almost sweet — heated olive oil gives up its grassy edge and becomes round and voluptuous with the garlic and shrimp juices dissolved into it.

name: Spanish Lentil Stew (Lentejas Estofadas)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Green or brown lentils (rinsed): 100 parts
  Alternatives: Puy lentils
Spanish chorizo (semi-cured, sliced 5mm): 40 parts
  Alternatives: smoked sausage; pancetta
Yellow onion (fine dice): 30 parts
Carrot (5mm rounds): 25 parts
Waxy potato (2cm dice): 40 parts
  Alternatives: turnip
Garlic cloves (minced): 5 parts
Smoked sweet paprika (pimentón dulce): 3 parts
  Alternatives: sweet paprika + a pinch of chipotle
Ground cumin: 1 parts
Bay leaves: 2 pieces
Olive oil: 8 parts
Water or light chicken stock: 280 parts
Fine sea salt: 2 parts
Sherry vinegar: 3 parts
  Alternatives: red wine vinegar
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 1 hr 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Earthy green lentils braised low and slow with coins of chorizo, smoked paprika, carrot, and waxy potato — the broth turns brick-red and silky, clinging to each lentil like a glaze.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Warm olive oil in a wide, heavy pot (at least 4L) over medium heat. Add chorizo slices and cook until the fat runs and the edges curl, about 3 minutes. Add onion and carrot. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the onion is completely translucent and the carrot is beginning to soften, 8–10 minutes. The oil should be stained deep orange from the chorizo.
Visual cue: Onion is soft and glassy, carrot is slightly yielding. The oil in the pan is vivid brick-orange from chorizo fat. No raw onion smell remains.
Underdone: Onion is still translucent-white with sharp raw scent. Carrot gives no give when pressed with a spoon. Lower heat and give it more time — rushing the sofrito base is the primary flavor error in lentil stew.
Perfect: Onion is golden at the edges and sweet-smelling. Carrot is pliable. Fat is visibly orange. Add garlic and spices.
Overdone: Onion is browning and sticking. Carrot edges are darkening. Bitter smell. Add a splash of water to deglaze and lower heat before proceeding.
Feel cue: Press a carrot round against the side of the pot — it should give slightly but not squash. The kitchen should smell of warm pork fat and onion sweetness.

Add minced garlic and cook 1 minute until fragrant. Add smoked paprika and cumin directly to the oil, stirring constantly. Cook for exactly 30–45 seconds — the spices toast in the fat, unlocking oil-soluble compounds. Do not let the paprika burn; it turns acrid instantly.
Visual cue: The pot is uniformly rust-red. The fat bubbles and sizzles around the spices. Fragrant, sweet-smoky steam rises.
Underdone: Spices look raw and powdery, not incorporated into the fat. No toasty aroma change. Stir vigorously and give it another 15 seconds — the oil must coat and activate the spice.
Perfect: Paprika has dissolved into the fat giving a uniform rusty sheen. Aroma shifts from raw to deep and smoky-sweet. Add lentils and liquid immediately.
Overdone: Paprika smells sharp or acrid. Dark spots appear on the pot bottom. Add the liquid now and scrape the bottom. A slightly scorched paprika can be managed but a burnt one cannot.
Feel cue: The spice bloom moment is instantaneous — you will smell the shift from raw powder to warm, toasty smoke. Act on it immediately.

Add lentils and bay leaves, stir to coat in the spiced fat. Pour in water or stock and bring to a boil over high heat. Skim any foam that rises. Reduce heat to a gentle simmer — small lazy bubbles breaking the surface, not a rolling boil. Simmer uncovered for 25 minutes.
Visual cue: A gentle, steady simmer with occasional bubbles breaking the surface. The broth is brick-red and beginning to thicken. Lentils are plumping visibly.
Underdone: Lentils are still chalky at the center when bitten. Broth is thin and watery. Continue simmering and check in 5-minute intervals.
Perfect: Lentils are just tender throughout but still hold their shape. Broth has reduced and lightly coats a spoon. Add potato and continue.
Overdone: Lentils are beginning to split and dissolve into the broth. Texture is porridgy. Add potato immediately and reduce heat to the lowest setting to prevent further breakdown.
Feel cue: Bite a lentil — it should yield cleanly with no gritty chalkiness at the center, but its skin should still be intact, not sliding off.

Add potato dice and season with salt. Continue to simmer for 20–25 minutes until potato is completely tender and the broth has thickened to a loose, cohesive stew consistency. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking. Remove bay leaves.
Visual cue: Potato cubes are completely soft, yielding to a spoon. The broth has reduced to a thick, glossy liquid that just covers the solids. The stew moves as one mass when the pot is gently shaken.
Underdone: Potato gives resistance at the center. Broth is still watery and thin. Continue simmering, stirring more frequently as it reduces.
Perfect: Potato is completely yielding. Broth is thick, glossy, and rust-red. When you drag a spoon through it, the line holds for a moment. Finish with vinegar.
Overdone: Potato has broken down and thickened the broth to a heavy paste. Lentils have disintegrated. Add a splash of hot water and stir vigorously — some breakdown is welcome but total dissolution loses texture.
Feel cue: Drag a wooden spoon across the bottom of the pot — the stew should flow slowly back to fill the gap, like warm caramel, not rush back like water.

Off the heat, add sherry vinegar and stir through. Taste and adjust salt. The vinegar wakes up the smoked paprika and lifts the whole stew from heavy to vibrant. Let rest 5 minutes before serving — the stew continues to thicken as it cools slightly and is always better the next day.
Visual cue: The colour deepens slightly when stirred. The scent shifts from purely meaty-smoky to bright and complex.
Underdone: Stew tastes flat and one-dimensionally meaty despite correct seasoning. Add another teaspoon of sherry vinegar and taste again — acidity is the missing bridge.
Perfect: The smokiness, richness, and acidity are in balance. Each lentil is seasoned throughout. Serve in deep bowls with crusty bread.
Overdone: Stew tastes sharp and sour — vinegar dominates. Add a pinch of sugar and a ladle of hot water, simmer 2 minutes to mellow.
Feel cue: The finished stew should feel substantial in a bowl — spoonable, not pourable — with a broth that coats your lips with a light savory gloss.

description: A whole chicken opened flat so it roasts evenly and fast, its skin shattering over garlicky herb butter while the potatoes underneath fry in the dripping schmaltz until crisp-edged and seasoned through.

ingredients.name: Whole chicken (about 2 kg / 4.5 lb), patted dry
柠檬（Lemon (zest into butter, halves roasted in pan)）
Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into 4 cm chunks

steps:
Set the chicken breast-side down. With sturdy kitchen shears, cut along both sides of the backbone and remove it (save for stock). Flip the bird, splay the legs out, and press firmly on the breastbone with the heel of your hand until you feel it crack and the bird lies flat. Pat dry, then sprinkle about 16 g of the salt evenly over both sides. Refrigerate uncovered on a rack for at least 1 hour, or up to 24 hours for the crispest skin.
Visual cue: A bird of even thickness, legs turned outward, breast flattened, skin dry and faintly matte.
Underdone: Breastbone not cracked — the breast still peaks high above the thighs, which will leave it overcooked by the time the legs are done. Press harder on the keel with both hands stacked until you hear a crack and the bird relaxes flat.
Perfect: Breast and thighs sit at roughly the same height; after resting uncovered the skin looks taut, dry, and slightly translucent over the fat. Proceed to the herb butter.
Overdone: Brined much longer than a day — skin is leathery and the thinnest edges have darkened. Still usable; skip any further salt on the chicken and rub the butter in generously.
Feel cue: After the dry brine the skin should feel like dry parchment under your fingertips — no tackiness, no beads of moisture.

Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) with a rack in the upper-middle position. Mash the softened butter with the garlic, thyme leaves, rosemary, the zest of the lemon, and plenty of black pepper. Slide your fingers under the skin of the breast and thighs to loosen it without tearing, then push most of the butter underneath and massage it out evenly from the outside. Smear the rest over the skin.
Visual cue: An even layer of flecked herb butter visible through the skin, covering breast and thighs.
Underdone: Butter sits in one lump near the neck opening; the thighs and far breast have none. Press from outside the skin and slide the butter down toward the legs and across the breast.
Perfect: A thin, green-flecked film shows through the skin everywhere, with the skin still intact. Proceed to the potatoes.
Overdone: Skin has torn open across the breast and butter is smeared on the outside only. Pull the loose skin back over the tear; a few holes will just brown a little unevenly.
Feel cue: The butter should be soft enough to spread like room-temperature cream cheese — if it resists, warm the bowl in your hands for a minute.

Toss the potatoes with the olive oil, the remaining salt, and pepper, and spread them in a single layer in a large rimmed sheet pan (about 33 × 46 cm / 13 × 18 in). Nestle the zested lemon, halved, cut-side down among them. Lay the chicken skin-side up on top of the potatoes, legs pointing toward the back of the oven. Roast 45–55 minutes, until the skin is deep golden and an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part of the thigh (not touching bone) reads 165°F (74°C); the breast should read at least 155–160°F (68–71°C).
Visual cue: Deep golden, blistered skin, juices running clear from the thigh joint, and potatoes crisp and browned where they touch the pan.
Underdone: Skin is pale gold and soft; pink juices seep when you pierce between leg and body; thigh reads below 165°F (74°C). Return to the oven and check every 5 minutes.
Perfect: Skin is mahogany-gold and crackled, thigh reads 165°F (74°C), and the potatoes are glossy with fat and browned on their undersides. Remove from the oven and rest.
Overdone: Skin has blackened at the wing tips and the breast reads well above 165°F (74°C); potatoes at the edges are dark and hard. Rest it anyway and spoon the pan juices over the sliced breast to help it along.
Feel cue: Wiggle a drumstick — it should move loosely in the joint. The skin should crackle audibly when tapped with a spoon.

Move the chicken to a cutting board and rest 10–15 minutes. Meanwhile, toss the potatoes in the pan juices and return them to the oven for 5 minutes if they need more crunch. Carve the chicken into legs, thighs, wings, and sliced breast, squeeze the roasted lemon over everything, and serve on top of the potatoes.
Visual cue: Breast slices that are moist and glistening, not puddling juice across the board.
Underdone: Carved immediately — juice floods the board and the slices go dry within minutes. Wait the full 10 minutes next time; spoon the board juices back over the meat now.
Perfect: Slices are glossy and hold their juices; skin stays crisp; potatoes are coated in savory drippings. Serve.
Overdone: Rested 40+ minutes — meat is lukewarm and the skin has softened. Flash the carved pieces skin-side up under the broiler for a minute.
Feel cue: Pressing a thumb into the rested breast should feel springy and firm, like the fleshy base of your thumb, with no liquid rushing out.

description: Granny Smith apples slow-cooked for hours with brown sugar, cinnamon, clove, and nutmeg in apple cider until they collapse and caramelize into a deep, mahogany-brown concentrate — velvety, intensely spiced, and almost impossibly fragrant.

ingredients.name: Granny Smith apples, peeled, cored, and roughly chopped
Fresh apple cider (unfiltered, not apple juice)

steps:
Place the roughly chopped apples and apple cider in a large, wide, heavy-bottomed pot (a Dutch oven or enameled cast-iron braiser is ideal — the wide surface area accelerates evaporation). Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the apples are completely soft and beginning to fall apart — about 25–30 minutes. You are not looking for texture here; the apples must become completely yielding, as they will be blended to a smooth purée. The cider provides both liquid for the initial cooking and a concentrated apple flavor that plain water cannot replicate. As the apples soften, they will release their own juice and the mixture will become more liquid before it begins to reduce.
Visual cue: Completely collapsed, soft apple pieces in a pale, frothy, apple-scented liquid — individual pieces yield instantly when pressed with a spoon.
Underdone: Apple pieces still hold their shape, resist the spoon, and have a chalky or starchy center. Continue simmering with the lid on to create steam and soften the pieces faster.
Perfect: Apple pieces completely collapse when pressed with the back of a spoon. The kitchen smells of warm, cooked apple. Liquid is frothy and pale. Add sugar and spices and begin the long reduction.
Overdone: Apple pieces are falling apart but the liquid has already reduced too far and is beginning to stick to the pot bottom. Add 50 ml of additional cider or water and reduce heat immediately.
Feel cue: Press a piece of apple against the pot side with a wooden spoon — it should smear completely with zero resistance, like pressing softened butter. Any springiness means more cooking time.

Add the brown sugar, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, allspice, apple cider vinegar, and salt to the softened apples. Stir to combine. Using an immersion blender directly in the pot, blend until completely smooth with no apple skin or chunk remaining. Alternatively, allow to cool slightly and blend in batches in a countertop blender (fill only halfway — hot liquid can erupt). If you prefer a very smooth, glossy butter, pass the blended mixture through a fine-mesh sieve, pressing firmly. Taste the sweetened applesauce base at this point: it will taste flat and too sweet because the sugar has not yet caramelized and concentrated — this is expected and correct. The transformation happens during the long, slow reduction that follows.
Visual cue: A smooth, uniform, pale caramel-colored sauce — no lumps, no skin pieces, smelling of cinnamon and apple.
Underdone: Sauce still has visible apple skin fragments or lumps — blending was insufficient. Blend for longer and, if needed, pass through a sieve for absolute smoothness.
Perfect: Completely smooth, flowing, pale tan to caramel color. Uniform spice fragrance throughout. Falls from the spoon in a smooth, even flow. Begin the slow reduction over low heat with the lid off.
Overdone: Over-blended and very foamy or aerated from the blender — surface covered in froth. Allow to settle for 10 minutes before beginning the reduction.
Feel cue: Rub a drop between your fingers — completely smooth, no grit, the spice fragrance should cling to your skin strongly. If you can feel any texture at all, blend longer.

With the pot uncovered, reduce the applesauce over the lowest possible heat for 2 to 3 hours, stirring every 10–15 minutes — particularly important in the final hour when the concentration is high and scorching can occur. As the butter reduces, it will pass through several distinct stages: pale caramel (1 hour), golden amber (1.5 hours), deep mahogany-brown (2 hours), and finally the thick, glossy, spreadable consistency of apple butter (2.5–3 hours). You will know it is done when: a spoonful dropped on a cold plate holds its mound shape and does not run; the surface has a glossy, lacquered sheen; and the color is a deep mahogany-brown. The volume will have reduced by roughly half. Transfer to clean jars immediately while still hot.
Visual cue: Deep mahogany-brown, glossy, thick enough to hold a ridge when a spoon is dragged across the surface, smelling intensely of caramelized apple and warm spice.
Underdone: Apple butter is still pale amber or caramel-colored, runs freely off the spoon, and tastes of sweet applesauce rather than concentrated, caramelized apple. Continue reducing. True apple butter takes patience. Stir more frequently to prevent scorching.
Perfect: Deep mahogany, glossy surface, holds its shape on a cold plate, does not run. Fragrance is intensely of cinnamon, clove, and caramelized apple. Tastes complex, deeply sweet with a bright acid finish from the vinegar. Transfer to jars immediately. Seal and refrigerate up to 1 month, or process in a boiling water bath for shelf storage.
Overdone: Apple butter has scorched on the pot bottom — bitter, dark caramel smell, very dark patches visible when stirring. Transfer immediately to a clean pot without scraping the scorched layer. Taste: if bitterness is not dominant, proceed.
Feel cue: Drag a spoon through the apple butter at the 2.5-hour mark — the channel it leaves should hold perfectly for 10 seconds
before slowly beginning to close. If it closes immediately, continue reducing.

name: Moroccan Slow-Roasted Lamb Shoulder
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: bone-in leg of lamb
Ras el hanout: 25 g
Garlic cloves: 30 g
Preserved lemon, rind only: 30 g
  Alternatives: 2 tsp lemon zest + 1 tsp salt
Extra-virgin olive oil: 60 g
Fine sea salt: 15 g
Fresh cilantro, roughly chopped: 20 g
  Alternatives: flat-leaf parsley
Fresh rosemary sprigs: 10 g
  Alternatives: thyme
Chicken or lamb stock: 300 g
  Alternatives: water with a squeeze of lemon
Saffron threads, steeped in 2 tbsp warm water: 0.5 g
Honey: 20 g
  Alternatives: date syrup
Fresh cilantro and flat-leaf parsley, mixed: 20 g
Toasted almonds or pine nuts: 30 g
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 5 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A bone-in lamb shoulder rubbed with a thick paste of ras el hanout, preserved lemon, and garlic, then slow-roasted until the meat yields to the lightest touch and falls from the bone in tender, perfumed shreds.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Saffron threads, steeped in 2 tbsp warm water
Fresh cilantro and flat-leaf parsley, mixed

steps:
Pound or blend the garlic to a paste with a pinch of salt. Finely mince the preserved lemon rind. Combine with ras el hanout, olive oil, cilantro, saffron water, honey, and salt to form a thick, aromatic paste. Taste — it should be salty, floral, pungently garlicky, and bright with citrus.
Visual cue: A thick, rust-orange paste with visible herb flecks and saffron threads. Should coat the back of a spoon without dripping.
Underdone: Paste is too thin and oily. Won't adhere to the lamb surface. Add more ras el hanout or pound the garlic more thoroughly to thicken.
Perfect: Thick enough to hold its shape on a spoon. Deeply aromatic with saffron, cumin, cinnamon, and preserved lemon all distinct. Apply to lamb immediately.
Overdone: N/A — this is a raw paste. Proceed.
Feel cue: Taste a fingertip of paste — the saffron should register as floral and faintly metallic, the preserved lemon as bright and saline, the ras el hanout as warm and complex.

Using a small sharp knife, make 12–16 deep incisions all over the shoulder, 3–4 cm deep. Push a sliver of garlic and a pinch of spice paste into each. Rub the remaining paste all over the exterior, working it into every crevice and around the bone. Tuck rosemary sprigs under the shoulder. Marinate covered in the refrigerator for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.
Visual cue: The shoulder is completely covered in a thick, fragrant orange-brown paste with no bare patches of meat visible. The incisions are stuffed with paste and garlic.
Underdone: Paste is only on the surface, no incisions made. The flavors won't penetrate deep into the thick shoulder. Cut the incisions — they are essential for a shoulder this large.
Perfect: All incisions stuffed, entire surface thickly coated. After overnight marination, the paste has darkened and adhered firmly. Bring to room temperature 1 hour before roasting.
Overdone: Over-marinated beyond 24 hours. Still excellent. Proceed.
Feel cue: After overnight marination, the paste should feel almost dry on the surface — it has bonded to the lamb and will form a crust in the oven.

Place the shoulder in a large roasting dish. Pour the stock around the base. Cover tightly with two layers of foil, sealing the edges completely. Roast at 160 C (320 F) for 3.5 to 4 hours. The shoulder is done when the meat pulls effortlessly from the bone when probed with a fork.
Visual cue: After 3.5 hours, lifting the foil reveals a shoulder that has visibly collapsed on itself. The bone is exposed at the end and the meat has pulled back significantly.
Underdone: Meat still clings to the bone and resists when a fork is inserted and twisted. The shoulder retains its original shape. Re-cover and continue at 160 C. Check every 30 minutes.
Perfect: Meat slides from the bone without effort. The shoulder has collapsed and is almost falling off the bone on its own. The fat is completely rendered. Remove foil and raise temperature for the crust.
Overdone: Meat has completely fallen off the bone and is shredding into the juices. Remove from oven immediately. Still delicious — serve as pulled lamb.
Feel cue: Push a fork into the thickest part of the shoulder and twist — at perfect doneness, the meat parts with no resistance and the fork comes out without effort.

Remove the foil. Raise oven to 200 C (400 F). Roast uncovered for 20–25 minutes, basting with the pan juices every 8 minutes, until the surface develops a deeply burnished, aromatic crust. The juices in the pan should have reduced to a rich jus.
Visual cue: The shoulder surface is deeply bronzed and crusted, the spice paste visibly caramelized into a dark, glossy coating. The pan jus is amber and syrupy.
Underdone: Surface looks pale and wet. No crust formation. Continue uncovered and baste more frequently.
Perfect: Dark, fragrant, crispy-edged crust over a shoulder that glistens with pan juices. The ras el hanout smells toasted and complex, not raw. Rest 15 minutes before serving.
Overdone: Crust has blackened and is crumbling off. Bitter smell. Remove immediately. Scrape darkest bits and serve with the good crust portions.
Feel cue: The crust surface should feel firm and slightly dry under a spoon — press and it should resist, not give way. The meat below will be completely soft.

Rest the shoulder for 15 minutes before serving. Scatter fresh herbs and toasted nuts directly over the shoulder. Serve at the table in the roasting dish, using two large forks to pull the meat apart. Spoon the pan jus over each portion.
Visual cue: A dramatically crusted shoulder on a platter, bright herb green and ivory nut contrast against the dark mahogany crust. Pan jus pooling at the base.
Underdone: Herbs placed before resting — they've wilted in the steam. Always add fresh garnish at the very last moment.
Perfect: Fresh, vibrant herbs on a rested, slightly cooled shoulder. Meat pulls apart in long, moist shreds with a tug of the fork. Serve with couscous or flatbread.
Overdone: Over-rested and too cool. Fat has solidified. A quick 5 minutes back in a hot oven will warm without drying.
Feel cue: The meat should pull apart in long, moist shreds with almost no effort from two forks — if you need to cut it, the shoulder needed more time in the oven.

name: Spinach and Ricotta Stuffed Shells

description: Jumbo pasta shells packed with a lemony ricotta-spinach filling, nestled in a quick garlic-basil tomato sauce and baked under a blanket of bubbling, browned mozzarella. Creamy, cheesy, and deeply comforting.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Frozen chopped spinach, thawed and squeezed very dry

steps:
Warm the olive oil in a saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the garlic and pepper flakes and cook 1–2 minutes until the garlic is pale gold. Add the crushed tomatoes, basil, 1 teaspoon salt, and pepper. Simmer gently 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until slightly thickened. Meanwhile, heat the oven to 375°F (190°C).
Visual cue: A slightly thickened, brick-red sauce with a sheen of oil at the edges.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and bright red, tasting raw and tinny. Simmer 5 minutes longer.
Perfect: Sauce has deepened in color and coats a spoon; tastes sweet and rounded. Remove the basil stems and set aside.
Overdone: Sauce is thick and spattering, sticking on the bottom. Stir in 60 ml water to loosen.
Feel cue: The garlic should smell sweet and toasty when the tomatoes go in — never sharp or burnt.

Boil the shells in a large pot of salted water for 2 minutes less than the package time (usually 7–8 minutes). Drain gently, rinse with cool water, and lay them open-side down on an oiled tray so they don't stick together. Cook a few extra — some always tear.
Visual cue: Pliable shells that hold their curled shape with no cracks.
Underdone: Shells are stiff and crack when opened. Boil another minute.
Perfect: Flexible and whole, still firm to the bite. Drain, rinse, and lay out.
Overdone: Shells are floppy and tearing, collapsing flat. Use torn shells to patch the dish; bake a few minutes less.
Feel cue: A shell should open under your thumb like a soft clam without splitting at the seam.

In a bowl, mix the ricotta, squeezed spinach, egg, grated hard cheese, lemon zest, nutmeg, 80 g of the mozzarella, 3/4 teaspoon salt, and pepper until evenly combined. Taste before adding the egg if you want to check seasoning.
Visual cue: A thick, pale filling evenly flecked with dark green spinach.
Underdone: White pockets of ricotta and clumps of spinach remain. Keep folding until uniformly speckled.
Perfect: Uniformly green-flecked and thick enough to hold a spoon upright. Fill the shells.
Overdone: Filling is loose and weeping green liquid — spinach wasn't squeezed enough. Stir in 2 tablespoons more grated cheese or breadcrumbs to firm it up.
Feel cue: Scoop some up — it should hold its shape like thick mashed potatoes, not slump.

Spread two-thirds of the sauce over the bottom of a 23 x 33 cm baking dish. Fill each shell with about 2 tablespoons of filling and nestle them open-side up in a snug single layer. Spoon the remaining sauce over and between the shells.
Visual cue: Tightly packed rows of plump shells sitting in red sauce, filling peeking out.
Underdone: Shells look thin and underfilled, and gaps are wide. Add more filling and push the shells closer together.
Perfect: Shells are generously filled and touching, sauce around and over them. Top with cheese and bake.
Overdone: Filling is mounded so high it's spilling over. Scrape back — it will puff and leak during baking.
Feel cue: Each shell should feel heavy and full in your hand, closing gently around the filling.

Scatter the remaining 120 g mozzarella over the top. Cover with foil and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 20 minutes. Uncover and bake 10–15 minutes more until the cheese is bubbling and spotted brown. Rest 10 minutes before serving so the filling sets.
Visual cue: Melted, blistered mozzarella with golden-brown spots and sauce bubbling at the edges.
Underdone: Cheese is melted but pale white; sauce not bubbling at the edges. Bake 5 minutes more, or broil 1–2 minutes watching closely.
Perfect: Cheese is bubbling with golden-brown blisters; sauce is thick and simmering around the edges. Rest 10 minutes and serve.
Overdone: Cheese is dark and leathery; shell tips are hard and crunchy. Spoon extra warm sauce over when serving to soften the tops.
Feel cue: A knife through the center should meet hot, steaming filling that holds together rather than running out.

  Alternatives: lemon juice; sherry vinegar
Flat-leaf parsley, chopped, and croutons: 0 to taste
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 2 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Green split peas simmered with a smoky turkey leg until they collapse into a thick, earthy, jade-green soup, studded with carrot and pulled smoked meat and brightened by a splash of vinegar.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Green split peas, picked over and rinsed
Kosher salt (add only at the end)

steps:
Melt butter in a 6 litre pot over medium heat. Add onion, carrot, and celery and cook 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft and the onion is translucent. Add garlic and cook 1 minute. Don't salt yet — the smoked turkey will season the pot.
Visual cue: Soft, glossy vegetables with the onion translucent and no browning.
Underdone: Onion white and firm; carrots crunchy. Cook 2–3 minutes more.
Perfect: Onion translucent and soft; carrots slightly softened; sweet aroma. Add peas, turkey, and water.
Overdone: Vegetables browned at the edges. A little browning is fine; it adds depth. Lower the heat and move on.
Feel cue: The onion should squash between the spoon and the pot with no crunch.

Add split peas, smoked turkey, water, bay, thyme, and pepper. Bring to a boil, skim the foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook partially covered 1 hr 15 min–1 hr 30 min, stirring the bottom every 15 minutes (split peas sink and scorch), until the peas have completely broken down and the turkey meat is soft.
Visual cue: Peas dissolved into a thick, olive-green soup; turkey meat pulling easily away from the bone.
Underdone: Peas still whole and distinct; liquid thin and watery. Keep simmering, stirring more often as it thickens.
Perfect: Peas have collapsed into a coarse purée that coats a spoon thickly. Remove the turkey to pull the meat.
Overdone: Soup is paste-thick and catching; brown flecks from the bottom. Don't scrape. Transfer to a clean pot, leaving the scorched layer, and add hot water.
Feel cue: Stir from the bottom — the spoon should move through thick velvet, not grab on a sticky layer.

Lift out the turkey, bay, and thyme stems. When the turkey is cool enough to handle, pull the meat into bite-size shreds, discarding skin, bones, and the thin, needle-like tendons in the leg. For a smoother soup, blitz briefly with an immersion blender. Return the meat and bring back to a simmer so everything is steaming hot (165°F / 74°C). Stir in vinegar, then season with salt only if needed. Thin with water to taste. Serve with parsley and croutons. To freeze: cool in shallow containers, refrigerate within 2 hours, and freeze up to 3 months. It sets almost solid when cold — add water as it reheats, stirring constantly.
Visual cue: A thick, jade-green soup with flecks of orange carrot and shreds of pink-tinged smoked turkey.
Underdone: Tastes heavy and muted; texture grainy. Add vinegar a few drops at a time, and blend briefly for smoothness.
Perfect: Earthy, smoky, gently salty, with a bright lift at the end; flows slowly off a ladle. Serve.
Overdone: Too salty from a very salty smoked leg. Add unsalted water and a potato cubed small; simmer 15 minutes.
Feel cue: Pour a ladleful back into the pot — it should fall in a thick, slow ribbon and settle gently, like loose porridge.
