ingredients.name: 天贝（Tempeh, cut into 3 cm cubes）
Dried red chilies, soaked and drained

steps:
Blend the soaked dried chilies, shallots, garlic, ginger, coriander, and cumin into a smooth paste in a food processor or blender. Add a tablespoon of water if needed to get it moving. The paste should be fine-textured, deep brick-red, and smell intensely of raw shallot and warm spice.
Visual cue: A smooth, deep brick-red paste with no large visible chunks. The color comes from the chilies, not from cooking — it should look vivid and raw.
Underdone: Rough texture with visible shallot and chili fragments. Inconsistent color. Blend longer, scraping down the sides. The paste must be smooth to cook evenly.
Perfect: Fine-textured, deep red paste. Presses through fingers without chunks. Smells sharp and raw. Fry in oil before adding coconut milk.
Overdone: Paste has liquefied to a thin puree. Will spatter excessively when fried. It will still work. Cook on slightly lower heat and stir more frequently.
Feel cue: The paste should feel like thick smooth hummus and smell sharp enough to make your eyes water — the raw allium bite will mellow during frying.

Heat coconut oil in a large wok or heavy pot over medium heat. Add the paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 8–12 minutes. The paste will first thin out as moisture evaporates, then darken and deepen in color, and finally begin to separate from the oil — a thin ring of clear oil appears around the paste. This is keluarkan minyak — the oil breaking out. This step develops the foundational flavor.
Visual cue: The paste has darkened from brick-red to a deep reddish-brown. A thin ring of clear reddish oil visibly separates around the edges of the paste mass in the wok.
Underdone: Paste is still bright red and wet. No oil separation visible. Raw shallot taste will persist into the finished dish. Keep frying — the paste needs to lose all its raw moisture. This takes patience.
Perfect: Deep reddish-brown, fragrant with cooked spice and toasted shallot. A clear ring of aromatic oil surrounds it. The paste presses into a rough dry mass when stirred. Add aromatics and coconut milk.
Overdone: Paste is very dark brown, approaching black at the edges. Smells slightly burnt. Add coconut milk immediately and reduce heat. The liquid will arrest further cooking.
Feel cue: At the point the oil separates, the paste will sound different — a dry sizzle rather than a wet hiss. Trust your ears as much as your eyes.

Add tempeh to the fried paste and stir to coat. Pour in coconut milk, add the lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves, turmeric leaf if using, salt, and palm sugar. Stir to combine. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a medium simmer. Cook uncovered, stirring every 10 minutes to prevent sticking.
Visual cue: A rich, fragrant coconut stew, gently bubbling with visible yellow-orange color from the turmeric and deep red from the chilies. Tempeh pieces are submerged.
Underdone: Still pale and thin. Coconut milk has not yet integrated with the paste. Raise heat to bring to a proper simmer and continue cooking.
Perfect: Unified dark coconut sauce, fragrant with lemongrass and kaffir lime. Tempeh is beginning to absorb color. Bubbling steadily. Continue simmering uncovered until coconut milk reduces significantly.
Overdone: Boiling hard. Coconut milk will break and become greasy rather than rich. Reduce heat to a gentle simmer immediately.
Feel cue: The aroma at this stage should be heady and multilayered — coconut, lemongrass, galangal, and chili all distinct and not yet merged. They'll unify over the next hour.

Continue simmering uncovered for 1–1.5 hours, stirring every 10 minutes with increasing frequency as the liquid reduces. The coconut milk will pass through several stages: creamy white, then pale yellow, then the coconut fat will separate and the paste will begin to fry in its own oil. This final stage — when the rendang is almost dry and the tempeh is frying in coconut oil — develops the characteristic dark, burnished crust. Keep stirring to prevent scorching. The rendang is done when the tempeh is dark and encrusted and the 'sauce' is more of a thick, dark coating.
Visual cue: The tempeh pieces are dark mahogany to nearly black on the outside, encrusted in a thick spice coating. The pot is nearly dry, only a slick of dark oil remains. The tempeh fries in this oil.
Underdone: Tempeh still looks pale and the sauce is thin. This is gulai stage — still a curry, not rendang. Continue reducing. True rendang can take 2 hours or more — patience is the ingredient.
Perfect: Tempeh pieces are dark, encrusted, and fragrant. The coating is almost dry and clings tightly to each piece. A wonderful nutty, spicy, caramelized smell fills the kitchen. Remove from heat and let stand 5 minutes.
Overdone: Tempeh has scorched, bitter smell, black powder at the bottom of the pot. Remove tempeh immediately. Discard the darkest bits from the pot bottom. The top pieces may be salvageable.
Feel cue: Lift a piece of tempeh — the coating should feel dry and slightly crumbly on the outside, never wet or saucy. Press it: the crust should yield and the tempeh inside should be firm but not hard.

Transfer to a serving plate or shallow bowl. Scatter fried shallots over the top. Serve with steamed rice, sambal, and pickled cucumber. Rendang improves overnight — the flavors deepen and the spice coating firms.
Visual cue: Dark, almost black-mahogany tempeh pieces on a white plate, each individually encrusted and separate. Crispy fried shallots add textural contrast.
Underdone: Rendang looks wet and saucy rather than dry and crusted. This is gulai — delicious but not rendang. Continue reducing next time.
Perfect: Dark, dry-coated pieces with visible spice crust and fried shallot. The rich, concentrated aroma is almost overwhelming. Serve with rice.
Overdone: Tempeh is too dark and has a bitter edge. Serve with cooling accompaniments: cucumber, coconut rice, plain yogurt.
Feel cue: A perfect piece of tempeh rendang should have a brittle, flaky outer crust that shatters slightly when bitten, giving way to the chewy, savory fermented interior.

name: Tempeh Sambal (Tempe Kering)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Tempeh, sliced 5mm thick: 100 parts
Red chiles (cayenne or serrano), sliced: 8 parts
  Alternatives: dried chile flakes
Shallots, thinly sliced: 15 parts
  Alternatives: red onion
Lemongrass, inner stalk only, bruised: 3 parts
Garlic cloves, thinly sliced: 3 parts
Kecap manis (sweet soy sauce): 10 parts
  Alternatives: soy sauce + palm sugar, 1:1
Coconut or neutral oil for frying: 15 parts
Fine salt: 1 parts
Fresh bay leaves (salam leaves if available): 2 parts
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 35 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Tempeh sliced thin and fried until golden and nutty, then tossed in a sambal of red chiles, shallots, lemongrass, and kecap manis that caramelizes to a lacquer in the pan — each piece of tempeh absorbing the sweet-spicy glaze while maintaining its characteristic firm, meaty bite. It is one of the great vegan preparations: deeply satisfying in a way that has nothing to do with mimicking meat.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Coconut or neutral oil for frying
Fresh bay leaves (salam leaves if available)

steps:
Heat 1 cm of oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. When the oil shimmers and a small piece of tempeh sizzles immediately on contact, begin frying the tempeh slices in a single layer, without crowding. Fry for 3–4 minutes per side until deep golden-brown and crisp on the outside. The tempeh should not be pale — it needs color for the later glazing step to work properly. Drain on a rack, not paper towels.
Visual cue: Tempeh slices are uniformly deep golden-brown on both sides. Edges are crisp.
Underdone: Tempeh is pale golden and still soft. Surface doesn't crackle when pressed. Continue frying 2 more minutes per side. The exterior must be properly fried before glazing.
Perfect: Deep golden-brown on all surfaces. Edges are crisp and audibly crackle when pressed. The smell is of roasted soybean and fried nutty goodness. Drain on a rack. Pour off excess oil from the pan, leaving about 1 tablespoon.
Overdone: Tempeh is dark brown with charred spots. Smells bitter. Lower oil temperature for the next batch. Use these pieces in the sambal — the glaze will mask some bitterness.
Feel cue: A properly fried tempeh slice should feel rigid and crackle audibly when you press it with a spatula — that crackle tells you the exterior has set and will hold up to the wet sambal without going soggy.

In the same pan with the remaining tablespoon of oil, add the shallots and cook over medium heat until golden and beginning to caramelize — about 5 minutes. Add the sliced chiles, garlic, lemongrass, and bay leaves. Stir-fry for 3 minutes until the chiles are softened and fragrant. The shallots should be well beyond translucent — approaching crisp and golden — before the kecap manis is added.
Visual cue: Shallots are golden and slightly crisp. Chiles are softened. The pan smells of sweet caramelized allium and chile.
Underdone: Shallots are still white and raw-smelling. Chiles haven't softened. Continue cooking on medium heat. Shallots need full caramelization before the glaze is added.
Perfect: Shallots are golden, slightly crisp, and jammy. Chiles are bright red and softened. Lemongrass is fragrant. The whole pan smells of Indonesian warung. Add kecap manis and return fried tempeh.
Overdone: Garlic has gone very dark and bitter. Shallots are beginning to burn. Add the kecap manis immediately to deglaze and halt the cooking.
Feel cue: When you drag a spoon through the sautéed shallots, they should feel jammy and slightly sticky against the pan — that stickiness is the natural sugars caramelizing, which is exactly what you want before the kecap manis goes in.

Add the fried tempeh to the sambal base. Pour the kecap manis over everything. Toss vigorously over high heat for 2–3 minutes until the kecap manis caramelizes and coats every piece of tempeh in a dark, glossy glaze. The liquid should reduce completely — the pan should be nearly dry. Season with salt if needed (kecap manis is quite salty already). Remove the lemongrass and bay leaves before serving.
Visual cue: Tempeh is coated in a dark, caramelized glaze. The pan is nearly dry. Each piece glistens.
Underdone: Kecap manis is still liquid in the pan. Tempeh is not glazed, just wet. Increase heat and continue tossing for another 60–90 seconds until the liquid reduces.
Perfect: Every piece of tempeh is lacquered in a dark, mahogany glaze. The pan is dry. Each piece glistens with the reduced kecap manis. The kitchen smells of caramelized sweet soy. Serve immediately over rice or as a side dish.
Overdone: Glaze has gone from caramelized to burnt. Black bits stick to the pan. Immediately remove from heat. The slightly bitter note from over-caramelization actually works in small amounts. Serve quickly.
Feel cue: The finished tempeh sambal should have a slightly sticky, lacquered exterior that resists the fork momentarily before the interior yields — that resistance is the difference between a glaze and a sauce.

name: Tempura Batter
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Cake flour or low-protein soft flour (sifted): 100 g
  Alternatives: 50g plain flour + 50g cornstarch for extra lightness; rice flour for gluten-free
Ice-cold water (with ice cubes in the jug): 160 g
  Alternatives: sparkling mineral water (adds CO2 bubbles for extra lift)
Egg yolk (1 large, cold): 18 g
  Alternatives: omit for a lighter, more translucent batter
Fine sea salt: 2 g
Neutral frying oil (rice bran, sunflower, or canola): 1000 g

Active time: 10 min
Total time: 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A barely-mixed slurry of ice-cold water and low-protein flour — intentionally lumpy, dangerously thin, and used immediately before gluten can form. In oil heated to exactly the right temperature, it sets into a crust so light and translucent it barely seems to exist, yet shatters at the bite to reveal whatever was inside.

ingredients.name: Cake flour or low-protein soft flour (sifted)
Ice-cold water (with ice cubes in the jug)
Neutral frying oil (rice bran, sunflower, or canola)

steps:
Fill a tall jug with cold water and add a generous handful of ice cubes. Measure 160g of this ice-cold water — include small slivers of ice if they fall in. The water temperature should be at or below 4 C. Cold water is the most critical variable in tempura: it slows gluten development (since gluten forms faster in warm water) and keeps the batter in a state of perpetual instability until it hits the hot oil. Place the jug in the freezer for 5 minutes if your tap water is not cold enough.
Visual cue: Water that is visibly cold — condensation on the outside of the jug, ice slivers drifting in the liquid, temperature at or near freezing.
Underdone: Water is cool but not icy — around 15 C. No condensation. Add more ice and wait 3 minutes. Tempura made with insufficiently cold water will be gluey and thick.
Perfect: Jug has condensation; water temperature is 2-4 C; ice slivers remain floating. Measure immediately and proceed to mixing. Speed is now critical.
Overdone: Water is partially frozen — too thick to pour easily. Let it sit at room temperature for 60 seconds and stir. You need a liquid, not a slush.
Feel cue: Touch the outside of the jug — it should feel like a cold windowpane in winter, distinctly chilling rather than merely cool.

Beat the cold egg yolk lightly in a bowl with chopsticks — just 3 or 4 strokes, enough to break it. Pour in the ice-cold water and stir with a single chopstick or the handle of a spoon, just enough to combine. Do not whisk. The goal is a yolk-streaked water, not a smooth emulsion — the streaks of yolk create micro-pockets of richness in the final crust.
Visual cue: A pale yellow water with distinct visible streaks of yolk that have not fully dispersed — like a very dilute egg drop soup before cooking.
Underdone: Yolk is still sitting as a whole broken dome on top of the water. Give two more gentle stirs with a chopstick to distribute.
Perfect: Yolk is dispersed in long, pale-gold ribbons through the water. Not emulsified — still streaky and inhomogeneous. Proceed immediately to adding flour. Every second matters from here.
Overdone: Yolk and water are fully emulsified into a uniform pale liquid. Still usable — the crust will be slightly less lacy but still light. Proceed with urgency.
Feel cue: The egg water should feel indistinguishable from very cold water on the fingertips — you are not trying to build body, only to slightly enrich a cold liquid.

Sift the flour and salt into the egg water all at once. Using chopsticks (not a whisk), stir with large, lazy figure-eight strokes — no more than 10 to 12 strokes. The batter should remain visibly lumpy with pockets of dry flour still floating on the surface. This restraint is the entire technique: every additional stir develops gluten and moves you toward a heavy, doughy batter that fries like calamari rings rather than light tempura. Use immediately — the batter deteriorates in minutes as gluten continues to develop even when unstirred. Keep the bowl over or within the tray of ice to maintain temperature.
Visual cue: A thin, pale yellow batter full of visible lumps and streaks of dry flour — it looks unfinished and wrong. When a skewer is dipped in and lifted, the batter drips off in a thin, irregular sheet.
Underdone: Large clumps of dry flour on top that haven't been incorporated at all — more dry than wet. Two or three more gentle strokes to wet the remaining dry pockets. Do not overmix to compensate.
Perfect: Thin, lumpy, and visually under-mixed. Drips in a thin sheet from a skewer with visible lumps passing through. Temperature still feels cold when you touch the bowl. Use within 5 minutes. Dip ingredients in a thin coat only — the batter should barely cling.
Overdone: Batter is smooth, uniform, and somewhat viscous — it coats a skewer thickly and drips in a slow, rope-like stream. Gluten has developed. You cannot undo gluten development. Make the best of it: fry immediately at the correct temperature and accept a slightly thicker, chewier crust.
Feel cue: The batter should feel ice-cold on your fingertips and drip off them almost as freely as water — if it drapes and clings in sheets, it has been over-mixed or is too warm.

Heat the frying oil in a heavy-bottomed pot or wok to 175-180 C — use a thermometer. Dip the ingredient (shrimp, sweet potato, broccoli, etc.) briefly in a light dusting of dry flour, shake off the excess, then dip into the cold batter and lower immediately into the oil. Fry in small batches — crowding drops the oil temperature catastrophically. Fry until the batter is set and pale gold, about 2 to 3 minutes. The key visual cue is when the furious initial bubbling subsides to a quieter, more intermittent sizzle. Remove with a spider strainer and drain vertically on a wire rack, never flat on paper towels (which steam the crust soft). Serve within 2 minutes.
Visual cue: A pale, almost translucent golden crust with irregular, airy bubbles across the surface — no thick, smooth-skinned coating, but an open, lacy texture like frozen sea spray.
Underdone: Batter is pale white, still looks raw. Bubbles are violent and the crust has not set. It tears off when you try to lift the piece. Return to the oil and do not agitate — let the crust set for 30 more seconds before touching.
Perfect: Pale amber-gold with a distinctly airy, blistered surface. Sizzling has subsided to occasional pops. Lifts cleanly from the oil with a spider strainer. Transfer to a wire rack. Serve within 2 minutes with tentsuyu dipping broth or just sea salt.
Overdone: Crust is deeply golden, almost brown. The light, translucent quality is gone — it looks opaque and uniform. The tempura is still crisp but the delicate flavour of the coating is compromised. Reduce temperature by 5 C for the next batch.
Feel cue: Listen to the oil — fresh tempura sounds like a sustained roar of a fast-flowing river. When that roar subsides to scattered pops, the piece is done. Trust your ears before your eyes.

  Alternatives: kombu dashi (vegan); light chicken stock

  Alternatives: fresh ginger, grated (very sharp — use sparingly)
Fresh ginger, grated (optional, for serving): 1 tsp

description: The clear, golden dipping broth served with tempura — a dashi-based tentsuyu seasoned with mirin and soy, sweet and savoury with a hint of the sea, served hot alongside grated daikon.

ingredients.name: 酱油（Soy sauce (koikuchi or usukuchi light soy)）

steps:
Measure the dashi, mirin, and soy sauce into a small saucepan and stir briefly to combine. The ratio of dashi to mirin to soy at 4:1:1 is the classic tentsuyu proportion for standard deep-frying. This ratio produces a broth that is savory but light — the dashi does the heavy flavor lifting, the mirin sweetens and rounds, and the soy colors and deepens. Place over medium heat and bring to a gentle simmer, stirring once. Let it simmer for 2–3 minutes to burn off the raw mirin alcohol and meld the three components. The sauce should smell deeply of the sea (from the katsuobushi in the dashi), sweet rice wine, and a clean, balanced soy.
Visual cue: A clear, light amber-gold liquid at a gentle simmer, translucent enough to see the bottom of the pan clearly, smelling of balanced dashi and mirin.
Underdone: Sauce is cold or barely warm, the mirin is still sharp and boozy-tasting, and the components haven't blended into a unified broth. Bring to a gentle simmer and hold for 2 full minutes. The heat is what marries the three components — cold tentsuyu is just three separate ingredients poured together.
Perfect: Gently simmering, crystal-clear amber-gold. Smells of the ocean (katsuobushi), sweet rice (mirin), and savory soy in equal proportion. No raw alcohol sharpness. Remove from heat and hold warm until ready to serve. Tentsuyu is always served hot alongside the tempura.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced significantly from a prolonged boil — it tastes salty and intensely concentrated, and the color has deepened from amber to dark orange. Add more dashi to dilute back to the correct ratio. Tentsuyu should be light and refreshing, not a glaze.
Feel cue: Cup a small amount in a tasting spoon and hold it to your lips without drinking: the steam should smell of the ocean, like standing at the edge of a dashi pot, with a caramel sweetness underneath. If the steam smells sharp and boozy,
simmer 1 more minute.

Peel a section of daikon and grate it on the finest setting of a Japanese oroshi grater (or the small holes of a box grater, or a Microplane) into a small bowl. Grate in gentle circular or back-and-forth strokes — pressing too hard will make the daikon watery and fibrous rather than fine and fluffy. Immediately gather the grated daikon with clean fingertips and press it into a small, clean hemisphere — the Japanese presentation always shows the daikon mounded neatly beside the sauce bowl, ready to stir in. The pungency of freshly grated daikon fades quickly — grate it immediately before serving, not ahead of time.
Visual cue: A mound of fine, fluffy, snow-white grated daikon with no fibrous strings — fine enough to look almost like soft-packed snow.
Underdone: Daikon has been grated coarsely — large, crunchy shreds that release too quickly into the broth and taste harsh and spicy rather than clean and mild. Use the finer side of the grater. Coarse daikon is not wrong exactly, but the traditional presentation is very fine and soft.
Perfect: Fine, fluffy, white mound with a fresh, faintly spicy clean scent. Each strand is barely visible, more of a soft paste than a shred. It dissolves into the broth almost instantly. Place the mound beside the tentsuyu cup and serve immediately. Daikon loses its pungency within 5 minutes of grating.
Overdone: Daikon has been sitting grated for 20 minutes — the volatile enzyme-created pungency has dissipated and the daikon is now waterlogged and flat-tasting. Grate fresh daikon. The whole point of oroshi daikon is the volatile contrast between pungent fresh grating and the sweet warm broth.
Feel cue: Press a small pinch of freshly grated daikon to your upper lip for 3 seconds: you should feel a faint prickling warmth — the isothiocyanate compounds that give daikon its pleasant bite. If you feel nothing, the daikon is old or the grater
is too coarse.

Ladle the hot tentsuyu into small individual dipping bowls — lacquerware or ceramic, ideally with a wide mouth that allows a full shrimp or vegetable piece to be dipped without splashing. Place the mound of grated daikon and a small amount of grated ginger on the rim or in a corner of a small condiment plate beside each bowl. The diner stirs the daikon and ginger into the hot tentsuyu themselves, controlling the intensity. To eat: dip a piece of hot tempura briefly into the broth — one to two seconds — so the batter absorbs a little broth without going soggy, and eat immediately. The salt, umami, and sweet of the broth complement the neutral crunch of the tempura batter.
Visual cue: A clear, hot, amber-gold broth in a small cup, steaming gently, with a small mound of white daikon and ginger beside it — simple and clean in presentation.
Underdone: Broth has cooled below 60°C before being ladled — it will cool further rapidly in the dipping bowl and fail to season the tempura properly. Reheat to a simmer and ladle immediately into warm bowls. Cold tentsuyu makes the tempura batter feel tough rather than yielding.
Perfect: Hot, steaming, crystal-clear amber tentsuyu with a clean sea-and-caramel aroma. One dip of tempura and the salt and umami penetrate the batter just enough. The daikon, stirred in, instantly softens the intensity with coolness. Serve alongside freshly fried tempura within 30 seconds of frying.
Overdone: Tentsuyu has been kept on heat too long and has reduced past the correct concentration — it's salty and too intensely flavored, overwhelming the delicate batter. Dilute with a tablespoon of warm dashi or hot water and taste again. Tentsuyu should feel refreshing, not heavy.
Feel cue: Taste a spoonful of the tentsuyu on its own, without any daikon. It should feel warm and light on the tongue — not the weight of a sauce, but the clean savory brightness of
a broth. The umami should hum rather than shout, leaving a long, pleasant aftertaste of the sea.

ingredients.name: Mixed vegetables: sweet potato (sliced), shiitake, green beans, lotus root, red pepper
Cake flour or all-purpose flour (very cold)
食用油（Neutral oil (sesame-sunflower blend or canola) for frying）

steps:
Prepare vegetables: slice sweet potato 6mm thick, clean shiitake and score the caps, top and tail green beans, slice lotus root 5mm thick, cut red pepper into wide strips. Pat all vegetables completely dry — any surface moisture prevents batter adhesion and causes dangerous oil splatter. Dust lightly with flour (the second function flour serves after structural gluten — it acts as a primer for batter adhesion). Keep everything cold until the moment of frying.
Visual cue: Dry, flour-dusted vegetable pieces arranged on a tray. No glistening moisture visible on any surface.
Underdone: Vegetables are still wet from washing — water beads on the surface. Batter will not adhere and will splash violently in the oil. Pat completely dry with paper towels and allow to air-dry for 5 minutes before flouring.
Perfect: All pieces completely dry, with a very thin, barely-visible dusting of flour. No bare, shiny wet patches. Keep refrigerated until the moment of frying.
Overdone: Too much flour — pieces are thick with a visible white coat. Shake off excess. Too much flour makes the batter thick and gluey rather than gossamer.
Feel cue: Rub a piece between your fingers after drying and dusting — it should feel dry like talcum powder, not damp or tacky. Cold vegetables hold batter longer before it slides.

This step must be done RIGHT BEFORE frying — never in advance. Combine the egg yolk with the ice-cold sparkling water and stir briefly. Add both flours at once and stir with chopsticks or a fork only 8–10 strokes. The batter must remain lumpy, floury, and obviously under-mixed. Large dry flour streaks are normal and desirable. Do not be tempted to mix until smooth — gluten development is the enemy of tempura.
Visual cue: A lumpy, barely-combined batter with visible dry flour streaks and clumps. Looks like it has been mixed by someone who didn't try very hard. This is correct.
Underdone: If somehow possible — batter is just flour and egg with no water incorporation. Won't adhere. Add the water and stir minimally.
Perfect: Lumpy, streaky, obviously under-mixed. Thin enough to drip off a chopstick in a thin, uneven stream. Barely holding together. Ice cold. Use immediately. Every minute it sits, gluten develops and the batter becomes less ethereal.
Overdone: Smooth, crepe-batter consistency with no lumps. Gluten has developed from over-mixing. Will produce a thick, chewy crust instead of a sheer, crisp shell. Cannot be un-mixed. Use it anyway but expect a less delicate result.
Feel cue: Dip a finger into the batter and hold it up — the batter should run off your finger in a thin, uneven stream with lumps, not in a smooth, even sheet. It should feel ice cold and barely there.

Heat the oil to exactly 170–175 C (340–345 F) — use a thermometer. Dip each vegetable piece briefly in the batter (let excess drip for just 1 second) and lower into the oil. Fry in small batches to maintain oil temperature — too many pieces cools the oil and produces soggy results. Fry 2–3 minutes until the batter sets to a very pale, almost white-gold. Drain on a rack. Serve within 2 minutes.
Visual cue: Pale, almost white-gold, sheer batter with a barely perceptible bubbled surface. Not dark golden. Looks nearly translucent in places where the batter is thinnest.
Underdone: Batter looks wet and is still softly bending around the vegetable. Hasn't fully set. Leave in the oil longer. The batter needs to set to a rigid, dry texture.
Perfect: Set to a sheer, barely-gold, rigid shell. Tiny bubbles on the surface. The oil has cleared. When lifted, the crust doesn't flex — it holds its shape. The vegetable inside is cooked through. Drain on a rack and serve within 2 minutes. Salt lightly at the table.
Overdone: Batter is deep golden or brown. The sheer delicacy is gone — it now looks like a thick-battered onion ring. Drain and serve. Still good to eat, but the essence of tempura — the gossamer veil — is lost.
Feel cue: Hold a piece of finished tempura by its thickest edge and wave it gently — a properly fried piece will feel almost weightless, and you should hear a faint rustling sound as the sheer batter shifts. It should feel as light as a crisp autumn leaf.

name: Mexican Tepache
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。

description: A barely-alcoholic fermented pineapple drink spiked with piloncillo and cinnamon — lightly fizzy, sweet-sour, and cooling, made from peel and core that would otherwise go to waste.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Pineapple peel and core (from 1 whole pineapple, washed well)

steps:
Warm about one cup of the measured water to 40°C (just warm to the touch, not hot). Add the piloncillo or brown sugar and stir until fully dissolved. Combine with the remaining measured room-temperature water in a large, clean jar or ceramic crock (at least 2-liter capacity). Never use cold water alone — cold does not dissolve piloncillo.
Visual cue: A clear to faintly amber liquid with no visible sugar granules. The water smells faintly of brown sugar and molasses.
Underdone: Piloncillo chunks or sugar granules still undissolved, sitting at the bottom of the vessel. Stir longer with warm water. Piloncillo in particular needs warm water and active stirring to dissolve fully.
Perfect: Uniformly amber-tinted water, completely clear with no undissolved material. Smells sweetly of raw sugar. Add the pineapple scraps and spices to the jar.
Overdone: Water has been used too hot — steam rising, water above 60°C. Risk of killing wild yeasts on the pineapple skin. Allow to cool to below 40°C before adding the pineapple. Wild yeasts die above 50°C.
Feel cue: Dip a clean fingertip — the water should feel pleasantly warm, similar to a warm bath, never uncomfortably hot. This temperature keeps the wild yeasts on the pineapple skin alive.

Scrub the pineapple skin thoroughly under running water before cutting to remove surface dirt, then cut the peel and core into rough chunks. Add them to the jar with the sugar water, followed by the cinnamon stick and cloves. The pineapple should be mostly submerged. Cover the jar with a clean cotton cloth secured with a rubber band — not a tight lid, as the fermentation produces CO2 that must escape.
Visual cue: A large jar filled with golden pineapple scraps, warm amber water, and spices. The cloth cover is taut and secured, allowing air exchange.
Underdone: Jar is sealed with a tight lid. No air exchange possible. Replace the lid with a cloth cover immediately — a sealed jar will pressurize dangerously or create conditions for off-flavors.
Perfect: Pineapple scraps mostly submerged in sugar water. Cinnamon and cloves visible through the liquid. Cloth cover secured and breathable. Set in a warm spot (22–28°C) out of direct sunlight for 2–3 days.
Overdone: Pineapple skin was not washed and carries surface contaminants or pesticide residue that can interfere with fermentation. Always wash pineapple well before using — soap is fine as long as rinsed thoroughly.
Feel cue: Push the pineapple scraps down into the sugar water — they should feel firm and float back up gently. The liquid should feel barely warm to the touch after combining.

Leave covered at room temperature (22–28°C is ideal) for 2–3 days, stirring once daily with a clean spoon. Bubbles will begin to appear in the liquid at the 24-hour mark. By 48 hours the tepache should be actively fizzing when the jar is gently tilted. Taste daily — it should move from sweet to lightly sour and pleasantly tropical. Stop when the tartness is to your liking.
Visual cue: After 48 hours: the liquid has taken on a deeper amber color, fine bubbles rise continuously from the pineapple pieces, and a thin white foam may sit at the surface (harmless wild yeast).
Underdone: After 24 hours: liquid is still clear and very sweet. No visible bubbles. No sour note when tasted. Wait — fermentation may be slow if the room is cool (below 20°C). Move to a warmer spot. Stir to redistribute yeasts.
Perfect: Lightly fizzy, pleasantly sour-sweet, with a tropical pineapple fragrance and a hint of cinnamon. Bubbles are active but not violent. The surface foam is white and clean-smelling. Strain immediately and refrigerate to slow further fermentation.
Overdone: Tepache is strongly sour or vinegary, has lost its sweetness entirely, and may smell of alcohol or kombucha. The liquid may be cloudy from over-active fermentation. Strain and dilute with sparkling water before serving. Or use as a cooking vinegar — excellent in salsas and marinades.
Feel cue: Dip a clean fingertip into the tepache on day 2 — you should feel the faintest tingle of carbonation, like very gentle sparkling water, not aggressive fizzing.

Strain the tepache through a fine-mesh sieve or cheesecloth into a clean pitcher or bottles, discarding the pineapple solids, cinnamon, and cloves. Refrigerate immediately to slow fermentation. Serve cold over ice. Tepache keeps refrigerated for up to 5 days and will continue to develop slightly in flavor.
Visual cue: A clear to lightly hazy amber-gold liquid with a persistent, fine effervescence. Smells tropical, slightly sour, and warmly spiced.
Underdone: After straining, liquid is barely carbonated — flat and purely sweet. No sour development. The fermentation was not long enough or the temperature was too cold. Serve as a sweet pineapple agua fresca, or allow the strained liquid to ferment 12 more hours in a sealed bottle in the fridge.
Perfect: Light, lively carbonation that tickles the glass. Color is a warm honey-gold. The nose is pineapple, brown sugar, and cinnamon. The palate finishes with a pleasant, refreshing sourness. Serve immediately over ice, or bottle and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
Overdone: Very strongly sour, minimal sweetness, heavy foam, possibly slightly alcoholic in taste. Dilute 1:1 with sparkling water or use as a base for cocktails. Still delicious — just more sour than the intended profile.
Feel cue: A sip of finished tepache should feel cooling and lively on the tongue — the mild carbonation gives it a slight effervescence that feels like spring water with a purpose.

name: Teriyaki Glaze
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Japanese soy sauce (koikuchi shoyu): 4 parts
  Alternatives: tamari for gluten-free
Mirin (hon-mirin, not aji-mirin seasoning): 4 parts
  Alternatives: dry sherry + 1 tsp sugar
Sake (dry Japanese rice wine): 2 parts
  Alternatives: dry sherry; dry white wine
White granulated sugar: 1 parts
  Alternatives: light brown sugar; honey
Fresh ginger (1 thin slice, optional): 0.2 parts
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 20 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A gleaming, lacquer-thick glaze of soy, mirin, and sake reduced to a syrupy consistency — sweet, savory, and deeply umami, brushed onto proteins in the final minutes of cooking.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine the soy sauce, mirin, sake, sugar, and ginger slice in a small saucepan. Stir briefly to help the sugar begin to dissolve. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring once more to ensure the sugar has dissolved completely before the liquid reaches a boil. Do not leave unattended at this stage — the sugar content means it can boil over quickly once it gets going. Remove the ginger slice after 2 minutes if using.
Visual cue: A dark, amber-brown liquid simmering gently, with small bubbles at the edges and a slight sheen beginning to develop on the surface. Steam carries a sweet, savoury sake-and-soy aroma.
Underdone: Sugar granules still visible on the spoon when you stir — the liquid hasn't reached a uniform temperature yet. Stir over the heat until sugar is fully dissolved and the liquid is uniform in color before reducing the heat.
Perfect: Uniformly dark, gently simmering, and clear — the sugar is dissolved and the alcohol is beginning to cook off. Smells deeply of caramelizing soy and sweet mirin. Reduce heat to medium-low and begin the reduction phase.
Overdone: Boiling too hard, with large bubbles and splattering — at risk of burning the sugar on the pan walls. Reduce heat immediately. Wipe down the pan sides with a wet pastry brush if sugar is caramelizing there.
Feel cue: The liquid at this stage should feel as thin as water when you test a drop between your fingers. The sweetness and salt should be equally assertive — if the soy dominates, add a tiny splash more mirin.

Reduce the simmering liquid over medium-low heat, without stirring, until it has reduced by roughly half and has reached a syrupy, glaze-like consistency. This takes 8-10 minutes. Watch carefully in the final 2 minutes — the sugar concentration rises sharply and the glaze can go from perfect to scorched in under a minute. To test: dip a cold spoon into the glaze and tilt it — it should flow in a slow, heavy sheet and coat the spoon in a thin lacquer. Off the heat, it will thicken further as it cools.
Visual cue: A glossy, mahogany-dark glaze that moves sluggishly in the pan when tilted. Small, slow bubbles pop at the surface. On a cold spoon, it coats in a thin, shiny, lacquer-like layer.
Underdone: Still thin and watery — runs off a spoon immediately without coating. Won't adhere to protein during brushing and will produce a pale, uneven finish. Continue reducing over gentle heat. The transition from liquid to glaze is gradual, then sudden — stay attentive.
Perfect: Thick, slow-moving, and lacquered-looking. Coats the back of a cold spoon in an even mahogany sheet. On the fingertip it feels distinctly syrupy and tacky. Remove from heat immediately. Use warm — brush over grilling salmon, chicken, or tofu in the last 2-3 minutes of cooking.
Overdone: Too thick — almost caramel-stiff when warm, hardens to a brittle glassy film when cool. Tastes intensely sweet with a bitter, burnt-sugar edge. Off the heat, stir in a few drops of soy sauce and warm water to thin to a workable consistency. Use immediately or it will over-set.
Feel cue: Touch a cooled drop on a plate: at the perfect reduction it should be tacky like a sticky note — adherent but not tooth-gluingly stiff. If it sets to a rigid, glassy bead within seconds, it has reduced too far.

ingredients.name: 玉米淀粉（Cornstarch (optional, for extra body)）

steps:
Combine soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small, heavy-bottomed saucepan. Stir briefly to dissolve the sugar. At this stage the mixture is thin, dark, and smells strongly of alcohol — the sake and mirin are raw. Set over medium heat and bring to a gentle simmer, stirring once or twice. Allow the alcohol to cook off before reducing: you will notice the sharp alcohol smell soften and sweeten as the sake and mirin cook out, replaced by a rounder, more caramelized fragrance.
Visual cue: A uniform, dark mahogany liquid with fine bubbles forming at the edges of the pan. The raw alcohol smell is fading.
Underdone: The liquid is still cold and the sugar hasn't fully dissolved — visible granules at the bottom of the pan. The smell is raw soy and raw alcohol. Stir gently and continue heating. Do not boil aggressively before the sugar dissolves.
Perfect: The mixture is uniformly liquid, gently simmering at the edges, dark brown, and smelling of warm soy and caramel rather than sharp alcohol. Proceed to reduce without stirring, just occasional swirling of the pan.
Overdone: The mixture has been brought to a hard rolling boil before the alcohol cooked off — the mirin has made the surface foam and the sugar may scorch on the sides. Reduce heat immediately and use a pastry brush dipped in cold water to dissolve any sugar crystals on the sides of the pan.
Feel cue: At the raw stage the liquid is thin and watery, barely coating a dipped finger. The smell of sake should be immediately noticeable — sharp and slightly floral. As it heats, the sharpness softens.

Maintain a steady, gentle simmer — not a hard boil — and reduce the sauce for 5–8 minutes, swirling the pan occasionally rather than stirring. The sauce is ready when it coats the back of a spoon thickly and a line drawn through the coating holds for 2–3 seconds. If using cornstarch: mix it with a tablespoon of cold water to form a slurry, then whisk it into the simmering sauce and stir for 30 seconds until thickened and glossy. Remove from heat — the sauce thickens further as it cools.
Visual cue: A glossy, mahogany-brown glaze that coats a spoon in an unbroken, shiny layer. When you draw a line through the coating with your finger, it holds clean for several seconds.
Underdone: The sauce runs off the back of the spoon like water. It tastes salty and sweet but thin, with no caramelized depth or body. Continue simmering. The sauce reduces quickly once it passes the halfway point — watch carefully and swirl rather than stir to avoid disturbing the reduction.
Perfect: The sauce coats a metal spoon with a glossy, lacquer-like layer. When cooled to room temperature, it will be thick enough to cling to proteins without dripping. The flavor is balanced: savory-sweet, with umami depth and no raw alcohol taste. Remove from heat and allow to cool slightly before using. The glaze will thicken further as it cools — if too thick when cold, thin with a splash of water or soy.
Overdone: The sauce has reduced too far — it looks syrupy and very dark, almost black. Tiny bubbles burst at the surface with a thick, toffee-like sound. It may smell slightly burnt. Add a tablespoon of water or soy sauce and gently swirl to re-incorporate. The sauce will loosen as it absorbs the liquid. Remove from heat immediately.
Feel cue: Dip a spoon and let the sauce run off your finger onto a cold plate — a properly reduced teriyaki sauce will set into a sticky, lacquer-firm film rather than a runny
puddle.

ingredients.name: 鸡腿（Chicken thigh, minced or coarsely ground）
Thai bird's eye chilies, sliced (adjust to tolerance)
Holy basil (krapow) leaves — NOT Thai basil

steps:
Combine oyster sauce, fish sauce, and dark soy sauce in a small bowl. Stir to blend. Taste — it should be powerfully salty and savory. This sauce goes in fast at high heat, so having it ready before you start is essential. Never season a stir-fry by shaking bottles over a hot wok.
Visual cue: Uniformly dark brown sauce, fully combined with no separation.
Underdone: Fish sauce and oyster sauce not yet blended — you can see two distinct layers. Stir vigorously for 10 seconds.
Perfect: Smooth, uniform dark sauce. Smells of fish sauce and sweet oyster sauce. Set next to the stove within arm's reach.
Overdone: Not applicable — this is a cold mix. N/A
Feel cue: The sauce should be thick enough to coat a chopstick — not runny like soy sauce, not thick like molasses.

Heat oil in a wok over high heat until smoking. Add garlic and bird's eye chilies together. Fry for 30-45 seconds, stirring constantly — the garlic will begin to golden at the edges and the chilies will turn the oil bright orange-red. Do not let the garlic burn or the dish will be bitter.
Visual cue: Garlic is pale gold at the edges with white centers; chilies have bloomed the oil to an orange-red. Fragrance fills the kitchen.
Underdone: Garlic is raw white, chilies still bright red — no color, no fragrance released. Increase heat and continue; stir constantly.
Perfect: Garlic edges are pale gold, centers still white. Oil is vivid orange-red from the chilies. Sharp, toasty aroma with chili heat visible as steam. Add chicken immediately.
Overdone: Garlic is dark brown or black, smells harsh and bitter. Discard and start over — burnt garlic cannot be saved and will ruin the dish.
Feel cue: The chili heat should hit the back of your throat even before the chicken goes in — if you are not tearing up slightly, either the chilies are mild or the wok is not hot enough.

Add minced chicken and break it apart with a spatula immediately. Stir-fry on high heat for 2-3 minutes, pressing the chicken flat against the wok to get color rather than steam. When no pink remains, pour the sauce around the edge of the wok (not over the chicken) — it will sizzle and char slightly before mixing in. Toss to coat.
Visual cue: Chicken is broken into varied, irregular pieces — some caramelized and darker, most pale golden. Uniformly coated in the dark sauce.
Underdone: Pink patches still visible in the chicken; sauce hasn't fully coated — looks pale and watery. Continue on high heat for another 60-90 seconds, spreading the chicken flat.
Perfect: No pink remains; some pieces have charred edges. Sauce clings to every piece in a glossy coat. Kitchen is filled with smoke and fragrant steam. Add holy basil.
Overdone: Chicken has dried out and shrunk significantly; the sauce is beginning to burn on the wok. Add a splash of water (1-2 tbsp) immediately and toss to deglaze.
Feel cue: Listen for the wok's roar — constant, aggressive crackling means you are stir-frying. Any drop to a gentle sizzle means the temperature has fallen and you are steaming.

Remove wok from heat (or reduce to minimum). Add holy basil leaves all at once and toss vigorously for 10-15 seconds. The leaves will wilt almost instantly from the residual heat. Do not overcook them — they should be wilted and dark green, not brown and mushy. Plate immediately over jasmine rice with a fried egg on top.
Visual cue: Basil leaves are wilted to dark, glossy green — not brown. They cling to the chicken pieces and the dish smells intensely of holy basil and caramelized fish sauce.
Underdone: Basil leaves are still bright green, upright, and raw — they haven't released their essential oils into the dish. Return to low heat for another 10-15 seconds, tossing constantly.
Perfect: Leaves wilted and darkened to a deep glossy green, completely integrated with the chicken. The aroma of holy basil — slightly clove-like, peppery — dominates the dish. Plate immediately.
Overdone: Basil is olive-brown and mushy; the aromatic oils have completely cooked off and it smells flat. The dish is still good — you just lost the herbal brightness. Serve immediately.
Feel cue: The basil should wilt with just a toss or two in the residual heat of the wok — if it needs more than 15 seconds, the wok was not hot enough to begin with.

ingredients.name: 猪肉末（Ground pork (or coarsely hand-chopped pork shoulder)）
Bird's eye chilies (prik kee noo), sliced or smashed (3–6 to taste)
Holy basil (bai krapao), leaves picked — Italian basil is a poor substitute
鸡蛋（Eggs, for frying (1 per serving)）

steps:
Heat a wok or large heavy skillet over the highest flame until smoke wisps from the surface — 2 minutes minimum. Add 30 g of the oil and swirl immediately. Add the garlic and chilies all at once and stir-fry for 20 seconds until the garlic is gold and the kitchen fills with a sharp, peppery fragrance. Add the ground pork, breaking it up with a spatula. Let it sear undisturbed for 30 seconds, then break and toss. Cook for 2–3 minutes total until no pink remains and the pork has some golden, crumbly edges rather than being pale and steamed.
Visual cue: Pork is golden-brown at the edges with visible caramelization, garlic is amber, chilies have softened and darkened. No pooled liquid in the wok.
Underdone: Pork is grey, wet, and releasing liquid. Steaming rather than frying. Garlic is still white. Drain excess liquid by tilting the wok, increase heat, and allow moisture to evaporate before continuing.
Perfect: Pork is golden-crusted in places, fragrant and dry. Garlic is toasty amber. Chilies are soft and bright red. Loud sizzle throughout. Add the seasoning sauces and rice.
Overdone: Pork is dried out and chewy, garlic is dark and bitter, edges are black. Add the rice immediately to stop the cooking and absorb excess char.
Feel cue: The wok should feel hot through an oven mitt held 15 cm above it. The sizzle of pork hitting the surface should be immediate and violent, not gradual.

Add the cold rice to the wok, breaking up any clumps with the spatula before it hits the heat. Pour the fish sauce, oyster sauce, and soy sauce around the edge of the wok (not directly on the rice) so the sauces hit the hot metal and sizzle. Toss everything together vigorously for 2–3 minutes, pressing the rice flat against the wok surface for 20 seconds at a time to allow contact browning, then tossing to redistribute. The goal is every grain coated and slightly toasted, not steamed.
Visual cue: Rice grains are uniformly amber and separate, each glossed with sauce. Visible slight char on individual grains. No wet spots or white grains remaining.
Underdone: Rice is pale and wet-looking, clumping in the center. Sauces are pooling at the bottom rather than coating the grains. Increase heat, press rice flat, and let it char undisturbed for 30 seconds before tossing again.
Perfect: Every grain is amber-coated, slightly separated, and smells of caramel and fish sauce. A few grains are darker where they touched the wok. The rice is dry enough to hiss when water is sprinkled on it. Add holy basil leaves.
Overdone: Rice is sticking to the wok in a crust and beginning to burn, black specks forming. Deglaze with a tablespoon of water, scrape the fond into the rice, and serve immediately.
Feel cue: Cold rice in a hot wok should bounce and rattle when you toss the pan — if it slides like porridge, your wok is not hot enough or the rice was too wet.

Remove the wok from heat. Add all the holy basil leaves at once and fold them through the rice with 4–5 broad strokes of the spatula. The residual heat of the rice and wok will wilt the basil in 20–30 seconds — you want it collapsed and glossy but not black or slimy. Holy basil wilts much faster than Italian basil and turns bitter if overcooked. The leaves should turn a deep, jewel-like green and release a wave of clove-anise fragrance. Taste and adjust with a few drops more fish sauce if needed.
Visual cue: Basil leaves are deep emerald-green and collapsed, integrated throughout the rice, releasing a vivid herbal perfume that fills the room.
Underdone: Leaves are still rigid and bright green, some standing upright in the rice. Keep folding — the heat in the rice is enough. If leaves remain stiff after 45 seconds, briefly return the wok to low heat.
Perfect: Leaves are wilted, deep green, slightly glossy. A clove-pepper-anise smell is unmistakable. Integrated evenly through the rice. Plate immediately and begin frying the eggs.
Overdone: Leaves are black, crispy, or smell burnt and bitter. If badly burnt, remove the worst pieces. The rice will still be good; the basil flavor has cooked into it.
Feel cue: The wilted holy basil should smell like someone crushed a clove between their fingers — peppery, floral, with a faint anise underpinning that is entirely unlike Italian basil.

In a small wok or skillet, heat the remaining 10 g of oil over high heat until it shimmers and just begins to smoke. Crack eggs into the oil and let them fry undisturbed for 60–90 seconds. The whites should blister and puff immediately on contact, forming golden lacey edges while the yolk stays barely set and glossy. Tilt the pan and baste the yolk with hot oil using a spoon. The egg is done when the white is fully set and golden-fringed, the yolk still deep orange and runny. Serve immediately atop the rice.
Visual cue: Egg whites are set but lacey at the frilled edges, golden-crisp in the outer ring, while the yolk is a dome of deep orange, opaque at the rim but still liquid at its crest.
Underdone: Whites are translucent and jiggly, no lace or color at the edges. The oil was not hot enough — wait until it shimmers visibly before cracking the egg.
Perfect: Whites are fully set with dramatic golden-brown lacey fringe. Yolk is orange and visibly liquid inside. Bottom of the white has a pale golden crust. Slide onto the rice immediately — do not let it rest in the pan.
Overdone: Yolk is pale, hard, and fully set. Whites are deeply brown and chewy. You've made a different dish — still tasty, but break the yolk over the rice for the best textural experience.
Feel cue: The lacey egg edge should snap when pressed with a spoon but the yolk should give like a water balloon — the contrast between crisp white and liquid yolk is the entire point.

Ground pork (or coarsely hand-chopped pork): 400 g
  Alternatives: ground chicken; ground beef; crumbled tofu
Bird's eye chilies, finely sliced: 5 whole

Neutral oil: 2 tbsp
Oyster sauce: 1.5 tbsp
  Alternatives: mushroom oyster sauce (vegan)
Fish sauce: 1.5 tbsp
  Alternatives: soy sauce + pinch salt
Soy sauce (thin, not dark): 1 tbsp
  Alternatives: light soy sauce

  Alternatives: white sugar
Thai holy basil (kra pao), leaves only: 1 cup (loosely packed)
  Alternatives: Italian basil (flavor differs significantly)
Water or chicken stock: 2 tbsp

description: Ground pork stir-fried over violent heat with bird's eye chilies and Thai holy basil until the meat caramelizes at the edges and the whole dish blooms with a peppery, clove-like fragrance that holy basil alone produces — a Bangkok street-food staple that takes 8 minutes, demands ferocious heat, and rewards with an intensity that formal restaurant versions rarely match.

ingredients.name: 猪肉末（Ground pork (or coarsely hand-chopped pork)）
Thai holy basil (kra pao), leaves only
Fried egg (kai dao), one per serving

steps:
Combine oyster sauce, fish sauce, soy sauce, and sugar in a small bowl. Stir until the sugar dissolves. Taste and adjust: it should be intensely savory, salty, slightly sweet, and smell powerfully of fermented seafood and caramel. Set beside the stove. In pad kra pao, there is no time for measuring once the wok is hot — everything must be ready before you start.
Visual cue: A dark, uniform brown sauce with dissolved sugar and no separation between the different sauces.
Underdone: Sugar crystals still visible. Fish sauce and oyster sauce not yet combined. Stir until completely homogenous.
Perfect: Smooth, dark, unified sauce. Smells powerfully of the sea and caramel. Ready at arm's reach of the wok. Prepare the wok.
Overdone: No such state. Proceed. Proceed.
Feel cue: Dip a finger and taste — the sauce should sting the tongue with saltiness and leave a sweet, umami aftertaste.

Heat a wok or large cast-iron pan over the highest possible heat until it begins to smoke. Add the oil and heat for 15 seconds. Add the chilies and garlic simultaneously. Stir-fry, keeping everything moving, for 30-45 seconds. The garlic should be fragrant and just beginning to color at the edges — not burnt. The chilies will release intense capsaicin vapor; ensure ventilation. This step is fast and violent.
Visual cue: Garlic with golden, just-turning edges surrounded by dark green chili pieces, in a haze of fragrant, spicy smoke.
Underdone: Garlic is still raw white. No color. No fragrance bloom. The wok may not be hot enough. Increase heat to maximum and stir constantly — the raw garlic flavor will dominate the final dish.
Perfect: Garlic edges are just golden. Chilies are slightly softened. The wok is smoking and smells of hot garlic and capsaicin. Add pork immediately — do not let garlic pass to brown.
Overdone: Garlic is dark brown and beginning to smell bitter. Discard and start again with fresh oil, garlic, and chilies — burnt garlic cannot be corrected in a dish this simple.
Feel cue: You will feel the heat of the capsaicin in your eyes and throat — this is the indication that the chilies are working. If you feel nothing, the wok is not hot enough.

Add the ground pork to the wok in one addition. Press it flat against the hot surface and let it sear without stirring for 30-45 seconds until the contact side turns grey-to-caramelized. Then break it up and stir-fry vigorously for 2-3 minutes, pressing and breaking apart any clumps. Pour in the pre-mixed sauce and the water. Continue stir-frying over maximum heat for another minute until the sauce has reduced and coated every piece of meat in a sticky, dark glaze. The pan should sound like it is sizzling furiously — not steaming.
Visual cue: Small, irregular pieces of pork coated in a dark, glossy, reduced sauce with caramelized edges — no grey, steamed-looking meat visible.
Underdone: Pork is still pale grey and steaming rather than sizzling. Sauce has not reduced. Too much liquid in the pan. Increase heat aggressively. Stop adding water. Keep stirring and tossing until the sizzle returns.
Perfect: Every piece of pork is dark, glossy, and caramelized at the edges. Sauce is reduced to a sticky coat. Pan sizzles loudly. Kitchen is fragrant with caramelized soy and chili. Kill the heat. Add basil immediately.
Overdone: Pork is dry and sauce has burnt to a bitter residue on the pan bottom. Deglaze immediately with a splash of water, stir quickly, and remove from heat.
Feel cue: Listen to the wok — pad kra pao is ready when it sounds like a roaring fire, not a boiling pot.

Remove the wok from heat. Add all the holy basil leaves at once and toss rapidly — residual heat will wilt the basil in 15-20 seconds. Holy basil releases its best aroma when it hits heat but is not overcooked: the leaves should be wilted but still intensely fragrant and not uniformly black. Serve immediately over jasmine rice, topped with a fried egg cooked in very hot oil until the edges are crispy and lacy.
Visual cue: Dark pork and glossy sauce with wilted-but-still-green basil leaves scattered throughout, topped with a crispy-edged fried egg.
Underdone: Basil leaves are still completely raw and stiff. The dish smells of raw herb rather than cooked basil's peppery, clove-like warmth. Return to low heat for 10 seconds with constant tossing.
Perfect: Basil leaves have wilted to a deep, glossy green with the clove-pepper perfume of kra pao released into the dish. A few crispy edges are acceptable and desirable. Plate immediately. The basil perfume fades within minutes.
Overdone: Basil has turned black and lost all fragrance. It tastes bitter. Nothing can recover burnt basil in the dish. Garnish with a few fresh raw leaves to restore some fragrance.
Feel cue: The finished dish should assault your nose with a spicy, sweet, clove-like intensity the moment you lift the lid — holy basil's fragrance is the dish's soul and it must be evident.

ingredients.name: White fish fillets (tilapia, Spanish mackerel, or snapper), pin-boned
Kaffir lime leaves, central stem removed, finely chiffonade
Long beans or green beans, cut into 3 mm rounds

steps:
Cut the fish into rough chunks. Pulse in a food processor until the fish breaks down into a coarse paste — approximately 15–20 short pulses. Do not blend to a smooth puree; you want some texture remaining. Add the curry paste, fish sauce, egg, and cornstarch. Pulse 10 more times to combine. Then switch from pulsing to processing: run continuously for 30–45 seconds. The mixture will visibly change — it begins to gather into itself, pulling away from the bowl sides and becoming sticky and elastic. This is the myosin protein network forming, the same mechanism that makes bouncy fish balls. This step is not optional.
Visual cue: A cohesive, slightly sticky orange-red paste that clings to the food processor bowl in one mass rather than splattering. The texture is like thick peanut butter with some small fish flakes visible.
Underdone: Wet and loose — splashes rather than gathers. Visible chunks of unprocessed fish. No elasticity; the mixture flows when the bowl is tipped. Continue processing for another 30 seconds. Scrape down the sides and process again. The transformation is abrupt.
Perfect: The paste has gathered into a single cohesive mass that barely moves when the bowl is tipped. Orange-red from the curry paste, slightly glossy from the egg. When you scoop some and stretch it, it pulls rather than tearing. Transfer to a bowl immediately — overprocessing will heat the fish from friction.
Overdone: Paste is warm from friction and has become extremely sticky and smooth, almost glue-like. Difficult to handle. Refrigerate the paste for 20 minutes to firm up before shaping. The texture will still produce good results.
Feel cue: Scoop a tablespoon of paste and slap it between your palms repeatedly — it should feel elastic and springy, stretching without tearing and snapping back with each slap. This 'slapping' technique further develops the protein network and is
traditional in Thai kitchens.

Transfer the fish paste to a bowl. Add the kaffir lime leaf chiffonade and sliced beans. Fold in firmly with a spatula — not gently, but with real pressure to distribute the additions without breaking the protein network already developed. At this stage, many Thai cooks slap the mixture against the bowl 10–15 times: lift and throw the paste back into the bowl to drive out air bubbles and further tighten the network. Refrigerate the paste for 15 minutes — chilling makes shaping much easier.
Visual cue: An orange-red paste with visible flecks of deep green kaffir lime leaf and bright green bean rounds distributed throughout. The paste should hold a peak when scooped.
Underdone: Kaffir lime and beans sitting on top, not incorporated. Paste is wet and not holding shape. Fold more firmly. If still too wet, refrigerate 10 minutes and fold again.
Perfect: Beans and kaffir lime evenly distributed. Paste holds a clear peak when scooped with a spoon and released. Chilled and easy to handle. Begin shaping immediately while cold.
Overdone: Paste overworked — very tight and hard to shape. Beans have started releasing liquid and making it wet again. Refrigerate 10 minutes. The brief rest will allow the gluten and myosin proteins to relax slightly.
Feel cue: Pick up a handful of paste — it should peel cleanly off your palm with a satisfying pop, leaving only a slight residue. If it slides off in a liquid sheet, the protein network is underdeveloped. If it stays glued, it is perfectly developed.

Heat the oil in a wok or deep pan to 175°C (350°F). Wet your palms with cold water. Scoop 2 heaped tablespoons of paste and form into a flat disc 1.5 cm thick and 7 cm diameter — they should look like hockey pucks, not balls. Slide gently into the oil. Fry 4–5 at a time without crowding. Cook 2–3 minutes per side until deep golden-brown all over. The cakes will float and puff slightly as they cook — a good sign. Test one by cutting in half: it should be cooked through with no translucent center and a dense, bouncy interior texture.
Visual cue: Evenly golden-brown discs floating at the surface of the oil, slightly puffed. Visible green flecks of kaffir lime and bean peeking through the crust.
Underdone: Pale, oil-saturated surface. Cakes are sinking rather than floating. Raw grey in the center when tested. Return to oil. Sinking cakes indicate the oil temperature dropped from crowding — remove some cakes and wait for oil to return to 175°C before continuing.
Perfect: Deep golden-brown, floating confidently, the surface crackled and slightly blistered. Bounce back firmly when pressed with a spoon. Interior: uniformly white, dense, springy. Drain on paper towels and serve immediately — they lose crispness quickly.
Overdone: Very dark brown, crust hard and brittle. The beans inside have turned army-green and lost their color. Drain well on paper towels and serve immediately with a cooling cucumber relish to offset the intensity.
Feel cue: Press the top of a freshly fried cake with a spoon — it should spring back decisively, like pressing a firm rubber eraser. A well-developed myosin network produces this distinctive bounciness. If it yields without springing back, the protein network was underdeveloped.

Drain on paper towels for 60 seconds only — too long and they cool and lose their crackle. Arrange on a serving plate. Serve immediately with Thai cucumber relish (ajat): thin-sliced cucumber and shallot in sweet vinegar with crushed peanuts and coriander. The cool, sharp relish is not optional accompaniment — it is the counterpoint the richness demands.
Visual cue: Glossy golden cakes on a white plate, still glistening slightly from the fry. Green herb flecks visible on the surface. Steam rising gently.
Underdone: Drained too long — surface has dulled to matte and the crust has steamed itself soft from internal moisture. Re-fry for 30 seconds in very hot oil to re-crisp the exterior.
Perfect: Golden, slightly glistening surface. Crisp sound when tapped with a fingernail. Interior still clearly hot — steam escaping when cut. Serve within 3 minutes of frying.
Overdone: Served after standing 10+ minutes — surface has gone soggy, green herbs have wilted and turned dark. Re-fry quickly. Next time, fry in smaller batches closer to service.
Feel cue: Pick one up — it should feel firm and rigid with a dry, crackly surface. Bite through: the resistance of the crust gives way to a dense, springy interior with an almost chewy quality from the developed myosin. The kaffir lime leaf should burst in individual floral-citrus hits.

description: Coconut cream and red curry paste in their essential dialogue — the paste blooms in oil until the room smells like a Thai kitchen, coconut cream added in stages to build a sauce that is simultaneously rich and electric with heat.

ingredients.name: Firm white fish (snapper or barramundi, skin-on, cut into 5cm pieces)

steps:
Spoon 4 tablespoons of the thick cream that has risen to the top of the coconut cream can into a wok or wide pan. Heat over medium-high until it begins to bubble and the cream starts to separate (the oil splits from the solids). Add the red curry paste and fry in the coconut cream for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly, until the paste darkens slightly, the oil separates fully, and the fragrance fills the kitchen. This frying step in coconut cream is the most important step — do not rush it.
Visual cue: The curry paste has darkened and is frying in released coconut oil around it. Oil has clearly separated and is visible pooling at the edges of the paste.
Underdone: Paste is pale and wet, sitting in coconut cream without frying. No separation, no darkening. Increase heat to medium-high. The cream must split for the paste to fry.
Perfect: Paste is deeper in color, fragrant, and surrounded by separated coconut oil. The smell is intensely of lemongrass, galangal, and chile. Add the rest of the coconut cream in stages.
Overdone: Paste is dark and sticking to the pan. Some pieces are beginning to burn. Acrid smell. Add remaining coconut cream immediately to stop the cooking.
Feel cue: When the curry paste is properly bloomed, the fragrance is extraordinary — layers of lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime, and chile rising together in one aromatic cloud.

Add the remaining coconut cream and stir to combine with the bloomed paste. Add fish sauce, palm sugar, and torn kaffir lime leaves. Stir and taste — adjust the balance of salty (fish sauce), sweet (palm sugar), and heat (curry paste) until it feels harmonious. Add the Thai eggplant. Simmer for 5-7 minutes until the eggplant is just tender but still holds its shape. The sauce should be rich, slightly thickened, and deeply colored.
Visual cue: A deep orange-red sauce with visible coconut cream richness — slightly glossy and uniform. Eggplant pieces are tender and have absorbed the sauce color.
Underdone: Sauce is thin and pale. Eggplant is still firm and white inside. Curry paste flavor is thin. Simmer 5 more minutes. The vegetables need time to release moisture and concentrate the sauce.
Perfect: Rich, orange-red, slightly thickened sauce. Eggplant is tender all the way through. Balanced flavor profile. Add fish and cook briefly.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced too far and is very thick and oily. Eggplant has collapsed into mush. Add a splash of water to loosen. Proceed to cook the fish.
Feel cue: A properly balanced Thai curry sauce should taste of four things simultaneously: heat, sweetness, salt, and the citrus ghost of kaffir lime. If any one dominates, adjust.

Nestle the fish pieces into the simmering curry sauce. Reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and cook for 4-6 minutes depending on thickness. Fish is done when it turns opaque throughout and flakes easily when a fork is pressed gently against the flesh. Do not stir after adding fish — the pieces are delicate and will break apart. Gently baste by spooning sauce over the exposed tops once during cooking.
Visual cue: Fish is opaque white throughout with a slight orange tinge from the sauce. The flesh flakes easily when a fork is pressed at the thickest point.
Underdone: Fish has a translucent center and resists flaking. The flesh is cool at the center. Cover and cook 2-3 more minutes. Check again by pressing gently with a fork.
Perfect: Opaque throughout, flakes with gentle pressure, and the sauce has infused into the surface layers. Remove from heat and add basil and lime juice.
Overdone: Fish is flaking apart on its own and crumbling into the sauce. Texture is dry and granular. Remove from heat immediately. Serve gently, spooning around the fish rather than through it.
Feel cue: Correctly poached fish in curry feels like it barely needs a fork — it yields at the touch and falls into large, moist flakes rather than small, dry crumbles.

Remove from heat. Tear in Thai basil leaves and stir gently once. Squeeze lime juice over the top. Taste once more for the final balance of salt, sweet, sour, and heat — this is the moment to adjust. Serve immediately over jasmine rice. The basil must go in off the heat to preserve its anise-clove fragrance.
Visual cue: Deep orange-red curry with wilted-but-vibrant green basil leaves and glistening fish pieces just visible beneath the sauce surface.
Underdone: No basil or lime juice added. Curry is flat and one-dimensional. Add both. The aromatic finish is what separates Thai curry from generic sauce.
Perfect: Basil has just wilted from the residual heat. Lime brightness cuts through the richness. Colors are vivid. Serve immediately over jasmine rice.
Overdone: Basil was added to the heat and has turned completely black and bitter. Lime was added too early and has faded. Add fresh basil torn over the top at the table instead.
Feel cue: The fragrance of Thai basil torn into hot curry is immediate and powerful — anise-forward with a sweet clove note that rises through the coconut and chile steam.

steps:
Dry-toast coriander seeds in a pan over medium heat, swirling constantly.
Visual cue: Seeds darken one shade and a thin smoke rises from the pan.
Underdone: Pale, raw color. No fragrance. Keep going — they need heat to bloom.
Perfect: Warm honey color, kitchen smells like an orange grove. Tip onto a cool plate immediately.
Overdone: Black flecks, acrid smoke. Discard. Burnt spices ruin the whole paste.
Feel cue: Smells intensely of toasted nuts crossed with citrus peel.

In a granite mortar, pound chilies, lemongrass, and galangal hardest first — fibers down to threads.
Visual cue: A coarse, pale-green fibrous mash with no recognizable chunks.
Underdone: Visible chunks of stem and seed. Pound longer, scrape the sides.
Perfect: Stringy paste; pestle leaves a clean trail. Add the alliums.
Overdone: Watery, juice pooling. Drain liquid, save for cooking the paste later.
Feel cue: Slow rhythm. The pestle should thud, not click. You feel the resistance shift from crunchy to wet-sandy.

Add shallot, garlic, and cilantro root. Continue pounding until alliums dissolve into the paste.
Visual cue: A wet, pale-green paste with no white or pink chunks.
Underdone: Pink shallot specks visible. Pound until they vanish.
Perfect: Glossy, uniform color, a single shade of bright green. Add zest, spice, shrimp paste.
Overdone: Soupy. Liquid pools at the edges. Strain off and save the liquid.
Feel cue: Smells sharp and oniony, with lemongrass perfume rising on top.

Add lime zest, shrimp paste, and ground toasted spices. Pound until the paste pulls cleanly from the mortar.
Visual cue: A glossy, deep-green paste that holds peaks like stiff frosting.
Underdone: Streaks of darker shrimp paste visible. Pound and fold until uniform.
Perfect: Single deep-jade color, glossy, holds shape. Use within 3 days, or freeze in tablespoon portions.
Overdone: Loose, oily, sliding off the pestle. Stir back together; flavor is still good.
Feel cue: Stings the eyes. Smells like a wet jungle floor at dawn.

description: Strongly brewed Ceylon tea stained to a vivid amber-orange by spices and food coloring, cooled over ice and crowned with a slow pour of sweetened condensed milk that sinks through the tea in billowing white clouds before it is stirred into a creamy, bittersweet drink. This is the beverage color of a Bangkok afternoon — the color of rust and sunshine simultaneously.

ingredients.name: Thai tea mix (cha yen blend — Ceylon with spices and orange food color)
Evaporated milk (for the white top layer)
Ground tamarind (optional — deepens color and adds slight sour note)

steps:
Bring the water to a full rolling boil. Place the Thai tea mix (and optional star anise and tamarind if using) in a tea sock, fine-mesh strainer, or paper coffee filter set over a large heatproof pitcher or measuring cup. Pour the boiling water over the tea in a slow, steady stream to ensure full saturation. Allow the tea to steep for 5 minutes without disturbing it — no stirring. The extraction time is critical: too short and the tea will be weak and watery with insufficient bitterness to balance the sweetened milk; too long and it becomes aggressively tannic and harsh. After 5 minutes, press the tea mix firmly through the strainer to extract the last of the liquid, which carries the most color and body. Add the sugar now if using — stir to dissolve in the hot tea. Allow the tea to cool for at least 10 minutes before chilling further.
Visual cue: A deep, opaque amber-orange tea — the color of rust or terracotta tiles — with a slight reddish tinge and no cloudiness.
Underdone: Tea is pale amber, almost the color of lightly brewed black tea. It lacks the vivid orange color and has insufficient body to balance the condensed milk. Steep for 2 more minutes and press the tea bag or sock more firmly when removing.
Perfect: A deep, vivid orange-amber that is almost opaque in the cup. Holds its color under direct light. Smells of spiced tea with a faint sweetness from the tea mix. Slightly bitter on its own but with body. Cool the tea to room temperature or use immediately over ice.
Overdone: Tea has steeped too long and is very dark — almost brown-black — with a sharp, astringent tannin bite that will not be masked by the condensed milk. Dilute with a small amount of hot water and reduce condensed milk slightly to compensate for the stronger extraction.
Feel cue: Press the back of a spoon against the steeped tea sock and run it down — the liquid that drains should stain the
spoon a deep amber-orange that is visible even in a thin film. That color intensity in a thin layer means the tea has full body.

Fill a large, clear glass completely with large ice cubes — the glass should be full to within 2 centimeters of the rim. Pour the condensed milk into the bottom of the glass first: it is heavier than the tea and will naturally settle to the bottom if you add the tea over it gently. Now pour the brewed Thai tea slowly over the ice, aiming for the side of the glass rather than the center to slow the pour and preserve the visual layering. The tea will be a vivid orange-amber column and the condensed milk will be a white layer visible at the bottom through the ice — this contrast is the visual signature of the drink. The condensed milk at the bottom has not yet been mixed in.
Visual cue: A glass of vivid orange-amber tea over ice, with a visible layer of white condensed milk settled at the bottom.
Underdone: The condensed milk has already been mixed in and the drink is a uniform pale cream-orange rather than showing the dramatic two-tone separation. Presentation has been lost but the flavor is correct. Add a small drizzle of condensed milk over the top to partially restore the visual.
Perfect: The glass shows a vivid orange-amber tea column over ice with a distinct white condensed milk layer visible at the bottom. The contrast is dramatic and the ice cubes are visible as a clear middle zone. Add the evaporated milk float and serve with a straw for the diner to stir.
Overdone: Too much ice has been added and the tea volume is insufficient — the drink will be very dilute. Top up with more brewed tea.
Feel cue: Hold the glass to the light — the tea should be translucent orange with enough depth of color that you cannot easily see your hand clearly through the glass. That opacity means the tea is properly concentrated to survive the ice dilution.

Pour the evaporated milk slowly over the back of a spoon held just above the surface of the iced tea. The spoon breaks the fall and spreads the milk in a thin layer across the top of the tea rather than sinking it immediately. The evaporated milk should form a distinct white cloud or layer floating on top of the amber tea — a visual that is as much a part of Thai iced tea as the flavor. Serve with a long straw and do not stir before serving — the diner stirs their own drink at the table, swirling the condensed milk from the bottom and the evaporated milk from the top into the tea, watching the orange darken and the white dissolve. That act of stirring is part of the ritual.
Visual cue: A tricolor glass: white evaporated milk floating on top, vivid amber-orange tea in the middle, and white condensed milk visible at the bottom through the ice.
Underdone: The evaporated milk has sunk into the tea and the top layer has merged with the orange tea. No visible white layer on top. Pour more evaporated milk over the spoon for a fresh float, very slowly.
Perfect: The three visible layers are distinct: white top, orange middle, white bottom. The evaporated milk float holds for at least 1 minute before slowly sinking. The glass is cold and condensation is forming on the outside. Serve immediately with a straw.
Overdone: Too much evaporated milk has been added — the top layer is thick and the tea tastes predominantly of milk rather than spiced tea. Stir in and top up with additional brewed tea.
Feel cue: When you stir the fully assembled drink and take the first sip through the straw — pulling from the bottom where the condensed milk is richest — the cold, sweet, creamy, slightly bitter tea should coat your throat with a warmth that begins cold and ends warm from the spice notes of the tea blend.

name: Thai Larb Gai
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

Total time: 25 min
