description: Quick-cooked minced chicken tossed with toasted rice powder, lime, fish sauce, and an avalanche of fresh herbs — bright, sharp, and texturally alive.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Dried chili flakes (prik bon), or to taste
Lemongrass, tender inner stalk only, minced

steps:
Place the raw glutinous rice in a dry wok or heavy skillet over medium heat. Toast, stirring constantly, for 5–8 minutes until each grain turns golden-brown and the kitchen fills with a popcorn-like, nutty fragrance. Do not walk away — the transition from golden to burnt takes seconds. Transfer to a mortar or spice grinder and grind to a coarse powder (the texture of fine breadcrumbs). This powder is the secret texture of larb: it absorbs the dressing and gives the dish its characteristic sandy bite.
Visual cue: Evenly golden-brown grains with no pale centers remaining. A column of nutty, popcorn-scented steam rises from the pan.
Underdone: Grains are still white or only lightly blond. Aroma is raw, starchy, faintly chalky. Continue toasting over medium heat, stirring constantly. You need full golden-brown color for the flavor to develop.
Perfect: All grains a deep, even golden-amber. Smell is intensely nutty and popcorn-like with no raw note. One or two grains have just begun to show the first hint of darker browning. Transfer immediately to the mortar — the residual pan heat will over-toast if left.
Overdone: Grains are dark brown or mahogany with a bitter, acrid smell. Smoke visible. Discard and start over — burnt rice powder makes the whole dish bitter. Reduce heat for the next batch.
Feel cue: Ground powder should feel like fine sand between your fingers — slightly gritty, dry, and warm. No damp clumping.

Heat a wok over high heat until smoking. Add the ground chicken with no oil — the natural fat in the meat is sufficient and oil would cause steaming. Break the meat apart rapidly with a spatula, spreading it thin across the hot wok surface. Cook until just no longer pink, about 3–4 minutes. Do not cook through completely — the residual heat and lime acid will finish it. The goal is barely cooked, still juicy chicken.
Visual cue: Chicken is pale ivory-white throughout with the barest hint of golden-brown on some pieces. No pink remaining, but no deep browning either.
Underdone: Pink or translucent flesh visible in the center of the crumbles. Raw chicken texture. Continue over high heat for another 90 seconds, spreading thin.
Perfect: Uniformly white and just cooked, still glistening with its own fat. Not browned. Juicy. Smells clean and meaty. Remove from heat immediately. Move quickly — it will continue cooking from residual heat.
Overdone: Dry, crumbly, slightly golden. Moisture has evaporated. Some pieces sticking to the wok. The larb will be less juicy. Compensate with extra lime juice and fish sauce in the toss.
Feel cue: A morsel pressed between your fingers should feel tender and moist, not rubbery or crumbly. It should fall apart easily but hold its shape when picked up.

Working while the chicken is still very hot (the heat helps the dressing penetrate), add fish sauce, lime juice, dried chili flakes, and sugar. Toss vigorously. Taste immediately — the balance is the dish. It should hit sour first, then salty, then heat building at the back of the throat. Adjust: more lime for brightness, more fish sauce for depth, more chili for fire.
Visual cue: The chicken has absorbed the dressing and glistens. The surface looks moist rather than wet. Chili flakes are evenly distributed.
Underdone: Dressing is pooling in the bottom of the bowl rather than coating the meat. Pale and under-seasoned. Toss more aggressively and add a touch more fish sauce to help emulsification.
Perfect: Each piece of chicken is coated and glistening. The liquid is absorbed, not pooled. The aroma is sharp lime and fermented fish, both distinct. Add herbs and rice powder immediately while still hot.
Overdone: Too much liquid has been added — the bowl is soupy. Flavors are diluted. Add extra rice powder (it will absorb the excess) and taste again for seasoning.
Feel cue: Smell the bowl — it should hit you with bright citrus first, then the deep funk of fish sauce underneath, then the heat of the chili rising into your sinuses. If any single note dominates, rebalance.

Fold in the shallots, mint, cilantro, scallion, and minced lemongrass. Scatter the toasted rice powder over the top and fold in gently — you want it distributed but not completely buried. Taste one final time. Serve immediately on a plate lined with cabbage leaves, with extra mint and raw vegetables on the side. Larb deteriorates quickly as the herbs wilt and the rice powder hydrates — this is a dish that lives in the moment.
Visual cue: A vibrant, herb-strewn mound of chicken. Mint leaves still bright green, shallot rings still slightly translucent and crisp. Rice powder visible as a sandy dusting on the surface.
Underdone: Herbs barely mixed in, sitting on top. Rice powder not distributed. Fold more thoroughly with two spoons, lifting from the bottom.
Perfect: Every element integrated but identifiable. Green herbs bright, shallots crisp, rice powder sandy throughout, chicken glistening. Serve within 3 minutes for peak texture.
Overdone: Herbs have wilted to dark green. Rice powder has fully absorbed the dressing and made the texture wet and heavy. Scatter a fresh handful of mint over the top and serve — it won't be the same, but it helps.
Feel cue: Scoop a bite — you should feel the slight crunch of raw shallot, the soft juicy chicken, and the sandy grit of rice powder all in a single mouthful. The mint leaves should feel cool and papery, not limp.

ingredients.name: Thai tea leaves (Cha Tra Mue brand preferred — orange-spiced blend)
Evaporated milk or full-fat coconut milk

steps:
Measure the Thai tea leaves into a fine-mesh strainer or muslin bag set over a heatproof pitcher or tall glass. Pour the boiling water directly over the tea leaves. Let steep for exactly 5 minutes — no less (the tea will be weak and pale) and no more (it becomes tannic and bitter, though Thai vendors often brew very strong by design). After 5 minutes, remove the strainer and press the leaves firmly with the back of a spoon to extract the last, most concentrated brew. The liquid should be a dramatic, almost improbable burnt orange — darker than any typical orange tea, with a rich spiced aroma of cardamom, star anise, and warm vanilla.
Visual cue: A deep burnt-orange to copper-brown liquid, visibly dark and opaque, releasing fragrant steam with a warmly spiced, almost chai-like aroma.
Underdone: Tea is pale amber or yellow-orange, thin and watery-smelling. No real spice aroma. Replace the strainer and steep another 2–3 minutes. Make sure water was truly at a boil, not just hot.
Perfect: Deep copper-orange, almost opaque. Smells of cardamom and vanilla with a tannin backbone. Tastes very strong, slightly bitter, and spiced — it is meant to be over-brewed by Western standards. Allow to cool to room temperature or speed-cool over an ice bath.
Overdone: Tea is very dark brown, not orange, and smells sharply tannic and astringent. Tastes aggressively bitter. Add an extra splash of water to dilute, and increase the condensed milk to compensate for the extra bitterness.
Feel cue: The brewed Thai tea should feel velvety on the back of the throat — the tannins coat your mouth like a black tea, but the spices leave a warm, vanilla-tinged trail after swallowing.

Allow the brewed tea to cool to room temperature (about 10 minutes) or place the pitcher in a bowl of iced water for 3–5 minutes of rapid chilling. Do not pour hot tea directly over ice — it dilutes the brew and produces a watery drink. The tea must be at room temperature or cooler before it meets the ice. If preparing ahead, the brewed tea keeps refrigerated for up to 3 days and actually improves as the flavors integrate and mellow.
Visual cue: Tea has cooled to room temperature. Still the same burnt-orange color, now without steam. No visible condensation on the inside of a cold hand test.
Underdone: Tea is still hot, steaming, and will melt the ice instantly when poured. Wait longer — an ice bath is the fastest method. Place the pitcher in a bowl of cold water and stir the tea.
Perfect: Tea is cool to the touch on the outside of the pitcher, room temperature or below. Still vividly orange-brown. Prepare the glasses with condensed milk and ice.
Overdone: Tea has been refrigerated and is now very cold — this is fine and actually preferred for efficiency. Proceed directly to assembly.
Feel cue: Touch the outside of the pitcher with the back of your hand — it should feel cool, not warm. If your hand wants to stay there rather than pull away from heat, the tea is ready.

Spoon 2 tablespoons of sweetened condensed milk into the bottom of a tall glass — this is not optional, it is the structural sweetness of the drink. Pack the glass completely with crushed ice. Pour the cooled tea slowly over the ice, filling the glass to about 2 cm from the top. Finally, pour the evaporated milk or coconut milk over the top from a height so it cascades down the side of the glass in white streams, clouding the orange tea in a slow, beautiful diffusion. Do not stir — present it swirling and let the drinker mix it, or stir at the table. Traditionally served with a straw.
Visual cue: A tall glass of brilliantly layered deep orange tea beneath swirling clouds of evaporated milk, condensed milk pooling at the base, ice visible above the tea line.
Underdone: Condensed milk hasn't been added or evaporated milk was stirred in — drink is uniformly beige-orange and tastes thin. Add more condensed milk and add the evaporated milk in a slow pour from height for the visual cascade effect.
Perfect: Dramatic orange tea, white milk swirling in plumes, condensed milk caramel visible at the base. Tastes sweet, tannin-rich, spiced, and deeply satisfying when stirred together. Serve immediately with a straw.
Overdone: Too much condensed milk makes the drink cloyingly sweet, and the tea flavor is lost. Add more tea to dilute, or add a squeeze of very light lime juice to cut the sweetness.
Feel cue: The first sip through a straw from the bottom of the glass is pure condensed milk — shocking sweetness. By the third sip, the layers are merging into something complex: tannin, caramel, spice, and fat richness all at once.

ingredients.name: Palm sugar or light brown sugar
Fresh cilantro leaves and tender stems

steps:
Place the raw white rice in a dry skillet or wok over medium-low heat. Toast, shaking the pan constantly, for 5–8 minutes until the rice turns an even golden-tan, like light caramel — every grain should be colored. The kitchen will smell of toasted popcorn and nutty warmth. Transfer to a mortar and pound to a coarse powder — not as fine as flour, but without whole grains. This khao khua is the signature element of Isaan cooking: it adds nuttiness, subtle crunch, and acts as a light thickener for the sauce.
Visual cue: Golden-tan rice grains, uniformly colored without burnt spots, pounded to a coarse, sandy powder with some larger fragments.
Underdone: The rice is still white and uncolored with no nutty aroma. It will taste starchy and raw in the sauce. Continue toasting. The color must develop all the way through — no white centers.
Perfect: Uniformly pale golden-brown. Smells nutty and lightly smoky. When pounded, produces a coarse, fragrant powder the color of light sand. Pound to a coarse powder and set aside.
Overdone: Some grains are dark brown and the powder smells of burnt popcorn. Discard the dark grains before pounding. Or proceed — a few dark grains add a subtle smokiness that some prefer.
Feel cue: Correctly toasted rice feels drier and lighter between the fingers than raw rice — less starchy, more hollow. When pressed between thumb and forefinger it should crumble easily.

Dissolve the palm sugar in the fish sauce and lime juice by stirring — if the sugar is in a hard block, grate or shave it first. Add the tamarind concentrate and stir to combine. Add the dried chili flakes, shallot slices, and toasted rice powder. Stir well. Add the cilantro last. Taste and adjust: the sauce should hit salty first, then sour, then sweet, then heat — the four pillars of Isaan seasoning. It should be just thick enough to cling to meat when drizzled, aided by the rice powder. Let it rest 5 minutes before serving so the rice powder absorbs the liquid and the shallots slightly pickle.
Visual cue: A dark, mahogany-brown sauce with visible shallot rings, green cilantro, and a slightly sandy texture from the rice powder — pourable but slightly thickened.
Underdone: The sauce is thin as water, the sugar unmelted, and the rice powder floating on top rather than integrated. Stir vigorously and allow 5 minutes for the rice powder to hydrate and the sugar to dissolve.
Perfect: A dark, complex sauce just thickened by the rice powder, with visible shallot, chili, and herb. Smells sour, umami, and aromatic. Coats the back of a spoon lightly. Serve immediately or within 2 hours. The sauce does not keep well refrigerated as the rice powder continues to thicken it.
Overdone: Sat too long — the rice powder has over-absorbed the liquid and the sauce has turned to a thick paste or the herbs have wilted. Add a few drops of lime juice and fish sauce to loosen. Serve immediately.
Feel cue: The sauce should feel slightly gritty from the rice powder — that sandy texture against the tongue is the authentic signature of Isaan cooking, not a flaw.

ingredients.name: Dried sen lek rice noodles (3mm wide)

steps:
Place the dried rice noodles in a large bowl and cover with room-temperature water. Soak for 25–30 minutes until pliable and flexible but still slightly firm — they should bend without snapping but still have a distinct resistance when bitten. Drain well. Do not soak in boiling water: boiling softens the noodles too much before they hit the wok, and they will turn to mush under wok heat.
Visual cue: Noodles are pliable and bend easily in a U-shape without cracking, but resist when bent past 90 degrees.
Underdone: Noodles snap when bent. Still opaque white. 10 more minutes needed. Continue soaking in room-temperature water.
Perfect: Noodles are translucent and flexible but have a firm bite at the center. Drain immediately. Drain and use within 15 minutes — soaked noodles continue to soften.
Overdone: Noodles are fully soft and limp, bending in any direction with no resistance. They will disintegrate in the wok. Cook them very briefly — 30 seconds maximum in the wok, add sauce quickly to arrest further cooking.
Feel cue: A properly soaked pad thai noodle should feel like a firm leather strap — flexible but with spine, not like a wet ribbon.

In a small saucepan, combine the tamarind paste, fish sauce, and palm sugar. Heat over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves completely and the sauce is uniform. Taste: it should be a balanced blend of sour, salty, and sweet — adjust with more tamarind for sour, fish sauce for salty, or sugar for sweet. The balance should lean slightly sweet-sour.
Visual cue: Dark brown, glossy sauce with no visible sugar crystals. The consistency of a thin, pourable caramel.
Underdone: Sugar crystals still visible; sauce has two distinct textures. Continue stirring over low heat until fully dissolved.
Perfect: Uniform dark-brown sauce that tastes balanced: sour front, sweet middle, salty finish. Pours like soy sauce. Set aside at room temperature — it will keep for weeks.
Overdone: Sauce has reduced too far and is becoming candy-thick. Add 1 tbsp of water and stir to loosen.
Feel cue: Dip your finger: the pad thai sauce should hit three notes in sequence — sour, sweet, then a long salty finish. Any one note dominating means the balance is off.

Heat a wok over the highest heat possible until it smokes. Add the oil. When the oil shimmers and wisps of smoke appear, add the garlic and shallots — they should sizzle immediately and vigorously. Stir-fry for 30 seconds. Add the dried shrimp if using, toss 15 seconds. Add the raw shrimp in a single layer. Cook 1 minute without moving, then toss. The shrimp should be nearly cooked through but not quite.
Visual cue: Shrimp are pink on the outside, barely translucent at the thickest point. Aromatics are lightly golden and fragrant.
Underdone: Shrimp are still grey and translucent. Aromatics smell raw. Cook 30 more seconds over maximum heat.
Perfect: Shrimp are 80% pink with a faintly translucent core. Aromatics are golden and the wok smells of wok hei — smoky and savory. Push to the sides and add the noodles.
Overdone: Shrimp have fully curled and gone rubbery before the noodles are added. Remove and add back at the very end to avoid overcooking further.
Feel cue: The wok should roar with sizzling when the ingredients hit — if it doesn't, the heat is insufficient and the dish will be oily rather than wok-charred.

Add the drained noodles to the wok. Pour the pad thai sauce over. Toss constantly for 1–2 minutes. Push everything to one side, crack the eggs into the empty side, and scramble quickly until barely set, then fold into the noodles. Add the bean sprouts and green onions, toss twice, and serve immediately. Garnish with peanuts. Serve with extra fish sauce, chili flakes, sugar, and lime wedges at the table.
Visual cue: Noodles are evenly coated in a caramel-brown glaze, with visible pieces of egg, pink shrimp, and flecks of green onion throughout.
Underdone: Noodles are pale and insufficiently coated in sauce. Egg is still wet and runny. Toss over maximum heat for 1 more minute — the noodles need direct wok contact to char slightly.
Perfect: Noodles are deeply golden-brown with occasional charred edges, sauce is glossy and evenly distributed, egg is in golden ribbons. Smells of wok hei and tamarind. Plate immediately and add garnishes.
Overdone: Noodles are sticking and breaking into short segments; sauce has completely absorbed and the wok is dry and scorching. Add a splash of water and toss quickly to release. Plate immediately.
Feel cue: The finished pad thai should steam aggressively when plated — the heat, the tamarind, and the wok char all arriving in one cloud of fragrance that is sour, smoky, and deeply savory at once.

ingredients.name: Smooth natural peanut butter (or freshly ground roasted peanuts)
Crushed roasted peanuts & sliced red chili

steps:
Pour half the coconut milk into a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the red curry paste and garlic and cook, stirring constantly, for 2 to 3 minutes until the paste is fragrant and the oil in the paste begins to separate as tiny slicks at the edge of the pan. This brief frying step — even in coconut milk rather than oil — cooks out the raw smell of dried spice and wakes up the aromatics. The smell shifts from raw and harsh to warm and toasty.
Visual cue: A reddish, aromatic coconut base with visible beads of red-orange oil floating at the edges; the smell has shifted from raw to fragrant and rounded.
Underdone: Paste still looks raw and bright red, smelling sharply of dried chili and raw garlic without any toasted depth. Keep stirring over medium heat — the paste needs at least 2 full minutes in contact with hot liquid to bloom.
Perfect: Oil beading at the surface, paste darkened slightly, a warm spiced aroma filling the kitchen with none of the raw garlic harshness. Add the peanut butter and remaining coconut milk.
Overdone: The coconut milk has reduced too far, the paste is sticking and scorching, and a burnt acrid note is rising. Immediately add a splash of the remaining coconut milk to stop the cooking.
Feel cue: The coconut milk should bubble gently around the paste, not splatter violently. Lean in — the aroma changes from something that stings the nose to something warm and appetizing, like walking into a good Thai kitchen.

Whisk in the peanut butter and the remaining coconut milk, stirring until completely smooth and uniform. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium-low heat, whisking steadily. The sauce will thicken considerably as the peanut proteins cook and the coconut milk reduces; if it tightens past a slow-flowing consistency, thin with a splash of water or coconut milk. Cook 5 to 8 minutes until the raw peanut taste mellow into a roasted, nutty depth.
Visual cue: A smooth, terracotta-toned sauce of medium thickness, gently bubbling with lazy blups, uniformly glossy with no lumps of peanut butter visible.
Underdone: Peanut butter still visible in streaks; the sauce tastes raw and beany rather than nutty and round. Keep whisking and simmering — 2 more minutes usually unify a lumpy sauce.
Perfect: Smooth, thick-but-pourable, uniformly colored. Coats the back of a spoon and drips slowly. Tastes nutty and rich. Add the seasoning ingredients off a vigorous simmer.
Overdone: Sauce is so thick it holds its shape like peanut butter and is catching on the pan bottom. Thin with water in small additions, stirring vigorously, and lower the heat.
Feel cue: The sauce should feel velvety and coatingly rich as you stir — the spoon should drag slightly as it moves through the thickened base. Listen for the slow, plopping blup of a properly thick simmer.

Off the heat, stir in the palm sugar until dissolved, then add the fish sauce and lime juice. Taste and adjust: this sauce should hit sweet first, then the savory-salty fish sauce depth, then bright lime, with the heat building slowly at the back. Tune each element in small doses — a teaspoon of lime lifts more than you'd expect, a few drops of fish sauce deepens without pushing it salty. Add water if needed to reach a consistency that clings to a skewer but flows off a spoon. Pour into a bowl, scatter with crushed peanuts and sliced chili, and serve warm.
Visual cue: A rich, glossy, terracotta sauce sitting in a bowl topped with crunchy peanuts and bright red chili, thick enough to slowly fill back in after a spoon draws through it.
Underdone: The sauce tastes flat or one-note — either too salty from fish sauce without brightness, or too sweet without the acid balance. Add lime juice a teaspoon at a time, tasting after each. Sweet-salty-sour must arrive in sequence; fix the one that's missing.
Perfect: Sweetness arrives first, followed by a savory depth, then lime brightness cuts through, and heat lingers last. The texture is thick but pourable. Garnish and serve at once with satay, crudités, or steamed vegetables.
Overdone: Cloying and one-dimensional — too sweet, or sharp and sour, or thin and watery from over-dilution. A pinch of salt and a little more peanut butter thickens and grounds an overseasoned sauce. Re-balance slowly.
Feel cue: A proper satay sauce should feel velvety and subtly gritty from the peanut when it hits the tongue — never glassy-smooth like commercial sauce. The heat should arrive slowly, warming the palate rather than attacking it.

name: Som Tum (Thai Green Papaya Salad)
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Green (unripe) papaya, peeled and shredded: 300 g
  Alternatives: green mango; kohlrabi + cucumber combination
Garlic cloves: 10 g
Fresh Thai bird's eye chilis: 6 g
  Alternatives: serrano (less heat); dried red chili
Fish sauce: 30 ml
  Alternatives: soy sauce + pinch of nori powder for vegan
Palm sugar (or light brown sugar): 15 g
  Alternatives: brown sugar; coconut sugar
Fresh lime juice: 45 ml
Dried shrimp: 20 g
  Alternatives: skip for vegan; fermented shrimp paste, tiny amount
Cherry tomatoes, halved: 100 g
  Alternatives: grape tomatoes
Long beans (yard-long), cut into 3cm pieces: 60 g
  Alternatives: green beans
Roasted peanuts, roughly crushed: 30 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 25 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Shredded raw papaya pounded with garlic and chili in a mortar, then tossed with lime, fish sauce, palm sugar, and dried shrimp — sour-hot-sweet-salty in such precise balance that each component disappears into a single electrifying punch.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
In a large granite mortar and pestle, add the garlic cloves and whole bird's eye chilis. Pound until they are bruised and broken — not a paste, but no longer whole. This releases the allicin in the garlic and the capsaicin oils in the chili without making them disappear into a paste. In som tum, you want visible shards of garlic and chili throughout, not a homogenous sauce. The technique is to pound and tumble, not grind.
Visual cue: Garlic in rough, torn pieces. Chili split open, seeds visible. The mortar smells of raw garlic and fresh chili heat.
Underdone: Garlic is still whole and hard. Chili is unbroken. Pound harder and more vigorously. You need to break the cell walls, not just move things around.
Perfect: Garlic is in irregular chunks with split fibers. Chili is cracked open with seeds exposed. The mortar smells sharp and intense. Add the dried shrimp and pound briefly, then add the papaya.
Overdone: Garlic and chili have been pounded to a smooth paste. Still good — the flavors will be more uniform and intense throughout the salad.
Feel cue: Each pound should feel like a controlled strike — firm and deliberate, using the weight of the pestle rather than brute force. The sound should be a sharp, woody thud with the pestle bottom hitting the mortar wall.

Add the dried shrimp to the mortar and pound briefly to break them up. Add the shredded papaya and the long bean pieces. Now use a combined pound-and-toss technique: pound gently with the pestle while using a large spoon to toss the mixture. The goal is to bruise the papaya strands so they absorb the dressing, not to mash them. You want the papaya strands to remain intact but softened and pliable from the pounding. Add the halved cherry tomatoes and give them 2–3 gentle pounds to lightly crush them so they release their juice.
Visual cue: Papaya strands that are slightly translucent at the edges from bruising. Tomatoes are lightly crushed and releasing juice. The mixture is beginning to pool liquid at the bottom of the mortar.
Underdone: Papaya strands are still completely raw and rigid. No liquid at the bottom of the mortar. Pound more — the papaya must be bruised to absorb the dressing. 20–30 strikes minimum.
Perfect: Papaya strands are slightly softened and beginning to turn translucent at the edges. Tomatoes are lightly crushed and bleeding juice. Juice is pooling at the base of the mortar. Add the dressing ingredients.
Overdone: Papaya has been pounded to mush. No texture remains. Still edible — the flavor will be fine but the texture is lost. For next time, pound less aggressively and use the toss technique more.
Feel cue: Pick up a strand of pounded papaya — it should bend without breaking and feel slightly moist rather than dry and crunchy. If it's still very stiff and dry, pound more.

Add the palm sugar, fish sauce, and lime juice to the mortar. Toss and lightly pound everything together to combine. Taste constantly — som tum is about precision balance between the four flavors: sour (lime), salty (fish sauce), sweet (sugar), and umami-hot (chili + fish sauce). Adjust one element at a time: more lime for brightness, more fish sauce for depth and salt, more sugar to soften if too harsh. No two batches are identical — the lime juice and papaya's natural acidity vary. The finished salad should be aggressively seasoned by Western standards — this is intentional.
Visual cue: A glossy, amber-tinted dressing coating every strand of papaya. The tomato juice and dressing have combined into a pool at the base of the mortar.
Underdone: Dressing ingredients haven't fully combined. Pools of fish sauce visible. Sugar granules still visible. Toss more aggressively. The sugar must fully dissolve before tasting for balance.
Perfect: A glossy, unified dressing coating everything. The papaya has absorbed flavor and is no longer neutral-tasting. Each bite delivers sour-hot-salty-sweet simultaneously. Transfer to a plate and finish with peanuts.
Overdone: Too much liquid — the salad is swimming rather than dressed. Lift the solids out with tongs and serve over rice, which will absorb the extra dressing.
Feel cue: Taste the dressing from the mortar — it should simultaneously make your mouth water (sour), make you reach for water (heat), and keep you coming back (umami). If any one sensation dominates completely, it is unbalanced.

Transfer the som tum to a plate using tongs, keeping the papaya strands intact and arranged loosely. Pour any remaining dressing from the mortar over the salad. Scatter the crushed roasted peanuts over the top. Serve immediately alongside sticky rice. Som tum does not hold — the salt and acid will continue to wilt the papaya and the salad will be soggy within 30 minutes. Make and eat.
Visual cue: A bright mound of pale papaya strands, vivid red tomato, and green beans in an amber dressing, topped with golden peanuts.
Underdone: Peanuts not added. The salad looks pale and lacks textural contrast. Add peanuts generously. They provide the crunch and richness that balances the salad's acidity.
Perfect: Vivid colors — pale papaya, red tomato, green beans. Peanuts golden and scattered. Dressing glistening on every surface. Serve within 5 minutes.
Overdone: Papaya has wilted to a soggy, pale mass. The dressing has fully absorbed and the colors have dulled. It has been sitting too long. The flavor is still good — serve over warm rice and it becomes an excellent warm salad component.
Feel cue: Bite into the salad — you should feel multiple textures simultaneously: the crunch of peanut, the slight resistance of papaya, the softness of tomato, and the pop of the long bean. If everything is uniformly soft, it needs to be eaten sooner next time.

ingredients.name: Whole firm fish (thiof, snapper, grouper), scored and cleaned
Yellow onion, one half sliced, one half in stuffing paste
Root vegetables: cassava, carrot, turnip, eggplant
Fermented locust beans (netetou) or dried shrimp

steps:
Blend the parsley, garlic, half the onion, half the scotch bonnet, salt, and pepper into a coarse green paste — this is the rof stuffing. Stuff the rof paste into the score marks of the fish, pressing it firmly into the cuts so the paste fills the incisions. Also rub a thin layer over the fish exterior. Let rest for 15 minutes. This step is the singular flavor signature of thiéboudienne — the rof perfumes the flesh from within as the fish braises.
Visual cue: Score marks are visibly packed with dark green paste. The fish exterior has a thin, even coating. The rof is inside and on the fish, not pooled around it.
Underdone: Rof paste is sitting on the surface only, not packed into the score marks. It will wash off during braising rather than penetrating the flesh. Use your fingers to push the paste firmly into each cut. Make the cuts deeper if needed — they should reach almost to the bone.
Perfect: Every score mark is filled flush with green rof paste. The fish exterior has a thin, uniform green coating. Paste is firm and packed, not runny. Let rest 15 minutes then proceed to frying.
Overdone: Too much rof applied — thick clumps are falling off the fish. The paste will burn in the pan before the fish is seared. Scrape excess to a thin, even layer. A thin coat is all that is needed; the interior stuffing carries the primary flavor.
Feel cue: Press the rof-packed score marks with your fingertip — the paste should feel firmly embedded, not yielding or loose. Bring the fish to your nose: you should smell parsley and garlic immediately.

Heat oil in a large, wide pot over medium-high heat. Fry the stuffed fish for 3 minutes per side until the exterior is golden and the rof has crisped slightly. Remove the fish and set aside. In the same pot, fry the remaining sliced onion until golden. Add the tomato paste and fry, stirring, for 10 minutes until it darkens and the oil separates. Add the locust beans or dried shrimp and the remaining scotch bonnet half. Add enough water to cover all vegetables and fish (about 1.5 liters). Return the fish to the pot and bring to a simmer.
Visual cue: The tomato base has darkened to a deep burnt-orange and the oil has clearly separated around the pot edges. The stock is a rich amber-red, deeply aromatic.
Underdone: Tomato paste is still bright red and raw-tasting. The oil has not separated and the base is wet and thin. Raw tomato acidity will dominate the final dish. Continue frying the tomato paste. This step requires patience — 10 minutes of active frying is the minimum.
Perfect: Deep orange-red base with oil clearly separated at the edges. The pot smells of caramelized tomato, onion, and a deep savory note from the locust beans. Add water, return fish, and bring to a simmer to cook the fish and vegetables.
Overdone: Tomato paste is dark brown with a bitter, acrid smell. Small black bits visible. Deglaze with water immediately. Taste the resulting liquid — if too bitter, add a pinch of sugar and proceed.
Feel cue: The aroma rising from the pot at this stage should be deeply complex — caramelized tomato, sweet onion, and the pungent, fermented depth of the locust beans all layered and distinct, yet harmonious.

Add the root vegetables (cassava, carrot, turnip, eggplant) to the pot around the fish. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook for 20–25 minutes until the fish is cooked through and the vegetables are tender. As elements finish cooking, remove them to a serving platter and keep warm — the cassava and turnip take longer than the eggplant. Reserve ALL the braising stock — it is the most important ingredient in the dish.
Visual cue: Fish flesh is fully opaque and flakes at the thickest part of the spine when pressed. Vegetables yield to a knife with no resistance. The braising stock is deeply colored and rich.
Underdone: Fish flesh is still translucent near the spine. Carrots and cassava resist a knife. Braising liquid looks thin. Cover and simmer for another 10 minutes. Root vegetables often take longer than expected — check them individually.
Perfect: Fish flakes cleanly at the spine with gentle pressure. All vegetables yield fully to a knife. Stock is deeply flavored and richly colored — almost like a consommé-rich broth. Remove fish and all vegetables to a platter. Strain and reserve every drop of stock for the rice.
Overdone: Fish has broken apart in the pot. Vegetables are very soft and some are beginning to dissolve. The stock has reduced significantly. Carefully scoop out the fish in pieces. Add water to bring the stock volume back up to the amount needed for the rice.
Feel cue: Taste a spoonful of the braising stock — it should be deeply savory, tasting of fish, tomato, and a complex background of fermented locust beans. This is the soul of the dish; it should make you want to drink it.

Measure the braising stock — you need a ratio of about 1.5 parts stock to 1 part rice. Top up with water if necessary and season the stock well (it should taste slightly salty). Bring the stock to a boil in the wide pot, add the rinsed rice, and stir once. Reduce heat to low. Cover with foil then lid (the tight steam seal from the jollof technique). Cook for 25–30 minutes until all liquid is absorbed and the rice is tender. Then uncover and increase heat for 3–5 minutes to develop the crust.
Visual cue: Rice is fully cooked and uniformly orange-red from the stock. The surface is dotted with burst steam bubbles. The bottom crust crackles audibly when the pot is shaken.
Underdone: Rice grains have a hard white center when bitten. Some liquid still pooled around the edges of the foil. Re-seal and cook for 5–8 more minutes. The tight seal is critical — steam escaping means uneven cooking.
Perfect: Uniformly cooked, richly flavored rice in a warm amber color. Grains are separate and fluffy. The base of the pot crackles like caramel when shaken — the crust has formed. Remove from heat, rest 2 minutes. Serve rice with fish and vegetables arranged on top.
Overdone: Rice is mushy and clumping. Crust has burned beyond smokiness to bitterness. Scoop the upper rice immediately, leaving the burned crust. Spread on a wide plate to stop cooking. Taste the crust before deciding whether to serve it.
Feel cue: Scrape the bottom of the pot with a spoon after the crust step — it should release in firm, caramelized chips that smell of toasted rice and spiced fish stock, not scorched or acrid.

Traditionally, thiéboudienne is served on a large communal platter: mound the rice in the center, arrange the fish on top (keeping it as whole as possible even if it has broken during cooking), and distribute the vegetables around the rice. Place the crust chips alongside or on top as a crispy bonus. Spoon any remaining braising liquid over the fish. Serve with lime wedges and a side of fermented onion-and-mustard dibi sauce if available.
Visual cue: A mountain of amber-red rice with a whole fish (or large pieces) on top, surrounded by richly colored root vegetables. The crust pieces are dark orange-brown, visible and appealing.
Underdone: The presentation is complete but the rice is still pale and the fish looks dry. The dish hasn't come together visually or aromatically. This is a plating note, not a cooking note — return to the previous step and check the rice and fish temperature and seasoning before serving.
Perfect: The platter is visually striking — deep warm colors, the fish as the centerpiece, vegetables like jewels around it. The kitchen smells of the sea, tomato, and toasted rice all at once. Serve at the table and let guests dig in communally.
Overdone: Fish has fully broken down into flakes scattered throughout the rice rather than sitting as a centerpiece. Vegetables have dissolved. Stir everything together into a more rustic presentation — it will taste identical, just less majestic. Present with the crust prominently.
Feel cue: Stand over the finished platter and breathe in — the aroma should be like standing at a Senegalese coastal market: sea salt, wood smoke, caramelized tomato, and something fermented and deep that you cannot quite name but cannot stop smelling.

name: 提拉米苏 · Tiramisù
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

Egg yolks (very fresh, room temperature): 90 g
  Alternatives: pasteurized egg yolks
Caster sugar: 100 g
  Alternatives: granulated sugar (blitzed fine)
Mascarpone (cold): 500 g
Heavy cream (cold, 35% fat): 200 g
  Alternatives: whipped egg whites (4 whites) for the classic non-cream method

description: Espresso-drenched savoiardi layered under a cloud of whipped mascarpone and sabayon — cold, boozy, and bitter-sweet, with a dusting of cocoa that breaks like dark snow under the spoon. The name means 'pick me up,' and it does.

ingredients.name: 蛋黄（Egg yolks (very fresh, room temperature)）

steps:
Combine the egg yolks, sugar, and salt in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water (a bain-marie). Whisk constantly and vigorously for 5-7 minutes. The mixture will thin, then pale, then thicken as the eggs gently cook to a safe temperature (about 70°C / 160°F). Never let the bowl touch the water or the yolks will scramble. Remove from the heat the moment it falls in thick, pale ribbons.
Visual cue: A pale, glossy, lemon-yellow sabayon that has tripled in volume. When you lift the whisk, it falls in a slow ribbon that sits on the surface for a few seconds before sinking.
Underdone: Still loose, dark yellow, and runny. The ribbon disappears instantly. Sugar feels gritty when rubbed between fingers. Keep whisking over the heat. The sugar must fully dissolve and the volume must build — it is not ready until it ribbons.
Perfect: Pale, thick, mousse-like, and warm to the touch. The whisk leaves trails that hold. Smooth, not grainy. Remove from heat and whisk off the heat for another minute to cool slightly before folding in mascarpone.
Overdone: Curdled flecks of cooked egg appear; the smell turns eggy and the texture grows lumpy. Strain immediately through a fine sieve to catch the curds. If badly scrambled, start over — there is no rescuing a fully cooked yolk.
Feel cue: The whisk should feel like it is meeting steadily increasing resistance — the moment your arm registers a thick, satiny drag, you are there. The bowl should be warm but never hot enough to hurt your hand.

Loosen the cold mascarpone with a spatula until smooth, then fold it into the cooled sabayon in two additions until uniform. In a separate cold bowl, whip the heavy cream to soft peaks. Fold the whipped cream into the mascarpone mixture gently, from the bottom up, until just combined. Stop the instant it is homogeneous — overworking will collapse the air and make it grainy or split.
Visual cue: A smooth, airy, pale cream that holds soft peaks and mounds softly on the spatula without running. No streaks of plain mascarpone or unmixed cream remain.
Underdone: Marbled streaks of white cream and yellow sabayon are still visible; pockets of stiff mascarpone hide at the bottom of the bowl. Fold a few more times, scraping the bottom of the bowl, until the color is even. Be gentle to keep the air.
Perfect: Uniform ivory color, light and billowy, holds a soft peak that slowly slumps. Spreadable but not pourable. Begin assembling immediately while it is at peak volume.
Overdone: The cream looks dull, dense, and slightly grainy or buttery; it may weep liquid. The air is gone. Stop folding now. It is still usable but will be denser — assemble quickly and chill well.
Feel cue: Fold like you are tucking the cream into bed — slow, deliberate strokes through the center and up the sides. It should feel light and yielding, never stiff or resistant.

Stir the Marsala (or rum) into the cooled espresso in a shallow dish. Working one at a time, dip each savoiardo into the coffee for ONE second per side — a quick in-and-out. Ladyfingers are thirsty; they keep absorbing after they leave the liquid. Arrange the soaked fingers in a single tight layer in the base of your dish, trimming to fit.
Visual cue: A ladyfinger that is moistened through but still holds its shape — darkened with coffee on the outside, with a faint dry core you can feel. It should sit firm in the dish, not slump.
Underdone: Pale dry patches remain; the biscuit is stiff and snaps. The finished layer will be hard and cakey. Dip a fraction longer next time — half a second more. You want moist, not crunchy.
Perfect: Evenly coffee-stained and supple, holding its log shape when lifted. Springs back faintly when pressed. Lay it down and move on quickly to the next.
Overdone: The finger sags, breaks apart, or drips coffee. It will turn the layer to mush and weep into the cream. Use it anyway pressed flat into the base, and dip the rest faster — a single quick pass per side.
Feel cue: Listen and feel: a properly dipped savoiardo gives a soft, pillowy squeeze without falling apart. If coffee runs down your fingers when you lift it, it has drowned.

Spread half the mascarpone cream evenly over the first layer of soaked savoiardi, smoothing it into the corners with an offset spatula. Build a second layer of dipped ladyfingers on top, then crown it with the remaining cream, swirling the surface smooth or into gentle peaks. Cover and refrigerate.
Visual cue: Two clean, level strata of biscuit and cream filling the dish to the rim, the top layer of cream thick and even with no biscuit poking through.
Underdone: Cream is spread too thin and patchy; soaked fingers show through the top, and the layers look uneven. Redistribute the cream so the top is fully covered — the surface should be an unbroken sheet ready for cocoa.
Perfect: Even, generous layers with a smooth cream top sitting just below the rim. Edges are clean and defined. Cover tightly and refrigerate for at least 6 hours, ideally overnight.
Overdone: Overfilled and bulging, cream squeezing out the sides; or so much coffee pooled at the base that the bottom swims. Tip out any pooled coffee from the base before chilling, and don't overfill — a clean rim sets better.
Feel cue: The assembled tray should feel cool and settled, with a soft give on top like a set custard. Resist the urge to serve early — patience lets the biscuit and cream marry into one tender whole.

After the tiramisù has chilled and set (6 hours minimum), dust the surface with cocoa powder through a fine sieve in an even, generous veil — but only just before serving, so it stays dry and matte rather than dissolving into the cream. Cut with a hot, wiped knife for clean slices.
Visual cue: An even, matte, dark-cocoa blanket over a set tiramisù that holds a clean edge when sliced, revealing two distinct cream-and-biscuit layers.
Underdone: Thin, patchy cocoa with pale gaps; the dessert still wobbles loosely and slices collapse. Dust a second pass for full coverage, and if it wobbles, return it to the fridge to set longer before cutting.
Perfect: Uniform velvety cocoa veil; slices hold their shape with defined layers and a cool, creamy, bitter-sweet first bite. Serve cold, straight from the fridge.
Overdone: Cocoa applied too early has gone damp and muddy, or so thick it forms a dry, bitter clump that puffs up when you take a bite. Scrape off the worst and re-dust lightly just before serving. A whisper of cocoa is enough.
Feel cue: The finished cocoa should sit dry on top — exhale gently across it and a faint dust should lift. The first spoonful should be cold, then bitter cocoa, then sweet cream, then the boozy coffee biscuit beneath.

name: Tkemali
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: sour cherry plums; damson plums picked green

Garlic cloves: 0.5 parts
Fresh cilantro (leaves and tender stems): 1 parts
Fresh dill fronds: 0.5 parts
Dried pennyroyal (ombalo) or fresh spearmint: 0.3 parts
  Alternatives: fresh peppermint, used more sparingly

  Alternatives: fresh red chile, minced

image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Georgia's indispensable wild plum sauce — shatteringly tart green or red tkemali plums simmered until collapsed, then pureed with garlic, pennyroyal, and cilantro into a sauce that is bracingly sour, herbaceous, and savory all at once, the Caucasian soul-mate to grilled meats and roasted potatoes.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Sour plums — green tkemali or firm underripe red plums

steps:
Place the whole plums and water in a wide, heavy saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover partially, and cook 20-25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until every plum has burst and the flesh has completely collapsed away from the pit. The water will turn deep pink or green depending on your plum variety and will smell intensely of cooked fruit and bright acid. Do not let the pot boil hard — a gentle simmer preserves the clean tartness; aggressive boiling muddies it.
Visual cue: All plums fully collapsed and mashed, pits clearly visible and bare, the flesh dissolved into a thick, jam-like slurry. The liquid is opaque and brightly colored — vivid pink-red or golden-green.
Underdone: Some plums are still whole or partially intact, and pits are still embedded in flesh that resists a spoon. Cover and simmer another 5-10 minutes. Every plum must surrender completely — any resistance means the flesh will not pass cleanly through the sieve.
Perfect: All flesh has collapsed into the liquid, forming a loose, bright-colored slurry with naked pits floating freely. The smell is intensely sour-fruity, clean and sharp. Remove from heat and pass through a sieve immediately while hot — it passes more easily warm.
Overdone: The liquid has reduced significantly and the plum slurry has darkened and begun to caramelize at the edges of the pot, losing its bright tartness for a cooked-jam sweetness. Add a splash of water and proceed to sieving. The sauce may taste slightly less sharp; compensate with a squeeze of lemon at the end.
Feel cue: Press a plum against the side of the pot with a wooden spoon — it should dissolve instantly into the surrounding liquid with no resistance whatsoever, like pressing cooked lentils.

Set a medium-mesh sieve over a clean saucepan. Pour the hot plum slurry in batches into the sieve and press firmly with the back of a large spoon or a silicone spatula, working the flesh through the mesh in circular motions. What passes through is the sauce; what remains in the sieve — skins and pits — is discarded. This step determines the texture of the finished tkemali: press until the residue in the sieve is almost dry and nothing of value remains.
Visual cue: A smooth, vivid, fruit-bright purée in the pan below — no skin fragments, no pit debris, uniformly silky in consistency. The sieve should hold only dry, spent skins and clean pits.
Underdone: The purée below contains visible skin fragments and small pit splinters, and the sieve residue is still wet and heavy with usable fruit. Continue pressing — circular motion with steady pressure. Rotate the sieve contents with a spoon to expose fresh flesh to the mesh.
Perfect: The purée below is completely smooth and uniformly colored. The residue in the sieve is a dry, wrinkled mass of skins and bare pits with no clinging flesh. Discard the sieve residue. Return the purée to the pan over low heat.
Overdone: You have pressed so long and hard that bitter compounds from the pits have begun to bleed through the sieve. Stop immediately. If you can taste bitterness, balance it with a very small amount of honey — though authentic tkemali carries no sweetness.
Feel cue: The purée passing through the sieve should feel like thick, wet paint — fluid but body-rich. When the material in the sieve starts dragging and resisting without releasing more liquid, it is exhausted.

Return the purée to medium-low heat. Finely mince or press the garlic and stir it into the purée along with the ground coriander and red pepper flakes. Simmer gently, stirring frequently, for 10-12 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly — it should coat a spoon rather than pool off it — and the garlic has cooked through its raw sharpness into a mellow, savory presence. The sauce will spit and pop as it thickens; lower the heat and keep stirring to prevent catching.
Visual cue: A slightly thickened, glossy purée that coats the back of a spoon with a thin but lasting film. The garlic smell should be savory and cooked, not raw and pungent.
Underdone: The sauce still tastes raw-garlicky and runs freely off the spoon. It smells more of raw garlic than of cooked fruit. Simmer longer, stirring. The garlic must cook into the sauce — raw garlic in a finished condiment is harsh and unpleasant.
Perfect: The sauce holds briefly on a spoon before flowing. The garlic taste is present and savory but soft. The coriander has bloomed into a warm, citrusy background note. Add the fresh herbs off the heat. Proceed.
Overdone: The sauce has reduced to a dense paste and the garlic has begun to brown at the edges of the pot. Add a splash of water to loosen and stir vigorously to incorporate. The texture of tkemali should be pourable, not paste-like.
Feel cue: Drag a spoon through the simmering sauce — it should part and close slowly, like a thin yogurt. The sound in the pot shifts from bubbling splashes to lazy, heavy blurps.

Pull the pan off the heat. Finely chop the cilantro, dill, and pennyroyal (or mint) and stir them into the hot sauce — the residual heat wilts and integrates them without cooking away their bright volatile aromas. Season generously with salt, stir thoroughly, and taste: tkemali should hit the palate with sharpness first, then herb-green complexity, with a savory, garlicky warmth underneath and heat at the back. It should taste aggressively tart — it is a condiment to cut through rich food, not a jam. Adjust salt and pepper as needed, then cool completely before serving or jarring.
Visual cue: A vivid, deeply colored sauce — apple-green if made from green plums, burgundy-pink from red — studded evenly with flecks of bright green herb throughout. It should smell intensely herbal and sour.
Underdone: The herbs are unevenly distributed and still visibly separate from the sauce. The salt is insufficient and the sauce tastes flat and one-dimensionally sour. Stir more vigorously to integrate. Season salt in small increments — salt lifts the tartness of tkemali without making it taste salty.
Perfect: Uniform color throughout, herb evenly suspended, the smell aggressively fragrant with cilantro and dill and an earthy pennyroyal undertone. On the tongue: tart-bright, herb-layered, savory, and warming. Cool to room temperature. The sauce thickens slightly as it cools. Serve or refrigerate.
Overdone: The herbs have sat in the hot sauce too long and turned dull olive-gray, with a cooked-herb flatness replacing the fresh brightness. The herb color loss is irreversible, but the flavor may still be good. Stir in a small additional handful of fresh chopped cilantro just before serving to restore the aroma.
Feel cue: Cool tkemali should pour like a thin, slightly textured yogurt — too thin and it has not reduced enough; too thick and it needs a splash of water stirred in. It should
leave a bright green-flecked stain on a white plate, not pool into a watery ring.

ingredients.name: 西葫芦（Zucchini, cut into 2 cm pieces）
茄子（Eggplant, cut into 2 cm cubes）

steps:
Place the farro in a large dry skillet over medium heat. Toast, stirring constantly, for 4–6 minutes until the grains smell nutty and are golden — some grains may lightly pop. This step is optional but transforms the flavor dramatically. The toasted grains will have a nuttier, more complex flavor after cooking.
Visual cue: Grains have deepened from pale tan to golden-brown. A cloud of nutty, almost popcorn-like aroma rises from the pan.
Underdone: Grains are still pale. No aroma change from raw farro. Continue toasting over medium heat — the color change is subtle but real.
Perfect: Golden-brown color on most grains. Clearly nutty, toasted smell. Some grains may have tiny cracks. Transfer immediately to a pot for cooking.
Overdone: Dark brown grains with a scorched, harsh smell. Discard and start over — burnt farro will make the entire salad bitter.
Feel cue: Pinch a toasted grain — it should be dry and hard, unchanged in texture but warm and fragrant. The aroma tells you more than the color — when the kitchen smells of toasted wheat and hazelnuts, you are there.

Transfer toasted farro to a pot. Cover with generously salted water or stock (3 parts liquid to 1 part farro by volume). Bring to a boil, reduce to a steady simmer, and cook uncovered for 30–40 minutes for whole farro (20–25 for semi-pearled) until the grains are tender but still have a distinct chew — al dente, like a well-cooked barley. Drain any excess liquid.
Visual cue: Plump, golden-brown grains that have roughly doubled in size. A clean bite reveals no white chalky center but a firm, pleasant resistance.
Underdone: White chalky center when bitten. Grains still tight and unswollen. Continue simmering — farro is notoriously slow to cook through.
Perfect: Fully swollen, uniformly golden. Definite chew but no hardness. Grains separate cleanly when stirred. Drain and toss immediately with half the olive oil to prevent sticking.
Overdone: Grains are splitting, soft, starchy. No chew. Drain immediately. The salad will be slightly mushy but the flavors will hold.
Feel cue: Bite through a grain of farro — you should feel a distinct, firm resistance before it gives, then a slightly creamy, starchy interior. It should chew like a very al dente pasta, not yield like rice.

Toss all the vegetables with a generous amount of olive oil, salt, and chili flakes on a large sheet pan. Spread in a single layer — do not crowd or they will steam. Roast at 220 C (425 F) for 25–30 minutes, turning once halfway, until caramelized and charred at the edges — particularly the cherry tomatoes, which should burst and concentrate.
Visual cue: Deeply caramelized vegetables with charred edges. Cherry tomatoes have burst, collapsed, and darkened. Zucchini is golden. Onion edges are dark and crispy.
Underdone: Vegetables are soft and pale — no caramelization, no charring. Raise oven temperature or continue roasting. Pale roasted vegetables taste boiled.
Perfect: Dark golden edges on all vegetables. Tomatoes burst and jammy. Zucchini golden with grill-mark-style char. Kitchen smells of sweet, concentrated vegetables. Transfer while hot to toss with farro.
Overdone: Vegetables are very dark or burnt. Tomatoes are dried out and hard. Pick out and discard any truly burnt pieces. The slightly over-charred ones add good flavor.
Feel cue: Press a piece of roasted zucchini — it should yield completely, offer no resistance, and feel soft but not wet. The skin should feel slightly blistered and papery, the interior like warm, collapsed softness.

While both the farro and vegetables are still warm, combine them in a large bowl. Drizzle with remaining olive oil and lemon juice. Add lemon zest, chili flakes, parsley, mint, and toasted nuts. Toss together gently — you want the warm farro to absorb the lemon and oil. Taste and adjust salt, acid, and oil. The salad is excellent warm, but also very good at room temperature.
Visual cue: A warm, golden-brown salad with vivid caramelized vegetables, bright green herbs, and glistening farro. Each component distinct but harmoniously combined.
Underdone: Salad looks dry and underdressed — herbs are dull and the farro looks starchy. Add more olive oil and lemon juice, toss again. Taste: it should sing with acid and fat.
Perfect: Gleaming, fragrant, herb-studded. The lemon oil has coated every grain. Warm steam rising from the bowl. Serve immediately as a main or allow to cool to room temperature.
Overdone: Salad is overdressed and soggy — pooling with oil and lemon at the bottom. Add more plain farro to absorb excess dressing.
Feel cue: Toss the finished salad with your hands — each grain of farro should move freely, coated in oil and lemon, clinging slightly to the warm vegetables but not clumping. The herbs should feel fresh and bright against the warm grains.

ingredients.name: Dried Japanese red chili (tōgarashi), ground or flaked
Dried mandarin or yuzu peel, finely ground
Sansho (Japanese pepper) or Szechuan pepper, ground

steps:
If making the orange or mandarin peel from scratch: use a peeler to remove only the colored zest (no white pith) from 2 mandarins or 1 orange. Dry in the oven at 90°C for 25 to 30 minutes until completely dry and brittle. Grind to a coarse powder. For the nori: toast a sheet of nori over a gas flame for 2 to 3 seconds per side until crisp and bright green. Crumble between your fingers directly into the bowl. Commercial pre-toasted nori is perfectly acceptable here.
Visual cue: Ground mandarin peel is a fine, pale orange-yellow powder with an intensely citrus aroma; crumbled nori is dark green, fine, and completely dry.
Underdone: Mandarin peel is still soft or leathery, not yet fully dried; it clumps when pressed rather than crumbling to a fine powder. Return to the oven for another 10 minutes. The peel must be bone-dry to grind and blend properly.
Perfect: Peel shatters to a fine, fragrant powder between the fingers; nori crumbles at a touch into fine, dark flakes. Both are completely dry. Proceed to combining all components.
Overdone: Mandarin peel has dried too long at too high a temperature and the volatile citrus oils have cooked off. The powder smells flat and bitter. Use store-bought dried mandarin peel for this batch. Fresh dried peel is always better if dried at a low temperature.
Feel cue: Properly dried mandarin peel snaps and shatters under slight finger pressure, crumbling into a fragrant citrus dust that immediately stains your fingertips orange-yellow. If it bends rather than snaps, it retains moisture and needs more drying.

Combine all seven (or eight, in this version) components in a bowl. Stir gently but thoroughly to distribute all elements evenly. The final blend should show visible diversity: the dark sesame and nori against the pale sesame and hemp seeds, the orange flecks of citrus peel against the red chili flakes. Stir for a full 30 to 45 seconds, lifting from the bottom of the bowl repeatedly.
Visual cue: A beautiful, heterogeneous blend showing visible red chili flakes, black and white sesame seeds, orange peel fragments, dark nori flakes, and pale hemp seeds.
Underdone: Heavy nori flakes have sunk to the bottom; red chili and sesame are clumped in one part of the bowl. Visual diversity absent. Fold more from the bottom up, gently rotating the bowl and cutting through the center of the blend.
Perfect: Every spoonful shows all seven elements. Smells of dried chili, citrus, and sesame simultaneously — bright, complex, warm. Transfer to a spice jar and seal. Ready to use immediately.
Overdone: Vigorous stirring has broken the nori and sesame seeds to fine dust. Texture is lost and the blend looks uniformly grey-brown. Fold in a fresh tablespoon of intact toasted sesame and crumbled nori to restore visual and textural contrast.
Feel cue: Cup a small amount of the blend in your palm and inhale. You should detect distinct notes arriving in sequence: first the sharp, dry-heat of chili, then the citrus lift, then the toasty sesame, then the numbing tingle of sansho on the tip of your tongue from the aromatic contact alone.

Transfer to a small glass spice jar with a tight lid. Label clearly with the date. Store at room temperature away from light and heat for up to 3 months — though shichimi togarashi is always at its most vivid in the first 3 to 4 weeks. Use directly at the table as a condiment, shaken over ramen, udon, yakitori, tempura dipping broth, grilled tofu, or mixed into ponzu. Never add it during cooking — the volatile oils in the sansho, citrus peel, and sesame dissipate with heat.
Visual cue: A compact, fragrant, visually diverse spice blend in a jar. No single color dominates — you can identify at least four distinct elements at a glance.
Underdone: The jar is not sealed and the blend is already losing its aromatic top notes to the air. Faint citrus smell that should be bright is becoming flat. Seal immediately. Togarashi's volatile aromatics are precious and dissipate within hours in an open container.
Perfect: Each time the jar is opened, a fresh, complex fragrance blooms — chili, citrus, sesame. Every pinch is flavorful and contains visible textural diversity. Keep at the table. Use generously.
Overdone: Stored for 4+ months, the blend is flat and dull. The citrus peel has become bitter and the sansho's numbing compounds have degraded. Toast the blend briefly in a dry pan for 30 seconds to revive the sesame and chili notes. The citrus will not recover — make a fresh batch soon.
Feel cue: The moment you shake shichimi togarashi onto hot food, its heat triggers a release of volatile oils — the aromatic compounds become airborne and the entire bowl smells of spice. This is the correct experience. If nothing happens when the spice hits the food, the blend has aged past its prime.

ingredients.name: 椰奶（Coconut milk, full-fat (canned or fresh)）
Lemongrass stalks, bruised and cut into 4 cm batons
Chicken thigh meat, sliced 1 cm thick
Oyster mushrooms or straw mushrooms, torn

steps:
Combine the coconut milk and chicken stock in a medium saucepan. Add the galangal slices, lemongrass batons, and torn kaffir lime leaves. Set over medium heat and bring to a gentle simmer — not a boil. A full boil breaks the coconut milk emulsion and makes the broth grainy and oily. Let it steep at a lazy simmer for 10–12 minutes, pressing the aromatics against the side of the pan occasionally with a wooden spoon to encourage them to release their volatile oils. The galangal should start to look slightly translucent at the edges.
Visual cue: A creamy ivory broth barely trembling at the surface, studded with pale galangal coins and bobbing lemongrass, steaming with a warm, intensely floral-citrus fragrance.
Underdone: The broth is hot but the lemongrass and galangal still smell raw and grassy rather than sweet and floral. The liquid is pale and watery. Continue simmering. The aromatic oils in galangal are released slowly at gentle heat — raise the heat slightly if needed, but maintain a simmer, not a boil.
Perfect: The kitchen smells of citrus blossom, pine, and a faint earthy warmth. The broth has taken on a faint ivory-gold tinge from the galangal. Pressing the lemongrass releases a final burst of fragrance. Add the chicken, mushrooms, and bruised chilies now while the heat is gentle.
Overdone: The broth has boiled — the surface shows an oily sheen of separated coconut fat and the liquid looks slightly curdled. The fragrance has become flat and cooked-out. Lower heat immediately. Add a splash of fresh coconut milk and stir to re-emulsify. The flavor may be slightly dulled but will still be acceptable.
Feel cue: Cup your hands around the steam rising from the pot and breathe in — you should smell kaffir lime above everything else, a cool, floral eucalyptus note undercut by the earthier warmth of galangal. If you mostly smell coconut, the aromatics need more time.

Add the sliced chicken thigh meat, mushrooms, and bruised bird's eye chilies to the simmering broth. Stir gently to separate the chicken slices. Maintain a gentle simmer and cook for 6–8 minutes until the chicken is just cooked through — it should feel firm when pressed with a spoon but not dry or stringy. The mushrooms will turn silky. Do not overcook the chicken or it will become rubbery; coconut broth continues to carry heat even off the flame.
Visual cue: Chicken slices have turned from raw pink to a matte, opaque white throughout. Mushrooms have softened and darkened slightly at the edges. Broth has taken on a very faint blush from the chilies.
Underdone: Chicken slices are still pink at the center when pressed apart with two spoons. The mushrooms are still firm and raw-tasting. Continue simmering for another 2–3 minutes. Check the thickest chicken slice by pressing it — it should offer no pink resistance.
Perfect: Chicken is just opaque all the way through, juicy and tender. Mushrooms have softened to a silky texture. Broth smells deeply aromatic with a faint chile warmth. Remove from heat. Season with fish sauce now before adding the lime — heat dulls lime acidity.
Overdone: Chicken has gone dry and is beginning to shred apart in the broth. Mushrooms are waterlogged and formless. Remove from heat immediately. The chicken will be less tender but the broth itself is still excellent. Serve quickly — further sitting will toughen the protein more.
Feel cue: Spoon up a piece of chicken and squeeze it gently against the edge of the saucepan — it should yield with slight resistance and spring back. If it collapses and falls apart, it has gone past the ideal window.

Remove the pot from the heat before adding the fish sauce and lime juice — lime acidity is volatile and the bright topnote evaporates when cooked. Stir in the fish sauce first, taste, and adjust. Then add the lime juice in stages, tasting after each addition. The balance of this broth is everything: it must be simultaneously salty, sour, and lightly sweet from the coconut, with a background warmth from the chilies. If it tastes flat, add more fish sauce; if it tastes thin and sour, a pinch of palm sugar rounds it out.
Visual cue: The broth is fully seasoned, bright, and aromatic. The surface shimmers with a fine bead of coconut oil and the color is a warm ivory-cream.
Underdone: The broth tastes flat, one-dimensional, and coconut-heavy — neither the saltiness of fish sauce nor the brightness of lime has opened it up yet. Add fish sauce a teaspoon at a time and taste after each addition before adding lime.
Perfect: The broth delivers four flavors in sequence: first salty, then sour, then a creamy sweet richness from the coconut, then a quiet building warmth. The lime fragrance is vivid and top-note. Ladle into bowls immediately, over rice if desired. Garnish at the table.
Overdone: Too much lime juice added over heat — the broth is aggressively sour and the coconut is overwhelmed. The lime fragrance has turned sharp and metallic. Add a splash more coconut milk and a pinch of palm sugar to pull back the acid. Next time, pull the pot off heat before adding lime.
Feel cue: Take a small sip straight from the ladle. The sour note should arrive at the sides of your tongue first, then the salt spreads across the middle, then the coconut richness coats the back of the throat. If any one of those arrives alone, the balance is off.

Ladle the broth into serving bowls, distributing the chicken and mushrooms evenly. Scatter fresh coriander leaves over each bowl just before serving — do not stir them in. Do not serve the galangal, lemongrass, or kaffir lime leaves as food; they are eaten around. Provide a small dish of extra lime wedges and fish sauce at the table so guests can adjust to their own taste. The broth is meant to be sipped, not just spooned.
Visual cue: A steaming ivory bowl with pale chicken pieces, silky mushrooms, and a scatter of bright green coriander floating on a creamy, fragrant broth.
Underdone: Garnish has been added too early and the coriander is wilted and olive-drab. The heat has cooked off the fresh top-notes. Add garnish only at the very moment of serving. Have the leaves ready and torn in advance.
Perfect: Vibrant green coriander sits on the still-steaming surface, its fragrance mingling with the coconut steam. The broth is hot enough to send a column of aromatic vapour upward. Serve immediately. This broth should be eaten at once — it does not improve with sitting.
Overdone: Bowls have sat waiting and the coconut fat has risen and solidified in a pale ring around the edge. The broth is lukewarm. Return the broth to a gentle simmer to re-emulsify and reheat, then garnish fresh.
Feel cue: Hold the bowl close before drinking — the steam should carry a dual signal of lime and galangal that makes you inhale involuntarily. That involuntary breath is the sign the broth is ready.

ingredients.name: 鸡腿（Chicken thigh, boneless, skinless, sliced 5mm）
Lemongrass stalks, bruised and cut into 5cm pieces
Fresh Thai bird chilies, lightly bruised (do not split)
Fresh cilantro (coriander), leaves and fine stems

steps:
Pour the coconut milk and chicken stock into a medium saucepan. Add the sliced galangal, bruised lemongrass pieces, torn kaffir lime leaves, and the lightly bruised (but whole) bird chilies. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat — never a rolling boil, which will break the coconut milk and make it grainy and oily. Simmer for 10 minutes, pressing the aromatics down occasionally with a spoon. The broth should carry a complex floral fragrance: the soap-citrus of kaffir lime, the hot-gingery punch of galangal, the lemon-grass green of the stalks. Do not remove the aromatics yet — they will steep through the entire cooking process and are removed before serving, not before. The chilies are left whole so they release mild background heat without the piercing intensity of split or chopped chili.
Visual cue: An ivory-white broth with a gentle quiver of movement at the surface — small bubbles drifting up at the edges, not a central boil.
Underdone: Broth is still cold and the aromatics have not released their oils. It smells faintly of coconut milk only — no galangal heat, no lemongrass fragrance. Increase heat slightly and allow 5 more minutes. The galangal fragrance should be detectable before you add the protein.
Perfect: The broth is a soft, creamy ivory and smells intensely of galangal and kaffir lime. Small fat droplets may be visible on the surface. The bird chilies have swelled slightly. Add mushrooms and chicken now.
Overdone: The coconut milk has separated — you can see a slick of yellowish coconut oil on the surface and the broth looks curdled and grainy rather than silky. Reduce heat to low and whisk gently to re-emulsify. Adding a splash of cold coconut milk can help bring it back, but work quickly — continued heat will make it worse.
Feel cue: Lean over the pot and breathe: the steam should carry a floral, almost soapy lemongrass fragrance that tingles the
back of your throat with the galangal's quiet heat — like inhaling through a Thai kitchen window.

Add the torn oyster mushrooms to the simmering broth and stir gently. After 1 minute, slide in the sliced chicken thigh pieces, spreading them through the broth so they cook evenly. Maintain a gentle simmer — barely trembling at the surface. Cook the chicken for 5 to 7 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the slices are opaque all the way through with no pink remaining. Chicken thigh at this thickness finishes in the time it takes the broth to return to temperature after the cold protein goes in. The mushrooms will soften and absorb the coconut broth. Do not increase the heat to rush this step — aggressive heat toughens the chicken and breaks the coconut base.
Visual cue: Chicken slices are uniformly white-opaque throughout. Mushrooms are silky and slightly translucent, collapsed softly into the broth.
Underdone: Chicken has a pink blush at the center when a thick slice is pressed open with a spoon. The flesh has a raw, dense look. Continue simmering for 2 more minutes. Thigh meat is forgiving — it will not dry out quickly.
Perfect: Chicken is fully opaque, white to its center. It separates easily when pressed with a spoon. Mushrooms have absorbed broth and look glossy and tender. Season with fish sauce, lime juice, and palm sugar immediately.
Overdone: Chicken slices are pulling apart into stringy fibres and the mushrooms have become completely soft and waterlogged. Season and serve at once — prolonged heat will continue to degrade both protein and mushrooms.
Feel cue: A piece of properly cooked chicken thigh, lifted on a spoon, should yield with gentle pressure — soft and juicy, not firm. The surrounding broth should coat the back of the spoon in a thin, creamy film.

Add the fish sauce, palm sugar, and lime juice off heat or over the lowest flame. Stir to dissolve the sugar. Taste and adjust — tom kha gai should be simultaneously rich (coconut), sour (lime), salty (fish sauce), with background sweetness (palm sugar) and slow heat (galangal and chili). Start with the listed quantities and adjust in small increments. The lime goes in last and must not boil after adding — boiling destroys its bright top note and turns it bitter. The correct flavor is silky-rich on the palate immediately, then sour and bright mid-palate, then a long trailing warmth from the galangal. If it tastes flat, it needs more lime; if it tastes harsh, it needs more palm sugar.
Visual cue: Broth is a smooth, uniform ivory-cream with a subtle golden tinge from the galangal and chili. No visible curdling or oil slicks.
Underdone: The broth tastes of coconut milk and stock but lacks brightness or complexity. The fish sauce and lime have not been added. Add fish sauce, lime, and palm sugar in the proportions listed, then taste and adjust.
Perfect: The broth delivers a layered rolling flavor: creamy and rich, then sour and bright, then slowly warming from galangal. It is impossible to taste any single ingredient in isolation. Ladle into bowls over the aromatics (which remain but are not eaten) and garnish.
Overdone: The broth tastes harshly sour or aggressively salty — lime or fish sauce was added too heavily. Balance with a small addition of coconut milk and palm sugar to round the edges.
Feel cue: The finished broth on a tasting spoon should feel silky and coating, like thin cream — not watery, not grainy. The lime's acid should make the edges of your tongue tingle slightly, while the galangal's heat settles warmly at the back of your throat.

Ladle the soup into deep bowls, ensuring each bowl gets equal portions of chicken, mushrooms, and broth. The aromatics — galangal, lemongrass, kaffir lime leaves, and bird chilies — remain in the bowl for visual beauty and ongoing aroma but are pushed to the side and not eaten. Scatter fresh cilantro leaves over the top of each bowl. Serve immediately while the broth is steaming. Provide a small spoon for the broth and chopsticks or a fork for the solids. At the table, diners may squeeze additional lime over their bowl. The soup does not improve on standing — the lime becomes bitter, the coconut milk may separate, and the chicken turns rubbery.
Visual cue: A beautiful ivory bowl with visible golden-white chicken, dark-gold mushrooms, and green cilantro scattered on a silky cream surface.
Underdone: The bowl looks pale and unadorned — no garnish, no color contrast. Add the cilantro immediately. The visual contrast is part of the eating experience.
Perfect: Steaming ivory broth, tender chicken and soft mushrooms visible below the surface, bright green cilantro floating on top. The galangal and lemongrass pieces rest at the edge of the bowl. Serve within 2 minutes of ladling.
Overdone: The soup has been held too long and a ring of coconut oil has formed at the surface rim. Cilantro has wilted into the broth. Skim the oil with a spoon, add fresh cilantro, and serve.
Feel cue: When you lift the bowl to your lips, the steam should carry the full aromatic profile — lemongrass, kaffir lime, galangal — before you taste a single drop. That fragrant cloud is the soup announcing itself.

description: A broth of such muscular clarity that every sip pricks the tongue with lime, burns with chili, and then retreats into the deep oceanic warmth of shrimp and fish sauce — the lemongrass and galangal floating in the bowl like aromatic driftwood, spent but still fragrant. This is the broth that defines hot-and-sour.
