ingredients.name: Lemongrass stalks, bruised and cut into 3cm pieces
虾仁（Shrimp, head-on if possible (shells reserved for stock)）
Fresh Thai bird chilies, lightly bruised

steps:
Combine the water or shrimp stock with the bruised lemongrass, sliced galangal, and torn kaffir lime leaves in a medium saucepan. Bring to a full boil over high heat, then reduce to a vigorous simmer. Simmer uncovered for 10 minutes, pressing the aromatics down into the liquid with a spoon every few minutes. The liquid will reduce slightly and, more importantly, it will extract the volatile aromatic oils from the lemongrass, galangal, and kaffir lime. After 10 minutes, the broth should smell powerfully of the three aromatics — the lemon-citrus of lemongrass, the camphor-hot of galangal, and the distinct floral-citrus of kaffir lime. If your water is very soft, the flavors will be more pronounced; hard water slightly mutes the aromatics. Do not strain yet — the aromatics continue to flavor the broth through the next steps.
Visual cue: A pale gold broth with a vigorous surface simmer and visible aromatic pieces floating throughout.
Underdone: Broth is still water-clear and the aromatics have not released their oils — it smells mostly of plain hot water. Continue simmering. The lemongrass must have time to release its oils into the liquid — 10 minutes is the minimum.
Perfect: Broth is a light golden color and the aroma hits you at arm's length from the pan — lemongrass, galangal, and kaffir lime, clear and vivid. The surface has a fine oily sheen from the released essential oils. Add the nam prik pao, chilies, and mushrooms.
Overdone: Broth has reduced by more than 25% and is concentrated to the point where the galangal's bitterness is coming forward and the lemongrass is harsh. Top up with water back to original volume. The aromatics are already well-extracted — do not continue reducing.
Feel cue: Lean over the simmering pot and cup your hands to direct the steam toward your face — the galangal and lemongrass should open your sinuses and make your eyes water slightly.
That sensory intensity is what you want in the finished bowl.

Add the lightly bruised bird chilies and the nam prik pao (roasted chili paste) to the simmering aromatic stock. The nam prik pao is the differentiator between tom yum nam sai (clear, pale broth) and tom yum nam khon (cloudy, richer, darker broth) — this recipe uses it for depth and color. Stir until the paste dissolves into the broth — it will turn the stock a warm amber-orange. Add the torn mushrooms and simmer for 3 minutes until softened. Taste the broth now — before adding the shrimp, fish sauce, or lime — and check that the chili heat is at your desired level. At this stage you can add more bruised chilies. The mushrooms will add an umami depth that bridges the gap between the sharp aromatics and the seafood.
Visual cue: An amber-orange, slightly cloudy broth with mushrooms softened and chili pieces floating through it.
Underdone: Nam prik pao has not fully dissolved and floats in dark clumps. Mushrooms are still raw and firm. Stir more vigorously and simmer for another 2 minutes.
Perfect: Broth is a uniform amber-orange, opaque with dissolved chili paste, fragrant with roasted chili and galangal. Mushrooms are soft and slightly translucent. Add the shrimp and season immediately.
Overdone: Broth has been simmering too long with the chili paste and has developed a sharp, almost burnt-chili bitterness. Add a splash of water and a pinch of sugar to moderate the bitterness.
Feel cue: Stir the broth and hold your hand close to the steam — you should feel the prickle of chili volatiles in your nose and on the soft skin of your wrist. That sharpness in the air around the pot mirrors the heat you want at the back of the throat in the finished bowl.

Bring the broth to a full rolling boil. Add the shrimp and cook for exactly 2 to 3 minutes, watching closely — shrimp in a hot broth cook far faster than expected. Remove the pot from heat the moment the shrimp are pink and curled into a relaxed C. Off heat, add the fish sauce and lime juice — never boil these after adding. The lime especially must not be cooked further or its bright top note becomes flat and bitter. Add the optional sugar now if the broth needs rounding. Taste for balance: tom yum should be aggressively sour and hot with a deep salty backbone and mild sweetness at the very end. Correct if needed. Ladle into bowls, leaving the aromatic pieces in the bowl (they are decorative and continue to aroma, but are not eaten), and scatter cilantro over the surface.
Visual cue: Vivid pink-orange shrimp curled to a gentle C in an amber broth, with green cilantro leaves on the surface.
Underdone: Shrimp are still translucent grey-blue and the bodies are straight, not curled. The broth tastes of aromatics without the seafood foundation. Return to a boil for 1 more minute. Shrimp finish very quickly.
Perfect: Shrimp are vivid pink, curled to a gentle C with just a hint of translucency at the very center. The broth is amber and aromatic, properly seasoned — sour, salty, hot, and faintly sweet. Serve immediately. Do not reheat.
Overdone: Shrimp are tightly curled into a full O, firm, and rubbery. The body has lost its glossy sheen and looks matte and dry. Serve at once despite the texture. Overcooked shrimp in a correctly seasoned broth are still pleasurable — the broth carries the dish.
Feel cue: The finished bowl of tom yum should hit you with heat before you even taste it — the steam from the surface carries chili volatiles that sting the eyes and nose from 20 centimeters away. That sting is the dish keeping its promise.

One tablespoon dissolved in hot broth conjures a bowl of sour, spicy, herbal brilliance.

ingredients.name: Lemongrass stalks, white part only, thin-sliced
Kaffir lime zest (from 2 leaves, or peel of kaffir lime)
Dried red Thai chilies, seeded and soaked
Shrimp paste (kapi), wrapped in foil and dry-toasted 2 min
Dried makrut lime leaves, crumbled (or fresh, very finely sliced)
鱼露（Fish sauce, for final seasoning）

steps:
Combine the sliced lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime zest, and salt in a heavy mortar. Begin pounding with a firm downward rhythm, rotating the pestle to drag fibers into the center. These aromatics are extremely fibrous — the lemongrass in particular has woody cell walls that must be completely crushed to release their volatile oils. Pound for 8–10 minutes until no visible strings remain and the paste smells explosively of lemon, pine, and something vaguely medicinal. Add a splash of water if it becomes too dry to pound effectively.
Visual cue: A pale yellow-green fibrous paste with no visible lemongrass strings. An intense citrus-medicinal fragrance that makes the eyes water slightly.
Underdone: Lemongrass rings still visible, galangal in recognizable chunks, paste appears stringy and poorly integrated. Keep pounding rhythmically — these are the hardest aromatics to break down. 10 minutes of work is not excessive.
Perfect: Smooth, cohesive, pale yellow paste. No strings. Smells vividly of fresh lemon, ginger, and a pine-like galangal note. Add the chilies and alliums.
Overdone: Paste is wet and watery, releasing too much liquid. Drain a little of the liquid off and continue — the oils are what matter, not the water content.
Feel cue: Run a finger through the paste — if it drags cleanly without strings catching on your fingertip, the lemongrass is sufficiently broken down.

Drain the soaked chilies and squeeze out excess water. Add the chilies, shallots, and garlic to the mortar. Continue pounding, working each addition in gradually — add the new ingredient, pound until integrated before adding the next. The paste will turn from pale yellow to a deep brick-red as the chilies incorporate. Work for another 8–10 minutes until the mixture is unified and smooth. The shallots and garlic will break down more easily than the initial aromatics.
Visual cue: A deep reddish-orange paste, dense and cohesive, with a fiery color and complex layered aroma of chili, garlic, and citrus aromatics beneath.
Underdone: Shallot or garlic chunks still visible, paste is two-toned with pale and red sections. Continue pounding with rotation — the alliums will break down quickly once they are fully pressed into the paste.
Perfect: Uniformly deep brick-red, smooth, cohesive. Smells of concentrated chili heat, raw garlic, and the underlying lemongrass. Leaves a single-color smear on the mortar wall. Add the shrimp paste and kaffir lime leaves.
Overdone: Paste has liquefied and is spattering when the pestle strikes. Add a small pinch of salt to help it re-cohere, and pound more gently.
Feel cue: The paste is ready when a smear on the back of your hand stains it red with no visible particles — and the heat from the raw chilies makes your skin tingle within 30 seconds.

Unwrap the toasted shrimp paste from its foil and add it to the mortar along with the crumbled kaffir lime leaves. Pound to fully integrate — the shrimp paste will add a fermented, deeply umami note that transforms the paste from simply spicy-aromatic to complex and savory. Add the fish sauce last and fold it in with a few strokes of the pestle rather than pounding. Taste: the paste should be intensely concentrated — hot, sour-aromatic, salty, and oceanic. When diluted in broth (1 tablespoon per 200 ml), it should produce a balanced tom yum. Store under a thin layer of oil in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks, or freeze in tablespoon-sized portions.
Visual cue: A dark brick-red paste, unified and dense, with visible specs of kaffir lime leaf and the darkening signature of the toasted shrimp paste throughout.
Underdone: Shrimp paste is still in identifiable chunks, fish sauce is pooling rather than incorporated. Pound more aggressively and fold with a spatula to bring the liquid into the paste.
Perfect: Fully integrated, dark, pungent, and deeply complex. The fermented aroma is present but not overwhelming. A tiny taste is hot, sour-aromatic, and umami-rich. The paste is finished. Store immediately.
Overdone: Paste is over-worked and oily, or the shrimp paste was too heavily toasted and tastes burnt. Add a few drops of lime juice to brighten. The bitterness will diminish slightly as the paste rests.
Feel cue: Finished tom yum paste should feel like damp potting soil — dense, slightly gritty, and uniformly textured. The smell should make you want to immediately heat a pan of water and make soup.

ingredients.name: Lemongrass stalks, bruised and cut into 5cm segments
Kaffir lime leaves, lightly bruised and torn
Large shrimp (head-on preferred), shell-on or peeled
Straw mushrooms or oyster mushrooms, halved
Fresh cilantro and spring onion, chopped

steps:
Combine water (or stock), lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves, and bruised chilies in a pot. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a vigorous simmer. Cook for 10-12 minutes to extract the aromatics fully. Do not strain yet — the aromatic solids continue infusing as you cook the rest of the soup.
Visual cue: Broth has taken on a pale golden-green tinge; the surface is fragrant with lemongrass, lime leaf, and a faint heat rising in the steam.
Underdone: Broth still smells mostly like plain water; lemongrass and galangal haven't fully released their compounds. Continue simmering for another 5 minutes; the aromatics need time and heat.
Perfect: Broth is pale gold, fragrant with lemongrass, citrus, and earthy galangal. Chilies have released visible orange-red color into the liquid. Add mushrooms and proceed.
Overdone: Broth has reduced significantly and may taste slightly bitter from over-extracted kaffir lime — the pithy stems contribute bitterness over time. Remove kaffir lime leaves; add a splash of water to reconstitute volume.
Feel cue: Lean over the pot and inhale — you should smell lemongrass, citrus, and something almost medicinal from the galangal. If the fragrance is faint, simmer longer with the lid off.

Add halved mushrooms to the simmering aromatic stock. Cook for 3-4 minutes until tender but still holding their shape. The mushrooms release their own umami into the broth, deepening the base.
Visual cue: Mushrooms are tender and have absorbed the broth color; the stock itself looks slightly more golden and opaque from the mushroom release.
Underdone: Mushrooms are still pale and resistant when pressed with a spoon. Cook another 2-3 minutes.
Perfect: Mushrooms yield slightly when pressed but hold their shape. The broth is a deeper golden with visible umami richness. Add shrimp immediately.
Overdone: Mushrooms are completely soft and beginning to disintegrate into the broth — texture is lost. Proceed quickly; they will still taste fine.
Feel cue: The broth at this stage should smell like the sea and the forest simultaneously — the mushrooms add an earthy depth that anchors the citrus aromatics.

Add shrimp to the simmering broth. Cook for 1-2 minutes only — until just pink and curled. Do not overcook. If using head-on shrimp, the heads release a burst of shrimp essence into the broth: press them gently with a spoon as they cook. Remove from heat immediately when the shrimp curl.
Visual cue: Shrimp are uniformly pink-orange throughout, curled into a C-shape — not an O, which indicates overcooking.
Underdone: Shrimp are still grey-translucent and limp. The color change hasn't completed. Cook another 30-60 seconds. Do not leave the pot.
Perfect: Shrimp are vivid pink-orange, curled to a loose C, and slightly firm when pressed. The broth smells strongly of sweet shrimp essence. Remove from heat and season immediately.
Overdone: Shrimp are curled tightly to an O-shape, opaque white throughout, and rubbery when pressed. Season and serve immediately — nothing further helps overcooked shrimp.
Feel cue: Touch a shrimp with your finger — it should feel firm and spring back slightly, like a pencil eraser. If it feels hard and doesn't spring, it is already overcooked.

Off heat (critical — lime juice loses brightness when simmered), add fish sauce and lime juice. Taste and balance: fish sauce for salt, lime for sour, and adjust chili level to taste. The soup should be bracingly sour and hot in equal measure. Ladle into bowls, add garnish, and serve immediately — this soup does not wait.
Visual cue: Clear, pale golden broth with vivid pink shrimp, green herbs floating, and orange chili specks — a soup that looks as electrifying as it tastes.
Underdone: Soup tastes flat, mostly of lemongrass water — fish sauce and lime haven't been added yet. Add fish sauce first (season), then lime juice little by little, tasting as you go.
Perfect: The flavors hit in sequence: first the heat from the chilies, then the sour brightness of lime, then the savory depth of fish sauce and shrimp. Each element is distinct and loud. Ladle and garnish immediately.
Overdone: Over-seasoned — either too salty (too much fish sauce) or too sour (too much lime). The flavors overwhelm each other. Add a small amount of water and a pinch of sugar to balance. The sugar should be barely perceptible.
Feel cue: The finished soup should make you draw a sharp breath from the heat, then exhale with the sour — that one-two punch is the soul of tom yum.

name: Tomatillo Salsa Verde
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Fresh tomatillos (husked and rinsed): 100 parts
  Alternatives: canned tomatillos (drained, skip boiling step)
Serrano chilis (or jalapeños): 12 parts
  Alternatives: jalapeños (milder); habanero (much hotter)
White onion (roughly chopped): 20 parts
Garlic cloves (peeled): 6 parts
Fresh cilantro (stems and leaves): 20 parts
Salt: 2 parts
Fresh lime juice: 10 parts
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Husked tomatillos boiled until they surrender their tartness, then blended with roasted serrano chilis and cilantro into a bright, herbaceous, acid-punchy green salsa that makes a carnitas taco into something you dream about.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Place tomatillos and garlic cloves in a saucepan. Cover with cold water by about 3cm. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook for 8–10 minutes until the tomatillos have changed from bright green to a dull, slightly olive-green color and have softened completely — they should look like they are about to collapse. Do not overcook to the point of disintegration. Reserve 1/4 cup of the cooking liquid in case you need to thin the salsa.
Visual cue: Tomatillos have turned from bright vivid green to a softer, more muted olive-green. They are visibly softened and some are beginning to split.
Underdone: Tomatillos are still bright green and firm, springing back when pressed with a spoon. Continue simmering. Undercooked tomatillos produce a harsher, more astringent salsa.
Perfect: Muted olive-green, fully soft when poked with a spoon, some showing cracks or splits. The water is golden-green and tart. Drain, reserving some cooking liquid, and proceed.
Overdone: Tomatillos have completely disintegrated into the water. The cooking liquid is very tart and the tomatillos have lost their structure. Drain immediately — the tomatillos still have flavor, they have just lost their shape. The salsa may be thinner.
Feel cue: Press a tomatillo against the side of the pan with a spoon — it should yield with almost no resistance and squish flat, releasing a burst of tart green juice.

While the tomatillos cook, char the serrano chilis directly over a gas flame or under a hot broiler, turning occasionally with tongs, until blistered and charred on all sides — about 5–8 minutes total. The skins should blacken and blister but the flesh should remain intact. Transfer to a bowl, cover with a plate for 5 minutes to steam, then peel, stem, and seed (or leave seeds for more heat). Charring the chilis adds a smokiness that offsets the tartness of the tomatillos.
Visual cue: Uniformly blistered and charred chilis — skin is bubbled and blackened but the chili underneath is soft and pliable, not burnt through.
Underdone: Chilis are lightly marked in spots but mostly green and still firm. Little smoke flavor has developed. Continue charring — turn more frequently for even coverage.
Perfect: Most of the skin is black and blistered. The chili is clearly soft and yielding. It smells of roasted pepper rather than raw capsicum. Steam in a covered bowl for 5 minutes before peeling.
Overdone: Chili flesh has collapsed and blackened through — not just the skin. Discard if completely carbonized. If only very dark, proceed with peeling — the interior may be salvageable.
Feel cue: After steaming, the charred skin should slip off between your fingers effortlessly — if it is pulling and resisting, steam for another 2 minutes.

Combine the drained tomatillos, garlic (cooked with them), charred chilis, raw onion, cilantro, salt, and lime juice in a blender. Add a couple tablespoons of reserved cooking liquid. Blend to your desired consistency: rough and rustic with 6 pulses, or completely smooth with 45 seconds on high. Taste immediately — adjust salt for savory depth, lime for brightness, and if too tart, a pinch of sugar to balance. The color will be a vibrant olive-green flecked with darker specks from the charred chili.
Visual cue: A bright, vivid olive-green salsa with herb flecks. Thick enough to mound slightly on a chip but pourable. Color is alive and herbal, not dull or grey.
Underdone: Still chunky with large pieces of tomatillo and cilantro stem visible. Flavors are not unified. Blend more — pulse until the desired consistency is reached.
Perfect: Smooth to medium-smooth, bright olive-green, intensely aromatic. The flavor is tart, herbal, and slowly spicy with a clean finish. Taste for salt and lime, then serve or refrigerate.
Overdone: Completely smooth and light-colored from over-blending — the color has turned from olive-green to a lighter, airier green from aeration. Let settle to allow air to escape. Color will deepen. The texture is thinner than ideal.
Feel cue: The finished salsa should smell so vividly of cilantro and tart tomatillo that it almost stings the inside of your nose — bright, green, and unmistakably alive.

ingredients.name: Aged balsamic vinegar (a few drops, optional)

steps:
Preheat the oven to 110 C / 230 F — low, slow, and patient. Halve the plum tomatoes lengthwise and place cut-side up in a single, tight layer in a roasting dish or on a rimmed baking sheet. They should fit snugly — they will shrink considerably. Scatter the unpeeled garlic cloves and thyme sprigs between the tomatoes. Sprinkle the sugar, salt, and pepper evenly over the cut faces. Drizzle the olive oil over everything generously — the oil must coat every tomato face and pool slightly in the dish; it acts as the confit medium, surrounding the tomatoes in fat and preventing them from drying out instead of concentrating.
Visual cue: Rows of bright red tomato halves, cut-side up, glistening with olive oil, evenly seasoned. The garlic cloves and thyme are distributed between them. The dish is full but not overcrowded — each tomato half has its cut face fully exposed.
Underdone: Tomatoes are stacked or overlapping — they will steam each other and never caramelize. Oil is insufficient and some faces are dry. Rearrange into a single layer, adding oil if needed. A crowded pan steams; a single layer roasts.
Perfect: Single layer, every face shining with oil, sugar and salt visible as a fine crust on each cut surface. Looks like a jewellery tray of rubies. Slide into the oven. Do not disturb for the first 2 hours.
Overdone: Not applicable at prep — proceed. Slide into the oven.
Feel cue: The tomatoes should feel firm and cool going into the oven — they are raw. By the time they come out, they will feel like deflated wine gums, yielding at the slightest touch: all their water gone, their sugar and umami intensified to a concentration the raw tomato could not hint at.

Roast at 110 C / 230 F for 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours, checking every hour. The tomatoes will slowly lose their water, shrink, and intensify. Their color will shift from bright red to a deeper, more muted red-burgundy. The cut faces will begin to wrinkle and caramelize into a sweet, tacky surface while the olive oil in the dish turns fragrant and gold. In the final 30 minutes, the surfaces may start to lightly caramelize at the edges. Do not rush this with higher heat — the concentration must be gradual to avoid drying to leather before the sugars develop.
Visual cue: Deeply shrunken, wrinkled, burgundy-red tomato halves — reduced to roughly half their original size. The cut surfaces are caramelized and tacky, the flesh translucent and jammy. The olive oil in the dish is golden and fragrant with thyme and garlic.
Underdone: Tomatoes have barely shrunk; they are still plump, bright red, and the surface looks wet and raw rather than caramelized and tacky. Less than 1 hour has passed. Continue roasting. The transformation is dramatic but happens slowly — be patient.
Perfect: Shrunk by 50–60%, deeply colored, the cut surfaces caramelized to a sticky, jammy finish. The flesh is entirely translucent. When pressed with a spoon, the tomato yields completely — all resistance gone. Remove from the oven. Add a drop of aged balsamic over each if using.
Overdone: Tomatoes have dried to leathery, shriveled husks — all moisture gone, the edges black and brittle. The oil in the dish has browned and smells slightly bitter. If only slightly overdone, the tomatoes are still usable as a very concentrated paste stirred through pasta. If fully dried to crisps, they are past saving.
Feel cue: Check a tomato at the 2-hour mark by pressing the edge with the tip of a spoon: the flesh should yield instantly and completely, like pressing a soft gel — no resistance, no bounce, just total
collapse. If there is any spring in the flesh, it needs more time.

Remove from the oven and add a drop of balsamic vinegar over each tomato if using — the residual heat will soften its edge and let it meld with the oil. Allow to cool in the dish. As they cool, the tomatoes will firm very slightly and the oil will thicken with their released sugars and pectins. The garlic cloves can be squeezed out of their skins and stored with the tomatoes — they will be soft, sweet, and completely transformed.
Visual cue: Cooled, jammy tomato halves in a golden-red oil that has thickened slightly as it cooled, with the balsamic darkening the edges of each tomato. The oil looks like a sauce unto itself.
Underdone: Still hot from the oven — the oil is very loose and the tomatoes are too soft to handle. Allow to cool at least 20 minutes before serving or storing.
Perfect: Cooled to room temperature: the oil has thickened to a syrup around the tomatoes, which now sit firm enough to lift intact but yield instantly to a fork. They taste intensely of concentrated tomato with a deep sweet-sour-umami complexity. Serve immediately or store covered in the oil in the fridge for up to 2 weeks.
Overdone: Left out for hours; the tomatoes are cold and the oil has solidified. Warm gently in a low oven or in a warm-water bath before serving.
Feel cue: Lift one confit tomato with a spoon: it should hold together but feel like a soft, filled water balloon — any pressure and it collapses. The oil beneath should flow slowly, thicker than fresh olive oil, carrying the concentrated flavors of hours of slow roasting.

Transfer the tomatoes and all the scented oil to a sterilised jar, ensuring the tomatoes are submerged. The oil is as precious as the tomatoes — use it to dress salads, drizzle over burrata, finish pasta, or brush on grilled bread. Refrigerate and use within 2 weeks. Serve the tomatoes at room temperature or warm for the fullest flavor expression.
Visual cue: A jar of deeply colored, jewel-like tomato halves suspended in amber oil infused with thyme and garlic. They look almost too beautiful to eat.
Underdone: Oil does not cover all the tomatoes — they will develop mold where exposed to air. Top off with fresh olive oil until all tomatoes are submerged.
Perfect: Fully submerged tomatoes in fragrant oil. Refrigerated, they keep beautifully for 2 weeks. Brought to room temperature before eating, they taste far more intensely of tomato than any can or tube could suggest. Use as a sauce, a topping, a condiment, or an ingredient.
Overdone: Stored beyond 2 weeks: the garlic in oil creates a botulism risk if not properly handled and stored cold. The flavor also fades. Discard after 2 weeks, or freeze portions in oil for longer storage.
Feel cue: A spoonful of the confit oil alone should taste extraordinary — the slow roasting has leached every flavour compound from the tomatoes, garlic, and thyme into it. If the oil tastes flat, the confit needed longer in the oven.

name: Tonkatsu Sauce
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Worcestershire sauce: 60 g
  Alternatives: Henderson's Relish for vegetarian; soy sauce + tamarind (3:1) as substitute
Tomato ketchup: 50 g
  Alternatives: tomato paste (30g) + 1 tsp sugar
Oyster sauce: 20 g
  Alternatives: hoisin sauce; mushroom oyster sauce for vegetarian
Rice vinegar: 10 g
  Alternatives: apple cider vinegar; white wine vinegar
Caster sugar: 8 g
  Alternatives: honey (use 6g)
Dijon mustard: 5 g
  Alternatives: English mustard (use half — it is sharper)
Garlic powder: 1 g
  Alternatives: freshly grated garlic (use half a small clove)
Active time: 5 min
Total time: 5 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A thick, glossy, dark-amber condiment that tastes like Worcestershire sauce's rounder, more harmonious Japanese cousin — fruit-forward, gently tart, and deeply savoury, with a sweetness that rounds every edge. Five minutes and a handful of pantry staples produce a sauce worthy of the best breaded cutlet, and confident enough to stand in for steak sauce, dipping sauce, or burger condiment.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Combine all ingredients in a small bowl or jar. Whisk vigorously until completely homogeneous — the mustard needs to be fully emulsified into the sauce so no yellow streaks remain. Taste and adjust: if it tastes too sharp, add 3g more sugar; if too sweet, add 5g more Worcestershire or a few more drops of rice vinegar; if too thin in umami, add 5g more oyster sauce. The sauce is ready to use immediately but improves significantly after 30 minutes of resting as the flavours meld.
Visual cue: A uniformly dark amber-brown, glossy sauce with no streaks, no floating oil, and a consistency that pours in a slow, controlled stream rather than dribbling freely.
Underdone: Yellow mustard streaks visible. Ingredients not fully combined. Separate thin liquid and thick paste layers. Whisk for another 30 seconds, paying attention to the sides and bottom of the bowl where mustard tends to cling.
Perfect: Uniformly dark amber-brown, glossy, pours in a controlled stream when the jar is tilted. Tastes complex: sour-sweet at first, then a deep, savoury, fruity base, then a gentle tart finish. Use immediately or rest covered for 30 minutes. Store refrigerated for up to 1 month.
Overdone: Not applicable for a no-cook sauce. If over-seasoned with too much of one component, balance it out with the opposing element. Add sugar to cut excess acid; add vinegar to cut excess sweetness; add Worcestershire to cut sweetness and add depth.
Feel cue: Dip a fingertip and taste — the first impression should be fruity and tart, the middle should be savoury and dark, and the finish should be mellow and sweet, all within 3 seconds. If any single note dominates for longer than that, it is out of balance.

Transfer the sauce to a clean jar or squeeze bottle and let it rest at room temperature for at least 30 minutes before serving. During this time, the raw garlic powder blooms, the mustard finishes emulsifying, and the competing sweet, acid, and savory notes knit into a unified whole. The sauce does not need cooking — heat would drive off the volatile acids and reduce the bright top notes that distinguish tonkatsu sauce from a cooked relish. Refrigerate any unused sauce. It keeps for 4 to 6 weeks and deepens in flavour over time, the way a good Worcestershire sauce does.
Visual cue: The rested sauce is slightly thicker than when first mixed — the mustard has absorbed moisture and the sauce has a more cohesive body when stirred. The colour has deepened very slightly.
Underdone: Sauce was used immediately without resting — the individual components are distinct rather than blended, and the garlic powder has a raw, astringent edge. The sauce is still usable — rest it next time. The flavour improves dramatically with even 20 minutes of standing.
Perfect: After 30 minutes: a glossy, homogeneous, dark sauce with a rounded, complex flavour. Pour from the jar onto a white plate — it should flow in a slow, controlled ribbon and hold its shape for 5 seconds before spreading. Serve at room temperature alongside katsu. Apply liberally to the cut face of the cutlet for maximum coverage.
Overdone: Sauce has been refrigerated for weeks and has separated into layers. Shake vigorously or re-whisk to recombine. The flavour will actually be better than freshly made.
Feel cue: Spread a small pool on the back of your hand and draw a finger through it — the trail should stay clean for 3 to 4 seconds before the sauce slowly flows back together, like warm chocolate sauce just before it sets.

name: 日式炸猪排 · Tonkatsu
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Pork loin cutlet (2.5cm thick): 100 parts
  Alternatives: pork tenderloin; chicken breast
Panko breadcrumbs: 20 parts
All-purpose flour: 10 parts
Egg (beaten): 8 parts
  Alternatives: aquafaba
Neutral frying oil: 60 parts
  Alternatives: vegetable oil; lard
Kosher salt and white pepper: 1.5 parts
Tonkatsu sauce (Bulldog or similar): 5 parts
  Alternatives: Worcestershire sauce blended with ketchup and soy sauce
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 40 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A thick pork cutlet entombed in craggy panko armor, fried to a shattering golden crust while the pork within stays barely blushed and juicy — yōshoku at its most satisfying, served with shredded cabbage and the sweet-savory sauce that makes it complete.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Use a meat mallet or the back of a heavy pan to gently pound the cutlet to an even 2cm thickness. Snip the fat and connective tissue band around the edge of the cutlet at 2cm intervals — this prevents the cutlet from curling during frying. Season generously with salt and white pepper on both sides. Let sit at room temperature for 15 minutes.
Visual cue: An evenly thick cutlet with a series of small cuts along the fat cap edge, seasoned uniformly on both sides.
Underdone: Cutlet thickness varies significantly across its surface — thick at the center, thin at the edges. Pound the thicker areas more to achieve an even thickness throughout.
Perfect: Consistent thickness from edge to edge. The fat cap shows neat snips at regular intervals. The seasoning is evenly applied. Set up the breading station.
Overdone: The cutlet has been pounded too thin or the snips in the fat cap go all the way through the meat. Proceed but be aware it will cook very quickly — check internal temperature early.
Feel cue: Run a finger across the surface of the cutlet — it should feel uniformly firm with no thin, floppy patches. The fat cap should feel intact but notched at regular intervals.

Set up three shallow containers in sequence: flour, beaten egg, panko. Dredge the cutlet in flour, shaking off every trace of excess — a thick flour coating creates a gummy layer that prevents the panko from crisping properly. Dip in egg, letting excess drip for a full 5 seconds. Press firmly into the panko, turning and pressing again, building up thick, jagged layers. The more aggressively you press the panko, the more dramatic the crust.
Visual cue: The cutlet is completely encased in a uniform, thick coating of panko with no egg or flesh visible. The panko stands up in jagged peaks and ridges rather than lying flat.
Underdone: Thin, patchy panko coverage with the egg coating showing through in places. Press additional panko onto the bare patches firmly, then let rest 5 minutes before frying.
Perfect: Thick, even panko armour with craggy, three-dimensional texture. The cutlet can stand on its edge without losing coating. Rest 5 minutes to allow the coating to set before frying.
Overdone: Panko is so thick and tightly pressed that it has become dense and uniform rather than craggy. Proceed — the crust will still be crisp, if slightly denser in texture.
Feel cue: Press the coated cutlet gently — the panko surface should feel like the surface of a coral reef, rough and three-dimensional, not flat and smooth. It should feel well-adhered when you shake the cutlet gently.

Heat oil to 170°C (340°F) in a pot deep enough for the oil to come halfway up the cutlet. Test with a panko crumb — it should sink, bob, then sizzle immediately without browning in under 10 seconds. Lower the cutlet away from you and fry for 4 minutes per side without disturbing. The lower temperature (versus standard deep frying) allows heat to penetrate to the center before the crust over-browns.
Visual cue: A steady, consistent stream of small bubbles rising evenly from all sides of the cutlet. The crust is gradually deepening from pale yellow to a rich, even amber.
Underdone: The crust is golden after only 2 minutes and the oil is aggressively bubbling and spattering. The oil is too hot. Remove the cutlet, reduce oil temperature to 170°C, and try again.
Perfect: After 4 minutes per side: deep amber-gold crust, steady moderate bubbling, internal temperature 63–65°C. The cutlet floats slightly as the fat in the meat renders. Remove and drain on a wire rack, not paper towels.
Overdone: The crust is dark brown and the bubbling has nearly stopped — the moisture has all been driven out. Remove immediately. The interior may be dry. Resting on a rack will help redistribute any remaining juices.
Feel cue: Listen to the oil — it should sound like a steady rain on a roof, not an aggressive crackling storm. When the bubbling begins to slow and quiet, the moisture is nearly gone and the cutlet is almost done.

Transfer to a wire rack and rest for 3 minutes — never paper towels, which trap steam and soften the crust from beneath. The carryover heat will bring the interior to a perfect 68°C. Slice into 2cm strips with a sharp knife using a single downward press — sawing shatters the crust. Serve immediately with tonkatsu sauce drizzled over or alongside for dipping, and finely shredded raw cabbage.
Visual cue: When sliced, the interior is pale white-pink and juicy, with a very faint pink blush at the very center. The crust is completely separate from the meat in texture — crackling, golden, and rigid.
Underdone: Interior is pink and the juices run clear-pink when pressed. The center feels soft and yielding. Return to the oil for 2 additional minutes per side, or finish in a 180°C oven for 5 minutes.
Perfect: Interior is white with the faintest blush of pink. Juices are clear. Crust is completely rigid. The contrast of textures — shatteringly crisp and tenderly juicy — is the goal. Serve immediately.
Overdone: Interior is fully white, no pink, and feels firm and dry when pressed. Juices are absent. Drizzle extra sauce to add moisture. Next time pull at 63–65°C internal temperature.
Feel cue: The first bite should present two sensations simultaneously: the crack of the panko shattering between the teeth, immediately followed by the yielding, juicy pork. The tonkatsu sauce should smell of Worcestershire and fruit — caramel and vinegar.

name: Tonkotsu Ramen Broth
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Pork trotters, split by butcher: 1000 g
  Alternatives: pork knuckles
Pork neck bones: 1000 g
  Alternatives: pork spine
Pork back fat, roughly chopped: 200 g
Dried shiitake mushrooms: 20 g
  Alternatives: dried porcini
Fresh ginger, thick slices: 50 g
Scallion, whole stalks: 4 stalks
Garlic cloves, unpeeled and crushed: 6 cloves
Cold water: 4 L
Fine sea salt, to taste: 10 g
  Alternatives: soy sauce (for color)
Active time: 1 hr
Total time: 14 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Milky-white, almost opaque pork bone broth from Fukuoka — boiled hard for twelve hours until collagen, fat, and gelatin emulsify into a bowl that looks and tastes like liquid silk.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Place the trotters and neck bones in a large stockpot and cover with cold water. Bring to a rolling boil over high heat and boil for 5 minutes — the water will turn grey and foul-smelling as impurities purge. Drain, rinse every bone under cold running water, and scrub away any dark clots or membrane. Clean the pot. This step is non-negotiable: skipping it produces a bitter, murky broth.
Visual cue: Bones are pale, clean, and free of grey scum. The rinsing water runs clear.
Underdone: Bones still have dark blood spots or grey patches. Scum clings to the surface. Rinse again under strong running water and scrub with your fingers — especially inside the trotter joints.
Perfect: Bright ivory bones, no discoloration, no off smell. Blanching water was discarded. Return bones to the clean pot and begin the long boil.
Overdone: Bones were blanched too long and look dry or chalky. Proceed anyway — over-blanching affects colour slightly but not flavour.
Feel cue: The blanched bones will feel slightly tacky when handled — that collagen is already beginning to loosen. Rinse until they feel slick and clean.

Return the clean bones to the pot with back fat, shiitake, ginger, scallion, and garlic. Cover with 4 litres of cold water. Bring to a hard, rolling boil and keep it there — the violent agitation is what forces fat and collagen into suspension, turning the broth white. Boil at full blast for 12 hours, adding water as needed to keep bones submerged. The liquid level will drop by nearly half. Partially cover to reduce splatter but maintain the boil.
Visual cue: An opaque, creamy-white liquid, resembling dilute milk. A vigorous rolling boil churning the surface. Visible fat droplets suspended throughout — not floating on top in a clear layer.
Underdone: Broth is still translucent or only lightly cloudy after 4 hours. Fat floats as a clear layer rather than emulsifying. Increase heat — tonkotsu requires a genuine hard boil, not a simmer. Turn it up until the surface is actively churning.
Perfect: Deeply opaque, milky-white broth after 10–12 hours. Coating the back of a spoon lightly. Smells of sweet pork and earth. Remove from heat. Allow to settle for 5 minutes before straining.
Overdone: Broth has reduced below the bones or turned a dark beige. Smells slightly scorched. Add a splash of fresh water and reduce heat immediately. Taste for bitterness — if bitter, the broth cannot be saved.
Feel cue: Dip a clean spoon and let a drop fall on the back of your hand — it should feel slightly heavier than water, almost velvety, coating the skin before sliding off.

During the 12-hour boil, skim away any thick grey foam that collects at the edges in the first hour. After that, resist the urge to skim — the white turbidity is collagen and emulsified fat that you want in the final bowl. Only remove solid flotsam (bone chips, mushroom stems). Check the pot every 2 hours.
Visual cue: Surface is actively churning white. Any grey foam at the pot's edges has been removed. White cloudiness remains intact.
Underdone: Thick grey scum still sits around the edges, leeching bitterness into the broth. Skim the grey carefully with a ladle, tilting the pot to pool the scum — but leave the white turbidity.
Perfect: No grey patches. Broth is uniformly milky and churning. Only white, creamy foam at the surface. Continue boiling and add water if level drops below bones.
Overdone: You over-skimmed and removed white emulsified fat along with the grey scum. Broth looks cleaner than it should. Add back fat (ing_03) and continue boiling — it will re-emulsify.
Feel cue: Grey scum feels slimy on the ladle and smells faintly metallic. White foam is creamy and smells rich — learn to tell them apart by smell.

Set a fine-mesh strainer lined with cheesecloth over a clean pot. Ladle the broth through — do not pour, as the bones shifting will cloud the liquid further. Discard solids. Season the finished broth with salt, tasting after each addition; it should taste deeply savoury on its own but mild enough to accommodate tare (seasoning sauce) and toppings. Cool and refrigerate if not using immediately — the broth will set into a firm ivory jelly.
Visual cue: A smooth, opaque ivory broth with no bone fragments. Under refrigeration, it sets firm enough to hold a knife cut — a sign of sufficient gelatin.
Underdone: Broth is thinner than cream and barely coats the spoon. Under refrigeration it stays liquid. Return to the pot and reduce by 20%, boiling hard for another 30 minutes.
Perfect: Creamy, velvety finish. Coats and clings to the spoon back. When cold, sets like soft panna cotta. Season carefully and store. Reheat gently — do not boil the finished broth.
Overdone: Broth is very thick and gluey at room temperature, dark beige rather than white. Dilute with hot water and re-season — it's concentrated, not ruined.
Feel cue: A few drops rubbed between thumb and finger should feel slick and slightly sticky — like a faint lip balm. That's the gelatin. If it runs off clean like water, boil longer.

name: Tonkotsu Ramen Broth
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Pork trotters, split lengthwise: 1000 g
  Alternatives: pork neck bones
Pork neck bones: 1000 g
  Alternatives: pork back bones
Yellow onion, halved and charred: 200 g
  Alternatives: leek tops
Fresh ginger, thick slices, charred: 60 g
Garlic cloves, crushed: 30 g
Cold water: 4000 g
Fine salt (for blanching water): 10 g
Active time: 45 min
Total time: 18 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A bone-white, viscous pork broth coaxed from split trotters and neck bones over 18 hours of rolling heat — collagen-rich, porky, and impossibly creamy without a drop of dairy.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Place bones in a large stockpot. Cover with cold water and bring to a rapid boil over high heat. Boil hard for 10 minutes — grey-brown scum and impurities will rise aggressively to the surface. Drain completely, then rinse each bone under cold running water, scrubbing off any remaining dark bits with your fingers or a brush. Clean the pot.
Visual cue: Rinsed bones that are clean and pale — no grey foam clinging to the marrow cavities or joint surfaces.
Underdone: Bones are still pink at the joints, substantial grey scum clinging to surfaces. Rinse more thoroughly and scrape out dark marrow if needed — residue clouds the final broth.
Perfect: Bones are uniformly pale ivory. Water runs clear when you rinse them. Marrow cavities are open and cleaned. Return cleaned bones to the pot with fresh water.
Overdone: Bones smell strongly cooked; surface texture feels chalky. Proceed — the subsequent long simmer will more than compensate.
Feel cue: The water should turn a murky grey-brown within 2 minutes — that visible purge is the reason the blanch step exists.

Place onion halves and ginger slices cut-side down in a dry cast-iron skillet or directly over a gas burner flame with tongs. Char until the cut surfaces are deeply blackened — nearly burnt. This caramelized bitterness sweetens as it infuses the broth over hours.
Visual cue: Cut surfaces are black and carbonized, with a ring of deep amber-brown around the char.
Underdone: Only lightly browned — translucent onion layers, golden ginger edges. Return to higher heat; the char is what flavors the broth.
Perfect: Jet-black carbon on cut surfaces with sweet, smoky aroma. Edges look nearly burnt but smell of caramel. Set aside until bones are ready.
Overdone: Entirely ash-grey with acrid rather than smoky smell. Discard and start over with new aromatics — true char is good; ash is not.
Feel cue: The onion should hiss and smoke when it hits the dry pan, and the kitchen should smell of sweet caramelized sugar within 30 seconds.

Return cleaned bones to the pot. Add charred onion, ginger, garlic, and all cold water. Bring to a full, rolling boil over high heat — do not reduce. Maintain a vigorous boil for the first 2 hours; the turbulent water emulsifies the collagen and fat into the opaque white broth characteristic of tonkotsu. After 2 hours, reduce to a strong simmer and cook for 14–16 more hours total, adding boiling water if the level drops below the bones.
Visual cue: Broth is opaque white — the color of whole milk — with no visible fat layer separating on top.
Underdone: Broth is light beige and clear, like a light chicken stock. Has not emulsified yet. Raise heat; you need that rolling boil to break down the collagen and emulsify the fat.
Perfect: Thick, creamy white with tiny bubbles churning the surface. Smells powerfully of pork fat and roasted bone. Maintain the boil; check water level every 2 hours.
Overdone: Broth has reduced past the bones; color turning yellow-grey and slightly scorched. Add 500g boiling water, reduce heat, and continue — watch more closely from here.
Feel cue: Rub a drop between your fingers after 10 hours — it should feel slick and slightly tacky from dissolved collagen, not watery.

After 16–18 hours, strain the broth through a fine-mesh strainer, pressing the solids to extract all liquid. Discard the exhausted bones and aromatics. You should have 2–2.5 liters of thick, white broth. Season to taste with salt or tare at the bowl.
Visual cue: Strained broth coats the back of a ladle thickly and drips slowly, like light cream.
Underdone: Broth runs off the ladle like water. Lacks body and smells thin. Return to the pot and boil down by 20%, then re-strain.
Perfect: Milky white, thick, coats a spoon with a sustained film. Aroma is deep, porky, and slightly sweet from the charred onion. Cool rapidly in an ice bath, then refrigerate. The broth will gel solid — that is exactly right.
Overdone: Broth is very dark and reduced to a paste-like consistency. Thin with hot water to your preferred richness level.
Feel cue: Cold tonkotsu broth should set to a firm, jiggly pork jelly in the refrigerator — if it stays liquid when cold, the collagen extraction was insufficient.

name: Tonnato Sauce
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Oil-packed tuna, well drained (quality matters): 100 parts
Anchovy fillets in oil, drained: 30 parts
Capers, rinsed (salt-packed preferred): 20 parts
  Alternatives: caper berries, halved
Mayonnaise (egg-yolk based, full-fat): 80 parts
  Alternatives: Greek yogurt for a lighter version
Fresh lemon juice: 30 parts
White wine vinegar: 15 parts
  Alternatives: Champagne vinegar
Extra-virgin olive oil: 30 parts
  Alternatives: light olive oil for a subtler flavor
Fine sea salt: 2 parts
White pepper, freshly ground: 1 parts
  Alternatives: black pepper
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A blender emulsion of oil-packed tuna, anchovy, capers, and mayonnaise — cold, silky, and unapologetically briny, the sauce that makes vitello tonnato what it is and transforms roasted vegetables into something quietly extraordinary.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Add the drained tuna, anchovy fillets, rinsed capers, lemon juice, and white wine vinegar to a blender. The quality of the tuna is the ceiling of this sauce — use the best oil-packed tuna you can find; water-packed tuna produces a grainy, dull result. Blend on high for 60–90 seconds until the mixture is completely smooth. There should be no visible tuna flakes, anchovy pieces, or caper skins. At this stage the mixture will be thick, blond-beige, and intensely savory — almost overwhelmingly salty and sour before the mayo is added.
Visual cue: A smooth, uniform pale-beige paste with absolutely no visible fish flakes, herb pieces, or caper skins — fine-textured enough to flow from the blender jar when tipped.
Underdone: Tuna flakes still visible as distinct pieces. The mixture is grainy and chunky rather than paste-smooth. Anchovy may still be identifiable as thin ribbons. Blend for another 30–45 seconds at full speed. If the blades are struggling, add a splash of the lemon juice or a tablespoon of cold water to free the mixture.
Perfect: Completely smooth, uniform pale-beige emulsion. The texture is fine and cohesive — closer to hummus than to pâté. The smell is intensely briny and savory, with a clean citrus lift from the vinegar and lemon. Add the mayonnaise and blend again briefly to create the finished emulsion.
Overdone: The tuna base has been blended so long it is warm from friction and starting to look slightly aerated — it will appear lighter and more foamy than a smooth paste. Proceed immediately to add the mayo; the colder, denser mayonnaise will cool and de-aerate the mixture.
Feel cue: Rub a small amount of the tuna base between fingers — it should feel perfectly smooth, dense, and slightly sticky from the proteins, with no graininess whatsoever. Any roughness means more blending is needed.

Add the mayonnaise to the blender with the tuna base. Blend on medium speed for 20–30 seconds until completely combined — do not over-blend at this stage, as the mayonnaise can break under prolonged high-speed blending. The sauce will transform from the stark, too-salty tuna paste into something considerably more rounded, creamy, and pale. The mayonnaise provides the emulsifying structure, fat, and body that ties everything together. Scrape down the sides and blend for 5 more seconds if any unmixed mayo is visible.
Visual cue: A smooth, pale ivory-cream sauce — noticeably lighter in color than the tuna base, with a uniform, creamy texture and a glossy surface.
Underdone: Streaks of white mayonnaise are still visible against the beige tuna base. The texture is uneven and the flavor tastes disjointed — salty tuna in one bite, flat mayo in the next. Blend for another 10–15 seconds, scraping the sides well beforehand. The two components will combine quickly once the blade reaches all surfaces.
Perfect: A smooth, homogeneous ivory-cream sauce with no visible streaks or variations in color. The flavor is now cohesive: savory, briny, creamy, and bright with acid. Stream in the olive oil and season with salt and white pepper to finish.
Overdone: The sauce has been blended too long and the mayonnaise emulsion is beginning to break — the surface looks greasy and the texture is separating. Transfer to a bowl and whisk in a tablespoon of ice-cold water to help re-emulsify. Do not return to the blender.
Feel cue: A properly emulsified tonnato should coat a spoon in a smooth, even layer that clings without running — similar to a slightly loosened mayonnaise. If it slides off like water, the emulsion needs more body.

Transfer the sauce to a bowl. Stream in the olive oil while whisking by hand — this adds a final layer of richness and adjusts the consistency. The olive oil will loosen the sauce slightly; add only as much as needed to reach the consistency you want: thicker for spreading on a platter of sliced veal, thinner for drizzling over roasted cauliflower or boiled eggs. Season with salt (taste first — the tuna, anchovies, and capers carry a great deal of salt) and white pepper. Taste and adjust acid if needed. Refrigerate immediately; tonnato sauce keeps for 3 days and is always served cold.
Visual cue: A pale ivory sauce with a light, drizzleable consistency and a subtle sheen from the olive oil — it should pour steadily from a spoon in an unbroken stream.
Underdone: The sauce is too thick and stiff — it mounds on the spoon rather than flowing. The flavor is flat and one-dimensional before the olive oil rounds it out. Add more olive oil a teaspoon at a time, whisking after each addition until the sauce reaches a slow-pouring consistency.
Perfect: The sauce flows in a slow, steady pour, coats the back of a spoon in a generous, even layer, and reveals complex flavor: first the creaminess of mayo, then the deep umami of tuna and anchovy, then the bright acid cut of lemon, then a gentle brine finish from the capers. Refrigerate until cold before serving. The sauce firms slightly when cold and the flavor deepens — made ahead by 2–3 hours is ideal.
Overdone: Too much olive oil — the sauce is thin and oily, running immediately rather than coating. It may also look slightly broken, with oil pooling on the surface. Whisk in another tablespoon of mayonnaise to re-emulsify and add body. If the oil has separated, do not blend again — whisk vigorously by hand instead.
Feel cue: The finished tonnato should feel silky and dense on the tongue — it coats the palate and releases flavor
slowly, the brininess and umami arriving in sequence rather than all at once. Serve it cold and generous.

description: A silky, pale-gold cold sauce from Piedmont — oil-packed tuna, anchovy, and capers emulsified with mayonnaise into something profoundly oceanic and savory, with a coolness that makes rich meats suddenly light. It is famously served with thinly sliced cold veal in vitello tonnato, but equally at home on roasted peppers or hard-boiled eggs.

ingredients.name: Cold water or cold veal poaching liquid
Capers and lemon zest, for serving

steps:
Combine the drained tuna, anchovy fillets, rinsed capers, and lemon juice in a food processor or blender. Process until the mixture becomes a smooth, homogeneous paste, scraping the sides as needed. There should be no visible chunks of tuna — the goal is a completely smooth, dense purée that will blend evenly into the mayonnaise.
Visual cue: A uniform pale-beige paste with a faintly grainy texture, the color of unbleached paper, smelling intensely of the sea — briny, savory, with a lemon brightness.
Underdone: Visible chunks of tuna and whole caper berries, the mixture still crumbly rather than paste-like. Continue processing, stopping to scrape down the sides. Add a teaspoon of olive oil if the blades are not catching.
Perfect: A completely smooth, dense paste — it falls off the spatula in a slow, heavy ribbon. The aroma is rounded and oceanic, not raw-fishy. Add the mayonnaise and olive oil.
Overdone: Over-processed until it smells metallic from the heat of the blender motor — the fat in the tuna may have slightly broken. Let it cool for a minute before adding the mayonnaise. The flavor will recover.
Feel cue: Spread a small amount on the spatula with your thumb — it should feel silky and uniform, like smooth hummus, with no grittiness or chunks.

With the processor running on low, spoon in the mayonnaise and drizzle in the olive oil. Process briefly — just enough to integrate. Over-processing after adding the mayo can make the sauce gluey. Scrape down and fold once by hand if needed. The sauce should be pale gold, thick, and absolutely smooth.
Visual cue: A pale, creamy gold sauce — the color of sea foam with a warm undertone — completely smooth and glossy, thick enough to spread but too loose to hold a peak.
Underdone: Streaks of white mayonnaise visible through the darker tuna paste — not yet fully combined. Process briefly in 3-second bursts until the color is uniform throughout.
Perfect: Uniform pale gold with a silky, glossy surface. It falls from a spatula in a smooth, unbroken curtain. No visible oil pooling. Adjust consistency with cold water or poaching liquid and season.
Overdone: The sauce has become gluey and slightly grayish; the mayonnaise has been over-worked and is starting to break. Whisk in a teaspoon of cold water and a drizzle of fresh olive oil to restore emulsification.
Feel cue: Dip a finger and taste — the sauce should feel smooth and coating on the tongue, with the fat of the mayonnaise carrying the tuna and anchovy. There should be no grittiness.

Add cold water (or cold veal poaching liquid for a more complex flavor) a tablespoon at a time to thin the sauce to a pourable but still coating consistency — it should coat the back of a spoon and fall in a slow ribbon, not run like water. Season with white pepper and salt, tasting carefully since the anchovies and capers have added significant salt. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes before serving to let the flavors meld.
Visual cue: A pale gold, pourable sauce that coats a spoon completely, falls in a ribbon, and has a slight glossy sheen. It should look like a very smooth, very refined cream sauce.
Underdone: Too thick — it clumps off the spoon and would need to be spread with a knife rather than poured over meat. Add cold water a teaspoon at a time, stirring gently, until it just reaches a pourable ribbon consistency.
Perfect: Pours in a slow, even ribbon over sliced meat and pools gently at the edges. Pale gold, gleaming, and utterly smooth. Tastes savory, slightly oceanic, with a clean lemon finish. Chill before serving. Pour generously over thin-sliced cold veal or roasted vegetables.
Overdone: Thinned too much — the sauce runs off the meat and pools on the plate, too fluid to cling. Whisk in a tablespoon of additional mayonnaise to restore body, then check seasoning again.
Feel cue: Pour a thin ribbon from the spoon onto the back of your hand — it should cling for a second before sliding, cool and silky, leaving a pale gold film. The aroma should be subtle: a whisper of the sea, a lift of lemon.

name: Torta Caprese
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Blanched whole almonds (or almond flour): 3 parts
  Alternatives: almond flour — skip grinding step
Dark chocolate (60-70% cocoa), roughly chopped: 3 parts
  Alternatives: bittersweet chocolate chips
Unsalted butter, cut into cubes: 1.5 parts
  Alternatives: cultured butter
Caster sugar (superfine): 2 parts
  Alternatives: light brown sugar
Large eggs, separated: 1 parts
Fine sea salt: 0.02 parts
Pure vanilla extract: 0.05 parts
  Alternatives: vanilla bean seeds
Icing sugar (powdered sugar), for dusting: 0.1 parts
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 1 hour 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The legendary cake of Capri that contains not one grain of flour — just dark chocolate, whole almonds, eggs, butter, and sugar collapsed into a dense, fudgy disc that is simultaneously a brownie, a flourless chocolate cake, and something entirely its own: cracked on top, trembling within, dusted white with powdered sugar.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
If using whole blanched almonds, pulse them in a food processor until they reach a fine, sandy consistency — the texture of coarse cornmeal. Do not over-process: if the almonds become warm and clumping, they are releasing their oils and will turn to almond paste rather than flour. Work in short 3-second pulses, scraping down the sides between each. The goal is a dry, free-flowing nut meal. If using store-bought almond flour, skip this step.
Visual cue: A dry, pale, free-flowing almond meal with a consistency between fine breadcrumbs and coarse semolina.
Underdone: Still grainy with visible large almond fragments that won't incorporate evenly. Continue pulsing in short bursts until the largest pieces are gone.
Perfect: Free-flowing, dry, pale almond meal. No large fragments. Smells nutty and fresh. Falls off a spoon cleanly. Set aside and proceed to melting the chocolate.
Overdone: Paste-like, sticky, and clumping — the fat has been fully released. Oily appearance. This almond paste will still work in the recipe but will produce a slightly denser, fudgier texture. Proceed.
Feel cue: Pinch the ground almond between your fingers — it should feel dry and slightly gritty, like fine sand, releasing no oil onto your skin.

Combine the chopped dark chocolate and butter cubes in a heatproof bowl. Melt together over a gentle bain-marie (a saucepan of barely simmering water, bowl sitting above but not touching the water) or in a microwave in 30-second bursts, stirring between each. The mixture should be completely smooth and glossy — no streaks of unmelted chocolate. Let cool to room temperature, about 10 minutes. Do not use the chocolate mixture while it is still hot, as it will cook the egg yolks in the next step.
Visual cue: A smooth, glossy, uniformly dark chocolate-brown liquid with no visible pieces of unmelted chocolate or streaks of butter.
Underdone: Chunks of chocolate still visible or streaks of unincorporated butter. Mix looks lumpy. Stir vigorously — the residual heat will usually complete the melting. Return to bain-marie briefly if needed.
Perfect: Perfectly smooth, uniformly dark, glossy liquid. Flows freely off a spoon. Smells of deep, roasted chocolate. Cool to room temperature before using — warm chocolate will cook the eggs in the next step.
Overdone: Chocolate has seized into a thick, grainy paste — overheated or water got in. Add a teaspoon of neutral oil and stir vigorously — this can sometimes rescue seized chocolate. If not, start over.
Feel cue: Touch a drop to the inside of your wrist — it should feel body-temperature or cooler before it goes into the batter. Warm chocolate will scramble the eggs.

Separate the eggs, placing the yolks in one large bowl and the whites in another clean bowl. To the yolks, add the caster sugar and whisk until pale, slightly thickened, and the sugar is mostly dissolved, about 2 minutes. Add the cooled chocolate-butter mixture and whisk to combine. Add the vanilla extract and salt. Fold in the almond flour with a spatula until fully incorporated. The batter will be thick, glossy, and dense. Set aside. In the separate clean bowl, whisk the egg whites with a pinch of salt until they reach soft peaks — they should hold a peak that droops gently at the tip. Gently fold one-third of the whites into the chocolate batter to loosen it, then fold in the remaining whites in two additions, using slow, sweeping strokes to preserve as much air as possible.
Visual cue: A thick, glossy, dark batter with no streaks of egg white remaining. Slightly lighter than the pure chocolate mixture due to the folded whites.
Underdone: Egg whites visible as unmixed white streaks or blobs throughout the dark batter. Continue folding with a large spatula using slow, sweeping strokes. Do not stir — folding preserves the air.
Perfect: Uniform dark, glossy batter with no white streaks. Slightly airy and moussey compared to the initial dense chocolate base. Pour into the prepared pan immediately.
Overdone: Over-folded: the egg whites have fully deflated and the batter looks completely flat and dense again. Proceed — the cake will be denser but still delicious. The torta caprese is naturally fudgy.
Feel cue: Lift the spatula and let the batter fall back — it should flow slowly and hold a slight fold on the surface before sinking, like thick lava.

Butter and line a 22 cm (9-inch) springform pan with parchment. Pour the batter in and smooth the top gently with a spatula. Bake at 170 C (340 F) for 30-35 minutes. The cake is done when the top is set and cracked, the edges are firm, but the center still has a very slight wobble when the pan is gently shaken — like a barely-set jelly. A toothpick inserted into the center should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter and not clean. The torta caprese is meant to be slightly underbaked by classical standards — the dense, fudgy center is a feature, not an error.
Visual cue: A cracked, matte dark surface with firm edges and a center that wobbles slightly — like a set ganache rather than a liquid. Edges have pulled away from the pan.
Underdone: Center wobbles dramatically, like liquid. Toothpick comes out completely wet. Edges have not set. Return to oven for 5 more minutes and test again. The center should jiggle, not wave.
Perfect: Top is cracked and matte. Edges firm and slightly pulled from the pan. Center has a gentle wobble — like set jelly, not liquid. Toothpick has moist crumbs, not wet batter. Remove from oven. Cool completely in the pan on a rack — at least 1 hour.
Overdone: Center is completely firm with no movement. Top may be uniformly puffed rather than cracked. Toothpick comes out clean and dry. The cake may be slightly drier than ideal but remains excellent. Serve with whipped cream or gelato to compensate.
Feel cue: Gently press the center of the baked cake — through the pan — it should yield softly, like pressing a firm ganache, rather than bouncing back like a sponge.

Allow the cake to cool completely in the pan on a wire rack — at least 1 hour, ideally 2. It will firm up significantly as it cools. Do not try to unmold it warm. Once completely cool, unmold from the springform. The cake is deliberately flat, dense, and cracked on top — this is correct and beautiful. Just before serving, dust generously with icing sugar through a fine-mesh sieve for the classic snowfall effect. Serve at room temperature cut in wedges — a warm knife (run under hot water and wiped dry) makes the cleanest cuts.
Visual cue: A flat, dense, dark chocolate disc with a naturally cracked top blanketed in a white snowfall of icing sugar.
Underdone: Cake too warm — it collapses when unmolded or is too soft to hold a clean wedge. Return to the pan and cool for at least another hour. Patience is the only tool here.
Perfect: Firm, dense, flat disc. Top is beautifully cracked. Icing sugar evenly dusted. Cuts into clean, fudgy wedges with a warm knife. Serve immediately or refrigerate for up to 3 days.
Overdone: N/A — dusting icing sugar cannot be overdone for a torta caprese. Serve.
Feel cue: The finished wedge should feel heavy and dense in the hand — almost like a slice of fudge. When you take the first bite, the outside gives a barely perceptible crust, then the interior is smooth, yielding, intensely chocolatey.

name: 西班牙土豆蛋饼 · Tortilla Española
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:

  Alternatives: fingerling potatoes
Large eggs, at room temperature: 60 %
Yellow onion, halved and sliced 3 mm thin: 40 %
  Alternatives: white onion; sweet onion
Extra-virgin olive oil: 50 %
  Alternatives: pure olive oil
Fine sea salt: 1.5 %
Active time: 40 min
Total time: 1 hr
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Spain's iconic egg-and-potato torta — thin potato and onion slices slow-cooked in olive oil until yielding, then bound in beaten egg and set on both sides into a golden, slightly runny disk that's Spain's answer to the omelette.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Waxy potatoes (Yukon Gold or similar), peeled and sliced 3 mm thin
Yellow onion, halved and sliced 3 mm thin

steps:
Pour the olive oil into a heavy 24 cm (9-inch) non-stick or well-seasoned cast-iron skillet — there should be enough oil to submerge the potato and onion slices at least halfway. Heat over medium-low until the oil shimmers lazily. Add the potato slices and onion together with a generous pinch of salt. The oil should surround them in a gentle, slow bubble — this is a confit, not a fry. Adjust heat so the bubbling is slow and the potatoes cook through without browning. Turn the mixture occasionally with a slotted spoon. After 20–25 minutes the potatoes will be completely tender, the onion will have turned translucent and sweet, and both will yield without resistance when pressed. Use a slotted spoon to transfer them to a colander set over a bowl, reserving the precious oil. Let them drain and cool for 5 minutes.
Visual cue: Potato slices are uniformly pale golden, completely pliable, and break apart easily at the edges; the onion is translucent and silky, with no browning on either.
Underdone: Potato slices snap or resist when pressed — there is still white starch at the core. The onion is still opaque. Continue confiting over low heat. Do not rush with higher temperature — undercooked potato makes a gritty, starchy tortilla.
Perfect: Potatoes slide apart with the gentlest pressure, completely tender throughout. Onion is sweet-smelling, silky, and fully translucent. Transfer to colander immediately, allow to drain and cool slightly before mixing with egg.
Overdone: Potato edges are brown and some slices have broken down to mush; oil smells of browning starch. Mashed potato pieces will make a denser tortilla but are not ruinous. Proceed with more care not to overmix with the egg.
Feel cue: Press a potato slice between your thumb and forefinger — it should yield completely and split apart like soft wax, with no crunch or resistance anywhere. The onion should feel like
cooked silk.

Crack the eggs into a large bowl and beat well with a fork — not a whisk — until the yolks and whites are fully combined. Season with salt. Add the drained, slightly cooled potato and onion to the beaten egg and fold gently together. Do not simply dump and stir: layer the potatoes into the egg, turning the mixture over a few times so the slices separate and are coated individually without breaking into mush. Press the mixture down so the egg covers the potatoes. Rest for 5 minutes — this allows the egg to penetrate between the potato layers and the potato starch to begin thickening the egg slightly, which is what gives tortilla its distinctive dense-yet-custardy texture.
Visual cue: Potato and onion slices coated in beaten egg with all air bubbles settled, the mixture looking dense, golden-yellow, and saturated throughout.
Underdone: Dry potato slices sitting on top of the egg without being coated — the egg has not had time to penetrate between layers. Press the mixture down firmly and fold again. Give it 5 more minutes to rest before cooking.
Perfect: Every potato slice is coated in egg, the mixture has a uniform pale gold color, and the bowl smells of egg and sweet onion together. Cook immediately while the mixture is at room temperature for even setting.
Overdone: Mixture has been stirred so aggressively the potatoes have broken down into a rough mash — the tortilla will be dense and homogeneous rather than layered. Proceed; the tortilla will taste fine but have less of the characteristic layered texture.
Feel cue: The mixture should feel heavy when you tilt the bowl — denser than beaten egg alone but not stiff. It should pour slowly, not pour freely. If it flows too freely, the egg-to-potato ratio is off.

Return 2 tablespoons of the reserved olive oil to the skillet and heat over medium until it shimmers. Pour in the egg-potato mixture and immediately shake the pan to spread it evenly. Reduce heat to medium-low and cook undisturbed for 5–6 minutes. Run a flexible spatula around the edge every minute or so to prevent sticking. The tortilla is ready to flip when the edges have set firm and turned pale gold, and the center — while still visibly wet and jiggly — no longer sloshes when you shake the pan. The underside should be a deep, even gold. This is the moment of the flip.
Visual cue: The edge of the tortilla is set solid and golden, the surface still looks wet and shiny at the center, and when the pan is shaken the whole disk moves as one piece rather than sloshing as a liquid.
Underdone: The tortilla is set only a few millimeters from the edge; the center sloshes freely when the pan is tilted. The underside may not have developed color. Continue cooking on medium-low. Do not flip yet — a too-soft tortilla will collapse or tear during the flip.
Perfect: Outer 3–4 cm are fully set; the center jiggles as one mass (like Jell-O, not water). The underside is a deep, even golden brown. Flip immediately using a plate or lid slightly larger than the skillet.
Overdone: The entire top surface has set dry and the center has puffed — the egg has fully cooked through on the first side, leaving nothing custardy in the middle. Flip anyway and cook the second side for only 1 minute to warm through. Accept a drier tortilla this round.
Feel cue: Slide the pan forward and stop it sharply — you should feel the tortilla move as a single mass, like a puck, not a wave. That unified movement tells you it's structurally sound enough to flip safely.

Place a flat plate or lid (at least as wide as the pan) over the skillet. In one confident motion, invert the skillet so the tortilla falls onto the plate with the cooked side facing up. Add a drizzle of the reserved oil to the pan and slide the tortilla back in, uncooked side down. Cook for another 3–4 minutes over medium-low. The ideal tortilla espanola is set on the outside and slightly runny — cuajada por fuera, jugosa por dentro — just set outside, juicy within. To check doneness, press the center gently: it should feel like a firm jelly — solid but with a slight give. Slide onto a board or plate and rest 10 minutes before slicing. Tortilla improves dramatically at room temperature and is traditionally served between 45 minutes and 3 hours after cooking.
Visual cue: Both flat faces of the tortilla are an even, deep golden-amber. The sides of the disk are set but the center yields to light pressure with a slight wobble — it should feel like a firm flan, not a cooked egg.
Underdone: When cut, the interior is fully liquid rather than custardy — the egg has not set at all at the core, and the slice collapses. Return cut halves to the pan briefly, cut-side down, to set the interior slightly. The classic runny center is a narrow target.
Perfect: Cut surface reveals layers of golden potato in a pale, custardy egg that holds its shape but glistens — not dry, not liquid, like soft scrambled egg that has just barely set. Let it rest 10 minutes for the residual heat to equalize before serving at room temperature.
Overdone: Interior is fully set, dry, and crumbles when cut — the tortilla tastes of cooked egg rather than the custardy, creamy meld of egg and potato. A drizzle of olive oil over the slice at serving helps compensate for the dryness.
Feel cue: Rest your palm flat on the center of the tortilla — it should give slightly and spring back slowly, like a mattress
under pressure. If it feels as firm as a hockey puck, it has overcookd. If your hand sinks through, it needs another minute.
