ingredients.name: Chinese cured ham (Jinhua or prosciutto di Parma)
Dried red chillies (árbol or tianjin), finely chopped
食用油（Neutral oil (rice bran, peanut, or grapeseed)）

steps:
Soak dried scallops in cold water for 2 hours; soak dried shrimp separately in cold water for 30 minutes. Reserve the scallop soaking liquid — it is intensely flavoured and will be added to the sauce. Drain and shred the rehydrated scallops by hand into thin strands along their natural fibres — they should pull apart like cooked chicken. Roughly chop the rehydrated shrimp. Finely dice the cured ham into pieces no larger than 5 mm.
Visual cue: Scallops are shredded into delicate pale gold strands. Shrimp are rough-chopped into small pieces. Ham is neatly diced. All three are ready and separate before frying begins.
Underdone: Scallops are still firm and resist shredding — they feel rubbery and dense. Soak for another 30 minutes. Under-soaked scallops will not shred into the right texture and will fry unevenly.
Perfect: Scallops pull apart easily into silky golden fibres. Shrimp are plump and yielding. The soaking liquid is amber and deeply fragrant. Begin frying immediately, or refrigerate the prepared components for up to 8 hours.
Overdone: Scallops have soaked so long they are waterlogged and falling apart into mush rather than strands. Gently squeeze out excess water and proceed. The texture will be less distinct but the flavour is unaffected.
Feel cue: A well-soaked scallop pulled along its grain should feel like wet silk — it separates into strands without resistance. If it tears in chunks, it needs more soaking.

Heat half the oil in a wok or wide, heavy skillet over medium-low heat. Add the shredded scallops first — they take longest. Fry slowly, stirring frequently, for 10–12 minutes until they turn golden and slightly crispy at the edges but remain tender inside. Add the shrimp and ham and continue frying for another 5–6 minutes until the shrimp are golden and fragrant and the ham's fat is rendered. The oil will turn orange from the scallop collagen. Remove all from the oil with a slotted spoon and set aside, reserving the flavoured oil.
Visual cue: Scallop strands should be a light, even gold — crispy at the outermost tips but still tender and yielding in the middle. The frying oil turns a warm amber-orange.
Underdone: Scallops are still pale and soft throughout — they have steamed rather than fried. Oil not hot enough. Increase heat to medium and continue frying. Underdone scallops will make the sauce taste steamed, not fried.
Perfect: Golden scallop strands with slightly crispy edges. The wok smells of caramelised seafood. Ham bits are rendered and lightly browned. Remove from oil and set aside. Keep the oil.
Overdone: Scallop strands are dark brown and brittle — they smell of burnt seafood. Taste a piece. If merely deeply toasted (not burnt), they may work. If bitter, discard and start this step over.
Feel cue: A fried scallop strand pinched between the fingers should have a slight crunch at the tips and yield softly at the center — the contrast of texture is the prize.

In the same wok with the reserved flavoured oil, reduce heat to low. Add the remaining oil. When the oil is shimmering but not smoking, add shallots and fry slowly, stirring constantly, for 8–10 minutes until they are deeply golden and beginning to crisp. Add garlic and fry for another 3–4 minutes — garlic burns faster than shallots, so watch carefully. Finally add the dried chilli and fry for 2 minutes. The entire allium-chilli base should be deeply golden, fragrant, and slightly crispy at the edges.
Visual cue: Shallots are a deep, even amber-gold — lightly crispy at the edges, still cohesive. Garlic is just turning golden. Chilli has darkened and is fragrant but not burnt.
Underdone: Shallots are still pale and soft — no colour has developed and they smell raw and sharp. Continue frying over low heat. Patience is essential — rushing the alliums makes harsh sauce.
Perfect: Deep golden shallots with slight crispiness. Garlic is golden and nutty-smelling. The chilli has opened up and made the oil red-orange. The wok smells extraordinary — sweet, sharp, oceanic, and spicy all at once. Return the fried scallops, shrimp, and ham to the wok.
Overdone: Garlic or shallots have turned dark brown and smell bitter. The oil is acrid. If slightly over, proceed quickly — the seafood and ham will balance some bitterness. If clearly burnt, start the aromatics step over.
Feel cue: Stand close to the wok — you should feel gentle warmth from the oil, not aggressive heat. Low and slow is the only way to build XO's complex allium base.

Return the fried scallops, shrimp, and ham to the wok. Add soy sauce, sugar, and Shaoxing rice wine. Add 2–3 tablespoons of the reserved scallop soaking liquid. Stir everything together and simmer over medium-low heat for 5–8 minutes, stirring frequently, until the wine has cooked off, the sugar has dissolved, and the sauce has come together into a cohesive, glistening, dark rust-red condiment. Taste and adjust salt.
Visual cue: A dark, rust-red, oil-glistening mixture where all components are distinct but unified — shredded scallop gold, orange-red chilli oil, amber alliums. The sauce should look rich and oily, not dry.
Underdone: The sauce still smells sharply of wine or soy. Components look separate and unintegrated. Continue simmering until the wine evaporates and the sauce comes together.
Perfect: A deeply fragrant, cohesive rust-red sauce. Everything is glistening in the oil. The flavour is intensely savory, slightly spicy, and impossibly complex — the sum is more than the parts. Remove from heat and cool completely before jarring.
Overdone: The sauce has dried out — the oil has been absorbed and the mixture looks crumbly and dry. Add a small amount of neutral oil and stir over low heat until glossy again.
Feel cue: A spoonful of finished XO sauce should feel slick and heavy — the oil should pool around the solids. If the spoon feels dry and the mixture is clumping, add more oil.

Cool the sauce to room temperature before transferring to sterilized glass jars. Ensure the sauce is fully submerged in the oil — add a thin layer of neutral oil on top if needed to seal it. Refrigerate. The oil will solidify slightly in the refrigerator — this is normal. XO sauce keeps refrigerated for 1 month and frozen for 3 months. Use a clean, dry spoon each time.
Visual cue: Jarred sauce should show a deep red-orange oil layer on top sealing the mixture below. When chilled, the oil layer will become slightly opaque and waxy.
Underdone: Sauce is still warm when jarred and the heat has created condensation in the jar lid, which will introduce moisture and reduce shelf life. Cool completely before jarring. Condensation introduces water, which risks spoilage.
Perfect: Room-temperature sauce fully submerged in oil. A clean, sterilized jar with a tight seal. The sauce keeps perfectly for a month in the refrigerator. Refrigerate and allow the flavours to meld for at least 24 hours before first use.
Overdone: Sauce has been left to cool too long and has congealed. Difficult to transfer cleanly to the jar. Warm very gently over low heat until just fluid again, then jar.
Feel cue: A cooled jar of XO sauce tilted to the side should show the oil moving slowly, like a viscous liquid — much slower than water. That viscosity is the rendered scallop collagen and flavored oil carrying weeks of work.

name: Yakitori Tare
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放

description: The dark, glossy soy-mirin glaze that defines yakitori — reduced to a lacquer that caramelizes on each pass over charcoal, building layer on layer of sweet-savory depth.

ingredients.name: 酱油（Soy sauce (koikuchi, standard dark soy)）
Chicken bones or chicken wings (for body)

steps:
In a small, heavy saucepan combine the soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar. Add the chicken bones or wings — these will render collagen into the tare as it reduces, giving it a glossy, lip-sticking body that plain soy-mirin reduction cannot achieve. Stir the sugar to distribute it. Set over medium heat and bring slowly to a simmer, stirring until the sugar has completely dissolved. You will notice the liquid becoming more fragrant as the sake alcohol begins to cook off, shifting from boozy to sweetly savory.
Visual cue: A dark amber liquid at a gentle simmer, with the sugar fully dissolved — no gritty texture when a spoon is drawn across the bottom of the pan.
Underdone: Sugar is still granular and the liquid is cold or barely warm — gritty when a spoon scrapes the pan bottom. Stir continuously over medium heat until no grittiness can be felt and the liquid is at a clear simmer.
Perfect: Smooth, glossy, uniformly dark amber liquid at a gentle bubble, smelling of caramel, soy, and sweet rice wine. Reduce heat to medium-low and begin the long reduction phase.
Overdone: Sugar has begun to caramelize on the sides of the pan in dark patches before the tare is reduced — heat was too high. Lower heat immediately, stir the dark patches back in (they add depth, not burnt flavor, at this stage), and continue.
Feel cue: Drag a clean spoon across the bottom of the pan — you should feel no graininess whatsoever. The liquid should flow smoothly off the spoon like warm, thin syrup.

Maintain a steady medium-low simmer, uncovered, for 25–30 minutes, stirring occasionally. The liquid will gradually deepen from amber to a dark mahogany and the surface will shift from a lively rolling bubble to a slower, thicker, more reluctant boil as the sugars concentrate. Watch the sides of the pan: a ring of syrupy residue will form and darken — this is normal. Keep the heat low enough that it never boils hard, which can make the tare grainy. The tare is reduced enough when it has lost roughly half its original volume.
Visual cue: A dark mahogany liquid that sheets off a spoon in a wide, slow ribbon rather than dripping in drops — thick but still pourable when hot.
Underdone: Still thin and drips off the spoon in a stream rather than a sheet — the sugars haven't concentrated enough to give the lacquer-coat quality at high heat. Continue reducing. Test by dipping a spoon and letting it cool for 10 seconds — only then will the thickness be apparent.
Perfect: Sheets off a cool spoon in a slow, wide, glossy ribbon. A drop on a cold plate sets to a sticky, glossy dot within seconds. Dark mahogany, deeply aromatic. Remove the bones, strain, and cool. The tare will thicken more as it cools — aim for maple-syrup consistency when hot.
Overdone: Tare has reduced beyond syrup to a thick, dark, semi-solid that sets stiff on a cold plate and smells of scorched caramel. Add 1–2 tablespoons of water or soy sauce and stir over low heat to loosen. Better to under-reduce and dip more frequently than to scorch.
Feel cue: Pinch a tiny amount between two fingertips and rub — you should feel a short, sticky pull before the fingers separate cleanly. That stickiness is the concentrated Maillard sugars that will caramelize beautifully on each pass over charcoal.

Remove the chicken bones with tongs and discard them — they've done their collagen work. Pour the hot tare through a fine-mesh strainer into a heatproof jar or container, pressing on any solids. Let it cool to room temperature; it will thicken noticeably as it cools to a consistency between maple syrup and molasses. Store in the fridge, where it keeps indefinitely. At service, reheat in a small saucepan or simply let it come to room temperature — cold tare is too thick to coat evenly. To use: dip skewers into the tare pot and return to the grill, repeating 3–4 times to build up layers of glaze.
Visual cue: A cool, dark-mahogany tare with a slow, glossy pour — thick enough to coat the back of a spoon with a mirror finish, thin enough to flow when tipped.
Underdone: Tare is thin and pale when cool, barely coating the spoon — will burn off on the grill before building any lacquer. Return to the pan and reduce further until the coating test is passed. A thin tare dries out on the grill instead of caramelizing.
Perfect: Rich mahogany, slow-pouring syrup with a glossy mirror surface. Coats a spoon completely, and runs off the tip in a single thick thread that coils when it hits the surface. Jar and store. Use at room temperature or slightly warm for best flow.
Overdone: Nearly solid when cool, cannot be poured without warming — has gone past the ideal reduction point. Thin with a tablespoon of soy sauce or mirin, warm gently, and stir until smooth.
Feel cue: Dip a clean finger and hold it up — the tare should drape and fall in a single, slow, unbroken thread. If it falls in drops, reduce more. If it sets like candy on your finger, thin it. The right tare feels as sticky as warm honey, not candy.

name: 扬州炒饭 · Yangzhou Fried Rice
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Day-old cooked jasmine rice, cold: 600 g
  Alternatives: Thai fragrant rice; long-grain white rice — must be cold and dry
Eggs: 3 whole
Medium shrimp, peeled and deveined: 150 g
  Alternatives: cooked crab meat; lobster
Char siu or honey-glazed ham, diced: 100 g
  Alternatives: smoked ham; Chinese sausage (lap cheong)
Frozen peas, thawed: 80 g
  Alternatives: corn kernels; edamame
Scallions, thinly sliced: 4 stalks
Light soy sauce: 30 ml
  Alternatives: tamari for gluten-free
Oyster sauce: 15 ml
  Alternatives: vegetarian oyster sauce; hoisin sauce
Toasted sesame oil: 5 ml
Ground white pepper: 2 g
  Alternatives: black pepper
Neutral oil (vegetable or peanut): 45 ml
  Alternatives: lard for a more traditional wok flavor
Fine sea salt: 3 g
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 20 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The most celebrated Chinese fried rice — day-old jasmine cooked over a blistering wok until each grain is separate and kissed with wok hei, bound with egg in two stages, studded with sweet shrimp, smoky char siu, peas and scallion. Prestige in a bowl.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。

ingredients.name: Char siu or honey-glazed ham, diced

steps:
This dish cooks in under 5 minutes once the wok is hot — everything must be ready before you touch the heat. Break up the cold rice with your hands, rubbing any clumps between your palms until every grain is separate and dry — clumped rice steams instead of frying. Beat the eggs lightly with a fork and a pinch of salt. Pat the shrimp dry with paper towels. Dice the char siu or ham into 1cm cubes. Have the sauces measured and combined in a small bowl. Slice the scallions with white and green parts kept separate. Line all components up beside the wok in the order they will be added.
Visual cue: Cold, dry, individual grains that fall apart when pressed. No wet clumps. All components portioned and within arm's reach of the wok.
Underdone: The rice is in large clumps and feels damp. It will steam rather than fry, turning the fried rice gluey. Spread on a tray and refrigerate uncovered for 30 minutes to dry out, then break up again.
Perfect: Every grain is individual and cold to the touch. When you toss a handful, they scatter and fall like pebbles, not mush. Heat the wok to smoking and begin immediately.
Overdone: The rice was frozen solid and now has ice crystals that will release water into the wok. Let thaw at room temperature for 10 minutes, then break up — it should be very cold but not frozen.
Feel cue: Cold, dry fried-rice rice should feel almost sandy between your fingers, individual grains slightly hardened on the outside from overnight refrigeration. That hardness is what allows each grain to fry without sticking together.

Heat a wok or very large, heavy skillet over the highest possible heat for 2 full minutes — it should be smoking before any oil goes in. Add 2 tablespoons of the oil and immediately add the shrimp in a single layer. Sear without stirring for 45 seconds until pink and curled, then toss and cook 30 seconds more. Remove from the wok immediately. Add the diced char siu for 30 seconds just to warm and slightly caramelize the edges. Remove and set aside with the shrimp.
Visual cue: Shrimp are uniformly pink and curled into a C shape, with slight char marks on their surface. Char siu pieces have caramelized, glazed edges.
Underdone: Shrimp are still translucent at the center and the meat feels soft and jellylike. Return to the wok for 30 more seconds — they should just be cooked through, not rubbery.
Perfect: Shrimp are pink through and through, with a light bounce when pressed. Not rubbery — just cooked, sweet and juicy. Remove immediately and set aside — they will continue cooking from residual heat if left in the wok.
Overdone: Shrimp have curled into tight O shapes and feel firm and rubbery. They are overcooked but will blend into the rice. Add them back at the very end of cooking for minimum further heat.
Feel cue: A properly hot wok makes the shrimp hiss and spit immediately on contact — if you hear a soft, wet sizzle rather than a sharp crackle, the wok is not hot enough. Remove what's in it and reheat.

With the wok still blazing hot, add the remaining oil and swirl to coat. Pour the beaten eggs into the center of the wok — they will set almost instantly. Scramble them very briefly, just until they are 70% set but still wet and glossy. Immediately add the cold rice on top of the wet egg, pressing it down into the egg. Toss vigorously — every 30 seconds pause to let the rice sit against the hot wok, then toss again. This alternation between contact and toss is what creates wok hei, the smoky 'breath of the wok.' Cook for 3–4 minutes total.
Visual cue: The rice grains are individually separated and some show golden-tan spots from wok contact. The egg has coated and clung to the individual grains rather than forming visible egg chunks.
Underdone: The rice is still clumping and looks steamed rather than fried. The egg is in visible pale chunks, not integrated. Keep tossing and pressing over high heat — the clumps need to break against the hot wok surface.
Perfect: Each grain is separate, golden, and lightly coated in egg. The rice smells of smoke and toasted starch — that is wok hei. Some grains have light char spots. Add the sauces, peas, white parts of scallion, seared proteins.
Overdone: The rice has dried out completely and many grains are very dark brown or black from prolonged contact with the wok. Add a splash of water and toss immediately to loosen — the steam will reconstitute some moisture.
Feel cue: Hold your hand 10cm above the wok — you should feel a fierce, dry heat radiating upward. That heat is what makes wok hei possible. A home stove is at a disadvantage; the answer is patience and good contact time.

Pour the combined soy sauce and oyster sauce over the rice and toss immediately and vigorously — the sauces evaporate quickly over high heat and should perfume rather than wet the rice. Add the peas and the white scallion parts, toss 30 seconds. Return the shrimp and char siu and toss just to incorporate and warm through. Finish with white pepper and a drizzle of sesame oil off the heat — sesame oil added to a hot wok becomes bitter. Scatter the green scallion tops over the top. Serve immediately — fried rice waits for no one.
Visual cue: A glossy, mahogany-tinged rice with visible peas, pink shrimp and char siu distributed through it. The grains gleam from the soy and sesame but are not wet.
Underdone: The rice tastes flat and bland. The soy and oyster sauce are pooled at the bottom of the wok rather than coating the grains. Toss more aggressively — the sauces need to hit the wok surface to evaporate and coat properly.
Perfect: Each grain is seasoned, separate, smoky and slightly glossy. The shrimp are sweet, the ham is savory, the peas are just warm. The sesame oil lifts everything into fragrance. Plate immediately in warm bowls and serve.
Overdone: The soy was added too early over too high heat and has caramelized into a bitter crust on the wok, transferring bitterness to the rice. Add a splash of water and toss to dissolve the crust, then taste — if bitter, it may need rescuing with a touch more soy and a pinch of sugar.
Feel cue: Yangzhou fried rice should feel light in the bowl — pick up a spoonful and it should scatter easily, not mound solidly. The aroma that rises is smoky, savory and faintly sweet from the char siu and sesame.

name: Homemade Yogurt
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Whole milk (not ultra-pasteurized): 100 parts
  Alternatives: 2% milk for a thinner set; goat's milk for a tangier, softer curd
Plain live-culture yogurt (active cultures, as starter): 4 parts
  Alternatives: a freeze-dried yogurt culture sachet (follow packet dose)
Nonfat dry milk powder (optional, for a thicker set): 3 parts
  Alternatives: omit for a looser, pourable yogurt
Active time: 25 min
Total time: 10 hours
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Whole milk scalded, cooled to blood heat, and seeded with a spoonful of live culture, then left to sleep in its own warmth until it sets into a trembling, tangy custard — pure white, clean-smelling, and faintly sweet, the everyday miracle of two ingredients turning into one.

ingredients.name: Plain live-culture yogurt (active cultures, as starter)
Nonfat dry milk powder (optional, for a thicker set)

steps:
Whisk the optional milk powder into the cold milk to dissolve any lumps, then pour into a heavy-bottomed pot. Heat over medium, stirring often and scraping the bottom so it doesn't catch, until the milk reaches 180 to 185°F (82 to 85°C) — just below a boil, with steam rising and a fine ring of foam at the edge. Hold it there for 5 minutes. This step is not about killing bacteria; it denatures the whey proteins so they cross-link into a thick, set curd instead of a thin, weepy one.
Visual cue: Wisps of steam lift off a glassy surface, a delicate skin starts to form at the rim, and the first tiny bubbles break at the edges without a rolling boil.
Underdone: The milk is warm but flat and silent, no steam or foam, well under 180°F on the thermometer. Keep heating and stirring. Don't rush the heat too high or the bottom scorches — medium is right.
Perfect: Steady steam, a foamy ring around the edge, and the thermometer parked at 180 to 185°F. The milk smells faintly sweet and cooked, like the top of warm rice pudding. Hold 5 minutes at temperature, then pull off the heat to cool.
Overdone: The milk has boiled over or a tough, leathery skin and browned, scorched bits have formed on the bottom. Strain out the skin and do NOT scrape the scorched bottom into the pot. A faint cooked note is fine; an acrid burnt one will carry through, so if badly scorched, start over.
Feel cue: Drag the spoon across the bottom — at temperature you'll feel it just starting to grip and thicken almost imperceptibly. The smell shifts from raw and milky to sweet and cooked.

Cool the milk to 110 to 115°F (43 to 46°C) — body temperature, warm but not hot to a clean fingertip. Stir gently now and then to keep a thick skin from forming, or set the pot in an ice-water bath to speed it up. This window matters: hotter than about 120°F kills the culture, cooler than 105°F and it works sluggishly or not at all. If a skin did form, lift it off so it doesn't make lumps.
Visual cue: The milk is still and warm with no steam, sitting steadily at 110 to 115°F on the thermometer.
Underdone: Still steaming, thermometer above 120°F. Too hot to seed. Wait, or use an ice bath. Adding culture now will scald the bacteria and the yogurt won't set.
Perfect: No steam, the pot's side is comfortably warm to hold, thermometer at 110 to 115°F. Move quickly to seed it with the starter before it cools further.
Overdone: The milk has dropped below 105°F and feels only lukewarm. Gently rewarm over low heat back into the window, stirring constantly, then proceed. Cool milk just ferments slowly rather than failing.
Feel cue: A drop on the inside of your wrist should feel pleasantly warm like a baby's bottle — never hot. If it stings, it's too hot; if you barely feel it, it's too cool.

Make sure the starter yogurt is fresh and labeled with live or active cultures. Whisk it together with a cup of the warm milk in a small bowl until completely smooth and lump-free, then stir that slurry back into the pot and whisk thoroughly so the culture is evenly dispersed. Don't overdo the starter — a little goes a long way, and too much actually crowds the bacteria and gives a sourer, thinner result.
Visual cue: A uniform, slightly frothy, pure-white milk with no streaks or floating clumps of starter — every spoonful looks identical.
Underdone: Visible ribbons or blobs of thick starter still float in thinner milk; it isn't evenly mixed. Whisk again. Uneven seeding sets unevenly, leaving thin and thick patches in the final yogurt.
Perfect: Smooth, homogeneous, faintly foamy warm milk that smells fresh and lightly tangy from the starter. Pour into clean jars or a container and move to the incubation step right away.
Overdone: The mixture looks broken or slightly curdled at the edges. The milk was likely still too hot. Whisk smooth and proceed anyway; it may set softer than ideal.
Feel cue: The slurry-first method is the key — mixing starter into a little milk before the whole pot prevents clumps. The milk still feels reassuringly warm to the jar's touch as you fill it.

Hold the seeded milk at a steady 105 to 115°F (40 to 46°C) for 6 to 10 hours, undisturbed — in a turned-off oven with the light on, a cooler packed with warm water jars, a wrapped warm pot, or a yogurt maker. Do not move, stir, or jostle it while it sets; agitation breaks the forming curd. Start checking at 6 hours: tip the jar gently and watch for a clean set. Longer means thicker and tangier. When it's set to your taste, refrigerate at least 4 hours to firm it fully and stop the souring. For Greek-style, line a sieve with cloth and drain the chilled yogurt 1 to 2 hours.
Visual cue: Tilted gently, the yogurt pulls away from the side in one trembling mass like soft custard, holding its shape, with maybe a thin film of clear yellow-green whey pooling at the surface.
Underdone: Tilting the jar, the contents still slosh as thin, soupy milk that hasn't gelled. Little to no tang. Keep incubating and check hourly. A weak set means low temperature, a stale starter, or simply more time needed — warmth and patience usually fix it.
Perfect: A clean, wobbling gel that holds a spoon's impression, smelling pleasantly sour and tasting bright and tangy with a creamy finish. Refrigerate at once for at least 4 hours. Chilling firms the curd and locks in the flavor; save a few spoonfuls as the starter for your next batch.
Overdone: Sharply, mouth-puckeringly sour with lots of separated whey and possibly a slightly grainy, cracked, or curdled surface. It's over-fermented but perfectly safe — stir the whey back in and use it for cooking, smoothies, or marinades. Next time, incubate cooler or for fewer hours.
Feel cue: Resist the urge to peek and prod — a single nudge in the first hours can wreck the set. Properly done, a spoon stands a moment before sinking, and the curd parts with a soft, custardy cleave rather than a watery slosh.

name: Yorkshire Pudding
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Plain flour (all-purpose): 1 part
Large eggs: 1 part
Whole milk: 1 part
  Alternatives: half milk, half water for a crispier result
Fine sea salt: 0.01 part
Beef dripping or lard (or neutral oil): 0.1 part
  Alternatives: duck fat; vegetable oil
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 1 hr 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The great British batter pudding — a thin, egg-rich batter poured into searingly hot dripping fat and baked until it billows into a dramatic golden crown, crisp-walled and hollow inside, the essential companion to roast beef.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。

ingredients.name: Beef dripping or lard (or neutral oil)

steps:
Measure flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the centre. Crack the eggs into the well and whisk them into the flour gradually, pulling in flour from the edges until a thick, lump-free paste forms — this is critical, because lumps introduced at the end never fully smooth out. Once the paste is smooth, pour in the milk in a thin stream, whisking constantly. The finished batter should be the consistency of single cream and absolutely smooth. Cover the bowl and rest it at room temperature for at least one hour, or up to overnight in the refrigerator. Resting lets the starch granules hydrate fully and the gluten relax, giving the batter elasticity without toughness.
Visual cue: A thin, smooth, cream-coloured batter with no visible lumps, pale and slightly aerated. When poured from a height it falls in a smooth, unbroken ribbon.
Underdone: Batter is lumpy or has visible streaks of dry flour. Too thick to pour smoothly. Whisk more vigorously and pass through a fine-mesh sieve to remove any stubborn lumps before resting.
Perfect: Silky and fluid, the colour of ivory. Coats the whisk but drops off cleanly. Smells gently eggy. Cover and rest at room temperature for at least 1 hour.
Overdone: Batter has been over-rested in the fridge and smells slightly sour, or was blended until foam-streaked and over-aerated. A mildly sour batter is still useable — it will puff well. Skim off excess foam before pouring.
Feel cue: Dip your fingertip into the batter — it should feel cool, silky, and leave a thin, even coat on your skin with no gritty flour specks. The mix should pour off your wrist in a clean sheet, not in drops.

Preheat the oven to 230 C (450 F) — this is not a suggestion, it is the entire reason Yorkshire puddings rise. Place a 12-cup tin or a large roasting tray in the oven with a teaspoon of dripping in each cup (or a generous pool in the tray). Heat the fat in the oven for at least 15 minutes, until it is shimmering, smoking lightly, and loud — you must hear it spit when a drop of batter hits it. The fat must be violently hot: it flash-steams the batter's liquid into a jet of steam that drives the rise before the structure sets.
Visual cue: The fat is visibly rippling and smoking, a thin haze rising from the tin. It shimmers with a heat mirage when the oven door is cracked.
Underdone: Fat is warm but not smoking. Batter will sizzle weakly when added and the puddings will not rise properly. Return the tin to the oven for another 5–10 minutes. Do not compromise on this step.
Perfect: Fat is sending up a faint blue smoke, shimmering violently, and a drop of cold water dropped into a cup spits aggressively. Temperature is around 230 C. Work fast: remove the tin from the oven, pour the batter immediately, and return to the oven without delay.
Overdone: Fat is burning, smoking black, or has started to ignite. Kitchen fills with bitter smoke. Remove the tin, discard the burnt fat, wipe the tin, add fresh fat, and reheat. Never pour batter onto burnt fat.
Feel cue: When you open the oven, a wave of fierce, dry, almost metallic heat should roll out at you. That intensity is what you need. If it merely feels warm, the oven is not hot enough.

Working with decisive speed, remove the searingly hot tin from the oven and set it on a heatproof surface. Pour the batter from a jug into each cup, filling each about one-third full. The batter should sizzle and immediately begin to cook around the edges on contact with the fat. Return the tin to the oven instantly — every second of delay costs rise. Bake at 230 C (450 F) for 20–25 minutes. Do not open the oven door for the first 15 minutes under any circumstances: a cold rush of air is enough to collapse them.
Visual cue: The puddings have climbed dramatically above the rim of the tin — tall, hollow crowns with deeply golden-brown, crisp walls and a lighter, custardy inner floor.
Underdone: Pale, flat, or only slightly puffed. The centres look wet and the walls are soft. Interior smells of raw egg. Return to the oven immediately. Do not remove until the walls are visibly rigid and golden. A wet centre means 5 more minutes minimum.
Perfect: Tall, dramatic, burnished gold with darker brown ridges. Walls are rigid and hollow-sounding when tapped. The cups have climbed at least 5 cm above the tin rim. Remove and serve immediately — they begin to deflate within minutes of leaving the oven.
Overdone: Walls are very dark brown approaching black at the tips. The base smells of burnt fat. Trim any truly charred edges. The interior is almost certainly still good — the dramatic colour is mostly on the outside crust.
Feel cue: Lift a pudding and tap the side with your knuckle — it should sound hollow and dry, like knocking on a ceramic pot. The walls should be rigid enough to hold their shape, not wobble. If it deflates when you touch it, it needed more time.

name: Yuzu Kosho
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Fresh yuzu zest (from 6–8 yuzu): 100 parts
  Alternatives: lemon zest + Meyer lemon zest (combined, less floral)
Green Thai or serrano chilis (stemmed): 80 parts
  Alternatives: red chilis (for red yuzu kosho); jalapeño (milder)
Fine sea salt (non-iodized): 25 parts
Fresh yuzu juice: 20 parts
  Alternatives: fresh lemon juice
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 7 days 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Yuzu zest and green chili ground together with salt and left to cure — a Kyushu condiment of almost impossible fragrance, equal parts floral, fiery, and saline, that transforms a simple bowl of noodles or a piece of grilled fish with a single small spoonful.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Zest the yuzu fruit using a fine microplane grater, working carefully to collect only the colored outer layer and avoid the bitter white pith beneath. A single yuzu yields a relatively small amount of zest — approximately 1–2 teaspoons. The oils in fresh yuzu zest are extraordinarily volatile and fragrant; work quickly and cover the zest as soon as it is collected to preserve those aromatics. If yuzu is not available, a combination of Meyer lemon and grapefruit zest approximates it loosely, though the floral complexity is quite different.
Visual cue: Fine, bright yellow-green zest with a distinctly wet, oily appearance from the natural oils released by grating. Intensely fragrant.
Underdone: Zest pieces are too large and the pith is visible in the mixture — white fragments mixed with yellow. Grate more finely, applying less pressure to the fruit so you take only the very surface.
Perfect: Fine, uniformly yellow-green zest with a wet, oily sheen and an intensely floral, citrus fragrance. No white pith visible. Cover immediately and move to processing.
Overdone: You have pressed the fruit repeatedly over the same section and white pith fragments are appearing in the zest. Pick out pith fragments with a toothpick, or rotate to a fresh section of fruit. Pith will make the finished yuzu kosho bitter.
Feel cue: The zest should coat your fingers in a faintly oily film that makes your skin smell like no other citrus — floral, almost herbal, with a complex top note that fades within seconds of leaving the skin.

For a traditional yuzu kosho, use a suribachi (Japanese mortar) or, if unavailable, a small food processor. The chilis should be finely minced, retaining most of their seeds for heat. Remove the stem but leave seeds. The finer the mince, the more evenly the heat distributes through the finished paste. If using a knife, mince to an extremely fine, almost paste-like consistency — tiny fragments, not visible chunks.
Visual cue: A very fine, wet green mince — almost a paste — with seeds evenly distributed. No large chili pieces remaining.
Underdone: Chili is still in visible chunks. Uneven mince means uneven heat in the final product. Continue mincing with a rocking knife motion, gathering and re-mincing until the texture is uniformly fine.
Perfect: Fine, wet, almost paste-like mince with seeds throughout. Color is a vivid, bright green. Combine with zest and salt.
Overdone: Chili is a smooth paste with seeds fully broken — some heat may have been lost from the capsaicin volatilizing. Proceed — the texture is smooth rather than slightly granular, but perfectly usable.
Feel cue: Mince the chili wearing gloves — at this fine a cut, the capsaicin is airborne and will sting eyes and skin. The smell should be a sharp, clean green-chili fragrance.

Combine the yuzu zest, minced chili, and salt in a suribachi or small food processor. Add the yuzu juice. Grind or process until the mixture forms a cohesive, slightly rough paste — the salt draws moisture from both the zest and chili, binding the paste together. Taste: it should be intensely salty, fiercely hot, and vibrantly citrus-forward. Transfer to a small sterilized jar.
Visual cue: A bright green, cohesive paste — smooth but slightly textured — that holds its shape when scooped on a spoon.
Underdone: Mixture is still loose and the elements haven't coalesced — zest and chili fragments are visible separately. Continue grinding or processing. The salt needs more time to draw moisture and bind the paste.
Perfect: A bright green, uniform paste with a slightly granular texture. Holds on a spoon, smells intensely of yuzu and chili. Transfer to jar and cure.
Overdone: Completely smooth paste with all texture lost and green color beginning to oxidize to olive-drab. Proceed — it will still taste excellent. Next time, use a mortar rather than a processor for better texture control.
Feel cue: The paste should feel wet and slightly sticky from the citrus oils and chili juice — like a very finely textured, very salty citrus jam that makes your tongue tingle before you even taste it.

Seal the jar and refrigerate for a minimum of 3 days, ideally 7. During this time, the salt continues to draw moisture, the flavors meld and deepen, and the sharpness of raw chili softens to something more complex. The color will shift from vivid green to a more muted olive-green — this is natural and desirable. Use in tiny amounts: a single teaspoon on grilled chicken, ramen, sashimi, or oysters. Store for up to 3 months refrigerated.
Visual cue: After curing, the paste is a deeper, more muted green-gold. The texture is uniform and slightly wetter than when packed. The aroma is deeply complex — floral citrus and chili integrated into one note.
Underdone: After only 1 day, the paste still tastes of separate raw chili and zest. The flavors haven't integrated. Reseal and return to the refrigerator. The integration happens between days 3–7.
Perfect: After 5–7 days, the flavors are unified: one complex, fiery-floral-salty note. Color is olive-green. The heat has deepened from sharp to slow. Begin using in very small amounts.
Overdone: After 3+ months, the color has turned an olive-brown and the citrus fragrance has faded. The heat and salt remain but the floral note is gone. Still usable as a chili-salt paste. Add fresh yuzu zest to revive the fragrance.
Feel cue: A fully cured yuzu kosho should smell like distilled citrus and chili — almost perfume-like in its intensity when you unseal the jar in a cool kitchen.

name: Za'atar Spice Blend
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Dried thyme: 100 parts
Dried oregano: 50 parts
Dried marjoram: 30 parts
  Alternatives: dried savory
Ground sumac: 60 parts
White sesame seeds: 60 parts
Fine salt: 10 parts
  Alternatives: flaked sea salt
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 15 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: The iconic Levantine herb-spice blend: dried thyme and oregano, sumac, toasted sesame seeds, and salt — stirred into olive oil, it becomes a dip; scattered over flatbread, it becomes a meal.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Rub the dried thyme, oregano, and marjoram between your palms over the mixing bowl, pressing firmly to break the leaves into coarse fragments and release their volatile oils. Alternatively, give them a brief pulse in a spice grinder. The herbs should retain some texture — do not reduce them to a fine powder.
Visual cue: Coarsely broken herb flakes with irregular edges, releasing a concentrated herbal aroma. The color brightens slightly from dull grey-green to true green as the cell walls break open.
Underdone: Leaves are still whole and rigid. No aroma has been released — the oils are sealed inside the intact leaves. Rub more firmly and longer between palms. The friction breaks the cell walls and releases the thymol and other aromatics locked inside.
Perfect: Irregular flakes ranging from fine crumbs to 3–4 mm pieces. The aroma is bright, resinous, and herbal. The bowl smells like a Levantine hillside after rain. Add the remaining ingredients and toss together.
Overdone: Herbs have been ground to a fine dust. All texture is lost and the aroma is already beginning to fade as the volatile oils evaporate. Add the sumac and sesame immediately to extend the shelf life of the oils. Powdered za'atar is still delicious — use it promptly.
Feel cue: Press a pinch between your fingers — it should feel coarsely textured like dried breadcrumbs, and your fingertips should come away lightly fragrant with thyme oil.

Place the sesame seeds in a dry skillet over medium heat. Toast, shaking the pan continuously, for 2–3 minutes until the seeds are golden — they will darken quickly once they start to color. Remove immediately to a plate to stop cooking.
Visual cue: Evenly golden sesame seeds with a warm, nutty aroma. A few will be slightly darker than the rest — this is normal and adds complexity.
Underdone: Seeds are still white and raw. No color change, no nutty aroma — just a raw grain smell. Continue over medium heat. The moment color starts to develop it moves fast — watch closely.
Perfect: Light to medium golden. Smell is warm, toasty, and faintly sweet. Seeds pop very slightly in the pan. Tip immediately onto a cool plate — they will continue cooking for 30 seconds from residual heat.
Overdone: Dark brown, some black edges. Smell has turned bitter and acrid, like burnt popcorn. Discard and start again with fresh seeds. Burnt sesame will make the entire za'atar bitter.
Feel cue: Toss a cooled sesame seed between your fingers — it should feel dry and slightly rough, with a detectable warmth from toasting still radiating from the surface.

Combine the crushed herbs, ground sumac, toasted sesame seeds, and salt in the bowl. Toss with a spoon or shake in a sealed jar to distribute evenly. Taste — adjust sumac for tartness, salt for seasoning. Store in an airtight jar away from light. Use within 2 months for peak flavor.
Visual cue: A heterogeneous blend of green herb flakes, deep burgundy sumac, ivory sesame seeds, and white salt crystals — no single ingredient dominant to the eye, the colors interspersed throughout.
Underdone: Sumac has clumped in one corner and the herbs are grouped separately — the blend is not evenly distributed. Shake the jar vigorously or stir for 30 seconds. Sumac is finely ground and tends to clump — ensure the bowl is completely dry before mixing.
Perfect: An evenly mixed, aromatic blend. Every spoonful contains visible herb fragments, sesame seeds, and the deep burgundy tint of sumac. The smell is complex: herbal, sour, nutty, and slightly floral. Transfer to a sealed jar. The blend needs no refrigeration.
Overdone: Over-mixed in a food processor — the blend has homogenized into a fine green-brown powder with no visible texture. Stir in a few whole sesame seeds for texture. The flavor is intact.
Feel cue: A pinch of za'atar should feel slightly gritty from the sesame and sumac, lightly oily from the crushed herb leaves, with an immediate sharp-herbal smell on the warm palm.

name: Lebanese Za'atar Flatbread
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
All-purpose flour: 3 cups
  Alternatives: bread flour
Warm water (38-40 C): 1 cup
  Alternatives: filtered water
Instant yeast: 1 tsp
  Alternatives: active dry yeast (proof first)
Fine sea salt: 1 tsp
  Alternatives: kosher salt
Extra-virgin olive oil (dough): 2 tbsp
  Alternatives: neutral oil
Dried za'atar blend (thyme, sumac, sesame): 4 tbsp
  Alternatives: dried thyme with sesame seeds
Extra-virgin olive oil (topping): 4 tbsp
Flaky sea salt (finish): 0.5 tsp
  Alternatives: Maldon salt
Active time: 30 min
Total time: 2 hr 30 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A dimpled, hand-stretched disk of yeasted dough blanketed in musky dried thyme, sesame, and sumac, then drenched in grassy olive oil before baking — the smell alone will pull your neighbors to the door.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, instant yeast, and salt. Make a well in the center, pour in the warm water and olive oil, and stir with a wooden spoon or your hand until the dough comes together into a rough, cohesive mass. The dough will be slightly sticky and uneven — resist adding more flour. Turn it out onto an unfloured surface and knead for 7-8 minutes using the heel of your hand, pushing the dough away from you and folding it back. The friction of the bare counter develops the gluten far better than a floured surface. After 7 minutes the dough should have transformed from sticky resistance to smooth compliance.
Visual cue: A smooth, slightly tacky ball that holds its shape, has a gentle sheen from the oil, and rebounds slowly when poked.
Underdone: The dough tears when pulled and leaves chunks on the counter. Surface looks rough and pockmarked like orange peel. Keep kneading — 3 more minutes, leaning your full body weight into each push.
Perfect: Smooth and supple, like soft chamois leather. The surface is taut and slightly translucent. A windowpane test reveals a thin, stretchy membrane that doesn't tear. Form into a ball, place in an oiled bowl, and cover with a damp towel.
Overdone: The dough is very tight and springs back almost instantly when poked. It feels rubbery rather than elastic. Cover and rest for 20 minutes — over-kneaded gluten relaxes. It will still make excellent flatbread.
Feel cue: By the end of kneading it should feel like warm earlobe skin — soft, pliable, and just barely yielding under gentle pressure. If your palm comes away clean, the gluten is developed.

Place the dough ball in a lightly oiled bowl and turn it once to coat. Cover with a damp kitchen towel or plastic wrap and set it in a warm, draft-free spot — an oven with just the light on (about 27-30 C) is ideal. Let it rise until doubled in size, roughly 60-90 minutes depending on your kitchen temperature. Do not rush this step: the slow fermentation builds the faintly sour, yeasty complexity that makes this flatbread taste like more than flour and water. You'll know it's ready when the dough dome is noticeably higher than the bowl rim and jiggles like gelatin when you gently shake the bowl.
Visual cue: The dough has clearly doubled in volume, is domed at the top, and has large bubbles visible through the walls of any clear container.
Underdone: The dough has grown by only a third. It feels dense and resistant when pressed, and the surface doesn't jiggle. Return to the warm spot and check again in 20 minutes. If your kitchen is cold, place the covered bowl over a saucepan of warm water.
Perfect: Exactly doubled. Pressing a floured finger in 2 cm leaves an indent that slowly springs back halfway. The dough smells of bread and faintly of yogurt. Divide and shape.
Overdone: The dome has collapsed inward. The dough is very slack and smells sharply sour, almost alcoholic. Gently fold it over on itself once, re-ball, and let it rest 15 minutes before shaping. The flatbread will be a touch more sour and slightly denser — still delicious.
Feel cue: A proofed dough pressed with a wet finger should exhale softly, like pressing on a fresh sponge, and leave a ghost indent that fades in 5 seconds.

While the dough proofs, combine the za'atar blend and olive oil in a small bowl and stir until you have a loose, thick paste, similar in consistency to pesto. The oil should fully saturate every dried herb and sesame seed — you're creating a spreadable slurry, not a dry sprinkle. Taste it: it should be herbaceous, nutty, and faintly sour from the sumac, with a grassy bitterness from the thyme. If your za'atar is very dry, add an extra teaspoon of oil so it spreads without tearing the raw dough. Let the paste sit and meld while the dough finishes proofing.
Visual cue: A dark green-brown paste that holds its shape on a spoon but spreads easily. The sesame seeds are fully coated and no dry pockets of herbs remain.
Underdone: Dry crumbs with pools of oil sitting separately. The herbs haven't absorbed the oil. Stir vigorously for another minute. The herbs will swell and drink the oil in.
Perfect: A uniform, glossy paste. Lifted on a spoon, it flows slowly and holds its shape at the edges. Cover and set aside at room temperature until the dough is ready.
Overdone: The paste has become so thin it is watery — too much oil was added. Stir in another teaspoon of dried za'atar to re-thicken. The ratio can flex; err toward drier.
Feel cue: The paste should smell powerfully of dried thyme and toasted sesame — earthy, faintly resinous, with a bright citric note from the sumac that hits the back of your nose.

Punch the risen dough down gently and turn it out onto a lightly floured surface. Divide into two equal portions (or four for smaller flatbreads). Working one at a time, press each piece into a flat disc with your palm, then use your fingertips — not a rolling pin — to coax it outward, rotating it a quarter turn after each pass. Aim for a roughly round disc 25-30 cm across and about 6 mm thick; slight irregularity is authentic and desirable. If the dough springs back, cover and rest it for 5 minutes, then try again — the gluten is tense and needs to relax. Transfer the shaped discs to parchment-lined baking sheets. Preheat your oven to 230 C (450 F) while you top them.
Visual cue: A rough oval or circle about 25-30 cm across, 6 mm thick, with slightly thicker edges and a thin center that you can almost see through when held to the light.
Underdone: The disc is thick and uniform — closer to a small boule than a flatbread. It will bake up bready rather than crackling and light. Keep pressing and stretching. The dough has more give than you think — trust the gluten.
Perfect: Thin and almost translucent in the center, with a rim about 1 cm thick. Laid flat, it relaxes without springing back. Proceed directly to topping.
Overdone: You've stretched too aggressively and the dough has torn through in one or two places. Pinch the tears closed and patch by pressing a small piece of raw dough over the hole. The baked result hides these scars under the za'atar paste.
Feel cue: At the correct thickness you can feel the slight resistance of the gluten network — it gives evenly across the whole disc without collapsing into one spot.

Spoon the za'atar paste generously over each disc and spread it to the edges with the back of the spoon, leaving a 1 cm border bare. Scatter flaky salt over the top. Slide the parchment directly onto the oven's lowest rack, or ideally onto a preheated baking steel or stone. Bake at 230 C (450 F) for 8-12 minutes, until the edges are golden brown, the center is set (not doughy), and the za'atar paste smells toasted and intensely fragrant. Watch carefully after the 8-minute mark — the thin center bakes quickly and the difference between perfect and scorched is 90 seconds. Serve immediately or within 20 minutes; the texture is best within the first half hour.
Visual cue: Golden-brown puffed edges with darker blistered spots. The center is set and matte, the za'atar paste is darkened and fragrant, and the underside is spotted with charred leopard-print marks.
Underdone: The edges are pale gold but the center still has a faint raw-dough sheen and yields softly when pressed. The za'atar paste smells of oil and herbs but not of toasting. Return to the oven for 2-3 more minutes. If the edges are darkening faster than the center, slide the tray to the middle rack.
Perfect: The edges are deeply golden and crackle when bent. The underside has dark charred spots. The za'atar paste is fragrant and dry at the surface, not wet or greasy. The flatbread flexes but holds its shape. Transfer to a cutting board and cut into wedges immediately.
Overdone: The edges have darkened to near-black and the za'atar paste has begun to smoke. The center may be stiff and cracker-like. Trim the burnt edges with kitchen shears. The interior is still edible and the za'atar flavor often intensifies attractively — call it 'twice-baked style'.
Feel cue: Fresh from the oven, the flatbread should crackle audibly when you press a corner — that sound is the crust shattering against the soft interior beneath.
The steam carries the perfume of dried thyme, sesame, and olive oil in a single warm gust.

name: Za'atar Spice Blend
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Dried wild thyme (or dried thyme): 100 parts
  Alternatives: dried oregano; dried marjoram; a mix of all three
Ground sumac (dried, tart red berries): 50 parts
White sesame seeds (toasted): 40 parts
  Alternatives: black sesame seeds
Salt (flaky): 10 parts
Ground cumin (optional): 8 parts
  Alternatives: ground coriander
Dried red chili flakes (optional): 5 parts
Active time: 15 min
Total time: 20 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Dried wild thyme, toasted sesame, tart sumac, and salt pounded into the Lebanese pantry's most essential blend — stirred into olive oil for bread dipping, scattered over labneh, or rubbed onto chicken before it hits the grill.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
Place sesame seeds in a dry skillet over medium heat. Toast, stirring constantly, for 3–4 minutes until the seeds turn golden and begin to jump and pop in the pan. Remove immediately from the heat and transfer to a plate to cool — they will continue to cook on the hot pan. This is the only ingredient that requires toasting; the sumac and dried thyme should not be heated, as warmth drives off the volatile aromatic oils that make za'atar fragrant.
Visual cue: Seeds are uniformly golden — not dark brown, not white. A light pop-and-jump activity in the pan is audible.
Underdone: Seeds are still white. No popping, no aroma change. Pan may not be hot enough. Continue on medium heat. The seeds take 2–3 minutes before any visible change — then it happens quickly.
Perfect: Uniformly golden, fragrant, with a few darker specks. A warm, nutty sesame aroma fills the kitchen. Seeds are jumping occasionally. Immediately off the heat and onto a cool plate.
Overdone: Seeds are dark brown to tan throughout. Smell is beginning to turn from nutty to bitter. Discard and re-toast. Dark sesame has a bitter note that will unbalance the entire za'atar blend.
Feel cue: Press a toasted sesame seed between your fingers — it should feel dry and crisp, crumbling slightly with pressure and releasing an immediate warm, nutty aroma.

Combine the dried thyme, sumac, cooled toasted sesame, salt, and optional cumin and chili flakes in a bowl. If the dried thyme is on the stem, strip the leaves first and discard the woody stems. Mix thoroughly with a fork or spoon. The blend should look evenly red-green from the sumac and thyme, with white sesame seeds distributed throughout. No grinding or processing is needed — za'atar is meant to be a loose, textured blend, not a powder.
Visual cue: A loose, evenly mixed blend of green thyme, red-purple sumac, and white sesame with visible texture. Not powder — it should look almost like a rough herbed salt.
Underdone: Thyme and sumac are sitting in separate clumps; the sesame is pooled at the bottom. Not mixed. Toss and fold more thoroughly. Za'atar is simply a mixing step — it just needs time and attention.
Perfect: Evenly distributed throughout. Green, red, and white are all visible in every spoonful. Aroma is herbal, tart, and nutty simultaneously. Taste, adjust salt, and store.
Overdone: Over-mixed with a spoon so vigorously that the thyme has broken to a fine powder and the sumac has clumped with moisture from the sesame. Spread on a plate to dry for 30 minutes, then combine again gently.
Feel cue: Rub a pinch between your palms and bring them to your nose — the combined aroma should be wildly layered: tart sumac, herbal thyme, warm sesame, all at once, like a hillside in Lebanon after rain.

Taste the za'atar dry, then mixed into a small pool of olive oil. Adjust: more sumac if you want more tartness (it is the most important flavor driver in a good za'atar), more salt if flat, more sesame for nuttiness. The blend should be balanced: earthy and herbal from the thyme, sour from the sumac, nutty from the sesame, and savory from the salt. Store in a sealed glass jar in a cool, dark place for up to 6 months. The sumac will slowly fade in color and tartness over time — use the freshest sumac you can find.
Visual cue: A bright, vivid blend. The sumac holds a deep burgundy-red color; the thyme is a rich, dry green; the sesame is warm gold. No clumping, no grey coloration.
Underdone: Za'atar tastes flat and primarily of thyme — the sumac note is absent or muted, suggesting old or poor-quality sumac. Add more sumac. The tartness of sumac is what distinguishes za'atar from simple dried thyme.
Perfect: Balanced: earthy-herbal first, then a clean sour note from the sumac, finishing with warm sesame and salt. Color is vivid and fresh-looking. Store in a sealed jar.
Overdone: Too much sumac dominates — the blend is aggressively tart and the thyme and sesame notes are buried. Add more dried thyme and sesame seeds to dilute the sumac and rebalance.
Feel cue: Pour a small pool of good olive oil and dip a piece of fresh bread through the za'atar before dipping into the oil — the blend should coat the bread in a thin, fragrant layer that makes the bread taste alive.

name: Zabaglione
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=parts）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Egg yolks, room temperature: 6 parts
Caster sugar (superfine): 3 parts
  Alternatives: honey (use slightly less)
Dry Marsala wine (Florio Secco or similar): 3 parts
  Alternatives: Moscato d'Asti; dry sherry; Vin Santo
Fresh seasonal berries or peaches, for serving: 1 parts
  Alternatives: amaretti cookies; pandoro
Active time: 20 min
Total time: 25 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: A warm Italian custard of just three elements — egg yolks, sugar, and Marsala wine — whisked over a bain-marie until they triple in volume and become an impossibly light, trembling foam that tastes simultaneously of sweet wine, warm custard, and something almost ethereal.

ingredients.name: Dry Marsala wine (Florio Secco or similar)
Fresh seasonal berries or peaches, for serving

steps:
Place the egg yolks and caster sugar in a large, deep, round-bottomed metal or glass bowl. Whisk vigorously by hand or with a hand mixer until the mixture turns pale ivory, triples slightly in volume, and falls from the whisk in a thick, slow ribbon that holds its shape on the surface for 2-3 seconds before dissolving. This pre-mixing — called 'blanchir' — begins the emulsification and ensures even, smooth cooking over the bain-marie. The sugar must be nearly fully dissolved before the bowl goes over heat — feel the mixture between fingers; it should feel smooth, not gritty.
Visual cue: Pale ivory, almost white mixture that has expanded in volume and falls from the whisk in a thick, continuous ribbon.
Underdone: Still deep yellow and liquid. Falls from the whisk in thin drops, not a ribbon. Sugar granules are visible. Continue whisking for 2-3 more minutes. The color change and volume increase are essential for a stable zabaglione.
Perfect: Pale ivory, nearly doubled in volume. Falls in a slow, thick ribbon that holds briefly on the surface before dissolving. Smooth to the touch, no grit. Add the Marsala and move to the bain-marie.
Overdone: Over-whisked without heat — very stiff and dry. Difficult to stir. This is fine; proceed to the bain-marie. The heat will loosen it.
Feel cue: Rub a drop between your fingertips — it should feel satiny and smooth, with no sugar crystals remaining. The mixture should be warm from the friction of whisking.

Add the Marsala wine to the ribboned yolk-sugar mixture and whisk to combine. The mixture will thin out significantly — this is expected. The Marsala should be at room temperature; cold wine can cause the eggs to cook unevenly. Taste the raw mixture: it should be sweet, winey, and slightly rich. This is your baseline — everything that follows is just cooking and incorporating air.
Visual cue: A thin, pale-gold liquid, evenly combined with no streaks of egg yolk or unmixed sugar.
Underdone: Streaks of dark yolk or unmixed sugar at the bottom of the bowl. Whisk more thoroughly until completely uniform.
Perfect: Uniform pale gold liquid, evenly combined. Smells of wine and egg. Position the bowl over the simmering bain-marie and begin whisking immediately.
Overdone: N/A — this step cannot be overdone. Proceed.
Feel cue: The mixture should smell delicately of Marsala — not raw egg, not alcohol burn, but a round, fruity, slightly caramelized wine fragrance.

Bring a saucepan of water to a gentle simmer — the water must not touch the bottom of the bowl, and it must not boil aggressively. Place the bowl of zabaglione base over the simmering water and immediately begin whisking continuously in a figure-eight pattern, making sure to reach the sides and bottom of the bowl. Whisk without stopping for 8-12 minutes. The mixture will slowly begin to thicken, increase dramatically in volume, and change from liquid to a thick foam. Watch the temperature: if you see any steam rising from the mixture or the eggs begin to look lumpy at the edges, remove the bowl from the heat immediately and continue whisking off-heat for 30 seconds, then return. The target temperature is 70-75 C (160-170 F). The zabaglione is done when it has tripled in volume and holds a soft mound.
Visual cue: A pale, voluminous foam three times the original volume, holding a soft mound when the whisk is lifted and dropped back in. Pale gold to ivory in color.
Underdone: Still liquid and thin. The mixture barely coats the whisk. Less than doubled in volume. The Marsala smell is still very prominent and raw. Continue whisking over the bain-marie. The transformation takes patience — 10 minutes of continuous whisking is normal.
Perfect: Tripled in volume, thick as softly whipped cream, and pale gold. Holds a soft ribbon or mound when the whisk is lifted. Smells of warm wine custard. Reaches 72 C on an instant-read thermometer. Remove from heat immediately and serve within 5 minutes.
Overdone: Lumpy, grainy, or scrambled appearance at the sides. A slightly sulphurous smell. The foam has deflated and the mixture looks dense and curdled. Remove from heat immediately. If just starting to scramble, strain through a fine-mesh sieve — the texture improves somewhat. Serve immediately, chilled, as a sauce rather than a foam.
Feel cue: Lift the whisk and watch the mixture fall
back: it should mound briefly on the surface before slowly sinking — like soft whipped cream, not liquid. Your arm will be genuinely tired at this point, which is how you know it's done.

Divide the warm zabaglione immediately among warm glasses or shallow coupes — it will begin to deflate and separate within 10-15 minutes, so speed matters. Spoon the fresh berries or sliced peaches alongside or beneath the foam. The warm foam against cold or room-temperature fruit is the defining contrast of the dish. Serve with a small spoon and a delicate biscuit such as a savoiardi or amaretto if desired. Zabaglione can also be chilled briefly and served cold, in which case fold in a small amount of softly whipped cream while it is still warm to stabilize the foam.
Visual cue: Pale gold foam billowing above the rim of the glass, glossy and trembling, with bright fruit alongside or beneath.
Underdone: Zabaglione served too cool and already deflating. Looks watery in the glass. Zabaglione must be served immediately from the heat. Prepare the glasses and fruit before you begin cooking.
Perfect: Warm, voluminous pale-gold foam barely contained in the glass. Trembles when touched. Fruit provides brilliant color contrast. Eat immediately.
Overdone: Served too late — foam has fully deflated into a thin, liquid custard layer at the bottom of the glass. It still tastes excellent — spoon it over the fruit as a sauce. For future reference, prepare glasses before starting.
Feel cue: The first spoonful should feel impossibly light on the tongue — a warm, sweet, winey cloud that dissolves before you expect it to, leaving behind a warmth that radiates from the chest.

name: Zhug
servings_note: 原文基准配方；人数未核对，保留原文用量，不自动缩放
quantity_notes:
原文基准用量（ratioSystem=weight）；不是经核对的人均用量。
Fresh coriander (cilantro), leaves and stems: 60 g
Flat-leaf parsley, leaves and stems: 30 g
Jalapeño peppers (stemmed, roughly chopped): 60 g
  Alternatives: serrano for more heat; green chilis
Garlic cloves: 15 g
Green cardamom pods, seeds removed: 4 g
Cumin seeds: 4 g
  Alternatives: ground cumin, 2 g
Black peppercorns: 3 g
Fine sea salt: 5 g
Extra-virgin olive oil: 30 g
Active time: 10 min
Total time: 10 min
image_alt: 餐桌风味示意图，并非本菜实拍
description: Yemen's incendiary green herb sauce — fresh coriander and parsley pounded ferociously with jalapeños, cardamom, and cumin into a thick, emerald-green paste that burns clean and bright. The most beloved condiment across the Yemeni diaspora and every Israeli market stall.
tip: 步骤保留英文原文；可向小厨询问中文做法。按原文份量与实际锅具判断火候。
adaptation: 由拾味厨房结构化整理；英文制作步骤保留原文，补充中文菜名、检索词和地区标签。© 2026 FoodML 与 ForkRecipe contributors；原文作者：ForkRecipe Kitchen。 本菜谱及其整理版本采用 CC BY-SA 4.0：https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/；改编时须署名并以相同许可分享。 用时、份量未明确则保持未知；饮食类型与过敏原未经逐条认证。
steps:
In a mortar, pound the cardamom seeds, cumin seeds, and black peppercorns to a fine, even powder. The cardamom seeds are the most important: they must be fully crushed to release the eucalyptus-floral oils that are zhug's signature. If using a spice grinder, run it for 30 seconds and check for any whole seeds remaining. The spice powder should be fine enough to not feel gritty on the tongue.
Visual cue: A fine, pale olive-green powder with a complex, almost medicinal-floral aroma from the cardamom.
Underdone: Whole or half seeds still visible in the powder. Cardamom has not opened and the aroma is flat. Continue pounding. Cardamom seeds are tough — they need sustained, focused pressure to release their oils.
Perfect: Fine, uniform powder with no whole seeds. The aroma is powerfully floral and warm, with the cumin's earthiness rising beneath the cardamom's high notes. Set aside and begin the main paste.
Overdone: Spices have been pounded so long they are warm and have lost their volatile aromatics. The powder smells flat. Proceed — zhug is robust enough to carry even slightly diminished spice, and the fresh herbs will provide most of the aroma.
Feel cue: Rub the spice powder between thumb and finger — it should feel silky and fine, not gritty with whole seed fragments. The moment the cardamom seeds crack open, the mortar fills with a eucalyptus-floral cloud.

Add the garlic and salt to the mortar with the ground spices and pound to a smooth paste. Add the jalapeño pieces in two batches, pounding each batch into the garlic base before adding more. Finally, add the coriander and parsley stems first (they are tougher), pound to a rough paste, then add the leaves. Work with a circular grinding motion against the mortar wall between pounding strokes. The paste will be wet and emerald green.
Visual cue: A thick, vivid emerald-green paste with a slightly coarse, fibrous texture from the herb stems.
Underdone: Paste is chunky with large herb fragments and jalapeño pieces clearly visible. The chili's heat hasn't fully integrated. Continue pounding and grinding. The texture should be cohesive enough that a spoonful holds together.
Perfect: Dense, wet, emerald-green paste. Not completely smooth — some texture from herb stems is correct and authentic. Smells intensely of fresh coriander and jalapeño. Stir in the olive oil to finish.
Overdone: The mixture has been pounded into a completely smooth, waterlogged puree. The herbs have released so much liquid the paste is soupy. Drain off excess liquid and proceed. The flavor will be fine but the texture will be thinner.
Feel cue: Pinch the herb paste — it should feel dense and fibrous, like a compressed herb bundle, releasing vivid green liquid when squeezed. The chili heat should already be warming your fingertips after contact with the jalapeño.

If you haven't yet, add the remaining herb leaves to the paste and work in. Pour the olive oil over the paste and fold it in with a spoon or a few more turns of the pestle. The oil should integrate but not fully emulsify — zhug is not a smooth sauce. Taste and adjust salt and heat. Pack into a clean jar, smoothing the surface, and press a thin layer of olive oil over the top to seal. Refrigerate. Zhug keeps for 1 to 2 weeks and the flavor deepens after 24 hours.
Visual cue: An emerald-green, oil-glossed paste that mounds on a spoon and releases green-tinted oil when pressed. Not a smooth emulsion — visibly textured.
Underdone: Oil is pooling separately at the top rather than integrating. The paste looks dry and dense underneath. Fold more deliberately with a spoon, working the oil down through the paste.
Perfect: Vivid green, glistening, coherent paste. Smells of green chili, coriander, and the floral warmth of cardamom. The heat on the tongue is immediate and clean. Pack into a jar and refrigerate. Serve alongside hummus, falafel, shakshuka, or grilled meats.
Overdone: Too much oil has been added and the paste is floating in oil, the two separating into layers instantly. Pour off the excess oil. Stir in a handful more fresh chopped herbs to reabsorb and thicken.
Feel cue: Zhug on the tongue is immediate — there's no build-up. The heat from jalapeños hits upfront and sharp, then the cardamom's eucalyptus note arrives as a high, floral contrast, and the coriander provides a long green finish. It should make you reach for bread immediately, not reach for water.
